summary: Two lines of activity touch this problem's own quantity (the balance constant delta(P)) since the frozen revision, neither of which resolves the general conjecture. (1) Max Aires and Jeff Kahn, in two 2025 preprints (arXiv:2509.11549, Sept 2025, and arXiv:2510.26134, Oct 2025), prove new asymptotic lower bounds on delta(P) for posets of large width (delta(P) -> 1/2 as n -> infinity under width/minimal-element conditions, delta(P) >= 1/e - o(1) under weaker width conditions) and study a related Kahn-Saks variance question for bounded-width posets. I fetched both abstracts directly; neither paper mentions the 1/3-2/3 conjecture by name in the fetched abstract content, and I found no statement of AI involvement in either paper's abstract or from search results on their acknowledgements. These are asymptotic bound improvements on the conjecture's own constant for a restricted class (large/bounded width), so they are genuine cases/progress under Section 3.1, but they leave the general conjecture (which needs delta(P) >= 1/3 for ALL non-chain posets, including small-width, bounded-size ones near the known worst cases) untouched, so status does not move to partial/resolved from these alone. (2) A July 2026 solo preprint by independent researcher Anish Gupta (arXiv:2607.23926, v1 2026-07-27, v2 2026-07-30) reports an exhaustive computer census of all order-14 posets (1,338,193,159,771 isomorphism classes, 4,096-way sharded exact-integer computation), verifying Peczarski's Gold Partition Conjecture -- which implies the 1/3-2/3 conjecture -- through n=14, one order beyond the prior exhaustive frontier of n=13 (De Loof, De Baets, De Meyer 2010) and n=11 (Peczarski 2006). This is a genuine case of the universally-quantified conjecture (restricting to posets of size <=14), so it counts under Section 3.1, and it is the event the status rests on. However, it is a single-author preprint with no journal acceptance, no traced expert digestion (no MathOverflow thread, no blog commentary, no citing follow-up found), so per Section 6.1 it is `claimed` rather than `resolved`, notwithstanding the exact-arithmetic, no-floating-point, independently-recomputed-witness design that makes the computation itself easy to check. Crucially, the paper's own text states plainly that 'Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family) were used extensively for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript' -- an explicit, first-person authorial disclosure, which is the required basis for an ai_role other than none. I classified this as assisted rather than none because 'computational experiment design' plausibly extends beyond mechanical coding/proofreading into the design of the verification approach itself (which sharding scheme, which independent-recomputation cross-checks to run), which is part of the mathematical/algorithmic content of the result, not merely code cleanup. Wikipedia's live article (checked for context, not as a substitute for primary sources) already cites this exact preprint for the '14 elements' claim, confirming the triage's find was on point.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of ai_role would put this at none rather than assisted: the quoted acknowledgement bundles 'computational experiment design' together with mundane items (software development/optimization, literature discovery, drafting/editing), and it is possible the phrase means only that the AI suggested which computations to run or helped script experiments -- i.e., an accelerant for human-directed work -- rather than that it originated any part of the mathematical argument that appears in the paper (the Gold Partition certificates, the recurrence, the sharding correctness argument). Under Section 6.2's test ('what did the model produce that appears in the final result?'), if the answer is that the census algorithm, certificates, and recurrences were all human-designed and the AI only helped implement/optimize/debug them and write prose, the correct code is none, with formalisation_only false (since this isn't formalisation, it's an empirical census). I did not find a more granular breakdown (e.g., a per-contribution list) that would let me disambiguate assisted from none with confidence; I lean assisted because 'computational experiment design' is a mathematical-methodology phrase, not a coding phrase, but this is a judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: The full paper text (methods/acknowledgements section, not just the abstract-page fetch) or the GitHub repository's commit history/documentation would show concretely which specific components (the sharding scheme, the independent witness-recomputation cross-check, the certificate logic itself) were AI-suggested versus human-designed, which would settle assisted vs. none. Separately, any MathOverflow/Peczarski/Kahn commentary on arXiv:2607.23926, or a published/refereed version, would let this move from claimed to resolved. For the general (all n) conjecture, only a full proof or an explicit counterexample at some finite n would change the status further.

outcome: No result found that changes the stated 1-factorization conjecture (that a k-regular graph on 2n vertices with k >= n (n odd) or k >= n-1 (n even) is 1-factorable) since 26 January 2024. The conjecture remains proved only for sufficiently large n (Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus & Treglown, 2016, arXiv:1401.4159 et seq.), a pre-window result. All post-window activity found concerns distinct, related conjectures (the perfect 1-factorisation conjecture of Kotzig, and the Overfull Conjecture), not this one.
summary: The 1-factorization conjecture as stated (a k-regular graph on 2n vertices is 1-factorable if k >= n for n odd, or k >= n-1 for n even) was proved only for sufficiently large n by Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus and Treglown in a four-part series (arXiv:1401.4159, .4164, .4178, .4183), all posted in January 2014 — well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, and already reflected in the pre-window Wikipedia text. I re-verified this is still the state of the art: the current Graph factorization Wikipedia article (fetched live, for context only) still describes the conjecture as proved only for 'sufficiently large n', with no update since 2016. I searched broadly for any 2024-2026 movement — full resolution, resolution for small n, or any bound improvement — and found none. The only post-window hits are: (1) 'The perfect 1-factorisation conjecture holds asymptotically' (Cheng & Sgueglia, arXiv:2607.09459, submitted 10 July 2026), which addresses Kotzig's conjecture — a genuinely different, stronger statement about decomposing the complete graph K_n specifically into n-1 perfect matchings that pairwise form Hamilton cycles, not about general k-regular graphs on 2n vertices meeting a degree threshold; this is a related problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated conjecture, since it changes the object (only K_n) and the requirement (Hamilton-cycle-pairing, not mere 1-factorability); and (2) 'Towards the Overfull Conjecture II' (arXiv:2607.02270), which is an unrelated edge-coloring conjecture (about overfull subgraphs forcing class-2 status) that does not cite or bear on the 1-factorization conjecture. I also checked for any multigraph-variant developments; the multigraph 1-factorization conjecture (Plantholt-Tipnis) was addressed asymptotically by Vaughan back in 2010 (arXiv:1010.5192), also pre-window and also a distinct variant (multigraphs with bounded multiplicity, not simple regular graphs). No AI system appears anywhere in this literature; all identified papers are conventional human-authored extremal/probabilistic graph theory arguments (absorption method, regularity method), with no mention of AI, machine learning, or automated proof assistance in any source I opened. I judge the search complete: I checked the current Wikipedia article, ran multiple targeted arXiv/web searches for the exact conjecture and its known variants, and opened every source that could plausibly bear on it.
competing_reading: None of substance. One could argue the Kotzig perfect 1-factorisation asymptotic result deserves mention as adjacent progress in the same research cluster, but by the letter of §3.1 it changes the stated question (restricting to K_n, and adding the Hamilton-cycle-pairing condition) rather than restricting it, so it is a related problem, not a case, and does not belong in `event`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving the conjecture for all n (removing the 'sufficiently large' restriction), or proving/disproving it for any specific small n not yet covered, would count as progress or resolution. No such paper was found.

outcome: Bernert, Browning, Lichtman and Teräväinen (arXiv:2410.12234, October 2024) improved the bound on the number of exceptional abc triples in a cube of side N from O(N^(2/3)) to O(N^(33/50)), the first power-saving improvement in over 60 years; the conjecture itself remains unresolved. [Hand-corrected 2026-09-24; the agent's original outcome follows.] Kirti Joshi published a series of arXiv preprints (2024-2025, culminating in a November 2025 FAQ and a May 2025 'Final Report on the Mochizuki-Scholze-Stix Controversy') asserting that combining his own 'Arithmetic Teichmuller Spaces' construction with Mochizuki's Inter-Universal Teichmuller Theory completes a proof of the abc conjecture and refutes every objection raised by Scholze and Stix; no expert digestion or journal has accepted this claim, and a 2026 independent Lean-formalization project (LANA, ZEN University) explicitly declined to conclude whether IUT theory constitutes a valid proof.

ai.basis_quote: It is essential for our project to distinguish between formal verification and generative AI prediction. Generative AI synthesizes text based on statistical patterns and can hallucinate. In contrast, Lean validates mathematical truth against strict logical rules.

disputes.summary: Joshi's 2024-2025 preprints claim to complete Mochizuki's IUT proof of the abc conjecture and to show that every objection Scholze and Stix raised (notably around Corollary 3.12) is mathematically false. Scholze and other experts remain unconvinced; the mathematical community has not accepted the combined Joshi-Mochizuki argument as a proof. A 2026 formal-verification effort (the LANA project at ZEN University, using Lean, with an interim report presented July 17 2026) reports narrowing down the specific disputed step (concerning whether a diagram commutes / an isomorphism can be regarded as the identity, in the q-pilot/multiradial-algorithm comparison) but explicitly withholds judgment on whether IUT theory constitutes a completed proof, neither confirming nor ruling out a genuine gap.

summary: Since 26 January 2024, the abc conjecture itself has not moved to accepted resolution. The dominant development is Kirti Joshi's claim (arXiv preprint 'Construction of Arithmetic Teichmuller Spaces IV: Proof of the abc-conjecture', submitted March 2024, with a November 2025 FAQ and a May 2025 'Final Report on the Mochizuki-Scholze-Stix Controversy') that his own Arithmetic Teichmuller Spaces construction supplies the missing ingredient in Mochizuki's Inter-Universal Teichmuller Theory and that every objection Scholze and Stix raised in their 2018/2021 critique is mathematically incorrect. This is a first-written-argument event within the window (first preprint March 2024), but no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or community consensus has followed; Scholze and other experts remain unconvinced, and no source found treats the conjecture as settled. I therefore code this 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' or 'open': a serious, human-authored claim exists and has been publicly circulated for over a year, but the community-acceptance bar for 'resolved' is unmet. The RIMS journal publication of Mochizuki's original IUT papers (2021) predates the frozen revision and is not itself a window event; it is mentioned only as background. Separately, a genuine narrowing of the exceptional-set bound occurred: Bernert, Browning, Lichtman and Teraevaeinen (arXiv 2410.12234, October 2024) improved the count of exceptional triples in a cube of side N from O(N^(2/3)) (a 1962 bound, per de Bruijn) to O(N^(33/50)) -- the first power-saving improvement in over 60 years -- and a related paper ('The abc conjecture is true almost always', arXiv 2505.13991, May 2025) surveys this and related density results. These are real quantitative progress on the abc conjecture's exceptional set, but per the DEEP_DIVE.md rule on existence/infinitude questions, narrowing where exceptions could hide is not itself resolving the (infinitude) question, so I treat this as supporting context for 'claimed' status rather than as an independent 'progress' event overriding it -- the Joshi claim is the more significant event and determines the status field. On AI: I found no AI involvement anywhere in this thread. The Joshi/Mochizuki preprints show no evidence of AI-assisted derivation, and a direct, dated quote from the 2026 LANA project (Johan Commelin, on ZEN University's Mathematics Center's IUT-verification project page) explicitly disclaims generative AI: 'It is essential for our project to distinguish between formal verification and generative AI prediction... In contrast, Lean validates mathematical truth against strict logical rules.' The bound-improvement paper (2410.12234) uses classical analytic number theory plus a linear program (with an appendix noting Python code for the LP) -- a computational-optimization technique, not a machine-learning or AI system, so it does not qualify for any ai_role other than none. Two search hits that surfaced during this research -- an OpenAI model disproving Erdos's unit distance conjecture (May 2026) and a Claude-assisted counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture (2026, Levent Alpoege/Anthropic) -- are unrelated conjectures entirely and are excluded as out of scope for this record.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is 'open' rather than 'claimed', on the view that Joshi's claim has gained essentially no traction (Scholze reportedly still unconvinced, no journal has accepted it, and it largely restates a 2012-2021 dispute) and so does not meet even the bar of 'a claim the field is taking seriously enough to evaluate'. Under DEEP_DIVE.md's definition, 'claimed' only requires 'a preprint, announcement or machine-checked certificate that experts have not yet digested' -- Joshi's preprint qualifies mechanically, and the ongoing 2026 LANA verification effort shows the field is at least engaging with the underlying IUT question, which supports keeping 'claimed' over demoting to 'open'. I have kept 'claimed' but flag this as a genuine judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: Either a journal publication of Joshi's completed argument accompanied by expert digestion accepting the combined Joshi-Mochizuki proof, or a further LANA-project report (beyond the July 2026 interim one) definitively locating and confirming (or refuting) the disputed step in IUT theory, would settle whether this moves to 'resolved' or reverts decisively to 'open'.

outcome: The general abundance conjecture for klt projective varieties over the classical (characteristic 0) setting in arbitrary dimension remains open, but several restricted cases were settled after 26 January 2024: Liu–Xu (arXiv:2505.05250, May 2025) proved abundance for klt/lc projective varieties in dimension ≤5 whenever κ≥0 and the numerical dimension ν≤1, and separately showed non-vanishing implies abundance in that numerical-dimension range in all dimensions; positive- and mixed-characteristic threefold cases (ν=2, char>3) and a Kähler-variety reduction strategy (dimension 4) also advanced, but these are either pre-window results with post-window arXiv revisions, or address a different ambient category (Kähler, not projective) or singularity class (slc, not klt).

disputes.summary: Swapnajit Das's arXiv:2604.28085 (submitted 2026-04-30) originally (v1) claimed a counterexample to abundance for compact Kähler slc threefolds. János Kollár pointed out the proposed counterexample admits an étale double cover with sdlt singularities, contradicting the v1 claims. The revised v2 (2026-09-13) instead proves abundance DOES hold for all compact Kähler slc threefolds (a positive result), and relocates the counterexample to non-Kähler varieties in Fujiki class C with slc (not klt) singularities. This is a withdrawn-then-corrected claim, but concerns slc singularities on a broader (non-Kähler, Fujiki class C) category, not the klt/projective statement in this bullet, so it does not itself change this problem's status.

summary: The Wikipedia statement is the general abundance conjecture: for a projective variety with klt singularities, K nef implies K semiample, in arbitrary dimension, classical (char 0) setting. This remains open in general — every source consulted (Wikipedia's own article, ProofAtlas, and every paper found) agrees the unrestricted higher-dimensional conjecture is unproved. Genuine post-window progress on CASES of the stated conjecture exists: Liu and Xu (arXiv:2505.05250, v1 2025-05-08, v2 2025-07-30) prove that the non-vanishing conjecture implies abundance whenever the numerical dimension ν≤1, and unconditionally settle abundance (in the lc case, using a refinement from Lazić–Peternell) for projective varieties of dimension ≤5 with κ≥0 and ν≤1 — a genuine, narrower case of the stated conjecture, classified `partial`/`confirmed`. Several other candidate results turned out NOT to be cases of the klt/projective statement: (1) the positive-characteristic threefold ν=2 result (arXiv:2307.03938) and the mixed-characteristic threefold result (arXiv:2111.08970) both had their substantive claims already made before the window (v1 2023-07 and v1 2021-11 respectively, the latter with no revision after 2022-11); their post-window arXiv revisions (v3 2026-04-17, publication-ready polish) do not add new mathematical content, so these are `open_stale` as individual events and are not used to date the record's status. (2) The Kähler-threefold log-abundance completion (Höring/Peternell-adjacent work, arXiv:2306.00671) for ν=2 was already claimed in v1 (2023-06-01), predating the window, and in any case Kähler (not necessarily projective) is a different ambient category from the Wikipedia statement, and an April 2023 erratum (arXiv:2304.10161, pre-window) had flagged a genuine gap in the underlying Campana–Höring–Peternell theorem that is not fully closed by that paper alone. (3) The April 2026 Kähler-variety reduction strategy (arXiv:2604.03879) explicitly reduces the Kähler case to the projective case and only settles some non-algebraic/trivial-K_X fourfold cases — a related-problem variant (different category), not a case of the stated klt/projective conjecture. (4) The 2026-04/09 slc-Kähler-threefold episode (arXiv:2604.28085, see `disputes`) concerns slc singularities, a strictly larger and different singularity class than klt, and after correction resolves positively for Kähler slc threefolds while placing the only counterexample in non-Kähler Fujiki class C — again a related problem, not this bullet's question. No source anywhere — not the papers themselves, not their arXiv listings, not searches crossing this problem with DeepMind/AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve/GPT/Claude/Lean formalization benchmarks (including the 'Formal Conjectures' DeepMind benchmark paper, arXiv:2605.13171, whose full text contains zero occurrences of the word 'abundance') — credits any AI system with any role in this problem. `ai_role` is therefore `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue the Liu–Xu fivefold result is narrow enough (a specific dimension bound and numerical-dimension restriction) that it barely moves 'what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry,' making `progress` a defensible alternative to `partial`; I chose `partial` because dimension ≤5 with κ≥0, ν≤1 is a genuine, fully-settled restriction of the exact stated question (klt/lc, K nef ⇒ semiample), which is what §3.1 defines as a case rather than a bound. A second competing reading is that the slc-Kähler dispute (arXiv:2604.28085) is close enough to klt that it should be logged as a near-miss `progress`/`incident` rather than excluded entirely — I judged slc to be a strictly different (broader) singularity hypothesis than klt, per the standard MMP hierarchy (klt ⇒ dlt ⇒ lc; slc is the non-normal analogue of lc), so it is a related problem under §3.1, not a case.
what_would_settle_it: A published, expert-digested proof of abundance for klt (or even just lc) projective varieties in arbitrary dimension over characteristic 0 would resolve the whole conjecture (`resolved`). Short of that, a case-settlement in a strictly higher dimension than 5, or removing the ν≤1 restriction in Liu–Xu's framework, would be further `partial` progress worth a fresh record.

outcome: The Agoh–Giuga conjecture itself (n prime iff pB_{p-1} ≡ -1 mod p) remains open, with no post-2024 change to the counterexample lower bound (still the 2013 Borwein–Maitland–Skerritt bound of 19,908 digits, itself pre-window). However, in 2026 an AI agent produced Lean-machine-checked proofs of two previously-open conjectures tightly bound up with the problem, listed on OEIS A309132 (the sequence whose 'a(n)=1 iff n prime' property is stated to be equivalent to Agoh-Giuga): (1) that this equivalence to Agoh-Giuga holds, and (2) that for composite n, a(n) is squarefree iff n is a Carmichael number (a 2019 Ordowski conjecture). Neither proof touches the truth value of Agoh-Giuga/A309132's primality conjecture itself, so the core problem is unmoved; the event is recorded as an instructive adjacent development.
credited_humans: Thomas Ordowski (2019, original squarefree/Carmichael conjecture statement)

ai.basis_quote: The proof that n is Carmichael iff n is composite and a(n) is squarefree was achieved by an autonomous AI agent, see the Tsoukalas paper and the Lean proof. ... Combining both directions yields the Carmichael equivalence (Summary by Opus 4.7).
ai.disclosed_cost: Paper's appendix records per-problem cost figures for this entry; WebFetch summaries of the PDF disagreed on the exact numbers across separate fetches (one pass reported $23 for the Agoh-Giuga-equivalence entry and $14 for the Carmichael/squarefree entry, both attributed to 'Claude Opus 4.8'; the OEIS comment itself credits a summary to 'Opus 4.7'). This inconsistency could not be resolved from a clean primary-text read of the PDF and is flagged as unverified rather than reported as fact.

summary: The frozen-revision statement of Agoh–Giuga is the primality biconditional pB_{p-1} ≡ -1 (mod p). This remains unproven and has no new counterexample-bound improvement since 26 January 2024 — the best bound (19,908 decimal digits / >10^19907, at least 4,771 prime factors) dates to Borwein, Maitland & Skerritt, 2013 (Zenodo record 10408952; also framed by some summaries as improving a 1996 bound), well before the window; the older Sorini 2001 figure of 10^36067 the triage found is likewise pre-window and in any case appears in some sources as a heuristic estimate rather than a rigorous bound, superseded by the 2013 rigorous result. In the window, the one genuine development is on OEIS sequence A309132, whose primality conjecture ('a(n)=1 iff n prime') is stated (informally, by Sondow/Ordowski circa 2019, and cited via Adamczewski 2026 on MathWorld) to be equivalent to Agoh-Giuga. As part of the 'OEIS Open' benchmark (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941, submitted 12 Aug 2026, v2 13 Aug 2026), which tested language models against 492 previously-open OEIS conjectures formalized in Lean by Tsoukalas et al., an AI agent produced machine-checked Lean proofs of two claims tied to A309132: the equivalence-to-Agoh-Giuga framing, and the previously-conjectured (Ordowski, 2019) fact that for composite n, a(n) is squarefree iff n is a Carmichael number. Both are recorded on OEIS A309132 in a comment by Ralf Stephan dated 25 May 2026, crediting an 'autonomous AI agent' and a Lean proof, with a summary line crediting a Claude Opus variant. I treat this as `progress` rather than `partial`: the squarefree/Carmichael claim is a structural fact about A309132's denominators that narrows nothing about whether the Agoh-Giuga primality biconditional itself is true (a composite Agoh-Giuga counterexample was already known, pre-2024, to have to be a Carmichael number that is also a Giuga number — this is old Borwein-era knowledge; the new proof formalizes a related but not identical characterization of a(n)'s squarefreeness). Also, I could not independently verify with full confidence the exact AI model name and cost figures, because repeated attempts to read the arXiv PDF's raw text via WebFetch produced inconsistent numbers across passes (a symptom of that tool summarizing a dense compressed PDF rather than a clean extraction); I report what was found with that caveat rather than asserting a single number as fact. No arXiv preprint, journal paper, or lab announcement in the window claims to prove or refute Agoh-Giuga's core biconditional, or to improve the digit bound. Also noted in searching: two September 2025 Zenodo postings ('The Arithmetic Geometry of the Giuga Condition...') are self-labeled speculative AI-generated content ('a creative exploration of a concept with AI — it should not be taken as correct mathematics') and carry no mathematical weight; they are mentioned only because they surfaced in searches and could otherwise be mistaken for progress.
competing_reading: One could argue the A309132 result is `partial` progress on Agoh-Giuga rather than merely `progress`/adjacent, on the grounds that A309132's conjecture is stated by mathematicians to be *equivalent* to Agoh-Giuga, so proving facts about A309132's structure is proving facts 'about' Agoh-Giuga by proxy. I did not adopt this reading because neither of the two things actually proved is the equivalence's non-trivial direction bearing on primality itself: proving 'this is equivalent to Agoh-Giuga' is a reformulation, not new information about which n satisfy it, and the Carmichael/squarefree fact narrows the composite side of a related sequence's structure without deciding a single new case of 'n prime iff pB_{p-1}≡-1 mod p'. If a reader takes the equivalence relation itself as sufficient to fold any A309132 progress into Agoh-Giuga's own record, `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` would be defensible instead.
what_would_settle_it: A primary, cleanly-extracted read of arXiv:2608.11941's full text and appendix table (rather than through a lossy PDF-to-text summarizer) to fix the exact system name, cost, and precise wording distinguishing what was newly proved versus previously known informally; and a statement from a number theorist on whether the A309132 Carmichael/squarefree proof is considered to bear on the Agoh-Giuga conjecture's open status.

outcome: No proof, disproof, counterexample, or narrowing of Agrawal's conjecture has appeared since 26 January 2024; the last substantive activity (the Primaboinca distributed search and the Pomerance-Lenstra heuristic) predates the window by years.
summary: I searched extensively for any post-26-January-2024 activity on Agrawal's conjecture (that (X-1)^n ≡ X^n - 1 mod (n, X^r-1) implies n is prime or n^2 ≡ 1 mod r) and found none. The current (2026) Wikipedia article on Agrawal's conjecture and on the AKS primality test both describe the same state of knowledge that existed before the window: computational verification for small ranges, the Primaboinca BOINC project (2010-2020, ended 31 May 2020, searched 10^10 < n < 10^17, no counterexample found), Popovych's modified conjecture (2008/2009), and the Pomerance-Lenstra heuristic argument that counterexamples should have positive density and are 'probably' infinite (this heuristic itself predates 2024 by roughly two decades and is unchanged in any of the sources I read). I also checked arXiv listings and general web search for any 2024-2026 preprints mentioning 'Agrawal's conjecture', 'cyclotomic AKS', or related search terms, and found only unrelated cyclotomic-polynomial papers with no connection to this conjecture. A 'Grokipedia' AI-generated encyclopedia page also exists on this topic but likewise reports no developments after January 2024 and is not itself a primary source. No lab, paper, or blog credits an AI system with any work on this conjecture. The Pomerance-Lenstra heuristic (an existence/infinitude-type argument about counterexamples) is not itself a resolution per §3.1 — 'are there infinitely many counterexamples' is not advanced by anything found here, and in any case it predates the window entirely. This is a clean 'nothing happened' case: the conjecture is exactly where it was in January 2024, with no narrowing, no case settled, and no AI involvement of any kind.
competing_reading: None found. The only mild wrinkle is that the Wikipedia article and AKS primality test article have presumably been edited since January 2024 (both were fetched as they exist in 2026), but their content shows no new mathematical claims postdating the frozen revision — they restate the same 2001-2020 facts. There is no plausible alternative classification other than open/no_change_found.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement (i) exhibiting an explicit n, r counterexample to the cyclotomic congruence, (ii) proving the conjecture true, (iii) proving/disproving Popovych's modified variant, or (iv) reporting a renewed/extended distributed or targeted computational search beyond the Primaboinca range (10^17) that either found a counterexample or extended the verified range — any of these dated after 26 January 2024 would change this record.

outcome: Daniel Cranston (arXiv:2512.08020, December 2025) extended the verified range of Albertson's conjecture from r≤18 to r≤24, and Fox, Pach and Suk (SoCG 2025) proved it for graphs with at most 1.4(k-1) vertices for large k; the general conjecture remains open. [Hand-corrected 2026-09-24; the agent's original outcome follows.] A solo-authored September 2026 arXiv preprint (Ankan Sadhu, v2) claims a full proof of Albertson's conjecture for every chromatic number r, superseding an earlier v1 of the same preprint that had claimed only r≤26; a separate concurrent preprint (Cao & Mehat) proves the restricted case r≤29 building on Cranston's r≤24 verification. Neither has been digested by an expert or accepted at a venue; the strongest claim (full proof) rests on a single preprint reviewed only by an automated review tool, not a human expert.

disputes.summary: Sadhu's preprint (arXiv:2609.01682) was posted 2026-09-01 as v1 claiming r≤26 only, then revised 2026-09-13 (v2) to claim a full proof for every r, retitled from 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26' to 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture'. A separate, apparently independent preprint by Cao & Mehat (arXiv:2609.04771, also September 2026) builds on Cranston's r≤24 result and Sadhu's r≤26 result (as of v1) to reach r≤29, without engaging Sadhu's later all-r claim. The two lines of work were not reconciled in any source found, and no expert commentary distinguishing/adjudicating between them was located.

summary: At the frozen revision the conjecture was verified for r≤18 (Albertson-Cranston-Fox for r≤12, Barát-Tóth for r≤16, Ackerman for r≤18). Since then, several independent lines of work have pushed the verified range and one preprint claims a full resolution. (1) Daniel Cranston (arXiv:2512.08020, submitted 2025-12-08, no AI disclosure) verified r≤24 and restricted possible counterexamples for r∈{25,26} to three residual orders. (2) Jacob Fox, János Pach and Andrew Suk (arXiv:2510.05893, SoCG 2025 version at drops.dagstuhl.de/.../LIPIcs.SoCG.2025.50, no AI disclosure) proved a genuinely restricted case: graphs of chromatic number k with at most 1.4(k-1) vertices satisfy Albertson's conjecture (via a weak-immersion argument going through the related Lescure-Meyniel conjecture), for k sufficiently large — this is a case, not a range-of-r extension, and does not itself resolve any full r. (3) Ankan Sadhu, solo author (arXiv:2609.01682), first posted 2026-09-01 as 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26' (a case extension eliminating Cranston's residual r∈{25,26} orders), then revised 2026-09-13 into 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture' claiming the full conjecture for every r, using Gallai decomposition, weak-immersion routing near r, and exact-certificate verification for a middle range, with 'exact verification certificates archived on GitHub and Zenodo.' The paper discloses that ChatGPT was used only for literature search, language editing and verification assistance, with the author stating he takes responsibility for all mathematical content — this is not AI-generated mathematics under the coding rules, so ai_role is none. (4) Sen Cao and Sanjit Singh Mehat (arXiv:2609.04771, September 2026) independently extended Cranston's r≤24 plus the (v1) r≤26 result to r≤29 using Kempe-chain/immersion, Gallai join structure and Tutte-barrier arguments; their AI disclosure states generative AI/LLMs were used 'substantially' for 'mathematical exploration, intermediate checking, and manuscript drafting,' again with the human authors claiming full responsibility — again coded none under the rule that checking, drafting-assistance and exploration-suggestion by itself does not make the role assisted or generated, since no specific piece of mathematics in the result is attributed to the AI by the authors. (5) Separately, the AI-agent research platform ProofAtlas hosts a live 'collaboration' workspace on this conjecture where AI agents pursue a 'globally minimal-counterexample' framework and report (unaudited, 'source-reported', explicitly marked unreproduced) analytic exclusion results for r≥5446 and adjacent exact-integer exclusions for r=5442-5445; an independent reader's guide to the platform explicitly warns that 'accepted in ProofAtlas' is not peer review and such claims should be treated 'as a lead, not a fact.' None of the ProofAtlas-internal claims have been published, checked by a human, or corroborated elsewhere, so they are not counted as an event here. Because Sadhu's full-r claim is only weeks old, solo-authored, and has so far been read only by an automated review tool (pith.science's 'Pith Review', itself an AI system, not a mathematician) rather than any named expert, journal, or the authors of the competing r≤29 paper, the overall status is coded claimed rather than resolved. The r≤24/26/29 case-extension work, taken on its own, would be coded partial, but the later, broader claim supersedes it as the decisive event for this record per instructions to describe the decisive event and note the others.
competing_reading: If one instead treats Sadhu's all-r claim as not yet a serious enough claim to be the decisive event (given it is solo-authored, unreviewed by any named mathematician, and its own v1/v2 history shows the scope ballooning within two weeks from r≤26 to 'all r' with no apparent independent check), the decisive event could instead be read as the r≤29 case-extension (Cao & Mehat / Cranston lineage), giving status partial with resolution_direction confirmed for the r≤29 range and leaving the general conjecture open. Under that reading ai_role is still none for the same disclosure reasons. I judged claimed to be the more faithful code because a full-scope proof claim exists in the primary literature dated within the window and 'claimed' is explicitly the status for exactly this situation (preprint or announcement not yet digested), rather than silently downgrading a found claim to a weaker status.
what_would_settle_it: A human expert digestion (a referee report, a blog post from a specialist in crossing numbers/chromatic graph theory such as Cranston, Fox, Pach, Suk, or Tóth, or journal acceptance) of Sadhu's arXiv:2609.01682 v2 either endorsing or finding an error in the all-r proof; alternatively, a retraction, a v3 narrowing the claim again, or a published refutation would settle it the other way.

outcome: The general conjecture remains open, but since August 2024 a series of papers using reinforcement learning (PPO), classical greedy/priority search, LLM-guided theorem discovery, and automated theorem proving (Prover9) have eliminated many long-standing potential counterexamples from the Miller-Schupp and Akbulut-Kirby families by exhibiting explicit AC-trivialization sequences, and separately shown the Akbulut-Kirby AK(3) presentation stably AC-trivial (a related, weaker STABLE-AC-conjecture result, not a resolution of the original conjecture as stated).

ai.basis_quote: The best-performing PPO agent solved two new presentations of the Miller-Schupp series that the greedy search had failed to solve.
ai.disclosed_cost: this entire project was carried out using relatively modest computational resources that a small academic research group can easily afford

counterexample.verified_how: The results eliminate specific presentations as potential counterexamples (i.e. confirm they ARE AC-trivial), rather than exhibiting a presentation that refutes the conjecture.

disputes.summary: Alexei Lisitsa's automated-deduction paper (Jan 2025, arXiv:2501.18601) presents an independent re-derivation of the stable AC-triviality of AK(3), explicitly crediting Shehper et al. (Aug 2024) with the original result and framing his own contribution as an alternative, human/Prover9-based proof rather than a new discovery. No dispute over who was first, but worth noting the two results used entirely different methods (RL vs. classical first-order automated theorem proving) to reach compatible conclusions.

summary: Wikipedia's bullet states the original (non-stable) Andrews-Curtis conjecture: every balanced presentation of the trivial group can be reduced to the trivial presentation by Nielsen transformations and conjugations of relators, with no extra generator/relator pairs allowed. Since the 26 January 2024 snapshot, the most substantial development is Shehper, Medina-Mardones, Fagan, Lewandowski, Gruen, Qiu, Kucharski, Wang and Gukov, 'What makes math problems hard for reinforcement learning: a case study' (arXiv:2408.15332, submitted 27 Aug 2024, revised 11 Feb 2025). Using a mix of classical greedy/priority search (not a learned model) and a PPO reinforcement-learning agent, they (a) proved by hand, after observing patterns surfaced by greedy search, that entire infinite families MS(1,w) and MS(n, y^-1xyx^-1) of Miller-Schupp presentations are AC-trivial (Theorems 2-3, Corollary 9) — genuine cases of the original conjecture settled, hence 'partial'; and (b) had their PPO agent directly discover AC-trivialization paths (lengths 205 and 1085, later shortened by removing trivial subsequences) for two specific Miller-Schupp presentations that classical greedy search had failed to solve (Theorem 10) — here the RL agent produced the mathematical object (the move sequence) itself, which the authors then verified and post-processed, making this ai_role 'generated' per §6.2's 'who did the mathematics' test. A companion result widely reported in press (Caltech news release, Aug 2024/Feb 2025; Scientific American) is that the Akbulut-Kirby AK(3) presentation — a roughly 40-year-old flagship potential counterexample — was shown 'stably' AC-trivial. Checking the primary paper directly: this is explicitly the STABLE Andrews-Curtis conjecture (which permits AC1-AC4 moves including adding/removing trivial generator-relator pairs), a related but distinct, weaker conjecture from the one in the Wikipedia bullet; the paper itself states AK(3) under the original, non-stabilized moves 'eludes all attempts at length reduction' and remains unresolved. Per §3.1 this stable-AK(3) result is a related problem, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not by itself move the bullet's status, though it is worth flagging as the single most publicized 'AI solves famous open problem' claim in this area and it is NOT actually a resolution of the bullet's conjecture. Alexei Lisitsa independently re-derived the same stable-AK(3) result using the classical first-order automated theorem prover Prover9 (arXiv:2501.18601, Jan 2025) — a non-AI, non-ML method (automated deduction, not machine learning) — and separately (ScienceDirect / Examples and Counterexamples, 2024) found new non-stable AC-trivializations for Miller-Schupp presentations MS_n(w*), n=3..8, again via Prover9, so 'ai_role: none' would apply to that specific paper's own new trivializations (they are not AI/ML-generated). A 2025 NeurIPS MATH-AI workshop paper by Zhang, Zhou, George, Gukov and Anandkumar ('AI-Driven Mathematical Discovery for the Andrews-Curtis Conjecture') extends the RL approach with an LLM-driven theorem-discovery loop and a deterministic Lean autoformalizer ('AC Certifier'), reporting 753 Miller-Schupp presentations solved/eliminated as counterexamples — this is a workshop paper, not yet digested by the wider expert community, so any status uplift from it would be 'claimed' rather than 'resolved'. Net effect: the overall Andrews-Curtis conjecture is still open, but a genuine, non-trivial slice of it (several infinite families and hundreds of individual Miller-Schupp presentations) has been settled in the confirming direction since the snapshot, with one theorem (Theorem 10 in the Aug 2024 paper) directly and explicitly credited by the authors to an RL agent's own search, satisfying the 'generated' bar under §6.2. I classify the overall status as 'partial' (a case/infinite-family of the problem settled, not the whole conjecture) with ai_role 'generated' anchored on that one clearly-attributed theorem, while noting in competing_reading that most of the total volume of eliminated presentations (753, and the hundreds solved by greedy search) either used non-AI classical search or an LLM+RL pipeline whose exact division of labor across those 753 cases I could not fully verify from the workshop paper alone.
competing_reading: One could argue ai_role should be 'assisted' rather than 'generated' at the level of the overall body of progress, since the two headline infinite-family theorems (Theorems 2, 3, Corollary 9) were proved by hand after humans noticed patterns in classical (non-learned) greedy-search output, and the large majority of solved presentations (533 via greedy search, 753 via the later LLM+RL+autoformalizer pipeline) involve either no AI at all or an entangled LLM/RL/human pipeline whose individual attribution per-presentation isn't spelled out in the workshop abstract I could access. If one weights by volume of presentations resolved rather than by the cleanest single attributable theorem, 'assisted' or even a mixed classification might be more representative; I chose 'generated' because Theorem 10 is the one instance where the authors are unambiguous that the agent itself produced a witness (the move sequence) that a classical method had failed to find, which is the cleanest test case under §6.2, but a reader weighting the aggregate progress differently could reasonably disagree.
what_would_settle_it: Full text access to the NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI workshop paper (openreview id lt3Lpa4d2d) to see exactly which of the 753 Miller-Schupp eliminations were LLM/RL-'generated' versus human-guided, and to arXiv:2607.23611 (Machine-checkable equivalence certificates at the length-14 Andrews-Curtis frontier, Carreras, Jul 2026) to see whether any AC(3)-adjacent length-14 presentations previously only 'claimed' equivalent to AK(3) without a published path now have machine-checkable non-AI certificates that would shift some 'claimed' work to 'resolved'.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or new computational progress on the square-freeness of Euclid numbers (E_n = primorial(p_n) + 1) has appeared since 26 January 2024; the question remains exactly as open as before, with computational verification still resting on Wagstaff's 1993 check of the first 43 terms.
summary: The question 'Are all Euclid numbers square-free?' — i.e., is E_n = 1 + product of the first n primes never divisible by any prime squared — remains open with no relevant activity found since the frozen revision date. The current Wikipedia article on Euclid numbers (checked live, not just the frozen 2024 revision) still lists this as an explicit open question, unchanged in substance from January 2024. The OEIS entry A006862 for Euclid numbers has one substantive comment added in the window, on 17 November 2024 by Antti Karttunen, but it establishes only that Euclid numbers are a subsequence of A048103 (numbers not divisible by p^p for any prime p) — a strictly weaker property than squarefreeness (squarefree numbers are themselves a proper subsequence of A048103, per the OEIS wiki page for A048103). This is consistent with, but does not advance, the squarefree question; it does not narrow which Euclid number could first fail to be squarefree. It is best read as incidental commentary rather than progress on the stated problem, so it does not change the status. Nyblom's 2008/2009 result (published as 'Euclid numbers are free from powers' in 2014, and referenced identically before and after the frozen date) predates the window and only rules out Euclid numbers being *perfect powers* — again a different and weaker-adjacent statement than squarefreeness, and it was already known before January 2024, so it is not new either way. Searches for arXiv preprints, Wagstaff-style computational extensions, and factordb records turned up nothing addressing squarefreeness specifically; a February 2026 arXiv paper ('A generalisation of the Euclid–Mullin sequences', arXiv:2601.21901) that surfaced in search results concerns the unrelated Euclid–Mullin sequence (where each term is a prime factor of one plus the product of previous terms) and cyclotomic residue-class questions, not squarefreeness of primorial+1 numbers — a related-but-distinct problem under §3.1's variant rule, so it is excluded from scope. No AI system involvement was found anywhere in the (nonexistent) progress. Confidence is high that nothing has happened: this is a narrow, well-defined, decades-old question in a well-indexed subfield (OEIS, Wikipedia, arXiv, MathWorld) with essentially no research traffic, and no source of any kind — preprint, blog, survey, database comment — post-dating 26 January 2024 touches it.
competing_reading: One could argue the November 2024 OEIS comment establishing Euclid numbers as a subsequence of A048103 constitutes minor 'progress' in a loose sense, since A048103 membership is a necessary (though far weaker) condition than squarefreeness, and it is new information about the sequence posted inside the window. But it does not narrow the actual squarefree question (a number can be in A048103, e.g. 5^4=625, without being squarefree), so under the case-vs-variant/no-narrowing test in §3.1 it does not count as touching this bullet's status. If a future record disagreed, it would most likely relabel this `progress` rather than `partial` or higher.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit proof that no Euclid number is divisible by any prime square, a single exhibited counterexample (an E_n divisible by some q^2), or even an extension of Wagstaff's computational verification (currently to n=43) to further terms would count as movement; none of these has been found.

outcome: No mathematical progress on the existence question was found since 26 January 2024; only routine discoveries of new prime factors of specific Fermat numbers occurred (e.g. Gary Gostin's November 27, 2025 discovery that 36812439837 · 2³¹⁴⁴ + 1 divides F(3135)), plus a bookkeeping fix to a Lean formalization of the statement, neither of which bears on whether any Fermat number is non-squarefree.
summary: The question is whether any Fermat number 2^(2^n)+1 is non-squarefree (equivalently, whether all are squarefree). This remains completely open. The only developments since 26 January 2024 are: (1) continued, routine discovery of new (single, first-time) prime factors of specific large Fermat numbers via the Proth/PrimeGrid/GIMPS-adjacent distributed search community, tracked at prothsearch.com/fermat.html — e.g. a factor of F(251) found 2024-05-24, factors of F(7220), F(414677), F(5798447) found across late 2024 and January 2025, and Gary Gostin's discovery on 2025-11-27 that 36812439837·2^3144+1 divides F(3135); none of these is a repeated (square) factor, so none bears on squarefreeness — they only extend the known factorizations of individual Fermat numbers, which is a search over a different axis (§3.1: this is an infinitude/existence-type question, and finding more distinct factors doesn't narrow whether a repeated factor exists). (2) A GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures#5702, closed via PR #5735) noting that a Lean formalization of the Wikipedia statement had the polarity of the question backwards (the Lean lemma name asked whether all Fermat numbers ARE squarefree, using `sorry`, i.e. unproved, while Wikipedia asks whether a non-squarefree one EXISTS). This is a pure bookkeeping/naming correction in a conjecture-cataloguing library, not a mathematical result, a proof, or an AI-generated finding — the statement is still marked `sorry` (unproved) after the fix. I confirmed this by reading the issue text directly rather than relying on the triage's note. The Wikipedia article on Fermat numbers itself still lists this as an open problem, citing only Björn and Riesel's pre-2024 heuristic argument (based on modeling square factors as behaving 'randomly') that non-squarefree Fermat numbers are unlikely, which is not a proof and predates the window. I found no arXiv preprint, journal paper, announcement, or AI lab result of any kind addressing squarefreeness of Fermat numbers, and no claimed counterexample. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case, consistent with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the steady stream of new-factor discoveries (a) constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense, since each new distinct prime factor found is one more factor confirmed to appear with multiplicity one, marginally narrowing where a repeated factor could be hiding within that specific Fermat number's factorization. But per §3.1, for an existence/infinitude-shaped question, narrowing where an answer could hide (or verifying more of a specific number's factorization) does not count as movement on the question itself, so I classified this as no_change_found rather than 'progress'. The GitHub issue could also be misread as evidence of a Lean formalization attempt at a proof; on inspection it is only a corrected problem statement, still unproved (`sorry`), so it does not change the classification.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that all Fermat numbers are squarefree, or the discovery of a single Fermat number divisible by the square of a prime, would resolve this. A completed (non-sorry) Lean proof or disproof in the formal-conjectures repository, or a peer-reviewed/expert-digested paper making either claim, would also count.

outcome: The conjecture (Borel's conjecture that every irrational algebraic number is normal, or at least normal in some base) remains completely open: no irrational algebraic number has been proven normal in any base since 26 January 2024. The one notable development is a December 2024 preprint (Kanado & Saito) that proves an equivalence between normality of a given algebraic irrational and the vanishing of a family of Riemann zeta function averages on vertical arithmetic progressions — a reformulation of the exact conjecture, not a resolution or a settled case of it, since the zeta-vanishing condition is itself unverified for any algebraic irrational.
summary: I traced this from the triage's found item, arXiv:2412.02337 (Kanado & Saito, 'Normality of algebraic numbers and the Riemann zeta function,' submitted 2024-12-03, revised 2024-12-17). I fetched the abstract and full text description directly: the authors prove that a positive algebraic irrational α is normal to base b if and only if a specific limit of Riemann zeta function averages over vertical arithmetic progressions vanishes for every integer k ≥ 0. This is a genuine mathematical result — an equivalence theorem — but it reformulates the exact conjecture in the bullet rather than settling any part of it: the zeta-vanishing side of the equivalence is exactly as unverified as the original normality question, so no case of the conjecture is removed and no bound moves. Per §3.1, this is scope-preserving (it's the same problem restated, not a restriction or a variant), but since neither side of the equivalence is established, it doesn't count as `partial` progress on the specific bullet — nothing has actually been settled. No journal publication or expert digestion (e.g., no Tao blog post, no Quanta coverage) of this paper turned up, and it has apparently not led to any follow-up proving the zeta condition for any specific algebraic number. Separately, I found a Google DeepMind 'formal-conjectures' GitHub repository (issue #2256, created 2025) that catalogues a Lean formalization of the *statement* of this conjecture as a benchmark target for automated theorem provers — this is explicitly not a proof attempt, just a formalized statement awaiting proof, and the repo's own text repeats that 'despite significant work, it is unknown whether even a single algebraic irrational number is normal in any base.' I also checked a 2017 paper on binary digits of algebraic irrationals (density bounds like √N growth in digit counts) but confirmed via its arXiv listing this predates the window and in any case only bounds digit density, which per §3.1's rule on existence/record questions doesn't move a normality question. The 2508.09319 paper on 'transcendentally normal numbers' is about transcendental numbers, a different class, and does not bear on algebraic irrationals. The current Wikipedia 'Normal number' article, fetched directly, confirms the conjecture is unresolved and cites no result past 2012 in its normality-of-algebraics section. No AI system appears anywhere in this chain: the zeta-equivalence paper is conventional human analytic number theory with no AI acknowledgement found, and the DeepMind repository's role is cataloguing/formalizing an unproved statement, not producing any part of a proof — so even that has no bearing on ai_role.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kanado-Saito equivalence deserves `progress` rather than `open`, on the theory that a clean equivalence to a well-studied analytic object (zeta function averages) is analogous to a bound moving — it changes the terrain future work would attack. But per the instructions a case must be *settled* (something removed from the open territory) to count as `partial`, and a bound must actually move numerically to count as `progress`; an equivalence where neither side is resolved settles nothing and moves no bound, so I classified it as `open` with `no_change_found` true. If a future update to this record found a paper verifying the zeta condition for a specific number (even conditionally), that would flip this to `claimed` or `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper verifying the Kanado-Saito zeta-vanishing condition for any specific algebraic irrational (which would prove that number normal in that base), or a direct proof/counterexample for any algebraic irrational, or expert digestion of 2412.02337 in a survey or blog confirming its correctness and importance.

outcome: No proof, counterexample, or new bound on the square-freeness of Mersenne numbers with prime index was found since 26 January 2024; the problem remains exactly as open as it was, resting on the same pre-2024 Wieferich-prime-based partial verification.
summary: The conjecture asks whether every Mersenne number M_q = 2^q − 1 with q prime is square-free. It is classical (Rotkiewicz-era work) that p^2 | M_q for prime p implies p is a Wieferich prime (2^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^2), so the conjecture is equivalent to a strong non-occurrence statement about Wieferich primes. Only two Wieferich primes are known (1093 and 3511), both found before 1922, and the relevant computational fact — that M_q is therefore square-free for all prime q below roughly 4×10^12 — predates 2024 (see primepuzzles.net's Conjecture 12 page and johnblythedobson.org's page on square divisors of Mersenne numbers). The main lever that could move this problem is an extended Wieferich prime search, but PrimeGrid's search completed its scan to 2^64 (~1.8×10^19) in December 2022 and has no plans to continue, so no bound moved inside the window (26 Jan 2024–present). A claimed full proof by Jacques Basaldúa (discussed on the primepuzzles.net page) was shown to contain a flaw in its treatment of the Wieferich prime 1093 well before the window and remains unresolved/withdrawn; it is not a 2024+ event. Searches for arXiv papers turned up Kovač–Luca, 'On the number of divisors of Mersenne numbers' (arXiv:2506.04883, June 2025, revised through Feb 2026), which studies the unboundedness of f(2n)/f(n) where f(n)=Σ τ(2^k−1) — a divisor-count growth question motivated by Erdős, not the square-freeness of individual Mersenne numbers. This is a related-but-different problem (§3.1): it says nothing about whether any M_q for prime q has a repeated prime factor, so it does not touch this bullet's scope, and does not even remove a case of it. No Lean/Coq formalization, no lab announcement, and no new named Wieferich prime candidate were found. This is an existence-type question (does any prime-index Mersenne number have a square factor) and, per §3.1, is not advanced merely by pushing verification limits further — and in any case no such push occurred in the window. I therefore agree with the triage's 'none' verdict and did not find anything it missed.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2022 completion of PrimeGrid's Wieferich search to 2^64, even though it finished before the window, has not been superseded and thus implicitly 'holds' the current bound into the window with no change — but this is not an event that happened in the window, so it correctly plays no role in the classification beyond providing background for why no progress was possible/attempted. There is no genuine ambiguity here between 'case' and 'variant' for the one adjacent paper found (Kovač–Luca): it is unambiguously a different question about a summatory divisor-count function, not about square-freeness of individual Mersenne numbers.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: (1) a new Wieferich prime discovered beyond 1093/3511 with a computation showing whether it divides some M_q; (2) an extension of the Wieferich prime search past 2^64; (3) a full unconditional proof (peer-reviewed or expert-digested) that no Mersenne number with prime index has a square factor; (4) a computer-verified counterexample exhibiting a prime q and prime p with p^2 | 2^q − 1.

outcome: Zhi-Wei Sun posted a preprint (arXiv:2609.04176, 3 Sep 2026) claiming to prove Catalan's constant — one of the constants named in this bullet — is irrational, explicitly crediting AI both for the proof strategy and for the numerical verification; a note by Dane Wachs (arXiv:2609.22339, 16 Sep 2026) identifies a specific numerical gap in the key estimate (Theorem 9.1) and concludes the derivation does not justify the claim, so nothing is currently established either way. No other constant named in the bullet (γ, π+e, π−e, πe, π/e, π^e, π^√2, π^π, e^(π²), lnπ, 2^e, e^e, Khinchin's constant) has had its rationality/algebraicity status settled since 26 January 2024; a March 2026 formal-verification writeup claiming to prove γ irrational (Zenodo, Jonathan Reed) is self-published, unreviewed, and not corroborated anywhere else.

ai.basis_quote: The author's many rounds of conversations with AI provide the basis of this paper. ... introducing 'weighted tails' made the proof practical and successful. ... The needed numerical data in the proof were produced by AI. The whole proof has passed the verification of Chatgpt 5.6 Solar.

disputes.summary: Dane Wachs's note (arXiv:2609.22339, 16 Sep 2026) reports that the lower bound Sun's Theorem 9.1 derivation actually controls is roughly +1.49 to +1.79 B² at tested indices (also stated on the Lean repo as converging to about +1.86), while Sun's derivation claims the quantity is at most −0.00966 B² + o(B²) — the opposite sign of what the argument needs. Wachs also flags an index-shift slip in Theorem 2.1 (repairable) and a missing term from the prime 2's contribution in the main ledger (not obviously repairable). Wachs concludes: 'the published derivation does not justify the claimed estimate, so the proof of the main theorem is incomplete... Nothing is concluded about the irrationality of G.' As of this research, Sun has not posted a v2 or public response; the paper remains at v1 on arXiv.

summary: The bullet asks about the rationality/algebraic status and irrationality measure of a list of thirteen named constants: gamma, pi+e, pi-e, pi*e, pi/e, pi^e, pi^sqrt(2), pi^pi, e^(pi^2), ln(pi), 2^e, e^e, Catalan's constant, and Khinchin's constant. Of these, only Catalan's constant has seen a serious claimed development in the window: Zhi-Wei Sun (Nanjing University) posted arXiv:2609.04176 on 3 September 2026 claiming a full proof that Catalan's constant G is irrational, using a 'weighted tails' variant of the determinant-based methods used in the 2024 Calegari-Dimitrov-Tang irrationality proof for a different constant (L(2,chi_{-3})). Sun's own acknowledgements state plainly that AI was used for more than clerical support: 'many rounds of conversations with AI provide the basis of this paper,' an AI-suggested pivot ('weighted tails') is what made the proof 'practical and successful,' and the numerical data underlying the proof was AI-generated and AI-verified ('Chatgpt 5.6 Solar'). That is a first-person account of AI contributing to the mathematical content itself (not just formalisation or proofreading), which is why ai_role is coded assisted rather than none — though the humans (Sun) still designed and wrote the overall argument, so this is not generated. However, a follow-up note by Dane Wachs (arXiv:2609.22339, 16 September 2026) performs a numerical check of the central inequality in Sun's Theorem 9.1 and finds the quantity the proof needs to be negative is empirically positive (roughly +1.5 to +1.9 B² versus a claimed bound of about −0.01 B²), and separately flags a missing prime-2 contribution in the main ledger. A partial, independent Lean 4 formalization of Sun's paper (github.com/chokmah-me/catalan-sun-lean) corroborates this: it formalizes the paper's early structural lemmas but explicitly disclaims proving the main theorem, and its own README states the measured quantity converges to about +1.86, consistent with Wachs's finding and inconsistent with what Sun's argument requires. No rebuttal or revised version from Sun has appeared. Because a human expert (Wachs) has examined the argument and found it does not currently establish the claim, and no correction has restored it, the proof is best classified as claimed (a preprint claim, unresolved, credibly disputed) rather than resolved, and the direction is coded confirmed for the claimed result itself (Sun's stated conclusion agrees with the long-suspected truth that G is irrational) while noting the claim itself is presently unsubstantiated. None of the other twelve constants in the bullet show any change: gamma's irrationality remains completely open in the peer-reviewed literature (confirmed via mathworld, Wikipedia's Euler-Mascheroni-constant article, and 2025-2026 arXiv papers on related generalized constants, none of which claim to settle gamma itself); one Zenodo preprint (Jonathan Reed, April 2026) claims a Lean-checked proof of gamma's irrationality, but it is self-published on a non-peer-reviewed repository, has no visible engagement from the number theory community, and its 'trap criterion' argument echoes the same pattern (bold claim, machine-checked, unreviewed) that turned out to be premature for Catalan's constant — it does not meet the resolved bar (no expert digestion) and is not corroborated elsewhere, so it is not made the basis of any status change here. Khinchin's constant's irrationality is explicitly stated as still open by MathWorld, Wikipedia, and all located 2024-2026 papers. The pi/e-family algebraic constants (pi+e, pi-e, pi*e, pi/e, pi^e, pi^sqrt(2), pi^pi, e^(pi^2), ln(pi), 2^e, e^e) have no irrationality or transcendence proofs in the window; the closest related work is a June 2026 no-go/obstruction paper (Runlong Yu, arXiv:2606.17303) showing why Apery-type and hypergeometric certificate techniques cannot resolve the irrationality of e+pi — this is a negative methodological result about proof techniques, not a case or resolution of the stated question, so per §3.1 it does not change this bullet and is mentioned only for completeness. Irrationality-measure bounds for pi did move in the window (Zeilberger-Zudilin's 7.103205334137 improved slightly to 7.101862832357 by Yufei Bai, arXiv:2609.11276, September 2026), but the bullet's irrationality-measure sub-question is about the measures of gamma, Catalan's constant, Khinchin's constant, etc. as named — pi's irrationality measure is not itself one of the thirteen named constants in this specific bullet's list (pi is used only as a building block for pi+e, pi*e, etc., whose measures are not addressed by a pi-only bound), so this bound improvement is a related development but out of the literal scope of the bullet and is not used to change status; it is recorded here for transparency. Overall this bullet's status is driven entirely by the Catalan's constant sub-claim, coded claimed with ai_role assisted.
competing_reading: One could argue the whole bullet should stay 'open' rather than 'claimed', on the view that Sun's proof has already been shown by Wachs's numerical check to fail, making it functionally indistinguishable from any other refuted/incorrect preprint that never should have moved the needle. Under that reading, an unrebutted but apparently-broken preprint is not really 'progress' worth a claimed status, and this would be closer to a progress/incident coding (an AI-linked claim that, on inspection, does not hold up) rather than claimed. I chose claimed over open or progress/incident because: (a) Sun has not withdrawn or corrected the paper, so it is not formally an incident/withdrawal; (b) the dispute (Wachs's note) is itself only a note, not a peer-reviewed refutation, and the field has not yet reached consensus; (c) the definition of claimed ("experts have not yet digested") fits a paper actively being checked and disputed better than open, which implies nothing happened. If Sun posts a corrected v2 that repairs Wachs's objection, or if the community consensus solidifies that the proof is unsalvageable, this record should be revisited: a solid rebuttal with no rescue would justify reclassifying as progress/incident dated to the claim.
what_would_settle_it: A revised version of Sun's arXiv:2609.04176 (or a follow-up paper) that either repairs the Theorem 9.1 estimate Wachs disputes (with the prime-2 ledger term accounted for) and survives expert scrutiny — which would move this to resolved or at least keep it claimed with the dispute resolved in Sun's favor — or a definitive rebuttal/withdrawal confirming the gap is fatal, which would move this to progress with ai_role incident. Watching Sun's homepage and arXiv for a v2, and watching for citations/commentary from established Catalan's-constant experts (e.g., Calegari, Dimitrov, Tang, or Rivoal) would settle it either way.

outcome: A September 2025 preprint by Han, Liu, and Zhuang proves that general-type minimal model programs (MMPs) terminate — i.e. no infinite sequence of flips exists — in dimensions 4 and 5, with the fivefold big-boundary case and the effective (explicit step-bound) fourfold case both previously open; the general (non-general-type) termination question and dimension >5 remain open.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether infinite sequences of flips are possible in dimension >3 — i.e. whether termination of the MMP (Kawamata's termination-of-flips conjecture) is known beyond the threefold case, where Mori/Shokurov settled it. Prior to the window, termination in dimension 4 was known unconditionally (Fujino/Kawamata-era results and Birkar's later work; the frozen-date state of the art already had dimension-4 termination for arbitrary flips, per Fujino 2004/2005-era results, and separately Kawamata's termination for terminal fourfold flips). The 2025 preprint arXiv:2509.01501 (Han, Liu, Zhuang, 'Effective termination of general type MMPs in dimension at most five', submitted 2025-09-01, replacing an earlier two-paper split of arXiv:2506.20183) proves effective (explicitly bounded) termination of general type MMPs in dimension ≤5, and states plainly that termination of fivefold MMPs when K+Δ or Δ is big was not previously known, and that even the fourfold case with an explicit step bound was new. I read the paper's introduction directly (via fetch of the arXiv abstract and PDF) and found no mention of AI, machine learning, automated theorem proving, or formalization anywhere in the text — the proof is a purely human argument using Birkar's induction technique together with a new uniform bound on the Cartier index of Weil divisors in a general-type MMP, then invoking termination of terminal fourfold flips. This is scope-restricted to 'general type' pairs (K+Δ big, or pseudo-effective with Δ big), so it is a case of the stated problem rather than a full resolution — it does not touch non-general-type MMPs in dimension ≥4, nor any dimension above 5. Because it is a single preprint less than a year old with no evidence of expert digestion, journal acceptance, or a subsequent verification I could find, I classify it as 'partial' (a case of the problem is settled) rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed'; had the paper's status been merely an unverified announcement I would have used 'claimed', but a written, technically detailed preprint with named authors and a concrete argument is treated here as the evidentiary basis for the 'partial' case-settled classification, while noting the lack of digestion in confidence/summary. resolution_direction is 'confirmed' because the settled case (dimensions 4-5, general type) confirms termination as conjectured (no counterexample; flips do terminate in this case).
competing_reading: One could argue this preprint should be logged as merely 'progress' rather than 'partial', since it is scoped to general-type pairs and gives an *effective* (bounded) version of a result whose non-effective avatar in dimension 4 was arguably already implicit in earlier work (Fujino's termination of flips for fourfold MMPs, and Birkar's 2007 work using boundedness of pairs). If the paper's dimension-4 contribution is read as 'only' adding explicit bounds to an already-known qualitative termination result, then dimension 4 is not new territory and only the dimension-5 general-type case is a genuinely new settled case — still 'partial' under the same code, but with a narrower scope than stated above. This does not change the status code, only the extent of what was newly settled, which is reflected in outcome/summary.
what_would_settle_it: An explicit statement in a survey or in Han-Liu-Zhuang's related papers pinning down exactly which fourfold termination facts (qualitative vs. effective/bounded) were already established before this preprint, and whether any journal referee report or expert blog commentary (e.g. a birational-geometry seminar write-up) has appeared digesting arXiv:2509.01501.

outcome: Guy's conjecture (that the Sprague-Grundy/nim-sequence of every finite octal game is eventually periodic) remains open; no case, counterexample, or bound relevant to this exact (impartial) conjecture was found dated after 26 January 2024.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet is Guy's conjecture for impartial octal games: every finite octal game's nim-sequence is eventually periodic. I checked the two standing reference resources for this problem — Achim Flammenkamp's octal-games database (wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/octal.html, last touched with a July 2026 note that a contributor 'extend[ed] the sgv-sequence of lots of octal-games,' i.e. computed further terms of already-known sequences rather than settling any new game's eventual periodicity) and David Eppstein's 'Octal periodicity' page — plus the current 'Octal game' Wikipedia article, none of which report any octal game's periodicity status changing since January 2024. The one live GitHub artifact the triage found, google-deepmind/formal-conjectures issue #3697 (opened 2026-04-05), is only a request/plan to state Guy's conjecture formally in Lean; it lists the Mathlib building blocks needed and explicitly leaves the proof open — no proof or disproof exists there. The triage's other lead, arXiv:2608.13273 ('A Finite Automaton Approach to Combinatorial Games,' 2026-08), does solve many two-digit games and states results toward a Guy's-conjecture analogue, but its abstract is explicit that this is a *partizan* version of Guy's conjecture ('we propose a partizan version of Guy's conjecture'), a different, non-impartial game class from the one this Wikipedia bullet states; per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated (impartial) conjecture, so it does not count as a change in scope. A tangential lead turned up while searching, arXiv:2512.24221 ('Node-Kayles on Trees,' 2026-01-01), proves periodicity results for Node-Kayles played on trees, but Node-Kayles-on-paths (the linear game, equal to octal game 0.137/Dawson's-Kayles-adjacent) is a different structure from Node-Kayles-on-trees, so this is also a related problem rather than a case of the finite-octal-game conjecture as stated (which concerns heap games on a line, not tree structures). No AI system appears anywhere in this search: the automaton paper uses classical finite-automaton construction and formal verification, not machine learning, and the formal-conjectures GitHub issue is human-authored planning text with no AI-generated content credited. I conclude 'open' with no change found, at high confidence for the impartial conjecture as literally stated, tempered slightly by the fact that the octal-games literature is scattered across personal pages and small journals that a search engine may not fully index.
competing_reading: If a reader takes 'octal games' broadly enough to include the automaton paper's partizan variant or the Node-Kayles-on-trees periodicity results as 'a case of' the conjecture, one could code this as `partial` with an AI role of `none`. I don't think that reading survives contact with the stated question, since both papers change the object (partizan payoff structure; tree adjacency structure) rather than restricting the same impartial, linear-heap game class — but the boundary between 'restriction' and 'variant' in combinatorial game theory is genuinely blurry when a paper explicitly frames its result as an analogue of the named conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or database update that (a) proves or disproves eventual periodicity for a specific unsolved impartial octal game (e.g. one of the ~65 unsettled 2-digit or 8 unsettled 3-digit games listed on Flammenkamp's page, or Grundy's Game / 0.6111...), or (b) exhibits a finite octal game whose nim-sequence is proven non-eventually-periodic, dated after 26 January 2024 — either would move this out of 'open.' Absent that, the conjecture stays open regardless of adjacent partizan or tree-game results.
