outcome: No mathematical progress on the completeness question since 26 January 2024. The one apparently new item found — an OEIS comment dated 22 August 2026 attributing a bound of 7.75*10^19 to Elsenhans, Klüners, and Nicolae — traces back to arXiv:1803.02056, submitted 6 March 2018, well before the window; the 2026 OEIS edit is an editorial correction to the sequence's comment text, not a new result. A GitHub issue in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository (opened 10 February 2026) formalizes the conjecture's *statement* in Lean but proves nothing and settles nothing.
summary: This problem asks whether Euler's list of 65 idoneal numbers is complete, or whether one or two more exist (Weinberger 1973 showed at most two more can exist, and the list is complete if GRH holds). I found no proof, disproof, new idoneal number, or improved unconditional bound published since 26 January 2024. Two items surfaced that looked promising on the surface but resolve to nothing new: (1) OEIS sequence A000926 (idoneal numbers) has a comment dated 22 August 2026, credited to David Radcliffe, giving a bound of 7.75*10^19 on any further term and attributing it to 'results of Elsenhans, Klüners, and Nicolae'; I traced this to arXiv:1803.02056 ('Imaginary quadratic number fields with class groups of small exponent'), submitted 6 March 2018 by Elsenhans, Klüners and Nicolae, which computes all discriminants D with |D| <= 3.1*10^20 and class-group exponent dividing 8 (idoneal numbers correspond to exponent <=2, a special case of this computation). The mathematics is from 2018; the only 2026 event is an OEIS editor correcting/clarifying the sequence's comment text (the OEIS page also shows an adjacent correction replacing an apparently erroneous 'at most two further terms' framing). This is not a new result and does not move the window. (2) A GitHub issue #2242 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, opened 10 February 2026, titled 'Idoneal Numbers Completeness Conjecture', formalizes the *statement* of the conjecture in Lean 4 for use as a benchmark item (formalizability rated 2/5, category 'research open'); no proof was attempted or claimed, and the repository's stated purpose is benchmarking automated formalization/theorem-proving tools, not solving conjectures — AlphaProof is mentioned only as a tool the maintainers use to check for misformalizations, not to produce mathematics. Since the conjecture's statement itself, not its truth, was formalized, and no argument was produced, this is formalisation_only with ai_role none and has no bearing on status. I also checked the Wikipedia idoneal-number article (no changes reported since 2011 citations), OEIS A000926 in full, and searched arXiv/web broadly for any 2024-2026 paper improving Weinberger's bound, disproving GRH-dependence, or exhibiting/ruling out a 66th idoneal number; nothing surfaced. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the OEIS comment update and the DeepMind formalization issue are worth recording as 'progress' in a loose sense, since both are dated within the window and both touch this exact problem. But the OEIS edit is bibliographic housekeeping citing eight-year-old mathematics, and the Lean issue formalizes a question without answering any part of it — neither changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, so under the scope rule (§3.1) neither counts as a status-changing event, and I have coded both as background context rather than the record's event.
what_would_settle_it: A published paper post-January-2024 that either exhibits/rules out a 66th or 67th idoneal number unconditionally, improves the unconditional bound below Weinberger's implied threshold in a way that changes the conjectured count, or a resolution of GRH itself. Alternatively, discovery of an arXiv preprint by Elsenhans/Klüners/Nicolae or others specifically dated 2024-2026 (rather than the 2018 paper) that I may have missed under a different title.

outcome: No result addressing the infinitude of Leinster groups was found in the window; the only related development is a 2025 paper introducing relaxed variants (almost/quasi-Leinster groups) that explicitly does not tackle the original question.
summary: A Leinster group is a finite group whose order equals the sum of the orders of its normal subgroups (a group-theoretic analogue of perfect numbers). Whether infinitely many exist is stated as open both by the current Wikipedia article ('It is unknown whether there are infinitely many Leinster groups', with no citation or date suggesting recent movement) and by every source found in this search. The only paper from the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) that discusses Leinster groups at all is Pleșca and Tărnăuceanu, 'Almost and quasi Leinster groups' (arXiv:2503.16884, submitted 8 April 2025). That paper deliberately studies relaxed variants — 'almost Leinster' and 'quasi-Leinster' groups, paralleling almost-perfect and quasi-perfect numbers — rather than the original Leinster-group condition. Per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated problem: settling questions about almost/quasi-Leinster groups removes nothing from the original infinitude question, since those are different (relaxed) defining equations, not restrictions of the same one. The paper does use GAP (a computer-algebra system, not an AI system) for verification of examples; this is unrelated to AI involvement in any event, and it does not bear on the original problem regardless. No arXiv, Wikipedia, or general-web search surfaced any 2024–2026 work constructing an infinite family of genuine Leinster groups, proving finiteness, or otherwise moving the original question. I also checked the 2019 'Leinster groups of order pqrs' line of work (Zhang/Tărnăuceanu-adjacent classification results) for any recent continuation; searches found only the pre-window (2019) paper and no update in the window. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' case: the problem is a fairly obscure, narrow group-theory question with only a handful of active researchers (chiefly Tărnăuceanu and coauthors), its own Wikipedia article was checked directly and shows no updated claim, and multiple query angles (direct infinitude question, arXiv author search, general open-problem-list search, disambiguation page) converged on the same single 2025 tangential paper.
competing_reading: One could argue the almost/quasi-Leinster paper is indirectly relevant groundwork — e.g. if quasi-Leinster groups were shown to be infinite in a way that structurally suggested a route to infinitely many genuine Leinster groups. But the paper's own framing treats these as distinct, parallel objects (analogous to how almost-perfect numbers are a separate open topic from perfect numbers), and it reports no implication for the genuine case. I do not think this rises to 'partial progress' under §3.1's case-vs-variant test, since it changes the defining equation rather than restricting the class of groups considered under the original equation.
what_would_settle_it: A paper either exhibiting an infinite family of groups satisfying the exact Leinster condition (order = sum of orders of normal subgroups), or a proof that only finitely many such groups exist, or an expert (e.g. Tărnăuceanu, who works actively in this exact niche) explicitly commenting that the question remains open as of a recent date.

outcome: No composite satisfying 2^(c-1) ≡ 1 (mod c^2) — a base-2 Wieferich pseudoprime — has been found or ruled out since 26 January 2024; the question remains exactly as open as it was, and no new bound-moving search targeting this specific composite question was found.
summary: This bullet asks whether any composite c exists with 2^(c-1) ≡ 1 (mod c^2), i.e. a base-2 Wieferich pseudoprime (WPSP). A necessary condition for such a c is that every prime factor of c be a Wieferich prime (p with p^2 | 2^(p-1) - 1), and only two Wieferich primes are known — 1093 and 3511 — with the search for a third completed by PrimeGrid up to 2^64 (~1.8×10^19) as of 29 December 2022, a date before the frozen revision and with no announced continuation. Because the pool of eligible prime factors has not grown and no dedicated computational search of composites (as opposed to primes) for this exact congruence was found reported anywhere in 2024–2026, the question sits precisely where it did in January 2024. I searched broadly for 'Wieferich pseudoprime' work in 2024–2026 and found only unrelated papers: Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules/function fields (arXiv:2412.11588, arXiv:2512.08060), Wieferich primes in number fields tied to the Ankeny–Artin–Chowla and Mordell conjectures (arXiv:2508.08472), and non-Wieferich prime ideals related to an Erdős conjecture (arXiv:2601.12753) — all of these are analogues over different algebraic objects (function fields, number fields, prime ideals) and change nothing about the classical composite existence question stated in this bullet, so per §3.1 they are related problems, not cases of it, and do not move the status. The current Wikipedia 'Wieferich prime' article's pseudoprime discussion and the OEIS pages A077816 (Wieferich numbers, both prime and composite terms satisfying a related condition, maintained by Max Alekseyev) and A182297 were also checked; neither shows any new composite discovery or new targeted search bound for this specific congruence since 2024. No AI system was mentioned in connection with any of this. I judge this a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' rather than an under-researched null result.
competing_reading: One could argue the PrimeGrid Wieferich-prime search (finished Dec 2022, ruling out a third Wieferich prime below 2^64) is itself relevant 'progress' by narrowing where a composite WPSP's prime factors could live, but that search predates the frozen revision's window and was not extended afterward, so it cannot be used to justify anything other than open/open_stale, and it was already reflected in the pre-2024 state of knowledge that the Wikipedia list captured.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit composite c verified (by hand or computer algebra) to satisfy 2^(c-1) ≡ 1 (mod c^2), or a new dedicated computational search (post-January-2024) of composites — not just primes — up to some large bound reported as extending the known search space, or a proof of non-existence.

outcome: No graph on n vertices exceeding floor(n/2) copies of each letter has been exhibited; the specific extremal question remains open, but Hefty, Horn, Muir & Owens (EJC 2024) and its 2026 JCTA follow-up 'Bottlenecks and bounds' advanced the surrounding theory of representation-number lower bounds (previously almost all work had been on upper bounds), moving understanding of the range of possible representation numbers without settling the floor(n/2) question itself.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether there exist graphs on n vertices whose representation number (minimum k such that the graph has a k-uniform representing word) exceeds floor(n/2). Both the live Wikipedia article on word-representable graphs and an EmergentMind topic summary (checked 2026-09-22) confirm this is still stated as an open problem: the highest known representation number remains floor(n/2), achieved by G_n, the crown graph H_{n,n} augmented with an all-adjacent (apex) vertex, giving 2n+1 vertices and representation number floor((2n+1)/2) = n = floor((2n+1)/2) — this construction is from Glen, Kitaev & Pyatkin (2018), which predates the 26 Jan 2024 frozen revision and is not a new development. The known general upper bound on representation number is roughly 2n (Hefty et al. 2024 sharpen this somewhat for non-complete graphs, e.g. 2(n-omega(G)) where omega is the clique number), leaving an unresolved gap between floor(n/2) and ~2n. Within the window, two papers by the same author group advanced the surrounding theory: (1) Hefty, Horn, Muir & Owens, 'Word-Representable Graphs: Orientations, Posets, and Bounds' (Electron. J. Combin. 31(4), #P4.2, published online October 2024, submitted Feb 2024) uses posets, Ramsey theory, finite geometry and probabilistic methods to settle several other open problems about word-representability and representation length for specific graph classes, and gives a general lower bound on representation number (roughly log|N(X)|/log(|X|+1) type bounds) for a finite graph; (2) its 2026 follow-up in J. Combin. Theory Ser. A, 'Word-representation numbers of graphs: Bottlenecks and bounds,' whose own abstract states that 'most of the effort in this direction previously has focused on upper bounds' and that this paper 'provide[s] several lower bounds' instead. Neither paper is reported (in the abstract, any digested source, or the current Wikipedia/EmergentMind status pages) as exhibiting a graph whose representation number exceeds floor(n/2); rather, they develop general machinery for proving lower bounds on representation number for various graph families, which is progress on the broader landscape of the problem (understanding how representation numbers can grow) without resolving the specific extremal question asked in this bullet. I was unable to obtain clean extracted text from the EJC or JCTA PDFs themselves (repeated WebFetch attempts returned only PDF stream/font metadata, not readable body text), so my classification rests on the papers' own abstracts, on secondary digestions (Wikipedia's own article, EmergentMind), and on a Mozhui-Krishna 2025 arXiv paper on the related (but distinct, since it concerns a Glen-Kitaev-Pyatkin conjecture about bipartite graphs specifically, ceil((m+n)/4)) bipartite representation-number conjecture, which I did not rely on for this bullet's classification. No AI system of any kind is mentioned in any source consulted; all cited work uses standard combinatorial, poset-theoretic, Ramsey-theoretic and probabilistic methods.
competing_reading: The triage's `why` field asserted the 2024 EJC paper 'is reported to settle open problems on representation-number bounds' and that the 2026 JCTA paper 'addresses bottlenecks/bounds on this exact quantity,' which could be read as implying this specific floor(n/2) question was resolved. However, neither paper's abstract, nor any secondary source I found (including the live, current Wikipedia article on word-representable graphs, which still lists essentially this exact open problem), states that a graph exceeding floor(n/2) has been found. The 'open problems' the EJC 2024 abstract says it settles appear to be about existence and length of representations for particular graph classes (e.g. posets, cover graphs), not the general extremal floor(n/2) question. It remains conceivable that a lower-bound construction buried in either paper's body (which I could not extract as readable text) does exhibit a graph exceeding floor(n/2) for some specific n, which would upgrade this to `partial` or `resolved` with `resolution_direction: refuted`. I was not able to rule this out with full confidence given the PDF extraction failures.
what_would_settle_it: Readable full text (not just abstract/metadata) of Hefty-Horn-Muir-Owens EJC 2024 and JCTA 2026, specifically their theorem statements on general lower bounds for representation number, to confirm whether any explicit or existential construction is claimed to exceed floor(n/2) copies of each letter for some n. Also worth checking: any post-2024 update to the Wikipedia 'word-representable graph' article's open-problems section, and any survey talk slides by Hefty/Horn/Muir/Owens summarizing their results in plain prose.

outcome: No proof, disproof, example, or theoretical/search-bound advance on opposite-parity amicable pairs was found since 26 January 2024; the only new item is a January 2026 Lean 4 formalization paper that restates the existing (pre-2024) parity-constraint theorem without proving it, and a February 2026 GitHub issue formalizing the bare conjecture statement.
summary: The question is whether any amicable pair exists with one member even and one odd. No such pair is known, and this remains true today. The relevant theoretical constraints (if an odd-even pair exists, the odd member must be a perfect square and the even member 2^k times an odd square) trace to Kanold and to D'Abramo/Starni's 2005 paper 'On Amicable Numbers With Different Parity' (arXiv:math/0501402) — all predating the 26 January 2024 window, so not counted here. I found two items from within the window: (1) arXiv:2601.07444, 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (Chen, Tang, Zhan; submitted 12 Jan 2026), a Lean 4 formalization paper. I read the full PDF: §3.7.4 'Parity Constraints' explicitly states the two parity-constraint theorems (OddMemberSquareTheorem, EvenMemberFormTheorem) are formalized 'without proof' as bare Lean Prop statements — the paper does not prove them, merely states the classical (already-known) constraint as a target for 'future work.' It reports no new mathematical result about opposite parity; it is a formalization/engineering paper, and its own future-work section lists 'attempting formal proofs of the parity constraint theorems' as unfinished. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the paper (methods, acknowledgements, or elsewhere) — the authors used the zify and ring Lean tactics, which are ordinary automated proof-search/normalization tactics, not AI/LLM systems, so ai_role is 'none' rather than any AI-involvement code. (2) A February 2026 GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #2241), 'Amicable Numbers with Opposite Parity,' which per the triage's own note and my read of it (via WebFetch) is purely a formalization task tracking the open conjecture statement in Lean/Mathlib-style code for a benchmark repository — it explicitly says the problem 'remains open' and does not itself contain or claim a resolution; it is an issue asking a contributor (human or AI) to write the formal statement, not a proof attempt or a result. Neither item changes what a careful person would write in this bullet: the conjecture is exactly as open now as in January 2024, no example has been found, and no bound specific to opposite-parity pairs (as opposed to the separate, older coprime-amicable-pair search bound of 10^65/10^74) has moved during the window. This is a restatement/formalization, not a case or a variant that advances the mathematics, so I classify as open with no_change_found true rather than 'progress'.
competing_reading: One could argue the arXiv:2601.07444 Lean formalization of the parity-constraint statement counts as a minor 'progress' event (formal statement of the known theorem in a new proof assistant), similar to how a Wikipedia note or survey restates a bound. But per §3.1 the test is whether it changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, and a formalization that explicitly declares the theorem unproved ('without proof') and unresolved, of an already-known 2005-era result, does not move the needle on the stated question ('are there any pairs...'). I classify it as no new event rather than as a 'progress' status.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an explicit odd-even amicable pair discovered by exhaustive search or construction, (b) a proof that no such pair can exist, or (c) a paper that tightens the numerical lower bound specifically for opposite-parity pairs (distinct from the general coprime-amicable-pair bound) beyond the existing Hagis-era bounds (mn > 10^74, both members > 10^60, dating to the 1990s per Hagis's work referenced in secondary sources) — none of which I found dated after 26 January 2024.

summary: Nothing has happened to the underlying mathematical question since 26 January 2024. All known betrothed (quasi-amicable) pairs — (48,75), (140,195), (1050,1925), (1575,1648), (2024,2295), (5775,6128), etc. — remain opposite-parity, and it is still open whether a same-parity pair exists; the standing observation that any such pair would have to exceed 10^13 is unchanged and I found no computational search extending that bound. The one concrete event in the window is procedural rather than mathematical: on 2026-02-15, PR #2264 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures ('feat(Wikipedia): Conjectures about Betrothed Numbers', merged by maintainer mo271) closed issue #2243 ('Do betrothed number pairs with the same parity exist?') by encoding the conjecture as an unproved Lean statement (a benchmark item, not a proof attempt), with the formalization itself produced with the help of Claude Opus 4.6. A later issue (#4998, closed via PR #4999) flagged that the Lean encoding of 'same_parity_betrothed' omitted the constraint m ≠ n, letting quasiperfect numbers (a separate, also-open conjecture) slip through the existential; that issue explicitly states 'the mathematics remains untouched' and both conjectures are still open. I also checked an unrelated arXiv preprint that surfaced in search, 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (arXiv 2601.07444, Chen/Tang/Zhan, Jan 2026) — a Lean 4 formalization of classical amicable-number theorems (Thâbit's formula, Euler's rule, the Borho–Hoffmann breeding method) that mentions betrothed numbers only in passing as an extension, again formalizing already-known facts, not advancing the same-parity question. Wikipedia's own article was edited in Jan 2026 (clarifying an OEIS A005276 cross-reference) and March 2026 (math markup formatting only) — no substantive change to the parity claim. Under §6.2, an AI system whose only contribution is formalising a human-authored (Wikipedia-sourced) conjecture statement, with no proof or new mathematics attributed to it, is ai_role none with formalisation_only true — this is exactly that case, not 'assisted', since Claude Opus 4.6 produced no mathematics that appears in any result (there is no result).
competing_reading: One could argue the formalization event itself deserves a `progress` label since a well-known lab (DeepMind's formal-conjectures project) touched this exact problem and it is now a tracked, machine-checkable benchmark item — a structural change in how the problem is pursued even though no mathematics moved. I read `progress` as requiring a bound to move or an instructive incident, neither of which occurred here (the 'incident' was a formalization bug, not an AI mathematical claim that was withdrawn), so I kept status `open`.
what_would_settle_it: A Lean proof or disproof replacing the `sorry` in the formal-conjectures repository's betrothed-numbers file, or a paper/preprint that either exhibits a same-parity betrothed pair or proves none can exist below some bound larger than 10^13.

summary: This is the general existence question 'are there any coprime amicable pairs?', which the frozen Wikipedia revision already stated as open with a computational lower bound (then >10^67 on the product; the current article states the same). Searching turned up two items of activity in the window, neither of which changes the mathematics: (1) GitHub issue #2244 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (opened 2026-02-10, closed via PR #3531) formalizes the question 'do there exist an amicable pair (a,b) with gcd(a,b)=1?' as a Lean conjecture statement — i.e. it states the open question in a proof assistant, it does not prove or disprove it. The PR's commit message says 'Formalization assisted by Claude Opus 4.6', but per the deep-dive rules a formalisation-only AI contribution is coded ai_role=none regardless of which model helped write the Lean statement, since no mathematics entered the result — the conjecture is still open before and after. (2) The January 2026 arXiv paper 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (arXiv:2601.07444) also formalizes classical amicable-number results in Lean 4 and, in the course of that framework, restates the empirical computational bound (searches have found no coprime amicable pair below roughly 10^65) without proving non-existence or finding a coprime pair. Per section 3.1, an infinitude/existence question is only advanced by an answer, and neither item answers it — they restate and formalize the same open question the frozen revision already recorded. Wikipedia's live 'Amicable numbers' article, checked directly, still states 'It is not known whether a pair of coprime amicable numbers exists' with no citation newer than 1969-1970 Hagis papers. I therefore classify this as status=open with no_change_found=true. This aligns with the triage's 'none' verdict; I did not disagree with it, though I went further by opening the actual GitHub issue/PR and arXiv paper rather than just search snippets, and confirmed the AI-assistance detail (Claude Opus 4.6 assisting the Lean formalization) that the triage pass did not surface.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind formal-conjectures repository activity constitutes a form of 'progress' in the broad sense that the conjecture is now machine-formalized and thus more tractable for future automated theorem-proving attempts. But per the rubric, a bare Lean statement of an already-known-open question, with no proof attempt or bound movement, is not a change to the problem's status — it would need to actually attempt or claim a proof to register as `claimed` or `progress`. I also considered whether the AI-assisted formalization should count as `ai_role: assisted`, but the rules explicitly carve out formalisation-only contributions as `none`, so I coded it that way despite the presence of a named, quotable AI system.
what_would_settle_it: Either an exhibited coprime amicable pair (settling it in the affirmative, likely via massive computational search or a novel construction) or a proof that gcd(a,b)=1 is impossible for an amicable pair (settling it in the negative). Short of that, a published improvement to the >10^65 (or >10^67 on the product) search bound would count as `progress`.

outcome: No progress on the existence question since 26 January 2024: no Wall–Sun–Sun prime has been found, none has been ruled out by proof, and the computational search bound (2^64, established by PrimeGrid's Wieferich and Wall-Sun-Sun Prime Search project, which concluded in December 2022) predates the window and has not been reported extended since.
summary: The existence of Wall–Sun–Sun primes (equivalently Fibonacci–Wieferich primes) remains open: none is known, and it is conjectured (not proved) that infinitely many exist. The only substantive activity in the record is PrimeGrid's 'Wieferich and Wall-Sun-Sun Prime Search' distributed-computing project, which extended the search bound to 2^64 (≈1.8×10^19) before concluding in December 2022 — this predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision date and is therefore not a change within the window; per §3.1, an infinitude/existence question of this type is not advanced merely by extending a search bound in any case, since the bound is not itself the question asked. I found no report of PrimeGrid or anyone else extending the search further after 2022, and no new theoretical result bearing on the existence question itself. Two arXiv papers turned up in searches — 'A new condition for k-Wall-Sun-Sun primes' (2023-02, predates window regardless) and 'The p-adic Valuations of Möbius Duals of Lucas Sequences' (Ross, Shen, Cai, arXiv:2512.03481, December 2025) — but both concern generalized/variant notions (k-Wall-Sun-Sun primes, a different Lucas-sequence-based construction) rather than the classical Wall–Sun–Sun primes as stated in the bullet; per §3.1 these are related problems, not cases of this one, so they do not count as movement on this bullet. No AI involvement of any kind was found in connection with this problem — the searching and the theoretical papers are entirely conventional distributed computing and human mathematics. This is a clean 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the k-Wall-Sun-Sun and Möbius-dual papers are close enough in spirit (they generalize the same congruence condition) that a reader might want them mentioned even though they don't count as progress on the stated existence question; I've noted them above but excluded them from the status per the case-vs-variant rule, since they change the object of study (introducing a parameter k, or a different dual construction) rather than restricting the original question.
what_would_settle_it: A published proof or disproof of existence, or (short of that) a credible report that PrimeGrid or another group has extended the search bound beyond 2^64 with a written announcement dated after 26 January 2024 — though per §3.1 even such an extension would not change the status of this existence question, only narrow where an answer could hide.

summary: The question is whether any base-47 Wieferich prime exists (a prime p, not dividing 47, with 47^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p²). This is a pure existence question, and per §3.1 it can only be advanced by an actual resolution, not by a search extended further with no result. I confirmed via the current Wikipedia articles on 'Wieferich prime' and 'Wieferich pair', OEIS's 'Wieferich primes' wiki page, and general search that no base-47 Wieferich prime is known — the base-47 case appears only as the dead-end term in the Wieferich sequence starting from 3 (3, 11, 71, 47, ?), where no successor prime is known, a fact unchanged since well before 2024. I found no arXiv preprint, PrimeGrid project page, OEIS sequence update, or blog post reporting any computational search specifically extending the base-47 bound, and no theoretical work resolving the existence question for this base. Two tangentially related 2024-2026 arXiv papers turned up (on Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules/function fields, and on number-field analogues tied to the Ankeny-Artin-Chowla conjecture) but both are generalizations to entirely different algebraic settings (function fields, number fields) rather than results about classical integer Wieferich primes in base 47, so per §3.1 they are related problems, not cases of this one, and do not change this bullet. No AI system was mentioned in connection with any base-47 Wieferich search. I therefore record no_change_found and status open, consistent with the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than dispute.
competing_reading: None found. The two adjacent arXiv papers (Drinfeld-module and number-field Wieferich generalizations) could in principle be stretched to bear on 'base 47' if one reads 'base' extremely loosely as any algebraic base, but neither paper mentions base 47 or the rational-integer case at all, so this reading is not defensible.
what_would_settle_it: A computational search report (e.g., a PrimeGrid subproject page, an OEIS sequence update, or a preprint) stating a base-47 Wieferich prime found below some bound, or extending the known search-exhaustion limit for base 47 specifically, or a theoretical nonexistence/existence proof for this base.

summary: The question 'are there infinitely many amicable numbers/pairs?' is still listed as open by every current source checked: the live Wikipedia article on amicable numbers explicitly states 'It is unknown if there are infinitely many pairs of amicable numbers,' and Carl Pomerance's survey makes the same point. No paper found in the 26 January 2024–present window claims a proof, a disproof, or even a non-trivial partial advance on the infinitude question itself. What does exist in the window: (1) S. I. Dimitrov's 'Generalizations of amicable numbers' (arXiv:2408.07387, Aug 2024), which defines (α,β)-amicable pairs and conjectures (does not prove) infinitude for that generalized family — a related/variant problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated problem, since it changes the definition rather than restricting it; (2) an English translation of Euler's 1750 paper on amicable numbers (arXiv:2409.08783, Sept 2024) — historical, no new mathematics; (3) 'Amicable numbers and their connection to the Euler totient function' (arXiv:2512.22319, Dec 2025), a structural characterization of amicable pairs whose gcd is a power of two — a case restricted by a structural condition, but it proves an identity/characterization, not a fact about existence of infinitely many such pairs, so it does not bear on the infinitude question; (4) 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (arXiv:2601.07444), a Lean 4 formalization of the classical Thabit and Euler generation rules and the Borho-Hoffmann breeding method, plus computational search bounds beyond 10^65 for coprime pairs — this formalizes known generation methods, not a proof of infinitude, and uses only Lean's built-in tactics (zify, ring), not any AI system; (5) the Sergei Chernykh/BOINC 'Amicable Numbers' distributed-computing project, which has extended the exhaustive search of amicable pairs (smaller member below 10^18, with over a billion pairs known in total across informal counts, and an active search pushing toward 10^21) — per the explicit rule in §3.1, extending a search to a larger bound narrows where a counterexample to finiteness could hide but does not touch whether infinitely many pairs exist, so this is not a change to the problem. No AI system was found associated with any of this work; the Lean formalization uses only the proof assistant's built-in automation, which is explicitly excluded from the AI-involvement codes. I am satisfied nothing has escaped this search: I checked the live Wikipedia article, a leading survey (Pomerance), the OEIS wiki, the active BOINC project's own site, and the arXiv listing for amicable-number papers 2024–2025, and every substantive hit either predates the window, is a variant/generalization, or is a computational extension that the stated rules exclude from counting.
competing_reading: One could argue the (α,β)-amicable generalization (Dimitrov 2024) is 'a case' rather than 'a variant' if the ordinary amicable pairs are recovered at α=β=1, making the classical conjecture a special case of Dimitrov's Conjecture 6. But Dimitrov's paper only conjectures infinitude for the generalized family; it does not prove anything, so even under that reading there is no settled result to record — the classification as 'no change' is unaffected either way.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude for the classical (1,1) amicable pairs specifically (not a generalized family), or a paper explicitly stating it resolves the classical conjecture, would settle the ambiguity and change the status away from open.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 addresses the infinitude of balanced primes; the conjecture remains open with no known proof, disproof, or targeted partial result.
summary: Balanced primes are primes equal to the arithmetic mean of the nearest prime above and below (e.g. 5, 53, 157, ...; OEIS A006562). It is conjectured, but not proven, that infinitely many exist. Searching for work since 26 January 2024, I found: (1) the current Wikipedia article on balanced primes, which cites no post-2024 progress on infinitude and whose most recent factual update concerns a 2023 record for a related but distinct object (largest known CPAP-3, three primes in arithmetic progression); (2) the OEIS sequence A006562 page, which received several comments in 2024-2025 — M. F. Hasler (2024-10-15) noted a characterization via vanishing second differences of the prime sequence, Peter Schorn (2025-04-30) restated the definition, and Alain Rocchelli (2024-03-21 and 2024-03-23) proposed two asymptotic-density conjectures about the growth rate and average spacing of balanced primes. None of these is a proof or disproof of infinitude, and none is even a restriction of the infinitude question to a special case (a 'case' in the sense of §3.1) — the Rocchelli conjectures are themselves unproven conjectures about a different quantity (asymptotic density/gap growth), so even if they were later proven they would not by themselves settle whether the set is infinite. Per the deep-dive rules (§3.1), an existence/infinitude question moves only when it is answered; density conjectures, definitional restatements, and record-largest-example searches do not narrow whether an answer exists. I also checked for any AI involvement broadly in prime-related work during this period (searches surfaced OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra work on largest known prime gaps, and general LLM-mathematics survey pages), but nothing in that AI-related work touches balanced primes specifically — it concerns a different, unrelated prime-gap record problem. I found no arXiv preprint, announcement, or forum discussion since January 2024 claiming progress specifically on the infinitude of balanced primes.
competing_reading: One could argue the OEIS comment activity (Hasler's second-difference characterization, Rocchelli's density conjectures) constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense, since it deepens the theoretical framing of the sequence. But under the scope rule in §3.1, these are restatements or entirely new, still-open conjectures about a different quantity (density/spacing), not a narrowing of the infinitude question itself, so they do not qualify as `progress` or `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof that the set of balanced primes is infinite (e.g., via a density/heuristic argument made rigorous, or a sieve-theoretic result specifically targeting this equal-gap condition), or a rigorous proof of one of Rocchelli's density conjectures that, as a corollary, implies infinitude.

summary: The Wikipedia article on betrothed numbers (checked as of this research) still lists the same known pairs as before and makes no claim about infinitude having been settled; it does not even frame infinitude as an explicit open question in its current text, but the mathematical literature and MathWorld both continue to treat it as unresolved. Two items of tangential activity were found in the window. First, a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures#2246, opened 2026-02-10 by user franzhusch) proposes formalizing the *statement* 'there are infinitely many betrothed pairs' as a target in the Lean/Mathlib-based formal-conjectures repository. The issue itself states 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' — so an AI agent produced the issue text (identifying and phrasing the conjecture as a formalization target), but this is not mathematical content: it is a request to state an unproved conjecture in Lean, rated formalizability 2/5, and it explicitly is not a proof or partial proof of anything. No comments or follow-up work resolving it were found. Second, an arXiv preprint 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (arXiv:2601.07444, Chen, Tang, Zhan) formalizes classical, already-known results about amicable, sociable, and betrothed numbers in Lean 4 (2076 lines, 139 theorems, zero `sorry`s) — including verified computational bounds (>10^65) and parity-constraint theorems — but its abstract gives no indication it proves or disproves infinitude of betrothed pairs; it is a formalization of existing mathematics, not new mathematics, and no AI/LLM involvement in producing the proofs is disclosed in the abstract. Under §3.1, neither item changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry: the first is a tracking issue for an AI-generated formalization *task*, not a result, and the second doesn't touch the infinitude question at all. No search turned up any preprint, blog post, or announcement claiming progress toward proving or disproving infinitely many betrothed number pairs exist since 26 January 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind formal-conjectures issue represents a form of 'AI activity' on this exact problem (an AI agent selected and phrased this specific open conjecture as noteworthy), which might be read as a very weak 'incident' of AI engagement. But per §6.2, identifying/phrasing a conjecture for a to-do list is not producing any mathematics that appears in a result — there is no result — so ai_role none and status open (not progress) is the correct reading.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint proving that infinitely many betrothed pairs exist (or do not), a proof that the set is finite, or even a partial/case result (e.g., infinitely many pairs within some restricted family) would move this off 'open'. Completion of the Lean formalization issue itself would not settle it, since the issue only asks for the conjecture's *statement*, not a proof.

summary: Cluster primes (Blecksmith, Erdős, Selfridge 1999) are primes p such that every even integer up to p−3 is a difference of two primes ≤ p; whether infinitely many exist is listed as Erdős Problem #17. Checking erdosproblems.com/17 (last edited 28 December 2025) confirms the problem is explicitly marked open and notes it 'cannot be resolved with a finite computation' — no proof, partial resolution, or new bound has been posted. Its single forum comment (from Ribenboim, historical, predating the window) adds no new information. The Wikipedia 'Cluster prime' article still states plainly that it is not known whether there are infinitely many cluster primes, with its most recent cited research from 1999 (Blecksmith reciprocal-sum finiteness) and 2003 (Elsholtz's improved density bound), both well before the window. I searched specifically for any post-2024 tightening of the Blecksmith–Erdős–Selfridge/Elsholtz density bounds (which would count as `progress` per §3.1, since the record for 'how sparse are cluster primes' is closer to the actual open question than a mere existence search) and found nothing: no arXiv preprint, paper, or announcement referencing 'cluster primes' appears from 2024 onward in any of several searches. Searches for AI involvement (theorem provers, LLM-assisted proofs, GPT/Claude-related number theory results) turned up only unrelated material (a Riecoin 'cluster' cryptocurrency-mining hit, general AI-theorem-proving surveys like APOLLO/SorryDB/Gauss's Lean formalization of the prime number theorem) with no mention of cluster primes specifically. This is a clean 'nothing happened' case: the denominator problem is real and well-defined, but no mathematical or AI-related event touched it in the window.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or scope-qualifying result on the infinitude of cousin primes has appeared since 26 January 2024; the only developments found are a December 2024 record for the largest known explicit cousin prime pair (which does not bear on infinitude per §3.1) and unrelated machine-learning work on empirical prime-density prediction.
summary: The infinitude of cousin primes (Polignac's conjecture for gap 4) remains an open problem with no resolution, partial resolution, or bound movement since 26 January 2024. The two pre-snapshot claimed proofs the triage pass found — Du's 2005 arXiv preprint (math/0510329, category math.GM, last revised 2005-10-24, never published in a peer-reviewed venue) and the 2019 arXiv preprint by [author of 1903.05410] claiming a proof of both the Twin Prime and Polignac/cousin-prime conjectures (category math.GM, revised 15 times through 2022-06-02) — remain unaccepted preprints with no subsequent endorsement, and neither has been withdrawn or formally reviewed; they predate the window regardless. The current Wikipedia 'Cousin prime' article (checked live, 2026-09) still states infinitude is unproven and conditional only on the (also unproven) first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, and lists no claimed proof as accepted. The one dated, verifiable event inside the window is the December 2024 update to the largest-known explicit cousin prime pair (S. Batalov, 86,138 digits, surpassing an earlier 51,934-digit record), reported on the Cousin prime Wikipedia article and prime-records sites. Under §3.1, a record extension narrows where an answer could hide but does not answer the existence question itself, so it is excluded as a status-changing event ('An existence or infinitude question moves only when it is answered ... A record counts only where the record is the question') — this bullet is not a 'largest known object' bullet, it is an infinitude bullet. I also found unrelated 2025-2026 work applying deep learning to prime classification: 'PrimeFamilyNet' (arXiv 2604.02383, Manik Kakkar) trains a residual network to recognize twin/cousin/sexy/Chen/etc. primes and reports that a version trained only to 10^9 'reproduced the correct asymptotic direction without density supervision, corroborating Hardy-Littlewood k-tuple predictions.' This is empirical/statistical corroboration of a density heuristic via a classifier, not a proof, a case settled, or a bound on the conjecture; it does not change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, so it is not counted as progress. I also encountered an unverifiable web-search summary claiming 'a 2026 preprint reformulated the cousin prime problem within a deterministic framework and showed that infinitely many cousin prime pairs exist' — I could not find this preprint under any independent search or by fetching candidate arXiv IDs, and the only paper resolvable at the cited ID (2604.02383) was the unrelated PrimeFamilyNet classifier paper. I treat this claim as unsubstantiated and it is not the basis for any finding in this record.
competing_reading: None of the candidate events (the two stale unaccepted preprints, the December 2024 record pair, or the PrimeFamilyNet paper) plausibly supports a status other than 'open'. The closest case for a different reading would be treating the December 2024 largest-known-pair record as 'progress', but the rules explicitly exclude record extensions on infinitude questions from counting, so I did not classify it that way.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed or expert-digested proof (or disproof) of Polignac's conjecture for gap 4, or an accepted preprint specifically addressing the cousin-prime case (as opposed to a general, unaccepted claim about twin primes bundled with a cousin-prime corollary).

outcome: No proof or disproof of infinitude, and no new base-2 Cullen prime, has appeared since 26 January 2024; the largest known Cullen prime remains 6679881·2^6679881+1, found in 2009.
summary: The question is whether there are infinitely many Cullen primes (numbers of the form n·2^n+1 that are prime). The current Wikipedia article on Cullen numbers, t5k.org's (Prime Pages) list of the largest known Cullen primes, and its top-20 Cullen primes page all still show exactly sixteen known Cullen primes, with the largest being 6679881·2^6679881+1, discovered in 2009 — no new base-2 Cullen prime has been found since the frozen revision, and no proof or disproof of infinitude has appeared. The one piece of related activity found in this window is PrimeGrid's Generalized Cullen Prime Search, which in April 2025 found a new largest generalized Cullen prime, 4052186·69^4052186+1 (base 69) — but generalized Cullen numbers (n·b^n+1 for general base b) are a distinct, broader family from the base-2 Cullen numbers this problem concerns, and per §3.1 a different base is a related/variant problem, not a case of this one (settling it removes no territory from the base-2 question). Even setting that scope issue aside, per §3.1 an infinitude question is not advanced by a new example or an extended search bound in any case — only an actual proof or disproof would move it, and none exists. As an aside, Hooley's 1976 result that almost all Cullen numbers are composite, and Caldwell's conjecture that infinitely many are nonetheless prime, both predate the window and are unchanged. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this space; the generalized Cullen search is conducted by PrimeGrid's traditional distributed sieving/PRP (Proth-type) testing infrastructure, not any AI/ML system. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the base-69 generalized Cullen prime result is worth noting as adjacent activity in the same research community (PrimeGrid) that also runs the (currently apparently inactive) base-2 Cullen search, suggesting the general topic is not dormant even though the base-2 problem itself hasn't moved. But this doesn't change the classification: it is a different base, hence a different (related) problem under §3.1, and even a genuine base-2 discovery would not resolve an infinitude question.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude of base-2 Cullen primes, or (short of that) an announcement from PrimeGrid's Cullen Prime Search (base 2 specifically) of a seventeenth known Cullen prime, which would still leave the infinitude question open but would at least update the 'known Cullen primes' record referenced in the article.

outcome: The infinitude of Euclid (primorial+1) primes remains an open problem; the only developments since 26 January 2024 are new record-holder terms found by conventional distributed/probabilistic computation, none of which bear on the infinitude question.
summary: The problem asks whether there are infinitely many Euclid primes (primes of the form E_n = 1 + product of the first n primes, i.e. primorial+1 primes, OEIS A006862/A014545). This remains fully open. Wikipedia's 'Euclid number' and 'Primorial prime' articles (both current as of this research) state plainly that it is not known whether infinitely many exist. Since 26 January 2024, the only concrete developments are: (1) the PrimeGrid distributed-computing project found new, larger Euclid primes — most notably 9562633#+1 (n=637,491, index a(28) in OEIS A014545), announced/verified around 29 June 2025 (per the Primorial prime Wikipedia article) and logged to OEIS on 21 Aug 2025 — using standard probabilistic PRP testing followed by deterministic N-1/Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge verification; and (2) an independent August 2025 Zenodo dataset (zenodo.org/records/16932166 and the related 16930308) that ran the Miller-Rabin and Pollard's Rho algorithms over a range of indices and reported 14 known Euclid primes among 1,406 candidates checked, with index 1391 the largest new one it turned up (already known via PrimeGrid/OEIS by that point). Neither of these results touches the infinitude question: per the task's scope rule (§3.1), 'are there infinitely many X?' is not advanced by finding one more X or extending a search to a larger range — it narrows where an answer could hide, not whether one exists. Both efforts used purely classical computational number theory (probabilistic and deterministic primality tests, integer factorization via Pollard's Rho); I found no mention of AI, machine learning, or LLM involvement in either the PrimeGrid announcements, the OEIS entries, or the Zenodo dataset's documentation. The triage record's verdict of 'none' and its conclusion are corroborated by this independent research.
competing_reading: One could argue that each new record Euclid prime is itself a 'case' of the existential question being partially settled (i.e., existence of a prime at that specific index is confirmed), which would justify a 'partial' status. However, per §3.1 this is precisely the pattern the rules exclude: an existence/infinitude question moves only when answered, and a record extension is not a change to the bullet's core question of infinitude. I classify as `open`/no_change_found rather than `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of infinitude of primorial+1 primes, or a proof that only finitely many exist — neither of which has been claimed or attempted in any source found.

outcome: The infinitude of Fibonacci primes remains an open question; nothing since 26 January 2024 has resolved it or settled any restriction of it. Only record-extension activity (larger probable primes found) and a general heuristic paper touching Fibonacci-like recurrences (finalized/aligned with publication in 2024 but originally from 2023) were found, neither of which changes the status of the bullet.
summary: Wikipedia's 'Fibonacci prime' article (checked live, September 2026) still states plainly 'It is not known whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes,' and no source found anywhere contradicts this. Three lines of activity turned up in the search, none of which change the status of the question. (1) Record extensions: F_201107 (42,029 digits) remains the largest *proven* Fibonacci prime, verified by Maia Karpovich in September 2023 — before the window. Within the window, a larger *probable* prime (Miller-Rabin PRP, not proven) F_10367321 was found in August 2024, and a still larger one, F_11964299, was found by Ryan Propper in June 2025. Per DEEP_DIVE.md §3.1, a record extension is explicitly excluded from counting as progress on an infinitude question — it narrows where an answer could hide, not whether one exists — so these are noted but do not move the status. (2) A 2018/2020 preprint and journal article by Fengsui Liu, 'There are Infinitely Many Fibonacci Primes,' claims a proof via a 'recursive sieve method.' This predates the window by several years and, more importantly, has never been accepted by the mathematical community: it appears only in a non-selective journal (Global Journal of Science Frontier Research) and on ResearchGate, with no digestion by experts, and Wikipedia's own article — which would be expected to reflect a genuine resolution — still lists the question as open. There is no evidence this claim was newly evaluated, endorsed, or reopened within the window, so it does not create an event to date inside 2024-2026. (3) A 2023 paper by Jon Grantham and Andrew Granville, 'Fibonacci primes, primes of the form 2^n-k and beyond' (arXiv:2307.07894), gives a heuristic framework for primality in exponentially growing linear recurrence sequences (including Fibonacci-like sequences) but explicitly does not resolve finiteness vs infinitude — the authors state only a conjectural dichotomy. Its only within-window activity is a v3 revision (September 2024) that the authors describe as 'minor changes to align with the published version,' i.e., a journal-formatting update to a 2023 preprint, not new mathematical content, so it is not a distinct in-window event. No AI or LLM involvement was found in any of this activity — the primality records are computational (Miller-Rabin/GPU-style search by individual hobbyist-mathematicians), and the Grantham-Granville paper is standard human number theory with no disclosed AI use. Given all this, the status is 'open' with no_change_found true, matching the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than contradict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Liu preprint deserves a 'claimed' status if reread charitably, since it explicitly claims a full proof of exactly this bullet's statement. I did not classify it that way because (a) it predates the window (2018/2020, well before 26 January 2024) so even if credited it would be open_stale rather than a live change, and (b) DEEP_DIVE.md requires that a 'claimed' status rest on some documented preprint/announcement/certificate that experts have not yet digested but that is at least being taken seriously; here there is no sign of even that — no citations engaging with its correctness, no digestion, and the Wikipedia article (checked live) still calls the question open years later, which is strong circumstantial evidence the claim was never found credible. I am confident 'open' is correct but note this as the closest call in the record.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: (a) a citation, review, or discussion by a recognized number theorist that seriously engages with Liu's claimed proof (either endorsing or refuting it) that I did not find; (b) a change to Wikipedia's Fibonacci prime or List of unsolved problems articles asserting resolution; (c) a new preprint post-January 2024 claiming a proof of infinitude that I did not encounter in these searches.

outcome: No progress toward the infinitude question was found since 26 January 2024: the count of known Giuga numbers (12, per OEIS A007850) has not changed since Fred Schneider's 2006 addition of a(12), no new example has been found, no bound on Giuga numbers themselves has moved, and the only 2026 documents that use the term 'Giuga number' are self-disclosed speculative/AI-generated explorations of a hypothetical Giuga number's consequences, not attempts on the infinitude question.
summary: The problem asks whether there are infinitely many Giuga numbers (composite n such that p | (n/p - 1) for every prime factor p of n; known examples are 30, 858, 1722, 66198, 2214408306, 24423128562, 432749205173838, 14737133470010574, 550843391309130318, 244197000982499715087866346, 554079914617070801288578559178, 1910667181420507984555759916338506). This is a pure existence/infinitude question, so per the scope rule (§3.1) it is only advanced by an actual resolution — not by finding one more example or narrowing a search range. I verified via OEIS A007850 that the list of known Giuga numbers is still exactly 12 terms, the same as after Fred Schneider's 2006 contribution; no new term has been added in the window and the sequence page (last touched September 2026 by routine maintenance) shows no substantive update. I initially mis-fetched OEIS A054377, which is a *different* sequence (primary pseudoperfect numbers, a related but distinct concept defined via the arithmetic derivative) and briefly appeared to show 2026 additions by 'Pedro Martins and Han M. Wang' — cross-checking against numbersaplenty.com and a fresh fetch of the correct A007850 page confirmed those 2026 additions belong to A054377, not to the Giuga numbers sequence, and are irrelevant here regardless since even a new example would not bear on infinitude. The two 2025-2026 items the triage pass surfaced are: (1) a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #2247, opened 10 Feb 2026) that only asks for a Lean *statement* of the open conjecture to be formalized — 'up for grabs', no proof attempted, formalization difficulty rated as needing only a simple predicate definition; and (2) two Zenodo preprints ('The Arithmetic Geometry of the Giuga Condition...', Sept 2025, and a related 'K-Theoretic Realization' variant) that explore hypothetical consequences if a Giuga number satisfying certain extra properties existed — the first explicitly labelled by its own authors as '[a creative exploration of a concept with AI - it should not be taken as correct mathematics]', and neither claims to settle whether Giuga numbers are finite or infinite; they only reason conditionally from a hypothetical. Wikipedia's own Giuga number article was edited in 2024 and 2026 only for formatting/citation cleanup and reorganizing the examples list, not for new mathematical content. I found no arXiv preprints, MathOverflow threads, or expert blog posts addressing the infinitude question in the window. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Zenodo 'Arithmetic Geometry of the Giuga Condition' preprints constitute 'progress' in the loose sense that they explore structural consequences of Giuga numbers using new machinery (motivic/K-theoretic). But they are explicitly conditional on a hypothetical Giuga number with extra properties, self-disclaimed as not correct mathematics (in the first case) or unreviewed and unusually speculative (in the second), and neither purports to move the infinitude question in either direction — restricting or extending the class of numbers considered is a different problem (existence of Giuga numbers with special structure), not the stated bullet, so under §3.1 this is a related/variant exploration rather than a case of the problem, and I did not code it as progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either a proof that infinitely many Giuga numbers exist (e.g. via an infinite parametrized family), a proof that only finitely many exist, or credible new terms found beyond the known 12 (which, per the existence-question scope rule, would still not settle infinitude but would at least be a search-space finding) accompanied by a peer-reviewed or widely-digested argument.

summary: A Kummer prime, as Wikipedia's list uses the term, is a prime of the form p_n# − 1 (a primorial minus one; OEIS A057704 lists the indices n for which this is prime). The question 'are there infinitely many?' is a pure existence question and remains completely open: no proof, disproof, heuristic breakthrough, or expert commentary addressing the infinitude of this sequence was found anywhere. What did happen since 26 January 2024 is that PrimeGrid's distributed sieving project found three new terms of the sequence: n = 334023, 435582, and 446895, credited to Jeppe Stig Nielsen and reported on OEIS A057704 (added 16 Dec 2024), with the largest (6533299# − 1, 2,835,864 digits) also documented on Wikipedia's Primorial prime article (dated to August 2024 by a search-engine synthesis citing Christian Wallbaum/PrimeGrid; the Wikipedia article itself gives a vaguer 'as of July 2025' framing, likely reflecting when the article prose was last edited rather than the discovery date). Per §3.1, a new record term of a sequence like this is not a narrowing of an existence question — it says nothing about whether the sequence is infinite, so it does not count as progress on this bullet. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this area: the new terms were found using conventional distributed sieving and primality-proving software (PrimeGrid's standard toolchain, e.g. MultiSieve/mtsieve and PRP/proof software), not any machine-learning or LLM system. Searches for any AI system engaging with Kummer primes specifically, or with the closely related (but distinct) conjecture on infinitely many regular primes, turned up nothing tying an AI system to either question. I am confident nothing was missed: the topic is a narrow, well-tracked computational sequence with an actively maintained OEIS entry and a Wikipedia article, both checked directly, and general web searches for AI-related activity on the term also came up empty.
competing_reading: One could argue that the ongoing PrimeGrid discovery campaign constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense (extending computational search), similar to how a bound moving counts as progress in other problems. But §3.1 explicitly excludes this: 'a search verified to a larger limit' is not progress on an infinitude question unless the record itself is the object of the question, which it is not here (the bullet asks about existence of infinitely many, not about the current largest known example).
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude for primes of form p_n# − 1, or a heuristic/asymptotic result specifically bearing on whether the sequence is finite or infinite (analogous to results on Mersenne or Fermat primes) — none of which currently exists.

summary: Kynea numbers have the form (b^n+1)^2-2; a Kynea prime is a prime of this form. The question 'are there infinitely many Kynea primes?' is an existence/infinitude question, so under §3.1 it moves only when actually answered, and record searches (finding a larger example, extending a search bound) narrow where an answer could hide without touching the question. Searches turned up no proof or heuristic argument published since 26 January 2024, no disproof, and nothing resembling a resolution. What did turn up was a confused set of 'largest known Kynea prime' claims scattered across secondary/mirror sites (Googology Wiki, HandWiki, EverybodyWiki, prime-numbers.info): one snippet cites a 169,553-digit example by C. Emmanuel that other sources date to November 2005 (an early hand/CPU search, well before the frozen date and using the original discoverer's own search rather than anything new); another cites index n=852770 (513,419 digits) found by Ryan Propper in July 2019 using CKSieve/PrimeFormGW; yet another cites index n=661,478 (398,250 digits) from June 2016. These are mutually inconsistent snapshots of an aggregator table that is evidently not being kept current by any of the mirror sites, and none of the dates fall in the 26 Jan 2024–present window regardless. The authoritative record source, Prime-Wiki (rieselprime.de), returned repeated 503 errors during this research and could not be fetched directly, so I could not confirm the exact current record holder or date from the primary source; this is noted as a dead end. The underlying search effort is a MersenneForum-coordinated distributed sieving/PRP-testing project (CKSieve, PrimeFormGW, LLR-type primality tools) opened in December 2015 and still active, which is classical computer algebra / exhaustive-search infrastructure, not an AI system by any of the codes in §6.2 — a targeted search for AI or LLM involvement in Kynea prime searches returned nothing relevant. No AI system of any kind appears anywhere near this problem or its associated record-search community.
competing_reading: None of the 'largest known Kynea prime' claims found actually fall inside the research window, so there is no genuine candidate event to weigh against the open/no-change classification here; the only live ambiguity is which of the three inconsistent record claims (2005/2016/2019) is currently accurate, which affects no field in this record since none postdate 26 Jan 2024.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or heuristic/probabilistic argument (analogous to the standard conjectures for Mersenne/Cullen/Woodall-type primes) establishing infinitude, or a rigorous disproof; short of that, a reliable current snapshot of the Prime-Wiki Carol-Kynea table would at least pin down the present record holder, though that would still not change the open status.

outcome: No progress on the question of whether there are infinitely many Lucas primes has been found since 26 January 2024; it remains an open conjecture with no rigorous proof for any Lucas sequence except the trivial cases.
summary: The question of whether infinitely many Lucas primes exist (Lucas numbers Lₙ that are themselves prime) is a long-standing open conjecture in number theory, analogous to the open questions for Fibonacci primes and Mersenne primes. It is a special case of the broader open problem of whether Lucas sequences Uₙ(P,Q) contain infinitely many prime terms: besides the trivial sequences Uₙ(2,1)=n and Uₙ(-2,1)=(-1)^(n+1)n, no Lucas sequence has ever been rigorously proven to contain infinitely many primes, though heuristic (probabilistic/Hardy-Littlewood-style) arguments support the conjecture for most coprime (P,Q). Broderius and Greene's related conjecture (that every Lucas sequence not in one of two specific exceptional families has infinitely many prime terms) remains itself unproven. I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 work bearing on this: (1) the Wikipedia 'Lucas number' article, which states the largest confirmed Lucas prime is L₁₄₈₀₉₁ (Sept. 2015, 30,950 digits) and largest known probable prime is L₅₄₆₆₃₁₁ (Aug. 2022), with no updates since; (2) The Prime Pages (t5k.org) 'Lucas Number' top-20 list, whose most recent entries (V(202667), V(193201), V(183089), V(159521)) all date to November–December 2023, i.e. before the frozen revision, with no post-window additions found; (3) OEIS A001606 (indices n with Lₙ prime), whose most recent substantive discovery comment dates to 2017; (4) recent arXiv papers on Lucas sequences (e.g. 'Shifting Lucas Sequences Away From Primes', INTEGERS 25 (2025); 'On members of Lucas sequences with bounded prime gaps', J. Number Theory 2025) address related but distinct questions — constructing sequences with few/no primes, or bounding prime gaps among Lucas-sequence members — none of which settle or narrow the infinitude question for the classical Lucas sequence itself, so under §3.1 these are related-problem results rather than progress on this bullet; (5) the Wikipedia 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' page, which comprehensively tracks AI-driven results on prime-related conjectures (e.g. OpenAI's bound improvement on the twin-prime-gap problem, DeepMind's work on Erdős problems, Anthropic's work on Riemann zeta zeros) and contains no mention of Lucas primes or Lucas sequences at all. I found no claim, preprint, announcement, or computational record update — by a human or an AI system — that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry. This matches the triage's 'none' verdict; I did not find any evidence to disagree with it, though I additionally verified the record-table angle (largest known Lucas prime) explicitly to rule out even a narrow reading of 'progress', and per §3.1 that record axis is not the relevant one for an existence question regardless.
competing_reading: None of the record-table facts (largest known Lucas prime/probable prime) would count as progress on this bullet even if a new record had appeared post-window, since per §3.1 an infinitude question is not advanced by exhibiting one more example. No plausible alternative classification presents itself here.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that some non-trivial Lucas sequence, or the classical Lucas sequence Lₙ specifically, contains infinitely many primes — or a preprint/announcement claiming such a proof, which would then need expert digestion to move from claimed to resolved.

outcome: The Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff conjecture (infinitely many Mersenne primes, equivalently infinitely many even perfect numbers) remains completely open. Since 26 January 2024 the only concrete developments are: (1) discovery of the 52nd known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1, on 12 October 2024 by Luke Durant via GIMPS using a GPU-based cloud infrastructure; (2) GIMPS completing exhaustive trial-checking of all exponents below 136,279,841 as of 18 June 2025, a search-completeness milestone; and (3) a stream of unvetted preprints (2024-2025) claiming a proof, none of which have been accepted, digested by experts, or survived scrutiny. None of these change the status of the conjecture itself.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent, uncoordinated preprint claims to have proved the conjecture have appeared since 2024 (e.g. a June 2024 ResearchGate paper 'Proof of the existence of infinite number of Mersenne primes' using a 'complementary prime sieve' / 'Dénes type Symmetric Prime Number theorem'; a June 2024 ResearchGate paper 'Proof of Mersenne Conjecture' via a Pigeonhole Principle argument; and an October 2025 preprints.org manuscript 'There Are Infinitely Many Mersenne Primes' by an independent researcher, Michael Mark Anthony, explicitly marked 'not peer-reviewed'). None have been accepted by a journal, digested by an expert, or received any public rebuttal/endorsement from a working number theorist; they appear to be part of the long-standing pattern of amateur claimed proofs of famous open conjectures that periodically surface on preprint servers.

summary: No change to the conjecture's open status has occurred since 26 January 2024. The conjecture (infinitely many Mersenne primes / infinitely many even perfect numbers) is an infinitude question, which under §3.1 only moves when it is actually answered — narrowing the search space or finding one more example does not count. Two genuine, verifiable developments occurred in the window: GIMPS/Luke Durant found the 52nd known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1 (41,024,320 digits), on 12 October 2024, using a distributed GPU cloud infrastructure across 17 countries; this is a new largest example, not progress on the infinitude question, and per §3.1 does not change the bullet. Separately, GIMPS completed exhaustive double-checking of all exponents below 136,279,841 by 18 June 2025 — again a search-completeness milestone, not a change to whether infinitely many exist. On the AI side, the Durant discovery is explicitly NOT an AI story: press coverage states Durant's stated motivation was to demonstrate that GPUs (typically associated with AI/ML workloads) are useful 'for more than AI' — i.e. the GPUs ran the deterministic Lucas-Lehmer primality test, not any learned model, so ai_role is 'none'. I also found and traced an unrelated news item (a ChatGPT-assisted resolution of a 60-year-old Erdős primitive-set conjecture) that a search briefly surfaced under similar phrasing; I confirmed by reading the source that it has nothing to do with Mersenne primes and excluded it. On the claimed-proof side, I found at least four independent unvetted claims of a proof posted to ResearchGate and Preprints.org between 2024 and 2025 (one flagged by triage, three found independently by me), none peer-reviewed, none digested, and none discussed by any credible source as correct — consistent with the long history of amateur 'proofs' of this exact conjecture (a genuinely retracted professional attempt by Janusz Czelakowski via Studia Logica exists in the literature, but that retraction was in October 2022, well before the frozen revision, so it is out of window and not part of this record's finding). No arXiv preprint, Terence Tao blog post, Quanta piece, or other expert-authored source discusses any progress on the actual infinitude question in the 26 Jan 2024–present window. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: None of the found preprints plausibly changes the classification, since none carry any indicium of correctness (no journal acceptance, no expert endorsement, no citation by credible sources) — but if any of the 2024-2025 preprint claims were later validated by an expert without my finding evidence of that, the record would need to move from 'open' to 'claimed' or better. I judge this unlikely given the total absence of any expert commentary treating these claims seriously.
what_would_settle_it: A citation of any of the preprint proofs by a credible number theorist (positive or as a debunking), or a retraction/correction notice on preprints.org or ResearchGate for the 2024-2025 claims, would confirm they remain dead ends; conversely, any digestion (blog post, MathOverflow thread, journal submission record) treating one as a serious candidate would change the status.

outcome: No proof, disproof, new large NSW prime discovery, or any other development bearing on the infinitude of Newman–Shanks–Williams primes was found since 26 January 2024; the question remains an open conjecture with no recorded change in the window.
summary: Newman–Shanks–Williams (NSW) primes are primes of the form ((1+√2)^n + (1-√2)^n)/2 for odd n, equivalently half of certain companion Pell numbers; the known terms correspond to OEIS A088165, with indices 3, 5, 7, 19, 29, 47, 59, 163 (and a 99-digit ninth term too large for the OEIS b-file entry). The largest known genuine (proven) NSW prime, for n = 9679 (3705 digits), was found in 2001, and the largest known NSW probable prime, for n = 172243 (65931 digits), was found in 2007 — both well before the frozen revision date, and no source found reports any new NSW prime, probable prime, or record extension since then, let alone since January 2024. I checked the OEIS entry A088165 for new terms or comments (none post-2008), the Wikipedia article on NSW primes (no dates past 2007 given, no mention of the infinitude question being addressed), t5k.org's 'largest known prime by year' history (no mention of NSW primes at all, largest-prime records dominated by Mersenne primes), and general web searches for any 2024/2025 NSW prime discovery, PrimeGrid announcements, or a proof/disproof of infinitude — all came up empty. This mirrors the closely related open questions for Fibonacci primes, Mersenne primes, and other primes-in-a-linear-recurrence sequences, none of which have been resolved either. No AI system appears anywhere in connection with this problem in the window. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record: the infinitude question is exactly the kind of existence question (§3.1) that is not advanced by finding another term or extending a search bound, and no such extension was even found to have occurred.
competing_reading: None found — no candidate event exists to argue about a different classification for. If an unreported PrimeGrid or GIMPS-adjacent project has found a new NSW prime or probable prime since 2007, it did not surface in searches or on the relevant OEIS/Wikipedia/t5k.org pages, which are the natural places such a record would be logged.
what_would_settle_it: A new entry in OEIS A088165 (or its b-file) with a post-January-2024 date, a PrimeGrid or similar distributed-computing project announcement of a new NSW prime/probable prime, an update to the NSW prime Wikipedia article's 'largest known' figures, or a paper addressing the infinitude of primes represented by the Pell/NSW recurrence.
