outcome: The conjecture itself (infinitely many palindromic primes in every base) remains unresolved; only weaker/adjacent statements about palindromes with restricted factorizations have been proven since January 2024.
summary: The bullet asks whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes in every base — an existence/infinitude question that, per §3.1, moves only when actually answered. It has not been answered. The Wikipedia article on palindromic primes (fetched at its current, live state) still says plainly that it is not known whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes even in base 10, and the conjecture for general bases is described in the literature as 'far out of reach with current methods,' the sparsity of palindromes (~√x below x) being the core obstruction. Since 26 January 2024 there has been a cluster of closely related but genuinely distinct results, each of which changes the question rather than the problem in this bullet: (1) Tuxanidy and Panario, 'Infinitude of Palindromic Almost-Prime Numbers' (arXiv:2307.16637, first submitted 31 July 2023 — before the window — with a revised v3 posted 23 July 2024 and journal publication in IMRN in September 2024), proving infinitely many palindromes in any base with at most six prime factors, each large; this is a genuine mathematical advance but is explicitly a weakening (almost-primes, not primes) that the authors themselves note their methods cannot push to square-free palindromes, let alone primes. (2) Johnston and Kerr, 'The infinitude of square-free palindromes' (arXiv:2601.07097, dated January 2026), proving infinitely many square-free palindromes in every base — again a different, weaker statement (no primality). (3) Chourasiya and Johnston, 'Power-free palindromes and reversed primes' (arXiv:2503.21136), which studies power-free palindromes and reversed-prime variants, not the stated conjecture. None of these settle any case of, or move a bound on, the actual conjecture that palindromic primes (not almost-primes, not square-free palindromes) are infinite in a given base — they are all related problems under §3.1's test, obtained by relaxing 'prime' to a weaker multiplicative condition, not by restricting the original statement. No AI system was found credited in any of these papers' methodology, acknowledgements, or metadata; all read as conventional analytic/combinatorial number theory. A broader search for any AI-driven attempt on this specific conjecture (e.g. via LLM theorem-proving pipelines, AI agents solving Erdős-style problem lists) turned up general AI-for-math activity (e.g. AI agents resolving some Erdős problems and OEIS conjectures) but nothing naming or touching this palindromic-primes conjecture. The triage's 'none' verdict is confirmed: this problem saw real progress in its neighborhood but no change to the bullet as stated, and no AI involvement anywhere in that neighborhood.
competing_reading: One could argue the almost-prime result (at most six prime factors) is a 'case' of the palindromic-primes conjecture in the loose sense that primes are almost-primes with exactly one factor, so the almost-prime result narrows the search space. But per §3.1 a case is obtained by *restricting* the stated question (e.g., a specific base, a specific digit length), not by *relaxing* the primality condition to a different, strictly weaker multiplicative condition; six-almost-primes are not a subset of primes, so proving infinitude of the former says nothing about whether primes among palindromes are finite or infinite. I classify all three papers as related-problem territory, not partial progress on this bullet, but flag the reasoning here since a differently-calibrated reader might score the almost-prime result as `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that for some fixed base b, the number of palindromic primes below x is unbounded (or is eventually zero) would resolve the case for that base; a paper explicitly closing the gap from 'six prime factors' to 'one prime factor' for palindromes, or any result stated in terms of prime palindromes themselves (not almost-primes or square-free palindromes), would be the marker to search for going forward.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or substantive new progress on the infinitude of Pell primes was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open and is believed to follow from Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture F, which is itself unresolved.
summary: Are there infinitely many Pell primes? remains open. Pell primes are Pell numbers P(n) = ((1+√2)^n − (1−√2)^n)/(2√2) that are themselves prime; as with Fibonacci primes, a necessary (not sufficient) condition is that the index n be prime. The conjecture that infinitely many exist is understood to be a consequence of Hardy–Littlewood's Conjecture F (on primes represented by binary quadratic/other low-degree forms related to the Pell recurrence), which is itself a decades-old open conjecture with no proof in the window. I checked: (1) the Wikipedia articles for Pell number and List of unsolved problems in mathematics, neither of which record any change; (2) OEIS A096650 (indices n for which P(n) is prime or probable prime), whose data (31 known indices, largest 90197) and comments were last substantively added to well before 2024 — the only 2025-era addition is an unrelated citing reference (Fan & Pollack, 'Extremal elasticity of quadratic orders', arXiv:2503.07801) that merely references the sequence in passing, not a result about the conjecture; (3) secondary summaries (Googology Wiki, MathWorld-derived search snippets) confirming the largest *proven* Pell prime (index 13339) dates to 2001 and the largest known *probable* Pell prime (index 90197) dates to 2004 — both well before the window, and in any case a new large (probable) prime would not bear on the infinitude question per the scope rules in §3.1, since finding one more term does not answer an existence question; (4) targeted arXiv/web searches for any 2024–2026 proof, disproof or conjecture-strength progress specific to Pell primes, which turned up nothing on point — the only 2024–2025 papers found involving 'Pell' and primality concern unrelated topics: a primality *test* built on the geometry of Pell's cubic (arXiv:2411.01638), pseudoprimality via the Pell conic (arXiv:2001.00353, pre-window), and general AI-for-number-theory surveys that do not mention Pell primes. None of these change what could be written in this Wikipedia bullet. I found no AI involvement of any kind in connection with this specific conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue that continued discovery/verification of larger probable Pell primes (the OEIS list, last extended pre-2024) constitutes 'progress' worth a `progress` status even though it doesn't touch the infinitude question, since it narrows nothing about the underlying existence claim. I judged this not to count, consistent with §3.1's rule that record extensions for an existence/infinitude question don't count unless the record IS the question (which it is not here — the question is about infinitude, not about the largest known example) — and in any case no such extension occurred inside the window.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture F (or a direct, unconditional proof/disproof of infinitely many Pell primes bypassing it) would settle this. Short of that, only a further-reaching heuristic/analytic result specifically about Pell primes (not merely citing the sequence) would count as `progress`.

outcome: The question remains open. By the Euclid-Euler theorem it is equivalent to whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes; no proof or disproof has appeared since 26 January 2024. A 52nd Mersenne prime (2^136279841-1) was found by GIMPS in October 2024 using GPU hardware, which is a new example but does not bear on the infinitude question per se. Two self-published preprints (Frank Vega, first posted April 2024; Ikorong Anouk Gilbert Nkodo/Nemron, posted September 2025) claim routes to resolving the question, but neither has been peer-reviewed, digested by experts, or gained any traction in the mathematical community, so neither meets the bar for `claimed` or higher. No AI system was found to be involved in any of this activity in a role beyond incidental mention.
summary: This bullet asks whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers, which (via the Euclid-Euler theorem) is equivalent to the still-open question of whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes. Nothing in the window (26 Jan 2024 - present) settles or narrows this question in the sense required by §3.1: the only concrete development is the discovery of the 52nd Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1, by GIMPS in October 2024 (the first GIMPS discovery found using an Nvidia GPU rather than Prime95/CPU, via a cloud VM volunteered by Luke Durant) — per §3.1 this is explicitly excluded ('a new example... does not narrow where an answer could hide'). I also examined two self-published preprint claims flagged by triage. (1) Frank Vega's 'Note for the Perfect Numbers' (first posted to EasyChair/ResearchGate/Cambridge Open Engage/ScienceOpen starting 22 April 2024, i.e. inside the window, with revisions through July 2024) claims to prove there are only finitely many Mersenne primes via an elementary argument on the sigma function. It has never been peer-reviewed or accepted by any journal, and search turned up no expert engagement, citation, or refutation discussion of it at all — it sits alongside a long history of Vega preprints on P vs NP, the Riemann hypothesis, and related famous problems that have not been accepted by the field (one exception, a Robin's-criterion paper, was accepted by the Ramanujan Journal, but that is a different problem). Given no expert has engaged with or endorsed the argument, and note that at least one version needed a self-acknowledged fix to a flawed upper-bound step, it does not meet the `claimed` bar for a serious contested claim so much as an un-digested fringe assertion; I record it as not changing the status. (2) Ikorong Anouk Gilbert Nkodo's 'A Curious Note around the Perfect Numbers Problem' (Zenodo, 27 August/6 September 2025) merely proposes a conjecture whose truth would imply a proof by contradiction — it does not itself claim a proof, and the author has a long history of similar self-published notes on twin primes, Goldbach, and other famous conjectures with no evidence of mathematical-community acceptance. I also checked whether any AI lab or system (DeepMind AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve, GIMPS software, etc.) has been involved: DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' GitHub repository tracks 'infinitude of Mersenne primes' as issue #134, but this is purely a formalization bookkeeping task (writing the open conjecture's statement in Lean/Mathlib for a benchmark corpus), not any attempt to prove it, and involves no AI-generated mathematics. A 2025 paper called 'The emergence of the Mersenne Star...bridging physics and artificial general intelligence' (Arab Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences, 2025; also on Zenodo/PhilArchive) describes geometric patterns among the finitely many known Mersenne primes and speculates about future AGI applications to prime-finding, but makes no claim about infinitude and involves no AI system producing any part of its content — it is patent-application-adjacent numerology dressed in AI branding, not a mathematical result in scope. GIMPS itself uses GPU compute (Prime95/Mlucas/Prime-Gpuowl) for primality testing, which is exhaustive/certified computation, not an AI system, consistent with §6.2's exclusion of computer-assisted search from AI-role coding. In sum: the problem is squarely open, nothing in the window changes that, and no genuine AI involvement was found anywhere near it.
competing_reading: One could argue Vega's preprint, despite lacking peer review, should be coded `claimed` on the grounds that it is a serious, structured resolution attempt by an author with at least one accepted paper in a reputable journal (Ramanujan Journal, on a different problem). I did not adopt this reading because (a) no expert digestion, citation, or engagement with this specific paper was found in any venue searched, (b) the author's oeuvre includes many parallel unaccepted claims on other famous problems (P vs NP, etc.), which is exactly the pattern §6.1 warns is 'not enough' for `claimed` even from a prestigious-seeming author, and (c) at least one version needed a self-described fix to a flawed bounding step, suggesting the argument was not robust even to its own author's later scrutiny.
what_would_settle_it: Either an accepted journal publication or a Terence-Tao-tier expert blog digestion working through Vega's or Ikorong's argument line by line and either endorsing or refuting it; alternatively, any future genuine proof or disproof of the Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff conjecture (which predicts infinitely many Mersenne primes) from a source that gets picked up by the number theory community.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or any mathematical progress toward the infinitude of Pierpont primes has been found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open and undisturbed.
summary: Pierpont primes are primes of the form 2^u·3^v + 1. Andrew Gleason's conjecture that there are infinitely many of them (per the count heuristic ~9n up to 10^n) remains unproven as of today, and every source checked (the current Wikipedia article on Pierpont primes, the Prime Pages glossary entry, and OEIS A005109) still states or implies this is an open conjecture with no resolution. The only concrete numerical fact in this area — the largest known Pierpont prime, 81 × 2^20498148 + 1 (6,170,560 digits), verified in June 2023 — predates the 26 January 2024 window and is in any case a record/search result rather than a statement bearing on infinitude (per §3.1, existence/infinitude questions move only when answered, not when the search frontier is extended). No newer record was found in searches of PrimeGrid-related coverage or general web search, and no arXiv paper, blog post, or announcement since January 2024 was found addressing the infinitude question directly — a search for arXiv papers with 'Pierpont primes' in the 2024-2025 window returned only unrelated number-theory papers (e.g. on primes p where p-1 is a sum of two squares) that merely appeared due to keyword overlap in sieve-theory search results. The one 2024-dated edit found on OEIS A005109 (a September 2024 formula restatement by Amiram Eldar) is a notational addition, not new mathematics, and does not bear on the conjecture. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem. This is a clean 'nothing happened' case, matching the triage's own conclusion.
competing_reading: None found. There is no plausible alternative classification here — no source suggests any movement, partial result, or bound relevant to the infinitude question in the window, and no case-restriction (e.g. a proof for a fixed v or u) was found either.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of Gleason's conjecture on Pierpont prime infinitude, or a partial result restricting the question to a sub-case (e.g. a density/lower-bound result specifically for numbers of the form 2^u·3^v+1) published as a preprint, journal article, or expert-digested announcement after 26 January 2024, would change this record.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 settles, narrows, or bears directly on whether there are infinitely many prime quadruplets {p, p+2, p+6, p+8}; the question remains completely open.
summary: The prime quadruplet conjecture (infinitely many p with p, p+2, p+6, p+8 all prime) remains open, and I found nothing in the window that changes it. Three candidate leads were checked and ruled out as not bearing on this specific problem under §3.1's scope rule. (1) A 2026 preprint, 'Prime Quadruplets and Jump Conditions on Arithmetic Functions' (arXiv:2606.10331, Roy Choudhury & Wei, first submitted 9 June 2026), poses a new conjecture about jump conditions on the totient and divisor-sum functions and states that IF that conjecture is proven true, infinitude of prime quadruplets would follow; the paper itself proves no case of the quadruplet conjecture, only an unproven conditional implication plus computational verification (no counterexamples) up to 10^12 of its own separate conjecture. This is not a case of the stated problem — it is a related problem (a different, new conjecture) whose resolution remains itself open, so nothing here changes what a careful reader would write in the quadruplet bullet. No AI involvement is mentioned anywhere in the paper. (2) OpenAI's August 2026 result (repository openai/PrimeGaps186, paper 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes') establishes DHL[40,2] and thereby liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) <= 186 for consecutive primes — a bounded-gaps result in the same Maynard-Tao/DHL sieve framework, using an AI system to help produce a Lean 4 formalization of a conditional theorem. However, this concerns gaps between *consecutive* primes for a 40-element admissible set with only 2 required primes (DHL[40,2]), which is a categorically different statement from the fixed, specific 4-tuple {0,2,6,8} needing *all four* shifts simultaneously prime (which would correspond to something like DHL[4,4], far beyond current sieve-theoretic reach — the best unconditional DHL[k,2] result only reaches k=50, let alone k=4 with m=4). This is a related/neighbouring problem under §3.1 (same conjecture family, different parameters and different tuple), not a case of the quadruplet conjecture, so it is excluded. (3) General Maynard-Tao/Polymath8 bounded-gaps literature since 2024 (e.g., 'On smooth gaps between primes using the Maynard-Tao sieve', arXiv:2403.19696) continues to refine k2 bounds for pairs of primes in admissible k-tuples, currently k2 <= 50; none of this addresses the specific 4-element admissible set {0,2,6,8} needing all four positions prime. (4) Records for the largest known explicit prime quadruplet (e.g. via Tony Forbes's k-tuplet records page or t5k.org) are search-verification records, which per §3.1 do not advance an infinitude question regardless of how large they get. No AI system was found to have produced, assisted with, or even touched any result that is a genuine case of this specific conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue the OpenAI DHL[40,2] result is close enough in spirit (same sieve machinery, same conjecture family) to count as 'progress' worth noting even though it targets a different tuple and different m. I judged it a related problem rather than a case, since it neither restricts nor touches the specific admissible set {0,2,6,8} with m=4 — the gap between DHL[40,2] and anything resembling DHL[4,4] is enormous and no technique currently bridges it. If a future reader takes a looser view of 'case', this could be reclassified as tangential 'progress' background rather than fully excluded, but the stated bullet's content would not change either way.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving DHL[4,4] (or equivalently, that the specific admissible 4-tuple {0,2,6,8} is realized as all-prime infinitely often), or any unconditional narrowing of the m=k=4 case of the prime k-tuples conjecture, would settle or advance this problem. Absent that, the question stays open.

outcome: No progress found on the question of whether there are infinitely many prime triplets (p, p+2, p+6) or (p, p+4, p+6); the conjecture remains fully open with no case settled and no bound moved on the specific triplet forms.
summary: The Wikipedia article on prime triplets (checked live, not the frozen revision, only to see whether the lead had been updated) still states the conjecture that there are infinitely many prime triplets of the forms (p, p+2, p+6) and (p, p+4, p+6) as open, and its most recent cited record dates to October 2020 (a 20,008-digit example), which predates the window and in any case is a record-size finding rather than a step toward infinitude (per §3.1, an existence/infinitude question is not advanced by a larger example). Broader searches for 'prime triplet conjecture proof', for AI involvement (DeepMind's AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve, other lab systems) touching prime constellations, and for related sieve-theory work in 2024-2026 turned up nothing that bears on this specific triplet conjecture. The closest adjacent results are: (1) Green and Sawhney's October 2024 proof that there are infinitely many primes of the form p^2+nq^2 for n ≡ 0,4 (mod 6) — a different problem (a binary-quadratic-form representation question, not the triplet-spacing conjecture) and thus out of scope under §3.1's case-vs-variant rule; (2) a July 2025 arXiv preprint ('Heuristic Bounded Prime Gaps via a Chaotic Multidimensional Sieve and Random Matrix Theory', arXiv:2507.17986) which is explicitly heuristic/conjectural, concerns general bounded prime gaps (not specifically the (p,p+2,p+6)/(p,p+4,p+6) triplet forms), has not been digested by experts, and makes no mention of any AI system in its methodology; (3) continued refinement of the Maynard-Tao/Polymath bounded-gaps machinery (the b ≤ 246 result) applied to prime constellations generally, none of which specifically resolves or narrows the triplet infinitude question, which requires a much stronger result than bounded gaps between some pair of primes. No case of the conjecture was settled, no bound specific to prime triplets moved, and no AI system was reported as involved in any of the adjacent work found.
competing_reading: One could argue that general prime-constellation progress (Maynard-Tao sieve methods, Polymath's b≤246 bound, or heuristic sieve extensions like arXiv:2507.17986) constitutes 'progress' on the broader project of proving infinitude of prime k-tuples, of which the triplet conjecture is a special case with k=3. However, none of this work proves infinitely many bounded-gap constellations of the *specific* required shape (differences of exactly 2-and-6 or 4-and-6), and the Hardy-Littlewood/Maynard-Tao apparatus for general admissible tuples is not sufficient to settle any specific triplet's infinitude without further work — so this remains general machinery rather than a case or bound on this problem, and I classify it as no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or heuristic/computational claim later confirmed) that either the bounded-gap methods can be specialized to show infinitely many prime pairs differing by exactly 2 and 6 (or 4 and 6) simultaneously, or any peer-reviewed/expert-digested result narrowing the specific triplet forms, would change this classification. Absent that, only a full proof of the Hardy-Littlewood prime k-tuple conjecture (or the specific triplet case) would resolve it.

outcome: The conjecture itself (infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1) remains completely open since 26 January 2024; only proxy quantities in the surrounding literature (the exponent c such that the largest prime factor of n^2+1 infinitely often exceeds n^c, and the Mahler-Chowla-type lower bound on the log-growth of that largest prime factor) have moved, and per the infinitude-only-moves-when-answered rule none of these settle or restrict the stated question.
summary: The stated question — are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem) — remains fully open, with no proof, disproof, or answered case since 26 January 2024. What has moved since the frozen revision is a cluster of closely related but distinct quantities in the surrounding research literature, none of which is the infinitude question itself and none of which restricts it in the §3.1 sense of settling a genuine case (they narrow where a large prime factor could be found, not whether infinitely many primes n^2+1 exist): (1) the exponent c for which the largest prime factor of n^2+1 infinitely often exceeds n^c — Merikoski's n^1.279 (Inventiones, published 2024 but first posted to arXiv in 2019, hence 'open_stale'-flavoured and pre-window in substance) was improved to n^1.3 by Alexandru Pascadi (arXiv:2404.04239, posted 5 Apr 2024, revised through Jan 2026), then to n^1.317 by Runbo Li (arXiv:2406.07575, posted 6 Jun 2024), and unconditionally to n^1.312 by Grimmelt & Merikoski (matching a value Merikoski had previously only obtained conditionally on the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture); and (2) the Mahler-Chowla-type absolute lower bound on the growth rate of the largest prime factor, improved by Hector Pasten from (log_2 n)^2/log_3 n (2023, pre-window) to (log_2 n)^2/log_4 n in arXiv:2609.01327, posted 1 Sept 2026. None of these move the needle on 'infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1' as such — even a hypothetical proof that the largest prime factor exceeds n^2 (Landau's original heuristic target) would not by itself prove infinitude, since a large prime factor is not the value n^2+1 itself being prime. I read this as squarely in §3.1's 'related problem/quantity' category rather than a 'case' of the stated bullet, so status is open/no_change_found rather than progress, even though the triage flagged real movement in the adjacent literature. The single most interesting item found is arXiv:2609.01327 (Pasten, 1 Sept 2026): its acknowledgements state, verbatim, 'Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof were first obtained in an autonomous way by the AI model ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro after a single prompt in July 2026. Theorem 1.1 was subsequently discovered by the author from interactions with the same AI model. The proof presented here is due to the author. Claude Opus 5 was used for proofreading an earlier version of the manuscript.' This is confirmed on both the arXiv HTML rendering and the independent Pith Review summary of the same paper, so it is not a fetch artifact. However this AI involvement (a) concerns the Mahler-Chowla log-growth bound, a quantity even further removed from the stated infinitude question than the n^1.3-type exponent chain, and (b) the paper is a preprint with no expert digestion yet found. Because the underlying mathematical event is not in scope for this bullet under §3.1, I am not coding this record as ai_role other than none — the AI involvement is real but attaches to a related-problem result, not to this problem. I record its existence here for transparency but do not let it drive the classification of this record, consistent with the instruction not to let a dramatic-looking result pull a no-change record toward a false positive.
competing_reading: A case could be made that the largest-prime-factor exponent bound (n^1.3, n^1.312, n^1.317) is a genuine 'case' of Landau's fourth problem in the §3.1 sense, since it directly measures how close the literature has come to Landau's own heuristic (exponent 2 would essentially force infinitely many primes via a Chebyshev-type argument on the cofactor). Under that reading this record would be 'progress' with ai_role 'none' for the exponent chain (Pascadi/Li/Grimmelt-Merikoski papers show no AI involvement), and the Pasten log-growth paper (arXiv:2609.01327) would still be a separate, more tangential item. Even under this more generous reading, however, the AI-touched paper (2609.01327) is about the log-growth bound rather than the exponent-c bound, so it would still not be the item that drives an 'assisted' or 'generated' ai_role for this specific bullet — at most it would be noted as adjacent incident-like context. I am fairly confident 'open'/'no_change_found' is the correct call for the bullet as literally worded, but flag this as the strongest alternative.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that n^2+1 is prime for infinitely many n, or an expert ruling that one of the largest-prime-factor bounds (e.g. reaching exponent 2, per Landau's own remark) is understood to formally imply the infinitude statement — no source found makes that implication explicit or claims it has been reached.

outcome: No proof or disproof of the infinitude of regular primes, and no progress on the conjectured e^{-1/2} density, has appeared since 26 January 2024; the problem remains exactly as open as Wikipedia's frozen statement describes.
summary: This is an infinitude/density existence question, so under §3.1 it moves only when actually answered — extending a computational record does not count. I searched broadly for any 2024-2026 proof, disproof, or substantive progress on (a) whether infinitely many regular primes exist, and (b) whether their density is e^{-1/2}, and found nothing. The current Wikipedia 'Regular prime' article (fetched live) confirms the infinitude question is still described as unsolved, states the same e^{-1/2}≈60.65% Siegel conjecture, and its most recent computational record is still Hart, Harvey and Ong's 2016/2017 'Irregular primes to two billion' (arXiv:1605.02398, published in Math. Comp. 86 (2017)) — no newer extension of that table was found, and even if one existed it would not change the status per §3.1 since a search bound is not an answer to an infinitude question. I also checked adjacent literature that surfaces under 'regular primes' searches — a 2023 Lean formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes (arXiv:2305.08955, formalized further in arXiv:2410.01466) and a 2023 paper on regular primes/non-Wieferich primes/multiple zeta values (arXiv:2310.06809) — both are about consequences of or related structures to regular primes (FLT for regular exponents; connections to Wieferich primes and MZVs), not about the stated question of infinitude or density, so they are out of scope under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 and do not change anything here. I found no AI system anywhere near this problem: searches for AI/ML work on regular primes turned up only tangential hits (a formal-impossibility result about ML and prime-generating formulas, an unrelated AI-verified Lean proof of the bounded-prime-gaps theorem, and AI-and-Goldbach's-conjecture experiments), none of which bear on regular primes' infinitude or density. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and reached the same conclusion independently.
competing_reading: None. The line between 'case of the problem' and 'related problem' is not in play here since nothing relevant was found at all; the only judgment call was whether the irregular-prime search-record extensions (which don't exist post-2024 anyway) would count, and per the existence/infinitude rule in §3.1 they would not even if found.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof that there are infinitely many regular primes (settling the first half), or a proof of the conjectured e^{-1/2} density (settling the second half, contingent on infinitude). Absent either, the entry stays open exactly as Wikipedia states it.

outcome: No proof, partial case, or moved bound has been found for the conjecture that there are infinitely many safe and/or Sophie Germain primes; the two 2025 items the triage flagged either prove a different statement or are unreviewed preprints with no expert uptake, and the record search for these primes was suspended in 2024 with no new large examples found since.
summary: The conjecture (are there infinitely many Sophie Germain primes p, equivalently infinitely many safe primes q=2p+1?) remains open. Two items surfaced by the triage pass turn out, on reading past the abstract/title, not to bear on the stated question. (1) Takashi Agoh, 'A Note on Sophie Germain Primes', Integers 25 (2025) #A83 (math.colgate.edu/~integers/z83/z83.pdf, read in full): its Theorem 3.1 proves that T — the set of primes that are NOT Sophie Germain — is infinite. This is a genuine, published, expert-reviewed result (journal of record, referee acknowledged, proof by Andrew Granville personally communicated to the author for one part), but it settles the complement of the stated question, not the question itself: infinitude of non-Sophie-Germain primes is nearly trivial (in fact almost all primes are not Sophie Germain, as the paper's own density computation in Section 4 shows: primitive density of S is 0), and is a different statement from 'are there infinitely many Sophie Germain primes'. Under §3.1 this is a related/different problem sharing a namesake, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not count as progress on this bullet. (2) A preprint titled 'There Are Infinitely Many Sophie Germain Primes' (preprints.org 202510.1213, October 2025) does directly target the stated question, claiming a trigonometric-product-identity proof. However: preprints.org is an unreviewed, not-peer-reviewed platform; I could not access the full text (403 Forbidden on direct fetch) but WebSearch summaries of the abstract describe a trigonometric/cosecant-power/Bernoulli-polynomial argument with no indication of review or acceptance anywhere. The same platform hosts a structurally similar unreviewed preprint 'There Are Infinitely Many Mersenne Primes' (202510.0673) by a different author, and there is a documented precedent of a near-identically-titled claim (Czelakowski, 'There are Infinitely Many Mersenne Prime Numbers', Studia Logica) that was formally RETRACTED after an error was found in the proof (Theorem 7.2) — establishing that this exact rhetorical pattern ('there are infinitely many X primes' on a low-barrier preprint venue) has produced at least one confirmed false claim in an adjacent problem. No citation, critique, digestion, or any secondary discussion of the Sophie Germain preprint could be found on MathOverflow, arXiv, Tao's blog, or elsewhere. A related preprints.org item, 'Infinitude Conditions for Sophie Germain Primes' (202510.1306), could not be fetched (403) but its title suggests conditional criteria rather than an unconditional proof. Given zero expert engagement and the strong base-rate warning sign, I treat the 202510.1213 preprint as an unverified/undigested claim that does not meet even the 'claimed' bar's practical threshold of visibility, and more importantly does not change what a careful person would write in this bullet today (the live Wikipedia article on safe/Sophie Germain primes, fetched today, still states the conjecture as open with no cited 2024-2026 developments). Separately, the empirical record: the largest known Sophie Germain prime (2,618,163,402,417 × 2^1,290,000 − 1, found Feb 2016) and corresponding safe prime remain the records; PrimeGrid's Sophie Germain Prime Search subproject was suspended in 2024 after exhaustive search of its targeted ranges, and no larger example has been found since. Per §3.1, a record search extension would not move this existence question anyway even had one occurred. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this search: none of the sources (Agoh's paper, the two preprints.org items, the Wikipedia article, the speculative blog post 'Beyond the Parity Barrier' from August 2026) mention any AI system, language model, or computer-assisted proof technique of the AI kind (as opposed to ordinary computational sieve search for prime records, which is not AI under §6.2).
competing_reading: One could argue the Agoh result, by pinning down exactly how the complement T relates to S via the explicit set A (Theorem 2.1), constitutes indirect structural progress toward understanding S — but the paper itself explicitly proves only facts about T's infinitude and S's density being 0, and never claims or implies anything toward S's infinitude; the author's own framing treats T's infinitude as the 'almost self-evident' but technically fiddly result, with S's infinitude left conspicuously untouched. I am confident this is a related/complementary result, not a case of the stated problem, but flag the reading here since it is the same author, same year, same paper as the triage's top lead.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the full text of preprints.org 202510.1213 (currently blocked to automated fetching) to check whether its trigonometric identity argument is complete and whether it has since been withdrawn, corrected, or picked up by any reviewer; and continued monitoring of arXiv/Integers/journals for any successor to Agoh's note that addresses S's infinitude directly rather than T's.

outcome: The sexy prime conjecture (infinitely many prime pairs differing by 6) remains completely open; no source claims a proof, disproof, or any result that narrows this specific case, despite a burst of activity in the adjacent bounded-gaps-between-primes problem during August-September 2026.
summary: The sexy prime conjecture asks whether there are infinitely many prime pairs (p, p+6). As of the frozen revision, the only known route to it was the Polymath group's 2014 result that the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture (GEH) implies infinitely many consecutive prime pairs differing by at most 6 (i.e. twin, cousin, or sexy primes) -- but GEH itself remains unproven, and no unconditional route reaches a gap as small as 6. I confirmed via the current Sexy primes and Polignac's conjecture Wikipedia articles that this is still exactly the state of the art: no proof, disproof, or narrowing of this specific case has occurred since 26 January 2024. Separately, I checked a recent flurry of activity on the *general* bounded-gaps-between-primes problem (the 'H1' constant, i.e. liminf of gaps between consecutive primes), since this is the natural place a case-6 result would show up. In this window: Polymath8b's H1<=246 (2014) stood until an OpenAI-credited result (dated around 30 August 2026, cdn.openai.com/pdf/.../short_gaps.pdf and the openai/PrimeGaps186 GitHub repo) claimed H1<=186 via a Lean formalization that is explicitly conditional on three unproven input axioms and contains three acknowledged theorem placeholders -- i.e. an unverified, incomplete, conditional claim, not a checked proof. Days later, Julia Stadlmann (human mathematician) posted an unconditional H1<=240 (arXiv 2608.31126, ~31 August 2026), and a further unconditional H1<=212 followed around 3 September 2026. None of these -- OpenAI's conditional 186, Stadlmann's 240, or the 212 result -- come remotely close to gap=6, and per the task's own scope rule an 'are there infinitely many X' question is not advanced by narrowing a bound unless the bound itself is the question asked; here the question is specifically about gap 6, and the general H1 constant is a different (much weaker, much larger) quantity. I therefore classify this as no_change_found: true. The OpenAI H1<=186 episode is itself an interesting AI-adjacent incident (an AI-attributed, Lean-formalized but axiom-conditional and admittedly incomplete claim, quickly overtaken by an unconditional human proof of a weaker bound) but it is not a result on this problem and I have not recorded it as an event here, since the sexy-prime bullet itself saw no movement at all.
competing_reading: One could argue that any tightening of the general bounded-gaps record is 'progress toward' sexy primes in a loose colloquial sense, since sexy primes are the case gap=6 of the same underlying liminf quantity. But per the task's rule, a case is only advanced when the specific case itself is settled or the general result's scope actually reaches it; H1<=186 (or 212, or 240) says nothing about whether gap-6 pairs are infinite, only that *some* gap <=186 recurs infinitely often. This is a related/general problem, not a narrowing of the sexy-prime case, so I did not code it as partial or progress.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (conditional or unconditional) that liminf of prime gaps is <=6, or a direct resolution of the sexy prime conjecture itself, or a proof of the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture (which the 2014 Polymath result shows would suffice), or a disproof/counterexample showing only finitely many sexy prime pairs exist.

outcome: No proof or disproof of the infinitude of Wagstaff primes has appeared since 26 January 2024; only record-extension and unrelated computational/related-problem work occurred.
summary: The question is a pure existence/infinitude claim, and per §3.1 it is only moved by an actual proof of infinitude, not by new examples, larger records, or verification to a higher computational horizon. I confirmed no such proof exists: the Wikipedia article's conjecture statement is unchanged and undated, and no paper claiming to settle the infinitude of Wagstaff primes was found on arXiv, in expert blogs, or in prime-number databases. What did happen since the frozen revision is entirely record-keeping and adjacent computation, none of which changes the bullet: (1) a new largest known Wagstaff (probable) prime, (2^141079+1)/3 with 42,469 digits, was found by ECPP in October 2025 (t5k.org/top20/page.php?id=67), surpassing the January-2024-era record of (2^138937+1)/3 (October 2023, already in Wikipedia's frozen text) — a record extension of an infinitude question, explicitly excluded by §3.1; (2) Alexey Dolotov, 'Three Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proofs for Wagstaff numbers' (arXiv 2605.18555, submitted 18 May 2026), gives classical N-1 primality certificates for three specific Wagstaff numbers (W_2617, W_10501, W_12391) as an alternative to ECPP, and states all Wagstaff numbers with exponents up to 42737 have now been proved prime or composite — pure classical/computational number theory with no AI, ML, or LLM component mentioned anywhere in the abstract or body; (3) Herbert Batte, 'On Wagstaff primes in the k-Lucas number sequence' (arXiv 2602.20387, submitted 23 February 2026), proves Wagstaff primes appear in generalized k-Lucas sequences only in finitely many specific cases, using linear forms in logarithms and LLL reduction — this is a related/variant problem (intersection with a different sequence family), not a case of or bound on the stated infinitude question, so it is correctly out of scope per §3.1's case-vs-variant rule. The 2019 vixra manuscript by Stephen Marshall claiming a proof of infinitude, flagged by triage, both predates the window (2019, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision) and remains unreviewed/unpublished, so even had it fallen inside the window it would not meet the resolved/claimed bar under §6.1. No AI system was found near this problem in any capacity — not in the record search, not in the primality proofs, not in the k-Lucas paper.
competing_reading: One could argue the Dolotov BLS paper's methodological contribution (giving primality proofs independent of ECPP) is itself 'progress' on the broader project of proving Wagstaff primality without conjectural tools, but it does not move the infinitude question itself, which is what this bullet asks, so I classified it as not a change to this problem rather than as `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint that proves (or disproves) that there are infinitely many primes p for which (2^p+1)/3 is prime — nothing short of that changes this bullet's status.

outcome: No change since 26 January 2024: still only two known Wieferich primes (1093, 3511), the search bound (a third must exceed 2^64, established by PrimeGrid in December 2022) has not been extended, and the infinitude question remains open and unproven. Several 2024-2026 papers study Wieferich-type conditions in number fields and function fields, but these are different (variant) problems, not the base-2 rational Wieferich prime question stated in this bullet.
summary: The stated question — whether there are infinitely many (base-2) Wieferich primes, i.e. primes p with p^2 dividing 2^(p-1) - 1 — remains completely open. As of the frozen revision and as of today, only two Wieferich primes are known (1093, discovered 1913; 3511, discovered 1922). The most recent search milestone, PrimeGrid's completion of a combined Wieferich/Wall-Sun-Sun search to 2^64 (~1.8x10^19), establishing that any third Wieferich prime must exceed that bound, occurred in December 2022 — before the frozen revision's date and thus not a change within the window; PrimeGrid has stated it has no plans to continue the search. I found no extension of that search bound and no new example in the 26 January 2024 - present window. Per §3.1, an infinitude question is not advanced by a larger verified search limit even when one exists (and here none post-dates the window at all), so this would not change the status even if a newer bound existed. I found several 2024-2026 papers that touch 'Wieferich' but all address different (related, not case-of) problems under §3.1: (1) arXiv:2508.08472 (Fellini-Murty, submitted Aug 2025, revised Feb 2026) proves, conditional on Masser's abc-conjecture for number fields, infinitude of certain non-Wieferich prime ideals in real quadratic number fields tied to the Ankeny-Artin-Chowla and Mordell conjectures — a number-field generalization, not the rational base-2 question. (2) arXiv:2607.15305 (Niedbala Giraudin, July 2026) exhibits a counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur about Carlitz-Wieferich primes in function fields (degree-5 irreducible c-Wieferich prime over F_19^3), verified independently via Magma (a computer algebra system) by Thakur — a wholly different (function-field, Carlitz-module) analogue, and no AI system was involved (Magma is CAS, not AI). (3) arXiv:2605.13460 (Jones, May 2026) relates classical Wieferich primes to monogenicity of a family of trinomials — a reformulation/application, not a case of the infinitude question. (4) arXiv:2412.11588 (Dec 2024) on Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules is likewise a function-field analogue. None of these change what a careful person would write in this bullet, none report AI involvement of any kind (no LLM, no AlphaEvolve/FunSearch-style system found in connection with Wieferich primes), and OEIS A001220's most substantive 2025 update (Jianing Song, June 2025) is an algebraic-number-theory remark about Z[2^(1/k)] rather than any advance on infinitude. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' case for the stated question, with the caveat that I cannot rule out an obscure preprint I did not surface.
competing_reading: One could argue the number-field generalization (arXiv:2508.08472) or the AAC/Mordell-conjecture connection is 'about' Wieferich primes closely enough to count, since it uses the same congruence condition and even proves infinitude results — but it proves infinitude of a structurally different object (prime ideals satisfying a generalized non-Wieferich condition in real quadratic fields, conditional on abc for number fields) rather than saying anything about the base-2 rational primes 1093/3511 and their kin. Per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem (changed hypotheses and ambient ring), not a restriction of the stated question, so it does not count as partial progress.
what_would_settle_it: A resolution of the base-2 rational question would require either an unconditional proof of infinitude of Wieferich primes, an unconditional proof of finiteness, or (short of full resolution) a proof of infinitude conditional on a named, well-regarded conjecture (analogous to how abc implies infinitude of non-Wieferich primes) — none of which has appeared for the base-2 case in the window.

outcome: No new Wilson prime, search extension, or theoretical progress on the infinitude question was found since 26 January 2024; only three Wilson primes (5, 13, 563) remain known, and the question is exactly as open as it was in the frozen revision.
summary: The question is whether there are infinitely many Wilson primes (primes p such that (p-1)! ≡ -1 mod p^2). Only three are known (5, 13, 563), and the last major search (Costa, Gerbicz, and Harvey, 2013/2014, arXiv:1209.3436) ruled out any further Wilson primes below 2×10^13 — a result that predates the frozen revision and would in any case be an `open_stale`-style search record, not a resolution of the infinitude question, per the rule that existence/infinitude questions move only on an answer, not on a larger search bound. I checked the Wikipedia Wilson prime article, MathWorld, AoPS wiki, and OEIS sequences A007540 (the Wilson primes themselves) and A002068 (Wilson quotients) for any update, and ran targeted searches for new Wilson prime discoveries, extended search bounds, PrimeGrid/Ibercivis/GIMPS search activity, and any 2024-2026 arXiv work on the conjecture. The only post-January-2024 paper I found that touches Wilson quotients at all is Bernd C. Kellner's 'Wilson's theorem modulo higher prime powers I: Fermat and Wilson quotients' (arXiv:2509.05235, submitted 5 September 2025) and its companion part II (arXiv:2509.05402). I opened the abstract/metadata directly: it proves supercongruences describing Wilson's theorem and the Wilson quotient modulo higher prime powers using Bell polynomials and Fermat quotient power sums — a purely theoretical, structural result about congruence identities, not a search extension, a new Wilson prime, or any statement bearing on whether infinitely many Wilson primes exist. Under §3.1 this is a related result (adjacent theory about Wilson quotients generally) rather than a case of the stated infinitude question, so it does not move the needle on this bullet. No AI system is mentioned in this paper or anywhere else I found related to Wilson primes. I found no evidence of any distributed-computing search (PrimeGrid, GIMPS, Ibercivis) being run or extended after January 2024 specifically targeting Wilson primes. The record is therefore `open` with `no_change_found` true, matching the triage's `none` verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kellner papers constitute 'progress' in a loose sense because they advance general theory around Wilson quotients that could eventually be useful to an infinitude proof or a more efficient search algorithm. But they contain no new bound, no new prime, and no argument bearing on infinitude, so under the scope rule (§3.1: a case restricts the question, a variant changes it) this is best read as adjacent background theory, not a change to this bullet.
what_would_settle_it: A new Wilson prime found beyond 5, 13, 563; a proof (or disproof) of infinitude; or, at minimum, a published extension of the search bound beyond 2×10^13 that explicitly targets Wilson primes.

outcome: No resolution, partial case, or bound extension found since 26 January 2024; the only two known Wolstenholme primes (16843, 2124679) and the >10^11 search bound (Booker, Hathi, Mossinghoff, Trudgian, 2022) are unchanged, and even a hypothetical new bound extension would not count under the scope rule for infinitude questions (§3.1).
summary: This bullet asks whether there are infinitely many Wolstenholme primes (primes p with C(2p-1,p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^4, a strengthening of Wolstenholme's theorem, which ordinarily holds only mod p^3). Only two are known — 16843 and 2124679 — and McIntosh's 1995 conjecture that infinitely many exist remains unproved. The most recent substantive computational result is Booker, Hathi, Mossinghoff and Trudgian's 2022 Ramanujan Journal paper 'Wolstenholme and Vandiver primes,' which extended the search bound to 10^11 (60 billion, per one summary) and predates the frozen revision, so it is not itself an in-window event; I found no successor paper extending this bound further in the 2024-2026 window. The current Wikipedia article, the Prime Pages glossary (t5k.org), and OEIS A088164 all still report only the same two known primes and the same pre-2024 bound, with the only 2025 OEIS edit (Thomas Ordowski, April 2025) being a cosmetic alternative characterization (a tanh/artanh identity equivalent to the existing congruence), not a mathematical advance. I also found a real but out-of-scope 2026 arXiv paper (Alexandre Linhares, 'Deep Vision: A Formal Proof of Wolstenholme's Theorem in Lean 4,' arXiv:2604.16507, submitted 14 April 2026) reporting an AI-assisted ('relational analogy engine') Lean 4 formalization of Wolstenholme's theorem itself — the classical 1862 congruence true for all primes p≥5 mod p^3, not the rare mod-p^4 Wolstenholme primes this bullet is about. Per §3.1 this is a related result sharing a name/topic, not a case of this problem, since it says nothing about the existence or count of Wolstenholme primes; I also note that even a genuine new search-bound extension would not count as movement on this bullet, since per the triage rules an infinitude/existence question is only settled by an actual proof, not by narrowing where a counterexample-type object could hide. No search turned up any 2024-2026 work claiming progress toward, or a proof of, the infinitude conjecture itself. Status is therefore 'open' with no_change_found true, matching the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than dispute.
competing_reading: One could argue the Linhares Lean 4 paper is adjacent enough (same theorem family, same 'Wolstenholme' name, uses AI) to be worth flagging as AI activity in the surrounding topic area, and a looser reader might conflate 'Wolstenholme's theorem' with 'Wolstenholme primes' as one search snippet did. But the bullet is specifically about the existence of infinitely many primes satisfying the stronger mod-p^4 congruence, and the Linhares paper neither states nor implies anything about that count; it formalizes the universal theorem that already held for all primes since 1862. I judge this to be a related/namesake result, not a case of the problem, and coded it as no AI involvement in this record's outcome.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint (i) proving infinitude of Wolstenholme primes, or (ii) at minimum extending the computational search past 10^11 with a stated new bound, dated after 26 January 2024, from a source such as arXiv, the Ramanujan Journal, Mathematics of Computation, or an update to OEIS A088164/t5k.org reporting a change in the known bound or a third example.

outcome: No change: the largest known Woodall prime (n = 17016602, found March 2018 by PrimeGrid) remains the largest known as of September 2026; the count of known Woodall primes (34) is unchanged; Suyama's result that almost all Woodall numbers are composite (pre-2024) still stands without further progress; the infinitude question remains open with no proof, disproof, or AI involvement found.
summary: This is the classic existence/infinitude question (§3.1): 'Are there infinitely many Woodall primes?' Per the deep-dive rules, this class of question moves only when actually answered — a new example, however large, narrows nothing about whether the set is infinite. I confirmed via t5k.org's list of largest known primes, the current Wikipedia Woodall number article, MathWorld, and the PrimeGrid forum announcement that the largest known Woodall prime (of the strict form n·2^n−1) remains 17016602×2^17016602−1, found by PrimeGrid volunteer 'ScOrPIoN' (credited to Diego Bertolotti in some secondary sources) in March 2018 — before the frozen revision date and thus not a window event even if it were the kind of event that counted. No new Woodall prime (strict form) has been discovered in the 26 Jan 2024–present window; t5k.org's current top-primes list shows the 2018 discovery as still the sole strict-form Woodall prime on the list, with several 'Generalized Woodall' primes (form n·b^n−1 for other bases b, or different exponent conventions) found in 2019 and 2024 — but these are a different, related problem (a different base family), not a case of this problem, so per §3.1 they do not count as narrowing this bullet even setting aside the infinitude rule. Suyama's theorem (pre-2024, extending Hooley's method from Cullen numbers) that almost all Woodall numbers are composite is unchanged and was not revisited by any 2024–2026 work I found. I found no arXiv preprint, announcement, or lab report claiming any progress — AI-assisted or otherwise — on this specific conjecture. A search for AI mathematical achievements touching prime-counting conjectures (e.g. Axiom Math, OpenAI's twin-prime-adjacent result) turned up work on unrelated problems (twin primes in function fields), not Woodall primes. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: None found. The 'Generalized Woodall prime' discoveries (2019, 2024) could conceivably be miscategorized by a careless reader as progress on 'Woodall primes,' but they concern a materially different number family (arbitrary base b instead of base 2, and often a different exponent relationship), matching the 'related problem produced by changing the question' pattern in §3.1 rather than a restriction of it. I classify them as out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude of strict-form Woodall primes (n·2^n−1), or an authoritative source explicitly stating the open status has changed in some other way (e.g., a proof of a positive-density or zero-density result stronger than Suyama's, which would still leave the status 'open' but might warrant 'progress' rather than 'open').

outcome: A preprint by Bai, Shelukhin, Wang and Xu (arXiv:2608.27242, posted 27 Aug 2026) claims a full proof of the Arnold–Givental conjecture in complete generality, combining integral Floer theory, a reduction to Hamiltonian Floer cohomology due to Lu, and a new ℤ/2-equivariant localization argument; the paper itself records a concurrent, independent announcement of a proof by Amanda Hirschi and Noah Porcelli one day earlier (26 Aug 2026) at a conference in Augsburg. Neither has been digested by the expert community yet; only an automated preprint-review service (Pith) has produced a report, which flags an analytic step (described as a 'thin point') needing careful checking.
credited_humans: Amanda Hirschi (concurrent independent announcement, unpublished as of this record)
Noah Porcelli (concurrent independent announcement, unpublished as of this record)

disputes.summary: The Bai–Shelukhin–Wang–Xu preprint (submitted 27 Aug 2026) explicitly notes in its Remark 1.2 a concurrent, independent proof announced by Amanda Hirschi and Noah Porcelli on 26 Aug 2026 (one day earlier) at the conference 'Symplectic Topology – in honor of Kai Cieliebak' in Augsburg. No preprint from Hirschi–Porcelli could be located as of this research (checked 2026-09-22); their work was described in the announcement as 'joint work-in-progress'. Priority and completeness of each claim is unresolved.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet bundles the Arnold conjecture (fixed points of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms) and the Arnold–Givental conjecture (a Smith-inequality-type bound on Lagrangian fixed-point sets of an anti-symplectic involution) as a single entry; the triage record and my research both center on the Arnold–Givental half, since that is where the dated finding sits. As of the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024), the Arnold–Givental conjecture was open in general, proved only in a list of special cases (Givental for (CP^n, RP^n); Oh for real forms of compact Hermitian spaces; Lazzarini for the negative monotone case; Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono for semi-positive (M,ω); Frauenfelder for certain symplectic reductions). On 27 August 2026, Bai, Shelukhin, Wang and Xu posted arXiv:2608.27242 claiming a full proof in complete generality, using integral Floer theory (methods of the 1st and 4th authors), a reduction to Hamiltonian Floer cohomology due to Lu, and a new ℤ/2-equivariant localization argument. I read the abstract and the paper's own text (via the arXiv HTML rendering) directly rather than relying on the triage's unopened snippet. The paper contains no mention whatsoever of AI systems, language models, or automated theorem-proving tools in its methods or acknowledgements — the acknowledgements section credits only NSF/NSERC/FRQNT/Simons funding, so ai_role is 'none'. The paper itself discloses a genuine priority dispute: it acknowledges a concurrent, independent proof announced one day earlier (26 Aug 2026) by Amanda Hirschi and Noah Porcelli at a symplectic-topology conference in Augsburg, described as work-in-progress; I could not locate a preprint from Hirschi and Porcelli as of 22 Sep 2026, so their claim remains an announcement only. Given the preprint is barely three weeks old at the time of this research, there is no evidence of expert digestion (no blog commentary from Tao, the Matroid/symplectic-topology community blogs, or journal acceptance). The only third-party assessment found is from 'Pith' (pith.science), which is explicitly an automated/machine preprint-review service (self-described as producing 'referee-style reports' via a 'machine reviewer'), not a human expert; its report flags an analytic step as a 'thin point' needing careful checking, i.e. it has not vouched for correctness. Per §6.1, a preprint with no human expert digestion is 'claimed', not 'resolved', however clean the exposition looks; the status here is 'claimed'. The stated result answers the conjecture as expected (confirming the conjectured inequality), so resolution_direction is 'confirmed'; this is not a counterexample. I disagree with the triage record only in nuance, not substance: the triage flagged 'likely' and found the same single arXiv entry; I confirmed by reading the abstract/full text, found the priority dispute the triage missed (it had not opened the paper), and confirmed no AI involvement rather than leaving it unchecked.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'resolved' given the identity/reputation of the authors (Bai and Shelukhin are established Floer theorists) and the existence of a machine-generated review that did not flag outright errors, only a step needing further scrutiny. But per §6.1 a machine review is explicitly insufficient for 'resolved' status — a human expert (named, working through the argument) or journal acceptance is required, and neither exists yet for a paper posted only ~3.5 weeks before this research date.
what_would_settle_it: A human expert's public digestion of the Bai–Shelukhin–Wang–Xu argument (a seminar report, a referee report, journal acceptance, or a named symplectic geometer's blog/MathOverflow commentary working through the proof), and/or the appearance of the competing Hirschi–Porcelli preprint and any reconciliation of the two claims, would move this to 'resolved' and settle the priority dispute.

outcome: A June 2026 preprint by Adams, Ionov, Mason-Brown and Vogan (arXiv:2606.01609) claims to prove in general the long-standing unitarity conjecture for Arthur packets of real reductive groups (that all Arthur packets consist of unitary representations), a core piece of Arthur's conjectures, using a new 'Jordan decomposition' technique that reduces the general case to the unipotent case established by earlier authors. As a byproduct they also claim a proof of Jiang's conjecture (wavefront-set bounds) for real reductive groups. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or blog treatment of this specific paper has appeared as of the search date (2026-09-22); a September 2026 follow-up preprint (arXiv:2609.19197, Jiawei Yang) builds on and extends the June paper's conjectured 'support equality', showing the community is actively engaging with it, but that is not itself an independent verification of the unitarity proof.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet for 'Arthur's conjectures' is unusually broad (Arthur's 1989 conjectures on automorphic representations, packets, and unitarity, with implications for the generalized Ramanujan conjecture), and the linked article is a stub that names no specific open sub-claim. Within the window, the clearest and most decisive event is arXiv:2606.01609 (Adams, Ionov, Mason-Brown, Vogan; posted 2026-06-01), which claims to settle in full generality the unitarity conjecture -- that every Arthur packet for a real reductive group consists of unitary representations -- a piece of Arthur's conjectures that had previously been established only for split real groups (Taïbi, 2019) and for unipotent packets by several groups of authors. The new paper's method is a 'Jordan decomposition' of an arbitrary Arthur packet into unipotent pieces via parabolic and cohomological induction, reducing the general unitarity question to the already-solved unipotent case. This is a genuine case of, and arguably a full resolution of, the stated unitarity component of Arthur's conjectures for real groups (as opposed to the still-conjectural non-archimedean/global cases). However, as of this search (2026-09-22, roughly 3.5 months after posting), I found no evidence of expert digestion: no acceptance notice, no coverage on expert blogs (Tao, Quanta, etc.), and the only 'review' found is an automated, non-expert machine-generated assessment from pith.science (explicitly self-described as 'machine-made and fallible... not journal acceptance and no substitute for expert scrutiny' -- itself a case worth flagging as an example of an AI system reviewing, but not producing, mathematics, so it does not count toward ai_role). A September 2026 preprint by a different author (Jiawei Yang, arXiv:2609.19197) extends a conjecture posed alongside the June paper ('Arthur-packet support equality'), which shows the paper is being read and built upon by the field, but is not itself a verification of the unitarity proof. Given the single-digit-month gap since posting and the absence of independent confirmation, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved'. No AI system is credited by the authors anywhere in this chain of papers; all work is attributed to human mathematicians using classical representation-theoretic and microlocal-geometric techniques.
competing_reading: One could argue the broad Wikipedia bullet 'Arthur's conjectures' should be treated as still fundamentally open even if the unitarity piece is settled, since the article names no specific sub-conjecture and other components (the full endoscopic classification and multiplicity formula for general reductive groups, especially non-quasi-split and non-archimedean cases) remain conjectural. Under a narrower reading focused only on 'the' unitarity conjecture as the decisive named result, 'claimed' (pending expert digestion) is the right call, which is what I used; under a broader reading treating the whole package of Arthur's conjectures as the bullet, the correct status might instead be 'progress' (a major piece moved, but the overall conjectural package is far from settled) rather than 'claimed'. I judged the unitarity result to be the single most decisive and specific event in the window, which is why I centered the record on it as 'claimed', while still status could arguably be read as 'progress' if one insists the bullet as a whole cannot be resolved by one sub-conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance of arXiv:2606.01609, a detailed expert digestion (e.g., a seminar write-up, a survey, or a blog post by a specialist in real reductive group representation theory working through the Jordan decomposition argument), or citations from subsequent papers that explicitly rely on and thereby implicitly vouch for the result, would move this from 'claimed' to 'resolved'. Conversely, if a flaw is found in the reduction to the unipotent case, this would become 'progress' with an 'incident' note.

outcome: The conjecture as stated (a fixed non-square, non-(-1) integer is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes) remains open and unproved unconditionally; the only claimed full proof found is conditional on a new, itself-unproven hypothesis, and other 2024-2026 work addresses related but distinct questions (refinements of the conjecture's finer structure, and an 'on average over a' version), not the stated conjecture for a fixed a.
summary: I found no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 - 22 Sep 2026) that changes the status of Artin's conjecture on primitive roots as literally stated: that a fixed integer which is neither a perfect square nor -1 is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes. The most significant candidate, flagged by triage, is Murty and Naik's arXiv preprint 'A non-abelian large sieve and Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2608.21573, submitted 25 Aug 2026), which states it proves the full conjecture 'assuming the non-abelian large sieve inequality' -- a new hypothesis the authors themselves have not proved (they only give partial/unconditional progress toward it via duality techniques). This is structurally the same kind of result as Hooley's 1967 GRH-conditional proof: a conditional proof resting on an unproved hypothesis, not a change in the conjecture's actual open/closed status, and I found no evidence of expert digestion or acceptance establishing the sieve inequality itself. I classified this as not changing the status (still `open`), by analogy with how Hooley's classical conditional proof does not make Wikipedia call the conjecture resolved. The second item triage found, Goldmakher-Martin-Peringuey's 'Refinements of Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2502.19601, Feb 2025), explicitly poses new, finer conjectures about the distribution of the multiplicative order that 'contain Artin's original conjecture as a special case' -- i.e. it changes the question (a related/refined problem), and proves its own refinements under GRH plus some unconditional partial results; it does not touch the literal conjecture as stated beyond what was already known via Hooley. I also found Klurman-Shparlinski-Teravainen, 'On Artin's conjecture on average and short character sums' (arXiv:2412.13355, submitted 17 Dec 2024, published in Bulletin LMS May 2025), which proves the asymptotic predicted by Artin's conjecture holds for almost all a in a growing range -- an average-case/variant statement over a, not a resolution for any single fixed a, and it explicitly improves on Stephens (1969), a pre-existing average-case literature distinct from the stated conjecture. None of these three papers, nor the current Wikipedia article on the conjecture, nor any other source I found, mentions any AI system, machine-learning tool, or automated theorem prover contributing to the mathematics; all read as traditional analytic/algebraic number theory. A search on AI benchmarks turned up only that Artin's conjecture appears as a test problem in the FrontierMath benchmark used to evaluate AI mathematical reasoning, with no claim that any model produced progress on it. Given the scope rule in section 3.1, I treat both the refinement paper and the 'on average' paper as related-but-distinct problems rather than cases of the stated conjecture, and the Murty-Naik preprint as a conditional result in the same unresolved pattern as Hooley's, so the conjecture's status has not moved: `open`, `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Murty-Naik preprint should be `claimed` with `resolution_direction` `confirmed`, on the reasoning that a genuinely new conditional proof of the *full* conjecture (rather than a further partial/average result) is itself a notable event even if the condition is unproved -- this would parallel treating Hooley's 1967 result as a landmark despite being GRH-conditional. Against this: Hooley's hypothesis (GRH) is a widely-studied standard conjecture with its own extensive support, while the 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' is newly introduced in this very paper with only partial unconditional support shown by the same authors, making the conditional proof considerably weaker evidentially and not yet vetted by any expert digestion. I judged this closer to a conditional-on-a-new-unestablished-hypothesis result (not yet a `claimed` proof of the actual conjecture, since the load-bearing hypothesis is itself open and unreviewed) than to a landmark conditional proof, but a future reviewer who finds independent scrutiny of the non-abelian large sieve inequality, or expert commentary treating this preprint as a serious conditional resolution, might reasonably upgrade this to `progress` or `claimed`.
what_would_settle_it: Expert commentary (a survey update, a blog post by a number theorist, or peer review) assessing whether Murty and Naik's 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' is a plausible/well-supported hypothesis comparable in status to GRH, which would clarify whether their conditional proof is comparable to Hooley's landmark result or a much weaker conditional claim; also, any later paper either proving or disproving the non-abelian large sieve inequality itself.

outcome: No result found, in any source, that settles or narrows this specific question in the 26 January 2024 to present window.
summary: This bullet's own citation (visible on both the frozen January 2024 revision and the current live article, confirmed identical) is Saharon Shelah, 'Borel sets with large squares', Fundamenta Mathematicae 159 (1999), arXiv math/9802134. That 1999 paper is the origin of the question: it introduces the cardinal invariant λ_{ω1}(ℵ0) and proves (⊗'_μ) that if a complete sentence ψ of L_{ω1,ω} (equivalently, by Chang's trick, an atomic class of a countable first-order theory omitting countably many types) has a model of cardinality μ ≥ λ_{ω1}(ℵ0), then it has a model of cardinality continuum, generated in a 'nice, absolute' way — and shows this is consistent with λ_{ω1}(ℵ0) itself being at or above ℵ_{ω1} (e.g. under MA + 2^ℵ0 > ℵ_{ω1}), so the Hanf-number-below-continuum phenomenon at exactly ℵ_{ω1} is not settled by that theorem alone; whether ℵ_{ω1} always suffices, or whether it can consistently fail, is left open. The Wikipedia bullet is a restatement of this residual open case. I searched extensively for any post-26-January-2024 progress on this exact question: model theorists who work in the closest surrounding territory (John Baldwin, Chris Laskowski, Shelah himself, and collaborators) have been highly active in the general area of atomic classes / L_{ω1,ω} categoricity and Hanf-number-type questions through 2024-2025 — e.g. Baldwin-Laskowski-Shelah, 'When does ℵ1-categoricity imply ω-stability?' (Model Theory 3 (2024) 801-823, arXiv 2308.13942, submitted Aug 2023 — before the window); Baldwin-Laskowski-Shelah, 'An analogue of U-rank for atomic classes' (arXiv 2502.00984, Feb 2025); and Baldwin's two 2024 and 2025 conference talks 'Can categorical classes in L_{ω1,ω} be bounded in size?' (AEC Conference, Baylor, July 2024; Shelah's 80th birthday conference, Vienna, July 16 2025) — but I read the 2025 talk slides in full and none of this work touches the ℵ_{ω1}-to-continuum question; it is about a different (though related) pair of questions: whether ℵ1-categorical atomic classes/AECs have models bounded in size at all (Grossberg's question, the WGCH(λ) theorem, and the (2^ℵ0)+ implies ω-stability theorem), not about the Hanf number for omitting-types classes at ℵ_{ω1} specifically. I also checked the Kurepa-tree/L_{ω1,ω}-spectrum literature (Bagaria-Cummings-... adjacent work; Lambie-Hanson and Stejskalová's Nov 2024 'Kurepa trees, continuous images, and perfect set properties') and Shelah's 'On what I do not understand' problem list (1999/2000) — all pre-window or off-target. No arXiv listing, Baldwin publication page, or Shelah archive entry from 2024-2026 addresses this exact statement. There is no AI involvement anywhere in this literature; it is entirely human set-theoretic and model-theoretic work using forcing, weak diamond, and pseudo-algebraic-closure techniques.
competing_reading: The Baldwin-Laskowski-Shelah 2024/2025 line of work (ω-stability from a model of size (2^ℵ0)+, and the general 'can categorical classes in L_{ω1,ω} be bounded in size' program) is close enough in subject matter that a very loose reading might count it as 'progress adjacent to this problem.' I judge it does not count under §3.1: it answers a different question (boundedness of ℵ1-categorical atomic classes, and ω-stability transfer) rather than moving the specific ℵ_{ω1}→continuum implication for theories omitting countably many types. It is a related problem, not a case of this one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that either (a) proves in ZFC that a class K of models of a countable first-order theory omitting countably many types with a model of cardinality ℵ_{ω1} must have a model of cardinality continuum, or (b) proves the consistency of ZFC + such a K having a model of cardinality ℵ_{ω1} but no model of cardinality continuum (a genuine independence/refutation result), or (c) an update to Shelah's own problem lists or the Shelah archive marking this specific sub-case as resolved.
