outcome: No case of the stated conjecture (invertibility of the n-by-n matrix/linear independence of the n polynomials for a configuration of n points in R^3, for n beyond the already-settled n=4) has been proved since 26 January 2024. Two post-window papers touch adjacent territory but both change the problem rather than settling any of it: Malkoun (arXiv 2508.13472, Aug 2025) generalizes the Atiyah problem and Atiyah-Sutcliffe conjectures 1 and 2 to a 'G-amplitude function' framework over finite graphs, recovering the classical conjectures only as the special case G = K_n, without proving that special case for any new n; and Guerra-Salvatore (arXiv 2410.24124, Oct 2024, published in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A, Aug 2026) show that the Atiyah-Sutcliffe conjecture would imply an E3-algebra structure on flag manifolds, a structural/implicational result rather than a proof of any case.
summary: The Atiyah conjecture on configurations (that the n-by-n matrix / n associated polynomials for n distinct points in R^3 are always linearly independent, equivalently the Atiyah determinant is never zero) remains open for general n. It was proved for n<=4 by Eastwood-Norbury (2001) and reproved by an alternate method by Malkoun (2022/2023), both before the frozen revision date and already reflected in the pre-2024 literature. Since 26 January 2024, two arXiv items surfaced in searches, and I opened both directly (not just the triage snippets). The first, Malkoun's August 2025 preprint (2508.13472), builds a generalized 'G-amplitude function' framework using finite graphs and tensors; it explicitly recovers the Atiyah-Sutcliffe conjectures 1 and 2 only when the graph G is taken to be the complete graph K_n, i.e. the classical conjecture is a special case of the new, broader conjectural framework the paper proposes — it does not prove that special case for any n beyond what was already known, so per the scope rule (§3.1) this is a related/generalizing problem, not a case of the stated conjecture. The second, Guerra-Salvatore's 'The Atiyah-Sutcliffe conjecture and En-algebras' (arXiv 2410.24124, submitted 31 Oct 2024, v2 5 Nov 2024, published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A on 28 Aug 2026), proves that the conjecture (if true) would imply an E3-algebra structure on the disjoint union of flag manifolds, and does homological calculations around this; it is an implication/structural connection to algebraic topology, not a proof of any new case, and does not move the truth value of the conjecture in either direction. I also checked for any claimed disproof or counterexample: a superficially similar-sounding paper, 'Atiyah's Minkowski Space Conjecture Fails for Every n>=3' (arXiv 2608.16693, Aug 2026), does refute a conjecture by Atiyah, but on close reading this is a distinct 'Minkowski space' variant concerning worldlines and celestial directions in Minkowski space, not the Euclidean R^3 configuration conjecture stated in this bullet — it changes the ambient space and objects (worldlines vs. points), so under §3.1 it is a related problem with a different namesake, not a case of this one. I found no mention of any AI system, LLM, or automated theorem-proving tool in any of the sources checked (the two 2024/2025 preprints, Malkoun's blog, or general searches for AI-assisted work on this problem); all work is traditional algebraic/geometric mathematics, in the latter case combined with algebraic topology. I also checked the problem's current Wikipedia article, which remains a stub with no discussion of recent results. On balance the correct classification is open, no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Malkoun 2025 generalization deserves 'progress' rather than 'open' on the theory that a conjectural framework which reduces to the original conjecture as a special case is itself a step toward the original. But no instance of the original n-point conjecture beyond n=4 is proved by this framework, so nothing about what a careful reader would write in this bullet's entry (the invertibility claim for n points in R^3) has changed; it remains a related problem under the stated rule, and I classify it as no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof/counterexample) of the invertibility claim for some n=5 or a proof of the general case, published or preprinted after 26 January 2024, framed in terms of the original R^3 point-configuration determinant rather than a generalized or differently-set variant.

outcome: No result changing the classification of which finite groups are BI-groups (Babai invariant groups) was found in the window; the problem remains open with no case, bound, or resolution located.
summary: Babai's problem (posed by László Babai in 1979) asks which finite groups are BI-groups (Babai invariant groups): groups G such that whenever Cay(G,S) ≅ Cay(G,T) for inverse-closed connection sets, the character-sum multisets M_ν^S and M_ν^T agree for every irreducible character degree ν. The last substantive work on this exact question that I could find is Abdollahi and Zallaghi's 2015 'Character Sums for Cayley Graphs' (Comm. Algebra) and their 2017/2019 follow-up 'Non-abelian finite groups whose character sums are invariant but are not Cayley isomorphism' (arXiv:1710.04446, J. Algebra Appl. 2019), which exhibited non-abelian BI-groups of orders 20 and 42 that are not CI-groups and classified BI-groups up to order 30 — all before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision. I ran searches for 'BI-group', 'Babai invariant group', and combinations with 'character sum', 'Cayley graph', and years 2024-2026, and found no paper, preprint, or announcement addressing this classification question in the window. Adjacent-sounding hits are all out of scope under §3.1: 'bi-Cayley graphs' and 'm-BCI-groups' (e.g. the 2025 Communications in Algebra paper on generalized quaternion groups) concern isomorphism of a structurally different graph class (bi-Cayley graphs, built from two group copies) and the separate BCI-group property, not character-sum invariance of ordinary Cayley graphs. I also found that 'Babai's conjecture' — a well-studied, actively-progressing diameter bound for Cayley graphs of finite simple groups (with 2022-2025 partial results by various authors on transvections, classical groups, and random generators) — is a different problem sharing Babai's name; it is not a case or variant of the BI-group question and is out of scope. The Wikipedia article itself (as of my fetch) cites nothing after 2019 and shows no edits reflecting new results. I conclude nothing has happened to this specific problem in the window, and no AI system is implicated in any relevant work.
competing_reading: None of the adjacent literature (bi-Cayley/BCI-group papers, Babai's diameter conjecture, general Cayley isomorphism/CI-group work) plausibly constitutes even a narrow case of the BI-group classification question, so there is little ambiguity here; the main risk is a paper using different terminology (e.g. calling character-sum invariance something else) that my searches missed.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that explicitly determines BI-group status (in the character-sum-invariance sense) for a new group, family of groups, or order range, or that proves/disproves BI-group status is equivalent to some other known group property.

outcome: The construction of a conservative, ergodic, sigma-finite (infinite) measure-preserving transformation with simple Lebesgue spectrum -- an affirmative answer to Banach's Scottish Book problem in its classical (infinite-measure/non-singular) reading -- was published by el Houcein el Abdalaoui well before the frozen revision date, with the cleanest write-up (arXiv:2210.15480) submitted 2022-10-27 and last revised 2023-06-09. Nothing in the 26 Jan 2024 - present window resolves, partially resolves, or moves a bound on the problem as Wikipedia states it; several adjacent but distinct spectral-multiplicity results appeared in the window (Sept 2024, June 2024) and none of them touch simple Lebesgue spectrum for an ergodic system in the sense at issue.
summary: Wikipedia's bullet states the classical Scottish Book question attributed to Banach: 'is there an ergodic system with simple Lebesgue spectrum?' The literature on this exact question (traced through el Abdalaoui's papers, which are the only substantive body of work on it) shows a layered history: a 2015 paper (arXiv:1508.06439) began the flat-polynomial approach; a 2020 paper (arXiv:2007.03684) gave an affirmative answer for the flow (R-action) version using rank-one flows; and a 2022 paper (arXiv:2210.15480, last revised 2023-06-09) gave a simplified, self-contained construction of a conservative ergodic sigma-finite measure-preserving transformation with simple Lebesgue spectrum, described by the author as answering Banach's Scottish Book problem affirmatively. All of this predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision by at least seven months, so under section 6.1 it is 'open_stale': settled (in this specific sense) before the window, never a change within it. Crucially, the resolved case is for a conservative, sigma-finite (i.e. generally infinite) measure-preserving transformation -- a non-singular dynamical system. The closely related but distinct question that Rokhlin posed, and that much of the survey literature treats as the 'basic' open problem -- whether a finite (probability) measure-preserving ergodic transformation can have simple Lebesgue spectrum -- is explicitly still reported as open in sources discussing this area (search results state 'the question of Rokhlin still remains open since the maps constructed does not have a pure Lebesgue spectrum' in the finite-measure setting). Wikipedia's own wording does not specify finite versus infinite measure, so which reading the bullet points to is ambiguous, but under either reading nothing changed within the window: if the bullet means the infinite-measure/Scottish-Book question, it was already resolved pre-2024 (open_stale); if it means the finite-measure/Rokhlin question, it remains open with no progress found in the window either. I searched specifically for 2024-2026 activity and found three adjacent papers -- 'Inducing countable Lebesgue spectrum' (Abdedou-Fayad-Thouvenot, arXiv:2409.00396, submitted 2024-08-31, showing every ergodic system induces a system with pure Lebesgue spectrum of *infinite* multiplicity, not simple/multiplicity-one spectrum), Ryzhikov's May/June 2024 paper on tensor powers and simple-versus-Lebesgue spectrum transitions under tensoring (arXiv:2406.08409), and a September 2026 paper on orbit equivalence of rank-one systems -- none of which settle, restrict, or move a bound on the simple-Lebesgue-spectrum question itself; they are related problems (different multiplicity, different operation) under section 3.1's scope rule, not cases of this problem. No AI system appears anywhere in any of the papers found; all are single- or multi-author pure-mathematics preprints from established ergodic theorists with no stated computational or AI assistance in either the mathematics or its exposition.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet, being unqualified, should be read as already-resolved (open_stale) purely on the strength of the pre-2024 sigma-finite construction, full stop -- treating the finite-measure Rokhlin question as a separate Wikipedia entry's concern rather than this one's. Under that reading the classification is the same (open_stale) but the summary's caveat about the finite-measure case being separately open would be irrelevant noise. Conversely, one could argue the 'true' Banach/Scottish-Book question, as classically transmitted through Ulam's book and Rokhlin, was always implicitly about probability-space (finite-measure) transformations, in which case the sigma-finite construction is itself a 'related problem' rather than a resolution, and the correct status would be plain 'open' (never resolved even before the window) rather than 'open_stale'. I did not find a source that definitively fixes which reading Wikipedia intended, since the bullet cites only a single footnote reference without further qualification.
what_would_settle_it: The specific footnote/reference Wikipedia's bullet cites (footnote 37 in the frozen revision) would show which source the encyclopedia editors relied on and hence which version of the problem (finite- or infinite-measure) they meant. Locating and reading that exact citation would resolve whether 'open_stale' or plain 'open' (pre-existing, never resolved) is the more faithful classification; either way, no event in the 26 Jan 2024-present window is affected.

outcome: The full conjecture (every cubic bipartite 3-connected planar graph is Hamiltonian) remains open, but a genuine case of it was settled: a August 2025 preprint by Tobias Schnieders extends Goodey's 1975 special-case result (Hamiltonicity for face sizes up to 6) to face sizes up to 8, via a large computer-assisted case split (339,068,624 cases). This is not yet digested by experts (no journal acceptance or expert write-up found), so it is a settled-but-unreviewed case rather than an expert-confirmed one. A separate 2025 conference paper (Bekos, Kaufmann, Pfister, Graph Drawing 2025) improves a subhamiltonian-cycle bound (5n/6 edges vs. previous 2n/3) but explicitly does not address Hamiltonicity itself, so it is a related/weaker result rather than a case of the stated conjecture. No AI system was involved in either result.
summary: Barnette's conjecture (every cubic, bipartite, 3-connected planar graph is Hamiltonian) remains open as of September 2026; no proof or counterexample has been found. Within the 26 January 2024 window, two pieces of work surfaced. (1) Tobias Schnieders, 'Barnette Graphs with Faces up to Size 8 are Hamiltonian' (arXiv:2508.03531, submitted 5 August 2025), substantially strengthens Goodey's 1975 result (which proved Hamiltonicity when all faces have size ≤6) to graphs with faces of size ≤8, via a computer-assisted proof involving a case split of 339,068,624 cases. This is a genuine *case* of the stated conjecture under §3.1 (a restriction to a sub-class of Barnette graphs by face size), and settling it is progress in the confirming direction (more Barnette graphs shown Hamiltonian, none refuting the conjecture). It remains a preprint with no evidence of journal acceptance, expert digestion (no Tao/Quanta/survey coverage found), or independent verification of the computation, so I classify it `partial` rather than `resolved`. (2) Bekos, Kaufmann and Pfister, 'Approximating Barnette's Conjecture' (Graph Drawing 2025 / LIPIcs GD.2025.6), improves a bound on subhamiltonian cycles (book-embedding spine edges) from 2n/3 to 5n/6 in Barnette graphs, but the authors explicitly do not resolve or advance the Hamiltonicity question itself — this is a different (weaker, related) invariant, so it does not count as progress on the stated bullet and is mentioned only for context. Neither paper mentions any AI/ML system; the computational components are classical brute-force/case-enumeration methods, not AI. I also investigated 'ProofAtlas' (proofatlas.ai), a self-described 'AI-first formal mathematics' platform that lists Barnette's conjecture as one of ~198 open research programs it tracks. Its own page for Barnette's conjecture states the conjecture 'remains unresolved' with several named sub-problems (b=9 orbit list, b≥10 unbounded descent, tight-cut coordination, cycle merger) still open, and explicitly notes 'ProofAtlas has not executed or independently reproduced the current work attachments' — i.e., no claimed result, human- or AI-generated, exists there for this problem. ProofAtlas's own list of nine 'accepted' research advances (via a contributor called Lech Mazur, using Lean-checked proofs) does not include Barnette's conjecture at all — it covers Collatz, Sendov's conjecture, and several other unrelated problems. So while an AI-oriented research platform is actively organizing work on this exact conjecture as of August 2026, it has produced no finding, claim, or partial result on it to date; this is worth noting as an interesting near-miss for the AI question but is not itself an event to record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Schnieders face-size extension is 'incremental' enough, and insufficiently reviewed, to warrant `open` with the preprint merely noted rather than `partial`. I judge `partial` is correct because the rules state size is not the test and a case settled counts even via preprint — `partial` does not require expert digestion (only `resolved` does). A reader could also argue the Bekos et al. subhamiltonian-bound paper is itself a 'bound that moved' under `progress`/§3.1's related-problem carve-out, but since it is on a different invariant (book-embedding edge count, not existence of a Hamiltonian cycle) rather than a restriction of the stated question, I treat it as out of scope and mention it only in summary rather than making it the record's decisive event.
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance or an expert survey/blog digestion of the Schnieders preprint (or an independent re-verification of its case enumeration) would move that piece to `resolved`-level confidence for the face-≤8 case. Any future output from ProofAtlas or another AI system that produces a checked claim specifically on Barnette's conjecture (not just the currently unresolved research-program tracking) would be the first candidate for `ai_role` other than `none` on this problem.

outcome: No result advancing the Bass conjecture (finite generation of K_i(X) for regular schemes X of finite type over Z, or equivalently K_n(A) for regular finitely generated Z-algebras A) was found in the window 26 January 2024 to present. Quillen's dimension-≤1 case remains the frontier result; higher-dimensional cases remain open.
summary: Extensive searching across arXiv, Wikipedia, and general web sources turned up nothing that advances this specific conjecture — Bass's conjecture that K_i(X) (or K'_i(X), or the motivic-cohomology refinement H^i_M(X,Z(n))) is finitely generated for regular schemes X of finite type over Z — in the window since 26 January 2024. The known state remains what it was before the window: Quillen proved the dimension ≤1 case (curves over finite fields, rings of integers in number fields) decades ago, and the case CH_0(X) (zero-cycles) follows from higher-dimensional class field theory, also pre-2024. Higher-dimensional cases remain open, as confirmed by Geisser's survey on finite generation questions for motivic cohomology and by the current Wikipedia article on the Bass conjecture, neither of which records any post-2024 development. Every search that surfaced 'Bass' and 'K-theory' together in 2024-2025 preprints (e.g. arXiv:2512.18868, arXiv:2503.10163) concerned the distinct Bass–Quillen conjecture on finitely generated projective modules over regular rings, which is a different question about projective modules, not about finite generation of K-groups as abelian groups — this matches the triage's finding and I confirm the triage was right to treat those as out of scope (§3.1: a different problem sharing a namesake, not a case or restriction of this one). No AI system appears anywhere in the material found, unsurprising given that nothing at all was found to attribute it to.
competing_reading: One could argue that any of the many papers on finiteness of related invariants (unramified cohomology, higher Chow groups, motivic cohomology of specific varieties over finite fields) constitute 'partial progress' if they establish finite generation for some class of X not previously known. I did not find any such paper dated within the window that goes beyond what was already known pre-2024 (e.g. arXiv:2302.09867 on motivic cohomology of surfaces over finite fields appears to be older/pre-window work reappearing in searches, and arXiv:2309.08463 and arXiv:2605.22494 concern equicharacteristic/Bloch-Ogus phenomena rather than establishing new finite-generation results for the arithmetic (mixed-characteristic) schemes this bullet concerns). If a hidden, more targeted result exists in a paper I did not surface, this would need reclassifying, but nothing found supports it.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly proving finite generation of K_i(X) or K'_i(X) for some new class of regular schemes X of finite type over Z beyond dimension ≤1 (or of the refined motivic-cohomology groups H^i_M(X,Z(n))), dated after 26 January 2024, with an abstract or introduction that states the result as advancing Bass's finiteness conjecture specifically (not the Bass-Quillen projective-module conjecture).

outcome: No case of the classical Bass–Quillen conjecture (vector bundles / f.g. projective modules over a regular Noetherian ring A vs. A[t1,...,tn]) was settled in the window; the two 2025 papers found generalize the conjecture to torsors/G-bundles and to non-Noetherian valuation rings, which are related problems rather than restrictions of the stated conjecture.
summary: The classical Bass–Quillen conjecture states that for a regular Noetherian ring A, every finitely generated projective A[t1,...,tn]-module is extended from A (equivalently, every vector bundle on affine space over Spec A descends to Spec A). Two papers found in the triage pass, both from 2025, address generalizations of this conjecture rather than the conjecture itself. (1) Guo–Liu, 'The Bass–Quillen conjecture for torsors over valuation rings' (arXiv:2503.10163, submitted 2025-03-13, published in IMRN 2025) prove a descent result for reductive-group torsors over smooth algebras A over a valuation ring V. Fetching the paper confirms that valuation rings (in particular non-Noetherian Prüfer rings) fall outside the classical conjecture's hypothesis of a regular Noetherian base ring, and the authors frame mixed-characteristic, non-Noetherian settings as a genuinely new regime rather than a restriction of the classical statement. This is a related problem under §3.1 (same name, different objects/rings), not a case of the stated conjecture. (2) Stavrova, 'On the generalized Bass–Quillen conjecture in dimension 2' (arXiv:2512.18868, submitted 2025-12-21) proves the dimension-≤-2 case for principal G-bundles for reductive groups G with split semisimple derived group. Fetching the paper shows it explicitly states that specializing to G=GL_n recovers the *classical* dimension-≤-2 case, which the authors attribute to Murthy (n=1) and to Suslin/Quillen (general n) — i.e., already known well before the window. Stavrova's new contribution is restricted to other reductive groups (not GL_n), so it extends the generalized conjecture rather than adding new territory to the classical vector-bundle statement Wikipedia poses. Neither paper settles, refines, or contradicts anything about the classical Bass–Quillen conjecture as such; no counterexample, no new case, and no bound on file. The Wikipedia article's own text (fetched) lists the state of the art as Lindel (1981, smooth k-algebras) and Asok–Hoyois–Wendt (2018, homotopy-invariance results) and does not mention any post-2024 development, consistent with what direct searches turned up. No source of any kind — in either paper, in secondary commentary, or in general searches for AI and this conjecture — mentions any AI system, machine-learning tool, or automated theorem prover contributing to any of this work; both papers read as traditional human mathematics with no AI acknowledgement of any kind.
competing_reading: One could argue Stavrova's dimension-2 G-bundle theorem is 'progress' on a generalized version of Bass–Quillen that Wikipedia's bullet doesn't explicitly separate from the classical one, since Wikipedia's own phrasing just says 'vector bundles' without foreclosing the torsor generalization by name. But the statement given names vector bundles over A and A[t1,...,tn] specifically, and both new papers' own contributions lie strictly outside that (either different objects — G-torsors for G ≠ GL_n — or a different ring class — non-Noetherian valuation rings), so under §3.1's test ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry?') the answer is no.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving a new case of the classical conjecture for GL_n vector bundles over a regular Noetherian ring not already covered by Lindel/Popescu/Murthy/Suslin/Quillen, or a counterexample to the general conjecture, would change this record's status.

outcome: The general statement — that the assembly map is an isomorphism — remains open in the coefficient-free form and was already known false in general with coefficients before the frozen revision (Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis, 2002). No result since 26 January 2024 changes the status of the statement as given; all activity found is either progress on special group classes (cases, not the general problem) or work on a related permanence-property question.
summary: I searched broadly for any development on the Baum–Connes conjecture (the general statement that the assembly map is an isomorphism) since 26 January 2024, and found nothing that changes the status of the problem as stated. Wikipedia's own current article confirms the conjecture (without coefficients) 'is still open,' and that the version with coefficients was already refuted before the frozen revision via the Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis counterexample (2002) — so nothing in the window bears on that either. The activity I found in the window consists entirely of case-restricted or related-problem work, none of which touches the general bullet: (1) Ellis, Rodríguez Cirone & Tartaglia, arXiv:2502.19111 (26 Feb 2025) — an expository writeup of the already-known proof of Baum-Connes for the infinite dihedral group D∞, following Higson–Kasparov; not a new result and, being an old case, would at most be `partial`/`open_stale` for that sub-case, not a change to the general problem. (2) A 'localization algebra approach to the Baum-Connes conjecture for extensions' (arXiv:2506.18446, ~June 2025) and (3) 'The Baum-Connes conjecture for extensions' by Ralf Meyer, arXiv:2508.05726 (submitted 7 Aug 2025, revised 29 Aug 2025) — the latter is a 2-page note giving a counterexample showing that Chabert–Echterhoff's permanence-property hypotheses for group extensions cannot be simplified; this is a negative result about a technical simplification of a proof technique, not about the Baum–Connes assembly map itself, and does not touch the general conjecture's truth value. (4) A December 2025 preprint on strong bolicity and Baum-Connes for relatively hyperbolic groups (arXiv:2512.21169) and an L^p/coarse Baum-Connes line of papers (2411.15070, 2311.05333) — all restrict to specific classes of groups or spaces (coarse geometry variants), which are cases or variants, not the stated problem. None of these results change what a careful reader would write in the bullet 'the assembly map is an isomorphism': that remains open in general and false with coefficients, exactly as before 26 January 2024. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this literature — all located papers are traditional human-authored pure-mathematics arguments, and a targeted search for any AI-assisted or Lean-formalization work touching Baum-Connes specifically returned nothing relevant.
competing_reading: One could argue the D∞ exposition (arXiv:2502.19111) or the relatively-hyperbolic-groups paper (arXiv:2512.21169) should be logged as `partial` progress on a case of the conjecture, since settling Baum-Connes for a specific group class does restrict territory from the general statement per §3.1's case-vs-variant test. I did not take this reading because (a) the D∞ result is explicitly an exposition of a pre-existing, decades-old proof (not new since 2024), and (b) results for specific group classes are a routine, continuous stream that predates the window by decades and does not represent a change in what is known about the conjecture's *general* truth value — the conjecture's own Wikipedia status line has not moved. If the strong-bolicity relatively-hyperbolic-groups result is judged genuinely novel and in-scope, the correct code would be `partial` / `progress` with `ai_role` still `none`, since no AI is credited in any of these papers regardless of classification.
what_would_settle_it: A published announcement, preprint, or expert digestion that either (a) proves or disproves the coefficient-free Baum-Connes assembly-map isomorphism for a substantial new class of groups not previously known, explicitly framed as new progress on the general conjecture (rather than an exposition or a permanence-technique note), or (b) any credible claim — refuted or standing — of a general resolution. No such source was found.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or partial resolution of Beal's conjecture has been established since 26 January 2024; only a steady stream of unrefereed amateur preprints claiming proofs, none accepted by the mathematical community, and Andrew Beal's $1 million prize remains unclaimed.

counterexample.verified_how: Extensive computational search (per Durango Bill's site and Norvig's earlier search) has found no counterexamples with C^Z up to at least 1.0E30 assuming an exponent > 4; no new counterexample search results found in the window.

summary: Beal's conjecture (A^x + B^y = C^z with x,y,z > 2 implies A, B, C share a common prime factor) remains open as of 26 September 2026. Wikipedia's article on the conjecture, checked directly, still describes it as unsolved, notes the $1 million Beal Prize (held in trust by the AMS) is unclaimed, and records only that the conjecture has been verified for many specific exponent cases and that the abc conjecture (itself unproven) would imply only finitely many counterexamples exist. In the 26 January 2024 - present window I found a large number of self-published, non-peer-reviewed preprints claiming proofs, all on venues with no mathematical vetting: SSRN ('Machine Learning Guided Proof of Beal's Conjecture', Jonathan Wilson, 11 March 2024; 'Beal's Conjecture: A Rigorous Proof', Jonathan Wilson, 30 June 2024 — explicitly a revision addressing the first paper's 'unproven lemmas, reliance on empirical data, circular reasoning, incomplete contradictions, misuse of number theory results, and lack of generality'), Preprints.org ('The Germany Problem for Beal's Conjecture', Feb 2024; 'Elementary Proof of Beal's Conjecture [v2]', Jan 2025), Zenodo ('A theoretical counterexample proof of Beal Conjecture', dated July 2026, which argues only that counterexamples 'should exist' and where to search for them computationally, without exhibiting one), ResearchGate, Academia.edu, ScienceOpen/HAL, and a small predatory-adjacent journal (IJDR, Mathematical Journal). None of these has been digested by an expert, accepted by a journal of record, or referenced by any mainstream number theorist; searches for commentary from figures such as Terence Tao turned up nothing specific to Beal's conjecture. The Wilson SSRN paper is the only item that invokes machine learning at all, and its own abstract describes ML only as having helped surface empirical patterns ('key lemmas derived with the help of patterns discovered through computational experiments') that guided a human-authored argument which the same author later needed to substantially rewrite to fix logical flaws — this is not an authors'-own-account claim that an AI system produced any piece of the mathematics that survived into a checked result, and no such result was ever accepted as correct. I also checked Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures Lean repository (arXiv 2605.13171 and the GitHub repo/README) since it is a legitimate AI-adjacent project formalizing conjecture statements for benchmarking; I could not confirm via search or the fetched README whether Beal's conjecture is among its ~2615 formalized statements, but even if present, that project formalizes statements only (not proofs) for benchmark use and would not itself constitute progress on the problem. No credible AI-generated or AI-assisted proof, counterexample, or bound exists for this problem in the window; the conjecture is exactly as open now as on 26 January 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the Wilson SSRN papers deserve 'claimed' status with 'ai_role: assisted' given their title explicitly invokes machine learning guidance. I reject this because (a) SSRN is not a refereed mathematics venue and hosts unvetted user submissions, (b) the author's own second paper acknowledges the first contained circular reasoning and unproven lemmas, i.e. it was not a valid proof even by its author's later admission, and (c) the abstract describes ML's role as pattern-spotting in computational experiments that fed a human-constructed argument, not as producing mathematics that appears in a valid final result — since no valid final result exists, there is nothing for the AI role to attach to.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement, from this window, that is digested by a professional number theorist, accepted at a refereed venue, or produces an explicit, verified counterexample or a machine-checked (and expert-reviewed) Lean/Coq proof; absent that, continued monitoring of arXiv number theory listings and the Wikipedia article's revision history would be the way to catch any future change.

outcome: Several narrow special cases of Beilinson's (and the closely related Beilinson-Bloch / Beilinson-Bloch-Kato) conjectures were settled in 2025: for certain K3 surfaces with an involution (Banerjee), for certain products of curves with powers of CM elliptic curves over function fields (Broe), for certain abelian surfaces conditional on BSD (Banerjee), and conditional progress on polarized motives (Peng). The general conjectures remain wide open; no AI involvement was found in any of this work.
summary: Wikipedia's bullet is unqualified 'Beilinson's conjectures' — the general statements relating orders of vanishing/special values of L-functions to ranks of motivic cohomology and regulators. These remain open in general; the article's own lead ('known to be true only in special cases') has not changed and has no post-2024 references. Since the 26 January 2024 freeze, four preprints have settled genuine special cases: (1) Kalyan Banerjee, arXiv:2502.09380 (submitted 2025-02-13, revised 2026-03-05), proves Beilinson's conjecture unconditionally for certain K3 surfaces over the algebraic closure of ℚ admitting an involution whose quotient is P² branched along a sextic; (2) Matt Broe, arXiv:2505.00696 (submitted 2025-05-01), gives a criterion for the Beilinson-Bloch conjecture over global function fields and deduces it for products of curves with powers of CM elliptic curves, via a proof of the Tate conjecture in that setting; (3) Kalyan Banerjee, arXiv:2509.24645 (submitted 2025-09-29), proves the Bloch-Beilinson conjecture for certain abelian surfaces over ℚ conditional on BSD holding for those surfaces; (4) Hao Peng, arXiv:2509.18615 (submitted 2025-09-24), makes conditional/partial progress on the Beilinson-Bloch-Kato conjecture for polarized motives. Each of these is a genuine restriction of the general conjecture (a specific variety type, or a specific base field) rather than a different conjecture altogether, so I classify this as 'partial' rather than 'open' with no_change_found — the territory covered by the general conjecture has been reduced, if only slightly and in some cases conditionally. None of the four papers mentions any AI or machine-learning tool in their abstracts, introductions, or (where checked) metadata; all are traditional single- or dual-author pure mathematics papers using classical techniques (Chow groups, regulators, Tate conjecture arguments, Iwasawa theory). A broad search for any AI system credited with progress on Beilinson's conjectures, the Beilinson-Bloch conjecture, or the Beilinson-Bloch-Kato conjecture (including checking Wikipedia's own 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence') turned up nothing. The dated event I anchor status to is the earliest of the four preprints (Banerjee, Feb 2025); the other three are described above rather than given separate records, per the instructions to describe multiple events in summary.
competing_reading: One could argue these four results are all instances of derivative/related conjectures (Beilinson-Bloch, Beilinson-Bloch-Kato) rather than 'Beilinson's conjectures' as Wikipedia's bullet names them, and that the bullet — being unqualified and pointing at the general L-function/regulator framework — is not moved at all by results confined to Chow groups and algebraic cycles on specific surfaces. Under that stricter reading the status would be 'open' with no_change_found true, since no result changes what a careful person would write about the general, unqualified conjecture. I lean toward 'partial' because Beilinson-Bloch and Beilinson-Bloch-Kato are standard extensions/refinements of the same conjectural framework attributed to Beilinson and treated by experts (e.g. Nekovář, Deninger-Scholl) as part of the same conjectural family that the Wikipedia bullet is gesturing at, and each paper explicitly proves cases of a 'Beilinson' or 'Bloch-Beilinson' conjecture rather than a conjecture with different hypotheses.
what_would_settle_it: A clear statement from an expert survey or the Wikipedia article itself on whether Beilinson-Bloch / Beilinson-Bloch-Kato are considered the same conjecture family as the bullet's 'Beilinson's conjectures' or a genuinely distinct (if related) conjecture; absent that, the classification rests on my own reading of the literature's naming conventions.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the shortest curve guaranteed to reach the boundary of an arbitrary shape from an unknown starting point and orientation — a problem still open in general. Since 26 Jan 2024 I found two distinct lines of work. (1) Zhipeng Deng's arXiv:2412.10686 (Dec 2024) proposes a general computational framework converting the problem into translation/rotation of the forest boundary and a discretized TSP/Hamiltonian-path-style optimization; per the paper's own text this recovers 'nontrivial results consistent with those from previous papers' (circle, equilateral triangle, infinite strip — i.e. confirms Finch/Wetzel/Zalgaller/Besicovitch results) rather than resolving new territory or the general conjecture. A follow-up, arXiv:2606.13987 (June 2026, v3 July 2026), claims to prove the validity of that general framework and adds Lean 4 formalizations of Theorems 1-7, plus further variations (closed paths, 3D, Wetzel's arc-covering connection); I found no AI-involvement disclosure in either Deng paper. Because this framework's claimed contribution is a solution *method* consistent with prior known cases rather than a newly settled case or the general problem, I read it as not a scope-qualifying advance under §3.1 (a related/derivative formulation, not new territory) — it belongs in the record for completeness but does not itself drive the status. (2) The status-driving event is Temerev and Doria's arXiv:2607.24483 (27 Jul 2026, GitHub: atemerev/gnomon), which proves the exact optimal escape curve for the golden gnomon (isosceles triangle, sides 1, apex 108°) — a symmetric seven-piece path of length C≈1.282676025459, described as 'the first proved exact optimum for an isosceles triangle whose base angle is below 45°.' This is a genuine case of the stated problem (a specific shape), so it counts as `partial`, direction `confirmed` (an escape curve was found and proven optimal, consistent with the problem being well-posed, not refuting anything). Crucially, the paper's own footnote states LLMs (Claude Fable 5, GPT 5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5) were used 'to search for the extremal curve, to draft the arguments given here, and to write the accompanying Lean development' — i.e., by the authors' own account, AI systems contributed to producing the mathematical argument and the formal proof, not merely checking or tidying human-produced work. That meets the bar for `assisted` (the authors' account describes AI producing part of the mathematics — the search for the extremal curve and drafting the argument — while humans verified via Lean's axiom audit restricting to the standard classical trio of axioms, and via Python audit scripts). I did not find evidence that the model produced the entire proof autonomously with humans only checking (which would push toward `generated`); the paper frames LLM use as embedded 'throughout' the discovery and drafting process alongside human-directed verification, which is squarely the `assisted` case. No expert digestion (journal acceptance, third-party mathematician review, or a Terence-Tao/Quanta-style writeup) was found for this two-month-old preprint, and Wikipedia's live article (checked 2026-09) has not been updated to mention any of this 2024-2026 work — it still cites only Finch and Wetzel (2004). A related paper by the same GitHub/arXiv cluster, arXiv:2608.01393 (Deng, Aug 2026) and arXiv:2609.04591 (worm problem, Sep 2026) extend similar covering-curve methodology but are either variants (worm problem is a different, though related, problem) or general frameworks rather than new settled cases of this exact bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue the golden-gnomon result is 'claimed' rather than 'partial'-with-confirmed-status, on the grounds that no human mathematician outside the two authors has yet reviewed or digested the proof (it is only ~2 months old, unpublished in any journal, and the only 'independent audits' are the authors' own Python scripts). Under the `resolved` vs `claimed` distinction that logic would apply to whether the *overall problem* is resolved, but since this is only a `partial` case-settlement, the resolved/claimed distinction is not squarely dispositive — the rules only make direction mandatory for partial, not additionally gating it behind an expert-digestion bar the way `resolved` is gated. I nonetheless flag this because a stricter reading might prefer to treat the golden-gnomon result as an unreviewed claim and downgrade confidence rather than accept it as a settled partial case. Separately, one could read Deng's framework papers as themselves partial progress (a new solution method, even if it only reproduces known cases) rather than a related/derivative contribution; I judged the framework itself doesn't settle any new case of the stated bullet, so it stays outside the scope-qualifying event, but this is a judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: An independent mathematician's review, referee report, or journal acceptance of arXiv:2607.24483 confirming the golden-gnomon proof is correct (upgrading it toward `resolved`-grade confidence in that case), and/or a citation or discussion of the paper in a survey, blog (e.g. Terence Tao's), or MathOverflow thread. Also useful: clarification from Deng on whether arXiv:2606.13987's 'proof of general solution' resolves any previously-unknown case beyond confirming known ones.

outcome: Tao Li, Yoav Moriah and Tali Pinsky's proof that tunnel number one knots satisfying a lens space surgery are Berge knots -- a restricted case of the stated conjecture -- was formally accepted and published in a refereed journal (Geometry & Topology, vol. 29, no. 6, 2025) within the window, and the arXiv preprint received a final revision (v7, 1 November 2024) also within the window; but the mathematical claim itself, and a proof of it, were already publicly posted as v1 in January 2017, well before the frozen revision date, so the substance of the result predates the window and only its expert vetting/publication falls inside it. The general Berge conjecture (for arbitrary knots in S^3) remains open.
summary: The bullet as stated ("the only knots in the 3-sphere which admit lens space surgeries are Berge knots") remains open in full generality; no result in the window settles it for all knots. What did happen in the window concerns a restricted case: Li, Moriah and Pinsky's paper 'Tunnel number one knots satisfy the Berge Conjecture' (arXiv:1701.01421), which shows that a tunnel number one knot in S^3 admitting a non-trivial lens space surgery must be doubly primitive, i.e. a Berge knot -- confirming the conjecture for that sub-class. This is a genuine case of the stated problem (a restriction to tunnel number one knots), not a variant, so under §3.1 it counts as `partial` progress toward the whole conjecture. The complication is dating: v1 of this paper, making exactly this claim with a purported proof, was posted 5 January 2017 -- seven years before the frozen revision. v3 was withdrawn in September 2018 (apparently over a gap), and the paper was repaired and reposted as v4 in December 2019, still years before the window. It sat as an unrefereed, long-standing preprint claim through the frozen revision date. What happened inside the window (26 Jan 2024 to today) is: a further arXiv revision (v6, April 2023, just before the window, followed by v7, 1 November 2024, inside the window) and, decisively, formal peer-reviewed publication in Geometry & Topology in 2025 -- a top journal in the field, which entails expert referee review of the argument. That refereeing is the event that converts a long-outstanding, twice-revised preprint claim into an expert-digested result, which is what makes `resolved` rather than `claimed` appropriate for this sub-case, and it happened inside the window even though the underlying mathematical content was substantially already public in 2017-2019. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this history: the paper's acknowledgements thank named mathematicians (Berge, Baker, Zupan, Rolfsen) for remarks, with no mention of any computational or AI tool. A tangential hit, a GitHub issue in Google DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' repository proposing to formalize the Berge conjecture statement in Lean, is purely a cataloguing request (the issue itself says knot theory is missing from mathlib, so it cannot even be stated yet) with no proof attempt, and the issue text discloses it was itself drafted by an AI agent and human-reviewed -- irrelevant to the mathematics and correctly ai_role `none`. I searched separately for any progress on the general conjecture (Floer-homology approaches by Baker-Grigsby-Hedden, Greene's simple-knot classification) and found nothing new in the window beyond restatements of pre-2024 work.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `open_stale`, on the reasoning that the decisive mathematical fact (tunnel-number-one knots satisfying the surgery are doubly primitive) was already established and publicly claimed with a full proof by 2019 (v4), so nothing new was mathematically discovered in the window -- only a paper that had been sitting on arXiv for years finally got a journal's stamp. Under a strict reading of §6.3 ("date the first public written argument... never the journal publication"), the first written argument is 2017/2019, which would make this `open_stale`. I did not choose that reading because `resolved` under §6.1 explicitly requires an argument that has been digested by experts (via journal acceptance or expert digestion), and that expert vetting genuinely did not occur until the 2024-2025 window -- the paper spent 2019-2023 as an unrefereed, once-withdrawn preprint, which is not equivalent in evidentiary weight to a refereed proof in Geometry & Topology. I treat the 2025 publication (preceded by the Nov 2024 arXiv revision, presumably incorporating referee-requested fixes) as the event that makes this specific case newly `resolved`-grade evidence, while flagging that the raw claim is much older.
what_would_settle_it: Access to the referee reports or a diff between v6 (April 2023) and v7 (November 2024) would show whether the November 2024 revision fixed a substantive gap found in refereeing (supporting dating the event to 2024-2025) or was a purely cosmetic change for publication (supporting `open_stale` with the real event dated to 2019/v4). Comment from the authors or the Geometry & Topology editors on the referee process would resolve this.

outcome: The general Berry-Tabor conjecture remains open, but two new cases were settled in the window: Kim, Marklof and Welsh (Jan 2026) proved the two-point Poisson spectral statistics for a quantum particle in a 3-dimensional rectangular box under a Diophantine condition on the side-length ratios, extending Eskin-Margulis-Mozes's 2005 two-dimensional result; and Lutsko (Sep 2026) proved Poissonian pair correlation for the relative spectrum of the three-particle trigonometric Sutherland model (an interacting many-body integrable system) under a Diophantine condition on the coupling constant, the first such result for an interacting system at the pair-correlation level.
summary: The Berry-Tabor conjecture (1977) asserts that generic integrable quantum systems have Poisson local spectral statistics, contrasting with random-matrix statistics for chaotic systems. It remains open in general as of September 2026, but the triage's lead — Kim, Marklof and Welsh, 'Values of ternary quadratic forms at integers and the Berry-Tabor conjecture for 3-tori' (arXiv:2601.03209, submitted 2026-01-06, v1 only) — checks out: they prove the two-point spectral density statement of the conjecture for a quantum particle in a 3-dimensional rectangular box under a Diophantine condition (κ close to 1) on the ratios of squared side lengths ℓᵢ²/ℓⱼ², extending the 2-dimensional case proved by Eskin, Margulis and Mozes in 2005 (which predates the window and is the prior state of the art, not a new event). This is a case of the general conjecture — a restriction to a specific class of integrable systems (rectangular 3-tori) under a technical Diophantine hypothesis — not a resolution, so it is classified `partial` with direction `confirmed` (the result confirms the conjectured Poisson statistics, it does not refute them). I additionally found a second, independent case settled within the window: Christopher Lutsko, 'Poissonian pair correlations for the three-particle Sutherland model' (arXiv:2609.03112, submitted 2026-09-02), which proves the conjecture's pair-correlation statement for a genuinely interacting integrable many-body system (three particles on a circle with inverse-square chord interaction) under a Diophantine condition on the coupling constant — described as the first such result for an interacting system at the pair-correlation level, reducing to Marklof's theorem on inhomogeneous quadratic forms via a finite-congruence/Weyl-sector argument. I checked both papers' full text/HTML and found no mention of AI, machine learning, automated theorem proving, or computer-assisted search in either the body or acknowledgements; both are conventional analytic-number-theory/homogeneous-dynamics proofs (Ratner theory, unipotent flows, quadratic form equidistribution). I also checked a third item the triage did not surface, arXiv:2605.06974 ('Poissonian correlations of α n^d mod 1' by Lutsko, Rome and Technau), which is a related-but-distinct problem (polynomial sequences mod 1, a number-theoretic analogue rather than a statement about quantum spectra of an integrable system) and does not count as a case of this bullet; I did not rely on it for status. The Wikipedia article on the conjecture, fetched directly, still describes it as open and mentions no recent proofs or AI, consistent with the frozen revision's framing and giving no reason to revise `status_sources` beyond the primary arXiv papers.
competing_reading: One could argue the 3-tori and Sutherland-model results are 'related problems' (different underlying integrable system) rather than 'cases' of the single conjecture as stated in the Wikipedia bullet, since the bullet's wording is generic ('generic integrable quantum systems') and doesn't specify a system. But per the DEEP_DIVE.md scope rule, restricting the general conjecture to a specific, well-defined sub-class of integrable systems (a class of tori, a class of many-body Hamiltonians) under an explicit Diophantine restriction is exactly the kind of restriction that counts as a case, not a variant — the underlying question (are the level statistics Poisson for this integrable system) is unchanged, only the system considered is narrowed. I judge `partial` is the correct reading, but flag this because the bullet names no specific system, unlike some Wikipedia bullets that name a precise sub-case.
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution of the Berry-Tabor conjecture would require proving Poisson statistics for a genuinely general class of 'generic' integrable systems (not restricted to Diophantine sub-families of tori or specific many-body models), or a counterexample showing genericity fails. Absent that, the record stands as `partial` with each new proved case adding to `status_sources`.

outcome: The smallest previously-open case of the conjecture (k=6, ℓ=4: every sufficiently large finite planar point set has 4 collinear points or a clique of 6 mutually visible points) has been settled in the confirming direction by a preprint whose author states the proof itself was produced by the AI system GPT-5.6 Sol Pro; the argument has also been formalized in Lean and passes a sorry-free kernel-checked build, but has not yet been digested in print by an independent human expert.

ai.basis_quote: After one fruitless attempt and the now customary generic encouragement, a relatively detailed proof of Theorem 1 was provided by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro after pondering for 222 minutes. [The author's] contributions were limited to checking the proof, simplifying some parts, and eventually writing the paper.

summary: The frozen Wikipedia revision states the big-line-big-clique conjecture of Kára, Pór and Wood is proved for k≤5 or ℓ≤3, and open for the first case k=6, ℓ=4 (its own naming convention differs slightly from the source papers' k/ℓ labels, but the case is described the same way in both). On 19 August 2026 Édouard Bonnet (CNRS/ENS de Lyon) posted arXiv:2608.19468, 'Large Finite Point Sets Have 4 Collinear Points or a 6-Clique,' proving every finite point set of size at least 10^11055931 contains 4 collinear points or a set of 6 pairwise-visible points — exactly the smallest open case, described in the paper itself as 'the first open case of the big-line-big-clique conjecture' resolved since 2009. Critically, the paper's own AI-disclosure section states in the author's words that after one failed attempt, 'a relatively detailed proof of Theorem 1 was provided by GPT-5.6 Sol Pro after pondering for 222 minutes,' with Bonnet's own role limited to checking, simplifying, and writing up — squarely meeting the bar for ai_role=generated (the authors' own account that the AI system produced the mathematics, with humans verifying). The proof was subsequently formalized in Lean by Bonnet and formalizer clemenskuske under the 'lax-56' submission in the Lax Lean Archive (github.com/EdouardBonnet/big-line-big-clique); as of a 15 September 2026 update (port to Lean v4.33), the FORMALIZATION.md states there are no sorry proofs, SAT calls, or native_decide calls, that the full Lake build (8574 jobs) passed, and that 'lax build --profile --replay' passed compilation, kernel replay, and statement inspection, resting only on standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). This is a strong machine-checked certificate, but I found no evidence of an independent human expert's public digestion of the informal argument (no Tao blog post, no Quanta coverage, no journal acceptance) as of 22 September 2026, about five weeks after posting — hence status=claimed rather than resolved, per §6.1's rule that a clean formal check alone is not sufficient without an expert reader. The triage's flagged item, the Sarkar preprint arXiv:2605.00918 ('Visibility cliques, cubic containers, and dense orchard cores,' posted 30 April 2026), is real but proves only structured special cases (points mostly on a real cubic curve, or with few ordinary lines via the Green–Tao structure theorem) — its own abstract says the full conjecture 'remains open otherwise,' and it explicitly states any AI tools it used were confined to LaTeX typesetting, literature search and proofreading, all mathematics verified by the human author — so under these rules ai_role=none for that paper and it is scope-relevant only as `partial` background, superseded in the k=6/ℓ=4 case by the later Bonnet/GPT-5.6 result which I treat as the decisive event. I also found the 11 September 2026 Fields Medallists' declaration 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,' which is a general reaction to the wave of AI math claims (including reportedly this kind of result) rather than a dispute of this specific proof's correctness, so I did not record it as a `dispute`.
competing_reading: One could argue status should be `resolved`: the Lean formalization is sorry-free and kernel-replayed, which is about as mechanically certain as mathematics gets, and one could read that as satisfying 'directly checkable by hand or computer algebra' even without a human expert's narrative digestion. I did not take this reading because §6.1 explicitly treats a machine-checked certificate with no expert reader as `claimed`, precisely because proof assistants can have soundness bugs and nobody outside the author/formalizer pair has yet vetted the mathematical content in prose. A second competing reading: since Wikipedia's own case boundary is 'k=6 or ℓ=4' (open) versus 'k≤5 or ℓ≤3' (closed), and Bonnet's theorem is stated as exactly '4 collinear or 6-clique', this is unambiguously the k=6,ℓ=4 case rather than a nearby variant, so I am confident this is a case of the stated problem, not a related one.
what_would_settle_it: A published expert digestion (a referee report, a blog post from a specialist in discrete/combinatorial geometry such as the co-authors of the original 2005 conjecture paper, or Quanta/Tao-level coverage) endorsing or disputing the correctness of the informal argument would move this from `claimed` to `resolved` (or surface a flaw and move it to `progress`/`incident`). Absent that, continued silence for many more months without any critique would itself be weak evidence in favor, but per these rules would not on its own justify `resolved`.

outcome: The conjecture remains open for n >= 3 (proved for n = 1, 2 since 1965); the only claimed advance against it — Bryant and Ferry's announced counterexamples for every n >= 6, first presented at the March 2018 Spring Topology Conference — has still not been published or posted to arXiv as of September 2026, and continues to be cited by working topologists as unpublished. No new mathematical result, published or preprint, moving the conjecture itself has appeared since 26 January 2024.
summary: The triage record correctly identified the only candidate event in this space: J. Bryant and S. Ferry's March 2018 announcement, at the Spring Topology Conference, of counterexamples to the Bing-Borsuk conjecture for every n >= 6 (infinitely many topologically distinct homogeneous ANR-compacta of dimension n, n >= 6, that are not topological manifolds). That announcement predates the frozen revision by nearly six years, so even if it were published it would be open_stale rather than a within-window event. But the more important finding is that it still has not been published anywhere, in any version, as of this research (September 2026). I checked: (1) Valov's 'Homogeneous metric ANR-compacta' (arXiv 2003.06907, March 2020) cites the Bryant-Ferry result as an unpublished announcement; (2) Valov's 'Homogeneous locally compact spaces' (arXiv 2401.00341, posted 2 January 2024, i.e. right before the frozen revision) again cites it as unpublished, with no arXiv identifier or journal reference for a Bryant-Ferry paper — a web-search summary in the triage record claimed this paper referenced a 'revised version' of the counterexample paper, but on actually opening and reading the PDF I found no such revised-version claim; it treats the result as it always has, an unpublished announcement; (3) Valov's newest paper on this cluster, 'Homology manifolds and homogeneous compacta' (arXiv 2505.07196, submitted 12 May 2025 — within the window), does not even discuss the Bing-Borsuk conjecture or the Bryant-Ferry counterexamples; it proves an unrelated characterization of almost-homology n-manifolds among homogeneous ANR-spaces, so it is not a case or a variant of this problem, just adjacent literature; (4) I could not locate a Bryant-Ferry preprint under any plausible title on arXiv directly. The Wikipedia article itself (English, current live version, opened for orientation only per the rules) still states the conjecture is proved only for dimensions 1 and 2 and mentions no counterexample at all — it appears not to have been updated even to reflect the 2018 announcement, let alone anything from the window. In short: no event in the 26 January 2024 to present window changes what a careful reader would write in this bullet. The pre-window 2018 announcement, were it ever published, would be classified open_stale, but since it has still not appeared in any citable form even by 2026, there is nothing to date and no status change to record; 'open' is the honest classification, and I record no_change_found rather than open_stale because there is no publication event to stamp a date on, only a standing unpublished announcement whose status is unchanged since before the frozen revision. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature; all authors are working topologists (Valov, Bryant, Ferry) doing conventional point-set/geometric topology.
competing_reading: One could argue for open_stale on the theory that the 2018 Bryant-Ferry announcement effectively settles the general conjecture (for n>=6) and that its non-publication is a technicality of academic norms rather than a live mathematical uncertainty, in which case the 'true' resolution predates the frozen revision and the record should be open_stale with the 2018 date noted. I rejected this because the rules for resolved/claimed require either expert digestion of a written argument or a manuscript at all, and here there is no manuscript to digest — an announced-but-never-written-up result is weaker than even a 'claimed' status, and every secondary source I found (2020, 2024, and implicitly 2025) continues to describe the conjecture as open precisely because the counterexample was never published. Treating an unwritten announcement as settling anything would overstate what happened.
what_would_settle_it: The actual appearance of a Bryant-Ferry (or successor) manuscript — on arXiv, in a journal, or as a citable preprint with a specific identifier — giving the construction of the n>=6 counterexamples, together with any expert digestion of it (e.g., a review, a citation that engages with its proof rather than merely citing the announcement). Absent that, the question is settled only for n=1,2 and remains genuinely open for n=3,4,5 and unpublished/unconfirmed for n>=6.

outcome: Burungale, Skinner, Tian and Wan (arXiv:2409.01350, 'Zeta elements for elliptic curves and applications', Sept 2024) proved the p-part of the BSD conjecture at supersingular primes for elliptic curves of analytic rank 0 or 1, which combined with prior results yields the first infinite families of quadratic twists of non-CM elliptic curves over Q for which the full strong BSD conjecture holds unconditionally. This is a partial result (infinite but density-zero families, not the general conjecture), by four leading experts in Iwasawa theory, but as of this research it remains a preprint with no journal publication, expert blog digestion, or Quanta-style writeup found — so it is classified as a strong, credible claim rather than a community-vetted resolution. A follow-up computational paper (Banwait-Huang, arXiv:2601.16044, Jan 2026, to appear at ANTS XVII) applied an explicit algorithm to the LMFDB to identify 36,687 elliptic curves of conductor ≤ 500,000 (about 0.1% of the database) admitting such infinite families, but this is an application/identification exercise, not new theory, and does not itself change the status. No AI system was involved in either paper.
summary: The main-line development on BSD since the frozen revision date is Burungale-Skinner-Tian-Wan's September 2024 preprint (arXiv:2409.01350), which constructs p-adic zeta elements for elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields and uses them to prove the ±-main conjecture of Iwasawa theory at supersingular primes (Kobayashi's 2002 conjecture) for semistable elliptic curves, together with the p-part of the BSD formula at supersingular primes for analytic rank 0 or 1. Combined with earlier ordinary-prime results (Skinner-Urban, Wei Zhang, Burungale-Tian p-converse theorems), this yields the first known infinite families of quadratic twists of non-CM elliptic curves over Q for which the full strong BSD conjecture (rank equality plus the exact leading-coefficient formula, including finiteness of Sha) is unconditionally true. This is squarely a case of the stated problem: it settles BSD for an explicit infinite (but density-zero, roughly 0.1% by the follow-up paper's count) family of curves, leaving the general conjecture open — a textbook 'case settled' rather than resolution, so under a stricter reading it would be `partial`; I classify it `claimed` instead because it also has not yet cleared expert digestion (no journal acceptance, no Tao blog post, no Quanta piece found via search) despite being four years past submission and by highly credible authors (Skinner and Tian are established BSD/Iwasawa-theory specialists), and per the DEEP_DIVE rules 'resolved versus claimed turns on whether a human expert has read the argument' — I could not confirm that has happened publicly. I checked for follow-on validation: a January 2026 paper by Banwait and Huang (arXiv:2601.16044, accepted to ANTS XVII, a peer-reviewed algorithmic number theory venue) explicitly builds on and cites BSTW's theorem as an input to an algorithmic search of the LMFDB, treating the BSTW result as an established fact — this is suggestive of acceptance by specialists but is not itself a digestion of the BSTW proof. No AI system is mentioned in either paper; both are purely human theoretical/computational number theory. I also checked the several 2025 preprints claiming full proofs of BSD found by the triage (Zenodo/Shimizu, SSRN/Svancara 'Relational Field Theory', preprints.org 'Iran Formula') — these show classic crank hallmarks (self-published, unreviewed, grandiose framing, solo authors, no institutional affiliation signals of note) and none disclose any AI involvement; the preprints.org page returned HTTP 403 and could not be directly verified, so I could not rule out AI involvement there, but there is no positive evidence for it either, and per DEEP_DIVE.md's rule on unreachable pages I note this as a dead end rather than a verified finding.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of §3.1/§6.1 would call the BSTW result `partial` rather than `claimed`: it is unambiguously a case of the problem (an infinite family of curves), and 'claimed' is defined primarily for results awaiting digestion of a claimed *resolution* of the stated problem, whereas here nobody is claiming the general BSD conjecture is proved — only a genuine partial result is on the table, and partial results by leading experts in a serious preprint are ordinarily accepted as fact by the field well before formal journal publication (as evidenced by Banwait-Huang treating it as citable, peer-reviewed-venue-accepted, established input). Under that reading the status should be `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed`, dated to the same September 2024 event.
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance of arXiv:2409.01350, or an expert digestion (a Tao-style blog post, a Bourbaki seminar writeup, an ICM survey lecture, or a Quanta/AMS Notices piece) explicitly discussing the proof, would move this from `claimed` to a confirmed classification (whether `partial` or `resolved` in nature) rather than leaving the human-verification question open.

outcome: No resolution, case, or bound-moving result specific to the Birch-Tate conjecture (relating #K2(O_F) to ζ_F(-1) for totally real F) was found in the window; only a formalization request with no proof content, and adjacent/generalizing work on the broader Quillen-Lichtenbaum framework and on tame kernels, neither of which addresses this conjecture directly.
summary: No result settling any case of, or moving a bound within, the Birch-Tate conjecture as stated (the equality/near-equality of #K2(O_F) to |ζ_F(-1)| up to powers of 2, for a totally real number field F) was found for the period 26 January 2024 to 22 September 2026. The conjecture was already known up to a power of 2 (Wiles's theorem on the Iwasawa Main Conjecture, plus Kolster's remark handling the 2-part for abelian fields) well before the window, and nothing in this window closes the remaining 2-primary gap or extends the abelian case to full generality. The closest candidate, Elmanto-Zhang's 'Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions' (arXiv:2405.03578, submitted 6 May 2024), generalizes the Quillen-Lichtenbaum conjecture (a related but distinct statement, itself a source of Birch-Tate-adjacent results) to Artin L-functions of Galois representations, proving cases integrally except up to powers of 2 in the non-abelian/totally real case — but its abstract and introduction do not mention the Birch-Tate conjecture, and its scope (general Artin L-functions with coefficients in Galois representations) is a different, broader statement, not a restriction of Birch-Tate's specific claim about ζ_F(-1) and K2(O_F). Under §3.1 this is a related problem, not a case, so it does not count as a change to this bullet. A second candidate, arXiv:2308.04099 (Lim, 'On the p-divisibility of even K-groups...', v1 August 2023, v3 corrections uploaded 5 August 2025, published in Ramanujan Journal 2025) predates the window in its substantive content (v1 2023) and in any case does not mention Birch-Tate in its abstract; its 2025 revision is corrections/rewriting, not new mathematical content within the window, so this is at most open_stale-adjacent noise and does not change the status. A third candidate, arXiv:2504.15767 ('Is there a Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for Dedekind zeta functions?', submitted 22 April 2025) is explicitly about an analogue of BSD for Dedekind zeta functions of number fields, a different question from Birch-Tate's K2 statement, and does not address Birch-Tate. Only one item was found that names the Birch-Tate conjecture directly within the window: a Google DeepMind 'formal-conjectures' GitHub issue (#1764, opened 18 January 2026) requesting Lean formalization of the Birch-Tate conjecture statement, tagged 'needs-prerequisites' because algebraic K-theory foundations are not yet built in that library. It contains no proof attempt, no claimed progress, and no AI-generated content — it is a formalization backlog item with zero comments. This is not a mathematical result and does not move the status; it is noted only because it is the sole hit naming this conjecture in the window. Overall: status remains open, no_change_found true, and there is no AI involvement of any kind (ai_role none) since no AI system produced any mathematics, bound, or even a formalization attempt for this specific conjecture in the window.
competing_reading: If a future reader considered the Elmanto-Zhang generalization of Quillen-Lichtenbaum to Artin L-functions as 'progress adjacent to Birch-Tate' worth noting even though out of strict scope, one could argue for `progress` with a null direction; I judged this a related/variant problem under §3.1 (a different, broader statement about general Artin L-functions and Galois-equivariant K-groups, not a restriction of the totally-real-field, trivial-representation Dedekind zeta statement that is Birch-Tate), so I kept status at `open`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint within the window that explicitly proves or narrows the 2-primary gap in the Birch-Tate equality #K2(O_F) = |ζ_F(-1)| · #K3(O_F) (up to sign/normalization) for totally real F, or extends the abelian-field case (already known via Mazur-Wiles) to a genuinely new class of fields, citing Birch-Tate by name.

outcome: The full Birkhoff conjecture (every strictly convex integrable billiard boundary is an ellipse) remains open, but two genuine cases were settled and published within the window: Illya Koval proved a local version (an integrable perturbation of almost every ellipse, preserving integrability near the boundary, must itself be an ellipse), published in Inventiones Mathematicae in December 2025; and Kaloshin, Koudjinan & Zhang proved that a domain close enough to a centrally-symmetric one with an integrable billiard is an ellipse, with a substantially revised version posted in September 2024.
summary: The triage correctly identified Koval's local Birkhoff conjecture result as the most decisive item, but its arXiv preprint (v1 Nov 2021, v2 Feb 2023) predates the frozen revision; what actually falls inside the window is the paper's appearance in Inventiones Mathematicae (published online 11 Dec 2025, vol. 244, pp. 221-298), which is when this result was digested/certified by a journal of record, so I treat it as the event that brought this case to `resolved-within-the-window` status for that restricted case, while keeping the record's overall `status` as `partial` because it only settles a case (integrable perturbations of almost every ellipse), not the full conjecture. A second, independently useful case restriction is Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang's 'Birkhoff Conjecture for nearly centrally symmetric domains' (arXiv 2306.12301): a domain sufficiently close to a centrally-symmetric one with an integrable billiard must be an ellipse. Its original submission (21 June 2023) predates the window, but a heavily revised v2 (19 September 2024, described in the arXiv changelog as an improvement to 'content and presentation' with the file size roughly halved) falls inside it; I dated the decisive `event` to this revision since it is the first written argument in the form now citable, though the underlying claim may have existed earlier in substance. I checked several other 2024-2026 papers that surface when searching 'Birkhoff conjecture': Kepler billiards (Baranzini-Barutello-De Blasi-Terracini, arXiv 2507.08446, July 2025) proves an analogous statement for billiards in a gravitational (Kepler) potential -- a different dynamical setting, so it is a related problem, not a case, and does not change this bullet. The 'rationally/polynomially integrable planar dual and projective billiards' line of work (Glutsyuk et al., e.g. arXiv 2112.07056, 2301.00464, and the newer Inventiones paper 'On rationally integrable planar dual and projective billiards') concerns dual/projective billiards, a distinct notion of billiard dynamics (reflections of tangent lines to caustics rather than the standard inner-billiard reflection law), so these too are variants rather than cases of the stated conjecture. Koval's separate paper on Gevrey divergence of Birkhoff normal forms (arXiv 2403.14448, submitted March 2024) is about analytic regularity of normal forms near periodic orbits, a related but distinct question, not a case restriction of the ellipse conjecture. No source anywhere in this search -- the papers themselves, the Wikipedia article (which returned 404 on fetch and could not be checked directly, though its content is mirrored in search-engine summaries), or general web searches for AI/machine-learning involvement in Birkhoff-conjecture work -- turned up any AI system contributing to any of these proofs; all are traditional human mathematical arguments (dynamical systems, KAM-type perturbation theory, complex-analytic and wave-trace methods) with no computer-algebra or numerical-verification component either, aside from illustrative numerical simulations of chaotic Kepler-billiard trajectories in the Kepler paper, which play no role in that paper's proof.
competing_reading: One could argue the `event` date should instead be Koval's Inventiones online-publication date (2025-12-11) rather than the September 2024 arXiv revision of the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang paper, since Koval's is arguably the more decisive/cited case restriction and per §6.3 journal publication dates are normally to be avoided in favor of first written argument -- but Koval's first written argument (the arXiv preprint) predates the window entirely, so if that paper is to count as an in-window event at all it can only be via its journal appearance, which is unusual under the dating rule. An alternative, more conservative reading is that Koval's result should be treated as `open_stale` for dating purposes (its substantive mathematical content was already public by Feb 2023) and only the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang September 2024 revision counts as a genuine in-window case-restriction event, which is the reading I adopted for `event`, while still describing Koval's Inventiones publication in `outcome`/`summary` as a second, independently useful data point about the field's overall progress.
what_would_settle_it: Access to the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang v1-to-v2 diff (or the authors' own account) to confirm whether the September 2024 revision changed the mathematical result versus only exposition, which would determine whether that revision is truly the first written argument for a new claim or merely a rewrite of an already-public 2023 result; and a full read of Koval's Inventiones referee reports or acknowledgements (not accessible without a subscription) to confirm no computational or AI-assisted component was used, beyond what the freely-available arXiv preprint shows.
