summary: The Wikipedia bullet states the arithmetic Bombieri-Lang conjecture: densities of rational points on algebraic surfaces/varieties over number fields (and their extensions). Searching for progress since 26 January 2024 turns up a genuine cluster of activity, but it is entirely about the *geometric* (function-field) Bombieri-Lang conjecture, a distinct problem posed over function fields rather than number fields. Junyi Xie and Xinyi Yuan (arXiv:2308.08117, submitted Aug 2023, so pre-window) proved the geometric conjecture for varieties with finite morphisms to abelian varieties of trivial trace; Guoquan Gao's Nov 2025 preprint (arXiv:2511.17010, updated Mar 2026) removed the hyperbolicity/non-isotriviality assumptions, extending this to all finite maps to abelian varieties over function fields of characteristic 0; and Junyi Xie's 2026 survey (arXiv:2607.02165) summarizes this cluster of results. I opened all three papers directly (via WebFetch) and confirmed each explicitly frames its result as the 'geometric Bombieri-Lang conjecture ... over function fields,' not the arithmetic/number-field version. Critically, the 2026 survey itself states outright that the arithmetic version (its Conjecture 1.1/2.2) 'remains very open in higher dimension,' explicitly distinguishing it from the now-partially-proved geometric analogue. Under the scope rule (§3.1), the geometric conjecture over function fields is a related problem obtained by changing the base field/setting, not a case obtained by restricting the number-field statement — proving it removes no territory from the arithmetic conjecture Wikipedia's bullet asks about. So none of this counts as progress on the stated problem, and status is 'open' with no_change_found true. On AI: the only AI mention found anywhere in this cluster is in the survey's acknowledgements, thanking an 'AI assistant Xiaozhua' for writing assistance and two people for providing an 'AI-agent environment' that resolved unspecified technical issues — this is writing/infrastructure support, not mathematical content production, so ai_role is 'none' per §6.2. I found no counterexample, disproof, or any other event touching the number-field statement; Terence Tao's blog posts tagged with this conjecture (Erdős-Ulam application, 2014; polynomial bijections, 2019; a related Bresciani preprint, 2021) all predate the window and concern applications assuming the conjecture, not progress toward proving or disproving it.
competing_reading: One could argue that proving the geometric analogue for an important test class (finite covers of abelian varieties) is evidence toward, or a strong heuristic analogue of, the arithmetic statement, since Vojta's dictionary treats the two as parallel conjectures and progress on one sometimes transfers proof techniques to the other. Under a looser reading of scope, a reviewer might code this as 'progress' (a related, structurally analogous problem making headway) rather than 'no_change_found.' I did not adopt this reading because the survey's own authors keep the two conjectures explicitly separate and say the arithmetic one is untouched by this work — the analogy is methodological inspiration, not a mathematical implication.
what_would_settle_it: A statement, by an expert or the original authors, that the geometric-case techniques (Nevanlinna theory / entire-curve constructions) have been shown to transfer to an actual arithmetic (number-field) result — e.g., a new case of the number-field Bombieri-Lang conjecture proved, cited as using ideas from Xie-Yuan/Gao. No such transfer has been reported as of this search.

summary: I could not find any result in the window (26 Jan 2024 – 22 Sep 2026) that resolves, partially resolves, or moves a bound on the stated conjecture: that closed aspherical manifolds are determined up to homeomorphism by their fundamental groups. The triage's lead, Davis & Hillman, 'The Borel Conjecture for manifolds with boundary' (arXiv:2501.12509, v1 21 Jan 2025, revised through v2 29 Jun 2026), proves a case of a *different* conjecture: the 'Borel Conjecture for manifolds with boundary' asks whether a homotopy equivalence of compact aspherical manifolds-with-boundary that is already a homeomorphism on the boundary is homotopic rel boundary to a homeomorphism — a statement posed for a different class of objects (manifolds with nonempty boundary) with an extra boundary hypothesis, not obtainable by simply restricting the closed-manifold statement in our bullet. Per Manifold Atlas and the paper's own framing, this is the standard related-but-distinct 'Borel Conjecture for manifolds with boundary,' developed in analogy with the closed case rather than as a special case of it. I also found a second candidate, Davis, Hayden, Huang, Ruberman & Sunukjian, 'Exotic aspherical 4-manifolds' (arXiv:2411.19400, v1 28 Nov 2024, v3 5 May 2026), which constructs closed, aspherical, smooth 4-manifolds that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic — a counterexample to the *smooth* analogue of Borel (diffeomorphism, not homeomorphism), which Wikipedia's own article already records as false (with the smooth-vs-topological distinction stated explicitly in the encyclopedia's wording of the conjecture we were given: 'This conjecture is false if topological manifolds and homeomorphisms are replaced by smooth manifolds and diffeomorphisms'). Because our stated conjecture is specifically about homeomorphism (the topological, not smooth, category), this result changes nothing about the bullet's status; it is a different statement and, moreover, one whose falsity in a related form was already known/expected before the frozen date. I also checked Lück's 'Survey on the Farrell-Jones Conjecture' (arXiv:2507.11337, 2025, to appear Bull. AMS): it is an expository survey with no new theorems of its own, and it frames the general Full Farrell-Jones Conjecture (whose truth for a torsion-free group implies Borel for that group's manifolds in dim ≥5) as still open, consistent with the general Borel conjecture remaining open. Lück–Macko's 2024 book 'Surgery Theory: Foundations' is likewise an exposition, not new research. The current live Wikipedia article on the Borel conjecture contains no mention of any 2024–2026 development. I found no AI involvement anywhere near this problem: none of the mathematical papers above mention AI assistance, and a tangential hit (an autoformalization-agent paper, 'Aria', arXiv:2510.04520) mentions using 'Borel's Conjecture in topology' only as a benchmark case for testing definition-retrieval in an automated formalization pipeline — it formalizes existing definitions/statements rather than proving or advancing anything, so it is not a mathematical event and not `ai_role` other than none even by inference (no authors' account ties it to a proof). A separate 'Human mathematicians are being outcounterexampled' post (Xena blog, Jul 2026) that surfaced in AI-adjacent searches discusses unrelated conjectures (Erdős unit-distance, a Grothendieck question, the Jacobian conjecture) and does not mention the Borel conjecture at all — a false lead from query overlap, not a finding. I therefore agree with the triage's underlying observation (the Davis-Hillman paper exists and is real) but disagree with treating it as progress on this stated bullet: it is a related problem under §3.1, not a case, so status remains `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the manifolds-with-boundary Borel conjecture is close enough in spirit — same conjecturer, same techniques (surgery theory, Farrell-Jones), same 'topological rigidity' slogan — that progress there is evidence-adjacent progress on the closed case, and some expositors (e.g., Manifold Atlas, which houses both under overlapping page structures) treat them as a family. If Davis and Hillman's technique is understood to eventually reduce to or imply results for closed manifolds via boundary-capping arguments, a future reader might argue for `partial`/`progress` instead of `open`. I did not find any explicit statement in the papers claiming implications for the closed-manifold case, so I did not adopt this reading.
what_would_settle_it: A published statement, by Davis, Hillman, or another expert, that their manifolds-with-boundary results imply a new case of the closed aspherical manifold Borel conjecture (e.g., via doubling or boundary-capping constructions extending fundamental-group classes for which the closed conjecture is now known); or any new paper directly proving/disproving a case of the closed conjecture within the window.

outcome: No result found in the window (26 Jan 2024 – present) that bears on the question of whether there exist three unknotted space curves, not all circles, that cannot be arranged to form the Borromean rings. All foundational work on this question (Freedman–Skora's 1987 proof that circles alone cannot form the rings, Cook's conjecture that any three unknotted curves not all circles can, Cantarella's proposed counterexample, and Howards' 2013/2014 weakening of the conjecture to planar curves) predates the frozen revision. Recent Borromean-rings papers found in the window address unrelated questions (hyperbolic geometry of the complement, ellipse-linking detection algorithms, quantum vortex dynamics, link Floer homology, gordian unknots under thickness constraints).
summary: Wikipedia's stated open problem is: 'Are there three unknotted curves, not all circles, that cannot form the Borromean rings?' — this is the open converse of Cook's conjecture (that any three unknotted simple closed curves, not all circles, CAN be combined to form the Borromean rings), as weakened by Hugh Howards after Jason Cantarella proposed a possible counterexample (a specific torus-parameterized curve). All of that history — Freedman–Skora's 1987 impossibility result for circles, Cook's conjecture, Cantarella's proposed counterexample, and Howards' 2013/2014 paper 'Forming the Borromean Rings out of arbitrary polygonal unknots' proving the planar-curve case — predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision and is out of scope. I searched extensively for any 2024–2026 work addressing this specific realizability question: direct searches on Cook's conjecture, Howards' name, Cantarella's proposed counterexample, arXiv listings for 'Borromean rings' across 2024–2026, and MathOverflow/survey-style queries. I found several genuinely new arXiv papers touching Borromean rings in the window (2404.02615 on the hyperbolic geometry of the Borromean rings complement; 2405.20874 on Borromean hypergraphs in random rectangles/percolation; 2506.04442 on 'gordian unknots' under curvature/thickness constraints, unrelated to this question as the triage also found; 2509.15104 on an efficient algorithm to detect Hopf/Borromean linking between ellipses, a computational-geometry question about a specific curve family rather than Cook's general realizability question; 2507.20903 on energy minimization of topological links; a February 2025 paper on quantum vortex Borromean-ring dynamics governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation; and an August 2026 paper on link Floer homology of the Borromean rings). None of these engage with the stated question of whether some non-circular unknotted triple fails to realize the Borromean link. I therefore agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and confirm status open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2509.15104 ellipse-linking-detection paper is adjacent, since ellipses are a natural non-circular curve family relevant to Cook's conjecture and Howards' planar-curve case; but the paper is a computational/algorithmic contribution to detecting whether given ellipses ARE linked, not a realizability or counterexample result bearing on the open question, so I classified it as out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (or proof) either exhibiting a specific non-circular unknotted triple that cannot be arranged into the Borromean link (settling the question affirmatively, likely building on Cantarella's proposed torus counterexample), or a general proof that every non-circular unknotted triple can always be so arranged (proving Cook's conjecture in full and thereby resolving the stated question negatively).

outcome: The minimum dimension in which a counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture is known to exist was lowered from 64 to 63 via a 321-point three-distance configuration in R^63 (proving b(63) >= 65), first produced by Max Grinsztajn using GPT-5.5 Pro in May 2026, with the construction independently reproduced by two other parties (one, Yibo Ji using a different model, posted and then withdrew an arXiv writeup once priority was clarified); separately, a 2026 preprint lowered the upper bound on the Borsuk number in R^4 from 9 to 8 by ordinary human construction.

ai.basis_quote: The example and proof were generated entirely by ChatGPT using GPT 5.6 Sol. The author has personally verified the result and assumes responsibility for that verification, but claims no credit for the originality of the construction.

counterexample.object: A 321-point three-distance configuration in R^63 (extending the Jenrich-Brouwer 320-point core with the G_2(4) Euclidean representation, plus one projected/rescaled point) that cannot be partitioned into 64 subsets of smaller diameter, proving b(63) >= 65
counterexample.verified_how: Verified by exact computation and formalised/checked into the Lean 'formal-conjectures' repository; the withdrawn arXiv writeup's author states personal verification of the construction

disputes.summary: The dimension-63 counterexample was apparently found independently by three parties in close succession: Max Grinsztajn (using GPT-5.5 Pro, credited as first, May 2026, per the formal-conjectures PR and the 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' Wikipedia article), a person/system referred to only as 'Konz', and Yibo Ji (using a different/later model, 'GPT 5.6 Sol', arXiv:2608.12561, submitted 12 Aug 2026). Ji's paper was withdrawn on 14 Aug 2026, two days after submission, apparently because the result had already been posted elsewhere (i.e., by Grinsztajn in May). I could not locate Grinsztajn's own primary write-up (blog post or repository) directly -- only secondary mentions of it in the formal-conjectures PR, a 'vibemathed' tracking-site PR, and the Wikipedia AI-discoveries list -- so I cannot fully verify the May 2026 date or the exact GPT-5.5 Pro attribution independent of these secondary compilations.

summary: Borsuk's problem asks for upper and lower bounds on the number b(n) of smaller-diameter pieces needed to cover any bounded set in R^n. Two distinct things happened in the window. (1) On the 'how low can a counterexample dimension go' side (the problem is known false for large n since Kahn-Kalai 1993, with the record dimension falling over decades), the minimum known failing dimension moved from 64 (Jenrich-Brouwer, pre-2024) to 63, via a 321-point three-distance configuration proving b(63) >= 65. Multiple sources converge on this: the arXiv preprint 2608.12561 (author Yibo Ji, submitted 12 Aug 2026, withdrawn 14 Aug 2026) states in its own abstract that 'the example and proof were generated entirely by ChatGPT using GPT 5.6 Sol' and that the author 'personally verified the result' but 'claims no credit for the originality of the construction' -- language suggesting the construction was already known. The google-deepmind/formal-conjectures Lean repository PR #5265 independently corroborates this, crediting 'Grinsztajn's 321-point configuration (May 2026, verified by exact computation and found independently by Konz and by Ji)', and states the PR itself narrowed the open range in the Wikipedia article to '4 <= n <= 62'. Wikipedia's 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' article credits Max Grinsztajn, prompting GPT-5.5 Pro, in May 2026, as the original discoverer. Because this is an explicit, exhibited counterexample object (not merely a bound moved on a search), and the authors' own account attributes the construction's origination to the AI system with humans checking/verifying it, I coded ai_role as generated. I classified status as claimed rather than resolved: the result is machine-verified by exact computation and appears in a Lean formalisation repository, but I found no evidence of a traditional expert digestion (a refereed paper, a survey, or an expert's blog post working through the argument -- notably absent from Tao's blog, which I checked directly) -- only the repository/preprint layer and Wikipedia's own compilation articles, which are not themselves expert peer digestion. This is a case of the problem (settling the minimal-counterexample-dimension question is a restriction/instance of the general upper/lower-bound question Wikipedia's bullet poses), so it counts under the scope rule, though it improves a specific quantity (min. failing dimension) rather than resolving the general conjecture, hence resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the counterexample direction, extending the known-false region) rather than a full resolution. (2) Separately, on the upper-bound side for a specific dimension, arXiv (announced as 2605.19068 per the triage record, but the fetched page shows submission 18 May 2026) by Alexander Tolmachev and Vsevolod Voronov reduces the upper bound on the Borsuk number in R^4 from 9 (Lassak, 1982) to 8, via an ordinary human hand-constructed partition of variants of the truncated Lassak cover; I found no mention of any AI system in this paper, so this half of the finding is ai_role 'none' and status 'progress' considered alone -- but since it is a bound movement on a still-open dimension it does not change the overall 'claimed' status driven by the dimension-63 counterexample, which is the more significant event. I flag a genuine oddity for the record: my search tool's synthesized summaries repeatedly and confidently attributed the arXiv paper 2608.12561 to 'Max Grinsztajn' with model 'GPT-5.5 Pro' and a May 2026 date, when the primary source I fetched directly clearly shows the paper's actual author is Yibo Ji, its named model is 'GPT 5.6 Sol', and its submission date is 12 Aug 2026 (withdrawn 14 Aug 2026). This is documented in the disputes/competing_reading fields; I trusted the directly-fetched primary arXiv page over the search engine's summary, per instructions, but the underlying Grinsztajn/May-2026 claim itself rests only on secondary compilations (the Lean PR and the Wikipedia AI-discoveries list), not a primary source I could independently open, so some residual uncertainty about the precise first-discovery date and exact model name remains.
competing_reading: If Grinsztajn's own primary account (a blog post or repository, which I could not locate or open directly) turns out not to substantiate the May 2026 date or the GPT-5.5 Pro attribution, the earliest verifiable primary-source event for the dimension-63 result would instead be Yibo Ji's arXiv:2608.12561 (12 Aug 2026, model 'GPT 5.6 Sol'), which was itself withdrawn -- in which case the event might be better classified as 'progress'/'incident' (a claim posted then withdrawn) rather than 'claimed', with the underlying mathematical fact of b(63)>=65 only resting on the Lean-formalised/exactly-verified construction in the formal-conjectures repository. It is also possible 'Konz' is the true first discoverer and Grinsztajn's priority, as recorded in secondary sources, is itself contested; I found no primary source resolving the three-way priority claim.
what_would_settle_it: Locating Max Grinsztajn's own primary write-up (repository commit, blog post, or paper) with a verifiable timestamp and exact model-name quote, and/or an expert (non-repository, non-Wikipedia) digestion -- a journal paper, a survey, or a mathematician's blog post -- working through the dimension-63 construction, which would move the status from claimed toward resolved and would settle the priority dispute among Grinsztajn, Konz and Ji.

outcome: No result found that advances the Bost conjecture (the l1-Banach algebra analogue of the Baum-Connes assembly map, as a case of the Farrell-Jones framework) since 26 January 2024; it remains open in general, with the pre-2024 known cases (word-hyperbolic groups, groups acting on trees, open subgroups) unchanged.
summary: The Bost conjecture in this bullet is the l1(G)-Banach-algebra analogue of the Baum-Connes assembly map (that the assembly map A_FIN^{l1}: H_n^G(E_FIN(G); K_{l1}^top) -> K_n(l1(G)) is an isomorphism), treated as a special/related case within the Farrell-Jones isomorphism-conjecture framework. I searched directly for the Bost conjecture by name (plain, with 'Farrell-Jones', with 'Baum-Connes', with 'Banach algebra', in French as 'conjecture de Bost', and restricted to arXiv and to 2024/2025/2026), and separately searched adjacent literature (Baum-Connes for relatively hyperbolic groups, coarse Baum-Connes, Banach KK-theory) for any paper that also addresses the Bost conjecture. Every hit is either (a) pre-2024 background (the 2009 Bost-conjecture-for-open-subgroups/tree-actions paper, the 2013 'Bost conjecture and proper Banach algebras' paper), (b) a same-name coincidence — an entirely different 'Bost conjecture' (J.-B. Bost's 1997 conjecture that tensor products of semistable Hermitian/Arakelov lattices are semistable, which is unrelated to the Farrell-Jones framework and not the subject of this bullet), or (c) work on the neighboring but distinct Baum-Connes conjecture itself (e.g. arXiv:2512.21169, December 2025, 'Strong bolicity and the Baum-Connes conjecture for relatively hyperbolic groups') that does not mention or extend the Bost conjecture specifically. I fetched the 2025 Lück survey 'Survey on the Farrell-Jones Conjecture' (arXiv:2507.11337, published in the Bulletin of the AMS 2026) directly and it contains no mention of the Bost conjecture at all, suggesting it has not been a locus of recent activity even in the most current comprehensive survey of the surrounding conjecture family. I also fetched the Farrell-Jones conjecture's current Wikipedia article, which describes the Bost conjecture but states no proof or new-case result. No AI system appears anywhere in this search. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict and its reasoning, and did not find anything it missed.
competing_reading: It is possible a paper proves the Bost conjecture for some further class of groups (e.g. some new class of non-positively-curved or acylindrically hyperbolic groups) without using the words 'Bost conjecture' prominently in its abstract or title, instead phrasing it purely in terms of the l1-assembly-map or K-theory of l1(G) — such a paper could be missed by name-based search. I did not find any such paper in the Baum-Connes/Banach K-theory literature I surveyed, but I cannot rule out its existence with certainty.
what_would_settle_it: A full-text search of arXiv's math.KT and math.OA listings for 2024-2026 for the phrase 'l1(G)' or 'K_*(l1(G))' combined with 'assembly map' or 'isomorphism conjecture', which would catch a paper that proves new Bost-conjecture cases without naming Bost explicitly; or a citation-graph check (Google Scholar 'cited by') on the two canonical Bost-conjecture papers (Lafforgue's original result, and the 2009/2013 papers found here) restricted to 2024 onward.

outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the full Brennan conjecture remains open, but several restricted cases have been settled: Aleman and Kouroupis (2024/2025) proved it for continuous semigroups of holomorphic functions; Jin (2025/2026) proved it for all univalent rational functions in the unit disk; and Zheng (2026) proved it for basins of attraction at infinity of certain monic polynomials. No AI system was involved in any of this work.
summary: The frozen-revision statement asks for a resolution of Brennan's conjecture: estimating the integral of |F'|^p over certain domains for conformal maps F onto the unit disk, for p in (4/3, 4). Wikipedia's own article (checked 2026-09-22) has not been updated and still reports the pre-2024 state: Brennan's original range 4/3<p<p0, Bertilsson's 1999 extension to 4/3<p<3.422, and 'the full result remains open' (the Hedenmalm-Shimorin improvement to p<3.75 is also pre-2024 and not part of this window). Three genuine cases of the conjecture were settled in the window, all confirming it (no case has been found false): (1) Aleman & Kouroupis, arXiv:2409.15074 (submitted 2024-09-23, revised 2025-04-14), prove the conjecture in full (all p in the stated range) for the restricted class of domains arising as images of continuous semigroups of holomorphic self-maps of the disk -- read via WebFetch, confirmed no AI/ML mentioned, uses classical complex analysis plus Bekolle-Bonami weight and integration-operator spectrum results. (2) Jin, arXiv:2512.09330 (first submitted 2025-12-10, 13 revisions through 2026-06), as a corollary of determining the exact integral means spectrum of all univalent rational functions on the disk, proves the conjecture holds for that entire class -- abstract fetched directly, no AI/ML mentioned, purely analytic/Teichmuller-theoretic methods. (3) Zheng, arXiv:2604.12240 (submitted 2026-04-14), proves the conjecture for basins of attraction at infinity of a broad class of monic polynomials z^m+a0 (m>=3) and polynomials with small non-leading coefficients, extending a known result of Baranski-Volberg-Zdunik -- these basins are simply-connected domains admitting a conformal map to the disk, so this is a restriction to a class of domains rather than a change of the question, though the framing in terms of dynamical basins rather than 'certain subsets' as worded on Wikipedia makes the classification a judgment call. None of the three papers mentions any AI system, machine learning, or computer-assisted search; all are traditional human proofs verified by classical complex-analytic argument. No AI-related result of any kind (generated proof, assisted argument, bound-moving computation, or withdrawn claim) was found for this problem in the window. I did not find any paper claiming or retracting a full proof of the general conjecture, nor any record-style or numerical result that would change status further. Status is 'partial' because multiple genuine cases were settled (all confirming the conjecture, hence resolution_direction 'confirmed'), while the general conjecture as stated remains open.
competing_reading: The Zheng basin-of-attraction paper could instead be read as a related/variant problem rather than a case: Brennan's conjecture is normally stated for domains arising from conformal Riemann mapping theory (quasidisks, Julia-set complements already studied by Baranski-Volberg-Zdunik), and one could argue that framing it dynamically (via polynomial iteration) changes the question's flavor even though the underlying object -- a simply-connected domain mapped conformally to the disk -- is unchanged. If read as a variant, only the Aleman-Kouroupis and Jin papers count as cases, and the status conclusion (partial, confirmed) is unaffected either way since both of those are unambiguous cases.
what_would_settle_it: A published taxonomy from Brennan-conjecture specialists (e.g. a survey or the next edition of Pommerenke-style geometric function theory literature) explicitly listing basin-of-attraction domains as an instance of 'certain subsets' in Brennan's original conjecture, versus treating dynamically-defined domains as a separate research thread.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or settled case of Brocard's conjecture (at least 4 primes between consecutive prime squares) was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open, with only computational verification extended and unrelated/distinct 'Brocard' work published in the window.
summary: Brocard's conjecture (at least 4 primes between (p_n)^2 and (p_{n+1})^2 for n≥2) remains unproven. The Wikipedia article and MathWorld both confirm this as of 2025-2026, with MathWorld noting only that computational verification has been extended to n=4×10^5 (E. Weisstein, 2025-01-12) — an extension of the record, which per §3.1 does not count as progress on a universal ('for every n') statement any more than it would for an infinitude question, since it narrows where a counterexample could hide rather than settling the question. I checked several arXiv papers surfaced by search that mention 'Brocard': arXiv:2606.23485 ('The Brocard Problem: Structural Invariants, p-Adic Density, and the Generative Sieve', submitted 2026-06-22) and arXiv:2004.09256 concern the *Brocard–Ramanujan problem* (n!+1=m², the existence of 'Brown numbers'), a different, only eponymously related problem — a case of §3.1's 'related problem, not a case' distinction, since the two share a name (Henri Brocard) but not a mathematical question. arXiv:2507.14410 (Matt Visser, submitted 2025-07-18) proves θ-analogues (using the Chebyshev θ function of primes) of Brocard's, Cramér's, Andrica's, Legendre's and Oppermann's conjectures as theorems, but explicitly for the transformed sequence θ_n = θ(p_n), not for the prime sequence itself — this is a variant/analogue, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not change what a careful reader would write in this bullet's entry. arXiv:2501.18048 ('Almost primes between all squares') proves an unconditional near-miss to Legendre's conjecture (a number with ≤4 prime factors between every n² and (n+1)²) but does not address Brocard's conjecture, which concerns primes between *prime* squares specifically, and Legendre's conjecture (even fully proved) would not itself establish Brocard's ≥4-primes requirement. arXiv:2508.08335 (the 2025 survey found by triage) discusses properties of primes and cyclic numbers but was confirmed not to advance Brocard's conjecture upon inspection. No AI system, language model, or automated theorem prover was mentioned in connection with any of this work; a general search for AI-assisted resolutions of open problems (Erdős problems solved by an AI agent per arXiv:2605.22763, ChatGPT-assisted results, etc.) turned up no connection to Brocard's conjecture specifically. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the θ-analogue theorems in arXiv:2507.14410 constitute 'progress' in a loose sense, since the transformed statements are structurally identical to Brocard's conjecture and are now proven theorems for θ_n. But the sequence θ_n = θ(p_n) is a different object from the primes p_n themselves, and Visser's paper explicitly frames these as analogues rather than as bearing on the original conjectures, so under §3.1's 'changing vs. restricting the question' test this is a related problem, not a case.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving that for every n≥2 there are at least 4 primes between p_n^2 and p_{n+1}^2 (or a counterexample for some n>3, since n=2,3 are already known exceptions), or a proof of Oppermann's/Cramér's conjecture (which are known to imply it), would settle the ambiguity around whether any progress exists.

outcome: Makki Naciri (2025, in Integers) proved that if x±1 is 7-free, then n = 4, 5, 7 are the only solutions of the exact equation n!+1=x^2, and more generally that the equation has only finitely many solutions whenever x±1 is k-free (k≥2) or a prime power — the strongest unconditional restricted result yet on the classical equation; the general conjecture remains open.
summary: Brocard's problem — whether n!+1=m^2 has solutions other than n=4,5,7 — remains open in general as of September 2026. The most substantial genuine progress in the window is Abderrahim Makki Naciri's paper 'On the Brocard-Ramanujan Equation with 7-Free Integers and Prime Powers' (Zenodo/arXiv preprint dated 2025-08-15, published in Integers, Vol. 25 (2025), and independently confirmed as the current best-known result by the erdosproblems.com database entry for this problem). Naciri proves that the classical equation n!+1=x^2 has only finitely many solutions when x±1 is k-free (k≥2) or a prime power, and specifically that if x±1 is 7-free, n=4,5,7 are the only solutions. This is a genuine restriction of the exact stated equation (a case, not a variant, since it constrains the same unknowns in the same equation rather than changing the equation), so it counts as `partial` with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the restricted case matches Erdős's conjectured answer). I could not access the full text of Naciri's paper (only the Zenodo/erdosproblems summaries), so I cannot directly quote methodology, but nothing in any secondary source suggests computer-algebra or AI assistance; this is standard analytic/algebraic number theory. Separately, a 2026 arXiv paper by Eric F. Bravo, 'On Brocard's problem with Padovan and Perrin numbers' (arXiv:2606.28577, submitted 2026-06-26), proves (n,x)=(4,5) is the only solution when x is restricted to being a term of the Padovan or Perrin sequence — also a genuine restricted case of the same equation, though narrower in scope than Naciri's result and not the basis for the status here since it postdates and is subsumed in spirit by the stronger, peer-reviewed Naciri result. A separate and unrelated development is Wataru Takeda's complete resolution of the *polynomial analogue* of the Brocard-Ramanujan problem (over F_q[T], published in Finite Fields and Their Applications, online 2025-09-30, print Feb 2026) — this changes the problem (integers to polynomial rings) rather than restricting it, so per §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case, and does not affect the status of the integer problem, which its own announcement explicitly states remains unsolved. A 2024 paper, 'Solution of Brocard's Problem' by Mohamed Imteaz Karimullah (Indian Journal of Advanced Mathematics, Vol. 4 Issue 1, April 2024, an APC-funded journal from Lattice Science Publication with no evidence of MathSciNet/zbMATH indexing or expert digestion, and whose claimed full resolution of a 150-year-old open problem in a minor journal without any subsequent citation, media coverage, or expert acknowledgement is a strong red flag), claims to prove there are no other solutions; I could not extract readable text from its PDF and found no independent verification, citation, or discussion of it anywhere (not on Wikipedia, not on erdosproblems.com, not in any survey). Given the complete absence of expert corroboration and the journal's profile, I do not treat this claim as a `claimed` or `resolved` event — it does not meet even the `claimed` bar of a credible, digestible preprint, and including it would overstate what happened. No AI involvement was found anywhere in the search: no lab announcement, no paper crediting a language model or other AI system with proving, assisting, or bounding any part of this problem. All identified work is conventional human mathematics in refereed or preprint venues.
competing_reading: One could argue the Karimullah (2024) IJAM paper should be recorded as a `claimed` resolution event since it explicitly asserts a full proof of the classical conjecture within the window. I did not adopt this reading because `claimed` requires a credible preprint or machine-checked certificate that experts simply haven't gotten to yet, and this paper shows none of the hallmarks of a serious attempt reaching that bar (no citations, no engagement from the number theory community, publication venue with pay-to-publish characteristics, and its claim would be one of the most significant results in elementary number theory in decades if genuine). Also arguable: whether the Bravo (Padovan/Perrin) 2026 paper should be cited as an additional supporting `partial` event alongside Naciri's — I mention it in summary but treat Naciri's as the decisive event since it is peer-reviewed, more general, and already independently verified by erdosproblems.com.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full text of the Karimullah (2024) paper's proof (I could only fetch raw PDF bytes, not rendered text) and checking whether it has since been cited, refuted, or corrected in the literature would resolve whether it merits inclusion as a claimed event. Reading Naciri's full paper in Integers would let me quote its methods directly rather than relying on the erdosproblems.com and Zenodo summaries.

outcome: A June 2026 preprint by Kothari and Tudose (arXiv:2606.12197) claims a full proof of Brouwer's conjecture by establishing an equivalence between the conjecture and the (previously proven) Grone-Merris-Bai theorem, restricted via split graphs; as of the research date (2026-09-22, about 3.5 months after posting) no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification has been found, and a July 2026 follow-up (arXiv:2607.03388) that builds directly on it to resolve the equality-case question (Li-Guo's 'full Brouwer conjecture') has likewise not been digested.

ai.basis_quote: We used GPT 5.5 Pro to simplify our proof that Brouwer's Inequality implies the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem. We also used it for a proofreading of our manuscript.

summary: The triage's pointer checks out on the facts but the classification needs tightening. Kothari and Tudose (arXiv:2606.12197, posted 2026-06-10) claim a full proof of Brouwer's conjecture on Laplacian eigenvalue sums, via an equivalence with the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem restricted to split graphs. I read the full HTML rendering of the paper: it is short (about 13-14 pages), has no acknowledgements section but does carry an explicit 'Statement of AI Use' reading verbatim 'We used GPT 5.5 Pro to simplify our proof that Brouwer's Inequality implies the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem. We also used it for a proofreading of our manuscript.' That is a disclosed, author-stated contribution of a specific named system to part of the mathematical content (simplifying one direction of the core equivalence), not merely proofreading, so I coded ai_role as assisted rather than none, with basis_quote and source as required. As of the research date (2026-09-22), roughly 3.5 months after posting, I found no expert digestion (no Terence Tao blog post, no MathOverflow thread, no journal acceptance notice), so the paper remains unverified by the mathematical community at large and status is claimed, not resolved. A July 2026 follow-up (arXiv:2607.03388, Cai/Chen/Yang/Zhang, v2 dated 2026-08-10) explicitly builds on the Kothari-Tudose proof ('Motivated by their perfect proof and methods...') to settle the equality-case characterization conjectured by Li and Guo (2022); it carries no AI-use statement of its own. I found no retraction, withdrawal, or identified error specific to the Kothari-Tudose paper itself, though I did find (via search snippets referencing an AI-review platform, Pith Review, at pith.science) that other, unrelated 2025-2026 preprints attempting partial proofs of Brouwer's conjecture were flagged with logical gaps by that automated reviewer -- those are different papers, not the Kothari-Tudose one, and I could not get Pith Review's page content to load to confirm whether it has reviewed 2606.12197 at all. Given the short elapsed time and the paper's brevity for such a major claim, I rate confidence medium: the mathematical claim is plausible and well-cited by fast-moving follow-up work, but the field has not yet had the years typical of digesting a 50-year-old conjecture's resolution.
competing_reading: One could argue ai_role should be 'none': the disclosed GPT contribution was to 'simplify' an already-established implication (Brouwer's Inequality implies GMB) rather than to originate new mathematical content, which is arguably closer to proofreading/tidying than to producing an argument, case, or bound that wasn't already there. I coded it as assisted because 'simplify our proof' is a step beyond pure proofreading -- it implies the model reworked part of the argument's presentation or structure, which is different from spell-checking prose -- but a stricter reading that requires the AI to have supplied genuinely new mathematical content (not just restructured existing content) would move this to 'none'. Separately, status could arguably stay 'open' rather than 'claimed' if one takes the view that a completely undigested, un-refereed, 13-page resolution of a 50-year-old conjecture with a short elapsed window carries too little epistemic weight to register as anything beyond noise; I judged 'claimed' more appropriate since the paper unambiguously exists, makes the claim in scope, and has already drawn serious follow-up work from other named mathematicians who treat it as correct.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (e.g., a referee report, journal acceptance, or a post by a recognized spectral-graph-theory expert such as Terence Tao's blog or a MathOverflow thread) confirming or refuting the Kothari-Tudose argument would settle status between claimed and resolved (or reveal a gap making it open/open_stale-adjacent). Getting Pith Review's or another automated/human reviewer's assessment specifically of arXiv:2606.12197 (not just of unrelated Brouwer-conjecture preprints) would also help. For the ai_role classification, seeing the actual before/after text of the 'simplified' proof step, or an author interview/talk describing what GPT 5.5 Pro changed, would clarify whether it contributed novel mathematical content or only restructured existing human-derived content.

outcome: Stanley Yao Xiao posted a preprint in December 2024 (revised through June 2025) claiming a complete proof that five integer squares with constant second difference 2 must be consecutive, which would resolve Büchi's problem (with M=5); as of this research the paper has not been accepted by a journal or worked through by an expert digestion, so it remains a claim rather than a settled resolution.
summary: Büchi's problem (the 'n squares problem') asks for the least M such that every sequence of M or more integer squares with constant second difference 2 must be a sequence of consecutive squares; it was known that M ≤ 5 works unconditionally is the target (Büchi/Vojta-type results had reduced this to needing M=5, with M=4 known to fail in general and various partial/conditional results existing before the frozen date). On 21 December 2024, Stanley Yao Xiao posted arXiv:2412.16740, 'Hilbert's tenth problem for systems of diagonal quadratic forms, and Büchi's problem,' which the abstract and body present as completing the proof that any five squares x1²,...,x5² with second differences all equal to 2 must be consecutive — i.e., establishing the M=5 case unconditionally, which is the statement of Büchi's problem as it is generally posed. The paper has gone through at least three arXiv revisions, the latest (v3) dated 7 June 2025, indicating active revision consistent with a claim still being refined rather than a finished, community-vetted proof. I checked the paper itself (via fetch), the live Wikipedia article on Büchi's problem, and searched for any journal acceptance, expert blog digestion (e.g. Terence Tao's blog, Quanta, or a number-theory survey), or peer-reviewed publication announcement — none was found. The current Wikipedia article for Büchi's problem states explicitly: 'A positive answer was claimed in 2024 by Stanley Yao Xiao and is awaiting peer review as of July 2025,' which matches what I found independently. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or formal verification (e.g. Lean/Coq) of the proof was located. I found no mention of AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving tools anywhere in the paper, in secondary coverage, or in searches combining Büchi's problem with AI/LLM terms — this appears to be conventional human mathematical work (analytic/algebraic number theory techniques building on Hilbert's Tenth Problem-style arguments). Given the proof is unrefereed and unreviewed by the expert community as far as I can determine, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved,' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' since the claimed result, if correct, proves the conjectured statement (M=5 suffices) rather than refuting it.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'resolved' if journal acceptance or an expert digestion occurred that I could not find (e.g., paywalled venue, or a talk/seminar digestion not indexed by general web search — the paper has been presented, e.g. in a 'Number Theory Web Seminar' (NTWS 259) YouTube talk by Xiao, which is the author's own presentation, not an independent expert's verification). Absent an independent referee report or published acceptance, 'claimed' is the more conservative and, I believe, correct reading. It is also possible a case could be made that the problem, as most commonly stated with unspecified M, is only partially addressed (Xiao's result is specifically for the second-difference-2 case with M=5, which is the standard formulation of Büchi's problem, so I do not treat this as a mere 'case' or 'variant' — it directly targets the stated conjecture).
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance of arXiv:2412.16740 (or a successor version) at a peer-reviewed venue, or a public expert digestion (blog post, MathOverflow consensus, or citation in a survey) explicitly confirming the proof is correct and complete, would move this to 'resolved.' Conversely, a retraction, identified gap, or published counterexample to a lemma would move it to 'progress'/'incident.'

corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, WITH DOUBT. Scope is right: Xiao claims the M = 5 case, which is Buchi's problem as usually posed. Credibility is the open question. Against: an unconditional proof would be a major result (previous routes needed the Bombieri-Lang conjecture), and in almost two years it has drawn no expert engagement, no journal acceptance, and no mention in the live Wikipedia article. For: the author is an established number theorist working in exactly this area, the paper has been actively revised, and nothing has knocked it down. That falls short of the grounds used to set claims aside in the non-credible-claims batch, so it stays `claimed`. It is one of the rows a planned 'doubtful claim' marker is for.

outcome: No mathematically accepted change to the Bunyakovsky conjecture since 26 January 2024; the only 'proof' claim (Jihyeon Yoon, July 2024, posted on TechRxiv/Zenodo/Authorea) is an unreviewed preprint on non-standard venues that has drawn no expert digestion, citation, or discussion, and both Wikipedia's live article and Grokipedia's page continue to state that no case of degree greater than 1 has been proved.
summary: The conjecture (posed 1857) remains completely open for all polynomials of degree greater than 1; the only proved case is degree 1, via Dirichlet's theorem, which long predates the window. Searching for developments since 26 January 2024 turned up exactly one candidate: a preprint by Jihyeon Yoon titled 'Proof of Bunyakovsky Conjecture', posted to Zenodo and TechRxiv on 2 July 2024 (Zenodo record 12616123, ORCID 0000-0001-9610-0994), which asserts the conjecture is 'proved to be true.' This is not a resolution under the rules here: it appears only on preprint-hosting sites with no peer review layer (TechRxiv and Zenodo host anything uploaded; Authorea is a self-publishing platform), it has not been picked up by arXiv math.NT, it has no citations, and no expert commentary, blog discussion, MathOverflow thread, or retraction notice could be found discussing it at all — it appears to have been ignored by the mathematical community rather than actively debunked. The current Wikipedia article and an independent encyclopedia (Grokipedia, fact-checked within the last 8 months as of access) both state plainly that no case beyond degree 1 has been proved, which is inconsistent with an accepted proof existing. I therefore classify this as no change (status open), not as claimed or resolved, since a genuinely serious full proof of a 167-year-old named conjecture would be expected to register at least some scrutiny or arXiv presence, and none was found. The only adjacent 2025 progress found is on Schinzel's Hypothesis H (which generalizes Bunyakovsky to systems of polynomials) — specifically 'Integrally Hilbertian rings and the polynomial Schinzel hypothesis' (arXiv:2502.09959, Behajaina/Dèbes/König, Feb 2025), which develops specialization-property machinery for a coprime/integral variant of Hypothesis H. This is a related problem under §3.1 (a different, more general question about systems of polynomials and ring-theoretic specialization), not a restriction of the Bunyakovsky statement itself, and it does not narrow or touch the single-polynomial primality question as worded in the frozen bullet. No AI system was mentioned in connection with the Yoon preprint, the Schinzel-H work, or any other source found; the 2026 AI-discovered counterexample events I encountered while searching (e.g. the Jacobian Conjecture counterexample found with the aid of a language model) concern an unrelated problem and have no bearing here.
competing_reading: One could argue the Yoon preprint should be coded 'claimed' on the theory that any standing, undisputed public proof claim of a major conjecture counts as 'claimed' regardless of venue prestige, since the rubric's 'claimed' bar is only a preprint or announcement not yet digested, not a peer-reviewed one. Against this: the DEEP_DIVE.md rubric's `claimed` category presumes a claim serious enough to attract eventual expert attention; this one has attracted none in over two years, appears formulaic/unreviewed similar to other undiscussed 'proof of X conjecture' preprints periodically posted to TechRxiv, and the Wikipedia/Grokipedia record of the field's consensus flatly contradicts it having succeeded. I judge 'open'/no_change_found is the better reading, but flag this as a genuine judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: Any expert commentary, arXiv posting, citation, or discussion thread engaging with the Yoon preprint's actual argument (confirming or refuting it) would settle whether it merits 'claimed' status; absent that, its total lack of uptake after two years supports treating it as noise.

outcome: No resolution or partial progress on B(2,5) specifically was found since 26 January 2024; it remains explicitly stated as open in every current source consulted (Wikipedia, Groupprops, Euler Circle expository papers, Encyclopedia of Mathematics). The only nearby movement in the broader Burnside problem — the Atkarskaya–Rips–Tent bound that free Burnside groups B(m,n) are infinite for odd n≥557 — was already present in v3 of that paper (submitted 22 June 2023), before the frozen revision date, and in any case concerns exponent ≥557, not exponent 5, so it does not touch this bullet's stated case.
summary: The bullet asks: for which (m,n) is the free Burnside group B(m,n) finite, in particular is B(2,5) finite? Extensive searching (arXiv, Wikipedia's current article, Groupprops, Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Euler Circle expository slides/papers from 2022 and 2025, and general web search) turned up no result, claim, or partial progress touching B(2,5) or the exponent-5 case since 26 January 2024. The current Wikipedia article (fetched live, for context only — not used as the frozen basis) still states plainly 'The particular case of B(2,5) remains open' and 'when the exponent is small and different from 2, 3, 4 and 6, very little is known.' The one piece of related motion in this area is Atkarskaya, Rips and Tent's result that B(m,n) is infinite for m≥2 and odd n≥557 (arXiv:2303.15997), improving the prior bound of 665. I checked its version history directly: the n≥557 bound was already the stated result in v3, submitted 22 June 2023 — before the window opens — with v4/v5 (March 2024) being later revisions of the same already-announced bound, not a new result. Even setting the date aside, n≥557 is a different case of the general problem (large exponents) from n=5, so it would not count as a change to this bullet's status under the scope rule (§3.1) even if it were newly dated. I also distinguished the free Burnside group B(2,5) (this bullet, unresolved) from the restricted Burnside group RB(2,5), whose finiteness (order 5^34) was settled by Kostrikin's theorem and computed by Wamsley in 1974 — a different, already-resolved object that some pages conflate with B(2,5); this predates the window by decades and is not the free group asked about here. No AI system appears anywhere in the sources I found relevant to the Burnside problem generally, including recent small-cancellation-theory and asymptotic-Burnside-laws papers (2024–2025) and the general AI-mathematics literature (AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, Lean formalization surveys) which never mention Burnside groups. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the 557-bound paper's final journal-of-record version or its v4/v5 arXiv revision (dated after 26 January 2024) should count as a fresh 'event' for the general Burnside problem bullet, since the paper was still being revised in the window and a careful reader dating by 'first written argument' could quibble about which version is the operative one. I reject this because the substantive numerical result (n≥557) did not change between v3 and v4/v5, and the case is exponent≥557, not exponent 5, so it would be `partial`/`progress` on a different case than the one asked about (B(2,5)), and dating rules (§6.3) call for the first public written argument, which was v3 in June 2023.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint, announcement, or computer-search result that explicitly determines whether B(2,5) is finite or infinite, or narrows the exponent bound below 557 into a range that includes or approaches 5, would settle or partially settle this. No such source was found.

outcome: A October 2025 preprint by Oscar Hill (arXiv:2510.08286) claimed an algebraic proof that no 3x3 magic square of nine distinct perfect squares exists, but an independent verification project (the CosmicWill GitHub repository) publicly refutes the proof's key step with an explicit counterexample witness; no expert digestion or journal acceptance of Hill's claim has been found. Separately, a September 2026 arXiv preprint by Auel and Singer studies the algebraic geometry of the surface parameterizing such squares, making genuine structural progress without resolving existence either way. The problem remains formally open.

disputes.summary: Oscar Hill's arXiv preprint 2510.08286 (v1 Oct 9 2025, v2 Oct 19 2025, v3 Apr 7 2026) claims a proof that no 3x3 magic square of nine distinct square integers exists, derived from properties of arithmetic progressions of odd numbers. An independent verification effort, the GitHub repository CosmicWill/magic-square-of-squares-3x3, publishes a dedicated refutation document (docs/refutations/2510.08286-hill.md) arguing that Hill's central equation (29) is merely an algebraic identity equivalent to an earlier lemma with 'no Diophantine content', and that the paper's final inference (that a certain coefficient must equal 1) fails on an explicit six-square-entry magic square witness with that coefficient equal to 6/5. No response from Hill, no journal acceptance, and no independent expert digestion (e.g. a blog post, review, or citation treating the result as established) was found on either side of this dispute as of the September 2026 v3 revision.

summary: The triage flagged Hill's October 2025 preprint (arXiv:2510.08286), which claims to prove that no 3x3 magic square of nine distinct perfect squares exists, via an algebraic contradiction built from arithmetic-progression pairs. Reading the paper (v1 full text) found no acknowledgement of any AI system, LLM, or automated theorem prover in its methodology or acknowledgements — the proof is presented as a hand-derived algebraic argument, checked, per the paper, by the author alone. Crucially, this claim is disputed: an independent GitHub research repository, CosmicWill/magic-square-of-squares-3x3, whose stated purpose is to rigorously investigate exactly this problem, contains a dedicated refutation document arguing Hill's key equation (29) carries no new arithmetic content beyond an earlier lemma, and that the paper's final step fails on an explicit witness square (six perfect-square entries, coefficient 6/5 rather than the required 1). That repository itself uses only conventional computational tools (SymPy, PARI/GP, gmpy2, Magma) for verification, and its README, RESEARCH_LOG.md, and refutation document contain no mention of any AI system either. Given a live, technically substantive, unrebutted dispute over Hill's proof, and no evidence any mathematician outside these two parties has digested or endorsed it, the claim cannot be treated as `resolved` nor even safely as `claimed` in isolation — I have classified the overall problem status as `progress` rather than `claimed`, since the one purported resolution is contested and not merely 'not yet digested' but actively rebutted on a specific technical point. Separately, and independently of the Hill dispute, a September 2026 preprint by Asher Auel and Benjamin Singer (arXiv:2609.09351, 'The algebraic geometry of 3-by-3 magic squares of squares') studies the singular complete-intersection surface in projective 8-space that parameterizes all 3x3 magic squares of squares, computing topological invariants, its automorphism group, and related del Pezzo/K3/Enriques surface structure. This is unambiguously about the problem as stated (the 3x3 case with distinct squares) and constitutes real mathematical progress — new structural understanding of the solution space — but the authors explicitly do not resolve existence either way, and no AI involvement is mentioned in its abstract. A related but distinct result, Rome and Yamagishi's proof (arXiv:2406.09364, published Research in Number Theory 2025) that n×n magic squares of squares exist for all n≥4, settling a conjecture of Várilly-Alvarado, is a different problem (n≥4) rather than a case of this n=3 bullet, so it is noted here but excluded from the status determination per §3.1's scope rule (changing n changes the question rather than restricting it, and here it goes the opposite direction — larger n, not a sub-case). I did not find any expert digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, or similar) of either the Hill preprint or the Auel–Singer paper.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is `claimed` rather than `progress`, on the reading that Hill's preprint is simply an unreviewed claim awaiting expert attention, and the CosmicWill repository — an anonymous/pseudonymous GitHub project rather than a named academic authority — should not be treated as the kind of 'expert' scrutiny that changes a classification. Under that reading the record would be `claimed`, `ai_role none`, with the dispute noted but not decisive. I preferred `progress` because the refutation is technically specific (an explicit numerical counterexample to a named inference step), unrebutted, and because treating an actively-contested claim as `claimed` risks implying a live, credible resolution exists when the strongest available evidence says it does not survive scrutiny.
what_would_settle_it: A response from Oscar Hill addressing the CosmicWill refutation (either a correction/withdrawal or a rebuttal of the witness counterexample), or an independent expert (a number theorist publishing a review, blog post, or citation) either endorsing Hill's proof or corroborating the refutation, would settle whether this is `resolved`, `open_stale`, or remains `open`/`progress`.

outcome: No result was found addressing whether a prime can be simultaneously a Wieferich prime base 2 (2^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p²) and base 3 (3^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p²); the question remains open with no theoretical or computational progress specific to it since 26 January 2024.
summary: This bullet asks whether a single prime p can satisfy both 2^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p²) (Wieferich prime base 2) and 3^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p²) (Wieferich prime base 3, a.k.a. Mirimanoff prime) simultaneously. As of the frozen revision, the only known base-2 Wieferich primes are 1093 and 3511, and the only known base-3 ones are 11 and 1006003, with no overlap, and a computational 'arms race' (culminating in PrimeGrid's completed search to 2^64, finished December 2022 — before the window) established that no such simultaneous prime exists below that bound. I searched extensively for any development since 26 January 2024: (1) whether PrimeGrid or another distributed-computing project extended the search bound past 2^64 — no such project was found; PrimeGrid's Wieferich search appears dormant since December 2022, and no new bound announcement was found; (2) whether any theoretical paper proved existence, non-existence, or any partial result narrowing this specific simultaneity question — none was found; recent arXiv papers on Wieferich primes (Wieferich primes in number fields, Aug 2025; Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules, Dec 2024; Wieferich and Mersenne primes for function fields, Dec 2025; Wieferich Primes and Monogenic Trinomials, May 2026) all concern generalizations to other algebraic settings (number fields, function fields, Drinfeld modules) or unrelated applications (monogenic trinomials), not the base-2/base-3 simultaneity question over the rationals; (3) whether any AI system (e.g., DeepMind's Gemini survey of Erdős problems, Feb 2026) touched this specific question — I found that a related but distinct object, 'double Wieferich prime pairs' (pairs of distinct primes p,q with p^(q-1)≡1 mod q² and q^(p-1)≡1 mod p²), has known examples, but this is a different concept (two different primes in a mutual relation, not one prime being Wieferich in two different fixed bases) and is not a case or variant relevant to this bullet. I also found that a Google DeepMind Gemini audit of Erdős problems surfaced an issue in the formal-conjectures repository concerning a *different* problem (Erdős-11, on whether non-Wieferich primes base 2 are infinite, via Granville–Soundararajan), and a related Erdős conjecture (Dupuy–Weirich, on digits of powers of 2 in base 3) connects both Wieferich bases 2 and 3 to a different question (digit patterns), not to simultaneity of one prime satisfying both congruences. None of this constitutes progress on, or AI involvement in, the specific problem stated in this bullet. I conclude the correct classification is 'open' with no change found.
competing_reading: None of the tangential results (double Wieferich pairs, Wieferich primes in number fields/function fields/Drinfeld modules, the Dupuy–Weirich digit conjecture) plausibly count even as a 'case' of this problem under §3.1, since they change the objects or question rather than restricting the stated one; I do not think a different classification is defensible here.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof that no prime can satisfy both congruences simultaneously, (b) discovery of an explicit prime satisfying both (which would also require it to individually be a Wieferich prime in each base, which is itself extremely rare), or (c) a new distributed-computing project extending the joint search bound past 2^64, which would be `progress` even though the question itself would remain open.

outcome: No progress on the four-cubes conjecture itself was found in the window; the two remaining unresolved residue classes modulo 18 (18x±4, 18x±5) are still open, as they were before January 2024.
summary: The sum-of-four-cubes problem (does every integer equal x³+y³+z³+w³ for integers x,y,z,w?) remains open. The Wikipedia article 'Sum of four cubes problem' (fetched live, reflecting content as of January 2026) still states the conjecture is unproven, with the same historical landmarks as before the frozen revision: Sierpiński and Schinzel (1959) and Demjanenko (1966) settled all residue classes mod 18 except 18x±4 and 18x±5, and the largest known non-representable integer remains 7,373,170,279,850 (Deshouillers–Hennecart–Landreau, 2000), still only conjectured to be the largest. No arXiv preprint, journal paper, blog post, or announcement dated after 26 January 2024 addresses either the two open residue classes or the finiteness of exceptions. Two tangentially related items were found and excluded as out of scope under §3.1: arXiv:2311.07325 (Choudhry, submitted Nov 2023 — predates the window anyway) proves results about sums of cubes of *polynomials*, a distinct algebraic framework, not integer cubes; and arXiv:2404.08193 (April 2024, revised March 2025) addresses the generalized Waring problem for *positive* k-th powers with 5≤k≤9, unrelated to k=3 with cubes of either sign. No AI-related coverage (DeepMind/AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve/Tao blog posts on AI math) mentions this problem among the conjectures those systems have tackled. This is a well-evidenced null result: the problem is niche, under-studied, and nothing in the primary literature, encyclopedic sources, or AI-mathematics announcements touches it in the window.
competing_reading: None found. The scope question (polynomial cubes vs. integer cubes; positive powers vs. signed cubes) was clear-cut in both excluded cases, not a close call.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement resolving the 18x±4 / 18x±5 residue classes, or a proof (or disproof, e.g. a new record non-representable integer beating 7,373,170,279,850) bearing on the Deshouillers–Hennecart–Landreau bound, dated after 26 January 2024.

The one notable event in the window — the September 2026 GNFS factorization of RSA-260 using an AI coding agent (Devin) for GPU implementation work — is a record factorization (largest number factored), not a change to the complexity of the problem, and the author explicitly states 'no algorithmic advancements' were made.
summary: No result changing this problem's status was found. The problem asks whether integer factorization can be solved in polynomial time on a classical computer; this remains open, with both the current (17 September 2026) revision of the Wikipedia article on integer factorization and multiple 2025-2026 sources confirming that 'no algorithm has been published that can factor all integers in polynomial time' and that existence/non-existence is unproven. I checked: (1) the triage's Zenodo find (Devashish Sonowal, 'Strongly polynomial-time integer factorization using Integer Linear Programming', 17 March 2025, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15041136) — this is an unreviewed self-published preprint with restricted-access files, no citations, no journal acceptance, and no corroboration anywhere; it does not rise even to 'claimed' status in a way that has moved the needle on expert consensus, and per §6.1 a claimed status requires at minimum a manuscript that is actually circulating and being discussed, which this is not (it is dated 2025-03, within the window, but I record it only as a non-credible claim, not as an event the status rests on). (2) The most substantively AI-related event in the window is the September 2026 factorization of RSA-260 (an 862-bit / 260-digit semiprime), the largest number factored in the public RSA Factoring Challenge to date, reported by Eric Lu of Cognition, who used Cognition's 'Devin' AI coding agent to build a GPU-accelerated implementation of CADO-NFS (general number field sieve), totaling about 4,900 GPU-days. This is a genuine and interesting AI-adjacent event, but by the authors' own account it involved 'essentially no algorithmic advancements' — GNFS is still the same sub-exponential (not polynomial-time) classical algorithm, and Devin's role was GPU performance engineering (writing a GPU lattice siever 'glas', optimizing linear algebra and polynomial selection for GPU memory systems) under close human direction (3,328 messages across 192 sessions), not producing new mathematics. Per §3.1, a factoring record (one more number factored, or a record table extended) is exactly the kind of narrowing move that does not advance an existence/complexity question like this one — the question is answered only by a proof or disproof that factoring is or is not in P. (3) Deterministic factorization complexity improvements (Hittmeir's N^(2/9+o(1)), Harvey's N^(1/5+o(1)), and later log-log refinements) are also sub-exponential-but-not-polynomial results, and in any case predate the window (2019-2021). (4) No AI system (AlphaEvolve, LLM-based theorem provers, etc.) was found to have made any progress specific to the factoring complexity question — AlphaEvolve's number-theory successes (minimum overlap problem, kissing numbers, matrix multiplication) do not include factoring. (5) Quantum computing results (Shor's algorithm implementations/records) are out of scope since the stated question is specifically about classical polynomial-time algorithms, and quantum hardware in the window remains far too limited to factor cryptographically relevant numbers regardless. I am satisfied nothing has changed this problem's open status in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the RSA-260/Devin event deserves a `progress` status with `ai_role: bound`, on the theory that record factorizations are evidence about the practical difficulty landscape even though they don't touch the P-time question. I rejected this because §3.1 explicitly says a record table extended does not advance an existence/infinitude/complexity question — 'Are there infinitely many X' and 'is this problem in P' are the same shape of question, answered only by resolving the universal claim, not by moving the frontier of known instances. The Sonowal preprint could alternatively be coded `claimed` since a preprint exists dated within the window; I did not do so because §6.1's `claimed` bar (a preprint or announcement that experts have not yet digested, but which is nonetheless a real currency in the field) implies a claim in circulation, whereas this is an unreviewed, uncited, access-restricted self-publication with no traction — treating every unverifiable independent claim as `claimed` would make that status meaningless as a filter.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed proof or disproof that FACTORING is or is not in P (or a widely-discussed preprint from a credible source making that claim, which would justify `claimed`); alternatively, evidence that the Sonowal preprint has been read, cited, or refuted by complexity theorists, which would change its evidentiary weight.

outcome: On 2026-08-19, Levent Alpöge announced an explicit C∞ (smooth) counterexample to the general Carathéodory conjecture — a smoothly embedded convex sphere with exactly one umbilic point of index 2 — via an X/Twitter post, with John-Paul Smith and Anthropic's Claude credited with checking the construction; a Lean formalization (8,013 lines, no sorry/axioms) exists but remains unmerged in the google-deepmind/formal-conjectures repository, with pull requests still marked draft and comments such as 'I'm currently checking this,' so no expert digestion or journal-level verification has yet been established.

ai.basis_quote: Alpöge credited John-Paul Smith and Claude with checking the construction.

counterexample.object: An explicit support function g₂ of a smoothly (C∞) embedded convex two-sphere in R^3 with exactly one umbilic point, of index 2 — the topologically minimal count rather than the conjectured minimum of two.
counterexample.verified_how: Human-constructed explicit support function, checked by a named human collaborator (John-Paul Smith) and by Claude; a Lean formalization (8,013 lines, no 'sorry' or declared axioms) was produced but has not been merged into the main branch of the google-deepmind/formal-conjectures repository, and associated pull requests remain in draft with reviewer comments indicating the check is still in progress.

disputes.summary: Brendan Guilfoyle and Wilhelm Klingenberg claim (2008, reaffirmed with further papers in 2025) to have proved the Carathéodory conjecture for surfaces of smoothness C^{3,α} (and, per Wikipedia's current article, for real-analytic surfaces per Hamburger 1940-41). The 2026 Alpöge counterexample is stated only for the strictly C∞ (smooth but not real-analytic, and below C^{3,α} in the relevant sense) category, so the two results are compatible rather than contradictory — the conjecture is claimed proved in the analytic/C^{3,α} regime and claimed false in the general smooth regime. Whether the Guilfoyle-Klingenberg proof itself is fully accepted by experts is a separate, longer-running dispute that predates the frozen revision and that this record does not attempt to adjudicate.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen (Jan 2024) wording of this bullet asks about 'any convex, closed, and twice-differentiable surface,' i.e. the general smooth case, which was open at the time modulo the disputed Guilfoyle-Klingenberg 2008 C^{3,α} proof. On 2026-08-19, Levent Alpöge (a mathematician who has since joined Anthropic) posted an explicit C∞ support function on X/Twitter giving a smoothly embedded convex sphere with a single umbilic point of index 2, directly refuting the conjecture in the C∞ category; per Wikipedia's current article on the conjecture and on Alpöge himself, he credited John-Paul Smith and Anthropic's Claude with 'checking the construction' — i.e., verifying a human-made construction rather than the AI producing the mathematics itself. A Lean formalization (8,013 lines, no sorry/axioms) was produced with help from Codex (OpenAI) for the formalization, but as of the check date it sits on an unmerged branch of google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, 11 commits diverged and 26 behind main, with draft pull requests and reviewer comments still saying the check is in progress; VibeMathed's own tracker labels the problem 'Candidate (review pending).' I found no expert digestion analogous to Terence Tao's write-up of Alpöge's earlier Jacobian-conjecture counterexample (Tao's post is explicitly about the Jacobian conjecture, not this one), and no journal acceptance or named-expert endorsement of the Carathéodory result. That combination — a clean explicit construction, informally checked by a named collaborator, with a Lean proof still unmerged and no independent expert digestion — is squarely 'claimed' rather than 'resolved.' Because the AI's documented role was checking/verifying a human construction rather than generating any of the mathematics that appears in the result, ai_role is 'none' under the rule that checking, proofreading or formalising does not count as AI involvement, however the announcement is publicized. This disagrees with the triage record's framing of the episode as straightforwardly 'AI-assisted,' so triage_disagreement is set.
competing_reading: One could argue for ai_role 'assisted' on the theory that an AI system checking a hard, delicate smooth-geometry construction before public announcement is itself a meaningful contribution that shaped whether the result was published — i.e., the check was load-bearing for the claim reaching publication, even if it didn't produce the construction. But the rule in §6.2 is explicit that checking/verifying, however much work it does, is 'none,' and no source I found has the authors saying the model produced any part of the mathematics (the construction, the choice of g₂, the index computation) — only that it checked what Alpöge had already built. A separate competing reading on status: if the unmerged Lean proof and Smith's check are treated as sufficient 'expert' verification, one could argue for 'resolved' rather than 'claimed'; I did not take this reading because Smith's own review comments ('I'm currently checking this') indicate the check was still open, and no independent digestion or journal acceptance was found.
what_would_settle_it: A merged, reviewed Lean proof in the formal-conjectures main branch; or a written expert digestion (Tao-style blog post, referee report, or journal acceptance) of Alpöge's construction; or public confirmation from John-Paul Smith or another named mathematician that the check is complete and the counterexample is correct.
