outcome: The main conjecture remains open, but a 2025 paper (published in Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics, also issued as a UNLV master's thesis by the same group) proved additional special cases of the conjecture, for totient values k = 2^t, 2p^s, 2^2 p, and 2pq (p, q distinct primes); no AI involvement is evident in either.
summary: The main conjecture — whether every value of Euler's totient function is attained by at least two integers — is still unresolved as of September 2026. Standard reference sources (the live Wikipedia article and MathWorld) both describe it as open, with the best-known lower bound on any counterexample still Kevin Ford's 1998/1999 result that a counterexample must exceed 10^(10^10) (equivalently, the conjecture is verified/true for all n below that bound); no sharper bound was found in the window. Within the window, a legitimate, peer-reviewed piece of progress appeared: 'On the special cases of Carmichael's totient conjecture' by Shannon, Shiue, He and Saito (Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics, received May 2025, accepted August 2025, published online 2025-08-15), which is the journal version of Christopher Saito's UNLV master's thesis (deposited 2025-05-15). This work proves the conjecture holds for all n with φ(n) = k in the specific forms k = 2^t, k = 2p^s, k = 2^2 p, and k = 2pq (p, q distinct primes) — a genuine restriction/case of the stated conjecture, so it is classified `partial` with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` (the settled cases go the way the conjecture predicts, i.e. multiplicity > 1 holds for them). Neither the journal article's fetched content nor the thesis abstract mentions any AI-tool assistance in deriving the results, so `ai_role` is `none`. The triage's two flagged items (an academia.edu page claiming a full proof, and a figshare 'note') were checked for accessibility: both academia.edu and figshare returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so their content could not be directly read; however, no secondary source, blog, forum, or citation anywhere in web search results treats either as a credible or discussed resolution — no journal acceptance, no expert digestion, no retraction notice, and no citation trail exists for the academia.edu 'proof' or the figshare 'note'. Given that the conjecture is a century-old, well-known open problem that would attract immediate expert attention if genuinely resolved, and given the complete absence of any uptake (no mention on Wikipedia, MathWorld, John D. Cook's number-theory blog which specifically discusses Carmichael's conjecture as recently as October 2025, or elsewhere), these are treated as uncredible/unreviewed amateur claims that do not constitute a resolution and are not separately counted as events. John D. Cook's blog post 'More on Carmethael' (2025-10-09) discusses only the existing verification bound (10^(10^10)) and makes no mention of any new proof, disproof, or AI involvement, corroborating that no headline change to the main conjecture has occurred.
competing_reading: One could argue the academia.edu/figshare claims deserve a `claimed` status entry of their own if their content could be read and shown to contain a genuine (if unreviewed) proof attempt — I could not fetch either page (403 errors) and found no secondary discussion of their content, so I cannot rule out that they contain something more substantive than the total silence around them suggests. However, the complete absence of any citation, discussion, or expert reaction to either item over the roughly 1-3 years they have been online strongly suggests they are not credible, and the correct default per the instructions is to not count an unreviewed, undigested, uncited claim as an event absent stronger evidence.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the academia.edu and figshare documents (e.g. via a logged-in session or an alternate mirror) to check whether they contain any coherent argument, combined with a search for any citations of either work in later papers or any mathematician's public comment on them.

outcome: Chen, Ghomi and Wang posted a preprint (10 Sep 2026, extended 17 Sep 2026) claiming to prove the Cartan-Hadamard conjecture in dimensions 3 through 9, extending the previously established range of dimensions 2-4; the claim is a preprint with no expert digestion yet.

ai.basis_quote: The AI tools Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) were used in the preparation of this manuscript. The authors have reviewed all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the final manuscript.

summary: The Cartan-Hadamard conjecture (sharp Euclidean isoperimetric inequality for Cartan-Hadamard manifolds) was known, at the frozen revision's date, for dimensions 2 (Weil 1926; Beckenbach-Rado 1933), 3 (Kleiner 1992) and 4 (Croke 1984); Ghomi and Spruck's widely-publicized 2019 claim of a full unconditional resolution was found to have a gap in early 2020, and their eventual published (2022, J. Geom. Anal.) result reduces the general conjecture to a total-curvature inequality rather than proving it outright — so the conjecture remained genuinely open in dimension >= 5 through the frozen date. In September 2026, Shibing Chen, Mohammad Ghomi and Peng Wang posted arXiv:2609.11005 (10 Sep 2026), proving the conjecture in dimension 5 via a sharp inequality for constant-mean-curvature hypersurfaces (in the spirit of Banchoff-Pohl) plus Jacobi-field estimates along geodesic chords, completed by a Kleiner-style isoperimetric-profile argument. A companion/extended paper by the same three authors, arXiv:2609.20517 (17 Sep 2026), extends the same method to give a unified proof covering all of dimensions 3-9 (also reproving dimension 3). One secondary source noted the dimension-5 argument leans on a regularity lemma (Ghomi-Spruck, Lemma 7.2) established only up to dimension 7, which is a detail worth flagging for anyone assessing the full 3-9 claim, but does not change the classification here. Both papers are very recent (5 and 12 days old at the time of this research) preprints with no journal acceptance, no Tao/Quanta/Terry Tao-blog digestion, and no independent expert verification found — hence `claimed` rather than `resolved`. The dimension-5 paper's acknowledgements disclose that 'The AI tools Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) were used in the preparation of this manuscript,' with authors stating they reviewed all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility; no detail is given on what the AI tools actually did, and nothing suggests they produced any mathematical content (a proof step, construction, or bound) rather than writing/editing assistance. Per the rules, a bare disclosure of this kind without the authors attributing any specific mathematical contribution to the AI is `ai_role: none`. Two further preprints found by triage are related-problem or partial results, not the (candidate) full resolution: arXiv:2609.14505 (Wheeler, 13 Sep 2026) proves the isoperimetric inequality only under an added curvature-pinching hypothesis relative to a reference radius of curvature — a restricted/conditional variant, not the stated conjecture; arXiv:2609.17093 (Agnoletto, Da Silva, Nardulli, Resende; 15 Sep 2026, rev. 21 Sep 2026) proves only the small-volume regime under an added lower Ricci bound, reducing the remainder to a rigidity question — also a restricted case with an extra hypothesis. Neither reports AI involvement.
competing_reading: One could argue the dimension 3-9 result should be treated as `partial` rather than `claimed`, on the reasoning that dimensions 3 and 4 were already resolved before 2024 and only 5-9 is new territory; I chose `claimed` because the paper's claimed scope (a unified proof for 3<=n<=9) is presented as, and would constitute if correct, a resolution of a large new swath of the conjecture including previously-unproven dimensions 5-9, which is closer to a leap in coverage than a single new case, and no expert has yet reviewed it to promote it to `resolved`. A different reading of the AI disclosure is also possible: an editor might argue that any acknowledged use of an AI system, however vague, should be flagged as `assisted` out of caution; I did not do this because the rule explicitly requires the authors' own account of the AI producing part of the mathematics in the result, and this disclosure states only 'preparation of this manuscript' with no claim that Claude or ChatGPT produced any proof step.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a referee report, journal acceptance, or a public write-up by another differential geometer such as on Terry Tao's blog or in a survey) confirming the dimension 3-9 argument is correct would move this to `resolved`; alternatively, a reported gap (as happened to Ghomi-Spruck in 2020) would keep it at `claimed`/`progress` or revert it. Clarification from the authors on exactly what Claude and ChatGPT were used for would settle whether `ai_role` should remain `none` or be reconsidered.

outcome: Soham Ghosh (University of Washington) posted a preprint in January 2025 claiming a complete proof of the Casas-Alvero conjecture for all degrees d>=3 over any characteristic-0 field, using Koszul homology; as of the March 2026 revision it remains an unreviewed preprint with no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification found. Separately, a genuinely peer-reviewed partial result (Schaub & Spivakovsky, Journal of Commutative Algebra, accepted January 2025) settled the conjecture's reformulated resultant-independence condition for the top three indices (i in {d-3, d-2, d-1}), and an earlier Ghosh preprint (Feb 2024) proved a finiteness result about the associated variety. No AI system was involved in any of this work.

disputes.summary: Ghosh's arXiv:2501.09272 claims a full resolution of the conjecture (confirming direction: every such polynomial is a d-th power of a linear polynomial) but has not been digested by experts as far as I could establish: it carries no journal acceptance, no cited independent verification, and was still being substantially revised (v1 15KB in Jan 2025 to v2 30KB in March 2026, described as 'major revisions') fourteen months after posting, which is itself a sign the argument was still being reworked rather than settled. Meanwhile the peer-reviewed Schaub-Spivakovsky paper only proves a restricted case (the top three resultant indices), leaving open whether Ghosh's broader claim is what actually closes the conjecture, a distinct result, or contains a gap the community has not yet flagged in searchable sources.

summary: Three distinct pieces of work touch this problem inside the window, none involving AI. (1) Soham Ghosh's arXiv:2501.09272 (submitted 2025-01-16, revised to v2 on 2026-03-21) claims a complete proof of the Casas-Alvero conjecture for every degree d>=3 over any characteristic-0 field, via Koszul homology and an analysis of 'almost counterexamples' using Brouwer degree techniques. I read the abstract and structure directly (fetched the PDF and abstract page); there is no acknowledgement of AI tool use, and no evidence the proof has been digested by an expert, accepted by a journal, or independently verified -- searches for retraction, error, or acceptance news turned up nothing, but the paper's own long gap between v1 and a 'major revision' v2 fourteen months later is itself evidence the argument was still being worked on, not settled. Given the standard here (resolved requires an expert digestion or journal acceptance; claimed is the right code for an unreviewed preprint however clean it looks), I classify this as claimed rather than resolved. (2) Independently, Daniel Schaub and Mark Spivakovsky published 'On the Casas-Alvero Conjecture' in the Journal of Commutative Algebra (received 2024-11-07, accepted 2025-01-12, published Summer 2025), a genuinely peer-reviewed result, but it only proves the reformulated resultant-independence condition for the top three indices i in {d-3, d-2, d-1} -- a partial case, not a full resolution. (3) Ghosh's earlier preprint arXiv:2402.18717 (submitted 2024-02-28) proved a finiteness result (the associated arithmetic Casas-Alvero scheme has finitely many rational points in any degree, and the variety is at most two-dimensional) -- also a partial, structural result predating and apparently feeding into the January 2025 full-proof claim. A later paper, arXiv:2608.14726 (Marashdeh, submitted 2026-08-12), gives further structural obstructions on any hypothetical counterexample (constraints on 'centred normal form', connections to MacMahon's determinant and 'bad primes') but explicitly does not claim to resolve the conjecture and does not reference Ghosh's work in the content I could access. I searched broadly for any AI system (LLM, AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, DeepMind formal-methods tools) touching this specific conjecture and found none; a 2025 'Gödel Test' LLM-conjecture benchmark and a 2026 'Formal Conjectures' verified-discovery benchmark were both checked directly and neither mentions Casas-Alvero.
competing_reading: One could argue the decisive event is the Schaub-Spivakovsky peer-reviewed partial result rather than Ghosh's unreviewed full-proof claim, since it is the only development in the window that has actually passed expert review, and under that reading status would be `partial` (direction confirmed, since the top-index cases matched the conjecture's prediction) rather than `claimed`. I chose `claimed` because Ghosh's paper, if correct, is a strictly larger event (full resolution vs. one case), and the rules ask for the decisive event the status rests on; but since I could not confirm expert acceptance of Ghosh's proof, a reader who weighs 'peer-reviewed but partial' above 'complete but unreviewed' would reasonably record this as `partial` instead.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from a specialist (a blog post, MathOverflow answer, or journal referee report) explicitly endorsing or rejecting Ghosh's Koszul-homology argument in arXiv:2501.09272, or a further arXiv revision/journal submission record showing acceptance, would settle whether `claimed` should become `resolved` (or be dropped if a flaw surfaces).

outcome: No proof, disproof, or scope-relevant progress on the conjecture itself was found; the only development since 26 January 2024 is a routine extension of the computational record for the aliquot sequence starting at 276 (to index 2157, exceeding 200 digits, as of November 2025), which per the existence/infinitude scope rule narrows nothing about whether the sequence is truly unbounded and does not count as progress on the conjecture.
summary: The Catalan–Dickson conjecture (every aliquot sequence eventually terminates at a prime-then-1-then-0, or cycles, i.e. no aliquot sequence is unbounded/non-repeating) remains fully open. I searched for proofs, disproofs, partial resolutions (e.g. a proof that some restricted class of starting values must terminate or must diverge), and any AI involvement, and found none. The main line of numerical evidence tracked by the community is the status of the 'Lehmer five' (276, 552, 564, 660, 966), the smallest starting values whose ultimate fate is unknown. The sequence starting at 276 — the most closely watched case — has had its computed trajectory extended further (OEIS A008892 records roughly 2145 terms/214 digits as of its last update, and a search result reports extension to index 2157 / >215 digits as of November 2025 via community computation, e.g. projects tracked at rieselprime.de and FactorDB), but this is a continuation of a decades-long manual/distributed-computing project (using standard integer factorization software), not a change to the mathematical status of the conjecture. Per the deep-dive rules (§3.1), an existence/unboundedness question like this one is not advanced by extending a numerical record further — the record narrows where an answer could hide, not whether the sequence is actually unbounded, so it is correctly excluded from 'progress'. The 2024 Guy–Selfridge counter-conjecture discussion (that aliquot sequences diverge for almost all even seeds) is unchanged background, not a new development. I found no arXiv preprints, journal papers, blog posts (Tao, Quanta, etc.), or lab announcements from 2024–2026 claiming any proof, disproof, or partial theoretical progress (e.g., a proven bound on how many even starting values could plausibly diverge), and no mention of any AI/LLM system being used in this area at all — only traditional distributed/manual computation (factorization software) for extending the 276 sequence. The Wikipedia article on aliquot sequences itself shows no update reflecting new developments beyond the same open-problem framing that existed before January 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the extension of the 276 sequence to a new record length/index is itself a form of 'progress' worth recording, since it is new computational work performed after the frozen date and is the kind of activity practitioners in this area consider meaningful. I did not classify it as such because the deep-dive rules are explicit that for an unboundedness/existence question, extending how far a sequence has been computed (a record) does not count unless the record IS the question being asked (e.g., 'what is the largest known X') — here the question is whether the sequence is infinite and non-repeating, and no finite amount of extension can answer that.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or heuristic-turned-rigorous argument) that some aliquot sequence is genuinely unbounded (confirming Guy–Selfridge and refuting Catalan–Dickson), or a proof that all aliquot sequences must terminate/cycle (confirming Catalan–Dickson), would settle the conjecture. Short of that, a rigorous theorem establishing that some explicit or provably-existing class of starting values must diverge (even without exhibiting one) would count as genuine progress; a longer computed trajectory for 276 or the other Lehmer-five numbers would not, per the scope rule.

outcome: No advance found: the primality/compositeness of the 6th Catalan-Mersenne number (and the general conjecture that all terms past some point are composite) remains undetermined; the number is too large for any known primality test or for GIMPS-style factor searches to have settled.
summary: Catalan's Mersenne conjecture concerns the sequence c0=2, c(n+1)=2^c(n)-1 (2, 3, 7, 127, 2^127-1, ...); the first five terms are known prime, and the conjecture (as Wikipedia frames it) is that some term becomes composite and all terms past that point are composite. Nothing in the window (26 Jan 2024 to 22 Sep 2026) advances this. The current Wikipedia articles for 'Catalan–Mersenne number' (fetched via the live page, last substantively updated per its own text and cross-checked against 'Double Mersenne number', updated 2 Jan 2026) both state plainly that no known method can establish the primality or compositeness of the 6th term (c5 = M(M127)) 'in any reasonable time' because of its size (~10^(10^37.7)), and that no factor below the searched bound has been found for the related double Mersenne candidate MM61. The only item the triage pass surfaced, a May 2024 preprints.org manuscript ('Hyperbolic Primality Test and Catalan–Mersenne Number Conjecture'), proposes a new primality-test heuristic and discusses the conjecture but does not establish compositeness of any further term; it is also unreviewed and, being posted May 2024, is inside the window but does not constitute a resolution, claim of resolution, or bound-moving result on this specific conjecture — I could not fetch the manuscript directly (403 Forbidden) but its title and abstract-level description (via search) confirm it is a proposed method paper, not a settled result, so nothing about it changes the status. A separate item found during this run, a Zenodo preprint by Chua Cheong Siong ('Catalan Mersenne numbers and discovery of the 53rd and 54th Known Mersenne primes', submitted to Inventiones Mathematicae 24 Sep 2025, still under review) claims to have found new (ordinary) Mersenne primes and even 'infinitely many Mersenne primes' — a vastly larger claim than resolving the Mersenne-prime-infinitude problem itself. This has zero uptake in any secondary source, no digestion, is not indexed on arXiv, and a claim of that magnitude going unremarked anywhere in the mathematical community strongly indicates it is not a credible mathematical result; in any case its abstract-level description does not claim to resolve the Catalan-Mersenne conjecture specifically (compositeness of the 6th term), so even taken at face value it would not count under this record's scope. No GIMPS or double-Mersenne search project (mersenne.org, doublemersennes.org) reports a new factor for MM61/MM89/MM107/MM127 in the window. No AI system was found associated with any activity on this problem. The status is 'open' with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: If the Zenodo/Chua preprint's claim of 'infinitely many Mersenne primes' were ever validated by experts, it would settle much more than this conjecture (it would resolve the classical Mersenne-prime infinitude question), and depending on its content it might also bear on double Mersenne numbers/Catalan-Mersenne numbers. But there is no evidence of expert engagement, no arXiv posting, and 'under review' at a journal is not evidence of correctness — extraordinary claims of this kind that lack any community discussion are conventionally treated as unverified/likely incorrect until shown otherwise. I could not open the PDF to check whether it even addresses c5's compositeness (the description only says it discusses Catalan-Mersenne numbers in the title, not that it resolves their conjecture), so this is treated as not counting, per §3.1 and the general evidentiary bar for 'claimed'.
what_would_settle_it: A digested proof or a machine-verified factorization/primality certificate for the 6th Catalan-Mersenne number (or any further term), accepted by number theorists (e.g., discussed on t5k.org/Mersenne Research pages, GIMPS/doublemersennes.org project results, or a peer-reviewed paper); alternatively, expert commentary (positive or negative) on the Chua/Zenodo preprint's claims would clarify whether that work has any bearing at all.

outcome: The general conjecture (that a d-degenerate graph's (d+2)-coloring reconfiguration graph has quadratic diameter) remains open, including the long-flagged d=2 case, but several papers in the window moved related bounds: a September 2025 preprint proves a *linear* recoloring diameter for d-degenerate chordal graphs and for bounded-treewidth graphs, though only at higher color counts (t≥2d+1, resp. t≥2k+1) than the conjecture's own threshold of d+2 colors, so it is a related strengthening at a different parameter regime rather than a resolution of a case of the conjecture as stated; a December 2024 paper pins down exact (not just asymptotic) recoloring diameters for complete bipartite graphs K_{p,q}; and a December 2025 paper determines extremal (max/min) 3-coloring diameters of trees, sharpening constants in the already-known linear d=1 case.
summary: Cereceda's conjecture, posed in Cereceda's 2007 PhD thesis and stated on Wikipedia as: for a d-degenerate graph G and any t ≥ d+2, the t-recoloring diameter of G is O(n²), remains open in general and specifically at the flagged easy-looking case d=2 (confirmed still open as of the Wikipedia article's current text, checked live). I found three papers with arXiv dates inside the 26 Jan 2024 – 22 Sep 2026 window that touch this cluster of problems. (1) Wang and Lu, 'Linear recoloring diameter of degenerate chordal graphs and bounded treewidth graphs' (arXiv:2509.15456, v1 18 Sep 2025), the paper the triage pass flagged: it proves an O(n) (linear, stronger than the conjectured quadratic) recoloring diameter for d-degenerate chordal graphs when t≥2d+1 colors are used, and for graphs of treewidth at most k when t≥2k+1 colors are used. I fetched the paper's HTML directly (not just the abstract) and confirmed it explicitly states Cereceda's conjecture in its introduction as the t≥d+2 quadratic-diameter statement, and frames its own results as exceeding that bound in strength (linear vs quadratic) but at a materially larger number of colors (2d+1 or 2k+1 rather than d+2). Because the conjecture is a statement about the specific threshold t=d+2, a result requiring roughly twice as many colors is progress on a closely related question (how many colors are needed for a linear, rather than merely quadratic, bound) rather than a proof of a case of the conjecture as Wikipedia states it — no case at the conjectured threshold t=d+2 was newly settled by this paper. I classified this as 'progress' rather than 'partial' for that reason; see competing_reading. (2) Cambie, Cames van Batenburg and Cranston, 'Sharp Bounds on Lengths of Linear Recolouring Sequences' (arXiv:2412.19695, v1 27 Dec 2024, published EJC 33(1) P1.18 in 2026): exactly determines (up to a small additive constant) the k-recoloring diameter of complete bipartite graphs K_{p,q} for all k≥3. This is a case of a related but distinct question (exact diameter constants for a specific graph family known to already have linear diameter) rather than new territory on the conjecture's own quadratic-vs-not question; I could not fully extract its acknowledgements/introduction text (PDF extraction failed) so I did not confirm from primary text whether it discusses Cereceda's conjecture explicitly, though the abstract and secondary description tie it to the same recoloring-diameter research programme. (3) Asgarli, Krehbiel, MacLean and Zaimi, 'Extremal diameters of 3-coloring graphs of trees' (arXiv:2512.03789, v1 3 Dec 2025): for trees (which are 1-degenerate, so this is the t=d+2=3 case), determines the exact maximum and minimum 3-coloring diameter over all n-vertex trees and the extremal trees achieving them. Its introduction explicitly invokes Cereceda's conjecture (quoted: 'Cereceda conjectured that the diameter of the k-coloring graph of a d-degenerate graph on n vertices is O(n^d)') and frames the tree work as refining the already-linear d=1 case (proved before 2024 by Bonamy, Johnson, Lignos, Patel and Paulusma) down to exact constants. None of the three papers' methods sections, acknowledgements, or any secondary source I found mentions any AI system, language model, or automated theorem-proving tool; searches for AI/LLM involvement specifically tied to Cereceda's conjecture returned nothing relevant. All work in the window is conventional human mathematics.
competing_reading: One could argue 2509.15456 deserves 'partial' rather than 'progress', on the reading that proving a *stronger* conclusion (linear diameter) at a *larger* color count is still 'about' the conjecture's graph classes (degenerate chordal, bounded treewidth) even though the color threshold differs, and that a linear bound at t=2d+1 trivially implies nothing about the quadratic bound at t=d+2 (fewer colors is a harder, not easier, regime), so strictly the paper doesn't settle any case of the stated conjecture at all — it answers a different, harder-in-one-sense/easier-in-another-sense related question. Under a stricter application of §3.1's case/variant test, this could even be classified as a 'related problem' (changing the number of colors changes the question) rather than a case, pushing toward 'open' with no_change_found note about the near-miss. I kept 'progress' as a middle reading: it is closely enough tied to the same conjecture (explicitly discussed by the authors as such) and to the same graph classes that dismissing it as wholly unrelated seems too strict, but it does not settle a case at the conjectured threshold, so 'partial' (which implies a case of the actual stated question was settled) seemed too strong.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving the O(n²) bound (or refuting it) at exactly t=d+2 colors for any degeneracy class beyond what was already known before Jan 2024 (trees, d=1; planar bipartite/degeneracy-3 case; treewidth-2) — in particular any progress on the flagged d=2 case, which as of the live Wikipedia article and my searches is still completely open, with no polynomial bound known even at the conjectured color count.

outcome: A May 2026 preprint by Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian gives a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for near-triangulations (planar graphs in which every bounded face is a triangle), settling a substantial subclass of planar graphs while leaving the general planar-graph characterization open.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Characterise (non-)word-representable planar graphs' is stated as the general problem of deciding word-representability for arbitrary planar graphs. As of January 2024, only partial results were known: triangle-free planar graphs are word-representable, and K4-free near-triangulations are word-representable iff 3-colourable. In May 2026, Roy and Hariharasubramanian (arXiv:2605.25733, 'Characterization of Word-Representable Near-Triangulations') obtained a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for the entire class of near-triangulations — including those containing K4, which the Wikipedia article explicitly flags as a previously open sub-question ('a characterisation is known for K4-free planar graphs' but not for K4-containing near-triangulations). The paper states it 'unifies previous findings across multiple subclasses—including polyomino triangulations, K4-free near-triangulations, and chordal near-triangulations—while also correcting errors in earlier research.' This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem (near-triangulations are a proper subclass of planar graphs, not a different problem), so under §3.1 it counts as a case settled, classified `partial`, direction `confirmed` (the characterization proves what was sought — a full description of the word-representable members — rather than refuting an expectation). The general planar-graph problem, and other planar subclasses beyond near-triangulations, remain open. I read the full PDF (via WebFetch) and found no mention of AI, machine learning, automated theorem provers, or SAT/computer search in the proof method or any acknowledgements section; the paper reads as traditional combinatorial/graph-theoretic argument (forbidden induced subgraphs via case analysis on triangulation structure). No retraction or dispute found; this appears to be a single, recent, undigested-by-experts preprint (no journal acceptance or expert digestion found), which is why it is classified `partial` rather than `resolved` for that piece — though note `partial` per the schema does not itself distinguish digestion status the way `resolved`/`claimed` do for full resolutions; I am treating 'digested' as not required for a `partial` case-result the way it is for a full `resolved`, since the schema's resolved/claimed distinction is specifically about full resolutions of the stated problem. The earlier arXiv:2508.15177 ('On the word-representability of Km-Kn graphs') found by triage studies a different graph family (complete multipartite-type graphs) and is not planar-specific, so it does not bear on this bullet — I did not rely on it.
competing_reading: One could argue near-triangulations, while formally a subclass of planar graphs, are close enough to being 'the interesting case' (triangle-rich planar graphs) that this is effectively most of the way to resolving the general problem — but the paper itself does not claim to settle general planar graphs, and non-near-triangulation planar graphs (e.g. those with larger non-triangular bounded faces) are untouched, so `partial` rather than `resolved` or a stronger characterization is the correct read. A stricter reading could also argue this is 'progress' rather than 'partial' since it's a preprint without expert digestion, but the schema's `partial` label is about scope (a case settled) rather than digestion status, which is orthogonal here since the case itself is fully and rigorously characterized (forbidden induced subgraphs), just not yet externally verified by other experts.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (survey citation, journal acceptance, or independent verification) of arXiv:2605.25733 would move this specific case toward being treated as solid; a further paper extending the characterization to all planar graphs (not just near-triangulations) would resolve the Wikipedia bullet itself.

outcome: The general problem (find the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs characterizing all word-representable graphs) remains open, but several restricted cases have been fully settled since 26 January 2024: word-representable split graphs, co-bipartite graphs, K_m-K_n (complete bipartite) graphs with a small side, and near-triangulations each now have complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterizations, all obtained by ordinary human mathematical proof with no AI involvement.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for a characterisation of word-representable graphs (a hereditary class defined via semi-transitive orientations) by minimal forbidden induced subgraphs, in general. This general problem is still explicitly open: the current live Wikipedia article on word-representable graphs (checked 2026-09) still lists exactly this sentence as an open problem, and no source found states or implies the general question has been answered. However, since the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) a cluster of papers has settled the analogous question for successively larger restricted classes, each a genuine restriction (case) of the stated problem rather than a variant: (1) arXiv:2507.08483 (Roy & Hariharasubramanian, submitted 11 Jul 2025) gives a minimal forbidden induced subgraph characterization of word-representable split graphs with an independent set of size 4, explicitly answering an open question posed by Kitaev and Pyatkin; (2) arXiv:2512.12259 (Srinivasan & Hariharasubramanian, Dec 2025) gives a complete forbidden induced subgraph characterization of word-representable split graphs generally, via a new 'I-circular property' on matrices; (3) arXiv:2512.12274 (same authors, Dec 2025) does the analogous thing for co-bipartite graphs; (4) arXiv:2508.15177 (Chen, Hameed, Kitaev, Aug 2025) characterizes word-representability of K_m-K_n graphs when the smaller side has size at most 4; (5) arXiv:2605.25733 (Roy & Hariharasubramanian, May 2026) gives a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representable near-triangulations, unifying and correcting earlier partial results and exhibiting a new minimal non-word-representable graph on 7 vertices. I opened and read all six papers the triage found (including arXiv:2502.06979 on minimal forbidden induced subgraphs relating word-representable and comparability graphs, Kenkireth/Sajith/Sasidharan, Feb 2025). None mentions any AI, machine learning, or LLM tool; all are proved by direct combinatorial/matrix-theoretic argument. A search result referenced a 2019 paper (arXiv:1909.09471, well before the window) that used a 'computational' (brute-force, non-AI) characterization for split graphs with clique size 5 — that predates the frozen revision and is unrelated to AI in any case, so it is noted here only to rule it out. Net: the problem is `partial` because genuine sub-cases have been fully settled since the window opened, each in the 'confirmed' direction (a characterization was found, matching the expectation that such classes admit finite forbidden-subgraph characterizations), with `ai_role` none throughout — this appears to be an active but entirely human research programme (much of it out of IIT Guwahati) with no AI contribution found anywhere in it.
competing_reading: One could argue each restricted-class paper (split graphs, co-bipartite graphs, K_m-K_n, near-triangulations) is a 'related problem' rather than a 'case' of the stated problem, since the stated bullet asks for a characterization of word-representable graphs in general and these papers work within proper hereditary subclasses rather than removing territory from the general class. But per §3.1 a case is what you get by restricting the stated question to a class of objects, which is exactly what split graphs, co-bipartite graphs, etc. are (subclasses of general graphs), so I classify these as genuine cases/partial progress rather than variants. The general characterization itself is unambiguously still open.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (or Wikipedia edit) explicitly claiming a complete minimal-forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization for word-representable graphs in general (not restricted to any subclass) would move this to resolved/claimed. Absent that, continued accumulation of solved subclasses keeps it at partial.

outcome: A May 2026 preprint by Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian ('Characterization of Word-Representable Near-Triangulations', arXiv:2605.25733) claims a complete forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization of word-representability for near-triangulations in general (not restricted to K4-free graphs), which would resolve the case this bullet names as open. It has not yet been digested by any expert, journal, or survey.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet (posed by the 2016 paper 'Colourability and word-representability of near-triangulations', arXiv:1605.01688, which characterised K4-free near-triangulations and left near-triangulations containing K4 as open, since K4 is non-3-colourable and the colouring-based approach used for the K4-free case does not apply) is squarely addressed by arXiv:2605.25733 (submitted 25 May 2026, single version, no later revisions or errata visible on arXiv). Its abstract states the paper gives 'a complete characterization of word-representable near-triangulations in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs' that 'unifies and extends the previously known characterizations for [polyomino triangulations, K4-free near-triangulations, face subdivisions of triangular grid graphs, triangulations of grid-covered cylinder graphs, and chordal near-triangulations], while also correcting inaccuracies appearing in earlier works.' The main result, Theorem 16 in the fetched HTML rendering, is stated for general near-triangulations ('Let G be a near-triangulation. Then G is word-representable if and only if it contains none of the graphs from Figure 8 as an induced subgraph'), with no K4-free restriction, so on its face it covers the K4-containing case this bullet asks about. I was not able to render the full PDF body (only metadata and an incompletely-decoded content stream came through two separate fetch attempts), so I could not independently verify the forbidden-subgraph list in Figure 8 or check the proof of Theorem 16 line by line; my reading of the theorem statement rests on an automated HTML extraction rather than my own read of the typeset proof. No journal listing, conference abstract, citing paper, or expert commentary (blog, Mathoverflow, Kitaev's own subsequent papers) discusses this specific preprint yet — it is four months old at the time of this research and appears to be genuinely unreviewed. A site called pith.science hosts an AI-generated review of the paper, but that is third-party automated commentary on the paper, not an expert digestion, and in any case I could not retrieve its actual review text (the fetch returned empty content twice). No acknowledgements section, methods statement, or any language anywhere in the paper, its arXiv listing, or secondary discussion indicates any AI system was used by the authors in producing the characterization or its proof; this appears to be ordinary human graph-theory research. Given a single, very recent, unreviewed preprint with a claim that (on its stated theorem) resolves the open case, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved', with resolution_direction 'confirmed' since the claimed result answers the characterization question rather than refuting the possibility of a clean characterization.
competing_reading: It is conceivable that Theorem 16's forbidden-subgraph list, despite being stated for 'near-triangulations' unqualified, is only actually verified/proved by the authors for the K4-free and previously-studied subclasses being unified, with the K4-containing extension resting on a gap or an implicit assumption not visible in the metadata-level extraction I obtained. Because I could not read the full proof (only the theorem statement, via an automated HTML-to-text extraction rather than my own direct read of the source), I cannot rule out that the 'K4-containing' generalization is weaker than the abstract suggests, e.g. restricted to a specific K4-containing subclass rather than fully general. If so, the correct status would still be 'partial' rather than 'claimed' for the full open problem, and 'claimed' for a case of it.
what_would_settle_it: A direct read of the full typeset PDF (Sections stating and proving Theorem 16 and the definition/enumeration of Figure 8's forbidden subgraphs), or an expert digestion (journal referee report, citing survey, or a specialist's blog/MathOverflow commentary) confirming the theorem's scope explicitly includes near-triangulations containing K4 as an induced subgraph, not just the previously-solved K4-free and named subclasses.

outcome: No progress on the general characterization (Hasse's problem) of which algebraic number fields admit a power integral basis. Research since 26 January 2024 continues in the same vein as before that date: family-specific monogenity criteria (trinomials, quadrinomials, pure cubic/octic fields, sextic fields with a real quadratic subfield, polynomial compositions), none of which advance the general classification question.
summary: The bullet asks for a characterization of all algebraic number fields admitting a power (integral) basis — this is the classical problem attributed to Hasse, of deciding for which number fields the ring of integers is monogenic (Z_K = Z[α] for some α). This is a genuine 'characterize all X' question, so per §3.1 it moves only when a general characterization is proved, not when another special family is settled. I searched arXiv, Google Scholar-style web search, and read I. Gaál's 2024 survey 'Monogenity and Power Integral Bases: Recent Developments' (arXiv:2407.00374, published in Axioms 13(7):429, July 2024) which is the standard up-to-date digestion of this subfield. The survey opens by stating the classical problem and then, rather than presenting any general characterization, catalogs decades of incremental, family-by-family results (pure fields, trinomials, quadrinomials, sextic/octic fields, etc.), and its 'Further Research' section explicitly poses open questions about even restricted cases (e.g., quartic and quintic fields in general, or arbitrary trinomials of degree ≤9), confirming the general problem is unsolved and was treated as such as of mid-2024. I then searched specifically for post-January-2024 work: results include a 2025 paper on quadrinomial monogenic fields (Chatterjee/Kumar, Springer Research in Number Theory 2025, arXiv:2408.14117), 2025 work on pure/octic fields, sextic fields with real quadratic subfields (arXiv:2505.04293), polynomial compositions (arXiv:2606.09739), and pure number fields with non-squarefree discriminants (arXiv:2506.16496). Every one of these is scoped to a specific polynomial family or field type — each is a 'case' in the §3.1 sense (restricting the question to a class), not a step toward a general characterization, and none of the papers claims to advance the overall classification. None of these papers, nor any secondary source found, mentions any AI system (LLM, neural network, or other machine-learning method) being used in obtaining these results; the methods described throughout (Newton polygons, Dedekind's criterion, Thue/index-form equation solving, Baker-type bounds) are traditional computational algebraic number theory, implemented in systems like Magma, not AI. This matches the triage record's conclusion of verdict 'none', and I did not find grounds to disagree with it.
competing_reading: One could argue that the accumulation of many family-specific characterizations over the years constitutes incremental progress toward a full characterization, since it maps out where monogenicity criteria are understood. But per §3.1, a case is a restriction of the stated question, and it does not move the general 'characterize all fields' status forward in the sense the status field tracks — it would only count as `partial` if it settled a scoping question. Wikipedia's bullet asks for a characterization of 'all' fields, and no source treats any of these family results as contributing to that general characterization (rather than being isolated special cases), so I classify as `open` rather than `partial`. If a future reader believes even one of these family papers should count as `partial` progress (settling monogenicity for an entire infinite class, e.g. all pure octic fields), that is a defensible alternative reading, but it does not change the overall open status of the general characterization problem, nor introduce any AI involvement.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or survey that proposes and proves (or substantially narrows) a general arithmetic criterion applicable across number fields of all/most degrees for admitting a power integral basis — as opposed to a criterion tied to one polynomial shape or field family — would settle whether real progress on the general problem occurred. Absent that, the status remains open.

outcome: The general conjecture remains open; work since January 2024 consists of survey/strategy papers and technical tools within the Borovik/Hrushovski program, plus resolutions of a distinct, differently-named conjecture (Borovik-Cherlin) that shares an author's name but is not a case of the Cherlin-Zilber algebraicity conjecture.
summary: The Cherlin-Zilber (algebraicity) conjecture — every infinite simple group of finite Morley rank is a simple algebraic group over an algebraically closed field — remains open, and I found no result since 26 January 2024 that settles the general conjecture, settles a new case (rank, type, or class) of it, or moves a bound on it. The current Wikipedia article's most recent cited progress is Altinel-Borovik-Cherlin (2008) plus Frécon's elimination of Morley-rank-3 bad groups, which appeared in JAMS in 2018 (arXiv work from 2016-2017) — well before the frozen revision, so it is not a window event. Since January 2024 I found: (1) Berkman & Borovik, 'Groups acting generically multiply transitively...' and related affine-type papers (arXiv:2405.07307, May-Dec 2024) which are structural lemmas in the Borovik classification program, not case settlements; (2) Kowalski & Uğurlu Kowalski, 'On generic and supertight automorphisms' (arXiv:2604.20415, April 2026), giving partial evidence for a Hrushovski-suggested principle ('fixed points are pseudofinite') used in the classification strategy, explicitly not a resolution; (3) Berkman & Borovik, 'The Şiş Kebap Theorem: A Generic Identification Theorem for Groups of Finite Morley Rank' (arXiv:2608.01161, August 2026), a conditional identification theorem (Theorem 1.2, under Prüfer-rank and torus-structure hypotheses A-C) intended as 'Step 6' of a six-step strategy in the Hrushovski Programme — a technical tool, not an unconditional case settlement, since its hypotheses are themselves open problems in the program; and (4) Katrin Tent's 'From the Cherlin-Zilber Conjecture via sharply 2-transitive groups to the Burnside problem' (arXiv:2606.18207, June 2026, to appear in ICM 2026 proceedings), an explicit survey that states no new result and instead discusses sharply-2-transitive groups as a potential source of counterexamples. Separately, I found a cluster of papers proving the 'Borovik-Cherlin conjecture' (arXiv:2106.02537, 2021/2025; arXiv:2609.02198, September 2026) — but per arXiv:2106.02537 and the Berkman-Borovik generic-transitivity literature, this is a distinct conjecture about generic multiple-transitivity bounds for definable homogeneous spaces (k ≤ RM(S)+2, and characterizing generically (n+2)-transitive actions as PGL_{n+1}), applicable across stable theories including ACF₀, differentially closed fields, and compact complex manifolds — not a restriction of the Cherlin-Zilber algebraicity statement about simple groups of finite Morley rank. It shares Cherlin's name (and, in the finite-Morley-rank case, overlapping authors and techniques) but is a different question under §3.1's related-problem/case-of-the-problem test, so its resolutions in ACF₀/CCM (2025) and now arbitrary characteristic (Karhumäki & Ramsey, arXiv:2609.02198, September 2026) do not count as progress on the bullet as stated. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature: none of the papers I opened mention AI, LLM, or machine-learning assistance, and broader searches for AI-assisted work touching finite-Morley-rank group theory turned up nothing intersecting this conjecture. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'no change' rather than a gap in my search: I checked the current Wikipedia article, the most recent arXiv listings under math.GR and math.LO citing Cherlin-Zilber or algebraicity conjecture, the 2026 ICM survey (which is itself a comprehensive contemporary account with no new result), and cross-checked the namesake conjecture that could plausibly be miscounted as a case.
competing_reading: Someone building the numerator from titles or acknowledgements alone could easily miscount the Borovik-Cherlin conjecture's 2025-2026 resolutions (arXiv:2106.02537's ACF₀/CCM cases and arXiv:2609.02198's extension to arbitrary characteristic) as progress on Cherlin-Zilber, since both share Cherlin as a co-namesake and both concern finite-Morley-rank-adjacent stable-theoretic structures. Under a looser scope reading where any theorem invoking 'finite Morley rank' groups counts, the Şiş Kebap Theorem (arXiv:2608.01161) might also be read as 'partial' progress rather than a conditional tool, since it does unconditionally identify a restricted class of groups as Chevalley groups under stated hypotheses A-C. I judge these hypotheses are themselves unresolved parts of the classification program (making the result a strategic lemma, not a case settlement of the conjecture as stated), but a reader who considers 'discharging one lemma toward a six-step program' sufficient for `partial` status could reasonably disagree.
what_would_settle_it: A precise reading (or a co-author's clarification) of whether Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2608.01161 applies unconditionally to a nonempty class of previously-unclassified simple groups of finite Morley rank (which would make it `partial`), versus applying only under hypotheses that are themselves still open (making it a conditional tool, as I've classified it); and confirmation from a model theorist that the Borovik-Cherlin conjecture is formally understood as conceptually distinct from, rather than a special case of, the Cherlin-Zilber algebraicity conjecture.

outcome: M. Cocos posted a long-dormant 2015 preprint (arXiv:1504.04852) through a series of major revisions from March 2025 through December 2025 (v4-v12), now titled 'A Proof of Chern's Conjecture for Flat Affine Manifolds,' claiming a proof for the flat (torsion-free, holonomy in GL(n,R) acting affinely) sub-case; the claim has not been digested, published, or endorsed by any expert source found, and the live Wikipedia article and other surveys continue to describe the conjecture as open.

disputes.summary: The claimed proof (arXiv:1504.04852) has undergone at least nine major revisions in 2025 alone (v4 in March through v12 in December), consistent with the author repeatedly patching gaps or errors found (by referees, readers, or self-review) rather than the claim being accepted as-is. No published referee report, journal acceptance, or expert blog/forum digestion (MathOverflow, Terence Tao's blog, etc.) was found endorsing or refuting the current version. The AMS Fall 2025 Western Sectional talk describing it as 'A posible [sic] proof' (not 'a proof') is itself hedged language from the author's own abstract.

A separate 2016 claim of a general proof by Huitao Feng and Weiping Zhang was found to have a serious flaw and was retracted (their corrected result instead gives an Euler-number formula for flat vector bundles); a 2020 claimed proof by Jianquan Ge (arXiv:2002.03105) was also withdrawn after errors were found (a Hessian-representation error identified by Andrea Clini, followed by the author's own discovery of an error in commutation of limits). Both of these predate the 26 January 2024 frozen revision and are recorded as history, not as events in the window.

summary: The problem as stated in this bullet is Chern's conjecture in full generality: the Euler characteristic of a compact affine manifold vanishes. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 - present), the only substantive development is Mihail Cocos's arXiv:1504.04852, a paper originally posted in 2015 (v1-v3, pre-window) that lay dormant until being extensively revised starting 31 March 2025 (v4) through 6 December 2025 (v12), now claiming a proof of the conjecture restricted to closed FLAT affine manifolds (i.e., manifolds admitting a flat, torsion-free affine connection) via a deformation argument on the Euler form using Stokes' theorem and a holonomy rigidity theorem. This is a genuine case of the stated problem (flat affine manifolds are a well-studied and important sub-class of compact affine manifolds, explicitly discussed in the problem's own Wikipedia article as the setting of Chern's original 1955 conjecture and of prior partial results by Kostant-Sullivan, Klingler, Hirsch-Thurston, etc.), so it counts under the §3.1 scope rule if credible - not a variant. However, I could find no evidence that any expert has read through and endorsed this proof: no journal acceptance, no MathOverflow or Tao-blog discussion, no citation as an established result in the one related paper I found citing it (arXiv:2510.09648, 'Affine-Orthogonal Manifolds and Deformation to Levi-Civita Connections,' Oct 2025), which cites Cocos's Theorem 2.3 only as 'evidence for Chern's conjecture,' not as a completed proof. The paper's own AMS Fall 2025 abstract is hedged ('A posible proof'), and the pattern of nine major revisions across nine months in 2025 is consistent with an unsettled, still-being-patched argument rather than a verified result. The current live Wikipedia article (checked today) still states the conjecture 'remains an unsolved mathematical problem' with no mention of Cocos's claim at all. Given all this, I classify status as 'claimed' (a preprint that experts have not yet digested) rather than 'resolved' or even 'partial' with confidence, and resolution_direction as 'confirmed' since the claimed result -- if correct -- would prove the flat case as conjectured (no counterexample, no refutation). I found absolutely no mention of AI/ML involvement anywhere in Cocos's paper, the AMS abstract, or any secondary source discussing it, and no lab or system is credited by anyone; ai_role is 'none'. I did also verify the pre-window history recorded in Wikipedia (Feng-Zhang 2016 retraction, Ge 2020 withdrawal) to confirm neither creates an open_stale situation -- both predate the window and neither was ever accepted, so they don't affect the window's classification.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be classified as 'open' with no_change_found, on the theory that an unrefereed, still-being-revised preprint with no expert uptake represents essentially no change to what a careful encyclopedia entry would say (which is exactly what the live Wikipedia article does -- it doesn't mention Cocos at all). Under that reading the nine-revision pattern is noise, not signal. I chose 'claimed' instead because the instructions define 'claimed' precisely as this situation (a preprint or announcement that experts have not yet digested) and distinguish it from 'open' specifically so that live, contested claims are visible in the dataset rather than folded into silence. The alternative classification names the same underlying facts but treats the lack of digestion as disqualifying rather than as the defining feature of 'claimed'.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance or a public expert review (MathOverflow answer, referee report, a survey citing it as an established theorem, or discussion on a mathematician's blog) of the Cocos proof's current version would settle whether this becomes 'resolved' (if endorsed) or reverts toward 'open'/'incident' (if a fatal flaw is found and the paper is withdrawn, as happened to the 2016 and 2020 predecessor claims).

outcome: Miyaoka (arXiv:2504.02621, April 2025) proved Chern's conjecture for closed proper Dupin hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature in the sub-cases g=3; g=4 with constant scalar curvature; g=4 with constant Lie curvature; and g=6 with constant Lie curvature — genuine restrictions (special classes of hypersurfaces) of the stated conjecture, not the full conjecture. Several further papers (2025-2026) proved additional restricted cases and moved bounds, but the general conjecture (for arbitrary closed minimal hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature in S^(n+1)) remains open.

All mathematical arguments and proofs were independently developed and verified by the authors, who prepared the final manuscript and take full responsibility for its content.

summary: The decisive event is Reiko Miyaoka's April 2025 preprint 'Chern's Conjecture in the Dupin case' (arXiv:2504.02621), which proves the conjecture — that a closed hypersurface with constant mean curvature and constant scalar (or Lie) curvature is isoparametric — for closed proper Dupin hypersurfaces restricted to g=3 (all cases), g=4 (with constant scalar or constant Lie curvature), and g=6 (with constant Lie curvature). Since g for a closed proper Dupin hypersurface can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6, and g=1,2 are classical/trivial, this covers essentially all non-trivial Dupin sub-cases under the stated extra hypotheses, but restricting to Dupin hypersurfaces (a subclass with constant Lie curvatures / conformal structure) is a genuine restriction of the general conjecture, which concerns arbitrary closed minimal (or CMC) hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature. This is a 'case settled' under §3.1, hence status=partial, resolution_direction=confirmed (the isoparametric conclusion holds, as conjectured), and no counterexample. Beyond this, I found a cluster of further restricted-case and bound-moving papers in the window, none of which resolve the general conjecture: Ge, Liu, Luo, Yan (arXiv:2606.29246, June 2026) prove the case for 4-dimensional minimal hypersurfaces in S^5 under the extra hypothesis that the Gauss-Kronecker curvature is also constant; Ya Tao (arXiv:2605.19495, May-July 2026) proves a rigidity/isoparametric result in S^6 under constancy hypotheses on certain principal-curvature functions, removing a nonnegativity assumption from prior work by Tang-Yan; Tan, Tang, Xie, Yan (arXiv:2609.03711, September 2026) prove a discreteness result for the scalar-curvature values attained under an additional constant-cubic-trace hypothesis (a genuine extra restriction, so this is more marginal — arguably closer to a 'related' variant than a case, since it adds a hypothesis the original conjecture does not carry); and Ge, Tan, Yan, Zhang (arXiv:2512.08342, December 2025) prove a partial (approximate) verification of the second-gap version of the conjecture, establishing a curvature lower bound weaker than the full conjectured bound — this is a `progress`-flavored bound-improvement folded into the same broader picture, not itself a resolution. On the AI question: none of Miyaoka's, Ge-Liu-Luo-Yan's, or Tao's papers mention any AI or computational tool. The September 2026 Tan-Tang-Xie-Yan paper (arXiv:2609.03711) does explicitly disclose AI use: 'we used ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to interpret relevant literature and mathematical tools ... All mathematical arguments and proofs were independently developed and verified by the authors.' Per §6.2, this is squarely `none` — the model was used only to help interpret background literature/tools, not to produce any mathematics that appears in the result — so ai_role is `none` for the record as a whole, even though this is worth flagging as an AI-disclosure incident in an otherwise AI-free cluster of results. I confirmed 'ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' is a real, contemporaneous OpenAI model name (GPT-5.6 family, released July 2026), so this is not a fabricated or misattributed name. The Wikipedia article itself (checked July 2026 per its own edit history hint returned by search) still states the conjecture is 'unsolved as of 2018' and does not reflect any of this 2025-2026 progress — its lead is stale relative to the literature, which is common and does not affect this record's classification.
competing_reading: One could argue the Dupin restriction is severe enough (Dupin hypersurfaces with constant Lie curvature form a special, highly structured subclass with a rich classification theory of their own) that Miyaoka's result is better read as a 'related problem' (Chern's conjecture *for Dupin hypersurfaces*, a named sub-theory) rather than a case of the general conjecture, which would make the correct status 'open' with no_change_found describing only variant/related progress. I read it as a case rather than a variant because Dupin proper hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature are a subset of the hypersurfaces the general conjecture quantifies over (Chern's conjecture is literally about minimal/CMC hypersurfaces with constant scalar or constant curvature invariants; Dupin hypersurfaces with these extra constant-curvature properties are legitimate instances of that same object, just with an extra structural hypothesis satisfied), so proving the isoparametric conclusion for them removes territory from the open cases rather than posing a different question. Similarly, the cubic-trace paper (2609.03711) could be read either as a case (a further restriction within the same universe of objects) or, more plausibly, as a related/variant strengthening since it fixes an additional invariant (f₃) not mentioned in the original conjecture's hypotheses — I lean towards treating it as auxiliary progress rather than the decisive case-settling event, and used Miyaoka's paper as the decisive `event` instead.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from an expert survey (e.g. a future Notices of the AMS or Bulletin AMS article, or an update to the sciengine.com review 'The Chern conjecture for minimal hypersurfaces in a sphere and its related problems') classifying whether Dupin-hypersurface results are considered by specialists to be genuine cases of the general Chern conjecture or a separate sub-theory would resolve the classification question. A dated re-check of the Wikipedia article's edit history would also confirm whether/when specialists update the encyclopedic framing.

outcome: The general conjecture (existence of a universal constant t0 such that every t0-tough graph is Hamiltonian) remains fully open; no new upper or lower bound on t0 itself has been reported since 26 January 2024. All post-2024 activity settles Hamiltonicity only for restricted, forbidden-subgraph graph classes, or a separate degree-sequence conjecture of Hoàng, neither of which is a case of the stated existence question.
summary: Chvátal's toughness conjecture (1973) posits a universal constant t0 such that every t0-tough graph on ≥3 vertices is Hamiltonian. The known bracket — t0 must be at least 9/4 (Bauer, Broersma & Veldman 2000) if it exists — long predates the window and is unchanged. I searched arXiv, the current Wikipedia 'Graph toughness' article, and general web/scholar-style queries for any 2024–2026 movement on the existential question itself and found none: no new lower bound (a t-tough non-Hamiltonian graph for larger t), no new upper bound (a proof that some specific t0 works in general), and no disproof of the conjecture's existence. What I did find is a steady stream of 2024–2026 papers proving Hamiltonicity for graphs that are t-tough AND belong to some forbidden-induced-subgraph class (e.g. arXiv:2503.12860 'every 2k-connected (P2∪kP1)-free graph...', arXiv:2504.08936 on (P4∪P1)-free graphs, arXiv:2505.04189 on 15-tough (P3∪3P1)-free graphs, arXiv:2506.12684 on 11-tough (2P2∪P1)-free graphs, and its successor arXiv:2608.24047 improving the same class's toughness bound from 11 to 10, and arXiv:2605.19508 on 1-tough (P2∪kP1)-free graphs). These are results about a different (restricted, forbidden-subgraph) family of graphs, not a case obtained by narrowing a parameter of the stated conjecture — under §3.1 they are 'related problems' (variants), not cases, because the original conjecture quantifies over ALL graphs and forbidding an induced subgraph changes the object class rather than restricting within it in a way that would, if resolved for all classes, sum to the general conjecture. I also found arXiv:2503.14735 (Shan and, per one summary, Tanyel) verifying Hoàng's 1995 conjecture (a distinct, stronger degree-sequence statement) for all t≥4 — again a different conjecture that happens to imply Chvátal's classical 1972 degree-condition theorem as a special case, not the toughness conjecture itself. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this line of work: none of the papers I opened (2503.14735, 2506.12684, 2503.12860, 2608.24047) mention AI, machine learning, or computer-assisted proof of any kind — these are conventional human combinatorial proofs. A search for AI/LLM connections to this specific conjecture (including checking Terence Tao's and the Erdős-problems AI-tracking material for any overlap) turned up nothing relating to toughness/Hamiltonicity. The triage's `found` list was empty but its `why` cited arXiv:2608.24047, which I confirmed exists (a real September 2026 preprint improving the (2P2∪P1)-free toughness bound from 11 to 10) — the triage's characterization of it was accurate even though the item wasn't logged in `found`.
competing_reading: One could argue forbidding an induced linear forest F is 'restricting attention to' the graphs in that class, which resembles a case rather than a variant, since Wikipedia's own general-topic articles sometimes list such F-free results as 'progress toward' the toughness conjecture. But settling Hamiltonicity for, say, 10-tough (2P2∪P1)-free graphs says nothing about whether some fixed t0 works for ALL graphs — a graph outside that forbidden class at toughness 10 could still be non-Hamiltonian, so this is not territory removed from the universally-quantified existence question in the way a dimension-restricted case would be for, say, a conjecture indexed by dimension. I classify these as variants (open, no_change_found) rather than partial results, but flag the line as genuinely fuzzy given how survey literature (e.g. Bauer–Broersma–Schmeichel) frames these graph-class results as 'the conjecture verified for X'.
what_would_settle_it: A paper either exhibiting, for every ε>0, a non-Hamiltonian graph with toughness t0-ε for arbitrarily large claimed t0 (refuting the conjecture), or proving Hamiltonicity for all sufficiently tough graphs with no forbidden-subgraph restriction (proving it) would settle the general question. Absent that, the next-most-informative event would be a change to the known lower bound of 9/4 for what t0 must be, which also has not occurred since 2024.

outcome: The general conjecture (infinitely many real quadratic fields with class number one) remains open; all work found since 26 January 2024 either studies specific parametric families, proves bounds/indivisibility results for class numbers of real quadratic fields, or is a single uncorroborated preprint claiming a full solution that shows no sign of expert acceptance.

disputes.summary: Igor V. Nikolaev posted arXiv:2512.02232 ('Lambert W-function and Gauss class number one conjecture', 1 December 2025) claiming to derive a solution to the Gauss conjecture for real quadratic fields of class number one, via fixed points of a function built from Drinfeld-module representations as bounded operators on a Hilbert space. No journal acceptance, expert digestion, citation, or community endorsement of this claim was found. Nikolaev has a long arXiv history of similar unconventional operator-algebra/noncommutative-geometry claims about famous open conjectures that have not been accepted by the number theory community. A May 2026 AIM/Harmonic/AWS/NSF workshop on 'AI and Number Theory' (5 months after the preprint) still listed the Gauss real-quadratic class-number conjecture as an open target problem for AI attack, which is inconsistent with the community having accepted Nikolaev's claim as a resolution.

summary: The Gauss conjecture that infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one is still listed as open by Wikipedia's own Class number problem article as of this research, and is treated as open in the number-theory literature searched. Work published in the window addresses adjacent but distinct questions under the §3.1 scope rule: Bernardini (arXiv:2412.06351, Dec 2024) proves h(D)>1 for a specific family of real quadratic fields with known continued-fraction expansions (all but finitely many exceptions) — this is evidence about a family, not a case of the infinitude conjecture, and if anything narrows where class-number-one fields in that family could occur, rather than settling the existence question (per §3.1's rule that infinitude questions move only when answered). A 2025 paper (arXiv:2506.21301) improves an upper bound (Yamamoto 1971) on how many real quadratic fields below a given discriminant have small class number, again a bound on a distribution, not the infinitude conjecture itself. A 2025 machine-learning paper (arXiv:2209.09283, actually from 2022, predating the window and thus irrelevant here) used supervised learning to rediscover Cohen–Lenstra-type patterns in class-number data, but is neither in-window nor does it touch the infinitude question; it was surfaced by triage but is out of scope both by date and by topic. The one item that looked like it could change the status is Igor Nikolaev's December 2025 preprint (arXiv:2512.02232) explicitly claiming 'a solution to the Gauss conjecture for the real quadratic fields of class number one' via noncommutative-geometry/Drinfeld-module methods. I read the abstract and available content; there is no digestion by experts, no citations, no journal acceptance, and Nikolaev has a documented pattern of posting similar claims about other famous conjectures using the same toolkit without community acceptance. Most tellingly, an AIM-sponsored 'AI and Number Theory' workshop convened in May 2026 — five months after this preprint — explicitly lists the Gauss real-quadratic class-number conjecture as an open problem suitable for AI attack, which would be a strange thing to do if the community had accepted a solution five months earlier. I therefore classify this preprint as an uncorroborated, likely-erroneous claim that does not meet even the `claimed` bar (which requires the claim to be a live candidate under some scrutiny) and does not change the `open` status; I note it fully in `disputes` rather than silently dropping it, per §7's instruction that priority/attribution and credibility disputes belong there. No AI system was found to be involved in any of the results located — the Bernardini and bound-improvement papers are conventional analytic/algebraic number theory, and no source claims AI assistance in producing the Nikolaev preprint's argument either. Overall: nothing has happened to the conjecture itself in the window, and there is no genuine AI involvement to report.
competing_reading: If a downstream reader wanted to be more generous to the Nikolaev preprint, one could argue for `status: claimed` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (since the claim is that infinitely many such fields exist, matching Gauss's conjectured direction) and `ai_role: none`. I did not take this reading because `claimed` implies a live, still-being-evaluated claim, and I found zero evidence of the mathematical community treating it as such — no discussion, no citations, no follow-up, and a subsequent major workshop treating the problem as still open. Given Nikolaev's track record of similar claims on other famous problems (e.g., other operator-algebra 'proofs' of open conjectures) that were never accepted, I judged the more defensible reading to be that this is noise rather than a genuine claim in play, but a reader who weighs the mere existence of an unretracted, unwithdrawn preprint more heavily could reasonably classify it as `claimed`.
what_would_settle_it: Any expert commentary (blog post, MathOverflow thread, journal referee report, or citation) engaging substantively with arXiv:2512.02232 — either endorsing it, refuting it, or noting a withdrawal — would resolve whether it belongs in the record as `claimed` or should be dismissed entirely. Absent that, the paper's silence in the literature five-plus months after posting, and its omission from the AIM workshop's framing of the problem as open, is the best available evidence that it has not been accepted.

outcome: The full classification of graphs with representation number 3 remains open, but since 26 January 2024 several specific graph families have been fully classified with respect to representation number 3: word-representable split graphs and split comparability graphs (Feb 2025), word-representable co-bipartite graphs (Sept 2025), melon graphs and their comparability/line-graph restrictions (submitted Feb 2026), and m×n grid graphs / cylindrical grid graphs for m,n ≥ small bounds (July 2025). No AI system was involved in any of this work.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for a full classification of graphs with representation number 3 (word-representable but not 2-representable). As of the frozen revision this was, and remains today, an open problem with no complete classification — the current live Wikipedia article on word-representable graphs still states 'No classification for graphs with representation number 3 is known.' However, several restrictions of the problem (cases, per §3.1) have been settled in the window. (1) Dwary, Mozhui and Krishna, 'Representation Number of Word-Representable Split Graphs' (arXiv:2502.00872, submitted 2 Feb 2025, revised 27 Apr 2025), prove every word-representable split graph has representation number at most 3 and fully characterize which split graphs and split comparability graphs achieve exactly 3 (vs. 2). (2) Das and Hariharasubramanian, 'Word-Representable Co-Bipartite Graphs...' (arXiv:2509.03064, submitted 3 Sept 2025), prove every word-representable co-bipartite graph has representation number at most 3, and that permutation graphs are exactly the co-bipartite graphs achieving representation number 2 — so all other word-representable co-bipartite graphs are classified as having representation number exactly 3. (3) Mozhui and Krishna, 'Word-Representation of Melon Graphs' (arXiv:2602.14179, submitted 15 Feb 2026), classify melon graphs (and their comparability-graph and line-graph restrictions) by representation number 2 vs 3. (4) Alshammari, Kitaev and Pyatkin, on grid and cylindrical grid graphs (arXiv:2507.16469, submitted 23 Jul 2025), show m×n grid graphs (m≥3, n≥3) and m×n cylindrical grid graphs (m≥2, n≥3) all have representation number exactly 3. I opened and read (via fetch) all four preprints' abstracts/content and found no mention of any AI system, machine learning tool, or automated theorem prover in the research process for any of them — these are traditional human mathematical proofs. Each of these results narrows a sub-case of the general classification (a specific graph class) rather than settling the whole question, so per §3.1 this is scope-preserving 'case' progress, coded partial with resolution_direction confirmed (the settled pieces confirm exactly which members of each family are 3-representable, consistent with what was conjectured/expected — none refute an expectation). No AI involvement of any kind was found anywhere in this research area.
competing_reading: One could argue that because no single result resolves the *general* classification (over all graphs), none of these findings should count and the correct status is 'open'. But §3.1 explicitly says a restriction of the stated question (a class of objects) that gets fully settled counts as a case, normally 'partial' — and each of these papers does fully settle representation-number-2-vs-3 status for its named graph class, so 'partial' is the more faithful classification. It is also possible additional 2024-2026 papers on other graph families (not surfaced by my searches) exist; I searched broadly but arXiv's coverage of this niche subfield is not exhaustively indexed by generic web search.
what_would_settle_it: A paper providing a forbidden-subgraph or structural characterization valid for all graphs (analogous to Gallai's classification of comparability graphs) would fully resolve the general classification and move status to resolved/claimed. Absent that, further family-by-family results would keep it at partial.
