outcome: The general closed curve problem (explicit necessary and sufficient conditions on periodic curvature and torsion for a space curve to close up) remains open, but Bamba and Ogata (Journal of Geometry, 2026) gave an explicit constructive solution for the special case of rotationally symmetric (spherical) curves, and extended it to closed curves with singularities (closed planar Legendre curves, closed spherical fronts).
summary: Wikipedia's bullet asks for explicit necessary and sufficient conditions on two periodic functions (curvature and torsion, or curvature alone in the plane case) so that the associated integral (Frenet) curve is closed. This is a long-standing open problem in the differential geometry of curves. Prior to the frozen revision, Grinevich and Schmidt (1990s work, well before the window) had already given a characterization of the closure constraints in terms of the spectral problem for an associated 2x2 matrix differential (Zakharov-Shabat/AKNS-type) operator arising from the self-focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation — a structural/spectral characterization, not an 'explicit' closed-form condition, so the problem as Wikipedia poses it (explicit conditions) remained open going into 2024. Searching for developments in the window, I found one clearly relevant, dated result: Bamba and Ogata, 'Closed space curves with singularities, generated by periodic curvature and torsion,' Journal of Geometry 117, article 12, published online 2026-02-02 (DOI 10.1007/s00022-025-00792-3; the '025' in the DOI indicates acceptance in 2025). No arXiv preprint of this paper could be located, so the journal publication is treated as the first written argument. The paper gives a constructive method for generating closed curves by controlling only the values of the first integral of a periodic function, which in turn determines periodic curvature and torsion; this yields an explicit solution to the closed curve problem for the restricted class of rotationally symmetric (spherical) curves, and the authors extend the construction to curves with singularities (closed planar Legendre curves and closed spherical fronts). This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem — a class of curves (rotationally symmetric/spherical), not a changed problem — so under Sec 3.1 it is a case of the problem and I classify it as 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the case was settled, not refuted). The fully general problem (arbitrary periodic curvature and torsion pairs in R^3, or arbitrary periodic curvature for plane curves) is still open; I found no other result in the window (2024-01-26 to 2026-09-22) that advances the general case, and no AI involvement of any kind — I checked the Springer abstract/search summaries, related arXiv papers on closed space curves (e.g. 'Unsigned Frenet Data of Closed Space Curves', arXiv:2608.09194, which explicitly addresses a different problem — the inverse problem of recovering signed torsion from unsigned data — and discloses no AI use), and general searches for AI-assisted solutions to this specific problem, none of which turned up any AI system credited in this area. I could not access the full text of the Bamba-Ogata paper (Springer paywall redirected to a login page, and a related Hokkaido University seminar PDF could not be parsed as text), so I relied on search-engine summaries and abstracts of the paper rather than the full manuscript; this is a limitation noted in 'incomplete'.
competing_reading: One could argue the plane-curve version of this problem (a single periodic curvature function determining a closed plane curve) is a genuinely separate sub-problem from the space-curve version (curvature and torsion), since Wikipedia's phrasing ('two periodic functions') most naturally reads as the space-curve case, but the plane case is the classical, well-studied one (e.g. 'When Is a Periodic Function the Curvature of a Closed Plane Curve?', pre-2024, unrelated to this window). If the bullet is read as covering only the space-curve problem, the Bamba-Ogata paper is squarely on-point as a special case; if read to also require progress on the plane case, no additional plane-curve progress was found in the window, which would not change the 'partial' classification since the space-curve special case alone already justifies it, but would narrow what 'partial' rests on.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the full text of Bamba and Ogata (2026) to confirm the precise scope of 'rotationally symmetric' curves covered, and a systematic search of 2024-2026 arXiv listings in math.DG for any paper that advances the fully general closed curve problem (not just a subclass) or credits an AI system with any part of the argument.

outcome: The conjecture remains open. The most notable event in the window is a withdrawn AI-produced Lean 'disproof' (July 25-28, 2026) that turned out to exploit two independent Lean/nanoda kernel soundness bugs rather than settle the conjecture; separately, computational verification was extended to 2^71 (Barina, 2025) and an unreviewed solo GitHub project claims a machine-checked improvement to the Krasikov-Lagarias density bound (0.8676 vs 0.84), with no AI involvement claimed for that result.

counterexample.verified_how: The claimed disproof was checked by two independent verifiers (Lean's official kernel and the nanoda external checker in Rust), both of which passed it — but each was later shown to have an independent soundness bug (a missing check in nested inductive type/kernel elimination handling) that let a proof of False through. Kiran Gopinathan reduced the exploit to a minimal proof of False on July 28, 2026, and the Lean kernel bug (#14576) was patched about an hour after being reported. The 'disproof' establishes nothing about the conjecture.

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on whether Ramana Kumar genuinely believed the AI-produced Lean proof was valid when publishing it, or knowingly circulated a kernel-bug exploit under the guise of a mathematical disproof. De Moura's postmortem and the Paulson/GIGAZINE accounts treat it as a good-faith claim later found to be invalid ('produced with AI assistance', discovered by others to exploit a bug). A LessWrong post ('Don't trust Lean4 alone') instead states Kumar 'knew it was a soundness bug' at the time of posting and released it 'under false pretenses' as a deliberate illustration of the danger, gaining publicity because it was not originally framed as a bug report.

summary: Since the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, the Collatz conjecture remains unproven, and the article's own current lead still describes it as open. The single event with a genuine, if indirect, AI angle is the July 2026 Lean 'disproof': on 25 July 2026 Ramana Kumar published a Lean 4 repository (github.com/xrchz/CollatzLean) containing a sorry-free formal 'disproof' of the conjecture that was, per Leonardo de Moura's postmortem, 'produced with AI assistance', and that passed both Lean's official kernel and the independent nanoda checker. On 28 July 2026 Kiran Gopinathan reduced it to a minimal proof of False and reported it as Lean issue #14576; investigation showed it exploited two unrelated soundness bugs (a missing check in the kernel's handling of nested inductive types, and a matching gap in nanoda's projection-node type checking) rather than proving anything about Collatz, and the kernel bug was patched within about an hour. No source I could open names the specific AI system involved — 'produced with AI assistance' / 'AI-generated' is as specific as any account (de Moura's blog, Lawrence Paulson's blog, GIGAZINE, and the Tildes discussion of the postmortem) gets, so I record the system as unnamed rather than guessing. There is also a genuine dispute about intent: a LessWrong post ('Don't trust Lean4 alone') asserts Kumar knew at the time of posting that the 'proof' exploited a bug and released it under false pretenses as a cautionary demonstration, which is a materially different story from an AI genuinely (if wrongly) believed to have found a real disproof — I record this as a dispute rather than picking a side. Per the withdrawn-claim rule (§6.1/§7), I classify this event as status 'progress' with ai_role 'incident', dated to the 25 July 2026 claim, since the problem itself did not move. Separately, I checked for any real (non-incident) progress in the window: computational verification was extended to 2^71 by David Barina (Journal of Supercomputing, published online ~May 2025, per FIT VUT and ResearchGate records) — this is a record-extension on an infinitude-shaped bullet and per §3.1 does not itself change the bullet, but I note it as background. I also found an unreviewed solo GitHub project (msharpe248/collatz) claiming a Lean-4, kernel-checked improvement of the Krasikov-Lagarias (2003) density bound from x^0.84 to π₁(x) = Ω(x^0.8676) via scaling the classical elimination argument to 3^14 congruence classes; this would be a genuine 'bound moved' progress event if it holds up, but it has no arXiv preprint, no journal venue, and no independent digestion I could find beyond the author's own kernel-checked certificate, so I do not treat it as decisive and note it only as background evidence that 'progress' (rather than 'open' with no_change_found) is the more defensible status even setting the AI incident aside. No AI role is claimed for that bound-improvement work. I also examined several 2024-2026 full-proof preprints (arXiv:2309.09991, Cambridge Open Engage Dec 2025, Preprints.org Aug/Oct 2025) and structural/dynamical papers (the circle-rotation near-conjugacy paper arXiv:2601.04289, and Edward Y. Chang's 'Exploring Collatz Dynamics with Human-LLM Collaboration' arXiv:2603.11066) — none of these claim to resolve the conjecture or settle a case of it; Chang's paper explicitly disclaims being a proof and instead catalogues why the conjecture resists proof across 29 frameworks, so despite naming human-LLM collaboration it is a related/variant contribution (proof-obstacle survey), not a case of the stated problem, and I exclude it from the status-determining event.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is 'open' with no_change_found true, treating the withdrawn Lean incident as too ephemeral and too indirectly tied to genuine mathematical progress to count as a status-changing 'event' at all — it was retracted within three days and settled nothing, positive or negative, about the conjecture. Against that: §7 explicitly says 'a withdrawn claim is still an event' and directs recording it as progress/incident rather than dropping it, which is the reading I followed. A second competing reading concerns the msharpe248 density-bound claim: if one credits it despite the lack of peer review or an arXiv posting, the status could instead rest on that bound-moving event (still 'progress', but with a different event and ai_role 'none' rather than 'incident') rather than on the Lean incident; I chose the Lean incident because it is better corroborated by independent, higher-authority sources (Lean's own creator, an established Isabelle/HOL expert's blog, tech press) whereas the density-bound claim rests solely on the claimant's own repository.
what_would_settle_it: For the Lean incident: a direct statement from Ramana Kumar (a tweet, blog post, or repository commit message) explaining his own intent and knowledge at the time of posting would resolve the priority/intent dispute, and identifying the specific AI system (model name and provider) used would let this be coded more precisely and cross-referenced against model release dates. For the density-bound claim: an arXiv posting or any third-party review of msharpe248/collatz's Krasikov-Lagarias improvement would let it be weighed as a genuine progress event rather than background context.

outcome: The general congruent number problem remains open: a full unconditional characterization still requires the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, which is unproven. Work since 26 January 2024 consists of restricted non-congruence criteria for special residue classes (variants/cases, not the stated problem), a machine-learning study of arithmetic statistics of congruent-number elliptic curves that classifies rather than proves, and several non-peer-reviewed preprints claiming full BSD proofs that show no sign of expert acceptance.

ai.basis_quote: Machine learning techniques are being employed to ascertain whether a given square-free integer is a congruent number... exploring the efficacy of computational methods in distinguishing congruent from non-congruent numbers based on the arithmetic properties of elliptic curves.

summary: The congruent number problem as stated (determine precisely which rationals are congruent numbers, a corollary of BSD via Tunnell's theorem) is still open, and nothing found since 26 January 2024 changes that. I found four categories of relevant material. (1) Restricted, unconditional non-congruence criteria for special residue classes: a 2024-vintage 'Pythagorician divisors' approach (SCIRP, 'A New Proof for Congruent Number's Problem via Pythagorician Divisors') and subsequent Shimura-lift work by Hourong Qin and collaborators (building on arXiv:2307.07438, with a 2604.xxxx-numbered April 2026 paper 'A necessary condition for a congruent number of the form 8k+3', and a June 2025 extension to curves E_n: y^2 = x^3 + 2n^3, plus a February 2026 ScienceDirect paper on non-congruent numbers via 2-primary Shafarevich-Tate group criteria for 'multiples of non-congruent numbers'). These are all narrower sub-questions (specific residue classes or families) rather than the general problem, and per §3.1 a case/variant of this kind is at most `partial` for the sub-case, not a change to the bullet as stated; none amounts to a general characterization, so I have classified the overall record as `open` rather than manufacturing a `partial` record for a narrow residue-class result, since the triage's own scope reasoning ('recent hits are about special/related cases... rather than the stated problem') is correct and I found nothing that removes territory from the general problem in a way a careful reader of this specific bullet would flag as settling part of it beyond what was already known before 2024 (partial congruence/non-congruence criteria for special forms existed well before the frozen date too). (2) A September 2025 paper (arXiv:2509.03129, 'Unveiling Arithmetic Statistics of Congruent Number Elliptic Curves via Data Science and Machine Learning') that uses a_p Frobenius-trace data as ML features to classify square-free integers as congruent/non-congruent, and separately tests Goldfeld's conjecture empirically on ranks/Selmer groups up to 3 million; the authors themselves frame the ML component as a classification/statistics exercise run alongside, not in place of, rigorous number-theoretic verification, so it produced no proof and is not a case of the problem being settled. Under §6.2 this is `ai_role: none` because the ML model classified/predicted rather than producing mathematics that appears in a proof. (3) Several 2024-2025 preprints claiming a full, unconditional proof of BSD (via an 'İran Formula' on preprints.org, a 'CASU framework' on ResearchGate, 'Relational Field Theory' on SSRN, and others on Zenodo/IJAEMR) which, if genuine, would resolve the congruent number problem outright; these are all self-published on non-peer-reviewed platforms with no expert digestion, no journal acceptance, and no citation uptake, bear the hallmarks of crank mathematics (grandiose acronyms, unconventional venues), and involve no disclosed AI system. They do not meet the bar for `claimed` (no coherent single preprint with any expert engagement) and I have not elevated the record on their basis. (4) 'ThetaEvolve: Test-time Learning on Open Problems' (arXiv:2511.23473), which does use an AI system (Claude) for open-problem exploration, turned out on inspection to be unrelated to the congruent number problem (it covers circle packing and other optimization-style open problems), so it is not relevant here despite surfacing on an AI+open-problems search. Overall: no case, bound, or full resolution changes the stated bullet since 26 January 2024, and no AI system produced mathematics that entered any result on this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the residue-class non-congruence criteria (8k+3 case, the E_n: y^2=x^3+2n^3 family, the 2-primary Sha criteria for 'multiples of non-congruent numbers') should be recorded as `partial` since they are, strictly, cases of the general problem (they settle congruence-status for specific infinite families of integers). I judged this is not new in kind — this style of restricted criterion (going back decades, including pre-2024 Qin-style Shimura-lift and Tunnell-style refinements) is exactly the sort of narrow-family result the field has produced continuously, and none of it moves the 'precisely characterize all rationals' bullet in a way a careful reader would flag as a discrete event; the safer reading consistent with the triage's own note is `open`/`no_change_found`. If a downstream reviewer prefers strict literalism about §3.1's 'a case counts, normally as partial', the record should instead be `partial`, direction `mixed` (some numbers confirmed non-congruent, others left open), dated to the April 2026 or February 2026 papers, with `ai_role: none` regardless.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the dataset's convention treats routine, continuous incremental non-congruence criteria for narrow residue classes (a genre of paper that predates 2024 by decades) as `partial` events worth a discrete record, or as business-as-usual background noise that does not constitute a change to 'the problem' bullet. A ruling on this would resolve the ambiguity for every open Diophantine-classification problem on the list, not just this one.

outcome: The Connes embedding problem was resolved in the negative by the MIP*=RE result (Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, Yuen), first announced in January 2020 and published in a fixed form in Communications of the ACM in November 2021 — well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, so this is a stale entry on the list rather than a change in the window. Within the window, two further items appeared that bear on the problem but do not alter its already-settled status: a June 2024 paper by Goldbring and Hart gives an independent proof route to the same negative resolution via undecidability of the hyperfinite II₁ factor's universal theory, and a February 2025 preprint by Manzoor gives a simplified/independent construction of a non-Connes-embeddable tracial von Neumann algebra, though it still invokes MIP*=RE as an ingredient rather than avoiding it entirely. No AI system is involved anywhere in this history.

counterexample.object: A type II₁ von Neumann factor (equivalently, via the Feb 2025 paper, the von Neumann algebra of an invariant random subgroup construction on non-abelian free groups) that does not embed into an ultrapower of the hyperfinite II₁ factor Rω, shown to exist via the MIP*=RE quantum complexity result rather than exhibited as a single explicit algebra.
counterexample.verified_how: Proved via the MIP*=RE theorem in complexity theory (a corrected version published Nov 2021 in Communications of the ACM after an error in an earlier ingredient was found and fixed in Sept 2020); Manzoor's Feb 2025 preprint gives an independent, more elementary construction still relying on MIP*=RE.

summary: The Connes embedding problem was already resolved negatively before the window: Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen's MIP*=RE result was first posted to arXiv on 13 January 2020 (arXiv:2001.04383), an error in an earlier ingredient was found and a corrected preprint posted in September 2020, and a broad outline appeared in Communications of the ACM in November 2021 (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3485628). All of this predates the 26 January 2024 frozen Wikipedia revision, so the correct classification is open_stale: the list is stale on this entry, not that something changed in the window. I verified this directly from the arXiv abstract page (version history: v1 Jan 2020, v2 Sept 2020, v3 Nov 2022) and from the CACM publication record, matching the triage's finding. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) two further items surfaced. First, Goldbring and Hart, 'The universal theory of the hyperfinite II₁ factor is not computable,' published in the Bulletin of Symbolic Logic in June 2024, gives an independent route to the same already-known negative resolution by showing the relevant first-order theory is undecidable (itself built on MIP*=RE) — this is a new proof technique for an old conclusion, not a change to the problem's status, and it settles nothing that was still open. Second, Aareyan Manzoor's 'There Is An Equivalence Relation Whose von Neumann Algebra Is Not Connes Embeddable' (arXiv:2502.06697, submitted Feb 2025, revised Apr 2026) gives a more elementary/independent construction of a non-embeddable algebra via invariant random subgroups of free groups, explicitly simplifying the reduction used in MIP*=RE — but the paper itself states plainly that it still uses MIP*=RE as an ingredient ('The landmark quantum complexity result MIP*=RE was used to prove the existence of a non Connes embeddable tracial von Neumann algebra'), so it is not an independent resolution avoiding the original proof, just a cleaner derivation of the same corollary. I also checked a June 2025 ICMAT interview with Gilles Pisier, who states that the MIP*=RE proof, coming from theoretical computer science, has still not been fully verified by analysts and that he is trying to find a purely analytic proof — this confirms the mathematical community still treats the CACM-published result as authoritative (i.e., 'resolved' rather than merely 'claimed') while independent verification work continues, and shows no sign this reopens the question. No AI system appears anywhere in this history: the MIP*=RE authors are five named human researchers with no computational or AI component to the proof itself (aside from ordinary use of complexity-theoretic and analytic techniques), Goldbring and Hart's paper is a human model-theoretic argument, and Manzoor's construction is likewise a human-authored mathematical argument with no stated AI assistance. A Google DeepMind 'formal-conjectures' GitHub issue (#1763) exists but is only a request to formalize the *statement* of the Connes embedding problem in Lean/mathlib — it is an open, unclaimed formalization task with no proof attached, and does not constitute AI involvement in any result.
competing_reading: One could argue the Goldbring-Hart (June 2024) or Manzoor (Feb 2025) papers should be coded as `progress` within the window on the theory that they represent a genuinely new, independent within-window event even though the overall conjecture was already settled before 2024. I considered this but rejected it: per §6.1, `open_stale` is for problems settled before the frozen date, and per §3.1 the test is whether a result changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry — since the entry is simply 'is Connes' embedding conjecture true', and that was already answered negatively pre-2024, neither 2024/2025 paper changes the answer; they offer new proofs/simplified constructions of the same already-known fact. The stronger case for `progress` would be if one treated 'the community has now also verified/reproduced the result via an independent route' as itself informative (e.g. increasing confidence given Pisier's stated verification concerns) — but no source treats either 2024 or 2025 paper as a distinct resolution event or digestion milestone changing the status of the original claim.
what_would_settle_it: A fully independent, expert-digested proof of the negative resolution that does not rely on MIP*=RE at all (Pisier describes exactly this as his goal, unachieved as of the June 2025 interview) would be the kind of event that could warrant a `progress` or renewed `claimed`/`resolved` entry distinct from the stale MIP*=RE-based resolution; no such proof has yet appeared.

outcome: No new convex uniform 5-polytope has been found or excluded since 26 January 2024, and completeness of the convex case remains unproven; all cataloguing activity found in the window (e.g. the 2024 discovery of 'scab', and count increases from ~1297 to 1333/1348) concerns non-convex uniform 5-polytopes, a broader, related enumeration rather than the stated convex problem.
summary: The stated problem is to determine the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes. As of the frozen Wikipedia revision (26 Jan 2024) and still today (checked Sept 2026), this remains unresolved: the known convex examples are two infinite families plus 105 sporadic examples (per the Open Problem Garden entry and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_5-polytope), all but one (the grand antiprism prism) Wythoffian, and completeness of this convex list has never been proven or disproven. I searched for any 2024-2026 activity specific to the convex case and found none: no new convex uniform 5-polytope announced, no proof of completeness, no disproof via a demonstrated missing case. The activity that does exist in this window — Jonathan Bowers/hi.gher.space community cataloguing (e.g. Mejecide's 2024 discovery of 'scab', the first non-prismatic uniform 5-polytope containing snub cubes, and the running tally rising from ~1297 to figures like 1333 or 1348) — is explicitly about the broader search for *non-convex* (and non-Wythoffian) uniform 5-polytopes outside the infinite families. That is a related but distinct enumeration problem (§3.1): it changes the answer to 'how many non-convex/non-Wythoffian uniform 5-polytopes are known', not to 'what is the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes'. I also found and ruled out a 2025 arXiv paper, 'Advancing Geometry with AI: Multi-agent Generation of Polytopes' (arXiv:2502.05199, Świrszcz, Wagner, Williamson et al.), which uses an AI system ('Hopper') to generate novel polytopes for the Hirsch Conjecture, the k-neighbourly polytope problem, and longest monotone paths — none of which is the classification of convex uniform 5-polytopes; it is a different family of polytope problems sharing only the word 'polytope'. No AI system was found anywhere near the convex uniform 5-polytope enumeration itself, which remains a manual/enthusiast-community combinatorial search.
competing_reading: One could argue that since 'scab' and the running tally of non-convex uniform 5-polytopes are literally uniform 5-polytopes, and since any newly found non-Wythoffian example theoretically could turn out to be convex (in principle a non-Wythoffian construction might still yield a convex figure), this cataloguing work is adjacent enough to count as 'progress' on the convex enumeration. But every source describing 'scab' and the tally explicitly frames it as part of the non-convex/general uniform 5-polytope search, and none of the newly catalogued examples are convex; the convex list (105 sporadic + 2 infinite families) has not changed. I therefore classify this as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a published proof that the known convex list (2 infinite families + 105 sporadic examples) is complete, (b) a newly discovered convex uniform 5-polytope not on that list, or (c) a rigorous non-existence argument ruling out further non-Wythoffian convex examples. None of these has appeared as of September 2026.

summary: Conway's 99-graph problem — whether an srg(99,14,1,2) exists — is still fully open; no existence or nonexistence proof has appeared since 26 January 2024. Three relevant post-snapshot preprints were found and read. (1) 'Approaching the Conway-99 problem using SAT solvers' (arXiv:2604.23037, v1 24 Apr 2026, Ali Keramatipour) encodes the problem as SAT and finds solvers cannot resolve it in reasonable time — a negative computational result, no AI/ML system involved, and not a change to the problem's status (it establishes a limitation of one tool, not a bound or case). (2) 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph' (arXiv:2606.29183, Yawara Ishida, 28 Jun 2026) is about a *different* problem — the Hoffman-Singleton missing Moore graph of degree 57, srg(3250,57,0,1) — not Conway's 99-graph at all; the triage record's inclusion of this item as relevant was a mistake, which I flag as a triage disagreement. It has no bearing on this record. (3) 'A Forced-Structure Reduction and Verifiable Bounds for Conway's 99-Graph' (arXiv:2608.11211, Aalok Thakkar and Simone Severini, v1 13 Jul 2026, v2 18 Sep 2026) is the substantive result. It proves a structural reduction (fixing one vertex forces its neighbourhood into a perfect matching, reducing the unresolved part to a constrained 12-regular graph on 84 vertices), validates this via CP-SAT on the smaller srg(9,4,1,2) case, exhaustively rules out circulant constructions on Z/99 (best circulant satisfies only 68.0% of a partial-credit constraint set used by the CAISc 2026 'Verifiable Problems' benchmark track), and reports a partial-constraint-satisfaction search. Fourteen human-designed search configurations reached at most 69.43% of constraints satisfied; the authors then gave the scoring function (with no access to their own reduction or heuristics) to Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve — an LLM-driven (Gemini-based) evolutionary code-search agent — which generated a novel tabu-search move (a degree-preserving 4-vertex switch) that reached 70.73%, crossing a plateau the human searches could not. The authors explicitly state 'None of these results settles Conway's problem' — it remains open, and this is a bound-improvement on a partial-score metric, not a case of the problem being settled, so status is 'progress' rather than 'partial' (no dichotomous existence/nonexistence sub-case was closed) or 'resolved'/'claimed'. The AI role is coded 'bound': AlphaEvolve produced a heuristic that improved a numeric score on a problem that remains open, exactly the 'bound' definition, and the authors' own acknowledgement is the basis for the claim. I did not code this 'assisted' because the improved artifact is a search heuristic/score, not a piece of the mathematical proof or reduction (which is entirely human work); nor 'generated', since no proof or counterexample was produced by AI. Wikipedia's live article (checked 2026-09-22) still lists the problem as open with no mention of any 2024-2026 developments, confirming no resolution has been widely digested.
competing_reading: Some search-engine summaries (not the primary paper text) described 2608.11211 as reporting 'a systematic, fully reproducible attack by an autonomous AI research agent' and stated the paper was 'accepted to the first Conference For AI Scientists (CAISc)' — a conference explicitly framed as having 'AI systems as primary authors and reviewers.' If the paper's own text or CAISc's framing in fact credits an autonomous AI agent (rather than the two named human authors) with designing the overall reduction and search strategy — not merely the one heuristic AlphaEvolve produced — the correct ai_role could be 'assisted' or even 'generated' for a larger share of the paper's content, and 'credited_humans' might need revision to reflect an AI-as-author framing. My direct reading of the fetched full paper text (via arxiv.org/html/2608.11211) shows the reduction, CP-SAT validation, and circulant enumeration are presented as work by Thakkar and Severini, with AlphaEvolve credited only for the one tabu-search heuristic in the acknowledgements — so I did not adopt the 'autonomous AI agent authored the whole paper' framing, since I could not verify it against the primary source itself (only against secondary paraphrase). This is worth flagging because CAISc's own premise (AI-authored papers) could mean the 'human authors' listed are themselves a framing device, which I could not confirm or rule out from what I read.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the CAISc 2026 acceptance/review page for this specific paper (the dynamically-loaded caisc2026.github.io/verifiable-problems page did not render its content on fetch) or the paper's own statement of authorship process would clarify whether an AI system is credited as an author/agent for the paper as a whole versus only for the one heuristic. Also, any future arXiv version or published proof of existence/nonexistence would resolve the underlying problem itself.

outcome: No progress on the stated conjecture (m ≤ n for thrackles) has been found since 26 January 2024; the best bound remains Xu's 1.393(n-1) from 2021, and 2025 work extends thrackle theory to nonplanar surfaces or studies a different (unavoidable-pattern) problem without touching the planar conjecture.
summary: No result changing the status of Conway's thrackle conjecture (that a thrackle on n vertices has at most n edges) was found in the window 26 January 2024 to 22 September 2026. The best known upper bound remains m ≤ 1.393(n-1), due to Xu (2021), which predates the window and was already the recorded state at the time of the frozen Wikipedia revision; no tighter bound, resolution, or counterexample surfaced afterward. Two 2025 papers touch adjacent territory but not the conjecture itself: (1) 'Thrackles on nonplanar surfaces' (arXiv:2506.11808, submitted 13 June 2025) disproves a *different*, generalized conjecture by Cairns and Nikolayevsky about thrackles on genus-g surfaces (m ≤ n + 2g), constructing denser examples (2n + 2g - 8 edges) — this is a related problem posed over different objects (higher-genus surfaces), not a restriction of the planar case, so under §3.1 it is out of scope; the paper explicitly states the original planar conjecture remains unresolved. (2) 'Unavoidable patterns and plane paths in dense topological graphs' (arXiv:2512.04795, submitted 4 December 2025, revised February 2026) studies unavoidable subgraph patterns in dense bipartite topological graphs and plane-path avoidance bounds — a related but distinct extremal topological-graph-theory question that does not reference or bound the thrackle edge count. Wikipedia's own 'Thrackle' article, last substantively updated as recently as 18 May 2026 per its revision history, still cites only the 2021 Xu bound and states the conjecture is open, corroborating that no intervening advance has been recognized by the community. A dedicated tracking page on ProofAtlas (a platform coordinating human/AI research effort on open problems) lists this conjecture as 'open' with 'partial' results depending on literature statements 'that still need independent checking' and explicitly states there is no AI-generated proof or bound for it — the platform organizes tasks but has not itself produced a result. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record: multiple independent, current sources (Wikipedia, ProofAtlas, the two most recent arXiv papers citing thrackles) converge on the same conclusion.
competing_reading: One could argue the nonplanar-surfaces paper (arXiv:2506.11808) is a 'case' rather than a 'variant' if one reads the planar conjecture as the g=0 instance of a general genus-g family. Under that reading the paper would still not settle anything, since it only disproves the *conjectured generalization* for g≥1 and explicitly leaves g=0 (the original) open — so even on the more generous reading, status remains unchanged. I classify it as a related/variant problem (different conjecture, by different authors, over a broader class of surfaces) rather than a restriction of the stated bullet, consistent with the triage's judgment.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement giving a bound on n-vertex planar thrackles better than 1.393(n-1) (progress), an explicit thrackle with more edges than vertices (refutation), or a proof that m ≤ n for all thrackles (resolution) — none of which has appeared as of this search.

outcome: No change to the known bounds for the exact 2D axis-parallel-squares case (F(Q²)) has been found since 26 January 2024; recent activity in this area addresses higher-dimensional generalizations (cubes, balls) rather than the planar square case stated in this bullet.
summary: The covering problem of Rado (as stated in the bullet: axis-parallel squares of total unit area, largest guaranteed area of a disjoint sub-collection) has the long-standing known bounds of a greedy lower bound of 1/9 (Radó, 1928), and Ajtai's 1973 disproof of Radó's 1/4 conjecture giving an upper bound of 1/4 − 1/1728 ≈ 0.2494, later refined by Bereg, Dumitrescu and Jiang (2008/2009, published in Algorithmica) to an upper bound of 1/4 − 1/384 ≈ 0.2474 and a lower bound of roughly 1/8.4797 ≈ 0.1179. All of these predate the frozen revision by well over a decade, so they are background, not events in the window. Searches for work since 26 January 2024 turned up two relevant recent preprints: a semi-survey 'Rado's covering problem for cubes and balls' (arXiv 2604.17509, 2026-04) and 'On the weighted hard-core model and Rado's covering problem for congruent Euclidean balls' (arXiv 2608.09744, 2026-08). I fetched both directly (not just abstracts). Both explicitly restrict their new contributions to higher-dimensional cubes and to Euclidean balls (of any dimension, including the plane disk case for the second paper) and general symmetric convex bodies — neither reports any new bound for F(Q²), the exact axis-parallel-square case in the plane that this bullet asks about. Both merely restate the classical 1/9, Ajtai's 1/4−1/1728, and the 1/4−1/384 / ~1/8.4797 bounds as historical context. Under §3.1, a result about squares/balls in dimension d>2, or about disks/general convex bodies in the plane, is a related problem (a changed hypothesis class), not a case of the stated square problem, so even if either paper had produced a new bound for balls or cubes it would not count as a change to this bullet. I also checked two false leads from search noise: 'Symbolic Sets for Proving Bounds on Rado Numbers' (arXiv 2505.12085) concerns Rado numbers in Ramsey theory (monochromatic solutions to linear equations under colorings), an entirely different Rado problem sharing only the name; and 'Covering a square by congruent squares' (arXiv 2601.16535) is the unrelated problem of covering one square by smaller congruent squares (Erdős–Soifer-type problem), not Rado's disjoint-subset-area covering problem. No AI system appears anywhere in either genuinely relevant paper (2604.17509, 2608.09744): both rely purely on classical combinatorial/geometric/probabilistic arguments (hard-core lattice gas models, Brunn–Minkowski, sphere-packing bounds). I found no arXiv preprint, lab announcement, or Wikipedia lead change indicating any AI involvement with this problem in any form. The Wikipedia article's own current content (fetched directly) still reports only the pre-2024 bounds. I am satisfied nothing has happened to the exact stated problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue that since Rado's covering problem is usually stated as a general family F(K) over convex bodies K, the 2026 papers on cubes/balls/general symmetric convex bodies are progress 'on the covering problem of Rado' in a broad sense. But the Wikipedia bullet specifically restricts to axis-parallel squares with unit area in the plane, which is the F(Q²) case; per §3.1 this is the stated question, and generalizing to other bodies or higher dimensions changes rather than restricts it, so it is a related problem, not a case.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or publication that specifically narrows the gap between 1/8.4797 and 1/4−1/384 for the planar axis-parallel-square case F(Q²), or that settles the exact value of F(Q²).

outcome: Two independent, non-peer-reviewed preprints in 2026 claim full proofs of Crouzeix's conjecture (sharp constant 2): a July 27, 2026 manuscript by neurosurgeon Shanmu Jin, produced with substantial assistance from OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and informally reviewed (but not formally refereed) by Anne Greenbaum, Alex Townsend and Michel Crouzeix himself; and an independent, differently-argued proof posted August 4, 2026 by Emiel Lorist and Felix Schwenninger, who used the same model only to explore proof strategies. Neither had completed conventional peer review as of the most recent secondary reporting (mid-August 2026), so the conjecture is not yet counted as resolved by these rules.

ai.basis_quote: Jin reportedly used 'OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol' in what was described as 'an autonomous run lasting about 16 hours' — 'a long-running research system exploring arguments, checking paths, and developing a candidate result.' Jin himself had to recognize relevance, convert findings into coherent proof form, and assume manuscript responsibility. Separately, the GitHub repository's README states: 'OpenAI ChatGPT contributed to proof development, manuscript preparation, and adversarial checking.'

disputes.summary: Two independent proofs of the same 22-year-old conjecture appeared eight days apart in 2026: Shanmu Jin's GPT-5.6-Sol-assisted proof (preprints.org, July 27, 2026) and Emiel Lorist and Felix Schwenninger's independently-derived, differently-argued proof (arXiv:2608.03841, August 4, 2026, revised August 17, 2026). The two used unrelated arguments (Jin's approach vs. Lorist-Schwenninger's double-layer-potential/2-dilation perturbation lemma), and neither cites the other as dependent. A third party, Qinyu Luo (ByteDance), separately published a 'Defect-Gram' proof and a Lean 4 formalization of a related candidate proof on Zenodo in August 2026, apparently as an independent reproduction/verification effort rather than a claim of separate priority.

summary: As of the most recent reporting (mid-to-late August 2026), Crouzeix's conjecture — that the matrix norm of f(A) is at most twice the sup of |f| on the field of values of A — has two independent, non-peer-reviewed claimed proofs, both from 2026, both post-dating the January 2024 frozen revision. (1) Shanmu Jin, a neurosurgery resident at Peking Union Medical College Hospital with no formal advanced-mathematics background, posted a manuscript on preprints.org on July 27, 2026 (preprints.org/manuscript/202607.1919; mirrored with a Lean 4 formalization and a public, privacy-filtered AI-conversation record at github.com/jinshanmu/CrouzeixConjecture). By his and secondary accounts (SIAM News essay by Alex Townsend, SCMP, remio.ai), the key argument was produced by an approximately 16-hour autonomous run of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, with Jin recognizing its relevance and converting it into a coherent manuscript; the repo's own README credits 'OpenAI ChatGPT' with 'proof development, manuscript preparation, and adversarial checking.' Numerical analysts Anne Greenbaum and Alex Townsend, and Michel Crouzeix himself, examined the proof informally and believed it correct, but this is expert digestion short of formal peer review or journal acceptance — so per §6.1 the correct code is `claimed`, not `resolved`. (2) Independently, Emiel Lorist and Felix Schwenninger posted a five-to-ten-page proof via a different operator-theoretic route (double-layer potential representation plus a perturbation lemma for 2-dilations) as arXiv:2608.03841 on August 4, 2026 (v2 August 17, 2026, expanded from 7 to 10 pages). Their own AI disclosure states GPT-5.6 Sol 'was used to explore proof strategies for this note ... to review previous approaches to the weaker spectral constant 1+√2 and to identify a possible source of improvement,' while the authors 'developed, verified, and wrote the complete proof themselves,' taking full responsibility — this is exploring-strategy assistance, which under §6.2 is not `generated` or `assisted` mathematics-production, so on its own this second proof's AI role would code as `none`. Because the two results are close in time and address the identical (not merely related) conjecture, I record the event as Jin's July 27 preprint (the one with substantive, authors'-own-account AI production of mathematics), note the Lorist–Schwenninger proof as a corroborating independent line in `disputes`, and set the overall `ai_role` to `assisted` reflecting the more AI-central of the two credited results. As of the latest secondary source found (an August 2026 SIAM News essay by Townsend, and remio.ai's summary), 'neither public manuscript had completed conventional peer review by August 15, 2026' — no journal acceptance, formal referee report, or full expert write-up (e.g., a Tao-blog-style digestion) was found. I searched for later developments (through September 2026) and found none beyond the ByteDance researcher's independent Lean formalization/reproduction efforts on Zenodo (records 22052523 and 22105428, published August 22 and 24, 2026), which likewise remain non-peer-reviewed. Absent a later peer-reviewed acceptance, `claimed` is the correct status.
competing_reading: One could argue the two proofs, having been informally vetted by leading experts in the field including the conjecture's own author (Crouzeix), and independently corroborated by a second, unrelated derivation within eight days, amount to de facto resolution and should be coded `resolved` — informal consensus among the small number of world experts on a niche numerical-analysis question may be the practical ceiling of 'expert digestion' this topic will ever receive, and waiting for a journal to catch up could be coding-by-formality rather than by substance. Against that: §6.1 explicitly requires 'acceptance by a journal of record, or a published verification by named experts' — an informal 'we reviewed it and believe it's correct' relayed through a SIAM News essay and press coverage is short of a published verification, and multiple contemporaneous sources (as late as mid-August 2026) explicitly flag that peer review was still pending for both. I also considered coding Lorist–Schwenninger's proof (arXiv:2608.03841) as the sole primary event with `ai_role: none`, since by their own account AI only suggested strategy; the alternate record would then treat Jin's proof only as a disputed corroborating claim. Both readings are defensible; I chose Jin's proof as primary because it is the more decisive test of AI involvement that this dataset is built to measure, and used `disputes` to preserve the alternative in full.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance notice, a detailed public referee report, or a thorough expert digestion (e.g., a Tao-style blog post or a survey/Notices article) for either the Jin or the Lorist–Schwenninger manuscript would move the status to `resolved`. Absent that, continued silence past several more months without retraction would still leave it `claimed`; an identified error or retraction of either preprint would move that line to `progress`/`incident` while leaving the other claim (if it survives) as the operative `claimed` status.

disputes.summary: The proof as formalized in Lean covers finite loopless bridgeless multigraphs (allowing parallel edges), which is a broader class than the traditional statement in terms of simple graphs; a commentator (toknow.ai) flagged that mathematicians must independently confirm the Lean definitions match the conventional conjecture's meaning before treating the formal check as settling the classical statement. This is a scope/definitional caveat rather than a rival proof or priority dispute.

summary: On 10 July 2026 OpenAI announced that GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra had produced a two-to-three-page proof of the cycle double cover conjecture (Szekeres 1973 / Seymour 1979) in under an hour using 64 subagents, releasing the proof PDF, the prompt used, and a Lean 4 formalization (github.com/openai/cdc-lean) that OpenAI reports builds cleanly with no 'sorry'/'admit' placeholders and no project-specific axioms. The proof reduces to cubic 3-edge-connected (multi)graphs, uses the Jaeger–Kilpatrick eight-flow theorem / a nowhere-zero F2^3-flow, and a linear-algebra duality argument to build an 8-cycle double cover (the stronger 5-cycle double cover conjecture remains open). Independent human expositions followed within days: Jim Geelen's arXiv note (2607.15399, submitted 16 July 2026, explicitly 'offers no new insights' but recasts the argument) and Sang-il Oum's arXiv exposition (2607.16356, submitted 17 July, revised through 1 August, v3 adding material on the small cycle double cover conjecture and matroid implications). Decisively, Johannes Carmesin — a graph/matroid theorist publishing in JCTB — wrote a guest post on The Matroid Union (21 July 2026) stating directly 'yes, the proof is correct,' after reviewing the argument's structure, the independent Lean 4 formalizations (by Krystal Guo's team, Carmesin's own team, and OpenAI's), and the Geelen/Oum expositions. This is the kind of expert digestion §6.1 treats as sufficient for `resolved` even absent journal publication, which as of my research (September 2026) has not yet occurred. TheoremDB lists the mathematical claim as 'Supported' citing these same expositions, though it separately notes it has not yet run OpenAI's Lean repository inside its own controlled verifier (a note about TheoremDB's own re-verification pipeline, not a doubt raised by any mathematician). The live Wikipedia article on cycle double cover has already been updated to describe the July 2026 preprint and its claimed resolution. Given a specialist's public, reasoned endorsement of correctness in a recognized expert venue, multiple independently-authored Lean formalizations, and no gap, retraction, or dissenting expert view found anywhere in my search, I classify this as `resolved` rather than `claimed`, while noting the caveat about journal non-publication and the multigraph-vs-simple-graph scope point in `competing_reading`.
competing_reading: A stricter reading would keep this at `claimed`: there is no refereed journal publication as of September 2026, Geelen's own note is explicitly not a verification ('no new insights'), and the toknow.ai piece raises a real definitional-scope question (multigraphs vs. simple graphs) that no source shows was formally closed. If Carmesin's blog post is read as a personal opinion rather than the kind of considered, venue-backed expert digestion §6.1 requires, or if The Matroid Union is judged not to rise to the level of a refereed check, `claimed` is the more conservative and defensible call. I weighed this and went with `resolved` because Carmesin's statement is unequivocal, made in a recognized subject-expert venue, backed by his own review of multiple independent formalizations, and unrebutted by any subsequent source I found.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance, or an explicit statement from a second independent expert (beyond Carmesin) confirming the multigraph-vs-simple-graph formalization gap is immaterial or resolved, would remove the remaining ambiguity.

outcome: No result settling Dade's conjecture, a case of it, or a counterexample was found in the window; the only closely-tied development is Rossi's reduction theorem for the (distinct) Character Triple Conjecture, which does not itself advance Dade's conjecture's truth for any group.
summary: I confirm the triage's `none` verdict. Dade's conjecture (as stated on the frozen page: character counts of blocks of G vs. local subgroups) has no resolution, partial resolution, or counterexample in the window 26 Jan 2024–present. The one substantive, clearly-dated development that is closely tied to Dade's program is Damiano Rossi's 'A reduction theorem for the Character Triple Conjecture' (arXiv:2402.10632, posted 15 Feb 2024, published Proc. London Math. Soc. 2025). Its abstract states it proves the Character Triple Conjecture (CTC) — a self-reducing refinement of Dade's conjecture introduced by Späth — holds for all finite groups once it is assumed for quasi-simple groups, thereby completing a reduction program Dade himself pursued in the 1990s. I read the full text via arXiv's HTML rendering: Theorem A is exactly this reduction; the paper does not prove the CTC (or Dade's conjecture) for any quasi-simple group, let alone for Dade's conjecture itself, so no group's status under Dade's conjecture actually changes. Per the scope rule (§3.1), the CTC is a related-but-distinct statement (a different, more restrictive/self-reducing formulation with its own hypotheses) rather than a restriction of Dade's conjecture to a sub-case, and a reduction theorem for it does not remove any territory from Dade's conjecture as stated. I also checked: (1) the Brauer's Height Zero Conjecture proof for odd primes by Malle–Navarro–Schaeffer Fry–Tiep (arXiv:2209.04736, published Annals of Math. 2024) — this is a related but distinct local-global conjecture, and in any case its arXiv preprint predates the frozen revision (Sept 2022), so even if it counted as a case it would be `open_stale`, not new progress; (2) a claimed 2024 verification of the inductive form of Dade's conjecture for Ree groups 2G2(3^(2m+1)) at p=3 (cited to Linear Algebra and its Applications vol. 697, 2024) — I could not locate the underlying arXiv preprint or confirm its actual submission/posting date despite several targeted searches, so I cannot verify whether the underlying work occurred inside or outside the window, and did not find the paper itself to read past a search-engine summary, so I am not using it to change the status; (3) the 'Bolzano' LLM-assisted mathematics paper (arXiv:2604.16989) that surfaced in a search — its problem list (data-structure lower bounds, tiling, cryptographic optimization, algorithm analysis) has no connection to Dade's conjecture or block theory, confirming this was a spurious search hit rather than an AI-related event for this problem. No AI system appears anywhere in the material I could verify as bearing on Dade's conjecture.
competing_reading: If one takes an expansive view of scope in which the Character Triple Conjecture is considered 'the modern form of Dade's conjecture' rather than a related-but-distinct statement (some secondary summaries do describe Rossi's result as 'completing Dade's program'), Rossi's reduction theorem could be read as `progress` on Dade's conjecture with `ai_role` none and `resolution_direction` null. I did not adopt this reading because Dade's conjecture as literally stated (character counts vs. local subgroups) is not itself proven, disproven, or reduced to a smaller open case by Rossi's theorem — the CTC has different, more general hypotheses (character triples rather than blocks directly) and remains unverified for quasi-simple groups, so nothing about Dade's conjecture's own open status changed for any single group.
what_would_settle_it: A clear statement from a survey or from Dade/Späth-school authors on whether the Character Triple Conjecture, once verified for quasi-simple groups, would be considered a literal proof of Dade's original conjecture as stated on the frozen Wikipedia page, or only of a related reformulation; and confirmation of the actual posting date and content of the cited 2024 Ree-group inductive-Dade verification.

outcome: Neither Danzer's original problem (existence of a Danzer set of bounded density) nor Conway's dead fly variant (existence of a Danzer set of bounded separation) has been resolved, refuted, or seen a case settled since 26 January 2024; the only post-window arXiv paper found in this area addresses a distinct, weaker problem (low-visibility dense forests) rather than Danzer sets themselves.
summary: Danzer's 1965 problem (does a Danzer set of bounded density exist?) and Conway's 'dead fly' variant (does a Danzer set of bounded separation exist?) both remain open as of September 2026. The Wikipedia article on Danzer sets, fetched directly, states the core existence question is still unsolved and that known constructions (e.g. growth rate O(T^d log T) by Solomon and Weiss, predating the window) do not have bounded density. Conway's $1000 prize for the separation variant remains unclaimed. The triage record flagged arXiv:2407.01633 ('A New Construction of Forests with Low Visibility', posted July 2024, revised through v3 in December 2024) as a possible lead. I fetched both the abstract page and the PDF: the paper's abstract and visible text contain no mention of 'Danzer', 'Danzer set', or 'Danzer's problem' at all. It constructs a set of points of finite density in R^d such that every sufficiently long line segment comes within distance ε of a point of the set, using at most O(ε^-(d-1) ln ε^-1) points per unit length — an improvement to the 'low-visibility dense forest' bound (previously O(ε^-(d-1) log(ε^-1) log log(ε^-1)^(1+η)) by Tsokanos). A dense/optical forest of finite density with optimal visibility would itself be a Danzer set, but this paper's construction is explicitly a weakening (finite density but not proven optimal/universal visibility against all convex bodies of unit volume) and per the Wikipedia article's own framing, dense-forest work of this kind is a standard relaxation of Danzer's problem, not a case of it — changing the question (bounded visibility for line segments) rather than restricting it. Per DEEP_DIVE §3.1, this is a related problem, not a case of the stated problem, so it does not move the status. No search turned up any AI system credited with progress on Danzer sets, dense forests, or Conway's separation problem; the search results that surfaced 'AI + math problem' matches (DeepMind's FunSearch/cap-set result, Erdős-problems-site tooling) concern unrelated problems. I therefore classify this as open with no_change_found true, and no AI role.
competing_reading: One could argue that improving the dense-forest visibility bound is 'progress' worth recording as `progress` with `ai_role none`, since dense forests are the standard relaxation researchers use precisely because Danzer's problem itself resists direct attack, and any improvement there is the closest thing to forward motion on this cluster of questions in the window. However, per the scope rule in §3.1, a dense forest of finite density is not a Danzer set (it need not intersect every convex body of unit volume, only get close to long line segments), so a bound on it does not change what a careful person would write in the Danzer-set bullet itself. I did not find any source stating that 2407.01633's construction achieves the Danzer property (visibility of every convex body of unit volume rather than long line segments), so I did not upgrade to `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A source (paper, survey, or updated Wikipedia article) explicitly stating either (a) a Danzer set of bounded density or bounded separation has been constructed or proven impossible, or (b) that a specific post-2024 dense-forest construction (such as 2407.01633) achieves the full Danzer property (finite density and universal visibility of every convex body of volume 1), which would make it a genuine case/instance of the problem rather than a related relaxation.

outcome: A June 2026 solo-author preprint (Ryosuke Mizuno, arXiv:2606.15860) reports improved lower bounds for two specific cases of the degree/diameter problem: N(12,5) >= 34,992 (up from the prior record 29,621) and N(16,5) >= 147,456 (up from 132,496), with the constructions explicitly credited to a dialogue with ChatGPT; the paper has not yet received an expert digestion or journal acceptance, though the community-maintained record table has already adopted the new values.

ai.basis_quote: explicit graphs, using a construction discovered through interaction with ChatGPT via its standard web interface ... ChatGPT was used as an interactive discovery engine. The author checked the mathematical claims, code, certificates, citations, final manuscript, and takes responsibility for contents. ... In Round 036 the LLM produced the initial 132-vertex controller combined with a universal chart on F_4^5, yielding N(16,5) >= 135,168. ... In Round 050, a 144-vertex exact-NB-5 controller was obtained from a 6-vertex 4-regular multibase and C4 x C6 voltage coverage. ... The search was conducted without an external orchestration layer around ChatGPT: no custom agent framework, automated evaluator-driven search loop, problem-specific search engine, or formal proof assistant was set up in advance by the author.

summary: The degree/diameter problem (given max degree d and diameter k, find the largest possible graph N(d,k)) is a live-record problem: most (d,k) pairs have no known optimal value, only improving lower-bound constructions tracked in a community table (Comellas's Degree-Diameter Table). Since the 26 January 2024 freeze, the only event I could establish as squarely within scope and within the window is Ryosuke Mizuno's arXiv:2606.15860 (submitted 14 June 2026, v1, no later revision found), which gives explicit 12-regular and 16-regular graphs of diameter 5 improving N(12,5) from 29,621 to 34,992 and N(16,5) from 132,496 to 147,456. This is squarely a 'record' case under this problem's own rule in §3.1 (an existence/infinitude question is not moved by one more example, but here the bullet's quantity IS the record itself, so a bigger explicit construction is a genuine advance on the stated question, classified as `partial` in spirit though because status also has to reflect review state I used `claimed`: the result is a case of the problem settled favorably but not yet digested by named experts or accepted to a journal — Google Scholar/arXiv show only the single v1 preprint, no journal venue, no blog digestion (searches for Terence Tao, Quanta, and general expert reaction turned up nothing about this specific paper — Tao's public ChatGPT-assisted work is a different, unrelated paper on Lebesgue constants). The Comellas maintained table (web.mat.upc.edu/francesc.comellas/delta-d/table_degree_diameter.html), which is the closest thing to an authoritative problem database for this exact quantity, has already updated to show 34,992 and 147,456 as the current entries as of my check (September 2026), which is meaningful community acceptance of the numeric record even without formal peer review; I weighted this together with the single-preprint status and settled on `claimed` over `resolved` because no named expert's independent digestion of the *proof/certificate* was found, only table adoption of the resulting numbers. On the AI side, the paper's own account (quoted in ai.basis_quote) is unusually explicit and mechanistic: the author describes a ~6-day, ~50-round dialogue with ChatGPT's standard web interface (no agent harness, no evaluator loop, no proof assistant) in which the human intervened only at a 'meta-level' (asking for novelty, abstraction, justification) while the LLM produced the actual combinatorial objects (a 'controller' route/chart construction using voltage graph coverage over finite fields) that became the final graphs, cases of the mathematics that end up in the certified result. The human's own contribution was steering the search direction and stopping criteria, and then independently verifying the resulting construction via three levels of computational certificate checks (voltage coverage, edge-list/generation consistency, and an independent diameter computation via igraph). Because the mathematics-that-ends-up-in-the-result (the specific graph construction) is authored-by-account to the LLM, while the human did not supply candidate components and instead verified/directed, I classified this `assisted` rather than `generated`: the paper frames the arrangement as a guided/interactive human-steered search rather than the LLM autonomously generating a finished, human-checked-only proof object, and the human's verification work is substantial and integral, not incidental proofreading. I also searched broadly for any other AI-relevant activity on this problem in the window (FunSearch-style program search, other LLM claims, withdrawn claims) and found none: FunSearch (DeepMind, 2023) is mentioned by Mizuno only as a contrast/related-work citation for a different AI methodology (evaluator-in-the-loop program search), not as itself having produced degree-diameter results, and I found no record of it being applied to this problem. I did not find any resolution of the general problem (which remains almost entirely open outside small/special cases), nor any withdrawal of the Mizuno claim.
competing_reading: One could argue this deserves `partial` rather than `claimed`, since a specific case (N(12,5) and N(16,5)) was genuinely settled in the 'a bigger explicit lower-bound construction now exists and is the current record' sense, and `partial` requires only that a case be settled, which arguably tracks the mathematics better than the 'has an expert reviewed it' axis that `claimed` vs `resolved` is about. I resolved this by treating `claimed`/`resolved` as an orthogonal review-status axis (per §6.1's own framing: 'resolved versus claimed turns on whether a human expert has read the argument') that takes priority when a result is this fresh and unreviewed, rather than `partial`, which I read as reserved for cases that are unambiguously settled and simply narrower in scope than the parent conjecture (which doesn't cleanly apply to a 'produce the largest known example' record-type bullet). A reader could reasonably prefer `partial` instead, or could argue this is `progress` (a bound moved) rather than a settled case at all, since neither N(12,5) nor N(16,5) has a matching upper bound proof — only the lower-bound record moved, and the exact value of N(12,5) or N(16,5) remains completely open. That `progress` reading is also defensible: nothing about the maximum possible size was 'decided' either way, only a better example was exhibited.
what_would_settle_it: An independent expert re-verification or acceptance of the Mizuno construction (e.g., journal publication, a survey or table maintainer's written endorsement beyond just updating the number, or a follow-up paper citing and checking it) would move this from `claimed` toward `resolved`; conversely a retraction or a found error in the certificate would move it to `progress`/`incident`. Also worth checking periodically: whether Comellas's own survey/table publishes an accompanying citation note (rather than just an updated number) that would count as a expert-authored acknowledgment of the result.

outcome: The conjecture as stated (an operadic/little-disks structure on the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra) was already proved by multiple independent methods well before the January 2024 snapshot (Tamarkin 1998/2000; Kontsevich-Soibelman 2000; McClure-Smith 2002; Voronov 2000; Lurie's ∞-categorical version). No development in the 2024-01-26 to present window resolves, reopens, or meaningfully narrows the classical (algebra-level) statement; the one within-window paper found extends the underlying technique to a different class of objects (algebraic schemes, including singular ones) rather than changing anything about the bullet's own statement.

This predates the window and does not affect the status classification, but is worth flagging since sources disagree on primacy.

summary: Deligne's conjecture on Hochschild cohomology (the operadic/little-disks structure on the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra) was resolved well before the frozen Wikipedia revision, with several independent proofs from 1998-2002 (Tamarkin; Kontsevich-Soibelman; McClure-Smith; Voronov) and a further ∞-categorical version by Lurie. The Wikipedia article itself, current as of a July 2026 edit, still describes the conjecture as proved by these authors and records no post-2024 resolution claim, consistent with the list simply being stale on this entry. Searching specifically for the 2024-01-26-to-present window, I found one relevant preprint: Sonja Farr, 'E2-algebra structures on the derived center of an algebraic scheme' (arXiv:2506.14069, submitted June 16, 2025), which recovers a canonical solution to Deligne's conjecture on Hochschild cochains 'in the affine and global cases, even for singular schemes' via an infinity-operadic-center argument. This is new work in the window, but it extends the conjecture's technique to a different class of objects (algebraic schemes, including singular ones) rather than resolving, reopening, or narrowing the classical statement about Hochschild cochains of an associative algebra that the Wikipedia bullet actually states -- per the scope rule (§3.1) this reads as a related/extended problem (different objects) rather than a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not change the status. I also found the 2023 Brav-Rozenblyum result establishing a 'cyclic Deligne conjecture' (arXiv:2305.10323) and its Calabi-Yau-structure applications; this is explicitly a variant with different hypotheses (cyclic structure, relative Calabi-Yau data) and predates the window regardless. No AI involvement was found in any of the sources checked: the Farr paper's acknowledgements thank only a human thesis advisor and an NSF grant, with no mention of AI, machine learning, or LLM tools anywhere in the text.
competing_reading: One could argue the Farr (2025) extension to singular schemes is a 'case' of the general conjectural picture in the broader sense that operadic Hochschild-cochain structures are being established in a strictly wider class of settings than the original algebra case, and that Wikipedia's own statement is loosely worded enough ('the operadic structure on Hochschild cochain complex') that it could be read as covering the geometric/scheme generalization too. Under that reading this would be `partial`, `ai_role` none, dated to 2025-06-16, direction `confirmed`. I judged this the weaker reading because the classical conjecture is specifically about associative algebras (per both the arXiv:9910126 solution and the Wikipedia article's own framing), and the scheme-level Deligne conjecture is treated in the literature (including by Iwanari 2020 and Brav-Rozenblyum) as its own strand of generalization rather than as an unresolved fragment of the original.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Wikipedia's own article or a mathematical survey treats the scheme-level/global Deligne conjecture as literally the same statement as the classical algebra-level one (in which case Farr's 2025 paper would count as a `partial` result in-window) or as a distinct, separately-posed generalization (as I read it, leaving the bullet `open_stale`).

outcome: The conjecture was fully resolved decades before the frozen revision: proved for classical groups by Lakshmibai, Musili and Seshadri (1979) via standard monomial theory, and extended to all reductive algebraic groups by Peter Littelmann in his 1998 paper 'Cones, crystals, and patterns' (Transformation Groups 3(2), 145-179) using the Littelmann path model. Nothing relevant happened in the 26 Jan 2024 - present window; the Wikipedia list entry is simply stale.
summary: The Demazure conjecture (1974) concerns whether certain Z-submodules of irreducible representations of algebraic groups are direct summands, i.e. whether Demazure's results on Schubert varieties extend from complex algebraic groups to algebraic groups over fields of other characteristics or over the integers. Both Wikipedia's own article on the conjecture and a corroborating Grokipedia summary state it was proved for classical groups (types A, B, C, D) by Lakshmibai-Musili-Seshadri in 1979 via standard monomial theory, and extended to all reductive algebraic groups by Littelmann in 1998 (identified via search as 'Cones, crystals, and patterns', Transform. Groups 3(2), 145-179) using the Littelmann path model. This is a fully digested, textbook-level result decades old, well before the 26 January 2024 window. I searched arXiv broadly for 'Demazure conjecture' activity in 2024-2025 and found only papers using the Demazure name for related but distinct combinatorial objects -- Demazure crystals, Demazure operators, Demazure products/atoms -- none of which are this conjecture (about integral structures / Z-submodule direct summands for algebraic group representations) restated or extended; they are different problems that happen to share the Demazure name (per the scope rule in §3.1, these are not cases or restatements of the stated conjecture). No AI system is involved anywhere in this history; the only credited work is by human mathematicians in 1979 and 1998. This is a clear case of the Wikipedia list retaining an already-solved problem, hence status open_stale rather than open or resolved (resolved would incorrectly imply resolution happened within or bears on the measurement window).
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is simply 'resolved' rather than 'open_stale' on the grounds that the result is settled and expert-digested. However, per §6.1, open_stale is specifically for problems settled before the frozen revision's date and never counted as a change in the window, which is exactly this case -- the resolution predates the 26 Jan 2024 snapshot by 26-45 years, so open_stale is the correct code, not resolved (which would misleadingly suggest the resolution is part of what happened since 2024).
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed to settle the classification; the only way this could change is if a source were found showing the 1979/1998 resolution was later found flawed or incomplete and reopened/refined within the 2024-2026 window, which no search here turned up.

outcome: The density hypothesis (A(σ) ≤ 2 for 1/2 ≤ σ ≤ 1) remains open, but the underlying zero-density bound moved for the first time in ~50-80 years: Guth and Maynard (arXiv:2405.20552, May 2024; now published Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 2) proved N(σ,T) ≤ T^(30(1-σ)/13+o(1)), lowering the classical supremum-type exponent from Huxley's 12/5=2.4 (1971) to 30/13≈2.31 in the range 1/2 ≤ σ ≤ 3/4, the first improvement on Ingham's 1940 bound there. Tao, Trudgian and Yang (arXiv:2501.16779, Jan 2025) subsequently obtained further zero-density improvements via a systematic, largely automated optimization over their newly built Analytic Number Theory Exponent Database (ANTEDB), without introducing new analytic inputs.

ai.basis_quote: In the longer term one could also imagine integrating the ANTEDB with other tools, such as Lean or AI systems, but for now we have focused primarily on collecting the data and optimizing the relations between the exponents.

summary: Two results moved the density-hypothesis quantity A(σ) since the frozen revision, but neither settles the hypothesis, and neither involves AI. (1) Guth and Maynard, 'New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials' (arXiv:2405.20552, submitted 2024-05-31), proved a large-value estimate for Dirichlet polynomials that yields N(σ,T) ≤ T^(30(1-σ)/13+o(1)) for 1/2 ≤ σ ≤ 3/4, the first improvement on Ingham's 1940 exponent in that range in over 80 years, and the first lowering of Huxley's 1971-era supremum bound (12/5=2.4 → 30/13≈2.31) in roughly 50 years. This is expert-digested — Tao devoted a detailed blog post ('A computation-outsourced discussion...', 2024-07-07) to working through the proof, and the paper has since been formally published in the Annals of Mathematics (vol. 203, no. 2, 2026), so treating it as `resolved`-grade digestion is warranted; however the *problem itself* (density hypothesis, A(σ)≤2 for all σ) is not resolved by it, so `status` is `progress` rather than `resolved` or `partial` — the bound moved but no case of A(σ)≤2 was newly settled beyond what was already known via Ingham/Huxley/Bourgain style bounds in adjacent ranges. (2) Tao, Trudgian and Yang, 'New exponent pairs, zero density estimates, and zero additive energy estimates: a systematic approach' (arXiv:2501.16779, submitted 2025-01-28), built the Analytic Number Theory Exponent Database (ANTEDB) and ran computer-assisted (but non-AI) linear/systematic optimization over known exponent relations to further improve several zero-density and related exponents 'in a largely automated fashion (without introducing any substantial new inputs from analytic number theory).' This is explicitly a database/optimization search, not machine learning — the authors themselves note that integrating the ANTEDB with 'AI systems' is a stated *future* goal, not something used here. On AI involvement specifically: I found no AI system credited with producing any part of either paper's mathematics. The one AI-adjacent detail I found is incidental: in his July 2024 blog post explaining the Guth-Maynard proof to a general audience, Tao mentions using Python 'with AI assistance, for instance via Github Copilot' to generate constraint-optimization graphs for expository/illustrative purposes — this is Tao's own digestion aid, not part of Guth-Maynard's proof or result, so it does not change `ai_role` for the event, which is coded `none`. I also checked a July 2026 expository/survey paper (Turnage-Butterbaugh, arXiv:2607.04632, a JMM Current Events Bulletin companion piece) which discusses the Guth-Maynard breakthrough but adds no new result and mentions no AI. A September 2026 paper (arXiv:2609.17875, 'Zero-Density Concentration for Dirichlet Polynomials') appeared in search results but concerns a different notion (deterministic concentration of normalized zero density via Bohr lifts) and does not engage with or improve on the Guth-Maynard/density-hypothesis exponent A(σ), so I treat it as a dead end rather than a case of this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Guth-Maynard result, now published in the Annals and thoroughly digested by Tao, plus its downstream consequences (improved short-interval prime results) constitute enough independent verification and importance to warrant a `partial` status if one reads the density hypothesis as a family of range-indexed sub-claims (A(σ)≤2 for each σ) and treats the newly-covered range as a 'case settled.' I did not take this reading because Guth-Maynard's bound (30/13≈2.31) is still strictly above the conjectured value of 2 for the range it covers — it improves the *known* exponent but does not establish A(σ)≤2 for any σ, so no case of the actual conjectured inequality was proved true or false. That keeps it as `progress` (a bound moved) rather than `partial` (a case settled), per §3.1's rule that record-type/bound-type problems move only when the record IS the question — here the question is an inequality, not yet met, so it stays open with only the surrounding bound narrowing.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that A(σ) ≤ 2 for some specific σ in (1/2, 1) — i.e., an exponent bound at or below 2 in some range — would settle a genuine case of the density hypothesis (as opposed to merely tightening a bound still above 2). Full resolution requires A(σ) ≤ 2 for all σ in that range.
