outcome: No proof, counterexample, new case, or bound improvement on the Marcus-de Oliveira determinantal conjecture was found in the window; the only post-snapshot item is a February 2025 survey paper that reviews pre-existing (largely pre-2024) partial results without adding new mathematics.
summary: The Marcus-de Oliveira determinantal conjecture (det(A+B) lies in the convex hull of n! points, for normal A, B) remains open. Searches for a proof, disproof, new special case, or bound improvement since 26 January 2024 turned up nothing new. The only item published in the window is Bebiano and da Providência, 'Revisiting the Marcus-de Oliveira Conjecture' (Mathematics, MDPI 13(5):711, published 22 February 2025), which is explicitly a survey: it 'reviews the main achievements relating to this open problem... and aims to bring attention... to stimulate the development of original approaches' — it establishes no new result, so it does not change status. The Khadejah Homadi Auburn thesis surfaced repeatedly in searches ('Progress on the Marcus-de Oliveira Determinantal Conjecture') is from 2017, well before the window, and compiles prior known partial cases (n-2 equal eigenvalues, essentially-Hermitian pairs, a class of normal dilations from a 2020/2021 paper) — none of that is new either and none postdates the frozen revision. A July 2026 arXiv preprint (2607.21163) that surfaced under similar search terms concerns a different conjecture entirely — a normal-matrix extension of a determinantal conjecture of Lin about det(A*A+|BA|^p) vs det(AA*+|A*B*|^p) — and does not touch the Marcus-de Oliveira sum-of-normal-matrices conjecture; it is excluded as out of scope (§3.1, a related/different problem, not a case of this one). The dedicated Wikipedia article 'Determinantal conjecture' is a stub with no post-2024 content. No AI system was mentioned in connection with this conjecture anywhere in the search results; general searches for LLM-solved conjectures returned unrelated problems (cycle double cover conjecture, Goldbach-related work), confirming no crossover. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 MDPI survey itself constitutes a form of progress by consolidating scattered partial results and explicitly restating open sub-questions (e.g., the n=4, X Hermitian/Y normal subconjecture) in a way that could focus future research — but a survey with no new theorem does not change what a careful reader would write in the Wikipedia bullet, so it does not meet the bar for `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or publication dated after 26 January 2024 that proves a new case of the conjecture (e.g., resolving the n=4 Hermitian/normal subconjecture), improves on the known partial results, or exhibits/rules out a counterexample; alternatively, explicit confirmation from a specialist survey (e.g., a future edition of the MDPI-hosted review) that no such result exists.

outcome: For k≥5, Leng, Sah and Sawhney proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) for some c_k>0, the first improvement to the upper bound on r_k(N) for k≥5 since Gowers's 2001 bound; the exact growth rate remains unknown and the problem is still open.
summary: This bullet asks for the growth rate of r_k(N), the size of the largest subset of {1,...,N} with no k-term arithmetic progression — a quantity for which the exact asymptotic order is unknown for every k≥3, so by the special carve-out in §3.1 ('a bullet asking for ... the value of a constant/record'), any bound improvement on this quantity is itself a change to what the bullet's entry would say, not a mere restriction of the question. The decisive event in the window is Leng, Sah and Sawhney's arXiv:2402.17995 ('Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem'), first posted 2024-02-28 (v2 2024-02-29), proving that for all k≥5 there is c_k>0 with r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}). This is the first improvement to the k≥5 upper bound since Gowers's 2001 result r_k(N) < N/(log log N)^{c_k}, and it was digested by experts: Quanta Magazine's 2024-08-05 feature quotes Ben Green (Oxford) calling it 'phenomenally impressive' and the authors' advisor Yufei Zhao calling it 'a huge achievement.' I classify this as `resolved`-adjacent but coded `progress` rather than `resolved` or `partial`, because the problem itself (determine the true growth rate) remains open — only the known bound moved; no case of the full problem was settled and no journal acceptance was found (as of this search the paper is still an arXiv preprint, not yet listed as journal-published). I found no involvement of any AI system in this work: the paper's own text (as much as could be extracted), the Quanta article, and general search turned up nothing about AI/ML/LLM assistance — this appears to be entirely human mathematical work built on companion paper arXiv:2402.17994 (quasipolynomial Gowers inverse theorem bounds) and prior work of Green, Tao and Ziegler. Separately, for k=3, Bloom and Sisask's r_3(N) bound (arXiv:2302.07211, originally 2023, revised to v3 in 2025-05) predates the window for its core result and is not treated as a fresh event; I found one small 2026 arXiv computational note (2606.04016, solo author Mehmet Ergezer) reporting a SAT/ILP/Lean computational search supporting the specific value r_3(212)=43, but this is a single finite-N computational data point, not a growth-rate bound, and its abstract discloses no AI involvement either — I judged it out of scope for this bullet (it doesn't move an asymptotic growth-rate bound) and did not use it as the basis for status or dating.
competing_reading: One could argue this bullet, being an open-ended 'determine the growth rate' request rather than a bullet explicitly asking for a record/constant value, should be treated like an ordinary existence/infinitude question where narrowing an unknown quantity doesn't count as a change (per the general rule in §3.1) — under that stricter reading the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true, since no one has determined the actual growth rate, only moved a bound. I judged the growth-rate/bound exception in §3.1 ('a bullet asking for a largest known object or the value of a constant') to apply here because r_k(N)'s asymptotic order is precisely a 'value of a function/constant' the bullet asks to pin down, and bound movements are the only kind of progress that can ever occur on such a bullet before full resolution.
what_would_settle_it: A published statement (or triage-level consensus) clarifying whether 'determine growth rate of X' bullets are to be scored like record/constant bullets (any bound movement counts) or like existence/infinitude bullets (only full resolution counts) would remove this ambiguity.

outcome: The overall structure of Keisler's order remains open, but a September 2025 expository paper by Malliaris (arXiv:2509.14068) discloses a new theorem, from a book manuscript in progress with Shelah, introducing a 'canonical Boolean algebra' construction and proving a chain-condition result for it (for the random graph, extended to simple theories with trivial forking); this is new machinery aimed at the structure problem, not yet published as a standalone refereed paper.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the overall structure of Keisler's order, a decades-old classification program in model theory. The triage record was correct that no result settling or substantially reshaping the overall structure appeared in the window; the two headline results it found (infinitely many classes, 2015/2018; continuum many classes / 'Keisler's order is not simple', arXiv:1906.10241, 2019) both predate 26 January 2024, as does the closely related 'Some simple theories from a Boolean algebra point of view' (Malliaris-Shelah, arXiv:2108.05314, posted August 2021, journal-published July 2023 despite carrying an 'Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 175 (2024)' volume label — I verified the PDF's own 'Available online 24 July 2023' date, so this is open_stale-adjacent and not counted as a within-window event). I searched further for anything genuinely new since the frozen date and found one item: Maryanthe Malliaris's September 2025 solo expository paper 'On ultrafilter construction' (arXiv:2509.14068, submitted 2025-09-17), which is a historical/pedagogical survey of the field but also explicitly discloses a new theorem (§14, Theorem 14.1) from a forthcoming Malliaris-Shelah book manuscript 'Ultrafilters and Theories' (cited as [Malliaris-Shelah], 'manuscript in progress'). This theorem introduces a newly defined 'canonical Boolean algebra' associated to a theory T and proves it satisfies a strong chain condition for the random graph, extending to any simple theory with trivial forking under mild parameter changes. This is squarely about the mechanisms underlying Keisler's order's structure (the algebra doesn't depend on choosing an ultrafilter jointly, unlike the 2021 construction) and is new mathematics disclosed within the window, so it counts as `progress`: a technical building-block result, not a resolution and not even a fully separate refereed paper yet. I classified it `progress` rather than `claimed` because it is not offered as a completed proof of a major open question but as an incremental theorem in an ongoing research program, presented by one of the two field-leading authors in an expository context; I did not find a subsequent standalone research paper stating and proving Theorem 14.1 in full detail, so no independent expert digestion of the full proof exists yet, but the informal nature and modest scope of the claim (a chain-condition lemma) makes 'progress' more apt than 'claimed' (which better fits a claimed resolution awaiting verification). No AI system is mentioned anywhere in any of the sources checked. I also checked and ruled out several other candidate 2024-2026 papers as out-of-scope variants (per the problem's scope rule, §3.1): Keisler measures / invariant Keisler measures (arXiv:2408.08370, arXiv:2406.00912, arXiv:2605.15870) and the Rudin-Keisler order on ultrafilters over measurable cardinals or P-points (arXiv:2601.10614, arXiv:2404.03238, arXiv:2511.19354) are distinct mathematical objects from Keisler's order (the ultrapower-saturation preorder on complete theories) despite sharing Keisler's name; none of these bear on the structure of Keisler's order itself. I also want to flag that an earlier WebSearch tool call hallucinated a '2026' date for Douglas Ulrich's 2018 paper 'Keisler's Order and Full Boolean-Valued Models' (arXiv:1810.05335) — I verified directly via WebFetch that this paper was submitted 2018-10-12 with a single version, so it is not a within-window event and I have excluded it.
competing_reading: One could argue the September 2025 survey paper's Theorem 14.1 should not count at all, on the grounds that it is announced in an expository/celebratory piece (dedicated to Shelah's birthday) rather than a dedicated research paper, and that the full proof lives only in an unpublished, unavailable book manuscript that I could not inspect — meaning this is closer to a preview or announcement than a citable, checkable result, and arguably the record should be `open` with `no_change_found: true` since no independently verifiable new theorem about the *overall* structure has actually landed. I lean toward `progress` because the theorem statement itself (with hypotheses and conclusion) is fully given in the paper, is new (not a restatement of prior work), and is clearly offered as an established fact ('Here is a first theorem from the book in progress'), not merely a promise of future work.
what_would_settle_it: Locating the full Malliaris-Shelah manuscript 'Ultrafilters and Theories' (or a subsequent standalone arXiv posting extracting Theorem 14.1 and its proof) would let me verify the proof directly and would also reveal whether later chapters of that manuscript make more substantial progress on the structure question than what is disclosed in the September 2025 survey.

outcome: No proof, disproof, case settlement, or bound movement on Dickson's conjecture itself has been found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open exactly as it was.
summary: Dickson's conjecture (1904) — that any admissible finite set of linear forms a_i + b_i·n is simultaneously prime for infinitely many n — remains completely open. It generalizes the twin prime conjecture (k=2) and Sophie Germain primes, and is itself a special case of Schinzel's Hypothesis H and equivalent to a restricted form of the Hardy-Littlewood prime k-tuples conjecture. The known partial results — Zhang (2013) proving bounded gaps between primes, Maynard and Tao (2013, independently) proving that admissible k-tuples of sufficient size contain infinitely many shifts with m primes for any fixed m, and Green-Tao-Ziegler's proof of the prime k-tuple conjecture for linear forms with no two satisfying a linear relation over the integers (giving infinitely many k-term prime arithmetic progressions) — all predate the 26 January 2024 window by roughly a decade, so none of them can count as an event in scope even under open_stale, since none of them settles the conjecture or a case of it in the first place (Green-Tao-Ziegler excludes exactly the parallel/coincident-form cases that make Dickson's conjecture hard, i.e. it proves a genuinely different, non-overlapping sufficient condition, not a case of Dickson's conjecture as literally stated for forms that can be linearly dependent). I searched arXiv listings, Google, and the current (2026) Wikipedia article on Dickson's conjecture directly — the live article's most recent citation is from 1996 and it contains no post-2024 status update. I also checked whether Dickson's conjecture appears as an AI target in the current wave of AI-driven Erdős-problem-solving (Google DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' Lean benchmark, the OpenAI unit-distance-conjecture disproof, and reports of ~100 Erdős problems moved to 'solved' since October 2025). Dickson's conjecture is not among the Erdős problems being attacked; the only hit connecting it to that ecosystem is a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #5672) reporting a misformalization bug in a Lean *variant* of an unrelated problem (Erdos 891, 'variants.weisenberg'), where the formal statement omitted Dickson's conjecture as a required hypothesis for a different, conditional result. That bug (found by an 'AI-powered audit' per the fetched summary and fixed in PR #5771) is about the correctness of someone else's formalization that merely cites Dickson's conjecture as an assumption — it does not touch Dickson's conjecture's truth, forge a case of it, or move any bound on it, so it is out of scope under §3.1 (a related/citing context, not a case or resolution) and is not recorded as an event. No preprint, announcement, or repository posting anywhere claims progress on Dickson's conjecture itself in the window. The correct classification is open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Green-Tao-Ziegler theorem (which does postdate Dickson's 1904 statement by a century but predates the 2024-01-26 window by ~18 years) is a 'case' of Dickson's conjecture already settled before the window and thus should be flagged as open_stale rather than plain open, since it does resolve the conjecture for a broad class of admissible forms (those with no two related by a rational affine dependency). I did not classify it that way because (a) it predates the window by so much that it was surely already reflected in the Wikipedia page's frozen 2024 wording, which still states the conjecture as fully open, and (b) more importantly, no new instance of this or a comparable case-settlement occurred inside the 2024-01-26–present window, so there is nothing to date as the 'first written argument' for an open_stale record — open_stale requires an event whose date needs recording, and the pre-existing, decade-old partial results don't constitute a discrete event in this window. If a reviewer wants the pre-window Green-Tao-Ziegler result explicitly logged, this record would become open_stale dated to 2006 (Green-Tao) / 2010s (Green-Tao-Ziegler) with the same no_change_found-in-window narrative in summary.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement, dated after 26 January 2024, that either (a) proves or disproves Dickson's conjecture in general, (b) proves it for some previously-unsettled class of admissible linear-form tuples not already covered by Green-Tao-Ziegler or Maynard-Tao, or (c) states a new quantitative bound specific to Dickson-type tuples (e.g. an improved density or size threshold for k in the 'infinitely many shifts with m primes' results) that a careful reading would say updates this bullet's text.

outcome: The upper-bound side (Huxley's 131/416 ≈ 0.3149 exponent for Δ(x)=O(x^θ+ε)) has not moved in the window: a claimed improvement to θ≈0.314483 by Li and Yang has existed as an arXiv preprint since August 2023 (before the frozen revision) and remains unpublished and undigested as of September 2026, so it does not count as a change. But the lower-bound (Ω) side of the classical k=1 problem did move in the window: Sourmelidis (arXiv:2411.14221, Nov 2024, accepted at Mathematika) and Mahatab (arXiv:2504.17032, Apr 2025, published in the Ramanujan Journal, 2026) independently improved Soundararajan's 2003 Ω-result for Δ(x) using the resonance method, and Lamzouri (arXiv:2605.21476, May 2026) then obtained a further, conjecturally sharp Ω+ result removing a log-loss factor that had persisted since Hafner's 1981 bound — the paper's own abstract calls it 'the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Ω+ result for the divisor problem.' These are genuine, peer-reviewed advances specifically on the classical (k=1) case, so the problem counts as partial progress, not open-with-no-change.

disputes.summary: Sourmelidis's improvement to Soundararajan's omega result and Mahatab's improvement were obtained independently using different resonator constructions; Mahatab's paper states the two efforts were concurrent and independent, with no priority conflict claimed by either side.

summary: The k=1 (classical Dirichlet) divisor problem has two live fronts: the upper bound on θ in Δ(x)=O(x^θ+ε), and the omega (lower bound / oscillation) side showing Δ(x) must be at least as large as some function infinitely often. On the upper-bound side, the triage record surfaced a Feb 2025 UIUC talk by Xuerui Yang and Xiaochun Li reporting θ≈0.314483, beating Huxley's 131/416≈0.31490. I traced this to arXiv:2308.14859, whose v1 was posted 28 August 2023 and v2 on 14 September 2023 — both before the 26 January 2024 frozen-revision cutoff. I checked Yang's own personal site listing her publications: as of the check, this paper is still listed as a 'preprint' with no journal, more than two years after posting, and the current (September 2026) Wikipedia article on the divisor summatory function still cites only Huxley's 2003 bound as the record, not Li-Yang's. There is no dated post-window re-submission, correction, or expert digestion (no Bulletin/Annals writeup, no blog digestion by e.g. Tao) that I could find. So this claim is excluded from the window under §6.3 (dated by first written argument, which predates the cutoff) and also fails the `resolved`/`claimed` bar since no expert has published a check of it. On the omega side, which is squarely the k=1 case and not a variant, three papers moved the bound within the window: Sourmelidis (arXiv:2411.14221, submitted 21 Nov 2024, revised 29 Apr 2026, noted as 'to appear in Mathematika' with an active DOI) and Mahatab (arXiv:2504.17032, submitted 23 Apr 2025, published in the Ramanujan Journal vol. 69, article 91, 2026) independently improved Soundararajan's 2003 omega result via the resonance method; Lamzouri (arXiv:2605.21476, submitted 20 May 2026) then sharpened this further, explicitly billing it as the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Ω+ bound. None of these papers' abstracts, and none of the secondary summaries I could extract, mention any AI or machine-learning tool in deriving the mathematics. Overall: `partial` progress, `ai_role` none, dated to the first (Sourmelidis) preprint in the chain, 21 November 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the omega-side improvements are a 'related' refinement rather than a case of 'the' problem, since Wikipedia's bullet (as commonly read) is usually about the upper-bound exponent θ, and the omega side is a different (though classical and well-established) sub-question about the same Δ(x). I read it as squarely in scope because the Piltz/Dirichlet divisor problem is standardly understood to include both the upper- and lower-bound sides of Δ(x)'s growth, and Wikipedia's own phrasing ('bounding Δ_k(x)') does not restrict to one direction. If a stricter reading confines the bullet to only the upper bound (θ), the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true, since the Li-Yang claim is pre-window and undigested.
what_would_settle_it: A clear statement, e.g. in the Wikipedia article's own wording or a canonical survey, of whether the bullet is meant to cover only the upper bound θ or both directions of Δ(x)'s growth. Also, any future journal acceptance or expert digestion (e.g., a referee report, a citation as an established result in a survey, or a Tao-style blog write-up) of the Li-Yang 2023 preprint would settle whether the upper-bound side has genuinely moved, and would push that event's classification toward `open_stale` (since dated pre-window) rather than remaining excluded as unverified.

outcome: No case of the general Hadwiger dissection conjecture beyond dimension 5 was settled, and no bound moved in this window; the only new 2024-2025 publication in this area re-proves an already-known special case (dissecting an orthoscheme itself into n smaller orthoschemes) rather than advancing the open conjecture about general simplices.
summary: The Hadwiger dissection conjecture (every n-simplex can be dissected into f(n) orthoschemes for some function f) remains open for dimension 6 and above, exactly as it stood on 26 January 2024: proven cases are only dimension 2 (2 orthoschemes), 3 (12), 4 (500), and 5 (~12.5 million). I checked the current Wikipedia article (last edited 27 December 2025 with no citations newer than 2009), the researcher-written survey at florestan.xyz (which discusses the conjecture in detail and mentions no progress past dimension 5, no dimension-6 attempts, and no computational/AI approaches), and searched broadly for any post-2024 arXiv or journal work claiming progress on the general conjecture. None was found. The one 2024-2025 publication I turned up in this space, István Lénárt's 'The Coxeter Trisection and the Hadwiger Conjecture in Multidimensional Spaces' (Journal of Applied Mathematics and Physics, Vol. 12, pp. 4301-4321, Dec 2024, DOI 10.4236/jamp.2024.1212264) and its follow-up 'Proving a Special Case of the Coxeter-Hadwiger Conjecture' (JAMP 2025, 13(8), 2700-2711), gives an algebraic proof that an n-dimensional Pythagorean simplex (i.e., an orthoscheme itself) can be trisected/dissected into n smaller orthoschemes of the same type. This is not a case of the stated conjecture in the sense that matters: the conjecture is about dissecting an arbitrary (general) simplex into orthoschemes, and the open frontier is dimension >= 6. Lénárt's starting object is already an orthoscheme, and the generalization of Coxeter's trisection of a path-simplex into n path-subsimplices for arbitrary dimension n was already established by Brandts, Korotov and Krizek in 2007 ('Dissection of the path-simplex in R^n into n path-subsimplices', Linear Algebra Appl.), well before the frozen revision date, so even read charitably as touching the conjecture's territory, this would be `open_stale`, not new progress. Because the scirp.org site returned 403 to automated fetching, I could not read the full abstract directly and relied on multiple independent search-result excerpts (consistent across four separate searches) describing the paper's actual content; I was unable to open the PDF or the paperinformation page myself. I found no mention anywhere of AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving involvement in any source touching this problem. I classify the record as open/no_change_found because no work in the window changed what a careful person would write about the stated conjecture (dissecting a general simplex, dimension >= 6 open).
competing_reading: One could argue the Lénárt papers deserve a `partial`/`open_stale` note rather than being folded entirely into 'no change', since they nominally invoke 'the Hadwiger Conjecture' in their titles and touch the same family of objects (orthoschemes, Coxeter trisection). But per the scope rule in §3.1, this is a related/variant construction (dissecting an already-orthoscheme simplex into orthoschemes) rather than a case of the stated question (dissecting a general simplex), and the underlying mathematical result it reproves predates the frozen revision by 17 years. I judged this insufficient to move the status off `open`, but flag the ambiguity since the triage pass's `found: []` did not surface these papers at all.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint claiming (with expert digestion) a bound f(6) for dissecting a general 6-dimensional simplex into finitely many orthoschemes, or a proof that no such finite bound exists in some dimension, would settle or move this record. Direct confirmation of the exact abstract text of the Lénárt papers (currently blocked by scirp.org's 403 response to automated fetchers) would also sharpen the classification, though based on consistent secondary descriptions I am confident it does not touch dimension >= 6 of the general conjecture.

summary: The frozen January 2024 statement of the Dittert conjecture (uniquely maximized at A=(1/n)Jₙ) had, before the window, already been settled for n=2 (Sinkhorn, 1980s), n=3 (Hwang, 1987) and n=4 (Divya K.U. and Somasundaram, arXiv:2312.00464, submitted 1 Dec 2023 — this is open_stale territory for that case, not a change in this window). Within the window: Zhekai Pang (arXiv:2606.01531, submitted 1 Jun 2026, Universitat Pompeu Fabra) proved the conjecture for every n≥17, combining the Knopp–Sinkhorn bound with a refined Cheon–Wanless scaling argument; no AI involvement is disclosed anywhere in that paper. Boris Kafidov (arXiv:2607.19439, submitted 21 Jul 2026) then closed n=16, explicitly disclosing that 'the proof strategy, the joint-deficit scaling lemma, and most of the original proof text' were produced by OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol (released 9 Jul 2026, confirmed via independent search) via ChatGPT, with Kafidov directing the process and taking authorship responsibility — this is squarely ai_role=generated per §6.2 (the model produced the mathematics that is in the result: the strategy, the central lemma, and most of the text). Together, Pang + Kafidov reduce the open range to 5≤n≤15. A third preprint (Li, Xiong, Yang; arXiv:2607.29191, ~Aug 2026) gives an independent exact sum-of-squares certificate, MOSEK-discovered and Lean-verified, for n=4 — but n=4 was already resolved in Dec 2023, so this is a re-proof of an already-settled case, not new territory, and discloses no LLM use (only SDP solving and Lean formal verification, which are not AI systems under §6.2). None of the three 2026 preprints have been digested by a named human expert (no Tao blog post, no Quanta piece, no journal acceptance found); the only 'review' located is an automated AI-reviewer site (Pith Review), which flagged a citation gap in Kafidov's equality-case argument (an unverified reliance on Hwang's Proposition 2.1(ii)) and recommended conditional acceptance pending a fix — this is not expert digestion and does not qualify the paper for `resolved`. Wikipedia's live article was checked directly and has NOT been updated to reflect any of the 2026 results: its most recent substantive edit is from 12 January 2026 (an authorlink fix), predating all three preprints; the triage's claim that 'the conjecture's Wikipedia article now reflects the n≥17 result' is not borne out and is flagged as a disagreement. Given this, status is `partial` (cases n=16 and n≥17 newly settled within the window, general conjecture for 5≤n≤15 still open) and the decisive event for ai_role purposes is the Kafidov n=16 paper, since it is the one carrying AI involvement.
competing_reading: One could argue the decisive `event` should instead be Pang's n≥17 result, since it is the larger and more consequential piece of progress (settling all but finitely many dimensions) and carries no AI involvement, which would leave ai_role as `none` for the 'main' event and relegate Kafidov's GPT-generated n=16 result to a secondary note. I chose to foreground the Kafidov paper because this record must reflect the AI question centrally, and it is the specific event this problem contributes to the AI-involvement count; both are reported and dated in the record.
what_would_settle_it: A named human expert (e.g. a specialist in permanent/doubly-stochastic-matrix combinatorics, or a Tao-style blog digestion) reading and either endorsing or rejecting the Pang and Kafidov arguments, including resolving the citation gap flagged in the Kafidov paper; a full proof or disproof for the remaining range 5≤n≤15; and a check of whether Wikipedia's article is ever updated to reflect these preprints.

outcome: An explicit three-variable counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture (announced 19-20 July 2026, credited by its announcer to Claude Fable 5) falsifies the Dixmier conjecture for the n-th Weyl algebra for every n≥3, via the well-known (easy-direction) implication DC_n ⇒ JC_n; the n=1 and n=2 cases remain open. Separately, Alexander Zheglov has an unreviewed preprint (arXiv:2410.06959, last revised Jan 2026) claiming a proof for n=1, which would be a full resolution of the original problem as usually stated but has not been digested by experts or accepted by a journal.

ai.basis_quote: hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil for asking about it and my other close friend fable for working during the world cup final

counterexample.object: An explicit polynomial self-map of C^3 with constant Jacobian determinant (−2) that is not injective (three distinct points collide); padding with untouched coordinates x_4,...,x_n extends it to a Jacobian-conjecture counterexample, and hence (via DC_n ⇒ JC_n) a Dixmier-conjecture counterexample, in every dimension n≥3.
counterexample.verified_how: Described by multiple sources as verifiable directly with any computer algebra system; Terence Tao's blog post is an expert digestion confirming the calculations, though a formal peer-reviewed paper had not appeared as of the sources checked.

disputes.summary: Secondary sources disagree on how to attribute the discovery: some (e.g. a commenter on Tao's blog) insist the correct order is 'Levent Alpöge, with Claude Fable 5' rather than crediting the model as primary discoverer, while other write-ups (kingy.ai, kingy.ai-style commentary, and Wikipedia's own phrasing) describe Fable as having 'found the map.' Alpöge's own X post credits Fable for 'working' on the problem without specifying whether the model produced the construction autonomously or under heavy guidance; no prompt log or discovery record is public.

summary: Two things happened to this problem since 26 January 2024. (1) Alexander Zheglov posted arXiv:2410.06959 in October 2024 claiming a proof that the Dixmier conjecture holds for the first Weyl algebra (n=1), and has continued revising it through a fifth version dated January 2026 (extending it from ~25 to 78 pages, still simplifying the final calculation) with no evidence found of journal acceptance or a published expert digestion — this is `claimed`, not `resolved`, and would only settle the n=1 case of the general conjecture in any case. (2) On 19–20 July 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced (casually, on X) an explicit three-variable counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, crediting Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 with 'working' on the problem alongside co-conspirator Akhil Mathew. Terence Tao's 21 July 2026 blog post digests the construction (an explicit map with constant Jacobian −2 sending three points to one) and confirms the calculations, though Tao also used an AI chatbot himself to check parts of his own digestion. Since the Dixmier conjecture for the n-th Weyl algebra (DC_n) is known (easy direction, pre-2024) to imply the Jacobian conjecture in n variables (JC_n) — established by Tsuchimoto (2005) and Kanel-Belov/Kontsevich (2007) — the falsity of JC_3 immediately falsifies DC_3, and padding with extra untouched variables falsifies DC_n for every n≥3. This is a genuine case-level result within the scope of the bullet as stated ('any endomorphism of a Weyl algebra'): it is a case of the general Dixmier conjecture across all n, and settling it negatively for n≥3 is a change to what a careful person would write about this problem, hence `partial` rather than `open`. The n=1 and n=2 cases remain open (n=1 only via Zheglov's unreviewed claim; n=2 depends on the still-open plane Jacobian conjecture). I coded the July 2026 event as `ai_role: generated` because Alpöge's own words credit Fable with 'working' on the problem in a context (secondary sources uniformly gloss this as Fable having found/produced the construction) that reads as the model producing the mathematical object rather than merely checking or formalizing a human-made one; but the primary quote itself is genuinely ambiguous about division of labor, and no discovery record or prompt log is public, so this is a judgment call flagged in `competing_reading`.
competing_reading: Alpöge's own words ('fable for working during the world cup final') do not unambiguously state that the model produced the counterexample unassisted; it is equally consistent with heavy human guidance (Alpöge and Mathew directing the search, checking candidates, or supplying the key ansatz) with Fable performing computation/search under close supervision, which would make this `assisted` rather than `generated`. No session transcript, prompt log, or authors' technical writeup has been published to settle which. If a future writeup states the humans supplied the construction and Fable merely verified it, the role would be `none`; if it states the humans set up a search framework and Fable's output was the exact witnessed map with essentially no further human mathematical contribution, `generated` is the better reading, which is what I chose.
what_would_settle_it: A discovery record, session transcript, or a written account by Alpöge/Mathew (paper, blog post, or interview) describing precisely what was given to Claude Fable 5 as input and what came back as output — i.e., whether the model was given the problem cold and returned the map, or was guided step-by-step to a human-supplied construction.

outcome: No progress found since 26 January 2024: no (2,5)-perfect number (n with σ(σ(n)) = 5n) has been found or proven not to exist, and no paper, preprint, or database update addressing this specific case was located.
summary: This bullet asks whether any (2,5)-perfect number exists, i.e. an n with σ(σ(n)) = 5n, in the (m,k)-perfect generalization of superperfect numbers (σ^m(n) = kn) documented on the Wikipedia 'Superperfect number' article and in MathWorld's 'Multiperfect Number' / 'Superperfect Number' pages. Both sources give a table of (2,k)-perfect numbers with known examples for k = 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 (with OEIS sequences A019279–A019291, skipping A019280 which would be k=5) but no entry and no known example for k = 5 — this is the specific gap the Wikipedia bullet is asking about. I searched arXiv and general web sources for any 2024–2026 work naming '(2,5)-perfect', 'σ(σ(n))=5n', or 'sigma_2(n)=5n' and found nothing addressing this case. Related but distinct recent papers were checked and ruled out as off-topic: 'On near superperfect numbers, the Goormaghtigh conjecture, and Mertens' theorem' (arXiv:2505.08160, May 2025) studies numbers with σ(σ(n)) = 2n + d (a near-(2,2)-perfect variant, not (2,5)); 'On Characterizing Potential Friends of 20' (arXiv:2409.04451) discusses '7/5-perfect'-type ratios of a single σ application, not the iterated σ(σ(n))=5n condition; 'Odd Spoof Multiperfect Numbers' (arXiv:2502.16954, Feb 2025) generalizes spoof/Descartes-style multiperfect numbers (single σ, k-perfect) rather than iterated (m,k)-perfect numbers. None of these, nor any other source found, discusses k=5 with m=2. The live Wikipedia 'Superperfect number' article's (m,k)-perfect table appears unchanged from the frozen revision in this respect (same gap at (2,5)), consistent with no update having been made. This is a small, obscure sub-case of multiperfect-number theory that appears to have attracted essentially no dedicated research attention in the window, and certainly none involving AI systems.
competing_reading: It is conceivable that a paper computing (2,k)-perfect numbers for a range of k (e.g. an updated computational survey of iterated-sigma multiperfect numbers) exists in a venue not indexed by the search engines used, and either extended the search bound for (2,5) or found none up to some limit without explicitly using the '(2,5)-perfect' phrase, using different notation (e.g. 'iterated sum-of-divisors' or a table without prose calling out k=5 by name) that these searches missed.
what_would_settle_it: A full-text search of the actual (not AI-summarized) content of arXiv papers on multiply-iterated sigma functions and multiperfect numbers published 2024–2026, and confirmation from OEIS that no sequence exists for (2,5)-perfect numbers (i.e., that A019280 is reserved for (2,2)-perfect/superperfect and no other identifier has been created for k=5).

outcome: No proof, disproof, or rigorous partial resolution of the base-10 Lychrel number existence question has appeared since 26 January 2024. The only in-window publication found (Kuitché, Advances in Pure Mathematics, August 2024) offers a probabilistic/heuristic argument, not a rigorous proof, and its own author explicitly states the characterization 'remains probabilistic' and that no particular natural number has been proven Lychrel.
summary: The question 'do any base-10 Lychrel numbers exist?' remains open. I checked the English Wikipedia article on Lychrel numbers (current version), which still states no base-10 Lychrel number has been proven to exist. I examined the one paper the triage flagged — Rostand S. Kuitché, 'Lychrel Numbers in Base 10: A Probabilistic Approach' (Advances in Pure Mathematics, Vol. 14 No. 8, August 2024) — by fetching the paper page directly rather than trusting the triage's title-only note. It proposes a probabilistic definition of 'Lychrel' (probability of ever reaching a palindrome falling below (1/10)^330) and a theorem relating this to a limiting growth ratio, and tests specific numbers (196, 879, 1997, 7059) computationally using ordinary iterative code ('Anaconda Navigator', no AI/ML). The author explicitly acknowledges the result is not a rigorous existence proof for any particular number and calls the probabilistic characterization a limitation to be addressed in future work. Under §3.1, a probabilistic/heuristic argument that does not settle any case or the general question is not a result that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet — it is at most an unproven conjecture-supporting heuristic, so it does not even rise to 'progress' on a bound (there is no bound here — this is a yes/no existence question, and per §3.1 an existence question only moves when actually answered). I also checked for any updates to the long-running '196 Palindrome Quest' record computations (Jason Doucette's world-records page, p196.org's news page): the most recent record and news entries found date to 2011–2016 (Romain Dolbeau's billion-iteration, ~414-million-digit computation; a 2016 note about a German student group), with nothing newer located, and in any case a longer non-palindromic run is a search-limit extension, not an answer to the existence question, so it would not count as an event even if a 2024–2026 update existed. I searched broadly for any AI/LLM/ML connection (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, GPT, general 'machine learning' searches) and found none tying any AI system to Lychrel numbers; all computational work found (the 2024 paper's code, the historical palindrome-quest programs) is ordinary iterative/brute-force computation, not an AI system under §6.2. I did encounter one WebSearch AI-generated summary that conflated an unrelated arXiv paper (on the Tribonacci sequence) with the Lychrel paper, and another that vaguely asserted existence had been 'proven in base 2, 11, or 17' — the latter refers to other numeral bases, not base 10, and predates the window in any case, so it is irrelevant to this bullet's base-10 statement. Overall: no change found, no AI involvement found.
competing_reading: One could argue the August 2024 paper constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense (a novel probabilistic framework and equivalence theorem), which might warrant status 'progress' rather than 'open'. I read it as not qualifying because 'progress' under this schema is reserved for a bound moving or an instructive incident on a question with a bound to move, whereas this is a binary existence question that only moves when answered (§3.1's existence-question rule), and the paper itself disclaims proving existence for any concrete number or in general. If a future reviewer judges the probabilistic theorem itself to be a form of admissible progress on the framework (even without an existence proof), 'progress' with ai_role 'none' would be the alternate classification.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous (deterministic) proof that some specific base-10 number is Lychrel (or a proof that no base-10 Lychrel numbers exist), published or preprinted after 26 January 2024 and ideally digested by an expert or verified computationally/formally; absent that, any credible claim — even an unresolved or later-withdrawn one — naming a specific number and a non-probabilistic argument would at minimum warrant a 'claimed' or 'progress'/'incident' status.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 changes the status of the conjecture; the only relevant events are (1) a 2025 paper by Jakimczuk that generalizes 'almost perfect' to an asymptotic condition σ(n)/n → β and is therefore a different, related problem, and (2) a February 2026 GitHub issue/PR in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository that formalizes the open conjecture as an unproved Lean statement (`sorry`), not a proof.
summary: The classical conjecture — that every almost perfect number (σ(n) = 2n − 1) is a power of 2 — remains open, and I found no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 – 22 Sep 2026) that settles it, settles a case of it, or moves a bound on it. The current Wikipedia article on almost perfect numbers still states only the pre-2024 constraint (an odd almost perfect number greater than 1 would need at least six prime factors, from Kishore 1978/1981) and contains no discussion of any post-2024 progress. Two items surfaced in searching deserve explicit mention because they are close to the topic but do not count as progress on this bullet. First, Rafael Jakimczuk's 'A Note about Almost Perfect Numbers' (ResearchGate, uploaded 4 September 2025) proves results about a generalized, asymptotic notion — for a real β > 1, infinitely many n with ω(n) arbitrarily large and σ(n)/n arbitrarily close to β, with β = 2 termed 'almost perfect' in his paper. This changes the defining condition from the exact σ(n) = 2n − 1 used in the Wikipedia bullet to an approximate ratio condition, so under §3.1 it is a related problem (a variant sharing the same name), not a case of the stated problem; it does not remove any territory from the original question of whether an exact non-power-of-2 solution exists. Second, a GitHub issue (#2240, opened 10 February 2026) and associated pull request in Google DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' repository formalize the exact classical conjecture as a Lean 4 statement — `∃ n, AlmostPerfect n ∧ ¬∃ k, n = 2^k` — but the proof body is `sorry`, i.e., unproved; the issue itself records a 'formalizability rating of 0/5' meaning it was judged trivial to state, not solved. This is bookkeeping/dataset infrastructure (a benchmark of open conjectures for formal-proof tooling), not mathematical progress, and involves no AI-generated proof content — it is a formal restatement of the already-known open question. No other 2024–2026 arXiv paper on near-perfect, superperfet, or within-perfect numbers touches the exact classical almost-perfect-number question either; each addresses a differently-defined class of numbers. I therefore record status `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Jakimczuk paper is a genuine generalization whose β=2 case literally re-derives the classical almost-perfect condition in a limiting sense, so a skeptical reader might call it a weak form of 'partial' progress (e.g., existence of infinitely many n with σ(n)/n arbitrarily close to 2, though not equal). But the stated problem asks about exact equality σ(n) = 2n − 1, and 'arbitrarily close' does not restrict or settle any case of that exact equation — it is a different question about density/closeness rather than about the discrete equality, so I classify it as out of scope rather than partial.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement giving either (a) an explicit non-power-of-2 integer n with σ(n) = 2n − 1, proved by hand or verified by computer algebra, which would resolve the conjecture in the negative-existence sense (refuted, i.e., such numbers do exist), or (b) a proof that no such n exists, which would confirm the conjectured characterization. Absent either, a completed (non-`sorry`) Lean proof of the formal-conjectures statement, checked and reviewed, would also count, at minimum as `claimed` pending expert digestion.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or new partial result on the specific question of odd noncototients was found; the conjecture that no odd number larger than 5 is a noncototient remains exactly where it stood in January 2024, resting on the same Goldbach-type heuristic (Browkin/Schinzel era).
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether any odd noncototients exist beyond the three small known cases (1, 3, 5), each disposed of by hand (1=2-φ(2), 3=9-φ(9), 5=25-φ(25)). The standing conjecture — that no odd number greater than 5 is a noncototient — rests on the (also open) strengthened Goldbach conjecture that every even number greater than 6 is a sum of two distinct primes p and q, since then pq - φ(pq) = p+q-1 expresses that odd number as a cototient. I searched the Wikipedia article on noncototients, the OEIS sequence A005278 (noncototients) and its comments, the erdosproblems.com entry, and general web searches for any 2024-2026 proof, disproof, or partial progress specific to the odd case; none of these show any post-January-2024 activity on this specific question. The only genuinely new and AI-relevant development I found in this neighborhood is unrelated to odd noncototients: Erdős Problem #418 ('are there infinitely many noncototients?', i.e. the density/infinitude question, already answered affirmatively by Browkin and Schinzel in 1995 for even numbers of the form 2^k·509203) was formalized in Lean in late 2025 as part of the erdosproblems.com/teorth formalization project, with the author (Boris Alexeev) reporting he 'asked ChatGPT to explain the proof by Browkin and Schinzel and then Aristotle [Harmonic's AI system] to auto-formalize the resulting LaTeX file.' That is (a) about a different question (infinitude/density of noncototients in general, not the odd case), and (b) a formalization of a 1995 result, not new mathematics in the window — so under §3.1 and §6.1 it is out of scope for this bullet and does not change its status; I record it here only as context so it isn't silently lost, and so a reader isn't misled by erdosproblems.com's page for #418 which could look at a glance like it bears on this problem.
competing_reading: None. The Erdős #418 Lean/AI formalization is unambiguously about the general (even) noncototient infinitude question, not the odd-noncototient question in this bullet, and even that underlying mathematical result (Browkin-Schinzel 1995) predates the frozen revision by decades. There is no plausible reading under which either the odd-noncototient conjecture or its supporting Goldbach-type heuristic moved in the window.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of the strengthened Goldbach-type statement (or a direct argument) establishing that every odd number greater than 5 either is or is not a noncototient; short of that, any paper explicitly exhibiting or ruling out an odd noncototient greater than 5, or any update to OEIS A005278's comments/references reflecting new work.

outcome: The existence question remains fully open, but the constraints any odd perfect number would have to satisfy were tightened in the window by at least two peer-reviewed, non-AI results: Zelinsky's new bounds on T(n) and H(n) in terms of the smallest prime factor (submitted 22 Feb 2024, published in Integers 25 (2025) #A59), and Stone's improved upper bound depending on the number of prime divisors (Integers 24 (2024) #A114, published Dec 2024, though originally received Dec 2021 and revised Feb 2024). Several self-published 'proofs' of full nonexistence surfaced on academia.edu, ResearchGate, SSRN and Zenodo, and a 2026 preprint claims to close some small-prime branches, but none of these are digested by experts or in a venue with peer review, so none change the status beyond 'progress'.
summary: The problem (does any odd perfect number exist?) is a pure existence question, so under §3.1 no amount of narrowing the search space settles it; the correct default remains 'open'. But real, dated, peer-reviewed progress on the necessary conditions occurred in the window, which the triage's cursory pass surfaced only indirectly (it found only non-credible nonexistence claims and one unverified 2026 preprint). I read the actual PDF of Zelinsky's 'The sum of the reciprocals of the prime divisors of an odd perfect or odd primitive non-deficient number' (arXiv:2402.14234, first submitted 22 Feb 2024 — six days after the frozen revision's 26 Jan 2024 timestamp, so squarely in-window; final version published in Integers 25 (2025) #A59, received 12/10/24, accepted 5/24/25). It proves new bounds on T(n) and H(n) (functions of the reciprocal-prime-sum and abundancy-related product) in terms of the smallest prime factor of a hypothetical odd perfect number, tightening prior Cohen/Suryanarayana bounds. No AI tool of any kind is mentioned in the acknowledgements or body — the paper credits only human mathematicians (Nielsen, Eve Zelinsky, a referee, and editors) for corrections. I also confirmed via search snippet and citation record that Andrew Stone's 'Improved Upper Bounds for Odd Perfect Numbers — Part I' (Integers 24 (2024) #A114) was published in December 2024, giving new upper bounds depending on the number of distinct prime factors; this is cited by Zelinsky's paper as [26], corroborating it is a real, distinct, peer-reviewed advance. I classify the decisive dated event as Zelinsky's Feb 2024 submission since it is the earliest clearly in-window, peer-reviewed advance I verified in full; Stone's result is a second, separately-dated (also in-window, if the Feb 2024 revision date is used rather than the Dec 2021 original submission) advance, noted here rather than given its own record per the instructions. I also checked the Ochem-Rao computational-bound webpage (lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/), which parenthetically claims the classic 10^1500 lower bound (Ochem-Rao 2012, predates the window) has since been 'pushed... to N > 10^2200', with file timestamps suggesting activity as late as February 2025 — but the page gives no clear date for when 10^2200 specifically was reached, there is no accompanying paper, and Wayback Machine access was unavailable in this environment to establish an archived timeline, so I could not verify this bound as an in-window, citable event and have excluded it from the record rather than guess a date. I found no evidence anywhere — journal papers, the Ochem-Rao site, or any of the self-published claims I checked (Mantovanelli's July 2026 arXiv preprint 2607.04365, academia.edu, ResearchGate, SSRN, Zenodo) — that any AI system was involved in this area's mathematics. The 2607.04365 preprint (single author, Marco Mantovanelli, submitted 5 Jul 2026) claims to close minimal-prime branches q=5,7,11,13,17 using 'JSONL certificate bundles, Python verifier scripts, and SHA256 hashes' — traditional computational verification, not AI, and unreviewed by experts, so even if legitimate it would only be 'claimed' status at best and doesn't change the overall picture. I disagree with the triage's implicit framing that this problem's post-window activity is dominated by dubious nonexistence claims: real incremental peer-reviewed progress (Zelinsky, Stone) exists and was findable, though it required opening full PDFs rather than relying on search snippets.
competing_reading: One could argue the status should remain 'open' rather than 'progress', on the theory that these are incremental technical bounds unlikely to interest a 'careful person' writing this bullet's one-line Wikipedia entry, which only states the existence question and the headline N > 10^1500 / nine-distinct-primes facts (both predating the window and unchanged on the live article). Since the live Wikipedia article itself has not been updated to reflect Zelinsky's or Stone's results, a stricter reading tied purely to what changed in the canonical one-line summary might prefer 'open'. I use 'progress' because §3.1 explicitly says size is not the test and a bound that moved even a little counts, and both papers are genuine, dated, peer-reviewed tightenings of necessary conditions on any hypothetical odd perfect number.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g. via an archived snapshot of lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/ from before 26 Jan 2024, or a dated arXiv paper) of exactly when the Ochem-Rao computational bound moved from 10^1500 to 10^2200 would let that be added as a further, likely more headline-worthy, progress event. Expert digestion or journal acceptance of Mantovanelli's 2607.04365 would upgrade that item from unverified preprint to citable partial progress.

summary: This is an existence question ('do any odd weird numbers exist?'), which under §3.1 is only advanced by an actual answer, not by extending a computational search. I searched broadly for any post-26-January-2024 developments — direct searches for the phrase 'odd weird number' combined with 2024/2025/2026, searches for updates or citations to Fang's 2022 paper (arXiv:2207.12906, the paper establishing the current best-known bounds: no odd weird number below 10^21, and none with abundance below 10^14 below 10^28), and a check of the OEIS sequence page (A006037) that tracks the history of this search. The Wikipedia 'Weird number' article's current text ('It is not known if any odd weird numbers exist. If so, they must be greater than 10^21') is unchanged from the pre-snapshot state and cites the same OEIS source. No new preprint, announcement, or computational search extending this bound was found anywhere. I therefore agree with the triage's 'none' verdict: nothing has happened to this problem in the window, and no AI system has been involved. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' result per §5, not an under-researched one.
competing_reading: None. The bound is a record-extension type quantity (largest verified search radius), but per §3.1 an existence/infinitude question ('do any exist') is not advanced by a larger search radius alone — it would need to be the type of bullet asking for the value of a constant or a largest known object, which this is not. There is no genuine ambiguity here about scope.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that no odd weird number exists, an explicit odd weird number exhibited and verified, or (short of resolution) a new preprint extending Fang's 10^21 / 10^28 computational bounds — none of which were found.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 answers, narrows, or moves a bound on whether a positive integer can be written as a sum of two positive fifth powers in more than one way; the last known computational bound (Ekl, 1998, sums checked up to roughly 4.01×10^30) and Guy's 1994/2004 statement of the open problem remain the most current record.
summary: The problem (Wikipedia's Taxicab(5,2,n), i.e. does any positive integer equal a sum of two positive fifth powers in more than one way) remains unresolved and no genuine progress toward it was found since 26 January 2024. The triage flagged Benfield, Lippard & Roy, 'End behavior of Ramanujan's taxicab numbers' (arXiv:2404.08190, published The Ramanujan Journal 2024/2025) as a possible lead. Reading the abstract and attempting the full text: that paper's framework fixes k (the exponent) and studies what happens as j (the number of summands) grows, asking for which m (number of representations) a smallest Taxicab(k,j,m) exists; it is not about fixed j=2 and varying n (our question's axis), and no passage found addresses k=5, j=2 specifically. Wikipedia's own 'Generalized taxicab number' article still states, unchanged, that no number is known to be a sum of two fifth powers in more than one way and it is not known whether one exists, citing Guy's 2004 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' — the same pre-window source. MathWorld's page on the 5th-power Diophantine equation and ProofWiki likewise still cite only Guy (1994/1997) for the 1.02×10^26 (later corrected/extended in the literature to Ekl's 1998 bound of roughly 4.01×10^30) exhaustive-search bound, both predating the window; no updated search bound was found. I also checked two adjacent December 2025 preprints by Valery Asiryan that surfaced via search for 'equal sums of like powers': 'The Linear Slicing Method for Equal Sums of Like Powers' (arXiv:2512.00551) and its companion 'Genus-One Fibrations and the Jacobian of Linear Slices in the Quintic Equal-Sum Problem' (arXiv:2512.11072). The second paper studies a^5+b^5=c^5+d^5 restricted to a single linear slice (c+d)-(a+b)=30 (the first admissible slice under a divisibility condition), and explicitly disclaims addressing 'the global open problem of non-trivial solutions ... without linear constraints'; moreover, even on that one restricted slice, the paper only bounds the Mordell-Weil rank of an associated elliptic surface at 1 and states this 'by itself ... does not decide the existence (or nonexistence) of integral solutions.' This is technical machinery-building on a narrow constrained sub-case that itself remains undecided — it does not remove any territory from the stated existence question, so it does not qualify as a case settled under §3.1. A third candidate, 'Ramanujan, the taxicab problem for polynomials, and the abc-conjecture' (arXiv:2604.25017), turned out on inspection to be about polynomial-ring identities p^n+q^n=r^n+s^n over ℤ[x]/ℂ[x], a formally different (variant) problem over different objects, not the integer question — excluded as a related problem rather than a case. No AI system was found credited in any of these papers; the Asiryan papers describe verification via the Magma computer algebra system, which is not an AI system under §6.2. Overall: status open, no_change_found true, confidence high that the specific existence question is untouched, though the broader 'equal sums of like powers' research area saw incremental structural work in 2024-2025 that does not bear on this bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue the Asiryan quintic-slice paper (arXiv:2512.11072) constitutes 'progress' in the loose sense that it is new mathematics narrowing possible solutions on one specific linear slice (h=30) of the same equation family. But the paper itself says this does not decide existence even on that slice, and a single slice out of infinitely many admissible h-values is a vanishingly small and non-exhaustive restriction; under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry?') the honest answer is no, so I classified as open rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an exhibited pair of positive integers with a^5+b^5 = c^5+d^5 and {a,b}≠{c,d} (would resolve as refuted/resolved), (b) a proof of nonexistence for all n>1 (resolved/confirmed), or (c) an extension of the exhaustive computational search bound beyond Ekl's ~4.01×10^30 published after 26 January 2024, which would count as `progress` under the record-is-the-question exception in §3.1 since Taxicab(5,2,n) as literally posed on Wikipedia's list is an existence/infinitude-style question but the underlying search-bound record is itself sometimes treated as the tracked quantity in this literature; I found no such updated bound.

outcome: The existence question remains open. Three lines of work appeared in the window: (1) a June 2025 preprint by Frank Vega claims a full proof by contradiction that no quasiperfect number exists, but it is unreviewed, has zero evaluations on Sciety/preprints.org, is on a non-peer-reviewed platform, and its author has a long track record of unaccepted claimed resolutions of famous open problems (P vs NP, generalized forms of the Riemann Hypothesis), so it cannot be treated as resolving anything; (2) a legitimate January 2026 arXiv paper by Max A. Alekseyev raises the numerical lower bound on a hypothetical quasiperfect number from 10^35 to 10^45 via classical computational number theory (SageMath, recursively enumerated sets, MapReduce), no AI involved; (3) an August 2026 arXiv preprint by Toyohara, Tao and Yao raises the minimum number of distinct prime factors from 7 (Hagis-Cohen 1982) to 8, via three elementary lemmas plus a large (79.75-million-leaf) computational elimination verified across CPU/GPU architectures and partially formalized in Lean (259 theorems, zero sorry); an independent 'Pith' desk review recommends peer review and release of computational artifacts before the result is trusted, since the enumeration cannot yet be independently replayed. None of these settles the existence question itself, and I found no credible AI involvement in any of the three: Vega's proof is claimed as human elementary number theory with no tool disclosure, Alekseyev's bound is explicitly classical computer algebra, and the Toyohara/Tao/Yao paper's own text mentions only classical HPC (CPU/GPU enumeration) and a Lean formalization, with no author statement crediting an AI system for producing any of the mathematics. A superficially related GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) is built heavily by an AI coding agent ('google-labs-stitch[bot]' via a tool called 'Jitro') but it is a distinct, unconnected project by a different author (Frederick de Ruiter) claiming a different, seemingly unfinished result (a bound with a literal unresolved template placeholder '10^{TelemetryMaxLog}' and a claimed omega(N)>=15 threshold) and must not be conflated with the arXiv paper.

disputes.summary: Frank Vega's June 2025 preprint claims full resolution (non-existence), which if accepted would supersede both later partial-progress papers entirely, but it has received zero independent evaluations and is by an author whose past claimed resolutions of famous problems (P vs NP, Riemann Hypothesis variants) have not been accepted by the mathematical community. I treat it as unverified rather than as the decisive event, and instead date the record to the most credible dated progress (the August 2026 prime-factor bound), while flagging that if Vega's proof were ever validated it would immediately make the whole record 'resolved'.

An unrelated GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) tackling the same problem is developed almost entirely through AI-agent-authored pull requests (bot 'google-labs-stitch[bot]', tool 'Jitro'), but its claimed result and authorship do not match the arXiv paper by Toyohara/Tao/Yao; there is no primary-source evidence linking the two projects, despite superficial topical overlap (both use Lean + GPU/CPU search on the same problem). I did not credit the arXiv paper's mathematics to this AI-heavy repository.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen statement asks only whether quasiperfect numbers exist; as of today they are still neither found nor ruled out by anything the mathematical community has vetted. Three results appeared in the window. Frank Vega (preprints.org, June 2025) claims a full proof by contradiction that no quasiperfect number exists; this would resolve the problem outright, but the venue is non-peer-reviewed, the article shows zero evaluations on Sciety, and Vega has a documented history (via ResearchGate, Cambridge Engage, and IPI Letters listings) of claiming resolutions to Millennium-Prize-tier problems that the field has not accepted, so I do not treat this as settling anything and classify it only as an unreviewed claim rather than the basis for 'resolved' or even 'claimed' status for the whole record — I nonetheless log it, since it is the most dramatic thing anyone has said about this problem in the window. Max Alekseyev (arXiv 2601.17832, submitted 2026-01-25) is a legitimate, established computational number theorist whose paper uses a general SageMath-based method to raise the known numerical lower bound on a hypothetical quasiperfect number from 10^35 to 10^45 — a real, if narrow, quantitative bound movement, done with classical computer algebra and no AI. Toyohara, Tao and Yao (arXiv 2608.02066, submitted 2026-08-03) raise the long-standing minimum-prime-factor bound from 7 (1982) to 8, via elementary lemmas plus a large computational elimination (381 'stems' expanding to ~79.75 million 'leaves', verified across seven independently closed computation ledgers on three CPU/GPU architectures) and a partial Lean formalization (259 theorems, zero 'sorry'); an independent desk review on pith.science calls the lemmas sound but flags that the core enumeration cannot yet be independently replayed and recommends peer review plus release of artifacts before full trust — this is 'partial'-grade progress on a case (a stronger necessary condition), not yet expert-digested, so I record the overall status as 'progress' driven by this dated, most-credible advance, while noting Vega's undigested stronger claim in `disputes` rather than letting it drive the record. On AI involvement: I read the arXiv abstract/metadata for both legitimate 2026 papers and found no author statement crediting an AI system with producing any lemma, proof, construction, or bound — the described tools are SageMath, Rust/GPU/CPU enumeration, and Lean, none of which are AI systems under the codes in this task. I could not fetch the full PDF text of either 2026 paper as clean prose (arxiv.org/pdf returns only partially-parseable binary via my fetch tool, and preprints.org/researchgate blocked me with 403s), so my reading of methodology and acknowledgements rests on abstracts, the Pith review's summary, and search-engine syntheses of the abstracts rather than a full read of the PDFs — this is disclosed as a limitation below. I also investigated a coincidentally similar GitHub repository (fderuiter/quasiperfect) that is heavily built by an AI coding agent ('google-labs-stitch[bot]', invoked via a tool named 'Jitro') and initially worried it might be the uncredited engineering substrate behind the Toyohara/Tao/Yao paper; on inspection its claimed result (omega(N)>=15, with an unresolved template artifact '10^{TelemetryMaxLog}' in its own abstract) and its sole author (Frederick de Ruiter) do not match the arXiv paper at all, and no primary source ties the two together, so I did not attribute any AI involvement to the arXiv paper on that basis.
competing_reading: If Vega's June 2025 proof is eventually validated by experts, the correct status becomes 'resolved' (with resolution_direction 'refuted', since the conjecture that they might exist would be answered in the negative) and this entire record should be superseded — the two 2026 papers would become moot, historically-interesting partial results en route to a resolution that had, in fact, already happened five months before either was written. Conversely, if Vega's proof turns out to contain the kind of elementary error that has been found in his other claimed resolutions of famous problems, 'progress' anchored on the August 2026 prime-factor bound is the right call, as I have made it. I lean toward the latter given the base rate of this author's claims, but flag this is a judgment call under uncertainty, not a settled fact — I was not able to obtain a substantive third-party critique of Vega's specific argument (only its absence of peer review), so I cannot rule out that it is correct on the merits.
what_would_settle_it: A named-expert digestion (blog post, MathOverflow thread, or referee report) of Vega's June 2025 argument that either validates or refutes it; alternatively, publication of Vega's paper in (or rejection from) a refereed journal. Separately, for the Toyohara/Tao/Yao result: release and independent replay of the computational artifacts behind the 79.75-million-leaf enumeration, and a completed (not partial) Lean formalization, per the Pith desk review's own recommendation.

outcome: No resolution occurred. An independent researcher (Akram Louiz) posted a self-published, non-peer-reviewed preprint on ResearchGate in October 2025 claiming to disprove the Twin Primes Conjecture and, via Heath-Brown's theorem, claiming this also proves no Siegel zeros exist; the claim used AI-generated Lean code and was self-promoted as 'AI validated,' but it is logically inconsistent with the theorem it invokes (which is a disjunction, not an implication), has not been digested by any expert, and search evidence indicates the paper was subsequently retracted/withdrawn. The pre-2024 Yitang Zhang claim (arXiv 2211.02515) remains unpublished and uncorrected, unchanged since before the frozen revision. The existence question remains fully open; unconditional computational and conditional theoretical work continues but does not touch existence.

ai.basis_quote: According to Louiz, he didn't type the Lean language code himself—it was generated by GROK or Gemini.

disputes.summary: Louiz's claim is internally inconsistent with the theorem it relies on. Heath-Brown (1983) proved a disjunction — 'Twin Prime Conjecture is true OR no Siegel zeros exist' — not an implication from twin primes to Siegel zeros. If Louiz's disproof of the Twin Prime Conjecture were correct, the disjunction would force the OTHER disjunct to hold, i.e. that no Siegel zeros exist would have to be true for a different reason than claimed — but the paper's chain of reasoning (as reported) treats the theorem as if disproving one disjunct further disproves Siegel zero existence directly, which does not follow from a disjunction's logical structure the way advertised. Search results also indicate the ResearchGate posting was subsequently retracted, and a companion 'formal verification' write-up describes AI (GROK) 'sometimes not understand[ing] the proof correctly.' No independent expert has endorsed the claim; it has not appeared on arXiv, only ResearchGate self-posts.

summary: The Siegel-zero existence question remains fully open since 26 January 2024; nothing has settled it and no legitimate, expert-vetted progress narrowed it. The one candidate event in the window is a October 29, 2025 self-published ResearchGate preprint by independent researcher Akram Louiz, 'A disproof of the Twin Primes conjecture proving also that there are no Siegel Zeros,' which claims to disprove the Twin Prime Conjecture and, via Heath-Brown's 1983 theorem, concludes no Siegel zeros exist. Heath-Brown's actual theorem is a disjunction (TPC true, or no Siegel zeros) rather than an implication; if a disproof of TPC were valid, the disjunction would force the surviving disjunct ('no Siegel zeros') to hold anyway for logical reasons, but nothing in the reported chain of argument independently establishes that beyond restating the disjunction — the paper's framing ('proving also') overclaims what follows. The Lean formalization used to lend the claim credibility was, by the author's own account, generated by AI systems (GROK and/or Gemini) rather than hand-written, and a companion 'Formal Verification and Endorsement' write-up (also self-posted, and itself apparently AI-assisted) concedes the AI 'sometimes' failed to understand the proof correctly. No arXiv listing, journal, or recognized expert (Tao, Granville, Soundararajan, etc.) has engaged with or endorsed this claim; search results indicate the ResearchGate posting was subsequently retracted/withdrawn, consistent with the pattern of an announced-then-abandoned claim. Separately, Yitang Zhang's arXiv:2211.02515 (Nov 2022), claiming L(1,χ) ≫ (log D)^{-2022}, predates the frozen revision, has never been revised or formally published, and is widely regarded by the community (per a Manifold prediction market resolving NO, and Peter Woit's/Terence Tao's commentary) as containing serious unresolved issues; it represents no new window activity and is recorded only as background showing the question was already contested pre-2024. Legitimate technical work continues in the window without touching existence: a February 2026 arXiv paper ('Numerical Computations Concerning Landau-Siegel Zeros', arXiv:2602.03626) extends computational verification of the absence of Siegel zeros for moduli up to 10^10 (a record extension, not an existence proof, per §3.1's rule that record extensions on an existence/infinitude-shaped question do not count as progress on the question itself), and an April 2024 paper ('Remarks on Landau-Siegel zeros', arXiv:2404.16003) proves a conditional strengthening (if certain L-functions have only real zeros near s=1, bounds improve) — conditional theoretical progress that does not bear on unconditional existence. Given the Louiz episode involves a real, dated AI-assisted claim that was publicly circulated and (per available evidence) subsequently withdrawn, I classify status as `progress` with `ai_role` `incident` rather than `open`/`none`, per §6.1's instruction that an announced-then-withdrawn AI claim is an instructive incident, dated to the claim, with resolution_direction null since the problem itself did not move.
competing_reading: One could argue this episode does not meet even the `progress` bar and the correct status is `open` with `no_change_found` true, treating the Louiz preprint as unsanctioned self-published noise with essentially zero credibility (never on arXiv, no citations from credible sources, apparently retracted) that a careful survey of 'what happened to this problem' would simply exclude. The counter-argument for keeping it as `progress`/`incident` is that §7's traps explicitly instruct that a withdrawn claim is still an event and should not be quietly dropped, and this is a genuine, dated, AI-assisted claim that entered public circulation and prompted secondary write-ups (including a self-styled 'formal verification' from an AI-assisted reviewer), matching the incident pattern described in §6.1 and §6.2 even though the claim was of low quality. I also cannot fully confirm the retraction via a primary source — ResearchGate blocked automated fetches of both the original preprint and the 'endorsement' companion piece — so this rests on search-engine summaries of those pages rather than direct reading of them, which is a real gap.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the ResearchGate pages (publication 394091238 and 397677244) to confirm the retraction notice, exact wording of the AI-use disclosure, and the precise chain of reasoning claimed to derive 'no Siegel zeros' from the TPC disproof; or an arXiv/journal submission of the same claim that would allow normal version-history tracking. Also useful: any explicit statement from Louiz or a third party confirming or dating a retraction.
