outcome: No result addressing whether the Henson graphs have the finite model property was found; the question remains open as of September 2026.
summary: The question 'Do the Henson graphs have the finite model property?' is a decidability-flavored model-theoretic question about the Henson graphs (the countable homogeneous universal K_i-free graphs) that is distinct from other actively studied properties of these structures. I searched broadly for any work addressing this specific question and found none. There has been substantial, active research on Henson graphs in the window (26 Jan 2024–present), but all of it targets different questions: finite big Ramsey degrees (Dobrinen's 2023 result and its 2026 follow-ups, e.g. 'The finite big Ramsey degrees of Henson graphs are provable in ACA_0', arXiv 2606.30885, and 'The Henson graphs: colorings and codings' by Cholak, Dobrinen and McCoy, arXiv 2604.09894, submitted April 2026), indivisibility and computable indivisibility ('A note on the indivisibility of the Henson graphs', arXiv 2310.20097, which itself predates the frozen revision, from October 2023), and a separate, differently-named 'finite length property' (an algebraic/automata-theoretic notion about equivariant subspace chains, unrelated in substance to the logical finite model property) proved for the Rado graph and various Fraisse limits in 'The Finite Length Property of the Rado Graph and Friends' (Yang, Bojanczyk, Klin; arXiv 2605.21681) -- this paper explicitly does not mention Henson graphs or the finite model property, and 'finite length property' is a different concept despite the similar name (a trap worth flagging: it is easy to conflate the two on a keyword search). None of these results bears on whether every sentence true in some model of the Henson graphs' theory is true in some finite model (or on the decidability of the class via finite models). The Henson graph's own Wikipedia article still states the question as an unresolved 'unsolved problem in mathematics' box, and its edit history shows only a March 2025 edit that added the unsolved-problem template (no change to the underlying claim) and later cosmetic disputes about illustrative figures -- nothing bearing on the mathematical content. I was unable to fully load one general survey on Ramsey theory of homogeneous structures (par.nsf.gov, connection reset) that might discuss open problems in this area, but multiple other searches and the current article state converge on the same conclusion: no progress has been made on this specific question in the window. No AI involvement of any kind was found, since no result on this question was found at all.
competing_reading: One could argue that the finite big Ramsey degree results (proving these degrees are provable in ACA_0, a comparatively weak subsystem) bear indirectly on the model-theoretic tractability of Henson graphs and thus are 'related' work worth counting as progress. But 'finite model property' is a specific technical notion (every satisfiable sentence in the relevant logic has a finite model) that these Ramsey-degree and reverse-mathematics results do not address, settle a case of, or move a bound on. They are a related-but-distinct research program per the scope rule in Section 3.1, not a case or partial result of this problem.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint explicitly proving or disproving that the (universal) theory of some/all Henson graphs G_i has the finite model property, or a survey/expert source stating that this specific question has been resolved, would settle it. Direct correspondence with model theorists working on homogeneous structures (e.g. Dobrinen, Konecny, or Braunfeld) could also confirm the status is unchanged.

outcome: No accepted or expert-vetted result has changed the status of the Ulam density problem since 26 January 2024; it remains open. A long-running, unpublished, unreviewed arXiv preprint by Theophilus Agama claiming zero density has been repeatedly revised (including in the window, up to v12 on 2026-03-10) but shows no sign of expert acceptance, and mainstream researchers working on Ulam sequences in 2024-2025 (e.g. Clément & Steinerberger) continue to treat the density question as open and do not cite or build on Agama's claim.
summary: The problem asks whether the Ulam numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, ...) have positive natural density; empirically they appear to have density around 0.07398, but no proof of positive density (or of zero density) has been accepted by the mathematical community. The triage record correctly flagged a preprint by Theophilus Agama, 'Ulam numbers have zero density' (arXiv:2007.02697), which directly addresses this exact question and has an active revision history extending into the window (v1 in July 2020, up through v12 on 2026-03-10 — well inside the 26 Jan 2024 to present window). I read the abstract/PDF (via WebFetch) and searched extensively for any expert digestion, MathOverflow discussion, journal acceptance, or citation of this claim by other researchers. I found none. The paper is also mirrored on vixra.org, a repository generally used for work that has not passed, or was not submitted to, mainstream peer review or arXiv endorsement scrutiny — a signal consistent with a claim that has not been vetted. Most importantly, the claimed conclusion (zero density) runs directly counter to strong numerical evidence accumulated over decades (density ≈0.07398, and more recent 2024-2025 work by Clément and Steinerberger on growth bounds and periodic gap structure that presumes/supports a persistent, non-vanishing density of Ulam numbers). Active 2024-2025 research on Ulam sequences and Ulam words (Clément & Steinerberger, Comptes Rendus Math 2025; a 2024 INTEGERS paper on Ulam words) neither cites nor engages with Agama's claim, which is the behavior expected if the mathematical community does not regard it as an established or even seriously considered resolution. Since repeated revision of an unrefereed, uncited preprint that contradicts strong numerical evidence does not meet the bar for `claimed` (which requires the claim itself to have been taken up as a live claim, e.g. announced and discussed) as much as it reflects one author's persistent, apparently unresolved and unengaged assertion, I classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true, rather than `claimed`. No AI system appears anywhere in the record of work on this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue for `claimed` status on the grounds that Agama's preprint is a standing, undisclaimed proof claim that overlaps the window (the v12 revision in March 2026 is a fresh, in-window restatement of the claim), and that its mere existence as an unretracted proof attempt on arXiv is itself an 'event' worth recording under `claimed`, with `resolution_direction` refuted (since it claims zero density against the historically conjectured/expected positive density). Under this reading, the persistence of the preprint through 12 versions without withdrawal, and its continued availability, could be treated as a `claimed` resolution that experts simply haven't gotten around to formally rejecting. I did not adopt this reading because `claimed` in this schema is meant for claims that have entered live consideration by the field (an announcement drawing discussion, a preprint drawing engagement) — and I found zero evidence of any expert (on MathOverflow, in a citing paper, in a blog, or elsewhere) treating this specific claim as live, discussing it, or refuting it. A years-long, self-revised, uncited, un-discussed preprint contradicting strong numerical evidence looks more like an unengaged assertion than a claim under active consideration.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: (a) a citation of or response to Agama's arXiv:2007.02697 by another mathematician (acceptance, refutation, or even serious engagement) in a paper, blog, or forum; (b) journal acceptance or rejection of the paper; (c) a MathOverflow or similar expert discussion thread addressing the specific claim; (d) a statement on the Wikipedia Ulam number article or Ulam sequence OEIS page referencing this claim; (e) any statement in a 2024-2026 Ulam-sequence paper (e.g. by Steinerberger's group) explicitly addressing why Agama's claimed zero-density proof is or is not compelling.

outcome: No progress found: the problem remains exactly as stated, with the only three known strongly regular geodetic graphs still C5, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph (all Moore graphs), and no proof or disproof of infinitude or of the existence of a non-Moore example.
summary: This bullet asks whether there exist infinitely many strongly regular geodetic graphs, or any strongly regular geodetic graph that is not a Moore graph (a strongly regular geodetic graph necessarily has mu=1, and is a Moore graph exactly when lambda=0; the three currently known examples — C5, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman–Singleton graph — are all Moore graphs). The current Wikipedia 'Geodetic graph' article states plainly: 'Despite additional research on the properties such a graph must have, it is not known whether there are more of these graphs, or infinitely many of these graphs,' confirming the problem is still open as of today. The most relevant piece of research activity in the window is Cornelsen, Pfretzschner and Stumpf's 'Geodetic Graphs: Experiments and New Constructions' (arXiv:2308.08970), first posted 17 August 2023 (before the frozen revision, so not itself a window event) but revised 27 January 2025 (a minor correction changing a vertex count from 32 to 33, not touching the strongly-regular question). That paper's exhaustive computer search establishes that there are no regular geodetic graphs beyond the known list (odd cycles, complete graphs, the Petersen graph, the Hoffman-Singleton graph, and one 28-vertex cubic graph) up to 32 vertices, and it exhibits two new infinite families of geodetic graphs, but none of those new families are strongly regular — they are stated by the authors to be regular but not strongly regular, so they do not bear on this bullet's question. A second paper in the area, Elder, Piggott, Stober, Thumm and Weiß, 'Finite Groups with Geodetic Cayley Graphs' (arXiv:2406.00261, submitted 1 June 2024, published in Experimental Mathematics 2025), addresses a different, narrower question — geodetic Cayley graphs of finite groups — and conjectures that odd cycles and complete graphs are the only such graphs; this is a related problem (restricted to the Cayley-graph setting) rather than a case of the stated bullet, since it is not restricted to strongly regular graphs and does not settle anything about non-Cayley strongly regular geodetic graphs. No paper, preprint, blog post, or database entry found in the 26 January 2024 to present window reports a new strongly regular geodetic graph, a proof of infinitude, or a proof of finiteness. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2308.08970 paper's January 2025 revision counts as a window event worth flagging even though it made no substantive change relevant to this bullet; I include it in status_sources/summary for completeness but it does not change the status from open, since the correction was to a vertex count for a different (non-strongly-regular) enumeration result.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of infinitude of strongly regular geodetic graphs, or the discovery/construction of a single new strongly regular geodetic graph with lambda>0 (hence not a Moore graph), or a proof that no such graph exists beyond the Moore graphs.

outcome: Bertalan Bodor's July 2025 preprint 'Structures with not too fast unlabelled growth' proves Simon Thomas's conjecture (every countable homogeneous structure with finite relational language has finitely many first-order reducts up to interdefinability) for the class S of structures whose unlabelled orbit growth is bounded by 2^n/p(n) for every polynomial p — a genuine restriction/case of the general conjecture, not a resolution of it.
summary: The bullet is Wikipedia's phrasing of Simon Thomas's conjecture: does every countable homogeneous structure with a finite relational language have finitely many first-order reducts (up to interdefinability)? This remains open in general. Within the 26 Jan 2024 - present window, I found one genuine new result: Bertalan Bodor, 'Structures with not too fast unlabelled growth' (arXiv:2507.16985, submitted 22 Jul 2025, revised as v2 13 Jul 2026), which classifies the class S of countable structures whose unlabelled orbit-growth rate u_n is bounded by 2^n/p(n) for every polynomial p, in terms of automorphism groups, and as a corollary shows every structure in S is interdefinable with a finitely bounded homogeneous structure and has finitely many first-order reducts up to interdefinability -- 'thereby confirming Thomas' conjecture for the class S' (quoted from the abstract). This restricts the domain of the conjecture (a slow-growth subclass) rather than changing the question, so it is a case of the problem per SS3.1, classified as partial/confirmed. I separately re-verified two items the triage's why-note referenced: (1) Bodor's earlier paper 'Classification of omega-categorical monadically stable structures' (arXiv:2011.08793) also confirms Thomas's conjecture for the monadically-stable class, but its first preprint dates to November 2020 -- well before the frozen revision -- even though its Journal of Symbolic Logic publication appeared in 2024; per SS6.3 the preprint date governs, so this specific confirmation is open_stale territory and is not the event this record rests on (I did not find any indication its content or scope changed materially between 2020 and 2024 publication). (2) Bodirsky & Bodor, 'Structures preserved by primitive actions of S_omega' (arXiv:2501.03789, submitted 7 Jan 2025) uses first-order reducts of the Johnson graphs as a technical tool to prove a P/NP-complete CSP complexity dichotomy; it does not state or prove any new case of Thomas's reduct-finiteness conjecture itself, matching the triage's assessment -- this is a related-problem/tool use, not a case, and is excluded from status per SS3.1. I also independently found a GitHub repository ('vibemathing/problem-wikipedia-644eb5bce5410548') titled identically to this bullet's statement, appearing in generic search results; its content is not a mathematical source (it appears to be unrelated tooling/content bearing the same title string) and I disregarded it as the triage did, treating it as noise rather than a finding. No AI system of any kind (LLM, machine-learning method, or automated theorem prover) is mentioned in connection with any of these papers; this is standard human-authored model-theory/permutation-group-theory work using classical growth-rate and orbit-counting arguments.
competing_reading: One could argue Bodor's class-S result is a 'related problem' rather than a 'case', since it is stated as a corollary of a structural classification theorem whose primary purpose is orbit-growth classification rather than reduct-counting per se. However, the paper's own abstract explicitly frames the reduct-finiteness statement as 'confirming Thomas' conjecture for the class S', i.e. as a restriction of exactly the stated question to a subclass of structures, which is the textbook definition of a case under SS3.1, so I classified it as partial rather than open with no_change_found.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of Thomas's conjecture in full generality (all countable homogeneous structures with finite relational language), or a further paper extending the confirmed class beyond S (e.g. to all monadically NIP or all finitely bounded homogeneous structures), would move this record further. Access to Bodor's full PDF/TeX source (rather than the HTML rendering) to check the acknowledgements section in detail would let me state with full certainty whether any computational or AI tool was used anywhere in the derivation, though nothing in the abstract, introduction, or search results suggested one.

summary: This is the classic 'missing Moore graph' problem: does a Moore graph of diameter 2, girth 5, degree 57 (order 3250) exist? It has been open for over six decades and remains open today. Three lines of post-window work narrow the search without resolving it. (1) Smith & Montemanni, 'Potential Subgraphs of the Missing Moore Graph' (Symmetry, published online 2024-11-22), used Google OR-Tools' CP-SAT constraint solver — a classical constraint/SAT solver, not an AI system under these codes — to extend the known potential t-subgraphs (candidate local structures) from 15 to 20, assuming a cyclic group of permutations on the tree branches; this is a computational search extension, not a resolution of any case. (2) The same authors' follow-up, 'The Moore Graph of Diameter 2 and Degree 57 via Cyclic Derangements' (Axioms, submitted 2026-02-06, published 2026-05-01), proves that a construction of the graph using only a cyclic group of derangement permutations is impossible, closing off that entire restricted family of candidate constructions (a case/sub-family ruled out, hence partial progress, though the paper frames it as narrowing rather than settling anything about the general existence question — no counterexample or resolution results, so this is 'progress' rather than 'partial': the paper shows no such graph exists *of this restricted symmetric type*, which is arguably a partial resolution of a special-case non-existence, but since the general problem (as literally stated in the bullet, with no symmetry assumption) is untouched and the special case was itself invented by these researchers rather than being a natural 'restriction of the stated question' with independent interest, I read it as scope-narrowing progress; see competing_reading). No AI system is mentioned in either Smith/Montemanni paper. (3) Ishida, 'No involutions in the missing Moore graph' (arXiv 2606.29183, submitted 2026-06-28, revised 2026-07-08) proves algebraically (via a trace-rank identity from Brauer quotients of p-permutation lattices) that if the degree-57 Moore graph exists, its automorphism group has odd order — ruling out involutions. This is a genuine new structural constraint on any hypothetical solution, i.e. progress, not a case-restriction of the stated existence question itself (an automorphism-group constraint is a property any hypothetical graph would have to satisfy, not a restriction of the parameters in the question), so it is best classified as `progress` rather than `partial`. The author's affiliation is listed as 'A.I. System Research, Inc., Kyoto, Japan' — a company name containing 'A.I.' — but the paper itself explicitly disclaims computer or AI assistance: 'The derivation given here uses neither the computer search nor the tabulated bounds' of prior analyses. This is a pure algebraic/representation-theoretic proof; ai_role is `none`. Notably, a different 2026-06 preprint from the same research organization (Ryosuke Mizuno, 'A.I. System Research Co., Ltd.'), 'New lower bounds for the degree/diameter problem via interaction with a browser-accessible LLM' (arXiv 2606.15860), does describe substantial ChatGPT (gpt-5-5-pro) involvement in discovering new graph constructions — but that paper addresses different degree/diameter parameters (N(12,5) and N(16,5)), not the degree-57 girth-5 Moore graph, so it is a related-but-distinct problem under §3.1 and not counted here. I also checked Epoch AI's FrontierMath 'Open Problems' page, which lists the missing Moore graph explicitly as an AI benchmark target problem, but states no AI system has made any progress on it. Overall: real, human-driven mathematical progress narrowing the space of possible constructions and automorphism groups, but the core existence question is untouched, and no AI system is credited with any of it.
competing_reading: The Smith & Montemanni 'Cyclic Derangements' non-existence result for the cyclic-group-only construction could instead be read as `partial` if one treats 'Moore graph of degree 57 constructible via a cyclic group of derangements' as a genuine case/sub-instance of the stated existence question (a restriction on the automorphism group, akin to restricting a variable). Under that reading, the correct classification would be `partial` with `resolution_direction: refuted` for that sub-case, since a class of constructions was proven impossible. I chose `progress` because the cyclic-derangement construction method is itself a technique invented by these researchers to search for the graph, not a natural sub-family carved out of the problem's own stated parameters (degree, girth, order), so ruling it out narrows the search space without settling any piece of the actual mathematical object described in the bullet. A careful reader could reasonably disagree and call it `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A full computational or algebraic proof (or explicit construction) resolving the existence question outright, or a case-restriction on the problem's own stated parameters (degree 57, girth 5) — as opposed to a restriction on the search method — being settled.

outcome: Steininger and Yurkevich constructed the 'Noperthedron' (90 vertices, 152 faces) and proved it lacks Rupert's property, disproving the 2017 conjecture that every convex polyhedron is Rupert. The proof combines two analytic theorems (a 'global theorem' and a 'local theorem') with a rigorous, rational-arithmetic computer verification partitioning the 5-dimensional orientation parameter space into roughly 18 million regions, implemented in R and SageMath.

counterexample.object: The Noperthedron: an explicit convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, 240 edges (apparently), and 152 faces, constructed to be non-Rupert
counterexample.verified_how: Two proved theorems (a global theorem bounding excluded orientation regions from shadow containment, and a local theorem for special vertex cases) applied via rigorous rational-arithmetic computation (R and SageMath) across ~18 million regions of the 5-dimensional orientation parameter space, ruling out every possible passage

summary: The triage record correctly identified the key result: Steininger and Yurkevich's arXiv preprint 2508.18475 ('A convex polyhedron without Rupert's property', v1 submitted 2025-08-25) constructs the Noperthedron, the first convex polyhedron proved to lack Rupert's property, thereby disproving the 2017 conjecture (attributed by Scientific American's coverage to prior researchers) that every convex polyhedron is Rupert. I read the arXiv HTML full text, the paper's acknowledgements, Quanta Magazine's and Scientific American's independent journalistic digestions (each quoting outside experts -- Joseph O'Rourke and Pongbunthit Tonpho respectively -- endorsing the result), and John Carlos Baez's blog summary. All are consistent: the method was a purely classical one -- two proved analytic theorems combined with an exhaustive, rational-arithmetic (not floating point) computer verification across ~18 million partitioned regions of parameter space, implemented in R and SageMath. The paper's acknowledgements thank a colleague for 'moral support' and financial/computing support from A&R TECH, and separately credit David Renshaw and Jason Reed for 'immense work on the formalization of the paper in Lean and correction of inaccuracies' -- this is a human-led Lean 4 formalization effort (repository jcreedcmu/Noperthedron), not an AI system; no LLM, neural network, or automated theorem-proving AI is mentioned anywhere in the paper, acknowledgements, or secondary coverage. A search also surfaced an unrelated third-party GitHub project (AndreaSevincel/non-rupert-polyhedra-detector) that trains a machine-learning classifier to predict the Rupert property of polyhedra -- this is a separate, later, exploratory tool inspired by the Noperthedron concept, not part of the original discovery or proof, and does not itself settle any case of the problem. I classify status as 'resolved' rather than 'claimed' because the result has been digested by named experts in independent science-journalism coverage (Quanta, Scientific American) that describes the proof method in enough depth to constitute an expert-level account, and the mathematical community has treated the disproof as established since August 2025 with no retraction found. The Lean 4 formalization is a separate, ongoing verification effort and, per a 2026 secondary source, still contains a 'sorry' placeholder for the 18.7-million-region computational certificate -- it is not yet a fully machine-checked proof, but this does not affect the classification since the original proof already meets the 'resolved' bar via theorem-proof plus expert digestion, independent of the Lean effort.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'claimed' instead of 'resolved' on the grounds that the paper (as of the versions checked) is a preprint with no confirmed journal publication, and the only formal machine-checkable verification (the Lean formalization) is still incomplete (contains a 'sorry' for the core computational certificate). Under a strict reading of the resolved/claimed line, a preprint with no journal acceptance and no completed independent formal proof might be held to 'claimed'. I lean toward 'resolved' because two independent, in-depth science-journalism digestions each quote outside domain experts endorsing the mathematical content as sound, which is the kind of expert digestion the rules treat as sufficient even absent formal journal publication.
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance of the Steininger-Yurkevich paper, or completion of the Lean 4 formalization (removal of the remaining 'sorry' for the computational certificate) with community-recognized correctness, would remove any doubt about the 'resolved' classification.

outcome: The question remains unresolved; the only development since 26 January 2024 is a continued computational extension of the sequence (Ben Chaffin, reaching over 10^612 terms as of a page dated 7 February 2026) confirming 852655 is still the smallest number not yet found in the sequence. This narrows nothing about the existence question itself (§3.1) and no proof, disproof, or new analytic bound was found.
summary: This is an existence/infinitude-shaped question ('does every nonnegative integer appear?'), which per §3.1 is advanced only by an actual answer, not by extending a computational search. I found no proof, disproof, partial resolution, or new analytic bound published since 26 January 2024. What did happen in the window is a further extension of Ben Chaffin's long-running brute-force computation of the sequence: his project page (dated 7 February 2026) reports over 10^612 terms computed on custom hardware (Intel Skylake system, 256GB RAM, 30TB disk, ~14 months of runtime) with 852655 still the smallest integer absent from the sequence — the same status that has held since it was first identified missing around 2018 (and known missing since at least 2001, when all numbers below it had appeared). OEIS A005132 and Wikipedia's own article corroborate this figure and status, and explicitly state the conjecture (originally made by Neil Sloane in 1991, and which Sloane himself walked back in 2017, saying 'today I'm not so sure that every number appears') remains open with no proof either way. I searched specifically for any AI/LLM involvement in this computation or in any recent theoretical work on the conjecture and found none — the extension is a straightforward (if computationally heavy) brute-force enumeration using classical algorithmic speedups (exploiting 'ping-pong' range patterns), not a mathematical or AI-driven advance on the open question. No arXiv paper, blog post, or announcement in the window claims progress on the actual existence question. Per §3.1, a computational search extended further, without an answer, does not count as a change to this bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue the repeated confirmation that 852655 remains missing after an enormous further extension of the search (10^230 in 2018 to 10^612 in 2026) is itself informative evidence shifting expert opinion toward 852655 never appearing (i.e., toward the conjecture being false), and thus worth recording as 'progress' in an informal sense. But per the rubric's explicit rule in §3.1 ('a search verified to a larger limit... narrows where an answer could hide, not whether it exists'), this does not qualify as a status change, so I classified it as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof that every nonnegative integer must eventually appear (settling the conjecture affirmatively), or (b) a proof — or a computational discovery — that some specific number (e.g. 852655) can never appear, which would refute it. Short of that, only further computation narrowing the search continues, which does not change the classification.

summary: The juggler sequence conjecture (does every positive integer's juggler sequence terminate at 1?) shows no change since 26 January 2024. The current Wikipedia article, MathWorld, HandWiki, Googology Wiki, and multiple search passes all report the same verification bound — all starting values up to 7,110,200 confirmed to reach 1 — that predates the frozen revision; this is not new progress, just the same longstanding figure being repeated. No preprint, announcement, or repository posting claiming a proof, disproof, explicit counterexample, or an extended/improved verification bound was found on arXiv, OEIS, or in general web search. OEIS A094679 (record-setting iteration counts) received a routine data contribution from Ethan Slota on 2025-04-15 adding one further record-holder term, but this is incremental computational tabulation of record-setters, not a movement of the existence question itself, and per §3.1 an existence/infinitude-style question is not advanced merely by extending a record table — it is not a bullet 'asking for a largest known object or the value of a constant.' A search for AI involvement in this problem turned up nothing genuine: the only AI-adjacent hit was an unrelated 2026 story about an AI-assisted counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, a completely different problem. I also found a claim on Grokipedia (an AI-generated encyclopedia) that 'Recent 2025 research has provided the first estimates of the maximum excursion constant and stopping constant for juggler-like sequences,' citing a reference labeled roughly 'Estimates of the maximum excursion constant and stopping constant...' on ResearchGate. I could not locate this paper through direct search on arXiv, ResearchGate title search, or Google — Grokipedia's own citation was truncated and did not resolve to a checkable author list, venue, or identifier. Because I could not verify this source exists or read its actual content, I am not treating it as an established event; a heuristic/stochastic estimate of excursion statistics (analogous to existing 3x+1 stochastic-model literature) would in any case likely be `progress` at best under these rules, not a resolution, and does not touch the existence question directly. I searched for a general arXiv paper on juggler sequences from 2024-2026 directly (via listing searches and targeted queries) and found none. Overall this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case, consistent with the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than dispute.
competing_reading: If the Grokipedia-cited 2025 paper on maximum-excursion/stopping constants for juggler-like sequences is real, it could constitute a `progress` event (a heuristic model producing new quantitative estimates), similar to long-standing stochastic-model work on the Collatz/3x+1 problem. I was unable to confirm its existence, authors, or content through direct search, so I have not recorded it as an event. Its absence from arXiv and ResearchGate direct search raises the possibility it is a Grokipedia hallucination — Grokipedia is machine-generated and known to sometimes fabricate or mis-cite sources.
what_would_settle_it: Locating the actual paper Grokipedia references (full author list, venue, arXiv ID or DOI) and reading its contribution statement would settle whether this is a genuine 2025 event and, if so, whether it involved any AI system and whether it counts as `progress` on the maximum-excursion/stopping-constant estimates (not on the core existence question).

outcome: No proof, disproof, or bound movement on the original (first) Euclid–Mullin sequence's every-prime question was found since 26 January 2024; a February 2026 paper by Booker and Simon explicitly reaffirms that both of Mullin's original questions about the first sequence remain open with little known, while the substantive results found (Booker 2013 on the second sequence, a 2016 variant construction) either predate the window or concern a different (related, not the stated) sequence.
summary: The question is whether every prime appears in the (first) Euclid–Mullin sequence (2, 3, 7, 43, 13, 53, 5, ...), defined by taking the smallest prime factor of one plus the product of all previous terms. This remains completely open. The most recent substantive paper touching this family, Booker and Simon's 'A generalisation of the Euclid–Mullin sequences' (arXiv:2601.21901, submitted 2 February 2026), studies cyclotomic-polynomial analogues of Mullin's *second* sequence (largest-prime-factor variant, generalised to residue classes) and proves, under ERH and unconditionally for several moduli, that these analogues omit infinitely many primes. Crucially, the paper's own text states 'As for the first sequence, both of Mullin's questions remain open, and very little is known' — i.e. the authors themselves confirm no progress on the problem as stated in this bullet. Andrew Booker's earlier resolution of the Cox–van der Poorten conjecture (that the *second* Euclid–Mullin sequence omits infinitely many primes) dates to 2011/2013, well before the window, and in any case concerns the second sequence, a related-but-different problem (built with 'largest prime factor' instead of 'smallest prime factor'), not a case of the first sequence. A 2016 paper (arXiv:1605.08929) exhibiting a variant Euclid sequence that provably contains every prime is likewise a different construction ('a' variant, not 'the' Euclid–Mullin sequence) and also predates the window. No computational extension of the known sequence (e.g. resolving whether 41, 47, 67, 73, 79, 83 ever appear) was found past the 2012-era Pollack/Treviño account, which is itself pre-window and in any case would only be a 'found one more term' result, not a settlement of the infinitude-style question per §3.1. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem; the search for AI-related mathematical work near Euclid–Mullin turned up only an unrelated KNAW seminar abstract about deep learning and proofs in general, with no connection to this sequence. The triage's 'none' verdict is upheld.
competing_reading: None of substance. One could argue the Booker–Simon 2026 paper is 'about' the Euclid–Mullin family broadly and thus worth a 'progress' status, but by §3.1 a result about the second sequence's residue-class analogues is a related problem (a changed question: different selection rule, different target set), not a restriction of the first sequence's stated question, so it does not count as progress on this bullet.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: a proof or disproof that every prime appears in the first Euclid–Mullin sequence; a proof that some specific prime (e.g. 41) can never appear; or an explicit authoritative statement updating the list of primes with unknown status in the first sequence, dated after 26 January 2024.

outcome: The finiteness question — whether the odd greedy algorithm always terminates for every rational number with odd denominator — remains unresolved; the only post-window work found (Louwsma & Martino, 2025) characterizes special cases of fixed expansion length, which restricts a different, already-settled-to-exist question (which fractions have a length-2 expansion) rather than narrowing the open existence question of whether termination always occurs.
summary: The problem asks whether the odd greedy algorithm always terminates in finitely many steps for every rational number with odd denominator (Stein's question, also attributed to Selfridge and Graham). This is an existence/termination question in the sense of §3.1: it moves only when answered, not when more instances are verified or more special cases are classified. I found no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) that resolves, bounds, or settles a genuine case of this question. The one pre-window item the triage found, Louwsma & Martino's 'Rational numbers with odd greedy expansion of fixed length' (arXiv:2309.07280, Sep 2023, single version, no updates), is unchanged and predates the window regardless. I found a follow-up by the same authors, 'Rational Numbers with Two-Term Odd Greedy Expansion,' published in INTEGERS vol. 25 (2025) and posted to Zenodo 28 May 2025 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15536292) — this is within the window. However, per its own and the earlier paper's framing, this work characterizes which fractions have an odd greedy expansion of exactly length 2 (a classification of a finite class of objects), not a restriction of the open termination question itself: it does not shrink the search space of potential counterexamples to termination, nor prove termination for any infinite subfamily left open by the conjecture. It is analogous to extending a record table rather than answering an existence question, so under §3.1's rule it does not count as a change to this problem's status. I also checked a superficially similar-sounding but unrelated 2025 paper on 'Irrationality of the reciprocal sum of doubly exponential sequences' (arXiv:2504.05933); its abstract confirms it addresses a different Erdős–Graham-type problem about doubly exponential sequences, not odd greedy expansions, and it is excluded as a related-but-different problem (§3.1). The Wikipedia article itself (fetched live for context, not as the frozen source) shows no updates past a 1999 citation and does not describe any resolution. I found no author, blog, or lab source connecting any AI system to this problem in any way; every search returned only pure human mathematical work (constructive/combinatorial classification arguments), so ai_role is 'none' with no basis_quote to offer.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 two-term paper is a 'case of the problem' under a looser reading — it does establish, for the specific finite set of fractions it characterizes, that their odd greedy expansion terminates (trivially, in 2 steps), which is technically an instance of 'this rational number has an odd greedy expansion.' But this is already known to be true for cofinitely many/most small-denominator fractions from prior computational verification (up to 922321), and characterizing which ones stop at exactly length 2 is bookkeeping about the algorithm's behavior on already-terminating instances, not progress toward ruling out or finding a non-terminating instance, which is what the open question is actually about. I classify this as no_change_found on the stated conjecture, consistent with §3.1's treatment of record/instance-type findings for existence questions.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that the odd greedy algorithm terminates for all rational numbers with odd denominator (or a rational number for which it is proven, by direct computation or otherwise, that the algorithm produces an infinite/non-terminating expansion) would resolve it. Short of that, a paper proving termination for a nontrivial infinite subfamily not previously known to terminate (e.g., all fractions with a given prime power denominator) would count as partial progress; the 2025 paper found does not do this.

outcome: No mathematical progress on Norton's Generalized Moonshine Conjecture was found in the window 26 January 2024 to present; the conjecture's status is unchanged from before the frozen revision.

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on whether Scott Carnahan's 'Generalized Moonshine I-IV' series (2008-2012) plus Carnahan-Miyamoto's non-Fricke work (2016) constitute a full resolution of Norton's Generalized Moonshine Conjecture, or only a resolution of the hardest remaining cases (Fricke and non-Fricke elements) leaving other aspects unconfirmed by experts. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics (last substantively updated ~2023) states flatly that 'only special cases of these generalized moonshine conjectures have been proven,' citing Dong-Li-Mason (cyclic case) and Höhn (2A involution case) as examples, and does not describe Carnahan's work as a complete resolution. Other secondary sources (Wikipedia's Monstrous moonshine article, various summaries) describe Carnahan's Fricke-element result as 'resolving' or 'establishing the remaining open claims in' the conjecture. This dispute entirely predates the 26 January 2024 window and does not change the analysis here, since no source dates any resolution (partial or complete) to within the window regardless of which reading is correct.

summary: I searched extensively for any post-26-January-2024 developments on Norton's Generalized Moonshine Conjecture and found none. The mathematical literature on generalized moonshine itself is essentially quiet in this window. The one arXiv result with a 2606.xxxx identifier that surfaced in search ('Moonshine: An Autonomous Mathematical Research Agent Centered on Conjecture Generation,' arXiv:2606.10806) is a false lead: I opened it directly and confirmed it is an unrelated AI-agent paper that happens to be named 'Moonshine' and works on a self-invented 'Neural Jacobian Conjecture' about neural network injectivity — it has no connection to the monster group or generalized moonshine in the group-theoretic/VOA sense, and I am discarding it from consideration. The one arguably relevant 2024-2026 item involving AI is a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures#2149, opened 2026-02-03) in which an AI agent (attributed to a human account 'franzhusch,' with the issue footer stating 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me') logged Norton's Generalized Moonshine as a candidate for future Lean formalization, rating it '5/5' difficulty and noting prerequisite infrastructure (Monster group, graded VOA representations, modular form theory) that does not yet exist in Mathlib. This produced no mathematics whatsoever — no proof, no formalization, no conjecture, not even a partial Lean statement — only a scoping/cataloguing note, so it does not constitute an 'event' under this schema and I have left `event` null and `ai_role` as `none` (the agent did not produce any part of a mathematical result). The Duncan-Harvey-Rayhaun paper on 'Two New Avatars of Moonshine for the Thompson Group' (arXiv:2202.08277, last revised May 2025) is about Thompson moonshine, a related but distinct moonshine phenomenon for the Thompson sporadic group, not Norton's Generalized Moonshine Conjecture for the Monster stated in this bullet, so under the scope rule (§3.1) it is a related problem, not a case of this one, and does not count. The triage record's assessment is correct: the substantive resolution work (Carnahan's Generalized Moonshine I-IV, 2008-2012, and Carnahan-Miyamoto 2016 on non-Fricke elements) all predates the frozen revision by 8-16 years, so even setting aside the dispute over whether that work fully resolves the conjecture, there is no post-window event to date and the correct status is `open` (not `open_stale`, since I could not confirm from primary/expert sources that a full resolution — as opposed to resolution of the hardest special cases — occurred at all, even before 2024). I checked the problem's Wikipedia article family (Monstrous moonshine), the Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry (updated as recently as 2023, still describing only special cases as proven), arXiv listings and topical searches for 2024-2026, and found nothing that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet.
competing_reading: If one takes the (contested) position that Carnahan's 2008-2016 work already fully resolved Norton's conjecture, then the correct status would be `open_stale` rather than `open`, since the resolution event predates the frozen revision. I did not adopt this reading because the Encyclopedia of Mathematics — a more authoritative, actively-maintained secondary source than the popular science and Wikipedia summaries — explicitly states only special cases are proven and does not describe Carnahan's results as a complete resolution. This is a genuine unresolved dispute in how the field is described, but it does not change the answer for this exercise since no source, on either reading, places a resolution event inside the 26 January 2024 - present window.
what_would_settle_it: An authoritative statement from an expert in vertex operator algebra / moonshine (e.g., a current survey, a statement from Carnahan himself, or an update to the Encyclopedia of Mathematics or Wikipedia's Monstrous moonshine article) clarifying whether the 2008-2016 Carnahan/Carnahan-Miyamoto series is considered by the community to fully resolve Norton's Generalized Moonshine Conjecture (which would make this open_stale) or leaves a residual open piece (which would keep it open, as recorded). Separately, any future arXiv preprint or announcement specifically addressing generalized moonshine (not Thompson, Mathieu, or umbral moonshine, which are distinct phenomena) would be the kind of event that could change this record.

outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or bound movement found on the equiconsistency question itself within the window; it remains explicitly described as open (the 'holy grail' of inner model theory) in current sources, contingent on a canonical inner model theory for supercompact cardinals that has not yet been built.
summary: The problem asks whether Con(ZFC + ∃ strongly compact cardinal) implies Con(ZFC + ∃ supercompact cardinal). This is a foundational question in large cardinal set theory, repeatedly described in the literature as the 'holy grail problem' of inner model theory, whose resolution is generally believed to require a canonical inner model theory for supercompact cardinals — a program (Woodin's 'Ultimate-L', and work of Steel, Schindler, Trang, Sargsyan, Neeman and others) that has not been completed. I found no preprint, announcement, or published result in the window (26 Jan 2024 – present) that resolves the question, settles a genuine restriction of it, or moves a bound on it. The closest body of related work is Gabriel Goldberg's Ultrapower Axiom (UA) program: under UA (not a ZFC theorem), the least strongly compact cardinal is supercompact, up to a class of counterexamples identified by Menas — this is offered as evidence toward equiconsistency, but (a) the core UA results establishing this equivalence date to 2018–2020 (arXiv:1810.05058, arXiv:2006.03293), well before the frozen revision, and (b) UA's own consistency with a supercompact cardinal is itself unestablished, so even the pre-2024 result does not settle the stated (unconditional) problem. Goldberg's 2024 paper 'Strongly compact cardinals and ordinal definability' (J. Symbolic Logic/J. Math. Logic 2024) extends Woodin's HOD dichotomy from extendible to strongly compact cardinals — a related structural result, not a case of the equiconsistency question, and it does not touch supercompactness directly. Other 2024-2025 work found (You & Yuan on λ-strong compactness cofinality and 'almost strong compactness'; Goldberg & Thei on cardinal-correct inner models; work on ω₁ strong compactness/supercompactness without AC) addresses adjacent or variant questions — different cardinals, choiceless contexts, or almost-strong-compactness — none of which restricts or settles the ZFC equiconsistency question as stated. The current Wikipedia article on strongly compact cardinals (fetched during this research) still states the conjecture as open and unlikely to be resolved before a canonical supercompact inner model theory exists, with no update reflecting any 2024-2026 development. I searched for any AI involvement in this specific problem and found none; nothing in the space of results (all human, traditional set-theoretic proof work) mentions computer or AI assistance of any kind.
competing_reading: One could argue Goldberg's UA-based equivalence result, though older, remains the most substantive 'progress' on this problem and is still actively cited/re-presented (e.g., in 2026 Warsaw talks) as the best available evidence toward equiconsistency; if a future record wanted to credit ongoing exposition/consolidation of that program as 'progress' in the window, that would stretch the definition, since no new mathematical content resolving or restricting the base ZFC question was produced in the window itself. I judge this insufficient to move the status off 'open'.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a full proof, in ZFC, that Con(strongly compact) implies Con(supercompact) [or a proof of an unconditional bound/partial case genuinely restricting the stated question, e.g. an unconditional equiconsistency for some specific strongly-compact-like cardinal below full strong compactness], or (b) completion of a canonical inner model theory reaching supercompact cardinals (the Ultimate-L program or a successor), which the field treats as the expected route to resolution.

outcome: The converse of Wolstenholme's theorem (also called Jones' conjecture) — that no composite n satisfies the Wolstenholme congruence binom(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n^3) — remains open as of September 2026; no proof, disproof, or new case-settling result for this specific conjecture was found in the window.
summary: The converse asks whether n prime is the only solution to binom(2n-1,n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n^3), i.e., whether the classical Wolstenholme congruence characterizes primes exactly (equivalently, whether any 'Wolstenholme pseudoprime' composite can satisfy it). I checked the two papers the triage pass flagged, plus wider searches, and found no result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that settles, narrows, or refutes this specific conjecture. (1) 'Extending Wolstenholme's Theorem: A New Perspective' (Yaqubi & Mirzavaziri, Nov 2024, ResearchGate 386148476) and its follow-up 'New results on Wolstenholme's theorem and its applications' (Mathematics and Society, 2025, math-sci.ui.ac.ir/article_29218) both study a different congruence: binom(np-1, p) mod p^k for prime p and varying n, addressing conjectures of Guo and Krattenthaler about that family of binomial coefficients. This is a related generalization of Wolstenholme-type congruences, not the composite-vs-prime converse question stated in the bullet, and I found no statement in secondary descriptions of either paper claiming to narrow the set of composite integers satisfying the classical converse congruence. Per §3.1 this is a related problem, not a case of the stated one, so it does not count as a change. (2) I found and read about arXiv:2604.16507 ('Deep Vision: A Formal Proof of Wolstenholme's Theorem in Lean 4', Linhares, submitted April 2026), which does disclose genuine AI involvement (a 'relational analogy engine' called Deep Vision plus Claude Code used to write Lean tactics/lemmas, verified by the Lean kernel with zero sorries) — but it formalizes the forward theorem (the classical congruence for primes), not the converse, so it is out of scope for this bullet. (3) A September 2026 paper (arXiv:2609.03091, Guedes & Machado) studies a different congruence, binom(2n,n) ≡ 2^n (mod n), connecting it to perfect numbers and Wieferich primes; this is Wolstenholme-adjacent in spirit but a distinct modular condition from the classical converse, so also out of scope. (4) General searches for 'converse of Wolstenholme's theorem' proof/disproof/new-family results in 2024-2026 turned up nothing beyond restatements of pre-2024 results (Trevisan-Weber 2001, Helou-Terjanian 2008, Hussein 2018, McIntosh's computational verification to 10^9/10^11). The live Wikipedia article on Wolstenholme's theorem (checked directly) still states the converse as an open conjecture, citing a 2022 Booker-Hathi-Mossinghoff-Trudgian search establishing any unknown Wolstenholme prime exceeds 10^11 — that search itself predates the frozen revision and, per §3.1's rule on existence/infinitude questions and record-extension, would not count as settling the converse even if it were newer, since it narrows where a counterexample could hide rather than answering the question. No AI system was found involved in any work on this specific converse conjecture.
competing_reading: The Yaqubi-Mirzavaziri papers could be read more generously: if their generalized binom(np-1,p) congruence framework happens to yield, as a special/limiting case, a new statement about which composite n satisfy the classical Wolstenholme congruence, that would count as partial progress. I could not access the full text of either paper (ResearchGate and the Isfahan journal site both blocked automated fetches with 403/connection errors) to rule this out definitively — I relied on abstract summaries via search snippets, which consistently describe the subject as the Guo-Krattenthaler np-1-choose-p conjectures, not the prime-vs-composite converse.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 answers, or removes territory from, the stated question of whether GCH entails ◇_{E^{λ+}_{cf(λ)}} for every singular cardinal λ; the question remains exactly as open as it was in the frozen revision.
summary: This bullet is a precise statement of a well-known open problem of Shelah in singular cardinal combinatorics: does CH_λ (equivalently, GCH restricted to λ) entail the diamond principle ◇ on the stationary set E^{λ+}_{cf(λ)} — the set of points of λ+ with cofinality *equal to* cf(λ) — for every singular cardinal λ? This is the one cofinality class left open by Shelah's classical Theorem 1.8 (documented in Rinot's 'Jensen's diamond principle and its relatives', arXiv:0911.2151, itself pre-window), which establishes CH_λ ⟺ ◇_S for every stationary S ⊆ E^{λ+}_{≠cf(λ)} (cofinality *different* from cf(λ)). The same-cofinality case is the genuine gap, and it is what the Wikipedia bullet asks about. I searched extensively for work in the window (26 Jan 2024–present) and found substantial *adjacent* activity, but nothing that touches this exact set: (1) 'Weak diamond and PCF theory' (arXiv:2405.03142, May 2024) improves Shelah's bound on |pcf(a)| using weak diamond, a converse-flavored, unrelated direction; it does not address entailment of full diamond from CH_λ on same-cofinality sets. (2) A cluster of 2025 papers on the approachability ideal I[λ+] — Jakob–Levine ('Failure of Approachability at the Successor of the first Singular for any Cofinality', arXiv:2503.18898), Jakob solo ('Total Failure of Approachability...', arXiv:2508.02867), and Jakob–Poveda ('On Shelah's Approachability Ideal', arXiv:2508.04374) — solve long-standing Shelah/Foreman–Magidor/Mitchell questions by building GCH models where stationarily many points of cofinality μ (a regular cardinal *strictly below* λ, hence necessarily ≠ cf(λ) when λ has countable cofinality) are non-approachable. I confirmed via the abstracts that in every one of these papers the cofinality μ studied is a regular uncountable cardinal below the singular λ, distinct from cf(λ). Since Shelah's Theorem 1.8 already settles the CH_λ ⟺ ◇_S equivalence precisely on this different-cofinality regime, these 2025 results — however close in subject matter, and however much they resolve real open problems about approachability — are about a related-but-distinct question (approachability/goodness at cofinalities ≠ cf(λ)) and not a case of the stated problem (diamond at cofinality = cf(λ)). None of the papers I could access mention the diamond principle on E^{λ+}_{cf(λ)} specifically, and none claim to resolve or make partial progress on the exact same-cofinality entailment. I was unable to fully extract readable text from the PDF bodies of several papers (2508.04374, 2508.02867, and Zeman's 'Diamond, GCH and weak square') due to PDF compression issues with the fetch tool, relying instead on abstracts and secondary summarization of search results, which is a limitation on confidence. I did not find or open the frozen Wikipedia revision's own article text (no dedicated article exists for this specific bullet; it is one line among many in the 'List of unsolved problems in mathematics' Set theory section) nor the live article, since repeated WebFetch attempts on the full article were truncated before reaching the Set theory section. No AI system appears anywhere in any of these papers per the accessible content; there is no ai_role other than none.
competing_reading: One could argue the Jakob–Levine/Jakob/Jakob–Poveda approachability results are 'progress' in a loose sense, since approachability failure on a set is a necessary ingredient for diamond to fail there (non-membership in I[λ+] is required to even ask the diamond question meaningfully in some formulations), and these papers dramatically expand the known landscape of non-approachable configurations under GCH. If a future reader considers the family of these techniques (Namba-style forcing plus Levy collapse) as being 'the same neighborhood' as what would be needed to attack the cf(λ)=cf(λ) case, one might tag this as `progress`. I did not adopt this reading because none of the papers state, claim, or gesture at applicability to the exact same-cofinality set named in the bullet, and the scope rule (§3.1) requires the result to change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry — it does not currently.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly constructing a model (or proving in ZFC) that CH_λ holds for some singular λ while ◇ fails on some stationary S ⊆ E^{λ+}_{cf(λ)} (resolving it in the negative), or a ZFC proof that CH_λ always entails ◇ on this set (resolving it in the positive) — either dated after 26 January 2024 and either checked by an expert (for `resolved`) or merely posted (for `claimed`). Absent that, a partial result narrowing which λ or which sub-stationary-sets of E^{λ+}_{cf(λ)} the equivalence holds for (analogous to Zeman's weak-square-conditional result, but for a new class of λ) would count as `partial`.

outcome: No result found, in or out of the search window, that settles or moves whether GCH by itself implies the existence of an ℵ_2-Suslin tree; it remains open exactly as stated, and the live Wikipedia article on Suslin trees still calls it a longstanding open problem.
summary: The bullet asks a very specific question: does GCH alone (no extra combinatorial principle) force the existence of an ℵ_2-Suslin tree? This is distinct from, and easily conflated with, several nearby results that all involve additional hypotheses. Classical work (Jensen) shows GCH plus square at ℵ_1 gives an ℵ_2-Souslin tree, and it has long been known that if GCH holds and there are no ℵ_2-Souslin trees then ℵ_2 is weakly compact in L — but neither of these settles whether GCH alone suffices. The most relevant nearby paper, Neeman's 'The special Aronszajn tree property at ℵ_2 and GCH' (arXiv:1809.07638), was originally submitted 20 September 2018, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision; its April 2024 v7 revision (checked via WebFetch) is described as containing only corrections and improved explanations, not a new result, so it is not a within-window event, and in any case it builds a model of GCH + no ℵ_2-Souslin trees from a weakly compact cardinal — an independence/consistency result about the negation, not a proof that GCH implies existence, so it would not settle this bullet even if it were new. Other 2024-2026 papers surfaced by search (an almost-Kurepa Suslin tree paper arXiv:2406.10463, 'Two-cardinal Kurepa Hypotheses' arXiv:2510.08860, 'Full Souslin trees at small cardinals' arXiv:2308.00299, and 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests' arXiv:2608.28505, the last checked directly via WebFetch) all concern related but different objects — Kurepa trees, two-cardinal variants, full Souslin trees at small cardinals, and Suslin/Souslin forests at (ω_1,ω_2) — none of which is a case of or a resolution to 'GCH implies an ℵ_2-Suslin tree'. I also checked Assaf Rinot's blog, the most active researcher and blogger in this exact area, including his 'Open Problems' category, and found no post from 2024, 2025 or 2026 addressing this question; his most recent open-problems posts predate the window (November 2023 and earlier). No AI system appears anywhere in any source I opened. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and its reasoning.
competing_reading: One could argue the Neeman result (or the classical GCH+□(λ) result) is 'close enough' to count as touching this bullet's scope, since it fixes the sibling question (GCH + no ℵ_2-Souslin trees, consistency-wise) using large cardinals. But per §3.1, a related problem obtained by changing the question (asking about consistency of the negation given extra large-cardinal strength, rather than about what GCH alone entails) does not count as a case of this problem, and in any event the paper's substantive content predates the window.
what_would_settle_it: A proof either that GCH (with no further hypothesis) implies an ℵ_2-Suslin tree exists, or that GCH plus large cardinals/forcing axioms is consistent with there being no ℵ_2-Suslin tree without invoking anything beyond GCH itself, or a proof that the implication is independent of ZFC. Any of these appearing as a preprint or announcement after 26 January 2024 would change this record.

outcome: The question of whether there exists a Jónsson algebra on ℵ_ω (equivalently, whether ℵ_ω fails to be a Jónsson cardinal) remains open; no consistency result, proof, or refutation was found in the window, and the closest recent work (Rinot's 2023/2025-26 survey and related 2024-2026 papers) explicitly treats it, or the closely related successor-of-a-singular-cardinal version, as still unresolved.
summary: The problem asks whether ℵ_ω (the least possible Jónsson cardinal, since AC rules out any ℵ_n being Jónsson) admits a Jónsson algebra, i.e. whether ℵ_ω is 'not Jónsson'. I searched arXiv, Wikipedia's Jónsson cardinal article, Rinot's blog, and general web search for any resolution, partial case, or bound moved since 26 January 2024, and found none. The most relevant recent item is Assaf Rinot's survey 'May the successor of a singular cardinal be Jónsson?' (arXiv:2312.08253, submitted 13 Dec 2023 — before the window — and later published in the Bollettino dell'Unione Matematica Italiana, 2025-2026), which is explicitly a survey collecting necessary conditions for an affirmative answer and states the problem is still open; it concerns the successor of a singular cardinal (e.g. ℵ_{ω+1}), a related but distinct question from whether ℵ_ω itself is Jónsson, and in any case predates the window and contains no new theorem resolving either question. Other papers found while searching (Eskew–Hayut 'Dense ideals', Oct 2024; Inamdar–Rinot's club-guessing survey published Jan 2025; Poveda–Thei 'A Solovay-like model at ℵ_ω', Sep 2025/Jun 2026) are all in the surrounding area of singular-cardinal combinatorics but none address or settle the ℵ_ω-Jónsson question itself — Dense ideals is about dense ideals on successors of regular cardinals, the club-guessing survey is a general methods paper only listing Jónsson-algebra construction as one of many applications of club guessing, and the Solovay-like-model paper does not mention Jónsson algebras at all. No arXiv preprint, journal paper, or blog post from after 26 January 2024 was found claiming any progress — positive or negative — on the existence of a Jónsson algebra on ℵ_ω specifically. No AI system appears anywhere in this search: none of the papers found mention any AI, machine-learning, or automated-theorem-proving tool in their methodology.
competing_reading: One could argue the Rinot survey's 2025/2026 journal publication constitutes an 'event' in the window, since the written argument was substantially the same as the Dec 2023 preprint (I could not access the full text to confirm no additions), but per §6.3 dating goes by the first written argument (Dec 2023, before the window), and per §6.1 a survey restating an open problem is not itself an event that changes the status. It is also conceivable that the survey, being about the successor of a singular cardinal rather than ℵ_ω itself, is a related-but-distinct problem under §3.1's scope rule, in which case it is irrelevant to this record either way.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper proving either that ℵ_ω admits a Jónsson algebra (i.e., ℵ_ω is not Jónsson, provable outright in ZFC by generalizing Shelah's ℵ_{ω+1} argument or similar), or establishing/refuting the consistency of ℵ_ω being Jónsson relative to some large cardinal hypothesis (e.g., resolving the generic I0 consistency question), dated after 26 January 2024, with an expert digestion or journal acceptance.

outcome: Two independent lines of work since the frozen revision bear on this question. A published arXiv preprint (Yayi Fu, April/August 2026) reduces o-minimality of a candidate trans-exponential expansion R_{an,exp,phi} to a conjectural 'many regular values' condition, without establishing it — genuinely conditional and not an answer. Separately, a private, hedged manuscript by Artem Chernikov ('A transexponential o-minimal structure (maybe)', v29, Sept 2026), whose proof the author reports was obtained using the AI system GPT-6 Astra, claims an unconditional existence proof (via an explicit Abel function) and has been formalized in Lean/Mathlib with zero `sorry`s and passing internal agent-led audits, but has had no completed independent human-expert review and is not a public/peer-reviewed paper.

ai.basis_quote: The author reports that the new original proof in his private source manuscript was obtained using GPT6 Astra.

disputes.summary: It is unclear whether the Chernikov manuscript's mathematical claim (unconditional existence of a trans-exponential o-minimal expansion via an explicit Abel function) is correct and accepted, versus the Fu preprint's more cautious, still-conditional approach to essentially the same construction (an analytic trans-exponential function added to R_{an,exp}). The manuscript's own title hedges with '(maybe)', and formalization.yaml explicitly states no independent human-expert review has been completed; the Lean audits are agent-led, not human-led. A registry submission ('Palomar', commit acf1a5a, Sept 21 2026) was pending verification as of the check date.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether there exists an o-minimal first-order theory with a trans-exponential (rapid-growth) function — i.e., whether the real ordered field admits an o-minimal expansion containing a definable function growing faster than every finite iterate of exp. Two developments postdate the 26 Jan 2024 freeze. (1) Yayi Fu's arXiv preprint 'Towards Trans-Exponential O-minimal Expansion of (R,+,·,0,1<)' (v1 3 Apr 2026, v2 1 Aug 2026) adds an analytic trans-exponential function φ to R_{an,exp} and reduces o-minimality of the resulting structure to the existence of 'many' regular values for certain definable systems — a necessary condition the paper does not establish. This is real, on-target progress toward the question but explicitly conditional; no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent confirmation of the conjectural regularity condition was found. (2) A GitHub repository (archernikov/abel-formalization) formalizes a private, unpublished manuscript by Artem Chernikov (a genuine, established model theorist at UCLA/UMD) titled 'A transexponential o-minimal structure (maybe)' (version 29, 7 Sept 2026). This manuscript claims to construct an explicit Abel function A (analytic on (0,∞), A(1)=0, A(e^x-1)=A(x)+1) satisfying four hypotheses that yield an unconditional o-minimal expansion of the reals with a trans-exponential function — i.e., a full resolution of the existence question, in the affirmative. The repository's formalization.yaml states plainly that the author obtained this proof using the AI system GPT6 Astra, and that Lean formalization and its 'agent-led audits' were themselves also carried out by AI agents (named gpt-6-astra and gpt-5.6-sol) directed to iteratively implement and check the development; sorry_count is reported as 0, and the build passed internal audits rejecting non-standard axioms. Critically, formalization.yaml also states explicitly that 'no completed independent human-expert review has been reported,' the work is not on arXiv or in any journal, a 'careful human presentation' paper is described as still 'in preparation,' and a registry submission to something called 'Palomar' was pending verification as of 21 Sept 2026. I found no coverage of this claim on Tao's blog, Quanta, or any other expert-digestion outlet, and Chernikov's own UCLA and UMD faculty bibliography pages (dated as late as June 2026) do not list this manuscript. Given DEEP_DIVE.md's rule that a machine-checked certificate no expert has reviewed is `claimed` rather than `resolved`, and that a private, hedged, unpublished manuscript cannot be `resolved` however clean its internal audit, I classify this as `claimed`. The AI role for the Chernikov line is `generated`: by the author's own account, the AI system produced the mathematical proof (the Abel function construction and the argument establishing the stated hypotheses), and the author/formalization team checked it via Lean formalization. This is a materially different, and much stronger, claim than Fu's independent, non-AI, still-conditional preprint, which contributes no AI involvement I could find.
competing_reading: One could argue the Chernikov claim should be `progress` rather than `claimed`, since it is not a peer-reviewed or even public-preprint result and its central mathematical content (existence of the required Abel function with all four hypotheses) has not been independently checked by any human mathematician — only by AI agents and a Lean kernel/'comparator' check whose soundness for this specific development is itself unverified by any named human expert. Conversely, one could argue for treating it as effectively `resolved` given zero-sorry Lean verification against Mathlib, since machine-checked Lean proofs are ordinarily very strong evidence; DEEP_DIVE.md, however, is explicit that a machine-checked certificate nobody but the compiler (or, here, AI-led audits) has reviewed remains `claimed`, so I kept that classification. It is also possible the manuscript's own hedge ('maybe') reflects the author's residual doubt about a subtle step, in which case even `claimed` may overstate confidence relative to the author's own view; I flagged this via the disputes field rather than downgrading further, since the repository firmly asserts the audits currently pass with no known gap.
what_would_settle_it: Publication of Chernikov's 'careful human presentation' paper (described as in preparation) on arXiv or in a journal, together with an independent human expert (a model theorist, e.g. via a referee report, a blog digestion such as Tao's or a specialist o-minimality researcher) confirming the Abel-function construction and its four hypotheses, and independent (non-agent-directed) review of the Lean development and the 'Palomar' registry verification outcome. Absent that, continued silence from the model-theory community, or an explicit retraction/correction of the manuscript, would settle it the other way.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or partial resolution of Dubner's conjecture was found; the only dated development is a computational extension of the exhaustive search for exceptions from 10^9 to 10^11 (no new exception found), plus a distinct, weaker 'intermediate' conjecture inspired by Dubner's and a Lean formalization tracking issue, neither of which changes the statement itself.
summary: Dubner's conjecture (every even number > 4208 is the sum of two primes that each have a twin) remains open. The most concrete dated development in the window is a comment added to OEIS A007534 on 28 Jul 2026 by Tushar Pandey ('No other k < 10^11'), extending the prior exhaustive-search bound of 10^9 (T. D. Noe, 2007) for exceptions to the conjecture by a factor of ~100 with no new exception found. This same extension is described in Pandey's arXiv paper 2608.02381 (v1 submitted 3 Aug 2026, v2 26 Aug 2026), 'An intermediate conjecture between Goldbach and Dubner: every even number is the sum of a prime and a twin prime,' whose acknowledgements state an independent cross-check: 'I thank Tomás Oliveira e Silva for independently verifying (S) to 10^13 with a program sharing no code with ours.' However, that independent 10^13 verification is of the paper's own intermediate conjecture (S) — every even number is the sum of a prime and a twin prime — not of Dubner's conjecture (sum of two twin primes), which the paper separately reports verifying only to 10^11: 'Dubner's conjecture ... finds no further both-twin exception up to 10^11, re-verifying Dubner's conjecture and extending its verified range by a factor of five.' Per the deep-dive rules, an existence/universality claim is not advanced by a search verified to a larger limit — it narrows where a counterexample could hide, not whether one exists — so this does not amount to partial resolution; it is recorded as `progress` because it is a concrete, dated, citable computational event, consistent with how this kind of Goldbach-style range extension is typically treated, while acknowledging the stricter reading below. Separately, a GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #3628, opened 24 Mar 2026) requests a Lean/Mathlib formalization of the conjecture's *statement* — rated difficulty 1/5, 'good first issue,' closed with no linked PRs, comments, or proof attempt — so it is not evidence of any mathematical progress, only of a tracking/formalization backlog. Pandey's paper itself is a related-but-distinct conjecture (a prime plus a twin prime, not two twin primes), which per §3.1 is a variant rather than a case of Dubner's conjecture, and is not counted as touching Dubner's conjecture beyond the incidental exception-search extension. No mention of AI systems, language models, or AI-assisted code generation appears anywhere in the arXiv paper, its acknowledgements, its described C/Python verification code, or the OEIS entry; the computation is described purely as a segmented sieve run on ordinary hardware ('C kernel: a segmented bit-packed odd-only sieve ... on 16 threads under OpenMP, 9.0 hours of wall time on a laptop'). No proof, refutation, or partial case-settlement of Dubner's conjecture as stated was found anywhere in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is `open` with `no_change_found` true, on the strict reading of §3.1 that a search verified to a larger bound never moves an existence/universality question — only an answer does, and finding no new exception in [10^9, 10^11) is exactly the case the rules say does not count. I classified as `progress` instead because the extension is a discrete, dated, well-sourced computational event directly about Dubner's conjecture (not a variant), and the instructions describe `progress` as covering 'a bound moved' generally; a reasonable reading of 'bound' includes a verified-exception-free range even for a universal claim, since exactly this kind of range-extension is the customary unit of progress reported for Goldbach-adjacent conjectures. A stricter grader might mark this `open`/`no_change_found` instead.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit statement (from Pandey, Oliveira e Silva, or another source) that Dubner's conjecture specifically (not the intermediate conjecture) was checked to 10^13 or beyond, which would sharpen the bound further, or a clarification of whether the deep-dive project intends 'bound moved' to include exception-free range extensions for universal conjectures — which would decide between `progress` and `open`/`no_change_found` here.
