outcome: The chromatic number of biplanar graphs is still unresolved (bounded between 9 and 12, unchanged since 1980/1959), but a 2026 preprint by Arjun Trivedi eliminates an entire candidate family — clique blow-ups of the 5-cycle C5[w] — as a possible source of a 10-chromatic biplanar graph, proving all such biplanar blow-ups are 9-colourable and giving a short proof that the specific candidate C5[4,4,4,4,3] is not biplanar. This narrows (but does not resolve) the search space Gethner's 2018 conjecture pointed to; no AI system is credited in any source found.
summary: The Earth-Moon problem (maximum chromatic number of biplanar graphs) remains open: the bounds are still 9 (Sulanke, 1980) and 12 (Ringel, 1959), exactly as before the frozen revision. No construction of a 10-chromatic biplanar graph has been found, and no expert digestion, journal publication, or arXiv listing of any new result was located. Two items of genuine post-window activity exist. (1) A GitHub repository by user 'EpsilonPhoenix' (earth_moon_small_order) gives a computer-assisted (Python/Z3/partial Lean 4) verification that every biplanar graph on at most 18 vertices is 9-colourable; this is explicitly a partial, unpublished formalization with unproved hypotheses, reconfirming rather than moving the known lower bound, and mentions no AI system. (2) A Zenodo self-archived preprint (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22074335, posted 2026-08-05) by Arjun Trivedi, 'Biplanar clique blow-ups of C5 are 9-colourable', proves χ(C5[w]) = max{max_i(w_i+w_{i+1}), ⌈n/2⌉}, shows every biplanar clique blow-up of C5 is 9-colourable (so this natural family, which includes several of Ellen Gethner's 2018-conjectured 10-chromatic candidates, cannot yield a counterexample), classifies the four 10-chromatic K9-free members of the family, and gives a short proof that C5[4,4,4,4,3] specifically is not biplanar (extending the 2023 arXiv result, predating this window, that showed C5⊠K4−v is not biplanar). This is a genuine case of the problem — it restricts the search space by ruling out a whole family of candidate constructions — so it counts as `partial` with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the family was confirmed to be 9-colourable, as conjectured/expected, not counterexample-producing). However, it has not been digested by experts: it is not on arXiv, has no citations, and its author has no visible institutional affiliation or other visible track record in this area (a Google Scholar page and GitHub profile under the same name were found but show no other related work). I classify this conservatively as `partial` rather than `claimed`+status-shift because the underlying mathematical content (a case elimination) is modest and mechanically checkable (a closed-form chromatic number formula for a well-understood graph family plus a routine biplanarity argument), similar in kind to the 2023 result already accepted as settling that specific graph. No source anywhere — the Zenodo record, the GitHub repo, Epoch AI's FrontierMath page, or the current Wikipedia article — credits any AI system with producing any part of this work; Epoch AI's page frames the Earth-Moon problem as an outstanding AI benchmark target (find a 10-chromatic biplanar graph) that remains unmet, not as a problem any AI system has moved.
competing_reading: One could argue the Trivedi result should be `open` with `no_change_found` true, on the grounds that ruling out one already-known-nonbiplanar-adjacent family (a variant class Gethner herself proposed only as candidates, never as confirmed 10-chromatic biplanar graphs) is closer to 'exploring where an answer isn't' than to settling any part of the stated question — the Earth-Moon problem asks for the maximum chromatic number, and narrowing candidate constructions without moving the proven bounds of 9-12 changes nothing a careful person would write in the bullet. Under that reading this is exactly the kind of narrowing search-space activity that §3.1 excludes for existence-style questions. I judged it as `partial` instead because the chromatic number question is not a pure existence question in the same sense as 'are there infinitely many X' — it is asking for an exact value, and formally settling that an entire well-defined subclass of biplanar graphs is 9-colourable is a genuine (if small) piece of the classification the problem calls for, analogous to case-by-case work on other coloring problems. Given the total absence of expert uptake, `open`/`no_change_found` is a defensible alternative.
what_would_settle_it: Whether an expert (a topological/chromatic graph theory researcher, or a citation/review of Trivedi's Zenodo preprint) treats this classification of C5-blow-up candidates as a real, correct contribution to the Earth-Moon problem's literature, or dismisses/ignores it as a minor self-published exercise; also whether the paper ever appears on arXiv or in a journal.

outcome: Matthew J. Colbrook (University of Cambridge) posted a preprint, 'Aperiodic maximisers of Lyapunov dimension: a counterexample to the unrestricted form of Eden's conjecture' (Zenodo, 21 September 2026), constructing a polynomial ODE on R^5 with a compact global attractor whose maximal Lyapunov dimension (4+4/c) is attained on an invariant two-torus carrying an irrational (aperiodic) linear flow, strictly exceeding the maximum (3) attained over equilibria and periodic orbits -- directly contradicting the unrestricted statement of Eden's conjecture as given in the Wikipedia bullet. The same maximizing set holds for the finite-time local dimension at every positive time and for the asymptotic Kaplan-Yorke dimension. The result is accompanied by a complete, from-scratch Lean 4 formalization (219 results in Solution.lean plus a 777-theorem supporting 'Eden' library) in a public GitHub repository, restricted to a small trusted axiom set (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) and checked by an independent 'Comparator' tool plus a third-party 'Palomar' verification pipeline.

counterexample.object: A polynomial vector field on R^5 with uniformly negative divergence and a compact global attractor, whose Lyapunov-dimension maximizer is an invariant two-torus carrying an irrational (hence aperiodic) linear flow, rather than any stationary point or periodic orbit.
counterexample.verified_how: Exact singular-value/exact-identity analytic argument in the paper, plus an independent, from-scratch Lean 4 formal verification (219 main results, 777 supporting library theorems) restricted to a small trusted axiom set and cross-checked by an automated Comparator tool and a separate 'Palomar' independent verification pipeline.

summary: The triage record (verdict 'none', checked 2026-09-20) missed this because the result was posted the day after its check (21 September 2026) -- a one-day gap that happens to fall right at the edge of triage timing rather than any error in its searches. I disagree with the triage verdict and set triage_disagreement, though the miss is purely a timing artifact, not a bad search. Colbrook's paper constructs an explicit polynomial ODE on R^5 whose global attractor's maximal Lyapunov dimension is achieved on an aperiodic invariant torus rather than on a stationary point or unstable periodic orbit, which is exactly and precisely a counterexample to the bullet as worded ('the supremum ... is achieved on a stationary point or an unstable periodic orbit'). This is squarely in scope under Sec 3.1: it directly negates the stated claim, not a variant or restricted case. I classify status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' because, as of today (22 September 2026), the paper is a one-day-old single-author preprint on Zenodo (not yet on arXiv at the time of my search, and not published in a journal); I found no expert digestion, commentary, blog discussion (Tao's blog, Quanta, Xena Project, etc. all silent on it), or third-party citation discussing or confirming the result. The accompanying from-scratch Lean formalization is extensive and methodologically serious (restricted axiom set, an independent Comparator/Palomar cross-check), which is strong self-verification evidence, but per Sec 6.1 a machine-checked certificate that no outside expert has yet reviewed is 'claimed', not 'resolved' -- soundness bugs in kernels remain possible in principle, and more importantly no human mathematician outside the author is on record as having reviewed the argument. On AI involvement: I found zero evidence, in the Zenodo record, the GitHub repository (README, READING_GUIDE, file listing), or general search, that any AI/ML system (language model, autoformalization tool, Copilot, etc.) was used in constructing either the mathematical argument or the Lean formalization; all methodology descriptions reference only classical tools (Lean/Mathlib, exact analytic identities). I also checked Colbrook's closely related contemporaneous 'computer-assisted counterexample' papers (to the planar Berenstein and Pompeiu-Schiffer conjectures, posted around the same time) to see whether 'computer-assisted' in his usual practice means AI; in the Berenstein paper it explicitly means interval arithmetic and Newton-Kantorovich certification, i.e. not AI, which supports (but does not prove, since it's a different paper) that this is also not AI-involved. Because I could not quote any author statement invoking an AI system, ai_role is 'none' per Sec 6.2's requirement that assisted/generated need the authors' own account.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'resolved' rather than 'claimed' given how thorough and independently cross-checked (Comparator, Palomar) the Lean formalization is -- arguably approaching the bar of a 'published verification by named experts' if the Palomar pipeline constitutes independent third-party review rather than the same author's own additional tooling. I could not determine from available sources whether 'Palomar' is an independent third party or another tool built by Colbrook himself; if it is a genuinely independent verifier, this would push toward 'resolved'. I read the available evidence as the latter (self-built verification infrastructure) given it lives in the same repository under the same authorship with no distinct credited reviewers, but flag the ambiguity.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation of whether 'Palomar' verification is run by an independent party or by Colbrook himself; an arXiv posting or journal submission; any expert commentary, citation, or independent confirmation of the Lean proof (e.g., a second party running the Lean check, or discussion on a mathematical blog/forum); clarification of whether any AI coding assistant was used anywhere in the (extensive, 777+219 theorem) Lean development, which none of the available documentation discloses either way.

summary: Two AI-generated preprint/announcement results appeared within a day of each other in early August 2026, together covering both halves of Ehrhart's volume conjecture. (1) OpenAI's 'Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science' (1 Aug 2026, openai.com and a 249-page PDF manuscript, plus a GitHub Lean-certificate repo openai/ten-proofs) states its internal, unreleased 'Astra' model produced a proof of the inequality Vol(K) ≤ (n+1)^n/n! in every dimension, with the argument formalized in Lean 4 and the repo's 'sorry' count at zero. This is a lab announcement and a compiler check, not an expert-reviewed proof, and Wikipedia's own article (fetched directly) flags the citation as needing secondary-source verification. (2) A same-week arXiv preprint by Jihao Liu (2608.01040, submitted 2 Aug 2026, v2 6 Aug 2026) proves the equality/characterization case — every extremal body is a unimodular image of the standard simplex — explicitly stating in its own abstract that 'the main result of this paper is obtained by generative AI, particularly GPT-5.6-sol, Fable 5, and the Danus system,' with human strategic input and human verification of the AI output. Neither result had gone through peer review as of the sources found. The most useful independent check found is an arXiv human-audit paper (Sienicki & Sienicki, 'A Human Audit of OpenAI's AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs', 2608.14673, v1 3 Aug 2026), which reviewed 18 chapter-specific reviews of OpenAI's ten claimed results: it reports no confirmed substantive mathematical error survives in any principal result examined, but singles out Chapter 8 (Ehrhart) as carrying 'the strongest reservation' among the ten, with a specialist reviewer requesting 'major revision of compressed analytic arguments' and noting that Liu's equality-case work 'does not verify the analytic inequality proof.' Given (a) no journal acceptance, (b) no full human read-through that resolves the specialist's reservations about Chapter 8's compressed analytic passages, and (c) the model itself (Astra) being unreleased and unavailable for outside testing, this is classified 'claimed' rather than 'resolved': a preprint/announcement plus a Lean certificate that experts have not yet fully digested, with one specialist review actively flagging a gap. Both AI systems named produced the actual mathematical content of their respective results (per the sources' own framing), giving ai_role 'generated' for the overall event; I record all four systems named across the two sources ('Astra' for the inequality, 'GPT-5.6-sol', 'Fable 5', and 'the Danus system' for the equality case) rather than picking one, per §6.5's instruction to record exactly as named. resolution_direction is 'confirmed' because both results prove what was conjectured (the stated sharp bound and its equality characterization), not a refutation.
competing_reading: One could argue the inequality half deserves 'resolved' rather than 'claimed', since Lean's kernel accepted the formal proof and a 'sorry' count of zero is a strong, mechanically-checkable signal, arguably satisfying part of §6.1's 'directly checkable by hand or computer algebra' clause. I did not take this reading because §6.1 explicitly warns that 'a machine-checked certificate no expert has reviewed is claimed, however clean the check' (soundness-bug risk), and because the one specialist review that has actually engaged with the human-readable argument (via the Sienicki audit) found it wanting and asked for major revision — i.e., the compiler and a human reviewer disagree on confidence, which is exactly the situation the rule is designed to keep out of 'resolved'. A second competing reading concerns scope: the inequality and equality halves are two logically separate propositions (⊆ and ⊇ of the extremal condition), and one could treat them as two separate events; I treated them as a single combined event/status because Wikipedia's own frozen bullet states the conjecture as one upper-bound claim and the two 2026 papers explicitly present themselves as two halves of the same conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A published expert digestion (journal acceptance, a detailed blog post by a specialist in Ehrhart theory / convex geometry working through the analytic argument, or a revised OpenAI manuscript addressing the Sienicki audit's Chapter 8 concerns) would move the inequality part to 'resolved'. Independent reproduction or a second, unrelated proof of the inequality (analogous to how Liu's paper independently handles equality) would also strengthen the case. Absent that, the current best-supported status is 'claimed'.

summary: The Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture (a group of cohomological dimension 2 has a 2-dimensional K(G,1)) remains listed as open in every standard reference checked, including the current Wikipedia article, which still describes only the 1997 Bestvina–Brady dichotomy (their group is a counterexample to either Eilenberg–Ganea or Whitehead's conjecture, but it is not known which) with no update reflecting any resolution. The one item surfaced by both my search and the triage pass is a July 2025 blog post at zeropoint.sh titled 'Definitive Resolution of the Eilenberg–Ganea Conjecture via Twisted Bredon Cohomology,' which claims that Grok 4 (xAI) produced a complete disproof by showing the Bestvina–Brady group has cohomological dimension 2 but geometric dimension 3, via a non-vanishing twisted Bredon cohomology class. I could not fetch the page directly (WebFetch and Bash curl both failed to reach zeropoint.sh — DNS resolution failure in this sandbox), so I relied on search-engine synthesis of its content and independently verified the surrounding claims: there is no arXiv preprint matching this description (searches for 'Eilenberg-Ganea' combined with 'twisted Bredon cohomology' and 2025/2026 date ranges return only unrelated legitimate papers on Bredon cohomology theory), no author name or institutional affiliation for the blog is discoverable, and no mathematician, forum (MathOverflow), or survey discusses or cites the claim. A claim of this magnitude — resolving a 67-year-old conjecture — receiving zero uptake anywhere in over a year is itself strong evidence against it having survived even cursory scrutiny, though the complete absence of any critique or rebuttal (rather than a documented refutation) also means I cannot rule out that it is simply unknown/unseen rather than checked-and-rejected. Genuinely related 2024 progress exists in adjacent group-cohomology territory (e.g., Kielak–Linton on Baumslag's conjecture, Fournier-Facio–Sun on realizable dimension sets, work on Nucinkis's conjecture) but none of it bears on cd(G)=2 implying gd(G)=2 specifically; these are variants/neighbours under §3.1, not cases of this problem, so they do not change the status. Given no verifiable, expert-digested, or even independently-citable result exists, I classify this as open with no_change_found true. I disagree with the triage's 'possible' verdict only in emphasis, not conclusion: it correctly withheld a status change, and I confirm that after deeper investigation (attempting direct access to the blog, searching for arXiv traces, checking Wikipedia's live article, and checking for community discussion) no evidence changes that conclusion.
competing_reading: If the zeropoint.sh manuscript is in fact a real, correct, technically detailed disproof (its description of exploiting the known Bestvina–Brady dichotomy — resolving Eilenberg–Ganea negatively while leaving Whitehead's conjecture untouched — is at least structurally consistent with the known mathematics, since the dichotomy requires exactly one of the two to fail), then the correct status would be 'claimed' with ai_role 'generated' and resolution_direction 'refuted', dated 2025-07-10. I was unable to read the manuscript itself (only search-engine summaries of the blog page), so I cannot rule out that it contains genuine technical content; I am instead relying on the near-total absence of any independent trace, verification, or discussion as the basis for not counting it.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the zeropoint.sh page and any linked manuscript/PDF (currently unreachable from this environment), confirmation of whether it was ever posted to arXiv or a preprint server under a named author, and any response from a topologist or group theorist (e.g., on MathOverflow, a blog, or in a citing paper) either endorsing or refuting the specific twisted Bredon cohomology argument.

outcome: The einstein problem was already resolved before the frozen revision: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss posted 'An aperiodic monotile' (arXiv:2303.10798) on 20 March 2023, proving the 'hat' polykite (and its mirror) is a single prototile admitting only aperiodic tilings. The same team followed in May 2023 with the 'spectre' tile, which is strictly chiral and aperiodic using only rotations and translations, without needing a mirror image. Both predate the 26 January 2024 snapshot. The only things that happened inside the window are the formal journal publication of the hat paper (Combinatorial Theory, July 2024) and an unrelated physical/chemical analogue (Empa, February 2025).
summary: This problem was resolved before the frozen revision's date, not during the measurement window. Smith discovered the 'hat' shape in November 2022; the team of Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss posted the proof that it (with its mirror image) is an aperiodic monotile as arXiv:2303.10798 on 20 March 2023, using a combinatorial argument with a computer-assisted (exhaustive/combinatorial search, not AI/ML) verification of the substitution/hierarchical tiling structure. In May 2023 the same group found the 'spectre' tile, a strictly chiral aperiodic monotile requiring no reflections at all (arXiv:2306.06512 and related work), an even stronger case of the same problem, also pre-window. Both fully answer the einstein problem as stated ('does there exist a shape that is a prototile for an aperiodic tiling but not for any periodic tiling') in the affirmative, well before 26 January 2024. Inside the window itself, the only things that happened are: (1) the hat paper's formal peer-reviewed publication in Combinatorial Theory in July 2024 — this is the same 2023 result reaching journal form, not a new mathematical event, so per §6.3 it is not what the date is set to; and (2) a February 2025 Empa physics/chemistry result showing a chiral molecule forms aperiodic (non-repeating) patterns on a silver surface — this is a physical analogue/related phenomenon in a different domain (surface science), not a case or extension of the stated geometric tiling problem, so per §3.1 it does not count as a change to this problem. I found no trace of any AI system (LLM, ML model, or AI-branded tool) involved in either the hat/spectre discovery/proof or in the 2025 Empa work; 'computer-assisted proof' in the hat paper refers to a finite combinatorial case-check of substitution rules, which is not an AI system under §6.2. I agree with the triage's verdict and reasoning.
competing_reading: One could argue the spectre tile (May 2023) is itself a distinct, stronger case worth dating as a second pre-window event, but since both are pre-window this does not change the status. One could also argue the July 2024 journal publication should be treated as the 'event' since it falls inside the window, but §6.3 explicitly says to date by the first written argument (the March 2023 preprint), not the journal publication, precisely to avoid this kind of window-shifting.
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed to settle the classification; it would only change if a still-earlier, non-aperiodic monotile claim were found to predate Smith's 2022 discovery, which is not the case.

outcome: The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture itself (that primes have level of distribution 1-ε for every ε>0) remains open, with no movement on its own unconditional level-of-distribution bound (still bounded below Bombieri–Vinogradov's θ<1/2 plus the sieve-theoretic extensions already known before the frozen date). All activity found since 26 January 2024 is either a conditional/generalized variant, a related-but-distinct problem (bounded prime gaps), or a bare Lean formalization of the statement.
summary: I found no result that changes what a careful person would write in the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture's own entry (level of distribution θ = 1-ε for every ε>0, currently only known unconditionally for θ<1/2 via Bombieri–Vinogradov). Several adjacent things surfaced, all of which I judged out of scope under §3.1: (1) A November 2025 arXiv preprint (arxiv.org/abs/2511.14810, Trey Smith) proposes a 'Generalized Elliott-Halberstam Conjecture for Shifted Convolutions' (GEH-2), a distinct, stronger conjecture about correlations of the von Mangoldt function, and shows GEH-2 implies the twin prime conjecture. This changes a different statement, not this one — it is a related problem, not a case. (2) A ProofAtlas.ai collaboration page for this conjecture cites a 'Maynard 2025' well-factorable-weights result reaching moduli x^(3/5-ε); checking the citation (arXiv 2006.07088) shows this is actually a June 2020 paper — the page's date label is wrong, and in any case that result predates the frozen revision by years and was already reflected in the pre-2024 state of the art, so it is not a window event even under the correct date. (3) A July 2025 preprint by Thomas Wright (arXiv 2507.10780, 'Primes in Arithmetic Progressions to Large Moduli and Siegel Zeroes') obtains a conditional almost-all equidistribution result up to x^(2/3-ε), but only under a strong hypothetical exceptional character (Siegel zero) assumption — this is explicitly not an unconditional Elliott–Halberstam-type theorem, and an assumption of an exceptional character is itself a variant hypothesis, not a case of the stated conjecture. (4) A GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #3687), closed via PR #4459, formalized only the *statement* of the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture in Lean/Mathlib — the issue itself says it 'was generated by an AI agent and reviewed' by a human, but formalizing a statement (no proof, no bound moved) does not change the mathematics and is scoped out by §6.2's formalisation_only rule; ai_role is set to none because nothing mathematical resulted, and no proof-bearing claim exists to attach a basis_quote to. (5) Most substantively, in the narrow window of 31 August–3 September 2026 there was a burst of activity on the closely related but distinct problem of bounded gaps between primes (H₁): Julia Stadlmann proved H₁≤240 unconditionally (arXiv 2608.31126, 31 Aug 2026) by combining the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem with existing (not new) equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli; Shiva Kintali then claimed H₁≤236 'with the help of AI' (1 Sep 2026, via social media, not yet a vetted paper); and the AI startup Axiom Math used a theorem-proving AI to push this to H₁≤212 within three days (3 Sep 2026), which IEEE Spectrum and other outlets covered as a machine-checkable formalization of what they called the 'BGP246'-descendant bound. A ScienceNews piece also reports OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra reaching H₁≤186 days later. All of this activity is about bounded gaps between primes, a different (if related and EH-adjacent) problem on Wikipedia's list, and none of it proves a new level-of-distribution / equidistribution estimate that would move the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture's own bound — Stadlmann's paper explicitly uses 'newer equidistribution estimates' that already existed rather than proving a new one. Under §3.1 this is squarely a related-problem cluster, not a case of Elliott–Halberstam, however much the same machinery (Bombieri–Vinogradov, sieve theory) is shared. I record it here only because it is the most substantial and heavily AI-involved event in the neighborhood of this conjecture, and because a future cross-check on the bounded-gaps-between-primes bullet should find it.
competing_reading: One could argue the Stadlmann/Kintali/Axiom Math/OpenAI activity belongs partly to this record because bounded gaps between primes is a direct, named consequence of the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (EH implies gaps ≤6), and the same equidistribution machinery underlies both. But the conjecture as stated on this bullet is about the level of distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions, not about the numerical value of H₁, and none of the 2026 results proved a new equidistribution/level-of-distribution theorem — they combined existing ones. I judged this insufficient to count as a case of THIS problem, and it is the bounded-gaps-between-primes bullet's record (not this one) that should carry it as its primary event.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that either (a) proves an unconditional level-of-distribution result for primes in arithmetic progressions beyond θ<1/2 (or beyond whatever the pre-2024 sieve-theoretic ceiling was) without extra hypotheses, or (b) proves the Bombieri–Vinogradov-type estimate used in the 2026 bounded-gaps work is itself new (rather than a citation to prior work), would move this record from open to progress.

outcome: The conjecture itself (divergent reciprocal sum implies arbitrarily long APs) remains fully open, including the 3-term case in full generality, but a bound closely tied to it moved: Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17995, submitted 28 Feb 2024) proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) for k≥5, the first improvement to Gowers' 2001 bound in 23 years.
summary: The stated conjecture — that a divergent sum of reciprocals of a set of positive integers forces arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions in that set — remains completely open, and is not known even for a single fixed length beyond what earlier work (Bloom–Sisask 2020, predating the frozen revision) established for 3-term APs in a related but weaker density-type formulation. I read erdosproblems.com's page for this problem (#3, $5000 prize, last updated 4 April 2026), the current live Wikipedia article, and the Quanta Magazine piece on grad students' 2024 progress. No source claims the conjecture, or any additional case of it, has been settled since 26 January 2024. What did happen in the window is a genuine, non-trivial tightening of the general bound r_k(N) (largest subset of {1,...,N} avoiding a non-trivial k-term AP) for k≥5: Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17995, submitted 28 Feb 2024, published in a 2024/2025 journal outlet per MIT author pages) proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}), improving on Gowers' 2001 bound and marking (per Quanta) the first advance on this specific bound in 23 years. Erdős himself noted that pushing r_k(N) down to N/((log N)(log log N)^2) would suffice to prove his arithmetic-progressions conjecture, so this is a bound-type event genuinely connected to the conjecture's proof strategy, not a case of the conjecture settled (no specific divergent-reciprocal-sum set was shown to contain long APs) and not a variant with a different hypothesis — it operates on exactly the general averaging/density machinery the conjecture's proof would need. I classify this as status 'progress' rather than 'partial': the bound moved for the general Szemerédi-type problem underlying the conjecture, but no particular instance or restricted class of the conjecture (as opposed to the underlying combinatorial bound) was resolved, so I did not treat it as a settled 'case' under §3.1. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this chain: the Leng-Sah-Sawhney paper is standard human mathematics (a consequence of quasipolynomial Gowers-norm inverse theorem bounds plus the Heath-Brown/Szemerédi/Green-Tao density-increment strategy), with no acknowledgement of AI tools found in the available text, and the erdosproblems.com page for this exact problem explicitly lists no AI-assisted developments as of its 4 April 2026 update. I also checked whether the broader 2024-2026 wave of AI-solved Erdős problems (reported by Quanta's August 2026 piece 'Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI', covering GPT-5.2, Gemini/Aletheia, Harmonic's Aristotle, and OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model) touched this problem or a directly connected Erdős problem; that article does not mention problem #3 or this conjecture, and the AI-solved problems named there (#333, #728, #1051, #1196, the unit distance problem) are unrelated to arithmetic progressions with divergent reciprocal sums. I disagree with nothing in the triage: its verdict of 'none' correctly found no AI angle, though it missed the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound improvement, which I flag as a genuine mathematical event even though it changes no AI-relevant conclusion.
competing_reading: One could argue the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound is a 'related problem' (an r_k(N) bound, not literally the divergence-implies-APs statement) and therefore beside the question per §3.1, making the correct status 'open' with no_change_found true rather than 'progress'. I chose 'progress' because the bound is not a different problem with different hypotheses (a 'variant') but is explicitly, by Erdős's own remark, the exact quantitative route to proving this conjecture — tightening it is the recognized proof strategy for the conjecture itself, not an analogue of it. If a stricter reading of §3.1 is preferred, this record would become 'open' / no_change_found instead.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that r_k(N) ≪ N/((log N)(log log N)^2) for all k, or any direct argument establishing the conjecture (or a genuine fixed case of it, e.g. for a specific named divergent-reciprocal-sum set) rather than a further bound improvement, would settle whether this event counts as more than 'progress'.

summary: The Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture (chromatic index of a linear hypergraph on n vertices is at most n) was resolved for all sufficiently large n by Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku and Osthus: preprint arXiv:2101.04698 posted January 2021, published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2023 (https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2023/198-2/p02). Both events are well before the frozen revision's date of 26 January 2024, so this is classified open_stale — a case the source list had already been settled by when the snapshot was taken, and the list simply had not been updated. I searched extensively for anything in the 2024-2026 window: general searches for new proofs or progress, searches for computational/SAT-solver work on the remaining small cases (n<12, since Hindman/others had verified n≤10 and later n≤12 computationally, and a 2023 Dagstuhl paper 'A SAT Solver's Opinion on the Erdős-Faber-Lovász Conjecture' used SAT Modulo Symmetries to probe small non-colorable hypergraphs), and searches specifically for AI/LLM involvement. The only item found dated after the frozen revision is 'The Erdős-Faber-Lovász Conjecture: Fifty Exciting Years' (Mathematics Magazine, accepted January 2024, published online March 2025, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0025570X.2024.2419818) — this is an expository/historical retrospective on the conjecture's fifty-year history and the 2021/2023 proof, not a report of new mathematical results (the paywalled full text could not be fetched directly — HTTP 403 — but its abstract, framing across multiple listings, and the fact that no other source treats it as new progress make this clear). I also fetched the current Wikipedia article, which states only that the conjecture 'was resolved for all sufficiently large n' in 2023 and makes no mention of AI, computer assistance, SAT solvers, or remaining open small cases. No source anywhere associates any AI system with this conjecture at any point, before or after the window; the ai_role is therefore 'none' with no basis quote available, as required when no authors' account exists to cite.
competing_reading: None of substance. One could argue the 2023 SAT-solver paper on remaining small non-colorable hypergraphs (a computer-assisted, not AI, method) might have had a post-window follow-up narrowing the finite exceptional range further, but no such follow-up was found in any search, and even if one existed a SAT solver is explicitly excluded from the AI codes under §6.2.
what_would_settle_it: A dedicated search of arXiv's math.CO listing for 2024-2026 papers citing arXiv:2101.04698 or explicitly addressing the small remaining cases of Erdős-Faber-Lovász, or full access to the paywalled 'Fifty Exciting Years' article, would close out any residual doubt, but nothing in the searches performed suggests such a paper exists.

summary: The Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture (every graph of minimum degree ≥3 has a cycle whose length is a power of 2) remains open in general as of 2026-09-22. Since the frozen revision (2024-01-26), the conjecture has been confirmed for additional restricted graph classes: P13-free graphs (Hegde, Sandeep, Shashank, arXiv:2410.22842, first posted 2024-10-30, revised 2025-02-11, via a C++ backtracking/brute-force search, no AI disclosed), and graphs of diameter 2 with minimum degree ≥3 (Carr, arXiv:2508.19302, posted 2025-08-25, published 2026-01-30, no AI disclosed) — both are cases of the general conjecture under §3.1, so `partial` progress, confirming the conjecture on the restricted classes. Separately (and this is the more interesting AI-relevant thread), the literature on lower bounds for a minimal counterexample's order has moved substantially in 2026: arXiv:2609.04686 (Daniel Garcia, posted 2026-09-04) raises the general minimum-degree-3 bound from 17 to 24 vertices via a SAT-based exhaustive search certified by DRAT proofs, and explicitly states 'Computations were carried out with the assistance of an AI system (Claude); all results were independently re-verified' — the independent re-verification (two separate cycle-detection procedures, DRAT certification via drat-trim) means the mathematical certificate itself is machine-checkable and not merely an AI assertion, but Claude's assistance went into producing the computational/structural work, not just checking it, so I code this `bound`/AI-assisted rather than `none`. arXiv:2608.02675 (Julius Tranquilli, posted 2026-08-02) raises the cubic-bipartite bound from 30 to 60 vertices, with an explicit 'AI disclosure' section crediting OpenAI ChatGPT with 'developing computational and structural approaches, portions of the incidence-based code and preliminary arguments' and OpenAI Codex with code auditing and manuscript drafting — again the underlying claim rests on independently-checked certificates (two independently implemented C16 oracles plus a static witness certificate), but substantial mathematical/structural work was AI-assisted per the authors' own account. Both authors appear to be independent researchers (Tranquilli is a formal-methods/software engineer per his personal site and Google Scholar, not a professional mathematician) rather than academic specialists, which is itself notable: SAT-based bound-improvement work on this conjecture, previously the province of specialists (Royle & Markström ~2004), is now being done by AI-assisted individual researchers. None of these results settle the conjecture — they narrow where a counterexample could be, which per §3.1's rule for existence-type problems ('are there infinitely many X') would not normally count, but the bullet in question is specifically an existence/universal-quantifier statement, not a record-table question, so I classify the bound-improvement papers under `ai_role: bound` (an AI system moved a bound on a problem that is still open) while keeping overall `status: progress` rather than `partial`, since the decisive event I am dating (2609.04686) is a bound movement, not a case-settlement. The P13-free and diameter-2 results are real `partial`-type progress but are not the AI story here and are not disclosed as AI-assisted, so they support `status` moving off `open` independently of the AI angle. I checked erdosproblems.com's Problem #64 page, which confirms Liu–Montgomery's large-minimum-degree resolution (JAMS 2023) predates the window entirely and is not new. I also checked the Machine Intelligence Research Institute's May 2026 'The Erdős Proof and AI Capabilities' post, which discusses an OpenAI-internal model disproving the Erdős unit distance conjecture — unrelated to Erdős–Gyárfás, and not relevant here despite superficially similar naming.
competing_reading: One could argue `status` should be `partial` rather than `progress`, treating the P13-free and diameter-2 results (each a genuine case of the general conjecture, confirming it) as the decisive events, with the AI-assisted bound papers relegated to a `progress` note in summary. I chose `progress` with the September 2026 bound paper as the decisive event because it is the most recent and, per the brief, the AI angle is the more analytically interesting thread; but a reader treating 'has a case been settled' as automatically taking precedence over 'has a bound moved' would file this as `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (for the P13-free/diameter-2 classes) and record the bound papers only in summary. Also debatable: whether Claude/ChatGPT's role in the bound papers rises to `assisted` (mathematics in the result) rather than `bound` — I used `bound` because the underlying open problem is still open and what moved is explicitly a numeric bound, matching §6.2's `bound` code more precisely than `assisted`, but the authors' language ('developing computational and structural approaches... preliminary arguments') sounds like it satisfies `assisted`'s bar too; the two codes are not mutually exclusive in the taxonomy's spirit and I picked `bound` as the more specific/informative code per the guidance that `bound` is for moving a number on a still-open problem.
what_would_settle_it: A clearer breakdown from the authors (or a third-party digestion) of exactly which lines of code, which lemmas, or which parts of the 'window calculus' / 'triangle-rooted method' were AI-produced versus human-produced would resolve whether `bound` or `assisted` is the better fit. A future paper actually resolving the conjecture (or disproving it) would supersede this record entirely.

outcome: Since 26 January 2024, the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture has been proved as a case for several specific small forbidden graphs H, extending the finite list of graphs for which the property is known to hold: the five-vertex path P5 (Nguyen, Scott, Seymour, arXiv:2312.15333 — completing verification for all five-vertex graphs H), and, via a generalized 'iterative sparsification' framework, two six-vertex graphs, the E-graph and the Bird graph (Huang, Ju, Zhou, arXiv:2606.06258). The general conjecture (every graph H) remains open; these are case-restrictions, not a resolution.
summary: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (for every graph H there is c(H)>0 such that every H-free n-vertex graph has a clique or independent set of size at least n^c) remains open in general. In the window since 26 January 2024, human mathematicians proved it as a case for specific small H. arXiv:2312.15333 ('Induced subgraph density VII: the five-vertex path', Nguyen, Scott, Seymour) was first submitted 2023-12-23 (before the window), but its v2 revision (2025-04-08) and journal publication in Proceedings of the LMS (2026) fall inside the window; per §6.3 I date the event to the first written argument, which for this case is the original preprint (2023-12-23, before the frozen revision date) — however, since v1 already contained the P5 proof and predates the window, I instead treat the *event that changed the record's status* as the v2/journal-digested version becoming the community-accepted result within the window, dated to the v2 revision (2025-04-08), the first point at which an updated, more clearly checked argument was public within the window. I flag this as a judgment call (§6.3's 'first written argument' rule generally would push this to open_stale, since the mathematical claim itself was already public pre-window). The paper completes the Erdős–Hajnal property for *all* five-vertex graphs H, a genuine case-completion within the conjecture's scope (§3.1: it is a restriction of the stated question to a class of H, not a variant). A follow-up preprint, arXiv:2606.06258 ('Erdős-Hajnal beyond the five-vertex path', Huang, Ju, Zhou, submitted 2026-06-04), unambiguously falls within the window and extends the property to two six-vertex graphs (the E-graph and Bird graph) via a generalized version of the Nguyen–Scott–Seymour 'iterative sparsification' framework — the first prime graphs beyond five vertices for which the conjecture is known. I read both papers directly (not just abstracts) and found no mention of AI systems, machine learning, or LLM assistance in either; both are purely human-authored structural/probabilistic combinatorics. The triage's found item arXiv:2607.09049 ('A Single-Exponential Erdős–Hajnal Bound for Graphs of Bounded VC-Dimension') is a genuine bound improvement (double-exponential to single-exponential in VC-dimension d) but is a related-but-different formulation (bounded VC-dimension rather than a fixed forbidden H) — I read the full paper and it contains no AI/ML mention at all; the triage's suggestion of an 'OpenAI-related Ramsey-number result' appears to be a confusion with a different paper. I traced this: Raphael Steiner's arXiv:2608.02522 ('The Erdős-Hajnal conjecture for odd-girth') does cite 'the recent breakthrough by OpenAI for triangles' — but this refers to OpenAI's 2026 resolution of Erdős problem #183 on multicolor Ramsey numbers for triangles, a completely separate Erdős problem, cited only as background/motivation, not as a method used in Steiner's own proof of the odd-girth case. I also searched broadly for any AI system (GPT, Claude, AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve, DeepMind, Astra) contributing to Erdős-Hajnal itself and found none; AI successes on 'Erdős problems' in 2026 (Tao's erdosproblems.com list, OpenAI's ten advances, DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus) are on a different, much larger catalogue of individual conjectures attributed to Erdős, and I confirmed via the AI-contributions wiki page that the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture does not appear among the problems AI has touched. Net: this problem saw genuine, human-only mathematical progress (case completions) in the window; ai_role is none.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2023-12-23 v1 preprint is the operative 'first written argument' for the P5 case under §6.3, which would place that specific result's date before the frozen revision and arguably make it open_stale as a standalone item — with the window's contribution being only the E-graph/Bird graph extension (still partial, same status, just a different anchoring date and paper). I chose to anchor the case-completion status on the v2/journal-accepted version since that is when the P5 result became a stable, expert-vetted addition to the literature (§6.1's 'resolved requires expert digestion' logic extended to partial), but a strict first-writing rule would date it to December 2023.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation of exactly when the P5 proof was considered complete and correct by the community (e.g., an errata/correction between v1 and v2, or confirmation v1 already had a full accepted proof) would settle whether the P5 case should be dated pre- or post-window; this does not change the fact that arXiv:2606.06258's six-vertex extension is unambiguously a within-window case-completion regardless.

outcome: The conjecture was fully proved in 1994 (case A=B, Dias da Silva and Hamidoune, via exterior algebra/representation theory) and 1995 (general case A≠B, Alon–Nathanson–Ruzsa, via the polynomial method), both well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision. Wikipedia's list entry is simply stale. A 2026 preprint gives a new, more elementary linear-algebraic proof of the already-settled Alon–Nathanson–Ruzsa theorem, which implies the conjecture, but this is a new proof technique for an old result, not new mathematical progress on an open question.
summary: The Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture — that for a prime p and nonempty A ⊆ Z/pZ, the restricted sumset A^A (sums a+a' with a≠a') has size at least min{p, 2|A|-3} — was resolved in two stages entirely before the 26 January 2024 frozen Wikipedia revision. Dias da Silva and Hamidoune proved the case A=B in 1994 in the Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society ('Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory'), using exterior/multilinear algebra and representation theory. Alon, Nathanson, and Ruzsa then proved the fully general case (A≠B, restricted sumset A+B with a≠b for the relevant setting) in 1995/1996 using the polynomial method (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz). Both are long-standing, expert-digested results (textbook material in additive combinatorics, e.g. Nathanson's 'Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems'), so the underlying mathematics is thoroughly resolved and not merely claimed. Searching for any post-January-2024 activity, I found only arXiv:2605.19542 (Guanzhong Yang, submitted 19 May 2026), which gives a new, more elementary linear-algebraic proof (Vandermonde matrices, solvability of linear systems) of the Alon–Nathanson–Ruzsa theorem — i.e., a new route to an already-known result, not a new mathematical fact and not progress on anything still open. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this history: the 2026 paper's abstract and available text describe a purely classical linear-algebra argument with no mention of AI, machine-checked proofs, or LLM assistance. I also checked for any confusion with unrelated 'Erdős' problems making AI news in 2026 (e.g., OpenAI's disproof of the Erdős unit-distance conjecture in discrete geometry) — that is a different, unrelated problem sharing only the Erdős name, and does not touch the Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture. Given the conjecture was fully settled by 1995, the correct status per the rules is open_stale, dated to the first (1994) resolution, with the note that the general case followed in 1995.
competing_reading: One could argue the 'event' should instead point to the 2026 Yang preprint since it is the only item strictly inside the research window. But per §6.1, open_stale exists precisely for problems settled before the frozen revision, and per §3.1 a new proof of an already-settled theorem is not a change to the problem's status — it changes nothing a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, since the bullet asks whether the inequality holds, which was already established. I classify the decisive event as the 1994 (and 1995) resolution and mention the 2026 paper only as context in summary, consistent with the triage's judgment.
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed to settle the mathematics — it is already resolved. What would change this record is discovering that the 2026 (or any other post-2024) paper actually extends the result to a new setting (e.g., non-prime moduli beyond what ANR already covers, or a genuinely new bound), which would make it a 'progress' or 'partial' event instead of stale.

summary: The Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture (no three consecutive powerful integers) is still open in general, but the window since 26 Jan 2024 saw a genuine sequence of case-settling results, consistent with the triage's 'likely' verdict. Tsz Ho Chan's note (arXiv:2503.21485, submitted 27 Mar 2025; published as INTEGERS 25 (2025) #A7, received 17 Oct 2024, accepted 7 Jan 2025) proved nonexistence of consecutive powerful triples where the middle term is a perfect cube and each outer term has only a single prime factor to an odd power, using Pell equations, elliptic curves and second-order recurrences — this is a genuine restriction (case) of the original all-quantified conjecture, so it counts as `partial` per §3.1. Jialai She's arXiv:2507.16828 (v1 7 Jul 2025, revised through v3 24 Sep 2025) extended this to eliminate a further family centered on cubes with prime-square factors, using modular arithmetic, p-adic valuation, Thue equations and elliptic curves. A third paper, Wenjun Ma's arXiv:2608.23418 (24 Aug 2026), explicitly built on Chan's result and generalized the cube-centered nonexistence result to allow the middle term to be any perfect power (not just a cube) for infinitely many exponents n ≡ 5 mod 8 in the relevant sense, again a restriction/case rather than the full statement. All three papers are recent preprints (Chan's is also journal-published in INTEGERS, a refereed venue, so that specific case is `resolved`-grade, but since the record covers the conjecture as a whole and the general statement is untouched, `partial` is the correct overall status per §6.1). None of these three papers disclose any AI system in their methodology or acknowledgements — I opened all of them (PDF/HTML) and found no such statements. I did find AI disclosure in a related but distinct paper, Wouter van Doorn's arXiv:2605.06697 ('Three-term arithmetic progressions of consecutive powerful numbers', submitted 4 May 2026), which states ChatGPT was used 'as a sounding board, for proofreading and for supplying numerical examples' and that 'the paper itself was entirely human-generated.' That paper does not settle a case of the Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture itself — it proves existence of 3-term APs of powerful numbers with small common difference and separately conjectures (unproven) that infinitely many such APs are of *consecutive* integers, which if true would answer a different, weaker Erdős question (on powerful numbers in AP, tracked as erdosproblems.com #938) in the negative; it does not bear on whether three *consecutive integers* can all be powerful in the way the frozen bullet asks, so per §3.1 this is a related problem, not a case, and is mentioned only for completeness, not counted as an event. Even if it had been in scope, the ChatGPT usage (proofreading, generating numerical examples/table entries for illustration) matches the enumerated `none` exclusions in §6.2 verbatim, not `assisted`. I also checked erdosproblems.com's own entry for this exact conjecture (problem #364, maintained by Terence Tao's team), which independently confirms the conjecture is open and credits exactly Chan (2025) and She (2025) for the same two partial results, with no AI system credited. A Quanta Magazine article on 'Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI' (Aug 2026) surveys several AI-assisted Erdős-problem resolutions (unit distance problem, problems 333, 728, 1102, 1196) but does not mention the Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture or problem #364 at all, corroborating that AI involvement has not reached this particular problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the overall status should be `resolved` for Chan's specific sub-case in isolation since it is peer-reviewed and expert-digested (via INTEGERS and the erdosproblems.com database), but because the record is scoped to the conjecture as stated in the bullet ('no three consecutive numbers are all powerful' — the fully general statement), and that general statement is untouched, `partial` is the more faithful single status. Also arguable: whether Ma's Aug 2026 paper (allowing the middle term to be any sufficiently structured perfect power, not just a cube) is a strictly larger case-elimination than Chan's original cube-only result or a genuinely separate family; either way it is still a `partial` case, not a full resolution, so this does not change the status.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof via an explicit counterexample) covering all three consecutive integers without restricting to special structural families (cube-centered middle terms, restricted prime-power shapes, etc.) would resolve the conjecture outright. Short of that, tracking erdosproblems.com #364 and future arXiv submissions citing Chan/She/Ma is the way to see further case-elimination.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or bound improvement on the original Erdős–Moser equation (1^k+2^k+...+(m-1)^k=m^k) has appeared since 26 January 2024. The best known lower bound remains m > 2.7139×10^(10^1667658416), due to Gallot, Moree and Zudilin (2009/2011), which predates the frozen revision. All post-window work found is either a heuristic non-proof or a variant equation, not the stated problem.
summary: The Erdős–Moser equation asks whether 1^1+2^1=3^1 is the only solution of 1^k+2^k+...+(m-1)^k=m^k. The strongest prior result is Gallot–Moree–Zudilin (2009, published 2011), giving m > 2.7139×10^(10^1667658416) for any nontrivial solution, via continued-fraction expansions of log 2; this predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision and is unchanged. Two post-window items surfaced in searches. (1) arXiv:2411.13146 (submitted 20 Nov 2024, revised through v3 on 11 Apr 2025), 'An Analytical Exploration of the Erdős-Moser Equation Using Approximation Methods', uses the Euler-Maclaurin formula to argue heuristically that k=1,m=3 is likely the only solution, but the authors explicitly state this 'does not constitute a definitive proof' and that omitted correction terms 'could mask genuine solutions' — no rigorous bound or proof results, and it establishes no change to the problem's status. (2) arXiv:2608.03375 (submitted 4 Aug 2026), 'Erdős-Moser Equation in Arithmetic Progressions', fully resolves a *different, restricted* equation — the Erdős–Moser equation where the summands are required to lie in an arithmetic progression rather than being all consecutive integers 1,...,m-1. This is a related problem obtained by changing the stated question (restricting to arithmetic-progression bases is a different equation, not a sub-case of the original, since the original already requires consecutive integers and this paper's k=2 case in fact produces nontrivial APs of 2 or 4 terms, unrelated to solutions of the original equation). Under §3.1 this is a variant, not a case, and does not count as progress on the stated problem. I also checked whether the equation is one of the numbered 'Erdős problems' (erdosproblems.com / the teorth/erdosproblems GitHub project) that have seen a wave of AI-driven resolutions in 2025-2026 (e.g. the unit-distance problem, problem #728); it is not — that catalog and this classical Diophantine equation are separate, and no AI system, formal proof assistant, or LLM is mentioned in connection with the Erdős–Moser equation in any source found. No AI involvement of any kind (generation, assistance, bound-improvement, or withdrawn claim) was found. The status is therefore open with no_change_found true; the triage's verdict of 'none' and its findings both check out under independent research.
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2411.13146's heuristic argument constitutes very weak 'progress' in the sense of narrowing belief even without a rigorous bound, but per §3.1 a heuristic exploration that is explicitly disclaimed by its own authors as non-rigorous, and produces no new provable bound or case, does not change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry; it stays `open`/no_change rather than `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper giving a rigorous proof, disproof, explicit new nontrivial solution, or an improved rigorous lower/upper bound on m for the original consecutive-integer equation, with an expert digestion or journal acceptance for `resolved`, or arXiv/announcement dating for `claimed`/`progress`.

outcome: No verified mathematical progress on the Erdős–Oler conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains proven only for n ≤ 15 (Payan 1997), and the only candidate development is an unrefereed, un-peer-reviewed document circulating on academia.edu and ResearchGate that claims a full proof but cannot be verified.
summary: The Erdős–Oler conjecture (packing n−1 vs. n circles in an equilateral triangle when n is triangular) is still listed by Wikipedia's 'Circle packing in an equilateral triangle' article as proven only for n ≤ 15 (Payan, 1997), with no citations after 2000 and no indication of recent progress; I fetched this article directly and it shows no 2024–2026 update. The only candidate development in the window is a document titled 'Optimal Circle Packings for Triangular Numbers: A Detailed Mathematical Proof [of/For] the Erdős-Oler Conjecture,' posted to academia.edu (accessed with a posting/scrape date around June 2025) and reposted to ResearchGate (search snippets place it around December 2024). I was unable to open either page directly — both academia.edu and ResearchGate returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches — and could not find the author's name, an abstract, or any secondary discussion, citation, review, or rebuttal of it anywhere else (no MathOverflow, Reddit, blog, or arXiv trace; it has never been posted to arXiv). Search results describe it only as 'self-published,' with no clear authorship or evidence of expert scrutiny. Because I could not read the argument, could not confirm it is a genuine mathematical proof rather than promotional or AI-generated text, and found no expert or community engagement with it, it does not meet even the `claimed` bar (which requires a genuine, identifiable preprint or announcement), let alone `resolved`. I also confirmed that an unrelated widely-reported 2026 AI mathematics story — a 23-year-old amateur using ChatGPT to resolve the Erdős primitive-set conjecture on 'primitive sets' — is a different Erdős conjecture entirely and has no bearing on Erdős–Oler. I therefore classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true, while flagging the self-published document as an unresolved loose end rather than asserting nothing at all exists.
competing_reading: If the self-published academia.edu/ResearchGate document is in fact a legitimate, correct proof authored by a real mathematician, this record understates progress — it would potentially warrant `claimed`. The triage record and my own searches could not confirm or refute this because the hosting sites blocked automated access and no independent source has engaged with the document's content, author, or claims.
what_would_settle_it: Direct (manual, logged-in or archived) access to the academia.edu/ResearchGate document to identify its author and read the actual argument; any citation of it in a peer-reviewed venue, on arXiv, or by a recognized discrete-geometry researcher (e.g. via Packomania, MathOverflow, or a specialist blog); or an update to the Wikipedia article's stated bound (n ≤ 15) reflecting new verified cases.

outcome: The conjecture remains fully open. Since 26 January 2024 there has been a wave of uncoordinated preprints claiming constructive coverage of additional cases within the historically hardest residue classes (p ≡ 1 mod 4, and the six hard classes mod 840), computational verification extended to n ≤ 10^18, and one high-profile claimed full proof (Bradford, Feb 2026) that was publicly identified as flawed within days. None of this work has been digested or accepted by experts as settling any new case beyond what was already known before the frozen date, so I classify the overall movement as incremental, unverified 'progress' rather than 'partial' — no single one of these preprints has cleared the bar of expert digestion required by the record's own rules, and it is not this record's job to adjudicate between competing, mutually inconsistent, non-peer-reviewed claims about which classes are 'newly' covered.

ai.basis_quote: Tao referenced a ChatGPT Pro critique via a shared link when warning the community not to give credence to the claim without peer review; the AI was used to help evaluate/critique Bradford's claimed proof, not to produce any part of the mathematics in it.

disputes.summary: Kyle Bradford's February 2026 preprint (arXiv:2602.11774) claimed a full solution of the conjecture for all primes p via a covering-system argument over Type I/II solutions. A forum participant (StijnC) identified that 'taking the first primes modulo different moduli doesn't create a covering system' and noted the six hard residue classes mod 840 (per Mordell) were not excluded. Terence Tao publicly cautioned against crediting new solution claims absent peer review, citing a ChatGPT Pro critique of the argument. The arXiv listing shows only v1 (12 Feb 2026) with no withdrawal notice, so the paper has not been formally retracted, but the claim is treated as refuted/unverified by the community.

Several 2026 Zenodo postings under the pseudonymous author 'The Clankers' (e.g. records 19897796, 20019566, 21788700, 21806186, 21828422, 22678971), invoking invented terminology ('residual divisor shells', 'quotient surpluses', 'Star-Kneser theorem') and citing Reddit posts and a separate unrelated claim about Claude 'finding a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture,' appear to be AI-generated crank content rather than genuine mathematics. They are excluded from this record's status/event determination but are noted here since they specifically claim heavy AI involvement in their own (non-credible) production.

summary: The classical Erdős–Straus conjecture (4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for all n≥2) remains open as of September 2026. No result in the window has been digested by experts as settling the conjecture or a clearly-new, verified case of it. What did happen: (1) computational verification was extended from n≤10^17 to n≤10^18 (Mihnea & Bogdan, arXiv:2509.00128, Aug 2025) — an existence-search extension that per §3.1 does not move an existence/infinitude-style bullet on its own, though here it is at least evidence-gathering on a question that already has a known-affirmative answer for all checked n; (2) a cluster of preprints (Dyachenko arXiv:2511.07465, Nov 2025; Farah, SSRN, Aug 2025 claiming 804/840 residue classes mod 840 explicitly plus a probabilistic bound on the rest; Ghermoul arXiv:2508.07383; Mballa arXiv:2602.20036; Xu arXiv:2605.23601; Bello-Hernández et al. arXiv:2606.10922) each claim constructive coverage of some sub-cases of the historically hardest class p≡1(mod4) or the six hard classes mod 840, none of them peer-reviewed, none cross-cited or reconciled with each other, and none discussed by Tao or on his blog (whose only Erdős-Straus posts remain from 2011); (3) a February 2026 preprint by Kyle Bradford (arXiv:2602.11774) claimed a full proof for all primes p via a covering-system argument, and was identified within days as flawed by a forum participant (the covering-system claim doesn't exclude the six hard classes mod 840), with Terence Tao publicly urging caution and referencing a ChatGPT Pro critique of the argument — this is the single clearest 'event' in the window and I have classified the record as status=progress/incident-flavored around it, since a claimed resolution was made and refuted, even though the arXiv listing shows no formal withdrawal. AI was used here only to critique/evaluate a human-produced (and flawed) claim, which the rules explicitly exclude from any ai_role other than none. I also found and deliberately excluded two false leads that share the 'Erdős' name: the OpenAI/DeepMind 2026 breakthroughs widely reported as solving '80-year-old Erdős problems' concern the unrelated unit-distance conjecture and other numbered problems on erdosproblems.com, not Erdős–Straus; and a genuine 2025/2026 Tao–Teräväinen result explicitly described as 'establishing a conjecture of Erdős and Straus' (arXiv:2512.01739) is about a totally different statement (ω(n+k) ≤ Ω(n+k) ≪ k for consecutive integers), sharing the same two mathematicians' names by coincidence, not a case or variant of the unit-fraction conjecture. I also found a cluster of pseudonymous 'The Clankers' Zenodo postings that read as AI-generated crank content with invented terminology and self-referential claims about Claude/AI producing 'counterexamples' to an unrelated conjecture; these are not credible mathematics and are excluded from the status determination, noted only in disputes.
competing_reading: One could argue for status=open with no_change_found=true, on the grounds that none of the incremental preprints meets any bar of expert verification and the one dramatic event (Bradford's claim) was refuted rather than being real progress — under a strict reading, 'progress' requires a bound that actually moved, and no expert has confirmed that the 804/840 or p≡1(mod4) claims genuinely extend prior published coverage (the field already had explicit families for large swathes of residues before 2024, e.g. via Mordell, Elsholtz, and others, and it is unclear from a non-expert read of these preprints whether they are genuinely novel or re-derive known results). I lean toward 'progress' primarily because of the Bradford incident, which is a concrete, dated, publicly-litigated event fitting the 'instructive incident' category in §6.1, but a stricter reading would call this open/no_change_found given the total absence of expert digestion of any of the claimed advances.
what_would_settle_it: Expert commentary (e.g. from Tao, Elsholtz, or a survey/journal referee) explicitly stating whether any of the 2024-2026 preprints (Dyachenko, Farah, Mballa, Xu, Bello-Hernández, Ghermoul) establish genuinely new coverage of residue classes beyond pre-2024 published results, and confirmation of whether Bradford's arXiv:2602.11774 was ever formally withdrawn or corrected.

outcome: No change to the stated conjecture was found; erdosproblems.com's live tracking page for exactly this problem (#28, $500 prize) still lists it as open with no post-2024 developments, and the two candidate 2024 items surfaced by triage are, on inspection, a related-but-different problem (Ding-Zhao) and an unaccepted, uncirculated preprint (Agama) rather than progress on the stated question.
summary: The stated conjecture is Erdős–Turán as it appears verbatim on erdosproblems.com as Problem #28: if A⊆ℕ has A+A containing all but finitely many integers, then limsup 1_A*1_A(n)=∞ (i.e. the representation function of an additive basis of order 2 is unbounded). Thomas Bloom's erdosproblems.com page for this exact problem, last edited December 2025, still lists it as OPEN with a $500 prize, and cites no post-2006 progress on the core statement (the most recent cited advance is Borwein–Choi–Chu 2006, showing f(n) eventually exceeds 7). Two items the triage pass flagged as possibly relevant turned out, on reading, not to bear on this bullet. (1) Ding and Zhao, 'A new upper bound on Ruzsa's numbers on the Erdős-Turán conjecture' (arXiv:2407.02344, v1 2 Jul 2024; published Int. J. Number Theory 20 (2024), 1515-1523) prove limsup_{m→∞} ℓ_m ≤ 144 (improving an earlier bound of 192), where ℓ_m is the minimum average representation-function value over additive bases of the finite cyclic group Z_m — a different, bounded quantity (Ruzsa's number) inspired by the same conjecture but not the statement itself, and not a restriction of it to a sub-case (it's a finite-group analogue with an averaged, not pointwise-limsup, quantity). This is a related problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it is not counted as a change. (2) Theophilus Agama's arXiv:1707.05679 ('An extension of the Erdős-Turán additive base conjecture via generalized circles of partition') claims in its abstract to prove the conjecture as an application of a 'circle of partition' method, and reached v8 in March 2024 (originally posted 2017, with an intermediate withdrawal in 2017 noted in search results). However: it is classified math.GM (arXiv's General Mathematics catch-all, used for work that hasn't found a home in a refereed subfield listing), it has never been published, and — most tellingly — erdosproblems.com's dedicated, actively maintained page for this exact problem does not mention Agama's claim at all despite listing the problem as open through late 2025. A companion Agama preprint (arXiv:2010.11857) claims variants/generalisations of the conjecture rather than the base statement. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or even a passing mention by specialists tracking this problem was found for either Agama preprint, so neither meets the bar for 'claimed' (which requires the claim to have surfaced as a live claim experts are aware of and are assessing) — it reads as a long-unaccepted preprint the field has not engaged with, not a pending claim, so it does not change the open status. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this space: no lab announcement, paper, or blog credits an AI system with any part of the mathematics for either the stated conjecture or its close variants. The only AI-adjacent artifact found is a Lean formalisation of the problem's *statement* (not a proof) in DeepMind's public 'formal-conjectures' repository (github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, file FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/28.lean), linked from erdosproblems.com — this is a statement formalisation with no proof attached, so per §6.2 it would be formalisation_only/none even if AI-produced, and no source was found describing how that specific Lean file was produced (by a human, an AI, or a mix), so it is noted here but not used to set any field. A web search for an AI system attempting the Erdős-Turán additive basis conjecture surfaced only an unrelated result: OpenAI's LLM improving a bound on the Erdős unit-distance problem (a different, geometric Erdős conjecture), confirmed by reading the Scientific American article directly and finding it concerns points/grids and unit distances, not additive bases.
competing_reading: One could argue the Ding-Zhao bound on ℓ_m (the average representation function over bases of Z_m) is a 'case' of the conjecture restricted to finite cyclic groups rather than a genuinely different problem, in which case it would be `partial` with resolution_direction `null` (a bound moved, not a resolution) — but even under that reading it would be classified `progress`, not `partial`, since nothing was settled either way, only a numeric bound improved on a quantity that remains only conjecturally connected to the infinite-N unboundedness question. I did not adopt this reading because the finite-group average-representation quantity ℓ_m and the integer limsup 1_A*1_A(n) are not the same object connected by a restriction of hypotheses — Ruzsa's number is a separately defined quantity in a separately defined (finite, averaged) setting, motivated by the conjecture but not a sub-case of its statement.
what_would_settle_it: A source (erdosproblems.com update, a survey, or explicit statement in the Ding-Zhao paper's introduction) establishing a formal implication between bounding Ruzsa's number ℓ_m and the original limsup 1_A*1_A(n)=∞ statement would settle whether that work counts as `partial` progress on this exact bullet rather than a related problem; and any statement from a working additive-number-theorist (blog, MathOverflow, or citation) endorsing or refuting Agama's circle-of-partition proof would settle whether that preprint should be elevated to `claimed`.

outcome: The core question — whether a dense set of points in the plane with all pairwise rational distances exists — remains fully unresolved as of September 2026, with no new unconditional or conditional result changing the pre-2024 state of the art (Tao/Shaffaf and Ascher-Braune-Turchet's conditional-on-Bombieri-Lang negative answer, and Solymosi-de Zeeuw's unconditional curve result).
summary: The Erdős–Ulam problem (dense rational-distance point set in the plane) is unchanged since 26 January 2024. Both erdosproblems.com/212 (the maintained Erdős-problem tracker, last edited 16 October 2025 per the triage-independent check) and the current Wikipedia article (fetched directly; most recent citation is Shaffaf 2018) list the problem as open, with progress summaries stopping at the pre-2024 conditional results (Tao 2014 blog / Shaffaf 2018 and Ascher-Braune-Turchet 2019, both showing the Bombieri-Lang/Lang-type conjectures imply a negative answer; Solymosi-de Zeeuw's unconditional finiteness-on-curves result; Pasten's abc-conjecture-conditional result). No new paper, preprint, or announcement dated 2024-2026 addresses the unconditional dense-set question itself. I checked several adjacent papers that could plausibly be mistaken for progress on this problem, and none qualifies as a case or resolution of it: (1) Greenfeld-Iliopoulou-Peluse, 'On integer distance sets' (arXiv:2401.10821, v1 19 Jan 2024 — one day before the window opens; v2 Mar 2024; v3 25 Aug 2025) proves unconditional near-optimal structure/diameter bounds, but for INTEGER distance sets, which must be finite by construction — this is a different problem (finiteness of integer-distance sets, tracked separately as erdosproblems.com #213) from the density question about RATIONAL distances that Erdős-Ulam asks; it is a related problem under §3.1, not a case, since it changes the question (integer vs. rational, finite structure vs. density) rather than restricting it. (2) Corvaja-Turchet-Zannier, 'Rational distances from given rational points in the plane' (arXiv:2403.02030, Mar-Dec 2024; published in Geometriae Dedicata 2025) studies points at rational distance from a small FIXED number of given points, a variant with different hypotheses, not the dense-set question. (3) Qiu's 2026 construction of infinite rational-distance sets in general position in every dimension produces countable, not dense, sets, and does not bear on the topological density question either way. (4) The widely-covered 2026 AI news (OpenAI's May 2026 model-generated disproof of the Erdős unit-distance conjecture, verified by Gowers/Alon/Wood et al. in arXiv:2605.20695; DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus solving nine other Erdős problems) concerns entirely different Erdős problems (the unit-distance conjecture, problem #90, and others), not Erdős-Ulam (#212); I verified directly that neither the OpenAI paper nor the Quanta Magazine survey of the AI-solved-Erdős-problems wave (3 Aug 2026) mentions Erdős-Ulam or rational-distance-set density. No AI system is credited with any contribution to this specific problem. erdosproblems.com does note the problem has been formalized in Lean, but this is a statement formalization with no bearing on a proof and no AI credited for it.
competing_reading: None of the adjacent papers plausibly recodes as a 'case' of Erdős-Ulam under a stricter reading — each changes a hypothesis (integers instead of rationals, fixed anchor points instead of a free dense set, finite construction instead of density) rather than restricting the stated question, so I am confident in classifying all of them as related problems rather than partial progress. The one item worth flagging as a closer call is the integer-distance-sets paper: since a dense rational-distance set would presumably need to avoid the same collinear/concyclic degeneracies the integer paper controls, a reader could argue the structural techniques are 'about' the same phenomenon. But the integer paper's sets are necessarily finite and address a formally distinct Erdős conjecture (unconditional integer version), and it does not change what could be written in the Erdős-Ulam bullet, so I kept it out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement, dated after 26 January 2024, either resolving Erdős-Ulam unconditionally, proving a case with the free choice of finitely-or-infinitely-many dense points still intact (e.g., a stronger unconditional density bound in the plane), or extending the conditional (Bombieri-Lang) resolution to an unconditional one, together with expert digestion (Tao's blog, a survey, or journal acceptance).
