outcome: Eremenko's conjecture (every component of the escaping set of a transcendental entire function is unbounded) was already disproved before the frozen revision's date. David Martí-Pete, Lasse Rempe and James Waterman constructed transcendental entire functions whose escaping set has a bounded (even singleton) connected component; the preprint appeared on arXiv in August 2021, the result was presented in seminar talks by 2023, and it was formally published in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society in 2025. No event affecting this problem occurred inside the 26 January 2024 – present window; the paper's journal publication in 2025 is a formal-publication lag on a result already established and circulated years earlier.

counterexample.object: A transcendental entire function f for which the escaping set I(f) has a bounded connected component (in particular, a singleton component, e.g. {0}), constructed via a general technique realising arbitrary full closed subsets of the plane as wandering sets ('wandering Lakes of Wada') of entire functions.
counterexample.verified_how: Explicit analytic construction (Runge/Arakelyan-type approximation and an inductive scheme) proved rigorously by hand; verified through peer review at the Journal of the American Mathematical Society (published 2025) and independently digested via conference/seminar talks (e.g. Lasse Rempe's 2023 Kiel seminar talk, ICMS talk by James Waterman) well before the frozen revision date.

summary: Eremenko's conjecture was disproved well before the Wikipedia snapshot of 26 January 2024, so this is a stale-list entry rather than a case of post-window progress. Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman posted 'Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points' (arXiv:2108.10256) on 23 August 2021, constructing transcendental entire functions whose escaping set has a bounded (indeed singleton) connected component, directly refuting the conjecture. The result circulated and was digested by experts well within the mathematical community prior to the frozen date: Lasse Rempe gave a seminar talk titled 'A counterexample to Eremenko's conjecture' at Kiel in 2023, and James Waterman presented related work at ICMS; Wikipedia's own 'Escaping set' article (a different, evidently better-maintained page) already states plainly that the conjecture 'has been disproved' and dates it to 2021. The paper underwent several arXiv revisions (v2 Feb 2022, v3 Jun 2022, v4 Apr 2024, v5 Oct 2024 as accepted manuscript) before its formal journal appearance in J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025), 877-918 — that journal date is a publication-lag artifact, not a new event, per §6.3's instruction to date by the first written argument. I found no trace of any subsequent, independent result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that would constitute new progress on this specific problem (the general question is now closed by this counterexample; later papers such as arXiv:2609.21977, a 2026 expository/accessible write-up by the same three authors sketching an alternative variant construction, and arXiv:2405.08811 on the separate 'strong Eremenko conjecture,' a different, already-2011-disproved conjecture about path-connectivity rather than boundedness, do not change the status of this bullet). I read the 2108.10256 preprint text directly for any computational/AI methods and found none: the construction relies entirely on classical complex-analytic approximation theory (Runge's and Arakelyan's theorems) and an inductive hand-built scheme. No AI system is credited anywhere in this chain.
competing_reading: One could argue the 'decisive event' for dataset purposes should be the 2025 JAMS publication, since that is the moment the result became a citable, peer-reviewed fact and the moment closest to the frozen revision's continued (stale) claim of an open problem. But §6.3 explicitly instructs dating by the first public written argument, not the journal publication which can lag by years — and here the lag is attributable entirely to ordinary review time on a paper whose mathematical content and community acceptance were already settled in 2021-2023. I also considered whether the 2026 arXiv:2609.21977 write-up (an accessible re-exposition/sketch of an alternative construction by the same authors) might count as a fresh in-window event, but it is explicitly presented as a more accessible account of the same 2021 result plus a sketched variant, not a new resolution of a previously-open case; it does not change what a careful reader would write in this bullet beyond what was already true in 2021.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g., from the authors or a citation tracker) that no version of the construction or its acceptance changed materially between 2021 and 2024 would remove any doubt; conversely, if arXiv:2609.21977 turned out to contain a genuinely new counterexample construction proving something the 2021 paper did not (rather than an expository variant), that could in principle be treated as a distinct, later confirmation event, though it would still not change the open_stale status of the original bullet.

outcome: Tutte's 5-flow conjecture remains completely open since 26 January 2024; the best known general bound is still Seymour's 1981 nowhere-zero 6-flow theorem, and no case, bound, or aspect of the conjecture's own statement has moved.
summary: I searched broadly for any movement on Tutte's 5-flow conjecture (every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 5-flow) since 26 January 2024, including any AI involvement, and found none. The Open Problem Garden page for the conjecture (fetched directly) still lists it as open with Seymour's 1981 6-flow theorem as the best general bound, and cites nothing from 2024-2026. Three items surfaced repeatedly in searches and by the triage pass, and I opened all three directly: (1) Gáborik et al., 'Manhattan and Chebyshev flows' (arXiv:2510.22234, submitted 25 Oct 2025) introduces a new 'flow-pairs' method inspired by Seymour's proof technique and proposes new conjectures the authors describe as potentially stronger than the 5-flow conjecture, but it does not prove anything about the 5-flow conjecture's own statement or move its bound -- it opens a new research direction, which is a related problem under the §3.1 rule, not a case of this one. (2) 'Nowhere-zero flow reconfiguration' (arXiv:2512.17342, submitted 19 Dec 2025, latest revision Jul 2026) studies a reconfiguration variant -- whether any two nowhere-zero 5-flows of a graph are connected by a sequence of small moves -- and proves that variant false for group and integer flows; this is explicitly a different question (about the space of solutions, not existence) and settling it leaves the original conjecture's truth value untouched. (3) A January 2026 paper (arXiv:2601.05692) proves Bouchet's 6-flow conjecture for signed graphs in the cyclically-5-edge-connected cubic case -- a distinct named conjecture about signed graphs, not a case of Tutte's unsigned 5-flow conjecture. None of the three, nor any other search result, discloses any AI or machine-learning involvement of any kind; all describe purely human, traditional combinatorial arguments. Given the frozen conjecture's own statement is about ordinary bridgeless graphs and 5-flows specifically, none of these results changes what a careful person would write in this bullet, so I classify it as open with no_change_found true, agreeing with the triage's verdict of 'none.'
competing_reading: One could argue the Gáborik et al. flow-pairs method, since it is 'inspired by Seymour's proof of the 6-flow theorem' and aimed at 'strengthening existing flow number bounds,' constitutes incremental progress worth recording as `progress` even though it does not move any bound on the 5-flow conjecture itself -- the paper is explicit that its new conjectures are merely proposed as potentially stronger, and no bound on the actual 5-flow number was tightened, so I did not adopt this reading. If a later, fuller version of that paper (or a citing follow-up) actually derives a concrete new bound implying progress toward the 5-flow conjecture, that would change the classification to `progress`.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that either (a) proves or disproves the 5-flow conjecture outright, (b) proves it for a new restricted class of bridgeless/cubic graphs (a genuine case, making it `partial`), or (c) improves the general upper bound below Seymour's 6-flow theorem toward 5 (making it `progress`), with the argument written up and, ideally, digested by experts (e.g., discussed on Open Problem Garden, in a survey, or on a research blog).

outcome: The general Tutte 4-flow conjecture (every bridgeless Petersen-minor-free graph has a nowhere-zero 4-flow) remains open, but two genuine sub-cases were settled in the window: (1) the cubic-graph restriction of the conjecture, equivalent to Tutte's three-edge-coloring conjecture, was completed by a July/August 2026 preprint proving the last outstanding 'apex' case (combined with the pre-2024 doublecross case), and (2) a July 2026 preprint proved the 4-flow property for the strictly smaller class of graphs excluding a proper minor of the Petersen graph (the P/e-minor-free case). Both are preprints, not yet digested by the expert community.

ai.basis_quote: GitHub Copilot was used to assist in implementing parts of the authors' verification software. All generated code was reviewed by the authors. ... ChatGPT Pro and Gemini Deep Think were also used to assist with exposition and to review the consistency between the mathematical descriptions and the pseudocode. ... independent implementations were reconstructed by ChatGPT Pro and Claude Code, directly from the pseudocode ... without access to the authors' source code. Both independently reproduced the computational results required in this paper. These reconstructions are not part of the mathematical justification of the theorem, but provide additional evidence for the reproducibility of the computations.

summary: The stated bullet is the general Tutte 4-flow conjecture: every bridgeless graph with no Petersen-graph minor has a nowhere-zero 4-flow. Both the arXiv preprint the openproblemgarden.org survey page (accessed 2026-09-22) confirm the general conjecture is still open. Within the 26 Jan 2024–present window, two case results were established, both remaining unread by the wider expert community. (a) Inoue, Kawarabayashi, Matsuo, Miyashita, Mohar & Sonobe, 'Three-edge-coloring apex cubic graphs' (arXiv:2608.22870, submitted 24 Aug 2026), prove the 'apex' case of the reduction Robertson–Seymour–Thomas set up for the cubic-graph restriction of the conjecture (which for cubic graphs is equivalent, via 3-edge-colorability, to Tutte's three-edge-coloring conjecture). The 'doublecross' case was already settled by Edwards–Sanders–Seymour–Thomas (2014/2016), which predates the window, so the only new event in the window is the apex case, completing the cubic special case. This is a genuine case of the bullet (cubic graphs are a restriction of 'bridgeless Petersen-minor-free graphs'), so it counts as `partial`, not a resolution of the general conjecture. The proof is computer-assisted (in the manner of the Four Color Theorem) and, as of this writing (~1 month after posting), has not been digested by an independent expert reviewer or accepted at a venue of record — an automated 'Pith Review' site flags that the computational/'cartwheel-search' part needs independent audit — so status is not yet `resolved`, though I am recording it as `partial` (a case was settled) rather than `claimed` because the case in question (cubic apex graphs) is itself fully specified and the reduction to it is an established, previously-published structural result; only the final case's verification is unreviewed. Readers should treat the cubic case as not-yet-fully-vetted. (b) Pintér, 'Nowhere-zero 4-flows in graphs excluding a proper minor of the Petersen graph' (arXiv:2607.22267, v1 24 Jul 2026, v2 9 Aug 2026), proves the 4-flow property for the class of graphs excluding P/e (Petersen graph with one edge contracted) as a minor. The paper's own introduction establishes that Q(=P/e)-minor-free graphs form a strictly smaller class than Petersen-minor-free graphs (Ex(Q) ⊊ ... in the minor order, i.e. excluding a minor of Petersen is a stronger restriction than excluding Petersen itself), so this is also a genuine, smaller case of the bullet, not a distinct/variant problem — I disagree with the triage's uncertainty on this point (see triage_disagreement). On AI: the apex-cubic paper explicitly discloses generative-AI use (GitHub Copilot for verification-software implementation, reviewed by the authors; ChatGPT Pro and Gemini Deep Think for exposition/consistency checking; and, notably, ChatGPT Pro and Claude Code used to independently reconstruct the verification code from pseudocode alone as a reproducibility check) — but the authors explicitly state these reconstructions 'are not part of the mathematical justification of the theorem.' No AI system produced any mathematics that appears in the theorem or proof; all AI use is checking/coding/exposition assistance, so ai_role is `none` per the rubric. The Pintér paper discloses using ChatGPT and Claude 'for literature research, editorial assistance, and help writing the accompanying code' for its finite (Python/Zenodo-archived) verification script — again none of this produced mathematics that appears in the result, so ai_role is `none` there as well.
competing_reading: One could argue the apex-cubic result, since it completes an entire named sub-conjecture (Tutte's three-edge-coloring conjecture) rather than merely narrowing a search space, deserves `resolved` status for that sub-conjecture even though the parent bullet (the full 4-flow conjecture) stays `partial`/open. I did not adopt this because the schema's `status` field tracks the bullet as given, and because the proof is a very recent (Aug 2026), computer-assisted preprint with no located expert digestion yet — under §6.1 an unreviewed computer-assisted certificate should be `claimed` rather than `resolved` even when it fully settles a sub-conjecture. A stricter reading could therefore call the cubic-case event `claimed` rather than folding it into `partial`; I chose `partial` because a `partial` status is about the parent bullet only having a piece settled, and that piece (the cubic restriction) rests on a currently-unreviewed proof, which the summary flags explicitly.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (e.g. a referee report, a Robertson/Seymour/Thomas-adjacent commentary, or acceptance at a journal/conference of record) of arXiv:2608.22870's proof and its computer-assisted verification would move the cubic-graph case from an unreviewed preprint to a properly vetted result. For the general bullet itself, only a resolution of the full Petersen-minor-free case (not restricted to cubic or to Q-minor-free graphs) would move status past `partial`.

outcome: The exponent pair conjecture — that (epsilon, 1/2+epsilon) is an exponent pair for all epsilon > 0 — remains unproven; the only activity since 26 January 2024 is (a) a January 2025 paper that finds new, incrementally improved exponent pairs via a systematic database/optimization approach, none of which approach the conjectured pair, and (b) a February 2026 AI-generated GitHub issue that merely proposes formalizing the conjecture's statement (not a proof) for a Lean benchmark repository.

ai.basis_quote: The issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me [franzhusch]

summary: The exponent pair conjecture (that for all epsilon>0, (epsilon, 1/2+epsilon) is an exponent pair, equivalent to beta(alpha)=alpha/2 and implying the Lindelöf hypothesis) is still open as of September 2026. The only substantive mathematical development in the window is Tao, Trudgian and Yang's 'New exponent pairs, zero density estimates, and zero additive energy estimates: a systematic approach' (arXiv:2501.16779, posted 2025-01-28), which launched the Analytic Number Theory Exponent Database (ANTEDB/expdb) and used it, together with computer-assisted (not AI) optimization search over known relations, to derive four new exponent pairs and improved zero-density/additive-energy estimates. Tao's blog post explicitly frames this as combining existing methods via automated/computer-assisted optimization, with no AI system credited; it only speculates about future integration with 'AI systems' as a possibility, not something used. I read the ANTEDB blueprint chapter on exponent pairs directly: it still presents the conjecture (there as 'Heuristic 5.6' / the statement beta(alpha)=alpha/2) as unproven, describing the convex hull of known exponent pairs as having gradually expanded but nowhere near closing the gap to the conjectured boundary. Separately, on 2026-02-08 a GitHub issue (#2213) was opened in DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' Lean benchmark repository proposing to add the exponent pair conjecture's *statement* (not a proof) to the repository, explicitly noting 'this issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me.' This is a formalization/cataloguing proposal for a benchmark of open conjectures — it does not touch the mathematics of the conjecture, has no linked pull request, and the conjecture is rated only 3/5 formalizable due to missing Mathlib infrastructure for phase functions and exponential sums. Under section 3.1 and 6.2's rules, neither event changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, and neither constitutes AI producing mathematics that appears in a result — the January 2025 exponent-pair improvements are conventional computer-assisted search (SAT/optimization-style, not a learned/generative AI system), and the February 2026 GitHub issue is AI-authored prose about the conjecture's formalizability, not a mathematical claim. I also searched broadly for any AI-driven attempt at the Lindelöf hypothesis or exponent pairs (e.g., LLM-driven formal proof search papers, the 'From Solvers to Research' and 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' papers) and found no claim touching this specific conjecture. Status is therefore open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the January 2025 Tao-Trudgian-Yang exponent-pair improvements are a 'case' of the general exponent pair conjecture in the sense that any newly-proved exponent pair is a single point confirmed to lie in the conjectured triangular region already known to be achievable (the region is a wedge, and known exponent pairs already populate parts of it away from the boundary (epsilon,1/2+epsilon)). But the conjecture as stated asks specifically about the extremal pair (epsilon, 1/2+epsilon) on the boundary of the region achieving the best possible exponent; the new pairs found are interior improvements to the known convex hull, not new points approaching that particular boundary pair, so I read this as general progress on the surrounding subject (which could be logged as 'progress' with ai_role 'none') rather than as partial resolution of the specific bulleted conjecture. If the harness's convention is to log any exponent-pair-database improvement as 'progress' toward the general conjecture regardless of whether it approaches the specific extremal pair, the correct status would be 'progress' rather than 'open' — I chose 'open' because the statement given is specifically about the pair (epsilon, 1/2+epsilon), and no source suggests the 2025 results move the frontier meaningfully closer to that particular point.
what_would_settle_it: A source (paper, ANTEDB update, or expert commentary) that explicitly states the January 2025 or later exponent-pair improvements narrow the gap to (epsilon, 1/2+epsilon) specifically, as opposed to improving other points on the known convex hull, would settle whether this should be 'progress' rather than 'open'.

outcome: The best known bound in the plane (d=2, dimension > 5/4, Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang 2020) has not been improved since 26 January 2024, and the best known bound in higher dimensions (d/2 + 1/4 − 1/(8d+4) for d≥3) was already fixed in a preprint submitted 8 September 2023 (arXiv:2309.04103 v1) — before the frozen revision's date — and was not mathematically changed by the October 2024 v2 revision, which the authors' own revision note describes as having 'slightly changed the introduction' only. The conjecture itself remains open in every dimension; only case-restricted or related variant results appeared inside the window.
summary: Falconer's conjecture (Hausdorff dimension > d/2 in ℝ^d implies a distance set of nonzero Lebesgue measure) remains open in every dimension as of September 2026. The only substantive advance anywhere near the window is Du–Ou–Ren–Zhang's improvement of the higher-dimensional (d≥3) threshold to d/2 + 1/4 − 1/(8d+4), but this bound was fixed in arXiv:2309.04103 v1, submitted 8 September 2023 — more than four months before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 timestamp. A v2 was posted 22 October 2024 (inside the window), but I fetched the arXiv abstract page directly and its own revision note says only '33 pages; slightly changed the introduction', with the file growing from 38KB to 40KB; the abstract and the stated bound are identical between versions, so no mathematics changed. The April 2024 Quanta Magazine article, read directly, is press coverage of the pre-existing 2023 result, not a report of new mathematics — it names no event past September 2023. The current Wikipedia 'Falconer's conjecture' article (fetched directly, last edited 18 September 2026) still cites this same 2023 Du–Ou–Ren–Zhang bound as the best known result in higher dimensions and 5/4 (Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang 2020, itself pre-2024) as the best known bound in the plane — confirming independently that nothing has superseded either bound in the window. A background research agent additionally found three papers submitted inside the window (arXiv:2503.15709 on nonempty interior, a strictly stronger and different property than positive measure; arXiv:2510.15118 proving the conjecture only for restricted hyperplane/product-set cases; arXiv:2607.05926 on the discrete finite-field Erdős–Falconer analogue, a different problem over vector spaces rather than ℝ^d) and a direct search of Terence Tao's blog and of Wikipedia's 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' page, both of which surfaced nothing relevant. None of the case/variant papers change the stated d/2 threshold or resolve any fixed dimension, so per §3.1 they do not move the status off open, and per §6.1 the correct code is open_stale rather than open, since the one bound-moving event on record predates the frozen revision even though it was still being publicized and lightly revised within the window. No AI system was mentioned in any source I or the research agent examined in connection with this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue for `progress` dated to 9 April 2024 (the Quanta article) or to 22 October 2024 (the v2 arXiv revision) on the theory that the bound only became widely known, or was formally re-submitted, inside the window. But §6.3 requires dating to the first public written argument, which is the 8 September 2023 v1 submission — press coverage and a cosmetic revision are not new events under that rule, so I classify as `open_stale` rather than `progress`. If a reader considers the widely-publicized Quanta coverage itself the 'event' that made the bound part of the record within the window, `progress` with event date 2024-04-09 and resolution_direction null would be the alternative record.
what_would_settle_it: A revision history diff of arXiv:2309.04103 v1 vs v2 showing whether the stated theorem, its dimension threshold, or its proof changed in any way beyond the introduction wording; this would confirm or overturn the open_stale classification. Also, any post-2024 paper improving the plane bound past 5/4 or the higher-dimensional bound past d/2 + 1/4 − 1/(8d+4) would move the status to `progress`.

outcome: The general Farrell-Jones conjecture remains open with no known counterexample, but several new classes of groups were proved to satisfy it since 26 January 2024, most notably the fibred Farrell-Jones conjecture for automorphism groups of one-ended hyperbolic groups (relative to virtually polycyclic subgroups) and suspensions of relatively hyperbolic groups (arXiv:2311.14036, published in Mathematische Annalen 2026), and Farrell-Jones for many hierarchically hyperbolic groups including extra-large-type Artin groups via new asymptotically CAT(0)/Z-structure techniques (arXiv:2504.17048, April 2025). No AI system was involved in any of this work.
summary: The Farrell-Jones conjecture (FJC), asking whether certain assembly maps in algebraic K- and L-theory are isomorphisms, remains unresolved in general as of September 2026, with no counterexample ever found. However, real mathematical territory was settled within the window (26 Jan 2024 to today) by extending the list of group classes known to satisfy it, which counts as `partial` under the case-vs-variant rule in §3.1: each new class is a restriction of the general statement, not a different question. Two results stand out. (1) arXiv:2311.14036 'Automorphisms of relatively hyperbolic groups and the Farrell-Jones Conjecture' was first submitted 23 November 2023 (before the frozen date), but a revised v2 was posted 2 March 2026 and the paper was accepted and published in Mathematische Annalen in 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s00208-026-03431-7, per Springer/PMC listing). Its core content -- proving the fibred FJC for suspensions of a large class of relatively hyperbolic groups and for all suspensions of one-ended hyperbolic groups, plus automorphism groups of one-ended groups hyperbolic relative to virtually polycyclic subgroups -- is a v1-era result predating the window; the 2026 journal appearance is dating by publication, which §6.3 explicitly says not to use. I therefore treat this paper as `open_stale`-flavored background rather than the load-bearing event, and instead date the record to (2) arXiv:2504.17048 'Asymptotically CAT(0) metrics, Z-structures, and the Farrell-Jones Conjecture', submitted 23 April 2025, squarely inside the window. This paper shows many hierarchically hyperbolic groups (including extra-large-type Artin groups) satisfy FJC, via a genuinely new technique (asymptotically CAT(0) metrics and Z-structures) and a genuinely new base fact (mapping class groups are asymptotically CAT(0), previously unknown). It is a preprint without a confirmed later journal digestion found in my search, so under §6.1 it would sit at `claimed` on its own, but it fits the broader pattern that a July 2025 survey by Wolfgang Lück (arXiv:2507.11337, also to appear in the Bulletin of the AMS per an AMS journal listing found in search) synthesizes: the survey states FJC is now known for 'a very broad, robustly closed class of groups' including hyperbolic groups, finite-dimensional CAT(0) groups, lattices, and fundamental groups of manifolds -- an expert digestion of the state of the art appearing in the window, which supports treating the overall body of new-case results as established (`partial`) rather than merely `claimed`. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this work: none of the papers I opened (2211.15523, 2311.14036, 2504.17048) mention machine learning, LLMs, or automated theorem-proving tools in their abstracts or visible metadata, and a targeted search for AI/Lean formalization tied to Farrell-Jones specifically returned only unrelated general AI-for-math papers. Triage's flagged Bunke-Kasprowski-Winges 'lax monoidal' result (arXiv:2211.15523) is confirmed to predate the window (final v3, 10 May 2023; the underlying BKW result itself is from 2021/2022), so it is correctly excluded as the driving event, matching triage's own hedge that its posting date was unconfirmed.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2026 Mathematische Annalen publication of arXiv:2311.14036 is itself the dating event under a 'journal acceptance = expert digestion' reading, which would push status toward `resolved`-for-that-case with event kind `journal` and date in 2026; I rejected this because §6.3 is explicit that journal publication should not be used for dating (it lags and can spuriously pull a stale result into the window), and the mathematical content of that paper is from the 2023 preprint. A second competing reading is that none of these results are substantial enough to move the needle and the record should be `open` with no_change_found -- I rejected this because §3.1 explicitly says size is not the test and a case settled (here, whole new classes of groups, established by new techniques within the window) counts as `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (e.g., a review in Mathematical Reviews/zbMATH, or a widely-cited survey explicitly crediting arXiv:2504.17048's specific new cases) confirming the hierarchically-hyperbolic-groups result has been checked and accepted by the community would move that particular result from an implicit `claimed`-adjacent status to solidly `resolved`-for-that-case. Confirmation of whether arXiv:2311.14036's 2026 Annalen publication reflects new content added in the 2026 revision (versus pure copy-editing of the 2023 preprint) would clarify whether it deserves its own within-window event.

outcome: The complex quadratic Fatou conjecture (density of hyperbolicity for the family z^2+c) remains open; no proof, disproof, or partial case settled it in the window, and the adjacent MLC-at-Feigenbaum-points result is a related but distinct question, not a case of this bullet.
summary: The bullet as worded is the classical complex Fatou conjecture: that the quadratic family f_c(z)=z^2+c is hyperbolic (has an attracting cycle) for an open dense set of parameters c. This is equivalent to 'density of J-stability' / 'density of hyperbolicity' in the complex quadratic family, and it remains wide open as of September 2026; the article's own Wikipedia page (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatou_conjecture) states only the bare definition and gives no indication of resolution, and no subsequent search turned up a proof, disproof, or partial resolution of the stated question itself. The triage flagged Dudko-Lyubich's 'MLC at Feigenbaum points' (arXiv:2309.02107, v1 Sept 2023 — before the frozen revision date of 26 Jan 2024 — with v2 Dec 2023 and a v3 in Dec 2025 timed to journal acceptance at Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS) and Dudko's December 2025 ICM survey note (arXiv:2512.24171) as possibly relevant. I read both. MLC at Feigenbaum points proves local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set, and hence of the corresponding Julia sets, at specific Feigenbaum (infinitely renormalizable, period-doubling and complex-tripling) parameters — points that lie on the boundary of hyperbolic components and are themselves non-hyperbolic. The logical chain in the field is: MLC (full local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set everywhere) implies triviality of fibers, which implies density of hyperbolicity for the whole quadratic family (via the Orsay notes / Douady-Hubbard framework). But MLC-at-isolated-points is not a restriction of the density-of-hyperbolicity statement to a sub-case — it establishes a structural/topological fact at specific non-hyperbolic parameters, not that a positive-measure or open set of nearby parameters is hyperbolic. It does not remove any territory from the 'is the hyperbolic locus open and dense' question, since Feigenbaum points are (measure-zero) boundary points, not intervals of parameters whose hyperbolicity status the conjecture asks about. This makes it a related result under the problem sharing intellectual machinery (renormalization theory) with the target conjecture, not a case of it under §3.1. I found no AI system credited in either paper — both are traditional human-authored proofs in the classical style of Dudko-Lyubich's prior work, with no acknowledgement of computational/AI assistance in the sections I could access. Also checked Kozlovski-Shen-van Strien-style results and other 2024-2026 arXiv listings for 'density of hyperbolicity' + quadratic/complex; all hits were either pre-2024 foundational papers (Lyubich 1997, Graczyk-Swiatek 1997, Kozlovski-Shen-van Strien for higher real degree) or tangential (Cantor Julia sets density-of-hyperbolicity paper from Sept 2025, arXiv:2509.09914, which is again a different class of rational maps, not the quadratic family itself, and hence a related problem, not this one). No withdrawn claims, no counterexamples, no bound movements found on the complex quadratic Fatou conjecture itself.
competing_reading: A looser reading could treat MLC-at-Feigenbaum-points as 'progress toward the machinery needed for Fatou' and classify status as progress with ai_role none, since it does chip away at open pieces of the broader renormalization program that the full Fatou conjecture sits inside. But the bullet asks specifically whether hyperbolicity is open and dense across parameter space, an existence/density claim (§3.1's rule that such claims move only when answered, not when the territory around them is mapped in more detail) — and a local-connectivity fact at isolated non-hyperbolic points does not narrow where non-hyperbolic parameters could hide in the way a case-restriction would. I judge 'open' / 'no_change_found' to be the better reading, but flag this as a genuine judgment call the triage pass also flagged.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that MLC holds everywhere on the boundary of the Mandelbrot set (full MLC), which the field agrees would imply density of hyperbolicity for the whole quadratic family via triviality of fibers; or a direct proof/counterexample of density of hyperbolicity itself, e.g. exhibiting a non-hyperbolic parameter with an open neighborhood of non-hyperbolic parameters, or a topological argument bypassing MLC.

outcome: A preprint posted 21 March 2024 on Preprints.org proves the Feit–Thompson conjecture holds when p and q are twin primes (p = q+2), a genuine restriction of the general statement; it remains an unreviewed preprint with no evidence of subsequent journal publication, expert digestion, or independent citation, and no other case, bound, or resolution of the general conjecture was found in the window.
summary: The triage flagged a preprint (doi:10.20944/preprints202403.1214.v1), titled 'The Feit-Thompson Conjecture: An Example for Mathematical Research Based on Contradictory Sources,' posted to Preprints.org on 21 March 2024 (within the window). I could not fetch the PDF directly (preprints.org and researchgate.net both returned HTTP 403 to automated fetchers), so I relied on search-engine-rendered abstracts and secondary summaries of the abstract/content from Google's indexing of both the preprints.org page and the ResearchGate mirror, which agree closely on wording: the paper's stated result is a proof that p^(q-1)/(p-1) does not divide q^(p-1)/(q-1) when p and q are twin primes (p=q+2), i.e. the conjecture holds on the twin-prime sub-case. Twin primes are a restriction of 'all distinct primes p, q,' so this is a genuine case of the stated problem (removes territory from it), not a variant — it satisfies §3.1's test directly, confirming the conjecture on that slice (resolution_direction: confirmed). Nothing in any secondary summary of the abstract or the paper's declared dual purpose (the second purpose being methodological, about navigating contradictory web sources on the topic) mentions any AI system, so ai_role is 'none' with no basis_quote — I did not manage to read the full text due to the 403s, which is the main gap in this record (see incomplete). I found no evidence of subsequent peer-reviewed publication, journal acceptance, or citations of this preprint by other researchers; it appears to remain a single unreviewed preprint two and a half years after posting, which pushes toward classifying this as more provisional than a fully 'resolved' case. However §6.1 defines 'resolved' as requiring digestion, journal acceptance, or a directly checkable-by-hand argument for problems in general, and reserves 'claimed' primarily for cases lacking human verification of any kind; a self-contained elementary number-theory divisibility argument of this kind is normally checkable by a competent reader, and the paper explicitly frames itself as a proof, not merely an announcement or machine output. Given I could not personally verify the proof's correctness (I don't have the full text) and there is no sign any third party has, I classify this conservatively as 'partial' (a case of the problem addressed) with lower confidence that it would upgrade to 'resolved' on full inspection. I separately confirmed via the live Wikipedia article and independent search that the general Feit-Thompson conjecture remains open, that no counterexample to it has been found (the known 1971 Stephens counterexample applies only to the strictly stronger 'always coprime' variant, and predates the window in any case), that prior known cases are q=2 (Stephens 1971) and q=3 (Le 2012), both pre-dating the window, and that no q=5, q=7, or other new case, nor any AI-related claim, disproof, or bound, appears anywhere in the 2024–2026 literature I could locate.
competing_reading: If the preprint were read in full and found to contain a rigorous, checkable elementary argument, and if independent researchers have quietly checked it without generating a citable trail I could find, the correct status could arguably be 'resolved' for the twin-prime case rather than 'partial' — the codes aren't mutually exclusive in spirit, but §6.1's own hierarchy suggests 'partial' fits a case-of-the-problem result regardless of verification depth, so this reading doesn't change my classification, only the confidence in it. A stricter reading could also treat this as 'claimed' rather than 'partial' on the grounds that an unreviewed preprint with no independent verification hasn't cleared even a low bar of scrutiny, but §6.1 defines 'claimed' by contrast with 'resolved' for preprints in general, while 'partial' is explicitly a scope category (a case settled) that can co-exist with 'claimed'-level evidentiary weakness; I judged scope (case vs. whole) as the primary axis per §3.1 and used the outcome/summary to carry the evidentiary caveat.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full preprint text directly (blocked by 403 responses from both preprints.org and researchgate.net during this session) to check the proof's correctness and look for any acknowledgements section; and checking Google Scholar/Semantic Scholar for citations or a later journal version of this preprint to see if it has since been formally reviewed or superseded.

outcome: Preda Mihăilescu (preprint, 22 Sep 2025) proved via a cyclotomic argument (Stickelberger ideal, Jacobi sums) that the equation (x^p+y^p)/(x+y) = p^e z^q has no solutions in coprime integers for p>3, q distinct odd primes, and states as a direct corollary that the classical Fermat-Catalan equation x^p+y^p=z^q has no solutions for that signature family — settling one infinite family of exponent triples (p,p,q), p>3, q an odd prime ≠ p. The general finiteness conjecture remains open. Separately, a December 2024 survey (Ratcliffe–Grechuk, published in Expositiones Mathematicae 2025) reports that Sikora's computational search of the classical Fermat-Catalan equation was extended to cover all coprime solutions with z^r ≤ 2^100, still finding only the same ten known solutions; this narrows where an eleventh solution could hide but does not itself settle the existence question (per the rule that a record/search-bound extension does not count as progress on a 'finitely many / are there more' question unless the record itself is the object of the bullet).
summary: The triage's `none` verdict correctly identified that no proof or disproof of the general finiteness conjecture, and no new qualifying solution, has appeared since 26 January 2024 — the conjecture as a whole is exactly as open as it was. But the triage mischaracterized Mihăilescu's September 2025 paper as 'unrelated cyclotomic work... on a different variant equation,' which I disagree with (triage_disagreement). Reading the paper directly (arXiv:2509.18275, HTML version), its Theorem 1 explicitly states two things in sequence: (1) the 'strong' quotient equation (x^p+y^p)/(x+y)=p^e z^q has no coprime solutions for p>3, q distinct odd primes, and (2) 'In particular, the Fermat-Catalan equation ... has no solutions with distinct odd primes p,q and p>3.' That second clause is a direct statement about the classical equation a^m+b^n=c^k with (m,n,k)=(p,p,q) — a restriction of the problem to a specific infinite family of exponent triples, which is a case of the stated problem under §3.1, not a variant with changed hypotheses (the object equation, coprimality condition, and exponent inequality 1/p+1/p+1/q<1 for p>3,q≥5 are all exactly the Fermat-Catalan setup). This is exactly the shape of result the deep-dive rules count as `partial`: a slice of the exponent-triple space is now provably solution-free, narrowing (removing territory from) the general conjecture, even though the conjecture as a whole stays open. Separately, the Ratcliffe–Grechuk survey (Dec 2024, revised Apr 2025, published in Expositiones Mathematicae) extended Sikora's exhaustive computational search to z^r ≤ 2^100, confirming no solutions beyond the known ten in that range and naming (2,5,7) and (3,5,7) as the smallest open signatures — this is real computational work but, per §3.1's rule for existence/infinitude questions, a larger search bound narrows where a counterexample could hide without answering whether one exists, so on its own it would not move status past `open`; it is reported here as context for the `partial` finding, not as an independent basis for it. No AI or machine-learning system appears in either paper: Mihăilescu's acknowledgements name only human colleagues and students, and both papers' computational work (ALICE HPC / University at Buffalo cluster) is exhaustive integer search, not a learned model. I also checked Sikora's October 2024 paper (arXiv:2410.21552), which proposes conjectural product-generalizations of Fermat-Catalan/Tijdeman-Zagier rather than proving anything about the classical equation itself — that one is correctly a variant, not a case, and contributes nothing to status. Anthropic's 2026 formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean is an unrelated problem (fixed equal exponents m=n=k, no coprime a,b,c<1 inequality structure) and does not bear on this record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Mihăilescu result is 'about' the strong/quotient equation and only mentions the classical Fermat-Catalan equation as an aside ('in particular'), so it might be read as a related/variant result rather than a case of the stated problem, especially since the paper's title and main technical machinery target the quotient form. Under that reading the correct status would remain `open` with `no_change_found` true (aside from the stale search-bound extension). I do not adopt this reading because Theorem 1 states the classical-equation non-existence result explicitly and unconditionally for that exponent family, and the deep-dive rule for a 'case' is about restricting the stated question, which is exactly what fixing (m,n,k)=(p,p,q), p>3 does — the route to the result (via the quotient identity) does not change what the result claims about the original equation.
what_would_settle_it: Expert digestion or journal acceptance of Mihăilescu's preprint would move this specific case from a preprint-only partial toward a firmly established partial result (it does not need 'resolved' since it only ever settles a case, not the whole conjecture). Any future paper explicitly extending or contradicting the (p,p,q) family result, or a full proof/disproof of the general finiteness conjecture, would supersede this record.

outcome: The full conjecture remains open, but two preprints since the frozen revision have moved the quantitative lower bound on the area of arbitrary (not just disk- or genus-one) isometric fillings of a length-2π circle: Briggs & Wells (Feb 2026) proved a bound of 1.36π via a discrete graph-theoretic analogue, and Chen, Li & Zhong (Sep 2026) improved this to 14ζ(3)/π ≈ 5.357 (about 1.706π) using a Fourier-coefficient method, with a stronger bound for orientable fillings — both still well short of the conjectured 2π.
summary: The filling area conjecture (Gromov, 1983) — that the hemisphere minimizes area among orientable Riemannian surfaces isometrically filling a boundary circle of given length — remains fully open since the frozen revision. The Wikipedia article itself has not been updated past 2011-era citations and still presents it as open. Two arXiv preprints from 2026 make genuine progress by proving quantitative lower bounds applicable to *arbitrary* isometric fillings (not restricted to disks or genus-one surfaces, where the conjecture was already known): Briggs & Wells, 'A discrete view of Gromov's filling area conjecture' (arXiv:2602.17859, submitted 19 Feb 2026), translate the problem into a discrete graph-theoretic analogue using Menger's theorem to get the first quantitative lower bound (1.36π) covering all fillings, not requiring orientability. Chen, Li & Zhong, 'A Fourier approach to Gromov's filling area conjecture' (arXiv:2609.08251, submitted 8 Sep 2026), use odd Fourier coefficients of boundary-distance functions plus a cubic resonant perturbation for the orientable case to push the universal lower bound to 14ζ(3)/π ≈ 5.357, with a stronger bound for orientable surfaces. Both results move the known lower bound closer to the conjectured 2π (≈6.283) but do not resolve the conjecture; neither has yet been digested by expert commentary (no Tao blog post, Quanta piece, or journal acceptance found), so both are correctly `claimed`-tier work but the record as a whole is `progress` since the bound moved without any single result being a full resolution — no case of the conjecture (e.g. a new topological class) was fully settled either. A related preprint, 'An Upper Bound for Discrete Isometric Filling of Cycles' (arXiv:2605.08909), explicitly notes its discrete construction 'cannot be used to settle Gromov's conjecture' — a related/variant result, not counted here. No AI system was mentioned in any of these papers, their abstracts, methods sections, or acknowledgements; all methods described (graph theory/Menger's theorem, Fourier analysis, cubic resonant perturbation) are classical continuous/discrete mathematics with no computational or machine-learning component disclosed. I found no news coverage, lab announcement, or AI system card referencing the filling area conjecture at all.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `claimed` rather than `progress`, since each individual preprint is itself an unresolved claim awaiting expert digestion. I chose `progress` because the rules describe `progress` as covering 'a bound moved,' which is the more specific and applicable code here, and because the conjecture proper is unaffected — both papers are explicitly about moving a quantitative bound on filling area, not proposing a proof of the conjecture itself.
what_would_settle_it: Expert digestion (e.g., a referee report, journal acceptance, or a well-known geometer's blog commentary) confirming the Briggs-Wells or Chen-Li-Zhong bounds, or — more decisively — a full proof (or disproof) of the conjecture in its stated generality (hemisphere as the area minimizer among all shortcut-free fillings, not just disk or genus-one cases).

outcome: The known unconditional upper bound on Λ has been pushed down twice by self-published, non-peer-reviewed computer-assisted works since the frozen revision (0.2 → 0.1787854 by Jude Gomila, July/August 2026; then → 0.149396 by Dale James Raymond, September 2026), both explicitly disclosing AI assistance; neither has been digested by the expert community or appeared on arXiv, and a separate unreviewed preprint claims Λ = 0 outright via a non-standard 'LCK Algebra' framework that shows strong crank hallmarks.

disputes.summary: Three independent, mutually inconsistent-in-status claims exist in the window: Gomila's Λ ≤ 0.1787854 (Jul–Aug 2026, human/AI collaboration, one named real expert reviewer mid-review), Raymond's tighter Λ ≤ 0.149396 (posted to Zenodo/GitHub 21 Sept 2026, explicit 'developed with AI assistance', not peer reviewed, superseding Gomila's numerically but with less external scrutiny so far), and Li Chuankai's claimed exact resolution Λ = 0 (preprints.org, Apr 2026, via a non-standard self-styled 'LCK Algebra'/'holographic extension' framework typical of fringe/crank submissions, also machine-verification-only). None of the three has been digested, published, or even posted to arXiv; only Gomila's has engaged a credentialed subject-matter expert (Dan Romik, UC Davis, author of the standard reference on the Riemann xi function's orthogonal-polynomial theory), and even that engagement is explicitly described as 'in-progress' with the write-up 'not yet peer reviewed.'

summary: Wikipedia's frozen (Jan 2024) statement of Λ's bounds was 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.2 (Platt–Trudgian 2020 upper bound, Rodgers–Tao 2018 lower bound); the live Wikipedia article as of my check still reports only these 2018/2020 figures and mentions nothing from the window. Independently, I found real activity: (1) Jude Gomila, a tech entrepreneur (Ultrametric/Golden/Heyzap founder, Cambridge engineering background, not a professional mathematician), self-published a 'computer-assisted proof' on his personal blog and a companion GitHub audit repo lowering the unconditional upper bound on Λ to 0.1787854, discovered 27 July 2026 with a release manuscript dated 20 August 2026. The work explicitly instantiates Polymath 15's Theorem 1.2 at new numerical parameters (Platt–Trudgian's verified RH height, a finite-window barrier certificate, and a tail lemma), and the author states plainly that it was 'developed through human-AI collaboration,' including a 'four-agent adversarial AI review panel' used to stress-test each proof component — but no specific AI systems are named anywhere in the post or repo. Crucially, Dan Romik, a genuine UC Davis mathematician and the author of the standard modern treatment of the Riemann xi function's orthogonal-polynomial expansions, is named as an independent reviewer who 're-proved every analytic lemma' and is reworking the material into 'journal-grade manuscripts' — but the repository itself states this is still 'in-progress' and 'not yet peer reviewed,' and no arXiv posting or journal publication has appeared as of my search (September 2026). This is real, non-trivial expert engagement short of digestion, so I classify it `claimed` rather than `resolved`. (2) A second, even tighter and even less-reviewed claim, Λ ≤ 0.149396 (0.149395073827688 exactly), was deposited to Zenodo by Dale James Raymond on 21 September 2026 (literally the day before my research date), also explicitly 'developed with AI assistance,' also not peer reviewed, and the record itself cautions that 'a successful replay verifies executable finite inequalities; it does not mechanically prove every analytic argument.' (3) A third claim, that Λ = 0 exactly (which would prove the Riemann Hypothesis outright), appears on preprints.org (April 2026) attributed to 'Li Chuankai,' built on a self-styled 'LCK Algebra' extending 'wheel algebra' with a 'universal absorbing element,' invoking 'holographic extension' and 'Gelfand-Naimark-Segal construction' language that is a strong stylistic marker of non-standard/crank mathematics (and plausibly LLM-generated prose); I found no evidence of any mathematician engaging with it, no arXiv posting, and it did not surface in any digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, MathOverflow). None of these three converge into a stable, expert-endorsed number, and no source I found (Wikipedia's live article, Tao's blog, Quanta) treats any of them as settled. I therefore anchor the `event` on the Gomila claim (July 2026) as the most substantively reviewed of the three, note the newer superseding Raymond claim and the outlying Li Chuankai claim in `disputes`, and set `ai_role` to `assisted` on the basis of Gomila's own account that AI collaboration produced parts of the proof apparatus (with an AI panel used for adversarial review of the mathematics, going beyond mere proofreading) — though I flag real uncertainty about whether this crosses into `generated` for parts of the construction, since the post is vague about exactly which pieces were AI-produced versus human-designed.
competing_reading: If Dan Romik's review, once completed and posted (to arXiv or a journal), confirms the Gomila bound, this would likely become `resolved` on a future check, and a stronger case could be made now that the substantial named-expert engagement already pushes it there. Conversely, one could argue `ai_role` should be `none` if the 'four-agent adversarial AI review panel' is read as only a checking/proofreading step (per §6.2's list of non-qualifying uses) rather than as producing mathematics — the blog post is not fully explicit about which specific lemmas or constructions were AI-authored versus human-authored, so `assisted` is my best reading of an ambiguous disclosure rather than a clean case.
what_would_settle_it: An arXiv posting or journal acceptance of Romik's reworked manuscript, or any digestion of the Gomila/Raymond bounds by a recognized expert venue (Tao's blog, Quanta, a Polymath-style collaborative wiki update, or the Wikipedia article itself being updated) would resolve the status question. A clearer authorial statement of exactly which analytic steps the AI panel produced (versus checked) would resolve the ai_role ambiguity.

outcome: No exact function, closed-form generating function, or resolution of the self-avoiding walk counting problem has been found since 26 January 2024; only incremental, traditional (non-AI) improvements to bounds and asymptotic estimates surfaced.
summary: The problem asks for an exact function (closed-form generating function or counting formula) for the number of n-step self-avoiding walks on a lattice — a classic unsolved problem in combinatorics/statistical mechanics, with no known formula except for degenerate or highly restricted cases (e.g. spiral walks on the triangular lattice, known since decades before 2024). I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 claim of an exact solution, a proof of the connective constant's value on the square (or other non-hexagonal) lattice, or any AI/ML-driven result, and found none. The Wikipedia article 'Self-avoiding walk' (checked as of its current revision) still states plainly that 'there is currently no known formula, although there are rigorous methods of approximation,' and that the exact connective constant is known only for the hexagonal lattice (Duminil-Copin & Smirnov, 2010/2012 — well before the window). Within the window I found only incremental, traditional-mathematics work: Qidong He's arXiv:2508.01993 (submitted Sept 2025) improves upper bounds on the *weighted* connective constant via dominant-eigenvalue matrix methods (no AI, no exact formula, problem remains open); and an arXiv:2504.13093 paper (April 2025) recasts SAW counting as a lattice-point-counting problem to derive *asymptotic* estimates for square-lattice SAWs across dimensions — again not an exact function and not AI-based. Neither paper changes what a careful person would write for this bullet: the exact enumeration function remains unknown. I also searched specifically for AI/ML angles (LLM-assisted conjecture generation, transformers, reinforcement learning applied to SAW counting) and found no work connecting any AI system to this specific problem; adjacent transformer-learning-random-walks papers (e.g. arXiv:2511.23239) are about learning simple random walks as a toy ML problem, unrelated to enumerating self-avoiding walks or contributing to the mathematical open problem. Given the volume and specificity of the search terms tried, and that the Wikipedia article itself shows no update to its 'no known formula' language, I am confident this is a genuine 'nothing happened, and no AI involvement' case.
competing_reading: One could argue the two 2025 bound/asymptotic papers constitute 'progress' worth a status of 'progress' rather than 'open', since a bound on the connective constant did move (He's paper) — but per §3.1, an existence/enumeration-type problem ('find a function to model n-step SAWs') is not the same as a 'largest known value' or 'value of a constant' bullet where a moved bound counts as the question itself. The bullet as phrased asks for an exact modeling function, not for the tightest bound on the connective constant (which is the separate, related open problem of determining μ exactly). Because no such function was found and the connective-constant bound movement is for a genuinely different (though closely related) question, I classified this as 'open' with no_change_found true rather than 'progress'. If the harness intends this bullet to be read as encompassing connective-constant bound improvements, 'progress' with ai_role 'none' would be the alternative classification.
what_would_settle_it: An exact closed-form counting function or generating function for n-step self-avoiding walks on a standard lattice (square, cubic, etc.) — which would itself resolve one of the most famous open problems in combinatorics — or, short of that, clearer evidence on whether the bullet is meant to include connective-constant bound movements as in-scope 'progress'.

outcome: The core k-set problem (matching Dey's O(n(k+1)^(1/3)) upper bound with Tóth's Ω(n·2^√log k) lower bound for general k-sets) remains completely open with no movement since January 2024. However, several narrower bounds within its scope moved: Rubin (SODA 2024 / arXiv March 2024) improved the bound on halving hyperplanes in dimensions d≥5; Alonso, López and Rodrigo (Symmetry, July 2024) improved the additive constant in the best asymptotic upper bound for planar halving lines (even n) and for small n in [106,336]; and Rodrigo, López, Magistrali and Alonso (Axioms, January 2025) improved the lower bound on the maximum number of halving lines for specific odd point-set sizes (n=35,59,95,97), with a consequent effect on rectilinear crossing number bounds.
summary: This Wikipedia bullet ('Finding matching upper and lower bounds for k-sets and halving lines') is the general open problem of closing the gap between Dey's 1998 upper bound O(n(k+1)^{1/3}) for the number of k-sets of an n-point planar set and the best known lower bound Ω(n·2^{c√log k}) (Tóth 1999/2001), together with the closely related halving-lines question of the maximum number of halving lines h(n). No paper found since 26 January 2024 closes or narrows this general asymptotic gap for k-sets in the plane. Three genuine but narrow pieces of progress occurred within scope: (1) Natan Rubin, 'Improved Bounds for Point Selections and Halving Hyperplanes in Higher Dimensions' (arXiv:2403.00412, submitted 2024-03-01, preliminary version at SODA 2024), which substantially improves the point-selection/halving-hyperplane bound in dimension d≥3 (particularly d≥5), a dramatic improvement over the 1991 Alon–Bárány–Füredi–Kleitman bound — this is the most significant single advance found and is squarely a case of the general 'k-sets/halving' bound-matching problem in higher dimensions, though the gap to matching lower bounds remains open. (2) Alonso, López and Rodrigo, 'An Improvement of the Upper Bound for the Number of Halving Lines of Planar Sets' (Symmetry 16(7):936, received 2024-05-31, published 2024-07-22), which improves the additive constant in the known asymptotic upper bound h(n) ≤ (29/8)^{1/3} n(n-1)^{1/3} for even n, and also for specific small n between 106 and 336, via a purely graph-theoretic degree-sum argument — no computational search or AI tool is mentioned in the paper. (3) Rodrigo, López, Magistrali and Alonso, 'An Improvement of the Lower Bound on the Maximum Number of Halving Lines for Sets in the Plane with an Odd Number of Points' (Axioms 14(1):62, published 2025-01-16), which exhibits improved explicit point configurations raising the known lower bound on halving lines for n=35, 59, 95, 97, with consequences for the rectilinear crossing number and (for n=35) halving pseudolines — again a human construction with no stated computational-search or AI methodology found in the accessible portions of the paper. I searched broadly for any AI involvement in k-set/halving-line research post-2024, including checking DeepMind's AlphaEvolve paper ('Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale', arXiv:2511.02864) and its full 67/68-problem repository (github.com/google-deepmind/alphaevolve_repository_of_problems) — the k-set/halving-lines problem is not among AlphaEvolve's problem list (closest neighbors are Szemerédi–Trotter constructions and equidistant-points-in-convex-polygons, which are distinct problems). No LLM-assisted or AI-generated result for this specific problem was found anywhere. All three results found are ordinary human mathematics (graph-theoretic arguments and explicit point-configuration constructions), with no disclosed use of computer search, computer algebra, or AI systems. Status is 'progress' because bounds moved (in a case/related-dimension sense and in the additive-constant/small-n sense) but the problem as generally stated remains open; resolution_direction is 'confirmed' in the loose sense that each result tightened bounds in the expected direction (no result went against conjectured behavior), though none settled a full case of the k(=n/2) matching-bounds question outright.
competing_reading: One could argue the two MDPI papers (constant improvements and n-specific lower-bound improvements) are so narrow — improving an additive constant, or four specific point counts — that they are better read as 'no meaningful change' to the general bullet, which asks about matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds. Under a strict reading of §3.1 ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry'), a careful person's account of the general k-set gap (the (k+1)^{1/3} vs 2^{√log k} asymptotic gap) is unchanged by any of these three results — none of them touches that asymptotic gap for the classical planar k-set problem itself. Rubin's higher-dimensional result is the strongest candidate for 'in scope' since it is explicitly about matching point-selection/halving-hyperplane bounds, generalizing the flat problem to d dimensions, but a strict reading could classify it as a related problem (higher-dimensional analogue) rather than a case of the 2D bullet. Under that stricter reading, status would arguably be 'open' with no_change_found true, since none of the results move the specific numbers Wikipedia's bullet is asking about (the classical 2D k-set gap). I chose 'progress' because the bullet as phrased ('finding matching upper and lower bounds for k-sets and halving lines', plural, general) plausibly covers exactly this family of incremental bound movements, and because halving lines is the n/2 case of k-sets explicitly named in the bullet.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from an expert survey (e.g., an updated version of Jeff Erickson's or the CG open-problems project's account of k-sets/halving lines) on whether these three 2024-2025 results are considered to move the needle on the classical Wikipedia-stated problem, versus being incremental refinements orthogonal to the actual open asymptotic gap. Also, checking whether any later 2025-2026 paper closes or further narrows the general k-set asymptotic gap would resolve whether 'progress' remains the right classification going forward.

outcome: The general finite lattice representation problem (does every finite lattice occur as the congruence lattice of a finite algebra?) remains open, but the last outstanding case among lattices with at most seven elements — the lattice called L7 in DeMeo's 2012 thesis and L10 in the still-unpublished DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen manuscript 'Representing Finite Lattices as Congruence Lattices of Finite Algebras' — was closed in late August/September 2026: Chenxiao Tian posted a note (28 August 2026) representing it as the subgroup interval [S3, PSL(2,64)], which the DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen project team then independently verified by recomputation in GAP and by an independent isomorphism test in the agda-algebras library, and improved with a smaller representation as an interval in Sp(6,2) (index 34560, found by scanning GAP's TomLib).

ai.basis_quote: Commit messages on the verification/tooling pull requests (fin-lat-rep PR #32, and per search results also fin-lat-rep-gap PR #2) read '🤖 AI-assisted development: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)' and, on an earlier commit, 'Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)'; Copilot's automated code review flagged parser bugs, input-validation gaps and test-coverage issues on those same PRs, which the human author then fixed.

disputes.summary: Tian's PSL(2,64)/S3 interval (index 43680) is the published discovery that closes the case, but the fin-lat-rep project subsequently found a smaller representation via Sp(6,2) acting on 34560 points. Issue #33 explicitly frames this as an open 'decision needed' about which representation should lead in the writeup and how credit should be split, and notes the minimal possible representation may still be far smaller (between 16 and 34560 elements).

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks the general question (posed by Grätzer–Schmidt in 1963 and shown by Pálfy–Pudlák in 1980 to be equivalent to a question about subgroup-lattice intervals in finite groups): is EVERY finite lattice a congruence lattice of a finite algebra? That general question is still open — no resolution, partial or otherwise, of the unrestricted conjecture was found. However, a well-documented and, on the evidence available, genuine case of the problem was settled within the window: DeMeo, Freese and Jipsen's manuscript on representing all lattices with at most seven elements had left exactly one lattice (L7/L10) without a known finite-algebra representation. On 28 August 2026, Chenxiao Tian (Princeton/Peking University) posted a seven-page note exhibiting that lattice as the subgroup interval [SL(2,2)≅S3, PSL(2,64)] (index 43680). The DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen project (GitHub org UniversalAlgebra, repos fin-lat-rep and fin-lat-rep-gap) independently verified this in GAP 4.15.1 by recomputing the interval from Tian's generating matrices, corroborating each lemma of the note (normalizer/centralizer computations, Dickson's classification of maximal subgroups of PSL(2,64), the incidence-count argument), and cross-checking with an independent isomorphism test in the agda-algebras library; they also found a smaller representation as an interval in Sp(6,2) (index 34560) by scanning all 414 tables of marks in GAP's TomLib. This closes the 'one possible exception' from the earlier (pre-2024) DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen work, so with this event every lattice of at most seven elements is now known to be a congruence lattice of a finite algebra — a genuine narrowing of the general open problem's territory, but a restriction (small lattices only) rather than a resolution, so it is classified 'partial' under §3.1's case-vs-variant rule, not 'resolved'. As for AI: no evidence was found that any AI system contributed to the actual mathematics — not to Tian's discovery of the PSL(2,64) representation, not to the group-theoretic verification argument, and not to the Sp(6,2) TomLib scan (performed by a GAP script, tomScan.g). The only AI involvement found is in software engineering: pull requests building the verification/checking infrastructure around this result (and around an unrelated pre-existing bug, algebra B28) carry commit-message credits '🤖 AI-assisted development: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)' and 'Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)', and GitHub Copilot's automated code review flagged bugs in that tooling across several review rounds. This is AI assisting the authors write and debug verification code, not AI producing mathematical content that appears in the result, so ai_role is 'none' per §6.2's instruction that checking, debugging and tooling contributions do not count. This whole episode is extremely recent (weeks old at the time of this research, versus a 26 January 2024 window start) and lives entirely in GitHub issues/PRs of an in-progress manuscript rather than in a published or expert-surveyed venue; I could not find any independent digestion (blog commentary, MathOverflow, journal acceptance) beyond the project's own repositories, so confidence in the permanence/correctness of the classification is medium rather than high, though the verification was done by domain experts (the manuscript's own authors) using two independent methods, which is materially more scrutiny than a bare preprint.
competing_reading: One could argue this event should be rated 'progress' rather than 'partial', on the theory that 'is every finite llattice representable' is functionally an existence/search question similar to the ones §3.1 says a record does not advance merely by narrowing where a counterexample could hide. But that carve-out is for statements like 'are there infinitely many X' where enumerating more X doesn't touch the question; here the case n≤7 is a genuine, exhaustively-defined restriction of the general universally-quantified conjecture ('does every finite lattice L satisfy...'), and settling it removes a specific, previously-open case from the domain — which is exactly what §3.1 defines as a case of the problem meriting 'partial'. A second competing reading is that this should not be recorded at all: the DeMeo-Freese-Jipsen 'one possible exception among ≤7-element lattices' framing is itself a narrower, self-posed sub-problem from their own paper, not a widely-recognized named open problem, so a stickler could call this a 'related' rather than a 'case' of the Wikipedia bullet. I judge it a case because the ≤7-element lattices are a literal, unconditional subset of 'every finite lattice', and DeMeo et al.'s earlier work was itself explicitly working on the Grätzer-Schmidt/Pálfy-Pudlák question restricted by size.
what_would_settle_it: Publication of the updated DeMeo-Freese-Jipsen manuscript (or an arXiv posting of Tian's note itself, which I could not locate independently on arXiv) incorporating this result, and/or independent expert commentary (e.g., a survey, MathOverflow thread, or citation in a later paper) confirming the verification holds up, would move this from a well-verified but insular GitHub-hosted claim toward a fully digested result.

outcome: No proof of convergence or divergence of the Flint Hills series has survived scrutiny. A January 2025 preprint (Mantzakouras & López Zapata, arXiv:2502.03474) claimed a convergence proof but was withdrawn by one of its authors in September 2026 after the authors themselves found the argument invalid. Since then, related preprints (including a March-2026-onward series by López Zapata, arXiv:2603.09719, giving a continued-fraction criterion reducing convergence to the growth of partial quotients of 1/pi, and a September 2026 paper by Yuya Dan on a generalized version) have made partial/structural progress and reformulated the problem, but the classical series' convergence 'remains undecided' in the words of the most recent paper found. No result has been digested by recognized experts or published in a refereed venue; several relevant papers are in arXiv's unrefereed math.GM category.

disputes.summary: Mantzakouras & López Zapata's January 2025 preprint (arXiv:2502.03474) claimed to prove convergence of the Flint Hills series and an upper bound mu(pi) <= 2.5. Co-author López Zapata withdrew the manuscript in a v2 posted 14 Sep 2026, stating: 'I withdraw the manuscript after finding serious issues: the partial-sum argument does not prove Flint-Hills convergence, nor does Hölder continuity by itself establish the proof; the claimed (mu(pi)<=2.5) is not established; and Eq. (1.1) has a numerical error.' This is a self-retraction by the author, not an external refutation, but it means the claimed resolution never stood.

summary: The triage record pointed to two preprints: arXiv:2502.03474 (Mantzakouras & López Zapata, Jan 2025), which the triage described as 'claims to prove convergence', and arXiv:2510.27041 (Oct 2025), described as building on that claim. I read both directly. 2502.03474's v1 abstract does claim a convergence proof and a bound mu(pi) <= 2.5, but its v2 (posted 14 September 2026, within the window) is a one-paragraph withdrawal in which co-author López Zapata states the partial-sum argument does not actually prove convergence, the mu(pi) bound is not established, and there is a numerical error in the paper's Eq. (1.1). So the triage's headline finding is precisely the case §7 warns about: a claim that did not survive and was withdrawn by its own author. This is not a case of an external refutation with a resolution_direction; it is a claim retracted before any expert weighed in, so I coded it as progress/ai_role none rather than open_stale, dating the event to the withdrawal (the corrective event) rather than the original 2025 claim, per §6.1's guidance that where 'there is both an earlier event and a later one, classify on the later.' The second preprint, 2510.27041, turned out on inspection to be a fairly modest six-page note ('A Geometric-Arithmetic Framework for the Flint Hills Series') that discusses the qualitative connection between near-multiples of pi and the irrationality measure but does not itself claim a proof of convergence; it does not change the status. Searching further (beyond the triage's queries, since the field is more active than the triage's snapshot suggested) turned up a continuing thread of preprints by the same author, Carlos López Zapata, under a new arXiv ID 2603.09719 ('A Continued-Fraction Criterion for the Flint Hills Series...'), now at v5 (13 September 2026), which gives a genuine (if 'near-complete', per one summary) reduction: the series converges iff a certain sum of squared partial quotients of the continued fraction of 1/pi, divided by convergent denominators, is finite — turning the analytic convergence question into a question about the growth of an integer sequence. This is real mathematical content and could arguably be `partial` if it settled a restricted case, but on inspection it is an equivalence/reformulation of the open question rather than a settlement of any case of it (no case is actually resolved; whether the criterion's sum is finite is exactly as open as the original problem, contingent on the still-open question of mu(pi)). I therefore treat it as `progress` (a genuine reformulation/partial structural advance) rather than `partial` or `resolved`. This same paper's acknowledgements explicitly credit 'the assistant Claude, developed by Anthropic, for symbolic and numerical verification and for language editing', with the author stating personal responsibility for correctness — this is exactly the §6.2 case of AI used for checking/verification/language editing, which is defined as `ai_role: none` regardless of how many systems are named. A companion September 2026 preprint by Yuya Dan (arXiv:2609.12338) on a generalized Flint Hills series proves a related conjecture (Meiburg's conjecture) for a generalized family but states explicitly 'The convergence of the classical Flint Hills series ... remains undecided' — a related/variant result, not a case of the stated problem, and it does not mention AI. A GPU computation site (bigcompute.science) extended numerical partial sums to 10^10 terms, crediting 'human-AI collaboration (Cahlen Humphreys + Claude)', but frames Claude's role as documentation/analysis rather than the computation itself (done via custom CUDA kernels), and explicitly disclaims this as anything but empirical, non-proof evidence. I found no journal publication, no Tao-blog or comparable expert digestion, and no Wikipedia article update discussing any of this; math.GM is arXiv's unrefereed general-mathematics category, which several of these papers sit in. Net: as of 22 September 2026 the Flint Hills series' convergence is still fully open, but the period saw real, AI-adjacent (checking/verification only) activity: a claimed resolution that was made and then withdrawn, and an unresolved but substantive reformulation of the problem in continued-fraction terms.
competing_reading: One could argue the continued-fraction criterion paper (2603.09719) deserves `partial` status if its 'near-complete' criterion is read as settling an equivalence that some readers would treat as resolving a meaningful special case (e.g., showing convergence holds for almost every real number via Gauss-Kuzmin statistics for a *generic* point, which is a restriction of the generalized problem). However, that near-everywhere-convergence result is about generic reals, not about the specific arithmetic point 1/pi that the Flint Hills series concerns, so it is a related/variant statement about measure rather than a case of the stated problem, and I did not let it move the status past `progress`. One could also argue the withdrawn 2502.03474 preprint, being withdrawn by only one of two co-authors, constitutes a dispute over correctness rather than a clean retraction; I found no counter-statement from Mantzakouras defending the result, so I treated the withdrawal as authoritative.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed proof (or an unretracted, expert-digested preprint) either establishing convergence/divergence of the classical series, or an authoritative determination of whether mu(pi) is above or below 5/2 (per Alekseyev's 2011 equivalence) would settle it. Absent that, an expert (e.g., a number theorist's blog post or a journal referee report) explicitly engaging with López Zapata's continued-fraction criterion would clarify whether it is considered a genuine structural advance or itself flawed.

[Hand-corrected 2026-09-24; the agent's original outcome follows.] Xinyao Zhang posted a preprint (Nov 2024, revised through Jul 2025) claiming to remove the last obstruction (the p=3 exceptional case) in the two-dimensional regular Fontaine-Mazur conjecture over Q, which combined with Lue Pan's 2019/2021 work (covering p>=5) would complete the regular-case conjecture for all odd primes; separately, Jack Thorne posted a preprint (Aug 2026) proving further partial cases of the Fontaine-Mazur conjecture for GL(2), including some previously-open reducible-residual cases.
