disputes.summary: A third-party automated preprint-review site (Pith, which describes itself as producing machine-generated, referee-style reports) assessed Zhang's paper as 'clos[ing] Pan's p=3 gap with a promising strategy, but the written proof is too sketchy at the local epsilon=+-1 case to accept as is.' This is not a human expert's verdict, but no human expert digestion (journal referee report, seminar writeup, blog post) was found either, so the paper's correctness is unconfirmed by any authoritative source as of this search.

summary: The triage correctly identified the two relevant preprints. Zhang's paper (arXiv:2412.06812, v1 2024-11-30, latest v4 2025-07-22) explicitly presents itself as a sequel to Lue Pan's arXiv:1901.07166 (which had already established the regular-case Fontaine-Mazur conjecture for p>=5) and claims to remove the last remaining obstruction, the p=3 exceptional case, thereby claiming the regular-case conjecture for all odd primes. I checked the arXiv admin note flagging 'substantial text overlap with arXiv:1901.07166, arXiv:1005.2008 by other authors' and confirmed via the paper's own introduction that this reflects Zhang building explicitly and extensively on Pan's and Kisin's established results and setup (a normal sequel relationship, citing what it extends), not an impropriety; the paper's stated new contributions are a potential-pro-modularity argument working uniformly for all odd primes and a generalized Greenberg-Wiles formula for the p=3 case. No journal acceptance, MathOverflow discussion, Tao-blog coverage, or other human expert digestion of this specific paper was found in searches; the only third-party assessment located is an automated review site (Pith) that itself is AI/machine-generated rather than a human referee, and it flags a possible gap in the local epsilon=+-1 case. Given the absence of human expert verification, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved', with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the result, if correct, confirms the conjecture in this case; there is no counterexample). Jack Thorne's separate preprint (arXiv:2608.07186, 2026-08-07) proves additional GL(2) cases (potentially crystalline ordinary, Hodge-Tate weights {0,1}, totally odd determinant, including some previously-open reducible-residual cases at p=2), explicitly a partial-progress paper per its own framing ('the vast majority of cases... are known'), so it is recorded as informing the same 'claimed' picture but does not itself change the status classification (it is genuinely a case/partial result, consistent with partial-type progress, but since the overall conjecture status here already rests on the not-yet-digested Zhang claim, I keep a single status field per the harness's instruction to describe the decisive event and discuss the rest here). Neither paper's acknowledgements, introduction, or any secondary source mentions any AI system, language model, or AI-assisted tool contributing to the mathematics; Zhang thanks his supervisor Takeshi Saito and Kojiro Matsumoto, Thorne credits only ERC grant funding. A separate ScienceDaily story about 'Claude Fable 5' and a mathematician named Alpöge (checked because it surfaced in search results) concerns an unrelated problem, the Jacobian conjecture (a counterexample in dimension >=3), and does not mention Fontaine-Mazur at all — I confirmed this by fetching the article directly and am ruling it out explicitly rather than silently.
competing_reading: One could argue Zhang's result should be classified as 'resolved' if one takes the mathematical content of a careful, sequel-style preprint from a specialist working under a named advisor at face value, especially since no substantive rebuttal or identified error (beyond the automated reviewer's flag) has surfaced in nearly two years since posting. Conversely, one could argue for 'open' if the automated reviewer's flagged gap at the local epsilon=+-1 case is treated as a live, unresolved correctness concern rather than routine preprint uncertainty. I chose 'claimed' as the middle reading most consistent with §6.1's literal test (no expert digestion, no journal acceptance) while acknowledging the claim is fairly mature (multiple self-revisions over 8 months, no public rebuttal).
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance, a human referee report, a seminar or conference talk with expert Q&A, a MathOverflow/blog discussion by a specialist in Galois deformation theory, or a follow-up paper by another author citing Zhang's p=3 result as an established input, would move this from 'claimed' to 'resolved'. Conversely, a substantive erratum, withdrawal, or identified error in the local epsilon=+-1 case would move it toward 'progress'/'incident'.

outcome: No progress found on the infinitude question itself since 26 January 2024: no Fibonacci-Wieferich prime, Pell-Wieferich prime, or Lucas-Wieferich prime for a general pair (a,-1) has been found by any search, and no unconditional or conditional theoretical result establishing infinitude of these primes (as opposed to infinitude of their complement, the non-Wieferich primes) has appeared in the window.
summary: The bullet asks whether, for a fixed integer a>0, there are infinitely many Lucas-Wieferich primes for the pair (a,-1) — i.e. primes p for which the Wieferich-type congruence *holds* (U_{p-e} ≡ 0 mod p²) for the Lucas sequence with parameters (a,-1); the a=1 case is Fibonacci-Wieferich primes and a=2 is Pell-Wieferich primes. I confirmed the triage's finding and extended its search. No new Fibonacci-Wieferich or Pell-Wieferich prime has been found since the frozen revision (the known bounds remain the pre-2024 PrimeGrid limits, roughly 9.7×10^14–1.9×10^17 for Fibonacci and below 10^9 for Pell, per the current Wieferich prime Wikipedia article, which itself contains no post-2022 developments on these variants). On the theoretical side, the active research program in this exact area (2021 Fang–Ren/Ribenboim-style paper on Lucas non-Wieferich primes in arithmetic progressions; a March 2025 paper 'The abc conjecture implies infinitely many non-Wieferich places for fixed bases in number fields' (arXiv:2503.19144); an August 2025 paper on Wieferich primes in number fields and the Ankeny-Artin-Chowla/Mordell conjectures (arXiv:2508.08472); and a December 2025 paper on p-adic valuations of Möbius duals of Lucas sequences and Wall-Sun-Sun primes (arXiv:2512.03481)) all address either (a) the complement question — infinitely many non-Wieferich (or non-Lucas-Wieferich) primes, which is the opposite congruence condition and does not bear on this bullet — or (b) number-field analogues/generalizations that are variants under §3.1, not cases of the rational-integer pair (a,-1) question as stated. None of these establishes, conditionally or otherwise, that there are infinitely many primes p with U_{p-e}(a,-1) ≡ 0 (mod p²) for any fixed a. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature or in the computational searches (which use classical sieve/modular-exponentiation methods, e.g. PrimeGrid's distributed computing project, not any AI/ML technique). I am satisfied nothing has happened to the stated question in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2512.03481 Möbius-dual paper's discussion of Wall-Sun-Sun primes is adjacent enough to count as 'progress' on the broader family of Wieferich-type conjectures, and one could argue the number-field papers (2503.19144, 2508.08472) are generalizations that 'contain' the rational case as a special instance. But in each case the actual theorem proved is about a different congruence (non-Wieferich, i.e. the failure of the congruence) or a different domain (number fields, Wall-Sun-Sun primes for Fibonacci divisibility by p rather than p²-Wieferich-type congruences for Lucas sequences), so under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 none of them changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or search result that either exhibits a Fibonacci-Wieferich, Pell-Wieferich, or general Lucas-Wieferich(a,-1) prime, or that proves (conditionally or unconditionally) infinitude of primes satisfying U_{p-e}(a,-1) ≡ 0 (mod p²) for some or all a, dated after 26 January 2024.

summary: The bullet, as Wikipedia words it, asks whether for a fixed integer a > 0 there are infinitely many primes p with a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p^2) — i.e. infinitely many base-a Wieferich primes (the exponent 'a^p − 1' in the extracted statement is Wikipedia's own rendering of a^(p−1) − 1; this is the standard base-a Wieferich prime definition per the Wieferich prime Wikipedia article and Fermat quotient article, and matches the triage's reading). This remains completely open: for base 2, only the two Wieferich primes 1093 and 3511 are known, and exhaustive search (last reported up to 6.7×10^15, a pre-2024 result) has found no others; no new Wieferich prime for any small base was reported as discovered in the 2024-2026 window. The only related developments found in the window are: (1) Graves & Weiss (arXiv 2503.19144, March 2025) and Fellini/related work culminating in arXiv 2508.08472 (Aug 2025), which prove — conditional on the abc conjecture (or Masser's number-field abc-conjecture) — that there are infinitely many base-a NON-Wieferich primes, in the classical and number-field settings respectively. These address the complementary question (primes where the congruence fails) and are conditional, so under §3.1 and §6.1 they are not a change to this problem's status: they neither settle nor narrow the stated infinitude-of-Wieferich-primes question, and even if they addressed the same object they would only support 'claimed' at best, not a real status change, since they are conditional on an open conjecture. No unconditional result, no computational discovery of a new Wieferich prime, and no AI-related work touching this specific question were found. I therefore agree with the triage's verdict of 'none' and its classification of the found papers as adjacent/conditional rather than resolving.
competing_reading: One could argue the conditional abc-conjecture results deserve a 'progress' status with ai_role none, on the theory that they represent movement in the surrounding theory even though they attack the complementary (non-Wieferich) question. I reject this because per §3.1 a 'related problem' (here, a different congruence direction, and conditional on an unproven hypothesis) does not count as scope for this bullet; the stated question about Wieferich primes themselves has seen no bound move, no case settled, and no conditional resolution offered anywhere in the literature I found.
what_would_settle_it: An unconditional proof (or disproof) that infinitely many base-a Wieferich primes exist for some or all a, or a new explicit Wieferich prime discovered by computer search extending the known range beyond 6.7×10^15, would count as progress or resolution.

outcome: Artin's primitive root conjecture remains open and unproven unconditionally for any single value of a; since 26 January 2024 there have been three genuine advances that move the surrounding landscape without settling the stated existence question: (1) Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen (Dec 2024) proved the predicted asymptotic density holds unconditionally for almost all a in a growing range, improving Stephens (1969); (2) Goldmakher-Martin-Peringuey (Feb 2025) proposed refined conjectures capturing finer distributional properties, proved under GRH plus unconditional weaker versions; (3) Murty-Naik (Aug 2026) gave a conditional proof of the full conjecture assuming a new 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' they themselves cannot yet prove, plus partial unconditional progress toward that inequality. None of these is a resolution or even a settled case (no single a is unconditionally known to be a primitive root for infinitely many primes); all are best classified as progress on the surrounding theory.
summary: The stated bullet is Artin's conjecture on primitive roots (posed 1927): for integer a, not a perfect square and not −1, are there infinitely many primes p with a as a primitive root mod p? This is still open in full generality and, as the current Wikipedia article states, 'there is no single value of a for which Artin's conjecture is proved' unconditionally (Heath-Brown 1986 only shows at least one of {2,3,5} works, a disjunctive result, itself pre-dating the window). Three pieces of work since the 26 Jan 2024 cutoff bear on the surrounding theory. (1) Klurman, Shparlinski and Teräväinen, 'On Artin's conjecture on average and short character sums' (arXiv:2412.13355, submitted 17 Dec 2024, published in Bull. LMS), prove unconditionally that the Artin asymptotic holds for almost all a up to exp((log log x)^2) — an average-case, not a general or per-a, result; it does not settle the existence question for any specific a, so per §3.1 an 'almost all' statement about an infinitude/existence question does not change the stated bullet, though it is a genuine improvement to the surrounding average-case theory and so counts as progress. (2) Goldmakher, Martin and Peringuey, 'Refinements of Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2502.19601, Feb 2025), propose finer conjectures on the distribution of ord_p(a) that specialize to Artin's conjecture, proving them under GRH and proving unconditional weaker versions; this refines rather than resolves the conjecture. (3) Murty and Naik, 'A non-abelian large sieve and Artin's primitive root conjecture' (arXiv:2608.21573, submitted 21 Aug 2026), claim a proof of the full conjecture conditional on a new 'non-abelian large sieve inequality' that is itself an open conjecture, plus some unconditional partial progress toward that inequality via duality techniques. This is a conditional proof analogous in spirit to Hooley's 1967 GRH-conditional proof — a genuine new conditional pathway, but not an unconditional resolution, and (being one month old at the time of this research) has not yet been digested by experts or seen any recorded reaction. None of the three papers mentions any AI or machine-learning system in their methods or acknowledgements — all are traditional human-authored analytic number theory. Separately, Artin's conjecture appears as 'Sample Problem 1' (Tier 3, authored by Olli Järviniemi) in the FrontierMath AI benchmark (Glazer et al. 2024, arXiv:2411.04872), but that benchmark problem asks for a specific computable density constant (⌊10^6 d_∞⌋ for primes where ord(2)>ord(3)) built using Artin-conjecture-style machinery, not the open existence conjecture itself — it is a related/variant well-posed numeric question, not a case of the stated bullet, and no source found indicates any AI model has actually solved it (aggregate FrontierMath scores are reported per-tier, not per-problem, and public commentary — e.g. Terence Tao's remark that Tier 3 problems would 'resist AIs for several years' — treats it as unsolved). No genuine case or resolution of the conjecture has any AI involvement; the only AI connection found is benchmarking, not mathematical progress on the stated problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen 'almost all a' result deserves `partial` rather than `progress`, on the reading that it settles the conjecture for a genuine (density-1-in-a-growing-range) subset of a-values. I did not adopt this because the underlying claim for each such a is still an infinitude-of-primes statement whose truth for that specific a is not established with certainty (it is a statement about the counting function's asymptotic matching the conjectured constant for almost all a, which is compatible with but does not by itself prove Artin's conjecture holds for those a — the density result is itself already conjectured as a corollary if Artin's conjecture were true, and proving it unconditionally for almost all a is more precisely a conditional-removal/quantitative average result than a case-by-case existence resolution). Given the ambiguity, a reader could reasonably classify this as `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` instead.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the Klurman-Shparlinski-Teräväinen paper's precise theorem statement to determine whether 'the asymptotic holds for almost all a' logically implies 'a is a primitive root for infinitely many p' for each such a (versus only implying the counting function's growth rate matches, which is a slightly weaker statement), and any expert digestion or citation record of the Murty-Naik paper once it has had time to be reviewed.

outcome: The generalized repunit-prime infinitude conjecture remains unproven for every base b; the only developments since 26 January 2024 are (a) a computational primality *certification* (not a new discovery) of the base-10 probable prime R(109297), completed 26 May 2025 by Andreas Enge using elliptic curve primality proving (ECPP), and (b) continued discovery of larger base-10 probable repunit primes (e.g. R(8177207), found by Ryan Propper in 2021 and still listed as a probable prime as of 2025). Neither result bears on whether infinitely many repunit primes exist in any base.
credited_humans: Harvey Dubner (original 2007 discovery of the probable prime)
summary: This bullet asks whether, for any base b that is not a perfect power and not of the form -4k^4, there are infinitely many base-b repunit primes (the generalized repunit/Wagstaff-type conjecture). This is a classic 'infinitely many X' question, which under §3.1 moves only when actually answered — not when a new example is found or a probable prime is upgraded to a proven prime. I confirmed via the current Repunit Wikipedia article, the Prime Pages (t5k.org) top-20 repunit list, and the specific record page for R(109297) that: the conjecture is still completely open in the literature (no proof or disproof for any base, including base 10); the sole event dated within the window is the 26 May 2025 ECPP primality certificate for R(109297) (a probable prime originally found by Harvey Dubner in 2007), computed by Andreas Enge over roughly 20 months on a 64-core machine — a certified, non-AI, deterministic-algorithm computation, and in any case only a proof that one specific number is prime, not a step toward the infinitude question. I also confirmed R(8177207), the largest known base-10 repunit probable prime (found 2021, still unproven as of 2025), has had no status change. Searches for any AI involvement in repunit-prime work (LLM-driven number theory searches, AI-assisted primality proofs) turned up general AI-and-mathematics stories (Erdős problems, OEIS conjectures, Theo-Conjecture) but nothing whatsoever connecting AI systems to repunit or generalized-repunit primes. I also noted, but did not open or rely on, a GitHub repository ('vibemathing/problem-wikipedia-...') that surfaced in search results and appears to be another research pass on this same dataset; per instructions I did not read it and it played no role in this record. Status is therefore open, no_change_found true, matching and confirming the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the ECPP certification of R(109297) deserves a `progress` classification as 'an instructive incident' of computational number theory, since it is a genuine new fact (a probable prime became a proven prime) dated within the window. But per §3.1, the bullet's question is existence of infinitely many primes, and a single case moving from probable to proven does not narrow or answer that question, so I classified it as `open` with `no_change_found` rather than `progress`. If the harness's convention is that any dated, sourced computational event on the topic should be surfaced as `progress` even when it doesn't bear on the infinitude question, this record would instead be `progress` / `ai_role none` / `resolution_direction null`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of infinitude of repunit primes for even a single qualifying base b would settle this bullet as resolved/partial; short of that, only a change in expert consensus or a new heuristic/proof-adjacent result (e.g., a proof of infinitude conditional on a major conjecture like GRH) would move the status away from open. No such result was found.

outcome: No proof, refutation, or partial resolution of this infinitude-of-primes question was found since 26 January 2024; it remains an open conjecture in the Bunyakovsky/Dickson/Schinzel-Hypothesis-H family, with only unrelated computational finds (new large probable/proven generalized-repunit-style primes) occurring in the window.
summary: This bullet is the generalized-repunit-style primality conjecture from the family of Bunyakovsky's conjecture / Dickson's conjecture / Schinzel's Hypothesis H: for fixed k≥1, b≥2, c≠0 with the stated gcd conditions, are there infinitely many n such that (k·b^n+c)/gcd(k+c,b-1) is prime? No case of this general family (beyond Dirichlet's theorem for degree-1 polynomials, which this is not) has ever been proved, and I found no claimed progress, partial resolution, or refutation dated in the 26 Jan 2024–22 Sep 2026 window. Searches for the exact expression, for 'generalized repunit prime conjecture', and for AI-related proof activity in this area returned nothing on point. Two tempting leads turned out to be irrelevant on inspection: (1) a 2025 arXiv/JIS paper by E. Cohen, 'Conjectures about Primes and Cyclic Numbers' (J. Integer Sequences 28 (2025), 25.4.7), which is about a different, unrelated family of 66 conjectures concerning cyclic numbers and Sophie Germain primes — not this conjecture — and one of whose sub-conjectures (a subadditivity conjecture, #66) was refuted by a human (Josué Alexander Ibarra) with a Lean-verified counterexample; (2) a November 2025 arXiv paper, 'Mathematics with large language models as provers and verifiers' (arXiv:2510.12829), reporting a GPT-5-based prover/verifier system that closed 22 of that same 66-conjecture list (17 proofs, 5 refutations) — but again this is the Cohen cyclic-number/Sophie-Germain list, not the generalized-repunit conjecture on our bullet, and I could not find our specific expression anywhere in that paper's Table 3 conjecture list. The only concrete events in the window relating to generalized repunit-style primes were computational discoveries — e.g. the repunit R(109297) being proven prime by elliptic-curve primality proving around May 2025 (t5k.org) — but per §3.1 a new record instance or verified-to-a-larger-limit search does not advance an 'are there infinitely many' question, so this does not change the status. No AI involvement of any kind was found in connection with this specific conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue that any progress on the broader Bunyakovsky conjecture, Dickson's conjecture, or Schinzel's Hypothesis H (of which this is a special/derived case) should count as 'progress' on this bullet under a generous reading of scope. I did not find any such progress in the window either (these remain fully open apart from Dirichlet's theorem, which predates the window by centuries), so this does not change the classification, but if any such general progress exists and I missed it, this record would need revision to `progress` rather than `open`.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement that either proves infinitude of primes for some fixed (k,b,c) instance of this family, proves a positive-density/lower-bound result specific to this parametrized form, or explicitly references this generalized-repunit primality conjecture (e.g. citing Guy's 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' or the Wikipedia bullet) with a claimed resolution.

outcome: Two independent teams settled the last open case of Hilbert's tenth problem for rings of integers: Koymans and Pagano (preprint, Dec 2024, using additive combinatorics and elliptic curves with full rational 2-torsion) and Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman (preprint, Jan 2025, using rank stability of abelian varieties in quadratic extensions) each proved that the problem has a negative (undecidable) answer for the ring of integers of every number field, closing the question the Wikipedia bullet asks.

disputes.summary: Koymans-Pagano posted first (arXiv, 2 Dec 2024) using additive combinatorics and 2-descent on elliptic curves with full rational 2-torsion. Alpöge-Bhargava-Ho-Shnidman posted a second, independent proof less than two months later (30 Jan 2025) via a rank-stability theorem for abelian varieties in quadratic extensions. Quanta Magazine reports both as independent, with Bhargava noting the two methods might be combinable for further results; no priority dispute is voiced by either team, and both are treated as full, independent resolutions of the same open case rather than a race with a single winner.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for which number fields Hilbert's tenth problem (decidability of Diophantine equations over the ring of integers) holds. Before the frozen revision, this was known to be undecidable ('the problem holds' in the negative-answer sense of undecidability) for various families -- e.g. number fields with an abelian Galois group over Q, and fields with exactly one pair of complex conjugate embeddings -- but the general case for all number fields was open. Within the window, two independent groups closed it. Koymans and Pagano (arXiv:2412.01768, submitted 2 Dec 2024, revised through v3 on 24 Nov 2025 with referee feedback incorporated per the acknowledgements) proved a negative answer for Hilbert's tenth problem over every infinite ring finitely generated over Z, which includes the ring of integers of every number field. Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman (arXiv:2501.18774, submitted 30 Jan 2025) proved the same conclusion specifically for rings of integers of number fields via a theorem that every quadratic extension of number fields admits a rank-stable positive-rank abelian variety; that paper has since appeared in Inventiones Mathematicae (published version confirmed via Springer, 2025/2026), a journal of record, and was digested at length by Quanta Magazine (3 Feb 2025), with named experts (Barry Mazur, Andrew Granville) commenting on its significance and no expert dissent found. A further paper by Bjorn Poonen (arXiv:2510.19553, 22 Oct 2025) gives an alternative, independently derived proof of the rank-stability-implies-Diophantine theorem underlying the ABHS result, which functions as additional expert corroboration of that key lemma. Given a journal-of-record publication plus an expert-digested account (Quanta) plus an independent alternative proof of the key technical theorem, and two independent full proofs of the same negative-answer conclusion, I classify this as 'resolved' rather than merely 'claimed.' Neither paper mentions any AI, machine-learning, or automated-proof-search methods; both are entirely human-authored, traditional number-theoretic arguments (additive combinatorics/2-descent, and rank stability of abelian varieties respectively), so ai_role is 'none' with no basis_quote available. The resolution_direction is 'confirmed' because the results confirm/answer the open question (undecidability holds for all number fields), matching what most experts in the area expected/hoped would eventually be shown, rather than refuting a competing conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue the Koymans-Pagano paper alone should be rated 'claimed' rather than folded into an overall 'resolved' verdict, since as of my research it is still formally an arXiv preprint (albeit heavily revised with referee comments incorporated) without a confirmed journal acceptance notice found. However, because the Alpöge-Bhargava-Ho-Shnidman paper independently proves the identical conclusion for the exact case this bullet asks about (all number fields) and is already published in Inventiones Mathematicae with expert digestion (Quanta) and an independent alternative proof of its key lemma (Poonen), the bullet's question is resolved regardless of the Koymans-Pagano paper's individual publication status. If a stricter reading required every contributing paper to be individually journal-published before calling the bullet 'resolved', this would instead be 'claimed' pending final publication of the Koymans-Pagano preprint.
what_would_settle_it: Direct confirmation of the Koymans-Pagano paper's journal acceptance (or continued preprint status), and any expert survey or Bourbaki-seminar-style digestion explicitly stating both proofs are fully verified and uncontested, would remove any residual ambiguity.

summary: Fortune's conjecture (no Fortunate number is composite) remains open, with no result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that changes the stated question. Three lines of activity exist. (1) Computational verification continues: OEIS A005235's data page shows a comment dated August 2026 (attributed to Brock Falfas) stating the first 4600 primorials have been checked and all corresponding Fortunate numbers are prime, extending the prior record of ~3000 (2017) / ~4600 terms already noted by the triage. Per the rules in §3.1, extending a verification record on an existence-type statement ('is there a composite Fortunate number') narrows where a counterexample could hide but does not answer the question, so this is not scope-changing progress on the conjecture itself — it is the routine continuation of a decades-long computational check, and I do not code it as `progress`. (2) A GitHub issue (#3688) was opened 2 April 2026 in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository by user franzhusch, proposing to add a Lean/Mathlib formalization of the conjecture's *statement* (not a proof or disproof). Its footer states plainly: 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' — this is AI involvement in tracking/formalization overhead only, producing no mathematics that bears on the truth of the conjecture, so ai_role is `none` per the formalisation_only rule (§6.2), even though I record the quote and mark formalisation_only true for completeness. (3) A partial/computational-evidence paper by Hayat Rezgui ('New explorations and remarkable inequalities related to Fortune's conjecture and fortunate numbers', Refaad) is dated 20 December 2023 — before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff — so even though it proves the conjecture 'in a particular case' by two methods and verifies an inequality across the first 3000 known terms, it is out of the window entirely (open_stale territory would apply only if it were the sole basis for a status change, which it is not, since it predates the window and no later paper restates or extends it). No AI system is mentioned in that paper. I found no arXiv preprints, no lab announcements, and no expert digestions of any new proof or disproof attempt in the window. The conjecture is coded `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the continued OEIS verification (2017's ~3000 terms to 2026's 4600 terms) constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense, since it is new computational work performed within the window. But per §3.1's explicit rule that record-extension on an infinitude/existence-type question is not scope-changing progress unless the record itself is the question (which it is not here — the question is whether a composite Fortunate number exists, not what the largest verified term is), I classify this as no_change_found rather than `progress`. A stricter reading might also want a `partial` credit for the Rezgui paper if one dates it to a later re-publication or indexing date rather than the original December 2023 preprint/publication date; I found no evidence of any 2024+ re-publication, so I keep it fully outside the window.
what_would_settle_it: A published proof or disproof of the general conjecture; a discovered composite Fortunate number (which would refute it); or, short of that, any peer-reviewed/expert-digested advance restricting composite Fortunate numbers to a provably finite or empty set. Also relevant: confirmation of whether the Rezgui paper's December 2023 date is a preprint date only, with a later 2024+ formal publication date that might bring it into the window (I found no evidence of this).

outcome: No proof, disproof, partial resolution, or bound movement on the four exponentials conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains fully open, exactly as it has been since the 1960s.
summary: I searched broadly for any development on the four exponentials conjecture — the statement that given ℚ-linearly-independent pairs {x1,x2} and {y1,y2} of complex numbers, at least one of e^(x1y1), e^(x1y2), e^(x2y1), e^(x2y2) is transcendental — in the window since 26 January 2024. This is a long-standing (Schneider 1957 / Lang-Ramachandra era) open problem in transcendental number theory, a special case of Schanuel's conjecture, and known to be very hard: the six-exponentials theorem's proof technique 'just misses' reducing to four. Searches in both English and French (for 'conjecture des quatre exponentielles', since much of the literature is French, e.g. Waldschmidt, Diaz) turned up only background/survey material: the current Wikipedia and MathWorld articles, Waldschmidt's 2023 survey chapter 'The Four Exponentials Problem and Schanuel's Conjecture' (Springer, in a 2023 volume, so before the window), a 1997 JTNB article by Guy Diaz that is entirely pre-window, and unrelated recent arXiv papers that surfaced only because they share incidental terms ('four exponential terms', Goldbach summatory function, etc.) with the query but do not address this conjecture at all. Waldschmidt's most recent publications (checked via his personal publication list) as of 2025 concern Schanuel's conjecture for elliptic/quasi-elliptic functions, an adjacent but distinct topic, not the four exponentials conjecture itself, and are about a related problem rather than a case or resolution of this one. I also checked for any AI-system involvement (AlphaProof, AlphaEvolve, LLM-driven formal proof search papers) and found no connection whatsoever to this specific conjecture — those systems' publicized work (IMO problems, algorithm discovery, other number-theoretic bounds) does not mention or touch the four exponentials conjecture. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' case: the conjecture is exactly as open now as it was in January 2024, and no AI system has been reported to have engaged with it at all. This agrees with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: None found. There is no genuinely ambiguous case or variant result that could plausibly be reclassified as a partial resolution of this specific conjecture within the window.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement proving the conjecture (or a genuine special case restricting the stated hypotheses, e.g. for specific algebraic number fields or additional constraints on x1,x2,y1,y2) with a submission date after 26 January 2024, or an expert digestion (Tao's blog, a survey, Zentralblatt/MathSciNet review) crediting such a result.

outcome: The conjecture remains open. Every genuine numeric improvement to the known lower bound (0.01 -> (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 -> ~0.38234 -> ~0.38271) was posted between November 2022 and June 2023, entirely before the 26 January 2024 freeze date. The only post-freeze events are a journal publication of already-known 2022 work, an arXiv metadata/write-up revision of an already-known 2022 bound, and a cluster of unverified 'full proof' preprints (2024 and 2026) that show no sign of expert acceptance and, in several cases, show clear hallmarks of low-quality or automated/crank submissions rather than mathematics.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent groups (Alweiss-Huang-Sellke, Chase-Lovett, Sawin, and separately Pebody) reached the (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 bound within days of each other in November 2022, and Yu and Cambie independently reached ~0.3823 within weeks in December 2022. All of this predates the frozen revision and is background, not a post-window event, but it explains why the same numeric progress is attributed to different author sets across different secondary sources.

summary: The triage flagged three items, all of which turn out not to be genuine post-2024-01-26 progress on the conjecture itself once traced to primary sources. (1) The Alweiss-Huang-Sellke paper (arXiv:2211.11731, the source the triage's Feb-2025 EJC link actually corresponds to) proving the (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 bound was submitted 21 November 2022 (v1-v3 all in Nov-Dec 2022); its only post-freeze event is formal journal publication in Electronic Journal of Combinatorics vol. 31(3) on 20 September 2024, which is a write-up/acceptance event for pre-existing 2022 mathematics, not a new result -- classified as open_stale territory for that specific bound, but since it was already public knowledge well before the freeze (and Wikipedia's Jan-2024 snapshot of this bullet doesn't cite a specific numeric constant to begin with), I record the problem's overall status as still open with no_change_found, folding this into background. (2) The 'improved bound' that the triage attributed to 'Cambie... Feb 2025' is arXiv:2212.12500, whose v1 was submitted 23 December 2022 and which reaches essentially the same ~0.3823 constant that Yu and Cambie both obtained in December 2022 (per Matthew Aldridge's timeline and cross-referenced against Liu's June 2023 paper, arXiv:2306.08824, which cites and improves on it to ~0.38271, itself also pre-freeze). The v2 revision dated 16 February 2025 is a metadata/text update to an already 2+-year-old preprint; I could not confirm it contains any bound beyond what existed in 2022, and no secondary source (survey, blog, or later citing paper) credits Cambie with a materially new numeric result after January 2024. (3) Two claimed full proofs were found: Roberto Demontis, 'The union-closed set conjecture is true' (arXiv:2405.03731, submitted 6 May 2024, single version, no retraction notice) and Jamolidin K. Abdurakhmanov, 'An Algorithmic Proof of Frankl's Union-Closed Sets Conjecture' (ResearchGate/HAL, dated 28 January 2026). Neither has any digestion, citation, or acceptance by an expert or venue that I could find (no Gil Kalai blog coverage, no Terence Tao mention, no MathOverflow discussion, no citing papers treating the conjecture as resolved) -- the conjecture continues to be described as open in every 2025-2026 secondary source I checked, including Gil Kalai's own 1 January 2026 'Combinatorics News' roundup, which discusses other combinatorics results but does not mention either claimed proof or treat the conjecture as settled. I also found a proliferation of Zenodo/ResearchGate/dev.to items around this problem ('The Reflection Restored -- A Machine-Certified Proof of Frankl's Conjecture via Collision-Restitution Invariants', an anonymous pseudonymous Zenodo upload tagged 'AI-augmented research'; 'A concavity obstruction and repaired support reductions in a Frankl entropy programme', an anonymous Zenodo record whose own description explicitly disclaims establishing any new bound, certificate, or peer review; and a GitHub repo 'frankl-conjecture-audit' cataloguing exactly this kind of claim) that read as automated or crank content rather than mathematics -- non-standard jargon ('collision-restitution invariants'), pseudonymous authorship, and self-disclaimed lack of any actual result. None of this constitutes a change to the problem under the scope rule of Section 3.1: an unverified, undigested preprint is not evidence the problem moved, and a self-disclaimed non-result certainly is not. No AI system was credited by any authors, in their own words, with producing mathematics that is part of a genuine, expert-accepted result on this problem -- the one AI-adjacent item found (the Zenodo 'AI-augmented research' tag) is on a paper that shows no sign of legitimacy and makes no first-person claim about what the AI produced, so ai_role is none rather than any of the AI-crediting codes.
competing_reading: One could argue the Alweiss-Huang-Sellke EJC journal publication (Sept 2024) or the Cambie arXiv v2 revision (Feb 2025) should be coded as 'progress' events with predates_frozen_revision noted, on the theory that a formal publication/revision date is itself a dateable event within the window even though the underlying mathematics is older. I chose not to do this because Section 6.3 instructs dating by the first public written argument, not the journal publication, specifically to avoid publication lag creating a false post-window event; treating a 2022 result's 2024/2025 formal write-up as 'progress' would overstate what happened since the freeze. If a future pass disagrees, the correct status would still be open_stale (not progress), since nothing about the bound changed.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a blog post by Kalai, Tao, or a subject specialist; a MathOverflow answer; or a citing paper treating the question as closed) of either the Demontis or Abdurakhmanov claimed proofs, in either direction -- confirming or refuting them -- would resolve whether this problem has moved past 'open'. Similarly, a citation trail showing Cambie's 2025 arXiv revision contains a numeric bound strictly better than Liu's 2023 ~0.38271 would establish genuine post-freeze quantitative progress, but I found no source making that claim.

outcome: Two post-window preprints settle further cases of Fröberg's conjecture on the Hilbert series of ideals generated by generic/general forms: Boij–Dannetun–Lundqvist (arXiv:2605.03872, May 2026) prove the conjecture in the second non-trivial degree for generic forms of degree d>2, and up to degree 2d-1 for sufficiently many variables; Wang–Zhang (arXiv:2608.24797, August 2026) prove it for general forms of degree 5 and 7 in four variables for every generator count r≥1, extending the previously known range (r≤5, and the equal-degree theorem through degree d+2). The general conjecture (arbitrary number of forms, degrees, and variables) remains open. Neither preprint has yet been digested by an expert (no journal publication, no blog/survey treatment found), so status is 'partial' rather than 'resolved' for either event.

The AI-assisted workflow used [these systems] for the formulation of mathematical ideas, generation of conjectures and proof strategies, derivation and checking of intermediate steps, construction of examples and exact certificates, comparison of literature and candidate proof approaches, organization of arguments, LaTeX drafting, and revision of the final text.

summary: Fröberg's conjecture (Wikipedia's 2024 wording: on the Hilbert function/series of an ideal generated by a set of generic forms) has not been resolved in general, but two preprints since the frozen revision settle additional special cases, which is squarely within scope under §3.1 since both restrict the same stated question (fewer variables/degrees/generator counts) rather than changing it. (1) Boij, Dannetun and Lundqvist, 'Independence of generic forms and the Fröberg conjecture' (arXiv:2605.03872, submitted 2026-05-05), prove the conjecture in the second non-trivial degree for generic forms of any degree d>2, and up to degree 2d-1 when the number of variables is large enough — a genuine, human-authored extension of the known range, with no AI involvement found in the fetched text (ai_role: none for that paper). (2) Wang and Zhang, 'Fröberg's Conjecture for Quintics and Septics in Four Variables' (arXiv:2608.24797, v1 2026-08-25, v3 2026-08-27), prove the conjecture for r general forms of degree 5 or 7 in exactly four variables for every r≥1, closing the previously-open generator-count gaps (6≤r≤11 for quintics, 6≤r≤21 for septics) beyond the classical r≤5 case and Boij–Dannetun–Lundqvist's degree d+2 bound. This second paper is the one carrying the AI signal: its own acknowledgements state the results were 'obtained through a generative-AI workflow' using three named systems for 'formulation of mathematical ideas, generation of conjectures and proof strategies, derivation ... of intermediate steps, construction of examples and exact certificates,' i.e. AI systems producing mathematics that appears in the final result (constructions/certificates), not merely checking or formalising human work — this clears the 'assisted' bar under §6.2. It could also be read as 'generated' (the AI produced the proof strategy and the certificates, and the human role appears reducible to running/rebuilding verification scripts), but the authors' own framing is 'computer-assisted' work by named human authors with AI as a tool within a structured workflow, not 'the model produced the proof and we verified it,' so I coded 'assisted' and flag the alternative. The paper is an unrefereed preprint (v3, dated 2026-08-27, revising only the AI-disclosure and acknowledgements, not the theorem or proof) with no evidence of expert digestion, journal acceptance, or treatment on expert blogs (Tao's site was checked and has no mention). An independent third-party site (VibeMathed, which catalogs AI-involved math results) reports it re-derived the Macaulay-matrix computations from the paper's printed data and reproduced all ten quintic endpoint rows exactly, but explicitly notes 'the mathematical reduction to endpoints wasn't independently checked' and 'the paper is unrefereed with no human expert review' — so this counts as partial computational corroboration, not expert digestion, keeping status at 'partial' rather than 'resolved'. Neither result is a counterexample; both confirm the conjectured Hilbert series formula in the cases they cover, hence resolution_direction 'confirmed'. The Wikipedia article itself is unchanged since 2024 (still a stub with only the statement and two 1980s/1990s references), consistent with this being progress not yet reflected in secondary digestion.
competing_reading: The Wang–Zhang paper could be coded ai_role 'generated' rather than 'assisted': the acknowledgements credit the AI systems with generating 'proof strategies,' 'exact certificates,' and doing the actual derivation of intermediate steps, with the named human authors' visible contribution largely limited to running verification scripts and drafting/revision oversight — arguably 'the model produced the proof and the humans verified it' per §6.2's generated/assisted distinction. I coded 'assisted' because the authors describe a 'workflow' they directed and do not say a model single-handedly produced the mathematics with the humans only checking it; but with only the arXiv HTML available (no access to any interview or supplementary methods statement), the line is genuinely close.
what_would_settle_it: A supplementary methods statement, author interview, or version-history comment from Wang and Zhang clarifying the division of labor (did a human devise the reduction to Macaulay-matrix endpoints, with AI filling in only the certificate search, or did the AI produce the whole strategy end-to-end?) would settle generated vs. assisted. Expert commentary (a review, Tao-style blog digestion, or journal referee report) on either preprint would allow upgrading status from 'partial' toward 'resolved' for the sub-cases, though the conjecture as a whole would remain open regardless.

No AI system involvement was found in either paper.

counterexample.object: Two explicit 60-point subsets of the finite Abelian group Z60 x Z12 (one a translational tile that is not spectral, the other spectral but not a tile), transferred via a finite-to-infinite transference principle to bounded subsets of R^2 that are finite unions of unit squares.
counterexample.verified_how: Direct construction in a finite Abelian group, claimed to lift to R^2 by an explicit transference argument; the lifting step for the non-tiling direction is disputed (see disputes).

disputes.summary: A review on pith.science of arXiv:2607.15632 states that the non-tiling direction of Zhang's construction 'rests on a notational error that must be fixed' in the transference proof, and that if patched, the result would resolve the two-dimensional case; as printed, the paper's claim for that direction is not established. No corrected version (v2) has appeared on arXiv as of this research, and no independent expert (e.g. a named mathematician's blog, a journal, or a citing follow-up paper) has publicly verified or endorsed the result.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks about nonconvex sets in R and R^2 (the last two open dimensions of Fuglede's conjecture; counterexamples were already known for d>=3 before the frozen revision). Two relevant preprints appeared in the window, both in July 2026. (1) Tao Zhang (arXiv:2607.15632, submitted 2026-07-17, Xidian University) claims both directions of the conjecture fail in dimension two, via an explicit construction in Z60xZ12 lifted to R^2. I read the full paper (via the HTML rendering): the construction is described in detail, the acknowledgements credit only Chinese NSF/Shaanxi grant funding, and there is no mention anywhere of computer search, machine learning, or AI tools in the discovery or verification of the result. However, a review on pith.science (an independent paper-review site) reports that the non-tiling direction's transference argument, as printed, rests on a notational error ('R_k notation error') that must be corrected before the two-dimensional case can be considered resolved. I could not find any later arXiv version (only v1 exists), any citing paper, or any established mathematician's public digestion (Terence Tao's blog has no post on this, and his only Fuglede-tagged post predates the window by 15 years and concerns a different topic, the Coven-Meyerowitz conjecture). Given a live, unretracted but disputed correctness issue and no expert digestion, I classify this as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' or 'partial'. (2) Ruxi Shi (arXiv:2607.24005, submitted 2026-07-27) proves that every bounded measurable subset of R that is spectral and a union of three intervals must tile R by translation — a genuine case of the R part of the bullet (restricting to three-interval sets), with no reported error and no AI mentioned. This alone would support 'partial' status (a case settled, direction=confirmed) for the R part, but since the dimension-two claim is the larger and more central event and carries an open correctness question, I record the record's overall status as 'claimed' and describe both events here rather than picking one arbitrarily, per the instruction to describe multiple events in summary rather than invent extra records. No AI system was found to be involved in either paper: not in acknowledgements, not in described methodology (both read as traditional analytic/algebraic constructions), and a broad search for AI-mathematics breakthroughs in 2026 (which turned up unrelated results — Jacobian conjecture via 'Fable AI', unit distance problem via an OpenAI internal model, Erdos problems via DeepMind's AlphaEvolve-like system) never surfaced Fuglede's conjecture. The Wikipedia 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' page, checked independently, also does not mention Fuglede's conjecture. A tangential GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #5703) flags a Lean misformalization of the (unrelated, d>=3) 'fails in every dimension' variant, found via an automated LLM audit — but this is bookkeeping on an already-settled higher-dimensional variant, not a result on the R/R^2 case, and the project's own README states AI (AlphaProof) is used only to catch misformalizations, not to produce proofs, so this is ai_role 'none' territory and not part of this record's core event regardless.
competing_reading: One could argue the Zhang paper should be scored 'partial' with resolution_direction 'refuted' on the grounds that the tiling-direction counterexample (a tile with no spectrum) may be unaffected by the notational error, which the review says affects only the non-tiling (spectral-but-not-tiling) direction — in which case one full direction of the conjecture in dimension two would already be established as false, while the other remains claimed-but-unverified. I did not have enough detail from the review to confirm that the error is isolated to only one direction with certainty, so I did not split the record this way; if the error is confirmed to affect only one direction, the correct status might be 'partial' (one direction refuted) rather than 'claimed' (whole result pending fix). Alternatively, one could argue the correct denominator-relevant status should rest solely on the Shi three-intervals result (clearly a case, clearly correct) and treat the Zhang claim purely as 'progress', since it is unverified; I judged 'claimed' more appropriate because the author explicitly presents a complete resolution of the last open Euclidean dimension, not merely a bound.
what_would_settle_it: A corrected version of arXiv:2607.15632 (v2 or later) fixing the flagged transference-proof error, together with either a citing paper, a named mathematician's public digestion (e.g., a blog post or MathOverflow answer working through the argument), or journal acceptance, would move the dimension-two claim to 'resolved' or clarify if only 'partial'. Absent that, watching for retraction or silent abandonment (no update for a long period after a flagged error) would support reclassifying toward 'open' or 'open_stale'-adjacent treatment of the dimension-two claim specifically.

outcome: The conjecture remains open in general, but the effective bound m in Fujita's freeness conjecture (K_M ⊗ L^⊗m globally generated for m ≥ dim+1) moved twice inside the window: a 2024 preprint claiming a full solution via analytic adjoint ideal sheaves was withdrawn after a flaw was found, and a September 2026 preprint by Jingjun Han claims a linear bound m ≥ ⌈1.776n⌉, improving on the previously best-known n·log(log n) bound.
summary: The triage's three finds check out but need care in dating and scope. (1) Ghidelli–Lacini's n·log(log n) bound was first posted to arXiv as 2107.11705 in July 2021 — well before the 26 Jan 2024 frozen revision — and only its Proceedings of the LMS journal version appeared in 2024; per §6.3 the event dates to the first written argument (2021), so this is open_stale and not a change in the window, despite the journal DOI carrying a 2024 date. (2) arXiv:2411.07129 (Tsz On Mario Chan, Nov 2024) claimed a full solution to the freeness conjecture using an extension theorem with analytic adjoint ideal sheaves; it was withdrawn after Professor S. Helmke identified a flaw in the construction of a local holomorphic section on p.31 that fails to preserve the required vanishing order under extension (illustrated with an {xy=z^2}-type counterexample to the construction). This is a genuine in-window event: an AI-free claim, announced and retracted, coded progress/incident dated to the November 2024 posting. (3) arXiv:2609.01574 (Jingjun Han, posted 1 Sep 2026, v2 on 11 Sep 2026) claims a linear bound m ≥ ⌈C₀n⌉ with C₀≈1.7763, a substantial improvement over the log-log bound, obtained via a new estimate for the multiplicity of a minimal log-canonical center; the paper is only three weeks old as of the check date and has not yet been digested by experts beyond an algebraic-geometry seminar presentation at the University of Michigan announcing it as 'after Jingjun Han' — not yet a vetted result. I read the full PDF (via fetch) and found no acknowledgement of any AI, machine-learning or language-model tool in the research, and none in the withdrawn Chan preprint either. The conjecture itself (full generality, all dimensions) remains open; the freeness conjecture is proved through dimension 5 (Ye–Zhu 2020, before the window) and the very-ampleness conjecture through dimension 2. No AI involvement was found anywhere in the trail. Status is coded progress because the best-known effective bound on an open conjecture moved (twice, net downward) within the window, with one intervening incident; no case of the conjecture was fully resolved.
competing_reading: One could argue the Han preprint, being unreviewed and only weeks old, should not yet count as 'progress' at all and the record should default to open/no_change_found — but §3.1 says size is not the test and a bound that moved counts, so I keep it as progress/claimed-bound territory rather than discounting it. Separately, one could read the PLMS 2024 publication as the operative event date since journal acceptance is itself a form of expert digestion of a result that was still informally circulating — but §6.3 explicitly instructs dating by first written argument, so I did not.
what_would_settle_it: Expert digestion (a referee report, a survey, or a blog treatment by an algebraic geometer) confirming or refuting Han's linear-bound argument, and confirmation of whether the paper has since been withdrawn or revised further.

outcome: The conjecture remains open. A June 2025 self-archived HAL preprint by Idriss Aberkane claims a full elementary proof, but it has received no expert digestion, no citations, no peer review, and no discussion in any mathematical venue I could find; its author has a well-documented history of discredited self-published claims to solve famous open problems (e.g. Collatz) in predatory venues. A March 2026 UBC seminar by Doug Lind and Mike Boyle produces counterexamples to a stronger variant of the conjecture (weak* convergence of ×3-iterates of a ×2-invariant continuous measure to Lebesgue), not to the original Furstenberg conjecture as stated in this bullet, so it is out of scope under §3.1. No AI involvement was found in any of this.
summary: The frozen bullet asks: is every invariant, ergodic measure for the ×2,×3 action on the circle either Lebesgue or atomic? I could not find any result since 26 January 2024 that changes what a careful person would write in this entry. The most up-to-date technical account is Matan Tal's survey (arXiv:2110.05989), whose v13 (17 Sep 2025) states the conjecture is still open in full generality, that 'contemporary knowledge... is more or less summarized by Rudolph's Theorem' (positive entropy case), and that 'not much is known about the case of zero entropy' — i.e. no narrowing of the survey's own account of the state of the art occurred in the window. The triage flagged a June 2025 HAL preprint by Idriss J. Aberkane, 'A Low-Tech Proof of Furstenberg's ×2–×3 Conjecture' (hal-05122193), which claims a complete elementary proof using Lucas's 2-adic congruence, binary digits of powers of 3 forming Sierpiński-gasket patterns, a finite-range cellular-automaton encoding, and entropy rigidity (Rudolph/Host). I was unable to open the PDF directly (it sits behind an Anubis bot-protection challenge on HAL and multiple fetch attempts, including a browser user-agent and a text-extraction proxy, were blocked), so I could not verify the argument or check for any AI-tool disclosure inside it; nothing in any secondary source or search result mentions AI involvement in this preprint. More importantly, I found zero evidence of any expert reading it: no citations, no MathOverflow or blog discussion, no journal submission, no rebuttal. That absence is itself informative given Aberkane's documented history — Wikipedia's own article on him records that he previously claimed to have solved the Collatz conjecture in a paper mathematicians say contains errors 'at the level of a high-school or first-year college student,' published in an MDPI journal described as predatory, and that a university sought to revoke his PhD for plagiarism. Under §6.1, a preprint with no digestion is at most `claimed`, and given the complete absence of any uptake at all (not even a critical response), and the author's track record, I judge the honest classification of this specific event to be indistinguishable from noise rather than a real claimed result worth elevating the status — so I record it as background context in this summary rather than as the decisive `event`, and keep `status` at `open`/`no_change_found`. I separately found a March 2026 seminar (UBC, speaker Doug Lind with Mike Boyle) building on 2024-era work by Badea and Grivaux that produces counterexamples to a *stronger* variant of the conjecture (about weak* convergence of ×3-pushforwards of a ×2-invariant continuous measure to Lebesgue measure), explicitly framed by the speaker as not resolving the classical Furstenberg conjecture. Per §3.1 that is a related/variant problem, not a case of this one, so it does not count as a change here. I also checked the current Wikipedia articles for Hillel Furstenberg and the 'List of unsolved problems' entry itself; neither reflects any resolution or update. No Lean/Coq formalisation effort, lab announcement, or AI system's involvement with this specific conjecture turned up in any search.
competing_reading: One could argue the Aberkane preprint should be coded as `claimed` (a preprint that experts have not yet digested) purely because it exists and explicitly claims to resolve the exact bullet. Weighing against this: a `claimed` status implies a serious claim in circulation, and this preprint shows no signs of having entered circulation at all (zero citations, zero discussion anywhere I could search), combined with the author's well-documented pattern of self-published, mathematically flawed 'solutions' to famous problems posted to preprint servers without peer review. If a future pass can access the PDF directly and confirms the argument is at least superficially serious (uses real, checkable machinery rather than being obviously circular or vacuous), the correct call would shift to `claimed`, dated June 2025.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the HAL PDF (currently blocked by bot protection) to assess whether the proof is a serious, checkable attempt or an obvious non-proof; any expert commentary, rebuttal, or citation of the Aberkane preprint; confirmation of whether it was ever submitted to or rejected by a journal.

outcome: Since 26 January 2024, several genuine cases of the Gan-Gross-Prasad (GGP) conjecture — which is really a family of restriction/period statements across group types — have been settled by conventional (non-AI) mathematics: most notably a three-paper series (Boisseau-Lu-Xue, arXiv:2404.07342, 2601.01727, 2601.01738; April 2024 to January 2026) completing the proof of the global GGP conjecture and its Ichino-Ikeda refinement for Fourier-Jacobi periods on unitary groups, and a combination of two 2025 papers (Chen-Chen arXiv:2507.04355, building on prior work of P. Boisseau) settling the non-tempered local GGP conjecture for Archimedean general linear groups. A separate item the triage flagged — the (U(2n),U(1)) case and its refinement, published in Mathematische Annalen in October 2024 — is a case of predates-the-window work: the arXiv preprint (2205.09471) was first posted 19 May 2022, and the 2024 event was only the journal's online publication, which per the dating rule does not count. No AI system was found to be involved in any of this progress.
summary: The Gan-Gross-Prasad (GGP) conjecture, as Wikipedia's frozen bullet words it, is a broad restriction/period problem spanning real and p-adic Lie groups (orthogonal, unitary, GSpin, etc.), local and global versions, tempered and non-tempered representations. It is not a single yes/no statement, so no event fully resolves it; what counts under §3.1 is a genuine case (a restriction of the stated family), which several results since 26 January 2024 supply. The clearest is the Boisseau-Lu-Xue trilogy: part I (arXiv:2404.07342, submitted 10 April 2024) sets up the relative trace formula comparison for Fourier-Jacobi periods on unitary groups; part II (arXiv:2601.01727, posted 5/6 January 2026) compares the trace formulae; part III (arXiv:2601.01738, posted 5 January 2026) explicitly 'end[s] the proof of the conjectures via a reduction to the corank zero case' — completing a proof of the global GGP conjecture and its Ichino-Ikeda refinement for the Fourier-Jacobi-period case for unitary groups. This is a case of the stated problem (a restriction to a specific group type and period), settled entirely within the window, so I classify it `partial` with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the case came out as conjectured). A second, independent case was also settled in-window: Chen and Chen (arXiv:2507.04355, submitted 6 July 2025) prove the 'period implies relevance' direction of the non-tempered local GGP conjecture for Archimedean general linear groups, and state this, combined with a prior result of P. Boisseau on the converse direction, settles that whole sub-case ('this conjecture for general linear groups over Archimedean local fields is settled'). I did not independently verify Boisseau's converse-direction paper, so I treat this as strong secondary evidence for a settled case rather than as the primary event my status rests on; the Fourier-Jacobi trilogy alone is sufficient for `partial`. By contrast, the triage's first `found` item — the Springer 2024 publication of the (U(2n),U(1)) proof and its refinement — turns out to be `open_stale` material misdated by the triage: I confirmed via the arXiv abstract page (2205.09471) that version 1 was posted 19 May 2022, well before the frozen revision, and the 2024 Mathematische Annalen appearance is only the journal publication, which §6.3 explicitly says not to use for dating. I therefore treat that item as not contributing a new in-window event (though it doesn't change the overall `partial` status, since the Fourier-Jacobi case independently qualifies). The other two triage `found` items — the local twisted GL(V)/U(V) case (arXiv:2504.21002, Le, April 2025) and the GSpin Rankin-Selberg paper (arXiv:2508.09066, Yan, August 2025) — are genuine in-window preprints proving further cases/one-directions of local and global GGP respectively, reinforcing that this is an actively moving family of results, but neither is a full resolution and neither mentions AI. I searched extensively and specifically for any AI/LLM/AlphaEvolve/AlphaProof connection to GGP and found none: all identified authors are individual mathematicians (Boisseau, Lu, Xue, Chen, Chen, Le, Yan, Haan, Kwon) publishing conventional human-authored proofs, with no acknowledgement of AI assistance in any abstract, arXiv metadata, or accessible full text. The `ai_role` is therefore `none` across the board.
competing_reading: One could argue the Fourier-Jacobi-periods case and the Archimedean-GL non-tempered case are 'related problems' (variants defined over a different group/period type) rather than 'cases' of the single bullet 'Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture', in which case the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true. I reject this reading because Wikipedia's own bullet describes GGP generically as 'a restriction problem in representation theory of real or p-adic Lie groups' without restricting to a particular group type, and the mathematical literature (including the papers themselves) treats these period/group-type specializations as cases of the single GGP conjecture, not as differently-posed problems — the trace-formula machinery and the conjectural framework (multiplicity formulas, Ichino-Ikeda refinements) is explicitly the same conjecture specialized to a subfamily of groups, matching §3.1's definition of a case as a restriction rather than a change of the question.
what_would_settle_it: A survey or expert digestion (e.g. a future ICM address, Bourbaki seminar, or Tao-style blog post) explicitly stating whether the Fourier-Jacobi trilogy and the Chen-Chen/Boisseau Archimedean-GL result are considered cases of 'the' Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture versus separate named results, would remove the ambiguity between 'case' and 'related problem' for this multi-strand conjecture family.

summary: The Gauss circle problem as stated (bounding the discrepancy between the integer-lattice-point count in a circle of radius r and πr²) remains open, and I found no result since 26 January 2024 that moves the classical error-term exponent. The best known bound predates the window: Bourgain and Watt's θ = 517/824 + ε ≈ 0.6274 (2017), refined slightly by Xiaochun Li and Xuerui Yang to 2θ* ≈ 0.6289 in arXiv:2308.14859, submitted 28 August 2023 (v2, 14 September 2023) — both before the frozen revision date, so neither is a within-window event even though the Li-Yang paper remains unpublished/uncited as a later journal version. The triage's two `found` items are both variants, not cases or progress on the stated problem: arXiv:2502.06804 ('Gauss Circle Primes', Feb 2025) studies the primality of the lattice-point count C(r), a wholly different question; arXiv:2412.05485 ('The Gauss Circle Problem and Fourier Quasicrystals', Dec 2024) generalizes the counting problem to Fourier quasicrystals (non-lattice point sets), an analogue rather than a restriction of the classical question. I additionally found arXiv:2604.23918 (Apr 2026, 'Gauss circle problem over smooth numbers') which restricts to a weighted sub-sum over smooth numbers — again a variant, not a case, since it changes the summand rather than restricting the domain of the original question. I also found a paper by Theophilus Agama ('On the error term in the Gauss circle problem', appearing on ResearchGate/Academia.edu around January 2025, using a self-styled 'compression method') claiming bounds of the form O(r log r) on the error term; this is not a genuine improvement — O(r log r) is far weaker than the 1906 Sierpiński bound of O(r^(2/3)) and even weaker than Gauss's own 1837 O(r) bound, so the claim, even taken at face value, is not progress on the problem and is not corroborated by any subsequent citation, journal placement, or expert digestion; I found no arXiv listing for it (only secondary aggregator pages), and could not verify it is not a case of a known-flawed circulating manuscript. I did not count it as an event under any status because it does not constitute a change to the stated exponent bound even by the author's own numbers. I searched specifically for AI involvement (DeepMind's AlphaEvolve/AlphaProof Nexus problem lists, general LLM-for-math coverage, Terence Tao's blog, MathOverflow) and found extensive AI-driven mathematical progress in this period (Kakeya conjecture in finite fields, Erdős problems, OEIS conjectures, kissing number bounds, Hilbert functions) but no source anywhere links any AI system to the Gauss circle problem specifically.
competing_reading: One could argue the Agama 'compression method' paper, if legitimate, would count as `progress` with a direction — but its claimed bound is mathematically weaker than results already known for over a century, which is strong evidence it is either erroneous or addressing a different/looser notion of error term than the standard one; absent any expert digestion or citation validating it, I classified the overall record as `open`/`no_change_found` rather than crediting it as progress.
what_would_settle_it: A citation, journal acceptance, or expert commentary (e.g. on MathOverflow or a survey) engaging with the Agama paper would clarify whether it should be counted at all, and if so at what status. Direct access to an arXiv identifier for that paper (I could only find aggregator mirrors) would also help confirm venue and revision history.

outcome: A preprint claiming a proof that no bounded-step infinite path exists was posted 16-17 January 2024 and withdrawn within a day when the author found the moat width had been miscomputed; no other paper, computational record, or claim touching this problem has appeared since. The problem remains open.
summary: The Gaussian moat problem (does an infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes exist with bounded consecutive gaps, i.e. can one walk from the origin to infinity through Gaussian primes with bounded step size) remains open. The only relevant written argument found anywhere in or near the window is arXiv:2401.08441, 'On the Gaussian Moat Problem' by Johann Christian Stumpenhusen, which claimed to prove no such bounded-step walk exists. It was submitted 2024-01-16, revised 2024-01-17, and withdrawn the same week -- the author's own comment states 'the width of the moat was not correctly computed.' This preprint predates the frozen revision (2024-01-26) by ten days, so under a strict reading it would be dated pre-window and hence irrelevant/`open_stale`-adjacent; however, because it never actually settled anything (it was retracted almost immediately after posting, before any expert digestion, and specifically because the core computation was wrong), it is best read as an instructive incident rather than a genuine (if stale) resolution, and I classify it as `progress`/`incident` per SS6.1's 'withdrawn AI claim' pattern generalized to any withdrawn claim -- dated to the claim itself. I found no post-2024-01-26 paper, announcement, or computational record touching this problem. Two much older preprints by Madhuparna Das (arXiv:1908.10392, 'A Note on The Gaussian Moat Problem', originally 2019; and arXiv:1901.10016, 'On the Extension of the Gaussian Moat Problem', originally 2019) each received a v2 on 2024-09-06 that is a withdrawal notice -- the author states the theorems in both were incorrect (Theorem 3 in the first does not actually cover all Gaussian primes and includes non-primes; Theorems 1 and 2 in the second conflate infinitude of rational primes with infinitude of higher-dimensional analogues). These are 2019 claims being formally retracted in September 2024, not new mathematics produced in the window, so they don't constitute a window event on their own, though I note them as background. The oft-cited computational record of a moat of width k=sqrt(36) (Tsuchimura, 'Computational Results for Gaussian Moat Problem') dates to 2004/2005 -- far outside the window -- and no larger record was found. No AI system of any kind is mentioned in connection with any of these papers or with the problem generally; all searches for AI/LLM involvement returned nothing relevant.
competing_reading: One could argue the Stumpenhusen preprint's event date (2024-01-16/17) falls entirely before the frozen revision and should therefore be excluded from the record altogether (treated as if it doesn't exist, rather than as `progress`/`incident`), since the rules define `open_stale` for pre-window resolutions but don't explicitly cover a pre-window claim that was withdrawn before the window began and never touched again. Under that reading the correct status would simply be `open` with `no_change_found` true, and the Stumpenhusen episode would be mentioned only as context predating the window. I lean toward `progress`/`incident` because the withdrawal notice itself (the operative fact -- 'the moat width was not correctly computed') and the paper's v2 are both timestamped 2024-01-17, still nine days before the freeze, so even this doesn't move it into the window; this makes the `open`/`no_change_found` reading the more defensible one, and I flag it as the stronger alternative.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the pipeline intends withdrawn pre-window claims to be recorded as `progress`/`incident` (as an instructive episode worth surfacing) or simply excluded as out-of-window noise under strict dating; a clarifying rule or example covering 'claim posted and withdrawn entirely before 26 Jan 2024' would settle it. Absent that, and given the entire episode's dates precede the freeze, the safer classification is `open` with `no_change_found` true.
