corrections.by: hand correction by a human reviewer, not the researching agent and not any automated pass
corrections.why: The event this status rested on, arXiv:2401.08441 (Stumpenhusen), was submitted 16 January 2024 and withdrawn by its author within the week, both ten days *before* the 26 January 2024 snapshot; the record's own `predates_frozen_revision` is true. It is therefore doubly disqualified as movement in the window: it predates the frozen revision, and it is a claim its author retracted, so nothing about the problem moved. Worse than the Novikov case in effect, because 2024-01 is the first month on the site's time axis, so this row was being drawn on the cumulative progress chart as though it were an advance. The preprint and its withdrawal stay described in `outcome` and `summary` as a note on a still-open problem. The agent's `competing_reading` proposed this same reading.

outcome: Chen–Chen–Chen (arXiv:2411.16146, Nov 2024) proved that every divisorial contraction to a curve between terminal threefolds is a weighted blow-up under a suitable embedding, and as Theorem 1.3 deduced that there exists a surface S containing the contracted curve C with at worst Du Val singularities — i.e. a general elephant with Du Val singularities — extending the previously known irreducible-fiber case (Kollár–Mori) to this broader class of contractions. Separately, Prokhorov's paper on general elephants for extremal curve germs with reducible central curve (arXiv:2002.10693) was revised to v5 in September 2024, adding an appendix, and Mori–Prokhorov (arXiv:2410.03165, Oct 2024, v2 Apr 2025) gave a rough classification of extremal curve germs with reducible central curve that the authors note has direct consequences for the general elephant conjecture via their earlier Theorem 1.3 in a companion paper. None of this resolves the conjecture in general — flipping contractions, contractions to points, and further conic-bundle/reducible-curve configurations remain open — but each is a genuine case of the stated problem being settled, so the overall status is `partial`.
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet asks whether 'general elephants have at most Du Val singularities' for threefolds — this is M. Reid's general elephant conjecture, a long-running program (Reid 1987 origin; Kawakita 2003 for divisorial contractions to points; Kollár–Mori for irreducible-fiber extremal curve germs; Prokhorov 1996+ for Mori conic bundles) that has been settled case by case over three decades, with genuine counterexamples known in the non-Gorenstein Q-Fano setting (Iano-Fletcher) predating the window. Since 26 Jan 2024, three pieces of progress fall in the window: (1) arXiv:2411.16146 (Chen–Chen–Chen, submitted 25 Nov 2024, v1 only) proves that divisorial contractions to curves between terminal threefolds are weighted blow-ups, and its Theorem 1.3 explicitly proves the general elephant conjecture for this class (confirmed directly by fetching the paper's HTML and reading the theorem statement, which contradicts an earlier automated summary that claimed no elephant/Du-Val mention — the terms are present and central to Theorem 1.3). (2) arXiv:2002.10693 (Mori–Prokhorov-adjacent; solo Prokhorov-line paper on extremal curve germs with reducible central curve) was revised to v5 on 23 Sept 2024, adding Appendix B and correcting one introductory sentence — a within-window event but a minor revision of a paper whose substantive case (condition (*) on the curve components) was already established in earlier versions predating the window, so I did not treat the v5 date as establishing new mathematical content, only used 2411.16146 as the load-bearing event. (3) arXiv:2410.03165 (Mori–Prokhorov, Oct 2024, v2 Apr 2025) gives a rough classification of extremal curve germs with reducible central curve, which the authors note has consequences for the general elephant conjecture via a companion theorem, but I could not confirm this paper itself states a Du Val/elephant conclusion directly (fetched content showed no 'elephant' occurrence), so I treat it as related but did not use it as the primary event. All three lines of work are classical algebraic geometry (minimal model program, extremal contractions, weighted blow-ups); no source mentions AI, machine learning, or any computer-assisted proof tool. This is a case of the problem, not the whole problem: the conjecture remains open for other classes of extremal contractions (flips, more general reducible-curve and conic-bundle configurations), so status is `partial` rather than `resolved`, with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` since the settled case went the conjectured way (Du Val singularities do occur, no counterexample in this class).
competing_reading: One could argue this is really an `open` record because the *general* conjecture (as loosely worded by Wikipedia, with no restriction to a class of contractions) is unresolved and always has been, and the incremental case-by-case literature has existed since the 1990s — so nothing distinctively new happened 'to the problem' in the sense a casual reader of the Wikipedia bullet would mean. Under §3.1's rule, however, a settled case of the stated question counts as `partial`, and Theorem 1.3 of 2411.16146 is squarely a case (divisorial contractions to curves) of the stated question (do general elephants have Du Val singularities), so I classify it as `partial` rather than `open`.
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution would require settling the conjecture for the remaining classes of extremal contractions (flipping contractions and the remaining reducible-central-curve / conic-bundle cases), or a counterexample within the terminal threefolds setting (as opposed to the known non-Gorenstein Q-Fano counterexamples, which are for a different, related global existence-of-elephant question rather than the local Du Val question).

outcome: GRH itself remains fully open with no resolution, disproof, or narrowing of the existential question; the only movement in the window is ordinary analytic-number-theory progress on zero-density and equivalence results for Dirichlet L-functions, all human-authored with no AI involvement, alongside one non-credible self-published 'AI-assisted proof' claim that never reached arXiv or gained any expert traction.
summary: Since the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, GRH — do the nontrivial zeros of all Dirichlet L-functions lie on the critical line 1/2+it — remains open, and I found no credible claim to the contrary. The Wikipedia article itself (fetched live, not the frozen revision, purely to check whether its lead now records any change) has not been updated with any 2024-2026 development and still describes GRH as unproven outside the algebraic function-field case; its most recent cited item (Dunn-Radziwill, 2021) predates the window. Two lines of genuine, human-authored analytic number theory moved bounds relevant to GRH within the window, both counting as `progress` rather than `partial` or `resolved` because they narrow error terms or establish conditional equivalences without settling any case of the existential question: (1) Bin Chen, 'Large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, and the density of zeros of Dirichlet's L-functions' (arXiv:2507.08296, submitted 11 July 2025, revised July 2026), which extends the Guth-Maynard large-value-estimate method (originally for the Riemann zeta function) to Dirichlet L-functions and improves the zero-density exponent from Huxley's 12/5 to 7/3 — an unconditional bound on how many zeros of Dirichlet L-functions can lie off the critical line at a given height, not a proof that none do. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the abstract or accessible metadata. (2) Kohji Suzuki, arXiv:2508.17701 ('Detecting zeros of Dirichlet L-functions via the Riemann zeta-function', August 2025), which — conditional on the ordinary Riemann Hypothesis — proves an equivalence between a distributional property of zeta zeros and GRH for Dirichlet L-functions. This is a related/conditional structural result, not unconditional progress toward or against GRH, and per §3.1 would not by itself move the classification; it is the triage's own found item and I confirm its characterization. I also investigated a self-published item the triage's queries did not surface: M. Sghiar's ResearchGate posting 'A Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Assisted by Artificial Intelligence: An Analytic Approach' (and an earlier 'Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis by ChatGPT'), which explicitly claims ChatGPT assistance in deriving a purported proof. This item never appeared on arXiv, has no journal acceptance, no expert digestion, and no evidence of even preliminary community engagement beyond the author's own postings — it sits alongside a long-running genre of crank RH proofs (Sghiar himself and others have posted many such claims over years). Because it never gained traction, was never checked by anyone besides the author, and concerns RH/GRH generally rather than being a distinct dated event that was 'announced then withdrawn', it does not meet the bar for `claimed` (no expert or institutional uptake at all) and does not fit `incident` cleanly either (nothing was ever accepted enough to need withdrawing). I record it here as color rather than as the event the status rests on; it does not change the classification. Net: the correct classification is `progress` (a real, human-only bound moved) rather than `open`/`no_change_found`, and `ai_role` is `none` because no AI system contributed to any result that actually changed the mathematical record — the only AI-attributed claim never entered the corpus of accepted results.
competing_reading: One could argue the status should be `open` with `no_change_found` true, treating Bin Chen's zero-density improvement as too incremental or too far from the existential GRH question (an 'are there any off-line zeros' question, which per §3.1's rule that record/bound movements don't count for existence questions might seem excluded). I read `progress` as correct because §3.1's exclusion is specifically for record-of-largest-known-object or verified-search-limit style non-events, whereas a zero-density theorem is a genuine analytic bound of the kind §6.1 explicitly assigns to `progress` ('a bound moved'). If a stricter reading is preferred, the honest fallback is `open` with `no_change_found` true and this progress noted as context that does not itself count.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the pipeline's status taxonomy treats an unconditional zero-density exponent improvement for the exact L-function family in the bullet's statement as a qualifying 'bound moved' (favoring `progress`) or as insufficiently connected to the existential question to count at all (favoring `open`/`no_change_found`).

outcome: No progress, partial result, or AI involvement was found for the generalized star-height problem since 26 January 2024; it remains open exactly as Wikipedia and the literature state.
summary: The generalized star-height problem (Brzozowski, 1980) asks whether every regular language can be described by a generalized regular expression (regular expressions plus complement) with bounded nesting depth of Kleene stars, and whether the minimum required depth is computable. It is a genuinely hard, narrow open problem: it is not even known whether a language of generalized star-height 2 exists (only height 0 and 1 are known to be realized). I checked the dedicated Wikipedia article 'Generalized star-height problem', which is a stub whose most recent citation is Sakarovitch (2009) and which was last touched only for routine maintenance (page last edited 2026-08-27, with no content change reflecting new research); the related 'Star height problem' article gives the same picture. I ran arXiv-focused searches (general and author-specific, e.g. for Tom Bourne and Nik Ruškuc, whose 2020-era work on Rees matrix semigroups and modular-subword languages is the most recent substantive progress I could locate, predating the window), checked the current cs.FL arXiv listing (16-22 September 2026) for any related submissions, and searched broadly for any claim of resolution, partial result, or AI-related work (including an AI-and-math angle) touching this problem. All searches turned up only pre-2024 material (1980s survey-era results through Bourne-Ruškuc's papers from the late 2010s/2020) or general encyclopedia pages restating the open status. One search result surfaced a GitHub repository under an org called 'vibemathing' titled 'problem-wikipedia-...: Vibe Mathing single-problem candidate research: Generalized star height problem' — this is evidently tooling/output from this same dataset-building effort (or a similar one), not an independent mathematical source, so I disregarded it per the instruction to work from primary sources only. No preprint, announcement, Lean/Coq formalization, or lab report addressing this problem in the 26 January 2024–22 September 2026 window was found. The triage's 'none' verdict is confirmed: this is a genuine case of 'nothing happened', and the record here documents that conclusion with the searches that support it.
competing_reading: None found. There is no genuine ambiguity here: no candidate result of any kind (resolution, case, bound, or AI-related incident) turned up in any search, so there is no alternative classification worth weighing.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper either (a) exhibiting a regular language of generalized star-height exactly 2 (settling the long-standing question of whether height >1 is ever needed), (b) proving no such language exists, or (c) giving an algorithm (or undecidability proof) for computing generalized star-height — together with expert digestion (e.g., citation/discussion in a survey, journal acceptance, or a specialist blog) confirming the argument holds up.

outcome: The conjecture itself remains open, but the best proven lower bound on the Steiner ratio moved twice: from 0.824168 (Chung & Graham, 1985) to a certified 0.8559 (Ke, Huang, Shu, He, Gai & Wang, arXiv 2601.22365, posted 29 Jan 2026), using an LLM-driven system to generate geometric lemmas verified by computer algebra, and then to a further, asterisked 0.860 (= 43/50) certificate-layer bound (J. Savva, PR merged into Terence Tao's optimizationproblems repo, 1 Sep 2026) that is conditional on unproven lemmas from the first paper and was itself produced largely by an AI system (Claude Fable 5) under human direction.

ai.basis_quote: Rather than directly prompting LLMs to solve the conjecture, we task them with generating rule-constrained geometric lemmas implemented as executable code... The LLM acts solely as a reasoning engine, offloading all validation tasks to Mathematica to perform exact computations... more than 80% of LLM-proposed lemmas are effective.
ai.disclosed_cost: Approximately 0.5M tokens (~35K per round) and 4.6 hours of reasoning across the run; total monetary cost of 'just a few hundred dollars' (Ke et al., arXiv 2601.22365). The Savva follow-up (GitHub PR #159) discloses no separate token/compute cost figure.

summary: The Gilbert-Pollak/Steiner-ratio conjecture (Steiner ratio = √3/2 ≈ 0.86603) remains open: no proof or disproof has appeared in the window, and Wikipedia's dedicated 'Gilbert–Pollak conjecture' article (checked live) still describes it as unproven, still referencing the retracted 1990 Du-Hwang PNAS proof (found to have a serious gap) and the follow-on Rubinstein-Weng work that inherits the same gap — all pre-2024 history, not counted here. What did happen in-window is movement on the best certified *lower bound* for the ratio, which had sat at ~0.824168 (Chung & Graham, 1985) for roughly four decades. On 29 Jan 2026, Ke et al. (arXiv:2601.22365, 'Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via Large Language Models') reported a system in which GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Pro generate candidate geometric lemmas as executable code, which are then validated deterministically in Mathematica; a layer of these machine-checked lemmas supports a certified new lower bound of 0.8559. The authors are explicit that the LLMs only propose lemmas (mathematical content that ends up in the certificate) while all verification is symbolic/exact — this is authors'-own-account AI involvement in producing part of the mathematics in the result, so ai_role is 'assisted' rather than 'generated' (the humans/algebra system, not the LLM, established correctness, and the LLM did not produce the whole proof/bound autonomously) and not 'bound'-only since the lemmas are genuine mathematical content, not just a numeric improvement produced by search. A second event, a GitHub pull request (#159) to Terence Tao's 'optimizationproblems' repository merged 1 Sep 2026, pushes the bound further to 0.860 (exact 43/50) via an independently-built, clean-room certificate layer verifying over 1.1 billion regions; but this second bound is explicitly asterisked in the repo's README and constants/43a.md as 'conditional on the lemma set of KHSHGW2026' (i.e., it inherits the first paper's not-fully-independently-vetted lemmas), so the repo itself treats 0.8559 as the safely certified value and 0.860 as provisional. The PR's own text states the software, analysis and paper were produced by 'an AI system (Claude Fable 5, Anthropic) working under my [Savva's] direction' — again an authors'-own-account claim of AI producing mathematics-bearing artifacts (the verification software and analysis), so this too is coded 'assisted' under the human submitter's direction rather than 'generated'. Neither event resolves any case of the conjecture in either direction (the ratio itself is still unknown, bounded strictly below the conjectured value), so resolution_direction is null and status is 'progress' (a bound moved on a problem that remains open), per §6.1/§6.4. I treat this as a single record with two AI systems groups reported (Ke et al.'s GPT-5/Gemini 3 Pro, and Savva's Claude Fable 5) since both are genuine in-window bound-moving events on the same problem; per the instructions I did not invent a second record for the second event.
competing_reading: One could argue the Ke et al. LLM contribution is better coded 'bound' rather than 'assisted', since ultimately what changed is a numeric constant on an open problem and the LLM's lemmas are themselves just inputs to a numerical/algebraic certificate rather than a human-legible proof step. I judged 'assisted' more faithful because the authors' own account frames the LLM as generating actual geometric lemmas (mathematical content, not merely search over parameters), and 80%+ of proposed lemmas were usable — closer to 'the model produced part of the argument' than to 'the model tuned a bound'. Similarly, one could read the 0.860 PR as 'incident' if one considers the conditional/asterisked bound to have been effectively later disowned by the repository maintainers as not fully certified — but the README does not withdraw it, it merely annotates it as conditional, so I kept it as 'progress' rather than 'incident'.
what_would_settle_it: Whether a later paper proves the KHSHGW2026 lemma set unconditionally (which would de-asterisk the 0.860 bound), and whether any subsequent work pushes the certified bound closer to √3/2 or, in the other direction, produces an actual proof or disproof of the full conjecture.

outcome: Gilbreath's conjecture itself remains open, but Chase, Hunter and Tao (arXiv:2607.08712, Jul 2026) prove the analogue of the conjecture holds almost surely for a Cramér random model of prime gaps, and give a deterministic inverse theorem showing the only ways a Gilbreath array can fail to have a {0,1}-valued first entry are (i) long blocks of zeroes or (ii) very long shallow {0,d}-valued blocks (d≥2) — a genuine structural narrowing of what would have to happen for the real conjecture to fail, though it does not settle any case of the conjecture for actual primes.

disputes.summary: A separate July 2026 preprint by Vincent Granville, 'Piercing Gilbreath's Conjecture: From Deep Number Theory Insights to Fintech and Cybersecurity' (arXiv:2607.04166), claims 'a precise path to the solution' via a 'reverse sieving' method. Independent assessment found the proof route runs through a conjecture (its Conjecture 5.1(4)) that is essentially as hard as Gilbreath's conjecture itself, so the paper does not deliver a genuine proof strategy despite its framing; its computational observations (reverse sieving, 'magic primes', forbidden constellations) are credited as novel but incidental. This is not counted as progress on the conjecture's scope under §3.1, since no case or bound was actually settled.

summary: Gilbreath's conjecture — that the leftmost entries of the triangular array of iterated absolute differences of consecutive primes are all 1 after the first row — remains unresolved as of September 2026. The most substantive development in the window is Chase, Hunter and Tao, 'Gilbreath's conjecture: a Cramér random model and a deterministic analysis' (arXiv:2607.08712, submitted 9 July 2026, also summarized on Tao's blog the same week). They prove that a probabilistic analogue of the conjecture (prime gaps replaced by independent geometric random variables per the Cramér heuristic model of primes) holds almost surely, and separately give an unconditional 'deterministic inverse theorem' (their Theorem 1.6) that pins down the only two ways an actual Gilbreath array could fail to be {0,1}-valued at the first entry: a long run of zero differences, or a long run of shallow {0,d}-valued differences for some fixed d≥2. This is structural progress that changes what a careful person would need to rule out to prove the real conjecture — it narrows the space of potential obstructions — but it explicitly does not resolve any case of the conjecture for actual primes; the authors state they 'cannot (personally) resolve Gilbreath's conjecture.' I classify this as status 'progress' rather than 'partial', since no case of the stated conjecture (a universal claim about primes) was settled, in either direction — the random-model result is a related/heuristic model, not a restriction of the actual problem to a sub-case, and the inverse theorem is conditional/structural rather than a settled instance. The paper's acknowledgements state plainly: 'Gemini was used to generate the code for Figure 1' (a Monte Carlo plot of constants in the continuous model) — this is not mathematics appearing in the result, only plotting code, so ai_role is 'none' per §6.2's instruction that code generation for figures does not count as AI involvement in the mathematics. No other AI system is mentioned anywhere in the paper, Tao's blog post, or secondary coverage I found. Separately, computational verification of the conjecture (not a resolution, per §3.1's rule that existence/pattern-search extensions don't count) was extended: Simon Plouffe verified up to 10^14 (arXiv:2510.06688, Oct 2025), and per the current Wikipedia article, Jean-François Colonna later extended this to 2×10^14 (2025) and 1.5×10^15 (2026) — these are recorded as background but do not change the status, being existence-type range extensions explicitly excluded by §3.1. I also found and read a second July 2026 preprint, Vincent Granville's 'Piercing Gilbreath's Conjecture' (arXiv:2607.04166), which claims to present 'a precise path to the solution'; an independent critical assessment I found concludes its proof route depends on an unproved conjecture of comparable difficulty to Gilbreath's conjecture itself, so it does not constitute genuine progress toward resolution despite the framing, and I have not counted it as a status-changing event. I checked the current (September 2026) Wikipedia article on Gilbreath's conjecture directly: it explicitly still states 'The conjecture remains an open problem,' and does not yet mention the Chase-Hunter-Tao or Granville papers, only the Plouffe/Colonna computational verifications. I also confirmed the triage's characterization of the Chase-Hunter-Tao paper is essentially accurate: it correctly distinguishes this from computational verification and correctly notes the conjecture remains open.
competing_reading: One could argue the Cramér random model result, combined with the inverse theorem, is close enough to a case of the conjecture (i.e., 'the conjecture holds under the Cramér heuristic model of primes') to count as 'partial' rather than 'progress', since a genuine mathematical statement was proved rather than merely a bound moved. Against this: the Cramér random model is a different (probabilistic) object, not a restriction obtained by narrowing the domain of the original statement about actual primes — it is closer to a 'related problem' under §3.1's variant test, since the model replaces the object of study (primes) with i.i.d. random variables. I lean 'progress' because the inverse theorem is the piece that most directly bears on the real conjecture (an unconditional structural fact about any Gilbreath array, prime-derived or not), and 'progress' better captures 'a bound moved, or an instructive incident'-adjacent structural narrowing without overclaiming a settled case.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that actual prime gaps cannot produce arbitrarily long zero-blocks or long shallow {0,d}-blocks in the Gilbreath array — which the paper notes would follow from (but is stronger than needed, and harder than) a Cramér-type bound on prime gaps — would resolve the conjecture outright via the authors' own inverse theorem.

outcome: No proof, disproof, partial resolution, or AI-related result affecting Gillies' conjecture on the distribution of prime divisors of Mersenne numbers was found between 26 January 2024 and today; the conjecture remains open with only empirical (pre-2024) support and continues to conflict with the also-open Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture.
summary: Gillies' conjecture (1964) concerns the distribution of prime divisors of Mersenne numbers M_p = 2^p - 1, modeling divisor counts as approximately Poisson-distributed; it is known to conflict with the widely-accepted but also-open Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture (predictions differ by about 11%). I checked the current Wikipedia article on the conjecture, which states plainly that it 'remains open' with only empirical support accumulated over past decades, and found no update reflecting any post-January-2024 development. I confirmed the triage's finding that Kovac–Luca's June 2025 arXiv paper 'On the number of divisors of Mersenne numbers' (arXiv:2506.04883) does not touch Gillies' conjecture at all — it proves an unrelated Erdos question, that the ratio f(2n)/f(n) (where f(n) is the cumulative sum of divisor counts τ(2^k-1) for k up to n) is unbounded. This is a genuinely different mathematical object (a cumulative sum of divisor counts across many exponents, not the distribution of prime divisors of a single Mersenne number) and a different question (boundedness of a ratio, not the Poisson-type distributional claim Gillies made), so per §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case of this one, and does not count as a change to this bullet. I found no other papers, preprints, announcements, or discussions from the window that engage with Gillies' specific conjecture, and no mention of any AI system in connection with it. The October 2024 discovery of the 18th Mersenne prime (M136279841, via GIMPS using an Nvidia GPU) is unrelated — it is a single new record prime, not a distributional or divisor-count result, and per §3.1 an existence/discovery event does not move a distributional conjecture. No credible source suggests any AI system has been applied to Gillies' conjecture specifically.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kovac–Luca paper is adjacent enough (same underlying arithmetic function τ(2^k-1), same author lineage citing Gillies' heuristic as motivation) that it constitutes 'progress in the surrounding area,' but it does not change what a careful reader would write in the Gillies'-conjecture bullet itself: the Poisson-type distributional claim about prime divisors of individual Mersenne numbers is untouched, so I do not think this rises even to 'progress' under §3.1.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint since 26 January 2024 that proves, disproves, refines the constant in, or settles a genuine restricted case of Gillies' own distributional/Poisson-model conjecture about prime divisors of M_p, or credible reporting of an AI system being applied to exactly that question.

outcome: The general problem (a combinatorial rule for all Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,mu,nu)) remains open, but Pak, Panova and Swanson (arXiv:2511.02312, first posted 4 November 2025) proved an explicit positive combinatorial interpretation, via counting certain marked trees, for the rectangular Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,(n^k),(n^k)) in the special case where lambda has at most two rows -- a genuine settled sub-case of the stated problem, not merely a related/variant problem.
summary: The stated problem -- give a combinatorial interpretation of the Kronecker coefficients in general -- remains open as of September 2026; the Wikipedia article on Kronecker coefficients still states this plainly and cites no resolution. Since the frozen revision date, two lines of genuine mathematical progress appeared. (1) Pak, Panova, Swanson, 'A combinatorial interpretation for certain plethysm and Kronecker coefficients' (arXiv:2511.02312, v1 posted 2025-11-04, revised through v3 on 2026-07-27), give an explicit positive rule -- counting certain marked trees -- for plethysm coefficients, which in the special case mu=(n) specializes to a combinatorial interpretation for the rectangular Kronecker coefficients g(lambda,(n^k),(n^k)) when lambda has at most two rows. This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem (a class of Kronecker coefficients, not a different question), so it counts as `partial` per the case/variant test in section 3.1: it removes real territory (all two-row-lambda rectangular cases) from the open problem, in the confirming direction (the object sought -- a positive combinatorial rule -- was shown to exist for this class). I read the full HTML/PDF text via WebFetch (introduction and available body text); no acknowledgements section or methods statement mentioning AI, machine learning, computer algebra search, or automated proof discovery appeared anywhere in the retrieved text, and the authors describe a traditional tree-theoretic proof technique. (2) Harman and Wilson, 'Kronecker Coefficients, Crystals, and Bitableaux' (arXiv:2507.14026, posted 2025-07-18), introduce 'bitableaux' as candidate combinatorial objects and reduce the general problem to a purified combinatorial conjecture, additionally proving a combinatorial expansion in the monomial-symmetric-function basis (weaker than a fully positive Schur-basis rule). This is progress/partial-flavored but is subsumed by the Pak-Panova-Swanson dating for the decisive event; I treat it as supporting context in `summary` rather than a second record, per the instruction to fold multiple events for one problem into the single decisive one. Separately, I found a cluster of machine-learning papers on Kronecker coefficients: Lee, 'Data-scientific study of Kronecker coefficients' (arXiv:2310.17906, 2023, predates the window) and Butbaia, Lee, Ruehle, 'Interpretable Machine Learning for Kronecker Coefficients' (arXiv:2502.11774, posted 2025-02-17), which train neural networks (including transformers, >99% accuracy) and interpretable models to predict whether a given Kronecker coefficient is zero or nonzero, and extract an ML-derived decision function in terms of 'b-loadings.' This is a different question from the stated problem: predicting vanishing is not a combinatorial rule for the value of g(lambda,mu,nu), and the paper itself does not claim to supply one -- it is a related/variant problem under section 3.1, not a case of this one, so it does not move the status and involves no claimed AI role in producing a result that is in scope here. No withdrawal, retraction, or dispute was found for any of these papers.
competing_reading: One could argue the ML vanishing-prediction papers (2310.17906, 2502.11774) are close enough to count as 'progress' with ai_role bound/assisted, since they do bear on Kronecker coefficients and use genuine AI systems (transformers). I judged them out of scope because the stated problem asks for a combinatorial interpretation (a rule explaining the value/multiplicity), whereas these papers only classify zero-vs-nonzero using black-box or semi-interpretable statistical models and do not produce, or claim to produce, a combinatorial formula -- so under section 3.1 they change a different bullet (nonvanishing/complexity questions), not this one. If a future reader takes a looser scope reading in which any AI-assisted numerical/structural insight about Kronecker coefficients counts, this record would need to add ai_role bound or assisted for those papers alongside a second, separate open question about vanishing.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the ML papers should be scoped into this bullet turns on the exact wording a careful reader would use for 'combinatorial interpretation' -- if that phrase is read broadly enough to include any explicit rule (even ML-derived heuristics) for a related invariant, the classification would need to change; a statement from the authors of the ML papers claiming their decision function constitutes a combinatorial interpretation (rather than a predictive classifier) would settle it in favor of inclusion.

outcome: The lower bound on HJ(3,3) — the Hales-Jewett number giving the smallest dimension in which a width-3 (3-in-a-row) n-dimensional tic-tac-toe board cannot end in a draw, hence guarantees X a winning strategy by strategy-stealing — moved twice in 2026: from the pre-existing van der Waerden-derived bound of 13 to 14 (Conlon, Farnsworth, Robertson, SAT-solver search), then superseded by a much stronger bound of 22 (Mouhib, Halbeisen, symmetric-coloring SAT search). The problem itself — the exact smallest dimension — remains open.

ai.disclosed_cost: Conlon/Farnsworth/Robertson report the SAT search required 8831 CPU hours (about 367 days), distributed across 15 cores, supported by Colgate University Research Computing and the Colgate Supercomputer.

disputes.summary: Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson's paper (arXiv:2607.18111, v1 submitted 2026-07-20) proves HJ(3;3)>=14 using a SAT-solver-based extension of van der Waerden constructions, but its Remark 9 explicitly notes that concurrent/prior work by Mouhib and Halbeisen (arXiv:2606.22155, v1 submitted 2026-06-20, one month earlier) already proved the much stronger HJ(3,3)>=22 using symmetric colorings, and that this was announced at Rutgers' Experimental Math Seminar before their own paper's results were presented. The two results are not in tension mathematically (22 is simply a better bound than 14), but the near-simultaneous, partly overlapping announcements are worth recording as a priority/overlap situation rather than two independent unrelated advances.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks: given the width of a tic-tac-toe board (i.e. the winning line length t), what is the smallest dimension n such that X is guaranteed a win — this is the n-in-a-row generalization tied to the Hales-Jewett theorem, since a coloring-free (draw-free) dimension implies a first-player win by strategy-stealing. For the classical width t=3 (three-in-a-row, as in ordinary tic-tac-toe), this is the Hales-Jewett number HJ(3,3) (using 3 colors/players' turn-parity coloring convention as in the cited literature) or more precisely the 3-color Hales-Jewett number relevant to the 2-player draw-avoidance question. Before the frozen revision date, the best known lower bound on HJ(3,3) stood at 13, obtained via classical van der Waerden number constructions (per arXiv:2607.18111's own account of 'Corollary 7'); no exact value is known and none has ever been computed for HJ(3,3). In the window, two SAT-solver-based preprints appeared in mid-2026: Mouhib and Halbeisen (arXiv:2606.22155, submitted 2026-06-20) proved HJ(3,3)>=22 (and HJ(4,2)>=14) via coordinate-symmetric colorings reduced to a polynomial-size constraint-satisfaction problem, certified by an explicit, hand-auditable table of under 600 cells; and independently, Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson (arXiv:2607.18111, submitted 2026-07-20) proved HJ(3;3)>=14 via a SAT-solver-extended van der Waerden construction (using CryptoMiniSat and Kissat, ~8831 CPU-hours), while explicitly acknowledging in Remark 9 that Mouhib and Halbeisen's concurrent/earlier-announced result already superseded their bound. Both papers rely exclusively on SAT solvers and exhaustive/constraint-based verification — no AI or machine-learning system (neural network, LLM, MCTS-guided solver such as AlphaMapleSAT, or similar) is used or mentioned anywhere in either paper; per DEEP_DIVE.md's own rule, SAT solvers and certified constraint search do not count as AI systems. I searched specifically for AI/ML tool usage (e.g. AlphaMapleSAT, which exists and has been used for related Ramsey/van der Waerden-type SAT problems) and found no evidence it, or any comparable AI-assisted SAT solver, was used for HJ(3,3) or HJ(4,2) in either 2026 paper. The problem — the exact minimal dimension for X's guaranteed win at width 3 — remains open; what moved is a lower bound, which is the correct classification as `progress` (an existence-type record like this only 'moves' the problem when the exact value or a matching upper bound is found, not when a bound is pushed further, per DEEP_DIVE §3.1's rule on records versus the underlying question — though here it is explicitly the bound itself, not a proxy record, that is asked about implicitly via HJ; I classify it as progress on the underlying Hales-Jewett dimension question, which the bullet is ultimately about).
competing_reading: One could argue this bullet is really an infinitude/exact-value question ("what is the smallest dimension") and that moving a lower bound is analogous to the disallowed case in DEEP_DIVE §3.1 of 'a record extended' not counting as progress on an existence question. However, that rule is aimed at record/witness constructions for existence questions (e.g. largest known prime), not at bounds on a well-defined finite quantity (HJ(3,3) is known to be finite and exact by the Hales-Jewett theorem itself); narrowing the interval in which that finite number must lie is direct, quantitative progress on the question asked, unlike, e.g., merely exhibiting one more example. I therefore classify as `progress` rather than leaving as strictly `open` with no_change_found, but flag this as the closest judgment call in the record.
what_would_settle_it: An exact determination of HJ(3,3) (matching upper and lower bounds), or an explicit winning strategy construction for X at a specific dimension n together with a proof that no strategy (or draw) exists at n-1, would settle the underlying bullet. Short of that, any further published bound (lower or upper) narrowing the interval would be the next relevant event to check for.

summary: The GNRS (planar embedding) conjecture, that every minor-closed family of graphs other than the family of all graphs has bounded-distortion embeddings into l1, remains open as of September 2026. The current Wikipedia article (fetched live, last edited 27 December 2025) still lists the conjecture as unresolved, with the only proved special cases being series-parallel/K4-minor-free graphs, O(1)-outerplanar graphs, bounded-pathwidth graphs, and 2-clique-sums of bounded-size graphs -- all results that predate the 26 January 2024 frozen revision (Lee-Sidiropoulos 2013, Lee-Poore 2013, Chekuri et al. 2006, Gupta-Newman-Rabinovich-Sinclair's own original partial results). No arXiv preprint, conference paper, or announcement in the 26 January 2024-September 2026 window claims to prove, disprove, or settle a new nontrivial case of the conjecture itself. Several adjacent papers surfaced in search but were checked and ruled out as variants rather than cases of GNRS: (1) Chang et al., 'Embedding Planar Graphs into Graphs of Treewidth O(log^3 n)' (arXiv:2411.00216, 2024-2025) addresses a different conjecture -- embedding planar graphs with (1+epsilon)-distortion into bounded-treewidth graphs, not l1 embeddings with O(1) distortion; confirmed via WebFetch that the paper explicitly treats this as a distinct problem. (2) 'Improved Lower Bounds on Multiflow-Multicut Gaps' (arXiv:2507.06576, 2025) improves a flow-cut gap lower bound for cactus graphs (a subclass of planar graphs) from 2 to 16/7, but this is a lower bound on a related but different quantity (the multiflow-multicut gap, which is bounded above by results implying GNRS-type embeddings but is not itself the l1-distortion constant), and the paper does not claim to move GNRS's own bound; it neither resolves a case of GNRS nor changes what would be written in this bullet. (3) Filtser's 'A face cover perspective to l1 embeddings of planar graphs' appeared in its journal form in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in 2025, but this is a journal publication of a SODA 2020 preprint (arXiv:1903.02758) -- the underlying result predates the window, and in any case only bounds distortion for planar metrics with bounded face-cover number, not full planar graphs, so it does not settle the planar case of GNRS either before or after the frozen date. No AI system was found associated with any of this work; none of the papers reviewed mention any AI/LLM involvement, and a targeted search for AI-related claims about GNRS turned up nothing.
competing_reading: None of the adjacent papers found are close enough calls to warrant a different classification; each addresses a demonstrably different mathematical question (bounded-treewidth stochastic embeddings, or multiflow-multicut gap lower bounds for a graph subclass) rather than restricting the GNRS statement itself. The one item worth flagging as a genuine boundary case is the Filtser ACM ToA 2025 publication: if a reader were to treat any 2025-dated appearance of a result as a 'change,' they might mark this as `progress`, but the mathematical content (face-cover-based distortion bounds) was already public via the 2020 SODA paper and 2019 arXiv preprint, so by the rule of dating to the first public written argument this is `open_stale` at most for that narrow sub-result, not a new development in the window, and it does not resolve a stated case of GNRS as posed (it bounds a parameter-dependent quantity, not distortion for all planar graphs).
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement that either (a) proves bounded l1-distortion embeddings exist for all planar graphs or all treewidth-3 graphs (long-open special cases), (b) exhibits a minor-closed family requiring unbounded distortion (a disproof), or (c) proves the general conjecture for all minor-closed families. Absent that, checking the current arXiv listings under math.MG and cs.DS for 'GNRS conjecture' or 'planar embedding conjecture' periodically would catch any future development.

outcome: The conjecture (every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes) remains open: no proof, disproof, or verified case-resolution has appeared since 26 January 2024. The strongest genuinely new result found in the window is an unrelated bound on Goldbach numbers in short intervals (a related problem, not a case of the stated conjecture), and every AI-adjacent item found is either non-credible, unmerged/unverified, or produced no mathematical content that changes the stated conjecture.
summary: The Goldbach conjecture (every even natural number > 2 is the sum of two primes) is untouched in the window 26 Jan 2024 - present: no proof, disproof, or settlement of any case was found. The conjecture is still verified computationally only up to 4×10^18 (a 2013-era bound; per §3.1, further verification would not count as progress on an existence/infinitude-type question in any case, and no extension of that bound was found or claimed). The closest thing to real mathematical progress found is Chirre & Hagen, 'On Goldbach Numbers in Short Intervals' (arXiv 2512.23534, a 2025-vintage preprint number under the 2512.* scheme), which assuming RH improves the constant for the shortest interval guaranteed to contain a Goldbach number from 9696 (Cully-Hugill & Dudek) to 123. This is a genuine, human-authored, non-AI advance, but it is about a different, related question (existence of a Goldbach number in a short interval, conditional on RH) rather than a case of the stated conjecture itself, so per §3.1 it does not change this bullet's status and is recorded here only for completeness — it does not count as `progress` on this record. On the AI side, three lines of 'evidence' were checked and all rejected: (1) an article ('GPT-6 Astra Unveils Major Breakthrough...', 36kr.com) claiming an AI model proved a 'weak Liouville form' of Goldbach; the article itself carries a publication date of 21 September 2026 in the future relative to when it was retrieved, cites no verifiable arXiv or Lean artifact, and reads as speculative/fabricated content, not a real result — discarded entirely. (2) A GitHub issue (#3952, opened 6 May 2026 by an outside contributor 'Suro-One') titled 'Erdős Problem 242 (Erdős-Straus) and Goldbach Conjecture resolved', linking to a personal repository (Suro-One/auro-zera_Erdos-Straus_proof) containing a file 'GoldbachZera.lean'. This is an unsolicited, unmerged, unreviewed external submission to DeepMind's formal-conjectures issue tracker; nothing indicates it was accepted, verified, or endorsed by DeepMind or any mathematician, and the repository's own open/closed status pattern (multiple other issues flag 'status mismatch' between the repo and problem-tracking sites) gives no indication Goldbach's status was ever changed to solved. Under §6.1 an unreviewed claim by an unknown party is not even `claimed`-worthy without further corroboration, and no corroboration exists — treated as noise. (3) A ScienceDirect article ('Bridging Mathematics and AI: A novel approach to Goldbach's Conjecture') and a dev.to post describing an 'AI research engine' finding a Chebyshev-bias-like pattern in Goldbach data are exploratory/heuristic studies using LLMs or search tools to look for patterns in already-verified computational data; neither produces a proof, a case-resolution, or a bound on the open conjecture, so under §6.2 they are `ai_role: none` even if they existed at the level of a 'finding' (which they do not, at the level of this conjecture). Overall: no status change, no credible AI involvement of any kind that touches the stated conjecture.
competing_reading: If the DeepMind formal-conjectures issue #3952 (or the underlying Lean file) turned out to compile without `sorry` and were independently confirmed as a sound proof, this record would need to move to `claimed` or higher with `ai_role` depending on how the proof was produced. This was not verified: the Lean file's contents could not be inspected in enough detail (10,000+ lines, page renders as GitHub metadata only) to rule out that it compiles, though an unsolicited, unmerged, unreviewed submission of this kind — bearing all the hallmarks of the many uncredited crank 'proofs' the triage record already flagged (ResearchGate, preprints.org, academia.edu, vixra) — is exactly the pattern the triage was right to dismiss.
what_would_settle_it: Independent compilation of Suro-One's GoldbachZera.lean against a trusted mathlib/Lean toolchain (checking for `sorry`, unsound axioms, or a mismatch between the formalized statement and the actual Goldbach conjecture), and/or any acknowledgement from DeepMind, a number theorist, or a math-news outlet that the issue was taken seriously rather than closed/ignored as spam.

disputes.summary: A September 2026 viral claim (via 36kr.com, KuCoin news, and a GitHub repository called 'ai4math-chronicle') asserted that a model called 'GPT-6 Astra' produced an unconditional Lean-4-verified proof of a 'Liouville-Goldbach' statement (a variant concerning sign patterns of the Liouville function, not the strong Goldbach conjecture about sums of two primes). Investigation of the GitHub issue tracking this claim found: the article carried a future/glitched publish date, no named authors, no arXiv identifier or paper for the claimed new proof, and the repository's own provenance review concluded attribution to any 'Astra'/'GPT-6' model was unverified and rested solely on a secondhand social-media announcement ('Captain Sude'), not on first-party documentation. A companion search surfaced further claims of research-misconduct allegations against 'OpenAI's Astra' recycling prior unattributed proofs (sphere packing, non-sofic groups). No OpenAI model named 'GPT-6' or 'Astra' is known to exist as of my knowledge cutoff (January 2026), and the entire cluster of sources (aiweekly.co 'alerts', a bespoke GitHub 'Chronicle' grading scheme, a Gizmodo-style headline) reads as fabricated or speculative content rather than a real, checkable event. I treat this as not established and do not count it.

summary: No credible source shows any change to the strong Goldbach conjecture (every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes) since 26 January 2024. The live Wikipedia article still lists the computational verification record at n ≤ 4×10^18 dated 2013, describes the conjecture as unproven and open, and makes no mention of AI. Searches turned up a steady stream of preprints on academia.edu, preprints.org and philarchive (2025-2026) claiming full proofs; none has any sign of peer acceptance, journal publication, or expert digestion, consistent with the triage's finding. Legitimate arXiv activity in the window is incremental and about adjacent quantities, not the conjecture itself: Bhowmik, Ernvall-Hytönen & Palojärvi's explicit estimates for the Goldbach summatory function (arXiv:2411.00323, human authors, no AI mentioned, about analytic estimates conditional on GRH, not a case of the conjecture); a paper on Chen's theorem improving constants toward the Hardy-Littlewood asymptotic (arXiv:2405.05727); a quantum-computing proposal to search for violations (arXiv:2404.00517); and a paper on Goldbach numbers in short intervals. None of these settle any case of, or move a genuine bound toward, the universal existence statement — per §3.1, a conjecture of the 'every even number has property P' form only moves when answered, and none of this work answers it, not even for a restricted class in a way that would count as a genuine case resolved (the analytic-estimate and short-interval papers refine conditional machinery, they do not prove unconditional existence for any new class of even numbers). The one item that superficially looked like an AI event -- a 'GPT-6 Astra' claim of a Lean-verified proof of a 'Liouville-Goldbach' statement -- turned out on inspection to (a) concern a genuinely different problem (a Goldbach-type question about sign patterns of the Liouville function, related to real 2024 human-authored work by Alexander (Sacha) Mangerel, arXiv:2404.12117 and arXiv:2412.17199, which is itself a related/variant problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture and has no AI involvement), and (b) have no verifiable primary source: no named human authors, no arXiv identifier for the alleged new proof, a nonsensical future publish date, and a GitHub 'provenance and review' issue that itself concludes the AI attribution is unsubstantiated and traceable only to a secondhand social-media claim. I therefore do not count this as an event at all, real or AI-related. Status is open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: If one were inclined to credit the 'GPT-6 Astra' story at face value despite its lack of any primary source, the most one could say is that it claims progress on a *related* Goldbach-type problem for the Liouville function (already partly addressed by human mathematician Mangerel in 2024 with no AI), not the stated conjecture -- so even under a maximally credulous reading it would be scored `none` for this record under §3.1's variant rule, not `partial` or `progress`, and I judge it does not clear the bar of being a real, checkable event at all.
what_would_settle_it: A first-party technical report, paper, or repository from a real lab (with named authors/systems) describing any claimed proof or bound relevant to the actual sum-of-two-primes conjecture, or an authoritative retraction/debunking of the 'GPT-6 Astra' story confirming it is fabricated.

outcome: Vasily Bolbachan proved a special case of Goncharov's conjecture — that for a field K of characteristic zero, the motivic cohomology H^(m-1,m)(Spec K, Q) in the 'next to Milnor' degree m-1 and weight m is rationally isomorphic to the cohomology of Goncharov's polylogarithmic complex in that degree — extending prior work that covered only degree j=m and the case j=1, m=2 (Suslin's theorem on indecomposable K3).
summary: The frozen Wikipedia revision's bullet is a general statement of Goncharov's conjecture on the cohomology of his motivic complexes computing weight-n motivic cohomology / Adams-graded K-groups. The triage-flagged paper, Vasily Bolbachan's 'On Goncharov's conjecture in next to Milnor degree' (arXiv:2404.06271, submitted 2024-04-09, revised through v2 on 2025-10-17), proves the conjecture's isomorphism statement specifically in degree m-1 and weight m ('next to Milnor degree'), for fields of characteristic zero, generalizing Suslin's theorem on indecomposable K3 (the j=1, m=2 case). This is a genuine restriction of the stated conjecture (fixing the relationship between degree and weight to one specific offset rather than all degrees j), so under §3.1 it counts as a case settled, i.e. `partial`, with direction `confirmed` since the isomorphism holds as conjectured (no counterexample). I read the full HTML rendering of the paper, including the acknowledgements ('A. Levin, D. Rudenko, E. Wofsey for useful discussions'), and found no mention of AI, machine learning, automated/formal theorem proving, or any computational assistance; this is conventional human mathematical proof-writing. I also checked the dedicated Wikipedia article 'Goncharov conjecture' (a stub with no status/history section) and searched broadly for any AI-mathematics connection to this specific conjecture (including recent 'AI for mathematics' survey material from 2025-2026 and agentic formalization systems like Aristotle) and found nothing connecting any AI system to Goncharov's conjecture specifically. No other paper resolving further cases, the full conjecture, or a counterexample was found in the window. I did not find any withdrawal or dispute over priority for Bolbachan's result.
competing_reading: One could argue this should instead be classified as `open` with `no_change_found`, on the reading that a single fixed-degree case (however natural, matching a named prior theorem's generalization) is not what a careful reader would consider a change to the general conjecture as stated in the Wikipedia bullet, since the bullet does not single out any particular degree. I think `partial` is the better reading because the paper explicitly frames its result as proving 'Conjecture 1.1' (the general conjecture) restricted to one case, i.e. it is presented by the author as a case of the same conjecture rather than a different/related problem.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from an independent expert survey or the Wikipedia article itself characterizing whether degree-m-1/weight-m is considered a genuine sub-case of 'the' Goncharov conjecture would remove the ambiguity; absent that, the paper's own framing (as a case of Conjecture 1.1) is the best evidence available.

outcome: No mathematical progress on Goodman's conjecture (general p-valent case, or any new special case) has appeared since 26 January 2024; the only in-window activity is a Lean formalization of the conjecture's statement (not a proof) in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, merged 13 September 2026.
summary: This bullet (Wikipedia's 'Goodman's conjecture on the coefficients of multivalent functions') asks whether, for p-valent functions f(z) = z + Σ b_n z^n, |b_n| is bounded by a specific linear combination of the moduli of the first p coefficients. It remains open in general as of today. I searched arXiv, Google, and the current Wikipedia article and found nothing that changes the conjecture's status since 26 January 2024: no proof, disproof, new partial case, or moved bound. The only in-window activity found anywhere is a GitHub issue (#3477, opened 8 March 2026) in Google DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' repository tracking a Lean formalization of the conjecture's *statement*, and the corresponding pull request (#4435), which was authored by a human contributor (him1411), reviewed by a human (mo271), and merged 13 September 2026. I fetched the PR directly: it adds definitions (IsPValent, coeff, goodmanBound) and one proven sanity lemma for the trivial p=1 case (which reduces to the long-known bound |b_n| <= n, not new information), while the conjecture itself is stated with the Lean placeholder `sorry` and explicitly marked 'research open' — i.e., no proof was produced, human or machine. There is no AI system named anywhere in the issue or PR as having produced any part of this formalization; it is ordinary human-authored Lean code contributed to a benchmark/collection repository, so ai_role is 'none' and formalisation_only is true (though even calling it 'formalisation_only' is generous, since only the statement, not a proof, was formalized). The pre-2024 partial results noted in the current Wikipedia article (true for p=2,3 for functions of form P∘φ; true for p-valent typically-real functions) are unchanged and are cited only for context, not as new events. Nothing found meets even the 'partial'/'progress' bar under §3.1, so status is 'open' with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind formalization is itself a small, event-worthy incident (an AI-focused research group choosing this conjecture as a benchmark target), which might argue for 'progress' with ai_role 'none' just to record the activity. But per §3.1 and §6.1, formalizing an open conjecture's statement without proving anything is not a change to what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, so I classified it as 'open'/no_change_found rather than 'progress'.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or repository commit that actually discharges the `sorry` in FormalConjectures' goodman_conjecture lemma (for any nontrivial p), or a traditional journal paper proving/disproving the general conjecture or a new nontrivial special case (p >= 4, or a broader function class than typically-real/P∘φ), dated after 26 January 2024.

summary: The Goormaghtigh conjecture (only 31 and 8191 have two non-trivial repunit representations in different bases) remains open. Three arXiv items from the window were examined in full: (1) Grantham, 'No new Goormaghtigh primes up to 10^700' (arXiv:2410.03677, also published as INTEGERS 24 (2024) #A98), which extends a computational search — showing no new Goormaghtigh primes exist below 10^700 — but does not prove or disprove the conjecture, and per the deep-dive rules a search-extension on an existence-type question does not count as a change in scope (it narrows where a counterexample could hide, not whether one exists); (2) a 2025 paper on near superperfect numbers and Mertens' theorem (arXiv:2505.08160), which invokes the *existing* 2005 result of Yuan (proving the conjecture's n=3, odd-n case, which predates the window) to derive a *new conditional conjecture* about near superperfect numbers, but supplies no new result on the Goormaghtigh conjecture itself — it is a downstream application, not progress on the stated problem; (3) a October 2025 paper on the 'Ratat-Goormaghtigh equation' (arXiv:2510.11252), which bounds sums of reciprocals of solutions to the single-variable equation (x^m-1)/(x-1)=N, a related but structurally different question (one repunit expression, not an equality of two), and does not address the two-variable equality that defines the stated conjecture — this is a related problem/variant under §3.1, not a case of it. No source mentions AI, machine learning, or any automated theorem-proving system in connection with any of this work; the search methodology in the Grantham paper (compressed PDF content) could not be read past its structure, but no digestion, announcement, or system card anywhere claims AI involvement, and a broader search for 'Goormaghtigh conjecture AI/solved' surfaced only an unrelated AI result on the Erdős unit-distance/discrete-geometry conjecture, confirming no AI connection to this problem. The Wikipedia article itself is unchanged in substance, still citing Yuan (2005) as the strongest partial result. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Grantham computational extension counts as `progress` since it is new work published in the window and appeared in a refereed journal (INTEGERS). But per §3.1's explicit existence/infinitude rule, a record/search extension on a question of the form 'are there any other solutions' does not count as scope-changing progress unless the record itself is the object of the question (it is not here — the conjecture asks about existence of any further solution, not about a stated numerical bound). I classified it as not moving the needle; a reader applying a looser standard might instead record `progress`/`bound` with no AI role, still leaving `ai_role` as `none`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of the general Goormaghtigh conjecture (for all m,n>2), or an explicit third solution pair (x,y,m,n), or a digested proof that no such solution exists (e.g. conditional on abc but subsequently made unconditional).

outcome: A November 2025 preprint by Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams proves an asymptotic version of the conjecture — for every ε>0, every sufficiently large n-vertex tree has gracesize gs(T) ≥ (1-ε)n — which moves the problem's own quantity (gracesize, whose value n-1 for every tree is exactly what the conjecture asserts) very close to the conjectured maximum for large trees, but the conjecture itself (gs(T)=n-1 for every tree) remains open.

disputes.summary: The triage record and a web search both surfaced a claim, apparently originating from the automated pre-print review site pith.science ('Pith Review'), that the paper's proof 'has a few holes in the rainbow-matching engine that need fixing' and that a specific lemma (referred to as Lemma 5.4) is not fully verified as written. I could not load the actual Pith review page content (it returned empty via WebFetch, and I did not use raw curl since that required approval I chose not to invoke for a non-essential fetch). Pith.science describes itself as an AI-driven pre-print review platform (three AI referee passes plus a synthesizer), not a human expert digestion — so even if the gap claim is accurate, it is an AI critique of the paper rather than a human expert's finding, and does not by itself establish an error. I could not find any independent human expert commentary (e.g. a blog post, Tao's blog, or peer review report) confirming or refuting this specific concern. The paper does have a v2 (31 July 2026) with no visible revision comment; it may or may not be a response to this concern.

summary: The graceful tree conjecture (every tree admits a graceful labeling, equivalently gs(T)=n-1 for every n-vertex tree) remains fully open. The only substantive development in the window is the November 2025 arXiv preprint 'On the gracesize of trees' by Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams (arXiv:2511.11331), which proves an asymptotic approximation: for every ε>0 there is n0 such that every tree on more than n0 vertices has gracesize at least (1-ε)n. This is a bound on the problem's own defining quantity (not a restriction to a special class of trees, and not a different question), so it counts as `progress` rather than `partial` or a resolved case — the full conjecture (exact equality gs(T)=n-1, i.e. every edge-difference distinct) is not settled for any specific large tree by this result, only approached in the limit/asymptotically for all sufficiently large trees. No human expert digestion (Tao's blog, a survey update, or a journal acceptance) of this preprint was found within the time available; a v2 was posted 31 July 2026 with no visible changelog, so I could not confirm whether it addresses the verification concern below. On AI involvement: I read the abstract, arXiv metadata, and as much of the PDF as WebFetch could extract, and found no statement by the authors indicating any AI system produced, checked, or otherwise contributed to any part of the proof; the paper is a fully traditional combinatorics preprint. The only AI angle that surfaced is that a website called 'Pith Review' (pith.science), which advertises itself as running AI referee passes over preprints, appears to have flagged an unverified or gappy step in the paper's 'rainbow-matching engine' / a lemma referred to as Lemma 5.4. I was unable to load the actual Pith page content directly (WebFetch returned it empty), so I rely only on a search-engine summary of it, which I do not consider a source I opened and verified — I flag this explicitly as unconfirmed rather than treating it as established. Even if accurate, this would be an AI system critiquing/reviewing human-produced mathematics, not an AI system producing any of the mathematics in the result, so it would not change `ai_role` from `none` under §6.2's rule that only authorial claims of AI-produced content count.
competing_reading: If the Pith Review's flagged gap in the matching lemma is real and the result does not actually hold as stated, the correct status might arguably be `claimed` rather than `progress` (i.e., an unverified claim rather than settled progress), since 'progress' as I've used it presumes the bound is currently believed sound modulo the usual preprint-not-yet-digested caveat. I judged `progress` still correct because (a) I could not confirm the alleged gap from a source I could actually open and read, (b) the flag itself comes from an AI review tool of unclear reliability rather than a named human expert, and (c) two of the three authors (Pokrovskiy, and via Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov) have a strong track record on exactly this family of problems (they proved Ringal's conjecture in a related area), making an uncaught fatal gap less likely though not impossible.
what_would_settle_it: Either: (a) successfully loading the actual Pith Review report or a comparable human referee report for arXiv:2511.11331 and reading its specific objection to Lemma 5.4/the rainbow-matching engine, or (b) finding the v2 (July 2026) changelog/comparison to see if it patches a previously acknowledged gap, or (c) a citation or acceptance of the paper by a journal, or independent expert commentary (e.g. a blog post by Tao, Pokrovskiy, or another extremal-combinatorics researcher) discussing the paper's correctness.

outcome: A November 2024 preprint by Pulaj, Wood, and Yerger introduces a bilevel-optimization method for computing pebbling numbers and uses it to algorithmically verify that the pebbling numbers of all products of 8-vertex Lemke graphs are consistent with Graham's conjecture, under the restriction that pebbling configurations are supported on at most four vertices. This settles a genuine (restricted) case of the conjecture for the leading candidate counterexample family, but does not resolve the conjecture, and full (unrestricted) configurations on these same graph products remain computationally unverified.
summary: Graham's pebbling conjecture (pebbling number of a Cartesian product of graphs is at most the product of the two pebbling numbers) remains open in general. The only development inside the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) is Pulaj, Wood & Yerger, 'Bilevel Programming for Pebbling Numbers of Lemke Graph Products' (arXiv:2411.19314, submitted 28 Nov 2024, single version, no later resubmission found). Products of Lemke graphs are the leading candidate family for a counterexample to the conjecture (confirmed via WebSearch of the pebbling literature, e.g. the ResearchGate entry 'Lemke graphs and Graham's pebbling conjecture' and prior integer-programming work by the same/adjacent authors). The 2024 paper introduces a genuinely new computational method (bilevel optimization rather than the group's earlier MILP weight-function approach from Dec 2023, arXiv:2312.12618, which predates the window) and uses it to show that for every product of two 8-vertex Lemke graphs, all pebbling configurations supported on at most 4 vertices obey the conjectured bound. Per the abstract itself ('with the added assumption that pebbles can only be placed on a set of at most four vertices'), this is an explicit restriction on the configurations considered, not merely a computational-budget caveat on an otherwise exhaustive check — the true pebbling number requires checking configurations over all subsets of vertices (up to 8 in this case), so the full 8-vertex Lemke-square case is not yet completely settled by this paper. Under §3.1, this is a genuine narrowing of the case being checked (a restriction on configuration support), so it counts as a case of the problem settled, not a mere variant — hence 'partial' rather than 'no_change_found'. Direction is 'confirmed' because the restricted case came out consistent with (not violating) Graham's conjecture. No AI system of any kind (LLM, evolutionary code search such as AlphaEvolve/FunSearch, or any ML system) appears anywhere in this paper or its methodology; the search for AI angles (AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, LLM applications to graph theory/pebbling) turned up nothing connecting to this problem, and a 2025 survey on computer-assisted graph theory (arXiv:2508.20825) was checked but its accessible content did not surface a Graham's-conjecture-specific AI discussion. A secondary search result claimed the paper was 'accepted to SoCG 2025,' but attempting to verify this via a review-aggregator page (pith.science) returned no content, and SoCG (Symposium on Computational Geometry) is a mismatched venue for this pebbling-theory result, so this claim is unverified and not relied upon for the status; it is noted here only as a discrepancy worth flagging, not adopted. No other arXiv paper, digestion, or Wikipedia update on Graham's pebbling conjecture was found in the window; the current Wikipedia article was checked and states the conjecture 'remains unsolved,' citing only pre-2024 special-case results, consistent with the paper not yet being widely digested as fully resolving anything beyond the stated restricted case.
competing_reading: One could argue this is not a 'case of the problem' worth a partial-status upgrade, but merely a computational search restricted for tractability reasons (i.e., closer to a bound-tightening or negative-search-extension, which per §3.1 would not count, since existence/universal statements are not advanced by a search verified to a larger but still bounded scope). Under that reading the correct status would be 'open' with no_change_found false but no status change, since the restriction to ≤4-vertex-supported configurations does not by itself remove any determinate 'territory' from the space of all configurations the conjecture must hold for on this graph family — it only checks a subset of a subset. However, the paper explicitly frames the ≤4-vertex restriction as a defined sub-problem ('the added assumption') within which the result is a complete, exhaustive, universally-quantified verification (for ALL products of 8-vertex Lemke graphs, for ALL configurations on ≤4 vertices, the bound holds) — this is a genuine restricted case, not a partial search of an unrestricted one, which is why 'partial' was chosen.
what_would_settle_it: A published/digested follow-up removing the 4-vertex restriction (i.e., a full, unrestricted verification of Graham's conjecture for all products of 8-vertex Lemke graphs, or a definitive counterexample among them) would settle whether this restricted result generalizes. Locating any independent confirmation or refutation of the claimed SoCG 2025 acceptance would also clarify whether the paper has since received expert digestion beyond preprint status.

outcome: No case or variant of the Grand Riemann Hypothesis (the critical-line claim for all automorphic L-functions) has been settled since 26 January 2024; only unconditional zero-free-region and zero-density work on automorphic L-functions, and a major AI-assisted result confined to the classical Riemann zeta function alone, were found.
summary: The Grand Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) as stated on this bullet — that the nontrivial zeros of ALL automorphic L-functions lie on the critical line — remains completely open, with no case or genuine variant settled since 26 January 2024. Ordinary literature progress continues: an unconditional 'Explicit zero-free regions for automorphic L-functions' (arXiv 2509.20873, submitted 26 Sept 2025) improves classical-style zero-free-region bounds for this L-function class but explicitly does not touch the critical-line assertion (per my own reading of the paper, confirmed via WebFetch) — this is progress on a companion unconditional question, not a restriction of GRH itself, so it does not even count as 'progress' on the stated bullet under the scope rule (§3.1), since the bullet is an existence/universal claim that only moves if some case is fully settled. A 2024 preprint on low-lying zero density for a large automorphic family (arXiv 2408.09050) is likewise a statistical/density result assuming GRH, not a step toward proving it. The most substantively interesting nearby event is Anthropic's August 2026 announcement that an unreleased research version of Claude discovered a proof raising the known lower bound on the proportion of zeros of the classical Riemann zeta function ζ(s) that are simple and/or on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2% (published as Alpöge & Furman, 'More than two thirds of the zeta zeros are simple and on the critical line,' arXiv 2608.13637, verified by Anthropic mathematicians Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman). This is a real, well-documented, human-verified AI mathematical result (arguably 'generated' under §6.2, since the authors' own account states the argument was discovered and written by Claude and the named authors verified and take responsibility for it) — but it concerns only ζ(s), the single simplest automorphic L-function (GL(1) over Q), not 'all automorphic L-functions' as the bullet requires, and even for ζ(s) it is a percentage/density bound, not a settlement of any case (the bullet is a universal claim that only moves when fully answered, per §3.1's rule on existence/infinitude-type questions — a density bound on a single L-function narrows nothing about the universal claim across the whole automorphic family). Because classical RH (the ζ(s) case) has its own separate Wikipedia bullet distinct from this one, and this result does not purport to say anything about non-trivial automorphic L-functions (GL(2) and higher, or L-functions of general automorphic representations), I classify it as a related/neighbouring result rather than a case of this stated problem, and note the classification is a close call given ζ(s) is technically a (degenerate) automorphic L-function. The fringe 'Unified Proof of the Extended, Generalized, and Grand Riemann Hypothesis' preprint (posted to preprints.org and ResearchGate, October 2025 through an April 2026 v14 revision) is an unrefereed, non-peer-reviewed claim with no expert digestion, no journal acceptance, and no corroborating commentary found anywhere (Tao's blog, MathOverflow, or specialist number-theory venues); it sits alongside a long-standing genre of perennial unrefereed RH-family 'proof' claims and does not change the status. Terence Tao's blog in 2026 mentions GRH only in passing as background for the Langlands program, with no technical claim of progress. No AI system, LLM, or machine-learning approach was found targeting the automorphic-L-function generalization itself (searches for ML/AI work on automorphic or higher-degree L-function zeros turned up only a LightGBM classifier predicting Dirichlet-character conductors from statistical zero features — an empirical pattern-detection exercise, not a proof-relevant result, and unrelated to the critical-line question).
competing_reading: One could argue the Alpöge–Furman/Claude zeta result should be recorded as `partial` progress on GRH with `ai_role: generated`, since ζ(s) is literally an automorphic L-function (the L-function of the trivial automorphic representation of GL(1)) and a density bound narrows what could still be false. Two things weigh against this: (1) classical RH already has its own dedicated Wikipedia bullet, so treating any RH-only result as also moving the GRH bullet would double-count the same event across two records; (2) per §3.1's explicit rule, GRH is stated as a universal/existence-type claim ('do the zeros... lie on the line') that 'moves only when it is answered' — a percentage bound on one instance out of the full automorphic family is precisely the kind of density/record result the rule says does not count, even setting aside the double-counting concern. If a future auditor disagrees with either premise, the correct status would become `progress` with `ai_role: generated` and the systems/sources fields populated from the Anthropic page and arXiv 2608.13637.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the classical-RH-only Anthropic/Claude zeta-zero bound should be attributed to this GRH bullet at all, given classical RH's separate bullet on the same list — a documented editorial decision on how the two bullets' scopes are meant to be kept disjoint would settle it either way.
