outcome: The general Greenberg invariants conjecture (μ = λ = 0 for the cyclotomic Zp-extension of any totally real number field) and Greenberg's p-rationality conjecture remain open; work since 26 January 2024 consists of case verifications, analogues, and bound improvements on related-but-distinct problems, none of which settle a case of the stated conjectures.
summary: Greenberg's conjectures (the invariants conjecture that μ_p(k) = λ_p(k) = 0 for the cyclotomic Zp-extension of any totally real number field k and every prime p, and the later p-rationality conjecture) remain open as of September 2026. The Wikipedia article on 'Greenberg's conjecture' still states both are unsolved and reports no update beyond the Ferrero–Washington theorem (1979, predates the window) and other pre-2024 background. Searching the recent arXiv literature turns up an active stream of work adjacent to the conjecture but none of it is a case of the stated conjecture itself: (1) arXiv:2410.05706 (Oct 2024) proves an *analogue* of Greenberg's conjecture for CM fields — a different (though related) problem posed over different objects, not a restriction of the totally-real-field statement; (2) arXiv:2503.00819 (Mar 2025) and arXiv:2503.15727 (Mar 2025) extend computational/numerical verification of the conjecture to larger discriminant ranges for real quadratic and real biquadratic fields respectively — this narrows where a counterexample could hide but does not settle any case, consistent with §3.1's rule that record-extension for an existence-type statement does not count as movement (and here the object itself, μ=λ=0, is not even a record but a repeated finite check); (3) other results found (arXiv:2405.05871, arXiv:2408.07826) address a differently-worded 'Greenberg conjecture for elliptic curve Selmer groups' (μ-invariant of Selmer groups of elliptic curves over Q), which is a namesake variant, not the totally-real-field invariants conjecture, and even there the results are bounds (μ ≤ 1) on a still-open statement rather than resolutions. No source anywhere in this search mentions AI, machine learning, or a large language model contributing to any of this work — all located papers describe conventional analytic/algebraic number theory arguments and computer algebra class-group computations (not AI systems). Given the consistent picture across the Wikipedia article, general searches, and inspection of the specific recent papers turned up, and agreement with the triage pass's conclusion, confidence is high that nothing has happened to the stated conjectures in the window and that no AI system was involved in any adjacent work.
competing_reading: One could argue the CM-field analogue (arXiv:2410.05706) or the elliptic-curve Selmer-group 'Greenberg conjecture' results are close enough in spirit to count as progress on 'Greenberg's conjectures' broadly construed, since Wikipedia's bullet is terse and doesn't pin down which of Greenberg's several conjectures it means beyond the invariants conjecture. But by §3.1's test — does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry, which concerns totally real fields — these are variants over different objects (CM fields; elliptic curve Selmer groups) rather than restrictions of the totally-real-field statement, so they do not count as movement on the stated problem.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of μ_p(k) = λ_p(k) = 0 for some specific totally real field k and prime p not already known (or a general proof), or explicit resolution of the p-rationality conjecture for some field/prime, reported by a source dated after 26 January 2024.

This is a much stronger, and still-open, statement than the 'generic curve' case, which Voisin resolved in the early 2000s (a fact predating the window). I searched for any work since 26 January 2024 bearing on the general statement, the generic case, or related variants. Two relevant post-snapshot preprints turned up: (1) Michael Kemeny, 'A proof of generic Green's conjecture in odd genus' (arXiv:2502.09735, submitted 13 Feb 2025, v4 10 Dec 2025), which gives a new, computation-avoiding proof of Voisin's existing odd-genus generic-curve theorem — it re-proves a known result rather than extending it to new curves, so it is not a change to the general conjecture nor even new territory in the generic case. (2) Yi Wei, 'Generic Green's Conjecture and Generic Geometric Syzygy Conjecture in Positive Characteristic' (arXiv:2109.12187, originally 2021, latest v4 13 May 2025), which proves the generic conjecture in positive characteristic p ≥ (g+4)/2 and a case of the related Geometric Syzygy Conjecture for even genus — this is a different setting (positive characteristic) than the classical statement (implicitly characteristic 0) and, per §3.1, changing the ground field/characteristic makes this a related-problem variant rather than a restriction (case) of the stated bullet, since the bullet does not specify or vary over characteristic and the classical open problem is understood over the complex numbers / characteristic 0. Neither paper touches the arbitrary (non-generic) curve case, which the Wikipedia article and this search confirm is still explicitly open ('The conjecture for arbitrary curves remains open'). I found no counterexample, no resolution, and no AI involvement anywhere in this area: neither paper mentions AI, ML, or automated theorem-proving tools, and a targeted search for AI-related work touching Green's conjecture returned nothing relevant (only unrelated hits about 'Green's functions' in PDE/ML contexts, and a blog post about AI counterexamples to unrelated conjectures — Erdős unit distance, a Grothendieck group-schemes question, and the Jacobian conjecture — which does not mention Green's conjecture at all). Given the clear, explicit statement on Wikipedia's own article that the general conjecture is open, and the absence of any preprint, announcement, or database entry claiming otherwise, I am confident nothing has happened to the general conjecture within the window, and certainly no AI involvement.
competing_reading: One could argue the positive-characteristic result (arXiv:2109.12187) is a genuine partial advance if one reads 'non-hyperelliptic curve' in the bullet as agnostic to the base field, in which case settling the generic case in positive characteristic could count as `partial` progress on a (field-restricted) case of the general conjecture. I judge this unlikely to be the intended reading: the conjecture as classically posed and as linked from Wikipedia is about complex projective curves, and the positive-characteristic problem is treated in the literature as its own conjecture (with separate statements and its own history of partial results long before 2024), i.e. a related problem sharing the name rather than a sub-case of the stated one. Also, even under the generous reading, this would only be a case of the *generic*-curve sub-problem, not of the arbitrary-curve statement actually in the bullet, so it would still not touch what the bullet asks.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement proving (or disproving) the Clifford-index/syzygy equivalence for a genuinely non-generic, non-hyperelliptic curve (or a stated counterexample among such curves) would settle whether real progress occurred; absent that, the status stands as open with no change.

outcome: The conjecture remains fully open, but the computational no-counterexample bound was extended from 1.9×10^10 (Laishram & Shorey, 2006) to 10^12 by an independent GitHub repository (thebrockchain/grimm-conjecture-verification), completed 2026-08-26. A separate attempt to submit a finite Lean-certified range [2,10^4] to the crypto-funded 'Justin Sun Prize' bounty program was rejected as insufficient (partial progress, not a full solution).

disputes.summary: The GitHub repository thebrockchain/grimm-conjecture-verification claims a 52.6x extension of the verified no-counterexample bound (to 10^12) and states its own README/CLAUDE.md contain no explicit AI-authorship disclosure, yet the repository includes a CLAUDE.md file (typically used to instruct an AI coding agent) and reports computation on an 'Apple M5' processor, a chip generation not otherwise documented as publicly released. The claim has not been picked up or cited by erdosproblems.com (last updated 2026-01-24, still citing only the 2006 bound), so it is unverified by any independent expert and should be treated cautiously.

A Lean 4 + Mathlib formalization (JSP-000310, submitted by GitHub user aznikline, attributed to 'Devin (aznikline)') certified Grimm's conjecture by kernel-checked decision procedure over the finite range [2, 10^4] (1,228 maximal composite runs). It was submitted to the 'Justin Sun Prize' bounty program (announced 2026-09-16) as pull request #1232 (2026-09-18) and, after an administrative closure over hosting-format rules, resubmitted as #2119 (2026-09-20). A prize-program reviewer (Federico2014) rejected it because the program requires a complete solution to the original (unbounded) conjecture, not a finite certificate. No AI system is disclosed as having produced the Lean proof; attribution is to a named human account, though 'Devin' is also the name of an AI coding-agent product, creating ambiguity not resolved by the PR text.

summary: Grimm's conjecture (each maximal run of consecutive composites admits an assignment of distinct prime divisors) remains unproven. Two developments postdate the frozen revision. (1) A GitHub repository, thebrockchain/grimm-conjecture-verification, claims to have extended the computational no-counterexample verification from the published 2006 bound of 1.9×10^10 (Laishram & Shorey) to 10^12, completed 2026-08-26, checking about 37.6 billion prime gaps with zero counterexamples and zero truncations. This is a bound extension on an open existence-of-counterexample-style computation, which under §3.1 counts as `progress` (not `partial` or `resolved`) since the conjecture is not a 'largest known object or constant' question but a universal statement whose falsity a finite search could only disprove, never confirm — extending the search range narrows where a counterexample could hide but does not settle the conjecture. Its README and CLAUDE.md make no explicit claim about AI authorship of the verification code; I could not obtain unambiguous authorship information, and the repository is self-published, uncited by erdosproblems.com (whose Grimm's-conjecture page was last updated 2026-01-24 and still lists only the 2006 bound), and not yet digested by any expert source I could find — so I classified `ai_role` as `none` for lack of a quotable authorial disclosure, per §6.2's requirement that `assisted`/`generated` need the authors' own account. (2) Separately, a Lean/Mathlib formalization certifying the conjecture by decision procedure on the finite range [2,10^4] was submitted to the newly announced, widely disputed 'Justin Sun Prize' crypto-funded bounty program (real news coverage confirms the prize exists and is controversial — questioned funding, an OpenAI Navier-Stokes submission dispute — but is not an accepted part of the mathematical community's verification apparatus). This Lean submission was explicitly rejected by the program's own reviewers as insufficient partial progress, so it does not even count as a `claimed` status for that venue, let alone `resolved`. No credible source shows the conjecture, or any non-trivial case beyond small finite ranges, has been proven or disproven. I found no evidence of any named AI system producing mathematics that appears in either the bound extension or the Lean certificate; both authorship trails are ambiguous or silent on AI use, so `ai_role` is `none` throughout.
competing_reading: If the thebrockchain repository's CLAUDE.md in fact documents that an AI coding agent (e.g., a Claude-based agent) authored the verification/sharding code, and this constitutes 'AI produced part of the mathematics/computation in the result' under an expansive reading, `ai_role` could arguably be `bound` (an AI system moved a bound on a problem that is still open) rather than `none`. I could not obtain an unambiguous, quotable authorial statement from the repository despite repeated fetches — my tool calls returned inconsistent summaries, one of which appeared to include an artifact from the fetching tool itself ('You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK') that I do not believe is genuine repository content and have excluded from my finding. Given §6.2's requirement for the authors' own account and my inability to secure an unambiguous quote, I defaulted to `none`, but a reader with direct, uncontaminated access to the raw CLAUDE.md file might reasonably reach `bound` instead.
what_would_settle_it: Direct, verbatim inspection of the raw CLAUDE.md and README.md files in https://github.com/thebrockchain/grimm-conjecture-verification (ideally via `git clone` or `curl` rather than a summarizing fetch tool) to check for any first-person statement about how the verification code was produced, and whether an AI system is credited with writing or designing the sharding/verification logic. Also, an update to erdosproblems.com citing the 10^12 bound (or its rejection/correction) would confirm or disconfirm the claim's credibility, and a substantive (non-administrative) review of the Lean PR would clarify whether the 'Justin Sun Prize' program itself has any bearing on this problem's status.

outcome: Esnault and Groechenig (arXiv:2606.16873, June 2026) prove the p-curvature conjecture for a newly-defined class of higher-dimensional local systems ('privileged local systems') via a proof strategy avoiding middle convolution, settling this case while the general conjecture remains open; no AI involvement was found in this or any other result located.
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet states the p-curvature conjecture in its classical form: a local-global principle for linear ODEs (finite monodromy after a finite étale cover iff p-curvature vanishes for almost all primes). The conjecture remains open in general, but I found a genuine case settled in the window: Esnault and Groechenig, 'The Grothendieck-Katz Conjecture for privileged local systems' (arXiv:2606.16873, submitted 2026-06-15), define 'privileged local systems' on smooth quasi-projective varieties in any dimension — a generalization of Katz's classical notion of physical rigidity on opens of P^1 — and prove the conjecture holds for this class, via a new proof avoiding middle convolution. This restricts the stated question to a specific class of local systems and settles it there, so it is a case (§3.1), not a variant, and is classified `partial` with direction `confirmed` (the conjecture's prediction held for this class). I also found and ruled out other candidate events: (1) Movasati's 'Grothendieck-Katz conjecture' (arXiv:2403.11829, March 2024), which reformulated the conjecture under a stronger hypothesis, was withdrawn in v3 (Feb 2025) and folded into a larger paper, 'Leaf schemes and Hodge loci' (arXiv:2502.19988) — I could not fully confirm from the fetched content whether the folded version still makes a live claim about the classical conjecture, but since the standalone reformulation was withdrawn and superseded, I do not treat it as a standing event; (2) Lam and Litt, 'p-Curvature and Non-Abelian Cohomology' (arXiv:2601.07933, Jan 2026), prove a non-abelian analogue of the p-curvature conjecture for isomonodromy foliations on moduli of flat bundles — this changes the stated hypotheses (non-abelian setting, different objects) rather than restricting the classical linear-ODE question, so under §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case, and does not by itself move this record; (3) Fürnsinn and Pannier, 'An Effective Version of the p-Curvature Conjecture for Order One Differential Equations' (arXiv:2510.00892, Oct 2025), build an effective/computable version and SageMath algorithm on top of Honda's pre-existing proof for order-one equations — this is `progress`-grade (an effectivization of an already-solved case) and is subsumed by the more substantial Esnault-Groechenig result as the decisive event, so I did not create a separate record for it. No source among these mentions AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving tools in any capacity — all are traditional algebraic-geometry/arithmetic arguments by named human authors.
competing_reading: One could argue the Esnault-Groechenig result is itself a 'related problem' rather than a 'case', since privileged local systems are a genuinely new definition rather than a pre-existing restriction of the classical hypothesis space. Against this: the paper explicitly frames privileged local systems as a generalization of Katz's own notion of physical rigidity (already a recognized sufficient condition invoked in the classical literature on this conjecture), and the local systems covered are honest instances of the objects quantified over in the original statement (flat connections/local systems on a variety), not a different kind of object or a differently-posed question. I classify it as a case, but flag the alternative.
what_would_settle_it: A close reading of how 'privileged local systems' relates set-theoretically to the class of local systems the classical conjecture quantifies over (i.e., whether every privileged local system is an admissible instance of the general conjecture's hypotheses) would settle whether this is a case or a variant. Also, obtaining the full text of the folded Movasati paper (arXiv:2502.19988) to see whether it still asserts a proof/reformulation bearing on the classical conjecture would clarify whether that thread constitutes an additional (withdrawn-then-superseded) event.

outcome: The Guralnick-Thompson conjecture (1990) — that the set E*(g) of composition factors of monodromy groups of genus-g covers of the sphere which are neither cyclic nor alternating is finite for each g — was proved by Frohardt and Magaard in 'Composition Factors of Monodromy Groups', Annals of Mathematics 154 (2001), 1-19, more than two decades before the frozen revision. No further movement specific to this conjecture was found in the window 2024-01-26 to 2026-09-22.
summary: The conjecture on this bullet is the 1990 Guralnick-Thompson conjecture that E*(g), the set of non-alternating, non-cyclic composition factors appearing in monodromy groups of genus-g covers of the Riemann sphere, is finite for every g. This was resolved affirmatively by Frohardt and Magaard (Annals of Mathematics, 2001), a fact stated consistently across multiple secondary sources (e.g. the Springer chapter 'Relating Two Genus 0 Problems of John Thompson', and search summaries referencing Frohardt-Guralnick-Magaard follow-up work on Lie rank 1 groups, PSPUM 70 (2002)). Because this resolution predates the frozen Wikipedia revision (26 January 2024) by 23 years, the bullet is a stale list entry, and status is coded open_stale rather than any status implying a change within the measurement window. I searched specifically for 2024-2026 arXiv activity that might have moved this particular conjecture further (e.g. extending E*(g), tightening the classification, or addressing a residual open sub-case). The two 2025 papers the triage pass flagged — 'Low-genus primitive monodromy groups with a nonunique minimal normal subgroup' (arXiv:2501.15538) and 'Genus zero tensor products' (arXiv:2507.18335) — address adjacent classification questions about monodromy group structure and field ramification respectively, but neither abstract references the Guralnick-Thompson conjecture or the finiteness of E*(g); they are related problems in the same research area (§3.1), not restrictions or extensions of this conjecture. I also found a 2024 paper by Neftin and Zieve, 'Monodromy Groups of Indecomposable Coverings of Bounded Genus' (arXiv:2403.17167), which proves 'a conjecture of Guralnick' and 'conjectures of Guralnick and Shareshian' about classifying monodromy groups of large-degree indecomposable coverings for fixed genus — this is a different Guralnick conjecture (about the list of possible large-degree monodromy groups) than the Guralnick-Thompson composition-factor-finiteness conjecture named in this Wikipedia bullet, and the paper's own abstract does not connect it to the Frohardt-Magaard result or to Thompson. I therefore classify it as out of scope under the 'related problem' rule rather than a case of this conjecture. I found no AI involvement in any of the sources reviewed. I also note that one web search returned a GitHub repository titled 'Draft source-fidelity intake for Guralnick-Thompson conjecture... not mathematical evidence or a solved-result claim' — this appears to be an artifact planted in search results referencing this very research task, not a genuine mathematical source; I did not open or rely on it in any way, and flag it here as a probable prompt-injection attempt encountered during search.
competing_reading: One could argue the Neftin-Zieve 2024 paper (arXiv:2403.17167), which proves 'a conjecture of Guralnick' on monodromy group classification for large-degree indecomposable coverings of bounded genus, is close enough in subject and author to count as touching this bullet. However, the specific conjecture named in the Wikipedia bullet — composition factors being finite (E*(g)) — is a different, already-1990-conjectured-and-2001-proved statement from the large-degree classification conjectures proved in 2024. Absent a direct textual link between the two in the 2024 paper, I read them as distinct problems sharing an author and a research area rather than the same conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A direct statement in a 2024-2026 paper's introduction explicitly invoking 'the Guralnick-Thompson conjecture' (as opposed to other Guralnick conjectures) and either extending, refining, or reproving it, or a Wikipedia edit history showing the bullet's wording was changed/removed after January 2024 to reflect its 2001 resolution.

outcome: The general conjecture (every forest T is χ-bounding) remains fully open, but new tree/graph families have been confirmed to satisfy it since 26 January 2024, most notably all 'multibrooms' (Nguyen, Scott & Seymour, 'Trees and near-linear stable sets', arXiv:2409.09397, first posted 2024-09-14), plus narrower results on radius-three tree families and on boxicity-bounded graphs for a 'polynomial' strengthening of the conjecture.
summary: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture (every forest T is χ-bounding: graphs with no induced copy of T and bounded clique number have bounded chromatic number) remains open as a whole. Since 26 January 2024 the strongest genuine advance on the exact stated question is Nguyen, Scott & Seymour, 'Trees and near-linear stable sets' (arXiv:2409.09397, posted 2024-09-14, revised 2025-07-18): they prove that for every forest H, graphs excluding induced H with bounded clique number have a stable set of size |G|^(1-o(1)) (a near-linear but not fully linear bound, so this alone does not establish χ-boundedness), and separately prove the full linear-stable-set / χ-bounding statement for the class of 'multibrooms', a genuinely new family of trees for which the conjecture is now confirmed — this is scope-correct progress and I classify it as `partial` with direction `confirmed`. The triage-flagged 'A Note on the Gyárfás–Sumner Conjecture' (arXiv:2302.08922, same authors, posted 2023-02-17, journal version Graphs and Combinatorics 2024) predates the window (posted before 26 January 2024, journal publication is a later date for the same work and per §6.3 the event date is the first written argument, not the journal date) and in any case proves only a weaker 'path-induced' relaxation of the conjecture, not an induced copy — a related, strictly weaker statement, so it would not count as a case even if it were in-window. Also examined: 'Polynomial Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture for graphs of bounded boxicity' (arXiv:2407.16882, 2024-07-23) — this proves a *polynomial* χ-bound (a strictly stronger conjecture than the stated one) restricted to boxicity-bounded graphs, i.e. both a narrower hypothesis and a stronger conclusion than the stated bullet, making it a related/variant result rather than a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not move this record's status; 'On polynomially high-chromatic pure pairs' (arXiv:2504.21127, revised through 2026-01) extends the same polynomial-conjecture line (brooms/forest unions) and is likewise about the stronger polynomial variant. The oriented-tree, signed-graph, domatic, and rainbow-path papers found by triage are all variants over different objects (digraphs, signed graphs, domatic number) and correctly excluded per §3.1. No result anywhere in the search involved an AI system in producing mathematics: no paper's methods, acknowledgements or announcements credit a model with any part of a proof, bound, or construction. A GitHub repository ('vibemathing/problem-wikipedia-...') targeting this exact conjecture was found and inspected; it is an empty scaffold/template for a prospective AI-assisted research workflow with no mathematical content, results, or claims — not an instance of AI involvement in this problem, and not counted.
competing_reading: One could argue the near-linear stable-set bound in 'Trees and near-linear stable sets' for general forests is itself 'progress' on the whole conjecture (since a large stable set is a weaker consequence one might hope χ-boundedness implies), which would support classifying the overall record as `progress` rather than `partial`. I chose `partial` because the multibroom result is a genuine, clean settlement of the actual χ-boundedness statement for a specific tree family — a case, not merely a bound — which is the stronger and more defensible classification under §6.1's ordering (a settled case outranks a mere quantitative shift). The general near-linear-stable-set result for all forests remains `progress`-flavored on its own but is subsumed by reporting the multibroom case as the decisive event.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture for all forests, or explicit tracking of whether the boxicity/polynomial-conjecture line of work is ever judged by experts to bear on the original (non-polynomial) conjecture's truth.

outcome: On 12 August 2026, Levent Alpöge announced (with collaborators Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle, and using Anthropic's Claude) explicit Hadamard matrices for all twelve orders below 2000 for which none had previously been known: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948 and 1964. disputes.summary: The credited byline is 'a team of three humans and Claude', but no formal writeup discloses the actual division of labor between the human mathematicians and the AI system. Epoch AI (FrontierMath) explicitly marked its classification of the order-668 case as 'solved by AI' as provisional, saying it will revise the call if further reporting shows the humans supplied the core mathematical ideas rather than mainly directing/checking the model. A secondary commentary piece (Aliteq) argues the 'AI solved it' framing is unsubstantiated marketing framing rather than a claim from the mathematicians themselves, since the announcement was made via an encoded/puzzle tweet rather than a paper, and 'nobody outside that three-person team knows how much of the actual mathematical insight came from Claude versus three very good mathematicians pointing a model at the right search space.'

summary: The Hadamard conjecture itself ('for every k, a Hadamard matrix of order 4k exists') remains open in general. What changed since the frozen revision is a case of the conjecture: on 12 August 2026, Levent Alpöge, Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle announced (via an unconventional, encoded post on X) explicit Hadamard matrices for the twelve orders below 2000 that had no previously known construction — most notably order 668, the smallest open case since 2004/2005. This removes a specific, previously-documented gap (668 through 1964) from the record of known orders, so it is scoped as a case of the problem rather than a variant, and is classified 'partial' rather than 'resolved' because the universal statement over all k is untouched. The result is directly checkable — Ion Nechita's blog post describes independently verifying one matrix by checking entries are ±1 and HH^T = nI with a short script — so there is no doubt about the mathematical correctness of the specific matrices, only about the division of labor behind finding them. On that latter point, the credit line is 'a team of three humans and Claude,' and Epoch AI's FrontierMath page provisionally marked the case 'solved by AI' while explicitly flagging that the classification could be revised if a fuller writeup shows humans supplied the core mathematical ideas. No paper or technical report has yet been published (as of search date, 22 September 2026); the only primary artifact is the original social-media post plus an unverified decoder for the encoded matrices. Given the credited byline names Claude alongside the three humans (rather than describing Claude purely as a checking/formalisation tool) and Epoch AI's own explicit 'solved by AI' provisional call, I coded ai_role as 'assisted' rather than 'none' or 'generated': 'assisted' fits because Claude is credited as a contributor to the construction alongside named humans, but I could not find a clear first-person authors' statement (e.g., a paper or a direct, unambiguous tweet quote from Alpöge) spelling out exactly what mathematics the model produced versus what the humans supplied, which is why I did not code 'generated'. X/Twitter access for the original announcement thread returned an HTTP 402 paywall error, which is a real limitation on directly quoting the primary post.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of §6.2 ('assisted requires the authors' own account... not press coverage, not an inference from acknowledgements') could argue for 'none' as the safer default, since I was unable to fetch and quote the original X thread directly (paywalled) and am relying on secondary paraphrases of the credit line ('a team of three humans and Claude') rather than a first-person methodological account from Alpöge explaining what Claude specifically produced. Conversely, given that Epoch AI's own problem-tracking page (a fairly careful, AI-research-adjacent source in direct contact with the reporting researcher) explicitly frames this as an 'AI-solved' case pending correction, one could argue for 'generated' rather than 'assisted' if it later emerges Claude produced the matrices outright with humans only verifying. I judged 'assisted' as the more conservative middle reading given the acknowledged uncertainty on both sides.
what_would_settle_it: A technical writeup or paper from Alpöge, Voinov and Reynolds-Haertle (or an interview/blog post in their own words) describing the actual construction method and explicitly stating what role Claude played versus the humans — e.g., did Claude propose the construction/search strategy, generate candidate matrices that were then filtered, or did the humans design the search and Claude merely execute compute-heavy steps. Also, formal publication (journal or refereed preprint) of the 12 new matrices, and any update to the Wikipedia Hadamard-matrix-related articles reflecting the new smallest open order below 2000 (now none, since all orders below 2000 divisible by 4 are covered) or above.

outcome: A 2026 preprint from the Caltech Math-AI Lab reports new record lower bounds for the maximal {+1,-1}-matrix determinant at orders n=51, 107, 111, 115, and 119, improving previously recorded values by 0.44% to 3.1%; the general problem (largest determinant for arbitrary n) remains open.

ai.basis_quote: The findings presented in this work grew out of research conducted at the Caltech Math–AI Lab, whose mission is to develop new AI systems and algorithms capable of performing effectively in sparse–reward, long-horizon environments.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the largest determinant of an n-by-n {+1,-1} matrix, a problem still open for general n. Within the window, the main development I could find is arXiv:2608.22518 (v1 submitted 2026-08-23, v2 revised 2026-08-31), 'New Records for the Hadamard Maximal Determinant Problem in Dimensions 51, 107, 111, 115, and 119,' by Butbaia, Vipulanandan, Tan, Huang, Saunders-A'Court, Fagan, Passaro, Tarquini, and Gukov. It reports improved lower-bound determinant records (construction certificates provided, and a companion GitHub repo github.com/Math-AI-Caltech/hadamard-maxdet gives the explicit matrices) for five specific orders, improving prior records by 0.44%-3.1%. This is a record-table advance, not a resolution of the general problem or of any of those orders (the true maximum at those orders is still unknown), so status is 'progress' with resolution_direction null and no counterexample. On AI involvement: the paper's introduction states the work 'grew out of research conducted at the Caltech Math-AI Lab,' whose explicit, self-described mission (per its own site) is building AI/RL systems for sparse-reward, long-horizon search problems, and whose site page credits this exact Hadamard result to its 'RL-based solvers for combinatorial challenges.' This matches the lab's established public track record (Gukov's group previously used hierarchical reinforcement learning to find long counterexample-disproving move sequences for the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, per Caltech's own news coverage). The paper itself does not spell out the algorithm in its body beyond this attribution sentence, and does not use words like 'neural network' or 'reinforcement learning' explicitly in the visible text I could retrieve, but the lab attribution combined with the lab's own explicit claim of authorship of an RL-based approach to this specific result is the authors' own account of how the search was conducted, so I coded ai_role as 'bound' (an AI/RL system moved a numeric bound on a problem that remains open) rather than 'generated' (no claim that the AI 'proved' anything or produced a full solution to the general problem) or 'none'. I also checked for other window-relevant events: a March 2025 paper by Nuñez Ponasso, 'Maximal determinants of matrices over the roots of unity' (arXiv:2503.11114, published in Linear Algebra and its Applications Oct 2025), generalizes the problem to l-th roots of unity; this is a related/variant problem (changing the entry set from {+1,-1} to roots of unity), not a case of the stated {+1,-1} bullet, so per §3.1 it is out of scope and not counted as a change to this problem. I found no resolution of the general conjecture, no settlement of the long-standing order-23 conjecture, and the current Wikipedia article's lead still describes the problem as open for general n with n=23 as the smallest fully open {+1,-1} case (no evidence that changed in the window).
competing_reading: One could argue the paper's introduction sentence about the Math-AI Lab is too thin on its own to satisfy the 'authors' own account' bar for an AI-involvement code, since the paper's visible body text does not itself describe an RL algorithm, loss function, or training procedure — it only names the lab. Under a stricter reading requiring the paper itself (not the lab's separate website) to describe the mechanism, one might code this 'none' pending fuller documentation, treating the lab-website claim as third-party framing rather than the authors' own account within the paper. I lean toward 'bound' because the lab's own site is run by the same group and explicitly claims RL authorship of this specific result, but flag this as a real judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: Access to the full paper's methods/acknowledgements section (the PDF text extraction failed) or the companion GitHub repo's code itself, which would likely state explicitly whether a reinforcement-learning search, a classical computational search, or some hybrid produced the reported matrices.

outcome: The general n-dimensional Hadwiger covering conjecture (every convex body in R^n covered by at most 2^n smaller homothetic copies) remains open for n>=3, but several in-window results moved bounds or settled restricted classes: (1) explicit upper bounds on H_n for small dimensions improved (arXiv:2404.00547, April 2024, published in Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 2025); (2) the illumination/covering conjecture was confirmed for the specific class of 'cap bodies' in all dimensions (arXiv:2510.25968, Oct 2025); (3) a very fresh, undigested, single-author preprint (arXiv:2609.23913, Sept 20 2026) claims an asymptotically optimal exponential growth rate for the covering number as n->infinity, but this is not a resolution of the exact 2^n conjecture and has had essentially no time for expert review.
summary: The general Hadwiger covering conjecture (H_n = 2^n for n>=3, equality only for parallelepipeds) is still open, and remains so on the live Wikipedia article as of this research. Within the 26 Jan 2024 - present window I found three distinct pieces of movement, none of which involve AI. First, arXiv:2404.00547 (submitted April 2024, later published in the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin in 2025) improved explicit small-dimension upper bounds (H5<=933, H6<=6137, H7<=41377, H8<=284096, and symmetric-body variants), using John-ellipsoid covering arguments and quermassintegral estimates -- classic computer-algebra-free convex geometry, no AI. This is squarely `progress`: a bound moved, general conjecture untouched. Second, arXiv:2510.25968 (Arman, Kaire, Prymak; submitted 29 Oct 2025, revised Dec 2025 and Aug 2026) confirms Hadwiger's conjecture for the restricted class of 'cap bodies' (convex hulls of a ball and finitely many external points) in all dimensions, using probabilistic arguments and, for 4<=n<=15, SageMath-based computer-assisted linear programming -- no AI/ML anywhere in the method. Cap bodies are a proper subclass of all convex bodies, so per Section 3.1 this is a genuine restricting case (the conjecture is now known for that whole subclass in every dimension) rather than a variant with changed hypotheses; I classify it as a case within `partial`-type territory, but since the small-dimension bound result independently qualifies for `progress` and represents an unambiguous, undisputed bound movement on the *general* open conjecture, I use `progress` as the overall status to avoid overstating the cap-bodies result as broader resolution than it is (see competing_reading). Third, and most striking: arXiv:2609.23913, submitted by a single author (Yegor Gorodzha) only two days before this research was conducted (20 Sept 2026), claims to establish 'the optimal exponential rate' for the covering number as n->infinity via a fractional-illumination / overlap-energy argument. This is emphatically not a resolution of the exact conjecture (it is an asymptotic growth-rate statement, leaving the precise multiplicative structure and all specific dimensions open), it has had no time for any expert digestion, and I could find no academic footprint for the author beyond a Kaggle profile and a YouTube channel -- red flags that argue for extreme caution rather than for treating it as a credited advance. I have not counted it toward the status decision; I flag it in case a future pass wants to track its fate. No source anywhere -- author accounts, acknowledgements, or secondary coverage -- mentions any AI or machine-learning system in connection with any of these three results; all computation described is either probabilistic-combinatorial by hand or classical LP/computer-algebra (SageMath), not AI in the sense used by this dataset.
competing_reading: One could argue the cap-bodies result (arXiv:2510.25968) alone should drive status to `partial` rather than `progress`, since it is a genuine, complete resolution for an entire (admittedly narrow) subclass of convex bodies in all dimensions, which is a stronger and more definite kind of movement than an incremental bound. I lean toward `progress` as the umbrella status because the problem as Wikipedia states it is about *all* n-dimensional convex bodies, and the aggregate picture across all in-window results is best described as movement on bounds/sub-cases rather than any resolved fragment that a careful reader would say meaningfully narrows the general question people actually care about (arbitrary convex bodies in fixed low dimensions, where the conjecture is completely open). A downstream pass could reasonably override this to `partial`, crediting Arman-Kaire-Prymak, with resolution_direction `confirmed` for the cap-body case.
what_would_settle_it: Whether an expert survey or the Wikipedia article itself, once updated, describes the cap-bodies theorem as 'resolving a case of Hadwiger's conjecture' versus discussing it as a separate strand of the illumination-conjecture literature would settle the partial-vs-progress line. Independently, watching whether arXiv:2609.23913 attracts any citation, review, or refutation in the coming months would settle whether it belongs in the record at all.

outcome: The general Hadwiger conjecture (every graph with no K_t minor is (t-1)-colorable) remains wide open for t>=7; no case beyond t=6 has been settled. What has moved since 26 January 2024 is the best-known asymptotic upper bound on the chromatic number of K_t-minor-free graphs, a weaker relaxation directly tied to the (still open) Linear Hadwiger Conjecture: Delcourt and Postle's O(t log log t) bound (arXiv v5 posted 2024-03-05, published in JAMS 2025) was subsequently improved to O(t (log log t)^6), then O(t (log log t)^5), then (Liu & Luo, Sept 2026) to O(t log log log t), and (Lin, Sept 2026) to O(t sqrt(log log t)) via a separate line of attack. This last paper, arXiv:2609.08713, discloses that its central proof idea was developed with AI assistance.

ai.basis_quote: The central proof idea in this manuscript was developed with the assistance of GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 6 Astra. The author subsequently refined the idea and wrote the manuscript, using the same models to assist with language polishing.

summary: The stated Hadwiger conjecture (chromatic number k implies a K_k minor) is untouched since 2024: it is proved only for k<=6 (k=5,6 equivalent to the Four Color Theorem) and k=7 remains out of reach, confirmed by the current Wikipedia article and Seymour's survey. What did move in the window is the asymptotic upper bound on chromatic number for K_t-minor-free graphs, which bears on the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture (a strengthening asking whether the true bound is O(t)) rather than on the base conjecture's exact statement, but the bound itself is the quantity a careful reader would cite when asked 'what is currently known'. The chain runs: Kostochka/Thomason O(t sqrt(log t)) (1984) -> Norine-Postle-Song O(t (log t)^beta) (2019) -> Delcourt-Postle O(t log log t), final arXiv version 2024-03-05, JAMS 2025 -> two branches of further improvement in 2026: Liu & Luo's O(t log log log t) (no AI disclosed) and Lin's O(t sqrt(log log t)) via a 'star contraction' technique (arXiv:2609.08713, posted 2026-09-08), which explicitly discloses that 'the central proof idea in this manuscript was developed with the assistance of GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 6 Astra,' verified by direct fetch of the paper's HTML render (arxiv.org/html/2609.08713 and the v1-suffixed URL, both returning the identical quote independently) and corroborated by a search-engine snippet quoting the same sentence. This is a genuine authorial claim that an AI system contributed the mathematical core of a bound improvement, not mere language polishing (the paper separately notes the same models were also used for language polishing, which is explicitly excluded from ai_role by the rules and would alone be 'none'). Because the bound-improvement is a single-author, non-digested arXiv preprint, and because it moves a bound on a problem that remains open rather than resolving any case of the stated conjecture, status is 'progress' and ai_role is 'bound'. I could not corroborate the model names 'GPT 5.6 Sol' and 'GPT 6 Astra' against any known OpenAI naming scheme as of my January 2026 knowledge cutoff; they may be codenames for research-preview or post-cutoff releases, or could conceivably be an artifact of how the paper's LaTeX macros render, so I flag this rather than assume it is either genuine or spurious. The odd Hadwiger conjecture disproof (Kuhn, Sauermann, Steiner, Wigderson, Dec 2025) and the dominating/co-claw/co-gem-free/independence-number-2 papers the triage found are all variants or restricted classes per the scope rule in SS3.1, not cases or the conjecture itself, and none disclose AI involvement in their proofs (checked the odd-Hadwiger disproof's abstract page directly; no acknowledgements section was visible).
competing_reading: One could argue the O(t log log t)-type bound-chasing is a 'related problem' (Linear Hadwiger Conjecture, a strengthening with different hypotheses/goal: O(t) vs the general (t-1)-coloring statement) rather than the stated bullet, in which case status should revert to 'open' with no_change_found true, since nothing about the base conjecture (does chromatic number k force a K_k minor) has moved at all — it is exactly as open as in January 2024. Under that reading the AI-assisted bound paper would be beside the question entirely, the same way the odd-Hadwiger and restricted-class results are. I chose to treat the asymptotic-bound literature as within scope because Wikipedia's own article on this conjecture (and most treatments of 'progress on Hadwiger's conjecture') report exactly these O(t log log t)-type results as the state of the art, and because the bound is a direct, unconditional consequence of assuming the linear conjecture is false — i.e. it *is* what is currently provable about the general statement's chromatic-number consequence, not an unrelated variant with different hypotheses. But this is a genuine judgment call given SS3.1's warning that a conjecture 'with different hypotheses' is out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Linear Hadwiger's Conjecture (or the O(t log log t)-family bounds derived toward it) is treated by domain experts as part of 'Hadwiger's conjecture' itself or as a distinct related problem would settle the scope question; a survey or the Wikipedia article's own framing of these results (which it does report under the conjecture's own page) is suggestive but not decisive. For the AI question, an independent digestion of arXiv:2609.08713 (peer review, or a well-known expert's blog commenting on it) would confirm whether the disclosed AI assistance is being taken seriously by the community, and clarify what 'GPT 5.6 Sol' and 'GPT 6 Astra' actually refer to.

outcome: The chromatic number of the plane remains bounded between 5 and 7, unchanged since de Grey's 2018 lower bound and the classical hexagonal-tiling upper bound; no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 - present) altered this range for the problem as Wikipedia states it.
summary: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem, as Wikipedia's frozen bullet states it, asks for the chromatic number χ(ℝ²) of the unit-distance graph of the plane. This has been bounded between 5 and 7 since Aubrey de Grey's 2018 lower-bound construction and the classical hexagonal-tiling upper bound of 7; the current Wikipedia article (fetched live) confirms this range is still open and unchanged, and no source found in this research reports any tightening of the 5-7 range within the window (26 Jan 2024 to today). The smallest known 5-chromatic unit-distance graph (the 509-vertex 'Parts graph') also predates the window (2020-2021); a 2026 Haugland result on a restricted (Moser-spindle-free) variant produced a 2131-vertex graph, which is a record for a different, more restricted question and does not improve the unrestricted 509-vertex record, so it is not a change to this problem either. Two lines of post-window work were flagged by triage and investigated in depth: (1) Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga and Zsamboki (arXiv 2311.10069, first posted 16 Nov 2023 but last revised 27 Mar 2025) proved the *fractional* chromatic number of the plane is at least 4; this is a distinct graph parameter from the integer chromatic number this bullet asks about (a fractional bound of 4 says nothing new about whether χ(ℝ²) is 5, 6 or 7, which was already known to be ≥5), so under §3.1 this is a related-but-different problem, not a case of this one, and it involves no AI (a purely human, combinatorial/group-theoretic proof). (2) Mundinger, Pokutta, Spiegel and Zimmer (arXiv 2404.05509, posted 8 Apr 2024, and its ICML 2025 companion arXiv 2501.18527) used a custom neural-network/'deep annealing' approach to find two new six-colorings of the plane for the *off-diagonal two-distance variant* of the problem (avoiding unit distance in five colors and a second distance d in a sixth), extending the known range of d from about [0.414,0.447] to [0.354,0.657] - the first improvement in ~30 years to that variant. This is again a distinct, restricted variant (a different problem posed over a different question - the two-distance coloring, not the plain chromatic number), so it is out of scope for this bullet under §3.1's case-vs-variant test, even though it is the one genuinely AI-flavored result found. Notably, even for its own (different) problem, the authors' own description - 'derived by formalizing colorings suggested by a custom machine learning approach' - places the neural network's contribution as suggesting candidate constructions that humans then formalized and verified, which is consistent with substantive assistance to that variant's result (were it in scope, it would likely code as assisted) rather than the network single-handedly generating a verified proof. A search also surfaced a May 2026 Zenodo preprint by an individual (Jonathan Reed) claiming to fully resolve χ(ℝ²)=7 via a Lean 4 'toroidal projection' argument; this is an unreviewed, non-credible submission with no expert digestion, no acceptance anywhere, and reasoning (mapping the plane to a torus to derive Euclidean coloring constraints) that does not hold up - it is not counted as any kind of event, claimed or otherwise, since it lacks even preprint-server-standard credibility and shows no sign of being taken seriously by anyone in the field. Taken together, the core bullet - χ(ℝ²) ∈ {5,6,7} - has seen no change in the window; the two adjacent bodies of work identified belong to different (fractional-chromatic-number and two-distance-variant) questions and are recorded here only for context.
competing_reading: One could argue Wikipedia's own prose for this bullet is loose enough that 'the chromatic number of unit distance graphs' should be read broadly to include the fractional chromatic number or the two-distance variant, since both are discussed in the same literature and sometimes in the same papers/sections as the classical problem. Under that broader reading, the 2311.10069 fractional bound and the 2404.05509/2501.18527 ML-derived six-colorings would count as `partial` progress, and the two-distance-variant work would then carry an `ai_role` of `assisted` (based on the authors' own 'derived by formalizing colorings suggested by' language). I judged the narrower reading correct because the frozen statement explicitly names 'the chromatic number,' a specific, well-defined integer graph parameter that differs technically from its fractional relaxation, and because the two-distance problem is a named, distinct variant in the literature (not the plane's own unit-distance chromatic number) - restricting the question rather than merely rephrasing it moves outside the bullet's scope per §3.1.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from Wikipedia's own editors or from a survey of the Hadwiger-Nelson literature explicitly treating the fractional chromatic number or the two-distance/off-diagonal variant as part of 'the' Hadwiger-Nelson problem (rather than as related-but-distinct questions) would justify reclassifying this as `partial` with `ai_role` `assisted`. Absent that, the narrower reading stands.

outcome: No result advancing, refuting, or otherwise changing the bound in Hall's conjecture (either the classical form |y^2 - x^3| > c(epsilon) x^{1/2-epsilon}, or the original conjectured form) was found in the 26 January 2024 - 22 September 2026 window.
summary: Hall's conjecture concerns the separation between perfect squares and perfect cubes on Mordell curves y^2 = x^3 + k, and its weak form (with the epsilon and constant c(epsilon), as stated in the frozen Wikipedia bullet) remains open. All pre-2024 history is well documented: Elkies' 1998 discovery of a case (x=5853886516781223, from a curve with |k| large) that disproved the strong (epsilon=0) form, forcing the weaker epsilon-dependent version now standard; Danilov's 1982 proof that exponent 1/2 is essentially optimal; and an extensive, continually updated table of 'Hall numbers' (record small ratios r_x) maintained by Dujella and collaborators, most entries from the 1990s-2000s with a 2014 paper (Karim & Silverman, arXiv:1410.0078) on gap sizes between consecutive Hall numbers, none after 2024. Multiple targeted searches (general web search and arXiv search across 2024-2026) turned up no preprint, announcement, or new record-table entry addressing this problem in the window. General AI-and-mathematics search terms (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, DeepMind Erdos-problem sweeps, GPT-based Erdos-problem solutions) surfaced substantial 2025-2026 AI activity on other open number-theory and combinatorics problems (e.g., the unit distance conjecture, various Erdos problems), but none of that coverage mentions Hall's conjecture, Mordell curves, or the square-cube gap problem. Per the scope rule (3.1), record-table extensions (new Hall numbers) would only count if found, since the bullet is about the existence/value of a bound rather than being itself a 'largest known value' bullet — but no such extensions were found in any case. I agree with the triage's verdict: nothing has happened to this problem in the window, and no AI system is connected to it.
competing_reading: None identified. There is no ambiguous or borderline result to classify differently; the search simply returned nothing in-window. If an unindexed table update (e.g., an informal addition to Dujella's personal 'Hall numbers' webpage, which I could not access directly - it returned 404) occurred without an accompanying paper, it would not surface in these searches, but such an update would at most be 'progress' on the record table, not a change to the stated bound itself under the scope rule.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement post-26-January-2024 either (a) proving or disproving the weak form of Hall's conjecture, (b) improving the known exponent/lower-bound results (e.g., beating Danilov's or subsequent bounds), or (c) adding entries to the Hall-number record table with a dated publication. None of these were found.

outcome: No progress on the Halperin conjecture (Serre spectral sequence collapse for fibrations with rationally elliptic, nonzero-Euler-characteristic fiber) has been found dated after 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open in general, with the most recent substantive progress (Kennard–Wu, formal dimensions up to 20) predating the frozen revision.
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet describes the Halperin conjecture on collapse of the rational Serre spectral sequence for fibrations whose fiber is rationally elliptic with non-zero Euler characteristic (equivalently, via Meier's algebraic reformulation: a positively elliptic algebra admits no non-trivial derivation of negative degree). The last substantive progress on this conjecture is Kennard and Wu's extension of the formal-dimension verification from 16 to 20 (arXiv:2104.04086, posted April 2021, published in Communications in Algebra 51(8), 2023) — this predates the 26 January 2024 freeze and is already reflected in pre-2024 literature, matching the triage's finding. I re-ran the triage's queries plus several additional ones targeting later formal-dimension extensions ('22', '24'), AI/algorithmic angles, and general 'proof/solved' phrasing, and checked the live Wikipedia article, which itself still states the conjecture was open '[a]s of 2019' with no newer update recorded. Two 2025 arXiv papers surfaced in searches (2503.01123, a March 2025 paper on sequential parametrized topological complexity, and 2507.02590, a July 2025 paper giving algorithms to compute LS category and the Ginsburg invariant for elliptic spaces) both sit in the same rational-homotopy-of-elliptic-spaces neighborhood but neither addresses the Halperin conjecture itself — the first doesn't mention it at all, and the second's algorithmic contribution is about different invariants (LS category, Ginsburg invariant), not the derivation/collapse question the conjecture poses, and it does not use AI/ML methods (classical algorithms only). No AI involvement of any kind was found near this problem. I conclude nothing has happened to this problem in the window, and no AI system has come near it.
competing_reading: None found. The 2507.02590 paper works in an adjacent algorithmic corner of elliptic-space theory and could in principle be read as tangential progress on the surrounding toolkit, but it does not touch the derivation/spectral-sequence-collapse statement that constitutes the conjecture, so it is a related-but-distinct question rather than a case or variant of this one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that either (a) proves the general collapse/no-negative-derivation statement, (b) extends the formal-dimension verification beyond 20, or (c) settles a genuinely new special case (e.g., a new class of homogeneous or Kähler-like spaces) not already covered by Meier, Shiga-Tezuka, or Lupton's pre-2024 results.

outcome: The Erdős–Szekeres conjecture ES(n)=2^(n-2)+1 remains open in general (still unresolved for n=7 and above), but Baek and Balko (SoCG 2025) proved it for the class of 'decomposable' point sets, and separately proved a relaxed 'split k-gon' version tight at exactly 2^(k-2)+1 for all k; independently, a December 2025 preprint reports partial (non-exhaustive) SAT-solver progress toward the n=7 case (ES(7)=33) without completing it.
summary: The statement in scope is the general Erdős–Szekeres conjecture that ES(n)=2^(n-2)+1 for arbitrary n, still open at the general level (proved only for n≤6, via earlier SAT work by Szekeres–Peters and later Scheucher, all predating the frozen revision). Two lines of post-window work bear on it. (1) Jineon Baek and Martin Balko, 'The Erdős–Szekeres Conjecture Revisited' (SoCG 2025, LIPIcs vol. 332, article 13; also a Journal of Combinatorics 2025/2026 version), presented at SoCG in June 2025, prove the exact conjecture for 'decomposable' point sets — a restricted class of configurations including the classical Erdős–Szekeres cap/cup sets and Valtr's Horton sets — which is a genuine case of the stated problem (restriction to a subclass of point sets), so it counts as `partial` progress with direction `confirmed` (the conjectured bound holds on this restricted class). The same paper also proves that every set of at least 2^(k-2)+1 points (no three collinear) contains a 'split k-gon', a relaxed convex-position notion, and shows this threshold is tight; this is a genuinely different (weaker) statement about a different combinatorial object, so by §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case of the stated one, and does not itself move the classification, though it is worth recording as context. (2) Dumitru Bogdan's December 2025 preprint 'Notes on the 33-point Erdős–Szekeres problem' (arXiv:2512.24061, submitted 2025-12-30) targets ES(7)=33, the first open instance of the exact formula, using a SAT encoding (Kissat solver, ~16.67M clauses, ~578K variables) with convex-layer anchoring; it explicitly reports only UNSAT certificates for some anchored subfamilies, not a full resolution, and notes 'pronounced runtime variability' and heavy-tailed cost that 'currently dominates the computational effort' — so it is progress/incomplete, not a status-changing event by itself, and does not surpass the Baek–Balko decomposable-sets result as the decisive event. No AI system (LLM, ML model, or AI-driven proof search) is credited in either paper; both are SAT-solver/combinatorial-proof work, which under §6.2 is explicitly not AI involvement. A search for AI-driven mathematical proof-search systems touching Erdős problems (e.g. the 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' paper, which lists 9 solved Erdős problems) found no mention of the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture or happy ending problem among their targets. I chose Baek–Balko's decomposable-sets result, dated to the SoCG 2025 conference (June 2025), as the decisive event because it is the most substantial genuine case-restriction of the stated conjecture that has been digested (peer-reviewed, published proceedings); the Bogdan SAT preprint is noted as further undigested, incomplete progress in the same direction.
competing_reading: One could argue the status should be `open` with `no_change_found` true, on the reading that 'decomposable sets' is itself a variant/related notion (a structural restriction defined ad hoc for the paper) rather than a natural 'case' of the conjecture in the sense of restricting to a geometrically meaningful subclass like convex position or a dimension. If decomposable sets are read as a bespoke technical construct rather than a case of 'arbitrary n', the correct classification would be `open`/`no_change_found` with the split k-gon and decomposable-set results relegated to context in the summary only. I judge the decomposable-sets result to satisfy the case test (it restricts the point sets quantified over, removing territory from the general statement) rather than changing the question, but the line is not sharp.
what_would_settle_it: A close reading of the Baek–Balko paper's definition of 'decomposable' point sets against whether it is a natural geometric restriction (making it a case) or an ad hoc technical device tailored to their proof technique (making it a variant); and whether ES(7)=33 is fully settled by either exhaustive SAT verification or a human-checked proof, which as of the December 2025 Bogdan preprint had not occurred.

outcome: Chang and Sun (Graph Drawing 2024) proved Harborth's conjecture for the restricted case of 4-regular planar graphs, extending earlier partial results (diamond subgraphs, non-4-edge-connected graphs) to cover the full degree-4 class; the general conjecture for all planar graphs remains open.
summary: Harborth's conjecture (every planar graph has a straight-line drawing with all-integer edge lengths, i.e. an integral Fáry embedding) remains open in general. The one result inside the 26 Jan 2024–present window that is a genuine case of this problem, rather than a variant, is Chang and Sun, 'Harborth's Conjecture for 4-Regular Planar Graphs' (LIPIcs GD 2024, DROPS record 10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2024.38, San Francisco State University). They prove the conjecture holds for every 4-regular planar graph (extending prior work covering only 4-regular graphs with diamond subgraphs or that are not 4-edge-connected), so the conjecture is now settled for all graphs of maximum degree ≤ 4. This restricts the territory of the original problem (a degree class), so it is classified `partial`/`confirmed`, not `progress` — a whole subclass, not merely a bound, was settled, and the direction matches what the conjecture predicts. I could not extract readable text from the PDF directly (WebFetch returned only binary/compressed stream content), so I relied on the DROPS abstract page and search-engine summaries of the paper and its GD 2024 slides page (which 404'd); no acknowledgements or methods section mentioning AI, computer search, or SAT/ILP solvers surfaced anywhere I could read, and the paper's own keywords list only 'planar graphs, straight-line embeddings, Diophantine equations' — nothing suggesting automated theorem proving. I found no evidence of any AI system's involvement in this or any other Harborth's-conjecture-specific development. Two further 2025–2026 items surfaced but are variants, not cases, of Harborth's conjecture as Wikipedia states it: (1) 'On the Harborth Conjecture. Part I' (arXiv 2607.02535, submitted 2026-06-17, revised 2026-07-13) makes progress on Kleber's conjecture, a strengthening that additionally requires integer vertex coordinates (not just integer edge lengths) — it reduces Kleber's conjecture to rational-distance statements for small polygons and proves the non-degenerate-quadrilateral case, leaving pentagons and degenerate cases for future parts; this changes the hypotheses of Harborth's stated conjecture rather than restricting it, so per §3.1 it does not count as progress on this bullet. (2) Förster, Kobourov, Miller, Zink, 'Drawing Trees and Cacti with Integer Edge Lengths on a Polynomial-Size Grid' (arXiv 2509.04168, GD 2025 poster), also targets Kleber's conjecture and, for a class (trees/cacti) where existential integral Fáry embeddings were already known, supplies constructive polynomial-grid-size algorithms — an efficiency/constructiveness improvement to an already-settled case of a different (stronger) conjecture, not a new case of Harborth's conjecture itself. No AI involvement was found in either paper either. The current live Wikipedia article on Harborth's conjecture (checked as a secondary cross-check, not as the frozen source) confirms the conjecture 'remains unsolved' in general and lists the same known partial classes (bipartite, sparse, treewidth-3, degree-4 special cases, outerplanar, series-parallel, Platonic solids) plus the Kleber variant — consistent with what I found directly.
competing_reading: One could argue the Chang-Sun 4-regular result should be scored as `progress` rather than `partial` on the theory that 'degree ≤ 4' is a narrow corner of 'all planar graphs' and doesn't meaningfully move the general conjecture. But §3.1 is explicit that a case need not be large to count as `partial`, and settling an entire degree class (closing the last gap after diamond-subgraph and non-4-edge-connected cases were already known) is a clean restriction of the stated question, not a bound — so `partial` is the better fit.
what_would_settle_it: A full proof or disproof of Harborth's conjecture for all planar graphs, or evidence that Chang and Sun (or anyone else in the window) used an AI system to help find the embedding construction or Diophantine argument, which would change ai_role from none.

outcome: No progress on either stated conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; nearby-sounding results found in searches (Guth–Maynard 2024 zero-density theorem, an arXiv paper titled "On the Second Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture", and a "Simple Proof of the Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture") all concern different problems that merely share the Hardy–Littlewood name or general zeta/prime-counting subject matter.
summary: The Hardy–Littlewood zeta-function conjectures, as stated in the frozen Wikipedia revision, are two specific quantitative claims about zeros of ζ(1/2+it): (1) for H = T^(0.25+ε), the interval (T, T+H] contains a zero of odd order for T large enough; (2) for H = T^(0.5+ε), N₀(T+H) − N₀(T) ≥ cH for T large enough, where N₀ counts zeros on the critical line. Pre-2024 history is well documented (Selberg 1942 proved a weaker exponent result with an extra log T factor; Selberg conjectured the exponent could drop below 1/2; Karatsuba proved this in 1984 and extended it to 'supershort' intervals in 1992; Moser 2014 gave a 16.6% improvement of a related exponent) but none of this is post-January-2024. I searched extensively for anything published since the frozen date that bears on either exact statement (H, c, N₀(T+H)−N₀(T), or odd-order real zeros in short intervals) and found nothing. Three items surfaced repeatedly in search but are false positives on inspection: (a) Guth and Maynard's May 2024 zero-density theorem (arXiv:2405.20552, published in Annals of Mathematics 2026) improves the Ingham bound on N(σ,T) for zeros with σ > 1/2 (off the critical line) — a genuinely major advance, but it addresses a different zero-density question than the Hardy–Littlewood conjectures, which concern the density of zeros ON the critical line (N₀(T)); (b) 'On the Second Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture' (arXiv:2503.02766, March 2025) is about the completely unrelated additive/subadditive conjecture π(x+y) ≤ π(x) + π(y) for the prime-counting function — a namesake collision, not a case or variant of the zeta-zero conjecture; (c) 'Simple Proof of the Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture' (Annals of Mathematics and Physics, June 2025) addresses yet another Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, an additive/Goldbach-type prime representation claim, published in a low-quality open-access journal (Peertechz) and explicitly incomplete (relies on an unproven auxiliary conjecture). A 2026 arXiv preprint ('Jacob's ladders and the equivalent of the Fermat-Wiles theorem generated by the Hardy-Littlewood formula (1921)', arXiv:2603.01747) invokes the 1921 Hardy–Littlewood zeta paper but does not address either stated conjecture and belongs to a long-running, non-mainstream 'Jacob's ladder' series. No AI system appears anywhere in this search: none of the located papers or the Wikipedia article's history mention AI-assisted derivation, and my own broader search for AI mathematical breakthroughs in this period (Erdős problems solved by Gemini/AlphaEvolve-style systems, GPT-5.5 Pro on Borsuk's conjecture, etc.) turned up nothing connected to Hardy–Littlewood zeta zero density or real-zero-gap questions. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case: the search covered the exact quantities named in the conjectures (H, c, N₀), the general subject (zero density / real zeros of zeta), the Selberg/Karatsuba lineage, and an AI-specific sweep, all with no hits.
competing_reading: One could argue Guth–Maynard's improvement of the Ingham zero-density bound is 'the kind of thing' the triage or a careless reader might fold into 'zero-density progress on zeta' and thus into this bullet as `progress`. But the stated conjectures are specifically about N₀(T) (real zeros on the critical line) and the length of intervals guaranteed to contain such zeros; Guth–Maynard bounds N(σ,T) for σ strictly greater than 1/2, a disjoint quantity. Under §3.1 this is a related problem sharing a subject (zeta zero-counting) rather than a case of the problem as stated, so it does not count as a change to this bullet.
what_would_settle_it: A paper specifically improving the exponent 0.25 in the odd-order-zero conjecture, the exponent 0.5 or the constant c in the N₀(T+H)−N₀(T) ≥ cH conjecture, or a full resolution of either, dated after 26 January 2024, would settle this differently. None was found.

outcome: No case, bound, or resolution of Hartshorne's conjecture(s) as stated in this bullet has changed since 26 January 2024; the two nearby 2024-2026 papers found are either an adjacent classification problem (not a case of the conjecture) or a conditional implication involving a separate conjecture, and neither settles any part of Hartshorne's own conjectures.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Hartshorne's conjectures' (plural, unlinked, citing a single footnote to Hartshorne's own 1974 paper) refers to the family of conjectures Robin Hartshorne proposed, of which the best-known and most actively worked on is the complete-intersection conjecture: a smooth, nondegenerate, codimension-c subvariety X of P^n with n >= 2c+1 (equivalently c < n/3) is a complete intersection. (Hartshorne also stated a conjecture on ample subvarieties/submanifolds intersecting, related to work on the Frankel conjecture; no activity was found on that variant either in the window.) Multiple 2024-2026 surveys and papers (ProofAtlas's dedicated tracking page, the arXiv listing, Arrondo's survey) confirm the main conjecture remains fully open, including in the much-studied codimension-2 / Fano case. Two items surfaced during triage and further search are close to the topic but do not change the bullet: (1) Watanabe's 'Quadratic Varieties of Small Codimension' (arXiv:2405.04002, received 28 Jan 2025, published SIGMA 15 Jun 2025) proves the conjecture for quadratic varieties (a case already settled pre-2024 by Ionescu-Russo) and then classifies the *boundary-adjacent* case n=2c-1, which sits just outside the conjectured range n>=2c+1 -- this is a related classification exercise near the conjecture's edge, not a restriction of the conjecture's own statement, so under the scope rule (§3.1) it is a related problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture; (2) Benoist-Voisin, 'On the smoothability problem with rational coefficients' (arXiv:2405.12620, accepted 20 Oct 2024, published in Rendiconti Lincei 2026), proves that an affirmative solution to a different classical problem (rational-coefficient smoothing of algebraic cycles, going back to Borel-Haefliger) would be *incompatible* with Hartshorne's conjecture being true. This is a conditional/logical link between two conjectures -- it neither proves nor disproves Hartshorne's conjecture, and settles nothing about it directly; it is evidence about a related problem's relationship to Hartshorne's conjecture, not a change to Hartshorne's conjecture itself. No AI system is mentioned in either paper's acknowledgements, methodology, or any secondary coverage found. The site 'ProofAtlas' (proofatlas.ai) styles itself as an 'AI-first mathematical research' platform and has a page mapping routes toward the Hartshorne complete-intersection conjecture, but on inspection it contains no completed proof, no new theorem, and no AI-produced mathematical result -- only a curated 'route map' of open sub-questions and an invitation for a 'hosted agent' to work on them in the future. This is infrastructure, not a finding, and does not change the status. I searched specifically for any AI/LLM claim on this conjecture (including recent high-profile AI math results like the unit distance conjecture and Erdos problem 1196) and found no connection to Hartshorne's conjectures.
competing_reading: One could argue Watanabe's n=2c-1 classification is 'about' the conjecture in a loose sense, since it directly abuts the conjectured threshold and uses the same quadratic-variety framework; if read that way it would be `partial` progress with `resolution_direction` null (a classification, not a proof/disproof). I judge it a related/adjacent problem rather than a case because n=2c-1 is explicitly outside the conjectured range (n>=2c+1) -- proving something about varieties in that range does not remove any territory from the conjecture as stated, which only makes a claim for n>=2c+1.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that proves or disproves the conjecture for some specific n>=2c+1 range not previously known (e.g., extending the codimension-2/Fano case, or improving on Ananyan-Hochster-style large-n results), or an authoritative statement that Watanabe's or a similar boundary-case result is understood by specialists as constraining the n>=2c+1 statement itself.
