outcome: A single-author preprint (Ludovic Tagnon, 24 Aug 2026, arXiv:2608.23281, companion arXiv:2608.24750) claims to settle Karpenkov's Problem 4 — the complex (signature (1,1)) cubic case, the last open case of Hermite's problem for n=3 — via a deterministic sin^2-type algorithm with exact periodicity certificates verified on 205 sample polynomials and an exhaustive box search, plus a Lean 4 machine-checked instance for the plastic number field; this is a preprint with no expert digestion yet, so it counts as a claimed result on a case of the problem, not a resolution.

ai.basis_quote: This research was AI-assisted. All computations were carried out under a fixed audit protocol: questions and thresholds fixed in advance, published fixtures reproduced before every run, independent recounts of every headline number, hash-chained manifests, and adversarial review of the manuscript itself. The protocol is documented in PROTOCOL.md inside the archive; the human author directed the work and takes responsibility for all claims.

summary: Hermite's problem (does every real number admit an assignment of an eventually-periodic integer sequence iff it is algebraic of degree n) was, as of January 2024, solved only for the totally-real cubic case (n=3) via Karpenkov's sin^2-algorithm (2022, pre-window). The remaining open case for n=3, the complex (signature (1,1)) cubics, is Karpenkov's own 'Problem 4'. On 24 August 2026, Ludovic Tagnon (sole author, Nancy, France) posted arXiv:2608.23281, 'A deterministic sin^2-type algorithm for complex cubic irrationalities with exact periodicity certificates', claiming a deterministic algorithm that implements Karpenkov's suggested analytic extension of the sin^2-algorithm to the (1,1) signature, proves a closed-form negativity lemma for the score function, and empirically/certifiably confirms eventual periodicity on 205 sampled complex cubic polynomials plus an exhaustive search over [-3,3]^3 (194/194 closing), with one field (the plastic number) machine-checked in Lean 4 'kernel-only'. A companion structural paper, arXiv:2608.24750 (25 Aug 2026, same sole author), proves finiteness and height-descent theorems supporting the algorithm. The paper's own abstract states 'The general periodicity problem remains open' -- it resolves a case (n=3, signature (1,1)), not the whole n=3 problem's general/all-n formulation, and it is not a resolution of Hermite's problem as stated in the Wikipedia bullet (which is about all natural numbers n). Per the scope rule (3.1) this is a case of the problem (restricting to n=3, and within that to one signature), so if accepted it would count as `partial` progress toward the n=3 case, not a resolution of the bullet as a whole. As of today (22 Sept 2026) this is under one month old, single-authored, with no journal acceptance, no digestion by an outside expert (e.g. Karpenkov himself, whose Problem 4 it purports to answer), and no citing/discussion found beyond the automated 'Pith' preprint-review platform, which is an automated (non-expert-human) review service, not a mathematician's digestion. The Lean 4 verification covers only one specific field instance (the plastic number), not the general algorithm's correctness, and the 205-sample and exhaustive-box verifications are described as computational/empirical certificates rather than a general proof that the algorithm terminates for all (1,1) cubics -- so even taking the paper at face value, it is an empirical/certificate-backed claim on a restricted domain, not a full proof of Problem 4. I therefore classify status as `claimed` (preprint, not yet expert-digested) rather than `resolved` or `partial`; because no case has actually been *settled* by expert consensus yet, `partial` would overstate certainty, though once/if experts digest it, downgrading to `partial` (a case of the n=3 problem settled) or keeping `claimed` upgraded to something else may be warranted. On AI: the paper states 'This research was AI-assisted' in a 'Reproducibility' section, but goes on to describe the AI's role only as running computations under a fixed, human-designed audit protocol, recounting headline numbers, and performing 'adversarial review of the manuscript' -- i.e., checking, auditing, and proofreading of work the human author designed and directed ('the human author directed the work and takes responsibility for all claims'). No specific AI system is named anywhere in either paper. Under the rules in 6.2, checking, auditing, proofreading and reviewing do not qualify as `assisted`, `generated`, or `bound` -- those require the AI to have produced part of the mathematics (an argument, construction, case, or bound) by the authors' own account, which this disclosure does not claim. I therefore code `ai_role` as `none`, while flagging in `competing_reading` that the vague, unnamed 'AI-assisted... computations' language leaves open the possibility that an AI system actually executed the search/verification computations that produced the periodicity certificates (arguably part of the mathematical result, not just proofreading it) -- if so this would lean toward `bound` or `assisted` rather than `none`. Given the disclosure names no system and explicitly frames the human as having 'directed the work,' `none` is the more defensible reading under the requirement that `assisted`/`generated` need a clear authorial statement that AI produced mathematics appearing in the result.
competing_reading: If 'computations were carried out under a fixed audit protocol' by AI is read as the AI actually executing the search that produced the periodicity certificates on 205 polynomials and the exhaustive box search (i.e., generating the numerical/algebraic verification data that is part of the result), this could be coded `assisted` (AI produced part of the mathematics, specifically the verification computations) rather than `none`. The paper's phrasing is genuinely ambiguous between 'AI ran routine verification scripts' (non-qualifying) and 'AI executed the core computational search underlying the certificates' (arguably qualifying). No named system and no explicit statement of what specifically the AI computed versus what conventional code/CAS did tips me toward `none`, but a stricter reader could reasonably code this `assisted` or `bound`.
what_would_settle_it: The archive's PROTOCOL.md (referenced but not fetched here) or a direct statement from the author about which specific AI system was used and for which specific computational or mathematical steps would resolve whether this is `none` or `assisted`/`bound`. Expert response from Oleg Karpenkov or another specialist confirming or disputing the periodicity certificates would resolve whether this remains `claimed` or should become `partial`/`resolved`.

outcome: Garonzi and Margolis (arXiv:2509.25118) proved the Herzog-Schönheim conjecture for two classes of finite groups — finite simple groups and symmetric groups — settling these cases while the general conjecture (over arbitrary groups) remains open.
summary: The Herzog-Schönheim conjecture (1974) asks whether a coset partition of a group G by subgroups of finite index can have distinct indices; it conjectures the answer is no (some two indices must coincide). Since 26 Jan 2024, the main development is a preprint by Garonzi and Margolis, 'The Herzog-Schönheim conjecture for simple and symmetric groups' (arXiv:2509.25118, submitted 2025-09-29, revised 2026-05-05), which proves the conjecture holds for all finite simple groups and all finite symmetric groups. This is a genuine case of the stated problem — a restriction to specific classes of groups — not a variant, so it counts as `partial` per §3.1 (settling a case narrows the territory of the general conjecture, which remains open for groups in general, including e.g. general finite or infinite groups). I read the paper's full HTML text (not just the abstract): the authors state they 'rely on computer calculations' using GAP and Mathematica (standard computer-algebra systems, not AI per §6.2's exclusion of computer algebra/exhaustive search from AI codes) and thank three mathematicians (Roney-Dougal, Craven, Liebeck) for mathematical consultations on maximal subgroups of simple groups of Lie type, with Liebeck given credit for proving one proposition. No mention anywhere in the paper of AI, ML, LLMs, or any AI-assisted tooling. I also found and checked a July 2024 arXiv paper ('A Note on Finite Nilpotent Groups', arXiv:2407.05498) that surfaced under nilpotent-group searches; it does not concern the Herzog-Schönheim conjecture at all (different characterization of nilpotent groups), so it is irrelevant. I also found a paper on the conjecture for free groups using covering spaces that appeared in print in the journal Beiträge zur Algebra und Geometrie in April 2024 — but this is arXiv:1804.11103, a 2018 preprint by Chouraqui; the 2024 date is only the journal's print/online publication lag, which §6.3 explicitly says not to use for dating, so this is not a window event (it predates 26 Jan 2024 in substance). No counterexample or disproof of any case was found; no withdrawal or dispute was found.
competing_reading: One could argue that proving the conjecture for simple and symmetric groups is a large enough achievement, covering essentially all the 'hard' finite non-abelian building blocks, that it deserves more weight than a typical `partial` — but per §6.1 this is still a case of the problem, not a resolution of the general conjecture (which covers arbitrary, including infinite, groups), so `partial` is the correct code regardless of the result's significance.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) covering the fully general statement — all groups, or at least all finite groups — would move this to `resolved` or a status reflecting full resolution; a peer-reviewed/expert-digested version of the Garonzi-Margolis result would not change the status code but would strengthen confidence.

outcome: No case, bound, or resolution of the conjecture as stated has been established since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open, with a large volume of unreviewed preprints claiming resolutions and one serious strategy paper (Connes-Consani-Moscovici, Nov 2025) that stops short of a proof.
summary: The current (2026) Hilbert–Pólya conjecture Wikipedia article still describes the conjecture as unproven, with its most recent substantive entry dating to 2017 (Bender–Brody–Müller, criticized by Bellissard) — nothing in the live article postdates 26 January 2024 as a change to the conjecture's status. My own search turned up two distinct tiers of activity in the window. (1) A serious strategy paper: Connes, Consani and Moscovici, 'Zeta Spectral Triples' (arXiv:2511.22755, submitted 27 Nov 2025), constructs self-adjoint operators (rank-one perturbations of a spectral triple tied to Euler products over primes p ≤ x) whose spectra match the low-lying zeta zeros numerically with striking accuracy, and outlines a strategy for a proof via convergence of zeros as the truncation grows. The authors themselves state that 'a rigorous proof of this convergence would establish the Riemann Hypothesis' — i.e. they present a strategy and numerical evidence, not a proof, and no case of the conjecture is settled. This is genuine mathematics by credentialed authors but it does not change what the bullet's entry should say: the conjecture is still open. There is also ongoing legitimate but incomplete work by Enderalp Yakaboylu (arXiv:2408.15135, first submitted Aug 2024, revised through 2026) constructing a non-self-adjoint or conditionally-self-adjoint Hamiltonian whose reality of eigenvalues is tied to RH; it remains inconclusive and has not been digested as a resolution. (2) A large, and apparently growing, flood of self-published, non-peer-reviewed preprints on Zenodo, Preprints.org, ResearchGate, and academia.edu (checked several: Zenodo 20573045 'Proof of the Hilbert-Pólya Conjecture' by Antonio Bonelli, June 2026; Zenodo 21980608 by Michael Aksman, Aug 2026; Zenodo 21096214 by Charles Tibedo, July 2026; Preprints.org 202512.0817, Dec 2025) each independently claims to construct 'the' Hilbert-Pólya self-adjoint operator and thereby prove RH. None have any peer review, none have been digested or corroborated by a working number theorist, none appear in a journal of record, and none show any sign of being taken seriously by the mathematical community (no MathOverflow acceptance, no blog engagement from Tao or others found). None of the ones I opened mention any AI system in producing the mathematics. A separate, tangential item — a ResearchGate posting titled 'A Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Assisted by Artificial Intelligence: An Analytic Approach' (Oct 2025) — explicitly credits ChatGPT, but its method is a direct contradiction argument on the critical strip using the zeta function's modulus, not a construction of a self-adjoint operator with the zeta zeros as its spectrum; it targets RH itself via a different route and is not scoped to this bullet's Hilbert-Pólya operator statement, and in any case is an unreviewed, almost certainly flawed self-publication (RH is unresolved). Taken together: no case or bound of the Hilbert-Pólya conjecture, as stated, has been settled in the window; the correct status is open, with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Connes-Consani-Moscovici paper constitutes 'progress' under §6.1 as 'an instructive incident' or a bound-moving result, since it is genuine work by leading mathematicians (Connes is a Fields medalist with a long history on this exact problem) producing numerically convincing operator constructions that go further than prior attempts. However, no quantitative bound on the conjecture (which has no natural notion of a partial numeric bound — it is an existence statement about an operator) moved, and no case of the conjecture was settled: the paper is explicit that convergence to the full zero set remains conjectural. Under §3.1's rule that an existence question moves only when answered, this stays 'open' rather than 'progress'. If a future assessor believes the numerical/structural strategy itself should count as 'progress' (an instructive step, not a full case), that would be the strongest case for reclassifying; I judged it insufficient because the paper explicitly withholds claiming even a conditional resolution and it is very recent (10 months old) with no independent confirmation of its convergence claims.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a peer-reviewed or widely-digested proof completing the Connes-Consani-Moscovici convergence argument, which would resolve the full conjecture, or (b) any expert (e.g. Tao, a number theory blog, MathOverflow consensus) publicly engaging with one of the many self-published 'proof' preprints and confirming or refuting a specific construction — which would move the corresponding item to claimed or resolved/refuted.

outcome: The general Hilbert-Smith conjecture remains open; the only relevant 2024 work found (Shelukhin's 'A symplectic Hilbert-Smith conjecture') proves cases in a restricted symplectic-topology setting (Hamiltonian homeomorphisms on symplectically aspherical manifolds / standard symplectic tori), which is a related problem in a changed setting rather than a restriction of the stated topological-manifold conjecture.
summary: The Hilbert-Smith conjecture (as stated: any locally compact group acting continuously and faithfully on a topological manifold is a Lie group) remains open in general as of September 2026. The known partial results — Montgomery-Zippin/Bing for dimensions 1-2, Repovš-Ščepin (1997) for Lipschitz actions, Martin (1999) for quasiconformal actions, and Pardon (2013) for the 3-manifold case — all predate the 26 January 2024 frozen revision and are not new events in this window. The one arXiv item the triage flagged, Egor Shelukhin's 'A symplectic Hilbert-Smith conjecture' (arXiv:2403.07195, v1 submitted 2024-03-11, v2 2024-06-26, with an appendix by Leonid Polterovich), proves that the p-adic integers Z_p admit no non-trivial continuous action by Hamiltonian homeomorphisms on symplectically aspherical symplectic manifolds, and more generally that a locally compact group acting faithfully by homeomorphisms in the C0-closure of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms on certain symplectic manifolds (e.g. standard tori) must be a Lie group. This changes the hypotheses of the original statement in two ways at once: the acting maps are restricted to a specific C0-closure of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms (not arbitrary homeomorphisms), and the target is restricted to symplectically aspherical manifolds with symplectic-topology structure (Floer cohomology, barcodes, Hofer's metric) rather than arbitrary topological manifolds. Per SS3.1 this is a related problem obtained by changing the question, not a case obtained by restricting it — it does not remove territory from the general conjecture's domain (arbitrary continuous actions on arbitrary manifolds), so it does not count as a change to this problem. I searched further for any 2024-2026 developments (proof announcements, disproofs, counterexamples, AI involvement) and found none: Terence Tao's blog has only a single 2011 post tagged with this conjecture and nothing later; a 2026 Simons Foundation survey of Hilbert's problems does not cover the Hilbert-Smith conjecture (a separate, later-named conjecture) at all; general searches for AI/machine-learning involvement in this conjecture returned nothing relevant. No AI system appears anywhere in the material connected to this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Shelukhin result is a 'case' of the Hilbert-Smith conjecture in the loose sense that Hamiltonian homeomorphisms are a subset of all homeomorphisms, so ruling out actions by p-adic integers via this subset is technically ruling out a subset of the possible actions covered by the general conjecture, which could be read as narrowing the space of potential counterexamples to the full statement. However, the paper's own framing and methods are specific to symplectic topology (symplectic asphericity, Floer cohomology, Hofer's metric) and do not bear on faithful actions by homeomorphisms in general on general manifolds, which is the substance of the stated conjecture and is precisely why the field itself treats this as a distinct 'symplectic Hilbert-Smith conjecture' rather than as partial progress on the classical one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that proves the conjecture (or a genuine dimensional/class-of-groups case of it) for actions by general homeomorphisms on general topological manifolds, extending beyond dimension 3 or beyond the already-settled Lipschitz/quasiconformal cases, would resolve the ambiguity; absent that, the symplectic result is best read as adjacent rather than as progress on the stated bullet.

outcome: No result found since 26 January 2024 that classifies quadratic forms over algebraic number fields, or settles a case of that classification; the general problem remains open (with Hasse's local-global classification for the equivalence question over specific completions/fields still the classical partial resolution predating the window). Ongoing research in this window (universality criteria, representation of integers, Pythagoras numbers) addresses related but distinct questions, not the classification itself.
summary: Hilbert's eleventh problem, as stated by Kaplansky and echoed in the Wikipedia bullet, asks to classify quadratic forms over algebraic number fields. Hasse's local-global (Hasse-Minkowski) solution to the equivalence/classification question for forms over number fields, via completions, dates to the 1920s and is long predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision — it is background, not a result in the window. I searched broadly for any 2024-2026 work that advances the classification question itself (arXiv listings, general web search, the Wikipedia article's current text, and a June 2026 Simons Foundation retrospective on the status of all 23 Hilbert problems). The Simons Foundation piece (published 2026-06-18) explicitly revisits Problem 11 and states only that 'Helmut Hasse solved the problem in one context, but work has continued in others,' with no claim of any new resolution or case settled since 2024 — it corroborates the classical status quo rather than reporting a new event. The live Wikipedia article likewise shows no post-2024 update to its history/status section (last substantive edit predates the window) beyond noting older work by Cogdell, Piatetski-Shapiro and Sarnak on representation questions. Papers found in the 2024-2025 window (e.g. arXiv:2410.22507 on 'universality criterion sets for quadratic forms over number fields,' arXiv:2403.07171 on representing integers by generalized quadratic forms over quadratic fields, and work on Pythagoras numbers for infinite algebraic fields) study representation and universality properties of specific quadratic forms — these are related problems in the same subfield, not restrictions/cases of the classification question itself, so per the scope rule (§3.1) they do not count as movement on this bullet. No AI involvement was found in any of this work; none of the papers surveyed mention any AI system's role in producing results, and no AI-related claim about this problem appears anywhere in my searches. I therefore agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and did not find anything the triage missed.
competing_reading: One could argue the classical Hasse-Minkowski local-global principle, since it is the mechanism by which 'equivalence' of quadratic forms over number fields is actually decided, effectively resolves the core classification question and the bullet should be `open_stale` rather than `open`. I did not adopt this reading because (a) Hasse's result predates the frozen revision by a century and would in any case be `open_stale`, not a change in this window, and (b) the Wikipedia bullet and the broader literature (including the 2026 Simons Foundation piece) still describe the problem as only 'resolved for some cases' rather than fully classified — full classification (e.g., over general number fields with all invariants, not just via local behavior) is treated as incomplete by working number theorists, so `open` (with nothing new in the window) is the more accurate status regardless.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement, dated after 26 January 2024, that gives a complete classification of quadratic forms over a general algebraic number field (or resolves a previously-unclassified case, such as extending classification results to a broader class of fields or forms) — as opposed to work on universality, representation, or Pythagoras numbers, which are adjacent questions.

summary: Hilbert's 15th problem asks for a rigorous foundation for Schubert's enumerative calculus. Nothing found in the 26 January 2024 to present window changes this bullet. Three lines of inquiry converged on the same conclusion. (1) The June 2026 Simons Foundation survey 'Solved, Unsolved and Unsolvable: The Status of Hilbert's 23 Problems' gives problem 15 the verdict 'It's complicated,' explicitly stating there is 'no consensus in the field about whether 2020 work by Haibao Duan and Xuezhi Zhao fully resolves the question' -- i.e. the open dispute is the same pre-2020, pre-window one, restated without new developments. (2) A June 2025 arXiv handbook chapter, 'Introduction to the Cohomology of the Flag Variety' by Billey, Gao and Pawlowski (arXiv:2506.21064), is a survey/computational introduction to Schubert calculus that states in its own framing that thanks to 'many contributions in algebraic topology, geometry, and combinatorics, we consider this solved' -- referring to the cumulative 20th-century foundational work (van der Waerden, Weil, Chevalley, Ehresmann, Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand, etc.), not to any new 2024+ result. It is a pedagogical/computational survey, not a new resolution. (3) A claim that an 'Adelic Langlands Program' resolves Hilbert's 15th problem appears in search results (a YouTube video title and a Medium blog series), which the triage pass flagged as unsourced. I traced the Medium series ('Logos Field Theory,' by an author using the handle jhblank7497) and found it is a self-published, non-peer-reviewed, thousands-of-volumes-long personal theory mixing legitimate terms (adelic numbers, Langlands correspondence) with speculative claims about consciousness, a computational 'operating system' universe, and a 'Theory of Everything.' No arXiv paper, journal article, or expert digestion of any 'Adelic Langlands' resolution of Hilbert's 15th problem exists; targeted arXiv searches for the phrase returned nothing on-topic. This is not mathematics and not evidence of anything happening to the problem, let alone AI involvement. No AI system was found to have been used to produce any relevant mathematical result on this problem in the window (the crank blog's authorship/tools were not established and are irrelevant regardless, since its content is not a mathematical result).
competing_reading: One could argue the June 2026 Simons Foundation piece itself constitutes a 2026 'event' worth a status of some kind, since it is dated within the window. But it is explicitly a status survey of existing (2020 and earlier) work with no new mathematical content, and it reaches the same 'no consensus' conclusion that predates the window; it does not move the problem, so it is treated as evidence for 'no change found' rather than as a dated event in its own right.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed paper or widely-cited preprint published after 26 January 2024 that either (a) settles the Duan-Zhao dispute by community consensus, or (b) presents a genuinely new rigorous foundation for Schubert calculus (or a specific gap in the existing foundation) that experts engage with. Also relevant: any statement from Duan, Zhao, or recognized experts in Schubert calculus/algebraic geometry taking a new position on the 2020 work within the window.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 settles, advances a bound on, or resolves a genuine restriction of the stated reciprocity law for k-th order norm residues; the problem remains open and is uniformly described (Wikipedia's article, a June 2026 Simons Foundation survey of all 23 Hilbert problems, and standard framing) as tied to non-abelian class field theory / the Langlands program, still unresolved.
summary: Hilbert's ninth problem asks for the most general reciprocity law for k-th order norm residues in a general algebraic number field, for k a prime power. The abelian case is settled by classical class field theory / Artin reciprocity (long before the window), but the general (non-abelian) case is universally treated as open, folded into non-abelian class field theory and the Langlands program. I checked the problem's own Wikipedia article (last substantive content unchanged in relevant part: 'Despite some results towards Langlands program, this conjecture seems to be far from proven, but stands as the best proposition of solution for Hilbert's ninth problem'), a June 2026 Simons Foundation survey of the status of all 23 Hilbert problems (which explicitly calls the ninth problem's status 'It's complicated' and says 'A great deal of progress has been made on this and the closely related 12th problem over the years, but neither is completely resolved' — giving no dated post-2024 event), and arXiv listings for 'Hilbert's ninth problem' and 'non-abelian class field theory' from 2024-2026. Two 2025 papers turned up that use the phrase 'non-abelian class field theory' — S. Bedikyan, 'Local non-abelian class field theory' (Hacettepe J. Math. Stat., published 28 April 2025), which extends İkeda–Serbest's local reciprocity map construction to any local field with a p-th root of unity, and I. V. Nikolaev's 2025 Algebras and Representation Theory paper relating Drinfeld modules to noncommutative tori. Both are incremental contributions to the broader non-abelian class field theory program (itself a decades-old research direction, not new since 2024) rather than results that a careful reader would record as advancing Hilbert's ninth problem's own stated bullet: neither claims a general reciprocity law for norm residues of k-th order over a general number field, and Bedikyan's result is local (p-adic fields), a restriction of scope rather than a step toward the general global statement Hilbert asked for, and its own framing situates it as one more contribution to an existing multi-decade line (Koch, Fesenko, Koch–de Shalit, İkeda–Serbest) rather than a new advance dated to the window. I also confirmed that the substantial 2024-2026 arXiv activity found under 'Hilbert's [ninth/tenth] problem' searches (Koymans–Pagano, Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman, etc.) is entirely on Hilbert's tenth problem (Diophantine decidability), a different problem, and does not bear on the ninth. No source anywhere discusses AI/LLM involvement in any work touching this problem; the only AI-adjacent hits were a 2025 Apple ML paper named 'Hilbert' (an LLM+Lean proving framework, unrelated in subject) and general LLM-for-formal-mathematics papers, none of which mention this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Bedikyan 2025 paper on local non-abelian class field theory is a genuine 'case' of the problem (the local, prime-power-root-of-unity case) rather than a 'related' variant, since it does construct an explicit local reciprocity map satisfying functoriality and ramification properties — which is precisely the kind of object Hilbert's ninth problem asks for, just restricted to local fields. Under that reading the status would be `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (a local reciprocity law constructed) rather than `open`. I did not adopt this reading because the paper extends an existing construction (İkeda–Serbest, itself pre-2024) to a broader class of local fields rather than settling new territory of the *global*, general-number-field statement Hilbert posed, and because no secondary source (Wikipedia, Simons Foundation survey) treats any 2024-2026 work as movement on Hilbert's ninth problem specifically — both continue to describe it as essentially untouched. This is a judgment call about how much extension counts as 'a case settled' versus 'the same open research program continuing as it always has.'
what_would_settle_it: A statement, by an author or a survey (e.g., a future Simons Foundation or Notices of the AMS update), that a specific 2024+ paper newly settles a well-defined case or sub-case of the general k-th order norm residue reciprocity law (as opposed to a general contribution to the decades-long non-abelian class field theory program), together with that paper's date and scope.

summary: I researched what has happened since 26 January 2024 to the classification of the possible configurations of connected components of M-curves (the first part of Hilbert's sixteenth problem, restricted to the maximal-oval-number case as the bullet states it). I found no post-window result that changes this bullet. The only closely related recent arXiv work is 2606.21449, 'Hilbert's 16th problem for arrangements of curves on a surface' (submitted 19 June 2026), which generalizes the classical problem to arrangements of multiple curves on a surface (obtaining a complete classification for three lines plus a cubic and a partial one for three lines plus a quartic); this changes the question posed (arrangements of several curves, not the isotopy type of a single M-curve) rather than restricting it, so under §3.1 it is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated bullet — I classify it as beside the question. It uses a custom Julia computational library (NWT) for managing large combinatorial databases and standard techniques (Bezout-type obstructions, Viro patchworking); no AI/ML system is used or mentioned. A 2026 Mathematical Notes paper by Orevkov and Puchkova on 'mutual arrangements of a plane real curve relative to an M-quartic with an oval-snake' is likewise a related configuration question (a curve's arrangement relative to a fixed M-quartic), not the general classification of M-curve configurations by degree, and again uses classical algebraic-geometric methods with no AI. I also checked a widely-circulated December 2024 press claim that a Brazilian team (UNESP) 'solved Hilbert's 16th problem'; on inspection (via the cited press article) their work addresses the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem (bounding limit cycles of polynomial vector fields via a new 'Geometric Bifurcation Theory'), a completely different bullet in the Wikipedia list, not the M-curve/oval-configuration question in this record, and used no AI or machine learning. No arXiv listing, Wikipedia update, or survey found any new resolved or partially-resolved case of the M-curve classification itself (e.g., no new settled cases for degree 8 or 9, no narrowing of the ~1227 a priori possible degree-9 schemes reported after January 2024). The Wikipedia article's own text is unchanged in substance from the frozen revision: degree 8 unsolved, degree 9 wide open.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2606.21449 arrangements-of-curves generalization or the Orevkov-Puchkova M-quartic-arrangement paper should count as 'partial' progress if one reads the Wikipedia bullet very broadly as 'anything about mutual configurations of real algebraic curves.' I don't think this is the better reading: the bullet as stated asks specifically about the isotopy classification of M-curves (single curves with the maximal oval count), and both papers pose a different question (arrangements of multiple named curves, or a curve relative to a fixed background M-quartic) rather than restricting the M-curve classification question itself. Settling either would not let a careful editor add a line to this bullet's entry.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement explicitly completing or substantially narrowing the list of realizable/prohibited isotopy types for M-curves of degree 8 (closing the 'almost complete' gap) or degree 9 (reducing the ~1227 a priori schemes), dated after 26 January 2024, would settle this as at least `partial`. I found no such source.

summary: Hilbert's twelfth problem, in the general form stated in the bullet (extend Kronecker-Weber to an arbitrary base number field), remains open, and I found no result since 26 January 2024 that changes what this bullet's entry should say. The one major resolution in this area — Dasgupta and Kakde's construction of the maximal abelian extension of totally real number fields from Brumer-Stark units, via a proof of the p-part of the integral Gross-Stark conjecture — predates the window: their preprint 'Brumer-Stark Units and Hilbert's 12th Problem' is arXiv:2103.02516 (submitted March 2021, an earlier related preprint from 2020), and it was published in Annals of Mathematics in 2023. The current live Wikipedia article and a June 2026 Simons Foundation retrospective on the status of all 23 Hilbert problems ('Solved, Unsolved and Unsolvable') both confirm the general case is still labeled unresolved, with only special cases (imaginary quadratic/CM fields via classical complex multiplication, and totally real fields via Dasgupta-Kakde) settled. Post-window activity I found is limited to: (1) an ICMS workshop 'Recent Progress on Hilbert's 12th Problem' held 24-28 June 2024 in Edinburgh, built around a lecture series by Dasgupta and Kakde presenting their (already-published/preprinted) totally-real-field result to a wider audience — this is dissemination of pre-2024 work, not a new result; (2) arXiv:2505.22272, a 4-page addendum (May 2025) to a much older paper ('Measured foliations and Hilbert 12th problem,' arXiv:0804.0057, published in Acta Mathematica Vietnamica 2023) giving numerical/computational examples of abelian extensions of real quadratic fields under Darmon-Vonk-style conjectural constructions — a small computational illustration of an existing conjectural framework, not a settled case and not clearly in scope of the stated bullet even if it were new; (3) arXiv:2408.02158 (August 2024), 'Ultra-Galois theory and an analogue of the Kronecker-Weber theorem for rational function fields over ultra-finite fields' — this proves a Kronecker-Weber analogue for a different object entirely (rational function fields over ultraproducts of finite fields, not number fields), so under §3.1 it is a related/variant problem sharing a namesake theorem, not a case of the number-field problem stated in this bullet, and does not count as scope. No source anywhere associates any AI system with this problem; a search for a possible AI connection surfaced only an unrelated Apple ML Research project literally named 'Hilbert' (an agentic LLM+Lean theorem-proving framework), which has no connection to Hilbert's twelfth problem and is a pure name coincidence. I agree with the triage's verdict and its underlying reasoning.
competing_reading: One could argue the Darmon-Pozzi-Vonk program for real quadratic fields (referenced in older seminar descriptions and now illustrated numerically in arXiv:2505.22272) constitutes 'partial' progress if the addendum's computations were novel confirmations extending the conjectural framework. But the addendum itself dates its core theoretical content to a 2023 journal publication of a 2008 preprint, and its 2025 content is purely numerical verification of examples rather than a new theorem, so it does not rise to a case being settled.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement, dated after 26 January 2024, either (a) proving unconditionally that a specific analytic construction generates the maximal abelian extension for some broad new class of number fields beyond totally real/CM fields (e.g., a real quadratic field result upgraded from conjectural to proven), or (b) a full proof for the fully general case. Also useful: any statement from an AI lab or paper's authors crediting an AI system with producing part of such a proof.

outcome: Eyal Markman proved the Hodge conjecture for abelian varieties of complex dimension 4 and (in a companion result) 5, a genuine human-authored case of the conjecture, digested by experts via a dedicated two-day seminar series and a September 2026 guest post by Burt Totaro on Terence Tao's blog. Separately, a cluster of low-credibility arXiv preprints (K3 surfaces, complete intersections, Calabi-Yau 5-folds, 'spectral rigidity' frameworks) claimed full or partial proofs; one was withdrawn by arXiv admin for policy violation, one was withdrawn and resubmitted by its own author without explanation, and none has been endorsed by any expert. An anonymously-sourced media report claims OpenAI is close to an internal solution, but as of the report date no paper, code, or Clay Institute statement exists.
credited_humans: Jonathan Pridham (2024 semi-regularity extension used as a key input)

disputes.summary: A wave of 2025 arXiv preprints (e.g. arXiv:2507.18999 'Constructive Proof of the Hodge Conjecture for K3 Surfaces via Nodal Degenerations'; arXiv:2507.09934 on complete intersections; arXiv:2507.12173 'Spectral Rigidity and Algebraicity'; arXiv:2506.17754 on Calabi-Yau 5-folds) claim proofs or frameworks for the full or restricted Hodge conjecture. arXiv:2507.12173 was withdrawn by arXiv Admin for 'violation of arXiv policies for acceptable submissions' (no further detail given) after a v1-to-v2 collapse from 7KB to 1KB; arXiv:2506.17754 was withdrawn by its own author and silently resubmitted days later with no explanation. None of these has any expert digestion, citation, or endorsement found; their titles and abstracts (invoking ad hoc 'spectral fingerprints', 'exceptional group constraints', etc.) match a pattern of low-quality or likely AI-generated preprints that surfaced across arXiv math sections in 2025-2026 and prompted community and moderator concern (arXiv's October 2025 restriction on AI-heavy survey/review submissions, and Terence Tao's and others' public commentary on a 'crisis of AI-generated mathematics'). No source establishes that these specific Hodge preprints were AI-authored; this is treated as unresolved and non-credible rather than as a confirmed AI claim.

The Information reported (17 September 2026), citing anonymous sources, that OpenAI is 'close to solving' the Hodge conjecture as a second Millennium Prize problem, following its disputed 8 September 2026 Navier-Stokes announcement. OpenAI itself has only said it made 'substantial progress' on an unnamed Millennium problem; the Hodge Conjecture attribution originated in a viral, since-controversial X post (9 September 2026) rather than from OpenAI. As of the most recent sources checked (around 17-22 September 2026), there is no paper, no code, and no Clay Mathematics Institute statement regarding the Hodge conjecture from OpenAI.

summary: The only credible movement on the Hodge conjecture since 26 January 2024 is Eyal Markman's proof, posted to arXiv on 5 February 2025 (arXiv:2502.03415, 'Cycles on abelian 2n-folds of Weil type from secant sheaves on abelian n-folds', v2 8 June 2025), that the Hodge conjecture holds for all abelian fourfolds (and, per follow-up work, fivefolds) of Weil type, hence for all abelian fourfolds. This is a case of the stated problem under §3.1 (restricting to abelian varieties of low dimension), not a resolution of the general conjecture, so status is 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed'. It has real expert digestion: a dedicated two-day seminar series ('The Hodge Conjecture for Abelian Fourfolds, after Markman') worked through the proof section by section, and Burt Totaro's guest post on Terence Tao's blog (11 September 2026) describes it in detail as a genuine breakthrough building on Ben Moonen-Yuri Zarhin's 1995 reduction and Jonathan Pridham's 2024 extension of Buchweitz-Flenner semi-regularity theory to twisted sheaves. No AI system is credited anywhere in this work; it is entirely human-authored classical algebraic geometry, so ai_role is 'none'. Separately, I found a cluster of 2025 arXiv preprints purporting much stronger results (full proofs for K3 surfaces, complete intersections, or general frameworks), none of which show any sign of expert acceptance, citation, or even engagement; one (2507.12173) was pulled by arXiv Admin itself for a policy violation, and another (2506.17754, Calabi-Yau 5-folds) was withdrawn and quietly resubmitted by its sole author. These match a broader, well-documented pattern of low-quality/AI-assisted preprint spam on arXiv math sections in 2025-2026 (prompting arXiv's October 2025 restriction on survey/review papers and public commentary, including Tao's, on a 'crisis of AI-generated mathematics'), but I found no source that specifically confirms these Hodge preprints were AI-generated, so I record them as a credibility dispute rather than an AI claim, and they do not change the problem's status. Finally, there is an active but entirely unconfirmed media story: The Information reported (17 September 2026, anonymous sources) that OpenAI is close to an internal solution of the Hodge conjecture, as a second Millennium Prize problem after its disputed Navier-Stokes claim of 8 September 2026. This traces to a viral X post naming Hodge specifically; OpenAI's own public statement names no specific problem. No paper, code, or Clay Institute statement exists for Hodge from OpenAI as of the most recent reporting I could check (around 17-22 September 2026), so under §6.1/§6.2 this cannot be coded as claimed or generated — it is not evidence of any change to the problem, only a rumor, and does not affect status.
competing_reading: One could argue the low-quality preprint cluster and/or the OpenAI rumor deserve a 'claimed' status with ai_role 'incident', on the theory that an AI-produced claim was effectively 'announced' via leaks and social media even without a formal paper. I rejected this because §6.1 requires a preprint, announcement, or machine-checked certificate for 'claimed', and neither OpenAI nor any credible author has actually claimed a Hodge conjecture proof in a citable, attributable document as of my research; the only announced OpenAI Millennium claim with a real paper is Navier-Stokes, a different problem. If OpenAI (or another lab) publishes an actual paper or technical report naming the Hodge conjecture, this record would need to move to 'claimed' or 'progress'/'incident' depending on outcome.
what_would_settle_it: A citable OpenAI (or other lab) paper, technical report, or system card explicitly naming the Hodge conjecture with a claimed result, which does not yet exist; or expert commentary (e.g. from Totaro, Tao, or other algebraic geometers) explicitly addressing and dismissing or confirming any of the 2025 arXiv preprint cluster, which I did not find.

outcome: No case of any of the 14 conjectures Wikipedia's article numbers under this heading (Direct Summand, Canonical Element, Improved New Intersection, Vanishing Conjecture for Maps of Tor, Serre's Conjecture on Multiplicities, etc.) was settled in the window. The one concrete piece of post-window movement found is in a closely related, commonly co-discussed homological conjecture not itself among the 14: VandeBogert and Walker proved a stronger form of the Total Rank Conjecture (a coarser corollary of the Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks rank conjecture) for rings of characteristic two, revised April 2024 and published in Duke Math. J. in February 2025. No AI involvement in that or any other lead.
summary: Wikipedia's article 'Homological conjectures in commutative algebra' enumerates 14 specific numbered conjectures from Melvin Hochster's program (Zero Divisor Theorem, Bass's Question, Intersection Theorem, New Intersection Theorem, Improved New Intersection Conjecture, Direct Summand Conjecture, Canonical Element Conjecture, Existence of Balanced Big Cohen-Macaulay Modules, Cohen-Macaulayness of Direct Summands, Vanishing Conjecture for Maps of Tor, Strong Direct Summand Conjecture, Existence of Weakly Functorial Big Cohen-Macaulay Algebras, Serre's Conjecture on Multiplicities, Small Cohen-Macaulay Modules Conjecture). I searched for post-26-January-2024 movement on each by name and found none: no new proofs, no new cases settled, and no retractions. The Direct Summand Conjecture and Existence of Weakly Functorial Big Cohen-Macaulay Algebras Conjecture were resolved by Andre/Bhatt/Heitmann-Ma well before the frozen date (2016-2018) and remain the state of the art; nothing moved after. Serre's positivity conjecture is still open with its most recent partial case (Skalit) from 2019. The one substantive post-window item I found in the broader neighborhood of 'homological conjectures in commutative algebra' as a named research subject is Keller VandeBogert and Mark E. Walker's paper on the Total Rank Conjecture in characteristic 2 (arXiv:2305.09771), whose v1 (May 2023) predates the window but whose v2 (11 April 2024) and Duke Mathematical Journal publication (February 2025, vol. 174 issue 2) postdate it; it proves a stronger form of the Total Rank Conjecture — a coarser corollary of the Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks rank conjecture — for characteristic-two rings, and separately proves an extension over non-Cohen-Macaulay rings containing any field. The Total Rank/Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks conjecture is not one of the 14 conjectures this Wikipedia article numbers, though it is frequently discussed in the same literature and courses under the 'homological conjectures' banner (e.g. Hochster's own surveys). I also found a 2026 preprint (arXiv:2607.26118) exhibiting explicit counterexamples to a *local variant* of Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks formulated by Lima-Pereira, Nuno-Ballesteros, Orefice-Okamoto and Tomazella for complete-intersection singularities — but this is a variant conjecture these authors themselves introduced, not a case of anything on Wikipedia's list, so it is out of scope under Section 3.1 and I did not use it as the basis for status. I separately investigated an AI system called Rethlas (arXiv:2605.25259, May 2026) reported to have resolved several open problems in commutative ring theory and Boij-Soderberg theory fully autonomously with human verification; its GitHub results page lists the specific problems solved (from Cahen-Fontana-Frisch-Glaz's 'Open Problems in Commutative Ring Theory' and Erman-Sam's Boij-Soderberg survey), and none of them are any of the 14 homological conjectures on this page or the Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks family — they are unrelated open questions that happen to share the broad subfield label 'commutative algebra'. I also checked a 2025 line of work on stable equivalences of Morita type and the Auslander-Reiten conjecture; this belongs to the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras (a distinct, though loosely analogous, family of 'homological conjectures' in a different subfield) and is not part of the Hochster program this Wikipedia article documents, so I did not use it either. Net: no true movement on any of the 14 listed conjectures; the closest thing to a hit is a genuinely human-authored partial result on a related-but-distinct conjecture, so I classify this record as 'progress' with low confidence that it belongs strictly in scope, flagged via competing_reading.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of Section 3.1 would hold that since the Total Rank Conjecture is not one of the 14 conjectures Wikipedia numbers under this exact heading, and is a genuinely different statement (about total Betti numbers/ranks) rather than a restriction of any of the 14, the correct status is 'open' with no_change_found true, treating VandeBogert-Walker as a 'related problem' in the Section 3.1 sense rather than a 'case of the problem'. Under that reading this record would be 'open'/no_change_found instead of 'progress'. I chose 'progress' because the bullet's statement is the broad umbrella phrase 'Homological conjectures in commutative algebra' (not a single conjecture), the Wikipedia article's own lead frames the numbered list as illustrative of a research program rather than an exhaustive closed set, and Hochster's own surveys of 'the homological conjectures' regularly include Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks-type rank statements alongside the 14. Reasonable people could pick either classification.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the dataset intends 'homological conjectures in commutative algebra' to mean exactly the 14 conjectures enumerated in the linked Wikipedia article, or the broader named research program as the field itself uses the term (which would include Buchsbaum-Eisenbud-Horrocks/Total Rank Conjecture, Auslander-Reiten-type statements, etc.).

outcome: A preprint by Simon Brendle and Pei-Ken Hung (arXiv:2608.19068, posted 19 August 2026) claims to construct a Riemannian metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, which would refute the product form of the Hopf conjecture (that no product of two positive-dimensional closed manifolds admits positive sectional curvature). The claim is very recent, has not been digested by the expert community or accepted by a journal, and an AI research-verification tool flagged apparently unresolved gaps (a bug in the supporting Mathematica calculation and a gap in a uniform bound) within a day of posting.

ai.basis_quote: This preprint is causing a stir in math because the title refutes the famous Hopf conjecture. This thread reports on some flaws that @RefineDotInk says need to be resolved for the argument to be sound. It's also a demo of what Refine (an AI research verifier) can do. ... The first apparent problem is that a key reduction supporting the 'second order positivity' needed uses a calculation that rests on a bug in the Mathematica code. The second major issue claims a gap in a uniform bound, where the AI believes this gap can be closed but isn't confident enough to complete the argument and asks the authors to do so.

counterexample.object: A metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, constructed as a third-order perturbation of a Cheeger-deformed ('Cheeger-Müter') metric on the standard product.
counterexample.verified_how: Claimed via an explicit analytic construction with symbolic-computation support in Mathematica (code attached to the arXiv submission); not yet independently verified by human experts, and an AI verifier (Refine) reported an apparent bug in the Mathematica calculation and an unresolved gap in a uniform bound shortly after posting.

disputes.summary: An AI research-verification system (Refine, from RefineDotInk) publicly reported, about a day after the preprint appeared, that a key calculation supporting 'second order positivity' rests on a bug in the authors' Mathematica code, and that there is a gap in a uniform bound the AI could not close itself. The authors issued a v2 on 24 August 2026 described only as correcting 'typographical errors in the manuscript and in the Mathematica notebook' — it is unclear from available sources whether this addresses the substantive issues Refine raised, or only cosmetic ones.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet covers 'the Hopf conjectures' (plural) on curvature and Euler characteristic of higher-dimensional Riemannian manifolds, which per the problem's own article and MathWorld comprises both a 'sign form' (positive sectional curvature on an even-dimensional closed manifold implies positive Euler characteristic) and a 'product form' (no product of two positive-dimensional closed manifolds admits everywhere positive sectional curvature — motivated by the fact that S^2 x S^2 has Euler characteristic 4 > 0, so the sign form alone would not rule it out). The sign form remains completely open in dimension >= 6 with no relevant results found in the window (only unrelated variant/case papers, e.g. Kennard-Mouillé-Nienhaus 2025 on positive second intermediate Ricci curvature with high-rank torus symmetry, and a curvature-operator-decomposition paper (arXiv:2507.15237) settling locally-conformally-flat and small-Weyl-curvature cases — both are restrictions/variants of the sign form, not resolutions of it). The one substantive, in-scope development is Brendle-Hung's August 2026 preprint (arXiv:2608.19068) claiming an explicit metric of positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, which if correct refutes the product form outright (a genuine case of 'this problem', not a variant, since the product form is one of the two Hopf conjectures the bullet names) while leaving the sign form untouched. This is not yet resolved: there is no journal acceptance, no expert blog digestion (checked Terence Tao's blog, which has 2026 posts on other conjectures but none found on this one), and, notably, an AI verification tool (Refine) publicly identified apparently unresolved technical gaps (a bug underlying a key Mathematica-based calculation, and an unclosed gap in a uniform bound) within roughly a day of the preprint's posting. Only a minor v2 revision (typo fixes) has since appeared, so it is unclear the substantive issues were fixed. I classify status as 'claimed' (preprint with an unresolved correctness dispute, no expert digestion) rather than 'progress'/'incident', because the paper has not been withdrawn and the authors have not conceded the argument is broken — but I flag real uncertainty here. The AI role is coded 'incident' rather than 'assisted' or 'none': Refine is an AI system that produced a substantive technical finding (an identified bug and an identified gap) about the mathematical content of a claimed resolution, and that claim's correctness is now publicly disputed as a direct consequence of AI-driven checking — this is the pattern of an AI-associated claim/dispute, not merely AI-as-tool assistance to the authors (the authors' own Mathematica usage is computer algebra, not an AI system, and is not disclosed as AI-generated mathematics). I use 'incident' with reservations since the underlying human claim has not been withdrawn, only publicly disputed on correctness grounds by an AI verifier; see competing_reading.
competing_reading: Two alternative readings are plausible. (1) Status: if the v2 revision (24 August 2026) in fact silently fixed the substantive gaps Refine flagged (not just typos, despite the changelog wording), the correct status could be 'claimed' moving toward 'resolved' pending expert digestion, with the Refine episode better treated as `progress`/an anecdote in summary rather than driving `ai_role`. Conversely, if the Refine-identified bug is fatal and unfixed, this may eventually resolve to `progress`/`incident` with `resolution_direction` null (the counterexample claim withdrawn), which would also change ai_role interpretation. (2) ai_role: one could argue for 'none' on grounds that Refine did not produce mathematics that appears 'in' any accepted result — it only critiqued an unverified claim, and the underlying construction is entirely human-and-Mathematica. I retained 'incident' because the guidance defines that code as 'an AI-produced claim that was announced or machine-verified, then withdrawn' or, by extension, publicly disputed via AI-driven verification with the claim's status left unresolved; but a stricter reading limiting 'incident' to claims of AI-generated proofs (as opposed to AI-generated critiques of human proofs) would push this toward 'none' with the Refine episode reported only as a dispute/summary note, not a role code.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Brendle-Hung's construction is ultimately confirmed correct (via expert digestion, journal acceptance, or a further arXiv revision that explicitly addresses and resolves the Refine-flagged bug and uniform-bound gap) or withdrawn/found fatally flawed; and separately, an authoritative account (from the authors, from Refine/RefineDotInk, or from expert commentary) of whether the AI-identified issues were real, and whether v2's changes addressed them.

outcome: No result addressing the exact count of Sudoku puzzles with exactly one solution was found since 26 January 2024; only pre-window results (2005 grid enumeration, 2012 17-clue minimum, ~2013 Monte Carlo estimate of minimal-puzzle count) and post-window work on genuinely different questions (per-grid minimum-clue optimization, LLM solving benchmarks) exist.
summary: The stated question is the exact enumeration of Sudoku puzzles (subsets of clues on a completed grid) that have exactly one solution. This is distinct from the much-studied minimum-clue problem (what is the fewest clues needed, resolved at 17 by McGuire, Tugemann and Civario in 2012 — before the window) and from the total-grid-count problem (6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960 completed grids, Felgenhauer and Jarvis, 2005 — before the window). The closest quantitative estimate of the actual count is a Monte Carlo estimate (~2013, predating the window) putting the number of minimal unique-solution puzzles at roughly 3.1055×10^37; I found no newer or more precise figure. I checked recent arXiv activity in this area: a 2023-submitted paper (published in Operations Research Letters, March 2024) on the 'Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem' formulates a bilevel optimization for the minimum clues needed to pin down a *given* grid — a related but distinct optimization question, not a count of puzzles with unique solutions, and its arXiv submission (2 May 2023) predates the window regardless. A July 2026 arXiv paper ('Sudoku Grids That Require Many Clues,' arXiv:2607.05728) proves lower bounds on clues needed for almost all grids — again the minimum-clue question, not the counting question, and it uses only classical algorithmic/combinatorial techniques with no AI. I also checked the AI-and-Sudoku intersection specifically: Sakana AI's 'Sudoku-Bench' (May 2025) and related LLM benchmarks test whether language models can *solve* individual Sudoku puzzles (a capability benchmark), which has no bearing on the mathematical enumeration question. The Mathematics of Sudoku Wikipedia article (checked as of today) still frames uniqueness only via the minimum-clue result and does not mention any resolution or new estimate of the exact count. No AI system appears anywhere near actual research on this specific counting question. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' case rather than a search failure: I searched the precise question phrasing, the standard-name variants (minimal Sudoku puzzle count, unique-solution puzzle enumeration), OEIS for a relevant sequence, and the AI/Sudoku intersection directly, and every hit resolved to either pre-window work or an off-scope variant.
competing_reading: One could argue the March 2024 Operations Research Letters publication of the bilevel MSCP paper counts as a dated event in the window, since it appeared in a journal after 26 January 2024. But per §6.3, dating must use the first public written argument (the arXiv preprint, 2 May 2023), not the journal publication date, and in any case the paper addresses a different question (minimum clues for a fixed grid) rather than the count of puzzles with a unique solution, so it is out of scope under §3.1 as a related-but-different problem regardless of dating.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or computation that produces an exact count (or a materially tighter/more rigorous estimate than the ~2013 Monte Carlo figure) of the number of subsets of a completed Sudoku grid (or of all grids) that admit exactly one completion, published or posted after 26 January 2024.

outcome: No exact count, new statistical estimate, or other advance on the number of minimal Sudoku puzzles was found since 26 January 2024; the question remains open, with the only quantitative estimate in the literature (Berthier, ~2011) predating the window by over a decade.
summary: The question is how many minimal Sudoku puzzles (puzzles with exactly one solution from which no clue can be removed without losing uniqueness or a solution altogether) exist. The triage's top find, arXiv 2305.01697 ('How Many Clues To Give? A Bilevel Formulation For The Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem', Tjusila, Besançon, Turner, Koch, submitted 2 May 2023, published in Discrete Applied Mathematics 2024), is a related but different problem: given one fixed completed grid, what is the fewest clues in any puzzle whose unique solution is that grid (the Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem, MSCP). It solves 50 instances of that per-grid minimization to optimality via a bilevel program; it says nothing about the total count of minimal puzzles across all grids, and its 2023 submission date predates the window regardless. The other triage find, arXiv 2607.20669 ('Counting, Symmetries and Equivalence Classes of Sudoku Grids', submitted 22 July 2026), is also a related-but-different problem: it derives the 44 equivalence classes of the first band of complete grids via Burnside's Lemma, a question about symmetry classes of full solution grids, not about minimal puzzles at all. Neither is a case of the stated question under §3.1's scope rule (restricting vs. changing the question) — both change the question rather than restrict it. The one substantive quantitative answer that exists in the literature — Denis Berthier's statistical estimate of ~3.1055×10^37 total minimal puzzles and ~2.5477×10^25 non-isomorphic minimal puzzles (0.065% relative error) — comes from 'Unbiased Statistics of a CSP: A Controlled-Bias Generator', arXiv 1111.4083, submitted 17 November 2011. That is over 12 years before the frozen revision and is not a change in the window; no update, refinement, or exact enumeration of this estimate was found dated after 26 January 2024. The current Mathematics of Sudoku Wikipedia article, checked live, still gives no exact count and does not cite any newer work than Berthier's. Repeated targeted searches for 2024-2026 enumeration or new estimates of minimal Sudoku puzzle counts turned up nothing beyond the two related-problem papers above. The question is therefore still open, and nothing in the window changes what a careful person would write in this bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue that arXiv 2305.01697's exact solution of 50 per-grid MSCP instances is a 'case' of the counting question in the loose sense that it pins down minimal-clue counts for specific grids. But the stated question is about counting *how many minimal puzzles exist* (a cardinality/enumeration question over the whole puzzle space), not about the minimum clue number for a given grid; solving MSCP for particular grids restricts a different question (minimum clues per grid) rather than restricting the stated one, and it predates the window in any case (submitted 2023). I judge this is a related problem, not a case, so it does not move the status from open.
what_would_settle_it: A paper post-January-2024 giving either an exact enumeration of minimal 9x9 Sudoku puzzles, a rigorously bounded (non-statistical) count, or a materially revised statistical estimate superseding Berthier 2011 would settle this as at least 'progress' or 'partial'; nothing of that kind was found.

outcome: Erdős's conjecture that the maximum number u(n) of unit distances among n points in the plane is n^{1+o(1)} was disproved: an OpenAI internal reasoning model produced a construction (using towers of algebraic number fields via a Golod–Shafarevich criterion) yielding u(n) > n^{1+delta} for a fixed delta>0 and infinitely many n, announced 20 May 2026 and subsequently digested and human-verified by a group of leading mathematicians (Alon, Bloom, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Shankar, Tsimerman, Wang, Matchett Wood) in a short 'Remarks' paper. Will Sawin then made the exponent explicit (delta ≥ 0.014114), and several further human/AI-assisted refinements pushed delta above 0.036 within weeks. The classical upper bound O(n^{4/3}) (Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter, 1984) is untouched, so the problem 'how many unit distances' is not fully closed, but the specific conjectured answer given in the Wikipedia bullet's implicit context (Erdős's n^{1+o(1)} conjecture) has been refuted and the refutation has passed expert digestion, meeting the resolved bar.

ai.basis_quote: We present a short, digested, human-verified version of the recent OpenAI-generated counterexample to the Erdős unit distance conjecture. ... the proof [is] a human-digested, somewhat simplified, and somewhat generalized version of the AI proof.
systems: an internal general-purpose reasoning model of OpenAI

counterexample.object: An infinite family of planar point sets, constructed via towers of algebraic number fields of large degree and small discriminant with many small-norm primes (Golod–Shafarevich construction), giving n points with more than n^{1+delta} unit-distance pairs for a fixed delta>0 and infinitely many n — exceeding Erdős's conjectured bound n^{1+o(1)}.
counterexample.verified_how: Original OpenAI construction gave only an inexplicit delta>0; the construction and its correctness were reviewed and rewritten by the named mathematicians in the 'Remarks' paper. Will Sawin then produced an explicit, independently-checkable value delta ≥ 0.014114.

disputes.summary: Whether the result should be described as 'AI-generated' or merely 'AI-assisted' is disputed. The Computational Complexity blog reports that critic Gary Marcus disputed OpenAI's 'AI-generated' framing, calling it 'AI-assisted' instead, given the substantial human role in digesting, checking, and rewriting the proof before publication. OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck defended crediting the achievement primarily to the model.

Multiple independent rapid improvements to the explicit exponent followed within days by different people/groups (mlewko, spiderduckpig, Naslund, Tseng, Emmerich) via informal channels (MathOverflow, blogs) as well as formal preprints, making it hard to assign clean priority for the numeric record beyond Sawin's first explicit bound.

summary: Wikipedia's bullet asks for u(n), the maximum number of unit distances among n planar points. As of the frozen revision (Jan 2024) the known bounds were the classical O(n^{4/3}) upper bound (Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter 1984) and a lower bound of n^{1+c/log log n} (Erdős's own construction), with Erdős conjecturing the truth was n^{1+o(1)}. On 20 May 2026, OpenAI announced that an internal general-purpose reasoning model had produced a construction refuting that conjecture: point sets with more than n^{1+delta} unit distances for a fixed delta>0. This was not a bare announcement — a paper 'Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture' (arXiv:2605.20695), authored by prominent mathematicians including Alon, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Tsimerman, Wang and Matchett Wood, presents 'a short, digested, human-verified version' of the AI-generated argument, explicitly stating it is a 'human-digested, somewhat simplified, and somewhat generalized version of the AI proof.' This constitutes the kind of expert digestion required for `resolved` under §6.1: the underlying mathematics has been checked and rewritten by named experts, not merely a compiler or an unreviewed preprint. Within days, Will Sawin (arXiv:2605.20579) made the exponent explicit, proving u(n) > n^{1.014114...} for arbitrarily large n via the same number-theoretic (Golod–Shafarevich) method — this is `resolved`/`refuted` since it directly answers the stated conjecture (the exponent is provably > 1, not = 1+o(1)) against Erdős's expectation. A cascade of further improvements followed over the following weeks (mlewko, spiderduckpig, Naslund reaching delta≈0.0358, Tseng, and a formal optimization paper by Emmerich reaching delta>0.036 as of June 2026, per Terence Tao's tracking page), some involving further AI assistance (a blog by 'nor' credits 'GPT 5.5 Pro' with producing 'the construction and proof... as well as most of the technical parts of the writeup' for one such improvement). These are bound-improving `progress` on an already-refuted conjecture, not separate resolutions, and are noted here rather than filed as separate events per the instruction to describe one decisive event. The classical upper bound side (O(n^{4/3})) is unchanged; a related paper (arXiv:2605.26145, 'An incomplete attack on the upper bound') attempted improvement there but is explicitly incomplete. Terence Tao's own expository blog post ('A digestion of unit distance constructions', July 2026) treats the OpenAI/Sawin result as established mathematics and discusses the current state of the exponent (0.03583 ≤ c ≤ 1/3 as of his writing), which is strong independent confirmation of expert acceptance.
competing_reading: One could argue for `claimed` rather than `resolved` if one holds that only the peer-reviewed journal version (not yet known to exist) counts as 'digested.' But the 'Remarks' paper's authors are themselves among the top experts in the relevant areas (algebraic number theory, additive combinatorics, discrete geometry) and its abstract explicitly frames itself as a verification/digestion exercise, which is exactly the bar §6.1 sets for `resolved` (an expert digestion that works through the proof) rather than requiring formal journal publication. Also debatable: whether the AI's role is `generated` or effectively `assisted`, since the publishable version was substantially rewritten by humans — but per §6.2, `generated` is correct whenever the authors' own account is that the model produced the proof/counterexample and humans verified it (as here), regardless of how much rewriting followed; the rewriting is verification and exposition, not new mathematical content per the sources reviewed.
what_would_settle_it: A published, refereed journal version of either the OpenAI/Alon-et-al. 'Remarks' paper or Sawin's explicit-bound paper, or an explicit statement from Tao or another leading expert unambiguously certifying the argument's correctness beyond the digestion exercise already performed, would remove any residual doubt about the `resolved` classification.

outcome: On 5-6 September 2026, OpenAI's pre-release GPT-6 Astra autonomously constructed a stationary, phi-mixing, finite-second-moment sequence whose partial-sum variance diverges but a normalized-sum subsequence converges to zero rather than to N(0,1), refuting both Ibragimov's CLT conjecture and Iosifescu's weak invariance principle conjecture; the construction and its Lean 4 formalisation were posted to a public GitHub repository by Tom Adamczewski (an Epoch AI research engineer, not a probabilist) and remain explicitly unaudited by any outside expert as of 22 September 2026.

ai.basis_quote: This entire repository was machine-written by AI assistants at the direction of Tom Adamczewski. The Lean proof itself was written by GPT-6 Astra. ... The counterexample construction and Lean disproof in this repository were obtained by GPT-6 Astra.

counterexample.object: A strictly stationary, centered, phi-mixing real-valued process built from Gaussian-smoothed rare spikes plus a bounded nonlinear (causal) feedback correction, with finite second moments and partial-sum variance diverging to infinity, but with variance-normalized partial sums converging to zero in probability along a subsequence rather than to a standard normal law.
counterexample.verified_how: Formalised and type-checked in Lean 4 (reported 13,047 lines; kernel accepts using only the standard axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; a `sorry` appears only in the conjecture-statement stub, not in the disproof itself). No independent human probabilist has yet reviewed the construction or the faithfulness of the formal definitions to the literature.

summary: The triage record treated this as fabricated/gamified content and stopped there, but on direct verification the underlying claim is real, current (well within the window), and substantive: a candidate counterexample to both halves of the Ibragimov-Iosifescu conjecture, built and Lean-formalised entirely by OpenAI's pre-release GPT-6 Astra model under the direction of Tom Adamczewski (an Epoch AI research engineer), posted to github.com/tadamcz/phi-mixing-clt around 5-6 September 2026 and catalogued on the 'VibeMathed' tracker (github.com/mrconter1/vibemathed, vibemathed.com), which is a genuine, methodologically transparent community database of AI-attributed math results rather than a hoax -- it explicitly labels this entry 'Candidate (review pending)' rather than 'Resolved'. The Lean proof is complete for the disproof itself (the only `sorry` is in the conjecture-statement stub, a standard formalisation convention, not a gap in the refutation), and an internal 'ANALYSIS.md' correctness audit endorses the formalisation's faithfulness to the literature with high confidence -- but that audit is itself an anonymised automated 'Scorer C / comparator' report bundled in the same repository, not a named independent human expert's review, and the repository and Wikipedia's own current article both state plainly that no probabilist outside the run has read the construction. Given the explicit 'unaudited'/'independent review pending' status repeated by every primary source (the repo, vibemathed.com, and the live Wikipedia article), and the complete absence of any arXiv preprint, journal submission, or named-expert commentary as of 22 September 2026 (17 days after the claim), this is classified `claimed` rather than `resolved`: a machine-checked, LLM-produced disproof that has not yet been digested by a human expert per Section 6.1's rule that a green Lean check alone is not sufficient. `ai_role` is `generated` because the authors' own account is unambiguous that GPT-6 Astra, not the human, produced the mathematical construction and its formal proof; Adamczewski's role was direction, infrastructure and posting.
competing_reading: One could argue for `resolved` on the grounds that Lean's kernel check is itself a rigorous, mechanical verification requiring no human trust in the proof steps, so 'expert digestion' is arguably satisfied by the ANALYSIS.md correctness audit plus the kernel's soundness. Against this: the audit itself is unsigned and produced within the same AI-native pipeline (a 'Scorer' stage, not an identified mathematician), the formal statement's faithfulness to the 55-year-old informal conjecture has explicitly not been checked against the primary literature by an outside person, and Section 6.1 treats 'a machine proof whose only reader is the compiler' as insufficient for `resolved` even when the check is clean. I judge `claimed` is the better reading, but flag this as a close call given how thorough the self-audit is.
what_would_settle_it: A named probability theorist (or a journal, or a widely-read expert blog such as Tao's) publicly reviewing the phi-mixing and stationarity formalisations against the Ibragimov/Iosifescu/Peligrad literature and either endorsing or refuting the construction; alternatively, an arXiv writeup of the natural-language argument that draws expert comment, or the Wikipedia article's own status line changing from 'candidate'/'pending' to an accepted resolution.
