outcome: Shimon Garti's May 2024 preprint 'Weak diamond and pcf theory' (arXiv:2405.03142) proves, from instances of weak diamond, that there exists a class of strong limit singular cardinals ℵ_δ for which 2^{ℵ_δ} < ℵ_{|δ|^{+3}} — one aleph-level better than Shelah's classical 2^{ℵ_δ} < ℵ_{|δ|^{+4}} bound that the Wikipedia bullet cites for ℵ_ω. The paper explicitly frames its motivation around the ℵ_ω case and Shelah's ℵ_{ω_4} bound, but its proved theorem (Theorem 3.3, conditioned on 'every limit cardinal is a strong limit cardinal') only asserts the existence of an unspecified class ℭ of such cardinals, and the paper itself poses as an open conjecture (Conjecture 3.4) whether this improved bound holds broadly across ZFC models. Nowhere does the paper state or prove that ℵ_ω itself belongs to the improved class; ω is a fixed point of the aleph function and the paper's proof machinery (built from weak-diamond-style club-guessing arguments) is standardly deployed at cardinals of uncountable cofinality, which ℵ_ω is not. No further paper since has closed this gap or otherwise moved the specific ℵ_ω bound.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether 2^{ℵ_ω} < ℵ_{ω_1} given ℵ_ω is a strong limit cardinal, and cites Shelah's PCF-theoretic bound 2^{ℵ_ω} < ℵ_{ω_4} as the best known. In May 2024, Shimon Garti posted 'Weak diamond and pcf theory' (arXiv:2405.03142), which derives bounds on |pcf(a)| from weak diamond principles and, as a corollary (Theorem 3.3, under the hypothesis that every limit cardinal is a strong limit cardinal), shows there is a class of strong-limit singular cardinals ℵ_δ with 2^{ℵ_δ} < ℵ_{|δ|^{+3}} — nominally one aleph better than Shelah's ℵ_{|δ|^{+4}}. The paper's introduction explicitly discusses the ℵ_ω/ℵ_{ω_4} case as its motivating example, which is why this looks at first glance like a direct improvement to the bullet. However, reading past the abstract, the actual proved statement (Theorem 3.3) only guarantees existence of an abstract class ℭ satisfying the bound, does not exhibit or confirm that ℵ_ω itself lies in that class, and the paper closes by posing as Conjecture 3.4 the very question of whether the improved bound holds broadly in ZFC — i.e., the authors themselves treat the general strengthening as open. Because the improvement's applicability to ℵ_ω specifically was not established, and because I could not confirm from any secondary source (no expert digestion, no published version, no citing paper) that ℵ_ω is covered, I classify this as `progress` rather than `partial`: something genuinely moved in the surrounding PCF machinery, and the paper directly targets Shelah's named bound, but it falls short of confirming the case named in the bullet was settled. This is very close to a `no_change_found` `open` classification, and I flag that possibility strongly in competing_reading. No later paper (checked through September 2026) revisits or improves further on this. No AI involvement of any kind was found in this niche of pure set theory — no author statement, no lab claim, nothing in the paper's acknowledgements (there is no acknowledgements section) or anywhere else.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of §3.1 would classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true: the bullet is specifically about ℵ_ω, and Garti's proved theorem never certifies that ℵ_ω belongs to the class ℭ for which the improved bound holds — it only proves existence of *some* class, motivated by but not shown to include ℵ_ω, and explicitly leaves the general statement as Conjecture 3.4. Under that reading, the paper's engagement with ℵ_ω is scene-setting/motivation rather than a result about the bullet's stated cardinal, making it a 'related' improvement in the surrounding PCF landscape rather than a case or bound-movement on the problem as stated. I lean toward `progress` rather than `open` because the paper's stated goal and framing is explicitly the ℵ_ω/Shelah-ℵ_{ω_4} gap, and a bound that provably holds for *some* strong-limit singular cardinals of this general shape is a nontrivial incremental result in the direction of the bullet's question, even without a certified answer for ℵ_ω itself.
what_would_settle_it: A published/expert-digested version of Garti's paper (or a follow-up) that explicitly states whether ℵ_ω is a member of the class ℭ in Theorem 3.3, or a resolution of Conjecture 3.4, would settle the classification. Absent that, checking whether any subsequent citing paper (via Semantic Scholar/Google Scholar forward citations) explicitly applies the ℵ_{|δ|^{+3}} bound to δ=ω would also settle it.

outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or bound on the stated conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; active adjacent structural work continues but does not settle whether categoricity in aleph_n for all n implies categoricity in every cardinal for atomic classes.
summary: This bullet asks whether an atomic class (the class of atomic models of a complete first-order theory, equivalently models of a complete sentence of L_{omega_1,omega}) that is categorical in aleph_n for every n < omega must be categorical in every cardinal. The classical background (pre-2024, hence not part of this window) is Shelah's theorem that under the weak continuum hypothesis below aleph_omega, a sentence of L_{omega_1,omega} categorical in aleph_n for every n is categorical in all uncountable cardinals for EXCELLENT atomic classes; excellence was the extra hypothesis needed, and whether it can be dropped (or derived) for general atomic classes was left open. Searching for developments since 26 January 2024, I found an active line of work by Baldwin, Laskowski and Shelah that is adjacent but does not resolve this question. 'When does aleph_1-categoricity imply omega-stability?' (arXiv:2308.13942, submitted 2023-08-26, published in Model Theory 3 (2024), 801-823) proves that an aleph_1-categorical atomic class with a model of size beth_1^+ (or, per one source's phrasing, (2^aleph_0)^+) is omega-stable -- a structural/stability result that is a step toward understanding the excellence-type hypotheses used in the older categoricity-transfer machinery, but it is a sufficient condition for omega-stability, not a resolution of the stated transfer conjecture, and its submission predates the window's start by five months in any case (it is itself open_stale territory as a pre-window event, though I am not using it as the decisive event since it does not settle the question). 'An analogue of U-rank for atomic classes' (arXiv:2502.00984, submitted 2025-02-03) develops an ordinal-valued rank for atomic classes and proves structural dichotomies (unranked types force 2^aleph_1 non-isomorphic models of size aleph_1; when all ranks are finite, the rank is additive and tuples are dominated by independent pseudo-minimal realizations). This is explicitly framed by the authors as part of a 20+ year program to either fill Shelah's gap or show no counterexample exists by proving aleph_1-categoricity implies omega-stability in general -- i.e. it is building toward the machinery that might eventually bear on categoricity transfer, but it neither proves nor disproves the aleph_n-for-all-n implies every-cardinal statement as such. No paper found addresses AI involvement of any kind; searches for funding/acknowledgement text on both papers surfaced only standard NSF/BSF/Simons grant lines, no mention of AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving. No withdrawal, no counterexample, and no claimed proof of the conjecture were found anywhere in the window. I therefore classify this as open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2023-08-26-submitted Baldwin-Laskowski-Shelah paper's 2024 journal publication constitutes an 'event' worth dating to the window under the journal-publication exception noted in the instructions (journal date normally excluded, but the paper's public preprint predates the window regardless, so by the first-written-argument rule (S6.3) it is correctly excluded). Also, a reader could see the U-rank paper as 'progress' on the broader categoricity-transfer program in a loose sense; I did not code it as progress because it does not move any bound or settle any case of the specific conjecture as stated (categorical in aleph_n for all n implies categorical in every cardinal) -- it is preparatory structural machinery for a related but distinct question (whether aleph_1-categoricity alone implies omega-stability), which is a case of a different, though closely related, conjecture in the same research program, not this bullet's conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving (or refuting, via a categorical-in-all-aleph_n-but-not-everywhere example) the transfer statement for general (non-excellent) atomic classes, or a paper proving that categoricity in aleph_n for all n forces excellence (which combined with the older Shelah/WCH theorem would settle it under that hypothesis), would settle the question. Absent that, continued structural papers in the Baldwin-Laskowski-Shelah U-rank program are the place to watch.

outcome: The implicit graph conjecture (every hereditary family of at most factorial speed admits an O(log n)-bit implicit representation) was refuted by Hamed Hatami and Pooya Hatami in a preprint posted 25 November 2021 (arXiv:2111.13198), published at FOCS 2022 and digested/cited widely since; a scaled-down version restricted to 'small' (slower-than-factorial) hereditary classes was also disproved before the frozen date, in Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk, Siebertz (arXiv:2307.11225, posted 20 July 2023, journal version SIAM J. Computing 2024). Both events predate the 26 January 2024 snapshot. No case, variant or restated form of the stated conjecture has been resolved inside the window; the only in-window activity is progress on a different, still-open conjecture (the 'Small Implicit Graph Conjecture' of Bonnet et al.) that narrows a bound but does not touch the statement given here.

counterexample.object: A hereditary family of graphs of factorial speed of growth (constructed via a probabilistic/counting argument, not an explicit family) for which every implicit (adjacency-labeling) representation requires labels of length n^Ω(1), refuting the requirement of O(log n)-bit labels.
counterexample.verified_how: Non-constructive probabilistic counting argument; the existence of such a family is proved but no explicit member family is exhibited (later work calls the search for an explicit counterexample the 'Explicit Implicit Graph Conjecture', which remains open).

summary: The bullet as given in this snapshot ('the implicit graph conjecture on the existence of implicit representations for slowly-growing hereditary families of graphs') is Wikipedia's own generic paraphrase of what is, in the literature, the single Implicit Graph Conjecture (IGC) of Kannan-Naor-Rudich/Spinrad: every hereditary graph family of at most factorial speed of growth admits an O(log n)-bit adjacency-labeling scheme. This was refuted by Hamed Hatami and Pooya Hatami in arXiv:2111.13198 ('The Implicit Graph Conjecture is False'), posted 25 November 2021 and published at FOCS 2022 -- a widely cited, expert-digested result (confirmed via the paper itself, its IEEE/FOCS publication record, and its treatment in later surveys and follow-up papers such as arXiv:2405.09011 and the ITCS 2025 paper arXiv:2409.04821, both of which state flatly that the IGC 'was recently refuted'). This event, and the conjecture's refutation, predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision by more than two years, so status is open_stale rather than any in-window code. I also checked whether a narrower, slower-growing restriction of the conjecture (matching the 'slowly-growing' wording more literally) might still have been open in January 2024 and settled afterward. It was not: Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk and Siebertz had already disproved the analogous conjecture for 'small' hereditary classes (growth rate n!^{c^n}, much slower than factorial) in arXiv:2307.11225, posted 20 July 2023 (journal version in SIAM J. Computing, 2024) -- again before the window. The only genuinely in-window development I found is arXiv:2409.04821 ('Adjacency Labeling Schemes for Small Classes' by Bonnet et al., posted 7 September 2024, published ITCS 2025), which improves the best known upper bound for small hereditary classes from polynomial (n^{1-epsilon}) to O(log^3 n) bits, and proves that small weakly sparse classes do admit full implicit representations. But this bears on a *different* conjecture -- the 'Small Implicit Graph Conjecture', a new conjecture introduced precisely because the original (and its small-class analogue) were already known false -- not on the statement given in this record. Under the scope rule (3.1), a bound moving on a distinct, subsequently-posed conjecture is a related problem, not a case of this one, so it does not change the status. No AI system appears anywhere in this line of work: none of the papers checked (Hatami-Hatami 2021/2022, Dawson et al. 2023/2024, Bonnet et al. 2024/2025) mention machine learning, LLMs, or automated theorem provers in their methods, and general searches for AI involvement in this specific conjecture turned up nothing relevant.
competing_reading: If 'slowly-growing hereditary families' in the Wikipedia bullet is read as pointing specifically at the small-class variant (rather than as generic wording for the standard factorial-speed IGC), the decisive event would instead be Dawson et al.'s arXiv:2307.11225 (posted 20 July 2023, journal version 2024) -- still open_stale, just with a different date and different credited authors (Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk, Siebertz instead of the Hatamis). Either reading keeps the status at open_stale and keeps all in-window activity (arXiv:2409.04821) as progress on a different, later-introduced conjecture rather than a case of the stated one, so the classification is robust to this ambiguity; I selected the standard/factorial-speed IGC as the primary reading because it is the one with its own dedicated Wikipedia article and the one virtually all secondary sources call 'the implicit graph conjecture' without qualification.
what_would_settle_it: The Wikipedia editors' intended referent for 'slowly-growing hereditary families' -- i.e., whether the bullet was written with the classical factorial-speed IGC in mind (in which case it is simply stale, refuted in 2021/2022) or with a specific slower-growth restriction in mind (in which case it is stale via the 2023 result instead). Either way, resolving the small implicit graph conjecture (open, and the subject of live 2024-2025 research) would be the next event actually worth tracking under this bullet going forward.

outcome: Cohen, Pohoata and Zakharov improved the upper bound for the Heilbronn triangle problem from Δ(n) ≤ n^(-8/7-1/2000) (their own 2023, pre-window result) to Δ(n) ≤ n^(-7/6+o(1)), first posted as arXiv:2409.07658 'Lower bounds for incidences' in September 2024 and now accepted at Inventiones Mathematicae; the lower bound (Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi, 1982) has not moved in the window, and the general asymptotic problem remains open.
summary: The bullet asks for movement on either bound of the Heilbronn triangle problem: the largest known lower-bound construction and the smallest known upper bound on the maximum guaranteed empty-triangle area Δ(n) for n points in the unit square. The upper bound moved in the window. Cohen, Pohoata and Zakharov's May 2023 paper (arXiv:2305.18253, pre-window) had given Δ(n) ≤ n^(-8/7-1/2000), the first improvement in 40 years over Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi (1981/82). Their follow-up 'Lower bounds for incidences' (arXiv:2409.07658, v1 11 Sep 2024, v2 18 Mar 2025, now published in Inventiones Mathematicae) proves the sharper upper bound Δ(n) ≤ n^(-7/6+o(1)) by establishing a new incidence bound between points and tubes; this attains what the authors call the 'high-low limit' of their method, i.e. a natural barrier for the current approach. This is squarely the quantity named in the bullet and is well past preprint into expert digestion (Inventiones acceptance, a University of Pennsylvania harmonic-analysis seminar talk by Cohen in Jan 2025, a Wikipedia lead that now states this as the state of the art), so I classified the September 2024 posting as the dated event and used the improvement itself — a bound moving on a problem that remains open — as `progress` rather than `resolved`, since the general problem (closing the gap between n^-2 and n^(-7/6+o(1))) is untouched. No source, including the Quanta profile of the 2023 result, the seminar-talk abstract, or the papers themselves, attributes any part of the mathematics to an AI system; the work is described throughout as a fusion of Roth's classical approach with recent harmonic-analysis/fractal-geometry incidence estimates, done by hand. I also checked adjacent Heilbronn-adjacent work for scope and AI relevance: Zakharov's 2024 higher-dimensional-Heilbronn paper and the October 2025 Maldague–Wang–Zakharov 3D Heilbronn paper (arXiv:2510.26644) are variants over different ambient spaces, not cases of this 2D bullet, and report no AI use. A May 2024 k-gons paper (arXiv:2405.12945) is about k≥4-gons, a different (related) problem, not this one. Gabor Ellmann's long-running preprint (arXiv:1703.03297, originally 2017, revised repeatedly through November 2025) gives an explicit lower-bound construction on a unit circle with bound Ω(n^-1.5 (log n)^-7/2); this construction predates the frozen revision (v1, 2017) and its exponent appears unchanged through the in-window revisions I could inspect (v6, Feb 2024, states the same O(n^-1.5(log n)^-7/2)), so I did not treat it as an in-window change to the lower bound, though I could not fully diff every revision's full text. Two December 2025/2026 computational papers (arXiv:2512.14505, and arXiv:2603.11107 'From Computational Certification to Exact Coordinates') use Gurobi mixed-integer optimization and Gröbner-basis symbolic computation to pin down exact optimal configurations for small n (5-9 points); these are a different, discrete/exact-optimization case of the problem (not the asymptotic bound the bullet is about) and explicitly use no machine learning or AI, only classical solvers and computer algebra.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2023 n^(-8/7-1/2000) paper and the 2024/2025 n^(-7/6+o(1)) paper are really one continuous program, in which case the 'event' could instead be dated to the 2023 preprint (pre-window, making this open_stale) with the 2024 paper as a mere refinement worth mentioning only in summary. I rejected this because the two papers state numerically and qualitatively different bounds, the second was posted and published entirely within the window, and the seminar/Wikipedia treatment of the two as separate results supports treating the September 2024 posting as its own event.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation from the Inventiones publication record of the exact acceptance/publication date, and a full read of all Ellmann revision diffs (2017-2025) to be certain no in-window revision changed the exponent on the lower-bound side.

summary: Two distinct threads occurred in the window, and neither settles the general problem, so status is `progress` rather than `resolved`, `claimed` or `partial`. (1) Genuine mathematics: Greene and Lobb, 'Square pegs between two graphs' (arXiv:2407.07798, submitted 10 July 2024), extended Tao's 2017 result to Jordan curves formed by two graphs with Lipschitz constant < 1+sqrt(2), a real bound-moving advance on a restricted case, with no AI involvement claimed anywhere in the paper. This is a case/bound within the window but, taken alone, would only warrant `partial`/`progress` with `ai_role` none; I folded it into one `progress` record with the more eventful AI incident as the dated event, per the instruction to describe multiple events in `summary` rather than open extra records. (2) The AI-linked item the triage flagged: independent researcher Yoshiki Ueoka published a Zenodo preprint (English: doi 10.5281/zenodo.18243635; also two Medium posts, Nov 2025 and a Jan 2026 follow-up) titled 'On the existence of squares inscribed in arbitrary C0 Jordan closed curves in the plane,' claiming to prove the fully general case via a topological-degree-theory argument, developed in collaboration with Gemini and ChatGPT. Critically, the Zenodo page itself carries the author's own caveat, fetched directly: 'An error was found in this proof, so we are considering an alternative approach. Once completed, we plan to submit it as a separate preprint.' So the claimed full resolution is a withdrawn/broken claim, not a standing one. On AI's role: per the author's own account (Zenodo metadata and Medium posts), the AI systems' contribution was English drafting/translation, structured proof-checking, and 'detecting missing links in arguments,' while Ueoka 'select[ed] and validat[ed] the final structure and mathematical content' — i.e., checking/proofreading/drafting, not producing the mathematics that ended up in the (broken) result. Under §6.2 that would ordinarily code as `none` (assistance limited to checking/proofreading/formalising), but because this is a claim that was announced and then itself invalidated by its author, I classified it under §6.1's 'instructive failure' clause as `progress` with `ai_role` `incident`, since the more load-bearing fact is that an AI-marketed claim was made publicly and collapsed, which is itself the kind of episode §6.2's `incident` code and §7's 'withdrawn claim is still an event' rule exist to capture. I also note Ueoka has a pattern of similarly self-published, AI-co-branded 'solutions' to other famous open problems (e.g. the Collatz conjecture), which is relevant context for weighing credibility but not dispositive on its own. I found no evidence any professional mathematician reviewed, endorsed, or even commented on the Ueoka claim; it has not been discussed on Tao's blog, in an arXiv listing, or in any digest I could locate. Wikipedia's own live article (checked via WebFetch on the current revision) still describes the general case as open, listing only pre-2024 partial results (Tao 2017, Chambers's 'close to C2' result). The Chambers paper the triage flagged (arXiv:2203.02613) was in fact first posted 4 March 2022 — well before the frozen revision — and its only in-window event is journal publication in Discrete & Computational Geometry (2025), which per §6.3 does not count as the dating event; I therefore treat it as `open_stale`-relevant background rather than an in-window advance, and it does not drive this record's status.
competing_reading: One could argue this record should be split, or that status should be `open` with `no_change_found` true on the grounds that the Ueoka claim is not a serious mathematical event at all (self-published, non-peer-reviewed, acknowledged-broken, by a non-specialist) and thus outside what should count as 'happened.' I judged that a publicly announced full-solution claim that named specific frontier AI systems as co-developers, went through two Medium posts and a Zenodo preprint, and was then retracted by its own author for an error, is exactly the kind of 'instructive failure' §6.1 and §7 ask to be recorded rather than dropped — dropping it would mean the record understates real AI-adjacent activity around this problem. A different reader might also argue `ai_role` should simply be `none` since the author's own description of AI's contribution (drafting, checking, translating) matches the `none` definition almost verbatim, and the 'incident' label overstates AI's causal role in the (broken) mathematics itself. I flag this tension rather than resolving it fully in one direction.
what_would_settle_it: A corrected version of Ueoka's preprint (or its retraction/silent abandonment) would settle whether this remains an open incident; and independent expert commentary (a blog post, MathOverflow thread, or citation) on the Ueoka claim would settle whether it merits any classification above 'incident'. For the Greene-Lobb thread, no further evidence is needed; it is settled as a genuine partial/bound advance with no AI role.

outcome: Khalil, Al-Hawawsha and Al-Zoubi published a claimed proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces (a case of the stated problem for general Banach spaces) in Axioms in September 2024; Ahmed Ghatasheh's preprint, submitted November 2024 and revised March 2025, identifies a specific false step (the Fourth Claim's constructed functional is not well-defined, because the sequence in question converges weakly to zero by Bessel's inequality, contradicting what the claim requires) and the claim is refuted. disputes.summary: Khalil et al. (Axioms, Sept. 2024) claimed a full proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces. Ahmed Ghatasheh's preprint (arXiv:2411.19409, submitted Nov. 2024, revised Mar. 2025) argues the proof's 'Fourth Claim' is invalid: the functional it constructs is not well-defined because the relevant sequence must converge weakly to zero (via a complete orthonormal basis and Bessel's inequality), contradicting the nonzero weak limit the claim requires. No retraction notice from Axioms was found as of this research; secondary sources report the editorial office was 'aware of concerns' and investigating, but I could not independently confirm or date any formal retraction.

summary: The only event in the window bearing on this problem is the Khalil–Al-Hawawsha–Al-Zoubi claim (Axioms, published Sept. 2024) of a proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces, followed by Ahmed Ghatasheh's refutation (arXiv:2411.19409, Nov. 2024, revised Mar. 2025), which pinpoints a specific gap: the Fourth Claim's functional is ill-defined because the underlying sequence converges weakly to zero, contradicting the claim's requirement of a nonzero weak limit. Since the claimed proof concerned separable Hilbert spaces specifically, it would have settled a case (restriction) of the stated Banach-space problem, so per §3.1 this is in-scope; because it was withdrawn/refuted rather than accepted, status is 'progress' with an 'incident' flavor rather than 'partial' or 'resolved' — no piece of the problem was actually settled either way, so resolution_direction is null and counterexample fields are empty. I found no evidence of AI involvement anywhere in this episode: I read Ghatasheh's refutation (which thanks two named individuals for feedback, no AI credited), searched for AI/LLM connections to the invariant subspace problem broadly (Terence Tao's o1 experiments, the 'Gödel Test' paper on LLMs and easy conjectures, 'From Solvers to Research' on LLM-driven formal mathematics, and a Google DeepMind formal-conjectures GitHub issue that catalogs the problem as a formalization candidate but shows no active AI work on it), and found nothing tying any AI system to this problem's claim, refutation, or any other development in the window. The Enflo (2023, pre-window) and Neville (2023, pre-window) Hilbert-space claims remain unverified preprints per Wikipedia's live article and are outside the window in any case (first posted before 26 Jan 2024; Enflo's only revision, in April 2024, is described by the author as 'a more detailed presentation' rather than a substantive change, so it does not constitute a new event). A 2025 survey by Chalendar and Partington ('Recent perspectives on the Invariant Subspace Problem', arXiv:2507.21834) exists but I could not extract its text (PDF was returned as binary/compressed to my fetch tool); I was unable to confirm whether it reports any other post-2024 development, which is a gap in this record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Khalil et al. episode does not belong in this record at all, since it was refuted and thus never became a genuine 'case settled' — under a strict reading of §3.1, a claim that turns out to be wrong changed nothing about what a careful person would write in this bullet, so the correct status might be plain 'open' with no_change_found true, treating the claim-and-refutation as noise rather than an event. I did not take this reading because §6.1 explicitly defines 'progress' to include 'instructive failures... an AI claim announced and then withdrawn is progress' by analogy, and more directly because this is exactly the kind of dispute the instructions ask to be recorded rather than silently dropped (§7: 'A withdrawn claim is still an event').
what_would_settle_it: An official retraction or correction notice from Axioms concerning Khalil et al.'s paper, and full read access to Chalendar & Partington's 2025 survey to confirm whether it records any other post-January-2024 development on this problem that I missed.

outcome: In August 2026, Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang gave an explicit degree-23 polynomial over Q whose splitting field has Galois group the Mathieu group M23, completing the realization of all 26 sporadic simple groups as Galois groups over Q; the general inverse Galois problem (every finite group) remains open, and the authors' own acknowledgements describe substantial AI assistance in the research process, though not in producing the mathematical text or final verification.

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on how central AI was to the mathematics. The paper's own acknowledgements list AI uses that read as auxiliary (literature search, code generation, hypothesis testing, ruling out approaches, computational strategy, checking, proofreading) and explicitly say no article text was AI-written and final verification was AI-free. A co-authored blog post ('Where to Point the Telescope', Proofs and Prompts) and Scientific American's coverage describe AI more substantively — 'multi-agent AI workflows... generate and test code, analyze data, ... organize large computations, and monitor and recover from failures', and AI 'numerically approximating' the Belyi map equations, with a human insight about switching coordinate systems (cutting required precision from 90 to 40 digits) being the decisive step. Epoch AI's FrontierMath Open Problems page went further, introducing a new 'human + AI' solved-status label specifically because 'comments from the authors make it clear that AI was instrumental in solving this problem' -- a stronger characterization than the paper's own wording of 'devising computational strategies'.

summary: The general inverse Galois problem (is every finite group a Galois group over Q?) remains fully open. What happened in the window is a case: an August 2026 preprint (arXiv:2608.08538, MIT mirror at math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/M23.pdf) by Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang exhibits an explicit degree-23 polynomial with rational coefficients whose splitting field over Q has Galois group the Mathieu group M23, the last of the 26 sporadic finite simple groups to be realized (the other 25 were done 1984-1989). This is squarely a §3.1 'case' -- it removes one specific finite group from the territory of the open problem without touching the problem as stated -- so status is partial, direction confirmed (the group is realized, as the inverse Galois heuristic expects). The AI question is the interesting part. The paper's own acknowledgements are explicit and are the primary basis for ai_role: they used Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8 and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol for literature search, code generation, hypothesis testing, ruling out approaches, devising computational strategies, checking results and proofreading, while stating plainly that no article text was AI-written and the final verification (in Magma and PARI/GP) was AI-free. Under the rubric's test -- 'what did the model produce that appears in the final result?' -- 'devising computational strategies' and 'testing hypotheses' sit right at the assisted/none boundary: they are more than pure checking or proofreading, since they describe the AI contributing to how the search for the polynomial/Belyi map was carried out, which is part of the mathematical route to the result, not just verification of a human-produced argument. A co-author's own blog post (Proofs and Prompts, 'Where to Point the Telescope', 2026-08-21) corroborates and elaborates: AI ran multi-agent workflows to generate/test code, organize large computations, and recover from failures, and separately produced initial numerical approximations of the Belyi map data -- work that fed directly into the mathematical construction, even though the post insists the decisive judgment calls (what to compute, when to stop, which coordinate system to switch to) were human. Scientific American's independent report corroborates this same account. Epoch AI's FrontierMath Open Problems page treated the authors' own account as strong enough evidence to retroactively relabel the problem from 'solved by humans' to a new 'human + AI' status, calling AI 'instrumental'. Weighing this, I coded assisted rather than none: the authors' own words describe AI producing parts of the computational/mathematical search process (hypothesis testing, computational strategy, and per the co-author's blog, generating the numerical approximations that were later recognized via PSLQ as algebraic coefficients), which goes beyond checking, proofreading or debugging alone.
competing_reading: A stricter reading would code ai_role: none. The paper's own list, read narrowly, is dominated by activities the rubric explicitly excludes ('checking, proofreading' and 'code generation' for computational infrastructure), and its clearest sentence -- 'No text in this article was written by AI' plus 'final results were verified... without the use of AI' -- could be read as the authors themselves drawing the line at 'auxiliary tool, not mathematical contributor'. On that reading, the PSLQ-based coefficient recognition and the actual Belyi map construction (the mathematics that appears in the result) were human/Magma/PARI-driven, and the AI-run numerical approximation was scaffolding that got discarded once humans found the right coordinates -- i.e., AI produced nothing that survives into the final argument. The gap between these two readings is exactly the gap between the paper's own wording and the co-author's blog post's more AI-forward narrative and Epoch AI's 'instrumental' framing; the blog and Epoch page are not the paper's official record and could be over-selling the AI angle for a general audience.
what_would_settle_it: A precise, first-person statement from the authors distinguishing exactly which numbers, coordinate choices, or intermediate objects in the final construction (the specific Belyi map, the degree-23 polynomial, the conjugacy-class triple) were first produced by an AI system versus by a human or classical CAS (Magma/PARI/GP/Sage), rather than a general list of AI-assisted tasks. The full, unredacted acknowledgements/methods text (ideally cross-checked against the published PDF once available, since the PDF text extraction here failed) would resolve whether 'devising computational strategies' refers to strategy for the mathematics or merely for software/infrastructure.

outcome: The question remains fully open: no proof or disproof that 10 is solitary. Since 26 January 2024, several papers have tightened necessary conditions any hypothetical 'friend' of 10 would have to satisfy (number and congruences of prime factors, structure of exponents, bounds on prime divisors), and an independent computational project (2026) established a certified lower bound that any friend of 10, if it exists, exceeds 10^32, improving on prior uncertified bounds by about two orders of magnitude. None of this settles or partially settles the existence question itself; it narrows where a counterexample could hide, which per the deep-dive rules (§3.1) does not move an existence/infinitude-type question. No AI system involvement was disclosed anywhere in this work.
summary: Whether 10 is a solitary number ('is 10 a solitary number' — equivalently, does 10 have a 'friend', i.e. another integer with the same abundancy index 9/5) is unchanged since 26 January 2024: no proof, disproof, or counterexample exists. What has happened is a run of papers and one substantial computational project that progressively tighten the necessary conditions any hypothetical friend of 10 would have to satisfy, none of which resolve or partially resolve the existence question. arXiv:2404.00624 (submitted 31 Mar 2024, latest v5 17 Jan 2025, Thackeray) shows any friend must be an odd perfect square with at least seven distinct prime factors including 5, plus several congruence conditions. arXiv:2412.02701 (submitted 10 Nov 2024, latest v4 16 Oct 2025) improves bounds on the 3rd and 4th smallest prime divisors of a hypothetical friend. arXiv:2504.08295 (submitted 11 Apr 2025, Sagar Mandal) proves further structural/modular constraints and a lower-bound inequality on the size of a friend in terms of its number of prime factors. arXiv:2503.11694 ('A note on solitary numbers', Mar 2025) is actually about 14, not 10, and does not address this problem — a related-but-distinct case, not evidence for this record. The most substantial recent item is a 2026 GitHub project by Caio Comitre Rossi (github.com/caioross/solitary10) which re-derives known necessary conditions mechanically via certified exact-arithmetic computation and establishes a new certified lower bound: any friend of 10 must exceed 10^32, about 100x tighter than the prior uncertified figure. I read the README, METHODOLOGY.md and RESULTS.md directly; none mentions any AI/ML/LLM system in deriving proofs, writing the certifiers, or designing the search — the methodology is explicitly classical exact-arithmetic computation (index pruning, valuation budgets, cyclotomic-polynomial arguments, Zsygmondy's theorem, Nielsen-style branching), with an internal 'proof / independent verification / adversarial review' discipline before anything is labeled proved. The author's own GitHub profile describes them as an individual developer (São Paulo, Brazil) working in 'local-first AI, XR, full-stack, hardware' — this describes their general work, not a claim that AI produced this project's mathematics, and no basis quote to that effect exists anywhere in the repo. I also found that Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures Lean repository contains a formal *statement* of this exact conjecture (FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/SolitaryNumber.lean, theorem is_ten_solitary), but it is stated with `sorry` — a benchmark placeholder with no proof attempt — so it is not an event that changes the problem's status. I also ruled out a same-name collision: a 2026 USAMO-style 'solitary integers' problem that appears in an AI-Olympiad-benchmark paper uses an entirely unrelated digit-based definition of 'solitary' and has nothing to do with abundancy/friendly numbers. No expert digestion (Tao's blog, MathOverflow consensus, OEIS updates) treats any of this as resolving the question; Wikipedia's own 'Solitary number' article (checked live, for context only) still lists 10 as an open, conjectured-solitary case with a raised lower bound. Given all this, status is `progress` (an instructive tightening of bounds/structure, not resolution of the open question), ai_role `none`, and resolution_direction null since the core question stayed open throughout.
competing_reading: One could argue the case-narrowing results (necessary structural conditions on any friend of 10) constitute a 'case of the problem' settled and thus warrant `partial` rather than `progress`. I read the rule in §3.1 as requiring that a genuine case be a *restriction* of the question that gets fully answered (e.g. 'is 10 solitary among numbers with ω(N)=7' answered yes) — but these results instead just narrow the search space for a still-fully-open existence question, which §3.1 explicitly says a bound or search-space narrowing does not move. If a future record-keeper disagrees, `partial` with `resolution_direction: null` would not fit either, since `partial` requires a direction; that internal inconsistency is further evidence `progress` is the better fit.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit friend of 10 exhibited and verified (refuted, counterexample), or a proof that no friend can exist (confirmed) — reviewed and digested by number theorists, or a machine-checked Lean proof (not just a `sorry` statement) that experts accept the soundness of.

outcome: In August 2024, Ryan Propper (working within the PrimeGrid distributed-computing project) found that 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1 is prime, eliminating k = 107347 as a candidate for a Riesel number smaller than 509,203. This is a case-elimination on the exact problem stated (whether 509,203 is the lowest Riesel number), reducing the pool of unresolved k values below 509,203 from 42 to 41. The conjecture that 509,203 is the smallest Riesel number remains open, and multiple sources confirm the count has stayed at 41 as of mid-2026, indicating no further eliminations occurred in the window.

counterexample.object: 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1, a 7,052,391-digit prime, showing k = 107347 is not a Riesel number and thus cannot be a counterexample to '509,203 is the lowest Riesel number' (it removes a candidate rather than exhibiting one)
counterexample.verified_how: Primality proved by Lucas–Lehmer–Riesel (LLR) test, standard for numbers of this form; distributed/verified through the PrimeGrid project infrastructure

summary: The problem asks whether 509,203 is the lowest Riesel number (a k such that k·2^n − 1 is composite for all n ≥ 1). As of the frozen Wikipedia revision (26 Jan 2024), the list of candidate k values below 509,203 not yet ruled out stood at 42 (57 of the original 101 candidates had been eliminated by finding a prime k·2^n − 1 for that k, as of December 2022, with no elimination recorded between then and the freeze date). In August 2024, Ryan Propper — working within PrimeGrid, the distributed-computing project that coordinates this search — found 107347 × 2^23427517 − 1 to be prime, which is a 7,052,391-digit number. This eliminates k = 107347 from the candidate pool, since finding any prime of the form k·2^n − 1 proves k is not a Riesel number. This is squarely a case-elimination on the stated problem (§3.1): finding one more prime among the remaining candidates directly shrinks the set of numbers that could be a smaller Riesel number than 509,203, which is exactly what the bullet asks about. I classify this as 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (the elimination is consistent with, and narrows in on, the conjecture that 509,203 is indeed the smallest). The list of 41 remaining unresolved k values (23669, 31859, 38473, 46663, 67117, 74699, 81041, 121889, 129007, 143047, 161669, 206231, 215443, 226153, 234343, 245561, 250027, 315929, 319511, 324011, 325123, 327671, 336839, 342847, 344759, 362609, 363343, 364903, 365159, 368411, 371893, 384539, 386801, 397027, 409753, 444637, 470173, 474491, 477583, 485557, 494743) has been reported consistently across sources from November 2024 through at least July 2026 (one search result cites 'as of July 29, 2026, there remain 41 uncertain candidates, and the coordinated search has currently reached n < 16984600'), which corroborates that no further eliminations occurred after the August 2024 one within this window — the underlying search (PrimeGrid's 'The Riesel Problem' subproject) has continued extending the tested range of n for the remaining k values without producing a new prime. On AI: this is a distributed-computing / GPU sieving and primality-testing effort (LLR/PRP testing, standard number-theoretic algorithms), and no source — Wikipedia's live article, PrimeGrid's project pages, or general search results on Propper's methods — mentions any AI or machine-learning system contributing to the search, sieving, or verification. Propper's other prime discoveries (Proth primes, etc.) are likewise attributed to conventional primality-testing software (LLR) run on CPU/GPU hardware. I therefore set ai_role to none.
competing_reading: One could argue the conjecture ('509,203 is the lowest Riesel number') is only truly settled when it is proven — i.e., when all 41 remaining candidates are eliminated or a smaller Riesel number is found — and that a single elimination is too incremental to register as anything beyond background progress on an open problem, arguably better captured as 'progress' rather than 'partial'. However, per §3.1, a case of the problem (here, one specific k value being ruled out) counts as 'partial' regardless of size, since it changes what a careful person would write about which k values remain live candidates for beating 509,203. I have followed that instruction literally.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (via exhaustive search or covering-set argument) that all 41 remaining k values are eliminated, or discovery of a Riesel number smaller than 509,203, would resolve the conjecture. Absent that, any future PrimeGrid/Propper/other announcement of a prime k·2^n − 1 for one of the 41 remaining k values would be a further 'partial' event to record separately.

outcome: On 1 August 2026, OpenAI announced that its then-unreleased model 'Astra' produced an explicit construction of a non-sofic countable discrete group, together with a machine-checked Lean 4 formalization (reported 'sorry' count of zero), disproving the soficity conjecture (Gromov 1999 / Weiss 2000). The construction has been read informally by several group theorists who find it credible, but as of late September 2026 it has not been digested by a refereed journal process, and it is under active dispute over whether key ideas were taken from mathematicians' private, unpublished conversations with OpenAI's chatbots, and over inadequate citation of prior work (Thom-Kun 2019 expander-decomposition results). OpenAI revised its announcement's language after these objections but has not withdrawn the result.

ai.basis_quote: the mathematical arguments 'originated with Astra' but ... 'OpenAI researchers then worked with the model to formalize them into publishable manuscripts' ... 'The precise division between what Astra contributed and what the research team contributed is not spelled out in the announcement.'
ai.disclosed_cost: Total compute for all ten proofs reportedly cost approximately $2,000 at GPT-5.6 (Sol) API prices, according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown, though this figure was described as deliberately conservative.

counterexample.object: An explicit finitely generated countable discrete group constructed by Astra that is not sofic (a subgroup of a unit group of a group algebra over a free group, per secondary summaries), refuting the conjecture that every countable discrete group is sofic.
counterexample.verified_how: Machine-checked in Lean 4, with a reported zero 'sorry' count across all ten formalized results in OpenAI's published repository; informally read by several group theorists (Henry Bradford, Michael Chapman, Alon Dogon, Francesco Fournier-Facio) who have not disputed the mathematical validity, though its provenance and citation of prior work are disputed.

disputes.summary: Andreas Thom (TU Dresden) publicly accused OpenAI in September 2026 of having derived key proof ideas from his and Gábor Kun's private, unpublished ChatGPT conversations about the 'extended/expander matching problem' relevant to soficity. OpenAI researcher Mark Sellke denied this ('that did not happen'), but Thom argued the denial addressed only direct access during proof-solving, not whether the conversations shaped training data; OpenAI has separately acknowledged (in a related dispute, Buckmaster/Alpöge) that it 'cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from usage of our products' influenced its models, a caveat not offered to Thom. A parallel attribution dispute arose over the announcement's insufficient citation of a 2019 Thom-Kun expander-decomposition paper and other prior literature (raised also by Francesco Fournier-Facio and Steven Miller); OpenAI revised its blog post's language (softening a claim that the problems had seen 'no progress for at least a decade') after correspondence, without withdrawing the mathematical result.

summary: The triage record is essentially correct: OpenAI's unreleased 'Astra' model, announced 1 August 2026, is credited with the first explicit construction of a non-sofic countable discrete group, directly refuting the conjecture (attributed to Gromov 1999 / Weiss 2000) that every countable discrete group is sofic — exactly the problem stated in this bullet, not a variant or restricted case. The proof ships as a Lean 4 formalization with a reported 'sorry' count of zero, and OpenAI's own account (echoed by tech press such as Pondero and TechTimes) states the mathematical arguments 'originated with Astra,' with OpenAI researchers (credited: Mark Sellke, Sébastien Bubeck) then working with the model to prepare the manuscript — meeting the bar for ai_role 'generated' since the authors' own account credits the model with producing the mathematics, not merely checking or formalizing human-derived arguments. However, I classify status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved': although several named group theorists (Bradford, Chapman, Dogon, Fournier-Facio) have informally read the non-sofic-groups chapter without disputing its mathematical soundness, there is no report of a completed refereed-journal digestion, and — more importantly — the result is under live, unresolved dispute as of September 2026: Andreas Thom's accusation (published 9 September 2026) that the construction may have drawn on his and Gábor Kun's private, unpublished research shared in ChatGPT conversations, and a separate, partially-resolved dispute over inadequate citation of 2016/2019 prior work that led OpenAI to revise (but not retract) its announcement. A machine-checked Lean certificate with a clean compile is strong evidence the construction is internally consistent, but per the task's own rule a clean check is evidence about the Lean kernel, not a substitute for settled expert and provenance review, especially while a live priority dispute is unresolved. The Wikipedia sofic-group article itself now documents the announcement alongside these very originality concerns, which supports treating the matter as claimed-but-contested rather than fully settled. Two items surfaced by triage are not evidence for this event: arXiv:2511.06586 ('Surjunctivity does not characterize cosoficity of invariant random subgroups', Bowen-Chapman, submitted 10 Nov 2025) is a related-but-distinct problem about invariant random subgroups, predates the Astra announcement, and does not bear on the base conjecture; it is a related problem, not a case of this one. arXiv:2608.02025 (Fournier-Facio, 'A torsion-free non-sofic group', posted early August 2026) is a human-authored follow-up strengthening Astra's result to a torsion-free, finitely presented example — itself a case/refinement of the same now-refuted conjecture, credited entirely to a human author with no AI role claimed in that paper's acknowledgements, and thus not itself an AI-involvement event, though it corroborates that the base result is being built upon by human mathematicians rather than dismissed. The GitHub google-deepmind/formal-conjectures issue #2153 is merely a tracking issue inviting someone to formalize this specific conjecture in Mathlib (rated formalization difficulty 3.5/5, marked 'up for grabs') and as of inspection contains no completed Lean proof — it documents that a from-scratch independent Mathlib formalization has not happened, distinct from OpenAI's own separately-published Lean repository.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'resolved' on the grounds that a Lean proof with zero 'sorry's is, per the task's own guidance, sometimes 'directly checkable by ... computer algebra' and that several named experts have read the chapter without objection to its mathematical content — the objections raised so far are about provenance/citation, not correctness. Under that reading the status would be 'resolved' with an ai_role note about the ongoing dispute recorded only in `disputes`. I did not adopt this reading because (a) 'reviewed informally by mathematicians who saw preprints' explicitly falls short of the 'resolved' bar's requirement of a digestion that works through the proof or acceptance by a journal of record, and (b) the live, unresolved priority dispute over the proof's origin bears on whether the published construction is what it claims to be, which is close enough to correctness-adjacent that treating it as fully settled seems premature.
what_would_settle_it: A refereed journal acceptance or a detailed public expert digestion (e.g., a Terence Tao-style blog walkthrough or a Bourbaki-seminar-style writeup) of the non-sofic group construction that treats it as correct and original; alternatively, resolution of the Thom dispute (either an independent finding that no private research was used, or a correction/retraction) would remove the main cloud over 'resolved' status.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or theoretical progress on the general conjecture; only continued discovery of individual new prime factors of specific, extremely large Fermat numbers, which narrows the search space but does not answer the universal question.
summary: The conjecture asks whether every Fermat number F_n = 2^(2^n)+1 is composite for n > 4. As of the frozen revision (Jan 2024) and still today, this is unproven in either direction: F_5 through F_32 are known composite (a status that predates the window), heuristic arguments (Boklan and Conway) suggest fewer than one in a billion chance of another Fermat prime existing, but no proof of the general statement exists, and no counterexample (a new Fermat prime) has been found. Since 26 January 2024, the only activity is continued distributed/individual factor-search work: on 27 November 2025 Gary Gostin found that 36812439837*2^3144+1 divides F3135, and on 3 December 2025 Sascha Beat Dinkel with PrimeGrid found that 1085*2^3943263+1 divides F3943261; prothsearch.com's tracking page records roughly 61 new such divisibility discoveries logged in 2026 alone. Each of these establishes that one more specific, very large Fermat number is composite, which is a case of the problem narrowing where a counterexample could hide, but per the deep-dive rule for infinitude/existence-type questions (an unbounded search that finds no counterexample does not advance the universal claim), none of this changes what a careful reader would write in this bullet's entry. The largest Fermat number known composite remains F_18233954 (factor found October 2020, before the window). No theoretical bound, partial classification result, or new proof technique bearing on the general conjecture was found. Separately, a WebSearch for 'Fermat AI' surfaced substantial 2026 coverage of Anthropic's Claude formalizing a Lean proof of Fermat's LAST Theorem (a completely different, already-proven 17th-century conjecture named after the same mathematician) — this is unrelated to Fermat numbers/Fermat primes and is noted here only to flag it as a namesake trap, not as a finding for this record.
competing_reading: One could argue that each new factor found (e.g., of F3135 or F3943261) constitutes 'partial' progress since it settles the compositeness of one more specific case. However, per the deep-dive rule (§3.1) on existence/infinitude questions, a bullet asking whether ALL F_n for n>4 are composite is not advanced by finding more composite examples — only a proof covering all n, or a counterexample (a new prime), would count. Since F_n for large specific n was already presumed/expected composite (and these searches only find factors, they do not even fully resolve compositeness for most of the enormous range of n with unknown character, e.g. n=20, 24, or the vast range beyond n=32), this is correctly classified as no_change_found.
what_would_settle_it: A general proof (or disproof via discovery of a new Fermat prime beyond F4) covering all n>4; short of that, any new theoretical bound, density result, or structural theorem specifically about the infinite family (rather than another individual factor) would count as progress.

summary: This is the Novikov problem (posed by A. Yu. Olshanskii, listed as Problem 8.52 'Do there exist infinite finitely presented periodic groups?' in the Kourovka Notebook, with the related type-(FP)_infinity version as R. Bieri's Problem 6.3, 'Is every periodic group of type (FP)_infinity finite?'). All known infinite periodic groups (Golod, Novikov-Adian free Burnside groups, Grigorchuk group, Gupta-Sidki groups, Tarski monsters) are only finitely generated, not finitely presented, so the question of whether an infinite finitely presented periodic group can exist remains open. I checked the most current authoritative source for open problems in group theory, the Kourovka Notebook's 21st edition (arXiv:1401.0300, version 40, dated 18 January 2026, well inside the window), and confirmed via its HTML rendering that Problem 8.52 is still listed without any solving reference or comment indicating progress; it is simply noted 'compare with 6.3.' I also checked arXiv listings in math.GR for 2024-2026 (searches for 'finitely presented periodic group', 'infinite finitely presented periodic group construction', and related terms), the Groupprops subwiki page on finitely presented periodic groups (last substantively edited 2014, still describing the conjecture as open, consistent with no change), Baumslag's 'Open problems in combinatorial group theory' survey, and general web/MathOverflow searches for any 2024-2026 activity. The only nearby results found were about weakly finitely presented periodic groups (a strictly weaker notion, pre-dating the window) and a 2025 paper on 'dice periodic groups' (arXiv:2504.00838, Petrogradsky) constructing new finitely generated (not finitely presented) infinite periodic groups — a related-but-distinct construction that does not bear on finite presentability, so it is out of scope under the case-vs-variant rule (§3.1) and does not change the status. No AI system was found associated with any activity on this problem in the window; no papers, announcements, or the Kourovka Notebook's own record credit any AI tool with work on this question. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 Petrogradsky 'dice periodic groups' construction (arXiv:2504.00838) is relevant progress, since it is a new construction technique for infinite periodic groups. However, it produces only finitely generated (not finitely presented) periodic groups, which is exactly the gap the Novikov problem is about — these constructions do not touch finite presentability, so under the scope rule this is a related problem (or at most tangential background), not a case of the stated problem, and should not move the status.
what_would_settle_it: A construction of an infinite finitely presented periodic group (resolving it in the negative direction relative to finiteness), a proof that all finitely presented periodic groups are finite, or an explicit comment/reference attached to Problem 8.52 in a future Kourovka Notebook edition indicating a solution or partial result.

outcome: Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture (is every group surjunctive?) remains open. The only claimed full proof (Cannizzo, arXiv:1912.00541, 'All groups are surjunctive') predates the frozen revision and was withdrawn by its author two days after posting in December 2019 due to a fatal gap in Lemma 5.3/Theorem 5.4; it was never resurrected. Post-window papers (2024-2026) extend surjunctivity-type results to sofic groups, non-uniform cellular automata, and invariant random subgroups, but none settles a new case of, or narrows, the general conjecture for all groups.
summary: The core question — is every group surjunctive (Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture) — remains open as of September 2026. The one attempt at a full resolution, Jan Cannizzo's December 2019 preprint claiming all finitely generated groups are surjunctive (arXiv:1912.00541), predates the frozen revision by over four years and, more importantly, was withdrawn by the author himself two days after the initial submission (v2, 2019-12-04), who stated the last sentence of Lemma 5.3 is unjustified and 'likely counts as a fatal flaw that invalidates the main theorem.' This is a pre-window, withdrawn claim, not a post-window event, so it does not move the status; I record it under 'event' only as the most recent substantive attempt on the conjecture, with predates_frozen_revision=true, and status is coded open/no_change_found rather than open_stale or progress/incident, since the withdrawal itself is also pre-window (no post-2024-01-26 development attaches to it). I searched for any 2024-2026 developments and found three papers, all variants under the §3.1 scope rule rather than cases or narrowings of the core conjecture: (1) arXiv:2403.05998 ('Generalized Gottschalk's conjecture for sofic groups and applications', March 2024) extends known surjunctivity-type theorems (Gromov-Weiss, Capobianco-Kari-Taati) to local perturbations of cellular automata and twisted group rings over sofic group universes — it assumes sofic groups are surjunctive (already known via Gromov-Weiss, itself pre-2024) and generalizes the automata/ring-theoretic apparatus around that fact, rather than settling surjunctivity for any group not already known to be surjunctive. (2) arXiv:2503.23435 ('On Gottschalk's Surjunctivity Conjecture for Non-uniform Cellular Automata', March 2025) proves a reversibility/invertibility result for non-uniform cellular automata over group universes that are already assumed surjunctive — a different (derived) question, not a case of 'is G surjunctive.' (3) arXiv:2511.06586 ('Surjunctivity does not characterize cosoficity of invariant random subgroups', November 2025) answers a related but distinct question in the negative — whether surjunctivity of an invariant random subgroup implies cosoficity — which is about IRSs, not about whether groups themselves are surjunctive. None of these three papers reduces the space of groups for which surjunctivity is unknown, and none is a restriction of the stated question in the sense of §3.1 (a case obtained by restricting the domain of the same question); they are variants that change the question (different objects: NUCA reversibility, IRS cosoficity) or extensions of the toolkit around an already-known class (sofic groups). The Wikipedia article on surjunctive groups, checked live, still states 'It is unknown whether every group is surjunctive' with no post-2014 developments mentioned. No AI involvement was found in any of the three post-window papers or in the withdrawn 2019 preprint; all rely on classical techniques in symbolic dynamics, descriptive set theory, and group theory, with no mention of machine learning, automated theorem proving, or AI assistance in any abstract, methodology, or acknowledgement section I could access.
competing_reading: One could argue the November 2025 IRS/cosoficity paper (arXiv:2511.06586) is close enough to the surjunctivity apparatus that it constitutes 'progress' in the broader research program around surjunctivity, since it resolves a natural companion question (does surjunctivity of an IRS imply cosoficity) in the negative. But the stated bullet is specifically 'is every group surjunctive', a question about groups, not about invariant random subgroups; the IRS question is a different mathematical object with its own conjecture (cosoficity vs. surjunctivity for IRSs), so under the change-vs-restrict test it is a related problem, not a case, and does not change what a careful reader would write in this bullet's entry.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement that either exhibits a non-surjunctive group (a counterexample, refuting the conjecture) or proves surjunctivity for a new class of groups not already covered by Gromov-Weiss sofic-group surjunctivity or other known classes (partial progress), or a corrected/re-submitted version of the Cannizzo argument (or an independent proof) that survives expert scrutiny (resolution).

outcome: No result advancing, restricting, or resolving Podewski's conjecture in characteristic zero was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains exactly as stated in the pre-2024 literature.
summary: Podewski's conjecture — every infinite minimal field (every definable subset finite or co-finite) is algebraically closed — was proved in positive characteristic by Wagner, and the characteristic-zero case has been open since at least the 2012/2013 paper 'Around Podewski's conjecture' by Krupiński, Tanović and Wagner (arXiv:1201.5709, Fundamenta Mathematicae 222 (2013)), which reduces the conjecture to a question about definable well-partial-orders and proves the 'almost linear' special case. I searched broadly for any post-January-2024 activity: general queries on Podewski's conjecture and minimal fields, targeted arXiv math.LO listing and site searches for 2024-2026, searches for the specific researchers active in this area (Wagner, Halevi, Hasson, Tanović, Krupiński) and their recent output, and a check of the closest-looking hits that turned up. None addressed the characteristic-zero case of Podewski's conjecture. Several near-misses were checked and ruled out as distinct problems under §3.1's scope rule: (1) Szachniewicz–Ye, 'Hyperbolicity and model-complete fields' (arXiv:2403.15300, published IMRN 2025) cites the already-known (pre-2024) Koenigsmann result on 'large fields' only in passing and does not engage with the characteristic-zero conjecture; (2) the classification of VC-minimal/dp-small fields as algebraically or real closed (Guingona's 2014 conjecture, proved by Guingona–Laskowski, published EMS/JEMS ~2022) concerns a different technical notion ('VC-minimal'/'dp-small', a combinatorial dividing-line condition) rather than 'minimal' in Podewski's strict model-theoretic sense (every definable subset finite or cofinite), and in any case predates the window; (3) 'On regular groups and fields' (Halevi–Hasson–Peterzil-adjacent work, arXiv:1211.3852, 2012) proving generically stable minimal/quasi-minimal fields are algebraically closed is also pre-2024 background, already known to the triage pass; (4) Acosta López–Hasson, 'On groups and fields definable in 1-h-minimal fields' (arXiv:2303.01127, published J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 2025) concerns Hensel-minimality ('1-h-minimal'), an unrelated valued-field notion, not Podewski-minimality; (5) a December 2025 survey by Jahnke and coauthors on tame valued fields' open questions does not mention Podewski's conjecture at all; (6) an ICM 2026 invited lecture 'Henselianity and NIP fields' (likely Jahnke) was found only behind a paywall (SIAM/epubs, 403 Forbidden) and could not be opened — noted as a source I could not reach. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and its underlying reasoning.
competing_reading: It is conceivable the paywalled ICM 2026 'Henselianity and NIP fields' survey or lecture contains a remark updating the status of Podewski's conjecture (e.g., citing a very recent unpublished result or restating it as still fully open), since ICM surveys of this kind often summarize the state of adjacent open problems. I could not access it to check. This is unlikely to change the classification given how much closer literature and researcher-specific searching turned up nothing, but it is the one unresolved gap.
what_would_settle_it: Access to the ICM 2026 'Henselianity and NIP fields' article (SIAM ebooks / epubs.siam.org, DOI 10.1137/25M1805412) to confirm it does not report new progress on Podewski's conjecture in characteristic zero.

outcome: No result found that resolves, partially resolves, or moves a bound on whether every reversible cellular automaton in three or more dimensions is locally reversible; the problem remains stated as open in the most recent secondary source found (the current English Wikipedia article on reversible cellular automata).
summary: The problem asks whether every reversible cellular automaton (CA) in three or more spatial dimensions is 'locally reversible' — i.e., realizable as a composition of local, reversible logic-gate-like steps (in the sense made precise by Kari 1996 and Durand-Lose 2001), analogous to what is known for one and two dimensions. I read the current (2026) English Wikipedia article on reversible cellular automata, which still lists this as an open problem under 'Billiard-ball computation and low-power computing': 'Kari (1996) showed that for one- and two-dimensional automata the answer is positive, and Durand-Lose (2001) showed that any reversible cellular automaton could be simulated by a (possibly different) locally reversible cellular automaton. However, the question of whether every reversible transition function is locally reversible remains open for dimensions higher than two.' No citation to any 2024-2026 work appears there. I then searched arXiv and the general web for any paper addressing local reversibility of 3D+ reversible CAs specifically, and found only tangential or unrelated work: (1) Durand-Lose's much older (pre-2024) theorem that any d-dimensional reversible CA can be written as a composition of d+1 block permutations (a block-cellular-automaton representation theorem, proving a 1990 Toffoli–Margolus conjecture) — this is a different notion (global block-decomposition, not local-gate reversibility) and predates the window regardless; (2) 'New classes of reversible cellular automata' (arXiv 2411.00721, Nov 2024, published in Designs, Codes and Cryptography 2026) — this concerns 'proper liftings' of Boolean functions parameterized by bit-width k, an unrelated notion of 'dimension'; (3) 'A Reversibility Characterization of Locally Finite Groups by Cellular Automata' (arXiv 2606.29958, 2026) — concerns CA over group shifts and locally finite groups, not the 3D local-reversibility question; (4) a 2025 AUTOMATA proceedings paper on number-conserving CA in three dimensions, which is a different conjecture (only trivial number-conserving reversible CAs exist) about a different notion of 'three-dimensional' constraint; (5) AutomataGPT (2026), an LLM-based system for forecasting and inferring CA update rules from data — this is unrelated AI-for-CA work but does not touch reversibility structure theorems, let alone this specific open problem. No preprint, announcement, or digested result of any kind addresses this problem in the 26 January 2024 - present window, and no AI system is credited with, or connected to, any progress on it.
competing_reading: None of the tangentially related papers found (block-CA representation, Boolean-function liftings, locally-finite-group CA, number-conserving CA, AutomataGPT) could plausibly be read as bearing on this exact scope question even under a generous reading; they concern different structures or different notions of 'dimension'/'reversibility'. There is no genuine ambiguity here to flag.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving or disproving that every reversible CA in 3+ dimensions decomposes into locally reversible (reversible-logic-gate) steps, or a paper narrowing the question (e.g., resolving it for a restricted class of 3D CAs), which would at minimum warrant a 'partial' classification. Absent that, continued citation of the problem as open in a current survey or the Wikipedia article itself is the best available confirmation of the status quo.

outcome: A June 2025 preprint by Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna proves the conjecture (attributed to Akgün et al.) that the crown graph H_{n,n} has the highest representation number among bipartite graphs on 2n vertices, for the case n odd (and for unequal-sized partite sets more generally); the case where both partite sets are equal and even remains open.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether crown graphs require the longest word-representants of all bipartite graphs — i.e., whether H_{n,n} has the maximum representation number among bipartite graphs on 2n vertices. This is precisely the conjecture attributed in the literature to Akgün et al. (building on the known fact, from Kitaev/Chen-type results on crown graphs, that H_{n,n} has representation number ⌈n/2⌉, the maximum possible for a comparability graph on 2n vertices). In arXiv:2506.01057 ("On the Conjecture of the Representation Number of Bipartite Graphs", submitted 1 June 2025), Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna prove that every bipartite graph is (1+⌈m/2⌉)-representable (m = size of the smaller partite set) and, when m is odd, that it is ⌈m/2⌉-representable — matching or falling below the crown graph's bound in all cases except when both partite sets are equal and even in size. The paper's own introduction and conclusion state this explicitly: the crown-graph-maximality conjecture is established 'when n is odd', leaving the equal-even-size case open. I could not find any journal acceptance, expert digestion (e.g. a survey or Tao-style write-up), or a later paper closing the remaining even case; the live Word-representable graph Wikipedia article (fetched today) still lists the bullet as an open problem with no mention of this 2025 progress, and a search of Mozhui/Krishna's subsequent 2025-2026 publications (an upper-bound paper in J. Information Processing 2025, and 'Word-Representation of Melon Graphs' in Graphs and Combinatorics 2026) did not turn up a resolution of the even case. No AI system is credited anywhere in the paper, its abstract, or surrounding coverage; the methods described (neighborhood inclusion graphs, direct combinatorial construction) are entirely classical human mathematics. This is therefore a `partial` resolution: a genuine case-restriction (all bipartite graphs except one symmetric family) of the exact stated conjecture, settled in the conjectured (confirming) direction, with `ai_role` `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `open` with `no_change_found` if one reads the Wikipedia bullet as asking only about the single extremal question (which specific graph is the unique maximizer) rather than about the general upper bound — under a very strict reading, the 'crown graphs are extremal' claim is only proven for a subfamily (n odd, or unequal partite sets), not universally, so the conjecture itself is still technically open in full generality. I judge `partial` is the better fit because the paper explicitly frames its result as (partially) proving that specific named conjecture, and a strict majority of cases (all except equal-even) are now settled in the confirming direction — this is a textbook case of 'a case of the problem settled' under §3.1, not a variant problem.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (or the same authors' follow-up work) resolving the remaining case of bipartite graphs with equal, even-sized partite sets — either proving H_{n,n} (n even) still has the maximum representation number, or exhibiting a bipartite graph on 2n vertices (n even) with a strictly larger representation number than the crown graph, which would refute the conjecture and directly answer the Wikipedia bullet in the negative.

outcome: The question of whether OCA (in the sense most sources mean by the bare name — Todorčević's OCA, OCA_T) is consistent with 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₂ remains open as of September 2026; no result in the window settles it either way for OCA_T. A distinct but easily confused variant, OCA_ARS (Abraham-Rubin-Shelah), was already shown consistent with 2^ℵ₀=ℵ₃ by Gilton and Neeman, but that paper (arXiv:1904.10516) was first posted in April 2019 and last revised May 2022, entirely before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, so it is not a change in this window even though it answers a closely related question. A January 2026 preprint by Lorenzo Notaro (arXiv:2601.01166) constructs a model of MA_ℵ1+OCA_T in which Baumgartner's Axiom and OCA_ARS both fail, answering a question of Farah — but this is about Baumgartner's Axiom, not about the size of the continuum, so it does not bear on this bullet.
summary: Wikipedia's bare 'OCA' most commonly refers to Todorčević's Open Coloring Axiom (OCA_T), and the specific open problem — first posed by Todorčević after he showed OCA_T implies b=ℵ2 — is whether OCA_T alone is consistent with 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₂. This is exactly the question addressed in a 2019 Fields Institute talk by Justin Moore ('Does OCA imply the continuum is ℵ2?'), which states that Moore showed in 2001 that OCA_T + OCA_ARS together force c=ℵ2, but whether OCA_T alone does so (or is consistent with a larger continuum) was open then and — per the 2021 survey 'Ken's colorful questions' (arXiv:2111.00632) and multiple recent secondary sources — remains open through the window. A separate, closely related axiom, OCA_ARS (Abraham-Rubin-Shelah), was shown by Gilton and Neeman to be consistent with 2^ℵ₀=ℵ₃, but that paper (arXiv:1904.10516) was submitted 23 April 2019 and its final revision (v5) posted 17 May 2022 — well before the 26 January 2024 snapshot — so even under a reading where OCA_ARS counts as 'a case of' the bullet's 'OCA', the result predates the window and would be open_stale, not a change in this window. I did not classify it as open_stale for the primary status because the bullet's 'OCA' is more naturally read as OCA_T given the article and survey usage, and the Gilton-Neeman work does not touch OCA_T at all (confirmed by direct fetch of the paper, which never mentions OCA_T). The one item that is new since the frozen date, Lorenzo Notaro's January 2026 arXiv:2601.01166 ('Open Colorings and Baumgartner's Axiom'), works with MA_ℵ1+OCA_T as a hypothesis but proves a result about Baumgartner's Axiom and OCA_ARS failing under that hypothesis — a different question (per §3.1, a related problem, not a restriction of this one) — and does not touch or move the continuum-size question. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this search: all sources are standard human-authored set-theory papers and surveys, with no AI system named, credited, or referenced in any capacity.
competing_reading: If 'OCA' in the Wikipedia bullet is read broadly enough to include OCA_ARS as a legitimate case falling under the same name (the article's own prose does say 'OCA' can refer to either the Todorčević or the Abraham-Rubin-Shelah axiom, and states 'Gilton and Neeman have announced that OCA[ARS] does not imply c=ℵ2'), then the Gilton-Neeman result is a settled case of the bullet — but even under that reading it is dated to 2019 (first posted) / 2022 (final version), both before 26 January 2024, so the correct status would be open_stale rather than any code reflecting a change in this window. Under neither reading does anything in the window (2024-01-26 to 2026-09-22) move this problem.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement that specifically constructs a model of full OCA_T together with 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₂ (or proves OCA_T implies c=ℵ2), postdating 26 January 2024, would resolve the open problem as stated. Short of that, any explicit new partial result narrowing exactly the OCA_T case (as opposed to OCA_ARS or combinations with Baumgartner's Axiom) would count as partial progress.
