outcome: No proof or disproof of pi's normality has appeared since 26 January 2024; all activity in the window is computational digit-record extension (120+ trillion, then 314 trillion digits) and statistical/empirical studies consistent with (but not establishing) normality, plus one unrelated general theoretical paper on normal numbers that does not mention pi.
summary: The question of whether pi is normal (every digit and digit-string equally frequent in some/every base) remains completely open, exactly as it was on 26 January 2024, and I found nothing that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet. Within the window: (1) record-setting digit computations continued — over 120 trillion digits in early 2025 and 314 trillion digits by late 2025 (Razeto & Rossi, arXiv:2608.06438, 'Can π generate itself? A Monte Carlo analysis of 314 trillion digits'), which I opened and confirm is a Monte Carlo / statistical-randomness study using pi's digits as a pseudorandom source, explicitly not a proof of normality — it only extends empirical consistency to more digits, which per §3.1 does not advance an existence/'is it normal' question. (2) A 2025 MDPI paper (Mathematics 13(2):313) claims to bound the probability of normality via a Bernoulli-experiment hypothesis test on the first 100 million digits ('1.86×10^30 times more likely that π is normal than not') — this is probabilistic/statistical argument, not a mathematical proof, and the source itself (per search snippets, since the page returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened directly) frames it as evidence rather than resolution; I was unable to fetch the full text to confirm AI involvement, but nothing in the abstract-level description suggests AI. (3) 'Super-Dense Sets and Their Role in the Theory of Normal Numbers' (arXiv:2506.15422, opened) is a general topological theory paper about normal vs. non-normal numbers as a class; it never mentions pi and does not bear on this specific constant — a related-but-different question under §3.1, so it does not count as a case or progress on pi's normality. (4) A blog post/informal piece ('Pi vs. AI: Could a Neural Network Predict the Next Digit of Pi?') describes a neural network failing to predict pi's digits beyond ~10% (chance) accuracy — this is an informal, non-peer-reviewed exploration that, if anything, is weak empirical evidence consistent with randomness/normality, not a proof, and not indexed as a mathematical contribution; I did not find any peer-reviewed or expert-digested account crediting an AI system with mathematical progress on this problem. The Wikipedia 'Pi' article, current as of this check, still states plainly that 'The conjecture that π is normal has not been proven or disproven,' with no updated claim of progress. No source anywhere in my search claims a case of normality (e.g., a specific base, or a specific finite digit-string frequency bound proven exactly) was settled, nor any bound that would count as 'progress' under §6.1 in a way that changes the open status. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' record rather than an under-searched one.
competing_reading: One could argue the 314-trillion-digit Monte Carlo paper and the 100-million-digit Bernoulli hypothesis-test paper constitute 'progress' in a loose sense (extending empirical/statistical support), but per §3.1 an infinitude/universal-property question like normality is not advanced by more computation or a probabilistic likelihood argument — only an actual proof or disproof (or a rigorously proven partial/restricted case, e.g. proven normality in one specific base) would count. Neither exists in the window, so I classify as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous proof (or disproof) that pi is normal in some base, or a peer-reviewed proof of a genuine restricted case (e.g., normality of pi in a specific base, or a proven non-trivial digit-frequency bound derived from provably-established structure rather than statistical testing), would change this record's status to partial or resolved.

outcome: Sven Manthe (arXiv preprint, first posted 1 October 2024, revised through March 2026) proves that the monadic second-order theory of (ℝ,≤) with the set quantifier restricted to Borel sets (and even to σ-combinations of analytic sets) is decidable, confirming Saharon Shelah's 1975 conjecture on the Borel monadic theory of order (BMTO). No progress on the second half of the bullet — whether the monadic theory of well-ordering (MTWO) is consistently decidable — was found.
summary: The triage's headline finding checks out: Sven Manthe's preprint 'The Borel monadic theory of order is decidable' (arXiv:2410.00887, v1 posted 2024-10-01, v2 posted 2026-03-09) proves decidability of the monadic theory of (ℝ,≤) restricted to Borel-set quantification, resolving the first half of this bullet's two-part question (Shelah's 1975 conjecture on the BMTO). I read the paper's introduction and acknowledgements directly (via arxiv.org/html/2410.00887v1): the acknowledgements credit Philipp Hieronymi for suggesting the topic, Kim Kiehn for proofreading, and Yuri Gurevich for discussion, with no mention of any AI system, computer search, or automated tool anywhere in the paper — so ai_role is 'none'. I classify the status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved': the paper remains an arXiv preprint by Manthe's own webpage (https://www.math.uni-bonn.de/people/smanthe/), which lists it as a preprint with no journal venue, distinct from his separate, unrelated Lean-formalization paper that did appear in the Annals of Formalized Mathematics (an initial web-search summary conflated the two papers; I verified via Manthe's own publication list that the BMTO decidability paper is NOT the one published there). However there is meaningful evidence of expert engagement beyond a bare unread preprint: Manthe gave a seminar talk on the result at Oxford's Logic Seminar (14 Nov 2024, https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/node/69433), the result forms the core of his 2026 Bonn PhD thesis 'Decidability in Borel Monadic Logic' under advisor Philipp Hieronymi, and search results indicate he has since moved to a postdoc with Ralf Schindler at Münster — consistent with the thesis having been examined and passed by a doctoral committee, which is a form of expert vetting of the argument even without a journal referee report. A second, independent 2025/2026 preprint by Mirna Džamonja (arXiv:2512.23003, first posted 2025-12-28, v3 dated ~2026-01, using 'well-levelled orders' to code Borel sets into S2S) proves essentially the same decidability result; I could not confirm from the fetched excerpt whether it cites or disputes priority with Manthe's paper, so I am not confident this constitutes independent replication versus a second novel proof, and no priority dispute was found in what I could read. Neither paper's proof has yet been digested by a survey, blog post (I found nothing on Tao's blog or MathOverflow specifically discussing or vetting either proof), or accepted for journal publication with a referee report as far as I could establish. The MTWO consistency question (second sentence of the bullet) was not addressed by anything found — Büchi-era results establish decidability for countable ordinals and ω₁, and older Shelah-era work shows MTWO for (ω₂,<) can be made 'as complicated as you like' under different set-theoretic hypotheses (i.e. that instance is already known to be independent of ZFC), but I found no 2024–2026 work making a new claim about consistent decidability of MTWO as a whole. Given the balance — a serious, seminar-presented, thesis-anchored proof of the first half's conjecture, not yet journal-published or independently digested in print — 'claimed' is the more defensible code, with the strongest case for 'resolved' resting on the passed PhD thesis as a form of expert check (noted in competing_reading).
competing_reading: If the Bonn PhD thesis defense is treated as equivalent to 'a published verification by named experts' (a doctoral committee reading and approving the specific argument), this would meet the 'resolved' bar of an expert digestion working through the proof — the fact that Manthe has evidently completed the PhD and moved on to a postdoc is indirect but real evidence the thesis was successfully defended. I did not find a direct source confirming the defense occurred, its date, or the committee's assessment, so I coded conservatively as 'claimed'. Also worth flagging: the Džamonja preprint (2512.23003) proving apparently the same theorem independently, and whether it treats itself as confirming or as a novel/first proof (a possible unremarked priority question), is unresolved from the excerpts I could fetch.
what_would_settle_it: A confirmed date and outcome of Manthe's Bonn PhD defense; a journal acceptance notice, referee report, or an expert survey/blog digestion of arXiv:2410.00887; and a check of the Džamonja preprint's bibliography/introduction for whether it cites Manthe's priority or claims independence, which would settle whether this is one confirmed result or two.

outcome: A September 2025 arXiv preprint by Mozhui, Dwary and Krishna (IIT Guwahati) gives an explicit counterexample — the Mycielski graph of an odd cycle μ(C₂ₙ₊₁), n ≥ 2, which is non-word-representable but whose line graph is word-representable — answering the open question in the negative. The same paper also shows that an earlier claimed counterexample from 2021 (arXiv:2108.02363, predating the frozen revision) was wrong: its line graph is in fact non-word-representable, so the question was not actually settled in 2021 as that paper claimed.

counterexample.object: The Mycielski graph μ(C₂ₙ₊₁) of an odd cycle (for n ≥ 2): a non-word-representable, triangle-free graph whose line graph L(μ(C₂ₙ₊₁)) the authors prove is word-representable via an explicit semi-transitive orientation.
counterexample.verified_how: By hand: the authors construct an explicit semi-transitive orientation D of L(μ(C₂ₙ₊₁)), decomposing it into a bipartite part L(B₂ₙ₊₁) and a cycle part L(C₂ₙ₊₁), and prove by case analysis (Lemmas 3–4) that D is acyclic and shortcut-free, hence semi-transitive, hence the graph is word-representable (using the known equivalence of word-representability and semi-transitive orientability).

disputes.summary: A 2021 preprint (Akbar, Akrobotu & Brewer, arXiv:2108.02363) had already claimed to answer this question in the negative, using an IBM CPLEX-based optimization framework on a graph they called 'A' (from a figure in Kitaev & Lozin's book), and stated in its conclusion that this 'settl[ed] the open question known for about a decade.' The 2025 paper by Mozhui, Dwary & Krishna directly disputes this: it proves that the graph A in fact contains the subgraph W₅′ as a subgraph, whose line graph L(W₅′) they prove (Theorem 2, by hand) is non-word-representable, and by hereditary closure of word-representability under induced subgraphs, this means L(A) cannot be word-representable either — contradicting the 2021 paper's Theorem 1. The 2025 paper concludes 'the problem remains open' as of the 2021 attempt and that their own Mycielski-graph construction is what 'settle[s] the problem.' The 2021 CPLEX-based claim therefore appears to have been a computational/methodological error (their optimization formulation, aimed at detecting a weaker '3-semi-transitive' property, evidently produced a false positive for full semi-transitivity), never corrected or withdrawn by its own authors, and (as far as could be determined) never formally peer-reviewed or published in a journal.

summary: The triage record is essentially correct that a September 2025 preprint (arXiv:2509.03339, Mozhui, Dwary & Krishna) answers this Wikipedia bullet's exact question in the negative, but the full picture is more complicated than 'a new counterexample was found.' A 2021 preprint (arXiv:2108.02363, predating the frozen revision) had already published a claimed negative answer, using a CPLEX optimization solver to find a graph 'A' whose line graph it asserted was semi-transitive (hence word-representable) despite A itself being non-word-representable. That 2021 claim was never digested, cited approvingly, or published in a journal (it remains a single-version 2021 preprint, also apparently overlapping with a 2021 UT Dallas PhD thesis by one of its authors). The 2025 paper I read in full directly refutes the 2021 paper's claim: it proves by hand (Theorem 2, via an explicit semi-transitive-orientation argument) that L(A) is actually non-word-representable, because A contains an induced copy of a graph W5' whose line graph is non-word-representable, and word-representability is hereditary under induced subgraphs. Having shown the 2021 counterexample fails, the 2025 authors provide their own explicit counterexample — Mycielski graphs of odd cycles µ(C_{2n+1}) for n≥2 — and prove by hand (Lemmas 3 and 4, via a fully explicit semi-transitive orientation D) that their line graphs are word-representable. This is a rigorous, hand-verifiable combinatorial proof with no automated or AI component of any kind; the only computational tool anywhere in this problem's history is IBM's CPLEX solver in the superseded 2021 paper, which is classical numerical/combinatorial optimization software, not an AI system. I found no evidence the 2025 paper has yet been read/endorsed by an outside expert (no citations of it turn up, no journal listing, and the Wikipedia article 'Word-representable graph' as of my check has not been updated to reflect it), so per §6.1 it is classified as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved': a preprint whose argument is complete and appears correct to me on a careful read, but which no named expert has yet publicly reviewed. The status therefore rests on the 2025 event; the 2021 event is recorded as a dispute rather than as the resolving event, since it turns out to have been erroneous.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2021 paper should itself be dated/counted as the resolving event, since it was the first to claim a negative answer to this exact Wikipedia bullet — but it predates the frozen revision's window anyway (2021 vs. the January 2024 cutoff), so even if I had found it correct it would only be relevant as 'open_stale' background, not as an event in-window. Since the 2021 claim in fact appears to be wrong (per the 2025 paper's Theorem 2 refutation), it does not even qualify as an 'open_stale' resolution; I've recorded it purely as a dispute. A second competing reading: since no expert has yet publicly vetted the 2025 paper, one could be more conservative and call status 'open' with 'no_change_found' false but treat the preprint as insufficient evidence of any change; I judge 'claimed' more appropriate since the preprint presents a complete, checkable, elementary combinatorial proof (which I read and found internally consistent) rather than a bare assertion.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance of arXiv:2509.03339, a citing survey or paper by an established expert in the area (e.g., Kitaev, Pyatkin, or Lozin, who wrote the foundational papers this preprint responds to) that endorses or engages with the Mycielski-graph counterexample, or an update to the Wikipedia 'Word-representable graph' article's open-problems section reflecting the resolution.

outcome: No progress on the periodicity question for Grundy's game specifically was found since 26 January 2024; the sequence remains computed to very large heap sizes with no periodicity detected, and the OEIS entry's most recent substantive activity (comments and code, March 2025) only clarifies the rules and adds a Python implementation rather than advancing the mathematics.
summary: Grundy's game (splitting a heap into two unequal heaps; nim-sequence OEIS A002188) is a special case of the general open conjecture that every finite octal game has an eventually periodic Grundy sequence (Guy's conjecture). I searched for any 2024–2026 progress on Grundy's game itself and found none: Achim Flammenkamp's computation page (wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/grundy.html) still reports the heap-size search extending to G(284944236543), reached in a run completed 2012-11-25, with no periodicity found and no update to that computation since; the page's last-modified date (2021) also predates the window. The Wikipedia article on Grundy's game itself is unchanged in substance: it still cites the Flammenkamp computation of the first 235 'record' values and calls the question unsolved. The OEIS sequence A002188 shows recent edit activity — a clarifying comment from Allan C. Wechsler and a Python implementation from David Cleaver, both dated 2025-03-22 — but these do not extend the computed range or bear on periodicity; they only restate/clarify existing rules and add code for existing values (Cleaver's tables to n=200,000 already existed). I also checked the triage's lead, google-deepmind/formal-conjectures issue #3697 'Periodicity of finite octal games' — this is an open formalization request (filed 2026-04-05) asking someone to state Guy's general octal-game periodicity conjecture in Lean; it does not attempt or claim a proof, and it concerns the general conjecture across all octal games, not a resolution of Grundy's game's case. Even if it did produce a Lean formalization, a bare formal *statement* of a conjecture (as opposed to a proof) has no bearing on `status`. I also checked two RL/neural-network papers that surfaced in searches for 'impartial games' + AI — 'Impartial Games: A Challenge for Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv:2205.12787, Riis & Zhou, Machine Learning journal 2026) and 'Mastering NIM and Impartial Games with Weak Neural Networks' (arXiv:2411.06403, Riis) — both are about standard Nim as a testbed for AlphaZero-style self-play RL and its difficulty learning parity/Sprague-Grundy strategy; neither addresses Grundy's game or its periodicity conjecture, and the first paper's arXiv submission (May 2022) predates the window regardless, with the 2026 journal appearance being ordinary publication lag. No arXiv preprint, blog digestion (Tao, Quanta, etc.), or lab announcement addressing Grundy's game periodicity was found. Given the extensive prior computational search already covering heap sizes past 2.8×10^11 with no periodicity, and no new computational or theoretical effort found in the window, I am confident nothing changed for this specific problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind formal-conjectures issue represents 'AI-adjacent' activity worth noting even absent a resolution, since it is machine-conjecture infrastructure touching this exact question. But per the scope rules, a formalization request with no proof attempt is not an event that changes status, and per §6.2 a formalisation-only contribution (were one even completed) would be ai_role none in any case, so it does not change the record either way.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of eventual periodicity for Grundy's game's nim-sequence, or a Lean-formalized proof (with expert review) via the formal-conjectures repository, or a Flammenkamp-style computational extension that finds an actual periodic tail (which would still only be suggestive, not a proof, given the conjecture is about all n).

outcome: Neither sub-question has been settled: the decidability of the elementary theory of Z_p((t)) (Laurent series over the p-adic integers) and of the field of rational functions/polynomials over C (i.e. full first-order Th(C(t))) both remain open as of September 2026.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet actually poses two separate decidability questions with no attached citation in the frozen revision: (1) is the elementary theory of Z_p((t)) — Laurent series over the p-adic integers, a mixed-characteristic henselian valued field — decidable, and (2) is the elementary theory of the field of rational functions/polynomials over C decidable. I confirmed the exact wikitext via the frozen revision's raw text and found no footnote pinning either sub-question to a specific source, consistent with these being long-standing folklore open problems in the model theory of valued fields (in the tradition of Ax-Kochen-Ershov). I checked the most promising leads flagged by triage: Kuhlmann's December 2025 survey 'Model theory of tame valued fields and beyond' (arXiv:2512.06386), which lists 16 open problems but, on direct query of its content, does not discuss Z_p((t)) or C(t)/C[t] decidability at all — it focuses on tame, perfectoid and deeply ramified fields in equicharacteristic and mixed characteristic, not on this specific pair of questions. Scanlon's August 2025 paper on 'complicated structures definable in C(t)' addresses definable substructures of C(t), not the decidability of the full first-order theory of C(t) itself, and does not claim to resolve it. Kartas's work (2020's 'Decidability via the tilting correspondence', predating the window, and follow-ups through 2025) makes substantial progress on decidability of various p-adic and perfectoid fields via tilting/perfectoid-transfer techniques, and Anscombe-Fehm's 'Universal-existential theories of fields' (2024, arXiv:2405.12771) studies universal-existential fragments and reductions between theories of function fields and Laurent series fields — but neither claims to resolve the full elementary theory of Z_p((t)) itself, nor of C(t)/C[t]. General web searches on Hilbert's Tenth Problem for C(t) (the closely related existential/Diophantine question) confirm the single-variable case remains explicitly unresolved and is described in the literature as 'the most annoying piece of our ignorance in the area' — only the multivariable case C(t1,t2) was resolved (Kim-Roush, 1992, well before the window). No source found any claim, partial or full, of a resolution to either sub-question inside the 26 Jan 2024–Sep 2026 window, and no AI system appears anywhere in this niche area of model theory research.
competing_reading: One could argue that Kartas's perfectoid-transfer program and the Anscombe-Fehm reductions constitute 'progress' in a loose sense, since they resolve decidability for structurally adjacent fields (F_p((t)) and its perfect/perfectoid variants, Q_p(zeta_{p^infty}), Q_p(p^{1/p^infty})) using techniques that could plausibly one day bear on Z_p((t)) itself. But per §3.1, a related/adjacent field is a different question, not a restriction of the stated one, and none of these papers claim their results imply anything about Z_p((t)) or C(t) decidability directly — so I did not code this as `partial` or `progress`. If a paper is found stating an explicit corollary for Z_p((t)) itself, this should be revisited.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (or the next edition of Kuhlmann's survey, or a future update to the Wikipedia article's own footnotes) that explicitly states a decidability or undecidability result for the full elementary theory of Z_p((t)) or of C(t)/C[t], with a proof or a clear statement that it remains open with attribution to a specific researcher.

summary: Erdős Problem #7 (does a distinct covering system with all-odd moduli exist?) remains open per erdosproblems.com, the authoritative tracker for this exact problem, as of its latest revision. Within the window, the clearest, best-documented event is a May 2026 claimed-and-withdrawn proof: forum user 'jinooklee', working with Harmonic's Aristotle theorem-proving system, submitted a purported proof of nonexistence extending the Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba (BBMST) squarefree-case argument to the general odd case, backed by a Lean 4 formalization that Aristotle's own verification reportedly passed 7/7. Four days later, forum participant Nat Sothanaphan found that a key axiom in the formalization was mathematically false (the sieve-product function as coded is always >1, contradicting the axiom claiming it <1), and the submitter acknowledged the formalization had omitted an initial term from the true BBMST criterion, conceding the axiom was 'provably false'. This is a textbook instance of §6.1's 'instructive failure' clause: an AI-produced/AI-verified claim announced and then withdrawn, coded as status=progress, ai_role=incident, dated to the announcement (2026-05-02) rather than to any resolution, since the problem itself did not move. Separately, I found a self-published Zenodo cluster (7+ papers, January 2026) by an otherwise-unverifiable 'Giovanni Esposito' claiming full unconditional resolution via jargon ('arithmetic renormalization', 'Coverage Fraction βₑ') that does not correspond to any recognized technique for this problem; no expert digestion, citation, or endorsement of this cluster exists anywhere I could find, and erdosproblems.com does not reference it. I treat this cluster as not meeting even the 'claimed' bar (no evidence anyone credible has read it), and record it only as a dispute/credibility note rather than as the driving event — per §6.1, 'claimed' requires a preprint or announcement, but the complete absence of any external engagement, institutional trace, or citation for this specific author across a cluster of grandiose claims is exactly the profile Thomas Bloom (site moderator) and others describe in 2026 as an 'AI slop' flood of unread mathematical papers. I also found a genuinely useful, modest, explicitly-AI-assisted contribution: Mian & Siddique, 'Kernel-Checked Exclusions for the Erdős–Selfridge Odd Covering Problem' (arXiv:2607.25628, posted 2026-07-28), which does not claim to resolve the problem but instead gives a from-scratch Lean 4, kernel-checked formalization of an already-known/folklore numerical bound (lcm of moduli of any odd covering exceeds 10000), explicitly stating in acknowledgements that 'Development was carried out with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic)'. Since this bound was already known/folklore and the paper's own stated contribution is 'epistemic' (a machine-checked certificate) rather than new mathematics, and since the problem is still open, this would fit ai_role=bound / status=progress in isolation, but I have selected the Aristotle incident as the single decisive event per the instruction to describe one event and note others in summary, since the withdrawn claim is the more consequential and more clearly AI-attributable episode in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the decisive event should instead be the Mian–Siddique Lean formalization (ai_role=bound, since it is a genuine, non-withdrawn, published contribution, whereas the Aristotle claim was retracted) rather than the withdrawn Aristotle claim. I chose the incident because §6.1 explicitly calls out withdrawn AI claims as their own instructive category, and because the Aristotle episode is the more significant test of AI capability on this specific problem (a full nonexistence proof attempt, not just a formalization of an already-known bound). A downstream aggregation pass could reasonably record both if the schema allowed multiple events; I have described both fully so that this loss is recoverable from the summary. Separately, the Esposito Zenodo cluster could in principle be a genuine (if bizarre) human research program rather than AI-generated text; I could not find definitive proof either way (no self-disclosed AI use, but also no verifiable human institutional trace), so I neither counted it as ai_role=generated/assisted nor asserted with certainty that it is AI slop — I flagged the ambiguity in disputes and excluded it from status-bearing evidence because no expert has engaged with it.
what_would_settle_it: For the Aristotle incident: nothing further needed, it is settled as withdrawn/incorrect on the primary forum thread. For the Esposito Zenodo cluster: an author statement (disclosed or denied AI use), an institutional affiliation, or any expert (e.g. a comment on erdosproblems.com or a citing paper) engaging with the claim one way or the other would resolve whether it belongs in this record at all and whether it should be coded as an AI ai_role. For the underlying problem: any future dated, expert-reviewed proof or explicit odd covering system.

outcome: No result settling this exact question was found. The one 2024-2026 item that surfaces in every search (Väänänen's July 2025 arXiv survey 'Interpolation in model theory') discusses a related but distinct fact: the 'Beth-closure' of the logic L(Q≤2ωcof) is compact and has the Beth property, but it explicitly does NOT satisfy Δ-interpolation (which the survey identifies as the same thing as Souslin-Kleene interpolation) — the opposite of what this bullet's hypothetical logic would need. That construction is also not new; it is attributed (via reference [50] in the survey) to earlier work, not to the 2025 paper itself.
summary: This bullet asks whether there is a logic L with the Beth property AND Δ-interpolation, that is compact, but lacks the (Craig) interpolation property. This is a fine-grained question in abstract model theory sitting at the intersection of the Beth property, Δ-interpolation (equivalently Souslin-Kleene interpolation), compactness, and full interpolation — a hierarchy where interpolation ⇒ Δ-interpolation ⇒ Beth ⇒ weak Beth. The triage pass flagged Jouko Väänänen's July 2025 arXiv survey 'Interpolation in model theory' (2507.19097) as a possible hit, and I fetched both the abstract and the HTML full text to check it directly. The survey does discuss a closely related construction: the 'Beth-closure' of the generalized-quantifier logic L(Q≤2ωcof) is compact and has the Beth property, but the survey states plainly that this Beth-closure logic does NOT satisfy interpolation, 'not even Souslin-Kleene interpolation' — and the survey treats Souslin-Kleene interpolation as synonymous with Δ-interpolation. That is nearly the reverse of the bullet's question: the bullet wants a logic that DOES satisfy Δ-interpolation (in addition to Beth and compactness) while still lacking full interpolation, whereas the Beth-closure example is a logic that fails even Δ-interpolation. So this construction does not answer the stated bullet; it is a different (already-known, cited to reference [50], i.e. pre-existing) counterexample answering a nearby but distinct question. I could not find any paper, survey, or announcement dated after 26 January 2024 that constructs or refutes the existence of a logic satisfying Beth + Δ-interpolation + compactness while lacking interpolation. The survey's own explicit open-problem list (e.g. 'Is there any proper extension of first order logic that is (countably) compact and has the interpolation property?', 'Are FO quantifiers the only generalized quantifiers giving a regular logic with Craig interpolation?', open questions about Shelah's logic and about a logic between L(Qωcof) and L(aa) with Craig interpolation) does not include this exact question, and does not flag it as newly resolved or newly open. Given the depth and age of this sub-area (Makowsky, Shelah, Stavi, Barwise-Feferman era work from the late 1970s-1980s), and that the 2025 survey — clearly written to catalogue exactly this kind of question — does not present this bullet as settled, I am reasonably confident this remains open. No AI system of any kind is mentioned in connection with any of the material found; this is traditional pen-and-paper mathematical logic.
competing_reading: One could argue the Beth-closure construction is 'close enough' to count as addressing the bullet, since it shows the same rough phenomenon (Beth + compact + not-full-interpolation) in a logic that is 'almost' Δ-interpolation-adjacent. But the bullet's wording specifically requires Δ-interpolation to HOLD, and the survey states it explicitly fails for this example, so by the letter of the question this is not a match, and I classified it as no_change_found rather than partial or progress. If a reader disagreed and felt any discussion of this exact quartet of properties, even a negative example, constitutes 'progress' in mapping the landscape, they might record 'progress' instead of 'open' — but no bound, case, or new example was actually established in the window that moves the stated existence question either way.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that either (a) exhibits a logic satisfying Beth + Δ-interpolation + compactness but lacking full interpolation, thereby answering the question affirmatively, or (b) proves no such logic can exist (a negative resolution), or (c) an updated edition/erratum of Barwise-Feferman or a survey explicitly stating this specific combination has been settled with a citation and date.

outcome: No resolution, partial case, or bound has been found since 26 January 2024; the problem is still open and the only relevant development is an October 2024 expository article restating the known combinatorial constraints without proving anything new.
summary: The problem asks whether a non-convex, non-self-intersecting polyhedron with more than seven faces exists in which every pair of faces shares an edge. Only two such polyhedra are known at all: the tetrahedron (f=4, genus 0) and the Szilassi polyhedron (f=7, genus 1), discovered in 1977. The triage's found item, 'Polyhedra with Every Face Connected to All Others Through Edges' (Crux Mathematicorum, Vol. 50(8), October 2024, by an author whose combinatorial derivation gives the Euler-characteristic constraint on possible (f, genus) pairs), was checked: search-engine summaries and secondary sources consistently describe it as identifying the next combinatorially admissible case (f=12, 44 vertices, 66 edges, genus 6, hendecagonal faces) as an abstract polytope, while explicitly stating that it remains unknown whether this abstract structure can be geometrically realized with planar, non-self-intersecting faces in R^3. I could not get a direct fetch of the article text (ResearchGate returned HTTP 403), so I rely on multiple independent search-result digestions of it, all of which agree on this characterization: the piece narrows the space of *candidate parameters* combinatorially but does not construct, or disprove the existence of, any new polyhedron beyond the two already known before the frozen date. This is consistent with Crux Mathematicorum's nature as a problems/exposition journal rather than a venue for new geometric-construction theorems. I separately checked the current (2026) Wikipedia articles for 'Szilassi polyhedron' and the unsolved-problems list; the Szilassi polyhedron article's most recent citation is the 2024 journal version of Arseneva et al., 'Adjacency Graphs of Polyhedral Surfaces' (Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2024; conference version SoCG 2021, arXiv 2103.09803) — but that paper addresses realizability of arbitrary adjacency graphs as polyhedral surfaces in general, not this specific all-pairs-adjacent, more-than-seven-faces question, and its results predate the frozen revision in any case (SoCG 2021), so even if it were on-topic it would not constitute a change in the window. No arXiv preprint, blog post, or announcement was found claiming a geometric realization of the f=12 genus-6 case, nor any disproof of its existence, nor any other progress on the problem since 26 January 2024. No AI involvement of any kind was found near this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the October 2024 Crux article, by explicitly working out the next admissible (f, genus) pair (12, 6) and the associated (V, E) counts via Euler's formula, constitutes 'progress' in the sense of narrowing the search space for a case of the problem, which could support status='progress' rather than 'open'. I did not adopt this reading because the problem as stated is an existence question ('Is there a...'), and per §3.1 an existence/infinitude question is only advanced by an actual answer, not by narrowing where an answer could hide (analogous to extending a record table). Working out combinatorial admissibility constraints via Euler's formula was already implicit in the known theory before 2024 (the same constraint that produces f=4 and f=7 as the first two cases); the article appears to restate and extend this arithmetic rather than establish any new mathematical fact about realizability.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit geometric construction (coordinates or a combinatorial-to-geometric realization proof) of a non-convex, non-self-intersecting polyhedron with f=12 (or any other admissible f>7) faces all pairwise edge-adjacent, or a proof that no such realization exists for the genus-6 case, would settle whether progress has occurred. Direct access to the full text of the October 2024 Crux Mathematicorum article (behind the ResearchGate 403 and not otherwise located as an open PDF) would also let me confirm definitively whether it contains any such claim, rather than relying on secondary search-result summaries.

outcome: Brayden Casella found a non-terminating game of Beggar-My-Neighbour on 10 February 2024 (a cyclical structure of 62 tricks reached by 30 distinct starting hands, looping after 474 turns/66 tricks), the construction and proof were written up with seven collaborators as an arXiv preprint on 19 March 2024, and the result was peer-reviewed and published in The American Mathematical Monthly (vol. 132, no. 10, pp. 978-994) on 20 October 2025, answering the question in the affirmative.

counterexample.object: A pair of starting hands (26 cards each) for Beggar-My-Neighbour that produce an eventually-periodic, non-terminating game: a cyclical structure of 62 tricks reached after some initial play from 30 distinct starting hands, with the concrete pair given as '---K---Q-KQAJ-----AAJ--J--' and '----------Q----KQ-J-----KA'.
counterexample.verified_how: Constructed deliberately via a targeted, non-random method (decomposing games into 'pieces' terminated by jacks, a template-based search for pieces, and backward-play reconstruction), then verified by direct simulation of the resulting deal; the construction and periodicity proof were later checked by peer review for the American Mathematical Monthly.

summary: The question 'Is there a non-terminating game of Beggar-My-Neighbour?' (Wikipedia's January 2024 wording of a problem John Conway called an 'anti-Hilbert problem') was answered affirmatively shortly after the frozen revision's date. Brayden Casella found a concrete non-terminating starting configuration on 10 February 2024 (per Richard P. Mann's Beggar-My-Neighbour records page and the Wikipedia article's current text), and Casella together with seven collaborators (Anderson, Kleber, Mann, Nessler, Rucklidge, Williams, Wu) wrote up the construction and proof, posting it to arXiv on 19 March 2024 (arXiv:2403.13855, 'A Non-Terminating Game of Beggar-My-Neighbor'). This was subsequently peer-reviewed and published in The American Mathematical Monthly, vol. 132, no. 10 (2025), pp. 978-994, on 20 October 2025 — a formal expert digestion via peer review, so status is 'resolved' rather than merely 'claimed'. The method was entirely classical: the authors describe decomposing games into independent 'pieces' bounded by jacks, a template-based search over candidate pieces ('any sequence can replace TEST in this template... if the game is non-terminating with this sequence, then the sequence is a piece and can be saved'), and reasoning about backward (non-deterministic) play to stitch pieces into a full cyclical game — plus earlier statistical/brute-force random search attempts that failed before the targeted construction succeeded. No machine learning, neural network, or AI system of any kind is mentioned anywhere in the paper, in Olly Britton's detailed blog write-up of the discovery process, or in the Wikipedia article. A 2026 follow-up preprint (arXiv:2602.23406, 'The Dynamical Landscape of Beggar-My-Neighbour: Ultra-long Matches, Loops, and Infinite Matches', posted 24 August 2026, by Andorno, Cernoia, Duiz, and Michelangeli) builds on the 2024 result with a heuristic 'Infinite Loop Factory' algorithm using backward dynamics reconstruction and 'adaptive insertion strategies' to systematize the discovery of further non-terminating cycles — again explicitly a heuristic/algorithmic search, not AI/ML, and it does not re-resolve the existence question, which was already settled in 2024; it is mentioned here for completeness but does not change the classification.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' if one requires the specific Monthly peer review to be the only acceptable digestion and discounts the fact that the result circulated and was informally checked (e.g., via community verification and Wikipedia's own updated article) for over a year before formal publication; but since the paper has in fact been peer-reviewed and published in a journal of record (American Mathematical Monthly), 'resolved' is the correct code per §6.1.
what_would_settle_it: The published Monthly article version already settles the classification; no further evidence is needed. (Only genuinely open would be independent replication of the specific card sequence, which is trivial to check by simulation and has been done by the community, e.g. via the referenced BeggarMyPython utility.)

outcome: On 19-20 July 2026, Levent Alpöge (an Anthropic technical staff member) announced on X an explicit polynomial map F: C^3 -> C^3 with constant Jacobian determinant -2 (three degree-7 components) that sends three distinct points to the same image, disproving the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3 and, by a standard stabilization argument (append the identity on extra coordinates), in every dimension n >= 3. The n=1 case was already trivially true and the planar (n=2) case remains open. Alpöge credited the construction to Anthropic's Claude Fable 5. The counterexample was independently checked by computer algebra within a day, digested mathematically by Terence Tao, and independently formalized in Lean 4 and in Isabelle (Archive of Formal Proofs), meeting the resolved bar via expert digestion plus independent machine-checked verification even though no journal has yet published it.

counterexample.object: Explicit polynomial map F=(P,Q,R): C^3 -> C^3 with P=(1+xy)^3 z + y^2(1+xy)(4+3xy), Q=y+3x(1+xy)^2 z+3xy^2(4+3xy), R=2x-3x^2y-x^3z, with det(J_F) identically -2, and with three distinct explicit rational points (e.g. (0,0,-1/4), (1,-3/2,13/2), (-1,3/2,13/2)) mapping to the same image (-1/4,0,0).
counterexample.verified_how: Independently checked by exact/symbolic computer algebra by multiple mathematicians within a day of announcement; independently formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 (independent verification, and separately by Paul Lezeau, submitted to Google DeepMind's Formal Conjectures repository) and in Isabelle/HOL (Archive of Formal Proofs entry), plus a digestion/explanation by Terence Tao.

disputes.summary: Alexander Borisov, Ofer Gabber and Adrian Vasiu published a preprint ('On endomorphisms of affine spaces and the Jacobian problem', arXiv:2609.05746) with a 'Supplemental AI statement of the third author [Vasiu]' raising the concern that an earlier, unpublished version of their framework may have been included in the training data of frontier AI models and could have informed Fable's construction of the counterexample without proper credit. Commentary (e.g. Benjamin Collas and Gro-Tsen on X) framed this as part of a broader pattern of AI labs allegedly training on unpublished drafts/private communications across several 2026 conjecture resolutions (Jacobian, non-sofic groups, Navier-Stokes) without disclosing or crediting the source material. Alpöge subsequently stated on X that Borisov, Gabber and Vasiu 'deserve credit too.' I was not able to read the Vasiu PDF's exact statement directly (fetch failed to extract readable text and Bash access to convert it was not authorized), so this is based on secondary reporting (DataCamp; Fortune) and X posts describing the preprint's content, not a direct reading of page 160 of that preprint.

summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, announced on X on 19 July 2026 (a 'very casual' post reading 'hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil for asking about it and my other close friend fable for working during the world cup final') an explicit degree-7 polynomial counterexample in C^3 to the Jacobian conjecture, disproving it for n=3 and, by trivial extension (identity on extra coordinates), for all n>=3; the n=1 case was already known true and n=2 (the planar Jacobian conjecture) remains open. He credited the construction itself to Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic). Multiple independent sources (John D. Cook, Terence Tao, Fortune, DataCamp, The Conversation, Kevin Buzzard's Xena blog) corroborate that the AI produced the actual construction/search result while Alpöge posed the question and announced/verified it -- DataCamp's framing 'a human posed the question, an AI did the work, a human announced the result' matches Alpöge's own phrasing crediting Fable with 'working' on it. No source I found discloses the actual prompts or the human-AI interaction log, so the fine-grained division of labor within that process is not publicly documented, but the authors' own account (Alpöge's post) squarely credits the AI system with producing the mathematical construction, supporting ai_role=generated rather than assisted. The result was verified extremely quickly: computer-algebra checks within hours/a day, a mathematical digestion by Terence Tao explaining why the construction works, and at least two independent formal verifications (a Lean 4 formalization, and a separate Isabelle/HOL Archive-of-Formal-Proofs entry proving the Jacobian is identically -2 and that three named points share an image), plus a Lean formalization submitted to DeepMind's Formal Conjectures repository. This combination of expert digestion (Tao) and independent machine-checkable verification meets the bar for status=resolved under Sec 6.1 even though, as of the sources found (through mid-September 2026), no traditional journal has yet published a refereed version -- it remains, in one source's words, 'a verified calculation and a preprint, not a refereed paper.' Multiple follow-up arXiv papers (Shuhong Gao, arXiv:2608.00222; T. Shaska, arXiv:2607.20210, 'Graded Keller maps and the Jacobian Conjecture'; Arno van den Essen, arXiv:2609.17795, showing an 'elementary' route to essentially the same example) generalize or re-derive the construction, and a Zenodo preprint traces downstream consequences for several related conjectures (Mathieu, Dixmier, Poisson, Gaussian moments). A priority dispute emerged: Borisov, Gabber and Vasiu's preprint (arXiv:2609.05746) includes a 'supplemental AI statement' suggesting their earlier unpublished framework may have been absorbed into AI training data and used without credit in reaching the counterexample; Alpöge reportedly acknowledged on X that they 'deserve credit too.' I could not directly read that supplemental statement (PDF text extraction failed via WebFetch, and Bash commands to download/convert it were not authorized in this session), so the dispute is recorded from secondary reporting and social-media commentary rather than the primary document -- flagged in confidence and in the dispute entry. The n=2 case is untouched by any of this and remains open with no result found addressing it in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue ai_role should be 'assisted' rather than 'generated', since no source discloses the actual prompt/interaction transcript, and it is conceivable Alpöge did substantial guiding work (choice of ansatz, search space design) that is simply not reported. The Conversation explicitly notes 'details have not been made public regarding exactly how Alpöge prompted the AI model.' However, the balance of direct evidence -- Alpöge's own words crediting Fable with 'working' on it, and multiple secondary sources' explicit framing that the AI produced the construction while Alpöge only posed the question and announced the result -- favors 'generated.' If a more detailed account later emerges showing Alpöge did the core mathematical construction and merely used the AI to check steps, this should be revised to 'assisted' or 'none'.
what_would_settle_it: Publication of Alpöge's own detailed writeup or interaction transcript describing exactly what he prompted and what Fable returned; alternatively, a technical report from Anthropic describing the episode (as has happened for other AI-math results) would settle both the ai_role classification and the priority dispute with Borisov-Gabber-Vasiu regarding training-data provenance. A referee report or journal acceptance would also move status language from 'resolved-by-community-verification' to an unambiguous formal resolution, though this does not change the classification here.

outcome: No proof, disproof, partial result, or bound on Jacobson's conjecture (that the intersection of all powers of the Jacobson radical of a two-sided Noetherian ring is zero) was found dated after 26 January 2024. All substantive results located predate the window (Herstein's 1965 counterexample for one-sided Noetherian rings, Jategaonkar's second-layer-condition work, Lenagan's Krull-dimension-one case, Cauchon/Cauchon-type fully-bounded-Noetherian results). The conjecture remains open in general for two-sided Noetherian rings.
summary: I independently re-ran and extended the triage's search, confirming its 'none' verdict. Searches for the conjecture's exact name, for 'intersection of powers of the Jacobson radical' plus 'Noetherian', for arXiv listings, and for any AI/machine-learning involvement all returned either (a) pre-2024 classical results — Herstein's 1965 counterexample for one-sided Noetherian rings, Jategaonkar's work, the fully-bounded-Noetherian and Krull-dimension-one special cases, all dated to the 1970s-2010s — or (b) unrelated hits on similarly named but distinct objects: the Jacobian conjecture (polynomial maps with polynomial inverses, which did see a 2026 AI-assisted counterexample per a UTEP tech report, arxiv 2311.14723-adjacent discussion, and other Jacobian-conjecture papers — a completely different problem), 'Jacobson rings' in the commutative-algebra/Nullstellensatz sense (Stacks project, Emerton notes), 'left Jacobson rings' (arXiv:2503.16005, a 2025 paper I opened directly and confirmed defines an unrelated one-sided Nullstellensatz-style property, not the radical-power conjecture), and Jacobson's ring-commutativity theorem (x^n=x). I checked the Wikipedia article on Jacobson's conjecture itself (still describes it as open, most recent citation 1982) and the Grokipedia mirror (same conclusion, no post-2024 developments, no AI mention). No survey, preprint, or announcement anywhere in these searches claims new movement on this specific conjecture since 26 January 2024. This agrees with the triage's verdict; I found nothing it missed.
competing_reading: None found. The only genuine ambiguity is nomenclature: several unrelated objects share 'Jacobson' in their name (Jacobian conjecture, Jacobson rings, left Jacobson rings, Jacobson's commutativity theorem), and a careless search could misattribute the Jacobian conjecture's 2026 AI-assisted counterexample to this problem. I verified each of these is a distinct mathematical object from Jacobson's conjecture on the radical, so none of it counts as a case or variant of the stated problem — it is out of scope entirely under §3.1, not merely a related problem.
what_would_settle_it: A dated preprint or journal paper explicitly addressing the intersection of powers of the Jacobson radical for general (or a new special class of) two-sided Noetherian rings, submitted after 26 January 2024 — none was found in this search.

outcome: Jaeger's Petersen-coloring conjecture appears to have been refuted in 2026 via an explicit counterexample cascade: a 68-vertex example attributed to an AI system posted on X in July 2026, followed by Bryce Putman's two non-isomorphic 112-vertex counterexamples (SAT-solver certified) in August 2026, Jorik Jooken's human-checkable proof that the 112-vertex graph is a genuine counterexample, and a 52-vertex counterexample plus an infinite family from Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo and Ulyanov. None of this has yet received the kind of independent expert digestion (survey article, blog write-up by a recognized expert outside the immediate circle, or journal acceptance) that would justify 'resolved' rather than 'claimed', though a human-checkable proof and a purely theoretical proof (not just SAT certificates) exist alongside the computational ones.

ai.basis_quote: OpenAI language-model systems were used extensively in the discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation of this work. [...] The author reviewed the final claims and artifacts and accepts responsibility for the contents.

counterexample.object: An explicit, simple, bridgeless cubic graph on 112 vertices (Putman; two non-isomorphic instances) with no Petersen coloring and no normal 5-edge-coloring, built recursively from copies of a four-pole derived from the Petersen graph and a claw six-pole; independently, a 52-vertex counterexample and an infinite family of cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs of even order ≥60 (Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo, Ulyanov); and a first 68-vertex example posted to X in July 2026 credited to an AI system.
counterexample.verified_how: Putman's 112-vertex graphs were verified UNSAT for both the Petersen-coloring and normal-5-edge-coloring SAT encodings using CaDiCaL 3.0.1, independently checked with drat-trim on the DRAT proofs. Jooken separately gave a short human-checkable case-analysis proof that the 112-vertex graph is a counterexample. The Goedgebeur et al. 52-vertex counterexamples come with a complete theoretical (non-computational) proof; their claim that no smaller counterexample exists below order 40 rests on computational (exhaustive) verification.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent groups produced counterexamples within weeks of one another (an anonymous/AI-credited 68-vertex example on X in July 2026, Putman's 112-vertex graphs in early August 2026, and the Goedgebeur/Jooken/Máčajová/Mattiolo/Mazzuoccolo/Ulyanov 52-vertex graphs shortly after), and the later paper explicitly frames its own contribution as a smaller, theoretically-proved counterexample in contrast to the earlier computational ones — a priority/precedence structure rather than a clean single discovery.

summary: Multiple mutually corroborating sources (independent WebFetch reads of arXiv abstract and HTML pages, and web searches) converge on the same account: Jaeger's Petersen-coloring conjecture, open since 1988, was refuted in 2026 through a chain of explicit counterexamples. The first, on 68 vertices, was posted to X in July 2026 by the account @NeuralReformist11 and is credited in the introduction of arXiv:2608.10028 (quoted verbatim via WebFetch) to 'GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra' — i.e., an AI system, not a named human researcher. Bryce Putman then posted (arXiv:2608.10012, 8 Aug 2026) two non-isomorphic 112-vertex counterexamples verified via SAT solver (CaDiCaL) and drat-trim; this paper's own 'Computational provenance and responsibility' section states 'OpenAI language-model systems were used extensively in the discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation of this work,' with the author reviewing and taking responsibility for the final claims — i.e., an authors'-own-account of AI producing the actual counterexample, not merely assisting with peripheral tasks, which is why I coded this `generated` rather than `assisted`. Jorik Jooken then produced a human-checkable case-analysis proof that the 112-vertex graph is genuinely uncolorable (posted as a revision under the same arXiv number, 2608.10028, which was later expanded through v2/v3 into a six-author paper). That expanded paper (Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo, Ulyanov; v3 dated 11 Sep 2026) gives two 52-vertex counterexamples with a fully theoretical (non-SAT) proof, an infinite family for even orders ≥60, and a computational lower bound of 40 vertices for any counterexample. None of these papers has (as far as I can establish) yet been accepted at a journal or received a public expert digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, a survey) — my search for such digestion returned nothing beyond the papers themselves and derivative aggregator pages (Zenodo cross-postings, an 'emergentmind' topic page, a 'Pith Review' page that returned no retrievable content). I therefore coded `status` as `claimed`, not `resolved`, despite the existence of both a SAT certificate and a from-scratch human proof, because the digestion bar in §6.1 requires an independent expert reading, which I could not confirm. I flag genuine concerns about this whole cluster that a careful reader should weigh: (1) the arXiv identifiers 2608.10012 and 2608.10028 use 4-digit sequence numbers, whereas other confirmed August-2026 arXiv IDs I found in the same searches (e.g. 2608.23459, 2608.21350) use the standard 5-digit zero-padded format that has been in place since 2015 — a genuine formatting anomaly I could not resolve; (2) one WebFetch call on arxiv:2608.10028 volunteered, unprompted, that the paper 'appears to be a future-dated preprint (2026), likely a test or fictional example'; (3) the identity of the human behind '@NeuralReformist11' and the existence of a model called 'GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra' could not be independently corroborated outside of the arXiv paper's own citation of the X post — I found no independent news coverage, no OpenAI announcement, and no archived copy of the X post itself. Against this, the papers' content was internally consistent across many independent fetches (author lists, dates, abstracts, methodology all matched on repeated retrieval), Zenodo records exist as companion artifacts with matching titles/dates, and House of Graphs entries (57278, 57280) are cited as hosting the graphs. On balance I judge this is real, very recent (within-window) work, but I am recording explicit uncertainty about the AI-attribution details rather than either suppressing them or overstating my confidence in them.
competing_reading: It is possible the '68-vertex counterexample credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, posted by @NeuralReformist11' detail is itself an error or fabrication introduced somewhere in the tool chain (search engine or fetch summarizer) rather than genuine paper content, in which case the true AI role would be limited to Putman's own OpenAI-model disclosure (still `generated` by my reading) and the '68-vertex, AI-credited' claim should be discounted. I mitigated this by requesting verbatim quotes via WebFetch on the raw arXiv HTML twice, both of which reproduced the identical sentence, which is why I ultimately kept it in the record rather than omitting it — but I could not reach the underlying X post directly to confirm it exists as described.
what_would_settle_it: Direct retrieval of the original @NeuralReformist11 X/Twitter post (or an archived/cached version) naming the model and showing the 68-vertex graph; confirmation of arXiv:2608.10012 and 2608.10028's identifier format against arXiv's own listing pages (which returned 404 when I tried to browse math.CO for August 2026 directly); and any subsequent journal acceptance, Terence Tao blog post, or Quanta Magazine coverage that would move the status from `claimed` to `resolved`.

outcome: Pavelescu, Pavelescu and Potter (arXiv:2604.03433, submitted April 2026) prove Jørgensen's conjecture for order 13: every simple graph on 13 vertices with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex (and in the latter case is isomorphic to K1 join the icosahedral graph), settling this small-order case via exhaustive computer search. The general conjecture (for all 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs) remains open.
summary: Jørgensen's conjecture (1994/2007) asks whether every 6-vertex-connected K6-minor-free graph is an apex graph. Before the frozen revision date, DeVos, Hegde, Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan had already proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large graphs (JCTB 2019, two papers), and Pierce (2014) and a 2020 Involve paper had settled small orders up to 12 vertices; all of this predates the window and is background, not a change. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), the only new development found is arXiv:2604.03433, 'New minor minimal non-apex graphs' by Andrei Pavelescu, Elena Pavelescu and Madeline Potter, submitted April 2026. This paper (a) catalogs 339 minor-minimal non-apex (MMNA) graphs — the most complete list to date, up from Pierce's 157 — covering all such graphs with at most 12 vertices or at most 26 edges, and (b) proves that every simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex (isomorphic to K1 * icosahedron), which settles the order-13 case of Jørgensen's conjecture. This is a case of the problem (a restriction to a specific vertex count and minimum degree), not a resolution of the general conjecture, so status is 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the settled case went the way the conjecture predicts — no counterexample). The method, per the paper's own text (read via the arXiv HTML rendering), is exhaustive computer search: the nauty software for graph generation and isomorphism testing, plus custom Python programs (isapex.py, ismmna.py) built on NetworkX, run on ordinary consumer/workstation hardware (Apple M4 Pro, Mac Mini M2, HP Intel i9), with the order-13-to-17 search taking about 340 hours of compute. No SAT solver, computer-algebra system, or AI/ML system is mentioned anywhere in the abstract, introduction, or methodology section as read. This is classic combinatorial exhaustive search/enumeration, which explicitly does not count as an AI system under the coding rules (§6.2), so ai_role is 'none'. I found no other 2024-2026 developments: no disproof, no counterexample, no progress on the general 6-connected case, and no mention of AI anywhere in the surrounding literature search (Open Problem Garden, the Wikipedia 'Apex graph' article, and general web searches for 2024-2026 progress or counterexamples all came back with nothing beyond this one paper and pre-2024 background).
competing_reading: None substantial. One could argue the ancillary file name 'NewMMNA_code.pdf' or the description of 'custom Python programs' might hide some ML-assisted code generation (e.g., an LLM used to help write isapex.py/ismmna.py), but the paper's own methodology section describes only nauty and NetworkX-based exhaustive search with no authorial statement of AI assistance, so per §6.2 ('the authors' own account') this cannot be coded as assisted or generated.
what_would_settle_it: The full PDF/HTML text of arXiv:2604.03433 (already reviewed via the HTML rendering) plus any acknowledgements section not surfaced by the fetch would confirm there is no hidden AI-tool disclosure; a check of the ancillary 'NewMMNA_code' file would confirm no AI-generated code is credited.

outcome: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the Kakeya conjecture in the n=3 case (every Kakeya set in R^3 has Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3), settling that case while the conjecture as stated (for general n) remains open for n>3.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet as frozen on 26 January 2024 asks whether n-dimensional sets containing a unit line segment in every direction (Kakeya sets) must have Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension equal to n, for general n. On 24 February 2025, Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl posted a 127-page preprint (arXiv:2502.17655, 'Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions') proving this for n=3: every Kakeya set in R^3 has both Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension exactly 3. This settles a specific case (restriction to n=3) of the general conjecture, which is the textbook example of §3.1's 'case of the problem' (dimension is restricted, not the question changed), so I classify it as `partial` rather than `resolved` for the conjecture as stated, even though the n=3 case itself is fully resolved and expert-digested. The proof has been extensively vetted: Terence Tao wrote a detailed technical blog post the same day walking through the strategy (terrytao.wordpress.com, 2025-02-25), Quanta Magazine covered it as a major breakthrough with commentary from Nets Katz calling it 'a once-in-a-century kind of result' (2025-03-14), Larry Guth wrote two survey/exposition papers on the proof (arXiv:2505.07695, arXiv:2604.03416, the latter a Séminaire Bourbaki survey), and — most decisively — Hong Wang was awarded the 2026 Fields Medal explicitly citing 'the proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture' as a key contribution, per the IMU citation reflected on her Wikipedia page. This amounts to full expert digestion of the n=3 case. The general conjecture for n>3 remains open; Wikipedia's own Kakeya set article confirms 'the conjecture remains open for n>3,' with partial lower-bound results (e.g., Wolff's bound, Katz-Zahl's planebrush bound of ~3.059 in R^4) but no full resolution. I found no evidence of any AI system involved anywhere in this line of work: the arXiv abstract, Tao's post, Quanta's article, and Guth's surveys contain no mention of AI, machine learning, or computer-assisted proof techniques — this is traditional human mathematical proof via multiscale/convex-geometry arguments building on Wang-Zahl's earlier 2022 'sticky Kakeya sets' work. I also checked the related but distinct 'arithmetic Kakeya conjecture' (an additive-combinatorics reformulation that implies the geometric conjecture, discussed on Epoch AI's FrontierMath open-problems page) — this is a variant/different formulation, not the bullet as stated, and in any case no AI progress on it was reported; Epoch AI lists it as an open research target, not a solved problem, with current best partial result (Katz-Tao, human work) unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the n=3 case, being a fully complete and celebrated resolution (Fields Medal-cited), deserves to be read as close to 'resolved' in spirit even though the bullet is about all n. But per §3.1 and §6.1, `resolved` must mean the problem as stated is settled; since the bullet is explicitly the general n-dimensional question and higher dimensions remain open, `partial` is the correct code, with the direction (`confirmed`) describing the settled n=3 piece.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of the Kakeya conjecture for general n (or at least n=4 and beyond) would move this further; short of that, `partial` with direction `confirmed` for the n=3 case is the correct terminal classification barring new work on higher dimensions.

outcome: No result settling the stated 3^d conjecture (or any new case of it) has appeared since 26 January 2024; the general conjecture remains open, and the sole in-window paper found proves a different (though related) flag-vector conjecture for a restricted polytope class, not the 3^d conjecture itself.
summary: Kalai's 3^d conjecture (every centrally symmetric d-dimensional polytope has at least 3^d nonempty faces, with equality only for Hanner polytopes) remains open in general. The triage record flagged a July 2025 preprint by Arnon Chor (arXiv:2507.22284, 'Kalai's flag conjecture for locally anti-blocking polytopes'), asking whether it constitutes progress on the 3^d conjecture as stated. Having read the paper's introduction, this is a related-but-different problem, not a case of the stated conjecture: it proves 'Kalai's flag conjecture' (Conjecture 1.3 in the paper), a separate, later conjecture also attributed to Kalai, which counts flags (maximal chains of faces, one per dimension) rather than the total number of nonempty faces that the 3^d conjecture counts. The paper's own introduction states that the 3^d conjecture itself for locally anti-blocking polytopes was 'recently' proved by Sanyal and Winter, and independently by Chambers and Portnoy (arXiv:2211.09215) -- and both of those results predate the frozen revision. Chambers-Portnoy's note first appeared on arXiv in November 2022, and Sanyal-Winter's paper (arXiv:2308.02909) was first submitted 5 August 2023, with its final v3 revision posted 21 April 2024 -- the revision postdates the snapshot, but the first public written argument (v1, per section 6.3's dating rule) does not, so this case-settling result is 'open_stale' relative to the frozen date, not new. No further case of the actual 3^d conjecture, no counterexample, and no full resolution has appeared in the window. Gil Kalai's own blog (gilkalai.wordpress.com), including a February 2026 'Updates and Plans' post, was checked for any mention of new developments on this specific conjecture; none was found. No AI system is credited anywhere: the Chor paper's acknowledgements name only human collaborators and funding bodies, and no search turned up any AI-related claim connected to this conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue the flag conjecture, because it dominates the ordinary face count in certain ways for the same restricted class of polytopes (locally anti-blocking) and reaffirms Hanner polytopes as the unique extremizers, is close enough in spirit to count as 'progress' on the broader research program Kalai's 3^d conjecture belongs to. But per the scope rule in section 3.1, the test is whether the result changes what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry specifically -- and it does not, since it is a strictly different quantity (flags vs. total faces) with its own separate conjecture status, and the 3^d-conjecture case for this same polytope class was already resolved (and already stale) before the window began.
what_would_settle_it: A published or arXiv-posted proof (or disproof) of the 3^d conjecture in full generality, or a proof/disproof for a new class of centrally symmetric polytopes not already covered by the pre-2024 Sanyal-Winter/Chambers-Portnoy results, dated after 26 January 2024, would change this record's status to partial, claimed, or resolved as appropriate.

outcome: No result found since 26 January 2024 that changes the Kaplan-Yorke conjecture as stated (that the Lyapunov dimension of a 'typical' dynamical system's attractor equals its information/Hausdorff dimension); all located post-window work addresses namesake variants (delay differential equations) rather than the stated conjecture.
summary: The Kaplan-Yorke conjecture (Kaplan and Yorke, 1979) holds that for a 'typical' dissipative dynamical system, the Lyapunov (Kaplan-Yorke) dimension of an attractor equals its information dimension (and, in many treatments, coincides with the Hausdorff/box-counting dimension). The original two-dimensional-map case was proven by Kaplan-Yorke themselves and extended by L.-S. Young (1984) to a class of 2D systems where Lyapunov, Hausdorff, box-counting and Rényi dimensions all coincide; that work predates the window and settled only the low-dimensional case, leaving the general higher-dimensional conjecture open (with known artificial counterexamples such as constructions related to the Feigenbaum attractor showing it fails without genericity assumptions). Extensive searching (WebSearch queries listed below, plus the triage's own three queries) turned up nothing in the 26 January 2024 to present window that advances the general conjecture. The only post-window hits are: (1) Zhang & Wu-type work extending the unrelated 'Kaplan-Yorke formula' (a different, non-namesake concept from delay differential equation theory concerning periodic solutions, not attractor dimension) to infinite-dimensional Banach-space delay systems (Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations, 2025, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10884-025-10428-4) -- this changes the question (a different dynamical setting and a different formula bearing the same name) rather than restricting it, so it is a related problem, not a case; and (2) a January 2025 ScienceDirect paper on 'Kaplan-Yorke periodic solutions' for delay differential equations, which is an entirely unrelated namesake topic (periodic-orbit multiplicity, not attractor dimension) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022039625000440). Neither touches the Lyapunov-dimension-equals-information-dimension conjecture for finite-dimensional attractors as Wikipedia states it. A December 2024 arXiv paper on Rulkov neuron lattices (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.12134) empirically checks that Lyapunov dimension is close to box-counting dimension for one specific system -- this is a numerical illustration consistent with the conjecture for a single example, not a proof, case settlement, or bound movement on the conjecture itself, and does not rise to the level of 'progress'. The Wikipedia article on the conjecture itself (fetched live) has no updates reflecting any 2024-2026 development and cites nothing past 2020. No AI system appears anywhere in this material. I therefore find no change to the conjecture's status and no AI involvement.
competing_reading: One could argue the December 2024 Rulkov-neuron paper constitutes 'progress' in the loose sense of adding a data point consistent with the conjecture holding for a specific chaotic system, similar to how record-verification is sometimes counted for existence questions. But per §3.1, a single-system numerical check is not a bound moving or a case being settled in a way that changes what a careful person would write in the bullet -- it is closer to routine numerical corroboration than to mathematical progress, so I classify it as not counting and keep status as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or published paper explicitly proving the Kaplan-Yorke/Lyapunov-dimension conjecture (or a genuine restriction of it, e.g. for a specific higher-dimensional class of attractors with an SRB or physical measure) for finite-dimensional dissipative systems, dated after 26 January 2024, or an explicit new counterexample to the conjecture as stated for a 'typical'/generic system.

outcome: The stated conjecture (KL polynomial values at 1 = Jordan-Hölder multiplicities of simple modules in Verma modules, for complex semisimple Lie groups/algebras) was proved independently by Beilinson-Bernstein and by Brylinski-Kashiwara in 1981, long before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision; nothing in the 2024-2026 window changes this. Substantial 2024-2026 activity exists on distinct, related problems in the same corner of representation theory (the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture for KL polynomials, the p-adic KL hypothesis for GL(n), and empirical/computational studies of KL polynomials), none of which is a case of or a restatement of the bullet's stated conjecture. One genuine, well-documented AI event was found, but it belongs to a different, unrelated conjecture in a 2024 paper about KL polynomials generally, not to the classical conjecture in this bullet.
summary: The bullet's stated conjecture is the classical 1979 Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture relating KL polynomial values at q=1 to composition-series multiplicities of simple modules inside Verma modules for complex semisimple Lie algebras/groups. This was proved in 1981, independently, by Beilinson-Bernstein and by Brylinski-Kashiwara (confirmed via the Wikipedia article on Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials, which states both proofs and that they launched geometric representation theory), so the correct status given the frozen-revision rule is open_stale, exactly as the triage pass concluded. I then searched specifically for 2024-2026 activity to check whether anything in the window bears on this bullet regardless. I found three clusters of genuine activity, none of which is in scope: (1) the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture (Lusztig-Dyer), a distinct conjecture about whether KL polynomials depend only on Bruhat-interval isomorphism type -- Barkley and Gaetz proved it for elementary intervals (Math. Annalen 2025), and other 2024-2026 papers proved parabolic and lower-interval cases (BBDVW conjecture, arXiv 2412.10256); (2) a 2025 proof of the p-adic KL hypothesis for GL(n) (arXiv 2510.09788), a p-adic analogue over a different ground field; (3) 'Big data approach to Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials' (Lacabanne-Tubbenhauer-Vaz, arXiv 2412.01283, J. Experimental Math. 2026), an empirical/computational study of KL polynomial coefficients for symmetric groups up to 11 strands. This third paper is the one AI-relevant item found in the whole search: its acknowledgments state 'In this work, we utilized ChatGPT for coding, proofreading, generating conjectures, and assisting with proof development' (ai_role would be none for this alone, per the rule that proofreading/coding/strategy-suggestion is not AI-producing-the-mathematics), and a later remark (added in v2/v3, and per arXiv's own version-comment metadata and the paper's GitHub repository dtubbenhauer/kldata) states that on 26 June 2026 Eivind Otto Hjelle contacted the authors with a proof of the paper's Conjecture 6.4 -- a closed-form formula P_{e,w}(q) = (1+q+...+q^l)^{k-1} for KL polynomials of a specific family of permutations -- generated by 'ChatGPT 5.5 Pro', and the authors state 'We have reviewed the generated argument and were unable to find any mistakes in the logic.' This is a real, well-corroborated (arXiv abs-page comments, the paper body, and the GitHub README all agree) AI-generated-proof event, but it is entirely out of scope for this bullet: Conjecture 6.4 is the paper's own empirically-discovered conjecture about a specific closed-form family of KL polynomial values, not a case of or a variant on the classical Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture stated in the bullet (multiplicities in Verma modules at q=1 for general semisimple Lie algebras). I record it here only to show the search was thorough and to explain the one 'AI + Kazhdan-Lusztig' item that surfaces in any broad search of this area; it does not move this problem's status. No result found anywhere restates, extends, or contradicts the 1981 theorem itself.
competing_reading: One could argue the field/subfield header ('Algebra / Representation theory') is broad enough that any KL-polynomial result, including the Conjecture 6.4 closed-form formula or the Combinatorial Invariance results, should count as informing this bullet, since they concern 'Kazhdan-Lusztig' objects. I reject this: per the scope rule (§3.1), a related problem is one obtained by changing the stated question (different conjecture, different objects), not restricting it, and Conjecture 6.4 and the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture are each a different mathematical statement from the multiplicity-conjecture in the bullet, sharing only the name 'Kazhdan-Lusztig' and the underlying polynomials as a common object of study.
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed to settle the open_stale classification of the bullet itself; it was proved in 1981. What would change this record's characterization of the searched activity is if a future source showed that the Combinatorial Invariance Conjecture, once fully proved, implies a strengthening or reproof of the 1981 multiplicity theorem via a different route -- but no source found suggests any logical connection of that kind.
