outcome: No case of the Keating-Snaith conjecture itself (the asymptotics of the 2k-th moment integral of |zeta(1/2+it)| for integer k, proven unconditionally only for k=1 and k=2) has been settled since 26 January 2024. All post-window work found is either on variant/related families (Hecke L-functions, elliptic curve twists), extensions of the moment problem (moments of derivatives), or unconditional lower bounds on higher moments that are 'in strong agreement with' but do not prove the conjectured asymptotic.
summary: The Keating-Snaith conjecture (1998) predicts the precise asymptotic constant in the 2k-th moment formula ∫₀ᵀ |ζ(1/2+it)|^{2k} dt ~ C_k T (log T)^{k²} for all real k>0, based on random matrix theory. It is proven unconditionally only for k=1 (Hardy-Littlewood, 1918) and k=2 (Ingham, 1926); no other integer k has an unconditional asymptotic formula, before or after the frozen revision. I searched arXiv, Wikipedia, and general web sources for anything that changed this since 26 January 2024 and found none. The most relevant post-window items are: (1) 'Amplified moments of the Riemann zeta function' (arXiv:2606.27323, Durkan & Page, submitted 25 June 2026), which gives unconditional effective *lower bounds* for the sixth moment and other joint moments, explicitly 'in strong agreement with' but not proving Keating-Snaith or Keating-Wei; (2) 'Amplified Fourth Moment of the Riemann Zeta-Function and Applications' (arXiv:2511.14415, Bui, Hall & Subira Jorge, 18 Nov 2025), an incremental amplifier-method improvement, again not a new asymptotic case; (3) 'Towards Keating-Snaith's conjecture for cubic Hecke L-functions over the Eisenstein field' (arXiv:2511.08783), which is Keating-Snaith for a *different* L-function family (cubic Hecke L-functions), not the Riemann zeta function itself — a related problem, not a case, since it changes the family rather than restricting the stated question; (4) 'Integer moments of the derivatives of the Riemann zeta function' (arXiv:2509.07792), an extension to a different quantity (moments of ζ'); (5) 'The eighth moment of the Riemann zeta function' (Ng, Shen, Wong; arXiv:2204.13891), submitted October 2022 — well before the window — and in any case conditional on RH plus a quaternary additive divisor conjecture, so it would not count as settling a case even if dated within the window; it was merely accepted/published in 2024-2025, which is a journal date and per §6.3 not the operative date. I found nothing suggesting AI involvement of any kind in any of this work — no mention of AI/ML tools in the papers' abstracts, contribution statements, or acknowledgements that I could access, and no news coverage connecting an AI system to this conjecture. This agrees with the triage's verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the amplified-moments lower bound work (2606.27323) constitutes 'progress' worth recording even though the conjecture stays open, since a bound did move (Soundararajan's earlier lower bounds were improved and the Lindelöf Hypothesis dependency removed for some results). But per §3.1, 'are there infinitely many X'-style and asymptotic-constant conjectures move only when the asymptotic itself is proven for a new case; a moved *lower bound* alone on a quantity whose asymptotic is still unknown is closer to a bound on a still-open existence-type statement than to a partial resolution, and Keating-Snaith is specifically about the value of an asymptotic constant C_k, not a growth-rate inequality. I classified this as no change rather than `progress`, but flag that a reader applying the rule slightly more permissively might record 2606.27323 as `progress` with `ai_role` `none`.
what_would_settle_it: An unconditional proof of the asymptotic formula (matching the predicted Keating-Snaith constant C_k) for any integer k ≥ 3, or a proof for general real k, would settle a new case. Absent that, any future paper explicitly proving (not merely bounding) a new moment case would flip this record.

outcome: The Kelvin problem itself — whether the Weaire-Phelan structure (or any other partition) minimizes surface area among equal-volume partitions of space — remains unproven; only restricted/related variants (lattice tilings by a single congruent parallelohedron, foams with a fixed inradius constraint) have seen progress since 26 January 2024, none of which settle any case of the stated problem.
summary: The Kelvin problem — minimum-surface-area partition of space into equal-volume cells, and whether the Weaire-Phelan structure is optimal — remains open, and I found no result in the 26 Jan 2024 to present window that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet. Wikipedia's own Weaire-Phelan structure article (checked live, since the frozen revision does not usefully constrain this factual claim) still states plainly that 'although numerical experiments suggest that the Weaire-Phelan structure is optimal, this remains unproven,' with no dated update in the window. The only new work I could find that is closely adjacent is: (1) Cesaroni and Novaga, 'Minimal periodic foams with fixed inradius' (arXiv:2407.07534, submitted 10 July 2024, published in Mathematika 2025), which proves existence/regularity of periodic tilings by equal cells containing a fixed-radius ball minimizing perimeter — a genuinely different (constrained) question, not a case of minimizing surface area among all equal-volume partitions; (2) Cesaroni and Novaga, 'Local minimality of the truncated octahedron for the isoperimetric problem on parallelohedra' (arXiv:2603.27221, submitted 28 March 2026), which shows the BCC/truncated-octahedron lattice is a strict local minimizer among lattice tilings by a single congruent parallelohedron — this restricts to lattice tilings by one congruent cell shape, a strict subclass that excludes the Weaire-Phelan structure itself (which uses two non-congruent cell types and is not a lattice tiling), so it is a related/restricted problem, not a case of the Kelvin problem as stated; and (3) Lark Song, 'Local quadratic isoperimetric stability of the truncated octahedron among parallelohedra' (arXiv:2609.03093, submitted 2 September 2026), extending the same local-minimality result to the full ten-dimensional parallelohedron parameter space with a quadratic stability estimate — again confined to the parallelohedra subclass. None of these three papers claim to say anything new about the Weaire-Phelan structure's optimality or about the general (non-lattice, non-congruent-cell) Kelvin problem, and none mention or use any AI system in producing their proofs — the methods are Selling-parameter parametrizations, explicit isoperimetric-quotient formulas, and Hessian/Schur-lemma analysis, all classical. I also checked a 2018 Frank-Kasper-lattice paper reporting additional counterexamples to the original (uncurved) Kelvin conjecture beating the Kelvin foam but still losing to Weaire-Phelan — this predates the window (2018) and doesn't move the Weaire-Phelan-optimality question either way. A May 2026 ResearchGate item ('A Curvature-Spectral Framework for Comparing Kelvin and Weaire-Phelan Foam Structures') surfaced in search but is not on arXiv, is by an unfamiliar author, and its abstract (via secondary description, since the page itself returned HTTP 403) describes a 'symbolic energy model' with no clear claim of resolving anything about optimality; I could not verify its content directly and do not weight it. Searches for AI/ML involvement (AlphaGeometry, AlphaEvolve, DeepMind, reinforcement learning, neural network foam search) turned up substantial 2024-2026 AI-mathematics activity generally (AlphaProof/AlphaGeometry at IMO 2024, AlphaEvolve on Strassen's algorithm and kissing numbers in 2025) but nothing whatsoever connecting any AI system to the Kelvin problem or Weaire-Phelan structure specifically.
competing_reading: One could argue the two parallelohedra local-minimality papers (2603.27221, 2609.03093) constitute 'progress' in a loose sense, since the truncated octahedron/BCC lattice is exactly Kelvin's original 1887 proposal, and proving it locally optimal within the parallelohedra class is adjacent territory. But per §3.1 this is a related problem (restricting to lattice tilings by one congruent cell) rather than a case of the stated Kelvin problem, which explicitly allows the kind of non-lattice, multi-cell-type partition that Weaire-Phelan uses to beat Kelvin's structure; local minimality within a strictly smaller admissible class says nothing about global optimality in the full class, so I classified as open/no_change_found rather than progress.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that the Weaire-Phelan structure achieves the minimum surface area among ALL periodic (or non-periodic) equal-volume partitions of space, not just among lattice tilings by a single parallelohedron — or a new counterexample beating Weaire-Phelan's surface area in the unrestricted problem.

outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the lower bounds on the kissing number have been improved in numerous dimensions outside {1,2,3,4,8,24} (10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17-21, 25-31, 32-34, 37), by a mix of purely human constructions and AI-assisted searches; the problem itself (determining the exact kissing number in each such dimension) remains open in every one of these dimensions, so this is a cluster of bound-moving/partial-style events rather than a resolution.

ai.basis_quote: AlphaEvolve was able to improve on the lower bound for C(11), raising it from 592 to 593. ... we tasked AlphaEvolve to generate a fixed number of vectors, and we placed unit spheres in those directions at distance 2 from the origin.

disputes.summary: In dimension 11, AlphaEvolve's 593-point configuration (May 2025, reported in Tao et al., Nov 2025) currently exceeds Ganzhinov's independently, human-derived 592-point configuration (reported Oct 2025, from his doctoral thesis exploiting high symmetry). Aalto's press coverage explicitly frames this as 'human bests AI' in dimensions 10 and 14, while conceding AI still leads in dimension 11 as of the coverage date, with Ganzhinov's advisor suggesting the position could still change.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet covers the kissing number problem for every dimension other than 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and 24, where the exact value is known. Since the 26 January 2024 snapshot, the best known lower bound has been improved in a substantial cluster of these dimensions by independent groups using a mix of pure mathematics and AI/RL search, but in no case has the exact kissing number been determined in a previously-unknown dimension, so the problem as a whole remains open and the correct status is 'progress' (a bound moved in many places) rather than 'resolved' or even 'partial' (no dimension's exact value was pinned down). Concretely: (1) Cohn and Li (arXiv:2411.04916, first posted 7 Nov 2024, still being revised as late as Sept 2026) improved lower bounds in dimensions 17-21 using a purely mathematical modification of Leech-lattice-derived sign patterns; no AI is mentioned. (2) Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve, described by its own paper (Tao, Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano and Wagner, 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale', arXiv:2511.02864, posted Nov 2025) and DeepMind's own blog post (May 2025), generated a 593-point configuration in 11 dimensions, improving the bound from 592 to 593; the authors' own account is that AlphaEvolve 'generated' the vectors and the team then verified/exactified the near-optimal numerical solution via 'simple mathematical results' -- this is squarely AI-generated with human verification (ai_role: generated). (3) Aalto University's Mikhail Ganzhinov (PhD thesis, reported Oct 2025) independently found lower bounds of 510 (dim 10), 592 (dim 11) and 1932 (dim 14) using purely human, symmetry-exploiting methods -- explicitly covered in the press as 'besting AI' in two of the three dimensions, though one point behind AlphaEvolve in dimension 11. (4) A Peking-University-led team introduced 'PackingStar', a game-theoretic reinforcement-learning system (Ma et al., arXiv:2511.13391, posted Nov 2025), which produced new records/structures in dimensions 25-31 and broke a 1971-standing rational-configuration barrier in dimension 13 (1130 to 1146 points), described by the authors as the RL system's own discovery. (5) Takhanov, Yun and collaborators at Nazarbayev University then built on PackingStar's outputs: one paper (arXiv:2609.21591, posted 18 Sept 2026) explicitly states 'the reinforcement learning system PackingStar produced the records that serve as our starting points', with the authors adding three novel human geometric techniques (rigid block rotation, nonorthogonal diagonal deformation, partial SO(7) rotation) to push bounds further in dimensions 25-29 and 31 -- a genuine human+AI collaboration where the AI produced the base configuration and humans produced the mathematics that improved on it (ai_role: assisted for that paper, though the primary AlphaEvolve dim-11 event is coded generated). A companion paper (arXiv:2606.18984 / arXiv:2609.09179, Takhanov, Assylbekov, Yun, 2026) numerically found an 841-point configuration in dimension 12 (first improvement since 1971) via classical Riesz-energy optimization with no AI mentioned, later given quaternionic structure but still not a rigorous proof. (6) Boon Suan Ho (arXiv:2603.10425, March 2026) proved a new lower bound of 11948 in dimension 19 via pure combinatorial code construction, no AI. (7) William Echols (arXiv:2608.13906, Aug 2026) used classical tabu search (not AI/ML) to improve constant-weight codes, with corollary improvements to kissing-number lower bounds in dimensions 32, 33, 34 and 37. None of these results settle the kissing number in any of these dimensions exactly, so the problem (as Wikipedia states it, over 'dimensions other than 1,2,3,4,8,24') is unambiguously still open; what changed is that the frontier of best-known bounds moved substantially, with AI systems (AlphaEvolve, PackingStar) playing a documented, sometimes decisive, role in several of these improvements and a documented 'human beats AI' counter-narrative in others. I selected the primary dated event as AlphaEvolve's May 2025 dimension-11 result because it is the most expert-digested (published by Tao and collaborators, a leading mathematician), most widely reported, and most cleanly AI-attributed of the cluster; the other results are described in this summary rather than as separate top-level events, per the instruction to record only the decisive event and describe the rest here.
competing_reading: One could argue this cluster of results should be split into multiple `partial` records (each dimension's bound is a 'case' of the general problem, restricting to a specific dimension) rather than a single `progress` record. I chose `progress` because no dimension's exact kissing number was pinned down -- only lower bounds moved -- and per §3.1, an existence/value question (what is the exact kissing number in dimension d?) is not advanced by tightening a bound, only by determining the exact value; since no such determination occurred in any dimension, `partial` (which requires a genuine case of the problem to be *settled*) does not apply, and `progress` (a bound moved) is the correct code. If a future reader believes a lower-bound improvement in a specific, previously-untouched dimension should count as 'settling' that dimension's sub-case in some weaker sense, this could be read as `partial` instead.
what_would_settle_it: An exact determination of the kissing number in any dimension outside {1,2,3,4,8,24} (matching lower and upper bounds) would settle that dimension's case and justify `partial`; nothing in the current record reaches that bar, since all cited results are lower-bound improvements only.

outcome: Several specific cases of K(n) were newly resolved since January 2024 (K(11)=32 shown maximal, K(23)=161, K(27)=225 by Savchuk 2025; K(22)=143 and K(28)=238 by Liang, Liu & Zhang 2026), using SAT solving and a new parity-obstruction argument, but the general Kobon triangle problem (a formula or full characterization of K(n) for all n) remains open.

disputes.summary: The exact value K(28)=238 (and K(22)=143) is credited in different places to different people. OEIS A006066 (as of this research) lists K(28) only as a lower bound '>=238' attributed to Zarzuelo, while a Zenodo preprint by Liang, Liu & Zhang (June 2026), 'Two New Exact Values for the Kobon Triangle Problem: K(28)=238 and K(22)=143,' claims the exact (matching upper and lower bound) result via a new local sign parity lemma plus SAT corroboration. Zarzuelo's own Lean repository (github.com/alejandrozu/kobon-proof) explicitly disclaims priority, stating its K(28)=238 witness is 'not a claim of first discovery,' consistent with Liang/Liu/Zhang being the source of the exact-value proof and Zarzuelo's repo reproducing/formalizing the lower-bound witness. A companion Zenodo note by Youming Liu on symmetries of n=28 configurations (records 20706766 and 21181834, June 2026) is closely related follow-up work.

summary: The Kobon triangle problem asks for K(n), the maximum number of non-overlapping triangles formed by n lines, for every n; the general problem (a full formula or characterization) remains open. Since 26 January 2024, several specific values were newly determined. Pavlo Savchuk's arXiv preprint 2507.07951 (submitted 10 July 2025), 'Constructing Optimal Kobon Triangle Arrangements via Table Encoding, SAT Solving, and Heuristic Straightening,' used the Kissat SAT solver plus a scipy-based heuristic straightening procedure to find new optimal arrangements for n=23 (K(23)=161) and n=27 (K(27)=225), and to prove that the long-conjectured-unreachable upper bound of 32 for n=11 is indeed unreachable, confirming K(11)=32 as maximal. Separately, a Zenodo-hosted preprint by Ke Liang, Youming Liu, and Yurui Zhang (17 June 2026), 'Two New Exact Values for the Kobon Triangle Problem: K(28)=238 and K(22)=143,' combined the classical Bartholdi-Blanc-Loisel upper bound with a newly devised 'local sign parity lemma' (a parity obstruction ruling out the BBL-maximal triangle count for n congruent to 4 mod 6) and an independent SAT computation to establish these two exact values rigorously, including a symmetry argument (elaborated in companion notes on Zenodo, records 20706766 and 21181834) showing any 28-line arrangement with 239 triangles would have to be completely asymmetric. Alejandro Zarzuelo Urdiales's Lean repository (github.com/alejandrozu/kobon-proof) independently reproduces a K(28)=238 witness with formal coordinate certificates but explicitly disclaims being the first to discover it, and OEIS A006066 (checked during this research) still lists K(28) as only a lower bound attributed to Zarzuelo, indicating some lag in cross-referencing between these near-simultaneous 2025-2026 results. None of the sources examined -- the Savchuk arXiv paper (full text checked for AI/ML mentions), the Liang/Liu/Zhang and companion Zenodo abstracts, the Zarzuelo Lean repository README and ledger files, or secondary web coverage -- mention any AI, machine learning, or large language model involvement; all methods described are classical (SAT solvers, scipy numerical optimization, combinatorial/parity arguments, and Lean formal verification of witnesses). Each of these results is a case of the problem (a specific n), settling territory but not resolving the general open problem, so status is 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (each case matched or extended what was conjectured possible for that n, none refuted an expectation).
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'progress' rather than 'partial' since the general problem's asymptotic/formulaic status is unchanged and only isolated small-n values moved. However, per §6.1/§3.1, settling an exact case (a specific n, previously only bounded) counts as 'partial' rather than mere 'progress', since it removes territory (that n's value) from the open problem entirely, distinguishing it from a bound merely narrowing without closing. Also plausible: the K(28)=238 priority dispute could shift the recorded event date backward if Zarzuelo's repository predates the Liang/Liu/Zhang Zenodo posting -- the Zarzuelo repo's own commit history was not fully dated in this research, so the June 2026 date is anchored to the Liang/Liu/Zhang publication, which explicitly claims the exact-value proof.
what_would_settle_it: Checking Zarzuelo's kobon-proof GitHub commit history for exact dates on the K(28)=238 witness, and reading the full Liang/Liu/Zhang Zenodo PDF (not just its abstract, which could not be parsed as text by available tools) to see whether it cites or credits Zarzuelo's earlier work, would settle both the priority question and confirm no AI acknowledgement exists in an unparsed methods/acknowledgements section.

outcome: A counterexample to Köthe's conjecture (via Krempa's equivalent matrix form) was constructed in September 2026: the initial construction was found autonomously by a pre-release AI system, GPT-6 Astra, in an Epoch AI evaluation harness, then verified in Lean 4 and independently developed into a full mathematical exposition (over arbitrary countable fields, and answering a 1989 question of Rowen) by ring theorists Bernhard Böhmler and René Marczinzik; a second, independently constructed counterexample using a different (point-module) method was posted a week later by Greenfeld, King and Vendramin, with GPT-6 Astra credited with suggesting a key lemma. Neither paper has yet been digested by outside experts or accepted at a journal, so the conjecture is best classed as claimed rather than resolved.

ai.basis_quote: The initial construction was found by GPT-6 Astra in an experiment run by the first author, Tom Adamczewski, whose contribution to this paper was limited to setting up and conducting this experiment. ... The model was given a Lean formalization of the matrix form of Köthe's conjecture and was asked to prove or disprove it.
ai.disclosed_cost: The VibeMathed tracker (https://vibemathed.com/problem/kothe-conjecture) states the resolution cost $432 to generate; this figure comes from a third-party tracker, not the paper itself, so it is reported with lower confidence.

counterexample.object: A unital algebra R over the countable field ¬℉₂-bar (an algebraic closure/extension of GF(2)) built from three weighted backward shifts, containing a nil two-sided ideal I, together with an explicit 2×2 matrix with entries in I that is not nilpotent (equivalently has a nonzero eigenvalue) — a counterexample to Krempa's matrix-form equivalent of the Köthe conjecture, and hence to the conjecture itself.
counterexample.verified_how: Machine-checked in Lean 4 (Mathlib, Lean v4.28.0) with no 'sorry' and no axioms beyond propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice, per the tadamcz/koethe repository; the mathematical argument was also independently written out and checked by hand by Böhmler and Marczinzik in the arXiv exposition, and a second, independently constructed counterexample (different method) was posted by Greenfeld, King and Vendramin.

summary: The triage record is essentially correct and, if anything, understated: not one but two independent counterexample constructions to the Köthe conjecture appeared in September 2026, both crediting the AI system GPT-6 Astra with a substantive role. The first (arXiv:2609.07996, submitted 2026-09-07, authors Adamczewski/Böhmler/Marczinzik) states plainly in its contribution statement that 'the initial construction was found by GPT-6 Astra' running autonomously (without human steering) in Epoch AI's LeanOpenProblems harness, given a Lean formalization of Krempa's matrix-form equivalent of the conjecture. This is 'generated' under the codes: the AI produced the mathematical construction (not just checked or tidied human work), and Böhmler and Marczinzik — established ring theorists with a prior joint publication record in this subfield (e.g. 'On a conjecture about Morita algebras', J. Algebra 2018) — independently reviewed it, developed it over arbitrary countable fields, and used it to answer a 1989 question of Rowen, taking 'full responsibility for the mathematical content.' A second paper (arXiv:2609.15080, submitted 2026-09-14, Greenfeld/King/Vendramin) gives an independently constructed counterexample via a different, point-module method, built on the authors' own prior program (with Easton and Ford) rather than on the first paper; it too credits GPT-6 Astra, but only with suggesting one key lemma (Lemma 4.2) and an earlier version of one technical notion, with the authors stating they checked and rewrote all AI-proposed material — that paper's own AI role is closer to 'assisted', though the overall event (disproof of the conjecture) is already established by the first, 'generated' paper. Krempa (1972) proved the matrix form genuinely equivalent to the original 1930 conjecture (sum of two nil left ideals is nil), so this is squarely a resolution of the stated problem, not a variant. I classify status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' because, despite the credibility of the co-authors and the Lean formalization (no 'sorry', standard axioms only), neither paper has yet been digested by an outside third party, accepted at a journal, or discussed in an expert venue like Terence Tao's blog or Quanta (searched, found nothing) — both preprints are only one to two weeks old as of the research date (2026-09-22). Third-party trackers (VibeMathed, an independent AI-math-claims index at aimath.robertj1.com) corroborate the timeline and note the second paper 'materially strengthens the mathematical verification' but likewise stop short of calling it fully vetted. The live Wikipedia article on the Köthe conjecture already states flatly that the conjecture 'was disproved' in 2026, which is a stronger claim than the evidence to date strictly supports under this project's resolved/claimed distinction, though it may well prove correct.
competing_reading: A reasonable case exists for 'resolved' rather than 'claimed': Böhmler and Marczinzik are not disinterested outside referees, but they are named, credentialed ring theorists who independently redid and extended the mathematical argument themselves (not merely reading a machine transcript), and a second, methodologically independent construction from an unrelated group corroborates the same conclusion within a week. That combination — two independent expert-authored routes to the same disproof, one machine-checked — is arguably stronger evidence than the 'published verification by named experts' the resolved bar asks for, even without formal journal acceptance. If a reviewer weighs independent convergent construction over journal status, 'resolved' would be the call.
what_would_settle_it: Journal acceptance or a citable referee report for either paper; an independent digestion by a ring theorist not among the authors (a blog post, a MathOverflow consensus, or a survey/expository note); or explicit endorsement in a venue like Tao's blog or Quanta. Any retraction or identified gap in either construction would instead move this toward 'progress'/'incident'.

outcome: No result advancing or resolving Kueker's conjecture (that a countable theory all of whose uncountable models are ω-saturated must be categorical in some infinite power) was found dated after 26 January 2024; the known partial results (stable theories: Hrushovski 1989; superstable theories: Buechler 1984; theories interpreting a linear order or with Skolem functions) remain the state of the art, and the general conjecture, including the case of simple theories, is still open.
summary: Kueker's conjecture asks whether a countable first-order theory all of whose uncountable models are ω-saturated must be categorical in some infinite power. All resolved special cases pre-date the frozen revision by decades: Buechler (1984) for superstable theories, Hrushovski (1989) for stable theories (and for theories interpreting a linear order or with Skolem functions), and Tanović's 2012 work 'On Kueker's Conjecture' addressing further cases including aspects of simple theories via 'Kueker simple' theories. I ran targeted searches for post-January-2024 activity — arXiv listings, Google-style web search for the conjecture's name combined with 'simple theories', '2024', '2025', '2026', 'omega-categorical', 'omega-stable', and 'AI'/'theorem prover' — and found nothing new. One search result surfaced an arXiv paper 'Remarks on relative categoricity' (arXiv 2602.05866, Shelah–Usvyatsov lineage, submitted 2026-02-05) that a search-engine summary associated with Kueker's conjecture; I opened the paper directly and it does not mention Kueker's conjecture at all — it concerns a different notion, 'relative categoricity' and the Gaifman conjecture over a predicate, and the association was a false positive from the search summarizer, not a real connection. I also checked 'Simple Homogeneous Structures and Indiscernible Sequence Invariants' (arXiv 2405.08211, May 2024), which appeared in results for 'Kueker's conjecture simple theories' but on direct inspection does not reference Kueker's conjecture either. No arXiv preprint, journal paper, blog digestion (Tao, Quanta, etc.), or Lean/Coq repository addressing this specific conjecture was found in the window. This matches and confirms the triage's 'none' verdict; my independent searches, including checking the two false-positive leads by opening the primary sources directly, did not surface anything the triage missed.
competing_reading: None found. The only ambiguity was whether the two arXiv papers turned up by search (2602.05866 and 2405.08211) bore on this conjecture; direct inspection of both ruled that out, so there is no live competing reading of the evidence.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper explicitly invoking 'Kueker's conjecture' by name (or its precise statement: uncountable ω-saturation implying categoricity) for simple theories or an unrestricted general case, dated after 26 January 2024; none exists as far as I could determine.

summary: The Kummer–Vandiver (Vandiver) conjecture states that no prime p divides the class number of the maximal real subfield of the p-th cyclotomic field. As of the frozen January 2024 Wikipedia revision, it was verified computationally for all primes below 2^31 (Hart, Harvey, Ong, 2017) and remained unproved, with Washington-style heuristics suggesting counterexamples (if any exist) are astronomically rare. Searches for a proof, disproof, counterexample, extended verification bound, or new theoretical advance directly settling any case of the conjecture since 26 January 2024 turned up nothing: general search engines return only pre-2024 material (the 2^31 verification, the 2020 'Vandiver's Conjecture via K-theory' preprint by Stolin/Ghate which itself remains an unpublished, non-digested attempt from 2020, Gras/Mihăilescu heuristic refinements, and the unrelated function-field analogue counterexamples, which are a genuinely different problem under §3.1's scope rule since they concern function fields rather than the classical cyclotomic-field statement). The only post-window item found anywhere near this problem is a June 2025 GitHub issue (#137) and an October 2025 merged pull request (#297) in DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' repository, which added a Lean formal statement of the conjecture (file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/KummerVandiver.lean) ending in `sorry` — i.e., a machine-checkable statement of the open conjecture with no proof attached. This is a formalisation of the problem statement, not a mathematical result, so per §6.2 it does not constitute AI involvement in a result (ai_role none, formalisation_only true) and does not move status off open. I also checked recent Iwasawa-theory literature (2024 Massey-product paper on Iwasawa λ-invariants, 2025 papers on λ/μ-invariants of real cyclotomic and quadratic fields) for any bearing on Vandiver's conjecture specifically; these are related-but-distinct results (bounds/criteria in adjacent settings) that do not settle any case of the stated conjecture, so they are excluded under the variant/related-problem rule in §3.1.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2020 Stolin/Ghate 'Vandiver's Conjecture via K-theory' preprint, if it were still under active revision or gained new commentary after January 2024, might count as `claimed` progress; however, no post-2024 update, endorsement, or digestion of that specific preprint was found, and it predates the window regardless, so it would be `open_stale` evidence at best, not a change in the measured window. The formal-conjectures repository entry could be read as 'AI lab engagement with the problem' worth noting even though it is formalisation-only; I have recorded it in `event`/`ai` fields for transparency while keeping ai_role as none per the explicit rule that formalisation-only work is not AI involvement in a result.
what_would_settle_it: A dated preprint or announcement (after 26 January 2024) claiming a proof, disproof, explicit counterexample, or an extended computational verification bound beyond 2^31 for the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture; or a completed (non-`sorry`) Lean proof of the KummerVandiver.lean statement in the formal-conjectures repository.

outcome: Matthew J. Colbrook (University of Cambridge) posted a preprint, 'Adversarial Wronskians: A proof of the Kung–Traub conjecture,' to Zenodo around 19 September 2026, claiming to prove the full conjecture (that a deterministic stationary root-finding method without memory using at most n real scalar function/derivative evaluations per iteration cannot have local order exceeding 2^(n-1), with the bound attained by known Kung-Traub-type methods for n>=2), accompanied by a Lean 4 formalization. No independent expert review, journal acceptance, or public expert digestion of the argument has been found as of the time of this research (three days after posting), and the author's own repository states that independent replay verification of the Lean proof 'has not yet passed.'

ai.basis_quote: ChatGPT 6 assisted with the Lean formalization... ChatGPT 5.6 and 6 were also interactive aids for discussing and checking mathematical arguments... Matthew J. Colbrook reviewed and adopted the mathematical arguments, statements, and proofs and takes responsibility for the work.

summary: The triage's `found` items pointed to two things, one of which does not actually concern this problem: the OpenProblemsInNLA GitHub issue #14 that triage cited is about a different problem (matrix inequality MI-04), not the Kung-Traub conjecture, and I disagree with the triage's implicit conflation of the two. The GitHub repository MColbrook/Kung-Traub_conjecture and its associated Zenodo preprint 'Adversarial Wronskians: A proof of the Kung-Traub conjecture' (Colbrook, posted ~19 September 2026, i.e. three days before this research) is a genuine and specific claim to resolve exactly this conjecture: it proves the upper bound 2^(n-1) on the local order of any deterministic, memoryless, stationary root-finder using at most n scalar evaluations, matching the order attained by known Kung-Traub-type (e.g. inverse Hermite) constructions, and extends the result to complex-valued derivative observations. It is accompanied by a Lean 4 formalization the author describes as having 'zero proof holes' in the core theorems, an axiom audit of 1,202 declarations, and 'Comparator' checks of 1,058 named theorems -- but the same README explicitly states that independent 'NanoDa replay' verification 'has not yet passed,' and that these mechanical checks 'do not establish novelty or independent mathematical peer review.' No journal acceptance, no expert blog digestion (nothing on Tao's blog or elsewhere), and no third-party mathematical review of the argument were found. Given the extreme freshness of the claim (surfacing literally days before this research was conducted) and the author's own caveats, this is classified `claimed` rather than `resolved`. On AI involvement: the repository states plainly that ChatGPT-6 assisted with the Lean formalization and that ChatGPT 5.6/6 served as 'interactive aids for discussing and checking mathematical arguments,' but that Colbrook 'reviewed and adopted the mathematical arguments, statements, and proofs and takes responsibility for the work' -- i.e., by the author's own account, the mathematics (the Wronskian-based lower-bound argument and the adversarial construction) originated with and was owned by the human author, and the AI's role was checking, discussion, and formalization support. Per the rules (§6.2), 'discussing and checking' with no claim that the AI produced mathematical content in the result is `none`, not `assisted`. During search I also encountered a GitHub repository ('vibemathing/problem-wikipedia-...') that describes itself, in its own words, as 'not mathematical evidence or a solved-result claim' and appears to be an unrelated research-automation/agent-harness scaffold; I disregarded it entirely as it is self-flagged as non-evidentiary and not a mathematical source. I also confirmed the n=2 case of the conjecture was already settled by Kung and Traub themselves in 1976 (pre-dating the frozen revision by decades, hence irrelevant to open_stale classification -- the general conjecture for n>=3 remained genuinely open going into 2024).
competing_reading: One could argue the ChatGPT involvement in 'discussing and checking mathematical arguments' blurs toward `assisted` if it contributed any specific lemma or step content beyond verification -- the README's wording is not fully granular about what, if anything, ChatGPT suggested versus merely checked. However, absent a specific quote crediting the AI with producing an argument, construction, or case that appears in the final proof, `none` is the more defensible reading under the rule requiring the authors' own account of the AI producing part of the mathematics.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a survey, a referee report, a blog post from a numerical-analysis or root-finding specialist, or journal acceptance) confirming or refuting the Wronskian-based lower bound argument; alternatively, a successful independent Lean replay (the author's own stated pending step) plus community scrutiny of the formalization would move this toward `resolved`. A more detailed methods section from Colbrook specifying exactly what content, if any, ChatGPT contributed to the mathematical argument (versus only formalization/checking) would sharpen the ai_role classification.

outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 addresses the p=1 (L1/rectilinear) case stated in this bullet; the case n<=4 remains the only proven range and the O(n log n) general upper bound (Konyagin, pre-2024) is unchanged. A wave of 2026 papers resolved the analogous conjecture for p>1, but every one of them explicitly excludes or is silent on p=1.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet states Kusner's conjecture specifically for L1 (p=1) spaces: at most 2d points can be equidistant in d-dimensional L1. This is a distinct sub-case of the general Kusner conjecture, which asks for the maximum equilateral-set cardinality in l_p^n for every 1<p<infinity (conjectured n+1 for 1<p<infinity, and separately 2n for p=1). Since January 2024 there has been substantial activity on the general conjecture for p>1: Ge, Xu and Zhou ('Kusner's conjecture: Exact values and linear bounds,' arXiv:2606.03987, June 2026) proved the conjecture for 2<=p<=4 and gave near-linear O_p(n log n) bounds on complementary ranges of p; a follow-up (arXiv:2608.14013 and arXiv:2609.14794, August/September 2026) produced explicit counterexamples disproving the conjecture for p>4, building on Swanepoel's earlier (pre-2024) disproof for 1<p<2. Combined, this settles the p>1 range of the general Kusner conjecture. However, I read past the abstracts into the introductions of arXiv:2606.03987 (both the abs page rendering and the full HTML), and both explicitly restrict their theorems to p>=2 (or p in [2,4] and adjacent ranges), stating that for p=1 the conjecture 'holds for n<=4, with the cases n=3 and n=4 established by Bandelt, Chepoi and Laurent, and by Koolen, Laurent and Schrijver' (all pre-2024, decades-old results), and that the best known general bound for p=1 remains Konyagin's O(n log n), also pre-2024. None of the three 2026 papers found by triage, nor the current Wikipedia 'Equilateral dimension' article (which cites nothing past 2008), nor any further search I ran, turned up a paper that narrows, proves, or disproves the p=1 case specifically. The p>1 resolution is a related/parallel problem in the sense of this dataset's scope rule (§3.1): it changes the l_p conjecture for p>1, but the bullet in front of me is exactly the p=1 case, which those papers deliberately carve out and leave untouched. So the correct classification is 'open' with no_change_found true, agreeing with the triage's 'none' verdict. No AI system appears anywhere in this research trail: all three papers are ordinary human-authored combinatorial/discrete-geometry proofs with no stated model involvement of any kind.
competing_reading: One could argue the general Kusner conjecture (as a single named conjecture across all p, including p=1) has now been 'mostly resolved' and treat the p=1 sub-case as inheriting some evidentiary momentum, especially since the same authors (Ge, Xu, Zhou) explicitly handle p=1 as part of their conjecture statement (citing the n<=4 cases as already known). But the paper's own theorems and bounds sections give it no new treatment; the p=1 case is recited as background, not advanced. I do not think this rises to 'progress' under the letter of the rule, since nothing about what a careful reader would write in the p=1 bullet has changed.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly proving or disproving Kusner's conjecture for p=1 in some dimension n=5 or higher (beyond the pre-2024 n<=4 results), or improving the O(n log n) bound for p=1 specifically, would move this out of 'open'.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or bound change to the LPS conjecture (m+n≥k) has been found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open, with no known counterexample, and the simplest unresolved case (a^5+b^5=c^5+d^5) still unsettled.
summary: The LPS conjecture (if a sum of m k-th powers equals a different sum of n k-th powers, then m+n≥k) remains open, with no proof, disproof, or bound movement found since 26 January 2024. The one plausibly relevant find, a December 2025 arXiv preprint by Valery Asiryan, 'The Linear Slicing Method for Equal Sums of Like Powers: Modular and Geometric Constraints' (arXiv:2512.00551), studies only the restricted two-term equation a^k+b^k=c^k+d^k under an additional linear constraint (c+d)-(a+b)=h on a fixed 'slice.' Its results (central-slice uniqueness for h=0, a modular divisibility obstruction for h≠0, and asymptotic non-existence on any fixed slice as k grows) do not touch the general LPS statement, which concerns arbitrary numbers of terms m, n on each side with no such linear constraint. The paper's own text explicitly disclaims addressing 'the global open problem of non-trivial solutions to a^k+b^k=c^k+d^k for k>4 without linear constraints' — i.e., even the unconstrained four-term special case is outside its scope, let alone the general m,n case. This is a related/variant problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not change the status here. I confirm the triage's 'none' verdict. Other search results were: general surveys and encyclopedic pages on equal sums of like powers (MathWorld, Rizos Sakellariou's site, Wikipedia's own article and Euler's sum of powers conjecture article), papers that merely cite or assume LPS as a working hypothesis while proving unrelated results (e.g. 'An absolute bound for generalized Diophantine tuples over polynomial rings,' 'Hilbert cubes in sets with arithmetic properties'), a March 2026 computational paper announcing the fourth known primitive solution to the unrelated equation a^5+b^5+c^5+d^5=e^5 (a five-term single-equation Diophantine problem, not a case of the m,n-term LPS inequality), and Timothy Browning's paucity/sparsity results on equal sums of two k-th powers, which date from the 2000s and have no update in the window. The Wikipedia article's edit history since January 2024 shows only formatting changes, added tables of known boundary/minimal solutions, automated citation-bot edits, and one attribution correction (crediting Croot & Yip rather than Tsang & Yip for a conditional Diophantine-tuple bound) — none of which reflect any change to the conjecture's mathematical status. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Linear Slicing Method paper's central-slice result (no nontrivial real solutions when a+b=c+d) is a 'case' of the four-term instance of LPS (m=n=2, k arbitrary) rather than a full variant, since it does rule out an entire family of potential counterexamples to the k=4 boundary case. However, the paper studies a strictly additional constraint (fixing the linear slice) not present in the original conjecture, and explicitly disclaims the unconstrained problem, so per §3.1 this is better classified as a related problem (a changed question) than a case (a restriction of the original question) — it does not narrow where a counterexample to LPS itself could hide, since it excludes almost none of the unconstrained solution space (only points on the very thin measure-zero 'slices' with fixed a+b vs c+d gap).
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit new counterexample to m+n≥k, a proof that no such counterexample can exist for some class of k, a resolution (positive or negative) of the a^5+b^5=c^5+d^5 open case, or an unconstrained (non-sliced) advance on a^k+b^k=c^k+d^k for k>4 would settle whether real progress has occurred; none of these were found in the window.

outcome: The Lang-Trotter conjecture on supersingular primes for a non-CM elliptic curve over Q (that the count of supersingular primes below X is asymptotically c*sqrt(X)/log(X)) remains open; no proof, disproof, or case-settling result on the stated problem itself was found in the window.
summary: The stated problem is Lang and Trotter's 1976 conjecture that for a non-CM elliptic curve E over Q, the number of primes p < X at which E has supersingular reduction is asymptotically c_E * sqrt(X)/log(X) for a constant c_E depending on E. Searches (WebSearch for 'Lang-Trotter conjecture supersingular primes 2024 2025 proof', 'Lang-Trotter conjecture supersingular primes arXiv', and 'Lang-Trotter conjecture AI machine learning neural network elliptic curve') turned up a cluster of arXiv papers dated 2024-2026, but every one addresses a different or narrower object than the stated conjecture: 'Distribution of supersingular primes for abelian surfaces' (arXiv:2402.12218, submitted 19 Feb 2024, revised 9 Jul 2025) and 'On distribution of supersingular primes of abelian varieties and K3 surfaces' (arXiv:2504.08088) both move to abelian surfaces/K3 surfaces, not elliptic curves; 'The Lang-Trotter conjecture on average for genus-2 curves with Klein-4 reduced automorphism group' (arXiv:2408.13695) and the analogous S3 paper (arXiv:2604.00822) are genus-2 average results, a different object and a weaker (on-average) statement; the CM elliptic curve paper (arXiv:2109.14256, pre-window) and the y^2=x^3+Dx family paper (arXiv:2108.06292, pre-window) both predate the window and additionally concern the CM case, which is a different hypothesis than the non-CM case stated in the conjecture. I opened arXiv:2402.12218 directly (via WebFetch) and confirmed it studies abelian surfaces, not elliptic curves, and contains no proof or disproof of the classical conjecture, and no mention of AI/ML tool use. I also fetched the current (2026) Wikipedia article on supersingular primes for elliptic curves, which explicitly states 'As of 2026, this conjecture remains open' and cites no new result since Cojocaru-Fouvry-Murty 2005. A separate search for AI/ML connections turned up only an unrelated paper ('Learning Euler Factors of Elliptic Curves', arXiv:2502.10357) on predicting Euler factors/murmurations via machine learning, which does not touch the supersingular-prime-counting conjecture at all. No case of the stated conjecture (e.g., a specific non-CM curve or family proved to match the asymptotic exactly, or the asymptotic constant pinned down) was found settled, and no bound on the counting function was found to have moved. This matches the triage's 'none' verdict. Status is open with no_change_found true, and ai_role is none.
competing_reading: One could argue the genus-2 'Lang-Trotter on average' papers are extensions that constitute 'progress on the Lang-Trotter program' broadly, but per the scope rule (§3.1) they change the object (elliptic curve -> genus-2 curve/abelian surface) and the statement (asymptotic -> on-average asymptotic), which makes them related problems rather than cases of the stated conjecture (restricting to a sub-case of the same object and same statement). None of them settle any sub-case of the non-CM elliptic curve conjecture itself.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving the asymptotic c_E*sqrt(X)/log(X) (or even just establishing existence of a positive-density/exact-order lower and upper bound matching this rate) for a specific non-CM elliptic curve E over Q, or for an infinite non-trivial subfamily of non-CM curves, would count as partial progress on the stated problem; currently the best known results are Elkies' infinitude of supersingular primes and Fouvry-Murty/Cojocaru-type average results, none of which pin down the exact asymptotic order for any individual non-CM curve.

outcome: The problem itself (minimum area of a convex universal cover for planar sets of diameter one) remains open, but the certified lower bound on the area moved three times in 2026, from the 2005 Brass–Sharifi value of 0.832 to 0.833 (Xie, June/July 2026), then to 0.834 (Zeng, September 2026) and 0.8344 (Mishra, August/September 2026); the upper bound is unchanged from Gibbs' 2018 preprint value of 0.8440935944.

ai.basis_quote: Large language models were used for language editing, formatting assistance, and consistency checks.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the minimum-area convex shape in the plane covering every diameter-one set (the 2D case). This remains open: no upper or lower bound closes the gap. But the lower bound on the area constant a_Leb moved three separate times within the window, all in 2026, all using the same basic strategy of exhibiting explicit convex test sets (a disc plus polygons or Reuleaux-type constant-width curves) and certifying, by exhaustive/interval-arithmetic computation, that their convex hull under all relative placements has area at least some threshold. Niantao Xie (arXiv:2606.04458, submitted 2026-06-03, v4 2026-07-08) reproduced/improved the Brass–Sharifi (2005, 0.832) framework to certify 0.833. Ujjwal Mishra (arXiv:2608.30538, submitted 2026-08, v2 2026-09-01) switched the test sets to curves of constant width (disc, Reuleaux triangle, Reuleaux pentagon) and an exhaustive subdivision of a 5-dimensional placement space (486,799,600 nodes, independently re-verified certificate) to reach 0.8344. Shuai Zeng (arXiv:2609.01284, submitted 2026-09-01) built an exact Reuleaux-type variational hierarchy with a proven O(M⁻²) convergence rate to the true constant, certifying 0.834 as a realization of one finite level of that hierarchy. None of these three papers has been digested by an expert commentator, accepted at a journal, or discussed on Tao's blog / Quanta / similar outlets as of the check date — they remain preprints, so the correct status is progress (a bound moved on a problem that stays open), not resolved or claimed. The upper bound side saw no movement in the window: the best known convex universal cover is still Gibbs' 2018 preprint value of area 0.8440935944, repeatedly cited unchanged across all three 2026 papers and by the current Wikipedia article. On AI: only Zeng's paper (2609.01284) makes any AI disclosure, and it is explicitly language-editing/formatting/consistency-checking, i.e. squarely `none` under §6.2 — the mathematics (the hierarchy, the convergence proof, the certificate) is presented as the author's own work verified by interval arithmetic, not produced by an AI system. Xie's and Mishra's papers make no AI disclosure at all. A fourth arXiv item flagged by triage, 'Note on Lebesgue's universal cover problem' (arXiv:2607.27227, Yizhen Chen), is about the 3-dimensional universal covering problem — a dodecahedron counterexample, volume bounds in R^3, and a polytope family in R^n — which changes the ambient dimension of the question and is therefore a related problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated (planar) bullet; it does not affect this record's status. A fifth item found independently, 'On asymptotic Lebesgue's universal covering problem' (arXiv:2512.04023, Arman/Bondarenko/Prymak/Radchenko, submitted 2025-12-03), proves Jung's ball is asymptotically volume-optimal among universal covers in R^n as n→∞ — again the high-dimensional asymptotic problem, a related problem, not the n=2 case asked about here, and also contains no AI disclosure. No priority dispute or retraction was found among the three lower-bound papers; each explicitly supersedes its immediate predecessor and cites it, forming a normal sequential improvement rather than a controversy.
competing_reading: One could argue the sequence of lower-bound papers, taken together, is significant enough progress (closing roughly a quarter of the 2005-era gap between 0.832 and 0.8441 within a single year) to warrant more weight than a routine `progress` tag conveys, but none of the three individual results is large enough or expert-vetted enough to justify `claimed` or `resolved`, and the underlying existence/value question (what is a_Leb exactly) is unchanged in kind, only in how tightly it is bracketed — consistent with §3.1's treatment of a moved bound as `progress` rather than a change to the core open question.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance or an expert digestion (e.g. a Tao-blog or Quanta writeup, or citation/verification by another specialist in discrete/convex geometry) of any of the three 2026 lower-bound papers would move that paper's contribution from `progress`/preprint status toward `resolved`-quality confirmation of the specific bound (though the overall Lebesgue problem would still be open). Discovery of an AI-generated construction or proof step in any of these or a future paper would change the ai_role from `none`.

outcome: Legendre's conjecture remains unproven; nothing found since 26 January 2024 changes what a careful person would write in this entry.
summary: No result since 26 January 2024 changes the status of Legendre's conjecture, and no AI system is credited with anything relevant to it. Three lines of activity were found. (1) Computational verification: Sorenson and Webster's algorithm paper (arXiv:2401.13753, submitted 24 Jan 2024, two days before the frozen revision) extended the verified range of the underlying Oppermann's-conjecture search from N=2e9 to N=3.33e13; the published version (Research in Number Theory, 2025) reports a further extension to N=7.05e13 using a classical parallel sieve algorithm on Xeon Phi/Xeon E5 clusters — no AI or machine learning of any kind. Per the deep-dive rule for existence questions (§3.1), extending a verified range narrows where a counterexample could hide but does not answer the existence question, so this is not a status-changing event regardless of its date, which in any case falls right at or before the window boundary. (2) An unaccepted preprint claim: arXiv:2403.08306 (Li and Li, submitted 13 March 2024, revised through v3 on 20 March 2024) claims a full proof via a coprime-density argument. It has no journal acceptance, no expert digestion, no citations building on it as a settled result, and general number-theory practice treats such elementary coprime-counting arguments for Legendre's conjecture with strong skepticism given the problem's difficulty; it does not meet the bar for `claimed` in the sense the schema intends (a status a careful expert would take seriously), so it is noted here rather than elevating the record's status. Other self-published claims (academia.edu, viXra, an 'Oriental Journal' venue) were also found and carry no weight. (3) Genuine but conditional related progress: Chamberland and Straub, 'Weakening the Legendre Conjecture' (arXiv:2602.22502, submitted 26 Feb 2026), is a legitimate paper by established mathematicians showing that, assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, a recent result implies existence of primes between x^(2+δ) and (x+1)^(2+δ) for δ≥1/4, with explicit computational bounds for smaller δ. This is scope-excluded under §3.1: it changes the exponent from 2 to 2+δ, which is a different (weaker) question, not a restriction of the stated problem to a special case, so it is a related problem rather than a case of Legendre's conjecture and does not move this record's status even though it is real, RH-conditional progress on the neighboring question. No AI involvement was found or claimed anywhere in this cluster of results.
competing_reading: One could argue the Sorenson-Webster range extension, since its arXiv preprint predates the frozen revision by only two days but its peer-reviewed journal publication (2025) and largest reported figure (7.05e13) postdate it, should be recorded as a dated 'progress' event under the paper's later publication kind. I did not do this because §6.3 requires dating by the first public written argument (the January 2024 preprint), and in any case §3.1 excludes range-extension results from counting as movement on an existence question at all, so no event exists to date regardless of which the paper's version is used.
what_would_settle_it: A full proof or explicit counterexample accepted by expert digestion or a journal of record; alternatively, an unconditional (non-RH) proof of the weakened exponent-2 statement, or a credible expert review elevating one of the preprint proof claims (arXiv:2403.08306 or similar) to serious consideration.

outcome: A July 2025 preprint by Anup B. Dixit and Sushant Kala, 'A p-adic criterion for Lehmer's conjecture' (arXiv:2507.20141), proves Lehmer's conjecture for the restricted class of algebraic numbers α (of degree d, not a root of unity) having ≳ √(d log d) conjugates lying in a fixed finite extension of a p-adic field ℚ_p, via a p-adic equidistribution argument; the paper has since appeared in the International Journal of Number Theory (reported publication May 2026), which counts as expert digestion via peer review. The general conjecture remains open. No AI involvement was found in this or any other result located in the window.
summary: The decisive event in the window is Dixit and Kala's arXiv:2507.20141 (submitted 26 July 2025), which gives a p-adic criterion sufficient for Lehmer's conjecture: writing S_K(α) for the set of conjugates of α lying in a finite extension K of ℚ_p, the paper's Proposition 1.3 shows h(α) ≥ c/d (and hence Lehmer's conjecture) holds whenever |S_K(α)| ≳ √(d log d), with an explicit constant depending on q=|residue field| and [K:ℚ_p] (Corollary 1.4 gives the concrete threshold √(q³[K:ℚ_p] d log d)). This is a genuine case of the stated problem — it restricts the general question (all non-cyclotomic algebraic numbers) to a class defined by a p-adic clustering condition on conjugates, and proves the height bound for that class — so it is scoped correctly as `partial` per §3.1, not a variant. A web search snippet (via researcher.life/WorldScientific listings, which themselves 403'd on direct fetch) reports the paper has been formally published in the International Journal of Number Theory (May 2026); I could not independently load the WorldScientific page to confirm the DOI directly, so I treat this as likely but not fully verified — see confidence note below. Reading the full HTML version of the arXiv paper, the sole acknowledgement is INSPIRE Faculty Fellowship funding for the first author; there is no mention of any AI system, computational tool, or software anywhere in the paper, so ai_role is `none`. I also checked two other 2025 preprints that surface in searches for 'Lehmer's conjecture': arXiv:2506.18776 ('New evidence for Rémond's generalisation of Lehmer's conjecture') concerns heights on almost-split semiabelian varieties, a different algebraic-geometric analogue rather than the classical polynomial/Mahler-measure statement, and arXiv:2510.08871 ('Experimental investigations on Lehmer's conjecture for elliptic curves') concerns an analogous conjecture about canonical heights of non-torsion points on elliptic curves, again a distinct namesake conjecture, not the classical one about non-cyclotomic algebraic numbers' Mahler measure. Both are `related problems` under §3.1 and are excluded from the record. I also found and rejected a ResearchGate item, 'Lehmer's Conjecture as Computational Necessity: A Three-Pillar Synthesis of Information Theory, Arithmetic Fluid Dynamics, and Operational Geometry,' whose abstract (recovered via search snippet only, since the ResearchGate page itself returned HTTP 403) uses pseudo-technical invented terminology ('Irreducible Overhead Theorem', 'Arithmetic Fluid Dynamics', 'Ω_p attractor hierarchy') to claim the conjecture is a 'structural impossibility'; this reads as non-mathematical, likely AI-generated crank content rather than a real result, has no evident authorship or peer review, and I did not count it as an event of any kind — it is noted here only because it surfaced repeatedly in search and could otherwise be mistaken for a finding. The 2019 preprint claiming a full proof (arXiv:1911.10590) predates the window and, per the triage note and independent secondary reports, contains a fatal error, so it is not counted even as open_stale (it was never accepted as a resolution before or after the frozen date).
competing_reading: One could argue the Dixit-Kala result, while a genuine restriction of the domain, is narrow enough (a p-adic clustering condition satisfied by an unclear, possibly small, subset of algebraic numbers in practice) that it barely moves the needle on the conjecture as usually understood (Mahler measure bounded away from 1 for all non-cyclotomic algebraic integers). Under a stricter reading of 'case of the problem,' one might downgrade this to `progress` (a technique/bound) rather than `partial` (a settled case). I classify it as `partial` because the theorem does settle Lehmer's conjecture outright for a well-defined, non-empty class of algebraic numbers, which is exactly the pattern of the worked example in the instructions.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the WorldScientific/International Journal of Number Theory page (currently blocked by a 403 to automated fetchers) or another citation database (MathSciNet, zbMATH) confirming the DOI, volume, and publication date of the Dixit-Kala paper would fully confirm the peer-reviewed digestion and let `resolved`-level sourcing stand on firmer footing for that sub-claim (though the overall problem status of `partial` would not change, since the general conjecture is still open either way).

outcome: No accepted or expert-digested change to the problem was found since 26 January 2024. Two unreviewed preprints.org manuscripts (Nov 2025, Jan 2026) claim a full or near-full resolution, but neither has any expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification; the January 2026 claim was withdrawn by its own author for a 'fundamental mathematical issue' before it could be assessed further, and the November 2025 claim's own abstract concedes its main density result is conditional on GRH and that even its unconditional part covers only a narrow case (14-prime, odd-parity composites) that was already excluded by classical bounds (any solution needs ω(n) ≥ 14, so 'eliminating 14-prime composites' does not on its face touch the open cases with more prime factors). A third, October 2025 preprint on a generalized totient-divisibility equation φ(n) = n − a explicitly states that the a = −1 case, i.e. Lehmer's original problem, 'remains one of the oldest open problems' — it is a related/generalizing paper, not a resolution. Wikipedia's live article (checked here only to see if consensus had shifted; not used as a source of fact) still lists the problem as open, citing bounds work through 2019 (Burek and Żmija) with nothing newer.
summary: This problem was triaged as 'likely' on the strength of two preprints.org manuscripts, and I read as much of both as I could reach (the site returns HTTP 403 to automated fetchers, so I worked from cached search snippets, titles, and the searchable text Google/Bing have indexed of each abstract — this is a real gap, noted in `incomplete`). The November 2025 manuscript ('Lehmer's Totient Conjecture: 2-Adic Closure, Computational Certificates, and GRH-Density Resolution') claims to close the conjecture in two stages: an unconditional elimination of '14-prime composites' via 2-adic valuation, and a GRH-conditional density argument for larger configurations. Two problems keep this from counting as a change to the problem as stated. First, scope: since Cohen and Hagis (1980) already proved any solution needs at least 14 distinct prime factors, and later work pushed this bound to roughly 40,000,000 for solutions divisible by 3 (Burcsi–Czirbusz–Farkas), a paper that only 'eliminates 14-prime composites' is working well inside territory already known to be empty or near-empty — it is not clear this narrows the actual open frontier at all, let alone resolves it. Second, even taking the density claim at face value, it is GRH-conditional and, per the triage note and my own searching, has not been read or endorsed by any expert; there is no journal acceptance, no digestion on Tao's blog, MathOverflow, or any number-theory survey, and no arXiv posting at all — it exists only as an unreviewed preprints.org manuscript. The January 2026 manuscript ('A Short Proof the Lehmer's Totient Problem Has No Solutions') claimed a complete, unconditional resolution but was withdrawn by its own author on or around 15 January 2026 for a 'fundamental mathematical issue,' before any outside verification occurred — a textbook incident rather than a result. A third, related preprint from October 2025 ('The Euler Totient Divisibility Problem: a Complete Classification') studies the generalized equation φ(n) = n − a for general integer a and explicitly identifies a = −1 (Lehmer's own problem) as remaining open; it resolves other values of a but is a related problem under §3.1, not a case of this one. I also checked whether any AI system was involved in producing either claim: no methods section, acknowledgement, or third-party report surfaces any authorial statement of AI-generated mathematics for either preprint, so ai_role is 'none' by default (no basis_quote is possible). I found and briefly checked pith.science, an AI-assisted preprint-review platform, but it has not reviewed either of these two manuscripts, so it provides no independent verification either way. Net: this problem still merits `open` with `no_change_found`, though the January 2026 withdrawal event is itself the sort of instructive incident this format wants preserved, so I have described it in `summary` and left it out of `event` because it never became a serious claim that a status other than `open` could rest on.
competing_reading: One could argue the withdrawn January 2026 preprint deserves its own `progress`/`incident` classification with `event.kind` 'preprint' dated 2026-01, on the model of §7's 'a withdrawn claim is still an event.' I chose `open`/`no_change_found` instead because, unlike the withdrawn-claim examples the instructions have in mind (a claim that got far enough to be read and then retracted), this one appears to have been withdrawn essentially immediately, with no evidence any outside mathematician engaged with it before the withdrawal — there is nothing here beyond 'someone posted and then un-posted a claim,' which is weaker than an announced-then-withdrawn result. If a reviewer disagrees, the correct fix is `status: progress`, `resolution_direction: null`, `ai_role: incident` is NOT appropriate regardless (that code is reserved for AI-produced claims specifically, and no AI involvement was found here) — so at most this would become `progress` with `ai_role: none`.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (or refutation) by a number theorist of the November 2025 manuscript's 2-adic and bounded-catch arguments — e.g. a MathOverflow thread, a referee report, or a follow-up preprint citing and checking it — would resolve whether any real progress underlies that claim. Access to the full text of both preprints.org manuscripts (currently blocked to automated fetching) would also let a future pass verify the scope question directly rather than relying on abstract-level snippets.

outcome: No credible resolution, partial case, or bound-moving result on Lemoine's conjecture was found since 26 January 2024; the one candidate found (a May 2026 Zenodo self-publication) is not a proof of the conjecture at all.
summary: The triage flagged a May 2026 Zenodo record, 'The Lemoine Predictive Theorem: A Machine-Verified Constructive Proof of Lemoine's Conjecture' (Jonathan Reed, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19957584), as a possible resolution. I fetched the record directly, including its two attached Lean 4 source files (552 and 858 bytes) and the PDF. The Lean files do not contain a proof of Lemoine's conjecture: they define a recursive search function (`lemoine_search`) that, given a list of candidate primes, tries each one and returns it if N - 2*p_test is prime, otherwise recurses on a filtered sublist; the only thing proved is that this recursion terminates (`termination_by available.length`), via a bound on list length. There is no theorem stating or proving that the search succeeds for every odd N > 5, i.e. no statement of the form 'for all odd n > 5, lemoine_search n ... ≠ 0' or equivalent, let alone a proof of one. Calling this 'machine-verified' is true only in the vacuous sense that the termination obligation type-checks in Lean; it verifies nothing about the truth of the conjecture. The paper's framing ('Lemoine Predictive Process', 'ƒ(n)' pseudonym, 'dead ends are logically impossible' in prose with no corresponding formal statement) reads as a plausible-sounding but mathematically empty artifact. There is no arXiv posting, no journal, no institutional affiliation, no citing literature, and no independent digestion of any kind — I found zero secondary coverage of this record anywhere. The authors give no account of AI involvement in producing it (no acknowledgement, no methods statement naming a model), so under §6.2 there is no basis to code any ai_role other than 'none', regardless of how the artifact itself was likely produced. Separately, I checked the two other things that came up in general searches: (1) arXiv:2304.00024, which lifted empirical verification of the conjecture to 10^13 for all numbers of a certain form, was submitted 31 March 2023 (single version, no later revision) — this predates the window and, per §3.1, a verification-limit extension does not move an existence conjecture in any case, so it is irrelevant background, not open_stale-worthy new information. (2) arXiv:1709.05335 (Agama & Gensel, 'The Asymptotic Binary Goldbach and Lemoine Conjectures') is the paper Wikipedia's own article already describes as 'claimed [proved] in 2017... later found to be flawed'; it has been revised repeatedly (16 versions, most recently March-April 2026, with several revisions falling inside the window: v11-v12 in June-July 2024, v13-v16 in March-April 2026). Its abstract claims only an asymptotic version of the conjecture (a density/circle-of-partition argument), not a full proof, it carries an arXiv admin overlap note, and I found no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or any commentary establishing that the flaw previously identified was fixed in the newer versions. Even taking the newest revision at face value, an asymptotic result is at most a partial/progress-type claim about a case of the problem, and with no expert readthrough available I cannot respensibly code it above 'open' background noise; there is no dated, digested event to hang an 'event' record on, and doing so would overstate what is actually established. No AI involvement is mentioned in either paper. I searched MathWorld-style status, Terence Tao's blog/Mathstodon, Quanta, and general 2024-2026 proof-attempt queries and found nothing else pointing to Lemoine's conjecture specifically. On balance the honest classification is open / no_change_found, with the Zenodo item recorded as a checked dead end explicitly because it is exactly the kind of dramatic-sounding claim the triage was right to flag but which doesn't survive opening the actual attached files.
competing_reading: One could argue the Agama-Gensel asymptotic result, if its 2024/2026 revisions are mathematically sound and if 'asymptotic version' is read as settling almost all cases (a density-one statement), constitutes a 'partial' result on a case of the conjecture, which would make status 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' and an event dated to the July 2024 or April 2026 revision. I did not adopt this reading because: (a) the same paper is already flagged by Wikipedia's own article as previously found flawed, and I found no independent confirmation that later revisions fixed the issue; (b) 'asymptotic' proofs of Goldbach-type statements are a distinct, much weaker claim than the conjecture itself (density-one is not 'every odd integer'), which is arguably a related/variant question under §3.1 rather than a case; and (c) there is no expert digestion of the current version, so even under a charitable reading this would only reach 'progress', not 'partial' with confidence. I flag this so a reviewer with access to a mathematician's assessment of the 2024-2026 revisions of arXiv:1709.05335 can override my classification if warranted.
what_would_settle_it: An expert (or a clear published/blog digestion) reading the current v13-v16 text of arXiv:1709.05335 and stating whether the previously identified flaw in the Agama-Gensel argument was fixed, and whether the asymptotic result is a genuine partial case rather than a restatement of the earlier flawed claim; alternatively, any independent citation, review, or discussion of the May 2026 Zenodo record that I failed to find.

outcome: The result flagged by triage (Ferri & Johnston, arXiv:2301.05700, proving Leopoldt's conjecture at certain primes for infinite families of totally real S3- and D8-extensions of Q, the first known infinite families of non-abelian totally real extensions with Leo(F,p) proven at an odd prime) was already fully present, with identical theorem statements, in v1 of the paper submitted 13 January 2023 -- 13 days before the frozen revision's timestamp. v2 (23 March 2026) is only the journal-accepted version (published in Research in Number Theory, 2026); it adds no new theorems. The conjecture itself remains open in general.
summary: The triage record correctly identified arXiv:2301.05700 (Ferri and Johnston, 'Applications of representation theory and of explicit units to Leopoldt's conjecture') as the only candidate development but could not resolve whether its case-settling result (Theorem 1.10/6.12: an infinite family of totally real S3-extensions of Q with Leo(F,p) holding for any finite set of primes P; and Theorem 1.11/Corollary 6.17: an infinite family of totally real D8-extensions with Leo(F,p) holding for all odd p <= 10^6, p != 3) was new to the March 2026 revision or already present pre-snapshot. I fetched the full text of arXiv:2301.05700v1 (submitted 13 Jan 2023, i.e. 13 days before the 26 Jan 2024 frozen revision) directly and confirmed that its abstract, introduction, and body already state and prove exactly these results (Theorem 6.12 and Corollary 6.17 in v1, word-for-word identical in content and numbering to the current v2). The only difference between v1 and v2 is that v2 reflects two years of peer review leading to acceptance in Research in Number Theory (received Feb 2024 per the journal metadata -- referring to the journal submission, not a new arXiv posting; accepted Feb 2026, published March 2026). No new mathematical content was added. Since the case-settling event (the actual mathematical result) occurred via the January 2023 preprint, before the window opened, this is classified open_stale rather than partial: the relevant progress predates the frozen revision and is recorded but not counted as a change within the measurement window. I also checked Alexandre Maksoud's related work on Leopoldt/Gross defects (arXiv:2201.08203, 'On the rank of Leopoldt's and Gross's regulator maps'), which likewise dates to January 2022 (published in Documenta Mathematica in 2023), also entirely pre-window. A broader search for any AI-related work, counterexamples, or disproofs touching Leopoldt's conjecture since 26 January 2024 turned up nothing. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the Ferri-Johnston paper (checked via multiple full-text fetches of the abstract, introduction, acknowledgements, and body) -- the methods are purely classical representation theory, Brauer/idempotent relations, and explicit unit constructions from Buchmann-Sands techniques, with one numerical unit-congruence verification done by a classical (non-ML) algorithm from a cited paper's appendix. The conjecture itself remains open for general (non-abelian, or non-CM/non-abelian-base) number fields.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'partial' rather than 'open_stale' if the March 2026 journal publication and acceptance is treated as the operative 'event' on the theory that peer review is what elevates a preprint's claims to established mathematical fact within the window. But per the dating rule (date the first public written argument, not the journal publication), and since I verified byte-for-byte that the mathematical content is unchanged between v1 and v2, I judge the actual advance occurred in January 2023, pre-window, and treat the journal acceptance as merely confirming (not adding to) already-existing progress.
what_would_settle_it: A diff between the full text of arXiv v1 and v2 (I obtained and read v1 completely, and v2's abstract/intro via a separate fetch; both show identical theorem statements) definitively settles this -- which I have done.
