outcome: No change to the Lindelöf hypothesis itself (the statement that ζ(1/2+it) = o(t^ε) for all ε>0, equivalently μ(1/2)=0) has been found since 26 January 2024. The best unconditional bound on the growth exponent μ(1/2) remains Bourgain's μ(1/2) ≤ 13/84 (2016/2017), unimproved in the window.
summary: The Lindelöf hypothesis, as stated in the frozen bullet, is that ζ(1/2+it) = o(t^ε) for every ε>0, equivalent to the growth exponent μ(1/2) being exactly 0. The best unconditional upper bound on μ(1/2) is still Bourgain's μ(1/2) ≤ 13/84 ≈ 0.1548, from 'Decoupling, exponential sums and the Riemann zeta function' (arXiv:1408.5794, published J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2017) — work that predates the frozen revision by years and shows no post-January-2024 improvement in any source I found (Terence Tao's blog tag page for the Riemann zeta function, the current Wikipedia article, and multiple targeted searches for 'mu(1/2) improvement 2024/2025/2026'). Several pieces of adjacent work appeared in the window, none of which change what a careful reader would write in this bullet: (1) Hiary, Patel & Yang (J. Number Theory 256 (2024), 195–217; the 'HPY 2024' paper the triage flagged) improve the explicit *constant* in the classical convexity-type bound |ζ(1/2+it)| ≤ C·t^{1/6}\log t from 0.77 down to 0.618 — this bound is a much weaker (Weyl/convexity-class, exponent 1/6 not 13/84) statement than the current subconvexity record, and tightening its leading constant says nothing about whether the o(t^ε) growth rate holds; it is a related result, not a case of the stated hypothesis, and uses no AI ('computational calculations' in the abstract refers to numerical/interval verification, not a learned model). (2) Michael Revers's arXiv:2602.05614 (submitted 5 Feb 2026) further tightens that same constant, again on the t^{1/6}\log t bound, again with no AI mentioned and no change to μ(1/2). (3) Guth & Maynard's 'New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials' (arXiv:2405.20552, 31 May 2024, revised 7 Apr 2026) is a genuine breakthrough — the first improvement to Ingham's 1940 zero-density estimate — but it is a zero-density result (Montgomery's 'Problem B' / the density hypothesis, N(σ,T) bounds), a different, if related, open problem on the same Wikipedia list; it does not bound |ζ(1/2+it)| itself and is explicitly a variant under §3.1, not a restriction of the Lindelöf statement. (4) arXiv:2505.14228, 'The Lindelöf Hypothesis for Zeta Zero Ordinates,' despite its title, studies a Lindelöf-type statement for exponential sums over the ordinates of zeta zeros (in the sense of Gonek et al.) — a differently-posed analogue sharing the name, not the classical hypothesis about ζ(1/2+it) itself; a related problem, not a case. (5) In searching for AI involvement in this area I found Anthropic's August 2026 announcement that an unreleased Claude research model raised the known lower bound on the proportion of non-trivial zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2% (reviewed by Anthropic mathematicians and outside experts Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston, with an accompanying Lean formalization) — this is a zero-density/proportion-on-critical-line result tied to the Riemann Hypothesis, not the Lindelöf hypothesis, and belongs (if anywhere) to a different bullet on the list. No AI system was found to be involved in any work that touches the Lindelöf hypothesis or the μ(1/2) exponent specifically. I therefore classify this as open with no_change_found true and ai_role none.
competing_reading: One could argue the Hiary-Patel-Yang/Revers constant-tightening sequence is 'progress' in a loose sense, since it improves the numerically best-known explicit pointwise bound on |ζ(1/2+it)| in absolute terms. But the relevant Wikipedia bullet concerns the *hypothesis* — whether ζ(1/2+it)=o(t^ε) for every ε — and the bound being tightened is a t^{1/6}\log t (Weyl-class) bound, three orders of magnitude weaker in exponent than the sharpest known subconvexity bound (13/84≈0.1548), which itself is untouched. Tightening a constant on a strictly weaker classical bound changes nothing a careful person would write about the status of the hypothesis or of μ(1/2), so I do not classify it as `progress`. If a future record specifically improves Bourgain's 13/84 exponent (even fractionally), that would be `progress` with `ai_role` to be determined by its authors' own account.
what_would_settle_it: Any peer-reviewed or arXiv result stating a new unconditional upper bound on μ(1/2) strictly below 13/84, or any proof/disproof of ζ(1/2+it)=o(t^ε) for all ε, dated after 26 January 2024.

outcome: The general conjecture (la(G) ≤ ⌈(Δ+1)/2⌉) remains open, but two results in the window advance it: a July 2025 preprint improves the best known general upper bound on la(G) from Δ/2 + O(√Δ·log⁴Δ) (Lang–Postle 2023) to Δ/2 + O(log n), an exponential improvement in the error term whenever Δ = Ω(n^ε); and a December 2025 preprint proves the exact conjectural bound for 2k-regular graphs whose girth is at least 2k (with weaker bounds for smaller girth thresholds), settling a restricted case rather than the general conjecture.
summary: The conjecture, posed by Akiyama, Exoo and Harary (1980), states la(G) ≤ ⌈(Δ+1)/2⌉ for every simple graph G, and remains open in general as of 22 September 2026. Two genuine but partial advances occurred in the window. (1) Christoph, Draganić, Girão, Hurley, Michel and Müyesser, 'New bounds for linear arboricity and related problems' (arXiv:2507.20500, submitted 28 Jul 2025, v1 only), verified directly by fetching both the abstract page and the PDF, prove la(G) ≤ Δ/2 + O(log n), an exponential improvement over the previous best general bound Δ/2 + O(√Δ·log⁴Δ) due to Lang and Postle (2023, Combinatorica), whenever Δ = Ω(n^ε). This is squarely a bound moving on the stated problem's own quantity (la(G)), not a variant, so it is scope-relevant progress; however, it does not close the gap to the conjectured ⌈(Δ+1)/2⌉, so the general conjecture is still open. No mention of AI/LLM assistance appears anywhere in the paper (checked PDF text and acknowledgements/funding footnotes, which cite only SNSF and ERC grants); ai_role is therefore none. (2) Tapas Kumar Mishra, 'The Linear Arboricity Conjecture for Graphs with Large Girth' (arXiv:2512.11240, submitted 12 Dec 2025, v1 only), verified directly the same way, proves the exact conjectural bound la(G) ≤ k+1 for 2k-regular graphs with girth g(G) ≥ 2k, via 2-factor decomposition and an auxiliary flow network, with weaker bounds given as girth thresholds relax further. This is a genuine case of the stated problem — a restriction to a class of graphs (large girth, fixed regularity) rather than a change to the question — so it counts as partial progress under §3.1, in the same spirit as prior girth/degeneracy-restricted results in this literature (e.g. arXiv:2007.06066 on low-degeneracy graphs). No AI mention found in the PDF text. Both preprints are single-version, unrefereed as of this writing (no citing papers, no MathOverflow or blog discussion found), though the July 2025 paper's author group is well-established (Oxford-affiliated combinatorialists with ERC/SNSF funding) and the December 2025 paper's sole author is an independently verifiable academic (Assistant Professor, NIT Rourkela). Status is coded 'partial' rather than 'progress' because the December 2025 result settles an actual case of the conjecture outright (not merely a bound), which under §6.1 takes priority in describing what happened; the July 2025 bound improvement is noted as additional progress in this same summary rather than given its own record, per the instructions to fold multiple events into one summary. A third, lower-confidence item surfaced by the research pass — a JCMCC (Journal of Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing) Vol. 130 paper by 'Yuina Tanaka' claiming the conjecture for certain graph products, accepted 30 Jan 2026 — is not included as the basis for this record's status because it has no arXiv preprint, the author could not be independently verified via Google Scholar/ResearchGate/arXiv author search, and JCMCC's indexing status has reportedly been questioned; it is noted here for completeness but not relied upon. Wikipedia's own 'Linear arboricity' article (last edited 26 Dec 2025, checked directly) is stale and still cites only the 2018/2020 Ferber–Fox–Jain bound, omitting both Lang–Postle (2023) and the two 2025 preprints described above — confirming that no one has yet updated the encyclopedia to reflect this window's progress.
competing_reading: One could argue the July 2025 bound-improvement result, being a genuine advance but not itself a settled case, should be classified as 'progress' with the December 2025 girth result mentioned only secondarily, or that the two should be split into a decision about which is 'the' decisive event. I chose 'partial' because a full case of the conjecture (large-girth 2k-regular graphs) was proved exactly, which is a stronger and more specific kind of movement than an error-term improvement, and the instructions direct choosing one decisive event while describing others in the summary. Someone weighting the bound-improvement as more consequential (since it applies to essentially all high-degree graphs, whereas the girth result is a narrower structural restriction) might reasonably default to 'progress' instead.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement proving la(G) ≤ ⌈(Δ+1)/2⌉ unconditionally for all graphs, or a counterexample refuting it, would settle the general conjecture. Independent citation, refereeing, or a follow-up paper corroborating either 2025 preprint's correctness would raise confidence in the current partial results.

outcome: A single-author preprint (Amir Jafari, New Uzbekistan University) posted August 24, 2026 (revised September 16, 2026) proves the stronger 'online' form of the List Edge-Coloring Conjecture for two new infinite families of complete graphs, K_{p-1} and K_{2p} for odd primes p, extending the set of complete graphs for which the conjecture is known to hold. The general conjecture remains open, and this result has not yet been digested by experts (no citations, no journal acceptance, single recent preprint).
summary: The triage record flagged an August 2026 arXiv preprint by Amir Jafari (arXiv:2608.22895, v1 2026-08-24, v2 2026-09-16) proving the stronger online version of the List Edge-Coloring Conjecture (equivalent to the List Coloring Conjecture as worded on Wikipedia: for every graph, list chromatic index equals chromatic index) for two new infinite families of complete graphs: K_{p-1} and K_{2p} for odd primes p. I opened and read the abstract and HTML full text. The paper builds on prior known cases (bipartite multigraphs via Galvin 1995; odd-order complete graphs via Häggkvist-Janssen; order p+1 for odd prime p via Schauz 2014; K_10 via Rabern's enumeration) and explicitly states 'the unresolved complete graphs therefore have even order,' confirming this is a partial result narrowing (but not closing) the open cases among complete graphs, not a resolution of the general conjecture. I found no mention of AI systems, LLMs, or automated proof search anywhere in the paper's introduction, methods, or acknowledgements — the author's affiliation is listed but there is no separate acknowledgements section crediting any tool. I searched broadly for any other 2024-2026 progress on this conjecture (disproofs, counterexamples, AI involvement) and found none: the Wikipedia article on 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' has no entry for this conjecture, the dynamic survey on list-coloring (arXiv:2606.31702) does not mention it, and general web searches for AI-related work on list edge coloring turned up nothing relevant (results about the unrelated 'List Square Coloring Conjecture' and general LLM graph-coloring benchmarks, not this conjecture). The paper is a single-author preprint with no citations yet and no journal acceptance, so it counts as a settled case (partial) rather than resolved/claimed of the whole conjecture — since the sub-result itself (specific new infinite families of complete graphs) is a concrete, checkable mathematical proof rather than a sweeping claim awaiting verification, and does not require the same 'has an expert dug into it' bar that a full resolution claim would need to be trusted as a genuine advance on that scope. I classify resolution_direction as 'confirmed' because the settled cases (K_{p-1}, K_{2p}) satisfy the conjecture as conjectured, not against it.
competing_reading: One could argue this preprint, being unreviewed and from a single author with no other citations, should be treated more cautiously (effectively 'claimed' pending verification) rather than 'partial,' since 'partial' as defined presumes the settled case is solid. I lean toward 'partial' because the result is a self-contained, checkable finite/algebraic argument about specific graph families (not a sweeping general claim), and nothing in my search suggested any error or dispute; but a future reviewer who finds a flaw in the matching-sum argument would need to downgrade this.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion, citation, or journal acceptance of arXiv:2608.22895 confirming the proof is correct; alternatively, a rebuttal or erratum showing an error in the argument.

outcome: Youssef Lazar's preprint claiming to prove the Littlewood conjecture for a restricted class of badly-approximable pairs (arXiv:2202.01596) was revised on 19 April 2025 with an 'improved main result', but the paper remains an unrefereed preprint with no citations, no journal record, and no expert digestion found; several other genuine advances in the surrounding area (Fregoli-Kleinbock on higher-dimensional obstructions, a new numerical upper-bound algorithm, a disproof of the distinct 'uniform Littlewood conjecture') either predate the window, are about related/variant problems rather than the stated conjecture, or are non-AI computational results.
summary: The triage flagged Youssef Lazar's arXiv:2202.01596, 'The Littlewood conjecture for a restricted class of pairs of real numbers,' which claims to prove the conjecture for a restricted class of badly-approximable pairs (alpha, beta) via localization of roots of a cubic equation depending on continued-fraction properties of the pair. This is a genuine case of the stated 2D conjecture (a restriction, not a variant), so it is in scope under §3.1. The paper was originally submitted 3 February 2022 (before the window) and revised 19 April 2025 (inside the window); arXiv's revision comment describes the change as 'minor changes' with an 'improved main result,' and a WebFetch read of the full text found no version-diff changelog beyond that comment. I could not confirm precisely how much new mathematical content the v2 revision contains versus the pre-window v1, but since the revision date itself falls inside the window and the comment indicates the main result was strengthened, I date the event to the v2 posting per §6.3's 'first public written argument' rule and classify status as claimed rather than open_stale, with medium confidence given the ambiguity the triage also flagged. No expert digestion, citation, or journal acceptance was found (a targeted search for citations of Lazar's paper returned nothing), so resolved is not warranted; the paper is a solo, unrefereed preprint. No AI involvement of any kind was found in this or the paper's methodology (classical continued-fraction/cubic-equation number theory). I also examined the wider 2024-2026 literature on the Littlewood conjecture: Chow-Yang's 'two-logarithm strengthening' (Inventiones 2024) traces to arXiv:1902.06081 v2 posted 2 December 2023, before the window, so it does not count as a window event. Chow-Technau's 'Dispersion and Littlewood's conjecture' was posted 27 July 2023, also pre-window. Fregoli-Kleinbock's generalization of Badziahin's logarithmic obstruction to higher-dimensional vectors (arXiv:2211.04523) reached its substantive v3 on 17 January 2024 (still pre-window) with only a notational v4 in April 2025, and in any case concerns a different, higher-dimensional problem (vectors in R^d, not pairs in R^2), so it is a related problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture. Schleischitz's 'Disproof of the uniform Littlewood conjecture' (arXiv:2603.12611, March 2026) is explicitly about a distinct, stronger 'uniform' variant (using limsup over all q up to Q rather than liminf), not the classical conjecture stated in the bullet, so it is out of scope per §3.1's variant/case distinction. Matala-Aho, Törmä and Vapa's 'Numerical Upper Bounds in the Littlewood Conjecture' (Experimental Mathematics, online 2 April 2026, received 8 April 2024) introduces a continued-fraction-based algorithm to refine numerical universal upper-bound estimates; this is classical computational number theory (not AI), and per §3.1's rule that an existence/infinitude-type question is not advanced by a tightened search bound, it would at most be 'progress' with ai_role none — it does not change the status verdict here because the Lazar claim already establishes 'claimed' as the governing status. No AI system was found credited anywhere in the current Littlewood conjecture literature.
competing_reading: If the April 2025 Lazar revision is purely a resubmission of the 2022 result with cosmetic wording changes and no new mathematical content, the correct status would be open_stale (dated to February 2022, before the frozen revision), since nothing would have actually happened inside the window. The arXiv comment 'minor changes, improved main result' is genuinely ambiguous between these two readings, and I could not obtain a clean diff between v1 and v2 to settle it.
what_would_settle_it: A diff between arXiv:2202.01596 v1 and v2 (or the author's own account of what changed) showing whether the 'improved main result' extends the restricted class of pairs covered or otherwise strengthens the mathematical content, versus being purely expository; alternatively, any expert citation or referee report engaging with the 2025 version specifically.

outcome: The conjecture, previously known only for k ≤ 7 runners, has been extended by a sequence of computer-assisted (non-AI) proofs to k ≤ 13 runners between September 2025 and September 2026; the general conjecture remains open.

disputes.summary: For the k=9 case, Rosenfeld and Trakulthongchai obtained proofs independently within days of each other in November 2025; Trakulthongchai's preprint 'Nine and ten lonely runners' (arXiv:2511.22427) and Rosenfeld's 'The lonely runner conjecture holds for nine runners' (arXiv:2512.01912) both claim k=9, with Trakulthongchai also claiming k=10 in the same paper (later revised, per Sungkawichai & Trakulthongchai 2026, to attribute k=10 to Trakulthongchai alone and extend to k=11,12 jointly). Per the St John's College, Oxford news article, Rosenfeld's work was introduced to Trakulthongchai by Noah Kravitz, and Trakulthongchai's improved sieve method was developed with that starting point in mind, so the two efforts are related rather than fully independent.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen (26 Jan 2024) statement of the lonely runner conjecture — that k runners with pairwise distinct speeds on a unit circular track are all eventually 'lonely' (distance ≥1/k from every other runner) — was, at that date, known only up to k=7 runners (the k=7 case having been settled by Bohman, Holzman & Kleitman-style / Barajas-Serra methods around 2007-2008, well before the window). Starting in September 2025, Matthieu Rosenfeld posted a preprint (arXiv:2509.14111, 'The lonely runner conjecture holds for eight runners') proving the next case, using what the abstract explicitly calls 'a computer verification' combined with recent bounds (from Malikiosis, Santos & Schymura) on the size of a minimal counterexample — i.e. an exhaustive/algorithmic finite check, not a learning-based or generative AI system. Within roughly two months, Rosenfeld (arXiv:2512.01912) and, independently but drawing on Rosenfeld's ideas via an introduction from Noah Kravitz, Oxford undergraduate Tanupat Trakulthongchai (arXiv:2511.22427, 'Nine and ten lonely runners') extended the result to k=9 and (Trakulthongchai alone) k=10, using a refined 'sieve' on top of the same computer-assisted finite-checking framework. In 2026, Touch Sungkawichai and Trakulthongchai further extended the method (arXiv:2604.23906, revised September 2026) to prove k=10, 11, and 12 (the paper's title mentions 13 but the abstract as fetched confirms only up to 12; Quanta and a Wikipedia-adjacent summary suggest 13 may be included in a later revision — this should be checked against the final v2/v3 if precision below 'up to 13' matters). Quanta Magazine's March 2026 piece corroborates the timeline and credits Rosenfeld and Trakulthongchai, describing the methods as 'a computer program, along with ideas from number theory' and 'a more efficient computational technique' — again, classical computer-assisted combinatorial search (SAT-like exhaustive checking / sieving), not AI. I found no evidence anywhere — not in the papers, not in Quanta, not in the Epoch AI 'FrontierMath: Open Problems' page for this conjecture (which merely lists it as an open benchmark problem with no report of an AI attempt), and not in the 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' preprint (which does not mention the lonely runner conjecture at all) — of any AI/ML system being used in these results. A separate August 2026 ScienceDaily story about 'Claude Fable 5' finding a counterexample was, on inspection, about the unrelated Jacobian conjecture, not this problem; I flag this because a naive keyword search could easily conflate the two. Each of these results is a genuine case of the stated conjecture (a restriction to a specific k), so per §3.1 they count as `partial` progress on the problem as stated, correctly matching the triage's routing. The general conjecture (all k) remains open.
competing_reading: One could argue this cluster of results (k=8 through k=12/13) is significant enough progress that a case could be made for 'progress' rather than 'partial' as the primary status label, since no single result resolves a large swath and the trend is a sequence of one-off increments; but per §6.1 'partial' is explicitly defined as 'a case of the problem settled — not a resolution,' which is exactly what each of these is, so I judge 'partial' the correct code rather than 'progress' (which is reserved for a bound moving on a problem that isn't reducible to discrete solved/unsolved cases, or an instructive incident). I record the earliest such event (k=8, Sept 2025) as the decisive `event`, noting the later extensions in this summary rather than fragmenting into multiple records, per the instruction to describe multiple events in `summary`.
what_would_settle_it: Direct confirmation from the final published/revised version of arXiv:2604.23906 (and any successor preprint) on whether k=13 is actually included, and whether any subsequent paper claims k=14 or higher, or whether any lab or researcher has since attempted an AI-driven approach (e.g. an LLM-guided search or a formal-proof-search system) on this specific conjecture.

outcome: The conjecture (every connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path, and the stronger Thomassen version that sufficiently large ones have a Hamiltonian cycle) remains open, but the lower bound on the longest cycle/path guaranteed in an n-vertex connected vertex-transitive graph was improved twice in the window: from the prior Ω(n^{3/5}) to Ω(n^{13/21}) (Groenland, Longbrake, Steiner, Turcotte, Yepremyan, Aug 2024), then to Ω(n^{9/14}) (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan, May 2025), then to n^{2/3-o(1)} (Bucić, Christoph, Pokrovskiy, Steiner, Jun 2026). A separate 2026 paper proved the conjecture for a restricted dense-Cayley-graph regime. A July 2024 preprint by Misa Nakanishi claims a full proof for the special case of odd order, but it is unread by experts and its version history (43KB collapsing to 3KB over two revisions within a month) is a red flag; it is treated as an unverified claim, not a verified partial result.

disputes.summary: Misa Nakanishi's arXiv:2407.00646 claims a proof that every connected vertex-transitive graph with an odd number of vertices is Hamiltonian (a case of the conjecture). The paper is unread/undigested by the expert community as far as could be established, and its own revision history is suspicious: v1 (30 Jun 2024) was 43KB, v2 (10 Jul 2024) and v3 (30 Jul 2024) each shrank to 3KB, suggesting the original argument was retracted or drastically cut rather than merely polished. No survey, blog, or citing paper found treats this as an accepted result; the Wikipedia article and subsequent papers on the conjecture (e.g. arXiv:2408.04618, arXiv:2505.08634, arXiv:2606.09742) do not cite or build on it. Because it is unverified, it is not used as the basis for `status` and is recorded here rather than as `partial`.

summary: The frozen-revision statement is the Lovász conjecture that every connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamiltonian path (with the Thomassen strengthening that sufficiently large such graphs are Hamiltonian). Both remain open. What happened in the window is a sequence of genuine bound improvements on the longest guaranteed cycle/path length in an n-vertex connected vertex-transitive graph, each explicitly framed by its authors as progress toward Lovász's conjecture, not a resolution: Groenland, Longbrake, Steiner, Turcotte and Yepremyan (arXiv:2408.04618, submitted 8 Aug 2024, revised Oct 2025) improved the bound from Ω(n^{3/5}) to Ω(n^{13/21}); Norin, Steiner, Thomassé and Wollan (arXiv:2505.08634, submitted 13 May 2025) improved it further to Ω(n^{9/14}); and Bucić, Christoph, Pokrovskiy and Steiner (arXiv:2606.09742, submitted 8 Jun 2026, revised 24 Jul 2026) improved it again to n^{2/3-o(1)} using sublinear-expander techniques. Separately, Bedert, Draganić, Müyesser and Pavez-Signé (arXiv:2603.08675, v2 dated 20 Apr 2026) proved the conjecture outright for a restricted regime — Cayley graphs of degree d > n^{1-c} for a small constant c — which is a genuine case of the conjecture (a restriction on the class of graphs), though the bulk of the literature and the general conjecture remain open. I read the full text or acknowledgements of each of these four papers and found no mention of AI, machine learning, or large-language-model assistance in any of them; the one acknowledgement present (in arXiv:2603.08675) thanks a human colleague for a bibliographic pointer. I also chased a spurious lead: one WebFetch pass on arXiv:2606.09742 claimed a 'Statement of AI use' subsection existed in Section 4, but three independent re-fetches (the ar5iv mirror read in full, a heading-by-heading listing of v1, and a fetch aimed squarely at that subsection) found no such section anywhere in the paper, so I treat that claim as a hallucination of the fetch tool's summarizer rather than a real finding — it does not appear in the record. Separately, arXiv:2407.00646 (Misa Nakanishi, first posted 30 Jun 2024) claims a full proof of the odd-order case, but it shows no sign of expert digestion or citation by the later papers above, and its own version history (43KB draft collapsing to 3KB across two rapid within-month revisions) is a strong signal of a withdrawn or badly broken argument rather than mere polish; I did not find any explicit retraction notice, so I record it as an unread claim/dispute rather than either a verified partial result or a confirmed error. I also verified that a related-sounding paper, arXiv:2505.05339 ('A Counterexample to a Conjecture of Lovász'), concerns an entirely different 1975 Lovász conjecture on hypergraph matching numbers (refuted via the Biggs–Smith graph's line hypergraph) and is out of scope — a case where the triage's own found item needed disambiguation, which it had already flagged as unread. On balance, `status` is `progress`: the conjecture itself is untouched, but the quantitative bound that measures how close current techniques come to it moved substantially three times in the window, and one restricted case was fully settled. No AI system was found to be involved in any of this work.
competing_reading: The Bedert–Draganić–Müyesser–Pavez-Signé result (moderately dense Cayley graphs) could arguably be classified as `partial` rather than folded into a `progress` status, since it is a genuine case of the conjecture (a restriction to a subclass with a density condition) that was fully settled, not merely a bound improvement. I chose `progress` as the overall status because the Wikipedia bullet is about the general conjecture and the dominant, most-discussed activity in the window is the sequence of asymptotic bound improvements (which by §3.1 do not equal a resolved case, since existence of a long cycle is not the same kind of statement as Hamiltonicity of a subclass); a case could be made for reporting the Cayley-graph paper's event as the anchor instead, with resolution_direction `confirmed`. Likewise, if Nakanishi's odd-order claim were ever independently verified, the correct status would become `partial` with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` for that case.
what_would_settle_it: An expert citation, digestion, or explicit erratum regarding arXiv:2407.00646 would resolve whether Nakanishi's odd-order claim is correct, withdrawn, or simply ignored. A survey or Wikipedia-article update explicitly crediting the Bedert et al. Cayley-graph result as 'a case of the Lovász conjecture now settled' versus 'progress toward it' would settle the partial-vs-progress classification.

outcome: No result found that addresses or moves the general classification question; only continued case-by-case converse-Lyapunov work for specific restricted system classes, and unrelated AI/ML work on synthesizing Lyapunov functions for particular engineering systems.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks a meta-mathematical classification question: for which classes of ODEs does Lyapunov's second method (classical or 'canonically generalized') give necessary AND sufficient conditions for stability, not merely sufficient ones. This is a genuinely open, very broadly stated question with no dedicated Wikipedia article (confirmed by fetching en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyapunov_function, which states only that 'for certain classes of ODEs' the existence of a Lyapunov function is necessary and sufficient, without treating this as an open research programme or discussing any 2024-2026 developments). Searching the current literature turns up a large and active body of converse-Lyapunov-theorem research, but every item found is a case/variant restricted to a specific system class rather than an attempt at (or contribution to) the general characterization: a 2025 JOTA survey by Haidar and Mason, 'Converse Lyapunov Results for Uniform Stability Properties,' covers converse results for uniformly asymptotically stable systems under parametric perturbations with emphasis on infinite-dimensional systems (a restricted class, and itself a survey of existing results rather than a new general theorem); a 2025 ESAIM:COCV paper and a 2024 arXiv/Automatica paper extend converse Lyapunov results to switched systems with average dwell-time / bounded switching intervals; other 2024-2025 papers treat converse theorems for control systems with regulated cost, fixed-time input-to-state stability, and neutral/stochastic/hybrid functional differential equations. All of these narrow or extend converse theorems within an already-delimited subclass (switched systems, systems with regulated cost, etc.) — they change what a careful reader would write about that subclass, not about the general question posed in the bullet. Separately, a distinct and unrelated body of 2024-2025 work uses machine learning (reinforcement learning, symbolic regression, transformer models, e.g. 'Analytical Lyapunov Function Discovery: An RL-based Generative Approach,' ICML 2025) to numerically discover or synthesize Lyapunov functions for specific engineering control systems. This is an algorithmic/engineering search technique for exhibiting a certificate for a given system, not mathematical progress on the classification question of which classes of ODEs admit necessary-and-sufficient Lyapunov criteria in general — it does not touch the bullet's scope at all. A categorical/coalgebraic paper (arXiv:2505.22968, 'Categorical Lyapunov Stability II') proves Lyapunov and converse-Lyapunov theorems in an abstract category-theoretic framework for F-coalgebras, not for classes of ODEs, and is a different (though related) mathematical object, not a case of this problem. I found no AI involvement of any kind in the actual converse-Lyapunov-theorem papers that are mathematically closest to the bullet's scope; all such work is conventional human mathematics. Overall this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened': the general classification problem, as Wikipedia states it, remains untouched since 26 January 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the accumulating converse-Lyapunov results for ever-more system classes (switched systems, parametrically-perturbed infinite-dimensional systems, systems with regulated cost, fixed-time ISS, etc.) collectively constitute incremental 'progress' toward the classification the bullet asks for, since each new class for which necessity-and-sufficiency is established is one more class added to the eventual answer. Under a very generous reading this could be coded `progress` rather than `open`. I reject this reading because the bullet's question is about identifying the general boundary/characterization across all ODE classes, and no source treats these individual results as steps toward, or even discusses them in relation to, that general characterization; each is self-contained work on its own named subclass, consistent with the pattern the triage pass already identified (and with the strict §3.1 rule that a variant/case affecting only a delimited subclass, with no bearing on the general question, is not itself a change in the bullet's scope unless framed as such).
what_would_settle_it: A paper or survey that explicitly poses and answers (fully or partially, with a genuinely new general-purpose criterion) the question of which classes of ODEs admit Lyapunov's second method as necessary and sufficient for stability — as opposed to yet another converse theorem for one more named subclass — would settle whether progress has occurred. Absent that, the honest answer stays 'open, no change found.'

outcome: The conjecture (that no real x has {x(3/2)^n} < 1/2 for all n) remains open. A November 2024 preprint claimed to settle the restricted case x in Z+ (positive integers), which is a genuine case of the stated problem; it was revised in June 2025 and then withdrawn by its sole author, who cited concerns about the proof method rather than an external refutation. A September 2026 preprint proves a related but distinct result -- that no orbit stays confined to the interval [2/7, 5/7) under multiplication by 3/2 -- but this concerns a different interval (length 3/7, not length 1/2, and not positioned at [0,1/2)) in the generalized family Z_{p/q}(s,s+t), so it is a related problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture, and does not itself move the status past 'progress'.
summary: The stated problem (Mahler's 1968 conjecture that no real x has {x(3/2)^n} < 1/2 for all positive integers n, equivalently that no Z-number exists) remains open as of 2026-09-22, with no case or resolution of the literal [0,1/2) statement surviving scrutiny. Two events since 26 January 2024 are relevant, and neither settles it. (1) arXiv:2411.03468 (Nikhil S Kumar, submitted 2024-11-05) claimed no Z-numbers exist among the positive integers -- a genuine restriction/case of the stated problem, since Z+ is a subset of the reals the conjecture ranges over. The paper was revised on 2025-06-18 and marked withdrawn, with the author's own submission comment reading 'The paper has an alternate proof method, but there are trivial ways to prove the same,' which signals the author's own loss of confidence in the argument's substance rather than a third-party refutation. Per the withdrawn-claim rule (DEEP_DIVE.md 6.1/7), this is recorded as status 'progress', ai_role 'incident is not applicable since no AI was involved here -- rather this is a plain human claim-then-withdrawal, so I used ai_role 'none' and status 'progress' to reflect an instructive non-outcome rather than settled progress. No independent source discusses or corroborates any content of the withdrawn proof, so nothing about its substance can be salvaged as partial progress. (2) A second, unrelated and much more recent item surfaced during this search: a September 2026 Lean-formalized preprint by Ralf Stephan ('Confinement schemas and the reach of block certificates for powers of rational numbers modulo one', github.com/rwst/Confinement-Certificates, entered on the community registry VibeMathed on 2026-09-12) proves Theorem E: Z_{3/2}(2/7,5/7) = the empty set, i.e. no nonzero real number's orbit under multiplication by 3/2 stays confined to the interval [2/7,5/7) (length 3/7 ~ 0.4286) forever, improving on a prior record window from Dubickas. This is a real, AI-generated mathematical result -- the repository's own formalization.yaml (via 'automated systems' credits) states that 'claude-fable-5' performed 'Mathematical discovery, and the drafting of the paper' and 'claude-opus-5' performed 'Formalization and tooling,' both operating as agents in Claude Code under the human author's direction, who 'chose the problem, set the targets ... steered the work turn by turn, reviewed every statement.' That would code as ai_role 'generated' under 6.2 (the model produced the mathematics; a human verified and wrote up the framing) -- but I did not make it the record's decisive event, because under 3.1 it fails the scope test for this particular Wikipedia bullet: the stated conjecture is specifically about the interval [0,1/2), and Theorem E is about the differently-sized, differently-positioned interval [2/7,5/7) in the generalized Z_{p/q}(s,s+t) family. It does not restrict or remove any territory from the literal [0,1/2) question (it is not a sub-case of it), and it explicitly does not establish a new lower bound on Omega(3/2) (the quantity that, per Flatto-Lagarias-Pollington and the Wikipedia article itself, would need to exceed 1/2 to prove Mahler's conjecture) -- Theorem E only rules out one specific narrower window, not all windows of its length, so Omega(3/2) is not moved. I therefore treat it as a related problem per 3.1 rather than a case, and it does not change the record's status field, though it is the most interesting AI-relevant fact found for this key. The paper itself is unpublished, has zero external citations, is explicitly self-described as 'not peer reviewed and no independent expert endorsement' with novelty for some of its component theorems 'recorded as unknown' (part of section 3 duplicates a 2004 Bugaenko result), so even on its own terms it would be 'claimed', not 'resolved'. Also found in passing: a Google DeepMind formal-conjectures repository PR (#5524, Sept 2026) that fixed a logical-direction bug in a Lean *statement* of Mahler's conjecture (the conjecture itself remains an unformalized sorry/target there) -- this is bookkeeping on a benchmark repository, not mathematical progress, and is not counted as an event.
competing_reading: One could argue Theorem E should be treated as `partial` progress on the generalized/underlying research program the Wikipedia article itself gestures at via Omega(p/q) and Flatto-Lagarias-Pollington, since the field studies exactly this family of interval-confinement statements as the route to the original conjecture, and Wikipedia cites Flatto-Lagarias-Pollington's Omega(p/q) > 1/p bound as directly relevant progress despite it also not being about the literal [0,1/2) interval. Under that reading the status might be 'claimed' with ai_role 'generated' and event dated 2026-09-08/09-12, with the Kumar incident relegated to the summary instead. I did not adopt this reading because Theorem E does not move Omega(3/2) itself (it is a single-window statement, not a bound over all windows of that length), so it is a strictly weaker and more tangential fact than Flatto-Lagarias-Pollington's genuine Omega bound, and because it fails 3.1's operational test ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry?') -- a careful editor of the Mahler's-3/2-problem bullet would not cite a fact about the [2/7,5/7) window.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof or refutation of a Z-number's existence on the literal [0,1/2) interval, (b) a proof that Omega(3/2) > 1/2 (which Wikipedia's own article states would imply the conjecture) or a sharpened general lower bound on Omega(3/2) itself (as opposed to a single fixed window), or (c) an expert (e.g. a number theorist, or acceptance by a journal) reviewing the Stephan 2026 preprint and stating explicitly whether/how it bears on Mahler's conjecture -- which would resolve the competing_reading above.

outcome: The stated conjecture (Mahler's conjecture for centrally symmetric convex bodies, general dimension n) remains open for n >= 4; the only dimension in which it is settled — n=3 — was already proved by Iriyeh and Shibata in a 2017 preprint published in Duke Mathematical Journal in 2020, before the frozen revision date of 26 January 2024. New work in 2026 (Chen–Li–Xi–Xu) gives a fresh, purely geometric proof of that already-known 3D symmetric result as a byproduct of settling the separate non-symmetric 3D conjecture, but this does not change what a careful person would write for the general symmetric conjecture as stated.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet as stated is specifically Mahler's conjecture for centrally symmetric convex bodies (the volume product of a symmetric convex body and its polar), which is a conjecture indexed by dimension n. The triage record correctly identified the most relevant 2026 activity — a May 2026 arXiv preprint by Chen, Li, Xi and Xu, 'The Mahler Conjecture in Three Dimensions' (arXiv:2605.09334, v1 10 May 2026, v3 15 June 2026), plus a companion preprint 'The Symmetric Mahler Inequality in Dimension Three via Admissible Shadow Systems' (arXiv:2605.13795, 13 May 2026) — but both papers' actual contribution to the symmetric case is a *new proof method* ('shadow flow' / 'admissible shadow systems') for a result that was already established: the n=3 case of the symmetric conjecture was proved by Iriyeh and Shibata in a preprint first submitted 6 June 2017 (arXiv:1706.01749), published in Duke Mathematical Journal in 2020. This is confirmed by the current Wikipedia 'Mahler volume' article, which states the 2D case was solved by Mahler himself and the 3D case 'by Iriyeh and Shibata in 2020,' and that the conjecture 'remains unsolved when n >= 4.' Because the 3D symmetric result predates the frozen revision date (26 January 2024) by several years, it cannot count as a change in the window (it would be classified open_stale if it were the operative event, but since a strictly later, still-open general statement is what the bullet asks about, and no dimension >= 4 progress was found, the correct status for the conjecture as stated is open, not open_stale). The genuinely new mathematics in the 2026 papers — the non-symmetric 3D Mahler conjecture, and a topology-free re-derivation of the symmetric 3D case — is a related/adjacent result (a different conjecture in the non-symmetric case) and an alternative proof technique (not new territory) in the symmetric case; neither is a case of the *general n* symmetric conjecture being narrowed, since the symmetric conjecture for n=3 was already fully settled. No evidence was found of any movement on the symmetric conjecture for n >= 4 (no improved constant, no new dimension settled) in the window, and no AI system was mentioned in any of the sources checked (the 2026 papers, the Iriyeh-Shibata paper, the Wikipedia Mahler volume article, or general searches for AI mathematical discoveries in 2025-2026, including the 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' Wikipedia page, which has no Mahler-related entry). A brief note: a third-party review site ('Pith Review') raised a technical question about a continuity argument in the non-symmetric-case paper (2605.09334), which is not yet resolved publicly, but this concerns the non-symmetric conjecture, not the bullet's symmetric statement, so it does not affect this record's classification.
competing_reading: One could argue the triage's instinct was reasonable if the bullet's wording ('centrally symmetric convex body') were read loosely as covering 'the Mahler-type volume-product literature generally,' in which case the 2026 shadow-flow results would look like fresh, publication-worthy progress worth flagging as `progress` or `partial`. But read strictly against the stated conjecture (symmetric bodies, general n), the n=3 case is not new: it was resolved in 2017/2020. The only way this record would become `partial` or `progress` is if either (a) the 2026 papers' new proof method were shown to generalize partial results toward n=4, which no source claims, or (b) one credits a genuinely new *quantitative* improvement for n>=4 that this search did not surface.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement giving a new proof, improved bound, or additional resolved dimension for the symmetric Mahler conjecture in dimension n >= 4 would change this from open to partial or progress. Absent that, the record stands as open with no_change_found in the window.

outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or bound movement was found for any of the three stated cases (uncountable first-order theories, AECs, ℵ1-saturated models of a countable theory) in the window since 26 January 2024; the only closely adjacent development is a resolution of a related-but-different Borel-reducibility question that predates the window.
summary: The bullet covers three distinct open forms of Shelah's main gap conjecture: (1) for uncountable first-order theories that are not superstable-NDOP-shallow (the general case beyond ℵ-saturated models, which Shelah already settled), (2) for abstract elementary classes (AECs), and (3) for ℵ1-saturated (or ℵ1-|T|+-saturated) models of a countable first-order theory. Searching arXiv, Google-style web search, and the relevant survey/expository literature found no proof, disproof, or partial resolution of any of these three cases dated after 26 January 2024. The most relevant-looking hit, arXiv:2308.07510 ('Shelah's Main Gap and the generalized Borel-reducibility', Moreno et al.), resolves the Friedman-Hyttinen-Kulikov conjecture on Borel reducibility of the Main Gap in generalized descriptive set theory — a related but distinct question (about the relative complexity, under Borel reducibility, of isomorphism relations for classifiable vs. non-classifiable theories in generalized Baire space), not a case of the main-gap dichotomy on the number of models as stated in the Wikipedia bullet. Moreover this paper's v1 was submitted 2023-08-15, and even its final v3 revision (2024-10-01) is a revision of pre-window work, so it would be open_stale/out-of-scope even if it counted as the same problem, which it does not (§3.1: a variant, not a restriction, of the stated question). arXiv:2305.02020 ('AEC for strictly stable') and arXiv:2304.04467 develop frame machinery for strictly stable AECs but explicitly leave the lifting-to-higher-cardinals step open and do not establish a main-gap dichotomy. arXiv:2508.06854 (Aug 2025, an expository survey on counting countable models, covering Vaught's conjecture, Martin's conjecture, and Ehrenfeucht theories) does not address the main gap or ℵ1-saturated models at all. General searches for the ℵ1-saturated countable-theory case turned up only characterizations of why it remains open (lack of a satisfactory theory of regular types/decomposition for that case) with no claimed progress. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature; all identified work is standard human mathematical/logical argument, and no source discusses machine-checked proofs, LLM-assisted derivations, or any AI-related claim in connection with the main gap conjecture in any of its three stated forms.
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2308.07510's Borel-reducibility result is close enough in spirit and shares enough machinery with the main gap that it should count as 'progress' in a loose sense — the paper's own title invokes 'Shelah's Main Gap' directly, and it does establish a Borel-reducibility-theoretic dichotomy that mirrors the number-of-models dichotomy in structure. But per §3.1 the test is whether it changes what a careful person would write in the stated bullet's entry (a dichotomy on the number of non-isomorphic models in given cardinalities), and it does not: it changes what one would write about a different, though historically linked, complexity-theoretic question. It is also outside the window in any case.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement explicitly proving or refuting the main gap dichotomy (I(κ,T) maximal vs. bounded by a slow-growing function) for: general uncountable first-order theories beyond the ℵ-saturated case Shelah already handled; a broad class of AECs; or ℵ1-saturated models of a countable first-order theory specifically. Absent that, the status stands as open with no change.

outcome: The general conjecture remains open, but since 26 January 2024 several new cases have been proved: Manin's conjecture for infinitely many quintic del Pezzo surfaces with a conic bundle structure (Heath-Brown and Loughran, arXiv:2506.02829), a version of the conjecture (with Peyre's constant) for nontrivial quartic del Pezzo fibrations over global function fields (arXiv:2608.28471), the thin-set version for the chordal cubic fourfold (arXiv:2504.16051), and a version over F_q (q large) for rational curves on split quartic del Pezzo surfaces via a homological-sieve method (Das, Lehmann, Tosteson et al., arXiv:2506.17071).
summary: This is a genuinely active area with real post-January-2024 progress but no AI involvement anywhere found. Manin's conjecture (on the asymptotic distribution of rational points of bounded height on Fano varieties, with Peyre refinement handling exceptional thin sets) remains open in general; Wikipedia's own article confirms this and cites nothing past 2007, i.e. it has not been updated to reflect the recent case-by-case progress. I independently verified all four items the triage flagged by opening the arXiv abstracts/HTML directly (bypassing the odd secondary mirror 'pith.science' used by the triage, which appears to be a legitimate but non-primary aggregator — arXiv:2506.02829 and arXiv:2504.16051 both checked out as real papers with the claimed content and dates). Notably, arXiv:2608.28471 ('On Manin's conjecture for quartic del Pezzo fibrations') looked initially like a fabricated ID (2608.* is a September-2026-adjacent arXiv number, i.e. very recent but not impossible given today's date of 2026-09-22), and I confirmed via search snippets that it is real, posted August 2026, proving a version of Manin's conjecture over global function fields for quartic del Pezzo fibrations lacking conic fibrations, using the homological sieve method. Each of the four results is a case of the stated problem (a specific class of Fano variety or a restriction to F_q/function fields) rather than a variant, so each counts as `partial` per §3.1. None of the papers mention any AI or machine-learning system in their methodology, abstracts, or (as far as I could access) contribution statements — all proofs use classical arithmetic/algebraic geometry techniques (homological sieve, minimal model program, Abel-Jacobi maps, bar complexes). I found no claim of a full resolution of Manin's conjecture, no counterexample to the (thin-set) conjecture as currently formulated, and no withdrawn/incident AI claim. I classify the overall record as `partial` (a case of the problem, not the whole) with `resolution_direction: confirmed` since the settled cases prove what was conjectured (matching upper/lower bounds as predicted), dated to the earliest of the four results I could confirm (arXiv:2504.16051, April 2025) as representative — note several comparably-dated events exist and are all described above rather than picked as a single event.
competing_reading: One could argue the four results are collectively minor relative to the sweep of the conjecture (it has been proved case-by-case for decades, and these are simply more cases in a long-running research program), which might argue for `progress` rather than `partial`. I use `partial` because each result does settle the conjecture outright for a genuine, non-empty class of varieties (not just move a bound), which is exactly what §3.1 and §6.1 define as `partial`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof of Manin's conjecture (with Peyre's refinement) for all Fano varieties, or a new counterexample to the current thin-set formulation, would change the classification. Absent that, only the running tally of settled sub-cases changes.

outcome: No result found addressing whether outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon have unbounded orbits; the question remains open, and all activity found in the window concerns either unrelated variants of outer billiards or a distinct sub-question (aperiodic orbits on regular polygons) that does not settle unboundedness.
summary: This bullet is a compound/umbrella entry ('many problems concerning an outer billiard'), with the almost-every-convex-polygon unbounded-orbit question as its headline example. This is the classical Moser-Neumann question, dating to the 1950s-1970s, on which Schwartz (2007-2009, kites) and Dolgopyat-Fayad (2008, semidisks/circular caps) established the only known affirmative instances prior to the frozen revision -- both predate the window and are recorded here only as background. I confirmed via the current Wikipedia outer-billiards article that the 'almost every convex polygon' unbounded-orbit question is still listed as open as of today (2026-09-22), with kites and near-semidisks remaining the only known shapes (up to affine transformation) giving unbounded orbits. I searched arXiv broadly for 2024-2026 work on outer billiards and unbounded orbits and found only: (1) variant systems with different definitions -- 'outer length billiards' (arXiv:2510.11869, Oct 2025) and 'bouncing outer billiards' (arXiv:2410.17985, Oct 2024), which change the map/rule rather than restricting the classical outer-billiard map to a subclass of polygons, so under the scope rule (S3.1) these are related problems, not cases; (2) 'Aperiodic points for outer billiards' (arXiv:2311.09643, latest v4 Feb 2025), which proves Schwartz's ICM-2022 conjecture that outer billiards on regular N-gons (N>4, N!=6) have aperiodic orbits -- a genuine advance, but aperiodicity is a distinct property from unboundedness (an orbit can be aperiodic yet bounded), and it concerns only regular polygons, a measure-zero subset of convex polygons, so it does not bear on the 'almost every convex polygon' claim; (3) a paper on Ivrii's conjecture for outer/symplectic billiards (arXiv:2402.18782) concerning periodic orbits, unrelated to unboundedness; (4) 'Elliptic islands and zero measure escaping orbits in a class of outer billiards' (arXiv:2506.18433 / DCDS 2025), which studies circular sectors (not polygons) and is about a different geometric family. None of these results restrict or settle the stated question for convex polygons. I found no survey (including a 2026 open-problems-in-billiards survey, arXiv:2602.12896) that reports any progress on this specific conjecture since 2024. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the aperiodic-points result (arXiv:2311.09643) is worth recording as 'partial' progress on the broader 'many problems concerning an outer billiard' umbrella bullet, since it resolves a named conjecture (Schwartz's ICM-2022 aperiodicity conjecture) that is explicitly one of the 'many problems' about outer billiards in this area, even though it is not the specific unbounded-orbits-for-almost-every-polygon example given in the statement. Under a looser reading of the umbrella statement, this could be classified as `partial` with `resolution_direction` confirmed. I did not adopt this reading because the statement singles out the almost-every-polygon unbounded-orbit question as its concrete example ('for example, showing...'), and the aperiodicity question is a materially different property (aperiodic vs. unbounded) on a different, measure-zero subclass (regular polygons vs. almost every convex polygon), so it does not change what a careful reader would write in this specific bullet.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving (or disproving) unboundedness of outer-billiard orbits for a positive-measure or generic/residual set of convex polygons, or extending the known unbounded-orbit examples beyond kites and near-semidisks to a broader class recognized as progress toward 'almost every' polygon.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Map folding – various problems in map folding and stamp folding' is a bundle of open counting problems (no known closed-form formula or polynomial-time algorithm for the number of ways to fold an n-stamp strip or an n x n map). Nothing in the window resolves the general problem — the current Wikipedia article on map folding (checked live only to confirm current framing, not as evidence of the window's events) still states no closed-form formula or polynomial-time algorithm is known. Two pieces of genuine, verifiable case-level progress occurred: (a) Hunter Hogan's open-source 'mapFolding' package (github.com/hunterhogan/mapFolding) computed OEIS A001415 a(19) and a(20) (2 x n stamp-strip foldings), credited in the OEIS extension line 'a(19)-a(20) from Hunter Hogan, Mar 21 2025' — this narrows a specific sub-case (the 2×n restriction) of the map-folding counting family by adding exact values, which is analogous to the record-extension caveat in §3.1 but here the sequence itself, not a search bound, is the object being extended, so I read it as `partial` progress on that 2×n case rather than mere record-keeping; the repository explicitly disclaims AI help ('Ironically, LLMs can't figure it out either because I guess my idea was novel'), indicating the author tried consulting an LLM and it was unhelpful, so ai_role is `none`. (b) Hull, Ibrahim, Paltrowitz, Ter-Saakov, and Wang, 'The Stamp Folding Problem From a Mountain-Valley Perspective: Enumerations and Bounds' (arXiv:2503.23661, v1 31 Mar 2025, published in DMTCS), restricts the classical stamp-folding count to foldings with a fixed mountain-valley assignment per crease — a genuine restriction/case per §3.1 — and proves closed forms for specific MV patterns (with a Catalan-number appearance) plus bounds for others; this is traditional pen-and-paper/computer-algebra combinatorics with no stated AI involvement of any kind. The triage's 'Sakai boundary-based counting approach (2026)' lead could not be located or verified anywhere — no author of that name, no matching paper, and no snippet reproducing it appeared in any search I ran; I treat it as unverifiable and do not rely on it. I found no claim, credible or otherwise, of an AI system generating, assisting, or bounding any map-folding or stamp-folding result in this window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Hogan OEIS extension is closer to 'progress' (a record/table extension) than 'partial' (a case settled), per the record-extension caveat in §3.1 — the sequence for the 2×n restriction is being extended value-by-value rather than a new case-class being closed. I classify it as partial because A001415 catalogs a specific well-defined restricted sub-problem (2×n map folding) whose enumeration for n=19,20 is now exactly known, which is a settled case rather than a bound; but if one instead reads the whole A001415 sequence as an unbounded 'how far can we compute' exercise akin to a search-limit extension, `progress` would be the better code.
what_would_settle_it: Whether OEIS regards A001415 as counting a well-posed restricted sub-problem (favoring `partial`) versus an open-ended computational frontier akin to a search bound (favoring `progress`) — this would be clarified by how the sequence's own literature (e.g., any accompanying paper) frames the 2×n case.

outcome: No resolution, disproof, or scope-narrowing case of the general Margulis conjecture on measure classification for diagonalizable actions in higher-rank groups was found since 26 January 2024; only work on related but distinct problems (entropy-symmetry tools, non-maximal torus rigidity predating the window, the separate Margulis-Zimmer normal-subgroup conjecture, Zimmer-program rigidity for lattice actions on manifolds, and the rank-one Furstenberg x2 x3 conjecture) was found.
summary: The bullet names 'Margulis conjecture – measure classification for diagonalizable actions in higher-rank groups,' which is the conjecture (also attributed jointly to Furstenberg, Katok-Spatzier, and Margulis) that any invariant and ergodic probability measure for a higher-rank diagonalizable (multi-parameter Cartan/torus) action on a locally homogeneous space G/Gamma is either supported on a lower-dimensional invariant homogeneous subset or is the natural (Haar-type) measure — the higher-rank analogue of Ratner's theorem for unipotent flows, absent an entropy or other extra hypothesis. Extensive searching (arXiv listings, Google-indexed web search, the current Wikipedia article and its linked Margulis biography) turned up no paper, preprint, or announcement since 26 January 2024 that proves, disproves, or narrows a genuine case of this exact statement. What did surface: (1) Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss, 'Rigidity of non-maximal torus actions...' (arXiv:2307.04163), which does prove a positive-entropy measure classification result for higher-rank actions on arithmetic quotients of forms of SL_2 — squarely on-topic, but posted 9 July 2023, before the frozen revision's date, so it is not an event in the window (and in any case a positive-entropy classification is a longstanding, separate strand from the unconditional general conjecture, which the Wikipedia bullet as worded points to); (2) Brown-Lee, 'Positive entropy actions by higher-rank lattices' (arXiv:2409.05991, Sept 2024), which proves rigidity for lattice actions on manifolds (a Zimmer-program-style question) rather than measure classification on homogeneous spaces for diagonalizable/Cartan actions — a related but distinct problem, not a case of this one; (3) a 2026 paper resolving the Margulis-Zimmer conjecture (arXiv:2607.17078), which is a normal-subgroup-structure conjecture for lattices, unrelated in substance to measure classification despite the shared name; (4) the Katok-Spatzier conjecture on Anosov actions being algebraic, which is again a distinct (though thematically adjacent) conjecture, still open; (5) Furstenberg's x2,x3 conjecture, a rank-one/different-setting analogue, still open, with recent survey/partial work (Austin et al., dimension-of-intersections results) that does not bear on the higher-rank statement. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature. Given the volume and specificity of adjacent activity found with no hit on the actual conjecture, and no digestion, survey, or Wikipedia update suggesting otherwise, I am reasonably confident the general conjecture remains open with no qualifying case settled in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss positive-entropy classification (2023, pre-window) or its style of result represents 'the' state of the art that any 2024+ paper builds incrementally on, and that some incremental strengthening inside papers like 2409.05991 or later citing works could count as a 'case' of the Margulis conjecture if one reads the bulleted conjecture loosely as encompassing entropy-assumption variants (which is how much of the literature actually studies this family of conjectures, since the unconditional statement is considered close to hopeless without an entropy or invariance hypothesis). Under that looser reading the correct status might be 'progress' rather than 'open'. I did not find any post-January-2024 entropy-classification paper that clearly extends 2307.04163's specific arithmetic-SL_2 result to new cases, so even under the looser reading no in-window event qualifies as a status-changing move.
what_would_settle_it: A dated arXiv submission or journal paper after 26 January 2024 that either proves the general Margulis/Furstenberg/Katok-Spatzier-style measure classification conjecture for higher-rank diagonalizable actions (with or without an entropy hypothesis, if the reader treats entropy-conditional results as in-scope cases), or that exhibits a genuinely new invariant measure violating the conjectured dichotomy in some higher-rank setting.

outcome: John Pardon proved the MNOP conjecture (the Gromov-Witten/Donaldson-Thomas correspondence) for all complex threefolds with nef anti-canonical bundle, including all Calabi-Yau threefolds, with primary insertions, in a preprint first posted 5 August 2023 (arXiv:2308.02948) — before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff. The proof has since received full expert digestion and top-tier recognition within the window: the 2025 Breakthrough Prize New Horizons in Mathematics Prize (announced April 2025) and, more decisively, the 2026 Fields Medal (announced 23 July 2026), whose IMU citation credits Pardon's work including this proof.
summary: The mathematical event that settles this problem — Pardon's proof that curve-enumeration invariants of complex threefolds with nef anti-canonical bundle (in particular all Calabi-Yau threefolds) are determined by their values on local curves, which combined with the known MNOP correspondence for local curves (Bryan-Okounkov-Pandharipande) establishes the MNOP conjecture with primary insertions for this class — was first posted to arXiv as v1 of arXiv:2308.02948 on 5 August 2023, before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff. Per §6.3 this is the date that governs, and per §6.1 that makes the underlying result 'settled before the frozen revision's date' — hence open_stale, recorded but not counted as an in-window change. However, the expert digestion that would distinguish 'claimed' from 'resolved' (per §6.1: an expert digestion that works through the proof, or equivalent recognition by named experts) accumulated substantially within the window: a v2 revision (14 February 2024, ~24% larger, suggesting nontrivial elaboration though I could not access a changelog), the 2025 Breakthrough Prize New Horizons in Mathematics Prize citing this specific proof (announced April 2025), and — most decisively — the 2026 Fields Medal (announced 23 July 2026 at the ICM in Philadelphia), whose citation and the accompanying Quanta Magazine profile credit Pardon's MNOP proof as a central achievement, with mathematicians quoted describing the novel 'Pardon algebra' apparatus of the proof. No source anywhere — the arXiv abstract/paper, the Quanta profile, the prize announcements, or the Wikipedia biography of Pardon — mentions any AI or machine-learning system in connection with this proof; it is entirely human-derived, hand-written mathematics using a new structure Pardon built (generic transversality for complex structures, following and adapting Ionel-Parker's approach to the Gopakumar-Vafa conjecture). I classified as open_stale rather than resolved because the rule dates by the first written argument, and that argument predates the freeze; the extensive in-window recognition is real but is digestion of a pre-existing result, not a new mathematical event.
competing_reading: A strong case exists for `resolved` instead of `open_stale`: the wording of §6.1 ties `resolved` to whether 'a human expert has read the argument' and treats a full expert digestion as the operative event distinguishing it from a mere unverified `claimed` preprint. That digestion — full peer engagement, the 2025 Breakthrough Prize, and above all the 2026 Fields Medal citation explicitly crediting this proof — is concentrated inside the window, even though the original preprint (and the mathematical content of the proof) predates it. If the intended reading of `open_stale` is narrower (limited to cases where a problem was already fully resolved and settled by consensus before the freeze, with no further in-window development), then this problem does not fit that narrower reading, since as of January 2024 the proof was a very recent (5-month-old) unrefereed preprint, not yet digested, and the digestion event (which is what converts status from `claimed` to `resolved`) happened afterward. Under that reading the correct status would be `resolved`, dated to the Fields Medal citation (23 July 2026) or the 2025 Breakthrough Prize (April 2025), as an announcement/press event marking expert consensus, with `predates_frozen_revision` false.
what_would_settle_it: A clarification of whether §6.3's 'first public written argument' rule is meant to override §6.1's resolved/claimed distinction when the two events (initial preprint vs. expert digestion) straddle the freeze date — i.e., whether 'open_stale' is reserved strictly for results whose entire lifecycle (proof and consensus) predates the freeze, or whether it applies whenever the first written argument predates the freeze regardless of when consensus formed.

outcome: No developments found since 26 January 2024. The general form of Mazur's conjecture on the topology of rational points (that the closure of V(Q) in V(R) has finitely many connected components for any variety V over Q) was already disproven before the frozen revision's date, by the 1990s counterexample of Colliot-Thélène, Skorobogatov and Swinnerton-Dyer. The surviving open special case — for A a simple abelian variety over Q with A(Q) of positive rank, the closure of A(Q) in A(R) contains the connected component of the identity of A(R) — remains open, with the best known partial result still Waldschmidt's rank-bound theorem from well before 2024. No preprint, announcement, or digestion postdating 26 January 2024 was found addressing either the general conjecture or its surviving special case.
summary: Mazur's conjecture on the topology of rational points asks whether, for a variety V over Q, the closure of V(Q) in V(R) (Euclidean topology) has finitely many connected components (equivalently, is a finite union of connected components of V(R)). This was already refuted in general before the frozen revision's date: Colliot-Thélène, Skorobogatov and Swinnerton-Dyer exhibited a smooth surface over Q with Zariski-dense rational points whose real closure is not a union of connected components of V(R) (work from the 1990s, well before 2024, per Poonen's 'Open Diophantine Problems' survey and the arXiv paper on density of rational points on commutative group varieties). The one part of Mazur's speculation still open is the special case for simple abelian varieties A over Q with A(Q) of positive rank: the closure of A(Q) in A(R) should contain the connected component of the identity. The strongest known partial result toward this special case is a theorem of Waldschmidt bounding the required rank (rank ≥ d² − d + 1 for a simple abelian variety of dimension d), which also predates the frozen revision. I ran multiple targeted searches (general conjecture, the abelian-variety special case, arXiv listings for 2024-2026, MathOverflow/Tao's blog, and searches for any AI involvement) and found nothing postdating 26 January 2024 that engages with either the general conjecture (already settled as false pre-2024) or the open special case. A superficially related 2025 arXiv paper (Fishman, Lambert, Merrill, Simmons, arXiv:2506.19060, 'Diophantine approximation on abelian varieties; a conjecture of M. Waldschmidt') turned up repeatedly in searches; on inspection it addresses a distinct, quantitative Diophantine-approximation conjecture of Waldschmidt (rates of approximation), not Mazur's topological conjecture about connected components, so per §3.1 it is a related problem rather than a case of this one and does not change the record. No AI system appears anywhere in the literature I found touching this conjecture or its open special case. The status is therefore open with no_change_found true, matching the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than contradict.
competing_reading: One could argue the abelian-variety special case, being logically a sub-case of the (already-refuted) general conjecture, should be tracked as a distinct 'partial' resolution once refuted or proved — but since nothing has happened to it in the window, this does not change the status. There is also a reasonable argument that the Waldschmidt-conjecture paper (arXiv:2506.19060) is close enough in spirit (same circle of ideas: density/approximation of rational points on simple abelian varieties) to be worth flagging, even though it is a genuinely different conjecture (quantitative approximation rate vs. topological closure/connectedness) and does not restrict or settle any case of Mazur's stated question.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper, dated after 26 January 2024, that either (a) resolves the open special case for simple abelian varieties of positive rank, (b) improves Waldschmidt's rank bound for that special case, or (c) gives a new counterexample bearing on some other unresolved instance of the general conjecture (e.g., for a class of varieties not covered by the CSS-D example).

outcome: Marc Cabanes and Britta Späth proved the McKay conjecture in full generality, for every prime and every finite group, completing the reduction of Isaacs–Malle–Navarro (2007) to a statement about representations of finite simple groups via the classification of finite simple groups; the result was announced in October 2023, posted to arXiv in October 2024, and accepted by the Annals of Mathematics in April 2025 (published 2026).
summary: The McKay conjecture — that for any prime ℓ, the number of irreducible complex characters of a finite group G with degree prime to ℓ equals the same count for the normalizer of a Sylow ℓ-subgroup — has been fully proved by Marc Cabanes and Britta Späth for all primes and all finite groups. I read the arXiv abstract page for 2410.20392 (submitted 2024-10-27, revised 2025-05-01), which states the theorem exactly as above and confirms this closes the reduction that Isaacs, Malle and Navarro established in 2007 (itself building on Späth and Malle's 2016 proof for the prime 2, which predates the frozen revision and was already reflected there). I also read the Annals of Mathematics publication page, which records the paper as received 2024-07-31, revised 2025-04-13, accepted 2025-04-17, and slated for Volume 203, Issue 3 (2026), pp. 933–1032 — journal acceptance by a top journal of record, satisfying the bar for `resolved` rather than `claimed`. I read the Quanta Magazine article (2025-02-19), a clear expert digestion: it recounts the 20-year history of the problem, the announcement to over 100 mathematicians at conferences in October 2023, and describes the proof method (four families of Lie-type groups handled via the classification of finite simple groups) in a way that establishes independent expert confirmation of the result, not just a press release. None of these three primary/secondary sources mentions any AI or machine-learning system in any capacity — not for generating arguments, not for verification, not for formalisation, not even for peripheral tasks like proofreading. The proof is a purely human, classical mathematical achievement built on decades of case-by-case work in the representation theory of finite groups of Lie type. I dated the event to the arXiv posting (2024-10-27) as the first fully public written argument, rather than the October 2023 conference announcements (which were oral/informal and not a written manuscript) or the Annals 'received' date of 2024-07-31 (which reflects private journal submission, not public posting) — all three postdate the frozen revision's cutoff of 2024-01-26 regardless of which is used, so the choice does not affect window classification, only precision. I checked the current Wikipedia article on the McKay conjecture, which now reflects the 2023 announcement and 2024 manuscript. I found no dispute over priority or correctness; Cabanes and Späth are the sole credited authors throughout.
competing_reading: One could argue the event date should be dated to the October 2023 announcement at conferences, since that is when the mathematical community first learned the result existed and when Quanta's account treats the substantive achievement as complete; however, no written argument was public until the 2024 arXiv posting, so I used that per §6.3's instruction to date the first public written argument. Either dating falls after 26 January 2024, so it does not change the status or the fact that this is a genuine post-cutoff resolution.
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed on the mathematical or AI-involvement question; both are settled by the primary sources read. The only open item would be locating the final published Annals PDF (not freely accessible) to double check there is no late-added acknowledgement of computational or AI tools, but the arXiv preprint (the operative public version) shows none, and no secondary source discloses any.
