outcome: No change to the McMullen problem (ν(d), the largest number such that any point set in general position in R^d admits a projective transformation into convex position) was found since 26 January 2024; the bounds 2d+1 ≤ ν(d) < 2d + ⌈(d+1)/2⌉ remain as established by Larman (1972) and Ramírez Alfonsín (2001), and the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 remains open for d≥5.
summary: The triage flagged a possible AI connection because a November 2025 AlphaEvolve paper (Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864, 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale') tests AlphaEvolve on a list of 67 problems in analysis, combinatorics, geometry and number theory, and search summaries speculated the McMullen problem might be one of them. I resolved this directly: the paper's companion repository (github.com/google-deepmind/alphaevolve_repository_of_problems) numbers its 68 problem pages (67 problems plus one split into two logic-puzzle pages), and I fetched the title of every single one (problems/1.html through 68.html). None of them is the McMullen problem or any close variant. The list covers Kakeya/Nikodym sets, autocorrelation and Sidon-set problems, sphere/circle packing, kissing numbers, Sendov/Schmeisser/Borcea/Crouzeix conjectures, the Heilbronn problem, the Erdős–Szekeres Happy Ending problem, the moving sofa problem, and others — but nothing on projective transformations of point sets into convex position or on ν(d). The triage's speculation is therefore refuted, not confirmed. Separately, I found one genuinely relevant piece of scholarship in the window's neighborhood: 'On k-neighborly reorientations of oriented matroids' (Knauer et al., arXiv:2306.00414; published European Journal of Combinatorics 2024), whose abstract explicitly frames the k=1 case as 'the original statement' of McMullen's problem and generalizes to k≥2. I fetched the paper's HTML rendering and confirmed it proves no new result for k=1 (the actual McMullen problem as stated in our bullet) — for k=1 it only restates the existing bound from reference [6] (Ramírez Alfonsín 2001) — and its new bounds and computer-verified cases (ν(5,2), ν(6,2), ν(7,3), etc.) are all for k≥2, a different, changed question (k-neighborly polytopes rather than plain convex position). Under §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated problem, so it does not count as progress here even though it is squarely about 'McMullen's problem' in the broader literature sense. Its v1 predates the frozen revision (June 2023) and its v2 (Feb 2024) is a minor revision shortly after; since the paper is out of scope regardless, the exact dating is moot. No source anywhere disclosed any AI/ML involvement in either the AlphaEvolve-repository check or the oriented-matroids paper (the latter mentions only 'by computer' exhaustive verification, i.e. classical computation, not an AI system). Wikipedia's own 'McMullen problem' and 'Convex position' articles both confirm the bounds are unchanged since 2001 and cite no post-2024 developments. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced no-change case: the natural AI-related lead was checked exhaustively and closed out negative, and no non-AI progress on the exact stated problem surfaced either.
competing_reading: One could argue the k-neighborly reorientations paper 'is' progress on McMullen's problem in a loose sense, since the literature commonly calls the whole family (all k) 'McMullen's problem' or its generalizations, and the paper explicitly invokes McMullen's name. But our bullet's statement is specifically the k=1 convex-position question, and the paper leaves that exact case exactly where it was (citing the 2001 bound, no new result), so under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 it is a variant (changing k) rather than a case (restricting the same question), and I classified it as out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint stating a new bound on ν(d) itself (k=1) for some or all d, or a resolution of the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 in any dimension d≥5, dated after 26 January 2024. Also, direct examination of the AlphaEvolve paper's full results tables (not just problem titles) would remove any residual doubt that a McMullen-adjacent problem was folded into one of the 68 listed under a different name — though the titles I retrieved (covering packing, autocorrelation, moving sofa, Erdős–Szekeres, etc.) leave essentially no ambiguity that convex position / projective transformation of point sets is simply not among them.

outcome: In a September 2026 autonomous evaluation run, a pre-release version of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra produced a Lean 4-verified disproof of the K=1 case of Smale's mean value conjecture (the exact statement given in this bullet, which has no free K and thus asks for K=1), exhibiting a polynomial p with p(0)=0, p'(0)=1 for which no critical point c satisfies |p(0)-p(c)|/|0-c| ≤ |p'(0)|. The proof is machine-checked but has not yet been read or endorsed by a human expert in complex analysis, so it is best classified as claimed rather than resolved.

ai.basis_quote: the Lean proof itself was written by GPT-6 Astra ... No human saw or steered the proof search. ... The proof was produced in the evaluation run wikipedia-vega-1000usd of Epoch AI's LeanOpenProblems harness (2026-09), in which a pre-release version of GPT-6 Astra attempted, autonomously and once each, all 222 research-open statements of the Wikipedia collection of Formal Conjectures under a budget of $1,000 and 96 hours of working time per statement.
ai.disclosed_cost: Attempts used 0.19 million input, 4.2 million output, 64 million cache-read and 12.4 million cache-write tokens, costing $432 at GPT-6 Astra's standard rates (within a $1,000 / 96-hour budget for the run).

counterexample.object: A complex polynomial p of very large, unspecified degree with p(0)=0, p'(0)=1, such that |p(c)/c| > 1 at every critical point c of p — i.e. at z=0 no critical point c satisfies |p(0)-p(c)| ≤ |p'(0)||0-c|. Constructed non-constructively via analytic approximation, disk-exclusion arguments and perturbation theory rather than exhibited with explicit roots.
counterexample.verified_how: Machine-checked in Lean 4 (Mathlib), with the repository's 'Comparator' tool checking that the formalized challenge statement matches the informal one and that the proof depends only on standard axioms (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice).

summary: Wikipedia's frozen bullet states the mean value problem with no free constant, i.e. it asks exactly the K=1 case: does every degree-≥2 complex polynomial f admit a critical point c with |f(z)-f(c)| ≤ |f'(z)||z-c| for every z? Smale proved this holds with the constant 4 in place of 1, and K=1 (the sharp conjectured constant) remained open as of the frozen revision. In September 2026, Epoch AI ran its LeanOpenProblems harness (evaluation 'wikipedia-vega-1000usd') giving a pre-release build of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra one autonomous, unsteered attempt at each of 222 open statements from a Wikipedia-derived collection in the 'Formal Conjectures' benchmark (arXiv:2605.13171, github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems), with a $1,000/96-hour budget per problem. For the mean value problem, the model produced a Lean 4-verified disproof of the K=1 case: a polynomial p with p(0)=0, p'(0)=1 at which every critical point c has |p(c)/c|>1, so the inequality fails at z=0 for K=1. This is published, with the Lean source, at github.com/tadamcz/mean-value-problem, directed by Tom Adamczewski, who states the repository was machine-written and that no human saw or steered the proof search. I independently confirmed: (1) GPT-6 Astra is a real OpenAI model released 2026-09-03/04 (multiple independent press sources: Al Jazeera, 9to5Mac, CNBC, OpenAI's own site and system card); (2) Epoch AI's LeanOpenProblems/Formal Conjectures infrastructure is real and documented in an arXiv paper and a GitHub org distinct from the tadamcz repo; (3) a sibling repository from the same evaluation run (tadamcz/koethe, disproving a case of the Köthe conjecture) corroborates that this was a batch run over many problems, not an isolated fabrication; (4) the registry whataifound.org, which specifically tracks AI mathematical claims, has an entry for this exact result and explicitly grades it 'Claimed' rather than 'Formally verified,' citing that it is 'days old at entry, unrefereed, with no expert in complex analysis on record as having read it,' that the witness polynomial has unspecified large degree and violates the bound only marginally (consistent with Smale's own K=4 bound), and that 'no third party has audited the statement against the literature.' Wikipedia's own live article header, by contrast, already reads 'disproved in 2026' and files the problem under solved problems — which is a stronger claim than the evidence I could verify supports, since a Lean type-check verifies internal consistency of the formalization, not that the formalization is a faithful rendering of Smale's informal conjecture (the repo itself flags that Lean's convention x/0=0 makes the formal statement 'if anything weaker' than the informal one, a discrepancy that if anything favors the disproof being valid, but one no complex-analysis expert has publicly signed off on). Given DEEP_DIVE.md §6.1's rule that a machine-checked certificate no expert has reviewed is 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' even when the check is clean, I classify this as claimed. Separately, and unconnected to any AI system, arXiv:2608.27047 (Oct 2026 preprint) proves the K=1 bound holds asymptotically for Schlicht-normalized polynomials with slowly decaying leading coefficients as degree d→∞ — a human-authored partial/asymptotic result on a restricted class, superseded in significance by the general disproof but worth noting as a second, independent line of work on the same problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'resolved' rather than 'claimed': Wikipedia's own live article now states the conjecture was 'disproved in 2026' and categorizes it as solved, and the proof is machine-checked against standard Lean/Mathlib axioms with a comparator tool verifying the formalization matches the informal statement, which is about as strong a guarantee as a proof-assistant check can offer for an unrefereed result. If one treats 'the Comparator confirmed the formalization is faithful' plus 'Wikipedia's own article treats it as solved' as sufficient digestion, 'resolved' would be defensible. I did not take this reading because no source I found shows a human complex-analysis expert who has actually read and endorsed the mathematical argument (as opposed to the machine check), and whataifound.org's registry — built specifically to track this class of claim — explicitly withholds 'Formally verified' status pending exactly that.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a complex-analyst's blog post, a Terence Tao-style writeup, or peer-reviewed publication/proceedings acceptance) confirming the Lean formalization faithfully captures Smale's K=1 conjecture and that the counterexample construction is sound, which would move the status from claimed to resolved.

corrections.by: hand review directed by a human reviewer (Alex Fogelson) and drafted on that instruction by Claude (claude-opus-5-5); not the researching agent and not any automated pass. Judged from this record's own findings and general knowledge of the field; no new sources were opened
corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, WITH DOUBT OF A SPECIFIC KIND. Scope is right: the disproof targets K = 1, the exact statement in the bullet. The risk is not the proof but the statement it proves. The Lean check is clean, so if the formal statement matches Smale's conjecture the result stands; the usual failure for an unsteered model working from a formal-conjectures statement is a mistranslated hypothesis (quantifier order over critical points, the degree condition, or the normalisation), which a kernel cannot catch. That matters more here than usual, because numerical evidence strongly supports K = 1 in low degree, and no human complex analyst has read either the construction or the formal statement. It stays `claimed`; what would settle it is a person comparing the Lean statement against Smale's, line by line.

outcome: No progress on the general n-vertex conjecture: the best known general upper bound on cop number remains n/2^{(1-o(1))√(log n)}, established independently by Lu-Peng and Scott-Sudakov (and Frieze-Krivelevich-Loh) in 2011, unimproved as of September 2026. All post-January-2024 work found either addresses restricted graph classes (algebraic/Cayley graphs, bounded vertex cover, diameter two), a hypergraph analogue, or uses machine learning to predict (not prove) cop numbers on small graphs — none of these change what should be written in the general conjecture's bullet.
summary: Meyniel's conjecture (cop number of a connected n-vertex graph is O(√n)) remains fully open for general graphs as of September 2026. The current Wikipedia 'Cop number' article confirms the best known general upper bound is still n/2^{(1-o(1))√(log n)}, the 2011 Lu-Peng/Scott-Sudakov(/Frieze-Krivelevich-Loh) bound; even the weaker 'soft Meyniel conjecture' (some constant c<1 with cop number O(n^c)) is unresolved. I checked every item the triage pass surfaced plus additional searches. 'On the cop number and the weak Meyniel's conjecture for algebraic graphs' (arXiv:2303.05381, v2 revised 2025-04-28, published EJC 2025) proves the *weak* Meyniel conjecture (cop number O(n) with a good constant, not O(√n)) for Cayley sum/generalized Cayley/twisted Cayley sum graphs — a different, weaker statement restricted to algebraic graph classes, not a case of the stated conjecture. 'Cops and robber in graphs with bounded vertex cover number' (arXiv:2602.07435, submitted 2026-02-07) proves a sublinear bound (k/2^{(1-o(1))√(log k)}) in terms of vertex cover number k rather than n — a genuinely different parameterization (a graph can have bounded vertex cover with unbounded n), so this is a related problem, not a restriction of the n-vertex conjecture. 'On Meyniel's Conjecture in Random Hypergraphs' (arXiv:2606.27066, submitted 2026-06-25) proves an analogous statement for hypergraphs, not the graph conjecture, and contains no AI-involvement disclosure. A 2026 paper, 'Predicting The Cop Number Using Machine Learning' (arXiv:2602.16600, submitted 2026-02-18), trains gradient-boosted trees and GNNs to predict (not prove) cop numbers of small graphs (≤13 vertices) with ~94-98% accuracy as a computational aid; its only substantive mention of Meyniel's conjecture is noting that the GNN's low false-positive rate for high cop numbers is desirable for avoiding spurious apparent counterexamples during search — it does not claim, find, or move toward any counterexample, and does not touch the proven bound. No AI system produced, checked, or contributed to any mathematical result bearing on the general conjecture. I also note (but exclude as non-primary) a GitHub PR (graph-theory-AI/graph-conjectures#10) that catalogs Meyniel's conjecture on a conjecture-tracking website with an 'AI-generated status review' summarizing existing literature; this is a secondary aggregation tool, not primary mathematical research, and its own AI use is limited to writing a literature summary, not to any mathematics that appears in a result.
competing_reading: One could argue the vertex-cover-bounded result is 'a case' of the general conjecture in a loose sense, since bounding a different graph parameter is philosophically similar to bounding n. But vertex cover number and n are genuinely different quantities (a star graph has vertex cover 1 but arbitrary n), so a bound in terms of vertex cover does not restrict or settle any instance of the O(√n) question as stated; it is a related/parameterized problem, consistent with how the triage pass and §3.1 treat it.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement proving or improving the general upper bound n/2^{(1-o(1))√(log n)} for all n-vertex connected graphs (moving it closer to O(√n)), or one exhibiting an explicit family of graphs with cop number ω(√n) (a counterexample), would change this record's status.

Each generation of AlphaEvolve was tasked with evolving a program representing a search heuristic... disputes.summary: Four separate AI systems from different groups (Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve, Together AI's EinsteinArena agents, Yuksekgonul et al.'s TTT-Discover, and Ye et al.'s SimpleTES) each claimed a new record upper bound within roughly a nine-month window (June 2025 to April 2026), each explicitly framed as beating the immediately preceding AI record. The exact chronological order between TTT-Discover's 0.380876 and TogetherAI's 0.380871 was not fully pinned down from primary timestamps; the current Wikipedia article and SimpleTES blog post both treat SimpleTES's 0.380868 as the most recent and tightest.

summary: This is a bound-type bullet (asymptotic constant c = lim M(n)/n for Erdős's 1955 minimum overlap problem), so under §3.1 a bound moving counts directly, and it moved several times. Before the frozen revision the state was: lower bound 0.379005 (White, arXiv 2201.05704, Jan 2022) and upper bound 0.380926 (Haugland 2016, 'The minimum overlap problem revisited', arXiv 1609.08000) — both pre-2024 and unchanged in the window as far as the lower bound goes. Starting mid-2025 a chain of AI systems repeatedly tightened the upper bound: Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., arXiv 2506.13131, submitted 16 June 2025) evolved a search-heuristic program that discovered a 95-piece step-function construction giving upper bound 0.380924, the first upper-bound improvement since 2016; the paper's own account (quoted in ai.basis_quote) describes AlphaEvolve evolving the search heuristic itself, with the paper's acknowledgements crediting mathematicians Javier Gomez Serrano and Terence Tao only with suggesting/formulating the problem, not with producing the construction — so this is `generated`, not merely `assisted`. Subsequently, Together AI's EinsteinArena agents produced 0.380871 (repository last updated 1 April 2026, 'purely obtained by AI agents'); Yuksekgonul et al.'s TTT-Discover (arXiv 2601.16175, test-time RL fine-tuning of an LLM) found an asymmetric 600-piece step function giving 0.380876, explicitly reported as surpassing AlphaEvolve's 0.380924 and verified by an outside human expert (Prof. Davide Torlo) who confirmed the bound but did not himself produce it; and Ye et al.'s SimpleTES (arXiv 2604.19341, using only the open-source gpt-oss-120b/20b models) reached 0.380868, described on the authors' own blog as ahead of the best human (0.380927), AlphaEvolve (0.380924), and TogetherAI (0.380871). All of these are upper-bound improvements on a problem that remains fully open (no exact value of the constant is known), so status is `progress` rather than `resolved`/`claimed`/`partial` — nothing was proved to be exactly true or false, a number simply moved, repeatedly. I used the earliest well-documented event (AlphaEvolve, June 2025) as the anchor `event` since it is the first AI-driven change from the pre-2024 baseline; the later improvements (TogetherAI, TTT-Discover, SimpleTES) are described in this summary rather than given separate records, per the instruction to keep one decisive event per record. `resolution_direction` is null because `progress` never takes a direction. `ai_role` is `generated` for all four systems on the authors' own accounts: in each case the construction itself (the step function achieving the bound) was produced by the AI system, with humans only verifying it, suggesting the problem, or running verification notebooks — none of the sources describe a human producing part of the mathematical content that ended up in the winning construction.
competing_reading: One could argue AlphaEvolve's role is closer to `assisted` since it 'evolved a search heuristic' rather than directly outputting the final numeric construction, and since named mathematicians (Gomez Serrano, Tao) were involved in problem formulation. But the paper is explicit that the program AlphaEvolve evolved is what searched for and found the improved construction — the humans' contribution was posing/formalizing the problem, not producing part of the mathematics in the result, which under §6.2 keeps this at `generated` rather than `assisted`. Also arguable: since four different AI systems each improved on the last with no single 'the' event, one could treat this as `open` with a `bound` role for the whole sequence rather than `progress`/`generated`; I judged AlphaEvolve's initial jump (first improvement since 2016) as the anchor `generated` event because it produced the qualifying construction itself, with `ai_role` describing that first and clearest case, and the subsequent chain narrated in `summary`.
what_would_settle_it: A primary-source timestamp resolving the exact order of the TTT-Discover (0.380876) and TogetherAI (0.380871) results relative to each other, and confirmation of whether any newer AI or human result has superseded SimpleTES's 0.380868 since April 2026.

outcome: The general MLC conjecture (is the Mandelbrot set locally connected everywhere?) remains fully open, but Dudko and Lyubich's proof of MLC at Feigenbaum-type (period-doubling and complex-tripling) parameters — a preprint already posted before the window — was published in a refereed journal (Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS, vol. 143, pp. 97–141, online 2 June 2026) during the window, and a further special-case extension (Kahn–Kapiamba–Lyubich, 'MLC for parabolically bounded primitive renormalization', June 2026) newly settled MLC for another class of renormalizable parameters.
summary: Two distinct events fall inside the window, both extending — not resolving — the MLC conjecture. First, Dudko and Lyubich's 'MLC at Feigenbaum points' (arXiv:2309.02107, v1 Sep 2023, v2 Dec 2023 — both before the frozen revision) received a v3 revision on 29 Dec 2025 and was then formally published, with a DOI and page numbers, in Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS vol. 143 (2026), pp. 97–141, online 2 June 2026 (confirmed by directly fetching the journal's article page). This upgrades the paper's status from preprint to expert-vetted (peer-reviewed, published in a top journal), so I record it, but the underlying mathematical result — MLC at Feigenbaum-type period-doubling and complex-tripling parameters — was already circulating before 26 January 2024 and is not itself a new event in the window; only its formal publication is. Second, and squarely inside the window on its own preprint date, Kahn, Kapiamba and Lyubich posted 'MLC for parabolically bounded primitive renormalization' (arXiv:2606.27272, submitted 25 June 2026, directly fetched), proving a priori bounds and local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set for a further class of infinitely renormalizable parameters (primitive renormalization type, approaching the cusp of M) using new tools (Thin-Thick Decomposition, Value Calculus, Wanderers Theorem, Wave Lemma). This is a genuine new case of MLC settled within the window — a restriction of the stated question to a specific parameter class, which is squarely a 'case of the problem' under §3.1, not a variant. Neither paper claims, nor is treated by any source as claiming, the general MLC conjecture (local connectivity of the entire Mandelbrot set). Wikipedia's live article and a Dec 2025 ICM 2026 survey by Dudko (arXiv:2512.24171, ICM survey, ~confirmed via search, framed explicitly as consolidating 'recent developments' rather than a resolution) both state the general conjecture is still open. No credible AI/LLM/automated-theorem-proving involvement was found in any of this work: the Dudko-Lyubich and Kahn-Kapiamba-Lyubich papers were directly checked (acknowledgements/full text) and contain no AI attribution; a crowdsourced Lean-formalization tracker (Prove2Me) lists MLC as an open target with no claim of AI-driven progress on it. I classify the record as 'partial' with 'confirmed' direction because the settled pieces (Feigenbaum-type and now parabolically-bounded-primitive-renormalization parameters) are additional territory carved out of the open general conjecture in the direction the conjecture predicts (local connectivity holds at these parameters), not a refutation.
competing_reading: One could argue this record should be 'open_stale' rather than 'partial', on the grounds that the only work whose mathematical content predates the window is the Dudko-Lyubich Feigenbaum result (posted Sept/Dec 2023), and that its 2026 journal publication is a purely bureaucratic event that shouldn't count as the decisive event. Under that reading the decisive event would instead be the June 2026 Kahn-Kapiamba-Lyubich paper alone, which is what I used to date `event` — so the two readings converge on the same status ('partial') and event date; the disagreement would only be about whether to also cite the IHÉS publication as a second, independent event. I chose to include it because it is itself dated inside the window (per §6.3, journal publication is normally excluded as a lagging indicator, but here the preprint's own underlying claim already existed before the window, so the publication date is the first point at which this specific fact — MLC proven and vetted at Feigenbaum points — became an established, expert-checked event) rather than to avoid double-counting a single underlying mathematical result under two dates.
what_would_settle_it: Direct confirmation (already obtained) of the IHÉS publication date and DOI, and of the Kahn-Kapiamba-Lyubich arXiv submission date, both independently fetched and cross-checked above; no further evidence is needed to settle the classification.

outcome: No resolution, disproof, or new case of the monomial conjecture (mixed-characteristic, dimension > 3) was found in the window 26 January 2024 to 22 September 2026; the conjecture remains open beyond Hochster's equicharacteristic proof and Heitmann's mixed-characteristic dimension-3 proof.
summary: I searched for any resolution, disproof, or newly-settled case of Hochster's monomial conjecture (the general mixed-characteristic case, dimension > 3, remains open; it is known in equicharacteristic by Hochster's original proof and in mixed characteristic dimension ≤ 3 by Heitmann) since 26 January 2024. Multiple searches for a proof, disproof, or extension to higher dimension in mixed characteristic turned up only pre-2024 literature (Hochster's and Heitmann's own papers, the 'Monomial Conjecture and Order Ideals' papers, the almost-Cohen-Macaulay-via-Fontaine-rings paper) and several 2024-2026 papers on adjacent homological conjectures in mixed characteristic — 'δ-rings, perfectoid towers, and lim Cohen–Macaulay sequences' (arXiv:2509.06527, Sept 2025) and 'Remarks on some Homological Problems regarding Infinite Integral Extensions' (arXiv:2608.09473) — neither of which mentions or proves any case of the monomial conjecture itself; they address the related but distinct positivity-of-intersection-multiplicities conjecture and Ext-module/NBIM-ring conjectures via lim Cohen-Macaulay sequences and perfectoid/contracting-endomorphism techniques. I opened both papers' full text/abstracts directly to confirm this rather than relying on titles. The current Wikipedia article on the monomial conjecture is a stub (flagged as relying on a single source) and states no change to the pre-2024 status. No AI, machine learning, or automated-theorem-proving involvement was found anywhere in this search space; general searches for AI-assisted resolutions of commutative-algebra homological conjectures in 2025-2026 turned up unrelated results (Erdős problems, OEIS conjectures, an unrelated geometry counterexample) with no connection to the monomial conjecture. I also encountered what appear to be spam/AI-generated Zenodo listings ('Monthly Mathematics Conjectures') in one search; I disregarded these as non-authoritative and did not cite them. This matches and confirms the triage's 'none' verdict — I do not disagree with it.
competing_reading: The adjacent 2024-2026 papers on lim Cohen-Macaulay sequences and perfectoid-pure/NBIM rings are close enough in subject matter (they descend from the same Hochster-school homological-conjectures program and use techniques, like Heitmann's, aimed at mixed characteristic) that a looser reading might count them as 'progress' on the broader conjecture family. But under the scope rule (§3.1), these are related problems — they change the question (different conjecture: Serre positivity, Ext-vanishing for NBIM rings) rather than restricting the monomial conjecture's own statement — so they do not count as a case settled or a bound moved on this specific conjecture.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly proving the monomial conjecture (or a specific new dimension/case of it) in mixed characteristic beyond dimension 3, or a preprint/announcement citing Hochster's monomial conjecture by name as its target and stating a settled case.

outcome: A single-author preprint by Yochay Jerby (arXiv:2511.18275) claims a conditional (RH-assumed) proof that the zeros of Hardy's Z-function — which under RH coincide with the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function — obey the GUE pair-correlation law, i.e. a conditional proof of Montgomery's conjecture as stated. It has not been digested, cited, or discussed by experts anywhere I could find, including the live Wikipedia article on this exact problem, which as of my check does not mention it at all.
summary: The triage's single strong lead is Yochay Jerby's arXiv preprint 2511.18275, 'Variations of the Hardy Z-Function and the Montgomery Pair Correlation Conjecture' (v1: 23 Nov 2025; v2: 19 Dec 2025). I fetched the paper directly: its Theorem C states that, assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, the nontrivial zeros of Hardy's Z-function obey the GUE pair-correlation law. Under RH the zeros of Z(t) coincide exactly with the imaginary ordinates of the nontrivial zeta zeros, so this is a claim to prove the conjecture as Wikipedia states it (conditionally on RH, which is itself the standard framing Montgomery used). This is single-author, very recent, and — critically — I found zero evidence of expert engagement: no MathOverflow thread, no mention on Terence Tao's blog or papers list, no citation by other 2025/2026 papers on the topic, and the live Wikipedia article on Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture (which does discuss other 2025 developments, e.g. Goldston–Lee–Schettler–Suriajaya's RH-free reformulation) does not mention Jerby's paper at all. That silence, for a claim of this significance sitting unremarked for ten months, is itself informative and weighs toward 'not yet vetted' rather than 'quietly accepted.' No errata, withdrawal notice, or retraction was found on arXiv; the paper is simply unreviewed. I therefore classify this as `claimed`, not `resolved` — a preprint with no digestion, per §6.1. Separately, the two-part Goldston/Lee/Schettler/Suriajaya papers (2503.15449, 2507.06823) and the related 2501.14545 paper all *use* PCC as a hypothesis to derive other unconditional consequences (proportions of simple/critical zeros) rather than proving PCC itself, so per §3.1 they are related work that does not change this bullet's status — I did not treat them as events. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the Jerby paper's visible text, nor in the Goldston et al. papers; all work presented is purely analytic/probabilistic with human authorship throughout, so ai_role is none for this record.
competing_reading: One could argue Jerby's result should be `resolved` if the field quietly treats RH-conditional results as citable science (RH-conditional proofs are common and often treated as effectively settling a question 'modulo RH'), or one could argue it doesn't even count as `claimed`-worthy progress if it turns out (on closer reading than I performed) to have a substantive gap — single-author, unreviewed proofs of hard old conjectures in this area have a history of not surviving scrutiny (e.g. periodic claimed RH proofs). Because I could not find any third-party mathematical vetting either way, I erred toward the conservative `claimed` rather than `resolved`, and did not downgrade to `open` since the paper itself is a genuine, specific claim that a careful reader would need to weigh, not nothing.
what_would_settle_it: A MathOverflow/blog discussion, a citation from a specialist (e.g. Steven Gonek, Brian Conrey, or the Goldston/Suriajaya group who work in this exact area), a referee report, or a subsequent version/retraction on arXiv would settle whether this stands as `resolved`, remains `claimed`, or should be downgraded to an `incident`.

corrections.why: The claim is not credible enough to be the event the status rests on. Full GUE pair correlation, even assuming RH, is far beyond current methods: Montgomery's own theorem and every later refinement reach only a restricted range of the Fourier variable, so a full-range proof conditional only on RH would be one of the major results in analytic number theory. It is a single-author preprint with no citation, commentary or uptake in ten months, and the live Wikipedia article, which does discuss other 2025 work on this exact conjecture (Goldston-Lee-Schettler-Suriajaya), does not mention it. The record's own competing_reading notes the history of such claims not surviving scrutiny. Nothing else in the window qualifies: the Goldston et al. papers assume the conjecture rather than prove it. DEPARTURE FROM THE INSTRUCTIONS, STATED PLAINLY: DEEP_DIVE.md 6.1 codes any undigested preprint `claimed` and the agent followed that correctly. This correction applies a stricter rule: a claim with no expert uptake, from outside or at the margin of the field, on a problem whose resolution would be a landmark, is set aside like a withdrawn claim, and the furthest genuine event that remains sets the status. The claim stays in `outcome`, `event` and `summary` as evidence; if it is ever digested this should revert to `claimed` or `resolved`.

outcome: Two independent, unpublished 2026 preprints moved bounds on the area of a convex universal cover for Moser's worm problem: Ethan Keller (arXiv:2609.21968, Sept 18 2026) raised the convex lower bound to 0.239 and lowered the convex upper bound to 0.24633..., cutting the gap between previously refereed bounds by over 75%, with the full proof formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4; Zhipeng Deng (arXiv:2609.04591, Sept 4 2026) separately claims a specific isosceles-triangle convex cover of area 0.257883595..., also Lean-formalized. The overall problem (exact minimum area) remains open, and neither preprint has yet received expert digestion or journal review.
summary: Moser's worm problem — the exact minimum area of a region covering every unit-length plane curve — remains open. Wikipedia's live article (checked 2026-09-22) still lists the best refereed bounds as of the frozen revision's era: convex lower bound 0.232239 (Khandhawit, Pagonakis & Sriswasdi 2013), convex upper bound 0.270911861 (Wang 2006), and nonconvex upper bound 0.260437 (Norwood & Poole 2003) / the 30° sector result of Panraksa & Wichiramala (2021, area π/12≈0.2618, settling Wetzel's conjecture) — all predating the window. Since 26 January 2024, two new, apparently independent single-author preprints have appeared in September 2026 that would move the convex bounds if they hold up: (1) Ethan Keller, 'Improved bounds for universal convex covers of unit arcs' (arXiv:2609.21968, submitted 2026-09-18), claims 0.239 ≤ α ≤ 0.24633..., a combined lower+upper bound improvement cutting the previously refereed gap by over 75%, with the full proof Lean 4-formalized and kernel-verified, code/certificates on GitHub. (2) Zhipeng Deng, 'Balanced Support Calibrations for Moser's Worm Problem' (arXiv:2609.04591, submitted 2026-09-04), claims a specific isosceles-triangle convex cover of area 0.257883595..., also with Lean 4 code and a Python symbolic replay verifier; this is a weaker (larger-area) upper bound than Keller's and appears to be superseded by it, though the two use different constructions and neither paper is aware of / cites the other given their near-simultaneous posting. Deng has an earlier, related preprint (arXiv:2412.10686, 'A General Solution to Bellman's Lost-in-a-Forest Problem', Dec 2024) proposing a general optimization framework said to extend to Moser's worm problem, but that paper only sketches a methodology and claims no numeric bound on the worm problem itself. None of these three preprints has been digested by a named expert (no Terence Tao blog post, no Quanta Magazine coverage, no journal acceptance found), and neither Keller nor Deng has a discoverable academic footprint tied to this specific subfield (search for 'Zhipeng Deng' turns up several different researchers in unrelated fields; no institutional affiliation is listed on either paper). I found no evidence of AI system involvement in producing either result: neither abstract, comments field, nor (for Keller) the linked GitHub README mentions any AI/LLM tool; both papers use Lean 4 (a proof assistant, not an AI system) and, for Deng, a Python 'exact symbolic replay verifier' (deterministic symbolic/rational-arithmetic code, not machine learning). A search for adjacent AI-mathematics activity turned up a Quanta Magazine piece ('Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI', Aug 2026) and a GitHub repo named 'clanker-solving-riemman-hypothesis-inator' (an LLM-agent scaffolding project using Claude and Codex) whose issue #142 asks an agent to reconstruct the 2013 Khandhawit–Pagonakis–Sriswasdi lower bound — but that repo explicitly states 'Scaffolding. No mathematical results yet,' and it is unconnected to either the Keller or Deng preprint. Because neither preprint is yet expert-digested, status is 'progress' rather than 'claimed'/'partial'/'resolved' — a bound on an open problem moved, but the problem itself (find the exact infimum area, convex or not) is unchanged and still open.
competing_reading: One could argue Keller's result should be 'claimed' rather than 'progress', since it targets the specific numeric bound the Wikipedia bullet's framing implicitly tracks ('smallest area... that can cover every unit curve') and comes with a machine-checked Lean certificate. I classified it as 'progress' because (a) it is only days old at the time of this research, unpublished, and un-digested by any named expert, and (b) per §6.1 a Lean certificate with no expert reader is only enough for 'claimed', and even 'claimed' felt too strong given zero external commentary exists yet to confirm the certificate is sound (a Lean proof can compile while encoding the wrong statement). If independent verification or expert commentary surfaces, this should move to 'claimed'. Also, both preprints appearing within two weeks of each other and citing no common lineage raises a small possibility that one or both could be retracted or found flawed — worth flagging as an open risk rather than a settled improvement.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (blog post, Quanta piece, or referee report) confirming the Lean formalization in either arXiv:2609.21968 or arXiv:2609.04591 actually encodes the stated theorem and is sound; or a follow-up preprint citing and building on either result; or evidence that one/both have been withdrawn.

outcome: Jineon Baek posted a 119-page arXiv preprint (Nov 29, 2024) claiming a proof that Gerver's 1992 sofa (area ≈2.2195) is the global optimum, resolving the problem as stated; the claim has been widely reported since Dec 2024 but as of the most recent sources found (mid-2026) is still under peer review at Annals of Mathematics and has not been formally accepted or digested by an expert review/verification, so it is coded as a claim rather than a resolution.

ai.basis_quote: We report two approaches, both supporting Gerver's conjecture that his shape is the unique global maximum... It turns out that the upper bound yielded by our models does converge to Gerver's area (within an error of 0.01% when the number of angles reaches 2100). We also improve their five-angle upper bound from 2.37 to 2.3337.

summary: Two distinct events occurred in the window, and they have different relationships to the problem and to AI. (1) In July 2024, Leng, Bi, Cha, Pinilla and Thiyagalingam (arXiv:2407.11106) used neural networks — a piecewise-linear network trained via physics-informed machine learning to model corridor rotation/trajectory, plus a discrete-optimization approach to the Kallus-Romik upper bound scaled to 10,000 angles — to produce numerical evidence that Gerver's sofa is optimal, and concretely tightened the best known five-angle upper bound from 2.37 to 2.3337. This is genuine AI involvement that moved a published bound, but the problem remained open afterward, so under the rules this is `progress`/`bound`, not a resolution, and does not by itself change `status`. (2) In November 2024, Jineon Baek (Yonsei University) posted a 119-page arXiv preprint, 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa,' giving a purely human, non-computer-assisted proof (representing sofas as points in an infinite-dimensional space and using a function Q) that Gerver's construction with 18 curve sections attains the maximum area exactly, which if correct fully resolves the problem as Wikipedia states it. This was widely reported (Quanta Feb 2025, Scientific American Dec 2024 and its 2025 'Top 10 Math Discoveries' list, NPR Dec 2024, Korea Herald, etc.) but every source consulted, including the most recent (a Jan 2026 Seoul Economic Daily piece and general 2026 searches), describes the proof as still under peer review at the Annals of Mathematics, with no announcement of acceptance, no published expert digestion working through the argument, and no errata or revised arXiv version (still v1) found. Because no human expert's review of the full argument was found to be complete and public, the decisive event is coded `claimed` rather than `resolved`, dated to the November 29, 2024 preprint submission (the first public written argument), with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the result proves the conjectured answer). The AI-involved paper is a separate, non-decisive event, recorded here as an example of AI moving a bound (`ai_role: bound`) but not driving the record's status, since the status rests on Baek's proof, which used no AI.
competing_reading: If Annals of Mathematics has in fact accepted the paper or a leading expert (e.g., a colloquium talk write-up, a detailed referee report made public, or a blog post working through the proof) has publicly and specifically vetted the full argument sometime after the searches reported here (last done via sources dated through mid-2026), the correct status would be `resolved` rather than `claimed`, still dated to the November 2024 preprint under the dating rule (§6.3: date the first public written argument, not the journal publication). I found no such digestion, but journal review timelines for a 119-page proof in a top journal can span years without much public signal in between, so I cannot rule out an acceptance that simply wasn't covered by press in the sources I could reach.
what_would_settle_it: An Annals of Mathematics acceptance notice or publication, a detailed public referee/expert write-up (e.g. a Tao-style blog post or a survey working through Baek's argument), or a revised arXiv version addressing referee comments, any of which would move the status from `claimed` to `resolved` (still dated to the original Nov 2024 preprint).

corrections.by: human review, not the researching agent
corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, and this record is the worked example for two rules about problems carrying more than one event. THE TWO EVENTS. (a) July 2024, Leng, Bi, Cha, Pinilla and Thiyagalingam (arXiv:2407.11106): piecewise-linear neural networks tightened the published five-angle Kallus-Romik upper bound from 2.37 to 2.3337 and produced numerical evidence for Gerver's sofa. Genuine AI mathematics, tier: progress. (b) November 2024, Jineon Baek alone (arXiv:2411.19826): a 119-page proof that Gerver's sofa is the global optimum, which this record describes as purely human and non-computer-assisted. Tier: resolution. The two are independent works by disjoint author sets four months apart; Baek did not verify, extend or build on (a) as far as any source here shows, and no quote exists in which he credits a model, which §6.2 requires before `assisted` is even available. RULE 1, DIFFERENT TIERS: THE FURTHEST EVENT WINS. `status` and `ai_role` both describe one event, and it is the furthest the problem has got: resolved/claimed over partial/progress over open. Here that is (b), which is human, so this row must not be read as AI involvement in the resolution. The stronger reason is supersession rather than seniority: once an exact optimum of about 2.2195 is proved, an upper bound of 2.3337 is not a lesser result but a dead one, so crediting the row to AI would credit a model with a bound the status itself obsoletes. RULE 2, SAME TIER: AI COUNTS IF AI DID ANY OF IT. Where two events sit at the same tier — two bounds moved on a still-open problem, one by a model and one by humans — neither supersedes the other, both stand, and the model did move the problem, so the AI credit holds. Rule 1 is about supersession, rule 2 about addition; they are not the same rule and this record only exercises the first. WHY `bound` IS RETAINED RATHER THAN RECODED: the code correctly describes what the AI did, and erasing it would lose the only record of event (a). The consequence is handled by scope instead: `bound` counts toward incomplete movement and never inside the resolution numerator. CONTINGENCY, AND IT IS LIVE: (b) is `claimed`, not `resolved` — under review at Annals of Mathematics since late 2024 and not digested by experts. If Baek's proof fails, the furthest event on this problem reverts to (a) and this row becomes an AI one, at tier progress. Re-examine this entry if the status of (b) ever changes. A tell that the two events are distinct: model_aliases.py deliberately maps `piecewise linear neural networks` and `physics-informed machine learning` to nothing, so this is the only resolved-or-claimed row carrying an AI credit with no canonical system behind it.

outcome: No result found that settles the original Browkin-Brzeziński n-conjecture (setwise-coprime n-tuples, no vanishing proper subsum) or any case/restriction of it as stated in the Wikipedia bullet. All 2024-2026 activity found concerns the 'strong n-conjecture', a related but distinct variant (Vojta 1998 / Ramaekers 2009) that replaces setwise coprimality with pairwise coprimality, which is a change of hypothesis rather than a restriction of the original statement.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet describes the original Browkin-Brzeziński (1994) n-conjecture: n>=3 integers that are coprime as a set (gcd of all n = 1), sum to zero, and have no vanishing proper subsum, satisfy an inequality (equivalently, quality limsup = 2n-5). Two lines of 2024-2026 activity were found, and both concern a different, stronger conjecture, not this one. (1) Hölzl, Kleine and Stephan, 'Improved lower bounds for strong n-conjectures' (arXiv:2409.13439, first posted 2024-09-20, journal version Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society, online 2025-06-02) prove lower bounds of 5/4 (n>=6) and 5/3 (odd n>=5) on the quality limsup for the 'strong n-conjecture' -- Vojta's 1998 variant requiring PAIRWISE coprimality of the n-tuple, with Ramaekers' (2009 thesis) further restriction that the limsup equals exactly 1. Their bounds disprove Ramaekers' conjecture for n>=5, but say nothing about the original Browkin-Brzeziński statement, which the paper itself explicitly distinguishes (their Definition 1.8/1.9 vs. the original setwise condition). I fetched the arXiv HTML (v2) and confirmed: acknowledgements thank Benne de Weger for correspondence and the referee for proofreading -- no computational or AI tool is mentioned anywhere in the paper; the proof method is polynomial identities (building on Darmon-Granville and Elkies) and Pell equations, entirely by hand. (2) Hölzl, Kleine and Stephan (or a related author set), 'Strong n-conjectures over rings of integers' (arXiv:2503.05296, posted 2025-03-07) extends the same strong/Ramaekers variant to Gaussian integers and Hurwitz quaternions -- again explicitly the strong variant, and again no AI or computational tool disclosed in the acknowledgements (only a Singapore MOE funding acknowledgement for F. Stephan). Neither paper is a restriction (case) of the original n-conjecture in the sense of Section 3.1: pairwise coprimality is a strictly stronger hypothesis than setwise coprimality, so a pairwise-coprime n-tuple is a special case of a setwise-coprime one, meaning the strong n-conjecture's truth or falsity constrains a strict subset of the tuples the original conjecture ranges over -- but the two papers' RESULTS (lower bounds on quality, disproof of Ramaekers) do not translate into any statement about the original conjecture's own inequality (2n-5), because the original conjecture is about a strictly larger, differently-shaped search space and its own best known quality bound is unaffected. This is why I classify it as a related/distinct problem rather than a settled case: the Wikipedia bullet's own numerical claim (limsup = 2n-5) is untouched by these results. Additionally, on 2026-09-22 I found a September 2026 entry on Wikipedia's 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' describing a Lean counterexample to 'the n=4 case of the N conjecture' by Tom Adamczewski (Epoch AI) using an unreleased OpenAI model referred to as 'GPT-6 Astra'. I traced this to its primary source, github.com/tadamcz/n-conjecture-strong, whose README states verbatim: 'A standalone Lean proof refuting the n = 4 case of the strong n-conjecture as stated in Hölzl-Kleine-Stephan, Conjecture 7' -- i.e. this AI-generated result is explicitly about the STRONG n-conjecture (the Ramaekers/Hölzl-Kleine-Stephan variant), not the original Browkin-Brzeziński n-conjecture of the Wikipedia bullet; the Wikipedia AI-discoveries list's shorthand 'N conjecture' is imprecise relative to its own linked primary source. The repo's own text states the entire repository, including the Lean proof, was machine-written by GPT-6 Astra at Adamczewski's direction -- this would be ai_role 'generated' if it were in scope, but because the object of the proof is the strong (pairwise-coprime) variant and not the conjecture as stated in this bullet, it is out of scope under Section 3.1 and I have not credited it to this record. I searched extensively for any work on the original setwise-coprime n-conjecture itself (by name, by the Browkin-Brzeziński names, and by the abc-conjecture-generalization framing) and found none since January 2024; all located activity is on the strong/pairwise variant.
competing_reading: One could argue that because pairwise coprimality implies setwise coprimality, every pairwise-coprime tuple counted by the strong n-conjecture is also counted by the original n-conjecture, so disproving Ramaekers' conjecture (a claim about the limsup over pairwise-coprime tuples) at least demonstrates large-quality examples that also lie within the original conjecture's domain, which could be read as 'progress' bearing on the original bound. Against this: the original n-conjecture's own claimed bound is 2n-5, far above the 5/3 or 5/4 lower bounds established, so these examples do not threaten or move the original conjecture's stated inequality, and the papers make no claim to. I judge the 'related problem, not a case with bearing on this bullet's own numerical content' reading as the stronger one, consistent with the triage's own uncertainty and with Section 3.1's instruction that a changed hypothesis (pairwise vs setwise) is a variant, not a restriction, when the settled result does not narrow the original bullet's own claim.
what_would_settle_it: A published result stating a bound, case, or disproof specifically for the original Browkin-Brzeziński n-conjecture's setwise-coprime, no-vanishing-proper-subsum formulation (i.e. explicitly relaxing pairwise to setwise coprimality), or an explicit statement by Hölzl-Kleine-Stephan or another author connecting their strong-n-conjecture bounds back to the original conjecture's 2n-5 claim.

outcome: No result changing the status of the Nagata-Biran conjecture (Seshadri constant ε(p1,...,pr;X,L) = d/√r for large r, on a smooth algebraic surface X with ample L of degree d) was found in the window 26 January 2024 to 22 September 2026.
summary: The Nagata-Biran conjecture generalizes Nagata's conjecture (on very general points in P^2) to an arbitrary smooth projective surface X with an ample line bundle L: for sufficiently large r, the r-point Seshadri constant equals the maximal possible value d/√r. As of January 2024 this was already known only asymptotically (verified as r→∞ up to lower-order terms, by Biran/Biran-Szemberg and, by different methods, by Harbourne), and it remains in that state today. Extensive searching (arXiv listings, Google/web search across many query variants, the Wikipedia articles for both 'Seshadri constant' and 'Nagata-Biran conjecture', and recent papers on Seshadri constants and symplectic embeddings) turned up no paper, preprint, or announcement in the 26 January 2024 - 22 September 2026 window that proves the conjecture for a general surface, extends the asymptotic verification, or narrows the class of surfaces for which it is open. Related but distinct work exists: a February 2025 paper on the 'valuative Nagata conjecture' (a strengthened variant of the classical, planar Nagata conjecture, not the surface-general Nagata-Biran statement); a May 2026 paper 'Weighted Seshadri constants and ellipsoid embeddings' (arXiv:2605.27574) that builds machinery from the McDuff-Schlenk staircase and speculates it might eventually be relevant to proving the classical (P^2) Nagata conjecture, but explicitly does not resolve it and does not address the general surface case; and continuing work on multi-point Seshadri constants on special surface classes (e.g. ruled surfaces) that gives explicit bounds/values in special cases but is framed as verifying expected behavior on those surfaces, not as new territory toward the general conjecture. None of this constitutes a case of, or progress on, the Nagata-Biran conjecture as stated (a general smooth surface and ample L), so status is 'open' with no_change_found true. No AI system appears anywhere in this literature; all identified work is conventional human mathematical research.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2026 weighted-Seshadri-constant paper's remark that its infinite sequence of divisors 'is precisely what one needs to prove the Nagata conjecture' constitutes 'progress' worth recording even though it is speculative and about the classical planar case rather than the general Nagata-Biran statement. I judged this a related/variant problem (the classical Nagata conjecture on P^2, which is itself a special case one level below the Nagata-Biran generalization, and the remark is prospective/speculative rather than an actual advance) rather than a case or resolution of the bullet as stated, so it does not change the status.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving the exact asymptotic (not just up-to-lower-order-terms) formula ε = d/√r for large r on a general smooth surface X with ample L, or extending the known asymptotic verification to a strictly larger class of surfaces than was already covered before January 2024, would count as progress; a full proof for arbitrary X and L would resolve it.

outcome: No result establishing, refuting, or narrowing any new case of Nagata's conjecture on curves was found in the window 26 January 2024 to 22 September 2026; the conjecture remains open for every non-perfect-square r ≥ 10, exactly as it stood in January 2024.
summary: Nagata's conjecture on curves (1959) predicts that a plane curve of degree d passing through r ≥ 10 very general points of P² with multiplicity at least m at each point must satisfy d > m√r; Nagata himself proved it when r is a perfect square, and every non-square case r ≥ 10 has been open for over 60 years. I ran searches for direct progress ('Nagata's conjecture proof/disproof 2024 2025 2026'), for the modern Seshadri-constant formulation, for the Nagata–Biran generalization, for bound improvements, and specifically for any AI-mathematics connection. The only post-2024 item that surfaced is Galindo–Monserrat–Moreno-Ávila–Moyano-Fernández, 'On the valuative Nagata conjecture,' published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences 12, no. 18 (2025) — but this is the journal publication of arXiv:2208.11041, whose only version was submitted 23 August 2022, well before the frozen revision. Per the dating rule (date by first written argument, not journal date), this event predates the window entirely and in any case is a different, weaker 'valuative' variant (concerning minimality of plane divisorial valuations w.r.t. an ample divisor, only implying the classical conjecture, not equivalent to or settling it) that gives equivalent characterizations of minimality rather than proving the valuative conjecture itself — so even setting the date aside it would not count as a case of this problem under §3.1. I also confirmed that a separate, distinctly named 'Nagata's conjecture' concerning wild automorphisms of polynomial rings (proved by Umirbaev and Shestakov in 2004, well before the window) and the triage-flagged September 2026 positive-characteristic automorphism variant are unrelated problems sharing only the name Nagata, not cases of this curves conjecture. No AI-mathematics coverage (OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, or other lab announcements about conjecture-solving) mentions Nagata's conjecture on curves; the AI breakthroughs I found in that space (Jacobian conjecture counterexample, cycle double cover conjecture, Erdős conjectures) are unrelated problems. The current live Wikipedia article's lead and body are unchanged in substance from the frozen revision and cite nothing later than 2004. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' result.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 journal publication of the valuative Nagata conjecture paper should be recorded as an 'event' under status progress, since it is the first fully peer-reviewed, expert-digested appearance of that variant's equivalent characterizations. But (a) the substantive mathematical content was already public via the 2022 arXiv preprint, before the window, and (b) the valuative Nagata conjecture is a distinct (stronger, implying) conjecture about divisorial valuations, not a case of the classical curves conjecture as restricted by prescribed multiplicities at finitely many very general points — it is a related problem under §3.1, not a case, since it changes the object (a valuation rather than a finite point set) rather than merely restricting it. Either way it would not move this record off 'open'.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement, dated after 26 January 2024, that either (a) proves or disproves Nagata's conjecture for some new non-square r ≥ 10, or (b) proves the general case, or (c) exhibits an AI system's involvement in either. None of these were found.

outcome: A February 2025 arXiv preprint by Rui Li, Zida Xiao and Huaiqing Zuo extends the Nakai conjecture to local domains and verifies it for isolated hypersurface singularities of modality ≤ 2, settling a restricted case of the conjecture (the general conjecture, and even the local-domain extension in general, remains open).
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet states the Nakai conjecture (1961): if the ring of differential operators of a complex algebraic variety is generated by degree-one derivations, the variety is smooth. The only development found in the window (26 Jan 2024–present) is arXiv:2502.04672, 'The Nakai Conjecture for isolated hypersurface singularities of modality ≤ 2' by Rui Li, Zida Xiao and Huaiqing Zuo, posted 7 February 2025 (single version, no later revisions). The paper explicitly frames itself as extending the conjecture to local domains and then verifying that extension for a specific, restricted class of singularities (isolated hypersurface singularities of modality ≤ 2), stating this 'extends the existing works.' This is a genuine case of the problem under §3.1: it restricts the class of algebras/varieties considered (to a specific singularity type and modality bound) rather than changing the question being asked, so settling it removes territory from the open problem. It does not resolve the conjecture in general — the Wikipedia article and all sources checked confirm the conjecture (equivalently implying the Zariski–Lipman conjecture) remains open outside a handful of known cases (algebraic curves, Stanley–Reisner rings, normal toric varieties). I read the arXiv abstract page directly (submission date, version history, MSC classes) and attempted to read the full PDF text; the PDF's text layer did not extract cleanly via the fetch tool, but the abstract, title, and all secondary discussion (a literature-review summary site, arXiv listing pages) are consistent and contain no mention of AI, machine learning, automated theorem proving, or computer algebra methods — this is a conventional human-authored proof in singularity theory. There is no evidence the paper has been digested by outside experts (no blog coverage, no citing survey found) or accepted to a journal of record as of this search, so it is classified `partial` rather than `resolved`: a genuine sub-case has been settled, using a status separate from the resolved/claimed distinction (which concerns the general conjecture, not this restricted result) — the case itself is a fully worked, verifiable mathematical proof in a preprint, not a machine-generated or machine-checked claim awaiting expert review, so it earns `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (the conjecture holds in the case verified) rather than being downgraded for lack of digestion. I also searched broadly for any other 2024–2026 work on Nakai/Zariski–Lipman and found only unrelated results: a GitHub tracking issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures#1822) requesting a Lean formalization of the (distinct, though related) Zariski–Lipman conjecture, which remains open/unformalized and does not mention Nakai at all, so it is out of scope and not counted.
competing_reading: One could argue the paper's 'extension to local domains' changes the object of study (global finite-type algebras over a field vs. local domains) enough to make this a related/variant problem rather than a case of the stated conjecture, in which case the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found: true` and this preprint noted only as beside the point. I judge it as a case rather than a variant because the authors present the local-domain extension explicitly as a natural strengthening/instance of the same conjecture (same hypothesis about the ring of differential operators being generated by first-order derivations, same conclusion of regularity/smoothness) applied to a narrower, well-defined class of rings, and prior literature on Nakai's conjecture routinely treats the local (singularity-theoretic) formulation as the natural setting for verifying cases — Wikipedia's own 'known to be true for algebraic curves' case is itself a local/specific-class result of exactly this kind.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full paper text (not just the abstract) to confirm the precise logical relationship between the 'extended to local domains' statement and the original finite-type-algebra statement, and checking whether any published survey or expert commentary treats this modality-≤2 result as a bona fide case of the classical Nakai conjecture or flags it as a distinct local variant.

outcome: On 2026-09-08 OpenAI announced that an internal (unreleased) AI system, coordinating roughly 10,000 concurrent agents over 88 hours, produced a proof — with an accompanying Lean formalization built afterward by GPT-6 Astra over 17 more hours — that a forced, initially smooth, finite-energy 3D Navier-Stokes flow can develop a finite-time singularity. This is a counterexample to smoothness/global existence only for the forced equations; the Clay Millennium Prize problem as officially stated (Fefferman's 2000 description) concerns the unforced/source-free case, so OpenAI explicitly did not claim the prize and the Clay Institute has kept the problem's status as 'active' rather than resolved. The result has not yet been digested or verified by the mathematical community: a joint guest post on Terence Tao's blog (De Toffoli & Duede, 2026-09-12) explicitly declines to certify it as an 'intelligible' mathematical proof, and NPR (2026-09-22) reports mathematicians still have not extracted understanding from it. A separate, human-led line of work by Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) and Levent Alpöge (Anthropic), building on Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa's earlier results, produced closely related (but not identical) finite-time blowup results for the Euler, Boussinesq and porous-medium equations around the same time (posted/announced 2026-09-07, per Tao's blog), using LLMs (both Anthropic's and OpenAI's) heavily to help write up arguments the humans devised; this touched but did not itself resolve the Navier-Stokes existence/smoothness question. A public priority dispute broke out between the two camps over alleged leakage of methods.

ai.disclosed_cost: OpenAI disclosed roughly 2.7-4.9 million inter-agent messages and approximately 130-300 billion output tokens for the effort; secondary reporting (e.g. Latent Space) estimates the compute cost at over $40 million.

counterexample.object: A forced (smooth external forcing), initially smooth, finite-energy solution of the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on the whole space that develops a singularity in finite time.
counterexample.verified_how: Formally checked in the Lean proof assistant (kernel-level type checking); the underlying informal manuscript (166 pages) has not undergone independent human peer review or expert digestion as of this record's date.

disputes.summary: Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) publicly alleged, in a statement posted roughly 12 hours before OpenAI's announcement, that OpenAI became aware of his and Levent Alpöge's (Anthropic) unpublished progress on the same underlying strategy (building on Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa's work) via leaked or de-identified data, and adopted a similar method for the full Navier-Stokes case. OpenAI (via Sébastien Bubeck) denied direct access to their proofs or prompts, said its model solved the related Euler problem by 'significantly different' methods, but did not deny that its Navier-Stokes solution followed a similar strategy. Charles Fefferman, author of the official Clay problem statement, credited Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa as the 'heroes' whose techniques underlie both efforts. Twenty-five Fields Medalists (including Tao and Scholze) issued a joint letter on 2026-09-11, 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,' criticizing the framing of unsolved problems as AI benchmarks and the erosion of attribution norms. The dispute over data usage and credit remains unresolved.

summary: OpenAI's 2026-09-08 announcement is a machine-produced (and Lean-formalized) proof of a counterexample to global smoothness/existence for the *forced* 3D Navier-Stokes equations — a related but not identical problem to the Clay Institute's official (unforced) Millennium Prize statement, which Wikipedia's frozen bullet points to. Because the problem as officially posed by Fefferman concerns the source-free (unforced) equations, and OpenAI itself says it is not claiming the prize, this is scoped as a case/near-neighbor result that bears directly on the stated existence-and-smoothness question in its forced variant rather than a full resolution of the frozen bullet. I classify status as `claimed` rather than `resolved`: the Lean kernel check gives logical certainty of internal consistency, but no human expert has yet published a digestion of the 166-page informal manuscript, and a guest post on Terence Tao's blog (De Toffoli & Duede, 2026-09-12) explicitly argues the community cannot yet call it an 'intelligible' mathematical proof; NPR (2026-09-22) reports mathematicians have extracted little insight so far. `ai_role` is `generated` because OpenAI's own account states an internal model (not GPT-6 Astra itself, but an unreleased more-capable model) produced the mathematics via a multi-agent process, with GPT-6 Astra doing only the subsequent Lean formalization; humans verified/reviewed the output but did not produce the mathematical content. Separately, a human-led effort (Buckmaster/Alpöge, building on Córdoba/Martínez-Zoroa) used LLMs heavily to help write up genuinely human-devised arguments for closely related equations (Euler, Boussinesq, porous medium) — that work is `assisted`-flavored AI use but did not itself settle the Navier-Stokes bullet, so I did not create a second status-bearing event for it; it is recorded in `disputes`/`summary` instead. A sharp, unresolved priority dispute and a 25-Fields-Medalist open letter followed, underscoring that no consensus verification exists yet.
competing_reading: One could argue the frozen bullet ('Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness') is broad enough, as commonly discussed in popular and even some technical accounts, to cover the forced variant loosely referred to as 'the Navier-Stokes problem,' in which case this would be `resolved` or at least a full case-settlement (`partial` with `confirmed`... but actually `refuted`, since existence/smoothness fails) rather than merely `claimed`. However, the officially cited problem description (Fefferman, 2000) that Wikipedia's article itself points to is specifically about the unforced equations, and OpenAI's own framing (not claiming the Clay Prize) supports keeping this scoped as directly on-point but not fully resolving, and as not-yet-expert-verified.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed publication or a widely-endorsed expert digestion (e.g., a detailed post by Tao, Buckmaster, Fefferman, or a Clay Institute-commissioned review) confirming the OpenAI manuscript's correctness and significance would move this to `resolved` (for the forced-flow case) or at minimum settle the `claimed` vs `resolved` distinction; resolution of the unforced case (which nobody claims yet) would be what actually closes the frozen bullet.

outcome: Negami's conjecture (equivalent to showing K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover) remains open, but the Dec 2024 preprint by Annor, Nikolayevsky and Payne narrowed the remaining case by proving K1,2,2,2 has no planar cover of ply below 14 (a case also proved in an earlier, pre-window 2023 preprint on n<14) and that any minimal planar cover of K1,2,2,2, if one exists, must be 4-connected.
summary: Negami's 1988 conjecture ('a connected graph has a finite planar cover iff it embeds in the projective plane') is known to reduce to a single remaining case: showing the seven-vertex graph K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover. As of the 26 Jan 2024 Wikipedia snapshot, 31 of 32 forbidden minors had been handled, leaving only K1,2,2,2 open. Within the window, the key development is arXiv:2412.19560 ('Three Theorems on Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture', Annor, Nikolayevsky, Payne), submitted 27 Dec 2024 (revised as late as 17 Jul 2026 per the search snippet, but the first written argument is Dec 2024). It proves (i) K1,2,2,2 has no planar cover of ply below 14, and (ii) any minimal planar cover of K1,2,2,2, if it exists, must be 4-connected — both restrictions on the space where a hypothetical cover could live, narrowing but not closing the case. This is a case of the stated problem (restricting properties of a hypothetical cover of the one remaining critical graph), so it counts as `partial` progress under the case-vs-variant rule, with resolution_direction `confirmed` since the result goes in the direction the conjecture predicts (no low-ply cover exists). A closely related but pre-window preprint (arXiv:2311.01672, submitted Nov 2023, proving the same ply<14 bound) was only published in the journal Graphs and Combinatorics in Nov 2025 — per the dating rule (§6.3), the journal date is irrelevant and the first written argument (Nov 2023) predates the frozen revision, so this specific result is `open_stale` relative to the window and is not what the window-status rests on; it is mentioned only for context, since the actual within-window advance is the Dec 2024 paper providing the additional 4-connectivity result plus a re-derivation/extension of the ply bound. A second Dec 2024 preprint (arXiv:2412.04420, 'On high genus extensions of Negami's conjecture') generalizes the conjecture to arbitrary compact surfaces; this changes the stated question (different surfaces) rather than restricting it, so it is a related problem, not a case, and does not affect the status of the projective-plane conjecture as stated. A June 2026 preprint (arXiv:2606.27703) gives a new, purely combinatorial proof of an already-known special case (rotation-compatible planar covers embed in the projective plane), explicitly described by its own authors as a re-proof of a result whose 'existing proof relies on advanced algebraic and topological methods' — this is a proof-technique contribution to an already-settled sub-case, not new territory, and does not change the classification. No AI system involvement was found in any of these papers: none mention computer search, SAT solvers, computer algebra, or AI/ML tools, and none have acknowledgements referencing such tools; all are described as hand-written mathematical proofs. A mention of 'Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture' on the AI-first formal-mathematics platform ProofAtlas was also checked: it lists the problem as an open workspace with '6 routes, 4 tasks' but no completed proof or claimed result, so it does not constitute an AI contribution to this problem as of this research.
competing_reading: One could argue the ply<14 result, having first appeared (for the same bound) in a Nov 2023 preprint, is not itself a new within-window fact, so the true within-window event is only the narrower 4-connectivity result. Either way the status classification (partial, confirmed) is unchanged; I dated the event to the Dec 2024 paper since it is the first written argument establishing the 4-connected structural constraint, which is new relative to the frozen revision.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof, i.e. an exhibited finite planar cover) that K1,2,2,2 has no finite planar cover at all — closing the single remaining case — would resolve the conjecture completely.

outcome: No proof, disproof, counterexample, or new instance satisfying all three New Mersenne conditions has been found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open and unrefuted.
summary: The New Mersenne conjecture (Bateman-Selfridge-Wagstaff, 1989) states that for odd p, any two of (p = 2^k ± 1 or 4^k ± 3), (2^p − 1 prime), and ((2^p + 1)/3 prime) imply the third. No proof, disproof, or new counterexample has appeared since 26 January 2024. The known set of numbers satisfying all three conditions remains {3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 31, 61, 127}, per The Prime Pages' 'New Mersenne Prime Conjecture' page and the Wikipedia 'Mersenne conjectures' article (fetched as it stands in 2026, no update noted regarding new qualifying numbers). The largest known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841 − 1, was discovered 12 October 2024 by Luke Durant using GIMPS, running Lucas-Lehmer primality tests on a cloud network of NVIDIA GPUs (A100/H100) — this is a purely computational/number-theoretic verification, not an AI/ML system, and it is simply a new large Mersenne prime consistent with (but not bearing on) the conjecture, since 136279841 is not of the required exponent form and does not settle any of the three-condition triples. I also found a July 2024 ResearchGate preprint by Pengcheng Niu and Junli Zhang, 'A Proof of Mersenne primes Conjecture,' but this addresses the classical (Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff) conjecture on the infinitude of Mersenne primes — a different, unrelated conjecture that happens to share the word 'Mersenne' — not the New Mersenne (Bateman-Selfridge-Wagstaff) conjecture that is the subject of this bullet; per §3.1 this is out of scope even if it turned out to be correct, and in any case it is an unreviewed preprint (the page itself returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch, so I relied on a search-engine summary of it, which is a limitation noted below). A May 2026 arXiv paper (2605.18555, 'Three Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proofs for Wagstaff numbers') gives certified primality proofs for three specific large Wagstaff numbers (exponents 2617, 10501, 12391); none of these exponents are of the New Mersenne conjecture's required form (2^k ± 1 or 4^k ± 3) and none appear among the nine known numbers satisfying all three conditions, so this is a related-but-distinct achievement (individual primality certification of Wagstaff numbers) rather than a case or resolution of the New Mersenne conjecture itself, and it involves no AI. No AI or machine-learning system was found associated with any work touching this conjecture specifically. This matches and confirms the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: None of the material found bears on this specific conjecture as stated; the only genuine ambiguity is whether the Niu-Zhang preprint's title ('Mersenne primes Conjecture') could be confused for the New Mersenne conjecture, but reading past the title, its content (infinitude of Mersenne primes via Lagrange multipliers on a characteristic-function inequality) addresses a different classical conjecture, so it is excluded under §3.1's 'related problem' rule rather than counted as a case.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed or widely-digested proof/disproof of the three-condition implication, or discovery of a tenth number (beyond 3,5,7,13,17,19,31,61,127) satisfying exactly two of the three conditions without the third (a counterexample), or a new number found to satisfy all three (extending the known list, which per the conjecture should not happen beyond 127).
