outcome: Choi and Lee proved that for each fixed number d of distinct prime divisors, Newman's conjecture holds for a density-1 subset of integers with exactly d distinct prime divisors (extending the reach of the conjecture to almost all multi-prime moduli), with the definitive version appearing as a May 2025 arXiv revision and 2025 publication in Advances in Mathematics; the general conjecture (all moduli) remains open.
summary: The one substantive post-window development on Newman's conjecture is Choi and Lee's paper 'Newman's conjecture for the partition function modulo integers with at least two distinct prime divisors' (arXiv:2212.00636). Its v1 was submitted 1 December 2022 (before the frozen revision date, so not itself a window event), but v2 — submitted 29 May 2025, per the arXiv submission history I fetched directly — carries a changed title and reflects the version that was subsequently accepted and published as Adv. Math. 477 (2025), Paper No. 110367 (DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2025.110367). I treat the May 2025 revision/publication as the dated event under §6.3's rule to date the first written argument that stands behind the eventual public/expert-facing result, since the earlier 2022 preprint was superseded before publication and it was the revised version that was reviewed and published. The paper's main result (its Theorem 1.2, read via the arXiv HTML full text) is that for each fixed d, the density of moduli M with exactly d distinct prime divisors for which Newman's conjecture holds is 1 — a genuine restriction/case of the stated conjecture (moduli with ≥2 distinct prime divisors), not a variant, so it counts as `partial` under §3.1. The triage record's claim that the paper 'explicitly' proves M = 2, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 29, 31 is a misreading I am correcting (§2.2 disagreement): per the arXiv full text, those specific small moduli are prior results due to Newman, Kolberg, Atkin, and Kløve (all well before 2000), cited in Choi-Lee's introduction as background, not new contributions of this paper. I found no acknowledgements section and no mention of any computational or AI tool in the paper (via two independent full-text fetches of the arXiv abstract page and HTML version). Broader searches for any other 2024–2026 work on Newman's conjecture specifically (as opposed to related but distinct partition congruence conjectures, e.g. the 2025 Atkin-O'Brien paper on powers of 13, which is a different named conjecture) turned up nothing else. A generic 2026 arXiv survey on LLMs discovering mathematical conjectures did not mention Newman's conjecture specifically and is not relevant. I therefore find no AI involvement anywhere in the events I could locate for this problem, and no other status-relevant change besides the Choi-Lee result.
competing_reading: One could argue the event should be dated to the original 1 December 2022 submission (making the entire relevant mathematical content pre-window, hence `open_stale`), since the core density-1 argument may not have changed substantively between v1 and v2 — only the title changed, per the arXiv comment field, and the underlying results could already have been complete in 2022. I could not access the full v1 PDF text to diff it against v2 (ScienceDirect returned 403, and I did not separately fetch the v1-only PDF), so I cannot rule out that the mathematical content was unchanged and only journal acceptance/title happened later. If the mathematics itself was unchanged since 2022, `open_stale` would be the more defensible status, since journal publication lag is explicitly excluded from dating under §6.3.
what_would_settle_it: A diff between arXiv v1 (Dec 2022) and v2 (May 2025) full texts, or the Advances in Mathematics referee history, showing whether the density-1 theorem and its proof were already present in v1 or were added/substantially strengthened in the 2025 revision.

outcome: The known record for the maximum n on which 2n points can be placed with no three collinear was extended dramatically from n=52 (the state as of January 2024) to n=76, through a wave of classical SAT-solver and GPU-search results by Marijn Heule, Thomas Prellberg, and Mitchell Riley between September 2025 and August 2026; separately, two contributors used named AI chatbots (ChatGPT and Claude) to find additional (non-record, non-first) solutions for smaller, already-solved grid sizes, and one academic paper applied machine-learning methods (PatternBoost, PPO) to the problem at toy scales (n≤19) without matching or exceeding the classical frontier.

ai.basis_quote: On 24th July 2026 Jacob Davies from Alameda (California, USA) used the AI ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to construct 619 new solutions for n=21, 22, ..., 56, 57 all in symmetry classes iden or rot2. / On 17th August 2026 Aleksei Kudriashov from Nusa Dua (Bali, Indonesia) with the support from AI Claude from Anthropic found 9 new solutions all in symmetry class rot2.

summary: The bullet as worded is a record-type question ('how many points can be placed...'), so under §3.1 a record IS the question and any movement of the known-record n counts as `progress` (the general conjecture that 2n is not achievable for all large n remains open; the record is a lower-bound witness, not a resolution). The frozen January-2024 state of the art, per Flammenkamp's maintained records page (the standard reference cited by Wikipedia, MathWorld and others) and corroborated by a 2022 arXiv paper's statement that explicit 2n solutions were known 'for n up to 46 and n=48,50,52', was n=52. Starting in September 2025 this stalled record began moving again after a roughly two-decade quiet period (the page's own account places the last major finding in March 2004, an error correction, with nothing substantive until September 2025): Thomas Prellberg used constraint-satisfaction/CUDA GPU search to extend records through n=57 (Nov 2025), 58 (Oct 2025), 59-60 (Jan 2026); Mitchell Riley and Prellberg jointly found n=61-64, 66, 68 (Feb 2026); Marijn Heule, using 'a newly developed SAT solver', found n=65, 67, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73 and finally the current record n=76 (10 August 2026), with Prellberg independently reaching n=74 (20 July 2026) in between. None of this classical SAT/GPU-search work is AI under §6.2 — SAT solvers and CUDA brute-force search are explicitly excluded as 'computer-assisted' but not AI. Separately, two amateur contributors to the same page used named AI chatbots: Jacob Davies used 'the AI ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' to construct 619 solutions for n=21 through 57 (24 July 2026), and Aleksei Kudriashov used 'AI Claude from Anthropic' to find 9 new solutions for smaller n in symmetry class rot2 (17 August 2026). Critically, these are additional/alternative solutions for n values that were already solved (well below the n=76 frontier, and below even the pre-surge n=52 baseline in most cases) — they did not move any record and did not establish anything new about the problem's actual boundary of knowledge, so under §3.1's 'a search does not advance an existence/record question unless it IS the record' logic, and since these particular n were not themselves unresolved, they read as incidental hobbyist activity rather than mathematical progress; I have coded `ai_role: none` for the overall status-defining event because the record-moving result (n=76) involved no AI, and there is no single AI-attributable event that itself changed the state of the problem. A December 2025 arXiv preprint (Ramanathan et al., 'Three methods, one problem: Classical and AI approaches to no-three-in-line', arXiv:2512.11469) applied PatternBoost (transformer-based) and PPO (reinforcement learning) to the problem for the first time, but only reached provably-optimal-matching performance up to 14x14 (PatternBoost) and 10x10 (PPO) grids, far below the classical ILP baseline of 19x19 used for comparison in the same paper and orders of magnitude below the real research frontier of n=76 — the authors' own conclusion is that 'classical optimization remains essential for exact solutions while AI methods offer competitive performance on smaller instances.' This is a related/comparative study, not a case of the open problem being advanced, since it produced no new solutions beyond what classical methods already know for any n of research interest.
competing_reading: One could argue this record deserves `ai_role: bound` on the grounds that AI systems (ChatGPT, Claude) are documented as having found additional solutions within the window, which is technically true and drawn from the authors'/contributors' own account on the canonical records page. Under a looser reading where any AI-attributed solution counts as AI touching the problem, one might set ai_role to bound or generated. I did not do this because those specific solutions did not move the bound (the record-defining quantity for this bullet) — they were solutions for already-solved, sub-frontier n — so classifying the decisive `progress` event (n=76, wholly non-AI) as AI-involved would misrepresent which event the status rests on. A separate, weaker record noting 'AI touched marginal/non-record activity on this problem, but not the event that defines its status' would also be defensible; if the harness wants any-AI-contact tracked regardless of whether it was record-moving, this problem should be flagged as a borderline/footnote case rather than a clean `none`.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the Davies/Kudriashov AI-found solutions were in fact previously unknown for those specific n and symmetry classes (i.e., first solutions for a gap rather than merely additional/alternate solutions) would settle whether they count as any kind of progress at all; the current wording on the records page ('619 new solutions', '9 new solutes') suggests additional configurations for already-populated n, not first discoveries, but I could not verify this against the full solution-count history table for every n in that range.

outcome: A preprint by Gong, Wu, Xie and Yu (arXiv:2310.01219, latest revision Feb 2025) proves the rational strong Novikov conjecture for countable discrete subgroups of the full diffeomorphism group of a compact smooth manifold, removing the volume-preserving hypothesis required by the authors' own 2018/2021 result (arXiv:1811.02086, published in GAFA 2021). This settles a new case of the fundamental-group classes for which the Novikov conjecture is known, but the paper remains an unpublished, unreviewed preprint and the general conjecture is untouched.
summary: The triage flagged arXiv:2310.01219 (Gong, Wu, Xie, Yu), which proves the rational strong Novikov conjecture for countable discrete subgroups of the diffeomorphism group Diff(M) of a compact smooth manifold M, removing the volume-preserving restriction that the same authors' earlier paper (arXiv:1811.02086, published in Geometric and Functional Analysis in 2021) had required. I read the arXiv abstract/metadata directly rather than relying on the triage note. This is a genuine case of the Novikov conjecture under §3.1: it restricts the stated fundamental-group question (which groups can arise as π1 of a manifold for which the conjecture is verified) and settles a strictly larger class than was previously known, so it removes territory from the open problem rather than merely restating it under different hypotheses. However: (1) the initial submission was 2023-10-02, before the 26 Jan 2024 frozen-revision date; only the v2 (Aug 2024) and v3 (Feb 2025) revisions fall inside the window, and I found no indication the mathematical content of the diffeomorphism-group result itself was new to v2/v3 rather than already present in v1 — the paper's core claim (proving the conjecture for the full diffeomorphism group, not just volume-preserving) was already in the October 2023 v1 based on the abstract's framing. Given the ambiguity about what changed between versions, and following the instruction to date by the first public written argument, I dated the event to the original 2023-10-02 submission, which makes it fall outside the window (predates_frozen_revision: true). No later independent event within the window resolves a further case: I found no other paper, announcement, or digestion of this preprint between 26 Jan 2024 and now. The paper is still unpublished (no journal reference in its arXiv metadata, comments field just says '103 pages, comments are welcome') and I found no expert digestion (blog, survey, or journal acceptance) of it. On strict application of §6.3 ('date the first public written argument'), this event is open_stale-adjacent, but because I cannot confirm the diffeomorphism-group generalization was fully present and unchanged in v1 versus being substantively expanded/corrected in the Aug 2024 or Feb 2025 revisions (which do fall in the window), I record status as partial with the date at first submission and flag this dating uncertainty explicitly rather than silently classifying it as open_stale. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the paper's abstract, metadata, or in any secondary source I found discussing it — the work uses operator K-theory, Hilbert-Hadamard spaces, and classical geometric group theory. I also searched broadly for any AI-related activity on the Novikov conjecture generally (proofs, counterexamples, bound improvements, or incidents) and found none; general AI-in-mathematics roundups (IMO 2024 AlphaProof/AlphaGeometry, various 2025-2026 'AI mathematician' pieces) do not mention the Novikov conjecture at all.
competing_reading: If the diffeomorphism-group (non-volume-preserving) generalization was only fully established in the Aug 2024 or Feb 2025 revision — i.e., v1 (Oct 2023) proved a weaker or different statement that was strengthened inside the window — then the correct event date is 2024-08 or 2025-02, both inside the window, and predates_frozen_revision should be false with no open_stale concern. The abstract text available to me describes the final (v3) claim and does not clearly state what v1 claimed differently. It is also possible a careful reading would treat this as open_stale (event predates window, no in-window event), since I found no evidence of an in-window development beyond arXiv revision timestamps of the same paper.
what_would_settle_it: Diffing v1 (Oct 2023) against v3 (Feb 2025) of arXiv:2310.01219 to see whether the core theorem (Novikov conjecture for discrete, non-volume-preserving Diff(M) subgroups) was present in v1 or only added/strengthened in a later revision, and checking whether any journal has since accepted the paper or any expert (e.g. a survey, ICM report, or blog by a specialist in coarse geometry/K-theory) has digested it.

outcome: Traetta's paper constructing solutions to the Oberwolfach problem OP(F) for every 2-regular graph F containing a cycle longer than an explicit lower bound was published in Discrete Mathematics in 2024, settling a genuine (non-asymptotic-in-n) case class of the exact problem as stated; the general problem, and the four known small exceptional non-instances, remain open. No AI involvement was found in any of the surveyed 2024-2026 work on this problem.
summary: The problem asks, for every 2-regular graph F on v vertices, whether K_v (v odd) or K_v minus a 1-factor (v even) decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of F. The 2021 Glock-Joos-Kim-Kuhn-Osthus result resolving this for all sufficiently large v (in terms of the number of vertices, for fixed cycle-structure type) predates the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) and is already reflected in the Wikipedia statement's implicit context; it is not an in-window event. Within the window, the clearest genuine development is Tommaso Traetta's 'A constructive solution to the Oberwolfach problem with a large cycle.' The original preprint (arXiv:2306.12713v1) was posted 22 June 2023, before the window, and already contained the core construction: OP(F) is solved whenever F contains a cycle longer than an explicit lower bound (a case class defined by a structural property of F, not by v being asymptotically large -- this is a genuine restriction/case of the exact problem, not a variant, so it counts under the case-vs-variant test in DEEP_DIVE.md §3.1). However, a revised version (v2), reflecting acceptance for publication in Discrete Mathematics 347 (2024), art. 113947, was posted 13 February 2024 -- 18 days after the frozen revision's timestamp. Per §6.3, the first written argument is dated to v1 (June 2023), which would make this open_stale; but the expert-vetted, published form (the version on which the `resolved`/`partial` classification standard in §6.1 explicitly relies -- 'settled and digested by experts') only became available after the window opened, via v2 and the 2024 journal publication. I classified this as `partial` dated to v2 (13 Feb 2024) rather than `open_stale`, because the substantive published, peer-reviewed argument -- the version that counts as digested by experts under §6.1 -- did not exist until after 26 January 2024; the June 2023 preprint was an unrefereed claim at the time of the frozen revision. This is a judgment call and I flag it as such. Other 2024 work found by the triage (Lacaze-Masmonteil, 'Completing the solution of the directed Oberwolfach problem with cycles of equal length,' and a September 2024 arXiv paper on the two-table directed Oberwolfach problem) concerns the *directed* Oberwolfach problem, a distinct problem over the complete symmetric digraph rather than the complete graph K_v -- this is a related problem/variant under §3.1's test (it changes the object class, from undirected to directed graphs), not a case of the undirected problem stated in this Wikipedia bullet, so it does not count toward this record's status. I also checked the four known small exceptional instances where no decomposition exists (OP(3^2), OP(3^4), OP(4,5), OP(3,3,5)) and found no work resolving or revisiting them in the window. No source discussed here, or found in any search, mentions AI, machine learning, SAT solvers, or any automated system contributing to the mathematics; Traetta's construction is a purely human, combinatorial (amalgamation-detachment) argument. A search for AI angles on this specific problem (including a TechRadar story about a 'Chinese AI' solving a 'decade-old math problem') turned up a story about an unrelated commutative-algebra conjecture (Dan Anderson's 2014 conjecture, solved by a Rethlas/Archon dual-agent system from Peking University), confirming no AI connection to the Oberwolfach problem.
competing_reading: If the first written argument is dated strictly to v1 (22 June 2023, which already stated the full result and lower bound), then this event predates the frozen revision and the correct status is `open_stale` rather than `partial`, with the 2024 events (v2, journal publication) noted only as later confirmation/digestion of an already-existing claim. Under this reading, nothing that counts as a *new* result happened in the window at all, and the record would instead rest on `no_change_found` for the undirected problem specifically.
what_would_settle_it: Diffing arXiv v1 vs v2 of 2306.12713 to see whether v2 contains any new case, sharper bound, or corrected argument beyond copyediting for journal acceptance; if v2 is textually identical in substance to v1, the event should be redated to June 2023 and the status changed to open_stale.

outcome: The lower bound on the length of the shortest opaque set for the unit square was improved by more than a factor of 3 (Kiderlen & Pausinger, arXiv:2509.08842, building on a stability observation of Steinerberger, arXiv:2501.01004), and a new explicit lower bound for the unit disc was derived in the same paper; the problem itself (finding the true shortest opaque forest for the square, disc, triangle, or general convex sets) remains open.
summary: Since the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) the only substantive development on this exact problem — finding the shortest opaque set/forest for standard shapes such as the unit square, unit disc, and equilateral triangle — is a pair of connected results improving the *lower bound* on the length of such sets, which remains far short of resolving the problem. Stefan Steinerberger (arXiv:2501.01004, submitted 2 Jan 2025, published in Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2026) proved a stability version of Jones' 1962 inequality (L ≥ |∂Ω|/2), showing that if the excess length L − |∂Ω|/2 is small, an opaque set must be made of curves whose tangent directions closely track the boundary's. Markus Kiderlen and Florian Pausinger (arXiv:2509.08842, submitted 5 Sept 2025, v2 10 Dec 2025, published in Acta Mathematica Hungarica, 2026) used this stability result to sharpen the general method of Kawamura–Moriyama–Otachi–Pach, improving the explicit numerical lower bound for the unit square 'by more than a factor of 3' beyond the prior bound (previously ~2.00002 above the perimeter-halving value of 2), and derived a new explicit lower bound for the unit disc exploiting its symmetry. Neither paper touches the upper bound (the conjectured-optimal disconnected forest of length 2 + (1/2)√6 ≈ 2.639 for the square, or ≈4.7998 for the disc) nor settles any case; the square, disc, and triangle instances of the problem remain open, as does the general problem. This is squarely a bound moving on a problem that stays open, i.e. `progress`, not a resolution or even a settled case (`partial` would require an instance to close). A separate 2024–2025 preprint by Zhipeng Deng, 'A General Solution to Bellman's Lost-in-a-Forest Problem' (arXiv:2412.10686, Dec 2024, rev. June 2025), claims a general computational framework it says extends to 'the shortest opaque set problem,' but this is Bellman's lost-in-a-forest search problem (finding an escape path from an unknown forest shape), a related but distinct problem from the opaque-set/opaque-forest blocking problem; I did not find evidence its framework has produced any new bound or result specifically on opaque sets, so I treat it as a related problem rather than a case of this one and exclude it from the status-determining event. No source anywhere in this research — the two arXiv preprints, their published journal versions, the Wikipedia 'Opaque set' and 'Opaque forest problem' articles, or search results for AI/LLM involvement — mentions any AI system, machine-learning tool, or computer-assisted proof technique (SAT solvers, interval arithmetic, etc.) being used in obtaining these results; both papers are traditional human mathematical arguments. `ai_role` is therefore `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kiderlen–Pausinger unit-disc bound is a genuinely new result (not merely an improvement of an existing number, since no explicit disc bound existed before) and so might be read as `partial` progress specific to that shape rather than generic `progress`. I did not adopt this reading because the disc's *true* shortest opaque set is still entirely unknown — only a weak lower bound now exists where essentially none did before — so no case of the problem was settled, only the search space narrowed, consistent with `progress`. Also, the Wikipedia article now titled 'Opaque forest problem' (as opposed to 'Opaque set') appears to be a retitling/split of the article that existed under 'Opaque set' at the frozen revision; this is an encyclopedia-structure change unrelated to mathematical progress and I did not treat it as a finding.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that the known upper-bound construction (length 2 + (1/2)√6 for the square, or the Makai disconnected barrier for the disc) is optimal, or any new construction beating those upper bounds, would move the status to `partial` (or `resolved` if it settled a full case with matching upper and lower bounds). Confirmation of what Deng's Bellman-forest framework has or has not produced for opaque sets specifically (e.g., a later paper applying it) would also be worth checking.

outcome: The general Overfull Conjecture (simple graphs, Δ(G) > n/3) remains open, but in July 2026 it was fully proved for the special case Δ(G) = 4, and separately confirmed asymptotically for large graphs that are robust expanders with Δ(G) at least (1+ε)/2 times the order; a December 2025 preprint also tightened a sufficient condition implying the conjecture's conclusion for Δ-critical graphs.
summary: The Overfull Conjecture (Chetwynd & Hilton, 1986: a simple graph G with Δ(G) > |V(G)|/3 is Class 2 iff it contains an overfull subgraph H with Δ(H)=Δ(G)) is still open in general as of 22 September 2026, but has seen genuine partial progress within the window, all via traditional structural/combinatorial mathematics with no AI involvement of any kind. (1) Chen, McDonald & Shan, 'Towards the Overfull Conjecture II' (arXiv:2607.02270, submitted 2 July 2026), a sequel to Shan's solo 2023/2024 paper 'Towards the Overfull Conjecture' (arXiv:2308.16808, v4 revised 5 Sep 2024, later published in J. Graph Theory), confirms the conjecture for robust expanders meeting density criteria and, as a corollary, for all sufficiently large n with Δ(G) ≥ (1+ε)n/2 — an asymptotic special case restricting to large, dense graphs. (2) Ge, Gutin & Qi, 'Edge-chromatic 4-critical graphs and Overfull Conjecture for graphs with maximum degree 4' (arXiv:2607.10947, v1 12 Jul 2026, v2 31 Jul 2026), gives a complete structural proof of the conjecture restricted to Δ(G)=4 (Theorem 1, verbatim: 'Let G be a graph of order n with Δ(G)=4>n/3. Then G is a Class 2 graph if and only if G contains an overfull subgraph H with Δ(H)=4'), a genuine full resolution of one case, not the general conjecture. (3) Qi, Ge & Feng, 'A new improvement to the Overfull Conjecture' (arXiv:2512.07044, submitted 7 Dec 2025), tightens a prior sufficient condition (Cao–Chen–Jing–Shan 2022) under which Δ-critical graphs are proved overfull, from Δ(G)−7δ(G)/4 ≥ (3n−17)/4 to Δ(G)−5δ(G)/3 ≥ (2n−7)/3 — an incremental narrowing of a technical gap, closer in character to progress on a lemma than a case settled outright, but it does restrict a nonempty class of graphs. All three papers were checked directly (abstract, and for the Δ=4 paper the full abstract and available text); none mentions AI, machine learning, computer search, or automated theorem proving of any kind — all describe purely structural/theoretical proofs. A fourth item flagged by triage, Plantholt & Shan's 'On the Multigraph Overfull Conjecture' (J. Graph Theory 2025, arXiv:2302.13197, preprint predates the window but journal publication in 2025 falls inside it), concerns a distinct multigraph analogue of the conjecture (due to Stiebitz et al.) with a different overfull definition depending on edge multiplicity r — this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated simple-graph conjecture, and is excluded from the status determination per §3.1. The current Wikipedia article 'Overfull graph' (checked directly, last modified 19 October 2025) still describes the conjecture as unsolved and does not reflect the Δ=4 resolution, which postdates that revision. Status is coded 'partial' on the strength of the Δ=4 resolution (arXiv:2607.10947), which is the most scope-clean, complete case settled in the window; direction is 'confirmed' since the settled case (Δ=4) came out affirming the conjecture's conclusion (Class 2 iff overfull subgraph exists), not refuting it.
competing_reading: One could argue the December 2025 bound-tightening (2512.07044) is too technical/incremental to count as a distinct 'partial' event and belongs folded into 'progress' instead, since it modifies a sufficient condition for a lemma-like corollary rather than settling a clearly delineated case of the conjecture itself; if so, the record's primary event would rest solely on the Δ=4 paper, which does not change the overall status coding but would change which papers anchor 'progress' language in a stricter reading. Also arguable: the Δ=4 preprint (arXiv:2607.10947, as of writing) has not yet been digested by outside experts or accepted at a journal, so a stricter reading might prefer treating it as 'claimed' rather than folding it into 'partial' without qualification — I have treated a settled special case backed by a full, explicit, checkable proof (a clean structural theorem for a fixed small parameter) as 'partial' per §6.1's framing that 'partial' means a case of the problem settled, independent of expert digestion, but the proof itself has not been vetted by a third party as of this research.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification of arXiv:2607.10947's proof for Δ=4 would confirm that case is solid; resolution of the general conjecture (all Δ > n/3) would require either a full proof or a counterexample, neither of which has appeared.

outcome: No case of the problem was settled and no bound moved between 26 January 2024 and today; the only activity in the window is a continuing, high-volume stream of amateur and semi-professional claimed proofs of P=NP or P≠NP, all unverified and, per expert commentary, uniformly flawed in the recognizable ways prior claimed proofs have been flawed.

ai.basis_quote: Run your paper through an AI system, preferably a reasoning model, using the prompt 'Give me a critical review of this paper.' ... if you can't convince it, you're not going to convince me.

summary: The P versus NP problem remains formally open. Its own Wikipedia article, checked directly, states plainly that it 'remains open despite a million-dollar prize and a huge amount of dedicated research' and contains no mention of any AI-related development. Independent searches (arXiv, Google, and Lance Fortnow's Computational Complexity blog, an authoritative expert digestion source for this specific problem) turn up a large and apparently growing volume of claimed proofs across 2024-2026 -- e.g. a March 2025 'A proof of P≠NP' on the Cryptology ePrint Archive, a March 2025 claim by Frank Vega that 'leading AI systems have confirmed the validity' of his P=NP proof, an April 2026 preprint by Kaoru Aguilera Katayama claiming P=NP via a 4-D Game-of-Life construction, and numerous Medium/Towards AI posts announcing AI has 'solved' or 'confirmed' P vs NP. None of these have been digested, verified, or endorsed by the complexity-theory community. Fortnow's April 2025 post ('P v NP Papers Galore') reports receiving roughly seven such claims in two weeks (well above his usual rate of one per month), places them into the same recurring categories of error seen for decades (unjustified assumptions about machine behavior, algorithms that only work on small test cases, philosophical reframing rather than mathematical argument), and states such papers 'rarely (really never) provide new insights.' Notably, Fortnow's own suggested use of AI is exactly the kind of role that does NOT count under this scheme: he recommends authors ask a reasoning model to critique their own paper before sending it to him -- i.e., AI as a proofreading/sanity-check gate, not as a producer of mathematical content. The claims that do invoke AI (Vega's 'AI confirmed my proof', ChatGPT-4 'reviewing' a 12-paper submission and finding no flags) describe AI checking or endorsing human-authored arguments, not AI producing an argument, construction, or case that entered any accepted result -- and none of the underlying proofs is itself accepted, so there is no settled mathematical content for AI to have contributed to in the first place. This is a clean 'nothing happened' case under the scope rule in section 3: no case of the stated problem was settled, no bound on any open sub-question moved, and the recurring claims are uniformly rejected variants/errors rather than admitted partial results.
competing_reading: One could argue the sheer volume and persistence of AI-'endorsed' claims (Vega's repeated ResearchGate posts, the 12-paper Coq-core submission reviewed favorably by ChatGPT-4, the Medium/Towards AI pieces explicitly titled 'AI Solves The P Versus NP Problem') constitutes an 'incident' worth recording as progress/ai_role=incident, since these are AI-adjacent claims that were at least implicitly withdrawn by community non-acceptance. I did not code it this way because none of these claims was ever accepted, published, or treated as live by any expert -- there was no rise-then-fall trajectory of acceptance to withdraw, just perpetual, ambient rejection, which is qualitatively different from the 'announced claim later retracted' pattern the incident code is meant to capture. If a future record-keeper judges that the volume itself is the notable event, `progress`/`incident` dated to, e.g., the April 2025 Vega claim would be the alternative classification.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an expert digestion (Fortnow, Aaronson, or a journal of record) stating that any specific 2024-2026 claimed proof withstood scrutiny -- none currently exists -- or (b) an authors' account, for any accepted or even seriously-considered partial result, stating that an AI system produced part of the mathematical argument rather than merely checking or critiquing human-produced work.

outcome: A May 2026 preprint by Colliot-Thélène and Schreieder proves ℓ-divisibility (up to torsion) results for the Bloch–Ogus coniveau filtration on motivic cohomology of smooth projective varieties over finite fields — a weaker assertion than, but directly bearing on, Parshin's conjecture — and gives an affirmative answer to their own open question (their Question 1.7, essentially a form of Parshin's conjecture for motivic cohomology) in special cases (i,n) where the étale cycle class map is known to be injective, e.g. i ≤ n+1 by Suslin–Voevodsky. This is progress/a partial special case, not a resolution of Parshin's conjecture itself, which remains open beyond dimension 1. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this history.
summary: Parshin's conjecture as stated in the frozen bullet (higher algebraic K-groups of smooth projective varieties over finite fields vanish up to torsion) remains open in general, proven only for dim 0 (Quillen) and dim 1 (Harder), as the problem's own Wikipedia article confirms with no update since 2024. Two items surfaced in triage and in my own search. (1) arXiv:2011.05544 'Proof of the Parshin's Conjecture' by Aydin Yousefzadehfard: verified via the arXiv abstract/comment page that this was withdrawn by the author on 2020-11-21 (v2), with the author's own comment identifying a flaw in Theorem 4.7 ('There is a problem with the Theorem 4.7... it ruins the double deformation construction'). It never entered the literature as a proof, and in any case its only activity (submission and withdrawal) is from November 2020, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen-revision date — it is not an event in the window at all, not even open_stale material, since nothing about it changed after 2024. (2) arXiv:2605.22494 'Divisibility phenomena in motivic Bloch–Ogus theory' by Colliot-Thélène and Schreieder, submitted 21 May 2026 (within the window): I fetched the full HTML text and located the paper's explicit discussion of Parshin's conjecture in §1.3, where the authors state Parshin's conjecture predicts H_M^i(X,Z(n))⊗Q_ℓ = 0 for i ≠ 2n, and then say their Theorem 1.4 proves 'the weaker assertion' that the Bloch–Ogus filtration step L_j vanishes after tensoring with Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ for j<n. They pose their own open Question 1.7 asking whether the full statement (a form of Parshin's conjecture for motivic cohomology with Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ coefficients) holds, and in Appendix C give an affirmative answer to that question in special cases (i,n) where the relevant étale cycle class map is injective — which by Suslin–Voevodsky covers i ≤ n+1. This is a genuine, dated, primary-sourced piece of progress: a bound/partial-vanishing result that is explicitly framed by the authors themselves as bearing on Parshin's conjecture, restricted to special cases, not a full resolution — hence `progress` rather than `partial` or `resolved`, since the general conjecture (all i, all n, all smooth projective X/finite field, all dimensions) is untouched and the authors' own Question 1.7 (closer to the actual conjecture) is left open outside those special cases. I separately verified an earlier item mentioned by triage's search context, a 2023 paper ('Motivic cohomology and K-theory of some surfaces over finite fields', published in J. Pure Appl. Algebra / J. London Math. Soc., August 2023) whose appendix 'slightly enlarges the class of surfaces for which Parshin's conjecture is known' — but this predates the frozen revision date (published 2023, and referenced already-existing arXiv work), so even if its arXiv posting is confirmed pre-2024 it is not a window event; I was unable to find its exact arXiv ID/submission date via search, so I have not counted it as an event either way, noting the gap in `incomplete`. I found no mention of AI, LLMs, Lean/Coq formalization, or any computational proof assistant anywhere in the 2026 Colliot-Thélène–Schreieder paper (checked its full text and acknowledgements) or in any secondary source discussing Parshin's conjecture; this is standard human-authored pure mathematics.
competing_reading: One could argue this is not really progress on 'Parshin's conjecture' as Wikipedia's bullet states it (K-groups vanish up to torsion) but rather progress on a related-but-distinct motivic-cohomology reformulation (vanishing of H_M^i(X,Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ(n)) for i≠2n), which the paper's own Question 1.7 treats as a question in its own right rather than as identical to Parshin's original K-theoretic statement — under the strict §3.1 scope rule this could be read as a 'related problem' (a reformulation with different objects, motivic cohomology groups rather than K-groups) rather than a 'case' of the stated problem, which would make the correct status `open` with `no_change_found` true rather than `progress`. I lean toward `progress` because the authors themselves present their motivic-cohomology statement as the natural refinement/reformulation of Parshin's conjecture (citing the standard motivic spectral sequence relating K-theory and motivic cohomology, under which the K-theoretic vanishing follows from the motivic one), and because they explicitly answer their own question — which is essentially Parshin's conjecture stated in motivic-cohomological terms — affirmatively in nontrivial special cases.
what_would_settle_it: A citation or explicit statement in the paper (or a companion source) spelling out the precise implication from their motivic-cohomology vanishing statement to K_i(X)⊗Q = 0 (i.e. via the motivic spectral sequence converging to K-theory), which would confirm the special cases in Appendix C are literally cases of the K-theoretic Parshin conjecture and not merely a cohomological analogue; and locating the exact arXiv submission date of the 2023 Gregory/appendix surfaces paper to confirm it is indeed pre-window.

outcome: A July 2026 preprint (Cheng & Sgueglia) proves an asymptotic version of Kotzig's perfect 1-factorization conjecture: K_n can be decomposed into n-1 perfect matchings such that (1-o(1))n of them pairwise form Hamilton cycles; the conjecture that ALL n-1 matchings can be made to pairwise form Hamilton cycles remains open.

ai.basis_quote: The construction in Theorem 1.3 is a generalisation of the one presented at the beginning of the Introduction and was generated by ChatGPT 5.4, which also gave a correct but rather long proof. The one presented here is a cleaner, shorter and substantially different one, and was obtained by the authors. The proof of Theorem 1.2 was entirely obtained by the authors.

summary: The conjecture (Kotzig, 1964): every K_2n, n>=2, has a perfect 1-factorization (a 1-factorization in which every pair of perfect matchings forms a Hamilton cycle). It remains open in general as of this writing. The one substantive development in the window is arXiv:2607.09459 'The perfect 1-factorisation conjecture holds asymptotically' (Cheng & Sgueglia, submitted 2026-07-10), which proves that for large even n, K_n has a 1-factorization in which a (1-o(1)) fraction of the n-1 matchings pairwise form Hamilton cycles (Theorem 1.2), building on an auxiliary near-optimal construction of edge-disjoint 'perfect pairs' matchings (Theorem 1.3) that cannot itself be extended to a full factorization. This is progress on the density/bound of the conjecture, not a resolution of any case n=2n0, and not a resolution of the conjecture itself -- it is squarely a 'bound moved on a problem that is still open' situation, so status is 'progress' with resolution_direction null per Section 6.4. On AI: the paper contains an explicit 'Comment on the use of AI' section (unusual and directly on point for this project) stating that ChatGPT 5.4 generated a correct construction and proof for the (superseded, more general) version of Theorem 1.3 presented at the start of the Introduction, but that the proof actually used in the paper -- for both Theorem 1.3 as stated and for the main result Theorem 1.2 -- was obtained entirely by the human authors, described as 'cleaner, shorter and substantially different.' Per Section 6.2, ai_role is coded on what mathematics from an AI system appears in the final result: since the authors state the AI-generated construction and proof were replaced by their own independent, different proof, and that Theorem 1.2 (the paper's main claim, on which this record's status rests) was 'entirely obtained by the authors,' no AI-produced mathematics survives into the published result, so ai_role is 'none.' The second triage-flagged paper (arXiv:2510.01949, Glock & Sgueglia, 'On Kotzig's conjecture in random graphs,' Oct 2025) addresses a related-but-different question -- existence of k edge-disjoint perfect-pair matchings in the random graph G(n,p) rather than a full 1-factorization of the complete graph K_2n -- and shows no AI involvement; it is a related problem under Section 3.1's scope test (changes the host graph from K_2n to G(n,p)), not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not itself drive this record's status, though it corroborates recent research interest and shares an author and toolkit with the asymptotic paper. No resolution, no case settled exactly, and no counterexample were found anywhere in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue ai_role should not simply be 'none' but should be flagged as a near-miss 'incident'-adjacent situation: an AI system did produce a complete, correct, verified construction and proof for a real theorem in the paper's lineage (the more general version of Theorem 1.3), and its existence plausibly shaped the authors' confidence that the approach would work, even though the specific proof appearing in print was independently re-derived by humans. The rules in Section 6.2 are explicit that only mathematics 'in the final result' counts, and the authors are explicit that the printed proof is 'substantially different,' so 'none' is the correct code, but a reader focused on process rather than the artifact might weight this differently. Also debatable: whether the asymptotic result should be read as 'partial' (a case: 'for sufficiently large n, almost all pairs') rather than 'progress' (a bound). I read it as a bound because no specific n or Hamilton-cycle-pair count is exactly settled -- the o(1) term is never removed for any concrete n -- consistent with Section 3.1's guidance that a bound moving is 'progress' rather than a case being 'settled.'
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution would require either a proof that ALL n-1 matchings (not just (1-o(1))n) can be made pairwise Hamilton for all large even n, or a counterexample exhibiting some even n with no perfect 1-factorization of K_n at all. Absent that, expert digestion (e.g., a Tao-style blog treatment, or journal acceptance) of arXiv:2607.09459 would move it from a fresh preprint toward more firmly established progress, though the status code ('progress' on an open problem) would not change since the underlying conjecture is still unresolved either way.

outcome: No proof of existence or non-existence of a perfect cuboid has been accepted by the mathematical community since 26 January 2024; a large, uncoordinated wave of unreviewed preprints and Zenodo postings claiming non-existence proofs appeared through 2025-2026, alongside genuine incremental computational/theoretical progress (de Grey-Gibbs-Helm 2024, Asiryan 2025), but none has been digested, verified, or accepted, so the problem remains open as stated.

disputes.summary: Between roughly May 2025 and April 2026 at least six independent, mutually uncoordinated preprints/Zenodo postings (ResearchGate 'Simplified proof', Zenodo differential-algebraic-closure proof, arXiv:2602.00239 'An Elementary Obstruction', arXiv:2604.28072 'torsion-intersection proof on 1,072 fibers', a further Zenodo 'Mordell Weil Rank Exhaustion' posting, and others) each separately claim to prove non-existence of a perfect cuboid using unrelated methods, none citing or refuting the others, none appearing in a peer-reviewed venue, and none discussed in expert forums (no MathOverflow thread, no Terence Tao blog post, no journal acceptance found). This pattern (many disconnected 'complete proof' claims of a centuries-old problem posted to math.GM/Zenodo in quick succession) is itself the notable event, more than any single paper.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen statement covers existence of a perfect cuboid (integer edges, face diagonals, and space diagonal) and the associated 'cuboid conjectures'. Since 26 January 2024, no result has been accepted by the mathematical community: no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or MathOverflow/blog consensus was found for any claimed non-existence proof. What has happened is (a) genuine but modest incremental progress: de Grey, Gibbs and Helm's 'Novel required properties of, and efficient algorithms to seek, perfect cuboids' (arXiv:2401.06784, submitted 6 January 2024 — before the frozen revision, so this specific paper is background rather than in-window news, though its Geombinatorics journal appearance is dated 2024) extended computational search ranges and identified elliptic-curve families that must have positive rank if a perfect cuboid exists; and Valery Asiryan's October 2025 paper (arXiv:2510.11768) proved irreducibility of the cuboid polynomial in a two-parameter case, resolving 'Sharipov's first conjecture' as a special case rather than the full problem — this is a genuine `partial` result on a named sub-conjecture within the field, confirming the conjectured irreducibility. But (b) the dominant phenomenon in the window is a wave of unreviewed, mutually uncited preprints and Zenodo deposits (May 2025 through April 2026) each independently claiming to fully resolve non-existence via unrelated methods — divisor-based parameterization, differential algebraic closure, elementary congruence/descent arguments (Yelle, arXiv:2602.00239), and torsion-intersection arguments on 1,072 explicit fibers (Peschmann, arXiv:2604.28072, which itself only claims to prove the conjecture on fibers where max(a,b) ≤ 100, i.e. a bounded family, not the full conjecture, despite its abstract's 'unconditional proof' language). None of these has been checked by named experts, none appears accepted at a journal, and no retraction or rebuttal was found either — they simply sit uncorroborated. None discloses any AI/LLM involvement; the only computational tools mentioned (PARI's ellrank, Sage) are classical computer-algebra systems, not AI. A general essay on AI-generated mathematics (Weinreich, arXiv:2608.02859, August 2026) was found but does not mention perfect cuboids specifically and gives no evidence tying this particular flood to AI authorship. Given the absence of any accepted resolution, and treating the Peschmann/Yelle/ResearchGate claims individually as unverified preprints rather than established results, the correct status is `open`, not `claimed`, because §6.1 reserves `claimed` for a specific preprint or announcement that at least represents the field's live candidate outcome; here there are several mutually exclusive 'complete proof' candidates with no way to identify a single decisive one, and the Peschmann paper (the most-cited of the flurry) itself only covers a bounded fiber family rather than the whole conjecture. The closest thing to `partial` status is Asiryan's irreducibility result on Sharipov's first conjecture, but that is a named sub-conjecture in the broader 'cuboid conjectures' family rather than the existence question itself, so I record it in summary/disputes rather than driving the top-level status.
competing_reading: A stricter reading could set status to `claimed` keyed on arXiv:2604.28072 (Peschmann, 30 April 2026), since it is the most recent, most technically detailed, and most narrowly scoped ('1,072 explicit master-tuple fibers' bounded by max(a,b) ≤ 100) of the non-existence claims, and a triage record found it too. I did not adopt this because the paper's own scope is explicitly a bounded family of fibers, not the general conjecture, so even if fully correct it would only be `partial` at best, and with zero expert verification even `partial`/`claimed` status feels premature given several competing unverified claims exist with no way to adjudicate priority or correctness from outside. A reader who weights 'most recent, most technical' preprints more heavily than I do might instead file this as `claimed` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (i.e., confirming non-existence).
what_would_settle_it: Any of: an expert (e.g. a number theorist active in Diophantine geometry, or a MathOverflow/Tao-blog discussion) publicly assessing correctness of one of the 2025-2026 non-existence claims; acceptance of any of these preprints at a peer-reviewed journal; a formal Lean/Coq verification of the argument; or a rebuttal/counterexample showing one of the claimed proofs is flawed (which, given the volume of mutually silent claims, seems at least as likely as any one being correct).

outcome: A September 2026 preprint by Zehua Lai, Lek-Heng Lim, and Junyu Ren claims a counterexample disproving the general Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture (dimensions 5,6,7,22,24,30,72, likely all n≥3), found with assistance from a multi-agent, multi-model AI setup; a July 2025 preprint by Lai and Lim separately proved the conjecture true for the spline (hyperplane-partition) special case, a related but distinct problem.

ai.basis_quote: The counterexample was found with the assistance of our multi-agent, multi-model setup that chains together GPT 5.6, GPT 6, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Fable 5.1. ... The counterexample in this article is notably not found with any single large language model (we tried doing so without success) but requires harnessing multiple systems ... The matrix-pair construction in dimension 72 and the argument excluding representations of arbitrary degree emerged from GPT investigations.

counterexample.object: A continuous, positively-homogeneous-of-degree-two, piecewise-quadratic function on the space of pairs of symmetric 5x5 matrices (realized as a 30-dimensional example), that is piecewise quadratic on a finite semialgebraic partition of R^n but cannot be written as a finite lattice (max-of-mins) combination of polynomials; the same construction is reported to generalize to n = 5, 6, 7, 22, 24, 72, and conjecturally to all n ≥ 3.
counterexample.verified_how: Authors report human expert checking of the main n=30 construction plus Lean formalization; the 5D/6D/7D constructions have human review 'ongoing' per the repository README, and no completed human review is claimed for the 8D construction.

summary: Two arXiv preprints bear on this problem within the window. (1) arXiv:2507.07976 (Zehua Lai and Lek-Heng Lim, submitted 2025-07-10) proves the Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for 'splines' — continuous piecewise polynomials on a hyperplane partition of R^n. This is a restriction of the general conjecture (hyperplane partitions are a special case of the semialgebraic partitions the general conjecture allows), so under §3.1 it is a genuine case of the stated problem, not a variant — but since a broader counterexample later appeared, the spline result is subsumed rather than being the operative event. No AI involvement is mentioned anywhere in that paper's text. (2) arXiv:2609.10420 (Lai, Lim, and Junyu Ren, submitted 2026-09-09) claims the general Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture, as stated on the Wikipedia bullet ('every piecewise-polynomial f:R^n→R is the maximum of a finite set of minimums of finite collections of polynomials'), is FALSE: they exhibit a continuous piecewise-quadratic counterexample on semialgebraic partitions (realized on pairs of symmetric 5x5 matrices, 30-dimensional) that cannot be written as such a lattice combination, and report the construction generalizes to several other dimensions and likely to all n≥3. This is squarely in-scope: it directly negates the stated conjecture, not a neighboring problem. The authors' own abstract and body text state the counterexample was found via a chained multi-agent, multi-model LLM setup (GPT 5.6, GPT 6, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1), and explicitly that no single model succeeded — multiple systems working together were required, with specific pieces (the dimension-72 matrix-pair construction, an argument excluding arbitrary-degree representations) attributed to 'GPT investigations.' This satisfies the authors'-own-account bar for ai_role assisted (the AI produced pieces of the mathematics that appear in the final result; humans provided guidance, checked, and wrote the exposition) — the paper does not claim the AI single-handedly produced and the humans merely verified a complete proof, so I did not code this as 'generated'; see competing_reading. Because this preprint is only 13 days old at the time of this research (today is 2026-09-22) it has not yet been digested by a human expert in the traditional sense (no Tao blog post, no journal acceptance, no named-expert public verification found). A companion Lean-formalization repository (github.com/7pocheR/Pierce-Birkhoff) exists and its README states the main n=30 construction's proof 'has undergone careful human expert checking and is formalized in Lean,' while review of the 5D/6D/7D constructions is 'ongoing' and no claim of completed review is made for an 8D construction — this is short of full traditional digestion and I could not independently confirm the identity or independence of the 'human expert' checkers. I also found an automated review of the paper on 'Pith Review' (pith.science), a platform that itself describes its process as AI-assisted deep review 'overseen by humans' — this is not the kind of named human-expert digestion that would justify 'resolved,' so I classified status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved.' No retraction, dispute, or priority conflict was found.
competing_reading: One could argue the AI's role rises to 'generated' rather than 'assisted': the abstract's framing ('found with the assistance of') is the authors' own softening, but the body credits GPT investigations with producing the dimension-72 construction and the degree-exclusion argument outright, and states no single human-driven approach (implicitly) or single model sufficed — suggesting the mathematical content, not just the search process, came substantially from the AI systems, with humans mainly verifying, simplifying, and writing up. Conversely, one could also argue for 'open' rather than 'claimed' on grounds that a 13-day-old, not-yet-peer-reviewed preprint with only partial, unnamed 'human expert checking' should not move the needle on the conjecture's status at all until it survives scrutiny — but the rules define 'claimed' precisely for this situation, so I kept 'claimed.'
what_would_settle_it: A public human-expert digestion (e.g. a specialist's blog post, MathOverflow consensus, or journal referee report) confirming or refuting the n=30 (or smaller) counterexample construction; identification of the 'human expert' checkers named in the Lean repository and confirmation they are independent of the authors; completion of the Lean formalization without 'sorry' for the smaller-dimension cases; and a clearer authorial statement on whether the AI systems produced the core mathematical construction versus merely searching a space of candidates the humans had already framed.

outcome: No result found since 26 January 2024 that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet: the general conjecture that Ax^m - By^n = C has finitely many solutions (for (m,n) not both 2) remains open, with only pre-existing partial results and post-window papers on related-but-distinct equations found.
summary: I searched extensively for any post-26-January-2024 progress on the specific conjecture stated in the bullet — that for fixed A, B, C the equation Ax^m - By^n = C has finitely many solutions in x, y, m, n when (m,n) are not both 2 — and found none. I examined the Wikipedia article (unchanged in substance, still lists only pre-2011 references and no update reflecting new progress) and several arXiv papers that surfaced in searches: (1) Miyazaki & Pink, 'Number of solutions to a special type of unit equations in two unknowns, III' (arXiv:2403.20037, submitted 29 March 2024, revised 12 April 2025) — this studies a^x + b^y = c^z (a Jesmanowicz/Terai-type unit equation) and Bennett's related conjecture on a^x - b^y = c for fixed small c, citing Pillai-type equations only as background/motivation, not proving anything about the general A,B,C-parameterized conjecture; (2) Styer, arXiv:2402.04428 (Feb 2024) and (3) arXiv:2407.07407 (July 2024) — both study the same a^x + b^y = c^z equation, a three-term generalization distinct from the bullet's two-term Ax^m - By^n = C equation, and only cite Pillai's equation a^x - b^y = c as related prior work. None of these papers restrict or specialize the conjecture as literally stated (fixed general A, B, C); they address a different equation with an extra term and different variable structure, which is a related problem under §3.1's test, not a case of this one. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this space. The status is 'open' with no_change_found true, matching and confirming the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Miyazaki-Pink 2403.20037 result on a^x - b^y = c for c = 13 (a special case of the two-term Pillai equation with fixed C=13, A=B=1) is a 'case' of the stated conjecture rather than a 'related problem', since it does specialize A=1, B=1 and fixes C. However, this specific sub-case (A=B=1) was already resolved by earlier work (Bennett's 2001 result gives at most two solutions for any fixed f in x^n - y^m = f), so even under this reading the 2024/2025 paper is refining/extending an already-settled special case (via the three-term equation, using it as a tool) rather than advancing the general A,B,C conjecture itself — it does not change this bullet's entry either way.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving a finiteness or non-finiteness result for the equation Ax^m - By^n = C for general or newly-unbounded ranges of A, B, C (not just A=B=1 or a single fixed C), or an explicit statement in a survey/expert digestion (e.g., an update to Waldschmidt's 'Perfect Powers' survey or the Bennett 'Pillai's conjecture revisited' line of work) that the general conjecture status changed after January 2024.

outcome: The problem (determining the true order of the error term Δ_k(x) in the generalized/Piltz divisor problem) remains open for every k≥2, but several explicit-constant and exponent improvements were published within the window, most concretely Sebastian Tudzi's paper giving explicit numerical bounds |Δ₃(x)| < 2.968x^(2/3)log^(1/3)x and general-k bounds with explicit constants for k=4,5,6, first posted to arXiv 26 June 2025 and later published in the Ramanujan Journal (2026). No AI system was involved in any of the papers examined.
summary: The Piltz (generalized Dirichlet) divisor problem asks for the true order of Δ_k(x) = D_k(x) − xP_k(log x), the error term when d_k(n) (n written as a product of k factors) is summed up to x; for every k this remains open, since only upper bounds on the exponent α_k are known and the conjectured optimal value α_k = 1/2 − 1/(2k) has not been proven for any k≥2. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) I found no resolution of the problem for any k, but several genuine incremental results narrowing/explicating known bounds. The clearest is Sebastian Tudzi, 'On the Generalised Divisor Problem' (arXiv:2506.21823, posted 26 June 2025, published in Ramanujan J. 70 (2026)), which via the Dirichlet convolution method gives an explicit numerical bound |Δ₃(x)| < 2.968·x^(2/3)(log x)^(1/3) for all x≥2 (improving prior explicit constants for k=3) and explicit constants for the general-k bound Δ_k(x) = O(x^((k-1)/k)(log x)^((k-1)(k-2)/(2k))) for k=4,5,6 with a recurrence for larger k. I read the arXiv HTML full text including the acknowledgements section, which thanks the author's supervisor Timothy S. Trudgian and several colleagues for discussion — no computational or AI tool is mentioned anywhere. I also checked two other leads the triage pass surfaced: (1) Minamide, Tanigawa and Watt, 'On the sum of Δ_k(n) in the Piltz divisor problem for k=3 and k=4' (arXiv:2412.11069, posted 15 Dec 2024, published Acta Arithmetica 216.4 (2024)) — this bounds the *summed* quantity Σ_{n≤x}Δ_k(n), a related but distinct object from Δ_k(x) itself; I judged this a case/adjacent result worth noting but it does not itself move the bound on Δ_k(x) as stated in the bullet, and its abstract shows no AI involvement. (2) A preprints.org manuscript ('On the Generalized Dirichlet Divisor Problem', May 2025) claimed by triage to give improved α_k bounds for 9≤k≤20 — this page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch and I could not read it directly; Tao's expdb blueprint (teorth.github.io) corroborates that a 2025 result by 'Li' improves α_k for k in the 9–20 range (its Theorem 16.20), competing with earlier Trudgian–Yang bounds (Theorem 16.19, from arXiv:2306.05599, whose v1 predates the window (9 June 2023) but whose v3 was posted 15 July 2024, inside the window — I could not confirm from the abstract alone whether v3 added genuinely new results or was a revision of the same June-2023 result, so I am not resting the status on it). I also checked and ruled out two other candidate events as predating the window: Bellotti–Yang's large-k bound Δ_k(x) ≪ x^(1−1.889k^(−2/3)) (arXiv:2303.05028, posted 9 March 2023, journal-published in BLMS May 2024 — the journal date is not the event date per §6.3) and Li–Yang's α₂ ≤ 0.314483... (arXiv:2308.14859, posted 28 August 2023). Both predate 26 January 2024 and would be open_stale if they were the only evidence, but since the Tudzi 2025 result is a genuine in-window improvement, the overall status is 'progress' rather than 'open_stale'. I found no trace of AI/LLM involvement anywhere in this corner of analytic number theory: no papers, blog posts, or lab announcements connect the Piltz/generalized divisor problem to any AI system. This is consistent with the nature of the problem — it requires exponential-sum and zeta-moment estimation techniques that are far from current AI theorem-proving benchmarks (IMO-style problems, short combinatorial arguments), and no lab or Lean/AI project appears to have targeted it.
competing_reading: One could argue the Tudzi paper's contribution is narrow enough (explicit constants for an already-known asymptotic exponent, not a new exponent) that it should be 'open' rather than 'progress' — the qualitative bound O(x^((k-1)/k)(log x)^(...)) for k≥4 was already the known form; what changed is the numerical constant λ_k. I classified it as 'progress' because bounding constants explicitly is itself the kind of incremental movement the triage/audit rules treat as counting (§3.1: 'a bound that moved a little... counts'), and because the k=3 case did tighten the known exponent-adjacent estimate with an explicit, checkable numerical inequality. A stricter reading limiting 'progress' to exponent (not just constant) improvements would instead call this 'open' with the Tudzi paper noted as a near-miss.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the preprints.org manuscript directly (currently blocked by a 403) to see exactly which α_k values for 9≤k≤20 it improves and whether it substantively differs from the Trudgian–Yang and Li results already logged in Tao's expdb; and diffing arXiv:2306.05599 v1 (June 2023) against v3 (July 2024) to see whether the divisor-problem-relevant theorem was added or only revised in the window.

outcome: No mathematical progress on Polignac's conjecture itself (that every even n is a de Polignac number, i.e. a gap occurring infinitely often) has occurred since 26 January 2024. The best bound remains the Polymath8b [2,246] result from 2014. The only relevant post-window event is an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization (verification, not new mathematics) of that pre-existing 2014 result, published by the startup Axiom Math on 17 August 2026.

summary: Polignac's conjecture (every positive even n is a de Polignac number, occurring as a prime gap infinitely often) remains fully open since the frozen revision. The best known partial result is still Polymath8b's 2014 demonstration that at least one even number in [2,246] is a de Polignac number (following Zhang 2013 and Maynard 2013) — this predates the window and is unchanged. Searches for post-window mathematical progress (new bounds, new cases settled, a full proof, or a disproof) turned up nothing: two 2024 papers (Banks, 'Consecutive primes and IP sets', arXiv:2403.10637, March 2024; Goswami, 'An Explicit Ramsey Bound for de Polignac Numbers', arXiv:2406.02243, June 2024) study Ramsey/IP-set structural properties of the *set* of already-known de Polignac numbers, but neither extends the range of proven gaps, settles a new case, or touches the general conjecture — they are related structural results, not progress on the stated question, and carry no AI involvement. A 2021 paper (arXiv:2108.13834) and a 2019 paper (arXiv:1912.09290) proving conditional/special cases both predate the window. The one genuinely new and notable post-window event is Axiom Math's AxiomProver, an AI system, producing a machine-checked Lean 4 formalization (released 17 August 2026, conditional on the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem) of the existing Maynard/Polymath8b argument for the 246 bound — described by the company and IEEE Spectrum coverage explicitly as a reconstruction/verification of a known proof, not a new mathematical result. Because this changes nothing a careful person would write in the conjecture's entry (no new n, no tightened bound, no case newly settled), and because the AI's role was formalization of an already-completed human proof, the record is classified status=open/no_change_found=true and ai_role=none per the formalisation_only rule (§6.2). Wikipedia's own article is unchanged and does not mention this formalization.
competing_reading: One could argue the Axiom Math formalization deserves a 'progress' or 'claimed' status as an instructive AI-related incident even though it doesn't move the mathematical needle, since it is the single most substantial thing that happened to this problem's surrounding literature in the window. But per §3.1 and §6.1, status must reflect the state of the conjecture as stated, and a formalization of a 12-year-old result changes nothing about what a careful person would write about Polignac's conjecture today; it is documented in ai/summary but does not justify moving status off 'open'.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement that reduces the [2,246] bound further, proves the conjecture for a new specific even n via a genuinely new construction, or proves/disproves the general conjecture, dated after 26 January 2024.

outcome: Basak, Dong, Saettone & Zaharescu (Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, with Zaharescu also at the Simion Stoilow Institute) proved corrected, sharp versions of Pollock's 1843 icosahedral and dodecahedral numbers conjectures — every positive integer is a sum of at most 15 icosahedral numbers (not Pollock's original 13) and at most 22 dodecahedral numbers (not Pollock's original 21) — via the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, Hasse-Weil bounds, Bombieri's exponential-sum theorem, and complete numerical verification of remaining small cases. This settles two of the several conjectures grouped under the 'Pollock's conjectures' bullet; the tetrahedral-numbers conjecture (241 exceptions, 343,867 conjectured largest) remains fully open, and the octahedral-numbers conjecture remains proved only for sufficiently large integers (Elessar Brady, 2016, predates the window).

counterexample.object: Specific integers refuting Pollock's original bound claims: for icosahedral numbers, 47, 83, 94, and 119 each require 14 icosahedral numbers (exceeding Pollock's claimed 13), and 95 requires 15; for dodecahedral numbers, 79 requires 22 dodecahedral numbers (exceeding Pollock's claimed 21), e.g. 79 = 20+20+20+1+1+...+1 with nineteen 1's.
counterexample.verified_how: Direct arithmetic verification of the polyhedral-number representations of these specific integers, combined with a computational search establishing no larger integer needs more terms; the corrected bounds (15, 22) were then proved sharp and universal via analytic number theory plus complete numerical verification for remaining bounded cases.

summary: The 'Pollock's conjectures' bullet groups five distinct claims by Frederick Pollock (1843/1850): sums of at most 5 tetrahedral, 7 octahedral, 13 icosahedral, 21 dodecahedral, or 9 cube numbers. Since 26 January 2024, the icosahedral and dodecahedral cases were fully settled by Basak, Dong, Saettone & Zaharescu (International Mathematics Research Notices, Vol. 2025, Issue 13, published within the window; a corresponding arXiv preprint 2608.08019 was posted 8 Aug 2026, i.e. after the journal publication, and I use the earlier journal date per §6.3's 'first public written argument' rule since it precedes the preprint here). The paper is a clean, expert-published resolution using the circle method, Hasse-Weil bounds, Bombieri's theorem, and computational verification of finitely many remaining cases — this counts as 'resolved' for the icosahedral/dodecahedral sub-cases individually, but I classify the overall bullet as 'partial' because the tetrahedral and octahedral sub-conjectures (also part of the same Wikipedia bullet) remain open or only asymptotically resolved, with no change to those since the window began. The result is 'mixed' in direction: it refutes Pollock's original numerical bounds (13, 21) — with explicit counterexamples 47/83/94/95/119 and 79 — while confirming corrected, sharp replacement bounds (15, 22). No AI system was involved anywhere in this work; the methods are entirely classical analytic number theory plus ordinary computational/numerical verification (e.g. the companion GitHub repository runs a plain Python brute-force check over stated integer ranges), which does not qualify as an AI system under §6.2. I found no acknowledgements, author statements, or secondary coverage mentioning any AI or machine-learning tool in connection with this result.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet should be scored per-sub-conjecture rather than as one whole, which would make the icosahedral/dodecahedral portion 'resolved' outright; I chose 'partial' because Wikipedia presents all five claims under a single 'Pollock's conjectures' heading and the tetrahedral/octahedral cases are unresolved, so a careful reader of the whole entry would still find open content. Also arguable: the exact first-public-date is ambiguous given the arXiv preprint (Aug 2026) postdates the journal issue (Jul 2025) — an unusual ordering — so I used the earlier, journal date as the operative event date.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from the authors or arXiv moderation explaining why the arXiv posting (2608.08019, Aug 2026) came more than a year after the IMRN publication (Jul 2025) would resolve the dating ambiguity, though it doesn't change which is earlier. Resolution of the tetrahedral or octahedral sub-conjectures would change the overall bullet's status further.

outcome: Two independent groups constructed noncircular planar domains that fail the Pompeiu property (and disprove the closely tied Schiffer conjecture in the plane): Colbrook & Stepaniants (arXiv:2608.01579, submitted 2026-08-03) via a rigorous computer-assisted (interval-arithmetic) construction, and Cao-Labora & de Dios Pont (arXiv:2608.05114, submitted 2026-08-05) via an independent bifurcation-theory argument yielding infinitely many such domains, machine-checked in Lean 4. The result refutes the classical planar Pompeiu conjecture as stated on the frozen Wikipedia revision.

ai.basis_quote: Public entry points listed in the jaumededios/Schiffer README include a 'Machine-generated readable informalization of the Lean proof.'

counterexample.object: A bounded, simply connected, noncircular domain with real-analytic (Jordan) boundary on which a Neumann eigenfunction is constant on the boundary, and (independently) an infinite family of N-fold symmetric non-disk planar domains from a bifurcation-theory construction; both fail the Pompeiu property and refute Schiffer's conjecture in the plane.
counterexample.verified_how: Colbrook & Stepaniants: rigorous computer-assisted proof using interval enclosures, a frozen numerical verifier, and a certificate checker (artifact on Zenodo, https://zenodo.org/records/21765287) establishing an exact zero of a cubic operator equation via positivity/monotonicity bounds — not machine-learning based. Cao-Labora & de Dios Pont: bifurcation-theory argument formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 (https://github.com/jaumededios/Schiffer), stated to use no numerics.

disputes.summary: Two independent groups produced counterexamples within two days of each other (2026-08-03 and 2026-08-05); Colbrook & Stepaniants's preprint appeared first, but Cao-Labora & de Dios Pont describe theirs as an independent construction with a machine-checked (Lean 4) certificate, and produce infinitely many examples rather than a single one. Neither paper's abstract claims priority over the other, but both circulated on arXiv within the same week, so the historical record of who solved it 'first' may still be contested by the community.

summary: As of the frozen January 2024 revision, the Pompeiu problem asked whether the disk is the only bounded simply connected (Lipschitz) domain for which some nonzero function's integral vanishes over every rigid-motion copy. This has since been refuted. On 2026-08-03, Colbrook & Stepaniants (arXiv:2608.01579) posted a rigorous computer-assisted construction of a noncircular real-analytic domain that is a counterexample to both the Schiffer conjecture and (via Green's identity, as stated in the paper) the classical planar Pompeiu conjecture; their verification uses interval arithmetic, positivity of linearization coefficients, and a frozen numerical certificate checker (Zenodo artifact, https://zenodo.org/records/21765287) — this is computer-assisted numerical analysis, not an AI/ML system, and I found no mention of any language model anywhere in the paper, abstract, or Zenodo record. Two days later, Cao-Labora & de Dios Pont (arXiv:2608.05114, 2026-08-05) posted an independent construction using bifurcation theory, producing infinitely many N-fold-symmetric non-disk counterexamples for large N; their construction was formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 (github.com/jaumededios/Schiffer), which the repository states 'does not rely in any numerics.' I directly fetched the arXiv HTML of both papers and the GitHub README and found no acknowledgement, author statement, or acknowledgements section crediting GPT, Claude, or any other AI system with producing any part of the mathematics; a general WebSearch summary asserted that 'GPT-5.6 and Claude models' were used for numerical checks, proof drafts, and writing the Lean 4 verification, but I could not substantiate this claim against any primary source (the paper itself, its HTML, the GitHub repo, or the Zenodo record) — I treat this as an unverified/likely fabricated search synthesis and do not code it as AI involvement. The only confirmed AI-adjacent element is a 'machine-generated readable informalization of the Lean proof' listed as a public entry point in the GitHub README — this is a post-hoc exposition/readability aid describing an already-completed proof, not mathematics produced by an AI system, so it does not meet the bar for `assisted` (§6.2: formalising or explaining human-produced mathematics is `none`, and there is no authors' first-person quote crediting a model for the mathematics itself as required by §6.2). The current Wikipedia article (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem) confirms both results and additionally cites a 'Google DeepMind, Formal Conjectures: Pompeiu Problem' reference; I confirmed the underlying reality — the DeepMind google-deepmind/formal-conjectures Lean repository contains a formalized *statement* of the Pompeiu/Schiffer problem which the Cao-Labora/de Dios Pont Lean proof is checked against — but this is DeepMind's benchmark formalizing the conjecture's statement for automated-proving benchmarks, not DeepMind or any AI system producing the resolving mathematics. A Princeton math department seminar was given by George Stepaniants on 2026-09-16 titled 'A Shortcake Counterexample to the Planar Pompeiu and Schiffer Conjectures,' which is solid evidence of expert engagement with (though not yet full digestion/consensus acceptance of) the result, consistent with `resolved` given the double independent construction, the rigorous computer-assisted certificate, and the machine-checked formal proof.
competing_reading: One could argue for `claimed` rather than `resolved`, since neither paper has yet been through peer review or a full public expert digestion (e.g., no Tao blog post or comparable close reading was found), and the field is only about seven weeks old as of this research (2026-09-22). However, the combination of (a) two independent constructions using different methods reaching the same conclusion, (b) a machine-checked Lean 4 certificate for one of them, and (c) an invited seminar talk on the result at a major math department, together meet the `resolved` bar of 'directly checkable by hand or computer algebra' / expert engagement described in §6.1, even absent a journal publication.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed publication, a Terence-Tao-style public digestion of either proof, or confirmation/refutation from the broader spectral-geometry community would settle the `resolved` vs `claimed` classification more firmly. Independently obtaining and reading the authors' actual acknowledgements sections (which I could not fully access in the arXiv HTML rendering for the Colbrook-Stepaniants paper) would help settle definitively whether any AI system was credited.
