outcome: No core model containing all large cardinals has been constructed or shown not to exist; the closest bearing result (Aguilera, Bagaria & Lücke, 2024-2025) is a conditional theorem about the technical Weak HOD/Weak Ultimate-L Conjectures, not a resolution of the general 'ultimate core model' problem, and it does not settle whether such a model exists.

disputes.summary: A MathOverflow thread (referencing the Aguilera-Bagaria-Lücke papers, labeled [ABL24]/[ABGL25] there) asks open questions about whether exacting cardinals are compatible with V = Ultimate-L at all, and what the correct large-cardinal hierarchy looks like if the HOD Conjecture holds instead. This shows the community treats the bearing of these papers on Ultimate-L/the core-model program as still unsettled and under active discussion, not as a closed matter.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet is the general, informal problem of constructing a single canonical inner model ('the ultimate core model') that contains all large cardinals present in V — Woodin's broad core-model-theory program, of which the Ultimate-L Conjecture is one concrete formalization. Nothing in the window (26 Jan 2024 to today) constructs such a model, proves it cannot exist, or otherwise settles the general problem; the article on Core model (fetched today) still describes this as an open, active research area and cites nothing newer than 2013. The one line of work that plausibly bears on it is a pair of papers by Juan P. Aguilera, Joan Bagaria and Philipp Lücke: 'Large cardinals, structural reflection, and the HOD Conjecture' (arXiv:2411.11568, first submitted 18 Nov 2024, latest v4 16 Sep 2025) and the companion 'Large cardinals beyond HOD' (arXiv:2509.10254, submitted 12 Sep 2025). These introduce 'exacting' and 'ultraexacting' cardinals and prove (Theorem B of 2411.11568, read directly from the arXiv HTML): 'Suppose that the theory ZFC is consistent with the assumption that there is an extendible cardinal below an exacting cardinal. Then, the Weak HOD Conjecture and the Weak Ultimate-L Conjecture are false.' This is a conditional (relative-consistency) result about the Weak HOD and Weak Ultimate-L Conjectures specifically — named, narrower conjectures in the Ultimate-L program — not an unconditional theorem, and not a statement about the Wikipedia bullet's own general question of whether an ultimate core model exists. Reading these Weak conjectures' refutation as bearing on the general problem stated in this bullet would be treating a related, more specific conjecture as if it were the stated question; per §3.1 that makes it a related-problem result rather than a case of this problem, so it does not move the status here. No search turned up any AI system (LLM, automated theorem prover, or otherwise) anywhere in this line of work: neither paper's text (fetched directly) mentions AI, GPT, Claude, Copilot, Lean, or any proof assistant, and a further search for 'exacting cardinal'/'ultraexacting' combined with AI terms returned nothing connecting them. Broader searches for AI-assisted work on the Ultimate-L program or core models generally (e.g. work on LLMs as provers/verifiers, autoformalization surveys) found generic AI-mathematics research unrelated to this specific problem. I am satisfied nothing has happened to the general 'ultimate core model' problem itself in this window, and that no AI was involved in the one adjacent development that exists.
competing_reading: A looser reading could count the Aguilera-Bagaria-Lücke result as `progress` on this bullet on the theory that the Ultimate-L Conjecture is the leading candidate formalization of 'the ultimate core model' and that conditionally refuting the Weak Ultimate-L Conjecture (and, if the exacting-cardinal consistency holds, the full Ultimate-L Conjecture and HOD Conjecture too) narrows the space of plausible ultimate-core-model programs. Under that reading the status would be `progress` with `ai_role` `none` and `resolution_direction` `null` (since the theorem itself is conditional, no direction is settled outright). I judged this a related-problem case rather than a case of the stated problem because (a) the result is explicitly conditional on the unresolved consistency of exacting cardinals with an extendible cardinal below them, so nothing is unconditionally refuted; (b) it targets the Weak versions of two named conjectures, not the general existence question Wikipedia poses; and (c) the MathOverflow discussion shows experts treat the relationship between exacting cardinals and Ultimate-L as an open question rather than a settled blow to the program.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an unconditional proof (or disproof) that an ultimate core model containing all large cardinals exists, (b) an unconditional (non-relative-consistency) refutation of the full Ultimate-L Conjecture itself, which would be a much stronger and squarely on-topic result, or (c) an authoritative expert account (e.g. from Woodin, Aguilera, Bagaria, or Lüücke) explicitly stating that their exacting-cardinal results settle, or are widely regarded by the field as settling, the general core-model existence question rather than only the named Weak conjectures.

outcome: The unconditional Linnik constant remains L=5 (Xylouris, 2011, pre-window). A March 2026 preprint by Matías Bruna proves a new conditional bound on the least prime p in an arithmetic progression mod q, p ≪_ε q^{2+ε}, under the generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GLH) — a hypothesis strictly weaker than GRH — nearly matching the bound previously known only conditionally on GRH. No AI system was involved.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Problems associated to Linnik's theorem' concerns the value of Linnik's constant L, the least exponent such that the least prime p(a,q) in an arithmetic progression a mod q satisfies p(a,q) ≪ q^L. As of the frozen revision (Jan 2024) the state was: unconditionally L=5 (Xylouris, 2011 PhD thesis, confirmed still current via the live Wikipedia article and multiple 2025-2026 secondary sources, e.g. arXiv:2511.05631), and conditionally on GRH, p(a,q) ≪ (φ(q)log q)^2, i.e. L=2+ε. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), I found no unconditional improvement to L=5 — it remains the record. I did find a genuine piece of progress: Matías Bruna's March 2026 preprint (arXiv:2603.25612, 'A conditional bound for the least prime in an arithmetic progression') proves p ≪_ε q^{2+ε} assuming only the generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GLH), which the paper's introduction explicitly states is weaker than GRH. This is new: it shows the strong GRH-conditional bound can be obtained from a weaker hypothesis, which is a real strengthening of the conditional landscape around this exact quantity (not a variant — it is literally the least-prime-in-AP function p(a,q) that the Wikipedia bullet is about). I read the HTML version of the paper directly (introduction and acknowledgements), which thanks only human collaborators (Asif Zaman, Andrew Granville, Université de Montréal) with no mention of any AI or computational tool. I also checked two adjacent but out-of-scope items that triage-adjacent searches surfaced: (1) Andrew Fiori's arXiv:2404.02329 (April 2024), a purely numerical/computational refinement of Wagstaff's 1979 conjectured bound 3φ(n)log(n)log(φ(n)), verified only up to 10^8 — this is a conjecture-refinement with numerical evidence, not a proof, and concerns a different (heuristic, average-case-flavored) quantity than Linnik's L, so it does not change this bullet's status by itself, though it is worth noting as adjacent computational work with no AI involved; (2) a 2024 Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal paper improving the least almost-prime (≤2 prime factors) bound from q^1.8345 to q^1.825 — this is about almost-primes, a genuinely different (relaxed) problem from the least-prime question in the bullet, so I classify it as a related/variant problem, not a case of this one. I found no AI system credited with any progress on Linnik's constant or the least-prime-in-AP problem in this window; a broad search for AI-assisted work in this specific area (least prime in AP) returned nothing relevant — the AI-and-mathematics hits that surfaced (Axiom Math's Lean proof of the 246 prime-gaps theorem, general AI-for-math surveys) are unrelated problems.
competing_reading: One could argue the Bruna result is 'beside the question' if one reads Linnik's constant narrowly as only the unconditional exponent — under that reading nothing at all has happened in-window and status would be 'open' with no_change_found true. I reject this narrow reading because the Wikipedia bullet and its own article explicitly discuss both the unconditional record and the GRH-conditional bound as part of 'problems associated to Linnik's theorem,' so a new, weaker-hypothesis derivation of essentially the same conditional bound is squarely in scope as progress on the conditional side of the same quantity, even though the unconditional constant L did not move.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g. via a later expert citation, a survey update, or citations to Bruna's paper) that the GLH-conditional bound is accepted as correct and non-trivial relative to prior conditional results, and whether any subsequent work improves the unconditional L=5 record within the window.

outcome: No result found addressing whether wild knots have infinitely many quadrisecants; the conjecture (attributed to Kuperberg, 1994) remains open exactly as stated in the frozen Wikipedia revision.
summary: I ran a broad set of searches for the wild-knot quadrisecant conjecture (that every wild knot has infinitely many quadrisecants, attributed to Kuperberg 1994) and found nothing addressing it in the window 26 Jan 2024 – present. The current live Wikipedia 'Quadrisecant' article still lists it as an unsolved problem with no update beyond the original attribution. Adjacent, pre-2024 background that repeatedly surfaced in searches — Kuperberg's theorem that every nontrivial tame knot has at least one quadrisecant, Denne's alternating-quadrisecant results for tame knots, the disproved 'quadrisecant approximation conjecture' (Denne/Sullivan et al., pre-2024), and the fact that every wild *arc* (not closed wild knot) has infinitely many quadrisecants — are all related-but-distinct results that predate the window or concern a different object (tame knots, or open arcs rather than closed wild knots), so none of them are cases of, or changes to, this specific bullet per §3.1. I also found genuine 2024-2026 wild-knot research — 'Knots Inside Fractals' (arXiv:2409.03639, Sep 2024) and 'Wild knots embedded in the Menger sponge' (arXiv:2602.20384, Feb 2026) — which construct new families of wild knots (in fractal/Menger-sponge settings) but do not mention quadrisecants at all; these are related problems (existence/classification of wild knots), not results on this conjecture. I found no preprint, announcement, or digestion — human or AI-assisted — that proves, disproves, or partially settles the infinitely-many-quadrisecants question for wild knots. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none': this is a case where nothing happened.
competing_reading: None of the adjacent results plausibly count as a case or partial resolution: the wild-arc quadrisecant result concerns arcs, not closed wild knots, and appears to predate 2024 in any case (it circulates as background in older quadrisecant literature, e.g. Denne's survey work), so even if it were on-topic it would be open_stale rather than a change within the window. I found no evidence it was newly proved or newly publicized in the window.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement explicitly proving or disproving that every wild knot (as a closed curve, not an arc) has infinitely many quadrisecants, or exhibiting a wild knot with only finitely many quadrisecants as a counterexample.

outcome: The general QUE conjecture of Rudnick and Sarnak — that all high-frequency Laplace eigenfunctions on a compact negatively-curved manifold equidistribute — remains completely open for arbitrary negatively-curved manifolds; only the arithmetic special case (already resolved before the frozen date by Lindenstrauss and Soundararajan) has seen further extension, to products of hyperbolic 2- and 3-spaces, and that extension is itself a variant/special case rather than a case of the general conjecture as stated in the bullet.
summary: The bullet states the general Rudnick–Sarnak QUE conjecture for arbitrary compact negatively-curved manifolds. This remains fully open: the current Wikipedia article on quantum unique ergodicity (checked live for context, not as a research source) discusses only the weaker quantum ergodicity theorem (Shnirelman/Zelditch/Colin de Verdière), which guarantees equidistribution for a density-one subsequence of eigenfunctions, not all of them, and does not report any resolution of the full QUE conjecture. Searches for progress since 26 January 2024 turned up three genuine results, none of which bear on the general conjecture as stated: (1) Shem-Tov and Silberman, 'Arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity for products of hyperbolic 2- and 3-spaces' (arXiv:2206.05955), first posted 2022-06-13, with a revised v2 posted 2025-01-26 and a 2025 journal publication in the Journal d'Analyse Mathématique — this proves AQUE (the arithmetic special case, using Hecke operators) for a specific class of arithmetic locally symmetric spaces; AQUE for the classical case (surfaces) was already settled by Lindenstrauss (2006) and Soundararajan (2010), well before the frozen revision, so even this is an extension of an already-resolved arithmetic sub-problem, not progress on the stated (non-arithmetic, general) conjecture, and per §3.1 counts as a related/variant result rather than a case of this bullet's conjecture; (2) Kim and Miller, 'Semiclassical Measures on Hyperbolic Manifolds' (arXiv:2503.01528, March 2025), which constrains the support of semiclassical measures (showing supports must contain the cosphere bundle of a totally geodesic submanifold) but explicitly does not resolve QUE — it is a related but distinct question about possible limit measures, not a proof or disproof of equidistribution; (3) an arXiv paper on QUE for magnetic Laplacians on the flat torus T^2 (arXiv:2411.18449, November 2024) which is a different operator on a non-negatively-curved space entirely. No AI or machine-learning involvement was found in connection with any of this work; broader searches for AI/ML activity touching QUE returned only unrelated physics applications (quantum-enhanced LLMs, quantum-informed ML for chaotic-system prediction) that use 'quantum' and 'chaos' in an unrelated sense and have nothing to do with the Rudnick–Sarnak conjecture. The record is therefore 'open' with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the Shem-Tov–Silberman extension to products of hyperbolic 2- and 3-spaces is a 'case' of the general QUE conjecture (since products of hyperbolic spaces are themselves negatively-curved-in-each-factor locally symmetric spaces) rather than a mere variant, which would make it `partial` progress with `resolution_direction` confirmed. I read it instead as confined to the arithmetic sub-conjecture (it relies essentially on Hecke operators, which have no analogue for a generic negatively-curved manifold), so it does not narrow the general conjecture's territory the way, e.g., resolving QUE for a specific non-arithmetic manifold would.
what_would_settle_it: A result proving or disproving equidistribution of eigenfunctions for a negatively-curved manifold or family of manifolds without reliance on arithmetic/Hecke structure would settle whether this counts as genuine progress on the stated (general) conjecture; absent that, the arithmetic-only results stay out of scope.

outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or scope-qualifying bound improvement was found since 26 January 2024; the Maass-form and general automorphic generalizations remain open, and the one long-running claimed proof for Maass forms of SL(2,Z) remains an unaccepted, undigested preprint.
summary: The Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture (for modular forms) was proved by Deligne in the 1970s; the bullet as given is the umbrella statement covering the still-open generalizations (Maass forms of SL(2,Z), and general automorphic forms on higher-rank groups). I checked the current Wikipedia article, which explicitly states 'As of 2025, the version of the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for Maass forms is still open' and that the automorphic-forms generalization also remains open — no post-2024 resolution is recorded there. The one item the triage flagged, André Unterberger's single-author arXiv preprint 2001.10956 ('The Ramanujan-Petersson and Selberg conjectures for Maass forms'), was first posted 29 Jan 2020 — before the window — and has been revised 16 times through v16 (12 Feb 2026), including two withdrawals (v2, v5) along the way. This long, contested revision history with no journal acceptance and no expert digestion found anywhere (no citation of it as settling the question in surveys, blogs, or subsequent literature) means it does not establish a change in status; per the resolved-vs-claimed rule, even 'claimed' would require the paper to still be a live, credible claim, and a 6-year unaccepted single-author preprint repeatedly withdrawn and rewritten does not meet that bar for either 'claimed' or 'resolved' — so the correct call is that the conjecture is still `open`, with this preprint noted but not counted. I searched for other results that might qualify as scope-appropriate progress (a case settled or a genuine bound improvement toward the generalized Ramanujan conjecture at pointwise/individual coefficient level, per Kim-Sarnak-style bounds). I found: (1) Yujiao Jiang's July 2025 preprint (2507.20653) proving 'Hypothesis H of Rudnick and Sarnak' for GL(n) over any number field in full generality — but this is an average/Euler-product statement about Rankin-Selberg coefficients, not a pointwise Ramanujan-type bound on individual Satake parameters, so it is a related-but-distinct statement (a 'related problem' under §3.1), not a case of this conjecture; (2) Liyang Yang's improvement to the Kim-Sarnak 7/64 bound for exceptional Maass forms, which is genuine bound-moving progress in scope, but the paper (arXiv:2011.09054) was first posted 18 November 2020 -- also before the window, so it is not a post-2024 event, whatever its later revision history; (3) Yuhao Cheng's 2025-2026 paper (arXiv:2507.09655) on 'Beyond Endoscopy for GL2 with ramification 2', which gives a *new proof* of the already-known 1/4 bound in a ramified case -- a new derivation, not a numerically improved bound, so it does not change what a careful person would write in this bullet. I also searched explicitly for any AI-system involvement (deep learning, LLM-driven proof search, AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve, or the 'Ramanujan Machine') in connection with this conjecture; the only AI-adjacent hits were the unrelated 'Ramanujan Machine' project (generates numerical conjectures for constants like pi, e) and its 2026 'Ramanujan Challenge for AI' benchmark paper, and AlphaEvolve's unrelated work on Ramanujan *graphs* (expander graphs, a different structure sharing only the name). None of these touch the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for automorphic/Maass forms. No AI system appears anywhere near this specific problem.
competing_reading: If a reader takes the Unterberger preprint's persistence and continued revision (through Feb 2026) as evidence of a live, increasingly refined claim rather than a stalled one, they might classify this as `claimed` with event dated to the most recent substantive revision. I do not take this reading because there is no evidence any expert has endorsed or even seriously engaged with the claim in six years, and repeated withdrawals (v2, v5) are a signal of substantive problems rather than routine polishing.
what_would_settle_it: A citation of Unterberger's paper by an independent expert (survey, seminar report, or journal referee) treating it as correct or substantively reviewed, or a journal acceptance, would move it to `claimed` or `resolved`. Absent that, continued arXiv-only revision does not count as movement.

outcome: Heinrich, Kiyomi, Otachi, and Schweitzer proved (arXiv 2504.02353, submitted 3 April 2025, revised May 2026) that interval graphs with at least three vertices are reconstructible, settling this case of the reconstruction conjecture and giving a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm for that class; the general reconstruction conjecture and the new digraph reconstruction conjecture remain open. A separate, unrelated 2024 claim of a full proof (O'Shea & Wilkins) predates the frozen revision and remains undigested/unaccepted by the field.

disputes.summary: O'Shea and Wilkins, 'Vertex-substitution framework verifies the reconstruction conjecture for finite undirected graphs' (Information Sciences vol. 654, article 119858; made available online 2 November 2023, formally issued in the January 2024 print volume), claims a complete algebraic proof of the full reconstruction conjecture for finite undirected graphs. This claim predates the frozen revision (26 Jan 2024) regardless of which of its two dates is used, so it cannot be the event this record's status rests on even if accepted. More importantly, as of September 2026 the claim has not been digested or endorsed by specialists: current surveys and the ProofAtlas tracking page for this conjecture continue to describe the general conjecture as open and record the O'Shea-Wilkins claim as an 'unverified resolution claim' rather than an accepted proof. No published refutation or counterexample to their argument was found either. This dispute is noted for completeness but does not change the record's status, since (a) it predates the window and (b) it remains undigested rather than accepted.

summary: Within the window (26 Jan 2024 – present) the clearest, verifiable change to this problem is Heinrich, Kiyomi, Otachi & Schweitzer's April 2025 arXiv preprint proving that interval graphs with at least three vertices are reconstructible (and reconstructible in polynomial time). This is a genuine case of the stated conjecture — interval graphs are a restriction of 'all graphs', so proving reconstructibility for them removes territory from the open general problem — and it has not (as far as I could establish) yet been digested by an independent expert account (no Tao-blog-level or journal-published discussion found), so it is classified 'partial' rather than 'resolved', resting on the preprint itself. No AI system is credited anywhere in this result; the authors' own account (per the arXiv abstract/HTML) describes purely human-derived combinatorial techniques. Separately, I found the most substantial AI-adjacent activity on this conjecture: Tsoukalas et al. (Google DeepMind, arXiv 2605.22763, 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search', submitted 21 May 2026), in which an AlphaEvolve-based agent 'helped formulate two bipartite variants of the graph reconstruction conjecture, along with a proposed full reconstruction algorithm' and 'produced a complete proof' for one of those variants, while only producing proof sketches/strategies for the other. Per the scope rule in §3.1, these are variants (bipartite incidence-deletion decks with different, self-formulated hypotheses such as biconnectivity and pairwise-distinct vertex types) rather than cases of the reconstruction conjecture as Wikipedia states it — they change the question rather than restrict it, and the agent itself devised the variants, which is a strong signal they are not simply narrower instances of the stated conjecture. I therefore do not let this AI work move the status, per the instruction that a related-problem result leaves status at 'open' (here 'partial', driven by the interval-graphs case) with the AI work noted as beside the question. I also verified O'Shea and Wilkins' 2024 Information Sciences paper claiming a full proof: it was made available online 2 November 2023 (DOI 10.1016/j.ins.2023.119858), before the frozen revision, so even if accepted it would be `open_stale`; but it is not accepted — ProofAtlas's tracking page and other 2026 sources still call the general conjecture open and describe the claim as unverified — so it does not change the status either way. The new digraph reconstruction conjecture: I found no result narrowing or resolving it in the window; it remains open per Wikipedia's own article and secondary sources (Ramachandran's 1979 conjecture, still open per the 'New digraph reconstruction conjecture' Wikipedia article as fetched). McKay's exhaustive verification up to 13 vertices predates the window and is unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind bipartite result should be coded as `ai_role: assisted` with `status: partial` if one reads 'a bipartite variant of the reconstruction conjecture' as a genuine case (e.g., if it can be shown that any counterexample to the stated conjecture restricted to bipartite graphs with the paper's extra hypotheses would also refute the general conjecture). I did not find the authors' precise theorem statement (the arXiv HTML excerpt did not include it), so I cannot rule out that their bipartite variant is literally a special case rather than a hypothesis-altered analogue. Given the paper's own language — 'AlphaEvolve experiments helped us formulate two bipartite variants' — and the added hypotheses (biconnected, pairwise-distinct vertex types) that are not merely 'graph is bipartite' but additional structural constraints changing the reconstruction problem (deck determines the graph 'up to bipartite graph isomorphism', a different equivalence than the original conjecture's graph isomorphism), I judge this to be a related problem rather than a case, but flag the ambiguity here since the full theorem text was not accessible to me.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full text (not just the HTML-extracted summary) of arXiv 2605.22763, once the companion paper 'currently in preparation' per the authors is posted, to see the exact statement of the bipartite reconstruction theorem and confirm whether it is a strict special case of graph reconstruction (same isomorphism notion, same deck definition, just restricted to a graph class) or a modified problem (different deck construction / different equivalence relation). Also, an expert digestion (journal acceptance or a survey/blog discussion) of the Heinrich–Kiyomi–Otachi–Schweitzer interval-graphs proof would upgrade its status from `partial` toward a more confidently 'expert-checked' partial result.

summary: This bullet ('Regularity of solutions of Euler equations') maps most naturally to the classical open question of whether the 3D incompressible Euler equations can develop a finite-time singularity from smooth data on all of R^3 (or the torus) with no boundary and no forcing. Two genuinely distinct strands of work since 26 January 2024 bear on it, and neither is AI-free nor AI-central across the board. (1) Chen & Hou (received 13 Jan 2025, PNAS 122(27):e2500940122, published 8 Jul 2025 as a NAS Inaugural Article) give a rigorous computer-assisted proof — interval arithmetic and numerical PDE analysis, explicitly NOT machine learning — of finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup for the 3D AXISYMMETRIC Euler equations with smooth initial data in a smoothly bounded domain, with the singularity forming at a boundary stagnation point. This is a genuine case of the general problem (restricted to axisymmetric flow with a boundary) and has been vetted by PNAS peer review, so it counts as `partial` with `ai_role: none`. (2) A September 2025 DeepMind preprint ('Discovery of Unstable Singularities', arXiv:2509.14185, 17 Sep 2025) used physics-informed neural networks to numerically discover new families of unstable self-similar singularities for 3D Euler-with-boundary (axisymmetric), Boussinesq, IPM and the CCF model; the authors are explicit that this is numerical discovery, not proof, and that a companion rigorous computer-assisted proof is 'in preparation' only for the simplified CCF case. (3) Most directly on-point: in September 2026, Ganeshram, Duruisseaux and Anandkumar (arXiv:2609.10867, 9 Sep 2026) used a PINN to find a candidate self-similar singular profile for the fully UNFORCED, UNBOUNDED 3D Euler equations on R^3 (the classical case), certified numerically via splines and interval arithmetic to ~1e-5/1e-3 precision, with a companion paper (Duruisseaux, Ganeshram, George, Anandkumar, arXiv:2609.10860) laying out a stability framework that reduces the remaining nonlinear-stability proof to a finite list of estimates. Both papers are explicit and repeated that the result is CONDITIONAL: 'Conditional on rigorous certification of the estimates and constants... the framework closes the stability proof,' and 'An unconditional blowup result would additionally require a local well-posedness and continuation argument.' The authors state LLMs played only a limited supporting role (references, checking derivations, Lean formalisation assistance) — the PINN did the profile discovery, not an LLM. Because this central, most-relevant strand is explicitly not yet a completed proof, and no expert digestion (e.g. Tao) treats it as resolved, the unforced/unbounded case of the problem remains `open`; only the Chen-Hou boundary case is settled and expert-reviewed, giving overall status `partial`. I separately confirmed that two other September 2026 results in this space — Alpoge & Buckmaster's finite-time blowup with SMOOTH FORCING for 3D Euler (and IPM, Boussinesq), and OpenAI's claimed finite-time blowup with smooth forcing for Navier-Stokes — are about a genuinely different (forced) equation and are related problems under Sec 3.1, not cases of the unforced Euler regularity question in this bullet; I did not use them to determine status, though they are extremely AI-heavy (heavy LLM use for proof-writing/Lean formalisation in the Buckmaster/Alpoge case, and an OpenAI 'internal multiagent system' producing the entire 166-page Navier-Stokes paper end to end) and are the subject of an active, unresolved priority dispute reported by TechCrunch, MIT Technology Review, and Scientific American as of mid-September 2026.
competing_reading: One could argue the bullet, as Wikipedia states it generically ('Regularity of solutions of Euler equations'), should be read broadly enough to fold in the Chen-Hou boundary/axisymmetric case as the dominant event and call the whole record `resolved` for that restricted but expert-vetted case, since it is the only fully non-conditional, peer-reviewed result in the window. I did not do this because the general 3D Euler regularity question (no boundary, no forcing) is what mathematicians and the Millennium-adjacent literature treat as 'the' open problem, and that piece is still explicitly conditional per the authors' own words in Sept 2026. A second competing reading: the Ganeshram/Duruisseaux/Anandkumar work could be scored `claimed` rather than `progress`, since it does assert a specific candidate singular profile with high numerical confidence; I chose `progress` because the authors themselves deny having a complete proof (no direction to resolve in either sense yet), which is a `progress`/`open` situation rather than a claim awaiting expert digestion of a completed argument.
what_would_settle_it: Publication (or a widely-read, expert-digested preprint, e.g. covered on Tao's blog as verified rather than merely reported) of the completed, unconditional nonlinear-stability certification promised by Duruisseaux/Ganeshram/George/Anandkumar (arXiv:2609.10860) for the unforced R^3 Euler case, or any comparably rigorous unconditional resolution of the classical (unforced, unbounded) 3D Euler blow-up question.

outcome: Global regularity for the classical relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system with large, general (non-symmetric) initial data remains open as of September 2026; all developments found in the window are either about restricted/symmetric cases whose core result predates the window, or about a distinct modified/related system.
summary: The bullet asks about regularity of solutions of the classical relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell (RVM) system, i.e. whether smooth solutions with large, general initial data remain smooth for all time. This is a long-standing open problem (Glassey-Strauss era continuation criteria, still the state of the art in spirit). I searched extensively for any 2024-2026 development and found three categories of activity, none of which changes the status of the general problem: (1) A 2025/2026 paper by Constantin and Grayer (arXiv:2504.01687, published in Communications in Mathematical Physics 2026) proves unconditional global regularity for large data, but for a 'Radiative Vlasov-Maxwell' system in which the Lorentz force is modified by an added radiation-reaction damping term. This is a different (related) system, not the classical RVM system this bullet refers to — per the scope rule (§3.1), a modified system with an added damping mechanism that the authors themselves note is what makes the problem tractable is a variant, not a case, of the stated question. (2) Xuecheng Wang's large-data global existence result for the RVM system restricted to cylindrical symmetry was originally posted to arXiv as 2203.01199 v1 in March 2022 — before the frozen revision date of 26 January 2024 — and already contained the full global existence claim. In July 2026 the author reformatted and split this into a two-part sequence (revised 2203.01199 as 'Part I' and a new companion arXiv:2607.14685 as 'Part II', which independently derives pointwise estimates that were treated as black boxes in the original). This is a restructuring and strengthening of rigor for an already-existing 2022 result, not a new mathematical event within the window; even if it were treated as new, cylindrical symmetry is a restriction (a case) of the general problem, which remains open outside that symmetry class. (3) A search for AI involvement turned up arXiv:2603.15929 ('Semi-Autonomous Formalization of the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau Equilibrium', Ilin, March 2026), a striking AI-assisted Lean formalization using Gemini DeepThink, Claude Code, and the Aristotle prover — but this addresses equilibrium characterization for the Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau system, a different question about a different (collisional, Landau-damping) system, not the regularity/global-existence question this bullet asks about. No AI system was found to be involved in any work on the classical Vlasov-Maxwell regularity problem itself. I did not find the problem's own dedicated Wikipedia article (the general Vlasov-Maxwell equations article does not discuss the regularity question), so I relied on the arXiv literature and continuation-criterion papers (e.g. Luk-Strain, Cheverry-Ibrahim) directly.
competing_reading: One could argue the July 2026 Part I/Part II restructuring of Wang's cylindrical-symmetry result constitutes a new 'event' worth dating to 2026 as `progress`, since Part II's independently-derived pointwise estimates were not previously public and arguably strengthen the original 2022 argument's rigor. Under that reading the status might be `partial` (a symmetric case newly solidified) dated to July 2026. I did not adopt this reading because the mathematical claim (global existence for large cylindrically-symmetric data) was already asserted and essentially argued in the 2022 v1, so the substantive resolution of that case predates the window; the 2026 papers are presentation/rigor work on a pre-existing result.
what_would_settle_it: A statement from Wang or independent experts on whether the 2022 v1 proof was considered complete/correct before the 2026 Part II estimates were supplied, or whether the pointwise estimates in Part II were a genuinely new, previously-missing ingredient without which the 2022 claim did not hold up. That would decide whether the cylindrical-symmetry case should be dated 2022 (open_stale) or 2026 (partial/progress).

outcome: Hales and Vajjha (arXiv, May 2024) proved Mahler's First conjecture (1947): the most unpackable centrally-symmetric convex disk in the plane must be a smoothed polygon. This narrows the class of candidate minimizers for Reinhardt's conjecture but does not identify the minimizer as specifically the smoothed octagon (Mahler's Second conjecture, equivalent to Reinhardt's conjecture), which remains open.
summary: Reinhardt's conjecture (1934) itself remains open: no source found since 26 January 2024 identifies the smoothed octagon as the packing-density minimizer among centrally-symmetric convex plane sets. What did happen in the window is a narrowing of the candidate class. A 260-page arXiv preprint/book by Thomas Hales and Koundinya Vajjha, 'Packings of Smoothed Polygons' (arXiv:2405.04331, posted 7 May 2024), proves Mahler's First conjecture (1947): that the extreme (most unpackable) centrally-symmetric convex domain must be a smoothed polygon — i.e. a polygon with corners rounded by hyperbolic arcs. This is a genuine restriction on the space of candidate minimizers for the same optimization problem that Reinhardt's conjecture concerns, so under this task's scope rule (§3.1) it counts as a case/partial result on the parent question rather than an unrelated variant: it removes territory (non-smoothed-polygon shapes) from consideration as the minimizer. It does not, however, settle which smoothed polygon (i.e., whether it is the octagon specifically) is optimal — Mahler's Second conjecture, equivalent to the Reinhardt conjecture as stated in the bullet, is untouched. Quanta Magazine (28 June 2024) and other secondary coverage (Brian Hayes' blog, Mathstodon, a 2024-11-01 Visual Insight post) confirm this reading and report informal expert engagement: Henry Cohn (Microsoft Research) and Greg Kuperberg (UC Davis) reviewed parts of the argument favorably, with Kuperberg explicitly noting the authors 'didn't really cross the finish line' toward the full Reinhardt conjecture. As of this research (September 2026), I found no evidence the 260-page proof has completed formal peer review or journal publication, nor a full third-party expert digestion working through the entire proof (only partial/informal review by named mathematicians is documented) — so I classify the underlying event as not yet fully 'resolved' by the §6.1 standard, though the informal expert engagement is substantial. Since the record concerns the parent conjecture (not Mahler's First conjecture as its own bullet), and only a sub-case/restriction was settled, 'status' is 'partial' rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed'. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the primary source, in Quanta's coverage, or in any other secondary source I found. The paper describes 'computer-assisted' proofs using a computer algebra system for verifying certain polynomial/algebraic inequalities — this is symbolic computation, not a machine-learning or AI system, so 'ai_role' is 'none' per §6.2's explicit carve-out for computer algebra and certified computation. I also searched for any later work (2025-2026) advancing toward identifying the octagon itself, or any AI-related attempt at Reinhardt's conjecture, and found none: search results consistently point back to the same May 2024 preprint as the most recent development, alongside an unrelated 2026 paper on a different 'Yau's conjecture on smooth Reinhardt domains' (a complex-analysis topic with only a name in common, not related to this packing conjecture).
competing_reading: One could argue the Hales-Vajjha result is a 'related problem' (Mahler's First conjecture) rather than a 'case' of Reinhardt's conjecture, since it is formally a distinct named conjecture with its own history (posed by Mahler in 1947, separate from Reinhardt's 1934 conjecture) and could be classified as 'open' with 'no_change_found' true, treating the Hales-Vajjha work as beside the specific question of whether the octagon is optimal. However, the two conjectures are widely treated in the literature (Wikipedia's own smoothed-octagon article, Quanta) as sequential steps toward the same optimization problem — Mahler's First and Second conjectures are the two halves of establishing that the octagon is optimal — so I favor 'partial' since the result strictly narrows the feasible set for the object Reinhardt's conjecture is about.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that among smoothed polygons specifically, the smoothed octagon (as opposed to a smoothed polygon with a different number of sides) minimizes packing density — i.e., a resolution of Mahler's Second conjecture / Reinhardt's conjecture itself. Also relevant: formal peer-review publication or a complete independent expert re-derivation of the Hales-Vajjha proof, which would move that underlying result from informally-vetted preprint status to fully digested.

outcome: A preprint by Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058, first posted 2 April 2026, revised 2 August 2026) constructs an explicit symmetric strategy ('FSD') that strictly beats the Anderson–Weber strategy for every n≥4 in the symmetric rendezvous search problem on n discrete locations, thereby settling — in the negative — the 1990 Anderson–Weber conjecture that their strategy is optimal for all n (the conjecture had already been confirmed for n=2,3 by Weber in 2012, and disproved specifically for n=4 by an earlier, pre-2024 paper). No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification beyond an AI-assisted 'Pith Review' has been found.

counterexample.object: An explicit symmetric strategy ('First-Same-or-Different', FSD) for n≥4 locations, correlating consecutive tours of non-home locations via a derangement-graph construction, whose expected meeting time is strictly smaller than that of the Anderson–Weber strategy for every n≥4.
counterexample.verified_how: Explicit construction with closed-form/asymptotic bounds on the improvement (e.g. an explicit ~0.00125 reduction for n=4, and an explicit lower bound on the improvement of order (n−1)⁻⁸ for n≥5); an independent (AI-assisted) review flagged one hand-checked monotonicity step (Lemma 11, covering n≥8) as the main point not fully automated/formally verified.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Rendezvous problem' links only to the general Rendezvous problem article, which (per the frozen January 2024 wording as fetched) covers several distinct sub-problems: the continuous 'telephone problem' rendezvous value on the line (bounds ~4.152–4.257, still open and untouched), and the discrete symmetric rendezvous game on n locations, where Anderson and Weber conjectured in 1990 that their round-based strategy is optimal for all n. That conjecture was confirmed for n=2,3 by Weber (2012, pre-window) and known to fail for n=4 specifically from an earlier paper (arXiv:0912.0670, 2009, pre-window). Since the January 2024 freeze, Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm posted 'Faster Symmetric Rendezvous on Four or More Locations' (arXiv:2604.02058, v1 2 April 2026, v2 2 August 2026), which generalizes the n=4 counterexample into an explicit strategy beating Anderson–Weber for *every* n≥4, closing the conjecture in full (negatively) modulo one hand-checked monotonicity lemma noted by an automated/AI-assisted review site ('Pith Review'). I treat this as within scope: the Wikipedia article explicitly frames the Anderson–Weber conjecture and its resolution status as part of 'the rendezvous problem played in n discrete locations,' so a full resolution of that conjecture for n≥4 is a change to what a careful reader of this article's content would now write, even though the specific numeric-bound sub-question (rendezvous value on the line, distance 2) is untouched. I found no evidence of any AI system contributing to the mathematical content: no acknowledgement, methods section, or author statement mentions AI/ML tool use in deriving or checking the FSD strategy or its analysis; the only AI-related item found ('Pith Review') is a third-party AI-assisted review of the paper, not an input to the result, so ai_role is none. Because the live Wikipedia article (last modified 20 February 2025, per fetch) still only mentions the n=3 resolution and says nothing about n≥4, and I found no journal acceptance, no blog treatment by rendezvous-search specialists (e.g., Alpern, Weber), and only the AI-assisted Pith Review as external commentary, I classify this as claimed rather than resolved: no independent human expert digestion was located.
competing_reading: One could argue the n≥4 generalization is a 'related problem' relative to the specific bullet, since the Wikipedia bullet points only to the general article and the frozen revision's own text emphasizes the n=3 resolution and the line-search bounds as the flagship open sub-problems, with the general-n Anderson–Weber conjecture mentioned only implicitly via 'even the symmetric rendezvous problem played in n discrete locations... has turned out to be very difficult to solve.' Under a stricter reading limited to the numerically-bounded line problem (distance-2 rendezvous value, 4.152–4.257), status would instead be open/no_change_found, since no source found any movement on those bounds since January 2024. I resolved this by treating the whole article's content as the scope, per the instruction that a bullet linking only a general article still requires researching the problem's own name and full scope; the Anderson–Weber conjecture is explicitly named and tracked in that article as an unsolved (at the time) sub-problem of 'the rendezvous problem.'
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation of whether a human expert (e.g., a referee report, journal acceptance, or a specialist's blog/survey treatment) has independently verified the FSD construction and its Lemma 11 monotonicity step, which would upgrade the status from claimed to resolved; alternatively, an explicit statement from Wikipedia editors or the rendezvous-search community on whether they consider the n≥4 case now closed.

outcome: The core problem (existence of resolution of singularities for varieties of dimension ≥ 4 over fields of positive characteristic) remains open. The only substantive AI-related development in the window is an exploratory 2026 paper by Gergely Bérczi using DeepMind's AlphaEvolve to evolve candidate termination-invariant ("ranking function") constructions for a simplified toy model of the canonical blow-up process in dimension 4, characteristic 3; the paper states two conjectures, not a proof, and does not resolve any case of the actual geometric problem. A separate, unrelated 798-page arXiv preprint (2608.20066, Aug 2026) claims a full resolution in all dimensions and characteristics, but shows strong hallmarks of being an AI-generated, non-peer-reviewed, likely nonsensical text (invented unexplained terminology such as 'total-Hasse activity packets', 'paid quotients', 'displayed parents', 'terminal truth'; the listed author has a Princeton 'Complex Infrastructure Systems' affiliation, not a mathematics one; no expert digestion, citation, or discussion of it exists anywhere).

ai.basis_quote: "the mathematical conclusions, conjectures, and counterexamples presented here arise from independent mathematical analysis" ... "this is a report ... describing a possible way to use AlphaEvolve as an experimental engine ... rather than as a finished mathematical theory" — AlphaEvolve (using gemini-2.5-pro / gemini-3-pro) evolved three explicit candidate ranking functions inside a fixed evaluation harness (a toy canonical blow-up simulator with human-designed features and benchmarks); the author then analyzed the outputs and formulated the paper's two formal conjectures about a discretized five-component lexicographic ranking function satisfying a bounded-delay descent criterion.
ai.disclosed_cost: Eleven experiments reported, with individual run durations ranging from 3 to 22 days (e.g. a first focused benchmark run of 26 hours and a discretization experiment of 24 hours).

disputes.summary: arXiv:2608.20066 (Chenxiao Tian, Aug 2026, 798 pages, 'Frobenius-Hasse Towers and Exceptional-History Descent') explicitly claims a full canonical strong embedded resolution and principalization construction over any perfect field of characteristic p>0 — i.e., a complete solution to the stated open problem. No expert digestion, review, citation, or discussion of this preprint could be found anywhere (no MathOverflow, blog, or forum commentary), it uses extensive invented terminology not found in the resolution-of-singularities literature ('total-Hasse activity packets', 'filtered coefficient cubes', 'semilinear Frobenius-Hasse sources', 'paid quotients', 'displayed parents', 'terminal truth', 'six-row defect calculus'), and the listed author's Princeton page (cis.princeton.edu) places them in a 'Complex Infrastructure Systems' lab, not a mathematics department, with no other mathematical publication record found. These are strong indicators of an AI-hallucinated or AI-generated preprint rather than genuine mathematics; it is treated here as uncredentialed noise rather than as a genuine claimed proof, and is not counted as 'claimed' status.

summary: The bullet concerns resolution of singularities in positive characteristic, open (as of Jan 2024) for varieties of dimension ≥ 4 over fields of characteristic p>0 (dimension ≤3 was already settled: surfaces by Abhyankar 1956, threefolds by Cossart–Piltant 2008–2009). Wikipedia's current article still states the higher-dimensional case as open, and I found no genuine proof or digested partial result advancing the general higher-dimensional problem in the window. The one substantive, verifiable AI-related development is Gergely Bérczi's Feb 2026 preprint (arXiv:2602.06553), which used DeepMind's AlphaEvolve (an LLM-driven evolutionary code-search system, built on Gemini models) to search for termination/ranking-function invariants in a deliberately simplified toy model of the canonical blow-up process (dimension 4, characteristic 3, monic purely inseparable leading term). This is honestly and explicitly framed by the author as exploratory: AlphaEvolve produced candidate ranking-function code within a human-built simulator and evaluation harness; the author independently analyzed the results, found a counterexample to an initial 'perfect' candidate, and formulated two conjectures about a five-component discretized ranking function. No proof of any case of the actual geometric resolution problem resulted — this is progress on a research programme (evolving ranking-function candidates as a heuristic-discovery tool) rather than a solved case, so status is `progress` and `ai_role` is `bound` (an AI system contributed to narrowing/exploring the landscape of a still-open problem, not to settling any part of it). Separately, I encountered a much more dramatic-looking claim: arXiv:2608.20066 (Aug 2026), a 798-page preprint by 'Chenxiao Tian' claiming to fully solve the stated problem in all dimensions and characteristics via a byzantine apparatus of invented terminology. I judge this very likely to be an AI-generated (hallucinated or LLM-authored) paper rather than genuine mathematics: the prose is dense with meaningless-sounding coined jargon uncorrelated with the literature, no expert has engaged with or cited it, and the listed Princeton affiliation is to an infrastructure-systems lab rather than mathematics, with no other mathematical track record found for this name. Because no human expert has validated (or even engaged with) this claim, and because its authorship/provenance itself is suspect, I do not count it as a `claimed` resolution — I record it only in `disputes` as a credibility flag rather than let it drive the status field, consistent with §6.1's requirement that even `claimed` status rest on a serious, engaged-with claim. I also checked the RIMS Kyoto Univ. 2024 publication on embedded resolution of surface singularities in arbitrary characteristic; this is an expository/summary account of an already-published 2020/2021 result (arXiv:2011.14443) with no AI involvement, and not new progress in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2608.20066 should be recorded as `claimed` with `ai_role` `generated`, since if genuine, it would fully resolve the conjecture and the writing style is consistent with an AI-generated proof attempt. I judge the evidence (invented terminology untethered to the literature, non-mathematical author affiliation, complete absence of any expert or community engagement even a year after typical circulation, and the sheer implausibility of a 798-page single-author solo resolution of a problem that has resisted the field for 60 years suddenly appearing with no preceding partial results from the same author) points toward this being unreliable noise rather than a genuine claim worth scoring, but I cannot rule out with certainty that it is a serious (if extremely dense) human-written attempt that simply hasn't been read yet.
what_would_settle_it: Any expert commentary, referee report, or citation addressing arXiv:2608.20066's validity; confirmation or denial from the named author regarding their identity/field and whether an AI system was used to draft the manuscript; or a retraction/withdrawal notice on arXiv. For the Bérczi AlphaEvolve line of work, a follow-up paper proving the conjectures for the toy model, or extending results to genuine (non-toy) resolution invariants, would move the status toward `partial`.

summary: The Riemann Hypothesis as stated in this bullet — do all nontrivial zeros of zeta lie on the critical line — is unchanged and remains open; per §3.1 an existence/universal-statement question of this kind moves only when fully answered, and nothing in the window answers it. What did happen is a genuine, well-documented movement of a *tracked partial quantity*: the best known unconditional lower bound on the proportion of nontrivial zeros proved to lie on the critical line (and be simple). This bound stood at roughly 41.6%-41.7% since around 2020 (Bui-Milinovich-Pratt-Zaharescu-type work referenced by both Anthropic and Lamzouri) and was raised to over 67.2% in a paper produced, by the authors' own account, by an unreleased internal research version of Claude in July-August 2026, announced by Anthropic on 2026-08-10 (https://www.anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta). The proof was reviewed by two Anthropic mathematicians (Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman) and, per secondary reporting, examined favorably by external experts Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston; Claude also produced a Lean formalization of the key result with help from Anthropic's Eric Easley, which passed the Lean checker. This human-checked, AI-produced mathematics is what the `ai_role: bound` code is for: an AI system moved a bound on a problem (the proportion of zeros) that is still open, without the underlying Riemann Hypothesis itself being settled. I coded `ai_role` as `bound` rather than `generated` because the improved quantity is a partial/auxiliary result about the problem, not a resolution or counterexample to RH itself — `generated` and `assisted` describe roles in producing 'the mathematics that is in the result' for the problem as stated, and here the relevant 'result' for the RH bullet is null (no change). The Anthropic paper itself (title reported as 'More than two thirds of the zeros lie on the critical line') was not, as far as I could determine, submitted to or accepted by a journal as of my research (the PDF at the Anthropic CDN link was unreadable as raw text via WebFetch, so I relied on the arXiv record of Lamzouri's independent paper and secondary press coverage that quotes it directly). Lamzouri's independent, human-authored paper (arXiv:2609.02882, submitted 2026-09-02) reproduces and slightly extends the same bound (>67.25% simple-and-on-the-line, >83.62% distinct) with a different, Hilbert-space-based proof, explicitly crediting Claude's earlier result and its verification by Alpöge and Furman in its own text — this is the strongest primary-source confirmation I have of the AI claim, since it is a human mathematician's own written acknowledgement rather than only a press release. Separately, I checked several 2024-2026 preprints claiming to fully prove or disprove RH (e.g. arXiv:2404.06306 'Disproof of the Riemann Hypothesis', posted in math.GM — a non-refereed arXiv category — with three revisions through January 2025 and no evidence of acceptance or expert engagement; and other Zenodo/journal-mill postings such as the 'Most Definitive and Comprehensive Disproof Ever Constructed' piece). None of these show any sign of community acceptance, so they do not change the status. I did not find any withdrawal of the Claude/Anthropic bound result, so this is not coded as `incident`.
competing_reading: One could argue this deserves `status: open` with `no_change_found: true`, treating the 41.6%→67.2% bound movement as beside the stated RH question entirely (a 'related quantity', not even a restriction/case of it, since 'the proportion of zeros on the line' is not itself the yes/no question posed). I chose `progress` instead because the rubric explicitly lists 'a bound that moved' as counting, and separately defines `ai_role: bound` for exactly 'an AI system moved a bound on a problem that is still open' — implying the intended reading is that such bound movements on RH's tracked quantities are in scope as `progress` events even though they don't touch the yes/no question itself. If a stricter reading is preferred, this record should be `open`/`no_change_found: true` with the same AI material moved into `summary` only.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Anthropic's own paper (or a version of it) is submitted to and accepted by a journal or given a public expert digestion beyond the two internal mathematicians and two informally-consulted external readers; and whether the rubric's own maintainers intend 'a bound that moved' to include proportion-of-zeros results on RH specifically, versus reserving `progress`/`bound` for bounds that are themselves the stated question (per §3.1's constant/record-table carve-out).

outcome: The general question (does strong mixing imply strong 3-mixing / mixing of all orders?) remains open, but Kanigowski and Ravotti (arXiv:2410.13686, Oct 2024) settled it affirmatively for a broad new class of parabolic systems by introducing 'locally uniformly shearing' (LUS) flows and proving all LUS flows are mixing of all orders, with Kochergin flows on the 2-torus and smooth time-changes of unipotent flows as consequences.
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet asks whether all strongly mixing systems are also strongly 3-mixing — Rokhlin's 1949 problem, still open in general as of today. Within the window, the clearest development is Kanigowski & Ravotti, 'Multiple mixing for parabolic systems' (arXiv:2410.13686, submitted 2024-10-17): they define 'locally uniformly shearing' (LUS) systems, formalizing the known 'mixing via shearing' mechanism behind essentially all known zero-entropy mixing examples, and prove every LUS flow is mixing of all orders (i.e. strongly mixing implies strongly k-mixing for all k within this class). They derive as corollaries that Kochergin flows on T^2 (for a.e. irrational frequency) and smooth time-changes of unipotent flows are polynomially mixing of all orders. This is a restriction of the stated question to a specific, well-motivated class of parabolic/zero-entropy systems, not a resolution of the general question, so I coded it `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (the settled case went the conjectured/expected way — mixing does imply multiple mixing there). I also read Ryzhikov's survey 'Multiple mixing, 75 years of Rokhlin's problem' (arXiv:2411.07234, submitted 2024-11-11), which explicitly states the general question 'remains open' after 75 years, catalogs the pre-existing classes where a positive answer was already known (singular spectrum, Ratner-property flows, positive local rank, finite rank automorphisms, Gaussian/Poisson suspensions) and the pre-2024 negative results for higher-dimensional actions (Ledrappier's Z^2 counterexample, predating the window), and cites a 2023 result of Ryzhikov's own on generic automorphisms deviating from multiple mixing — none of which are new results inside the window and none of which resolve the stated bullet. The survey does not mention the Kanigowski-Ravotti paper (likely a scheduling/overlap coincidence given the one-month gap between the two arXiv postings) or any AI/computer-assisted methods. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this area: no lab announcement, no author statement crediting a model with any part of either paper's mathematics, and no machine-checked or formalized proof. The current live Wikipedia list article's Rokhlin entry is worded identically to the frozen revision, consistent with the problem still being open in general.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kanigowski-Ravotti LUS result is close enough to 'the' answer that it deserves a stronger status than `partial`, since LUS captures essentially every known mechanism for zero-entropy mixing and the authors present it as unifying prior special-case results. But the stated bullet is the fully general question over all strongly mixing systems, and LUS is explicitly a sufficient condition, not a characterization — non-LUS mixing systems are not excluded from being counterexamples, so the general problem is unambiguously still open and `partial` is the correct scope-respecting call per §3.1.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof that every strongly mixing system is strongly 3-mixing (or a counterexample showing some strongly mixing but not 3-mixing Z-system, resolving the general problem), or (b) a proof that LUS (or some other checkable condition) is not just sufficient but necessary for multiple mixing, which would at least clarify how much territory the general problem still covers.

outcome: A case of Rosa's conjecture (Dutch windmills of any order with three pendant triangles are graceful or nearly-graceful) was settled by Alkasasbeh, Dyer and Shalaby using Skolem-type sequences, but the underlying mathematical result was first posted to arXiv in June 2020 (revised August 2021) and only appeared in a journal (Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 91(2), 2025) after the frozen revision date; no result actually occurring inside the 26 Jan 2024 - present window was found, and the general conjecture remains open.
summary: The triage's found item — 'Applying Skolem Sequences to Gracefully Label New Families of Triangular Windmills' (Alkasasbeh, Dyer, Shalaby), which the triage saw published in Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 91(2) (2025), pp. 242-265 — is the same paper as arXiv:2006.16396, first submitted 29 June 2020 and revised 9 August 2021 (confirmed via WebFetch on the arXiv abstract page, which shows [v1] 2020 and [v2] 2021). The paper proves that any Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles (a family of triangular cacti, i.e. connected graphs whose blocks are all triangles) is graceful or near-graceful depending on its residue mod 4, settling a case (not the whole) of Rosa's conjecture, via Skolem-type/Langford sequence constructions across eleven sub-types. This is a genuine case of the parent problem under §3.1 (a restriction to a specific sub-family of triangular cacti, not a variant), so if the result had appeared inside the window it would be classified 'partial'. But the mathematics itself long predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision — the AJC 'publication' in 2025 is only the journal's belated formal print of a five-year-old arXiv preprint, a lag explicitly anticipated by §6.1's rationale for 'open_stale' and by §6.3's instruction to date by the first written argument rather than the journal date. I found no other paper, preprint, or announcement addressing Rosa's conjecture (or any triangular-cacti sub-case of it) with a first-written-argument date after 26 January 2024; a November 2025 arXiv paper ('On the gracesize of trees', arXiv:2511.11331) addresses the sibling graceful tree conjecture (an approximate/asymptotic version for trees), not Rosa's conjecture on triangular cacti, and is a different problem in this dataset's terms. No source anywhere mentions AI, machine learning, automated theorem proving, or computational search in connection with this paper or with Rosa's conjecture generally — the method is classical combinatorial construction (Skolem/Langford sequences) by hand. Confidence is high that nothing happened to this specific problem inside the window, though I could not fully render the two PDFs' raw text (WebFetch reported binary/compressed content for both ajc_v91_p242.pdf and a related Memorial University thesis PDF) and instead relied on the arXiv abstract page, ResearchGate listing, and multiple independent search-engine summaries, all of which agree on authorship, dates, and content.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 AJC publication itself is the 'event' that counts, on the theory that the paper was not authoritative/expert-vetted mathematics until it passed peer review and appeared in a journal of record, and that the 2020 arXiv posting was merely a claim. Under that reading the status would be 'partial' with event date 2025 (journal) and the case would count as in-window progress. I reject this reading because §6.3 explicitly instructs dating by the first written argument, precisely to prevent journal lag from moving results across the window boundary, and because there is no evidence the mathematical content changed between the 2021 arXiv v2 and the 2025 journal version — this looks like an ordinary long peer-review queue, not new work.
what_would_settle_it: A diff between arXiv v2 (2021) and the published AJC version would confirm whether the journal version added any new mathematical content after 26 January 2024 (e.g. an additional family of cacti, a strengthened bound); if it did, that increment would be a genuine in-window 'partial' result dated to the journal publication.

outcome: The conjecture itself remains open, but two papers since the frozen revision moved the best known asymptotic bound toward it: Montgomery & Sauermann (Aug 2025) proved (1-o(1))n disjoint transversal bases can always be packed (and (1+o(1))n suffice to cover), up from the prior (1/2-o(1))n; Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, Swamy & Zlatin (Apr 2026) then gave the first polynomial-time constructive algorithm achieving an asymptotic version of this packing result for arbitrary matroids.
summary: Rota's basis conjecture (rank-n matroid with n disjoint bases can be arranged into an n×n matrix whose rows and columns are all bases) remains fully open as of September 2026. The most substantial development since the 26 January 2024 frozen revision is Montgomery & Sauermann, 'Asymptotically-tight packing and covering with transversal bases in Rota's basis conjecture' (arXiv:2508.05601, submitted 7 August 2025), which improves the best known asymptotic packing bound from (1/2-o(1))n disjoint transversal bases to the asymptotically-tight (1-o(1))n, and the covering bound from 2n (and later 2n-2) down to (1+o(1))n. I read the abstract and full text via fetch; it contains no reference to any AI or machine-learning system in its methods, acknowledgements, or elsewhere — this is a purely human, pen-and-paper (probabilistic/combinatorial) argument. A follow-up preprint, Arndt, Moseley, Pruhs, Swamy & Zlatin, 'Approximation Algorithms for Matroid-Intersection Coloring with Applications to Rota's Basis Conjecture' (arXiv:2604.03735, submitted 4 April 2026), constructivizes the Montgomery-Sauermann asymptotic packing result into the first polynomial-time algorithm achieving it, extending from representable matroids to arbitrary matroids; this is also purely human work with no AI mentioned. Both results are quantitative narrowings of the gap between the best proven packing/covering number and the full n the conjecture demands — they are bound-improving progress on the conjecture's own question (not a restriction to a special case, and not a different conjecture), so I classified the record as 'progress' rather than 'partial'. I also checked a 2024 result, Sauermann's 'Rota's basis conjecture holds for random bases of vector spaces,' but its arXiv submission (2203.17121) is dated 31 March 2022 with no later revision — only its European Journal of Combinatorics publication landed in 2024, which per the dating rule (first public written argument, not journal date) puts the actual event before the frozen revision date, so it is excluded (not counted, not even open_stale, since the actual submission genuinely predates the article's freeze and is irrelevant to what changed in the window). I also found a 2024 paper on the 'Latin Tableau Conjecture' (Chow & Tiefenbruck, arXiv:2408.04086), a generalization (wide partition conjecture, in the free-matroid case) of Rota's basis conjecture with computational verification of low-order cases; this changes a different, more general question rather than the stated bullet, so under §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case, and I did not let it affect the status here. No source anywhere — triage's own found item, the Wikipedia article, EmergentMind, Open Problem Garden, or my own searches — surfaced any AI system near this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Montgomery-Sauermann and Arndt-et-al results are significant enough progress on a 30-year-old conjecture to warrant more prominence than 'progress' conveys, but per §6.1 'progress' is exactly the code for a bound that moved while the problem stays open, which is precisely what happened; there is no case of the conjecture (e.g., a specific matroid class or fixed small n) that was newly settled, so 'partial' would overstate what occurred.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) removing the o(1) term entirely — i.e., establishing exactly n disjoint transversal bases (or a counterexample) for arbitrary matroids — would resolve the conjecture itself; short of that, any paper explicitly crediting an AI system with producing part of the combinatorial argument in a future preprint would change the ai_role.

outcome: A July 2026 preprint by Saša Novaković proves that for arithmetic progressions whose step q is polynomially bounded in the length N (q ≲ N^r for any fixed r > 0), the number of squares is N^{1/2+ε} for any ε>0 as N→∞ — matching Rudin's conjectured exponent O(√N) — but only for this restricted class of progressions, not for arbitrary step size, so the general conjecture (Q(N) over all progressions) remains open.
summary: The triage pass (verdict 'none') found nothing post-January-2024 and its searches (generic phrasings of 'Rudin's conjecture' plus year filters) missed this because the relevant work does not use the phrase 'Rudin's conjecture' at all. I found arXiv:2607.15895 ('A comment on the number of k-th powers inside arithmetic progressions', Saša Novaković, submitted 17 July 2026), a 4-page note extending Bourgain and Demeter's 2018 theorem (arXiv:1811.11919) on k-th powers in arithmetic progressions whose step has O(1) divisors. Novaković's Theorem 1.4 shows that for progressions whose step q grows at most polynomially in the length N (q ≲ N^r for any fixed r>0), the number of k-th powers among the first N terms is N^{1/k+ε} for any ε>0 and N large enough; for k=2 this is N^{1/2+ε}, matching Rudin's conjectured O(√N) exponent up to the ε. This restricts the class of arithmetic progressions considered (bounding the step's growth) rather than changing the question, so under §3.1 it is a case of Rudin's conjecture, not a variant: it removes a large swath of arithmetic progressions (all those with sub-polynomial-in-N step, which includes the vast majority of practically considered cases) from the space where the conjecture could still fail, while progressions with faster-growing steps (e.g. the extremal example 24n+1, whose step is a small constant, is actually already covered by the even older Bourgain-Demeter O(1)-divisor case) are the ones for which the full-strength O(√N) bound is not newly established here — the general Q(N) bound over ALL arithmetic progressions (Bombieri-Zannier's O(N^{3/5+o(1)}), still the best known for the fully general case) is untouched. No expert digestion, citation record, or journal acceptance was found for this July 2026 preprint (posted about two months before this research date), so it is not yet 'resolved' — it is a `claimed`-quality single-case result, hence overall problem status `partial` (a case settled, general conjecture still open). No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the paper's introduction, results, or (nonexistent) acknowledgements section; this appears to be conventional solo human mathematics extending a known induction argument, explicitly described by the author as work that 'should be known' but which the author is formally writing up.
competing_reading: One could argue this is closer to a `related problem` / variant rather than a `case`: Bourgain-Demeter's original theorem already covered the O(1)-divisor case, and Novaković's extension to polynomially-bounded steps, while broader, still excludes the general Q(N) problem (unbounded step growth) that Rudin's conjecture is actually about, and the paper itself is presented as an incremental technical comment rather than a targeted attack on Rudin's conjecture (it barely mentions Rudin by name, if at all, in the accessible text). Under a stricter reading, since the extremal near-optimal examples for Q(N) are believed to have small, fixed steps (already covered pre-2024 by Bourgain-Demeter), this new result adds coverage mainly to progressions that were never candidates for the extremal cases anyway, so its practical import for the conjecture as usually discussed is arguably closer to `progress`/`bound` than a genuine `partial` resolution of a case.
what_would_settle_it: A published/peer-reviewed version of arXiv:2607.15895, or an expert digestion (e.g., a citing survey or blog post) explicitly framing the polynomial-step-growth case as settling part of Rudin's conjecture, would confirm the `partial` classification and let it be upgraded toward `resolved` for that case. Absent that, direct confirmation (via the full paper PDF, which I could not cleanly OCR/extract past the abstract and a WebFetch-generated summary) of whether the paper explicitly cites Rudin's conjecture by name would also sharpen the scope call.

outcome: An arXiv preprint (2609.14281, Sept 2026) by independent researcher Patrick White claims to prove that every 4-partite 4-uniform hypergraph with matching number ν(H)=2 satisfies τ(H)≤6, confirming an unpublished 1979 claim of Tuza and closing the case (r,ν)=(4,2) of Ryser's conjecture, improving the prior best bound τ≤7 due to Haxell and Scott (2012). The proof is explicitly stated by the author to have been found through AI-driven reasoning (GPT-5.6 Sol) with independent computational verification (MILP/enumeration) by the human author; it has not yet been digested by any expert, accepted by a journal, or covered in survey/blog literature.
