outcome: Lower bounds on a(n), the longest induced path (snake) in the n-dimensional hypercube, were repeatedly improved for dimensions 9-17 during the window via heuristic/pruned search, most substantially by T. Ace (2025, dims 10-13), Orland, Fagan, Tarquini, Passaro, Manko, Heyes, Gruen, Butbaia, Tan and Gukov (arXiv:2607.15270, July 2026, dims 9-13), and Bernatonis (2026, dims 14-17); none of the sources located disclose any AI/ML method for the search itself.

disputes.summary: For dimensions 9-13, the improved bounds are attributed to at least three independent, overlapping efforts within the window: T. Ace (Zenodo, Nov 2025, dims 10-13, values 732/1439/2854 for 11/12/13), the Orland et al. arXiv paper (July 2026, dims 9-13, values 191/379/746/1476/2924 for 9-13), and the live minortriad.com records table (checked 2026-09-22, showing still-higher values 191/379/750/1480/2934 for 9-13, apparently reflecting further post-paper updates credited informally to Ace/Echols collaboration). No single source resolves current priority/attribution cleanly, and the live table already supersedes the July 2026 preprint's own numbers.

summary: The problem asks for a(n), the length of the longest induced (snake) path in the n-dimensional hypercube graph Q_n, known exactly only for n≤8. Since 26 January 2024, no resolution of the general problem occurred (it remains open for all n≥9), but the best-known lower bounds moved several times, which is squarely within scope per §3.1 since the bullet's quantity (the record length itself) is what changed. In order: T. Ace published 'New Lower Bounds for Snake-in-the-Box in 10-, 11-, 12-, and 13-dimensional Hypercubes' on Zenodo (6 November 2025, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17538015), reporting 732/1439/2854 for dimensions 11/12/13 using, per the abstract, 'simple heuristics' (a pruned breadth-first search per the companion GitHub tool docxology/snake) — no AI/ML disclosed. Then a ten-author paper from Sergei Gukov's Caltech group (Orland, Fagan, Tarquini, Passaro, Manko, Heyes, Gruen, Butbaia, Tan, Gukov), 'A Census of New Snake-in-the-Box Records' (arXiv:2607.15270, submitted 16 July 2026, revised 20 July 2026), reported new records in every dimension 9-13 (191/379/746/1476/2924), with a companion GitHub dataset (Math-AI-Caltech/Snake-in-the-Box). I read the paper's full HTML text directly (introduction, results, example, data, acknowledgements, and section list); it contains no methods/algorithm section at all describing how the authors found their snakes — it is a pure results 'census', citing predecessors' methods (genetic algorithms, evolutionary search, Monte Carlo tree search) but never stating its own. The acknowledgements credit DARPA, NSF, and a philanthropic gift, plus (per one fetch) Google Cloud TPUs and NVIDIA GPU compute grants — hardware normally used for training neural networks. This is suggestive given that several co-authors (Fagan, Tarquini, Manko, Gruen, Butbaia, Passaro, Gukov) are simultaneously authors of explicit reinforcement-learning-for-mathematics papers from the same lab in the same period (e.g. 'The Two-Hump Problem: Bridging the Difficulty Gap in Mathematical Reinforcement Learning', ICML 2026, on the Andrews-Curtis conjecture; 'RLGT: A reinforcement learning framework for extremal graph theory', on Ramsey/Turán problems) — but neither of those companion papers mentions the snake-in-the-box problem, and no source I found (paper text, GitHub READMEs for either Math-AI-Caltech/Snake-in-the-Box or Math-AI-Caltech/ACSolverX, alphaXiv digestion, Pith Review digestion) states or quotes that RL or any AI system was used for the snake search specifically. Meanwhile a separate 2026 paper by Kristijonas Bernatonis (Notre Dame) extended pruned-BFS heuristic records to dimensions 14-17 (5750/11249/21411/40835), again with no AI claimed. The live minortriad.com records table (T. Ace's own site, checked 2026-09-22) now shows even higher values for 11-13 (750/1480/2934) than the July 2026 paper, crediting continued 'sustained computational efforts of Ace and Echols' with no dates or method given in the FAQ. Wikipedia's own (non-frozen, current) Snake-in-the-box article, last touching this figure around 2026-07-23, cites minortriad.com for 191/379/746/1476/2932 and does not mention any of these researchers or any AI angle; its most recent methodologically-notable citation is a February 2023 AAAI paper (Dang, Bazgan, Cazenave, Chopin, Wuillemin, 'Warm-Starting Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation with Optimal Stopping') that did use a genuine RL-adjacent method (Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation) to improve snake-in-the-box bounds — but that result predates the window (Jan 2023) and is not counted here. Net: real, repeated, in-scope progress on the record bound (a(n) for n=9-17) occurred throughout the window, but the strongest textual evidence available describes it as heuristic/pruned search rather than AI, so ai_role is coded none under the rule that a role requires the authors' own account, which I could not find despite reading the primary paper directly and its surrounding ecosystem (GitHub, Zenodo, alphaXiv, Pith Review).
competing_reading: The TPU/GPU acknowledgement in the Orland et al. paper, combined with the fact that several of its authors are core members of an AI-for-mathematics research program (RL for Andrews-Curtis and extremal graph theory) publishing in the same months, is real circumstantial evidence that the snake search itself may have used a learned (RL or neural) heuristic/policy rather than a purely hand-coded pruning rule. If an unlocated methods appendix, supplementary material, or follow-up blog post confirms this, the correct coding would likely be ai_role 'assisted' or 'bound' (a bound moved by AI search) rather than 'none'. I was unable to access the raw PDF (binary/compressed, not parseable by my tools) and could not find a separate methods writeup, so I am not confident this circumstantial reading is wrong.
what_would_settle_it: A methods/supplementary section of arXiv:2607.15270 (or a talk, blog post, or code repository beyond the bare data-only Math-AI-Caltech/Snake-in-the-Box repo) that states in the authors' own words what search procedure produced the record snakes — specifically whether it involved a trained model (RL policy, neural network, or similar) versus a purely combinatorial/heuristic pruned search. Also, direct correspondence or a changelog on minortriad.com dating and crediting the current (750/1480/2934) records beyond the July 2026 paper's numbers.

outcome: The general-dimension asymptotic sphere packing problem remains open, but several distinct results moved bounds since January 2024: Klartag (Apr 2025) proved a new lattice lower bound of order n²·2^-n (up from the Campos–Jenssen–Michelen–Sahasrabudhe n·log n·2^-n bound of Dec 2023, which itself predates the frozen revision); a Huawei Noah's Ark/UCL team (Dec 2025) used a Bayesian-optimization + Monte Carlo Tree Search pipeline to find new state-of-the-art upper bounds for dimensions 4-16 via the Cohn–Elkies three-point method; and OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model (Aug 2026) is claimed to have determined the exact asymptotic exponent of the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound, capping what that method can ever achieve — the first improvement to the general high-dimensional upper-bound exponent since 1978. None of the problem's core open question (the true asymptotic packing density in general dimension) has been resolved; the densest classification is 'claimed' because the most significant single result (Astra's Cohn-Elkies exponent) is Lean-verified and has an informal mathematician digestion (Seewoo Lee) but has not cleared traditional peer review, and is under an active, unresolved priority/attribution dispute.

ai.basis_quote: Astra works on the problem, sometimes for a long time, and produces the core insight and strategy for a proof; human mathematicians then write that strategy up as a traditional, readable manuscript, and the model translates the manuscript into the strict formal syntax of Lean.
ai.disclosed_cost: OpenAI reported that finding all ten proofs (including this one) cost the equivalent of roughly $2,000 in AI usage fees, a figure that omits the cost of unsuccessful attempts and is not broken out per problem.

disputes.summary: Steven Miller (Yeshiva University) says Astra's sphere-packing (Cohn–Elkies exponent) proof reuses an argument from his own 2016 paper without adequate attribution; a similar unattributed-prior-work complaint was raised by Fournier-Facio (Cambridge) about a different one of the ten results (nonsofic groups). OpenAI's response: 'We take responsibility for the correctness of these results and are meeting the same standards generally expected of human mathematicians.' As of six weeks after release (per Scientific American, published in the Sept 2026 window), the dispute is unresolved and none of the ten results has cleared traditional peer review.

summary: Three separate, unrelated developments touch this bullet's asymptotic sphere-packing-density question since 26 January 2024, and none of them settles the general problem. (1) Boaz Klartag (arXiv:2504.05042, submitted 2025-04-07, v2 2026-01-25) proved a new lattice sphere-packing lower bound of order c·n²·2^-n via a 'stochastically evolving ellipsoid' construction, a quadratic-in-n improvement over the previous best construction (Campos–Jenssen–Michelen–Sahasrabudhe, arXiv:2312.10026, Dec 2023 — which itself predates the frozen revision and is not counted as an in-window event, though it is the baseline Klartag improves on). Gil Kalai's blog (2025-04-09) calls it 'an amazing breakthrough'; a Lean formalization of Klartag's result also appears to exist (per an issue on the leanprover/lean-eval-submissions repo), giving this piece close to 'resolved'-level digestion, though it is only a lower-bound improvement, not a resolution — classified as `progress` in isolation. No AI system produced this mathematics; it is pure human work by Klartag. (2) A Huawei Noah's Ark / UCL AI Centre team (arXiv:2512.04829, submitted 2025-12-04) used a Bayesian-optimization-plus-Monte-Carlo-Tree-Search pipeline to search for polynomial pairs in the Cohn–Elkies three-point semidefinite-programming method, reporting new state-of-the-art upper bounds on packing density for dimensions 4-16 (excluding 8). This is `ai_role: bound` in isolation — an AI system moved a numerical upper bound on a still-open problem, not a proof. (3) The most significant event, and the one this record's top-level fields describe, is OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model (announced 2026-08-01, in a 249-page manuscript plus Lean 4 certificates), which is claimed to have determined the *exact* asymptotic growth rate of the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound itself (exponent √(e/2π) ≈ matching an exponent decay rate), the first improvement to the general high-dimensional sphere-packing upper-bound exponent since 1978. This caps what the Cohn–Elkies method can ever prove, but is not itself a resolution of the sphere-packing problem (it supplies no new packing and does not pin down the true asymptotic density) — mathematically this is best read as `progress`/`claimed` on the upper-bound side rather than a full resolution. Authors' own account (via secondary reporting, since the primary PDF could not be parsed by the fetch tool) describes a pipeline where Astra 'produces the core insight and strategy for a proof,' humans write it up, and the model formalizes it in Lean — squarely `ai_role: generated` under §6.2, since the mathematics in the result originated from the model rather than from checking/proofreading a human argument. As of six weeks post-announcement, the claim has an informal mathematician digestion (Seewoo Lee spent two weeks reconstructing and explaining the proof, though his post explicitly says he does not yet understand how the upper- and lower-bound exponents match) but no traditional peer review, and is under an active, unresolved priority dispute with Steven Miller over uncredited prior work. This combination — Lean-checked, informally digested, not peer-reviewed, disputed — is exactly the profile of `claimed` rather than `resolved`. I also checked and excluded DeepMind's AlphaEvolve result (new kissing-number lower bound in dimension 11, 592→593, announced 2025) as out of scope: the kissing number problem is a related-but-distinct problem from sphere-packing density, with its own separate Wikipedia bullet, so under §3.1 it is a related problem rather than a case of this one.
competing_reading: One could argue the overall record should be `progress` rather than `claimed`, on the view that the Astra result, however striking, is an upper bound on a bounding *method* rather than the packing problem itself, so the strongest single move is really Klartag's `progress`-level lower bound. I chose `claimed` because it is the most classification-relevant status the frozen bullet's asymptotic behavior has seen: the Cohn–Elkies exponent result is a genuine mathematical resolution of a sub-question (the ultimate power of the linear-programming method), it is the event with an actual (if incomplete) AI-authorship claim requiring adjudication under §6.2, and `claimed` still correctly signals 'not yet settled by peer review' rather than overclaiming `resolved`.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a completed peer-reviewed publication or widely-accepted expert consensus (e.g., a second independent 'digestion' post or a journal referee report) on the Astra Cohn–Elkies exponent result, resolving the Miller priority dispute one way or the other, or (b) a genuine resolution of the asymptotic sphere-packing density itself (as opposed to a bound on a bounding method), which remains fully open.

summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet just names 'the spherical Bernstein's problem, a generalization of Bernstein's problem' with no statement of which cases remain open; the problem's own article (checked directly, not the live version but consulted for background as permitted when a nested/linked article is needed to make sense of the bullet) explains that Chern's problem asks whether equators are the only smooth embedded minimal hyperspheres in S^(n+1), that n=3 was resolved by Almgren-Calabi, that Hsiang resolved it negatively for n in {4,5,6,7,8,10,12,14}, and that Tomter (1987) extended the negative resolution to all even n -- leaving it open only for odd n>=9 (equivalently even ambient dimension n+1>=10). This matches the triage's own summary of the state of the art. The one item found in the window, arXiv:2602.03984 (Wang, Wang & Zhou, submitted February 2026, revised August 2026), gives a new min-max-theoretic construction of a non-equatorial minimal hypersphere in S^4 specifically, calling it 'a new resolution of Chern's spherical Bernstein problem in S^4.' Since S^4 (n=4, even) was already settled in the negative by Hsiang decades before the 26 January 2024 snapshot, this is a new proof technique for an already-closed case, not new territory, so it is dated 'open_stale' with respect to the genuinely open cases (odd n>=9 / even ambient n+1>=8+2). I found no work in the window that touches the actually-open odd-n>=9 cases: searches for progress there surfaced only work on the superficially similarly-named but distinct 'stable Bernstein problem' (Chodosh-Li 2023-2024, Chodosh-Li-Minter-Stryker 2026, Mazet 2024), which is a different problem about stability of minimal hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, not Chern's spherical Bernstein problem, and was correctly not conflated here. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the 2602.03984 preprint's methods, acknowledgements, or in secondary discussion found; the work uses purely classical equivariant min-max variational methods.
competing_reading: One could argue the new 2602.03984 construction, even though S^4 was already known to admit non-equatorial minimal hyperspheres, still counts as 'progress' because it introduces a new equivariant min-max machinery (regularity theory for the G-equivariant Plateau/isotopy problem in manifolds with 3-dimensional orbit space) that the authors may intend to extend to the genuinely open odd n>=9 cases -- the triage's `why` field raises exactly this possibility. However, the paper itself only claims the S^4 result; no extension to higher/open dimensions is proved or even conjectured concretely in the version I reviewed, so I did not classify this as `progress` on the open cases. If a follow-up paper by the same or other authors applies this machinery to an open dimension, that would change the classification.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (from these or other authors) that applies equivariant min-max theory, or any other technique, to construct or rule out a non-equatorial minimal hypersphere for some odd n>=9 (or even ambient dimension n+1>=10), which is the actual open frontier of the problem.

outcome: The problem (the asymptotic growth rate of wasted space W(x)) remains open, but the rigorously-established upper bound moved during the window: Chung and Graham's 2019 claim of W(x)=O(x^0.6) was discovered in 2025 (Arslanov & Bui) to contain a calculation error, temporarily reverting the proven state of the art to the weaker W(x)=O(x^{(3+sqrt(2))/7} log x); two independent papers then re-established W(x)=O(x^0.6) rigorously by new methods (Bui, Aug 2025; McClenagan, preprinted Feb 2026 from a 2024 thesis). A third paper (Bui, Apr 2025) simplified the Roth-Vaughan lower-bound proof technique without changing the bound. No AI system was involved in any of this work.

disputes.summary: Bui (arXiv:2508.04603, submitted 2025-08-06, v2 2026-03-15) and McClenagan (arXiv:2602.01484, submitted 2026-02-01) independently proved the same bound W(x)=O(x^{3/5}) (equivalently O(x^0.6)) by different constructions. McClenagan's result derives from his 2024 UNBC master's thesis (DOI 10.24124/2024/59553); the arXiv writeup itself states that 'since submission [of the thesis], a similar result by a different method was published in 2025 (arXiv:2508.04603 by Bui),' i.e. McClenagan's own account places his result first but its public arXiv posting second. I could not establish the exact month of the 2024 thesis defense/deposit, so I cannot determine whether the thesis itself was completed before or after the 26 January 2024 cutoff.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet as frozen on 26 Jan 2024 is bare ('what is the asymptotic growth rate of wasted space?'), with no bound cited. Checking the frozen revision confirms this. The problem itself -- the precise asymptotic growth rate of W(x) -- remains fully open; nothing in the window resolves it or narrows it to a single answer. What happened in the window concerns the best known *upper* bound, and it is more complicated than the triage summary suggested: Chung and Graham had claimed in a 2019 paper (Discrete & Comput. Geom. 64(3):690-699) that W(x)=O(x^0.6) (equivalently x^{3/5}), improving on Wang et al. (2016)'s O(x^0.625). As best I can tell from later sources, this claim was the believed state of the art as of January 2024. In 2025, Arslanov and Bui (Discrete & Comput. Geom., DOI 10.1007/s00454-025-00767-w) identified a technical error in Chung-Graham's calculation of a quantity W_5, invalidating the 2019 proof and reverting the rigorously-established bound to the earlier, weaker W(x)=O(x^{(3+sqrt(2))/7} log x) (Chung-Graham 2009). Two papers then closed this gap independently: Hong Duc Bui (arXiv:2508.04603, first submitted 2025-08-06) gave a new construction rigorously proving W(x)=O(x^0.6); Rory McClenagan (arXiv:2602.01484, submitted 2026-02-01, extracted from a 2024 master's thesis) gave a different construction (via 'stacks' of unit squares plus trapezoidal sub-packings) proving the same bound, explicitly framing the result as confirming that 'the bound claimed by Chung and Graham... is, in fact, correct, using a new algorithm.' A third paper, Bui (arXiv:2504.09489, submitted 2025-04-13, presented at CCCG 2025), proved that only 'good squares' (inclination <= 10^-10) need be considered when establishing the Roth-Vaughan lower bound W(x) not-in o(x^{1/2}), simplifying that proof's case analysis without changing the bound itself -- this is `progress` on proof technique, not a moved bound, and by itself would not change status. I read all three papers (HTML/PDF) in full or via careful extraction, including abstracts, introductions, and acknowledgements, and found no mention anywhere of AI, machine learning, neural networks, computer search, or automated/computer-assisted proof techniques; the acknowledgements in the two substantive papers thank a human proofreader and anonymous reviewers only. I classify the overall status as `progress` rather than `partial` or `resolved`: no case or sub-instance of the open growth-rate question was settled, and the open problem (the exact asymptotic rate) is untouched; what moved is the best known upper bound, which is exactly the `progress` category, and I use the Bui paper's 2025-08-06 submission as the dated event since it is the first public written argument re-establishing O(x^0.6) rigorously (McClenagan's underlying thesis may predate this, but I could not establish its month, and its own arXiv writeup postdates Bui's). `resolution_direction` is `confirmed` because the re-proof confirms (rather than refutes) the previously-believed-but-then-invalidated Chung-Graham bound.
competing_reading: One could argue this is `open_stale`-adjacent: the O(x^0.6) bound was already the publicly believed state of the art before the frozen revision date, so the 2025-2026 papers merely repair a gap rather than advance genuinely new mathematics beyond what was already assumed true in January 2024. Under that reading the 'progress' is illusory -- the field is only catching back up to where everyone already thought it was. I did not adopt this reading because between the January 2019 claim and the 2025 papers there was a period (starting with the 2025 Arslanov-Bui erratum) where the rigorously-known bound was strictly worse than O(x^0.6), and restoring a result after a genuine, published invalidation is itself a real mathematical event (a new, different, correct proof was required, not a correction of the old one) rather than a non-event. A second, narrower competing reading: the Bui 'good squares' paper (2504.09489) could be read as `partial` if one considers the reduction to good-square packings itself a nontrivial partial characterization result rather than pure proof-simplification, but the paper's own framing ('allows the lower bound proof... to be simplified') supports treating it as technique-simplification, which does not by itself change `status`.
what_would_settle_it: The exact month (or day) of deposit/defense of McClenagan's 2024 UNBC thesis (DOI 10.24124/2024/59553) would settle whether an argument for W(x)=O(x^0.6) existed publicly before or after 26 January 2024, which would matter if the thesis itself (as opposed to its 2026 arXiv writeup) counts as the first public written argument. It would not change the `progress` classification (the open problem itself is untouched either way) but could shift the `event` date earlier and add nuance to the `open_stale` question for the upper-bound sub-thread.

outcome: The only substantive advance on this conjecture — that large stable fields are separably closed, a case obtained by restricting to 'large' fields — was proved by Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye in a preprint posted 4 September 2020 (arXiv:2009.02319), well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, and later appeared in the Journal of the European Mathematical Society (online June 2023, print issue 2024). A July 2026 preprint by Kaplan, Matthews and Walsberg ('Building trees in large fields', arXiv:2607.16942) gives a substantially simpler proof of the same case (and of the related fact that large simple fields are bounded) but does not extend the result to any new case and does not touch the general conjecture, so it is not itself a scope-changing event under §3.1. The general stable field conjecture — every infinite field with a stable first-order theory is separably closed — remains open.
summary: The stable field conjecture (every infinite stable field is separably closed) is a long-standing open problem in model theory, with partial progress predating the window: Scanlon (1999) showed infinite stable fields are Artin-Schreier closed, and Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye (arXiv:2009.02319, posted 2020-09-04, published in JEMS with online publication 2023-06-15 and a 2024 print issue) proved the case of 'large' stable fields, via a new étale-open topology. Both the decisive preprint and its journal appearance (dated by first written argument, per §6.3, not by journal print date) predate or straddle the 26 January 2024 freeze in a way that keeps the underlying mathematical event pre-window, so this is classified open_stale rather than a fresh partial result. Within the window, the only new item found is arXiv:2607.16942 ('Building trees in large fields', Kaplan, Matthews, Walsberg, posted 2026-07-18), which gives a substantially simplified, more conceptual proof of the same 'large stable fields are separably closed' result (and a companion result on large simple fields being bounded) using an explicit tree-building technique. I read the full abstract/HTML of this paper and found no claim of a new case, no extension of the boundary of what's known, and no mention of AI or machine-learning tools in the research. Because it re-derives an already-known case rather than restricting the conjecture's scope further, it does not constitute a new event under §3.1's case-vs-variant test — it is a proof simplification, not new mathematical territory. The general conjecture (for arbitrary infinite stable fields, not just 'large' ones) remains fully open, and I found no work in the window addressing it directly. I also checked arXiv:2508.10886 ('Large implies henselian', Johnson-Tran-Walsberg-Ye, 2025-08-14) which is about characterizing large fields via henselianity and does not mention the stable field conjecture at all. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this research area.
competing_reading: One could argue the JEMS publication (online 2023-06-15, print 2024) should count as the dating event since journal acceptance is when the result becomes 'digested by experts' (resolved-tier evidence), and since the print issue is dated 2024, arguably later than the frozen revision's January 2024 timestamp. But §6.3 is explicit that journal publication date should never be used for dating since it lags the real event and would spuriously pull pre-window results into the window; the first written argument (the 2020 preprint) is what governs, and it was already digested (via peer review) well before 2024 regardless. I am confident in open_stale here.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture for the general (not necessarily large) infinite stable field case would resolve or refute the conjecture outright; a paper explicitly extending 'large' to some broader class would count as further partial progress and change the status to partial with a new dated event.

outcome: A preprint by James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik claims a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, using an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, in which forking cannot always be witnessed by a stable formula. The authors state the counterexample was found using ChatGPT 5.6. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification of the argument has yet surfaced.

ai.basis_quote: Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. ... This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol. Specifically, we prompted ChatGPT to construct a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture with a detailed series of prompts which took into account the many restrictions and likely restrictions such a counterexample would have to satisfy. ... The proofs of the relevant facts around the counterexample as well as some aspects of the specific setup have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript. (AI was used for proofreading, with the edits performed and evaluated manually by the authors.) ... In retrospect, it seems unlikely that this counterexample would have been found in the near term without the use of generative AI.

counterexample.object: The theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, in which forking (governed by an abstract independence relation encoding the order property of the random graph) cannot always be witnessed by a stable formula, contrary to the conjecture.
counterexample.verified_how: The authors state they independently wrote the proofs of simplicity (via the Kim-Pillay abstract-independence criterion) and of the failure of stable forking by hand; no independent third-party verification or expert digestion has yet been found.

summary: On 2026-08-31/2026-09, James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik posted arXiv:2609.00436, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture,' claiming to refute the 1996 conjecture of Hart, Kim and Pillay that every simple theory has stable forking (i.e. that forking is always witnessed by a stable formula). The counterexample is a specific simple theory (an infinite-dimensional vector space over a division ring of fractions of a quantum graph algebra of the random graph) in which the random graph's order property is encoded into the independence relation, so that no stable formula can witness all forking. Multiple independent checks corroborate this is a genuine, real preprint rather than a fabricated result: Scott Mutchnik's own academic homepage (sites.google.com/berkeley.edu/scottmutchnik) lists 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, with James Freitag (using ChatGPT 5.6), preprint' among his own works, and both authors are established, active model theorists with a real, independently verifiable 2025 co-authored paper (with John Baldwin) findable via web search. This is enough to establish the event and the AI-attribution as coming from the authors' own account, satisfying the bar for `ai_role: generated` and `status: claimed`. However, I flag real uncertainty in the secondary sourcing: several page fetches of the arXiv abstract page returned mutually inconsistent bibliographic details (a 'submitted 31 Aug 2026' notice attached to an arXiv identifier, 2609.00436, whose YYMM prefix denotes September 2026, and one listing-page fetch that did not contain the paper in an August 2026 listing but did in a September 2026 listing), and a PDF fetch returned unreadable binary content rather than text, so I could not read the manuscript's full body directly — only reconstructed abstract/section-1.1 quotes via secondary tool fetches of the abstract/HTML page, which I cross-checked against each other and against the author's own homepage listing for consistency. The model name 'ChatGPT 5.6' / 'GPT-5.6 Sol' is unfamiliar to me (my knowledge cutoff is January 2026), which is expected for a system released after cutoff but is also a reason for caution given the fetch inconsistencies above. No expert digestion (a Tao-style walkthrough, journal acceptance, or independent re-derivation by a third model theorist) has surfaced; a companion blog post (Kevin Buzzard's Xena blog, 2026-07-20) discusses a wave of similar 2026 AI-found counterexamples to other conjectures (Erdős unit distance, a Grothendieck group-scheme question, the Jacobian conjecture) with emphasis on Lean-checked verification, but does not mention this problem, so the stable forking result has not received that level of independent scrutiny. Status is therefore `claimed` rather than `resolved`: a preprint with a clear authorial account of AI involvement in constructing the counterexample, not yet digested by the field.
competing_reading: If the bibliographic inconsistencies in the fetched arXiv metadata (date vs. identifier mismatch) reflect an actual data problem rather than tool/fetch noise, there is a small chance this record is describing a paper that does not exist as described, or exists with different details than reported here. I weighed this against corroboration from Mutchnik's own institutional homepage, which independently lists the same paper with the same AI attribution, and judged the corroboration sufficient — but a reader with direct arXiv access should re-verify the raw abstract page and PDF text before treating this as fully settled.
what_would_settle_it: Direct, verified access to the raw arXiv abstract page and PDF text of 2609.00436 (rather than reconstructed tool summaries), and evidence of expert digestion or peer review — e.g. a referee report, journal acceptance, or a model theorist's independent write-up confirming the proof of simplicity and the failure of stable forking.

outcome: The general standard conjectures (Grothendieck's conjectures B, D, and the Hodge standard conjecture) remain open, but Thomas Agugliaro proved the standard conjecture of Hodge type unconditionally for new classes of abelian varieties (powers of abelian threefolds, powers of simple abelian varieties of prime dimension over finite fields, and other Frobenius-rank cases) in a preprint posted 24 October 2025 (arXiv:2510.21562), extending his own 2024 paper (arXiv:2401.17445, to appear in Documenta Mathematica) which constructed infinitely many abelian varieties of dimension g≥5 satisfying the same conjecture.
summary: The triage correctly flagged two 2025 preprints and correctly hedged on whether they count. Having read both in full: arXiv:2508.13882 (Truong, 'Standard conjecture D and some conjectures around Weil's Riemann hypothesis') is explicitly conditional — its main result is 'If Standard conjecture D holds ... then all polarised endomorphisms on X are semisimple,' i.e. it assumes the conjecture and derives consequences, and settles no case of it. This is not a change to the stated problem and is excluded under §3.1. arXiv:2510.21562 (Agugliaro, 'Standard conjecture of Hodge type for powers of abelian varieties'), by contrast, is an unconditional proof of the Hodge standard conjecture (one of the several conjectures collectively called the standard conjectures) for concrete new classes: powers of abelian threefolds, powers of simple abelian varieties of prime dimension over finite fields, and cases characterised by Frobenius rank. This is a genuine restriction of the stated problem (a specific class of varieties) proved true, so it is a case of the problem under §3.1, not a variant — it counts as `partial`, direction `confirmed`. It builds on the same author's 2024 preprint (arXiv:2401.17445, forthcoming in Documenta Mathematica), which had already produced infinitely many g≥5 abelian varieties over finite fields satisfying the conjecture, using a theorem of Ancona on rank-2 motives; that 2024 work is itself in the window (submitted 2024-01-30, after the 26 Jan 2024 freeze — checked and it is one day after, not stale) but the October 2025 paper is the more recent and more general event, so it is the one dated. Neither paper has yet been digested by an expert community (no citations found, no published version, no blog commentary), so under §6.1 this stays short of `resolved`; but it is also not a bare unrefereed claim of a headline result — it is routine, incremental special-case literature of the kind the field regularly produces, and I classify it as `partial` (a case settled) rather than `claimed`, since `claimed` is meant for claims of resolving the (sub)problem that await verification, and here the case genuinely is proved by ordinary rigorous means with no room for a 'the argument might be wrong' concern of the kind `claimed` exists to flag. I also checked adjacent literature that could be mistaken for progress on this problem: Floccari–Varesco (arXiv:2308.04865, v2 Nov 2024, published in Mathematische Annalen 2024) proves the Hodge and Tate CONJECTURES (not the standard conjectures) for 4-dimensional generalized Kummer varieties — a different, related problem, correctly out of scope. Foster (arXiv:2512.04114, Dec 2025) proves the Lefschetz standard conjectures for 4-dimensional Kummer-type varieties, but conditionally on an unproven Buchweitz–Flenner conjecture, so like Truong's paper it does not settle an unconditional case and is excluded. Ito–Ito–Koshikawa's Hodge standard conjecture for self-products of K3 surfaces (arXiv:2206.10086) was posted in June 2022 and has only one arXiv version; its 2025 appearance is solely a journal publication (Journal of Algebraic Geometry) lagging the preprint by three years, which §6.3 explicitly says must not be used as the event date — this result is `open_stale` in isolation, predating the window entirely, and is not the basis for this record's status. No AI system was found anywhere in this literature: none of the four preprints checked (2510.21562, 2508.13882, 2401.17445, 2512.04114) or the two journal papers (2308.04865, 2206.10086) mention any AI system, language model, or automated theorem prover in their abstracts, methodology sections, or (where visible) acknowledgements. Targeted searches for AI/LLM/theorem-prover involvement specific to this problem returned nothing. ai_role is therefore 'none' with an empty basis_quote, as required when no authorial statement exists.
competing_reading: One could argue Agugliaro's result is close enough to routine incremental special-case literature (as the triage worried) that it should not move the status away from 'open' at all, on the theory that the standard conjectures article is really asking about the conjectures in general and cataloguing every proved special case would never let this record read 'open' even though the headline conjecture never moves. I judge against this reading because §3.1 explicitly instructs that 'a single case settled' counts, normally as partial, and does not carve out an exception for fields (like this one) where special cases are proved frequently; the volume of special-case literature is a fact about the field's ordinary variety, not a reason to disregard the instruction.
what_would_settle_it: A citation, referee report, or acceptance of arXiv:2510.21562 by a journal would move it toward being folded into 'resolved for that case' with more confidence, though the status code would still be `partial` since it is not the general conjecture. A subsequent survey or Wikipedia edit explicitly listing this case would also help confirm the classification.

outcome: The Brumer–Stark conjecture (the case of the Stark conjectures this bullet names) was proved by Dasgupta–Kakde in 2020 (away from p=2) and extended to a full proof over Z by Dasgupta–Kakde–Silliman–Wang in October 2023 — both before the frozen revision. The general (non-abelian, higher-rank) Stark conjectures remain open. Post-window activity found is confined to a distinct, related question: explicit p-adic formulas for the already-proven-to-exist Brumer–Stark units (Honnor 2023/2024/2025; Dasgupta–Honnor–Spieß 2022/2025), which is a refinement/constructive-formula question tied to Hilbert's 12th problem, not a further resolution of the existence conjecture itself.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet names 'Stark conjectures (including Brumer–Stark conjecture)'. The Brumer–Stark conjecture — that certain Brumer–Stark units exist with p-order equal to a partial zeta value — was proved away from p=2 by Dasgupta and Kakde (arXiv:2010.00657, submitted 2020-10-01, published in Annals of Mathematics 2023) and extended to a full unconditional proof over Z by Dasgupta, Kakde, Silliman and Wang (arXiv:2310.16399, submitted 2023-10-26). Both events predate the frozen revision (2024-01-26), so this case of the general Stark conjectures is correctly status open_stale, dated to the October 2023 full proof (the later, more complete event, per §6.1). The broader Stark conjectures (arbitrary rank, non-abelian settings) remain open; I found no post-window result settling any further case of those. What I did find post-window is a cluster of papers on a related but distinct question: explicit formulas expressing the (already known to exist) Brumer–Stark units p-adically. Matthew Honnor's paper (arXiv:2302.12332) had v1 in Feb 2023 (pre-window) but v2, posted 2024-01-11, proved a strictly stronger result resolving an additional root-of-unity ambiguity at p=2 and removing an assumption from Dasgupta–Kakde's formula — this is a genuine post-window strengthening, but it targets the Dasgupta–Kakde explicit-formula conjecture, not the Brumer–Stark existence conjecture itself. A companion paper, Dasgupta–Honnor–Spieß 'On the Equality of Three Formulas for Brumer–Stark Units' (arXiv:2211.01715, v1 Nov 2022, substantially revised Dec 2025, published in J. London Math. Soc. Oct 2025) proves three conjectural p-adic formulas for the units agree; this too is about the explicit-formula/Hilbert's-12th-problem side of the theory, not the existence conjecture. Neither paper's abstract or introduction (as accessible) frames the formula question as a literal restatement of the Brumer–Stark conjecture as Wikipedia states it; the existence question was already closed before the window, and the formula question is a related, Hilbert-12-flavored refinement that a careful reading of the bullet would not fold into 'the Stark conjectures' entry as newly resolved or newly partial. No AI system was found anywhere in this cluster of work — all papers are traditional human-authored algebraic number theory (Iwasawa theory, Hilbert modular forms, Ritter–Weiss modules, Eisenstein congruences); searches for AI/ML involvement in Stark or Brumer–Stark work returned nothing relevant.
competing_reading: One could argue the Dasgupta–Spieß explicit-formula conjecture is close enough to 'the Brumer–Stark conjecture' in spirit (both are about pinning down these units completely and both trace to the same research program aimed at Hilbert's 12th problem) that Honnor's Jan 2024 strengthening and the Dec 2025 equality-of-three-formulas result should count as `partial`/`progress` post-window movement on this bullet, with event date 2024-01-11 (Honnor v2) rather than open_stale. Under that reading ai_role would still be none.
what_would_settle_it: A careful reading of Tate's original Brumer–Stark conjecture statement and the Dasgupta–Kakde papers' own framing of whether the explicit p-adic formula is presented as part of the conjecture's statement or as a separate conjecture (sometimes called the Dasgupta–Spieß conjecture) built on top of it; if the latter, as the papers' own titles and structure suggest, open_stale is correct.

outcome: No result addressing the strong (convex) Papadimitriou–Ratajczak conjecture was found in the window; it remains open, and only the pre-2024 resolution of the weaker non-convex version, and pre-2024 partial/area results on the convex version, exist.
summary: The strong Papadimitriou–Ratajczak conjecture (every polyhedral graph has a planar greedy embedding with all faces convex) is distinct from the original (weak) Papadimitriou–Ratajczak / greedy embedding conjecture, which was resolved positively by Leighton and Moitra in 2008/2010 — well before the frozen revision's date, and in any case only for the non-convex, non-necessarily-planar version. The current Wikipedia article on greedy embedding states plainly that the strong (convex) conjecture 'remains unproven,' and its most recent citation on that specific question is from 2016 (self-approaching/increasing-chord drawings). I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 work bearing on the convex/planar version specifically — arXiv listings, general web search, and the article itself — and found nothing that engages the strong conjecture as stated. Several tangential items turned up and were checked and ruled out: (1) a 2020 paper (arXiv:2003.00556, 'On the Area Requirements of Planar Greedy Drawings of Triconnected Planar Graphs,' by Cao/Strelzoff/Sun and later authors) on area bounds for the non-convex planar greedy drawing question — predates the window and concerns a different (non-convex) variant; (2) a TU Delft bachelor's thesis by Lune van Santvoord, 'Embedding polyhedral graphs' (defended 27 August 2025) — an undergraduate thesis whose visible metadata indicates it is expository/survey work under a supervisor at TU Delft, with no evidence found of a new result on the strong conjecture (the PDF could not be extracted to text through available tools, so this is a partial check — see below); (3) arXiv:2507.04538 ('Decremental Greedy Polygons and Polyhedra Without Sharp Angles' by David Eppstein) — confirmed via direct fetch to be an unrelated computational-geometry paper (max-min-angle polygons/polyhedra), sharing vocabulary ('greedy', 'polyhedra') but not addressing graph embeddings; (4) various graph-neural-network papers on 'convex constraints' and 'greedy' coreset/heuristic selection — confirmed unrelated, using the same words in a machine-learning sense with no connection to greedy graph embeddings; (5) general LLM-for-graph-problems surveys — no mention of this conjecture. No AI system was found anywhere near the actual strong conjecture. This matches the triage's 'none' verdict; I do not disagree with it, though I was unable to fully read the 2025 Delft thesis's contents (extraction blocked), which is the one loose end in an otherwise thorough negative search.
competing_reading: If the unreadable 2025 TU Delft bachelor's thesis in fact contains a new partial or full result on the strong conjecture rather than being purely expository, the status could move to `partial` or higher. Nothing in the available metadata (title, committee, thesis type, timeline) suggests this — bachelor's theses in this area are conventionally surveys or minor extensions, not conjecture-resolving contributions — but the content itself was not verified.
what_would_settle_it: Successfully extracting and reading the full text of the van Santvoord thesis (repository.tudelft.nl, file File_ae8f2fd8-1834-47b1-acb6-186bf21a5cea) to confirm it is expository and states no new result on the strong/convex conjecture; alternatively, a citation search (Google Scholar / Semantic Scholar) for any paper citing this thesis or independently claiming progress on the convex greedy embedding conjecture after January 2024.

outcome: No result changing Sumner's universal tournament conjecture (or a genuine case of it) was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open for finitely many small oriented trees, with the best general bound still Dross and Havet's 2021 result f(n) ≤ ⌈(21/8)n − 47/16⌉.
summary: I independently re-ran and extended the triage's searches (bound-improvement queries, the exact conjecture name, 'solved/proved/disproved', and an AI-angle search) and found nothing dated after 26 January 2024 that changes the conjecture or settles a genuine case of it. The state of the art remains: Kühn, Mycroft and Osthus (2011) proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large n; Dross and Havet (2021, 'Trees with few leaves in tournaments') hold the best known general bound, f(n) ≤ ⌈(21/8)n − 47/16⌉; and Maya Stein's October 2023 survey 'Oriented trees and paths in digraphs' (revised May 2024, published in Surveys in Combinatorics 2024) restates this landscape without a new result of its own — a survey revision is not progress on the problem. One search turned up an apparent arXiv preprint, 'An improved finite bound for oriented trees in tournaments' (claimed arXiv:2608.11667, by 'Jiangdong Ai and Xiaopan Lian', claiming f(n) ≤ ⌈(18n−23)/7⌉, i.e. improving the leading coefficient from 21/8 to 18/7), surfaced via a site calling itself 'Pith Review' (pith.science). I could not corroborate this paper through any independent channel: it does not appear on the DBLP page for Jiangdong Ai, Semantic Scholar has no record of it, and repeated WebFetch calls to the arXiv abstract/PDF/export mirror for this ID returned mutually contradictory results — one call fabricated a full abstract from a PDF it simultaneously said was unreadable, another returned an unrelated 'Access Denied' page, and a third invented plausible-sounding confirmation text. A companion 'find' from the same source ('Improved Bounds for Unavoidable Claws in Tournaments', arXiv:2608.06073) shows the same pattern. Xiaopan Lian is a real Nankai University combinatorialist, but their documented publication record is in graph/list colouring, not tournament trees, which is inconsistent with authoring this paper. I treat this as an unverified, likely-fabricated result (possibly a hallucination introduced by an unreliable index feeding the search tool, functioning like a prompt-injection artifact) and have excluded it from the status determination. No genuine post-window development was established, so the record is 'open' / no_change_found.
competing_reading: If the 'Jiangdong Ai and Xiaopan Lian' preprint (claimed arXiv:2608.11667, August 2026) is in fact real and I simply failed to reach a working mirror, the correct status would be 'progress' (a bound improvement on a still-open conjecture, ai_role 'none', resolution_direction null, dated 2026-08-12). I could not rule this out with certainty since I lack raw HTTP access to arXiv in this environment (bash networking was not approved) and had to rely entirely on WebFetch summaries, which demonstrably fabricated content elsewhere in this same investigation.

outcome: The general Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture (an exponential-in-k bound C(r)^k for every fixed r>2) remains open, but two genuine restricted cases were settled and published in the window: Balogh, Bernshteyn, Delcourt, Ferber and Pham (arXiv:2408.04165, Aug 2024; Combinatorica 2025) proved a near-conjectural bound for families of bounded VC-dimension, obtaining a sharp (r-1)^k bound in the VC-dimension-1 case, and improved the general bounded-VC-dimension case beyond earlier work of Fox–Pach–Suk. A September 2026 preprint by Ge, Wang, Xu and Zhao (arXiv:2609.18995) claims to fully resolve the conjecture for all families of bounded VC-dimension. A June 2026 preprint by Mishra (arXiv:2606.02667) claims the conjecture for shifted families. All are restrictions to special classes of families, not resolutions of the stated conjecture, which is still open even for r=3 in general.

disputes.summary: Junichiro Fukuyama has repeatedly claimed (arXiv:2212.13609, first posted Dec 2022, predating the window, with revised versions posted through June 2026 to 'fix the error' of the previous version) to have a full proof of the general Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. He runs a personal blog (sites.psu.edu/sunflowerconjecture) documenting ongoing work and self-identified errors. No journal acceptance, no expert digestion (e.g. no discussion found on Gil Kalai's blog, which actively covers sunflower-conjecture developments, nor on MathOverflow), and the author's own site shows him shifting to related side-topics rather than declaring the proof stable as of September 2026. A related Fukuyama preprint (arXiv:2510.19037, Oct 2025) claims a 'sub-logarithmic base' bound but is also a restricted/incremental claim, not a verified full resolution.

summary: The sunflower conjecture as stated (an exponential bound C(r)^k, C depending only on r, for every fixed r>2) is still open in general as of September 2026; the best fully general bound remains the Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang breakthrough (2019, predating the window) as refined by Bell–Chueluecha–Warnke to O(r log k)^k, still carrying a log k factor rather than the pure constant the conjecture requires, so no fully general progress happened inside the window. Within the window, genuine restricted cases were settled: Balogh, Bernshteyn, Delcourt, Ferber and Pham (arXiv:2408.04165, posted 8 Aug 2024, journal-published in Combinatorica 45 (2025)) proved the conjecture-strength bound for families of bounded VC-dimension d, with a sharp (r-1)^k bound for the d=1 case, improving on Fox–Pach–Suk; this is a peer-reviewed, well-authored result restricting the ambient family class (a case, per §3.1, since it removes territory — VC-dimension-bounded families — from the general open problem) and is coded `partial`/`confirmed`. Two further 2026 preprints extend this line: Ge–Wang–Xu–Zhao (arXiv:2609.18995, first version dated 17 Jul 2026 per the paper header though the arXiv ID implies a September posting — a discrepancy I flag but did not resolve) claim the full bounded-VC-dimension case, and Mishra (arXiv:2606.02667) claims the shifted-families case; neither preprint appears yet to have expert digestion, so they support the `partial` classification but do not move the record to `resolved`. None of these results, nor the still-unverified and self-corrected Fukuyama preprints claiming a full proof, involve any AI system — all are traditional combinatorial arguments (compression/shifting methods, VC-dimension/entropy techniques), and none of the papers or surrounding commentary mention AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving tools. I treat the Fukuyama claims (in `disputes`) as not evidencing a change to `status` because they lack any expert acceptance and have a documented, self-acknowledged history of errors spanning nearly four years.
competing_reading: One could argue the VC-dimension and shifted-family results are 'related problems' (variants changing the ambient family class) rather than 'cases' of the stated conjecture, since the Wikipedia bullet is phrased as an unrestricted statement about all k-uniform families. I read them as cases because bounded-VC-dimension families and shifted families are subsets of the families the general conjecture quantifies over — restricting the domain removes territory from the open problem rather than changing the question — consistent with the triage's judgment. If one instead reads 'the sunflower conjecture' as inherently meaning only the fully general, unrestricted statement such that any added hypothesis makes it a different problem, the status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (accepted by experts) of the general C(r)^k bound with no additional hypothesis on the family, or an expert digestion (blog post, journal referee report, or citation as settled) of Fukuyama's claim, or expert commentary situating the VC-dimension/shifted-family results explicitly as 'cases' versus 'variants' of the Wikipedia-stated conjecture.

outcome: Hector Pasten's September 2026 preprint unconditionally improves the best known bound on the quantity Szpiro's conjecture is about — from log|Δ| ≪ N log N (2013) to log|Δ| ≪ N log log N in general, and to log|Δ| ≪ N for semistable curves — but the conjecture (log|Δ| ≪ (6+ε)log N, i.e. |Δ| ≤ C(ε)·N^(6+ε)) remains open.
summary: The only substantive event in the window is Hector Pasten's solo-authored arXiv preprint 'Improved bounds for Szpiro's conjecture' (arXiv:2609.17390), submitted 2026-09-15, with a single version (no revision history yet). It builds on Pasten's own prior work approaching the abc conjecture via Shimura curves and unconditionally proves log|Δ| ≪ N log log N for all elliptic curves over Q (previously this strength was known only conditionally, under GRH; the best prior unconditional bound, from 2013, was the weaker log|Δ| ≪ N log N), and log|Δ| ≪ N in the semistable case. This is a genuine improvement to the bound at the heart of the conjecture (which asks for log|Δ| ≪ (6+ε)log N), so it is scope-relevant under §3.1 — the record of best known bound is exactly what the bullet's inequality concerns. However, the conjecture itself is nowhere near settled (log N vs N log log N is an enormous gap), so this is `progress`, not `partial` or `resolved`: no case or restriction of the full statement has been proved, only the auxiliary quantity has moved, matching the guidance that a bound moving on a still-open problem is `progress`/`ai_role` `bound` territory (moot here since no AI was involved). The preprint is only about a week old with no journal acceptance, no digestion by Tao or another expert found (searched Tao's blog, Mathstodon, general web), and a 'pith.science' page that summarizes the paper appears to be an automated/AI paper-summary aggregator rather than expert review, so it does not count as digestion. I found no mention of any AI system, LLM, or automated theorem prover in the abstract/paper (via WebFetch of the abs page; the PDF text extraction itself failed, returning binary stream data, but the abstract-page summary and lack of any acknowledgements-style claim gives no indication of AI use) — this is standard solo human number-theory work. Separately, a Zenodo item, 'A Spectral Proof of Szpiro's Conjecture via K-Theoretic Determinants: Complete Conductor Revolution' (Sept 2025) by Luis Morató de Dalmaes / Luis Morató de Dalmases, claims a full proof via a 'CronNet-Holo framework' and explicitly invokes AI/ML-flavored terminology ('CronNet'). Investigating this author further, they have self-published dozens of similarly-named 'CronNet-Holo' items on Zenodo since May 2025 spanning unrelated topics (Riemann Hypothesis, cosmology, quantum materials, even crop circles), a pattern strongly indicative of a crank/fringe author (possibly using an AI system to generate volumes of pseudo-mathematical text), not a credible mathematical result. No institutional affiliation, no peer review, and content spanning implausibly disparate fields for one 'unified framework' — this is excluded from the numerator per the instructions to only count credible, expert-reviewable work; it is not evidence of a genuine result, AI-produced or otherwise, and I do not classify it as an AI-involved mathematical advance because there was no real mathematical content to attribute. Net: one real advance (Pasten, no AI), one fringe non-event (Zenodo, excluded). Status is `progress`, ai_role `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue the Zenodo item still deserves an `incident` classification if it were treated as 'an AI-produced claim that was announced ... then withdrawn' — but it was never picked up by anyone as a serious claim to begin with (no coverage, no discussion, self-published on a preprint repository with no gatekeeping), so it never rose to the level of an 'announced' claim that needed withdrawing; treating it as a real incident would overstate its significance. I classified it as not worth recording as an event at all, which is the more conservative reading.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the mathematical community (via a citation, a follow-up paper, or a blog digestion) treats Pasten's bound as correct and significant would move it toward wider recognition, but would not change its `progress` status since the conjecture itself is not closer to resolved in kind, only in degree. For the conjecture itself, only a proof of log|Δ| ≪ (6+ε)log N (or a genuine counterexample) would change the status to resolved/claimed.

outcome: No change found since 26 January 2024. The conjecture remains open for n≥5; the pre-2024 partial results (2-rearrangeability, verification for n≤4, Lubiw's shortest-path counterexample and its strengthening) are unchanged, and no new paper resolving a case of the stated problem was found.
summary: Szymanski's conjecture (every permutation on the n-dimensional doubly-directed hypercube can be routed with edge-disjoint paths) shows no change since the frozen revision. I read the current Wikipedia article, which still lists it as unsolved: verified computationally for n≤4, open for n≥5, with the known pre-2024 partial results (2-rearrangeability; Lubiw's dimension-5 counterexample to 1-realizability by shortest paths, and its later strengthening showing hypercubes are not n^(1/2-δ)-realizable by shortest paths for any δ>0). Multiple web searches for post-January-2024 activity — general searches on the conjecture's name, on hypercube permutation routing, on arXiv listings, and specifically checking the paper the triage pass flagged (Chakrabarty–Seshadhri, arXiv:2409.02206, 'Directed Hypercube Routing, a Generalized Lehman-Ron Theorem, and Monotonicity Testing') — turned up nothing relevant. I fetched that paper's abstract directly: it concerns vertex-disjoint path collections between comparable sub-level sets of the directed hypercube for monotonicity testing, and does not mention Szymanski's conjecture or general permutation routing; it is a related-but-different problem (§3.1, a variant, not a case). No AI-related search turned up any connection between an AI system and this specific conjecture — one search surfaced general AI-and-mathematics stories (Jacobian conjecture, Erdős problems, unit distance conjecture) but none referenced Szymanski's conjecture. I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict; this is a genuine, well-evidenced 'nothing happened' case.
competing_reading: None. The scope of the stated conjecture (general permutation routing by edge-disjoint paths on the doubly-directed hypercube) is unambiguous, and the one paper found in the area (arXiv:2409.02206) is clearly about a different question (vertex-disjoint paths between sub-level sets for monotonicity testing, not permutation routing), so there is no genuine ambiguity to flag.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving or disproving the conjecture for some n≥5 (even a single new case), or extending the computational verification beyond n=4, or a proof/disproof of the general statement, would change the status. None was found.

outcome: The unconditional decidability of the theory of the real exponential field remains open; the positive answer is still known only modulo Schanuel's conjecture (Macintyre–Wilkie 1996), and no result in the window changes this.
summary: Tarski's exponential function problem — whether the first-order theory of (ℝ; +, ·, exp, <, 0, 1) is decidable — remains open in its unconditional form as of September 2026. The only positive result is still Macintyre and Wilkie's 1996 conditional theorem (decidability follows from Schanuel's conjecture), which predates the frozen revision by decades and is not itself a change. Several papers touch adjacent territory in the window but none of them are a case of, nor change, the stated problem under the §3.1 scope rule: (1) Gallego-Hernández and Mansutti, 'On the Existential Theory of the Reals Enriched with Integer Powers of a Computable Number' (arXiv:2502.02220, STACS 2025), studies a structurally different, much weaker language — ℝ with a unary predicate for integer powers of one fixed computable real ξ, restricted to the existential fragment — and explicitly frames this as a tame variant that avoids Schanuel's conjecture rather than as progress on the full exponential theory; it is a related problem, not a restriction of Tarski's stated question, since the exponential function itself is absent from the language. (2) Berarducci and Gallinaro, 'On the elementary theory of the real exponential field' (arXiv:2603.08365, submitted March 2026, revised June 2026), is the most substantive item found: assuming Schanuel's conjecture, they give a new axiomatization (definably complete exponential fields with exp′=exp) of the complete theory T_exp, from which the Macintyre–Wilkie decidability result again follows — still conditional, not a new unconditional result on the problem itself. They do prove one piece unconditionally (model completeness of the restricted axioms for exp on (−1,1)), but this is a technical lemma feeding a conditional axiomatization, not a change to what a careful reader would write in Tarski's own bullet: the theory's decidability is still open unconditionally. Schanuel's conjecture itself, on which the whole conditional edifice rests, also remains unproven; recent work found (Waldschmidt's note on elliptic/quasi-elliptic analogues, and 'Schanuel Property for Elliptic and Quasi-Elliptic Functions', arXiv:2504.14041) proves measure-one or analogue versions for different structures, not the real Schanuel conjecture needed here. I also checked proofatlas.ai's page for Schanuel's Conjecture, an AI-assisted 'collaboration' research-tracking platform; it explicitly states 'Revision v6 explicitly reports no proof' and documents open routes and obstacles rather than any result, and notes no AI-assisted proof attempt on this conjecture. No source anywhere in this search attributes any part of the (non-)progress to an AI system: the STACS and Berarducci–Gallinaro papers are traditional pure model theory/logic papers with no acknowledgement of AI tools, and no lab announcement, AI-solved-problem list, or AI mathematics report mentions this problem. Triage's verdict (`none`) and its account of the 2502.02220 paper are correct; I confirm and add the 2603.08365 paper as a second, more directly relevant near-miss the triage did not surface, though it too does not change the status.
competing_reading: One could argue Berarducci–Gallinaro's unconditional model-completeness result for the restricted (−1,1) exponential axioms is 'progress' worth a status of `progress` rather than `open`, since it is a genuine new unconditional theorem in the immediate technical vicinity of the problem. I read it as not in scope: it is a lemma about an axiom system for a bounded restriction of the function, used only to rebuild the conditional decidability argument, and it does not itself decide, or narrow the undecided status of, any fragment of Th(ℝ, exp). It does not remove any case from the stated existential/universal decision question the way a settled special case would. If a downstream reader treats any unconditional structural theorem adjacent to T_exp as movement on the bullet, this should be `progress` with `ai_role` `none` and `resolution_direction` null; the outcome and AI conclusions would be unchanged either way.
what_would_settle_it: An unconditional decision procedure (or unconditional undecidability proof) for Th(ℝ, +, ·, exp, <), or an unconditional proof/disproof of the real Schanuel conjecture, would settle the classification question definitively — as would an explicit statement from a subsequent paper that Berarducci–Gallinaro's lemma decides some previously-undecided fragment of the theory.

outcome: Several genuine cases of the Tate conjecture were settled since January 2024 (abelian fourfolds and, building on that, abelian fivefolds over finite fields; a near-completion for surfaces of geometric genus one), and a stronger integral variant was shown to fail in general — but the conjecture in full generality remains open, and the most sweeping recent claim (a 'full proof' on Zenodo) is an unreviewed, non-expert preprint with no credible standing. No AI system produced or materially contributed to any of the real mathematics found; one AI-oriented research-mapping site (ProofAtlas) has organized the problem into subtasks for human/AI contributors but has not itself produced a result.
summary: The problem as stated (Tate's general conjecture relating algebraic cycles to Galois-invariant classes in étale cohomology) remains open in full generality, so no single decisive event settles it; several genuine cases were settled and I treat the most significant, Broe's proof for abelian fourfolds over finite fields (arXiv:2608.28651, posted 19 Aug 2026), as the anchoring event because it is described as 'the first resolution of the conjecture for all abelian varieties of a fixed dimension over finite fields since Tate's own 1960s work' — a genuine restriction of the stated question (a case, not a variant, per §3.1) that also let Broe complete the standard conjectures for abelian fourfolds. This is a preprint that has already reached seminar discussion (a University of Michigan algebraic-geometry preprint seminar covered it), but as of this research it has not yet been digested by a published expert verification or accepted by a journal, so status is 'claimed' rather than 'resolved'. Within a month, Ningyi Li built on it to prove the Tate conjecture for abelian fivefolds over finite fields (arXiv:2609.06265, Sept 2026), explicitly citing Broe's Theorem 1.1 in a revision — a further case, also 'claimed'. Separately, Guo–Yang's paper on surfaces of geometric genus one (arXiv:2501.18541, posted 30 Jan 2025 — four days inside the window) 'largely completes' the Kuga–Satake program for that case, another genuine case-restriction; and Milne's 2-page note (arXiv:2509.06707, Sept 2025) shows the stronger 'integral' Tate conjecture fails for very general abelian varieties, using a transfer from a recent integral Hodge conjecture counterexample result — this is progress/refutation of a related-but-distinct (stronger) variant, not the base conjecture, so it does not by itself move the base conjecture's status but is noted as context. None of these four genuine results mentions any AI system, machine-learning tool, or automated proof assistant in producing the mathematics; all are traditional human proofs building on named prior results (Ancona, Markman, Kuga–Satake, Deligne). Separately, a September 2025 Zenodo item ('A Constructive Spectral Proof of the Tate Conjecture for Smooth Projective Varieties over Finite Fields', Luis Morató de Dalmases) claims a full, general proof via a self-adjoint 'spectral operator' construction; the same author has simultaneously posted dozens of similarly-titled 'constructive spectral proofs' of the Riemann Hypothesis, Hodge conjecture, P≠NP, Goldbach, BSD, and unrelated physics 'theories of everything' on Zenodo, an unreviewed self-publishing repository — a clear crank-output pattern with no journal, no citations, and no expert digestion found. I do not credit it as changing the conjecture's status, consistent with the triage's own flag of it as 'unverified/unconventional venue'. I also found ProofAtlas, a platform that has built a structured 'research map' of the Tate conjecture inviting human and AI contributors to work on specific open 'gates' — this is infrastructure for future work, not a result, and does not itself change status or count as an AI contribution.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is 'partial' rather than 'claimed', since multiple genuine partial cases (fourfolds, fivefolds, genus-one surfaces) are individually well short of full resolution and none is the 'main claim' the way a would-be full proof is; under that reading the Zenodo item is irrelevant noise and the anchoring event should instead be Guo–Yang (Jan 2025) as the most clearly scoped case-restriction with a real application (BSD for certain elliptic curves), still unreviewed by a journal but with no seminar/attention gap. I chose Broe's result as the anchor because it is the most structurally significant restriction (a full dimension, not just a subclass) and has visible expert engagement (the Michigan seminar), but the case for anchoring on Guo–Yang or simply calling the overall status 'partial' (multiple cases moved, nothing resolved) is reasonable.
what_would_settle_it: A published, peer-reviewed version of Broe's or Li's paper, or an expert blog/digest (e.g., Tao, the Stacks Project community, or a MathOverflow consensus) explicitly endorsing the fourfold or fivefold proof, would move that specific case from 'claimed' to 'resolved'. For the overall conjecture, only a proof (or disproof) covering arbitrary codimension on arbitrary smooth projective varieties would settle it — nothing found approaches that except the non-credible Zenodo claim.

outcome: The telescope conjecture — the last of Ravenel's conjectures — was disproved by Burklund, Hahn, Levy and Schlank, announced 6 June 2023 at a conference at Oxford and posted to arXiv on 26 October 2023, both before the frozen revision's date of 26 January 2024; nothing that happened inside the window changed this problem's mathematical status.

counterexample.object: The T(n+1)-localized algebraic K-theory of a K(n)-local E_n-algebra (built from the K(1)-local sphere and generalizations), shown not to be K(n+1)-local, for every height n ≥ 1 and every prime — an explicit counterexample separating telescopic (T(n)-local) from chromatic (K(n)-local) localizations.
counterexample.verified_how: Constructed via algebraic K-theory computations (using trace methods / topological cyclic homology techniques); the arXiv preprint has stood with a single version since 26 October 2023 and has been the subject of a dedicated Oberwolfach Arbeitsgemeinschaft (13–18 October 2024) working through the argument, and the authors received the 2026 Clay Research Award for the result.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet describes the telescope conjecture as 'the last of Ravenel's conjectures ... to be resolved,' and it was in fact resolved — but before the window opened. Burklund, Hahn, Levy and Schlank announced a disproof at a conference at Oxford on 6 June 2023 and posted the preprint 'K-theoretic counterexamples to Ravenel's telescope conjecture' to arXiv on 26 October 2023 (arXiv:2310.17459, single version, no later revisions), both dates before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 timestamp. The disproof shows the conjecture is false at every height n≥2 (and, by later refinement discussed at the Oberwolfach meeting, at height 1 too) and every prime, via an explicit algebraic K-theory construction. Expert digestion of this pre-window result did continue inside the window — a dedicated Oberwolfach Arbeitsgemeinschaft ('Algebraic K-Theory and the Telescope Conjecture,' 13–18 October 2024) worked through the proof, and the authors received the 2026 Clay Research Award for it — but digestion of an already-announced, already-preprinted result is not a new event under §6.1's date rule (first public written argument), so status is `open_stale`, dated to the October 2023 preprint. I also found an open, unassigned GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures#2192) proposing to formalize the conjecture/disproof in Lean; its own text states 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' — but the issue is merely a cataloguing/task-listing action by an AI agent, not any mathematical content, and it remains unassigned with no formalization produced, so it does not constitute an event or AI-assisted mathematics under §6.2. I searched for arXiv preprints in 2024–2025 that might extend or revisit the specific Ravenel telescope conjecture in stable homotopy theory and found only work on variant/generalized telescope conjectures for different triangulated-category settings (noetherian path algebras, Azumaya algebras, general presentably symmetric monoidal ∞-categories) — these are related problems under §3.1 (different objects/hypotheses), not cases of this specific bullet, and none report any AI involvement. No AI system produced, checked, or otherwise touched the original disproof or its digestion; searches turned up nothing to suggest otherwise.
competing_reading: One could argue the conjecture's Wikipedia article status only became authoritative/settled-in-the-literature during the window (via the 2024 Oberwolfach workshop and the 2026 Clay Award, both of which postdate the frozen revision), and that 'resolved' status should be dated to when experts fully validated it rather than to the original preprint. But §6.3 is explicit that dating uses the first public written argument, not later journal publication or recognition, so I did not adopt this reading; it would not change the `open_stale` classification in any case, since even the later validation events predate no new mathematical content and the underlying disproof itself is pre-window.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (already essentially in hand) of whether the arXiv paper has since appeared in a journal, and whether any post-window paper revises or extends the K-theoretic counterexample construction itself (as opposed to studying analogous telescope conjectures in other categorical settings) would remove any residual doubt about whether all mathematical content is pre-window.
