outcome: No resolution, partial resolution, or moved bound on the stated problem (the minimum-energy configuration of n mutually-repelling particles on the unit sphere, for general or specific n) was found since 26 January 2024; work found in the window either studies variant domains (disk, spherical cap) or explores the local-minima/stationary-point landscape rather than the global minimum.
summary: The Thomson problem asks for the minimum-energy configuration of n mutually-repelling charges on the unit sphere. Exact solutions remain known only for n=1-6,12 (per the current Wikipedia article, unchanged since before the window); for all other n the state of the art is numerically 'best known' configurations. I found no result since 26 January 2024 that resolves the general problem, proves a new exact case, or otherwise changes what the stated bullet would say. The closest candidates are: (1) 'Exploring the energy landscape of the Thomson problem: local minima and stationary states' (arXiv 2506.08398, June 2025, published Journal of Statistical Physics 2025) — this explicitly targets cataloguing local minima and stationary points for N up to ~150ish, not the global minimum, and uses only classical numerical optimization (Newton-conjugate-gradient, basin-hopping-style perturbation in Python/scipy/numba) with no AI/ML; (2) 'Thomson problem on a spherical cap' (arXiv 2508.17625, Aug 2025) — a genuinely different domain (a bounded cap with curvature and a border, interpolating between disk and sphere), makes no claim about the full-sphere problem, and uses only basin-hopping; (3) two 2025-2026 disk-confinement papers (arXiv 2609.20777, arXiv 2609.24722, and the 'pith.science' 2609.20777 listing) that report new record configurations for N up to 100,000 — but these are for charges confined to a flat disk, a different domain from the sphere, using quenched molecular dynamics, not AI; (4) 'Shannon Entropy as an Order Parameter for the Two-Dimensional Confined Coulomb Systems' (arXiv 2609.15428, Sept 2026) — this does include a genuine sphere dataset (N=5000, 7500, 10000, claimed as new largest-N sphere configurations), but it is an entropy/order-parameter analysis, not a Thomson-problem resolution, its large-N data for N up to 40886 is drawn from prior published (largely pre-2024) datasets, and no AI/ML method is described anywhere in the paper (classical basin-hopping/divide-and-conquer style methods are referenced). None of this work changes what a careful person would write in the bullet: the general n minimum-energy configuration is still open, no new n has been solved exactly, and no AI system has been applied to the problem itself. I also checked whether the AlphaEvolve mathematical-discovery paper (arXiv 2511.02864, Nov 2025, Georgiev/Gómez-Serrano/Tao/Wagner), which covers 67 geometry/combinatorics/number-theory problems including sphere-packing-adjacent questions, touches the Thomson problem — it does not mention it. Separately, 'Learning towards Minimum Hyperspherical Energy' (NeurIPS 2018, well before the window in any case) uses the Thomson problem as *inspiration* for a neural-network regularizer, i.e. math informing ML rather than AI solving the math problem, and is out of scope regardless of date.
competing_reading: One could argue the large-N sphere dataset in arXiv 2609.15428 (N=5000-10000, described by its own authors and by Zenodo as 'never before achieved for the Thomson problem on a sphere') constitutes 'progress' in the loose sense of extending the range of numerically-known best-known configurations. But per §3.1, an existence/optimization record like this moves only where the record itself is the question; the Thomson problem as stated asks for the minimum-energy configuration (implicitly for general or specific n), not for a running list of largest-N numerical solutions, and improving numerical approximations for particular large n without proof of optimality does not settle a case of the stated problem. I classified this as no_change_found rather than `progress`, but flag it as the closest call in the record.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous proof of the optimal configuration for some previously-unsolved n (e.g. n=9 or n=11), or a resolution/disproof of a specific well-known conjectured configuration for a given large n, dated after 26 January 2024; or, for the AI question, an explicit authorial statement that a machine-learning/AI system (as opposed to classical numerical optimization, basin-hopping, or molecular dynamics) produced a new configuration or proof for the sphere Thomson problem.

outcome: The general conjecture remains open, but Dalal, McDonald and Shan (arXiv:2405.07382, posted 12 May 2024; published Journal of Graph Theory 110(3):249-262, 2025) proved a new general upper bound χ_T(G) ≤ Δ(G)+2⌈|V(G)|/(Δ(G)+1)⌉ for every finite simple graph (improving Hind's 1992 bound by one color), and used it to confirm the conjecture outright — χ_T(G) = Δ(G)+2 — for a class of sufficiently large, sufficiently dense r-regular graphs (r ≥ (1+ε)n/2). A related 2025 preprint (Henderschedt, McDonald, Shan, arXiv:2507.05548) extends the dense-regular result to large minimum degree rather than regularity.
summary: The general Total Coloring Conjecture (χ_T(G) ≤ Δ(G)+2 for every finite simple graph) remains open. Since the frozen revision date, the substantive development is Dalal, McDonald and Shan's paper 'Total Coloring Graphs With Large Maximum Degree' (arXiv:2405.07382, first posted 12 May 2024, published in Journal of Graph Theory 110(3):249-262 in 2025 — a peer-reviewed venue, so this passes the 'digested by experts' bar). It (a) improves the best known general bound by one color over Hind's 1992 result, and (b) fully confirms the conjecture (proves the exact Δ(G)+2 bound, not just an upper bound) for a restricted class: r-regular graphs on n vertices with n large and r ≥ (1+ε)n/2 for any fixed ε>0. Part (b) is a genuine case of the stated conjecture settled — dense regular graphs are a restriction of 'every graph' — so this record is coded 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed'. A follow-up 2025 preprint (arXiv:2507.05548, Henderschedt/McDonald/Shan, not yet independently confirmed as journal-published) extends the settled case to large minimum degree instead of regularity, which is the same kind of contribution and does not change the classification. Separately, the 2020 Murthy preprint (arXiv:2003.09658) claiming a full proof of the general conjecture remains unaccepted as of its June 2021 v3 and September 2026: no retraction notice was found, but no journal acceptance, expert digestion, or citation as settled was found either — it continues to be treated as open by these 2024-2025 papers themselves, consistent with the triage's assessment. I found no AI system anywhere in this line of work: the papers are standard combinatorial/probabilistic arguments (degree/regularity conditions, no mention of computer search, SAT solvers, or machine learning in any accessible page or abstract).
competing_reading: One could argue the dense-regular-graph result is closer to a 'related problem' (an asymptotic density condition rather than a natural sub-case named in the literature) and should be scored 'progress' rather than 'partial', since the density/large-n threshold is somewhat artificial and no one graph or finite family is exhibited. But because the theorem proves the exact conjectured bound (not just a weaker bound) for an actual, non-empty subclass of graphs satisfying the stated hypothesis (Δ(G) as maximum degree, over all finite simple graphs), it reads as a genuine case settled rather than a different question, so 'partial' is the better fit.
what_would_settle_it: A resolution (or explicit counterexample) for the fully general conjecture with no density, degree, or regularity restriction; alternatively, expert acceptance (citation as proved, or journal publication) of the 2020 Murthy preprint would change its status from unaccepted claim to resolved/claimed.

outcome: No result changing the stated bounds or resolving any case of tripod packing was found published or announced between 26 January 2024 and today (22 September 2026).
summary: Tripod packing asks how many disjoint tripods (Stein's 'semicrosses'/'Stein corners') can have their apexes packed into an n×n×n grid. As of the current live Wikipedia article, the best lower bound is Ω(n^1.546) (Gowers and Long, 2021) and the best upper bound is n²/2^Ω(log* n), derived via the Ruzsa–Szemerédi problem — both established before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision date. I ran searches for a proof, disproof, new bound, or any case-settling result on tripod packing (also trying the historical names 'semicross' and 'Stein corners'), searches specifically for post-2024 arXiv papers, and searches for any AI-system involvement (e.g., DeepMind AlphaEvolve/FunSearch-style results, which have recently touched circle-packing and sphere-packing variants but not this problem). None turned up any post-January-2024 development on this problem's own bounds. The only 2024+ hits were irrelevant homonyms (camera/photography tripods, an unrelated deep-learning model named 'Tripod', unrelated packing papers on spheres, cylinders, and bin packing). I also checked the Wikipedia article's own edit/citation history via the live page (most recent citations are 2021 and 2019) and confirmed no newer citations appear. Note the triage record's stated lower bound, Ω(n^(2/3)), does not match the Ω(n^1.546) figure I found on both the live and (per the triage's own citation trail) presumably the frozen-era article; Ω(n^1.546) is the Gowers–Long 2021 result and is the figure that should be treated as the pre-2024 baseline. This appears to be a triage transcription/recall error rather than a substantive disagreement about post-2024 events, since no matter which baseline is used, no post-2024 movement was found either way.
competing_reading: It is conceivable a paper improving the bound exists in a venue not well indexed by general web search (e.g., a discrete geometry conference proceedings or a national mathematical society journal not on arXiv), given this is a fairly niche problem with a small community. I could not rule this out with certainty, though the problem's visibility (it has its own Wikipedia article and is referenced in surveys) makes it likely that any improvement would surface in general search results or in citations to the Gowers–Long paper.
what_would_settle_it: A citation search (e.g., via Semantic Scholar or Google Scholar, which were not directly queryable here beyond web search) specifically for papers citing Gowers & Long's 'On the density of tripod-packings' or Aronov et al.'s work, filtered to 2024 onward, would give the most authoritative confirmation that no citing improvement exists.

outcome: No result found since 26 January 2024 changes what a careful person would write in this bullet: the Zarankiewicz crossing-number conjecture for complete bipartite graphs remains open, with the same pre-2024 verified small cases (m ≤ 6, and K7,7, K7,8, K7,9) and the same pre-2024 lower bounds (Brosch–Polak's semidefinite-programming bound, arXiv:2206.02755 v2, October 2023; a flag-algebra bound giving cr(Kn,n) ≥ 0.9118·Z(n,n), September 2023).
summary: Searches for post-January-2024 activity on Turán's brick factory problem / the Zarankiewicz crossing-number conjecture (cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n)) turned up no result that changes the bullet as stated. The live Wikipedia articles for both 'Turán's brick factory problem' and 'Zarankiewicz crossing number conjecture' still describe the conjecture as open, verified only for min(m,n) ≤ 6 and for K7,7, K7,8, K7,9 (Kleitman 1970, Woodall 1993), with the best lower bound still the pre-window 83%-of-Zarankiewicz-bound result. An AI-search summary tool asserted, without a traceable source, that K8,8/K8,9/K8,10 had also been verified; I could not substantiate this in either Wikipedia article or any paper found, so I treat it as a search-synthesis artifact rather than a fact, and it would predate 2024 in any case since it rests on the same Kleitman/Woodall parity argument. The one genuinely new, AI-adjacent 2026 item found — 'New Bounds for Zarankiewicz Numbers via Reinforced LLM Evolutionary Search' (arXiv:2605.01120, submitted 1 May 2026), which used an LLM-driven evolutionary search (OpenEvolve) to find new bipartite-graph constructions — is about a different problem that merely shares Zarankiewicz's name: the extremal Zarankiewicz number Z(m,n,s,t), the maximum edges in a bipartite graph avoiding K_{s,t} as a subgraph. That is not the crossing-number quantity Z(m,n) in this bullet's conjecture (cr(K_{m,n})); the two are unrelated except by naming coincidence, per §3.1's 'related problem, not this problem' rule (same trap as the disambiguation note in the triage's own scope logic). No arXiv listing, survey, or Terence Tao / graph-drawing blog post found in this window reports a new exact case, an improved bound on cr(K_{m,n}) itself, or any disproof. I therefore agree with the triage's 'none' verdict; my independent search additionally surfaced and ruled out the LLM/Zarankiewicz-number paper as a false positive, which the triage's narrower queries did not encounter.
competing_reading: If a reader conflates 'Zarankiewicz number' (extremal forbidden-subgraph problem) with 'Zarankiewicz's conjecture' (crossing number of K_{m,n}, i.e. this bullet), the arXiv:2605.01120 LLM-evolutionary-search paper could be mistaken for AI progress on this problem. It is not: the quantities, the theorems, and the entire mathematical content are unrelated aside from both being attributed to Kazimierz Zarankiewicz. I am confident in excluding it, but flag the naming collision explicitly since a shallower pass could code this problem as ai_role 'bound' in error.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or repository posting, dated after 26 January 2024, that either (a) verifies Zarankiewicz's formula for a new pair (m,n) beyond the existing small cases, (b) improves the constant in the lower bound cr(K_{m,n}) ≥ c·Z(m,n) beyond the pre-2024 flag-algebra/semidefinite-programming results, or (c) exhibits a drawing of some K_{m,n} with fewer crossings than Z(m,n), thereby refuting the conjecture.

outcome: Anish Gupta posted a preprint (arXiv:2608.06538, 6 Aug 2026) extending the proven case of Tuza's conjecture from graphs of maximum average degree less than 7 (Puleo 2015, covering max degree at most 6) to graphs of maximum degree at most 7, closing the gap left by 7-regular graphs; this is a case of the original conjecture, not a variant, but it is a fresh, unreviewed preprint from an independent researcher with no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or blog commentary found as of the check date.

summary: The triage flagged arXiv:2608.06538 (Anish Gupta, submitted 6 Aug 2026), which extends the known case of Tuza's conjecture from Puleo's 2015 result (maximum average degree < 7, i.e. covering max degree ≤ 6) to graphs of maximum degree exactly 7 — closing the 7-regular gap. I read the arXiv abstract page and the full HTML text (v1), and the accompanying GitHub repository. This is a genuine case of the stated conjecture (a restriction to a bounded-degree class), so per §3.1 it counts, and I classify it as `partial` progress on the case, but the overall record status is `claimed` rather than `resolved` because no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification by named experts turned up in any search — the author is an independent researcher (contact details and an ORCID are given on the preprint) and the paper is six weeks old as of the 2026-09-22 check date with no blog commentary (checked Terence Tao–style discussion, found none) or citations yet. On the AI question: the paper's own acknowledgements state plainly that Claude Code and OpenAI Codex were used 'extensively' for 'proof exploration, software development, exact computational checks, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript,' but the same sentence states the author 'selected the arguments and methods' and 'takes full responsibility for the content.' Critically, the paper explicitly disclaims that the 1,144-certificate catalogue — the one piece of mathematics in the result that was machine-produced — came from AI: 'The certificates were originally found by an integer-constraint search; no property of that search is used, only its output, which is checked independently.' An integer-constraint search is a classical combinatorial-search technique, not an AI system, and its output is independently, exactly verified by Python code (not by an LLM). Per §6.2, uses of AI for exploration, drafting, literature search, and computational checking/verification are explicitly `none`-coded regardless of how extensively they were used, since none of that output is mathematics that appears in the final proof; the actual mathematical content (the reducible-pair argument and the certificate catalogue) was produced by the author's own theoretical work and a non-AI search procedure. I therefore code `ai_role` as `none`. I also found a second, independently in-scope but smaller preprint: Chahua & Gutierrez, 'On Tuza's Conjecture in Dense Graphs' (arXiv:2405.11409, submitted 18 May 2024), which proves the original conjecture for split graphs with minimum degree ≥ 3n/5 and for complete 4-partite graphs — also genuine cases of the stated conjecture, using a probabilistic argument with no AI mentioned. Since the Gupta result is later, larger in scope (an entire degree class rather than a special graph family), and is what the triage flagged, I use it as the decisive `event`; the Chahua–Gutierrez result is additional confirmatory evidence that the conjecture keeps advancing case-by-case with no AI involvement, and I mention it here rather than making it a separate record. I checked the live Tuza's conjecture Wikipedia article, which as of my check states the conjecture is still open and does not yet mention any 2024-2026 development (it is not kept current). The second triage `found` item (arXiv:2406.06501, hypergraph generalization) is a related-but-different problem (the Aharoni–Zerbib hypergraph generalization) and is correctly excluded from scope per the triage's own note; I confirm that exclusion.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `resolved` rather than `claimed` if one judges the paper's own from-scratch, independently-verifiable Python certificate checkers (with SHA256 checksums, `make check-full`) as equivalent to expert digestion, since anyone can mechanically re-verify the 1,144 certificates and the human-readable argument in Sections 1-8. But §6.1 requires either an expert digestion that works through the proof, journal acceptance, or a published verification by named experts — a reproducible computational check by the author's own tooling does not meet that bar, especially for a result this recent and from a researcher not previously established in this subfield. I judge `claimed` to be the correct, conservative reading given the six-week-old, un-digested status of the preprint.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance, a written expert digestion (e.g. on a graph-theory blog, MathOverflow, or by a named expert such as Puleo or Tuza specialists), or an independent group reproducing/checking the 1,144-certificate catalogue and the reducible-pair argument would move this to `resolved`. Absent that, continued silence for another several months while the paper is cited or discussed would still leave it `claimed`.

outcome: The twin prime conjecture itself remains open, but the associated bound H1 (the smallest gap between primes proven to recur infinitely often, equal to 2 iff the conjecture is true) moved dramatically in a rapid, contested sequence in late August/early September 2026: 246 (2014, pre-window) -> 240 (Julia Stadlmann, human, arXiv 31 Aug 2026) -> 236 (Shiva Kintali, AI-assisted, X announcement 1 Sep 2026, unreviewed, no preprint) -> 212 (Axiom Math's AxiomProver AI system, ~2-3 Sep 2026, Lean-formalized but unreviewed by experts) -> 186 (OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, dated to a paper released with the model on/around 3 Sep 2026, Lean formalization conditional on three unproven Lean axioms). None of these post-Stadlmann bounds has been digested by an independent human expert as of this writing (22 Sep 2026); the situation is treated by the mathematical community itself as unsettled and contested.

ai.basis_quote: "Announcing that GPT-6 Astra has pushed the prime gap to 186, with Lean formalization!" (OpenAI researcher Weijie Su); the OpenAI paper states the proof 'is due to GPT 6 Astra' and that the improvement combines equidistribution estimates of Polymath 8a and Stadlmann with 'complementary factorization conditions ... and an improved numerical optimization'. Separately, AxiomProver is described by Axiom Math as an 'AI system under development ... [that] autonomously generated from natural-language specifications a Lean certificate' for the H1<=212 result, with the underlying mathematics credited to named human co-authors (Charton, Hong, Lau, Ono, and others). Shiva Kintali stated on X: 'I showed that H1 <= 236 with the help of AI, building on Julia Stadlmann's work,' without naming the model or describing the division of labor.

disputes.summary: In the space of about four days (31 Aug - 3 Sep 2026), four different bound-improvement claims (240, 236, 212, 186) were announced by different parties (a human mathematician, an individual claiming AI-assisted work with no preprint, an AI startup's theorem-proving system, and OpenAI's flagship model), each explicitly building on the previous. The exact chronological ordering of the 212 (Axiom) and 186 (OpenAI) results is unclear from secondary sources: one search summary places OpenAI's preprint date as 30 Aug (before Axiom's 3 Sep announcement) while the Lean development for 186 appears to have posted around 2 Sep, and OpenAI's own framing ties the 186 announcement to the GPT-6 Astra model release event on/around 3 Sep. None of the AI-derived bounds (236, 212, 186) has yet been reviewed or endorsed on the record by an independent human expert not affiliated with the producing organization.

Experts publicly criticized the AI-driven race as harmful to the field even where the results are not in mathematical dispute. Andrew Granville said OpenAI should have contacted Stadlmann directly rather than only her advisor Kevin Ford; Ford worried the dynamic could discourage young researchers; Terence Tao criticized prioritizing benchmark numbers over human mathematical understanding. Number theorist Thomas Bloom explicitly flagged Stadlmann's 240 result as notable specifically for being '(by a human!)', implying the subsequent bounds were viewed differently by the community.

summary: This bullet (a nested sub-case of Landau's problems) asks whether there are infinitely many twin primes. That remains completely open: no source claims to have proven or disproven it. What did happen in the window is the Wikipedia article's own headline auxiliary fact — the best known unconditional value of H1 = liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n), the smallest gap proven to recur infinitely often (2 iff the conjecture holds) — moved for the first time since 2014, and moved four times in about four days. Julia Stadlmann (arXiv:2608.31126, submitted 31 Aug 2026), working alone with traditional methods and no AI, proved H1 <= 240, improving the Polymath8b/Maynard bound of 246 that had stood since 2014; this is squarely 'progress' on a record-type sub-question, confirmed by expert reaction (Granville, Soundararajan, Bloom all publicly praised it as a genuine, human-authored advance) even though it has not yet gone through full peer review, so I treat it as the anchor human result. Within days, Shiva Kintali announced H1<=236 'with the help of AI' on X with no preprint, no named model, and no review (VibeMathed logs it as an unreviewed, thin claim). Axiom Math's AxiomProver system then produced H1<=212, credited to named human co-authors (Charton, Hong, Lau, Ono, et al.) with the AI system generating the Lean formalization/certificate from natural-language specification — per Axiom's own site this is a case where the mathematics is attributed to the humans and the AI's contribution is described as formalization, though the underlying mathematical derivation process is not fully disclosed either. Almost simultaneously, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra had reached H1<=186, with OpenAI's own paper stating the proof 'is due to GPT-6 Astra' — the strongest authorial claim of AI-generated mathematics among the four bounds — but the accompanying Lean formalization is explicitly conditional on three unproven axioms (two Kloosterman-sum bounds from Deligne/Fouvry-Kowalski-Michel, cited but not formalized, plus numerically-verified-but-unproven integral bounds), and by the Hacker News discussion's own characterization, 'the proof file is roughly 10MB of Lean with no independent human semantic review yet.' None of the three post-Stadlmann bounds (236, 212, 186) meets this dataset's bar for `resolved` (expert digestion) or arguably even stable `claimed` status, since the whole sequence is still shifting and disputed; I classify the overall event as `progress` (an instructive, ongoing incident on a still-open problem) and set ai_role to `bound` because, taking the clearest and best-documented AI claim (OpenAI/GPT-6 Astra), an AI system is credited by its own developers with moving an unconditional-looking (but formally conditional) numerical bound on a problem that remains open — this is exactly the `bound` category's definition, not `generated` (which would require a settled result, and this is a live-record contest, not a resolution) and not `assisted` (Axiom's account attributes the mathematics to humans). I could not find a single authoritative source resolving the exact chronological order of the 212 and 186 claims, or any expert consensus on which (if any) is currently considered the valid record; multiple sources call the whole episode unresolved/contested as of writing.
competing_reading: One could argue this record-chasing episode is entirely a 'related' quantity (H1, a bound on gaps) rather than a case of the twin prime conjecture itself, and that per SS3.1's rule that record-table extensions on an infinitude question ('are there infinitely many X') don't count unless the record is the question, this whole event should be `open`/`no_change_found`. I judge H1 is not a pure record table narrowing search space (like 'largest known twin prime pair') but is the specific auxiliary constant Wikipedia's own article cites as the state of the art on this exact conjecture (DHL[k,2]-type results are the standard proxy for progress toward the conjecture in the literature and on the page itself), so a change in H1 is the kind of bound-movement SS6.1's `progress` category is designed to capture. If a stricter reading is taken, the correct status would be `open` with `no_change_found` true and this entire episode relegated to `summary` as context.
what_would_settle_it: An independent, on-the-record verification (a peer-reviewed paper, a widely-endorsed blog post by a named expert working through the Lean formalization line-by-line, or explicit acceptance by the Polymath-style community) confirming which of the 212 or 186 bounds (or a further one) is the actual current unconditional record, and clarification of whether OpenAI's three unproven Lean axioms have since been discharged.

outcome: No result addressing Ulam's packing conjecture (whether the ball is the worst-packing convex solid) was found published or announced between 26 January 2024 and today; the conjecture remains open with the same partial results (Kallus's local-minimum theorem, and simulation verification for various solid classes) that predate the frozen revision.
summary: I ran a broad set of searches covering the conjecture directly ("Ulam's packing conjecture" with 2024/2025/2026), the underlying mathematical question (worst-packing convex solid, worst packer, asphericity, local minimum), potential counterexamples, and an AI-specific angle. All searches returned only pre-2024 material: Kallus's 2012–2015 local-minimum results for point-symmetric bodies and the ball's local pessimum status in 3D, the Kallus–Nazarov dimension-dependent result (arXiv 1212.2551, from December 2012, showing dimensions 4,5,6,7,8,24 admit small-asphericity bodies that pack worse than balls — this is a pre-window result the triage's 'why' field also surfaced), and simulation-based verification extended to prisms/antiprisms, Johnson solids, and Catalan solids (also pre-2024 work). Two 2024–2026 papers that surfaced in searches — Schildkraut's 'Lower bounds for sphere packing in arbitrary norms' (arXiv 2406.07479, June 2024, revised April 2025) and Han/Henk/Xue's 'Packing minima of convex bodies' (arXiv 2601.13937, January 2026) — were opened directly and neither mentions or relates to Ulam's conjecture: the first is about density lower bounds for sphere packing in general normed spaces (a related but distinct question), and the second is about a different notion of 'packing minima' unconnected to the worst-packer question. A search for AI/ML connections surfaced only a reinforcement-learning paper on kissing numbers (arXiv 2511.13391), which is an unrelated problem (kissing numbers, not Ulam's packing conjecture). The current (2026) Wikipedia article for the conjecture was fetched directly and its full reference list contains no citations after 2015, confirming no update has been logged even informally. I am satisfied nothing has happened to this problem in the window.
competing_reading: None of the tangentially related 2024–2026 papers (sphere packing in arbitrary norms, packing minima, kissing-number RL) constitute even a 'related problem' finding worth recording as `progress`, since none of them mention or bear formally on the specific claim that the ball is the worst-packing convex solid — they address different, only thematically adjacent packing questions. There is no genuine ambiguity here to flag.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement that either proves/disproves Ulam's conjecture in full, exhibits a convex solid packing worse than the ball (a global counterexample), extends the local-minimum result to a broader class of shapes, or explicitly discusses the conjecture by name with a dated 2024+ result.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or partial resolution of the stated conjecture (a bound N(K,g) on the number of K-rational points on any genus g≥2 curve over a number field K) was found in the window; all located post-2024-01-26 activity concerns distinct, differently-scoped conjectures that happen to share the name "uniform boundedness."
summary: The stated conjecture asks for a bound N(K,g) on the number of K-rational points on any genus g≥2 curve over a number field K, depending only on K and g, not on the curve's height, degree, or embedding. I searched extensively for anything bearing on this exact question since 26 January 2024 and found none. Several literature threads use the phrase 'uniform boundedness conjecture' or closely adjacent language but address genuinely different mathematical objects, per the scope rule of §3.1 (a related problem, not a case of this one): (1) the dynamical Uniform Boundedness Conjecture of Morton-Silverman, about preperiodic/torsion points of rational maps or polynomial dynamical systems (arXiv:2105.05240 on polynomials over number fields, Doyle-Faber on rational maps with automorphisms arXiv:2401.11309, Doyle-Poonen work referenced in surveys, and follow-ups through 2025); (2) uniform boundedness of torsion/small points on abelian varieties over function fields, resolved in that function-field setting by Looper-Yap (March 2026, arXiv preprint) and related work by Gao — these concern abelian varieties over function fields of characteristic 0, not curves of genus g≥2 over number fields; (3) the 'dimension growth conjecture' / Bombieri-Pila-type bounds on rational points of height ≤ H on a curve of given degree, most recently sharpened by Binyamini-Cluckers-Kato (Proc. LMS 2025, arXiv:2401.03982, submitted 8 Jan 2024 — itself before the window) and by a 2024 IMRN paper of Binyamini-Cluckers-Novikov — these bound points by height and degree, not a height-independent bound depending only on genus and field, so they do not touch the stated conjecture even though they are much closer in spirit; (4) Bremner's conjecture on arithmetic progressions on elliptic curves (arXiv:2604.04850), which is about rank, not point-count uniformity for genus ≥2 curves. I also checked whether the conjecture has been formalized or attacked via proof assistants: a Google DeepMind formal-conjectures GitHub issue (#1820) proposes adding the exact statement to a Lean formalization corpus, but it is an open formalization request (labeled 'needs-prerequisites' and 'new conjecture'), not a proof of any kind, and involves no AI-generated mathematics — it is a request for a Mathlib-target statement. The Wikipedia article itself (checked directly) still lists the same partial results predating the window (Caporaso-Harris-Mazur 1997 conditional on Bombieri-Lang, Stoll's and Katz-Rabinoff-Zureick-Brown's work on the weaker Mazur Conjecture B, and the 2021 Dimitrov-Gao-Habegger resolution of Conjecture B) with nothing added since. No AI system was found anywhere near any of this work; the Doyle-Faber and Looper-Yap papers are ordinary human-authored proofs with no stated AI assistance.
competing_reading: One could argue the Binyamini-Cluckers-Kato dimension-growth bound is 'close enough' to count as progress, since uniform (in height) point-counts are the classical tool (Bombieri-Pila/Heath-Brown determinant method) used to attack uniform boundedness, and the sharpened d² factor is a genuine advance in that toolkit. But the bound is explicitly height-dependent (grows with H) and per-curve rather than uniform over all curves of a fixed genus, so under the stated question (a bound N(K,g) with no height parameter) it remains a related-but-distinct problem, consistent with the triage's judgment.
what_would_settle_it: A paper proving, for some or all g≥2 and some class of number fields K, a bound on the total number of K-rational points on a genus-g curve that does not depend on the height, degree, or any other invariant of the specific curve beyond g and K itself — or a counterexample showing no such bound exists for some (K,g).

outcome: The classical uniqueness conjecture remains open, but a genuine (if narrow) necessary condition was proved in the window — Markov's equation is not partition regular (Tao & Yang, Oct 2025) — while the only paper claiming a full resolution (Gore, June 2025) is an unreviewed, uncredentialed math.GM preprint with circular reasoning and no engagement with the literature, and a widely-repeated 'May/June 2026 Heffern 3-adic lifting proof' turned out on verification to be a search-tool hallucination with no corresponding arXiv record.

disputes.summary: Robert A. Gore's 'Patterns Within the Markov Tree' (arXiv:2506.04299, filed under math.GM — arXiv's unendorsed/general-mathematics category, and listing only 'Cheyney, PA' rather than an institutional affiliation) claims in its abstract that analysis of a Pell equation 'leads to the resolution of the Uniqueness Conjecture.' On reading the full text, the argument is circular: it uses Mathematica to observe that solutions to an auxiliary Pell-type equation exist exactly when the parameter equals a Markov number, then treats this observed correspondence as a proof that the parameter must be a Markov number, without independently establishing uniqueness of the corresponding triple. It cites no foundational literature (Frobenius, Aigner, Cohn, Christoffel-word / cluster-algebra work) beyond a single Quanta Magazine article, and has not been digested, endorsed, or cited by any specialist. It has not been treated as a resolution by the community and does not meet the bar for `resolved` or even `claimed` credibility, but is recorded here as a claim that surfaced in the window.

summary: The classical uniqueness (Frobenius/unicity) conjecture for Markov numbers is still open as of this research. Several genuine but non-resolving pieces of work appeared in the window (26 Jan 2024 – present): (1) David Fisac's 'Markov's Conjecture on integral necklaces' (arXiv:2501.15550, submitted 26 Jan 2025, revised Feb and Aug 2025) reformulates the geometric simple-length-spectrum version of the conjecture into purely combinatorial terms — a reformulation, not a proof, and its own abstract makes no resolution claim; this is a related restatement rather than a case settled, so on its own it would not move status. (2) Daniel Martin's 'A new proof of Chen's theorem for Markoff graphs' (arXiv:2502.15960, Feb 2025) is not about the uniqueness conjecture at all — it gives an alternate proof that connected components of the Markoff mod-p graph have size divisible by p (Chen's 2021 result), which bears on graph connectivity/Baragar's conjecture, a different problem; the triage's uncertainty about its scope is resolved here as 'not this problem.' (3) Tianyi Tao and Bohan Yang, 'Markov's equation is not partition regular' (arXiv:2510.10151, submitted 11 Oct 2025), prove that no finite coloring of the positive integers has every color class containing a solution of the Markov equation, and state explicitly that this 'confirms a necessary condition for the Uniqueness Conjecture' — this is genuine incremental progress narrowing what any full proof must be compatible with, though it does not settle any case of the conjecture itself (no specific Markov number's uniqueness is newly established), so it is coded `progress` rather than `partial`. (4) Robert A. Gore's 'Patterns Within the Markov Tree' (arXiv:2506.04299, math.GM, June/Aug 2025) explicitly claims in its abstract to resolve the Uniqueness Conjecture, but on reading the full text the argument is circular (observing via Mathematica that an auxiliary equation's solutions correspond to Markov numbers, then treating that correspondence as the proof), engages with essentially no specialist literature, and has had no expert digestion or endorsement — it does not meet the bar for `resolved`, and given how far short it falls of even a serious unreviewed claim, it is noted as a dispute/curiosity rather than driving the status to `claimed`. No AI system is credited with any mathematics in any of these four items: Gore explicitly credits Mathematica (a computer algebra system, not an AI system under §6.2) for exploratory pattern-finding, and Tao & Yang's paper shows no sign of AI involvement in its methodology section. Separately, an initial web search returned a confident-sounding claim that 'Elleard Heffern' published a proof of the unicity conjecture via 3-adic lifting in May/June 2026; this was checked directly against the arXiv API (search for author Heffern) and returned zero results, and the named 'Elleard Heffern' is verifiably a biology PhD student (bird-flock phase transitions, Royal Society B) with no known number-theory work — this claim is a hallucination produced by the search tool's synthesis and is excluded from the record entirely per instructions to verify primary sources. No DeepMind/OpenAI/Anthropic system (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, etc.) has been reported working on this specific conjecture; those systems' 2025-2026 results (Kakeya, Erdős problems) are on unrelated problems. Because the only event that is both real and squarely on-topic (Tao & Yang) is a necessary-condition result narrowing the space rather than settling a case, status is coded `progress` with `ai_role` `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue Fisac's reformulation should also be logged as an `event` alongside Tao & Yang's, since a successful reformulation can be instrumental to eventual resolution; it is described in `disputes`/summary instead of as a second `event` per the instruction to describe multiple events in `summary` rather than invent extra records. One could also argue the Gore paper, despite its flaws, should be coded `claimed` rather than left out of `status` — the record instead treats it as a dispute over credibility because it shows no sign of having been taken seriously by anyone (no citations, no digestion, unendorsed category), which is different from a serious claimed proof awaiting review.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (blog post, referee report, or citation by a specialist) either endorsing or debunking the Gore paper's argument would resolve whether it belongs in the record at all; a subsequent paper building on Tao & Yang's partition-regularity result to settle an actual case of uniqueness (e.g., for a new infinite family of Markov numbers) would move status to `partial`.

outcome: A September 2026 preprint by Taylor Gordon claims an explicit construction of universal point sets for general planar graphs of size n^{1+o(1)} (n·exp(O(sqrt(log n)))), improving the quadratic upper bound that had stood as the state of the art through the 2025 Dujmović–Morin survey and through the frozen Wikipedia revision. This is not yet an expert-digested resolution: the preprint is 12 days old, has a single arXiv version, no journal reference, and the only secondary commentary found treats it explicitly as unverified.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen January 2024 revision states that closing the gap between the linear lower bound and quadratic upper bound for universal point sets of general planar graphs is open, and the general (unrestricted) case remained quadratic as of the 2025 Dujmović–Morin survey 'Free Sets in Planar Graphs: History and Applications' (arXiv:2403.17090), confirming nothing changed between the frozen date and late 2025. On 10 September 2026, Taylor Gordon posted arXiv:2609.10916, 'Almost Linear Universal Point Sets for Planar Graphs,' claiming an explicit construction of size n^{1+o(1)} via a reduction to superpatterns for 213-avoiding permutations (building on the Bannister–Cheng–Devanny–Eppstein reduction), represented through ordered rooted forests and layered intervals. The abstract and conclusion both explicitly credit GPT-6 Astra with assisting in developing the construction and the proof itself ('the model helped develop the construction, formulate and revise the proof, check finite examples, and draft the exposition') — this is authors'-own-account language describing the model contributing to the mathematics, not merely checking or formalizing human-produced work, so ai_role is coded 'assisted' rather than 'generated' (a human, Gordon, is credited as directing/producing the result with substantial AI help) or 'none'. The paper includes a Lean 4 formalization, but by the authors' own statement this formalization covers only 'an earlier construction' and explicitly does NOT cover 'the layered proof presented here' — so the Lean check does not certify the actual theorem as stated. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification of this specific result was found. The one piece of secondary commentary located, an article on llmrumors.com surveying September 2026 GPT-6-Astra-credited arXiv papers, explicitly discusses this paper and cautions that 'a model name cannot carry a theorem,' that arXiv moderation is not peer review, and that the linked Lean code covers the earlier construction, not the new near-linear result — i.e., it treats the paper as an unverified claim, not a resolution. No retraction, refutation, or identified flaw was found either. Given all this — a very recent single-version preprint, explicit disclosure that the formal verification does not cover the claimed result, and no expert working through the argument — this is coded 'claimed,' not 'resolved.' The direction is 'confirmed' because the claimed result, if correct, answers the open question in the direction of existence of a subquadratic (indeed near-linear) universal point set, matching what was conjectured/hoped rather than refuting it; there is no counterexample involved.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'progress' rather than 'claimed', on the theory that an unverified single-author preprint with heavy but partial AI assistance and an admittedly incomplete formalization is closer to an unconfirmed rumor than a checkable claim. I coded 'claimed' because the preprint does present an explicit, fully written construction and proof (not just a bound-improvement sketch), which is what distinguishes 'claimed' from 'progress' in §6.1 — but confidence that this preprint will hold up under scrutiny is low given the total absence of independent human review at the time of writing, and given that other GPT-6 Astra proof attempts surveyed in the same news piece (Quang Hung Tran's geometry conjectures) turned out to be incomplete.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) an expert in graph drawing (e.g. Dujmović, Morin, Eppstein, or another author in this specific subfield) publishing a review, a conference/journal acceptance, or a blog post working through Gordon's construction and confirming or refuting the n^{1+o(1)} bound, or (b) a full Lean/Coq formalization of the actual layered-interval proof (not just 'an earlier construction') that compiles without `sorry`, or (c) a follow-up preprint identifying a gap or counterexample to the construction.

outcome: No result addressing the general question of which finite sets C admit a countable universal C-free graph under strong (induced) embeddings was found in the window; the closest 2023-2025 work (Krill, universal graphs with forbidden wheel minors) uses a different containment notion (minors, not induced subgraphs) and was submitted before the window opened.
summary: The bullet is Cherlin's universality problem for C-free countable graphs under strong (induced) embeddings: for which finite sets C of forbidden connected graphs does the class of countable C-free graphs have a universal member under strong embeddings? This traces to Cherlin's long-running program (with Shelah, Komjath, Tallgren, Shi and others), organized around the Solidity Conjecture (if C has an incomplete block, no universal C-free graph exists) and related conjectures about tree/path/near-path cases, most recently advanced in Cherlin-Shelah's 'Block path solidity' (Combinatorica 2016). I found no paper in the 26 Jan 2024 - present window that resolves, extends, or meaningfully moves this general question or the Solidity Conjecture itself. Cherlin's own Rutgers publications page (sites.math.rutgers.edu/~cherlin/Paper/) lists nothing on universal graphs since 2016; his 2024-2025 papers are on unrelated model-theoretic topics (algebraicity, separably closed fields). The most relevant candidate found, Thilo Krill's 'Universal graphs with forbidden wheel minors' (arXiv:2309.12473, published in Journal of Graph Theory 2025), proves universality results for classes defined by forbidding a minor (cycles, theta-graphs, wheels) under a different containment notion than the Wikipedia bullet's 'strong embeddings' (which mean induced-subgraph embeddings in this literature); more importantly it was submitted 21 September 2023, before the 26 January 2024 window opens, so even if judged a case of the stated problem it would be open_stale, not a window event. Krill's paper explicitly frames its own open Conjecture 1.2 as distinct from and only 'lending support to' ideas in the Cherlin program, underscoring that it is not a direct advance on the Wikipedia bullet. A June 2025 paper on 'Infinite induced-saturated graphs' (arXiv:2506.08810) addresses a related but different saturation question and does not bear on universal C-free graphs. No arXiv, Google Scholar, or web search turned up any 2024-2026 paper directly addressing the general universality-for-C-free-graphs question or citing new progress on the Solidity/Pathlike conjectures. I therefore agree with the triage's 'none' verdict; no disagreement.
competing_reading: One could argue Krill's wheel-minor paper is close enough in spirit (same universality-for-forbidden-substructure paradigm, explicitly citing and building on Cherlin-Shelah-Tallgren results) to count as adjacent progress worth flagging, and that if it were somehow read as bearing on the subgraph/induced version of the problem it would predate the window regardless (open_stale). But minors and induced subgraphs are different containment relations addressed by different (if related) conjectures in the literature, and Krill's own paper treats them as separate open problems (his Conjecture 1.2 concerns minor-freeness specifically), so I classify it as a related-but-distinct problem rather than a case or resolution of the stated one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper by Cherlin, Komjath, Shelah, or others explicitly proving or disproving a case of the Solidity Conjecture or the general classification for finite C under strong (induced) embeddings, dated after 26 January 2024, would settle whether anything has happened. Checking Cherlin's personal page periodically and monitoring arXiv math.CO/math.LO for 'universal graph' + 'forbidden subgraph'/'C-free' would be the way to catch it.

outcome: No result addressing whether a first-order theory with minimum universality spectrum exists was found in the window; the only substantive Shelah paper on this exact question (SH1164, 'Universality; new criterion for non-existence') predates the frozen revision by over two years.
summary: The universality spectrum problem asks whether some complete first-order theory has a minimum universality spectrum among all such theories (a theory Tceq — an equivalence relation with a family of choice functions — is the leading candidate believed to be minimal or near-minimal among non-simple theories). The last substantive contribution I could find is Shelah's SH1164, 'Universality: new criterion for non-existence,' posted to arXiv as 2108.06727 on 2021-08-15 (v2: 2022-03-14) and published in Bollettino dell'Unione Matematica Italiana in 2023 — this gives new sufficient conditions for non-existence of universal models for Tceq at various cardinals, but does not settle the minimality question and predates the frozen revision (26 January 2024) regardless. I searched broadly for any 2024-2026 work continuing this line — direct searches on 'universality spectrum,' searches for Shelah's more recent papers, and searches for the specific candidate theory Tceq/Tfeq — and found nothing addressing the stated question. I did find two adjacent but distinct 2025 papers, 'On the spectrum of limit models' (Beard & Mazari-Armida, arXiv:2503.11605) and 'The spectrum of limit models in a first order setting' (Beard, arXiv:2510.03459); I opened the abstract/content of the first and confirmed by direct inspection that it concerns the isomorphism spectrum of limit models in abstract elementary classes (a different, though terminologically similar, question about when limit models are isomorphic to each other) rather than the existence of universal models or the universality spectrum ordering of theories. This is a related-problem/different-question case under §3.1, not a case of the stated problem, so it does not count. I was unable to fully render Shelah's SH1164 PDF as text via the fetch tool (it returned raw PDF markup), but I independently confirmed its arXiv posting date and abstract content through the arXiv abstract page and a published-journal citation, which is sufficient to establish it predates the window. No AI system appears anywhere in any of the sources found. This agrees with the triage's 'none' verdict; I did not find its dismissal of the Tceq/limit-model adjacent work to be wrong.
competing_reading: If the Beard–Mazari-Armida 'spectrum of limit models' line were judged to be close enough in substance to the universality spectrum (both concern classifying models of a theory by an ordering related to embeddability/isomorphism across cardinals), one could argue it deserves a 'partial'/'progress' classification with a caveat. I do not think this is the better reading: the universality spectrum problem specifically concerns universal (embedding) models, and the limit-model spectrum concerns isomorphism types of models built by increasing chains — these are different mathematical objects studied with different techniques (types/independence relations vs. combinatorial non-embeddability arguments), and neither paper mentions universal models or Shelah's SH1164 line of work in what I reviewed.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that either exhibits a first-order theory provably minimum in the universality spectrum ordering, proves no such minimum exists, or narrows the class of candidate minimal theories (e.g. further sufficient/necessary conditions for Tceq or Tfeq specifically) would settle or advance this. Direct access to Shelah's personal publication list (shelah.logic.at) with working links, which returned a 404 for the listing page I tried, could also surface a newer unlisted preprint if one exists.

outcome: No source establishes any change to whether unknot recognition is in P. Marc Lackenby's 2021 quasi-polynomial-time algorithm remains an unpublished announcement with no arXiv preprint found and, per multiple 2025-era sources, still not in the peer-reviewed literature. AI/ML work found in the window (a Google DeepMind/Oxford reinforcement-learning paper and a follow-up RL paper) targets the unknotting number and hard unknot diagrams, a related but distinct question, not the polynomial-time recognition question stated in this bullet.
summary: The bullet asks specifically whether unknots can be recognized in polynomial time — i.e., whether unknot recognition is in P. Nothing found in the 26 January 2024–22 September 2026 window changes the status of that question. Lackenby's 2021 announcement of a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm (n^{c log n} steps) predates the window and, per the Oxford Mathematical Institute page and searches run for this record, remains unpublished with no arXiv preprint located as of the check date; it would not settle the P question even if published, since quasi-polynomial time is weaker than polynomial time. A 2026 arXiv paper on incompressible surfaces, hierarchies and unknot recognition (2607.23350) gives a new proof of the already-known NP membership result via a different route, not new progress on P-membership. Two machine-learning papers turned up repeatedly in searches: (1) 'The unknotting number, hard unknot diagrams, and reinforcement learning' (arXiv:2409.09032, submitted 13 September 2024, authors including Applebaum, Blackwell, Davies, Edlich, Juhász, Lackenby, Tomašev, Zheng — a Google DeepMind/Oxford collaboration), which uses an RL agent to find minimal unknotting-crossing-change sequences and determine unknotting numbers for many knots; and (2) a March 2026 follow-up, 'RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number' (arXiv:2603.07955, Dranowski/Kabkov/Tubbenhauer), which extends this with a self-improving RL pipeline for Reidemeister-move simplification. Both are squarely about the unknotting number (minimum crossing changes to reach the unknot) and about heuristic diagram simplification, not about the computational-complexity question of whether recognizing an unknot diagram as trivial can be decided in polynomial time. Per the scope rule (§3.1), a different question about the same objects is a related problem, not a case of this one, so these do not count as movement on this bullet even though they are squarely 'about unknots' and do involve AI. A separate, unrelated 2025 result (Brittenham and Hermiller, arXiv preprint posted ~June 2025, digested in Quanta Magazine 22 September 2025) disproved the long-standing additivity conjecture for unknotting numbers under connected sum — again the unknotting-number question, not recognition complexity, and involves no AI. The 2020 'Learning to Unknot' paper (arXiv:2010.16263, Gukov et al., CALT-2020-046/CERN-TH-2020-179) that keeps surfacing in searches predates the window (submitted 28 October 2020) and is itself a heuristic ML classifier/RL-move-finder, not a complexity proof, so it is out of scope on both counts. No source found claims, disputes, or withdraws any polynomial-time algorithm for unknot recognition in this window; the honest answer is that the problem is unchanged and open.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind/Oxford RL papers on hard unknot diagrams are close enough to count as 'progress' on unknot recognition broadly, since they do produce practical algorithms that recognize (and prove) unknottedness for large classes of hard diagrams via explicit Reidemeister/crossing-change sequences, and Lackenby himself is a co-author bridging both the complexity work and the ML work. If the bullet were read loosely as 'progress on algorithmically recognizing unknots' rather than strictly 'is the decision problem in P', these papers would be `progress` with `ai_role` `assisted` or `bound`. I did not adopt this reading because the papers' own framing and results are about the unknotting number and empirical/heuristic performance on specific diagram classes (up to 200 crossings, or engineered 'very hard' unknots), not about worst-case polynomial-time bounds or the complexity class P, which is what the Wikipedia bullet asks.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed publication or well-digested preprint proving (or disproving) a worst-case polynomial-time upper bound for the general unknot recognition decision problem — as opposed to a quasi-polynomial bound, a heuristic/empirical algorithm, or a result about a different quantity such as the unknotting number.

outcome: A single-author arXiv preprint (Owen Root, Aug/Sep 2025) claims to prove that the fractional-part condition 2^k·{(3/2)^k} + ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ > 2^k never occurs, which — combined with prior work of Dickson, Pillai, Rubugunday and Niven — would fix a fully general closed-form expression g(k) = 2^k − ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ − 2 for all k. As of this writing (over a year after posting, two versions, no journal submission or expert digestion found), it has not been checked or accepted by the mathematical community; the only public assessment found is a fully automated ('machine-made') review flagging that the abstract does not even state the condition being proved, making it hard to evaluate even provisionally.
summary: Waring's problem bullet on this list covers two separate open quantities: g(k), for which a conjectural general formula g(k) = 2^k − ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ − 2 has long been known to hold except possibly when a specific fractional-part condition occurs (it is known not to occur for all currently checked k, and never for large k by results of Mahler-type arguments, but not proved impossible for all k), and G(k), for which only bounds are known for k ≥ 7 or so. Searching the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), I found one candidate event: arXiv:2508.17950 by Owen Root (a physics PhD candidate at CUNY, per their alphaXiv profile — not previously known in this subfield), first posted 25 Aug 2025 and revised 4 Sep 2025, titled 'Expression for g(k) Related to Waring's Problem'. Its abstract states it proves the outstanding condition never occurs, which would settle g(k) in closed form for every k — a full resolution of that half of the bullet, not just a case, if correct. However, I found no evidence any human expert has read through and endorsed the argument: no journal listing, no digestion on blogs (Tao's blog, Quanta, etc. — none found), and the one public review is from Pith Review, an explicitly 'machine-made' (automated/LLM) review platform that itself flags the paper as unverifiable from the abstract alone and 'important enough to warrant expert review', i.e. a request for human checking that (as far as I can determine) has not yet happened. Per §6.1 this is squarely 'claimed', not 'resolved': a preprint that no digestion has verified. On the AI question: the paper's own text contains no acknowledgement of AI/ML tool use in producing the proof (checked via full-text fetch of the HTML version), so there is no basis for 'assisted' or 'generated'. The only AI system anywhere in this problem's timeline is Pith's automated reviewer, which only assessed/critiqued the preprint — a checking function, not a mathematics-producing one — so per §6.2 that is 'none', not 'assisted' or 'generated', regardless of how central Pith's critique is to the current epistemic status of the claim. Separately, one of the triage's found items, arXiv:2401.13436 ('Further Improvements on Waring's Problem G(k)' by An-Ping Li), was submitted 21 Jan 2024 — four days before the frozen revision's 26 Jan 2024 timestamp — so it is not an in-window event and is excluded from consideration (it would in any case not involve AI, being a classical exponential-sums/Hardy-Littlewood-circle-method argument). I found no other G(k) bound improvements, small-k value determinations, or g(k) work in the window besides Root's preprint. The Wikipedia article's live lead (checked, though not authoritative for this project) still cites only pre-2003 literature and does not mention Root's or Li's work, consistent with no accepted change yet.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'progress' rather than 'claimed', on the theory that an unverified single-author preprint on an open problem with this track record (many false or flawed claimed proofs of number-theoretic closed forms circulate on arXiv) is closer to 'nothing has really moved' than to a live claim awaiting adjudication. I kept it as 'claimed' per §6.1's literal definition ('a preprint, announcement or machine-checked certificate that experts have not yet digested') since the preprint's proof, if it holds up, would be a full resolution of the g(k)-formula question, not a partial bound — that is a meaningfully different situation from a mere incremental bound (which would be 'progress'). Also arguable: whether Pith Review's automated critique itself, being a form of AI-driven mathematical review, deserves separate notice as a 'progress'/'incident'-flavored data point about AI infrastructure entering the peer-review pipeline for this problem; I judged it does not rise to an event about the problem's mathematical status and is better treated as part of the evidentiary picture for 'claimed' vs 'resolved', not as its own event.
what_would_settle_it: A human expert's digestion of arXiv:2508.17950 (blog post, MathSciNet review, or journal referee report) either confirming the proof of the fractional-part condition or identifying an error; alternatively, any independent proof or disproof of that same condition; or any new arXiv preprint on G(k) small-value determinations or asymptotic bounds dated after 26 Jan 2024 that I did not surface.

Proving that 2^k{(3/2)^k} + floor((3/2)^k) > 2^k never occurs is a statement about the distribution of the fractional parts of (3/2)^k, the territory of Mahler's 3/2 problem, where only 'for all sufficiently large k, ineffectively' (Mahler 1957) is known; a proof for every k would be a landmark in Diophantine approximation, not a closing lemma. outcome: M(10) and higher Dedekind numbers remain exactly uncomputed since 26 January 2024; two 2026 preprints produced statistical (non-rigorous) estimates of M(10) through M(15) using Monte Carlo / Markov-chain layer-ratio methods, narrowing where the true values plausibly lie but not settling any of them.
summary: The bullet asks for the exact values of the Dedekind numbers M(n) for n ≥ 10; as of 26 January 2024 only M(n) for n ≤ 9 were known exactly (M(9) was computed in 2023, before the window, and is not itself in scope since the bullet is about n ≥ 10). Since the frozen date, no exact value of M(10) or any higher Dedekind number has been computed or claimed — this remains far beyond current computational reach (the gap between known rigorous lower and upper bounds for M(10) spans roughly 230 orders of magnitude). Two 2026 preprints move the needle on the surrounding mathematics without settling the question: 'Finite-n Estimate of Dedekind Numbers by Layer-Ratio Monte Carlo' (arXiv:2606.09795, submitted 2026-06-08, Chen/Feng/Wang/Chen/Zhang) gives a statistical estimate M(10) ≈ (8.9360 ± 0.0010)×10^78 using reversible fixed-layer Markov chains to estimate layer ratios; 'Statistical Estimation of higher Dedekind Numbers' (arXiv:2607.08446, Fihman/Van Hirtum/Plessl) extends this to statistical estimates of D(10) through D(15) with several algorithmic variants (pair matching, reference subsets, weight-layer branching). Both papers are explicit that these are statistical/Monte Carlo estimates, not exact values or even rigorous bounds — they narrow uncertainty about where the true value likely lies but do not constitute a resolution, a new proven bound, or a case of the problem being settled (an 'exact value' question is not advanced by a probabilistic point estimate, per the rule that existence/value questions move only when actually answered). I read both papers' abstracts and available body text and found no mention of any AI or machine-learning system contributing to the estimation methodology; the techniques described are traditional statistical/algorithmic (Markov chain Monte Carlo, combinatorial counting), not learned models. A GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #2360) merely proposes formalizing the open problem statement in Lean/Mathlib for tracking purposes — it was itself generated by an AI agent in February 2026 as a repository-maintenance action, but it reports no mathematical progress and its 'AI agent' authorship is about issue-filing, not about producing any mathematics, so it does not count as AI involvement in the problem itself. I classified status as 'progress' rather than 'open' because the two 2026 papers represent an instructive advance in estimating quantities the bullet is directly about, even though no bound or exact value was proven — this is closer to the 'a bound moved, or an instructive incident' sense of progress than to true silence, though I flag this as a judgment call (see competing_reading).
competing_reading: One could argue this should be classified as plain 'open' with no_change_found true, since a statistical Monte Carlo point estimate is neither a proven bound nor a settled case — it does not change what a careful person would write in the bullet's entry (the exact value of M(10) is exactly as unknown now as in January 2024), and 'progress' risks conflating an estimate with a bound movement. I lean toward 'progress' because the statistical estimates are the first substantive quantitative narrowing of belief about M(10)–M(15) since the (in-window-irrelevant) 2023 M(9) computation, and because it is an instructive computational advance in methodology directly targeting this exact question, but 'open' / no_change_found is a defensible alternative reading.
what_would_settle_it: An exact computation of M(10) (or any n ≥ 10) verified by independent recomputation or expert digestion, or a rigorously proven (non-statistical) narrowing of the lower/upper bound gap, would move this further; either would need to appear as a peer-reviewed or expert-vetted result rather than a preprint estimate to reach 'resolved'.

outcome: A preprint by Dutour Sikirić and van Woerden (arXiv:2508.20719) computes all 2,237,251,040 perfect lattices in dimension 9 via Voronoi's algorithm and derives that the Hermite constant γ9 equals 2, extending the set of dimensions with a known value beyond {1-8, 24} for the first time since 24 was settled. The result has not yet received independent expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent reproduction of the computation.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asserts the Hermite constant is known only for dimensions 1-8 and 24. The triage pointer was correct: a preprint posted 28 August 2025 (revised 7 February 2026) by Mathieu Dutour Sikirić and Wessel van Woerden, 'The lattice packing problem in dimension 9 by Voronoi's algorithm' (arXiv:2508.20719), completes Voronoi's algorithm in dimension 9 for the first time, enumerating all 2,237,251,040 perfect lattices up to similarity, and concludes as a corollary that γ9 = 2 (with the laminated lattice Λ9 achieving the densest packing). This is squarely a case of the stated problem (it fills in exactly the 'dimensions other than 1-8 and 24' the bullet names), not a variant, so it counts under §3.1. I read the full text (via the arXiv HTML rendering) and confirmed the methodology is entirely classical: Voronoi's 1908 algorithm, graph-isomorphism software (Nauty/Traces), polyhedral computation libraries (PPL, LRS), and MPI-parallelized enumeration, with completeness certified by the algorithm's own termination criterion (no new perfect-form neighbors found) and a consistency check against a prior partial enumeration for high-incidence forms. No machine learning, neural network, or other AI system is mentioned anywhere in the text or acknowledgements, so ai_role is 'none'. I classified status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved': the paper remains an arXiv preprint with no journal submission/acceptance noted, and I found no expert digestion (no Terence Tao or comparable blog treatment, no citing survey, no independent reproduction of the 2.2-billion-lattice enumeration) as of my search on 2026-09-22 — only the authors' own account and secondary paraphrases of the abstract. The 'directly checkable by computer algebra' clause of the resolved definition is a genuine complication: the computation is deterministic and the authors' code/data are on Zenodo, so a suitably resourced expert could rerun it, but no evidence I found shows anyone has done so, and a computation of this scale is not 'directly checkable by hand' in the way the rule seems to intend for a quick verification. I therefore treat it as claimed rather than resolved, pending independent confirmation.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'resolved' on the grounds that the result rests on a deterministic, reproducible enumeration algorithm (not a probabilistic or heuristic method) with data published on Zenodo, so it is 'directly checkable ... by computer algebra' per the resolved criterion even without a human having independently redone it. Under that reading the status would be 'resolved', direction 'confirmed', with ai_role and all other fields unchanged.
what_would_settle_it: An independent reproduction or audit of the dimension-9 perfect-lattice enumeration (or of the derived γ9 = 2 claim) by another group, a journal acceptance, or a digestion by a recognized expert commentator (e.g., a blog post, survey, or update to the Hermite constant / sphere-packing literature citing and endorsing the result) would move this to 'resolved'.

outcome: Angeltveit and McKay proved R(5,5) ≤ 46 (down from the previous best upper bound of 48, which they themselves established in 2017), narrowing the known range from 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 48 to 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46. The exact value of R(5,5) remains unknown.
summary: The decisive event for this bullet is Angeltveit and McKay's arXiv preprint 'R(5,5) ≤ 46' (arXiv:2409.15709, submitted 2024-09-24, v2 2025-09-01), which improves the upper bound on R(5,5) from 48 (the same authors, 2017) to 46, via 'a combination of linear programming and checking a large number of cases by computer' — no AI system of any kind is mentioned, and the WebFetch of the abstract/paper confirmed no ML, neural network, or SAT-solver framing; this is classical computational combinatorics (LP + exhaustive case-checking, independently re-implemented by both authors as a cross-check). The result was subsequently published in the Journal of Graph Theory 112 (2026): 198–208 (DOI 10.1002/jgt.70029), so it has passed peer review by experts in the field — enough for 'resolved' status if the result had settled the whole problem, but since R(5,5)'s exact value remains open (only the range narrowed, from 43–48 to 43–46), the correct code is 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (the bound moved in the expected/conjectured direction, no violation of expectation). The current Wikipedia article on Ramsey's theorem confirms this is the state of the art: 'it is known to lie between 43 (Geoffrey Exoo (1989)) and 46 (Angeltveit and McKay (2024)).' Separately, and NOT folded into the status/date above, I found a closely related but distinct result: Nagda, Raghavan and Thakurta (Google DeepMind), 'Reinforced Generation of Combinatorial Structures: Ramsey Numbers' (arXiv:2603.09172, submitted 2026-03-10), used AlphaEvolve — described by the authors as 'an LLM-based code mutation agent' that 'uses LLMs...to iteratively evolve code-snippets to generate better lower bounds' — to improve lower bounds on nine classical Ramsey numbers: R(3,13), R(3,18), R(4,13), R(4,14), R(4,15), R(4,16), R(4,18), R(4,19), R(4,20). This is squarely an AI-generated result on 'the values of the Ramsey numbers' in general (this bullet's broader statement covers all Ramsey numbers, with R(5,5) singled out as 'particularly' notable), but it does not touch R(5,5) or any case/restriction of R(5,5) specifically — it is a related result on different index pairs, not a case of the R(5,5) sub-problem, and is still an unreviewed 'working paper' (their own label) with no independent verification of the lower-bound constructions described in the text I read (only that the graphs were 'made public on Github'). Because the specific named quantity in this bullet is R(5,5), and the AlphaEvolve work does not change that number, I have not made it the decisive event, but it is highly relevant context for the general Ramsey-numbers problem this bullet also names.
competing_reading: If the bullet is read at its broadest — 'the values of the Ramsey numbers' as a whole, with R(5,5) as merely the illustrative example rather than the exclusive target — then the AlphaEvolve result (arXiv:2603.09172, 2026-03-10) is itself a qualifying 'case settled' (nine Ramsey-number lower bounds moved) and would make ai_role 'generated' or 'bound' for at least part of this bullet's scope, since the authors' own account is that AlphaEvolve produced the constructions/search algorithms that yielded the new bounds. Under that reading, this record would need two co-existing events: R(5,5)≤46 (no AI) and the AlphaEvolve lower-bound improvements (AI-generated/bound, still unreviewed preprint). I judged the narrower reading — that 'particularly R(5,5)' makes R(5,5) the operative target of this specific bullet, since it is the only value actually named — to be the better fit, consistent with treating other-index Ramsey numbers as a related/different problem rather than a case of 'the R(5,5) problem.' A different annotator could reasonably weight the AlphaEvolve preprint as the more AI-relevant event for this bullet given its 'values of the Ramsey numbers' framing.
what_would_settle_it: Clarification of whether this bullet's denominator is 'the value of R(5,5) alone' or 'the values of Ramsey numbers generally, exemplified by R(5,5)' would settle whether the AlphaEvolve preprint counts as a qualifying event here. Separately, peer review or independent computational verification of the AlphaEvolve lower-bound constructions (currently just a working paper with GitHub-posted graphs) would move that result from 'claimed'-type evidence to something more solid, though it would still not change the classification of this specific R(5,5) record.
