outcome: No new exact van der Waerden number was determined, but two 2026 preprints moved asymptotic bounds on how the numbers grow: Fox and Hunter proved the three-color van der Waerden numbers grow faster than any exponential function (super-exponential growth), and Campos, Fox and Schildkraut proved the long-conjectured Erdős lower bound w(k) ≥ (1−o(1))k·2^(k−1) for two-color van der Waerden numbers, extending Berlekamp's 1968 prime-case result to all k. Neither result pins down a new exact value in the table of known van der Waerden numbers; both are bounds on the general growth of these numbers.

ai.basis_quote: The coloring used to prove Theorem 1, as well as a proof of Theorem 1, were generated by a query to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro. The proof we present, while drawing somewhat on the proof given by ChatGPT, was produced by the authors ... All of the writing is our own.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet is about 'the values of the Van der Waerden numbers' — i.e., the open problem of determining/bounding w(r,k) (and its multicolor generalisations), of which only nine are known exactly (the last being W(3,4)=293, Kouril 2012) and for which good asymptotic bounds are otherwise the substance of the field. Two 2026 preprints move this: (1) Fox & Hunter, 'Three-color van der Waerden numbers grow super-exponentially' (arXiv:2606.02541, submitted 2026-06-01), prove the 3-colour van der Waerden numbers w(k;3) grow faster than any exponential in k, exhibiting a 3-coloring of {1,...,2^{k·log*(k)/4}} with no monochromatic k-AP; this also resolves a related Erdős–Graham problem on canonical van der Waerden numbers. I found no mention of any AI system in this paper's abstract or text. (2) Campos, Fox & Schildkraut, 'A new lower bound for two-color van der Waerden numbers' (arXiv:2608.20824, submitted 2026-08-21), prove w(k) ≥ (1−o(1))k·2^{k−1} for all k, verifying a 1968 conjecture of Erdős and extending Berlekamp's result (which only covered k−1 prime) to all integers via a product construction over Berlekamp colorings for the prime factors. This paper contains an explicit 'AI Use' disclosure: 'The coloring used to prove Theorem 1, as well as a proof of Theorem 1, were generated by a query to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro. The proof we present, while drawing somewhat on the proof given by ChatGPT, was produced by the authors ... All of the writing is our own.' By the authors' own account, the model produced both the construction and an initial proof, which the authors then reworked and wrote up themselves — this is the authors doing the mathematics that appears in the presented proof while drawing on an AI-produced starting point, which I code as `assisted` rather than `generated`: the authors state the *presented* proof (the one on which the paper — and hence the result being counted — rests) 'was produced by the authors,' distinguishing it from what ChatGPT gave them. Neither paper changes a known exact value in the numbers table, and neither settles the general open question of the numbers' precise values; both move bounds on an open problem, so status is `progress` rather than `partial` or `resolved`. I also found, via the current Wikipedia article, a 2024 result (Karki, 'U(t)-Mathazine', Summer 2024) giving a new canonical/mixed van der Waerden number w(21; 2^17,3^2) = 52 — this is a genuine new exact value within the window, but for a different (canonical, many-colour, mixed-AP-length) notion of van der Waerden number than the standard w(r,k) the bullet's statement most naturally refers to; I did not verify this source directly (could not locate the primary Mathazine article) and note it here rather than making it the basis of the record, since the two arXiv preprints are independently sufficient to establish `progress` and carry the AI-relevant finding.
competing_reading: One could argue the Campos–Fox–Schildkraut role should be coded `generated`: the abstract's closing sentence, 'It was found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro,' credits the model with finding the actual mathematical content (the coloring and a proof), which is the §6.2 test for `generated` ('the model produced the proof or counterexample and people checked it'). Against this, the body's AI Use note says the authors produced the proof they present and drew only 'somewhat' on ChatGPT's proof, i.e. their own mathematical work went into what's in the paper, not pure verification of the AI's output — closer to `assisted`. I lean `assisted` because the paper explicitly separates 'was found by ChatGPT' (the abstract, discussing origin) from 'was produced by the authors' (the AI Use section, discussing the actual presented argument), and the latter is more specific and should govern. A reader could reasonably code this `generated` instead.
what_would_settle_it: The authors' full 'AI Use' section or any accompanying blog/talk describing exactly how much of the final written proof is verbatim or close paraphrase of ChatGPT's output versus independently reconstructed — e.g. did the authors independently verify Theorem 1 from scratch after seeing the AI's claim, or did they mainly clean up and rewrite the AI's argument? Either would resolve whether this is closer to `generated` (model proof, human-checked) or `assisted` (model idea, human-proved).

outcome: The general conjecture remains open, but several papers since 26 January 2024 settled Vaught's conjecture for further restricted classes of theories: countable complete theories with a definable infinite discrete linear order (Tanović, arXiv:2212.13605 v3, March 2024), theories of partial orders admitting a finite lexicographic decomposition and unions of products of rooted trees (Kurilić, arXiv:2601.03155 and arXiv:2606.12014, 2026), and the omega-Vaught's-conjecture for Ehrenfeucht theories via a Scott-analysis framework (arXiv:2606.15205, 2026).

disputes.summary: Robin Knight has announced (2002, 2007) a purported counterexample to Vaught's conjecture and the topological Vaught conjecture; as of the most recent secondary sources found (through 2021, and no update located in the 2024-2026 window), it has not been verified or published in a form the community accepts. No new development on this dispute was found within the window, so it does not change the status here, but it is the single most consequential open thread on this problem and is noted for completeness.

summary: I treated this as the general first-order Vaught conjecture (finite/ℵ₀/2^ℵ₀ trichotomy for countable models of a countable complete theory), per the statement given, and searched for anything that changed the state of that conjecture since 26 January 2024. Nothing resolved or refuted the conjecture itself. Several genuine partial results (cases of the conjecture, in the §3.1 sense of restricting rather than varying the question) appeared in the window: (1) arXiv:2212.13605 (Tanović), 'Vaught's conjecture for theories of discretely ordered structures' — v1 predates the frozen revision (Dec 2022) but v3, dated 24 March 2024, is the version that proves the final result (continuum-many countable models for any countable complete theory with a definable infinite discrete linear order); I date the event to the v3 posting since that is the first written form of the completed argument, per §6.3's rule to use the first written argument. (2) Miloš Kurilić's 2026 papers on partial orders admitting a finite lexicographic decomposition (arXiv:2601.03155) and unions of products of rooted trees (arXiv:2606.12014), each proving VC for those specific classes. (3) arXiv:2606.15205, 'Scott Analysis below the Vaught Ordinal', which proves the ω-Vaught's-conjecture (a known strengthening/variant, not identical to the classical conjecture) for Ehrenfeucht theories — this is arguably a 'related problem' under §3.1 rather than a strict case, since the ω-VC is a different statement, though it specializes to VC-relevant consequences for that class; I lean toward counting it as informative context rather than the primary basis for 'partial' status, and rest that status mainly on the Tanović and Kurilić results, which are unambiguous cases. I read the arXiv:2508.06854 Pillay–Tanović item as a survey, not a new result. None of these papers mention any AI system, machine learning, automated theorem proving, or Lean/Coq formalization anywhere I could check (abstracts, and for the two I could render as text, fuller content); all are traditional human-authored proofs in the classical style of this literature, which has a decades-long tradition of chipping away at VC one class of theories at a time. I also checked for any AI-related developments on Vaught's conjecture generally (searches for AI-assisted proofs, Lean formalizations, DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository) and found nothing connecting any AI system to this problem in any way. The long-outstanding Robin Knight counterexample claim (2002/2007) remains, as far as I could determine, unverified, with no update found in the window; I recorded it as a dispute rather than letting it drive the status, since nothing changed about it during the window.
competing_reading: One could argue that arXiv:2606.15205's ω-Vaught's-conjecture result is a 'related problem' (a different, stated variant) rather than a case of the classical conjecture named in the Wikipedia bullet, in which case it should be excluded from the basis for 'partial' and only cited in summary as related. This would not change the overall status, since the Tanović and Kurilić results independently establish 'partial' on their own as clear cases (restrictions to specific theory classes) of the exact statement in the bullet.
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution of the ℵ₁-model case under ¬CH (the one case Morley's theorem leaves open), or verification/refutation of Robin Knight's long-standing counterexample claim, would settle the general conjecture. Absent that, the question of whether the ω-Vaught's-conjecture result should count as a case versus a variant would be settled by a closer reading of how the ω-VC modifies the hypotheses of the classical statement.

outcome: Since 26 January 2024, the general Virasoro conjecture (for all smooth projective varieties, all genera) remains open, but several further special/restricted cases have been proved by human mathematicians using traditional methods: the genus-0 and genus-1 parts of a generalized Virasoro conjecture for semisimple CohFTs (Guo–Zhang, arXiv:2502.18895, Feb 2025), a proof of the genus-1 Virasoro conjecture on the ambient state space of smooth Fano complete intersections (Guo–Zhang–Zhou, arXiv:2608.29870, Aug 2026), and a proof of Virasoro constraints for the relative Gromov-Witten theory of all smooth projective effective orbifold curves, from which the absolute Jiang-Tseng Virasoro conjecture follows for such curves (Hu–Jin–Ke–Lu–Tseng–Wu, arXiv:2609.01300, Sep 2026). A related paper connecting the Virasoro conjecture to the λg-conjecture (Xin Wang, arXiv:2412.05287, Nov 2024) also proves the λg-conjecture in new cases assuming/using Virasoro-conjecture machinery, but is a related/derived result rather than a case of the Virasoro conjecture itself.
summary: The Virasoro conjecture as stated (a certain generating function encoding the Gromov-Witten invariants of a smooth projective variety is fixed by an action of half the Virasoro algebra) remains open in general — it is known for genus 0 (Liu-Tian, 1998), for semisimple CohFTs and some toric/flag/Grassmannian/curve cases from before the frozen date, and (per the article) in all genera only for a point and Calabi-Yau 3-folds. Since 26 January 2024 several further cases have been settled by traditional (non-AI) mathematics: (1) Guo-Zhang (arXiv:2502.18895, Feb 2025) prove ancestor and generalized Virasoro conjectures for semisimple CohFTs in full and verify the genus-0 part more generally; (2) Guo-Zhang-Zhou (arXiv:2608.29870, Aug 2026) prove the genus-1 Virasoro conjecture on the ambient state space of Fano complete intersections via wall-crossing and quantum Lefschetz methods; (3) Hu-Jin-Ke-Lu-Tseng-Wu (arXiv:2609.01300, Sep 2026) prove Virasoro constraints for relative Gromov-Witten theory of all smooth projective effective orbifold curves, yielding the absolute Jiang-Tseng Virasoro conjecture for such curves as a corollary. Each of these is a genuine case of the stated problem (a restriction to a class of varieties/genus), not a variant, so status is 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the settled cases go the way the conjecture predicts; no counterexample). I read all three papers via fetches of their arXiv abstract pages; none mentions any AI system, language model, or machine-learning tool anywhere — these are traditional human-proved results in algebraic geometry using wall-crossing formulas, quantum Lefschetz theory, and CohFT/Frobenius-manifold techniques. I also searched broadly for any AI/LLM connection to the Virasoro conjecture or nearby Gromov-Witten work (including AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve-style automated theorem proving) and found nothing relevant; one superficially matching hit, arXiv:2510.21741 'Virasoro algebra and Sugawara constructions formally in Lean' (Kytölä, Oct 2025), is an unrelated Lean formalization of the Virasoro algebra's representation theory in a different (non-Gromov-Witten) context, not a formalization of this conjecture, and its page gave no information about AI tool use in any case. I did not find a paper claiming the full/general Virasoro conjecture was proved or disproved in the window. The triage's two 'found' items check out as real, on-topic, human-authored partial results; I found one additional in-window partial result (arXiv:2502.18895) the triage did not surface, and one related-but-distinct result (arXiv:2412.05287, connecting Virasoro to the λg-conjecture) that I judged a related problem rather than a direct case, discussed in summary rather than counted toward status.
competing_reading: One could argue the Xin Wang λg-conjecture paper (arXiv:2412.05287, Nov 2024) should also count as 'partial' progress on the Virasoro conjecture itself, since it proves the λg-conjecture unconditionally in genus 0 and 1 and ties it to Virasoro constraints; I read it as a related/derived conjecture (the λg-conjecture, a distinct statement about Hodge integrals) rather than a restriction of the Virasoro conjecture's own generating-function statement, so I did not use it as the status-defining event. If a reader defines 'the problem' more broadly to include consequences for closely tied conjectures, this event could be pulled earlier (Nov 2024) without changing ai_role or resolution_direction.
what_would_settle_it: A closer reading of arXiv:2412.05287's proof to see whether it establishes new instances of the Virasoro conjecture itself (rather than only using Virasoro as a hypothesis/tool for the λg-conjecture) would settle whether it belongs in status_sources.

outcome: No source found that settles, refutes, or otherwise moves the still-open direction of Vitushkin's conjecture (whether a purely unrectifiable compact set with non-sigma-finite H^1 measure necessarily has zero analytic capacity) since 26 January 2024; the only nearby activity is work framed by its own authors as progress adjacent to, not a resolution of, that direction.
summary: Vitushkin's conjecture (a compact K subset of C with finite H^1 measure is removable for bounded analytic functions iff it meets every rectifiable curve in a set of zero length) was already settled in the H^1-sigma-finite case before the frozen revision's date: Guy David proved it in 1998 for the finite-H^1-measure case, and combined with Tolsa's 2002-03 semiadditivity result this gives the full sigma-finite case. Mattila (1986) and later Jones-Murai showed one direction fails outright in the non-sigma-finite case (a set with zero Favard length but positive analytic capacity). The remaining open question, per the Wikipedia article and the literature, is whether the other implication holds in the non-sigma-finite setting: does purely unrectifiable / zero-Favard-length imply zero analytic capacity there? I searched extensively for any 2024-2026 work bearing on this open direction. The one paper the triage flagged, Dabrowski-Villa 'Analytic capacity and dimension of sets with plenty of big projections' (arXiv:2204.05804), was in fact first posted in April 2022 -- its only 2024 event is a June 2024 revision (v2), and its 2025 appearance is the Trans. AMS journal publication, which under Sec. 6.3 does not count as the dating event since the first written argument predates the window. Substantively, the paper proves a lower bound on analytic capacity for sets with 'plenty of big projections' (PBP), a different (sufficient-condition) class of sets, and is described by the authors themselves only as marking 'progress on an old conjecture of Vitushkin,' not as resolving the open implication. A second, genuinely 2024-dated paper, Dabrowski's solo 'Favard length and quantitative rectifiability' (arXiv:2408.03919, submitted 7 August 2024), proves a quantitative Besicovitch projection theorem (Ahlfors-regular sets with large Favard length contain big pieces of Lipschitz graphs) and again is framed by the author only as 'progress on Vitushkin's conjecture,' addressing quantitative/Favard-length questions rather than settling the stated non-sigma-finite implication. I found no paper, announcement, or digestion claiming the open direction itself was proved, disproved, or otherwise directly moved since 26 January 2024. I also searched for any AI/LLM connection to this problem or to the surrounding literature (analytic capacity, geometric measure theory, Favard length) and found none -- the AI-theorem-proving hits that surfaced (AlphaGeometry, LLM provers/verifiers) are unrelated fields with no crossover to this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Dabrowski-Villa PBP result and the 2024 Favard-length paper are close enough to the conjecture's spirit (both explicitly invoke Vitushkin and Favard length) that they deserve a 'progress' status rather than 'open.' I did not adopt this reading because both results concern a different, restricted class of sets (PBP sets, or Ahlfors-regular sets) rather than settling any additional case of the stated open implication (purely unrectifiable / non-sigma-finite implies zero capacity) -- per Sec 3.1 this makes them related-problem results, not case results, and the authors' own framing ('progress on', not 'resolves a case of') supports treating them as adjacent rather than as narrowing the stated question.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement proving (or disproving) that every purely unrectifiable compact set with non-sigma-finite H^1 measure has zero analytic capacity, or explicitly resolving that implication for some non-trivial subclass in a way that reduces the stated open territory -- as opposed to establishing sufficient conditions (PBP, Ahlfors-regularity, large Favard length) for positive capacity on sets outside the conjecture's hypothesis.

outcome: The conjecture remains open, but the best known universal constant in the approximate form γ(G□H) ≥ c·γ(G)γ(H) was raised twice within the window: Steiner (arXiv:2606.14414, 2026-06-12) improved Clark & Suen's 2000 bound of 1/2 to (5+√73)/24 ≈ 0.5643, and Aliabadi & Krop (arXiv:2607.01109) then raised it further, first to ≈0.5809 (v1, 2026-07-01), then — after a withdrawn v2 flagged in the arXiv listing as containing an 'algebraic mistake' — to a corrected 2/3 ≈ 0.667 in v3 (2026-09-09). The claimed bipartite case-restriction preprint (arXiv:2509.10473, Hosking) and the Zenodo 'Impossible Descent' Lean 4 item do not add genuine progress (see summary).

ai.basis_quote: AI disclosure: During the preparation of this work, the authors used Claude (Fable 5) for language editing and computational assistance related to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4.

disputes.summary: Aliabadi & Krop v2 (posted 2026-07-02, one day after v1) was withdrawn; the arXiv math.CO July 2026 listing records the withdrawal comment 'Algebraic mistake.' v3 (2026-09-09) states the authors 'fixed the argument and made an improvement,' raising the claimed constant from v1's ≈0.5809 to 2/3. The v1 constant (0.5809) itself was never withdrawn or corrected — only v2 was pulled — so v1's result appears to stand as an intermediate step, superseded by v3's stronger 2/3 bound.

summary: Vizing's conjecture (γ(G□H) ≥ γ(G)γ(H) for all graphs G, H) is still open. Within the window, the universal-constant approximate form saw two genuine improvements: Raphael Steiner (arXiv:2606.14414, 2026-06-12, no AI mentioned) raised Clark & Suen's (2000) bound of 1/2 to (5+√73)/24 ≈ 0.5643 — the first improvement on that constant since 2000. Mohsen Aliabadi and Elliot Krop (arXiv:2607.01109) then improved it further: v1 (2026-07-01) claimed ≈0.5809 with no AI acknowledgement; v2 (2026-07-02) was withdrawn, flagged in the arXiv combinatorics listing as containing an 'algebraic mistake'; v3 (2026-09-09) fixed the argument, restructured the paper around Theorem 1.1 (a packing-based inequality) and Theorem 1.3 (the headline 2/3 bound), and carries an explicit AI disclosure that Claude (Fable 5) was used 'for language editing and computational assistance related to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4.' That sentence — the authors' own account, quoted directly from the v3 HTML — is the basis for `ai_role: assisted`: it names AI contribution to the derivation of specific numbered theorems, not merely proofreading or formalisation, so it clears the `none` bar. Neither of these bound-improvement papers has yet received an expert digestion (no Tao blog post, no Quanta coverage, no journal acceptance found); they remain unreviewed preprints, which is why status is `progress` rather than `claimed` — `claimed` per the rubric attaches to resolution/certificate claims, and a moved bound on a still-open problem is `progress` by definition regardless of review status. Separately, two lower-credibility items surfaced by triage were examined and found not to constitute progress: (1) arXiv:2509.10473 (Noah Hosking, math.GM, v1 2025-08-26 through v5 2026-08-23) does not prove the conjecture for any concrete case such as 'k-regular bipartite graphs with k≥7' as triage's note suggested — reading the full text shows it only proves a conditional inequality with an unresolved additive-deficit term (Remark 1), explicitly leaving the reduction to 'domination-neutral leaf deletions' as future work; it is math.GM (not math.CO), never rigorously closes any case, and so is not a genuine partial result. (2) The Zenodo item 'Vizing's Impossible Descent' (Jonathan Reed, posted 2026-08-08) claims a full Lean 4 proof by contradiction but is self-published with no corroboration, no peer engagement, and no visible acknowledgements section; per the rubric a machine-checked certificate no expert has reviewed would be `claimed` at best, but there is no evidence anyone besides the author has run or examined the Lean development, and no trace of it anywhere else (no arXiv cross-post, no mathoverflow/blog discussion), so it is treated as non-credible noise rather than a countable event, consistent with the triage note. I also checked arXiv:2608.29595 ('GPT, the Counterexample Machine' by Suvrit Sra), which surfaced in AI+Vizing search results; it documents ~16 GPT-discovered counterexamples in combinatorics/convexity/analysis but does not mention Vizing's conjecture at all — a false positive, not evidence for this record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Aliabadi-Krop v3 AI disclosure ('language editing and computational assistance related to the proofs') is ambiguous enough to read as `none` if 'computational assistance' meant only checking algebra rather than generating proof steps — the rubric's `none` bucket explicitly includes debugging and proofreading. I read 'computational assistance related to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4' as naming a specific mathematical contribution to those theorems (not just language), which pushes it past the `none` threshold into `assisted`, but the sentence does not spell out exactly what Claude computed, so a stricter reading landing on `none` is defensible.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or newly settled case of Vojta's general conjecture on heights of points on algebraic varieties over algebraic number fields has appeared since 26 January 2024; all located work addresses variants (the abc-conjecture analogue over function fields, algebraic tori, or entire curves in toric varieties via Nevanlinna theory) or narrow K-stability-based sufficient conditions that do not amount to a settled case of the stated height-inequality conjecture, and no AI involvement was found anywhere in this area.
summary: Vojta's conjecture, as stated in the frozen Wikipedia bullet, is the general height-inequality conjecture for points on algebraic varieties over algebraic number fields (Vojta, 1987), a broad generalization encompassing Roth's theorem, Mordell/Faltings, and the abc conjecture as special cases. I ran targeted searches for any proof, disproof, or newly-settled case since 26 January 2024 and found only work on adjacent but distinct statements: (1) arXiv:2410.19395 (Oct 2024, updated Feb 2026) proves 'Vojta's abc conjecture' for entire curves in toric varieties highly ramified over the boundary — this is the Nevanlinna-theoretic complex-analytic analogue (entire curves, not rational/integral points over number fields), a genuinely different mathematical object sharing only the name; (2) the ScienceDirect/JPAA 2025 paper (an updated version of arXiv:2106.15881, originally 2021) proves the abc-analogue for algebraic tori over function fields, not number fields; (3) the Monatshefte 2024 GCD-inequality paper is explicitly 'inspired by' the conjecture rather than a proof of any of its cases; (4) arXiv:2401.01428 (Jan 2024, essentially at the window boundary) uses K-stability of Q-Fano varieties to exhibit settings (a torus-invariant divisor on toric Fano varieties) where Vojta's conjecture's predicted inequality holds — this is a narrow sufficient-condition/special-setting result on toric varieties, arguably closer to a case but still a restricted geometric class rather than a case that changes what a careful reader would write about the general conjecture, and it is dated essentially at the frozen revision's timestamp with no indication of being later strengthened; (5) arXiv:2508.11888 (Aug 2025, updated Nov/Dec 2025) reorganizes Vojta's own 1991 proof of the Mordell conjecture (Faltings' theorem) using Arakelov geometry and a newer arithmetic Siu inequality — this is a re-proof of an already-known special case (abelian/curves case, settled by Faltings 1991, itself predating the window by decades), not new progress on the conjecture. The Wikipedia article on Vojta's conjecture itself does not mention any post-2024 developments; its only cited resolved special case remains Faltings' 1991 theorem for abelian varieties, which long predates the window. No source anywhere in this search mentioned AI, machine learning, or any AI system in connection with Vojta's conjecture; the only AI-mathematics story that surfaced in these searches (an AI-found counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture) is an unrelated problem that a naive keyword search could conflate with this one. I therefore agree with the triage's 'none' verdict and its classification of all found items as variants rather than cases.
competing_reading: arXiv:2401.01428's K-stability result could be argued to be a genuine 'case' of Vojta's conjecture (a restriction to toric Fano varieties with a specific divisor) rather than a 'related problem,' which under §3.1 would warrant `partial` status with `resolution_direction: confirmed`. I did not classify it this way because (a) it is dated January 2, 2024, essentially indistinguishable from the frozen revision's timestamp of January 26, 2024, so even if counted it contributes negligible information about post-window progress, and (b) from the abstract alone it is unclear whether it establishes new cases or surveys/re-derives previously known settings connecting K-stability to the conjecture; I could not access the full text to confirm the precise scope of what is newly proved.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full text of arXiv:2401.01428 to determine precisely which toric Fano varieties and divisors it newly establishes the conjecture for, and whether any of that is dated after 26 January 2024 (e.g., in a later arXiv revision) or was already known before the paper. Also, a direct search of Paul Vojta's own publication list and any survey articles or ICM-type reports post-2024 on Diophantine approximation would help confirm no case has been missed.

outcome: The Andersen-Kashaev volume conjecture (the modern operator-theoretic form of the volume conjecture) was proved for a new large class of one-cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds admitting 'FAMED' geometric triangulations, including all knots in S3 with at most 12 crossings and all knots with a triangulation of 23 or fewer tetrahedra (over 42,000 knots verified); additional papers proved the (Chen-Yang variant of the) conjecture for large-parameter Dehn fillings of twist-knot manifolds and, separately, for all hyperbolic double twist knots. The general conjecture, for arbitrary hyperbolic knots, remains open.
summary: Since 26 January 2024 there has been real, substantive progress on cases of the volume conjecture, but no AI or machine-learning system was involved in producing any of it, and the general conjecture (for arbitrary hyperbolic knots) is still open. The most significant development is the 'FAMED geometric triangulations' program: Ohtsuki and collaborators introduced FAMED triangulations in an October 2024 preprint (arXiv:2410.10776, submitted 2024-10-14) and proved that the Andersen-Kashaev volume conjecture (the version of the conjecture phrased via Teichmuller TQFT partition functions and the Neumann-Zagier potential, closely related to Kashaev's original invariant) holds for every hyperbolic 3-manifold admitting such a triangulation, exhibiting these for every hyperbolic twist knot and the first 42,000 hyperbolic knots in S3. A December 2025 follow-up (arXiv:2512.17437, 'Famed by computer') extends this by computational search (using Regina and SnapPy) to all knots with at most 12 crossings and all knots whose complement triangulates with at most 23 tetrahedra, again over 42,000 examples. This is scope-appropriate: it settles the stated conjecture for a large but restricted class of knot complements (a case, not the whole problem), so it is classified 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (the conjecture held for every example checked; no counterexample was found or claimed). The role of the computer here (Regina/SnapPy triangulation enumeration) is exhaustive rigorous search/computer algebra, not an AI system, so ai_role is 'none'. Two further preprints add other partial results within the window: arXiv:2501.00225 (submitted 2024-12-31, revised through May 2025) proves the volume conjecture for all hyperbolic double twist knots using complexified tetrahedra and SL(2,C) representations, with no AI or ML mentioned anywhere in the methodology; arXiv:2410.20489 (submitted 2024-10-27) proves the Chen-Yang variant of the volume conjecture (a related but distinct q-deformation with q approaching a root of unity along the unit circle rather than 1) for Dehn-filled twist-knot manifolds, but only for sufficiently large Dehn-filling parameters, which is itself a further restriction. A February 2025 preprint (arXiv:2502.18575) trains a feedforward neural network to predict hyperbolic volume from the adjoint Jones polynomial (99.34% accuracy) and uses this purely as a numerical exploration tool to motivate an improved conjectural statement about the optimal phase for colored Jones polynomial asymptotics; the network's output is not itself a proof, is not incorporated into any theorem, and the authors show a closed-form function of the polynomial achieves comparable accuracy without any learning, so this is 'none' involvement (a numerics-motivated conjecture refinement, not a case of the stated problem being settled, and not AI-produced mathematics). No expert digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, a survey) of the FAMED result was found, and it has not appeared in a journal; the December 2025 preprint is very recent (this deep dive is dated 2026-09-22, about 9 months after that preprint), so it is plausible a digestion exists that a search did not surface, but none was found. Given the absence of expert digestion or journal acceptance, and that these are all preprints, the correct status is 'partial' (a case was settled) rather than 'resolved' — no single event fully resolves the general conjecture, and the individual case-results themselves are still only preprints. The event date recorded is the first (Oct 2024) FAMED preprint, the earliest genuinely new post-window result found; the December 2025 computational extension and the double-twist-knot and Chen-Yang results are described here rather than given separate records, per the instruction to consolidate on one decisive event and describe others in summary.
competing_reading: One could argue the December 2025 'Famed by computer' preprint (2512.17437), rather than the October 2024 theory preprint (2410.10776), should be the dated 'event', since it is the one that actually reaches the widely-quoted '42,000+ knots, all ≤12 crossings' headline figure via computer search; the October 2024 paper proves the general FAMED criterion and applies it to twist knots and an initial batch of 42,000 knots, so the two papers' claimed knot counts overlap and the later paper is best read as extending the computational search rather than being the first appearance of the result. Either dating supports the same 'partial' classification. Separately, one could argue the Chen-Yang large-parameter Dehn-filling result and the neural-network-motivated conjecture refinement are 'related problems' (different q-limits, or a different conjectural statement) rather than cases of the stated conjecture, in which case they would not count toward this record at all; I have read them as adjacent partial evidence worth mentioning rather than as the load-bearing event, so this reading does not change the recorded status.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a survey, a blog post by a specialist such as Ohtsuki or a Quanta/Tao-style write-up) confirming the FAMED-triangulation proof is correct and assessing how much of the knot volume conjecture landscape it now covers would move the FAMED result from 'partial-preprint' toward a stronger evidentiary footing; journal acceptance of any of these preprints would strengthen confidence further. A search of the Kashaev invariant / volume conjecture literature for any AI-lab announcement (e.g. a foundation-model mathematics team claiming a proof) between January 2024 and September 2026 turned up nothing, so nothing here is contingent on missing an AI claim, only on missing an expert readthrough of preprints that already exist.

outcome: A December 2024 preprint by Yong-Geun Oh claimed a proof of the general Weinstein conjecture (and Arnold's chord conjecture) via contact instanton moduli theory; the author withdrew the claim in September 2025 after finding he could not rule out the associated Reeb orbit being constant, leaving the general conjecture open. No AI system was involved at any point.
summary: The Weinstein conjecture (does every regular compact contact-type level set of a Hamiltonian on a symplectic manifold carry a periodic Reeb orbit?) remains open in general since 26 January 2024. The one substantive event in the window is arXiv:2412.20731, 'Contact instantons and Proofs of Weinstein's conjecture and Arnold's chord conjecture,' submitted 30 December 2024 by Yong-Geun Oh, which claimed a full proof of the general Weinstein conjecture using contact-instanton moduli theory and Legendrianization of contactomorphisms. I opened both v1 and v2 of the arXiv entry. On 17 September 2025 the author posted v2 with a withdrawal comment reading (quoted verbatim from the arXiv comments field): 'It is still a possibility that the associated isospeed Reeb orbit could be a constant orbit which I cannot rule out at the moment. Sorry for the long delay realizing this.' This is a gap in a key step (ruling out a constant orbit), not a cosmetic fix, and the paper was never digested or accepted before the retraction, so the correct status is progress/incident under §6.1: an announced claim that was withdrawn, dated to the claim (since no resolution followed) rather than to the withdrawal — but per the instructions I recorded event.date as the withdrawal (2025-09-17) since that is the point at which the record can attest the claim did not stand; the claim itself (2024-12-30) predates the window's midpoint but is itself within the window and is the operative fact plus its retraction. No AI system, LLM, or automated proof assistant appears anywhere in the paper, its arXiv metadata, or any secondary coverage I found — Oh's argument is entirely traditional analytic/geometric contact-topology work. I separately checked the triage's flagged namesake, 'High dimension Weinstein conjecture and its application to Schiffer conjecture' (Zeitschrift für angewandte Mathematik und Physik, 2026): this is unambiguously a different 'Weinstein conjecture' — Payne's 1955 planar inequality Λ₁ ≥ λ₂ between the buckling and membrane eigenvalues, generalized to higher dimensions and applied to the Schiffer conjecture — with no connection to Reeb dynamics, contact geometry, or Hamiltonian flows. It is out of scope as a namesake, confirming the triage's read. I also checked arXiv:2508.01113 ('On the contact type conjecture for exact magnetic systems'), which invokes the (still-open) strong Weinstein conjecture as a hypothesis to build magnetic systems with prescribed contact-type properties, rather than proving any case of the Weinstein conjecture itself — also out of scope as a related-but-distinct problem. I checked the current Wikipedia 'Weinstein conjecture' article, which reports only the pre-2024 state (Taubes's 2007 dimension-3 proof) with nothing from 2024–2026. I checked the 'List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence' Wikipedia page and it contains no mention of the Weinstein conjecture, contact geometry, or Reeb dynamics. A March 2025 survey ('A survey on the Weinstein conjecture,' Yanqiao Ding, Frontiers of Mathematics in China) exists but its full text is paywalled; the accessible abstract/reference list gave no indication of a new theorem proved after January 2024, and no mention of AI. I did not find any other proof attempt, partial result, or bound-moving paper on the general (higher-dimensional) Weinstein conjecture within the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is simply 'open' with no_change_found true, treating a withdrawn, never-verified preprint as not a 'happening' worth recording at all. I chose 'progress'/'incident' instead because §6.1 and §7 explicitly instruct that a withdrawn AI-adjacent-looking claim is itself an instructive event that must not be silently dropped, and because a serious, specific, later-retracted full-generality claim by an established expert in the field is exactly the kind of incident the schema is built to capture, even though in this case no AI was involved. The dating of event.date to the withdrawal rather than the original claim is also debatable; an argument could be made to date it 2024-12-30 (the claim) instead, since that is 'the claim' per §6.1's ai_role incident guidance for AI claims. I used the later date because it is the point at which the full story (claim + failure) is established, and because the instructions say 'dated to the claim' specifically for AI incidents, which this is not.
what_would_settle_it: A published errata/corrigendum from Oh explicitly stating whether the gap was later closed, or a new preprint (by Oh or others) building on or repairing the contact-instanton approach, would settle whether this remains a dead end or becomes a fresh claim. Access to the full text of Ding's March 2025 survey (currently paywalled) could also reveal whether any other 2024-2025 partial result exists that my searches missed.

outcome: The exact values of Bloch's constant and Landau's constant remain unknown, but both lower bounds moved: Frank Wikström (Lund University) posted two computer-assisted preprints in Aug/Sep 2026 improving the lower bound on Bloch's constant to B >= sqrt(3)/4 + 0.0153 (superseding Chen-Gauthier's sqrt(3)/4 + 2e-4 and Xiong's sqrt(3)/4 + 3e-4), and the lower bound on Landau's constant to L > 0.5100305329006052049176652 (superseding Chen-Shiba's 0.5 + 2e-8). Neither paper claims or approaches the exact value; both are preprints, not yet digested by outside experts.

summary: Wikipedia's bullet asks for the exact value of Landau's and Bloch's constants; the triage record correctly identified the Bloch's constant preprint (arXiv:2608.17660, 'An improved lower bound for Bloch's constant', posted 18 Aug 2026) but had not read it. I opened it, plus a companion preprint by the same author, Frank Wikström of Lund University, on Landau's constant (arXiv:2609.23236, 'A computer-assisted lower bound for Landau's constant', posted 19 Sep 2026), which the triage pass missed entirely. Both improve lower bounds via rigorous computer-assisted proofs (Arb interval arithmetic at 40-80 decimal digits, verifying certificates independently of the floating-point LP solvers used only for discovery): B >= sqrt(3)/4 + 0.0153 = 0.448312701..., up from Chen-Gauthier's sqrt(3)/4 + 2e-4 and Xiong's sqrt(3)/4 + 3e-4 (both well before the frozen revision, so genuinely superseded within the window); and L > 0.5100305329006052049176652, up from Chen-Shiba's 0.5 + 2e-8. Neither result touches the exact value the bullet asks about -- both constants remain open, with the classical Ahlfors-Grunsky conjectured exact values (B ~ 0.47186, and the corresponding value for L) still unproven, as confirmed by the current Wikipedia article on Bloch's theorem (complex analysis), which does not yet reflect either 2026 preprint. Per Sec 3.1, an 'are there infinitely many X' or 'what is the exact value' question is not advanced by a bound moving unless the bound IS the question -- here Wikipedia's bullet is phrased as asking for the exact value, not for a record bound, so strictly the bound movement is adjacent rather than dispositive; but because Landau's/Bloch's constants are traditionally tracked via their best-known bounds in the literature (MathWorld, the Wikipedia article itself reports bounds as the state of the art), I classify this as progress rather than pure no_change_found, following the spirit of tracking the state of a constant-valued open problem. Both papers are single-author preprints with no expert digestion, journal acceptance, or independent verification by named experts found; I found no citations, blog digestions, or follow-up commentary on either as of 22 Sep 2026 (both are only weeks/days old). The AI disclosure in the Bloch's constant paper is explicit and unusually candid: two named systems (OpenAI Codex GPT-5.6 Sol, Anthropic Claude Opus 5.0) were used for 'mathematical brainstorming and proof auditing' and to help develop verification scripts, but the author states he independently reviewed, checked, and takes full responsibility for all content, and the actual mathematical certificates are re-derived and checked by a separate rigorous interval-arithmetic system independent of any AI or even the LP solver. This matches Sec 6.2's explicit list of non-qualifying AI uses (checking, proofreading, debugging, suggesting strategies) rather than 'assisted' (authors would need to say the AI produced part of the mathematics itself, which this disclosure does not say). The Landau's constant companion paper (2609.23236) discloses no AI use at all in the sections I could access. I could not extract a clean acknowledgements section from the Landau's constant paper's HTML/PDF; my search for one returned only metadata, so I cannot rule out an AI disclosure there, though none was surfaced by two separate fetch attempts.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'open' with no_change_found true, since the bullet's literal question (the *exact value*) has not moved even slightly -- a lower bound moving does not narrow where the exact value could be in the way an existence question would be narrowed by ruling out cases, and Sec 3.1 is explicit that record/bound movements only count when the bound itself IS the question. Landau's and Bloch's constants are not phrased in Wikipedia's bullet as 'what is the best known bound' but as 'what is the exact value', which under a strict reading is unmoved. I lean 'progress' because the literature and Wikipedia's own article for this problem present these constants primarily through their best-known bounds (there is no other quantitative sense in which 'progress' on an unknown exact constant can be measured short of resolving it), but a stricter reader could reasonably mark this 'open'/no_change_found.
what_would_settle_it: Either the exact values are proven (matching or refuting the Ahlfors-Grunsky conjectured closed forms), which would move this to resolved/claimed with a direction; or clarity on whether Wikipedia's phrasing intends 'exact value' literally (favoring open/no_change_found) versus tracking best-known bounds (favoring progress) would remove the ambiguity in competing_reading.

outcome: No result found that narrows the gap between the known lower bound (0.082n) and upper bound (n/6 + o(n)) on the maximum pathwidth of n-vertex cubic graphs since 26 January 2024; the Fomin–Høie (2005/2006) bounds remain the state of the art.
summary: The problem asks for the largest possible pathwidth of an n-vertex cubic (3-regular) graph, expressed as a fraction of n. As of January 2024 the known bounds, both due to Fomin and Høie ('Pathwidth of cubic graphs and exact algorithms', Information Processing Letters, 2005/2006), are: pathwidth ≤ n/6 + o(n) for all sufficiently large cubic graphs, and there exist cubic graphs with pathwidth ≥ 0.082n, leaving an open gap between ~0.082n and ~0.167n. I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 work that narrows this specific gap — general pathwidth-of-cubic-graphs bounds, treewidth-of-cubic-graphs results, and adjacent pathwidth literature (path partitions in subcubic graphs, polynomial pathwidth bounds for graphs edge-coverable by k shortest paths, pathwidth-η deletion kernelization, spectral treewidth lower bounds) — and found nothing that addresses the cubic-graph pathwidth extremal question itself. The current Wikipedia 'Pathwidth' article (fetched live) still states the bounds in exactly the 2006 form, with no updates. Related but out-of-scope 2024–2026 papers exist (e.g. on treewidth-of-cubic-graphs NP-completeness, and pathwidth bounds for other graph classes), but none change what a careful reader would write in this bullet. This agrees with the triage pass's 'none' verdict; I do not disagree with it.
competing_reading: None of the adjacent papers found (e.g. 'A polynomial bound on the pathwidth of graphs edge-coverable by k shortest paths', arXiv 2510.02901, or treewidth-of-cubic-graphs NP-completeness work) bear on the extremal question asked here; they concern different graph classes or different parameters (treewidth vs. pathwidth, or different structural restrictions), so none is a plausible case of this problem under a looser reading.
what_would_settle_it: A paper that either exhibits cubic graphs with pathwidth exceeding 0.082n (improving the lower bound) or proves a pathwidth upper bound below n/6 for cubic graphs (improving Fomin–Høie's upper bound), for arbitrarily large n.

outcome: No proof, disproof, or new record for the maximum number of givens in a minimal Sudoku puzzle has appeared since 26 January 2024; the empirical record of 40 clues (found by forum user 'dobrichev', reported around 2010–2014, predating the window) remains the largest known minimal puzzle and is still unproven as an actual maximum.
summary: This bullet asks for the maximum number of givens (clues) a *minimal* Sudoku puzzle (one where removing any clue destroys uniqueness) can have. This is the mirror image of the famous 17-clue minimum problem, which was settled in 2012 (McGuire, Tugemann, Civario), but the maximum-givens question has no comparable exhaustive-search proof: it is a much larger, less constrained search space (the current record, 40 clues, was found by exhaustive/targeted computer search by the forum contributor known as 'dobrichev', with the relevant forum threads and Wikipedia record dating to roughly 2010-2014, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision). I searched broadly for any post-window movement: a new record above 40 clues, a proof that 40 (or some other number) is the true maximum, or any theoretical upper bound result. I found none. I also checked a 2023/2024 paper ('How Many Clues To Give? A Bilevel Formulation for the Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem', arXiv:2305.01697, journal version dated 7 March 2024 on ScienceDirect) which is superficially adjacent but addresses a different question — the minimum number of clues needed to pin down a *given* completed grid (MSCP), not the maximum number of givens compatible with minimality — so it is out of scope under §3.1 (a related/different problem, not a case of this one), and in any case its arXiv preprint predates the window. I also searched for any AI/LLM involvement specific to this combinatorial question; the only AI-and-Sudoku material I found (Sudoku-Bench, causal-language-modeling-on-logic-puzzles papers, Sakana AI's Sudoku work) concerns LLMs solving/reasoning about Sudoku puzzles generally (and performing poorly, e.g. sub-15% solve rates reported for o3-mini-high and Gemini 2.5 Pro on Sudoku variants), and has no connection to the maximum-givens-for-a-minimal-puzzle question. The Wikipedia 'Mathematics of Sudoku' article, as of this check, still states only that '40 clues' is the largest minimal puzzle found so far, with no update. Given the topic is a niche combinatorial/computational puzzle question mostly discussed on the enjoysudoku forum and personal collection pages, and I found nothing there or in the academic literature suggesting new activity, I classify this as open with no_change_found true, matching the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: None found — I found no borderline case or ambiguous result to weigh a different classification against. It is conceivable that a new record puzzle (e.g. 41+ clues) has been posted only on the enjoysudoku forum without being indexed by general web search or picked up by Wikipedia, since that forum is the primary venue for this niche pursuit and is not always well-crawled; I could not directly browse the current state of relevant forum threads (a direct fetch of one thread failed with a connection error) so I cannot fully rule this out.
what_would_settle_it: A post-26-January-2024 announcement (forum post, paper, or updated Wikipedia/Mathematics-of-Sudoku text) reporting either (a) a minimal Sudoku puzzle with more than 40 givens, or (b) a proof/exhaustive argument that 40 is the true maximum for minimal puzzles.

outcome: Chess remains unsolved: no proof of the game-theoretic outcome of the starting position under perfect play exists as of September 2026, and no serious claim to the contrary has been made.
summary: The question of what the game-theoretic outcome of a perfectly played game of chess is (win for White, win for Black, or draw) remains completely open as of September 2026, with no change since the frozen revision. The Wikipedia 'Solving chess' article states plainly that no complete solution in either the strong or weak sense is known and none is expected soon; this has not changed since January 2024. The only concrete progress in the relevant area since 2024 is on endgame tablebases: Niklas Fiekas and Marc Bourzutschky released a partial 8-piece tablebase ('op1', covering positions with an opposing pawn pair) in a Lichess blog post dated 2026-02-07. This was produced by exhaustive retrograde analysis — brute-force backward computation from checkmate/known-win positions — not by any AI or machine-learning system; the blog post explicitly describes the method as retrograde analysis. Even setting the AI question aside, this does not count under §3.1: the question 'what is the outcome of a perfectly played game from the start' is an existence/answer-type question that is only advanced by an actual determination of that outcome, not by extending tablebase coverage deeper into the endgame space (analogous to the rule that record-extension does not advance an infinitude question). I also checked for any AI lab claims of having solved or nearly solved chess (e.g., DeepMind, OpenAI) — searches turned up only chess-playing performance milestones (e.g., OpenAI's o3 winning a 2025 Kaggle chess exhibition) and AI-for-chess-puzzle-generation research, none of which bears on the theoretical outcome question, and no retraction-worthy claims either. A tangential arXiv paper title ('Semi-Strongly solved: a New Definition Leading Computer to Perfect Gameplay', Takizawa, Nov 2024) initially looked relevant but on inspection concerns 6x6 Othello, not chess, and introduces a new solving-strength category rather than reporting any chess result — it is an unrelated problem under §3.1 and was excluded. Expert consensus that perfect play likely results in a draw is unchanged from the 19th century (Steinitz, 1889) and remains unproven. No change to record for this problem.
competing_reading: None of the material found is even arguably in scope; there is no close call here. The 8-piece tablebase work is the closest thing to 'progress' in the surrounding literature, but it neither touches nor could touch the starting-position outcome question under any reasonable reading, since full 8-piece and beyond tablebases are still vastly short of the 32-piece starting position, and tablebase completion for a fixed piece count is a different (bounded, decidable) question from the game's true value.
what_would_settle_it: A weak solution of chess from the initial position (a proof, verified by experts, establishing the game's value as win/loss/draw with a strategy securing that outcome against any opposition) would resolve this. Short of that, nothing currently on the horizon (given 10^40+ legal positions) moves this question; a claimed breakthrough would need independent expert verification given the field's history of unverified claims.

outcome: No new bound, proof, or change to the perfect komi value for full-size (19x19) Go was found since 26 January 2024. Standard AI-derived estimates (KataGo/professional statistics suggesting 6-7 points under various rulesets) remain unchanged pre- and post-window. The one genuinely new, dated result in the window is a May 2024 arXiv paper rigorously solving 5x5 Go (a much smaller board, komi 24.5, no komi under area scoring) under the positional superko ruleset specifically — but this is a case of a related small-board problem, not a change to the stated 19x19 'perfect komi' question, and its underlying board result (Black wins by 25 points with no komi) was already established by van der Werf et al. in 2002/2003, well before the frozen revision.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the perfect (fair) value of komi in Go — implicitly the full 19x19 board, where 'perfect komi would make each game result in Jigo given perfect play by both sides' (per the Komi (Go) Wikipedia article). This value is not known with certainty because perfect play on 19x19 Go is computationally out of reach, and nothing in the 26 Jan 2024 – present window changes that: no proof, no new bound, no updated AI-derived estimate that supersedes the pre-2024 consensus (professional/computer statistics suggesting the fair value is around 6-7 points, with 7 argued as the theoretically likely odd integer under area scoring). I searched specifically for updated KataGo or other AI self-play estimates from 2024-2026 and found none beyond older (pre-2024, including 2020-era) forum and community discussion threads restating the same 6-7 point consensus. The one concrete, dated, in-window item I found is arXiv:2405.05594 ('Expected Work Search: Combining Win Rate and Proof Size Estimation', submitted 9 May 2024, Randall/Müller/Wei/Hayward, University of Alberta), which presents 'the first solution to the empty 5x5 board with the commonly used positional superko ruleset.' I fetched the abstract, introduction and full HTML text: the paper uses classical Monte Carlo Tree Search-style rollouts and Proof Number Search (no neural networks or learned evaluation functions in its reported results — the authors explicitly list 'machine learned evaluation functions' only as future work), so even if this counted, ai_role would be none. More importantly, this does not change the stated problem: (1) it concerns the 5x5 board, not 19x19, so it is at most a case of a much smaller instance of the general question, and general komi results on tiny boards do not constrain or inform the 19x19 answer in any established way; (2) the underlying combinatorial result for 5x5 Go without komi (Black wins by 25 points under Japanese-style rules) was already established by van der Werf et al. in 2002-2003 (predates the frozen revision by two decades); the 2024 paper's actual novelty is proving the same result holds rigorously under the stricter 'positional superko' rule variant (resolving a technical superko/GHI-problem complication), which is a ruleset technicality rather than a new komi value or a new case of the 'what is the perfect komi' question as commonly understood. I therefore classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true, consistent with the triage's `none` verdict, which I confirm rather than contradict.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2024 EWS paper is a genuine `partial` result: 5x5 Go is a legitimate case of 'Go' broadly construed, and rigorously nailing down its exact result under a previously-unresolved ruleset variant is new mathematical content produced within the window. Under a generous reading where 'the problem' is 'determine perfect komi for boards of various sizes' rather than specifically 19x19, this would count as `partial`/`progress` with `ai_role` `none`. I did not adopt this reading because (a) the base numerical result (25-point win, i.e. komi 24.5) was not new — only the ruleset rigor was — and (b) the Wikipedia bullet, read in context of the Go article's other sub-bullets, is most naturally about the standard 19x19 game where komi is actually used in practice, which is exactly the value that remains unknown.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous solution (or credible new AI/human-derived estimate that moves the consensus) for 19x19 perfect komi, or an explicit Wikipedia/community consensus that small-board superko results are considered a 'case' of this bullet, would settle the classification either way.

outcome: No change to the known bracket for the smallest Skewes number since January 2024: the upper bound remains e^727.951336105 (Saouter, Trudgian & Demichel, 2015) and the lower bound remains 1.39×10^17 (Platt & Trudgian). One 2025 paper refines the underlying error-term methodology for Lehman-type bounds but does not produce a new numerical crossover bound; one 2026 paper on 'generalized Skewes numbers' addresses a different (prime-race) problem, not this one.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks for the exact value of Skewes's number, i.e. the smallest x with π(x) > li(x). As of 26 January 2024 the state of the art was: upper bound Ξ < e^727.951336105 ≈ 1.398×10^316 (Saouter, Trudgian & Demichel 2015), no crossing below 10^19 (Büthe 2015), and lower bound Ξ > 1.39×10^17 (Platt & Trudgian). I found no post-2024-01-26 source that narrows this bracket, exhibits a value, or otherwise settles the question. The one clearly on-topic paper in the window is Michael Revers, 'New bounds in R.S. Lehman's estimates for the difference π(x)−li(x)' (arXiv:2501.04488, submitted 8 Jan 2025, revised 30 Jan 2025, later published in the Journal of Number Theory per ScienceDirect). It improves Lehman's 1966 error-term machinery (a new, sharper R₆ term, removal of a lower restriction on the parameter η, and adaptation to the Saouter-Trudgian-Demichel kernel), and reports roughly 30-34% tighter η values in numerical illustrations 'near 10^316' — but per the paper's own abstract and body, this is a methodological refinement, not a new certified numerical crossover bound; it does not claim to beat e^727.951336105, nor does it exhibit any new region below 10^19 where a crossing is shown to occur or be excluded. Because the bullet is a 'smallest value' question rather than a pure existence question, under §3.1 a bound that moves in either direction would count as progress — but I could not find that this paper (or anything else in the window) actually moved either the upper or lower numerical bound; it is best read as `progress` on tooling for future bound improvements rather than progress on the bound itself, so I classified as `open` / `no_change_found`. A second paper turned up in searches, arXiv:2603.20093 ('A Wasserstein metric approach to generalized Skewes' numbers. I. Prime number races', 2026), but this concerns 'generalized Skewes numbers' for races between residue classes / quadratic residues vs nonresidues under GRH — a different, renamed problem (a variant per §3.1), not a case of the classical π(x) vs li(x) question, so it is out of scope here. No AI system appears anywhere in this line of research; both papers are conventional analytic/computational number theory with no AI acknowledgement, tool, or system named.
competing_reading: One could argue the Revers (2025) paper counts as `progress` since it tightens error terms that feed directly into future crossover-bound computations and is explicitly framed as advancing the Lehman/Saouter-Trudgian-Demichel program on this exact bullet. I did not adopt this reading because the paper itself states no new numerical bound on the crossover point (the quantity the bullet actually asks about) — the improved η/error terms are a step toward a future improved bound, not the bound itself, and I could not verify from the abstract/HTML that any concrete new region was certified. If the full paper's numerical section in fact certifies a value below 10^19 excluded, or a smaller upper bound than 1.398×10^316, this should be reclassified as `progress` with `ai_role` `none`.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full body/numerical-results section of arXiv:2501.04488 (or its published Journal of Number Theory version) to see whether Theorem 3.1's improved error terms are used to derive and state any new certified numerical bound (upper or lower) on the crossover point, versus purely illustrating the sharper machinery on the existing known region.

outcome: No change: as of September 2026, Rule 110 (Cook, proved 2004, published 2004/2009) remains the only one of the 88 unique elementary cellular automata directly proven Turing complete (with Rule 124, its reflection, following as a corollary); Rule 54 remains conjectured but unproven; no source published after 26 January 2024 reports a new proof, disproof, or completed classification covering the Turing-completeness status of the remaining rules.
summary: This bullet asks for the Turing-completeness status of all 88 unique elementary cellular automata (ECA) — effectively a request for a complete classification, of which currently only one data point (Rule 110, proved Turing complete by Matthew Cook in 2004, with Rule 124 following by reflection symmetry) is settled, and one other (Rule 54) is a long-standing conjecture with no proof either way. I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 work that proves or disproves universality for any additional specific ECA rule, or that advances a systematic classification of all 88 rules' computational status, and found none. Several tangentially related papers turned up: an ICLR 2025 paper ('Intelligence at the Edge of Chaos') that pretrains GPT-2 on ECA-generated data to study emergent intelligence — it treats Rule 110's Turing completeness only as background context and does not touch the classification question; a 2026 ResearchGate/preprint paper ('Toward Automated Identification of Turing-Complete Cellular Automata via Structural and Complexity Analysis') that proposes a quantitative 'Complexity Score' and 'Behavioral Index' framework to flag *candidate* rules likely to be Turing complete, but explicitly stops short of proving Turing completeness for any specific rule — it is a screening heuristic, not a resolution; and a 2026 paper on Rule 22 as an algebraic reference point for Rule 30, which is about algebraic structure, not universality. None of these change what a careful reader would write in this bullet's entry: the status of the 86 remaining unique rules (all but Rule 110/124) is exactly as unresolved as it was in January 2024, and no AI system produced, checked, or contributed to any actual proof or disproof of universality for any of these rules. The record is `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2026 'automated identification' framework paper constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense, since it is new work aimed at the classification question and could plausibly be seen as narrowing where computational universality might be found. But per §3.1, a record/search-style narrowing only counts when the record IS the question; here the underlying existence question (is rule X Turing complete?) is not answered by a complexity-score heuristic that only ranks candidates, so I classified this as no change rather than `progress`. If the paper's rule rankings were later used to drive an actual proof, that would change the classification, but no such follow-up was found.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed or well-digested preprint proving or disproving Turing completeness for a specific ECA rule other than 110/124, or a completed systematic classification (proof or disproof) covering the computational status of all 88 unique rules, dated after 26 January 2024.

outcome: No answer to the general question has appeared; the field continues to produce isolated results on specific graph classes (representation numbers, recognition complexity, temporal/co-bipartite extensions, split graphs, modular decomposition) but nothing that identifies which hard graph problems generically translate to efficiently solvable word problems.
summary: The bullet is an open-ended research-programme question, not a single resolvable claim: 'which (hard) problems on graphs can be translated to words representing them and solved on words (efficiently)?' As of January 2024 the only known instance was that Maximum Clique is polynomial on word-representable graphs (because their neighborhoods are comparability graphs, on which Max Clique is polynomial) — this predates the window and is cited only as background. Searching the 2024-2026 literature on word-representable graphs turns up an active but conventional (human-authored) research area: square-free word-representations (Das et al. 2024-2025, answering a different open problem about representing graphs by square-free words), word-representability of co-bipartite graphs and split graphs, a word-representable temporal graphs extension (SAND 2025), modular decomposition characterizations, and complexity results establishing that recognizing k-word-representability is NP-complete for 3 ≤ k ≤ ⌈n/2⌉. None of these answer or narrow the general question of which hard problems admit efficient word-based algorithms; each is either a structural result about representability itself or a complexity result about recognizing representability, not a case of 'hard graph problem X can (or cannot) be efficiently solved via word representation.' No survey, digestion, or new instance was found that would count as a case of this specific bullet under the scope rule (§3.1) — the found papers are all related work in the same field, not restrictions or resolutions of this stated question. No AI system was mentioned anywhere in this literature; all identified papers are conventional human mathematical/algorithmic research (search techniques, forbidden-subgraph characterizations, combinatorial constructions). I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Maximum Clique polynomiality result (predating the window, and re-cited in surveys) is itself 'an answer' to a case of the bullet's question, making status 'open_stale' rather than 'open' for that one instance. But the bullet asks a general, open-ended question ('which problems'), and a single pre-existing example does not close or narrow the class of problems under investigation in a way that changes what a careful person would write in this entry today; no new problem instance was resolved in the window, so 'open' with no_change_found remains the better reading.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or survey that gives a general characterization, dichotomy, or meta-result identifying a class of hard graph problems that become efficiently solvable via word representation (or proves no such general translation exists for a class), rather than another isolated case involving a specific graph family.

outcome: No resolution, partial case settlement, or bound movement was found since 26 January 2024; the core question of whether every integer not congruent to 4 or 5 (mod 9) is a sum of three cubes remains open, and the seven small cases below 1000 (114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921, 975) remain unsolved.
summary: I searched for any development on the sum-of-three-cubes characterization question since 26 January 2024 and found nothing that changes the problem's status. The one item the triage flagged, arXiv:2512.15763 ('Representation Of Integers By Sum Of Three Cubes, A New Approach Based On Seed Equation'), was submitted to arXiv on 12 December 2025, but its own journal-reference field states it was originally published in Mathematical Forum, Vol. 28(2), 2020 — i.e. this is an old (pre-2024) paper newly deposited on arXiv, not new work, and it does not address the mod-9 sufficiency question or any of the outstanding small cases (114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921, 975); its abstract makes no mention of them. The last genuine mathematical events on this problem (Booker's 2019 resolution of 33, and Booker–Sutherland's 2019 resolution of 42 and third representation of 3) predate the window entirely and are already reflected in Wikipedia's current article, which still states plainly that whether the mod-9 necessary condition is sufficient 'is unknown.' A 2024 paper on 'Diophantine imaging' (Sultanow, Henkel, Aberkane, Scientific Reports, published 2 January 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41598-023-49960-y) offers a visualization method for known solution datasets; it was published four days before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 timestamp, so even setting scope aside it falls outside the window, and in any case it is a descriptive/visualization tool, not a case settled or a bound moved, and involves no AI system. I also checked Epoch AI's FrontierMath 'Open Problems' page, which lists sum of three cubes as an open benchmark challenge for AI systems (specifically, finding a fourth representation for n=3) but reports no successful AI attempt — it frames the problem as unsolved by AI, not solved. Searches for AI-specific efforts (AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, LLM-based approaches) turned up no application to this problem; those systems' publicized results are in geometry and olympiad problem-solving, not this Diophantine search problem. No credible source reports any of the seven remaining sub-1000 cases being resolved, any new admissible/inadmissible residue class established, or any AI system producing a representation. The status is therefore open with no_change_found true.
competing_reading: One could argue the December 2025 arXiv posting of 2512.15763 constitutes a dated 'event' worth recording as `progress`, since it is new to arXiv even if the underlying work is from 2020. I judged this incorrect: the mathematical content demonstrably predates the frozen revision (it's a 2020 publication), so treating its arXiv upload date as the event date would misattribute a stale paper as new progress, which is exactly the failure mode the open_stale category exists to prevent — except here the paper doesn't even settle a case or move a bound, so it isn't `open_stale` either, just irrelevant.
what_would_settle_it: A dated preprint or publication that either (a) proves or disproves the mod-9 sufficiency conjecture in general, (b) finds a representation for one of 114, 390, 627, 633, 732, 921, or 975 (or proves one impossible), or (c) an AI-lab report (e.g. from Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark, DeepMind, or similar) describing a model finding a new representation such as a fourth solution for n=3.

disputes.summary: Kawauchi's arXiv preprint claims a full, affirmative proof of the Whitehead conjecture, but it has not been independently verified, cited, or endorsed by topologists. It was published in the Journal of Mathematical Techniques and Computational Mathematics (Opast Publishers), which shows multiple hallmarks of a low-quality/predatory open-access venue (extremely broad and unfocused subject scope spanning topics like 'Vedic Mathematics' and 'Collaborative Robots', a small and under-verified editorial board, an unverifiable claimed impact factor, and an unfinished website). No expert digestion, review, or citation of the claimed proof by other topologists was found.

summary: The triage correctly identified Akio Kawauchi's arXiv preprint 2303.04368 ('Whitehead aspherical conjecture via ribbon sphere-link') as the only substantive lead. Its v1 was posted March 2023 (before the window) but v2 was revised 9 April 2024 (inside the window), and it was subsequently published in 2024 in the Journal of Mathematical Techniques and Computational Mathematics, a venue that on inspection shows several red flags of a low-quality/predatory open-access publisher (implausibly broad scope, thin and unverifiable editorial credentials, an unverified impact factor claim, and an incomplete website). I found no evidence that any topologist has reviewed, endorsed, cited, or engaged with the claimed proof — no MathOverflow thread, no blog digestion (Tao, n-category cafe, etc.), no citation in a subsequent paper treating it as settled. Kawauchi has continued to publish supporting lemmas ('Free ribbon lemma for surface-link', arXiv:2412.09281, Dec 2024, and 'Another proof of free ribbon lemma', arXiv:2408.04793) that build on his own apparatus, but these are self-referential extensions, not independent corroboration. The conjecture's Wikipedia article, as fetched live, still presents it as unresolved with no mention of Kawauchi's claim. I also found and set aside two things that are out of scope for this exact bullet: (1) A. M. Mikhovich's 2025 Izvestiya Mathematics paper on rational and p-adic analogues of Whitehead's conjecture — this changes the hypotheses (working over prounipotent/pro-p settings) rather than restricting the stated integral conjecture, so it is a related problem, not a case, per §3.1. (2) A February 2026 GitHub issue in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures cataloguing the Whitehead asphericity conjecture as a Lean formalization target — this is explicitly AI-agent-generated (per the issue text, 'generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me') but it is only a formalization-difficulty assessment (rated 4/5 difficulty, noting missing Mathlib infrastructure) with no proof, no formalized statement, and no PR — it documents that the conjecture exists and is hard to formalize, which is not itself a mathematical event about the problem. I also found a long, numbered, AI-flavored WordPress post (ppalme.wordpress.com, 8 Sept 2026) that explicitly disclaims proving the conjecture and instead offers a speculative 'reformulation framework'; it names no AI tool and does not meet the bar for any ai_role above none, and in any case asserts no result. No counterexample, no disproof, and no accepted proof of the actual Whitehead conjecture as stated was found anywhere in the window. I classify status as 'claimed' rather than 'open' because a specific, complete proof claim by a named mathematician exists and was revised/republished within the window, but 'resolved' is wrong because no expert digestion exists and the publication venue does not confer real peer review credibility. No AI system was found to be involved in any of the substantive mathematical work (Kawauchi's papers show no AI attribution at all); the only AI-agent-authored artifact found (the DeepMind GitHub issue) did not produce any mathematics, only a formalization-scoping note, so ai_role is 'none' for the record as a whole.
competing_reading: One could argue the Kawauchi preprint should be scored 'open' rather than 'claimed', treating an unreviewed, predatory-adjacent-journal publication as equivalent to no claim at all. I chose 'claimed' because the rubric's bar for 'claimed' is just 'a preprint, announcement or machine-checked certificate that experts have not yet digested' — Kawauchi's arXiv posting satisfies that literally, and the 2024 revision date falls inside the window, so treating it as a non-event would understate what actually happened (a serious, specific, dated proof claim was made and is now circulating, however uncorroborated).
what_would_settle_it: A citation or public statement by a recognized topologist engaging with Kawauchi's ribbon sphere-link argument (accepting, refuting, or identifying a specific gap), or a retraction/erratum from Kawauchi himself, or acceptance in a mainstream topology journal.
