outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 changes the classification of pairs of n×n matrices under simultaneous conjugation; the two candidate papers found by searches both address distinct, related problems (a different equivalence relation, and a finite-field algorithmic variant), and the classical wild problem itself is a long-standing complexity benchmark rather than an active open conjecture with a research program aimed at resolving it.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet describes the classical 'wild problem': classifying pairs of n×n matrices under simultaneous conjugation (A,B) ↦ (S⁻¹AS, S⁻¹BS). This is not an open conjecture in the usual sense but a decades-old benchmark of representation-theoretic complexity, formalized by Yu. A. Drozd's tame/wild dichotomy: a classification problem is 'wild' precisely when it contains (is at least as hard as) this matrix-pair problem, which is considered intractable/'hopeless' to classify explicitly because it is known to encode the representation theory of arbitrary finitely generated algebras. Nothing in the mathematical literature treats this as a problem awaiting resolution — its content (that no tractable classification exists) was established well before 2024, so there is no pending resolution for a 2024-2026 result to deliver. Triage found two 2024 papers: arXiv:2408.04244 ('Polynomial similarity of pairs of matrices', published in Linear Algebra and its Applications vol. 708, 2025) proves that classification under a different, weaker equivalence relation ('polynomial similarity', involving polynomial coordinate changes plus similarity, restricted to commuting nilpotent pairs) is itself wild by reduction to the classical problem — this is a related problem (a different equivalence relation), not a case of the stated problem, and it does not change the classical statement. arXiv:2409.12457 ('Canonical forms for matrix tuples in polynomial time', FOCS 2024) gives polynomial-time algorithms for computing canonical forms of matrix tuples over finite fields under conjugation and left-right actions — this is an algorithmic/computational question about a specific setting (finite fields, isomorphism/canonical-form testing) that coexists with wildness (wildness is about the impossibility of a tame parametrized classification, not about computational infeasibility of canonical-form algorithms) and is a related but distinct problem, not a resolution or partial resolution of the stated classification problem. I opened both papers directly (via WebFetch) rather than relying on titles/snippets, confirming triage's reading in both cases. I also checked the current Wikipedia 'Wild problem' article, which contains no update reflecting any 2024-2026 development. No source anywhere mentions AI, machine learning, or automated theorem proving in connection with this problem or either paper. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and its scope classification of both found items as variants rather than cases.
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2409.12457's polynomial-time canonical-form algorithm for matrix tuples over finite fields is a 'case' of the stated problem restricted to finite fields — if so it would be `partial` progress with `ai_role` none. I reject this reading because the stated problem is about classification (a normal-form/parametrization question showing the parameter space structure, which wildness says is intractable in a technical representation-theoretic sense), whereas the FOCS paper is about the different question of algorithmically computing/testing canonical forms and isomorphism given specific matrix tuples over a finite field — a computational complexity question that is compatible with, and does not resolve or restrict, the classification-theoretic wildness statement (the paper itself does not claim to make progress on or resolve any case of the wildness classification). It also is not confined to n×n conjugation of pairs (it covers general tuples and multiple groups of actions), further indicating a different-but-related problem rather than a restriction of the exact stated one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly reducing part of the classical simultaneous-conjugation classification problem to a tame/tractable sub-case (e.g., a bounded-dimension case proven tame where previously open) would settle the ambiguity in favor of `partial`; absent that, the current reading (both found papers are related-but-distinct problems) stands.

outcome: The literal Williamson conjecture (that Williamson matrices — quadruples of symmetric circulant ±1 matrices A,B,C,D of order n with AA^T+BB^T+CC^T+DD^T=4nI — exist for every positive integer n) was disproven before the frozen revision, by Đoković in 1993 (order 35 counterexample) with further counterexamples (orders 47, 53, 59) found in 2008. No result since 26 January 2024 reopens, extends, or otherwise changes this settled status; nothing found in the window is a case of this specific bullet.

counterexample.object: Order 35 (and later orders 47, 53, 59): no Williamson matrices exist at these orders, contradicting the conjecture that they exist for every n.
counterexample.verified_how: Exhaustive computer search (Đoković, 1993; MathCheck SAT-solver verification of the nonexistence, independently reproducible per the MathCheck page).

summary: The Williamson conjecture as stated in the frozen Wikipedia revision (Williamson matrices exist for every positive integer n) was already refuted in 1993 by Đoković, who found via exhaustive computer search that no Williamson matrices exist at order 35 — the smallest known counterexample at the time — with further counterexamples at orders 47, 53 and 59 found by 2008. Both of these events predate the 26 January 2024 snapshot, so status is open_stale and no post-window change to the conjecture itself was found. I checked two lines of post-2024 work the triage flagged as possibly relevant, and both turn out to be results about neighboring problems rather than this bullet, per the §3.1 scope rule (a related/variant problem does not count): (1) Kharaghani, Mohammadian and Tayfeh-Rezaie, 'A search for Hadamard matrices of Williamson type' (arXiv:2605.08661, submitted 9 May 2026), which studies 'near Williamson matrices' — a deliberately relaxed definition (only A is required circulant; B, C, D are symmetric circulant but the joint structure differs from classical Williamson matrices) — and classifies all inequivalent near-Williamson quadruples for odd orders up to 35 and proves existence up to 63, plus a new quaternary Hadamard matrix of order 118 as a corollary. This is a variant construction with a changed definition, not a case of the stated conjecture (which is already settled/refuted), and I found no AI/ML involvement in this paper — its abstract, methodology, and metadata show only computer search (no mention of AI or ML models). (2) The August 2026 announcement by Levent Alpöge (Anthropic), Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle, using Claude, of Hadamard matrices for the 12 previously-open orders below 2000 (668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948, 1964), posted as an encoded puzzle on X on 12 August 2026 and tracked (provisionally, as 'solved by AI') by Epoch AI's FrontierMath open-problems tracker. This is a result about the parent Hadamard conjecture, not the Williamson conjecture: the search frontier for order 668 specifically is described (via Đoković and Kotsireas' reduction, and corroborated by an independent paper 'Order 668 in the Hadamard conjecture: structural bottlenecks and a certified local-search obstruction') as Goethals-Seidel difference families over Z/167Z in the quadratic-residue-anchored skew supplementary-difference-set regime — a fundamentally different construction from Williamson matrices, which the same source-family explicitly notes are 'too sparse to generate Hadamard matrices of all feasible orders.' No source ties the order-668 (or the other 11) construction to Williamson-type matrices. This belongs to the hadamard-conjecture record, not this one. I could not fully verify the order-668 claim's own status: TheoremDB (accessed via WebFetch) states 'No real Hadamard matrix of order 668 is known, and no nonexistence proof is known,' crediting only Eliahou's 2025 64-modular (not exact) construction, while Epoch AI describes the August 2026 Claude-assisted construction as an actual solution, marked 'provisionally' as AI-solved pending confirmation of how much mathematical insight came from Claude versus the three-person human team. This dispute (and the AI-role classification) is properly a finding for the hadamard-conjecture record, since it is about the parent conjecture, not this one — I note it here only because the triage record raised it under this key.
competing_reading: One could argue the near-Williamson-matrices paper (2605.08661) is close enough in name and spirit to count as progress on 'the problem of finding Williamson matrices' as loosely worded in the Wikipedia statement. I read the statement as referring to the specific mathematical object (Williamson matrices proper, as defined by Williamson in 1944 and by the Wikipedia article's own definition), for which the near-Williamson class is an explicitly different, relaxed structure introduced by the authors themselves as a new object — a related problem, not a case, under §3.1. If a future reader considers 'near Williamson matrices' close enough to count, this would shift to progress/partial with ai_role none (since no AI was used in that paper regardless).
what_would_settle_it: A source explicitly stating that the near-Williamson-matrices existence results are understood by the field as bearing on the classical Williamson conjecture (rather than as a distinct relaxed construction), or a source tying the order-668/Claude construction specifically to a Williamson-type (symmetric circulant quadruple) matrix rather than a Goethals-Seidel/difference-set construction.

outcome: The full question (does a nontrivial elementary embedding j:V→V exist consistently with ZF alone) remains open, but a major necessary sub-case moved: Farmer Schlutzenberg proved (arXiv:2006.01077, decisive version v4 posted 2024-03-18, published in Journal of Mathematical Logic 25(2), 2025) that ZF plus the existence of a Kunen-type embedding j:V_{λ+2}→V_{λ+2} (for λ even) is consistent relative to ZFC + I0, contrary to the natural expectation (from the ZFC Kunen inconsistency) that ZF alone might already refute it. Since any Reinhardt embedding j:V→V restricts to give such a V_{λ+2}→V_{λ+2} embedding, this removes what many set theorists expected to be an easy obstruction and is widely treated as the most significant recent movement on this question, earning Schlutzenberg the 2026 Hausdorff Medal of the European Set Theory Society.

disputes.summary: Rupert McCallum posted an arXiv preprint (2601.10231, v1 2026-01-15) claiming the next level up, inconsistency of a nontrivial Σ1-elementary embedding j:V_{λ+3}≺V_{λ+3} with ZF — a stronger and more directly relevant claim toward refuting the full V→V question. The author withdrew it (v3, 2026-08-23) after finding an error in the 'continuity of Skolem functions' argument in the final section. This is a withdrawn claim, not a settled result, and is recorded here as an instructive incident rather than as the record's main event; McCallum made and withdrew a similar claim in 2017-2018 as well (predates the window, not counted).

summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet asks whether ZF alone (without choice) can consistently admit a nontrivial elementary embedding j:V→V. This remains fully open as stated: no proof of consistency or inconsistency of the full V→V embedding with ZF alone has been published or claimed since 26 January 2024. However, a closely related necessary sub-case did move. Any Reinhardt embedding j:V→V restricts to an embedding j↾V_{λ+2}:V_{λ+2}→V_{λ+2} for λ = sup_n j^n(κ), so the existence of such a 'Kunen cardinal' embedding is a necessary consequence of (and hence a genuine case of) the full question. Farmer Schlutzenberg's paper (arXiv:2006.01077, originally posted 2020 but decisively revised as v4 on 2024-03-18, inside the research window, and published in the Journal of Mathematical Logic in 2025) proved that ZF + 'there is an elementary embedding j:V_{λ+2}→V_{λ+2}' is consistent relative to ZFC + I0 (for λ even) — i.e. this weaker embedding is NOT refutable from ZF alone the way Kunen refuted it from ZFC, a genuinely surprising result that won the 2026 Hausdorff Medal. This is a `partial` result in the sense of §3.1: it settles (positively, modulo relative consistency) a necessary case of the stated question, without resolving the full V→V question itself, so status is `partial` and resolution_direction is `confirmed` (the natural conjecture that ZF alone might refute even this weaker embedding was refuted; the embedding's consistency was confirmed relative to I0). Separately, in January 2026 Rupert McCallum posted a preprint (arXiv:2601.10231) claiming to prove inconsistency of ZF with a nontrivial Σ1-elementary j:V_{λ+3}≺V_{λ+3}, one level stronger and directly bearing on the general question; he withdrew it in August 2026 after finding a flaw, and it is recorded as an unresolved incident in `disputes` rather than as the primary event, since a withdrawn claim carries no result. No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the Schlutzenberg paper, the McCallum preprint, or the other 2024-2025 papers I examined (Mohammd 2025 on eventually dominating functions, Jeon 2024 on cofinal Reinhardt embeddings without Powerset) — this is standard, entirely human, pen-and-paper large cardinal set theory with no LLM, theorem-prover, or automated-search component disclosed by any author. The triage's verdict of `none` for AI involvement is correct, but I disagree with treating the problem as having seen no relevant movement: the Schlutzenberg result, though dated by preprint history to 2020-2024 with a 2024 decisive revision, is squarely inside the window by its operative posting date and is a substantial, high-profile case of this exact bullet.
competing_reading: One could argue Schlutzenberg's result is really about a different, weaker statement ('Kunen cardinal' / V_{λ+2} embeddings) rather than a case of 'the' Reinhardt/V→V question, since the Wikipedia bullet's literal object j:V→V is a proper-class embedding of the whole universe, and no first-order formalization of that exists without moving to NBG/KM (a point the Reinhardt cardinal article itself makes). Under a strict reading, V_{λ+2}→V_{λ+2} is a related-but-distinct, weaker large cardinal notion, and settling it would be a related problem, not a case, making the correct status `open` rather than `partial`. I judge `partial` to be the better reading because the restriction relationship is not merely analogical: existence of a full Reinhardt embedding provably implies existence of a Kunen-cardinal embedding (this is the actual mathematical content of Kunen's own inconsistency argument), so 'is ZF-with-Kunen-cardinal consistent' is a logically necessary condition for 'is ZF-with-Reinhardt-cardinal consistent', which is exactly what makes it a restriction/case in the sense of §3.1 rather than a change of the question. Also worth flagging: I could not fully extract the Schlutzenberg PDF text (encoding issues) and relied on WebFetch's markdown-converted renderings plus the Hausdorff Medal citation for corroboration, so there is a small residual chance of an inaccuracy carried over from the fetch tool's summarization rather than my own reading of primary text.
what_would_settle_it: A published proof (peer-reviewed, or at least surviving expert scrutiny for a couple of years) either constructing a nontrivial j:V→V (in some workable class-theoretic sense, e.g. NBG/KM) consistent with ZF, or refuting it, would resolve the bullet outright. Short of that, a non-withdrawn version of a V_{λ+3}-level or higher inconsistency result (of the kind McCallum attempted) would be the next incremental case to watch, since the chain of decreasing embedding strengths (V_{λ+2}, V_{λ+3}, ..., V→V) forms a natural ladder toward the full question.

outcome: Woodall's conjecture itself (general, unweighted digraphs) remains fully open with no resolution, no disproof, and no genuinely new bound first announced inside the window; the one true bound on the unweighted conjecture (Cornuéjols, Liu, Ravi, 'Approximately Packing Dijoins via Nowhere-Zero Flows') was first posted to arXiv on 2023-11-07, before the frozen revision, and only its IPCO 2024 conference presentation (2024-07-03/05) and later journal publication (Combinatorica, 2025) fall inside the window; everything else found in the window (chordal-digraph result, p-adic relaxation, dual-conjecture partial-3-trees result) settles a related-but-different conjecture rather than a case of Woodall's own statement.
summary: Woodall's conjecture (1976) as stated in the bullet — for a general digraph, minimum dicut size equals maximum number of disjoint dijoins — is still open. Nothing in the window resolves it, disproves it, or produces a genuinely new bound whose first written argument falls inside the window. Four pieces of related work surfaced: (1) Cornuéjols, Liu, Ravi, 'Approximately Packing Dijoins via Nowhere-Zero Flows' (arXiv:2311.04337) is the one paper that actually bounds the unweighted Woodall conjecture directly, proving a digraph with minimum dicut size τ contains ⌊τ/k⌋ disjoint dijoins whenever the underlying graph admits a nowhere-zero k-flow (giving ⌊τ/6⌋ unconditionally via Seymour 1981). Its v1 was posted 2023-11-07, before the frozen revision, so under §6.3 the event is dated to that preprint and the status is open_stale; its IPCO 2024 Best Paper presentation (Wrocław, 2024-07-03 to 07-05) and its 2025 Combinatorica journal publication (and arXiv v2, 2025-05-22) are the only window-internal traces of it, representing further vetting/digestion of an already-existing result rather than a new one. (2) Cornuéjols, Liu, Ravi, 'A Min-Max Relation on Dicuts and Dijoins in Weighted Chordal Digraphs' (arXiv:2501.10918, Jan 2025) resolves the weighted Edmonds-Giles conjecture (a distinct, related conjecture already known to be false in general) for chordal digraphs; per its own abstract 'the unweighted version conjectured by Woodall remains open' — this is a related problem, not a case of Woodall's own statement, so it does not count under §3.1. (3) Abdi, Cornuéjols, Liu, Silina, 'Strongly connected orientations and integer lattices' (arXiv:2410.13665, Oct 2024, in window) proves a p-adic (fractional/relaxed) packing relaxation of Woodall's conjecture — this changes what is being packed (p-adic rather than integer dijoins), making it a variant rather than a restriction, so it also does not count as a case. (4) Gutiérrez, 'Towards a Dual Version of Woodall's Conjecture for Partial 3-Trees' (arXiv:2408.05703, Aug 2024) explicitly addresses a dual conjecture (shortest dicycle vs. disjoint feedback arc sets in planar digraphs), which is a different, though related, statement. A separate 'Seymour and Woodall's conjecture' (2001, on chromatic number and complete bipartite minors) is an unrelated conjecture sharing Woodall's name and was excluded. No AI system was mentioned in any of the primary sources checked; all listed results are conventional human-authored combinatorial proofs. Net: no in-window event changes what a careful person would write in this bullet; the closest thing to real progress on the unweighted conjecture predates the window and only received further vetting (conference award, journal publication) inside it.
competing_reading: One could argue the IPCO 2024 Best Paper presentation (July 2024) or the Combinatorica 2025 journal publication of arXiv:2311.04337 should itself be treated as the 'event' under the conference/journal-postdate exception discussed in §6.3 ('announced at a conference before the frozen date but written up after') — but here the arXiv preprint already existed before the frozen date, so this exception (meant for results only written up after being announced) does not apply, and the paper is more naturally treated as fully predating the window, hence open_stale rather than progress. If one instead credits the paper's continued life (award, journal version) as evidence the community's understanding of the bound genuinely firmed up within the window, `progress` with the later date could be argued instead.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the field would consider a paper 'new' for dating purposes when its first arXiv posting predates the window but its peer-reviewed publication and major award fall inside it; and whether a future paper actually restricts Woodall's own unweighted statement (e.g., to chordal digraphs, without changing weighted/unweighted or integer/p-adic character) rather than a neighboring conjecture.

outcome: No result found in the window (26 January 2024 – present) that settles, partially settles, or moves the ZFC question of whether GCH holding below a strongly compact cardinal implies GCH holds everywhere. The only adjacent development, a negative answer under the negation of full AC (ZF, not ZFC), is both (a) a changed hypothesis rather than a case of the stated problem, and (b) mathematically published before the frozen revision date.
summary: The problem asks (in ZFC, as is standard for this list): if κ is strongly compact and GCH holds for all cardinals below κ, must GCH hold everywhere? Extensive searching (general web search, arXiv listings, Wikipedia's own 'Strongly compact cardinal' article, and targeted author searches for Apter, Gitik, Goldberg, Usuba, and others who work in this exact area) turned up no result in the ZFC setting that resolves, partially resolves, or moves a bound on this question since 26 January 2024. The one genuinely close-sounding item is Arthur Apter's work titled 'A Choiceless Answer to a Question of Woodin', presented as talks at the CUNY Set Theory Seminar (22 March 2024) and the Rutgers Logic Seminar (25 March 2024) — both inside the window. However, per multiple independent search syntheses, the underlying mathematical result is a negative answer to Woodin's question obtained in the *absence of the full Axiom of Choice* (i.e., in ZF rather than ZFC), and the underlying paper — 'A Note on a Question of Woodin', Bulletin of the Polish Academy of Sciences (Mathematics), vol. 71(2), 2023, pp. 115–121 — was published in 2023, before the frozen revision date of 26 January 2024. Two things follow. First, dropping full AC changes the hypotheses of the question rather than restricting its scope (it is not obtained by narrowing the domain of κ or the class of models within ZFC), so per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated one, and does not count as a change to this bullet even on its own terms. Second, even setting that aside, the actual first written argument predates the window; only the seminar talks recapitulating already-published 2023 work fall inside it, which is not itself a new result. Other adjacent literature found (Goldberg's 2021 'Strongly compact cardinals and ordinal definability', settling a different question of Woodin's — nonexistence of an elementary embedding from HOD to itself under the HOD hypothesis and a strongly compact cardinal; the Ultrapower-Axiom-implies-GCH-above-a-supercompact result, which is conditional on UA, a different and stronger hypothesis than 'GCH holds below a strongly compact cardinal', and predates 2024 in any case) is all either off-topic for this specific bullet or outside the window. No AI system appears anywhere in any of the sources checked; this is a purely human, and in fact largely inactive, corner of set theory in the relevant window. I judge the record complete and well-evidenced for a 'nothing happened' conclusion, with confidence high.
competing_reading: If one reads the Wikipedia statement as not implicitly restricted to ZFC (the statement as given doesn't say 'ZFC' explicitly, only 'strongly compact cardinal' and 'GCH'), one might argue the choiceless negative answer is a legitimate case of the stated problem rather than a variant, since it is literally a model where the antecedent (strongly compact κ, GCH below κ) holds and the consequent (GCH everywhere) fails. Under that reading the status would be `open_stale` (negative answer, but the underlying paper is from 2023, before the frozen revision) rather than `open`. I judge the ZFC reading more faithful to how this list and the surrounding literature treat the problem — Woodin's question is uniformly stated and discussed in the ZFC context in every secondary source found, with the choiceless work explicitly framed by its own author as a distinct, weaker-hypothesis question — but flag this as the strongest case for a different classification.
what_would_settle_it: A definitive resolution would require either (a) locating the original source in which Woodin posed this question (a talk, paper, or problem list from the 1980s/1990s) to see whether it explicitly assumes full AC/ZFC, which would settle the competing_reading question, or (b) finding a genuinely new ZFC-context paper or preprint dated after 26 January 2024 that addresses the strongly-compact-cardinal GCH question directly — none was found despite multiple search strategies.

summary: No result since 26 January 2024 settles, refutes, or moves Woodin's Ω-conjecture as stated (that a proper class of Woodin cardinals implies Ω-logic satisfies an analogue of the completeness theorem). Searches on the conjecture directly, on Ω-logic, and on adjacent absoluteness/large-cardinal work turned up only tangential set-theory papers: 'On (Σ²₁)^uB Absoluteness Between V and HOD' (arXiv 2505.01393, submitted 2025-05-02), which proves a downward-absoluteness result between V and HOD under a proper class of Woodin cardinals but does not mention or bear on the Ω-conjecture itself; a 2025 characterization of Woodin cardinals via compactness/Henkin models (arXiv 2505.15574); and general surveys/course notes on Ω-logic and the generic multiverse that predate 2024 or restate known background (e.g. that the conjecture is known to hold in all currently known core models, and that it is generically invariant so unlikely to be independent the way CH is). None of these constitute a case of the Ω-conjecture being settled, a bound moving, or even a narrowly restricted variant being resolved — they are papers using or characterizing Woodin cardinals for other purposes. The English Wikipedia Ω-logic article (fetched as it stands, last edited 2026-02-01) still presents the conjecture as open and unchanged in status, with no mention of any post-2024 progress. No AI system appears anywhere near this problem: a search crossing 'Ω-conjecture' with AI/LLM terms returned only unrelated papers about LLMs proving other conjectures (e.g. the OpenAI discrete-geometry counterexample, math benchmarks), none touching Ω-logic or Woodin's conjecture. This matches the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than contradict.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 V-HOD absoluteness paper (2505.01393) is 'about' Ω-logic in a loose sense since it operates in the same conceptual neighborhood (Woodin cardinals, absoluteness, third-order definability), and a very generous reading of scope might credit it as incremental context-building toward the Ω-conjecture program. But per §3.1 it changes a different, related question (V/HOD absoluteness of Σ²₁ statements) rather than restricting or settling the Ω-conjecture's own completeness-theorem statement, so it is a related-problem result, not a case of this one, and does not change the classification.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement that either proves the Ω-conjecture from a proper class of Woodin cardinals (or a comparably strong hypothesis), proves it false under some large-cardinal assumption, or settles a genuine restriction of the completeness-theorem-for-Ω-logic statement itself (e.g. for a restricted class of sentences or a specific inner model in a way that counts as a case rather than a variant).

outcome: The Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem remains unsolved and unaccepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute. Since January 2024 there has been a large proliferation of self-published preprints (arXiv, Zenodo, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org, academia.edu) claiming full or partial proofs; at least one (Agawa, March 2025) was posted and then retracted by its own author, and one arXiv submission (Jacobsen, May-June 2025) was withdrawn by arXiv administrators for failing content-quality standards. The single most substantive AI-related event is an April 2026 Zenodo report by a human author with three named AI systems as co-authors, describing an 'intensive campaign' using 'adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models' to attack the problem; it produced some genuine partial mathematical constructions (e.g. a mass-gapped noncommutative 4D gauge theory, confinement at all couplings) but explicitly failed to prove the continuum mass gap and reframed the question rather than answering it. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or Clay Institute recognition of any of this work exists.

ai.basis_quote: We report the results of an intensive campaign to prove the Yang-Mills mass gap --- one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems... using adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models.

disputes.summary: Dozens of mutually inconsistent self-published preprints across Zenodo, arXiv, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org and academia.edu each independently claim a complete or 'unconditional' proof of the mass gap (e.g. Silva-Filho's Lean-4-certified 'Unconditional Trilogy', Toupin's celestial-holography proof, the withdrawn Jacobsen and Agawa preprints, and others using names like 'Darkon-Yang-Mills', 'Big Boot Gauge Theory', and 'Quantum Cell Theory'). None has been reviewed or endorsed by any recognized expert, journal, or the Clay Mathematics Institute; several show hallmarks of low-quality or AI-generated text, and Zenodo itself has reported being flooded with bot/AI-crawler traffic during this period.

summary: The problem itself has not moved: the Clay Mathematics Institute's own page and the current Wikipedia article both still describe it as unsolved, and no proof or partial result here has received expert digestion, journal acceptance, or prize recognition. What has changed since January 2024 is the surrounding landscape: a large and growing volume of unreviewed, mostly self-published 'proof' preprints appeared on Zenodo, arXiv, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org and academia.edu, several with titles claiming complete or 'unconditional' resolutions (e.g. a Lean-4-'certified' trilogy by Silva-Filho, September 2026; a celestial-holography proof by Toupin, January 2026), one of which (Agawa, March 2025) was retracted by its own author after readers mistook it for an established result, and one arXiv submission (Jacobsen, May-June 2025) was withdrawn by arXiv administrators for not meeting content-quality standards. None of these has been accepted or verified by any recognized expert or institution, so none qualifies as resolved, claimed, or even partial under the scope rule: they are unverified assertions, not results a careful expert would treat as changing the bullet. The one event worth recording under `event`/`ai_role` is the April 2026 Zenodo report authored by John Henry Watt together with three AI systems listed as co-authors (Claude Opus 4.6 Extended, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.20), which explicitly describes 'adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models' used to systematically attack the mass gap problem. This is the clearest primary-source account of AI systems doing mathematical work (not just checking or formatting) that I found anywhere in this space: the systems are credited with producing matrix-model, noncommutative-gauge-theory, and lattice arguments as part of the campaign. But the campaign's own conclusion is that it failed to prove the continuum mass gap - it hit 'a factor-of-23 discrepancy between lattice and continuum formulations' and pivoted to arguing the question itself is 'not a dynamical mystery... but a geometric fact', i.e. it reframed rather than solved the problem. I classified this as `status: progress` (an instructive incident, not a resolution of any part of the stated problem) and `ai_role: incident`, per the rule that an AI-driven claim that surfaces and does not survive scrutiny (here, self-reported non-resolution rather than a formal retraction) is `progress`/`incident` dated to the claim. I treated `no_change_found` as false because this AI campaign is itself a recordable event even though the underlying mathematical problem is unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is plain `open` with `no_change_found: true`, treating the Watt/Claude/Gemini/Grok Zenodo report as just more unreviewed noise indistinguishable from the dozens of crank preprints, on the grounds that it produced no result that survives scrutiny and was never meant as a serious claim of resolution. outcome: Two 2026 preprints improved the known lower bounds on the first eigenvalue of embedded minimal hypersurfaces in the unit sphere (Yuhang Zhao, arXiv:2603.20890, March 2026, improving the Choi-Wang bound; arXiv:2606.10962, June 2026), both treating Yau's conjecture as open. [Hand-corrected 2026-09-24; the agent's original outcome follows.] Lingzhong Zeng posted a single-author arXiv preprint (2508.06123, 8 Aug 2025) claiming a full, affirmative proof of Yau's conjecture, but over a year later it remains an unreviewed single version (v1), has drawn no visible citations, expert commentary, or journal acceptance, and later 2026 preprints on the identical question (e.g. 2606.10962, June 2026) still describe the conjecture as open and do not cite or engage with Zeng's claim — so the claim has not been digested by experts and does not warrant `resolved`.
summary: The triage correctly flagged Lingzhong Zeng's arXiv preprint 2508.06123 ("The First Eigenvalue of Embedded Minimal Hypersurfaces in the Unit Sphere I: Yau's Conjecture", submitted 8 Aug 2025) as claiming a full proof that the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on any embedded compact minimal hypersurface of the unit sphere S^{n+1} equals n, via a minimizing sequence in a suitable Sobolev space and the variational principle, with rigidity theorems as applications. I fetched the abstract and full text directly: it is a genuine claim to resolve the conjecture as stated, not a restricted case or a variant, so it is squarely in scope under §3.1. However, it carries only one arXiv version (v1, unchanged since posting, comment field reads only 'Any comment is welcome'), no journal reference, and I could find no citing papers, no MathOverflow/blog/expert discussion, and no acknowledgement of it anywhere. Critically, two later 2026 preprints on the exact same narrow topic — Yuhang Zhao's arXiv:2603.20890 (21 Mar 2026, improving the Choi-Wang bound on the same eigenvalue problem) and an anonymous-to-me author's arXiv:2606.10962 (10 Jun 2026, 'On the First Eigenvalue of Embedded Minimal Hypersurfaces in the Unit Sphere', giving an improved partial lower bound) — both still frame Yau's conjecture as an open problem and neither cites nor mentions Zeng's claimed resolution at all. That silence from directly adjacent, contemporaneous work is strong indirect evidence the field either has not noticed the claim or does not regard it as settling the question. Per §6.1, a preprint with no expert digestion is `claimed`, not `resolved`, however clean the argument looks on the page — and here there is additionally a live signal (continued 'open' framing by close successors) suggesting doubt rather than mere lag. I found no AI involvement anywhere: Zeng's paper is a traditional single-author variational-methods argument with no mention of AI/ML/computational assistance, and the two 2026 follow-up papers likewise show no AI involvement. Wikipedia's own article on the conjecture (last substantively updated before Zeng's preprint) still calls it unsolved, consistent with the frozen revision's framing, and is not itself evidence either way about the post-cutoff period.
competing_reading: One could argue Zeng's is a serious, detailed single-author proof by an established researcher in this exact subfield (he has prior papers on partial results toward this same conjecture going back over a decade), and that arXiv preprints in this area sometimes go uncited for a year before slower-moving referees catch up — in which case `claimed` might understate confidence that the proof is probably correct. But the silence from Zhao (Mar 2026) and the Jun 2026 paper, both narrowly on-topic, tips this toward genuine non-acceptance or at least non-notice rather than mere citation lag, so I did not upgrade to `resolved`.
what_would_settle_it: A citation, review, or explicit endorsement/refutation of Zeng's 2508.06123 by another expert in minimal-surface spectral geometry (e.g., in a paper, MathOverflow thread, or Tao/Matroid-Union-style digestion), or a journal acceptance record for that preprint, or an explicit statement in a later preprint that the conjecture is now considered proved (or that Zeng's argument has a gap).

outcome: The general Zarankiewicz problem remains open, but a cluster of results since November 2024 has moved specific Zarankiewicz numbers z(m,n;s,t): Davies, Gill & Horsley (arXiv 2411.18842, published Discrete Mathematics 349 (2026), art. 114924) improved upper bounds on z(m,n;s,t) via a strengthened linear program; and Bhan, Nobili & Langer (arXiv 2605.01120, May 2026) used an LLM-guided evolutionary search (OpenEvolve) to find matrix constructions that pin down three previously-unknown exact values (Z(11,21;3,3)=116, Z(11,22;3,3)=121, Z(12,22;3,3)=132), 41 new lower bounds, and 4 matched closed cases. Several further preprints (Aug-Sep 2026, by other independent authors) report additional exact-value determinations and bound improvements on z(m,n;3,3) and z(43;2) using purely classical/computational methods, with LLMs used only for writing/exploratory assistance or not at all. None of these results settle the general asymptotic conjecture z(n,n;s,t) = Θ(n^(2-1/s)); each moves specific finite instances.

ai.basis_quote: The results are obtained using OpenEvolve, an open-source evolutionary algorithm based on Large Language Models (LLMs) that iteratively improves algorithms for generating mathematical constructions by optimizing a reward signal tailored for this specific problem.
ai.disclosed_cost: Approximately $15 to $30 per m×n parameter case, per the paper's cost analysis, with each search phase completing in around 10 minutes.

counterexample.verified_how: The LLM-generated matrix constructions (candidate extremal bipartite-graph/binary-matrix constructions) were checked programmatically against the K_{s,t}-free constraint and compared to known upper bounds; exact values were confirmed when a construction's edge count matched a previously established upper bound.

summary: The classical Zarankiewicz problem — the general question of z(m,n;s,t) — remains open, and no result since 26 January 2024 resolves it or the standard asymptotic conjecture z(n,n;s,t)=Θ(n^(2-1/s)). But this is a problem whose 'entry' is really a large family of specific extremal numbers, and several of those specific instances moved in the window. The clearest and most load-bearing change is Davies, Gill & Horsley's improved linear-programming upper bounds (arXiv 2411.18842, submitted 28 Nov 2024, published in Discrete Mathematics 349 (2026) — a purely classical, non-AI result, now expert-reviewed via journal publication). Independently, Bhan, Nobili & Langer (arXiv 2605.01120, submitted 1 May 2026, revised 7 May 2026) used OpenEvolve, an LLM-guided evolutionary program-search framework, to discover binary-matrix constructions that pin down three new exact Zarankiewicz values and 41 new lower bounds; by the authors' own account the LLMs (named as Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 3.7, and — in later search phases — 'Claude Opus 4.6') proposed the constructions/generating programs, which were then verified deterministically (not by another LLM) against known upper bounds. This is coded ai_role 'generated' because the LLM produced the actual construction that appears in the result, with humans/code only checking it — not merely assisting, debugging or proofreading a human-authored construction. Status is 'progress' rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed' at the whole-record level because the overall problem is still open and no expert digestion of the May 2026 preprint has appeared; the specific closed cases it reports are best read as claimed-not-yet-digested exact values sitting inside an otherwise-open problem. A cluster of further Aug-Sep 2026 preprints (Saurabh 2608.26603, Afrasyab 2608.08154, Hou 2608.08549, Sadhu 2608.01606, Liu & Song 2609.07227) report further bound improvements or exact values on related z(m,n;3,3)/z(43;2) instances; most explicitly use classical/computational methods with no learned component, one (Afrasyab) discloses generic LLM (GPT) use for 'exploratory reasoning, implementation, verification, manuscript integration' — i.e. author-facing tooling, not a source of the mathematical content — which the rubric codes as ai_role none, and Liu & Song's paper concerns a related but distinct 'limited augmented Zarankiewicz number' tied to sums-of-squares rank of biquadratic forms rather than the classical bullet, so I treat that one as a related problem, not a case of this one.
competing_reading: One could argue the whole record should be 'open' with no_change_found, since the Wikipedia bullet is phrased as the fully general question and none of these results touches its asymptotic form. I instead read finite exact-value/bound results on z(m,n;s,t) as genuine cases of the stated problem — restrictions to specific (m,n,s,t) — which per §3.1 count as partial/progress rather than being dismissed as a different problem, so 'progress' rather than 'open' is the more defensible code. A second uncertainty: WebFetch's extraction of the arXiv 2605.01120 text gave inconsistent detail across repeated fetches (once omitting named models entirely, twice reproducing an identical three-phase model schedule including 'Claude Opus 4.6', a tier name I cannot independently confirm exists) — I report the names as given because they recurred verbatim across independent fetches, but flag that this could be a fetch-tool artifact rather than the paper's actual text.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the arXiv 2605.01120 PDF/LaTeX source (not mediated by a summarizing fetch tool) to confirm the exact model names and cost figures verbatim, and any subsequent expert commentary (e.g. a Discrete Mathematics or combinatorics-blog digestion) on whether the three new exact Zarankiewicz values have been independently verified.

summary: I searched extensively for any post-26-January-2024 progress on the Zariski-Lipman conjecture (that a complex/perfect-field variety with locally free module of derivations must be smooth) and found none. All substantive special-case results predate the window: complete intersections (Källström), log canonical spaces (Druel 2013; Heuver 2015), normal algebraic surfaces (Biswas et al. 2014), low-genus surface singularities (Graf 2018; Bergner–Graf 2019), toric varieties (Tipler, arXiv:2202.02109, Feb 2022), and the positive-characteristic counterexample/violation results (arXiv:2201.06646, Jan 2022) are all 2022 or earlier. Two items surfaced in the window: (1) a January 2026 GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #1822) proposing to formalize the conjecture's *statement* in Lean for a benchmark repository — the issue itself says 'Created by AI, reviewed and edited by me,' meaning an AI system (per formal-conjectures' own convention, an LLM) drafted the issue text, which a human then reviewed; this is not mathematical progress, just a benchmark-tracking issue for an open statement, so I coded it formalisation_only with ai_role none (the AI's contribution is tracking/drafting an issue, not producing mathematics). It is also open/unstarted (Formalizability Rating 4/5, blocked on missing mathlib infrastructure), so no proof or even formalization exists yet. (2) arXiv:2510.07607 ('The blow-up of a singularity at the module of derivations,' Barajas–Chávez-Martínez–Romano-Velázquez, submitted October 2025), which studies resolving singularities via blow-ups of the derivation module and explicitly invokes the Zariski-Lipman conjecture as a known true statement in the log-canonical/rational-singularity cases (already settled by Druel and others pre-2024) to conclude smoothness after blow-up. It does not extend the conjecture's proven scope to any new case — it is downstream applied use of prior results, so under the scope rule (§3.1) it does not count as a change to this problem. No expert digestion (Tao's blog, Quanta, survey), no new arXiv preprint proving a new case or a new counterexample, and no AI-generated or AI-assisted proof of any part of the conjecture was found. I judge this a genuine 'nothing happened' case rather than a search failure.
competing_reading: One could argue the October 2025 blow-up paper's Corollary 2.4/Theorem 3.5 results (resolving curve and log-canonical surface singularities via iterated derivation-module blow-ups) constitute 'progress' adjacent to the conjecture's spirit, since they deepen understanding of when the derivation module's freeness controls smoothness. But the paper does not settle any new case of the conjecture itself (it relies on, rather than extends, the log-canonical/rational cases already proved by Druel in 2013), so under the scope rule this is a related problem (resolution of singularities via a different construction) rather than a case of Zariski-Lipman, and I classified it as no_change_found.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or announcement proving the conjecture in a new class of varieties not already covered pre-2024 (e.g., general normal surface singularities beyond the pg-g-b≤2 bound, or higher-dimensional cases beyond complete intersections and toric varieties), or a full general proof/disproof, or an expert survey/blog explicitly stating new movement since January 2024.

outcome: The general Zariski multiplicity conjecture (homeomorphic hypersurface germs have equal multiplicity) remains open, but a central and long-studied case — the 'multiplicity conjecture in families' (a family of isolated hypersurface singularities with constant Milnor number has constant multiplicity) — was proved by Fernández de Bobadilla and Pełka; the proof was finalized and published in the window (final arXiv revision v5, 5 March 2024; journal publication in Annals of Mathematics, online 3 July 2024). Two further special cases (a metric/bi-Lipschitz version for multiplicity two, and the 1-parameter quasihomogeneous surface-germ case) were proved in preprints posted September 2025.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet states the general 1971 Zariski multiplicity conjecture: that topological (homeomorphism) equisingularity of two reduced complex hypersurface germs implies equal algebraic multiplicity. That general statement is still open — no counterexample and no general proof exists. However, the most heavily studied restricted case, the 'multiplicity conjecture in families' (a 1-parameter family of isolated hypersurface singularities with constant Milnor number has constant multiplicity), was resolved by Javier Fernández de Bobadilla and Tomasz Pełka in 'Symplectic monodromy at radius zero and equimultiplicity of μ-constant families.' The arXiv preprint (2204.07007) was first posted 14 April 2022, well before the 26 January 2024 frozen-revision date, so the mathematical argument itself predates the window. But the paper underwent substantial revision through review: the final, accepted version (v5) was posted 5 March 2024, and the peer-reviewed article appeared in the Annals of Mathematics (Vol. 200, Issue 1), published online 3 July 2024 — both inside the window. Following §6.3's rule to date by the first written argument, and given that the argument continued to be revised until the version accepted for publication, I date the event to the final arXiv revision (5 March 2024), noting the July 2024 Annals publication as confirming expert digestion (this is what makes the classification 'partial'/resolved-in-scope rather than merely 'claimed'). The BCAM and Ikerbasque press releases (undated but clearly post-publication, referring to it as solving a '54-year-old conjecture') publicized the result but added nothing new to the underlying proof or AI question. Because the family case is a restriction of the general conjecture's scope (constant Milnor number is a special hypothesis, not present in the general statement), this counts as a 'case settled' under §3.1, hence status 'partial' rather than 'resolved' for the bullet as stated — the general conjecture is not closed. Two further, narrower special cases were resolved in September 2025 preprints (not yet digested by outside experts as of this research): Fernandes, Jelonek and Sampaio (arXiv:2509.03447, submitted 3 September 2025) proved a metric/bi-Lipschitz version of the conjecture for hypersurfaces of multiplicity exactly two (this paper does not use the name 'Zariski multiplicity conjecture' itself but proves the analogous bi-Lipschitz statement for multiplicity-two germs, framed as part of the Arnold corank problem); da Silva and Messias da Silva Júnior (arXiv:2509.01634, submitted 1 September 2025) proved Zariski's multiplicity conjecture for 1-parameter families of quasihomogeneous, corank-1, finitely-determined surface germs, a case not covered by the 2024 Annals paper (which is limited to isolated hypersurface singularities in the μ-constant-family setting; the quasihomogeneous surface germ case involves non-isolated map germs from (ℂ²,0) to (ℂ³,0)). None of the sources examined — the two 2024/2022 arXiv versions, the Annals publication page, the BCAM and Ikerbasque press releases, the two September 2025 preprints, or the related August 2023 TQFT re-proof of the family case (arXiv:2308.13925, using Floer cohomology) — mention any AI system, machine learning tool, or computer-assisted search. All proofs are traditional human mathematical arguments (symplectic geometry, Floer-theoretic/TQFT methods, weighted-degree/transverse-slice arguments). AI role is therefore 'none'.
competing_reading: One could argue the entire event should be classified 'open_stale' on the theory that the substantive mathematical content was already complete and essentially public via the April 2022 arXiv v1 preprint, making the 'event' predate the frozen revision and the later revisions/publication merely bureaucratic. Under that reading the correct status would be 'open_stale' rather than 'partial', since nothing new was mathematically discovered after January 2024, only certified/published. A stricter reader could reasonably classify this as open_stale instead.

outcome: Zauner's conjecture remains open. The most substantial development is a January 2025 preprint (Appleby, Flammia, Kopp) giving an explicit construction of SICs in every dimension d>3, valid conditional on the order-1 abelian Stark conjecture for real quadratic fields and a new 'Twisted Convolution Conjecture' the authors introduce — this reduces Zauner's conjecture to other open conjectures rather than proving it. A January 2026 preprint (Stefan Joka) claiming a full unconditional proof for all finite dimensions was found flawed on review (a false vertex identification and circular induction) and was withdrawn by the author himself in a fifth revision in May 2026. A September 2026 preprint (McConnell) proves a structure theorem for SIC dimension towers, a further piece of number-theoretic scaffolding, not a resolution.

disputes.summary: Stefan Joka's arXiv:2601.13475 (submitted 20 Jan 2026) claimed a full unconditional proof that SIC-POVMs exist in every finite dimension. Reviewers (per pith.science's review of the paper) found that the central identification between moment-polytope vertices and rank-one projectors is false and that the paper's induction argument is circular. The paper went through five revisions (v1 20 Jan 2026, v2 22 Jan 2026, v3 7 Feb 2026, v4 7 Mar 2026, v5 31 May 2026) and was ultimately withdrawn by the author in v5, with the withdrawal itself confirming 'the proof the paper gives is not correct.'

summary: Zauner's conjecture (do SIC-POVMs exist in all finite dimensions?) is still open as of September 2026, and I found no evidence that any AI system contributed to any of the mathematics attempted on it in this window. The genuinely substantial event is Appleby, Flammia and Kopp's 'A Constructive Approach to Zauner's Conjecture via the Stark Conjectures' (arXiv:2501.03970, submitted 7 Jan 2025, revised to v2 17 Mar 2025). It gives an explicit construction — a 'ghost SIC' built from real-multiplication values of the Shintani-Faddeev modular cocycle — that the authors prove yields a valid SIC in every dimension d>3, but only conditional on (1) the order-1 abelian Stark conjecture for real quadratic fields, itself a major open conjecture in number theory, and (2) a new identity they call the Twisted Convolution Conjecture, whose difficulty a third-party review (pith.science) notes 'may be comparable to the target result' itself. Because Zauner's conjecture is not proved outright, and because the reduction is to other unproved conjectures (not a restriction to a sub-case), I classify this as `progress` rather than `partial` or `claimed`: it is a structural advance / conditional roadmap, not a settled case of the stated existence question. No AI involvement is mentioned anywhere in the paper, on ResearchGate, or in third-party commentary I found. Separately, a January 2026 preprint by Stefan Joka (arXiv:2601.13475) claimed a full unconditional proof for every finite dimension; this is the kind of dramatic claim that would matter a great deal if correct, but expert review (via pith.science, a paper-review aggregator) identified a false identification between moment-polytope vertices and rank-one projectors and a circular induction step, and the author withdrew the paper himself after five revisions spanning January-May 2026 — the arXiv withdrawal notice states plainly 'the proof the paper gives is not correct.' This is recorded as the instructive-failure branch of `progress` (an announced/preprinted claim that came to nothing), dated to the original claim (20 Jan 2026) per §6.1's rule for incidents, though I use ai_role `none` (not `incident`) because there is no evidence any AI system was involved in producing or checking Joka's proof — it appears to be an ordinary (mistaken) human mathematics preprint, not an AI-produced claim. A third paper, Gary McConnell's 'SIC dimension towers via cyclotomic polynomials' (arXiv:2609.04431, submitted 3 Sep 2026), proves a structure theorem situating the known SIC dimension towers within a broader cyclotomic/arithmetic framework; it neither resolves any case nor moves a numerical bound on the conjecture itself, so on its own it would not even rise to `progress`, but the overall problem status of `progress` is carried by the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp reduction. I found nothing suggesting the January 2024 Wikipedia lead ('do SIC-POVMs exist in all dimensions?') needs updating: SIC-POVMs are still only known/verified in specific dimensions (exact solutions to d=53 and scattered higher values, numerical solutions further out), and the general existence question is unresolved.
competing_reading: One could argue the Appleby-Flammia-Kopp paper deserves `claimed` rather than `progress`, on the reasoning that it is a nearly-complete proof modulo well-regarded, independently-motivated number-theoretic conjectures (the Stark conjectures have their own long history and community credibility) — under that reading it is closer to 'a proof, conditional on X' being treated as a serious claim awaiting X. I did not adopt this because the paper's own second condition, the Twisted Convolution Conjecture, is new and unproved elsewhere, is acknowledged by reviewers as possibly as hard as the target, and Zauner's conjecture itself is not asserted to be proved by any human expert digestion I found — the paper's own framing is constructive/conditional rather than a claimed resolution.
what_would_settle_it: A proof of the order-1 abelian Stark conjecture for real quadratic fields, or of the Twisted Convolution Conjecture, that experts accept as closing Appleby-Flammia-Kopp's construction — or any independent unconditional proof of Zauner's conjecture that survives expert review (which Joka's attempt did not).

outcome: A August 2026 preprint by Ivan Dynnikov proves a structural reduction of the Zeeman collapsibility conjecture (ZCC): any counterexample to ZCC would yield a 'standard' counterexample, and ZCC holds for polyhedra embeddable in 3-manifolds; the general conjecture remains open, and no case of it (in the sense of a class of complexes previously undecided) was settled outright.

summary: Since 26 January 2024, no resolution, partial case, or counterexample to Zeeman's collapsibility conjecture (ZCC) has appeared. The most substantial development is Ivan Dynnikov's preprint 'On Zeeman's collapsibility conjecture for non-standard polyhedra' (arXiv:2608.23331, submitted 24 August 2026), which proves that (Theorem 2.5/1.4) any compact contractible 2-dimensional polyhedron can be transformed via 3-deformability moves into a 'semi-standard' polyhedron, so that if a counterexample to ZCC exists at all, a standard one exists; it also shows (Theorem 1.5) ZCC holds for polyhedra embeddable in 3-manifolds, leaning on the (proven) Poincare-Perelman theorem. This is a genuine narrowing of where a counterexample could be found for the exact problem as stated (contractible 2-complex K, is K x [0,1] collapsible?) — it is about the same object, not a variant — but it does not decide any previously-open sub-case in either direction: standard polyhedra were already the hardest and most-studied case, and the reduction leaves the truth value of ZCC on those exactly as open as before. I therefore classify this as 'progress' rather than 'partial': the theorem narrows the search space (akin to a bound moving) rather than settling a restriction of the stated question. The paper itself flags that part of its argument (a transfer of Matveev's 1987 technique to a new case) is asserted rather than independently re-verified, which the triage record also flagged as worth checking. Separately, a December 2024 preprint by Fagan, Qiu and Wang, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis Conjecture via Fake Surfaces and Zeeman Conjecture' (arXiv:2412.12293), relates the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture to a reformulation via 'fake surfaces' and proves a small case (complexity < 6) of that reformulation; this is about the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture, a related but distinct problem, not a case of ZCC itself, so it does not count as a change to this bullet and I treat it as background context only. No AI system played any role in either paper's mathematics: the Dynnikov preprint explicitly discloses that Google Gemini's web version was used 'solely for the purpose of final language editing,' which is exactly the kind of contribution (proofreading/tidying) that these codes classify as ai_role 'none'. No search turned up any AI lab announcement, LLM-produced proof or counterexample, or withdrawn AI claim concerning the Zeeman conjecture specifically (distinct AI results exist for other named problems, e.g. the unit distance conjecture and Jacobian conjecture, found incidentally while searching, but those are unrelated problems and not applicable here).
competing_reading: One could argue Dynnikov's Theorem 1.5 (ZCC holds for polyhedra embeddable in 3-manifolds) is a genuine 'case settled' and thus warrants status 'partial' rather than 'progress', since it restricts the stated question (all contractible 2-complexes) to a concrete sub-class (those embeddable in 3-manifolds) and answers it affirmatively. Under a stricter reading of §3.1 ('a case of the problem... settling it removes territory from the original... normally partial'), this would push the record to 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' for that sub-case. I lean 'progress' because the practical content of the paper is understood by the author primarily as a reduction/scope-narrowing result (the abstract and framing emphasize the standard/non-standard reduction, with the 3-manifold-embeddable case presented as a corollary of a lemma relying on the unverified Matveev transfer), but this is a genuinely close call.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (e.g. a survey, MathOverflow discussion, or citation with commentary from a topologist) characterizing whether Theorem 1.5 is regarded by the community as a real settled sub-case of ZCC or merely a technical corollary en route to the main reduction; also, verification of whether Dynnikov's reliance on 'transfer of Matveev's technique' has been checked by anyone since posting.

outcome: The general Zilber-Pink conjecture remains open, but several genuine restricted cases were proven in the window: Dogra (self-products of curves with degenerate reduction, submitted Mar 2024), Daw-Orr (curves in Y(1)^n under multiplicative degeneration — published in Duke Math. J. Sept 2025, though first posted to arXiv in 2022), Klingler-Tayou (subvarieties not defined over Q-bar, Apr 2025), and Daw-Orr-Papas (further cases in Y(1)^3, Oct 2025). No AI system produced or contributed to any of these results; the only AI-related touchpoint is a Jan 2026 GitHub issue requesting a Lean formalization of the conjecture's statement, with no proof attempt.
summary: The Zilber-Pink conjecture (finiteness of atypical/maximal atypical subvarieties in a mixed Shimura variety or semiabelian variety) is a broad unifying conjecture in unlikely intersections theory, and it remains open in general as of September 2026 — the Wikipedia article on it (last touched 7 Nov 2025) still describes it as 'wide open' with only special cases proven, which matches what I found independently. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to today), several genuine restricted cases were proved, each narrowing (not varying) the stated question by restricting the class of X or V, which under the deep-dive's §3.1 rule makes each a 'case of the problem' rather than a related/variant problem: (1) Netan Dogra, arXiv:2403.05481, submitted 8 March 2024 (v1; a v3 was posted 7 July 2026, well within the window), proves Zilber-Pink for n-fold self-products of a curve inside the self-product of its Jacobian under degenerate-reduction and no-extra-endomorphism hypotheses, for n sufficiently small. (2) Christopher Daw and Martin Orr's paper on curves in a product of modular curves under multiplicative degeneration was first posted to arXiv in August 2022 (predating the window) but was formally published in the Duke Mathematical Journal (vol. 174, no. 13, pp. 2877-2926) on 15 September 2025 — I confirmed this date directly via Project Euclid. Per §6.3, I date the underlying event by first written argument (2022, out of window) but the paper was actively revised inside the window (v2 Apr 2024, v3 Jan 2025, v4 Mar 2025) and only reached expert-vetted journal form in Sept 2025; I treat the Duke publication as the in-window event supporting a 'partial' status rather than 'open_stale', since a careful reader in Jan 2024 would not yet have had the peer-reviewed, final-form result. (3) Klingler and Tayou, arXiv:2504.00865 (submitted 1 April 2025), prove Zilber-Pink for subvarieties of mixed Shimura varieties not defined over the algebraic closure of Q in a strong sense, plus an analogous VHS statement. (4) Daw, Orr and Papas, arXiv:2510.09603 (submitted 10 October 2025, revised Feb 2026), extend the Y(1)^n line of results to further cases in Y(1)^3. I independently verified all submission dates, abstracts, and the Duke publication date by opening the arXiv abstract pages and the Project Euclid record directly (not relying on the triage's dates or notes). None of the four papers, nor any of the other in-window papers found (Barroero-Dill on distinguished categories, Bhatta on PEL types, Pila on Schanuel+Zilber-Pink, Daw's June 2025 survey, etc.), show any AI/ML involvement in the mathematics — no acknowledgement, method section, or abstract mentions a language model, automated theorem prover, or AI-assisted search, in what full-text I could access (extraction was degraded for three of the four PDFs, so absence-of-mention confidence is high but not absolute for those). The one AI-related touchpoint found anywhere near this conjecture is GitHub issue #1824 in DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, opened 21 January 2026, titled 'Zilber-Pink Conjecture', which asks contributors to formalize the conjecture's *statement* in Lean 4/Mathlib (rated difficulty 4/5, tagged needs-prerequisites, still open and unassigned as of the check). This is not a proof attempt, a bound, or any mathematical contribution — it is an infrastructure request so that AI theorem-provers could eventually be pointed at the problem — so it does not change ai_role from none for the mathematical progress itself; I mention it here rather than assigning it its own event because it produced no mathematical result. I classify the overall status as 'partial' (a case of the problem settled) rather than 'progress' or 'open', because multiple genuine special cases were proved with a clear direction of confirmation (the finiteness statement was proved, not refuted, in each restricted setting), and rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed' because the general conjecture named in the Wikipedia bullet is untouched.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'open' with no_change_found if one reads the Wikipedia bullet as asking only about the fully general statement over arbitrary mixed Shimura/semiabelian varieties with no restriction — under a very strict reading, none of the four papers touch 'the conjecture' itself, only proper sub-cases, and an observer could say nothing changed about the open problem as such. I reject this reading because §3.1 explicitly says a case obtained by restricting the stated question counts, normally as partial, and that is exactly the shape of all four results (restricting X, restricting V, or restricting the field of definition). A second competing reading concerns the Daw-Orr paper's date: one could argue for 'open_stale' since the underlying mathematical result was already known (posted to arXiv) before 26 January 2024, and only the journal's peer-reviewed publication happened in the window — under that reading the paper would not represent a new event at all, just a formality. I lean toward 'partial' with the Duke publication as a supporting (not primary) event because the paper underwent substantive revision within the window and its expert-vetted, citable form only existed from September 2025.
what_would_settle_it: Full text access to the acknowledgements sections of the Daw-Orr, Daw-Orr-Papas, and Dogra papers (PDF extraction was degraded) would firm up the 'no AI involvement' finding to high confidence. A check of whether GitHub issue #1824 has since been formalized or closed would clarify whether the AI-formalization effort progressed beyond a stub request.
